During the night of the fifteenth to the sixteenth, the weather was very fine and clear. The winds remained to the south-east very weak. We continued the course to the north-east by east which I had signalled to the Naturaliste.
1801-03-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SW to SE. At daybreak the cheeks of the main topgallant crosstrees were found broken; the crosstrees were at once lashed under the cap with a stout seizing. The rigging was set up. At noon in 30° 31' 47" of latitude observed and in 54° 44' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 47' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 21' 30" of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 56° 15' E.

1801-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light variable air from SE. At 4.30 made all sail and trimmed close-hauled.
1801-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, at dawn, the weather continued fine and the winds remained to the south-east, but so weak that there was every appearance that we should have a calm. The sea was extremely smooth and yet a long south-east swell caused us to roll considerably. There is every appearance that a few gales must have passed through these regions from this quarter which must have been vigorous.
At noon, our observed latitude was 29° 44' south and the longitude following dead reckoning was 51° 35'. That indicated by our timekeepers placed us at 53° 28' 50" following No. 38, and at 53° 57' 58" following No. 38 (sic). On board the Naturaliste they signalled 54° 30', which gave a difference all the more considerable in that our timekeepers had always placed us more to the east than that of this vessel, which was then ahead.
In the morning, we took more than thirty distances of the sun to the moon to verify the observations of the day before and their result, according to a mean term, gave for the observed longitude 55° 28' 48", consequently a difference east of 1° 59' 58" with the mean of our timekeepers. The agreement of this observation with the preceding one which had given 2° 7' 40" confirmed to us that the movement of our timekeepers was behind by this quantity and if to-morrow the weather permits we shall verify by new observations this discrepancy which we did not even suspect.
During the evening, the winds varied from south-east to south-south-east, the sky always very fine and the winds weak. We took to advantage of the fine weather different sorts of molluscs and especially a small chambered nautilus with its fish, which gave us all the more pleasure in that there is every reason to believe that the animal is not known although its shell is found almost everywhere.
During the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth, the weather was very fine and the sky clear, but the winds drew towards the east, and we had them sometimes at east-south-east very weak. We continued to make the course north-east, all sail set.
1801-03-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE and SSE. At noon in 29° 43' 12" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 27' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 10' of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 45° E. At 6 the Naturaliste asked to pass under our stern, which we granted. At 7 we spoke, and Captain Hamelin gave us the result of his lunar observations.

1801-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, the wind SE to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, the winds came back to the south-east and to the south-east by south almost calm. The sky was nebulous and fine. Squalls were formed at different times from various points of the horizon, but none came to us and the heat of the sun seemed to have absorbed them before they had risen to a certain height above the horizon.
In the morning, we multiplied the observations by distances and their results placed us at 56° 8' 45". The mean longitude of the timekeepers at the same time was 53° 59' 19", so that we found to within a few minutes the same difference as the preceding days and which seemed to affirm well affirmatively the retardation of the movement of our timekeepers.
We saw during the morning and for only the second time since our departure from Teneriffe, three or four tropicbirds that came to play above the ship's weathercock. But they remained at too great a height to be shot at with the musket. Since thirty-two degrees we had lost sight of the albatross.
At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 41' and the longitude following dead reckoning was 51° 59'. Timekeeper No. 31 placed us then at 53° 46' 56" and No. 38 at 54° 11' 42" which gave us for the course made a difference to the north of 4' 43" and a second to the east of 6' 42".
During the evening, the weather was fine, but there was but little wind and although we had all sail set we did not make great progress.
The mean result of several azimuths and amplitudes gave for declination north-west 18° 27' 30".
The night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth was fine and although the sky was sometimes covered with clouds coming from the south, they passed over our heads without giving us wind. They were moving fairly quickly to make us believe that at a more southerly latitude, it should be blowing fresh from this quarter. Although all our observations of longitude placed us at that of Île de France, I did not wish to change course and continued to steer north-east, not believing myself sufficiently certain that our timekeepers which had shown so regular a movement until the Cape of Good Hope, could have experienced from the Cape to the place where we find ourselves a difference as considerable as that which we have just perceived in these three days.
1801-03-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from SE to SW. At noon in 28° 40' 40" of latitude observed and in 55° 52' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 58' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 38' of longitude. Light rain during the night.

1801-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SW, WSW, NW and SW. The sea smooth. At 10 we had a squall which brought the winds round to SSW.
1801-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth at dawn, the winds remained to the south-west and the calm continued until eight o'clock. There were squalls in the morning from almost every point of the horizon all agitated by different winds. We received several on board which gave us abundantly rain and without wind. In the intervals we repeated our observations by distances whose result gave again 2° 27' 42" to the east of the timekeepers, but the weather had not been very favourable and we made little account of these last results.
At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 3' 32" and the longitude by dead reckoning was 52° 15' 5". That which was then indicated by our timekeepers was for No. 31 of 54° 4' 54" and at No. 38 of 54° 34' 12". We found in the 24 hours a difference to the east of 1° 16' and to the north one of 7' 7 seconds.
Scarcely was it noon when we had a squall which made the winds shift to south-south-east and it blew fine breeze. We thought that after the squall passed we should have calm again, but we were deceived this time to our advantage for the winds having settled to the south, were always increasing. We even feared the weather might become bad during the night, so loaded was the sky with dark clouds and had bad appearance. The barometer seemed inclined to fall and we took accordingly our precautions for the night by hauling our mainsail and our topgallant sails which we did not need to keep the Naturaliste in company which nevertheless had all sail set.
The night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth we did not have the bad weather that appearances had announced. On the contrary, it blew very fresh from the south to the south-south-east, and we made good progress steering north-east. For, although our observed distances placed us much more to the east than the timekeepers, I had difficulty in believing that their movement had experienced the retardation of which we thought ourselves aware. During the night the weather was very nebulous and some good gusts passed, nevertheless we brought in our topsails from time to time only to wait for the Naturaliste which was forcing sail to follow us.
1801-03-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At noon in 28° 3' 32" of latitude observed and in 56° 49' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 18° 8' NW. The lunar distances gave 56° 2' of longitude.

1801-03-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy and the winds a strong breeze from SSW to south. The mizzen topsail sheet having parted, we clewed the sail up to leeward to repair it.
1801-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, we had very fine weather and a fine breeze variable in the morning from south to south-south-east and we made good progress. The winds continued thus in the afternoon and during the night so that the twenty-four hours were the best course we have made since doubling the Cape of Good Hope. It was beyond question the finest day of our voyage, since the good wind we had was accompanied by a fine sky.
At noon, the observed latitude was 25° 2' south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 53° 54' 51". That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 31 of 55° 31' 9" and by No. 38 of 56° 8', which gave us in the twenty-four hours a difference to the north of 9' 30" and one to the west of 17' 18".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and at four o'clock I signalled to the Naturaliste that at midnight we would shape course to the north-north-east finding myself advanced enough to the east to have no fear of making the land under the lee of Île de France and I feared on the contrary to find myself too much to windward if our longitudes observed by distances were better than those indicated by our timekeepers.
On board the Naturaliste the timekeepers gave 30' more east than ours, which appears to us all the more astonishing in that they had always indicated a longitude more west and it will only be on our arrival at Île de France that we shall truly be able to know which shall have had the most regular movement. I am inclined to believe, as I have already remarked, that the great damp we have long experienced may have somewhat altered their daily movement, although very little difference has been observed in the comparisons.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the weather continued fine and the winds came round to the south-east, the breeze was less strong. Nevertheless we made passable progress, having only enough sail to enable the Naturaliste to overtake us which had all she could carry.
1801-03-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 25° 2' 50" of latitude observed and in 57° 29' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 14° 17' NW. At noon the course was signalled and given N 33° 45' E. At 4 signalled the course N 22° 30' E for midnight.

1801-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea and the wind light from south, SE and SSE. At noon the course was signalled us NE by N until midnight, when we were to steer NNE.
1801-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, the weather continued fine, but the breeze was much less strong than the day before and we had these twenty-four hours only a very ordinary day. The winds in the morning came to the south-east by south and in the afternoon they returned to the south-south-east and towards evening to the south.
After sunrise we had a visit from quite a large number of tropicbirds which remained around us quite long and then disappeared.
In the morning, we began to caulk our boats which were found to require it and we prepared the capstans which were engaged by our plant boxes which I had had secured around, as being the place most suited to their security.
At noon, the observed latitude was 22° 50' and the longitude according to dead reckoning was 54° 34' 51". That of No. 31 was then 55° 54' 12" and that of No. 38 was 56° 20' 54". There was in these twenty-four hours 56 seconds difference to the north and 17' 8 seconds difference to the east.
In the afternoon the breeze was very weak, the Naturaliste which was at half cannon-shot distance asked to pass astern and we spoke together. It was agreed to continue the course to the north-north-east until the next day at noon and that during the day of the twenty-first the anchors should be prepared for mooring. The longitude indicated by her timekeepers was 30' more east than ours and that by six observations of distances of 36° 58' (sic) which gave her a small difference from ours which placed us a little more to the east.
The mean result of two amplitudes and two azimuths gave for variation north-west 13° 30', on board the Naturaliste they had 14° 30'.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first, the sky was very nebulous and the wind almost calm, in a few hours they were then to the south and even to the south-south-west. There were some clouds which gave a little rain, but it was in small quantity. The sea was quite fine and yet the ship rolled considerably being wind-astern.
1801-03-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 2 a.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the second time, in 58° 6' of longitude. The rigging was set up. At noon in 22° 48' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 9' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 55' NW. At 5.30 we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander told Captain Hamelin to bend his sheet cables without waiting for the signal.

1801-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind light from SE, south, SSW and south. We asked the commander whether we should bend the cables without waiting for a signal; he answered no.
1801-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, we had very little weather and the winds singularly variable from south-south-west to south-east by the south. As there was but little wind we rolled considerably. The sea, although fine, had a heavy swell from the south and quite high. We saw during the morning a great quantity of tropicbirds but we remarked that they never showed themselves in the afternoon which appeared to us all the more singular in that from the morning at sunrise they were to soar above the weathercock.
In the morning the cables were sent down and the anchors were disposed to be put in mooring when the time came.
At noon we observed the latitude of 21° 49' 54" and the longitude following dead reckoning was 54° 59' 58". That of No. 31, reduced to noon, was 56° 13' 48" and for No. 38 of 56° 42' 0. We found ourselves to have in the twenty-four hours a difference to the north of 7 minutes 47 seconds and one to the east of 5 minutes 54 seconds.
In the afternoon the winds were to the south gentle breeze and I signalled the course to the north by north-east finding myself by the movement of the timekeepers advanced enough to not miss Île de France and much too far advanced if our observations of longitude are good since they give us near two degrees to the east of the timekeepers.
The mean result of two ortive and occasive amplitudes joined to that of two azimuths gave for declination north-west 12° 30' for the evening and 12° 45' for the morning, which seemed to confirm that we were much to the east of our timekeepers since this declination is to within a small matter that which is observed at present at Rodrigue.
At the beginning of the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second it blew quite fine breeze from the south-south-east, but during the night the wind abated considerably. We continued the course to the north by north-east all sail set in order to gain way to the north and place ourselves in the latitude of Îlot Rond which M. d'Après places at 19° 50' south latitude.
1801-03-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SSE. We bent our cables and got the anchors ready to let go. At noon in 21° 29' 40" of latitude observed and in 58° 14' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 49' NW. At 1.30 the course was signalled and given N 11° 15' E.

1801-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from south, SSE and SSW. At 3 the winds shifted all at once to WSW. At sunrise land was thought to be seen in the WNW; the wind fell light. Saw a great number of tropic birds.
1801-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, at dawn, we had fair weather and winds variable from south-south-west to south-south-east gentle breeze. At six o'clock I signalled to steer to the north-west and to carry the most sail possible in order to try to have knowledge of land before nightfall should a fresh breeze come during the day. But we lost this hope for it blew but little throughout the morning during which we saw a great quantity of tropicbirds. The calm of the morning was very fortunate for us since we caught two small fish of so bizarre a form that I hope no similar ones have ever been seen. These fish were lodged under tufts of fucus which the sailors call bunches of grapes. They were the first we had encountered since our departure from Europe. It appears that the season in which we passed, the trade winds and the trade winds was not the epoch when this plant detaches itself from the bed of the sea which is ordinarily found covered in fair weather.
At noon, the south latitude observed was 20° 20' 19" and the longitude following dead reckoning was 54° 33' 51". We found ourselves, following the movement of the timekeepers at 55° 56' 54" at No. 31. Citizen Bissy having made no observation this day I had none of No. 38. There was in the 24 hours 10' 24 seconds difference to the south and 2' 30" difference to the east.
During the evening it blew fine breeze and we forced sail until evening to try to have knowledge of the land, being to have knowledge of it before night according to the movement of the timekeepers.
At sunset the weather came on to squalls and we had at times some rain. I signalled the Naturaliste to pass astern and when she was within hail I told her that we should regulate the sail during the night so as to make only three knots and that I should lay-to if the horizon were not extended enough to see at a certain distance.
At eleven o'clock, the sky being very nebulous and covered we took reefs in the topsails and the offing until four o'clock in the morning when we shaped course for the land, all sail set.
1801-03-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to ESE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and given N 45° W. Saw a great deal of weed. At noon in 20° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 1' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 35' NW. At 3 the weather turned overcast, with light rain. At 4.45 signalled the Naturaliste to pass under our stern; at 6, being within hail, the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to steer N 67° 30' W, that at 8 he would regulate his canvas so as to run only 3.5 knots, and that if the weather turned bad he would heave to on the starboard tack, of which he would warn him by two lights. After speaking the Naturaliste we bore up N 67° 30' W. At 11 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under close-reefed topsails; the breeze light, with lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SE, N, NE, east and SE. At 5 passed under the commander's stern; he gave us verbal orders to run no more than three and a half knots to the WNW, and that if the weather turned bad we should heave to. At a quarter past eleven the commander hove to on the starboard tack. We did the same. At 4 a.m., the wind having shifted to the north, we went onto the port tack.
1801-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-third at dawn, the winds suddenly came to the north-east fine breeze. As we had shaped course we forced sail towards the land to obtain sight of it during the day, not doubting to have sight of it before night unless there should be some change in the movement of the timekeepers. Throughout the morning we had sight of a great number of birds of different species which indicated to us that we were not far from it. Nevertheless at noon we had no knowledge of it. The observed latitude at the same time was 19° 54' and the longitude following dead reckoning was 53° 6'. That indicated by the timekeepers was then 54° 47' 17" at No. 38 and 54° 15' 19" at No. 31. There was a difference in the 24 hours of 54" to the north and of 8' 38" to the west.
In the afternoon it continued to blow fine breeze and we forced sail until sunset.
At five o'clock the lookouts from the mast-head announced the land and we were not long in perceiving it from below. After sunset we made the bearing as follows.
Bearings of the land at six o'clock in the evening:
The northernmost land to the west 22° north!
The southernmost land to the west 19° 31 south!
Îlot Rond to the west: 2° south! all of the compass.
At seven o'clock we hauled in our topgallant sails and all light sails and at eight o'clock we came close-hauled on the starboard tack.
The Naturaliste having passed astern asked me what were my intentions for the night. I replied that we should keep in the position we were in making different tacks in order to pass tomorrow early through the passage between Îlot Rond and Coin de Mire. It was also agreed that we should keep a light astern all night and that the changes of tack would be indicated according to the usual practice of signals. During the night we had several squalls of rain with some wind and many flashes of lightning though we did not hear thunder.
1801-03-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to SE. At 5 a.m. shaped our course west, crowding sail. At noon in 19° 54' 0" of latitude observed and in 56° 34' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 53' NW. At 5 p.m. the land was sighted in the S 75° W. At 6 took the bearing of Round Island N 68° W, the southernmost point of Mauritius in sight S 70° W, and the most conspicuous peak S 88° W. At 8.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 9.30 the Naturaliste passed under our stern; Captain Hamelin asked the commander his intentions for the night, and he told him he would stand off and on until daybreak. During the night overcast and squally weather, with rain and lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.30 we made the land, and a moment later the commander signalled us the course WSW. At 1 a.m. went about, the weather stormy and squally. At daybreak we sighted the land WNW, distant about 6 leagues. The commander hailed us to steer for Round Island and to keep in his wake as close as possible. He asked whether we had anyone on board who knew the passage; we answered that we had Citizen Piquet, ensign.
1801-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth at four o'clock in the morning I signalled to the Naturaliste to take tacks on starboard and we came towards the land. At daylight we were greatly astonished to see that the current had carried us considerably to the south, but as there was no remedy and we must regain the way lost, we forced sail to close with Îlot Rond which we had much difficulty in doubling on account of the force of the current and the little wind. Nevertheless the weather was in squalls with rain and we had some that gave us a little wind while they lasted.
Bearings at noon
Îlot Rond at the north-east
The highest part of Île Plate at the north-west by north all of the compass
Pointe des Canonniers at the west by south-west
The northernmost land to the south
We followed the Neptune Oriental in passing between Îlot Rond and Coin de Mire and we hugged the latter at a distance of a cannon and a half shot. We experienced in passing a set of current which nearly threw us athwart on the starboard side although we had all sail set and fresh breeze.
After passing Coin de Mire we steered for Pointe des Canonniers by which we hoisted our colours which was assured by a powder shot. The fortress which is there did the same but when we doubled it the colours were struck a powder shot was fired and they were hoisted again. Not knowing what this manoeuvre meant we did the same in any case and continued our course to reach the anchorage of the Two Brothers.
At four o'clock we obtained knowledge beyond Île aux Tonneliers of the vessels which were in the harbour and we counted on reaching the anchorage in less than half an hour but the winds coming to the south-south-west failed us and obliged us to take the offing. From four o'clock until eight they were very variable from south-south-west to south-south-east. We beat about in short tacks to reach the anchorage but we could not succeed and as the calm took us we dropped one of our sheet anchors in nineteen fathoms coral bottom opposite Baie du Tombeau.
As soon as we were at anchor I signalled this to the Naturaliste but she did not reply having not perceived it because she had run too far off shore.
During the night the weather was absolutely calm and the ship lay very quietly on her anchor. We kept until daylight a light at each of our masts so that the Naturaliste might perceive them when she came back towards the land. This vessel anchored at eleven o'clock at half a league from us.

Citizen Péron observes in his note that the variations of the barometer corresponded fairly generally with those of the atmosphere especially in the first days of the decade during which the weather was very uncertain and the state of the sky variable. He concludes and doubtless with reason that the hygrometric state of the air sensibly influences the lowering of the mercury in the barometer tube. It is almost certain that the barometer would always remain at a great height if the sky free from vapours and damp were always pure and as it is only when it is overloaded with vapours that bad weather occurs it is quite natural that the weight of the air should lower the barometer so much the more as the atmosphere is charged with these same vapours which are the first and principal cause of its variations.
General observations. Thermometer
By a continuation of the observations of Citizen Péron it appears that this decade is one of those which gave us the most heat since our departure and especially that it sustained itself in a manner constant and uniform. By the little difference which the results of each noon or midnight of the same day produced he maintains that it is his uniformity that is the cause that we perceived it less than at other times when although less strong it sometimes appeared very unbearable to us. This reasoning is perhaps not without foundation.
General observations. Hygrometer
According to the remarks of Citizen Péron it appears constant that we always found a greater quantity of damp in the atmosphere when the winds reigned in the east quarter variable to the north than when we had them from east variable to south. The explanation of this phenomenon will not be difficult if we consider the great quantity of land to the north as well as its proximity to us relative to that which we might have to the south. It appears to me quite simple to believe that the vapours lifted from the earth by the sun must be in much greater quantity than those it can lift from the sea and it is doubtless in consequence of this principle that the north winds constantly gave us a greater degree of damp than the south winds which having much less land to cross to reach us encountered on their route only the vapours which the sun was able to lift from the sea.

General observations on the temperature of the waters of the sea
The very multiplied experiments which Citizen Péron made appear according to his report to have fully convinced him that the temperature of the waters of the sea at the surface is generally warmer than that of the atmosphere at least in the regions we traversed. He reserves to make known by a detailed memoir the cause of this phenomenon not finding sufficiently satisfying what those who until now have occupied themselves with seeking the true cause have said about it. He does not believe moreover that the observations which have been made before this voyage have been sufficiently multiplied and it is for this reason that he has never failed to make them every day we have kept the sea and in all the different variations where we have found this element during four consecutive months of being at sea.
This work will doubtless be interesting and new and the natural philosophers will find in the account of Citizen Péron all the information they could desire.
State of the atmosphere during the month of Ventôse.
In the first decade the weather was generally warm rainy and damp. Winds from the north reigned sometimes but they came to us more frequently from east towards south moderate.
There were no electrical phenomena nor meteors of any kind in this decade. Although we had fairly often rain and many black and thick clouds in the air we did not hear thunder and the weather became fine without a shift of wind.
Second decade Up to the 25th Ventôse
The sky during these fifteen days was fairly generally fine with but little damp in the air but very hot. The winds were very variable in the first days and we had then a covered sky and in appearance stormy. Once we had reached the general south-east winds the sky then brightened and fair weather succeeded. Nevertheless we had at times rain but it was never of long duration.
It was remarked that as soon as we had the south-east winds the gusts were very abundant and it was for this reason that the crews who enjoyed the best of health were forbidden to sleep in the open although it was very hot below the decks.
On the thirteenth in the morning we had the sight of a double rainbow perfectly well formed but on the 23rd following a strong squall of rain we had a triple one. It was the first time such a phenomenon had struck our eyes and we much regretted that it was not of longer duration than it was.
1801-03-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.15 a.m. shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7 the commander gave verbal orders to Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at a cable's length. At 8 took the bearing of Serpent Island N 24° W, Mauritius from N 75° W to S 50° W; signalled the Naturaliste to make ready to let go a bower anchor. At noon Round Island N 45° E, Flat Island N 34° W, Pointe aux Canonniers S 79° W. At 1.30 we hoisted our colours and confirmed them with a gun. The fort of Pointe aux Canonniers hoisted the national flag and confirmed it. At 2, being abreast of it, it saluted us with the flag; we returned the salute. At 3 the breeze drew round to SSW, variable to W. We stood on whichever tack served us best, firing guns to call the pilot. At 4 took the bearing of Pointe aux Canonniers N 75° E and Pointe aux Tonneliers S 24° W. At 8, being almost becalmed, we anchored under the coast in 20 fathoms, coral bottom, the light of Île aux Tonneliers bearing south and that of Fort Diane S 22° 30' W. The shore under which we lay anchored sent up two rockets every two hours.

1801-03-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and a fresh breeze from ESE. After doubling Coin de Mire the commander signalled us to follow his movements; he was lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 3, the commander having fallen calm under the land, he went onto the starboard tack. A moment later the winds shifted to SSW; we stood on on our tack and went about a moment afterwards to run in for the land. We struggled all along against the fickleness of the winds to reach the anchorage under Île aux Tonneliers, but their weakness did not let us come near enough to the land to let go the anchor. At nightfall we fired a gun and hoisted our ensign at half mast to call a pilot. At 8.30 p.m. we stood off to seaward, the currents setting us WSW. At 10.30 p.m. we went onto the starboard tack. The winds having shifted, we ran in for the land and sounded without finding bottom; it was not until 10.35 that we found 26 and 17 fathoms. We let go the anchor in 14 fathoms, coral bottom, and veered 36 fathoms of cable. We sent a boat to sound all round the ship, Port Louis bearing from us S by E at a short distance, the commander in the NE by E at a great distance; the weather fine, a flat calm. At daybreak we showed our colours and our ensign at the stern half mast. At 6.45 we sighted a boat coming off from the shore towards us, approaching only with caution; when within hail she called to us, and on our answer she came aboard. The captain of the port, who was in her, left us a pilot and gave us a signal to identify ourselves from the shore. We were visited by the health officers and by the colonial assembly; the said captain of the port went aboard the Géographe. At 7.30 hove up, broke the anchor out and catted it. We got under way, casting to port. Favoured by a breeze off the sea, we shaped our course for Port Louis, doubled the Deux Frères at 9, leaving them to port, and doubled Île aux Tonneliers. At 10 we anchored in five fathoms and a half; shortly afterwards the Géographe came and anchored ahead of us.
1801-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
(The month of Pluviôse is here an error and so until the 30th: read Ventôse)
Entry into the north-east port of Île de France
On the 25th, after sunrise, seeing no boat coming from land, we set sail to reach the entrance of the port which we would have attained without encountering a canoe, had the breeze not failed us. However, around seven o'clock, being about one league from the Two Brothers, a canoe was sighted which we judged to be that of the pilot. It came alongside the Naturaliste first, who was ahead of us, and shortly after it came to meet us. When the officer commanding it came aboard and the first compliments were over, I asked him why he had not come the previous day to the various signals that had been made. But he excused himself by saying that the lookouts had signalled us as enemy vessels and he added that our appearance had caused such alarm in the island that all troops and national guards had been ordered to their respective posts where they had spent the night to oppose the landing that was supposed we had designed to effect. I could not help laughing at the fright that vessels as peaceful as ours had occasioned. And I observed only to this officer that our manœuvre should make us all the less suspect, as we had had all night, at the anchorage we occupied, lights at all our masts, which is not ordinarily done by vessels which, wishing to commit hostilities, must at least hide their position in order not to be incommoded by the artillery of the forts under which they find themselves.
Be that as it may, the port officer and the pilot arranged the course that had to be made to reach the Pavilions. But before manœuvring accordingly, we had to make a conventional signal with the land to make known that the vessels came from France.
(in a note at the end of the page: It is expressly forbidden to port officers and pilots to allow, within the Two Brothers, vessels coming from France to enter before the Commission of which I have just spoken has come aboard and seized all the public letters or papers that may be found there. This measure extends even to letters addressed to the administrators and it was seen with regret that I handed over to the aide-de-camp of the General-in-Chief those that were meant for him).
When it was made, we steered under easy sail in the direction of wind indicated so as to give time to the Intermediate Commission, representing the colony, to come aboard, seeing that no vessel coming from France can enter the passes before the members of this Commission come aboard to learn the news that is brought and the motives of its port of call.
At half past nine, a boat from the port bearing flag displayed at the stern came into view. We were at once informed that it was that of the Intermediate Commission and we prepared to receive it. The Naturaliste received its first visit and half an hour later we saw four persons arrive, two of whom wore the tricolour sash.
The officer of the guard having received them according to custom, I then invited them to pass into my cabin where I was informed of the subject of their visit. The conversation turned at first on the situation of France, but soon more particular inquiry was made concerning the intentions of the Government towards the Colony &c. I was especially questioned on the nature of the expedition I was about to make, and finally, whether there was not aboard some secret agent charged with carrying out the decree on the freedom of negroes. Having answered as best I could all these questions, I was required to hand over all the letters that might be found aboard.
I was assured on word of honour that they would be exactly delivered to their addresses. I made no difficulty about those I was carrying but, not content with this particular deference, I was invited to give a whistle signal so that the officers and crew would conform to this measure which they called a security for the safety of the Colony. I did not think I should refuse this request and the order was given as they desired. After the handing over of the letters came that of the public papers and finally we set course to enter the port.
As soon as the vessels were at anchor in the port, the members of the Intermediate Commission proposed that I should go ashore with them, which I accepted. At eleven o'clock we landed and I was conducted to the Government where I arrived not without difficulty, so encumbered was the road with the quantity of people whom curiosity or the desire to learn news had gathered. All questioned me at once and I had no other means of satisfying them than to announce that, having handed over to the Commission the public papers I had brought, they should address themselves to it for political news, but as for those particular to France, I assured them that everything was in the best possible order and that they would soon learn that a glorious peace would assure the stability and prosperity of the Republic.
My interview with M. Magallon, Governor General, had nothing remarkable about it. The assembly, besides, was too numerous for him to speak to me of business matters. This first meeting was limited to making known to him the motive of my arrival and the mission I had to accomplish. He invited me to dinner as well as M. Hamelin, and we parted.
On leaving the residence of the Governor General, I was conducted to the place where the Intermediate Commission holds its sessions. I found several of its members assembled there who no doubt counted on my visit. After the first compliments on my safe arrival, the inspection of all the letters I had handed over was made in my presence. I noticed that several were set aside when the others were sent to the post. Having asked why this retention was made, I was answered that the tranquillity of the Colony depended on it and that those to whom they were addressed would receive them as soon as their contents had been known.
After having answered the various questions that were put to me, I went to the municipality where I found the hall full of people who were waiting impatiently to hear the news I was bringing. I was placed beside the mayor who, having announced in a loud voice the motives of my port of call in the Colony and the short stay I counted on making there, then read a letter which was written to him by the brother of General Villaret (de) Joyeuse.
This letter contained, in substance, that General Villaret would soon arrive in the Colony as Governor-in-Chief, that he would bring with him a considerable sum for the payment of the salaries of the Government and that he himself would go to Lima to take additional funds which would soon restore to the Colony the state of splendour which it had formerly enjoyed. His arrival was to take place six or eight months after that of the General and cetera and cetera.
From the municipality, I went to the Intendancy and I did not find in the Administrator who resides there that honest and gracious reception that I had met with everywhere else. I learned afterwards that he had taken it badly that, leaving the residence of the Governor, I had gone to the Intermediate Commission before paying my respects to him. I do not know whether the course I followed compromised the dignity of M. the Intendant, but as I was always accompanied in these visits by a member of the Commission and a municipal officer, it seemed to me quite simple to follow the course they indicated to me.
Moreover, M. the Ordonnateur should rather have blamed my conductors than me if I committed this blunder, and not have revenged himself in the way that he did.
The rest of the day had nothing remarkable about it. M. Hamelin and I dined at the General's where nothing happened that deserves to be mentioned.
1801-03-16.journal_breton_geographe: The wind a light breeze from SE. At 5 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7.30 an officer of the port and a pilot came out to us; they did not come aboard until they had asked whether there was any contagious sickness. At 10 we anchored in the North West Port in 4 fathoms, black mud mixed with grey sand, the flagstaff of Île aux Tonneliers bearing N 18° W, that of the Discovery Hill S 30° W, Le Pouce S 15° E and Pieter Both S 40° E. Several members of the colonial assembly and of the municipality came aboard. Orders were given to hand over all letters for the colony. The commander and Captain Hamelin went ashore shortly afterwards; leave to communicate with the shore was brought out to us, and many boats loaded with people, who had been waiting only for that leave, came alongside. The port's longboats helped us to moor; the boats were put in the water. Continuation. At 9 p.m., being charged with the duty of the roads as commanding ship, Citizen Ronsard, officer of the guard, went the rounds; Citizen Le Bas, frigate captain, went with him, knowing the usage of the service at Mauritius. He hailed a Danish ship that had a fire burning; a man who was on deck answered him rudely, and, having said he was a petty officer, Citizen Le Bas had him put into his boat. On reaching the ship he wanted to make him go first. The stranger then told him he was an officer like himself; in spite of which he pushed him by the shoulder. The gunner's mate tried to do the same; the unfortunate man's feet caught in the lashings that were on the gangway and he fell into the hold and was badly bruised on the shoulder. He was dressed and sent back to his ship. The 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1801]. The brig L'Utile got under way for Réunion. An officer from La Cayenne came to tell us that we should no longer be charged with the duty of the roads. A water lighter came out to us. The topgallant masts were got down.

1801-03-17.journal_anonyme: During the day, the pilot being on board, we weighed to warp further in; by nightfall we were moored in six fathoms with 70 fathoms of cable out to starboard and the port cable made fast to a mooring buoy. On the morning of the 26th we laid a third anchor astern. Stay at Mauritius, Germinal to the 5th Floréal [Year 9, 25 April 1801]. During our stay at Mauritius we were busy overhauling the rigging and caulking the ship, and fresh provisions were embarked. The nights were cool enough and the days calm. By day the winds were fairly regularly from SE to SSE, and by night from NW to WNW. We had many deserters, and several officers and scientists of the two corvettes stayed behind at Mauritius. To prevent desertion the commander made us get under way to lie at the outer anchorage. On the morning of the 28th [Germinal, Year 9, 18 April 1801] the officers of the Naturaliste were assembled aboard the Géographe by the commander's order. They all went with the captain to the appointed place. The commander said he had held a council to determine what measures it would be best to take to bring back our deserters; and at the same time he read out the petition addressed to the constituted authorities of the colony to reclaim them. The commander having asked each man's opinion, all were of the view not to sign this petition; and by unanimous agreement among the officers of both ships the following declarations were entered in the Géographe's log: The officers forming the wardrooms of the two corvettes Géographe and Naturaliste, convened in council by the commander-in-chief of the expedition of discovery to deliberate on the most effective means of bringing back the deserting seamen of both ships, have declared that the commander alone had the right to take whatever measures should appear most fitting. All the officers signed this declaration, but Citizen Hamelin stated that he would not sign it, and the commander said he ought not to do so. Captain Baudin having announced that the purpose of the meeting was fulfilled, we took leave of him and all our officers returned on board; we hoisted in our longboat and our large boat. At 6 a.m. on the 2nd Floréal [Year 9, 22 April 1801] a naval gendarme brought us ten men by order of the fitting-out office. On the 3rd Floréal [Year 9, 23 April 1801] a boat sent by the fitting-out office brought clothing and money for various seamen shipped the day before. At 3.30 p.m. on the 5th [Year 9, 25 April 1801] the commander gave the order to unmoor; we at once sent a longboat to weigh our kedge anchor. At 5 a.m. on the 5th the winds ESE, a light breeze; at a quarter to seven the commander made us the signal to get under way. We at once hove short and hoisted our topsails to the mastheads, and as soon as the anchor was aweigh we filled and stood on. Bearings at eight in the morning: Coin de Mire NE by E; Île aux Tonneliers E by S 5° S. The winds variable from east to ESE and to west. Noon bearings: Coin de Mire N 60° E; the discovery hill of the port E by S; Morne Brabant SSW 5° S.
1801-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe: On the twenty-sixth, most of the naturalists disembarked their effects and took lodgings in different quarters of the town. Aboard, we occupied ourselves with placing the vessel on four moorings according to the custom of the port. The small means given to us for this work caused it to last the whole day, so that it was entirely lost for the particular works we had to do aboard. However, I had a statement drawn up of the replacements in provisions of the campaign that I needed, having resolved to make the request the next day of the General Administrators.

1801-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, I addressed to the General Ordonnateur a statement of my requirements and wrote to him the letter which is found in the correspondence that I had occasion to hold with the Administrators during the time of my port of call.
Aboard, we occupied ourselves with unrigging the vessel and as it was fitting to give a little rest to these men who had kept the sea for seven months, six months, it was arranged that every day twelve would have permission to go ashore and that the others would only go when the first had returned.

1801-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, the provisions clerk carried to the Ordonnateur the statement of our daily provisions, but the request was refused. I made my way in the morning to M. the Intendant to urge him to grant us some refreshments in bread and fresh meat. But I was no more successful nor better received than the provisions clerk had been. I represented to M. the Ordonnateur the inconveniences of his refusal and the discontent that the crew would experience, but all was useless and I obtained nothing, under the pretence that there was no money in the cashbox to pay the butcher and the baker.
The consumption of our campaign provisions was too precious for me not to make him feel that it would be less costly to him to feed us fresh meat than to replace the biscuit and salted meat that he wanted us to consume. (In the margin: his answer) was that we could make such consumption as we pleased, but that he would replace nothing. I then invited him to reply to the letter that I had had the honour to write to him concerning our needs, so that I would make my decision when he had made known to me officially his intentions. And I withdrew, truly, very discontented, seeing clearly that there was more ill humour in his refusals than inability to grant me my requests.
On leaving the Ordonnateur, I went to the General-in-Chief to whom I made known what had just happened. He promised to see the Intendant during the day and assured me that he would do his best so that we would not have the unpleasantness that I was already beginning to foresee and which I did not conceal from him.
In the evening, returning aboard, I learned of a poster that had been put up at the corner of some streets and on which was written in large letters: "VOYAGE OF DISCOVERIES FAILED". I ignore the motive that could have given rise to this bad joke and I am pleased to believe that it will not come true.

1801-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, I handed over to the Swedish Captain commanding the ship the Kent, a letter which announced to the Minister of the Navy our arrival in the Colony. A copy of this letter will be found in my correspondence with the Administrators of the Colony and following that which I addressed to him at the time of my departure for New Holland.
In the morning, I received from the port twenty-six caulkers whom I had requested the previous day to cover the vessel to its flotation line. We needed all the more to do this work as the vessel, being new, had suffered so much from the heat that all the oakum had come out of the seams, which caused us to make a considerable amount of water whenever the sea was rough.
In the course of the day, no one went ashore, having been obliged to lend the longboat of both vessels to the ship the Kent which was leaving for Europe. We employed our time aboard in resetting the mast of the topsail yard and in unbendin our sails.

1801-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, as no one had gone ashore the previous day, permission was given to half the crew to go ashore, some to wash their clothes and others to take a walk. As it was, besides, a day of decade and consequently of rest, we did nothing aboard. In the morning, three Arab vessels left the port and one of them ran on to the rocks which are to port of the pass when leaving. It would no doubt have remained there if, as soon as I became aware of it, I had not sent my longboat and that of the Naturaliste with each a cable and an anchor to extricate it from the embarrassment. For in the port, no movement was made to give it assistance.
At three-thirty in the afternoon, seeing that it was not yet out of danger, I wrote to M. the Ordonnateur, the General being absent, to express to him how surprised I was at the indifference with which a vessel was seen to be lost and I invited him to send it new assistance before nightfall.
At four o'clock and before the port had made any movement, this vessel extricated itself from the rocks on which it had run. I received a letter of thanks from the Captain who commands it by the return of my longboat. But it cost me a cable and an anchor. The anchor moored amongst the rocks was broken in raising it, and the cable much damaged. I gave notice of this to the Administrators begging them to replace these two objects for me since they had served to fulfil the duties of the port. I await the reply to my letter.
The rest of the day had nothing remarkable about it.

1801-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 1st germinal, we reset the topsail yards and they were at once uncapped to inspect the rigging. Our lower yard suspenders were found broken in two places and the shrouds were so damaged that they had to be changed.
The caulkers continued their work and I prepared to have placed, in a warehouse which M. the Intendant had been kind enough to lend me, the articles of trade and even the provisions that were aboard for greater facility in taking on our water.
In the course of the day, I received from M. the Intendant, the letter of which a copy is found in my correspondence with this Administrator concerning the requests I had made to him for our replacements in provisions. On reading them, one will see his good dispositions towards us and I do not doubt that the Government will thank him in the manner he deserves for the interest he took in the health of my crew and in the success of the expedition.
At ten o'clock, I went to see the harbour master to ask him to lend us the place called "The Tower" to establish our observatory. He lent himself with the best grace in the world to our requests; it was arranged that the next day we would have our instruments carried there so as to determine well the running of our timekeepers.
In the course of the day, the longboat which the port had lent me, armed with fifteen negroes to relieve the work of the crews, made two trips in the port and we deposited in the warehouse which had been lent to us, the articles of which the officers' journal makes mention. It is at this time that several of the savants asked the chief physician of the ship for hospital passes to go refresh themselves there. One of the officers of the Géographe named Baudin had for two days taken lodgings in the town and I was not informed of it until his absence at the moment when he was to take the watch. This conduct seemed to me somewhat extraordinary and I resolved to express to him my surprise at our next meeting.

1801-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, we continued the disembarkation of our effects, whilst the caulkers, carpenters and sailors occupied themselves, each in his own department, to accelerate our work and put us in a condition to leave quickly. We worked likewise aboard the Naturaliste which was found to have greater needs than us, having one of its davits to change and part of its knightheads to repair. It received the same number of caulkers as we did and the carpenters that it needed for its other work.
In the morning, the crew made complaints to me about the manner in which they were fed at the roadstead. I carried their representation to M. the Intendant whom I found as little accommodating as on the previous days. I represented to him that a measure so unsuitable would surely be a pretext for desertion and that, if once it took hold among my crew, it would be difficult to stop the consequences, nothing could make him change the resolution he had taken not to give me anything. At last, having pushed him to the limit, he told me that the Minister of the Navy, in announcing my arrival, had also announced to him that we needed nothing and that consequently he would give us nothing.
I thought I should observe to him that the need of nothing concerned only what was necessary for the rigging of the vessels, but that this could not be understood in the same way for the usual ration following long navigations. This reasoning was no more successful than the others and I was obliged to find another way to obtain some refreshments.
Eight men entered the hospital this day, alleged of severe colics with fevers. The ship's physician attributed the cause to the quality of the water and immediately I ordered that for the daily ration, a drink composed of rum, sugar and water mixed together be prepared, in order to prevent the illnesses that raw water could occasion.

1801-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, seeing that I was to expect nothing from the Administration for the replacements in campaign provisions of which I had such essential need, nor yet for the daily ration, I thought it fitting to stop the murmurs of the crew, at least for a part of their complaints. Accordingly, I went to find the butcher who serves the Government for the supplies of the hospital. I explained my position to him and the manner in which I set about it, urging him to promise me fresh meat, three times a decade, and he consented only to receive payment when the Administrators should be in funds. It seemed to me that I had won a great victory and I at once went to the Intendant to announce to him the success of my efforts. But what was not my surprise to see him immediately make a written order to the purveyor to furnish us nothing except for ready money, declaring to him that he would not account to him for any advances that he might make to us. I confess that this conduct on the part of the Intendant gave me all the more ill humour, as I saw in it a well-marked design to harm us so that I asked him whether it was he who had had "Voyage of Discoveries Failed" posted up and whether he truly persuaded himself that he would succeed. However, to terminate all discussion, the conversation becoming too serious, I withdrew and again went to find the butcher with whom I made a formal engagement to pay him before my departure. And by this means I procured for the crew fresh meat three times a decade. On the other days, I procured at the market a little fish and some vegetables. Nevertheless, I had the unpleasantness of seeing many of my people enter the hospital where they cost the Government, to treat them as sick, three times more than it would have cost to have kept them in the good health that they had brought into the Colony.
From what had just happened, I made it my duty to no longer present myself at M. the Ordonnateur's and I proposed only, whenever circumstances should require it, to make my requests to him in writing so as better to establish his conduct towards us.
During the day we continued to occupy ourselves aboard with the work we had to do and with the inspection of our rigging. Our instruments were also carried ashore and the astronomers took possession of the place that had been lent to us. We also disembarked the sails that needed repairs and they were deposited for greater safety and ease in the workshops of the Republic which could not, under any pretext, be refused to us for no one worked there for the account of the Government, but the sailmakers attached to this establishment were in town for the account of the Administrators in finance.

1801-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the hope of being more fortunate in addressing myself to the Intermediate Commission representing the Colony, I sent it a statement of requests which I restricted as much as was possible for me. Several people had already urged me to take this step, but I had always refused so that the Administration would have no cause to complain. However, as it was the only means left to me and as I truly was beginning to perceive that one wished to force my crew to renounce the continuance of the expedition, I hesitated no longer and sent to the members composing this Commission the letter which is found annexed to my correspondence.
I was very impatient to know what the result would be, when one of the members and an old acquaintance of mine in this country came and told me that I should expect nothing from it, seeing that the fear of seeing the English appear at any moment made it desirable that I should remain longer in the Colony, so as to take possession of my people if they should appear. This news, which was the result of a secret deliberation, became known to me and I judged it fitting, while appearing to ignore it, to take a decisive step as soon as the reply to my letter should reach me. Supposing, as I ought to have expected, that nothing would be given me, I had decided in my own mind to at least put the vessels out of the port and as soon as they had been ready, I would have set course for Batavia or Manila where I was well assured of not experiencing the same difficulties.
The conduct of the Intendant towards the crews had caused several, persuaded that I would not be able to leave, to begin to become disorderly and even impertinent. Several were put in irons aboard to serve as an example but they made little account of this punishment.

1801-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, the administrative assembly of the Colony, in replying to my letter, made it known to me that I was to expect no more assistance from its part than I had obtained from the administration of the Government and from that moment, I began to see that it would be difficult for me to get out of Île de France, where I sincerely regretted, but too late, having anchored.
In the course of the day, I handed over into the hands of the Government the Chinaman A-Son, in accordance with the instructions which the Minister of the Navy had given me concerning him. I likewise saw with regret that several officers of the General Staffs of both vessels took rooms ashore and had their effects carried there, content to appear aboard only once or twice a decade to do what they call their guard duty to which they believe themselves solely bound during the stay of the vessels in the port. I complained to several about this conduct; they replied to me that the care of their health was their first duty and that the chief physician of the hospital had judged it thus. The truth is that these gentlemen were much healthier than I was for at this time I had caught a draught of air which made me suffer greatly.
Be that as it may, given up to my anxieties about the consequences of my voyage, I prepared to leave Île de France as soon as possible with the only means left to me and I gave orders to press more vigorously than ever our work of all kinds, but I could not obtain from the administrators a supplement of workers, whether caulkers or day labourers. However, the Government has two thousand workers and more at its disposal for the service of its Navy and workshops. But they are more often employed for the account of private individuals than for anything else. My intention was, on leaving Île de France, to come and seek New Holland by the latitude of the lands of Concord and to call at some one of the Molucca islands so as to be able, next summer, to visit the south coast of the land of Diemen and the strait which separates it from New Holland.
Being, the same day, at dinner at the house of the Danish Consul, Pelgrom, my friend for a long time, I confided my sorrows to him and the regret I had of having entered this Colony. After a few moments of reflection, he asked me to what sum the replacements of which I had need for both vessels might amount.
As I had on me the statement of them I communicated it to him. It came, according to the estimate I had made of it, to twelve thousand strong Spanish piastres. After he had taken cognisance of it, he told me that he hoped to procure them for me and to achieve this, he invited the next day to dinner all the Danish captains who were in the Colony, assuring me that he had a certainty assured that they would make among them all this sum for me, all the more so as several had remittances to make in Europe and they could not find a better opportunity. This idea pleased me so much that, forgetting all my sorrows, I already regarded my business as settled and the continuance of my voyage assured.
The rest of the day had nothing remarkable about it and I awaited the issue of that of the next day with much impatience.
During the night of the fifth to the sixth, the weather was very bad. Abundant rain mixed with heavy claps of thunder incommoded us much at the roadstead and the variety of winds caused us to fear experiencing some squall. All the moorings of the vessels were doubled for greater safety.

1801-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, in the morning, the weather cleared and the sunrise brought back the land winds. The swell that prevailed in the port indicated that it had been blowing fresh outside from north to north-north-west.
When the caulkers and day labourers returned aboard, we continued our work aboard. We were short four men this day, the third master being among them.
At eleven o'clock I went ashore and made a visit to the hospital to see the officers and naturalists who, according to the slip given me, were supposed to be there. This visit was entirely useless for I met no one there. The Sisters of Charity who carry on its management assured me that these gentlemen went there sometimes in the evening and even quite late, but that ordinarily they spent the day in town where, no doubt, their amusements were more varied than they would have been by remaining in such a place.
At one o'clock I went to the house of Consul Pelgrom, and I found gathered there twelve Danish captains and three Swedish ones. The Consul told me that he had not yet spoken to them of anything and that he was reserving the moment of dessert to make known the motive of the invitation he had made to them. At two o'clock we sat at table and although the dinner was of great magnificence, I sighed only to desire to see the moment of dessert arrive. It arrived at last. The first toast was to the success and entire success of the voyage I was about to undertake and in which all the nations of Europe had taken the most lively interest. This toast was proposed by the Consul. The second toast was to that of all the individuals who would contribute to give us all the assistance of which we might have need and without which the voyage could not take place. Then the Consul explained that, having addressed myself to the Administrators for the Government and to the Intermediate Commission for the Colony, I had been unable to obtain any assistance from them. Under the pretence that the Colony being threatened with an imminent attack on the part of the English, the Government had need of all its means and that, besides, they had (no) funds at their disposal. He then proposed to several who had remittances to make in Europe to give me a sum of ten thousand piastres at the ordinary exchange rate of the Colony, representing to them that these remittances would be more agreeable and profitable to their principals than to make them in any other way.
All the Danish captains found this sum so small that all wished to complete it by equal portions, but one of them having greater need to send funds to Europe than any other, asked the preference for everything of which I might have need and it was not without great discussions that the others consented to grant him this preference.
I confess that I did not expect such complete and prompt success. I testified to each one in particular my gratitude. But I could not help seeing with regret that the French and especially the capitalist merchants were going to cover themselves with shame in the eyes of all Europe by refusing me such a modest sum.
On leaving the table, the Consul went into his cabinet with the Danish captain who had obtained the preference and there he signed a formal engagement to give us what we should need in money for the purchase of our replacements, and the Consul for his part undertook to give him bills of exchange drawn by me at four months at an exchange rate of thirty-three and one-third per cent profit, the rate of the Colony even in time of peace. I judged it fitting to forewarn the Administrators of my changed position and addressed to them the letter which is found in my general correspondence with them.

1801-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh germinal, we had a continuation of fine weather. We occupied ourselves aboard with the disembarkation of our effects and the packages in the hold were partly emptied. The four men who had not appeared the previous day did not appear this day either and I postponed until the next day declaring them deserters.
The caulkers continued to cover the top of the vessel which was found to be entirely empty of oakum. The same work was taking place aboard the Naturaliste.
In the course of the day, I handed to the chancellor of Consul Pelgrom the note of the provisions I needed in replacement of those consumed during the campaign and it was he who was charged with gathering and finding them.
During the night of the seventh, the weather was very rainy and we often had strong gusts without thunder.

1801-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, the weather continued rainy and the winds were at east-south-east with strong squalls. As it was not possible to work at caulking outside, the caulkers were occupied inside on the second deck. The ship's carpenters repaired our topgallant yards which were broken and work was done on stowing the hold. I had twelve pieces of two put ashore during the day which were intended to contain the arak that I wished to embark.
The four sailors who were missing were declared deserters at the harbour master's office and I handed their descriptions to the police.
The rain that we had during the day continued into the night and the south-east winds blew with strong squalls mixed with a few claps of thunder.

1801-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, the weather was fine and work was done outside the ship at caulking. Part of the crew was occupied with the inspection of the rigging, while the rest worked at stowing the hold and emptying our water casks.
I have forgotten, until this moment, to make mention of Citizen Gutte. This individual was found aboard two days after our departure. When I questioned him on the motives that had led him to take this step, he replied to me that, having been deported from Île de France, where he had wife and children, he had arrived in Europe without resources and that, not having been able to find an opportunity to return to his family, he had thought he should take advantage of this one, in order to get out of the misery in which he had lived for six months. When the Intermediate Commission came aboard, I made known to it the declaration which this man, very well known in the Colony, had made to me. I was asked to keep him aboard, confined until the Assembly had deliberated on what it would have to do concerning him. All the efforts which the friends and acquaintances of Citizen Gutte have been able to make have not been able to have him admitted into the Colony. All that he has been able to obtain is the permission to go ashore under the condition that he would be confined to the quarter and I know that it is proposed to send him to the Seychelles by the first opportunity. It is from this day that an invitation was received aboard from the Municipality to allow him to go ashore. His wife and children came to see him often aboard during the time he was confined there. Besides, he conducted himself very well whilst he was with us and appeared to us in all respects to be a man who could not be dangerous to any party.

1801-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, half the crew had permission to go ashore for the day of the decade with orders not to fail to return to sleep aboard. Despite the rain that there was in the morning, most of the officers supposedly at the hospital for illness and to refresh themselves, went to walk on various plantations, and when I made my visit of the sick, I found no one, as had happened to me every time I had presented myself there.
In the morning, a brigantine arriving from Bourbon entered the port.
In the evening at the cannon shot, only four men of the party of the crew that had gone ashore were missing; they returned during the night.

1801-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, after the caulkers and carpenters had begun work, we commenced to take on water, our hold being arranged for this purpose. We had been obliged to change part of our stowage to clear our spare anchors which were found right at the bottom, underneath. We put two from the davits at the opening of the main hatchway and a third aft in order to have them ready in case of need.
The rest of the day had nothing remarkable about it and the night was very fine.

1801-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, everyone being at work, I went ashore to see whether serious efforts were being made to gather together the campaign provisions of which I had given the list. On my arrival at the port I saw with pleasure that efforts were being made to deliver aboard a lighter that was intended for us our salt meat as well as the beer that I embarked in place of wine, the price of wine being too high to take the quantity that I needed.
When half the objects that were in the lighter had been taken aboard, the remainder was sent to the Naturaliste which embarked them likewise.
In the afternoon we had no caulkers aboard and I do not know why. At night the water tank was sent ashore to fill up, having been emptied during the day.

1801-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth, we occupied ourselves with hoisting up the topsail masts and lower yards and we embarked the remainder of our beverages in wine and in country arak. I took only forty barrels of wine for both vessels in case we should have sick people during the campaign, for my intention is not to give it as a ration but only one meal a decade. As I will subject myself first to this rule, I am pleased to believe that everyone will conform to it willingly and with good grace.
In the course of the day, a foreign vessel entered under Prussian colours, coming from Bordeaux. This vessel having left France eighteen days before us brought nothing new. It had aboard forty-four passengers who, during the crossing, had not lived in very good understanding.
A rather singular adventure occurred aboard this vessel and which merits that I make mention of it. In making for Île de France, it came to sight the island of Rodrigue in the part the part (sic) of the south. The French who were aboard took at first this island for Île de France but on approaching it more closely, they recognised from its appearance that it was not that. Nevertheless, no one recognised the island of Rodrigue and all maintained that it was surely Saint Jean de Lisboa which, for a very long time, many sailors have uselessly sought. According to this persuasion, they approached land as closely as was possible and finally, as the weather was fine, they cast anchor on a coral bottom in forty fathoms. The boats were at once sent ashore with fifteen armed men in case the island was inhabited by some nation hitherto unknown.
The boats put ashore in a cove where they met no one and then they advanced about one league into the interior of the country. But as the day was about to end, they thought to embark, putting off to the next day a more extensive visit. However before quitting the island, they took possession of it in the name of the French Republic, and they put a copy of the act of possession in a bottle which was hung to a tree so that if hereafter some vessel should land on this part of the island, it would learn that it would not be the first to have come there.
When the boats returned aboard, the Captain learned that the island did not appear to be inhabited and that formal possession had been taken of it in the name of the Republic and a copy of the deed of ownership was handed to him. A great dispute then arose aboard and the Prussian captain claimed with reason that the island, having been discovered by a Prussian vessel, should belong to the King of Prussia and not to the French Republic. But as this right was contested to him, he decided to pass the night at anchor and the next day he sent again one of his boats ashore which planted on an eminence a Prussian flag and he enclosed in a well-sealed bottle a second act of possession in the name of his master the King, reserving to himself upon his arrival at Île de France to assert his rights. The vessel then set sail and continued its course for this port where it arrived three days later, not yet well persuaded that it had seen only Rodrigue instead of Saint Jean de Lisboa.
The report that this new discovery made occasioned searches and after having examined the journal of this vessel, the variation it had observed, the latitude of the place and the course travelled since the time of its discovery, it was demonstrated to them that the land which they had visited was nothing other than the island of Rodrigue, belonging truly to the French Republic.

1801-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, we embarked part of our firewood and what was found ready of our campaign provisions. The crew was entirely occupied in rigging the vessel and we hoisted our topgallant masts. The weather was very fine all day but we suffered greatly from the heat, the breeze having failed.
Ashore, great preparations were being made to receive the English whom one expected to see appear at any moment, having been informed that a considerable armament was being made in India the destination of which was unknown.

1801-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, all our water casks being filled, we began to embark the various objects that we had put ashore for our greater convenience in the disarrangement of the hold that had to be made to remove our spare anchors and several other objects which it was necessary to have at hand for the continuance of the campaign.
In the course of the day, our caulking was at last completed outside and inside and we got rid with pleasure of 28 men who had greatly inconvenienced us for the other work we had to do. I am persuaded that ten Europeans would have done in eight days what twenty-six negroes had difficulty in doing in twenty.

1801-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, we began to clean the vessel which the caulkers had left in a pitiful state. Most of the negroes on fatigue duty were employed to scrape inside whilst the crew worked on the rigging and splicing the ropes.
We embarked few objects this day concerning our campaign provisions, because we had to stow in the hold those which had come on the previous days so as not to encumber ourselves too much.
In the visit that I made to the hospital, I was no more fortunate than I had been every time I presented myself there, that is to say I found no one there.
In the afternoon I went to the observatory under the direction of Citizen Bernier, our chief astronomer having appeared there only once or twice since our arrival. But as Citizen Bernier is much more capable of this work than the other, I rejoiced at his absences.

1801-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, we embarked a large part of our campaign provisions which were placed aboard in different places in the vessel until such time as we would be in a condition to put them in fixed positions, our stowage not being yet completed.
At noon I went ashore to attend a great dinner which my old acquaintances in this Colony gave me. We drank freely there to the success of the voyage and each one congratulated me on having been able to obtain by the means of Consul Pelgrom the replacements of which I had need, but I was warned to be on my guard with the crews and was assured that several people had already made efforts to engage them to desert and that perhaps they would fail me at the moment when I should least expect it. This fear on the part of my friends appeared to me to be ill founded in that until this moment they had generally departed little from their duties.
