1801-04-08.journal_baudin_autographe: On the eighteenth, we embarked fifteen thousand weight of wheat and the Naturaliste the like. As we have aboard convenient mills to reduce it into flour, I preferred to take it thus because I am persuaded that it will keep very well. It would besides have been very difficult to have it ground ashore at the mill of the Republic. I had requested permission to do so from M. the Intendant who replied to me that this mill was not working, that is to say for us, for having gone there myself, I found it in full activity for the public who pay the Administration for this.

1801-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, little work was done aboard, the weather having been rainy almost the whole day. However in the intervals of the squalls the longboat made different trips ashore to take from the warehouse where our effects were those which did not fear rain and we embarked the pitch, the tar, the vinegar and various other objects of less importance. I had resolved to lose no time in endeavouring to leave at least the port. For I had just been informed that the Intermediate Commission had resolved to retain the vessels there if the English should appear in order to divide the crews among different posts. Although this conduct would have been against the law of nations, I have no doubt whatever that it would take this step if the case should arise before my departure from the port.
In the evening I informed the General-in-Chief of what I had learned; he replied to me that it would be nothing and that he did not presume that one would resort (to) such an extremity.

1801-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, two-thirds of the crew had permission to pass the decade ashore. They had behaved themselves too well until this moment to give me anxiety about their future conduct.
Nothing new happened in the day and among the various vessels that entered the port, there was found a large English prize coming from India and laden with masts. This vessel, which the owners of the privateer that captured it made little account of, was a real loss for the English.
At the cannon shot, all those who had been ashore with the exception of three people had returned aboard.

1801-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, we continued our preparations for departure and during the day we embarked the greater part of the objects that were ashore.
The three men who had not returned the previous day arrived aboard in the morning. There arrived in the port two small brigantins coming from Madagascar having as cargo rice and slave negroes.

1801-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, we embarked our sails on deposit and under repair in the workshops of the Republic. We also stowed our spare masts which, (for) greater convenience, was placed differently than it had been on leaving Le Havre.
The stowage of the hold was found to be very advanced, so that I saw the moment of departure approaching with a satisfaction which it would be difficult to express.
As from the tenth germinal, I had ceased to keep table for the general staff and the naturalists, I began the embarking of my provisions. It is a great mistake that was made in France to want me to be charged with this.

1801-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third the sails were put on yards and those of spare, in the places which were destined for them.
I was forewarned during the day that eight people had the project to desert. As I did not have a well-assured certainty of this plot, I did not think I should take any other measure than to double the guard of the gangways during the night and to confine to the sentinels the boats. However, six men of the eight which had been pointed out to me deserted by swimming. Their comrades learned us that they had passed by the knightheads.

1801-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the corvettes were hove-to and in the afternoon they were, to my great satisfaction, brought into anchorage outside the Pavilions. I was then in safety and no longer had anything to fear from the intentions of the Intermediate Assembly should the English appear.
All that remained for me to do was to bring back ashore the men who were in hospital and the deserters whom it seemed to me easy to find. I had a statement of their descriptions drawn up and sent it to the office of classes and to the police.
In the anchorage, the ships were moored on a pendant and afforchès with a stout cable and a drift anchor, 18 fathoms, bottom of sandy mud.
Bearings of the anchorage:
The point of the Cannoneers at NE 1/4 N
Coin de Mire at NE 5° N
Le Pouce at SE 1/4 S 4° South
The Mountain of the Port at South 5° East
The land to the West at SW 1/4 W all by compass.
At seven o'clock, I went ashore in the boat of the harbour master who had come to bring the vessel into anchorage.
As the Naturaliste had not set sail despite the signal I had made her, I presumed her anchors had become fouled. But on passing alongside this vessel, I was informed that the cayenne or pontoon commanded by Citizen Mangin had prevented her from getting under way on the pretext that no vessel was permitted to sail at sunset.
I was much displeased with M. Hamelin for having complied with such an order and not having executed the signal I had made, having to receive orders only from me.

1801-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, the vessel began to be painted, having had no time to do this work in port. At seven o'clock, the Naturaliste set sail with a fine south-east breeze and came to anchor alongside us.
I was informed that during the night, despite all the precautions he had taken, three men had deserted from him by swimming. I lodged complaints with the General against the conduct of the officer commanding aboard the cayenne on the previous day and held him responsible for the desertion of the three men who had left the day before in that this would not have happened had he not prevented this vessel from going to the Pavilions. The General, without altogether approving the conduct of the pontoon officer, did not appear to pay much attention to my representations.
In the morning, I went to the hospital to make an exact inspection of our sick and their situations. I was not surprised not to find the officers and naturalists there, for they only went when they were not on some pleasure expedition or did not know where to go to dinner. But I was greatly astonished to learn that during the night eight of my best sailors had deserted by going over the walls. I pretended to believe this statement but after making more exact enquiries, I learned with certainty that, far from having gone over the walls, they had left by the main gate with their baggage, on a note from the Commissary in charge of that part of the service.
This conduct made it clear to me that there was regret at seeing us outside port and an intention to delay our departure, which they supposed could not take place owing to lack of men. They believed, moreover, that I could not do without the officers who remained ashore and persisted in the belief that the voyage was lost in that they were ignorant of the means I intended to employ to obtain men if those I claimed were not returned to me.
At sunset, I went aboard to consider the means of having our deserters arrested.

1801-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe: On the twenty-sixth, work continued aboard on staying our fore and aft shrouds. Several boats from port brought us the remainder of our stores and I requested the Ordonnateur to have the accounts, though not considerable, which I had to sign, prepared.

1801-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, we continued with activity the preparations for departure and as it was known ashore that I was short of men, they began to be anxious about thirty blacks in corvée whom I kept aboard both vessels for the daily service of the boats that were constantly going to and from the anchorage to port and from port to anchorage.
In consequence of these fears, M. the Intendant sent me a harbour officer to demand them back but I refused to return them for the reasons set out in the letter I wrote to him on this subject.
At ten o'clock, I hoisted the order flag having decided to assemble in council the officers of both corvettes to communicate to them my intention and the letter I intended to address to the Commander-in-Chief, the Administrator and other constituted authorities of the Colony. The council assembled having left me the choice of means to employ, I addressed to them the one to be found in my correspondence, persuaded that it could only have a good effect.
The rest of the day had nothing particular about it but at eight o'clock there arrived for the second time the harbour officer who had come in the morning and twelve men from the cayenne, six of whom were for the Naturaliste. On handing these over, I was given a letter from M. the Intendant, who, claiming that I no longer had any reason to retain the blacks in corvée, was persuaded that I would have no difficulty in returning them. I kept the six men intended for me and sent aboard the Naturaliste those who were for him. But I kept the blacks no less, writing again to M. the Intendant the reasons on which I based myself for acting thus.

1801-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, at four o'clock in the morning, I sent my boat armed with ten blacks to port to take the items that might still remain for us ashore. She returned at ten o'clock laden entirely with all manner of things.
I sent word to the astronomer Bernier on this same occasion to pack all his instruments and to dismantle the observatory, my intention being that everything should be aboard by the next day.
During the day, I received from the Commander-in-Chief a reply to the letter I had written to him the day before concerning our deserters and our position. It appeared to me from a paragraph of his letter that he was not very satisfied with the measures I was asking him to put into execution. Nevertheless, I do not think my letter had anything offensive about it for him in particular and I wrote to him again on this subject.
The rest of the day had nothing particular about it and I put off until the next day going ashore to sign the accounts and to find out what would finally be the result of my requests to all the administrations of the Colony.

1801-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, I went ashore at dawn and gave orders on leaving the vessel to send the boat on shore at nine o'clock with the master gunner to take our powder.
On arriving ashore, I was informed by my friends that my letter to the Intermediate Commission had not been received with pleasure there. I was all the less surprised at this in that I was persuaded beforehand that they would not be content with the course I was taking which was to place under their responsibility and even under that of the whole Colony the safety of the vessels and the continuation of the expedition. It is certain that if they did not give hidden asylum to our deserters, they could not fail to find them very quickly. In a rather heated conversation I had occasion to have with some members of this assembly, I did not hide from them that it rested with them to have the men who were missing returned to me. And although they excused themselves on the difficulties of finding them, I did not let them remain ignorant that I knew from good authority that when they had had someone to deport, they had certainly found the means to have him arrested, even in the middle of the woods, and that it was easier to recover forty men and more who were missing from us than a single individual.
After this conversation, I went to the police and by means of some rewards that I promised to the constables, they assured me they would set about tracking my men.
In the afternoon, two blacks were executed. The nature of their punishment attracted many curious onlookers and not doubting that some of our sailors might be there, I invited the chief of police to take measures accordingly.
What I had foreseen actually happened and twenty-two were arrested. But the guard with which they were entrusted to conduct them to the port prison being composed only of tavern-keepers and sutlers, they allowed fourteen to escape on the way and brought only eight to port. It appears that those they allowed to escape were their debtors for among those they brought none owed them anything.
I received, as I was at the Commander-in-Chief's, a letter from the Intermediate Assembly in reply to that which I had addressed to them as well as a copy of the deliberations to which it had given rise.

1801-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, all offices being closed we could do nothing ashore. Around ten o'clock, the General requested me to call on him and in the conversation we had together, he informed me of the administration's anxieties concerning the thirty blacks who were still aboard the corvettes. M. the Intendant had persuaded him that my intention was to take them with me, which would have greatly displeased some of his entourage or perhaps himself, for they know very well how to turn them to account for considerable revenue. I assured the General that this idea had never occurred to me, but that I was absolutely determined to keep them aboard until I had a sufficient crew to set sail. I added that if M. the Ordonnateur was so eager to have back the government blacks, it rested with him to furnish me with men and he had the means at his disposal by having me given from the cayenne those kept there for the arming of a corsair in whom he was not indifferent and who was only waiting my departure to arm himself as a privateer with a number of my deserters.
The General promised me he would make to the Chief of the administration the representations he thought suitable and we parted.
The rest of the day had nothing particular about it. No one came from the vessel ashore and not even the blacks although it was the day of the decade.

1801-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Floréal, early in the morning, we embarked aboard the great boat and three of our small boats. During the night of the thirtieth to the first, two men taking advantage of the darkness attempted to swim ashore in the hope of reaching land although we were more than a league distant from it. The sentinel having noticed them, we at once armed the small boat to go after them. One was arrested, but the second escaped.
He who was brought back was exhausted and would undoubtedly have drowned before reaching land. There is every reason to suppose his companion experienced this fate.
At ten o'clock in the morning, I was informed of the whereabouts of sixteen of our deserters by a Spanish sailor who promised to deliver them to us if I would give him twenty piastres. I accepted his proposal and even offered him thirty if he would tell me the truth. Having gone at once to the police, I asked for a sufficient guard and had the Spaniard who served as guide accompanied by the master gunner of the Naturaliste who happened to be ashore. The guard I had obtained immediately set off for the quarter called Grande Rivière and returned in the evening with twelve whom I had put in prison until the next day. Except for three, all belonged to the Naturaliste. Having had them questioned in the presence of the officer of the guard at the harbour gate as to the reason for their desertion, they declared that recruiters for the corsair I have mentioned had offered them one hundred and fifty piastres advance and that they could not resist such a fine offer.
I informed the General of this discovery and urged him to put an end to the abuses which have hitherto been the consequence for the vessels of the Republic. He promised me he would take measures accordingly, but as he is not master to do as he wishes, there is every reason to believe things will remain for the present in the state they are.
He informed me that, following the steps of M. the Intendant, I would receive the next day twelve men from the cayenne whom he had told him were sailors.

1801-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, I addressed myself to M. the Intendant or rather I addressed to him the letter the copy of which is to be found in my correspondence to obtain some livestock to deposit in some place which I intended to visit. I do not know if this request will prove as fruitless as those I had previously made to him, but I have reason to believe he will grant it in that I have managed to interest his vanity in not refusing it me. It is besides too inconsiderable.
During the morning, I settled most of the business that was in arrears ashore and I was informed by a boat from the vessel that the twelve men, six of whom were for the Naturaliste, had been brought aboard.
During the night, two of these same men deserted by swimming but they were intercepted by our boats which I sent after them.

1801-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, I received from M. the Intendant a most satisfactory reply to the request I had made to him the day before.
During the day, I returned to him all the blacks in daily corvée who were aboard both vessels and he was all the more pleased at this in that those who derived revenue from them had persuaded him that my intention was to take them with me, which would truly have caused them great loss since their revenue would have diminished by about twenty-five to thirty piastres a day.
As I had announced to the Commander-in-Chief that I had decided to set sail on the fifth in the morning, he sent me an invitation as well as to M. Hamelin to come to dinner with him on the fourth, which we both accepted.
During the course of the day, we occupied ourselves entirely with the arrangements for our departure and everything was put to position and in order aboard the corvettes.
In the afternoon, all the boats were embarked, with the exception of one which was kept for the daily service of the vessel.
The two men who had deserted the day before caused me to redouble precautions during the night and the watch of the gangways and the hawseholes was doubled with orders to fire on whoever should attempt to escape.

1801-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the morning, Captain Hamelin and I went ashore and called on the Governor to whom I gave a nominal list of the number of men aboard both vessels. There were fifteen people missing from the Géographe, not counting the learned men to have the number who were with me on my arrival. But I observed to him that I found myself sufficiently provided and that I only begged him to give us each three Malays from those at the cayenne who were to be sent back to Batavia which he granted and the order was given at once to send them aboard. By this means I had one hundred men in all and the Naturaliste eighty-five. Thus we were in a state to put to sea with tranquillity.
On leaving the General's office, we went to the bureaux for the signatures we had to give, but the accounts not being entirely completed, we had to return at four o'clock in the afternoon.
At one o'clock, we went to the General who gave us a very good dinner. M. the Intendant was there as well as several other officials. Everything went off as well as possible and there was not a word about the small difficulties I had experienced during my stay in the Colony; only I was congratulated on having had the good fortune to find resources to be able to leave. M. the Intendant protesting constantly his regrets at not having been able to help us for want of means.
After dinner, I handed to the General the packages in duplicate which I addressed to the Minister of the Navy. My despatches contain: 1) an extract from my navigation journal since France. 2) the account of our expenses in the Colony, 3) a copy of my correspondence with the Administration, 4) a private letter to the Minister of the Navy. All under cover.
All these documents are in duplicate and the General promised me to take advantage of the first favourable opportunities that might present themselves to send them to their destination.
Having taken leave of the General around four o'clock, we parted and I went to the Danish Consul to whom I gave him the 3rd and 4th duplicate of the letters with which the General had charged himself.
At seven o'clock, having nothing more to do ashore, I returned aboard, firmly resolved not to return there except on my return. On my arrival, I found the vessel on an anchor and had there not been a calm, we should at once have set sail, having that same day embarked the livestock that the Intendant had given us.
Journal of Navigation. Departure from Île de France.

1801-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth of Floréal, year 9, at six o'clock in the morning, we hove-to head up to take advantage of the land winds as soon as they should come. At seven o'clock we had the breeze and although it was still weak, we got under way at once and to my great satisfaction, for until this moment I had always been anxious not only for the safety of the crews but also as to the manner in which I should leave a Colony where I had experienced so many different annoyances. I had certainly managed to replace most of the deserters with men of truly ill will, but I at least had enough for the working of the vessels and I was little troubled by the officers and learned men who had abandoned the expedition.
At ten o'clock we fell calm and it was not until afternoon that we could get clear of the coast with the help of a small south-east breeze which lasted long enough to take us well away so that at sunset there was nothing to fear from the currents had there been a calm during the night as there appeared likely.
Bearings at six o'clock in the evening:
Mount Brabant at South 3° East
The peak of the northern ravine to the East 16° N
The most northern point of the island at N 44° E all by compass.
During the evening, we occupied ourselves with forming the watch-bill for service and we also made the sale of several objects belonging to the deserters we were leaving in the Colony. The crew, once under sail, seemed content enough to me and I have no doubt that all will perform their duties well.
The greater part of the night of the fifth to the sixth passed in a calm. However at midnight, we could stand south, Mount Brabant remaining to the East 5° North at an estimated distance of four leagues. We then had a fairly nice breeze from the East variable from East 1/4 South-East, but we found the sea very rough from the South.
The rest of the night had nothing particular about it; we regulated our canvas to that of the Naturaliste which in spite of the change he had made to his stowage during our stay at Île de France was found to sail no better than usual.
1801-04-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. At 6 a.m. made the signal to get under way. At 7 got under way and shaped our course west. At noon Coin de Mire bore from us N 55° E and Le Pouce S 70° E; shaped the course S 45° W, running along the land at 4 miles' distance. At 4, Le Pouce N 67° 30' E, the Piton of Rivière Noire N 80° E and Morne Brabant S 10° E. At midnight, Morne Brabant N 85° E, 12 miles off. The 6th [Floréal, 26 April 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ESE. At 8 took the bearing of Morne Brabant N 5° E, 24 miles off, from which I took my point of departure in 21° 8' of latitude and 55° 7' of longitude. The anchors were secured in their stowage and the mizzen topgallant mast struck. At noon in 21° 19' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 12' of longitude by account. Variation 13° 26' NW. At 2.30 took the bearing of Réunion S 67° 30' W, at the limit of sight.

1801-04-26.journal_anonyme: The winds from the WNW, light. Bearings taken at 5.30 p.m.: Morne Brabant south 5° E, estimated distance 3 leagues and a half; the signal hill of the NW port NE by E. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze.
1801-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the sixth in the morning, we took our point of departure from the bearings of Mount Brabant which at six o'clock remained north 5° east at an estimated distance of eight leagues.
I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south by east observing that we would always give in the close-hauled courses a quarter in the sails, as much to have less drift as to go faster.
At seven-thirty, we had a squall which gave us some rain and a fair amount of wind. We were obliged to bear away several points and to reef the topgallant sail until it was passed. It lasted about half an hour.
In the morning, I had the mizzenmast rigging struck to relieve the head of the fore-topgallant mast which is too weak for its great height. We had been obliged to do the same on coming from France, but as the mast and its sail were very useless to us, this in no way delayed our progress and on the contrary only served to make the working of the aft sails quicker and easier.
At noon, the estimated longitude from the point of departure in the morning was 54° 43' 48", there was no observation of latitude nor hour angle for the watch march.
In the afternoon, we occupied ourselves with striking the cables down below and placing the anchors to their stations. The battery was cleaned and prepared being somewhat encumbered by the departure.
Our livestock was placed in comfortable pens to preserve them in case of bad weather and everything was arranged for the best.
During the evening, the weather was fair. There was a fairly nice east breeze variable to east-south-east, and we alone should have made fair way.
The night of the sixth to the seventh was fine, the winds in the same quarter, and we found the sea a little more manageable than the day before.
Note. In the arrangements made for service at sea, it was settled that the frigate captain Ste Croix le Bas should command the first watch, Ensign Freycinet the second, Ensign Picquet from the Naturaliste the third, Ronsard and the chief helmsman the fourth, and Bonnefoy with Maurouard the fifth. By this means nobody had to complain except me, who found I had two to oversee.
Citizen Bernier, astronomer of the Naturaliste, passed aboard the Géographe to replace M. Bissy, left ashore and in hospital, either for form's sake or until he had assembled a sufficient number of pupils, intending to teach drawing.
Citizen Bernier wished to have with him the two timekeepers whose march he had been following aboard the Naturaliste and we returned to Citizen Faure those which had served us aboard.
M. Le Villain, pupil zoologist, passed aboard the Naturaliste on which only two learned men remained and I had replaced, aboard the Géographe by Citizens Petit and Le Sueur, the places uselessly occupied by MM. Milbert and Garnier. One will judge from the work of these two young men if the choice I made was a good or bad one.

1801-04-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the wind a strong breeze from east to ESE, the sea running from the south.
1801-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the seventh, the weather continued fair and we advanced south as much as we possibly could while always regulating our canvas to that of the Naturaliste. During the morning, the weather was somewhat variable and we sometimes had squalls of rather heavy wind; nevertheless, we found the sea much better than we had had it before and the vessel was more tranquil.
I settled with the provisioner the manner in which I wished the distribution of those we had aboard and so that the articles we had in small quantity should last longer, we agreed that distribution should be made in the following manner, namely:
Two rations of arrack a day and one ration of beer at noon,
On meat days, a meal of rice,
On vegetable days, a meal of peas at noon and rice in the evening,
Coffee twice a decade on the 5th and 10th,
Fresh bread once a decade for the wardroom as for the crew,
Six bottles of wine from the store for the wardroom on the 5th and 3 on the 10th of each decade.
As from what had happened on the way from France I had discontinued keeping table, I arranged matters so as to invite two people each day, an officer and a naturalist, so that with my secretary I always had four persons at my table and at my expense. I had foreseen from the start when leaving France that there would be discontented persons and however good my ordinary was there would always be someone who was not satisfied with it. Nevertheless I must acknowledge that the learned men never complained of it and whatever discontent this arrangement has caused me, it was only M. Bissy and the officers who complained of it. So I am very happy they saw fit to remain ashore.
At noon, the observed latitude was 22° 44' 49" South and the longitude according to dead reckoning was 55° 12'. That indicated by No. 27 was 55° 25' 18" and that of No. 35 was 55° 21' 9". We found in the 48 hours a difference north of 8 seconds and an east one of 9' 13".
During the evening, the weather was the same as in the morning, the breeze was not well established but in general the winds were from the east to east-south-east, moderate and often weak. The course was the same.
At sunset, we closed with the Naturaliste which was much to leeward and during the night we made way at a quarter of a league's distance from one another, this vessel having all sails set. The night had nothing particular about it. From time to time a few small squalls passed with rain but they were of little consequence and short duration.
Note: according to the report of the chief medical officer, there was aboard only one man sick with a tertian fever and I learned with pleasure that no one had yet been attacked by venereal disease. I am in this much more fortunate than at my departure from Teneriffe, for the day after our sailing I had more than ten aboard the Géographe.
1801-04-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At noon in 22° 40' 30" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 29' NW.

1801-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from ESE. The sea smooth enough. The weather fine and the sky serene. At 10 a.m. we found the third forward shroud of the mainmast had parted above the futtock shrouds; the damage was repaired at once.
1801-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the eighth, during the day, the weather was fairly fair, although the horizon was very limited and the sky heavy with humid vapours producing a dull and whitish haze which was nothing pleasant to the sight. The winds which had been for some time at the east varying a little towards the south and we continued to make way close-hauled. The vessel was somewhat strained during the day in that there was a fairly strong swell from east-south-east to south-east which made us roll considerably.
At noon, we observed latitude 23° 59' 50" South and longitude, according to dead reckoning, was 55° 18' 42". That indicated by the timekeepers reduced at noon was for No. 27 of 55° 36' 57" and for No. 31 of 55° 30' 27". We had in the 24 hours 1' 4" difference north and 12' east.
During the evening, the sky became clearer than it had been in the morning and we had the appearance of a fine night. The winds varied a little from east towards north but this was not for long.
At four o'clock, the Naturaliste which was about three quarters of a league to leeward of us made signal of damage in one of her main shrouds; we bore away over her to better ascertain what it was and after speaking to M. Hamelin, he informed us that one of his main mast shrouds had broken but that this damage was repaired.
He also informed us that he was satisfied with his crew which numbered eighty-seven men in all and all in good health. After separating, I made him signal that we would govern south-east by compass if the winds would permit before quitting the trade wind latitudes.
The night of the eighth to the ninth was very fine as we had had reason to expect at sunset. As it was the day of the full moon, it was so clear that our horizon was more extended than it had been during the day. The winds during the whole night varied little from the east and the breeze was weak.
1801-04-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 23° 58' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 53' NW. At 2 the course was signalled S 45° E should the wind draw aft. At 3.45 the Naturaliste signalled us damage to her main shrouds; we bore down on her and spoke.

1801-04-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 the course was signalled SE, and we signalled the commander the damage to our lower shrouds.
1801-04-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the ninth, in the morning, we had the winds at the east variable to east-south-east, fairly nice breeze, but the sea continued to be rough and the vessel was somewhat strained. After breakfast, the crew was employed in staying our fore shrouds and our topmast shrouds fore and aft in that they had great need of it. The seizings not being sufficiently tight in the manner they had been kept the day before our departure from port.
At noon, the observed latitude was 25° 4' 50" South and the longitude according to dead reckoning was 56° 2" which gave a difference north of 8' 24 seconds and one east of 5' 30 seconds. The longitude indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 56° 7' 32" and for No. 35 of 55° 59' 16".
In the afternoon, the weather continued fair and the winds varied a little from east towards north. We had fairly nice breeze until sunset when it varied and diminished somewhat and for a short time.
By two azimuths taken in the evening and morning, we found that the declination of the magnetic needle was 13° 32' 30" NW. At four o'clock, the Naturaliste signalled us a new damage in her fore shrouds which was soon repaired. And we continued to make way south taking of the east as much as it was possible for us.
During the night of the 9th to the 10th, the weather was fairly fair but the winds were very variable and obliged us to make different manoeuvres until daylight.
Nota. On the ninth in the morning, the water-men being engaged in taking water for the day's ration, a plaintive voice was heard in the hold which attracted their attention. Coming to report this to the officer of the watch, a search was made in the light in that part of the forward section from where the groans that had been heard came. After a quarter of an hour's search without discovering anything, the same sound of voice was heard again which had come to one's notice a little while before and finally a young black was discovered lying almost unconscious.
The doctor was at once brought down who, having judged from the weakness of the pulse that lack of food was the sole cause of the state in which he was, ordered that he should be given air by different gradations and then had him take something light.
When this black had recovered consciousness and some strength, he was questioned about the time of his arrival aboard and to whom he belonged at Île de France.
His reply to the first question was that he had been aboard for five days and had absolutely taken no food during all that time. His master, according to his declaration, is M. Gloux, living at Île de France.
1801-04-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SE. At 6 a.m. a young Black man was found in the hold, where he had hidden himself at Mauritius. Want of food had left him so weak that he could not stand; he said he belonged to M. Gluaux, an inhabitant of Mauritius. At 9.45 the Naturaliste made us a signal that could not be understood. At noon in 25° 6' of latitude observed and in 56° 2' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 0' NW. At 5 we spoke the Naturaliste; she told us that at 9.45 she had signalled us the height of her masts, 106 feet 8 inches from the truck to the gun deck.

1801-04-30.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from east; the sky cloudy. At 1 bore away to close the commander. By three we were near enough to him. The commander having worn ship, we went onto the starboard tack. At 5 p.m. the mist having kept us from seeing the commander, we shortened sail to wait for him; and at 7.30 we went about, supposing he had gone onto the port tack.
1801-04-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the tenth, before daylight, the variety of winds which had come for a moment from the south nearly caused us to lose the Naturaliste. The officer who had the watch having brought her head into wind, taken the braces to larboard and the Naturaliste which was close by us having seen this manoeuvre did the same. But at five o'clock, the winds being back at south-east, we at once changed tack. Persuaded that the other vessel would do the same, we did not make her the signal. At daybreak we had good sight of the Naturaliste in our waters, at a great distance. Persuaded that she was on the south tack, I contented myself with taking in the mainsail and putting the fore-topgallant mast in place to give her time to rejoin us. The sky, which was fine at this period, became covered with mist and all the rest of the day the weather was squalls and rain.
At eight o'clock, not seeing the Naturaliste whom we had borne away to the north-east, I went about to go to meet her. But it was not until about ten o'clock that we sighted her in a clearing, indeed on the south-south-west tack. She was then about three leagues to windward of us. As I persuaded myself that she must have seen us as well as we had seen her, I went about again and lay-to to wait for her.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, she having overtaken us, made her signal of recognition to which we replied. I had during the mist fired several cannon shots of which, doubtless, she had no knowledge since she did not reply to them, or if she did reply, we did not hear them.
I was all the more pleased that she had closed with us in that the weather became so bad and misty in the evening that there is every reason to believe we should not have met again before the coasts of New Holland had she failed to see us in the clearing which occurred in the morning when I was running north to look for her.
At noon, there was no observation of latitude and the estimated longitude was 56° 6' 12" east.
At four o'clock in the afternoon, the weather having very bad appearance for the night, I had the topgallant sails struck. The sea was already heavy and the vessel was pitching considerably. I also made signal to the Naturaliste to do the same and to show an hourly fire during the night if the vessels were not to keep each other in sight. At the same time, a second reef was taken in the topsails.
During the night of the tenth to the eleventh, the weather was fairly bad until about ten o'clock in the evening, but then the moon having gained strength, the squalls and mist dispersed. The sky became clear and we had fair weather for the rest of the night. The winds were from the east quarter variable to east-south-east strong breeze and we found the sea fairly rough and agitated.
1801-04-30.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, a very thick fog, with rain. The wind light and then a strong breeze from SE to E. Lay to from 8.45 until half past noon on account of the fog. Fired several guns, as did our consort. At noon in 25° 50' of latitude by account and in 55° 27' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-01.journal_anonyme: The wind very variable and in gusts. At noon a thick mist came up and we lost sight of the commander. We fired two guns to which he did not answer. At 1.30 we sighted him and fired a third gun, and he at once answered our signals. We at once trimmed close-hauled on the port tack.
1801-05-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the eleventh, in the morning, the weather was fine, only we had the sea somewhat rougher and agitated by the very strong breeze of the day before. However, we took in a reef in our topsails and dried our other sails. In the morning, we fitted the running backstays which I had had prepared for the solidity of our lower masts which I did not find sufficiently well supported and I am persuaded that it is necessary to give them another shroud in the after part.
At noon, we observed latitude 27° 28' 30" South and the longitude according to dead reckoning was then 56° 12'. That of the timekeepers put us at No. 27 by 55° 57' 10" and according to No. 35 by 55° 51' 15". So that in the two days we had a difference north-south of 1' 12" and a second and west of 12' 50".
In the evening, the weather became dark without however appearing likely to become bad. The sea on the contrary had become much improved so we took in a reef in our topsails and rigged the topgallant sails. The winds were in the east quarter variable to east-south-east light breeze.
After the crew's dinner, a distribution of rope tobacco and twisted tobacco was made to those who had need of it. Wool garments were also given to the men we had taken at Île de France as replacements for our deserters, those they had beginning to be too light for the temperature we were experiencing.
At sunset, the weather was very dark without bad appearance, we continued to make way close-hauled all sail set except the topgallant sails which were furled so as not to get too much ahead of the Naturaliste.
During the day we saw an albatross, which indicated to us the approach of the variable winds for it is rare to find them further north than 28° south latitude.
During the night of the eleventh to the twelfth, the weather became quite fair and although there was much moisture in the air and a sort of mist, all dispersed as the moon rose above the horizon.
1801-05-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At noon in 27° 29' 18" of latitude observed and in 55° 53' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 18° 1' NW.

1801-05-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south. The sea smooth, the sky rather dark. At half past five the commander signalled the course ESE.
1801-05-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twelfth, in the morning, we had the finest weather in the world and a breeze from the north-north-east. As soon as day broke, I signalled to the Naturaliste, which was a little to windward of us and at a short distance, to steer east-south-east, and I brought myself round to that point of sailing. The sea having become very smooth, we made good way until noon.
In the morning, the crew were occupied on board in preparing, for the mizzen mast which was not solidly secured, two preventer shrouds, as had been done in the days before for the main mast. And by means of this precaution, I think I have made our masting as solid as it can be, and in a state to withstand whatever gales we may happen to meet with.
In the At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 37' 15" south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 58° 14'. That indicated by the timekeepers placed us, according to No. 27, at 57° 51' 57", and by No. 35, at 57° 46' 0". We found that, in the twenty-four hours, we had a difference to the south of 1' 21" and one to the west of 22' 3".
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine, but the breeze was a little less strong than it had been in the morning. The Naturaliste made all the sail she possibly could to take advantage of it, and we kept her under our principal sails with a reef in the topsails and the staysails, which, from time to time, we were obliged to take in so as not to leave her too far astern.
The night of the twelfth to the thirteenth, the weather continued fine, but we found a great deal of dampness in the air. The winds having shifted to the north-north-west and to the north-west, a pleasant breeze, we judged that we had left the general south-east winds.
1801-05-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NW. At 6 the course was signalled and given S 67° 30' E. At noon in 28° 35' of latitude observed and in 57° 51' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 17° 0' NW.

1801-05-03.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from NNE to NNW and north. The commander very close in the SE 5° E.
1801-05-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the thirteenth, we had continuation of fine weather and we advanced during the day as much to the east as we possibly could by forcing sail on the Naturaliste to take advantage of it.
In the morning, I had our wheat mill hoisted and it was placed under the sterncastle in a convenient place and sheltered from all accident. I hope we shall derive good service from it and I put off until tomorrow trying it out. We have conformed for the arrangement of the parts to all that the instruction given us provides and it appears to us beforehand that it will work very well.
At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 53' 17" South and the longitude according to dead reckoning of 60° 58' 30" east. According to the march of our timekeepers that of No. 27 was 60° 36' 43" and that of No. 35 was 60° 30' 40", which gave us a difference of 0° 21' 50" east and by the observed latitude there was another one to the south of 0° 0' 55".
During the evening, it continued to blow a nice breeze and we were obliged to decrease much sail to wait for the Naturaliste which however was covered with it.
At sunset we observed 16° 34' 20" variation NW, mean result of amplitudes taken with three different compasses.
After sunset, the sky became covered in different parts of the horizon with dark and misty clouds which seemed to announce a change of weather. But after the moon rose, all dispersed and it was very clear. During the night the breeze was weak and the winds passed to west-north-west. The Naturaliste not having caught up with us until about nine o'clock in the evening, we began to make more sail so that she would not have to decrease hers the weather being very fine and the sea fine.
On the thirteenth, at daybreak, I sent my boat well armed and under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy to visit a place to leeward of us whose configuration of land made me believe there might be found some ravine or small river emptying into the sea. This aspirant who was then acting as an officer aboard had also orders to skirt the bay in which we found ourselves and to take soundings of it. When the boat was gone, we set sail and followed her fairly closely, always keeping the lead in hand, and very fine bottom of fine sand mixed with shells and some fragments of corals.
In the morning, the winds were extremely variable from east to south-east and from east to north-east, which made the tack we were on as bad on one tack as the other. However, around ten o'clock, they remained until noon at east towards the north and by this means we went deeper into the south-south-east part of the bay to a small distance from the land. The boat constantly signalled us an easily landing coast and good anchorage from ten to twenty fathoms.
At noon, the observed latitude was 33° 33' 26" and the longitude deduced from the march of the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 111° 55' 5" and for No. 35 of 112° 4' 31". I no longer used, since our landfall the estimated course from the log.
At one o'clock, we went about to stand offshore having only fifteen fathoms, fine bottom. The coast then offered us a beach of fine white sand on which the sea broke very little. This cove had about two leagues opening and again a league in depth from where we were. All the coast in this part is low and even, covered with fine green trees and of easy access as are all those we have traversed so far. Having cast the dredge several times in this cove we obtained several shells of the genus of scallops fairly fine and especially stars of the sea of a new species.
During the evening, we continued to work to windward tack on tack to advance as much as possible to the east, but the wind was so weak we advanced very little. However around six o'clock, we had until eight o'clock a fairly nice south-south-east breeze by means of which we advanced two leagues east. Then the calm coming again, we anchored in eighteen fathoms, bottom of sand but finer than that we had had before.
During the night the weather was fine and the winds passed to the east.
Report of Aspirant Bonnefoy commanding the boat.
"The Commander having given me orders to sound near the land in the boat, I left the vessel at seven o'clock in the morning and ran on a point which remained south by south-west of our anchorage.
"At about a cannon shot distance from the ship, I found 20 fathoms, very fine and reddish sand and at 9 o'clock, a league from the coast, 19 fathoms, fine sand and black mud mixed with much small particles of talc or at least which appeared to me to be such.
"At 9 o'clock and a half, heading south-west, we had before us a very easy bay for landing, the sea not breaking at all on the rocks which were there, nor on the sand beach with which it is surrounded.
"At 10 o'clock, we found 16 and 17 fathoms always same sandy bottom and at ten o'clock and a half we had nine fathoms, same bottom at a cable's length from the coast.
"At noon, finding ourselves in the bottom of the bay, by two fathoms almost ashore, we manoeuvred to get out and in half an hour the bottom increased to 5 fathoms, white sand.
"I observed that the soundings could be seen even at ten fathoms so clear and bright it is.
"The coast, near the sea, is low and covered with wood. I saw nothing which could lead one to suspect one might find fresh water there.
"At one o'clock, finding myself near the south-east point of the bay, I took from there my point of departure to return to the vessel sounding every 10 minutes.
"From one o'clock until two, the bottom increased regularly from five fathoms to ten, bottom of sand mixed with mud and from two o'clock until two-thirty from 10 to 12 fathoms, very fine gravel, the soundings then increasing gradually. At three o'clock, I found myself in 15 fathoms, bottom of sand and black mud. At three-thirty, I had 16 and 17 fathoms, same bottom.
"We saw in the bay a very large turtle which the noise of our oars caused to dive.
"Note: of the different bearings taken with the boat.
"At eight o'clock, two miles from the anchorage of the Géographe, the land furthest to the west of the coast west of our first anchorage remained to me at west 7° 15 south.
"At nine o'clock at a distance of four miles from the first point, that is to say from the corvette, the same point remained to me at west 11° 15 north.
"At 9 o'clock and a half, at 5 miles from the corvettes, the same point at west 22° 30' north.
"At eleven o'clock, an isolated rock from the coast of about a mile and from the boat a cable's length remained to me at north 39° 45 west,
"a rock whitened by the droppings of sea-birds and on which there were a great many, being at a distance of half a cable's length, remained at north 67° 30 west,
"the rock which forms the beginning of the bay at south 5° west.
"The sea at this hour seemed to me to have ebbed two feet on the rocks.
"At eleven-thirty, being abreast the rock which remains at south and half a cable's length from it, it remained to me at SW.
"At noon, the isolated rock remained to me at N NW.
"The south point of the great bay at SE at a distance of 4 and a half to 5 miles.
"the middle of the same bay at SW distance of a mile and a half.
"The Géographe at NE four to five miles distance.
During the whole day we clearly and distinctly saw three considerable fires at a small distance and about in the direction of the first anchorage we had occupied. These fires were, or at least appeared to me, too considerable and extensive for me to believe that the natives of the country were near. I am moreover persuaded that if there had been any they would not have failed to come and show themselves on the shores of the coast and at the small distance we were from it would have been difficult not to see them. I therefore think these fires could well have been lit by them but I doubt that when we passed they were assembled there.
Soundings of the day and nature of bottom
H Fathoms
1 25 fine grey sand 5 25 fine grey sand
2 26 same bottom 6 23 same bottom
3 26 same bottom 7 24 same bottom
4 26 same bottom 8 21 same bottom
1801-05-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to WNW. The hand mill was rigged and we ground wheat. At noon in 28° 53' 42" of latitude observed and in 60° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 30' NW.

1801-05-04.journal_anonyme: Winds from N to NNW. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8.45 the captain signalled the commander the longitude by lunar distances.
1801-05-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the fourteenth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the winds varied from west-north-west to south-south-west, nice breeze. We continued to govern east-south-east regulating our canvas to the march of the Naturaliste which had caused us to lose much way for two days. We found in the morning a heavy swell from south to south-east which made the sea somewhat elevated and agitated but as there was a good breeze, the vessel was not made uncomfortable.
At noon, the observed latitude was 29° 14' 21" and the longitude according to dead reckoning was 63° 44'. That indicated by the timekeepers at the same hour was for No. 27 of 62° 17' 58" and for No. 35 of 62° 11' 42". We had in the 24 hours a difference to the south of 0° 2' 19" and one to (no figures nor direction).
In the afternoon, the breeze calmed much and the winds passed from south-south-west to south and appeared to want to fix at south by south-west. The sky became dark and humid and we had appearance of a change of weather.
We saw in the course of the day an albatross and three or four storm petrels having the belly and underside of the wings a fine white and the upper part of body and wings a clear grey.
At sunset, the sky remained dark and there was much moisture in the air, the winds remaining at south by south-west.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth, the winds calmed still more. At the rising of the moon, or at least shortly after, the darkness which covered our view of the stars dispersed entirely and the sky became very clear. The sea was very rough from south to south-south-east and agitated by different waves. The vessel was strained so much the more in that there was little wind and was not supported by its canvas.
1801-05-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to south. At noon in 29° 11' 20" of latitude observed and in 62° 12' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 19' NW.

1801-05-05.journal_anonyme: Winds NNW, very light, the weather very unsettled, a swell running from SW to SSW. Saw many birds.
1801-05-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the winds were variable from the south to the south-west and there was almost a calm. The vessel suffered greatly from the agitation of the sea and especially from the heavy swell from the south to the south-south-east which, striking us athwart, caused us great oscillations. The sky was very clear throughout the day, and no sign upon the horizon indicated to us from what quarter the wind would come when it decided to blow.
In the morning, we took advantage of the calm to fumigate the vessel in all its parts and accordingly made a general muster.
We also took a great quantity of distances from the sun to the moon, the average result of which gave for easterly longitude 64° 6' 15", which occasioned a difference of 0° 17' 36" by which the timekeepers were found to be more to the east.
At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 59' 51" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 65° 14'. We had, in twenty-four hours, a difference of 12' 8" to the south and one to the east of 32' 5". No. 35 gave us 64° 30' 3" and No. 27 64° 23' 51".
In the afternoon, the weather continued fair and the breeze was always very slight and the sea heavy and elevated. In the evening, the winds varied from the south to the south-east, and then it began to blow a little and the vessel suffered much less.
During the night of the fifteenth, the sky became covered with clouds and the winds seemed to settle in the southern direction towards the east which (caused) us to make some way to the north. I would not change tack until the winds had settled and, as I was gaining something to the east, I continued to keep the wind close-hauled on the same tack. Although the sky was laden with clouds during the night and they even appeared quite threatening in appearance, we had very little wind and much moisture without rain or mist.
1801-05-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 28° 57' 20" of latitude observed and in 64° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 48' NW.

1801-05-06.journal_anonyme: Winds SE, variable to ESE. The weather fine, a swell running. At 9.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-05-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the winds were extremely variable from the south towards the east and the sky had a bad appearance; we had squalls, mist and sometimes rain during almost the whole morning.
At ten o'clock, the tack we were holding being worth nothing, I signalled to the Naturaliste that we were about to go to the other tack and we put the vessel about and at the same time went about and oriented ourselves on starboard tack with the course to the south.
At noon, the observed latitude was 28° 37' 2" south and the longitude following dead reckoning 66° 22'. That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 63° 23' 9" and for No. 35 of 63° 17' 2", so that dead reckoning already put us 58' 51" more to the east.
In the afternoon, the weather continued in squalls and the breeze increased considerably. However, as it appeared to want to clear up in the evening, I delayed taking a second reef in the hope that after sunset it would become calm. But at seven o'clock, although the sky had become clear and fair, the breeze, which was then east-quarter-south-east to east-south-east, increased so much that we were obliged to take a second reef in the topsails and to furl the main stay sail. The Naturaliste, which found herself near us, did the same.
During the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth, it continued to blow a fresh breeze from the east-south-east direction and the sea became heavy. Nevertheless, the sky was clear and fair without any appearance of bad weather, which led us to believe that a breeze so strong could not last long and that surely it would end soon and perhaps with the rising of the moon. This conjecture proved false, for it blew all night and in fine manner. We were obliged several times to let out our main sail to allow the Naturaliste, which was falling too far astern, to keep up.
1801-05-06.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 28° 35' 36" of latitude observed and in 65° 17' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-07.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea high and with a little swell. Wind ESE in gusts.
1801-05-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventeenth, in the morning, the winds were almost as strong as the previous day and only varied sometimes a little towards the east. The sea was beginning to become heavy and we experienced pitching movements from time to time. The sky was cloudy and fair without any appearance of bad weather.
We had, in the morning, a visit from quite a large number of albatrosses of two species, that is those that are entirely grey and those that are almost white. We remarked especially upon the damier petrel because it was the first one of these we had caught sight of since our departure from France, having met none to the east of the Cape of Good Hope after doubling it although we had been in a latitude more south than that where we are. We also saw several storm petrels or birds of the tempest which appeared to us much smaller than those ordinarily encountered.
At noon, the observed latitude was 30° 28' 31" south and the longitude following dead reckoning 65° 28' 42". That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 65° 14' 6" and for No. 35 of 65° 8' 9".
In the afternoon, the sea appeared to us a little calmer and the breeze had also fallen although it was still blowing a fresh breeze.
At sunset, we saw with pleasure that the winds were taking a little from the east by the north and we hoped soon to have them from the north-east.
During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth, the winds were in squalls and the sky sometimes cloudy and fair and sometimes misty. It blew a strong breeze from the east to the east-south-east and we continued to keep the wind with two reefs in each topsail.
At ten o'clock, the Naturaliste having closed with us, hailed but the force of the wind prevented us from hearing what she said. The rest of the night had nothing particular. Only, we remarked that the sea was not heavy in relation to the force of the wind.
1801-05-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. Saw albatrosses and pintado petrels. At noon in 30° 29' 10" of latitude observed and in 65° 8' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-08.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ENE, the sky cloudy, a high sea.
1801-05-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the eighteenth, the weather was fair and the sea became fine. Nevertheless, we changed little or nothing in our canvas, as we had enough to outpace the Naturaliste despite her having let out a reef in her topsails and set her topgallant sails and stay sails. The winds having varied towards the north, we were able to steer to the east-south-east, which was the course I intended to make and which I signalled to the Naturaliste.
At noon, the observed latitude was 31° 37' south and the longitude by dead reckoning 67° 40'. That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 66° 20' 34" and for No. 35 of 66° 14' 51". We found that we had, in twenty-four hours, a difference to the north of 0° 4' 47" and one to the west of 0° 16' 32" according to the dead reckoning of the distance and courses run by the vessel.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fair and there was a fine breeze from the north-east. We greatly regretted not being able to take full advantage of it by making more sail, but as I did not wish to leave the Naturaliste behind, I confined myself, as usual, to regulating my course by her slow progress.
During the whole day, we had the company of several damier petrels and other petrels who came to play about the vessel. We tried to catch some on the line and often they took the bait offered to them while avoiding the trap we had set for them. The naturalists were much amused by this sport.
The night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth was fair and the breeze well settled, the sea was no longer heavy and we hoped that the north-east winds would not abandon us soon. The atmosphere was very damp all night and the horizon had a dingy white colour which was not pleasant to the eye.
1801-05-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. At noon in 31° 39' 30" of latitude observed and in 65° 15' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 27' NW.

1801-05-09.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NE by E. The sea smooth, the weather fine and the sky very clear. Sailing a short distance from the commander. At two in the morning the sea was covered with luminous molluscs.
1801-05-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the nineteenth, in the morning, the fair weather of the previous day disappeared. We had a sky heavily laden with vapours and covered, having a bad appearance in all points of the horizon. Nevertheless, the breeze was moderate throughout the morning and we had the winds from the north-east direction variable to north-north-east.
A heavy swell from the north-west, which had begun to be felt from the previous night, seemed to announce to us that we would soon have winds from that quarter or that they had already blown hard from that point of the horizon.
At noon, we saw, for a moment, the sun show itself through the misty clouds we had above our heads. The latitude which we observed, although doubtful, put us at 32° 9' 29" south and the longitude following dead reckoning was found to be 69° 41' 30" easterly. There was no hour angle that day to know that indicated by the timekeepers.
In the morning, the barometer fell suddenly to 28.3 from 28.4,5, the height at which it had been for two days. This sudden decrease seemed to announce to us some squalls and the state of the atmosphere seemed equally to confirm it.
However, in the afternoon, the winds increased little but they turned more towards the north and (we) had them, even, at north-north-west where they remained little.
At eight o'clock in the evening, the winds being at north-east, the sky became more laden with vapours and mists and rain began to fall. We then furled all our light sails and did well, for at nine o'clock it began to blow a fresh breeze. And during the rest of the night, squalls succeeded one another with such rapidity that barely had one passed when we began to feel the effect of the one that followed. At midnight, we furled our mizzen topgallant sail and the topsails were hauled down entirely so as not to leave the Naturaliste too far astern, to whom we showed a light every hour to indicate our position.
1801-05-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with mist and squalls. The wind a strong breeze and blowing hard from NE to N. At noon in 32° 10' of latitude by account and in 67° 19' of longitude by account.

1801-05-10.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from NE by N in gusts, attended with rain.
1801-05-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, in the morning, the weather became worse and worse. We had such an abundance of rain that it would have been quite easy for us to fill all our empty casks had we been in need of them, but we were content to gather some for the consumption of the livestock and for washing the crew's linen when fair weather should return. In the morning, the winds appeared quite steady from the north-north-east and we remained under the fore sail and the two topsails, all reefs taken, the Naturaliste with only her lower sails and only two reefs in her topsails, so as to make more progress, the sea being moreover not very bad.
At noon, the longitude following dead reckoning of the course run was 71° 21' 30" and we found ourselves at 32° 51' 18" of south latitude.
In the afternoon, the movement of the barometer announced to us that the bad weather would not end with the day, in that it was descending continually, but not with as much speed as it had done when the bad weather began. At eight o'clock, it was at 27 inches eleven lines and during the night, it was not below 27.9. Before the night, I caused the cape stay sail to be set and signalled to the Naturaliste that both vessels would carry a light all night so as to better observe each other. This vessel furled his main sail at five o'clock and took a third reef in his topsails. This manœuvre caused him to fall much astern so that, to give him time to rejoin us, I put to and lay to at eight o'clock, especially as I could not see the light we had agreed upon; in consequence we furled the topsails and I came broadside to the wind, under the fore sail and the mizzen stay sail.
At half past nine, the weather having cleared a little, we saw to my great astonishment the Naturaliste within pistol shot, trying to double us to windward. I immediately hailed that vessel to bear away and she passed under our lee. This manœuvre surprised me all the more in that I do not see why M. Hamelin sought not to make his position known to us, by showing at least from time to time the light he had been ordered to carry all night.
When that vessel had passed us, I bore away and steered the signalled course, using only the main topsail.
It blew a fresh breeze from north-quarter-north-east to north-north-east throughout the rest of the night, but the rain ceased and the sky became a little less dark, the sea beginning to be bad and the waves high.
1801-05-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from NNE. At noon in 32° 46' 30" of latitude by account and in 70° 2' of longitude by account. We signalled the Naturaliste to keep a light all night; she did so, as did we. The 21st [Floréal, 11 May 1801]. Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from NNE to NW and SW. At noon in 33° 32' 20" of latitude by account and in 73° 37' of longitude by account. At 6 p.m. we lost sight of the Naturaliste.

1801-05-11.journal_anonyme: The same winds and squally. Continual rain; by the commander's order we kept a light burning all night. But no longer seeing the commander, we sent up a rocket; at 6 he was sighted in the SE by E. The ship labouring a great deal from the violence of her pitching and rolling. The wind NNE, a strong breeze.
1801-05-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, in the morning, the weather was much the same as the previous day except that we found the sea much worse and the gusts stronger. Nevertheless, we had very little rain, but the atmosphere was filled with dark and misty clouds which were driven by the wind with a liveliness that the eye could scarcely follow.
At daylight, the Naturaliste found herself very far from us, which made it seem likely that that vessel had made very little canvas during the night. Scarcely could one see her from the deck. Nevertheless, I continued on my course with the same canvas, convinced that if she increased some of hers, she would soon rejoin us. Besides, the weather did not permit me to reduce canvas as the sea would have greatly inconvenienced me. Nevertheless, at eleven o'clock, seeing that she was not approaching, I decided to lay to, and by this means she soon closed with us.
We caught sight of the sun sometimes in the morning but that was only in very brief intervals.
In the evening, the winds varied from west-north-west to south-west and always in squalls and in gusts. The barometer keeping always below 27 inches (sic) there was no appearance that the bad weather was at an end.
Although the vessel was strongly tossed about by the agitation of the sea, I saw with pleasure that our masts ran no risk and I greatly rejoiced at having taken the trouble early to secure them.
At noon, our estimated longitude was found to be 74° 52' 30" easterly and the latitude likewise estimated was 34° 18' 38" south.
During the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second, the barometer began to rise and we had hope of a change.
Nevertheless, I dreaded this change because if it came too promptly and calmed down, we would be tormented in a manner far more disagreeable than we had been by the bad weather, the sea being very heavy. We kept, all night, the stern light burning to make known to the Naturaliste our position, but (we) could not see the light of that vessel although sometimes our horizon was fairly extensive, the sky having cleared from time to time, but as we had changed nothing in our canvas, I was convinced she could not be far away. The vessel suffered greatly during the night from the violent movements which the heavy sea caused her to experience.

1801-05-12.journal_anonyme: A heavy wind from SSW and SW, blowing hard. We struck our topgallant masts and the jib boom and lowered the mizzen gaff. On the morning of the 22nd, the weather having cleared, we swayed up our topgallant masts, ran out the jib boom and hoisted the gaff.
1801-05-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-second, the weather became fair from the morning and it was the south-west winds which brought us this change. The Naturaliste found herself far away, in our waters and, as we had suffered greatly during the previous night, I feared that something untoward might have befallen her masts if, like us, she had not taken the precaution of lashing her masts. Nevertheless, one could very well distinguish with the long glass that she had all her masts high, which led me to continue my course, convinced that by making sail as the weather then permitted, she would soon catch up with us.
The barometer, which had risen in less than twelve hours from 27 inches ten lines to 28 inches four, announced to us the end of the bad weather and the sky had also cleared itself of all those misty and thick clouds which had brought us such violent squalls and gusts.
However, seeing that the Naturaliste was not approaching us and was always at the same distance, I came broadside to the wind to wait for her. When she had closed with us to be able to distinguish her signals well, she signalled to us damages in her main shrouds which we were occupied in repairing. At two o'clock, she was abeam of us and I signalled to her that we would steer to the east-quarter-south-east. We oriented ourselves one and the other to this course.
Having had a fair sun at noon, we observed the latitude of 33° 42' 27" south and the estimated longitude was 77° 54' 30". That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 77° 17' 13" and for No. 35 of 77° 11' 42", so that we found ourselves with a difference from dead reckoning in the past three days of only 4' 19" to the south and 21' 19" more to the east by the result of the timekeepers.
In the afternoon, the weather became quite fair, but the sea being very heavy and the winds almost astern, the vessel suffered greatly. We had then the main sails, two reefs in each topsail and the Naturaliste carried her topsails with only one reef and her bonnets.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, the weather continued fair but we were no less inconvenienced by the agitation of the sea which caused such violent movements to the vessel that our masts could not have resisted them without the precautions we had taken to secure them.
1801-05-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to WSW. At daybreak the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake at a great distance; at 11.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack to wait for her. At 1 she had closed; we signalled her the course S 78° 45' E and shaped it. At noon in 33° 39' 40" of latitude observed and in 77° 12' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW. The 23rd [Floréal, 13 May 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze and light from SW to WNW. At noon in 33° 34' 0" of latitude observed and in 79° 50' of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, being almost becalmed with a heavy swell from the SW, our masts were labouring greatly from the rolling; we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and signalled the Naturaliste to follow our movement. At 5 we spoke her; the commander informed Captain Hamelin that if it freshened we should shape the course S 78° 45' E.

1801-05-13.journal_anonyme: Wind SSW to SW. The wind a strong breeze, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, a very high sea and the ship rolling extremely. The course was signalled E by S.
1801-05-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, we had continuation of fair weather and a fine sky, but we saw with regret that the wind, which was from the south-west variable towards the west, was gradually falling calm and that we would be greatly inconvenienced by the swell which was extremely long and high. The waves were so high that the two vessels, although within half cannon shot of one another, could not see each other when they found themselves amid the waves and although there was still a fine breeze, our sails were entirely becalmed between the waves.
We saw in the morning several albatrosses and damier petrels, but among others a small gull of which the upper part of the body was a fine light grey-linen colour and the underside of the belly a very fine white with a black circle around the eye which made this bird very pleasant to look upon. It was the first of this species we had encountered and we judged it to be an inhabitant of the Amsterdam and Saint-Paul islands which were, for us, the nearest known lands we had.
At noon, the observed latitude was 33° 41' 49" south and the longitude following dead reckoning was 79° 16' 30". That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 79° 54' 54" and for No. 35 of 79° 49' 16". We had, in twenty-four hours, a difference of 4' 38" to the north and a second one of 7' 29" to the west.
In the afternoon, the wind calmed in such a manner that we could not keep the course for fear of losing our masts. We experienced oscillating movements so violent that I was in continuous anxiety which only ceased when I decided to take the swell head on, steering the course south-quarter-south-west. I signalled to the Naturaliste, who was rolling at least as much as we, to do the same and we steered one and the other to this course until the breeze was strong enough to counteract the effect of the swell.
At sunset, we caught on the line a damier petrel which greatly amused the naturalists; it was given to Maugé to stuff.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth, the calm lasted until one o'clock, when the winds having passed to the north began to freshen. The two vessels then resumed their course and we steered to the east-quarter-south-east of the compass, the Naturaliste carrying all canvas and we under our four main sails with two reefs in each topsail.

1801-05-14.journal_anonyme: Winds light from SW to north. A heavy swell running. The course signalled south.
1801-05-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the winds varied from north to north-north-west, fine breeze and the heavy swell from the south-west no longer inconvenienced us so that we continued to steer to the east-quarter-south-east of the compass, the Naturaliste making as much sail as possible to take advantage of the fair wind.
In the morning, the sky, although cloudy and heavily laden in different parts of the horizon, was fairly fair and we had the sun in view from time to time.
At noon, the observed latitude was 33° 31' 21" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 82° 22' 50". That indicated by the timekeepers, referred to the same hour, was for No. 27 of 81° 11' 30" and for No. 35 of 81° 7' 1", which gave us, in twenty-four hours, a difference to the west of 30' 44" and one to the north of 6' 45".
During the evening, it continued to blow a fair breeze and the winds varied sometimes to the west-north-west.
The sea was beginning to become fair and the heavy south-west swell which had agitated us so much became much less elevated.
We had the whole day the company of a great quantity of albatrosses and different species of petrels, but we caught only one on the line and that too was lost to us for, in hauling it on board, the line broke.
