At the beginning of the night, the weather had a bad appearance and the sky became laden with vapours and very thick clouds in all parts of the horizon and, although a strong breeze was blowing, they changed little in position. The Naturaliste furled all her bonnets and we furled our stay sails.
The night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth was finer than the appearance we had been given and we observed a rather singular phenomenon. The sky was sometimes clear and without any cloud, whilst two or three minutes afterwards it was suddenly obscured. This happened to us three or four times during the watch from eight o'clock to midnight which I kept entirely due to fear of bad weather and the little experience of him who commanded it. The winds, during the night, varied sometimes towards the north, but they remained there little and always returned to the west-north-west, fine breeze.
1801-05-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At midnight we shaped our course. Saw several albatrosses and many pintado petrels. One of the latter was taken with a line. At noon in 33° 35' of latitude observed and in 81° 7' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-15.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NW, variable to SSW.
1801-05-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the winds were north-west, fine breeze until five o'clock when they suddenly jumped to the south-south-west without losing any of their force. We immediately oriented ourselves on the starboard tack and continued our course to the east-quarter-south-east of the compass.
In the morning, the weather was fairly fair although with a very cloudy and misty sky. We had from time to time the sun in view and at noon we observed the latitude of 33° 18' 47" south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 86° 16' 50". That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 85° 18' 28" and for No. 35 of 85° 14' 16". We had in twenty-four hours a difference to the north of 4' 16" and an easterly difference of 12' 58".
In the afternoon, we encountered once again a very heavy swell from the south-west and it appeared to us that a great force of wind must have blown in these waters before our arrival. We had, as in the previous days, quite a large quantity of petrels and albatrosses for travelling companions. We caught another of the former on the line, but the hook having broken in hauling it on board, it was lost to us.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth, the weather continued fair but the winds calmed greatly and ended by settling to the south-east and sometimes even to the east-south-east. Nevertheless, I did not change tack and wished to wait, on the same tack, to see where they would settle. It seemed besides that they would not be long in returning to the north-west, the clouds being driven from that course with sufficient speed.
Since the wind had calmed, the vessel suffered greatly but nevertheless not as much as the swell made me fear.
1801-05-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to south. At noon in 33° 22' 50" of latitude observed and in 85° 14' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW.

1801-05-16.journal_anonyme: The winds south, variable to SSE and ESE. At 7 a.m. on the 26th we sent a boat aboard the commander with an officer to set the marine timekeeper, which had not been wound the day before.
1801-05-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, we spent the greater part of the day in calm and the vessel as well as all of us were greatly tormented by a very heavy (swell) from the south-west which caused us violent oscillating movements.
At eight o'clock, the Naturaliste asked, by a signal, that we send a boat on board. In consequence we hove to to receive her. The officer which she sent to me being arrived, I was informed by him and by the letter which M. Hamelin wrote to me that his two timekeepers had stopped because the day before someone had forgotten to wind them. We restarted No. (no figures) which he had sent to me and I had a note conveyed to him with the difference of hours with our No. 27. When all (was) settled, the boat returned on board and I invited M. Hamelin, in the reply I sent to him, not to leave both timekeepers to the same person to prevent, for the future, anyone forgetting to wind them both at the same time.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 32° 54' 1" south and the longitude according to dead reckoning was 87° 32' 50".
That indicated by the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 86° 47' 14" and for No. 35 of 86° 43' 35". We found that we had in twenty-four hours a difference to the south of 6' 12" and one to the east of 12' 46".
During the evening, the sky became covered with fairly dark and thick clouds and there was no appearance of calm for long. However, at the beginning of the night, we had no wind that the appearances announced to us.
The night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh passed almost in calm and it was only around two o'clock in the morning of the twenty-seventh that (we) had winds from the north-east direction, quite weak and nevertheless sufficient so that we were no longer rudely tormented as we had been during the whole time it was calm. We took, as soon as the breeze came, the closest course on the port tack.
1801-05-16.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the breeze light from SE to NE. At 7.15 the Naturaliste asked to send a boat aboard; we at once hove to. At 8 Citizen Saint-Cricq brought one of the Naturaliste's marine watches; they had stopped, Citizen Faure, who had charge of them, having forgotten to wind them. At 9, the boat having left, we filled and stood on. At noon in 32° 51' of latitude observed and in 86° 44' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-17.journal_anonyme: Winds NE to NNE in gusts. A swell running. At 7 a.m. the course signalled ESE.
1801-05-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, the breeze was very fine during the day, and we had very fair weather although the sky was covered in such a way as not to be able to see the sun. The Naturaliste being ahead of us at daylight, we let out one of the reefs of our topsails and set all our stay sails to join her more quickly.
In the morning, we saw a great quantity of damier petrels, albatrosses and other seabirds. We were fortunate enough to catch four of the former on the line, independent of all those we missed, but the others did not approach the bait offered to them.
We observed in the damier petrels we caught a thing which is perhaps not without interest. The first which was caught having been given to Citizen Maugé to stuff, he suffocated it as he had done the first. But in taking this bird, it rendered a quite large quantity of oily substance which congealed immediately and represented to us perfectly melted yellow wax which would have been spread on paper or in a vessel, which led our Gentlemen to say that this bird rendered wax. The three others offered us the same spectacle which the first had not (done). We gathered quite a large quantity of this substance which I am preserving for anatomy. It would doubtless be quite curious to know what is the principal food of these birds for it to convert into so much oil as they have rendered, for I think it is nothing else.
At noon, having had no sun, the estimated latitude was for us 33° 30' 1" south and the longitude 88° 33' 45" easterly.
In the afternoon, the birds which had been such good company to us in the morning, although at their expense, abandoned us and in the evening we saw them no more. It continued to blow a fine breeze from the north to the north-east and the sky remained covered. The hygrometer nevertheless announced much humidity in the air, but as the barometer was very high, we did not fear bad weather for the night which, indeed, was fair although the sky remained always very dark and covered.
1801-05-17.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NNE. At 7.15 signalled the course S 67° 30' E, which had been given since 4 o'clock. Saw albatrosses, petrels and many pintado petrels; several were taken. At noon in 33° 20' 10" of latitude by account and in 87° 43' of longitude by account.

1801-05-18.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts. Laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the commander, who was astern.
1801-05-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, the weather remained covered all day, but a fine breeze blew from the north-north-east to the north-north-west and we made good progress. The heavy south-west swell which had accompanied us for so long was beginning to diminish greatly and the sea was very fair.
The Naturaliste, having all canvas set and her bonnets, obliged us to rig our topgallant sails, but they were not of use to us for long and we soon had to furl them to wait for her. We did not have, during this day, the company of the damier petrels on which we had nevertheless counted the previous evening in order to complete the dozen which I proposed to preserve for the Museum collection. Among the birds we encountered, there was a species new to us, but we do not know to what genus to assign it. It was a bird the size of a sea snipe and having absolutely its flight. Its body above was a light grey and the underside of the belly very white as well as the lower part of the wings. The tail was also grey above and white beneath with a black border at the extremity.
At noon, we had no solar altitude but the latitude by our dead reckoning was (no figures) south and the estimated longitude (no figures).
In the evening, the sky became a little less covered than it had been in the morning, we saw the sun appear sometimes through the clouds, but it was for so short a time that one could say we did not see it at all. The (winds) passed to the north-north-west and the breeze was moderate and fairly steady.
During the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth, the winds were the same, we saw from time to time a few stars shine and we had the appearance of a fair day for the morrow. We continued on the course to the east-south-east in conformity with the canvas of the Naturaliste.
1801-05-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh and then a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At noon in 33° 55' 50" of latitude by account and in 91° 28' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-19.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts, the commander far ahead of us. We sent up a rocket, and at 3 he answered with a light at the masthead. We took his bearing SE. Saw whales.
1801-05-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the winds were variable from the north-north-west to the north-west, fine breeze, but the sky had a very bad appearance: the whole horizon, in the direction of the wind and under the lee, being extremely laden with large black and thick clouds which sometimes gave us strong gusts. The sea was also beginning to become a little heavy so that we unrigged our topgallant sails and took a second reef in the topsails.
In the morning, the barometer suddenly fell to 28p 2l 6 from 28.5,6 at which it had been for some time, which led us to think that we would have again some squalls. Nevertheless, the weather appeared to want to become fair and we had sight of the sun, which had not happened to us for three days.
At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 29' 38" and the longitude following dead reckoning was 95° 26' 50", whilst that indicated by our No. 27 was only 94° 31' 33" and at No. 35 of 94° 30' 40". We found since the last observations a difference to the south of 13' 25" and one to the west of 9' 51".
During the evening, the weather appeared to want to become fair. Most of the misty and low clouds which obscured our view of the sky dispersed and we could contemplate it at our ease, which had not happened to us for a long time.
At sunset, we had an amplitude of which the result gave for the declination of the needle (no figures) north-west.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth, the weather became covered again with dark and misty clouds. After the setting of the moon, it continued to blow a fair breeze from the north-north-west and we made good progress, having the Naturaliste at a short distance from us and straining every sail to follow us. As there was no appearance of squalls and the wind was fairly uniform, I allowed her to set her main topgallant sail.
1801-05-19.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 30' 40" of latitude observed and in 94° 31' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 11' NW.

1801-05-20.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, the sea rather high, the wind a strong breeze from ESE. Saw many albatrosses.
1801-05-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, the winds were much the same as the previous day and it continued to blow a fine breeze. Although the sea was beginning to become heavy, the vessel was no less performing well and we made good progress.
At eight o'clock, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to the east-quarter-south-east and I myself steered to this direction.
In the morning, the weather appeared to want to become quite fair, although the barometer had fallen greatly and the hygrometer announced a considerable quantity of moisture in the air. We had almost all the morning a fine sun and fair sky although cloudy. Nevertheless at noon we could not observe its meridian altitude because at that time it was enveloped in a cloud which hid it from us until three o'clock in the afternoon.
According to our dead reckoning, our latitude should have been 35° 5' south and the longitude 99° 54' 50". The distance run during twenty-four hours was the greatest we had made since our departure from France.
In the afternoon, the weather did not have a fair appearance. We sometimes had a few small squalls with rain, but they were not of long duration nor was the wind they brought to us too strong.
At four o'clock, not wishing to go too far to the south, I ordered the course to the east and signalled this direction to the Naturaliste. We saw in the day only very few damier petrels and a single albatross. But we perceived fairly often the bird of which I spoke yesterday and whose flight perfectly imitates that of the snipe. It appeared to us that this bird has the same habits on the sea when it is agitated as the storm petrel or bird of the tempest, that is to say it beats the water with its feet and seems at first glance to walk on it.
At the beginning of the night, the sky became covered with a thick mist and soon after it became rainy. At nine o'clock, the winds suddenly jumped to the south-west and masked us. We immediately oriented ourselves on the port tack and continued our course. Several signals were made during the night to the Naturaliste which appeared to us to have greatly reduced her canvas. She answered some and not others, which obliged us to furl, for some time, our lower sails in order to wait for her.
During most of the night, the weather was very rainy and the winds weak. The sea was a little heavy and we began to perceive that we would not be long in seeing fair sky, the horizon brightening greatly in the west-south-west direction.
Meteorological observations made on board the corvette the Géographe

General remarks: Barometer.
Citizen Péron observes that the results he obtained from his observations are much the same as those he had obtained previously. However, he believes that the north winds which prevailed during the fifteen days have influenced the mean terms he obtained and which he thinks ought to be greater by reason of the change of latitude.
In the last decade, he also found the extreme of the barometer variations much greater than he had expected and he attributes the cause to our having long followed the same parallel without any kind of bad weather.
General remarks: Thermometer.
According to Citizen Péron, the north winds which brought us warmth, have also influenced the extreme variations of the barometer thermometer since despite a change of 13° in latitude, the results gave him only 7° in sixteen days, four of which were very bad.
During the last decade, the mean term of the temperature of the atmosphere was even less strong than that of the previous decade: he explains the cause to be the quality of the winds which prevailed as well as two strong squalls which we experienced in the last days of the decade.
General remarks: hygrometer.
The mean term of the hygrometer being fairly considerable, the squalls and frequent rains we had are truly the cause.
The disproportion which Citizen Péron found in the results of the third decade appears to him to be explainable only by the nature of the winds which did not allow (the) humidity which was in the air to descend to a lower region, for it is a fact that there was much of it.
Temperature of the sea water.

General remarks on the temperature of the sea water.
Citizen Péron, who at the time of his departure from Europe could not imagine that the temperature of the sea water was higher than that of the atmosphere, is finally beginning to believe it. All observations and experiments having almost constantly given him results contrary to his opinion.
Electricity, meteors.
There were none of any kind in the first fifteen days, although we had rain sometimes and a stormy sky. It was the same in the third decade.
1801-05-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NNW. At 8 the course was signalled and given S 78° 45' E. At noon in 35° 10' 20" of latitude by account and in 98° 42' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 31' NW. At 4 the course was signalled and given east. During the night sent up rockets.

1801-05-21.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, fresh enough. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8 shortened sail to wait for the commander, who had fallen to leeward. At 8.30 p.m. went about and signalled our tack to the commander.
1801-05-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the first of Prairial, the day was extremely fair and resembled perfectly a fine summer's day in Europe. Nevertheless, the sea, although calm, was extremely heavy from the west-north-west, but as we took the swell almost astern, we were only slightly inconvenienced by it. The weakness of the wind prevented us from making much progress and sometimes the vessel had difficulty in steering.
We saw during the day several large birds having much resemblance by their flight and even by their plumage to albatrosses and we judged them to be such in the distance. But when they drew near us and we were able to observe them well, we clearly saw that it was a new species, in that they had the beak, the head and the tip of the tail black. We greatly regretted not to have the opportunity of procuring one of them but perhaps by and by we shall be more fortunate.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 34° 47' 52" to the south and the longitude following our dead reckoning was 102° 32' 50". That indicated by our timekeepers at the same time was for No. 27 of 101° 29' 59" and for No. 35 of 101° 30' 57". In consequence of this observation we found that we had since the last meridian altitude a difference of 2' 26" to the north and one to the west of 15' 34".
In the evening, the weather continued to be fair and we took several observations from distances of the moon to the sun which gave as result 102 degrees 37 minutes of easterly longitude which put us 57 minutes to the east more than the timekeepers. But the weather not being favourable, the observation is doubtful.
At sunset, the winds passed to the east. Nevertheless we held the northern tack until eight o'clock to allow time for the wind to settle. At this time, it began to freshen from the north-east and we took the port tack, signalling to the Naturaliste to do the same. This vessel was then far ahead of us and went about.
During the night of the first to the second, the weather was fairly fair and the breeze increased gradually until daylight. The sky, after the setting of the moon, became covered with clouds and became dark, but the breeze was no less settled and moderate.
1801-05-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW, SW, SE, E and NE. At noon in 34° 47' 0" of latitude observed and in 101° 20' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 53' NW.

1801-05-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind a light breeze from NNW. Saw many birds and fish of various kinds.
1801-05-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, the winds varied from the north-north-east to the north and we continued our course to the east of the compass to place ourselves at forty-four degrees of south latitude. The sky, although very cloudy, was fairly fair and a fine breeze blew all the morning. Without the heavy swell from the west-north-west which agitated the sea, it would have been very fair.
In the morning, we saw on several occasions those grey and white birds whose flight so well imitates that of the snipe. They were indeed in fairly numerous flocks, but we drew no conclusion from it regarding the approach of land since we had already encountered quite a large quantity more than two hundred leagues to the west of the point where we found ourselves when we saw these last ones. Nevertheless, it appeared to us quite astonishing that a bird, which appeared so weak in appearance, should go so far from land.
At noon the observed south latitude was 34° 37' 28" and the longitude according to our dead reckoning was 104° 15'. That indicated by the timekeepers put us according to No. 27 at 103° 12' 17" and No. 35 at 103° 14' 10". There was in twenty-four hours a difference to the south of 5' 3 seconds and one to the east of 18 seconds.
During the evening, the weather was fair. The winds took a little from the north by the west and we made fairly good progress, always steering to the east of the compass. The result of the amplitudes and azimuths gave (no figures) of north-west declination.
After sunset, the sky became covered with misty clouds, but the night was no less fair and even fairly clear until the setting of the moon. We made sail all night to take advantage of the fair weather; the winds passed to the north-west and to the west where they appeared to want to settle.
1801-05-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 103° 12' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 9° 20' NW.

1801-05-23.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, a light breeze, heading east. At 7 the commander made us the signal to bend our cables. At 7.30 p.m. we sounded without finding bottom.
1801-05-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, in the morning, the weather was fairly fair and the winds passed from the west-north-west to the west, gradually falling calm; we continued our course to the east with all canvas set.
We had in the morning points (sic) of so many different kinds, occasioned by the clouds spread around the horizon that we could not help making several observations of them. We had indeed remarked for three or four days that they presented to us an appearance quite different from that which we had seen in other climates, but it falls far short of them not having presented forms as bizarre and picturesque as those which they have offered since some time. This is, without doubt, an effect of mirages and of the position in which they are found with respect to the sun.
At ten o'clock, I signalled to the Naturaliste to set and establish her cables and we did the same on board.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 34° 13' 37" south and the longitude made by our dead reckoning was 107° 9' easterly. That of the timekeepers was then for No. 27 of 105° 44' 54" and for No. 35 of 105° 47' 31".
There was in twenty-four hours a difference to the north of 3' 45" and one to the west of 14' 23".
In the evening, the weather continued fair but the breeze was always diminishing so that we made very little progress. As the Naturaliste was ahead, I caused the topgallant sails and the bonnets to be rigged. It was the first time since our departure that we had occasion to set so much canvas.
Around four o'clock, the Naturaliste having hove to, launched a boat to the sea, doubtless to take some birds or other object of natural history which she would have spotted on the water.
At sunset, the weather was fair but the horizon in the west-south direction was extremely laden with dark and thick clouds which seemed to indicate that winds would come to us soon from that quarter.
At seven o'clock, they indeed passed to the south-south-west and brought us a squall which in an instant enveloped the whole horizon. It lasted until eight o'clock and brought us a fair amount of rain, but little wind. The weather then became fair again and the sky became very clear. We then remained in calm until ten o'clock and we then had a slight breeze from the south which allowed us to continue our course with all canvas set during the rest of the night. The sky was fair with a few small squalls but which gave only a little rain and even less wind.
1801-05-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW, SW, SE and south. We signalled the Naturaliste to bend her cables, and bent ours. At noon in 34° 13' 30" of latitude observed and in 105° 45' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 31' NW. In the evening the Naturaliste signalled 105° 57' of longitude and asked leave to shorten sail.

1801-05-24.journal_anonyme: The winds WNW, variable to south and SW. We hove to to wait for our boat, which was aboard the commander. At 4.30 we filled and stood on under all sail, the weather misty and rainy.
1801-05-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, in the morning, we had winds from the south, a light breeze, variable to the south-south-east and to the south-east by south. The sky was fine in the morning, and as the sun rose above the horizon, the breeze increased so that at nine o'clock we had to reef our topgallant sails, though less from the strength of the wind than to await the Naturaliste which remained far astern.
At ten o'clock, this vessel made me a signal to inform me of its estimated longitude and which placed it at 106° 50' and at the same time requested me to reduce sail, at seven o'clock in the evening. I replied to its signal with the attention ensign but not at all to its request to reduce sail which I thought even most singular. In the morning we made as much easting as possible.
At noon, the observed latitude was 33° 45' 38" south and the longitude, according to our dead reckoning, was 109° 18'. That indicated by the timekeepers was, at the same time, for No. 27 of 107° 51' 1" and for No. 35 of 107° 54' 14" so that this timekeeper which had always been behind No. 27 had for several days been ahead and had finally passed it.
In the afternoon, a fine breeze continued to blow from the south-south-east. The sky was fine until sunset but the horizon, in the south-east to north-east part, was very laden with clouds and everything announced to us that we would soon have winds from that quarter.
At four o'clock, the Naturaliste being somewhat ahead of us, I made it the signal for general and absolute rally and, having brought it within hailing distance, I gave it orders to keep, during the night, two miles from us, in our waters and beginning at eight o'clock to sound every two hours until four o'clock in the morning. Although we had had during the day no sign of the approach of land, this precaution seemed to me all the more necessary since, according to one of our charts, at the latitude where we were, the bottom (was) at nearly fifty leagues from the coast.
After sunset, the sky became overcast with haze and at eight o'clock the weather turned to rain, so that our horizon was very limited. At the same time, we sounded, but a line of two hundred and fifty fathoms gave us no bottom which however we should have found according to M. Bellin's chart which places the westernmost point of New Holland, at our latitude at 110 degrees 30' east longitude whilst the other charts place the same point at 113° 20'.
At ten o'clock, the winds having shifted to south-east variable to south-south-east with a very overcast and hazy sky, I made signal to the Naturaliste to take the southern tack and having executed the same manoeuvre myself, we both laid ourselves with the ship under close-hauled on the larboard tack and remained there until the following morning.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth, the weather was very changeable, we sometimes had a fairly extended horizon but it was mostly dark and hazy, the winds shifted from south-east to east, so that we did not lose much by making little headway.
1801-05-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 33° 42' 40" of latitude observed and in 107° 51' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 4' NW. At 12.15 the course was signalled S 78° 45' E. At 4.30 made the signal to close. Shortly afterwards we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander ordered Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at half a league and to sound every two hours, and to warn us by two vertical lights should he find bottom, adding that we should warn him in the same way if we found bottom. At 8 hove to and sounded without finding bottom at 265 fathoms. At 8.30 filled and stood on. At 10.30 lay to on the port tack under the mizzen topsail, the mizzen and its staysail, the main staysail and the fore staysail.

1801-05-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind SSE. At 3 the course signalled E by S. At 4 we shortened sail to wait for him; being within hail he ordered us to keep in his wake at half a league's distance and to sound every half hour. Hove to at 7, 8 and 10 and ran out 120 fathoms of line without finding bottom. The commander having gone onto the port tack, we did the same. At midnight, two and four o'clock ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, with winds from the east, a light breeze, we held as close as we could on the southern tack. The sky became quite fine in the morning, and we had a fairly extended horizon and we wanted only for the winds to be favourable. The breeze increased a little as the sun gained strength, but in general it was very moderate.
We saw, in the morning, several flocks of birds, but all were of the same species as we had encountered for several days and at a great distance from the coast, so that up to this point nothing announced to us that we were near the lands of New Holland.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 33° 51' 16" south and the longitude, for the same time, was for No. 27 of 108° 27' 33" and for No. 35 of 108° 33' 20", so that according to the chart which seems to merit the most confidence, we still have 4° 47' of distance to make to the east before reaching land.
According to our dead reckoning, the longitude arrived was 110° 1' east and we found ourselves to have in 24 hours a difference to the south of 2' 15" and one to the west of 3' 54" which differed very little from the estimate of the course.
After having observed the meridian altitude, not wishing to advance further to the south, I made signal to the Naturaliste to go about and we both took the northern-north-east tack. The sky was so fine in the evening that it could be compared to that ordinarily encountered under the tropics and we ourselves were astonished to find it so clear in this season of the year.
From the azimuthal observations and rising amplitudes taken during the day, the mean result of all observations gave (no figures) and as the weather was very favourable, there is every reason to believe that it differs little from the true declination of the needle in the waters we are traversing.
The night of the fifth to the sixth was one of the finest and clearest we have had since our departure from Europe. The moon, which was approaching full, lit us without the least interruption.
At ten o'clock in the evening, the winds having shifted to east-north-east, signal was made to the Naturaliste to go about and to hold as close as possible until the winds permitted us to bear away to east by south-east. We executed the same manoeuvre ourselves and made course all night taking advantage of the winds which shifted more and more toward the north-east.
1801-05-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to NE. At 5 filled and stood on. At noon in 33° 51' 40" of latitude observed and in 108° 29' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 8' NW.

1801-05-26.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind variable from NE to NNE. At 1 p.m. wore onto the starboard tack, and at 10 p.m. went about. At 1 a.m. ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, we had winds from the east-north-east, a fine breeze and a calm sea. After sunrise I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to east by south-east and I then made all sail to chase ahead in order to sight the land before night, in case the longitude of New Holland in the part where I wished to attack it did not differ much from that given it by M. Bellin's chart. But it was labour in vain for at night, although the weather was fine and the horizon fairly extended, we perceived nothing, nor even any sign which could make us suspect that (we) were at a small distance from it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 50' 49" south and the longitude, according to our dead reckoning from the distance indicated by the log, was 111° 15'. That of the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was for No. 27 only 110° 1' and for No. 35 of 110° 6' 31". We found, in the twenty-four hours, a difference to the south of 5' 49" and one to the east of 1° 5' 29" (?) which was very considerable.
In the afternoon, the weather continuing fine, we left the Naturaliste astern to press sail toward the land, but the sea becoming somewhat rough and taking the swell in our teeth, we reefed, about three o'clock, our topgallant sails which seemed badly maintained.
At sunset, having no sign of the approach of the coast, I would have continued to press sail but the Naturaliste being too far away since one could scarcely distinguish it from the main top, I made less sail to wait for it.
During the night of the sixth to the seventh, the weather was fine and the sky fairly clear. However we constantly had flashes of lightning in the south-south-west to south-east part which, following one another without interruption, seemed to announce winds from that quarter. Our expectation was disappointed for they remained constantly at north-east varying sometimes to north-east by east, which made them unfavourable to our course by bearing us too far to the south of the course I wished to hold.
At midnight, we hove to in order to sound but a line of two hundred fathoms gave us no bottom. After recovering the lead, two rockets were fired to indicate to the Naturaliste our position. As I thought this vessel would have continued under sail, I supposed from how little we ourselves had made that it should not be far from us. Nevertheless, no reply was made to this signal and then I lay under the topsails, almost aback to make less headway.
At two o'clock, sweeping the horizon with my night glass, I perceived this vessel astern of us and to windward. I ordered a light to be set at the mizen peak and when it had closed with us, we increased sail.
1801-05-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. At 7 signalled and shaped the course S 78° 45' E. At noon in 33° 49' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 44' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. The Naturaliste, far astern, was lost sight of at nightfall. Sent up rockets and showed a light at the gaff to give her our position. At midnight we sounded and ran out 200 fathoms without finding bottom.

1801-05-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NNE. The commander standing in for the land. At 5 it bore from us east 9° S, distant about 5 leagues, the commander out of sight. At 3.30 a.m. we had closed him within hail. At 7 he signalled us land without giving the bearing. At 7.30 we took its bearing in the SSE, with two detached points. At 10 took the bearing of the northernmost land ESE. Noon bearings: the furthest point to leeward that could be seen, east 25° 30' N; the point at which the land seemed no longer to continue, east 33° 10' N; the middle of the land which to windward appeared separate from the first, east 37° 45' N. None of these corrected for 6° 30' of NW variation.
1801-05-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & remarks. View of New Holland.
On the seventh, from four o'clock in the morning, we began to make all sail, except for the topgallant sails and at seven-thirty, as the sailors were setting them, they announced to us the land remaining to the east by north-east. As the winds were then north-north-east variable to north-east by east, we had great difficulty in closing with it and it was not until about ten-thirty that it began to be distinguished from the deck.
The first view we had of it is absolutely conformable to the coloured drawing I give of it and any vessel that makes landfall at the same latitude as us will recognize it easily. The southern part of Cape Leeuwin, seen in the distance, offers to the view a fairly even coast and seems, at a distance of nine to ten leagues, to form several islands or, at least, indentations of which the depth is not visible. The middle of the most apparent land is fairly high and terminates in two low points followed by the other lands shown in figure No. 1. One can easily, in fine weather, see it at a distance of ten leagues. At the moment we sighted it, our estimated latitude was 34° 25' 55" south and the longitude arrived was 112° 51'. We deferred drawing closer to the land to determine the error of the timekeepers which appeared to us to show a westerly difference.
At noon, the observed latitude placed us at 34° 35' 58" and the longitude, reduced to noon, by dead reckoning was 112° 57' 42" east.
That indicated by the timekeepers was at the same time for No. 27 of 111° 42' 7" and for No. 35 of 111° 47' 19".
Bearings of the land at noon:
The easternmost point of the land in sight to the east 22° north)
The point of that to the north to the east 47° north) the whole by compass
A point to the north of the former to the east 35° north)
A point of the same land to the east 43° north)
After taking the bearings, I made sound and we found bottom at one hundred and four fathoms, broken and articulated coral. The Naturaliste, which had sounded at the same moment, signalled to us 117 fathoms, fine white sand. This vessel was then about two miles astern of us and somewhat to windward.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine, but we were almost becalmed until four o'clock in the evening, when the winds shifted to south-east variable to south-south-east. We immediately laid the starboard tack and closed with the land which, according to the bearing taken at sunset, presented itself to us in the form shown in drawing No. 3.
Bearings of the land at sunset:
The land to the north most in view to the north 5° east) the whole by compass
The middle of the same land to the N. NE 4° east)
The easternmost point to the NE 5° east)
After sunset, we continued our course to the N. NE to close with the land and work northward, sounding often and at eight o'clock I hove to for the night in this position if the weather continued fine. We then distinguished the land very clearly, and our dead reckoning placed us at five leagues from it.
Throughout the whole night the weather was fine and the winds south-east variable to east, a light breeze. We sounded every two hours and the soundings showed, sometimes, several irregularities of bottom. Each sounding announcing us a good sandy bottom sometimes mixed with small points of coral, I decided, to make the night less long and to satisfy my curiosity, to have one of our dredges put out, persuaded that despite the great depth of the water, I could encounter some fine shells or other curious objects. In consequence we got ready to dredge. We had then a fine bottom of seventy-two fathoms, grey and white pure sand. At ten o'clock, we cast out the dredge, and we paid out one hundred and fifty fathoms of rope. Half an hour later, it was hauled in and to our great satisfaction, it was found to be quite full of different objects which we were most eager to know. Having had a bucket prepared in advance, everything was emptied into it and it was not without astonishment that we saw a great variety of things new to us.
After it was emptied, it was cast out again and we (we) set about reviewing what we had just brought up from the bottom. The greater part of the objects consisted of sponges and pieces of soft corals, several fine marine plants and a great quantity of small sponges resembling, in form, potatoes.
Among living animals we found only two species of worms which were immediately put in alcohol.
The marine plants and different species of coral seemed to us the most precious, and we made an ample collection of them as well as small branches of corals but, except two small white nerites and a limpet, we took no shells.
At ten-thirty, we hauled in our dredge which was found to be even more full than the first time and of nearly the same objects. We much regretted that different lithophytes which we had had the good fortune to encounter were broken. But this misfortune seemed without remedy from the pressure caused by the water and the accumulation of the different objects caught in the dredge.
In any case, the first trial at such a great depth seemed to us so satisfactory that I resolved to, whenever the opportunity presented itself, to make good use of the time we would lose by not making headway.

At eight o'clock in the evening, the Naturaliste having passed within hailing distance, I hailed it that my intention was to remain hove to during the night if the weather remained fine, and asked it for permission to send aboard to compare its timekeepers which it had been unable to use since the last time it had come aboard to compare them.
At nine o'clock, M. de St Criq arrived and he regulated their rate anew with M. Bernier, our astronomer who, in all respects, is worth a hundred thousand times more than the one who, happily for us, remained at Île de France.
I took the same opportunity to send to M. Hamelin the table of our conventional signals for the boats which I accompanied with an instruction on the conduct that the officer to whom he entrusted his longboat should hold, if we are sometimes obliged to send it for several days on reconnaissance.
Note: at eleven o'clock in the evening, a spirit thermometer encased in a wooden frame filled then with tallow was immersed in the water. This thermometer remained at about fifty fathoms depth until the next day at five o'clock in the morning. We found it, after withdrawing it from its case, at 17°9, the air of the atmosphere was then at 17°, which gave 0°9 more for the temperature of the sea-water at this depth. We had noticed before that the objects withdrawn with the dredge gave off considerable heat but the eagerness to examine them prevented us from thinking of placing the thermometer there.
View of New Holland. Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, in the morning, we were much astonished not to see the land of which we still had a perfect view at four o'clock. It was only then visible from the main top and we concluded rightly that a strong and violent current or, at the very least a change of tide, must have carried us to the south-east, since the bearing we took of it then gave us:
The northernmost lands at N ¼ NE ) the whole by compass
The middle of the same lands at N. NE )
and the easternmost point at NE 6° N )
After recognizing our bearings, we made sail, but with the winds then at E. SE, very weak, the course we were obliged to hold brought us little closer to the land.
We saw, in the course of the morning, several whales of ordinary size and much like those encountered south of Madagascar. They passed close enough to the vessel to give our gentlemen a spectacle quite new to them, by their manner (of) spouting the sea-water.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 34° 46' north south, whilst that of the dead reckoning gave us 34° 9' south so that we had, from the dead reckoning to the observation, a difference of 35' to the south.
The longitude indicated by the timekeepers was then 111° 45' 59" for No. 27 & 111° 41' 55" for No. 35, which gave 4' 6" of distance to the east in 24 (hours), so that the current or the tide carried us (us) directly to the south 6° east. This small mishap was a lesson for us and I hope that the currents in this direction will not play us such a trick again.
After the observation of the sun, the lands of which we then had perfect view from the deck remained for us according to the following bearing:
The northernmost land at: north 16° east ) the whole by compass
A low point on which one could distinguish )
two small peaks at north 22° east, at north 30° east ) The land in view most to the east, at N E. )
The sounding, at the same moment, indicated 104 fathoms bottom of sand and fine coral.
Figure No. 5 gives an exact view of the aspect which the land presented to us then which, in this part, is found, as I have already observed, of mediocre height and easily to be seen from 10 or 12 leagues in fine weather.
During the evening, the winds having shifted to east-south-east, a fine breeze, we pressed sail toward the land of which we were no more than two leagues from at most at sunset. We then reduced sail to wait for the Naturaliste which was far astern and we took the following bearing by taking the view shown in figure No. 6.

At the same time, the bottom was 87 fathoms, sand and decayed shells.
At seven-thirty, we laid the main topsail aback, and we waited for the Naturaliste which joined us shortly after, and hove to on the same tack as us.
So as not to waste our time doing nothing, I ordered the dredge to be cast to see if we would be as or more fortunate than the previous day. We took some madrepores, sponges of different colours and even some curious pieces of soft coral on which were found different plants and lithophytes. This first trial encouraged us to make another despite that I was not (without) anxiety about the fate of my dredge since the quality of the bottom indicated by the sounding which I was having taken every half hour announced it to be bad. However we hauled it in without accident but either that it had been badly guided or for some other reason, we took nothing this time.
At about ten o'clock, the Naturaliste, which was more toward the land than us, went about and came to warn me that it had found a strong current bearing, according to its dead reckoning, to the east-south-east and which had brought it so close to the coast that it had been as much as twenty-five fathoms, rocky bottom, and that it had perfectly recognized the breakers ashore.
We had taken, like the Naturaliste, our marks ashore at the beginning of the night. One remained at E. 22° N and the other at E. 5° N, and at the moment when the Naturaliste spoke to us, one remained at E. 11° N and the other at N 10° west which led me to believe that the currents were carrying us more toward the NW than toward the south-east.
In any case, we made sail, one and the other, and ran about an hour to the N. W under our topsails, after which we hove to again on the starboard tack.
Throughout the whole night the weather was very fine and by the light of the moon, we distinguished the land perfectly and all the white patches with which it (is) marked in this part. Our dead reckoning placed us at about two leagues from it.

1801-05-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE and light from SSE to E. At 1.30 the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake. At 7.30 the land was sighted; it stretched from S 78° 45' E to N 67° 30' E and appeared to be divided in two parts. We signalled it to the Naturaliste. At noon the land from N 43° E to N 68° E, being in 34° 35' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 42' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 15' NW. At half past noon the lead gave 104 fathoms, coral and sand. At 7.30 hove to on the starboard tack; the Naturaliste passed under our stern and the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to lie to all night; he gave him leave to send aboard to compare his watches. At 8.30 Citizen Saint-Cricq arrived with the marine watches and left at 9. At 10.30 the boat came back to bring us hay. The dredge was put over and brought up marine specimens; the lead gave from 92 to 100 fathoms, coral, sand and shell. At midnight the land N 15° E.

1801-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind varying from SE, SSE and ESE. At half past noon hove to to sound. The lead brought up 93 fathoms, white sand mixed with broken shell. We thought we noticed that the winds set to the south. Bearings taken at sunset: the southern end of a stretch of land we judged to be an island, east 47° N; the furthest part to the north bore N 23° 40' E. At 7.30 passed under the commander's stern and asked his leave to communicate in order to set our marine timekeepers; he granted it and warned us that if the weather stayed fine we should lie to heading north. Soundings: at 9 p.m., 89 fathoms, reddish sand and broken shell; at 10, 11 and 12, 90 fathoms, the same. We lay to on the starboard tack until four o'clock, when we filled and stood on. At daybreak took the bearing of the land east 27° N. At 10, east 38° 10' N.
1801-05-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ENE. Shortly after midnight the land was lost sight of. At 7 we filled and stood on, and the land was seen from aloft. From midnight to noon the lead gave from 100 to 105 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon the land bore from us N 33° E to N 38° E, being in 34° 45' 0" of latitude observed and in 111° 46' of longitude by No. 27. The variation 6° 90' NW [sic]. By the reckoning we had made way to the north and west, and by the observation we had made it to the south and east, which can only be put down to the violence of the currents, which set south and SSE. At 5 took the bearing of the north point in sight N 11° E, the south point in sight N 67° 30' E, and an islet lying near the latter N 78° 45' E. From 5 until midnight the lead gave from 45 to 33 fathoms, sand and coral. During the night we lay to, in sight of land.

1801-05-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ESE. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 took the bearing of the easternmost part of the land in sight N 23° 20' E, the westernmost part N 45° E, estimated distance 16 miles. Passed under the commander's stern; he ordered us to heave to. At 8.25 sounded and found 25 fathoms, sand and broken shell. At five in the morning the commander having filled, we did the same. At noon sounded and found 28 fathoms, rock and coral. At the same hour took the bearing of the southernmost point of the land east 38° 30' S and the northernmost N 21° 30' E.
1801-05-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, at daybreak, we pressed sail to close with the land which our dead reckoning then placed at four leagues distance. The weather was very fine, and the sunrise announced a fine day. We had only to regret that the winds were from the east variable to east-north-east and very weak. But, as on the previous days they had varied from the east toward the south when the sun gained strength, we hoped the same would happen to us during the day.
At sunrise, the following bearing was taken:
The northernmost land relative to our position, at N ¼ NE)
A cape in front of which lay a great white patch at NE ) the whole by compass
The southernmost lands relative to us at east ¼ SE )
From the bearing and the dead reckoning of the reduction of the different courses since yesterday noon, our estimated latitude was 34° 3' 46" which brought us very close to that which almost all charts, both old and modern, indicate for the latitude of this cape.
From the morning, the view presented to me by the coast made me suspect that the point we had in view could well be it, but to fix my opinion on this subject with greater certainty, I deferred to the observation of the sun's altitude at noon the verification of this conjecture.
The breeze having increased somewhat and the winds directing toward the east, we came closer to the land on which the tide also seemed to carry us so that at eight o'clock noon, we were at most three leagues from it. The observed latitude then was 34° 10' 35" for the greater part of the instruments, and those which the observation placed most to the south differed by only 2' 15 seconds. So that the mean result of our observations gave 34° 7' 6" 3"' for the observed latitude at noon. The sky was then very fine and the horizon so clear that there can be no doubt about the result of the observations.
From this latitude and the position assigned to Cape Leeuwin by most of the charts we have, it would therefore appear certain that the advanced point athwart of which we found ourselves and which then remained at east 17° south, no more than 3 leagues distance, would truly be this cape and moreover very easy to recognize by the great white patch which is found near it and somewhat more to the south. Mean longitude of the timekeepers at noon 111° 37' 57".
Having then joined the Naturaliste which was about a quarter of a league ahead of us and to windward, I asked it for its observed latitude. It was (no figures), consequently differing from ours by only (no figures). I then questioned it to know which of the points we had in view it believed to be Cape Leeuwin. Its reply was that it presumed it was the point remaining at SE 5° south. It based its reasoning on the fact that yesterday evening we had sighted this same point at the extremity of which one thought they had seen the small island placed on the charts.
I had seen as M. Hamelin did yesterday this small island which, according to all those who climbed to the top of the masts is not an island, but rather low land joined to another coast which extended out of sight to the south-south-east. Besides, if the cape remaining at south-east 5° south which we had in view was truly Cape Leeuwin, it would result that its latitude would be thirty-four degrees thirty-three minutes six seconds, which I am far from believing.
It appears demonstrated to me by the extent of coast we have travelled south of Cape Leeuwin that the place where M. St Aloüarn could have anchored cannot be at the estimated latitude he indicates in his journal, for supposing we had not perceived his island, we would have at least had knowledge of some of those he speaks of since we made landfall at 34° 35' 58". Thus prolonging the south coast of New Holland, we made to the north twenty-eight minutes fifty-two seconds in latitude to arrive at 34° 7' 6" still close enough to the land to be able to distinguish islands, islets and banks of rocks, if any had existed. The entire coast we have travelled since 34° 35' 58" is sound and even very sound. It is far from being low and submerged as far as (no figures) it is on the contrary full of elevations which succeed one another fairly rapidly and it can only be at eight or ten leagues distance that, not perceiving the lower lands which join them together, one could mistake these elevations for islets. Undoubtedly it was at a great distance that M. St Aloüarn saw the coast and the islets he announces.
In the evening, we had winds from the south-east and south-south-east as we had expected, which made us approach the coast to four miles distance, and we continued after sunset to follow it contouring all the sinuosities presented to us by the different indentations it could offer us. We saw with regret that it offered no shelter nor anchorage for vessels. And, excepting two small sand coves where the sea appeared somewhat calm, it broke with great force all along the coast which is extremely precipitous and steep.
As we followed the coast, the astronomers and geographers were constantly occupied in taking angles and bearings to draw its chart and I believe this work will be well done from the diligence with which they pursued it and our small distance from the land.
All the country we explored appeared arid as to the lands nearest us which are located facing the edge of the sea. The most remarkable elevations for us were, for the greater part, covered with a species of heather which offered little elevation and one could sometimes distinguish some plateaux of trees of fairly fine green, which only served to make more disagreeable to the view the places which were bare of them. One of the things which struck me most was not to perceive, in the fairly considerable extent of land we visited so closely, any ravine which appeared to have an outlet to the sea for the waters.
The mountains, for there are many which are not as high and bear this name, were little advanced into the land and terminated at the sea by a slope which appeared to us fairly gentle, but at the edge of the sea, the coast was, as I have already said, precipitous and little accessible.
These lands will be easy to recognize thereafter by navigators who frequent these waters. The different white patches more or less large found there are disposed with enough symmetry not to be mistaken. They are indicated in the view which I had drawn (and) coloured expressly for this purpose. There will be seen equally the wooded parts and those which are not.
We were long in believing this coast was uninhabited, but we were not long in having proof to the contrary, for at night we perceived in different places fires which indicated to us that it was not without inhabitants.
If, during the day, I had perceived some places suitable for bringing the vessels there, I would not have failed to return the next day but independently of the fact that no anchorage is found, the bottom is bad, having found almost everywhere only sand mixed with coarse coral or a hard bottom of pure coral and rocks.
As I had taken the lead of the Naturaliste, I found myself at sunset to have explored a much greater extent of coast than it and so that it could know the course I would be obliged to make during the night, I kept my stern light burning until it had reached me.
I am ignorant whether the coast we have just visited can offer anything of interest for natural history since we did not land there but at least, what appeared to me rather extraordinary, is that we had the visit of no land bird, and two petrels are the only sea birds we encountered which is almost sufficient indication to establish the aridity of the land and the few resources the sea can offer to others.
A thing equally rather singular and which I did not give credence to, is that the look-outs from the top of the masts stoutly maintained having seen come out of a small wooded grove fairly high which we then had in view, several large quadrupeds which they said were oxen or at least appeared to be. They appeared to it, at different times, to enter and leave the grove of which I have just spoken.
In the night of the ninth to the tenth, the weather continued fine. We passed it partly hove to and partly under sail at about four leagues from the coast. The following table indicates the nature of the soundings we had during the twenty-four hours, as well as the sounding which was fairly regular.

1801-05-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SE. At 5 we filled and stood on, running along the coast at about 6 miles. It seemed to me to offer no safe anchorage: it is fringed with reefs on which the sea broke with force; the dunes are covered with heath and a few bushes are to be seen here and there. The lead giving from 30 to 40 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon, being in 34° 11' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 44' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 4' NW. The northernmost point in sight bore from us N 20° E, the southernmost S 45° E, and a white cape (taken for Cape Leeuwin) S 78° 45' E. At 5 we saw a fire on the shore, which convinced us that the coast is inhabited. At 7.30 we hove to. The Naturaliste passed under our stern and spoke us. The trend of the coast is roughly north and south. Note: Cape Leeuwin lies further south than this white cape.

1801-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; we ran along the coast to the north. At 4 p.m. took the bearing of Cape Leeuwin south 15° 30' E, distant about six leagues. Running along the coast we saw a fire ashore and then several more. We hoisted a lantern at the gaff to make ourselves known to the inhabitants. Soundings: at 8 and 9, 30 fathoms, rock and coral; at 10, 38 fathoms, fine sand; at 11 and 12 the same, mixed with broken shell. At 1 the commander having altered course we did the same. At 2 filled and made all sail. At 6.25 a.m. went about to close the commander, who was far to leeward. At 6.40 sounded in 28 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon we saw that the land stretched away all along to starboard and formed a bight, of which several points could be seen at noon from the quarterdeck. Noon bearings: Point P ahead of us S 2° E; Point N furthest astern S 3° 30' E; Point O which we had doubled S 27° W. These points are so named after the surveying engineer's work.
1801-05-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, at four o'clock in the morning, the weather being very fine and the sea calm, we oriented ourselves as close-hauled on the larboard tack, the winds being then at SE ¼ E variable to E. SE and at daylight we made all sail. The Naturaliste did the same and we closed with the land of which we were three leagues distant.
Bearings of the Lands at Sunrise
The northernmost land in view at east 18° N)
The southernmost land in view at south 5° east ) the whole by compass.
The middle of the land formed by these two points at SE )
At eight o'clock, we went about and closed well with the land which we skirted at one league distance until its northernmost point relative to our position and which is very remarkable for a reef which extends a good quarter of a league offshore and on which the sea broke with great force.
When we had doubled this cape, the easternmost lands began to show themselves and continuing the tack which bore us to the north-east, we obtained knowledge of a great bay of which the cape we had just doubled formed the southern point whilst that of the north extended to the W ¼ NW. And scarcely could one see, from the top of the masts, the end of the indentation it takes to the east, so that this extent presented to us an immense bay which, according to our dead reckoning, had more than fifteen leagues from one cape to the other. After doubling the southern point of which I have spoken, the winds being at south-east, we had no other tack to hold than that of north-east. And as it was moving us away from the coast, I thought we were over great depth which made me sound often so as not to venture too far, but I was much astonished to see that instead of the soundings we had been in ordinary proximity to which usually diminished, they decreased gradually and that from thirty-five fathoms which we had when doubling the point, it was no more than 33 when we were at six or seven leagues distance. The Naturaliste, which was then under the lee of us, had about the same bottom, fine sand.
At noon, the estimated latitude was 33° 32' 42" south and that observed was 33° 23' 49" which gave us for difference in the dead reckoning of the courses during the twenty-four hours, 8' 53" distance to the north. The longitude indicated by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was for No. 27 of 112° 13' 38" and for No. 35 of 112° 20' 29", our great cape then remaining at south 38° west.
Shortly after the observation, the Naturaliste signalled to us that it did not believe the course we were making good to follow in that it perceived a danger in the N. NW. I replied with the attention ensign but I continued to hold the same tack so that it could assure itself more positively being persuaded that the danger was surely, like those often announced to us, nothing else than whales which were playing on the water and making it leap to a great height.
At two o'clock, so as not to move too far from our great cape marked at south 38° west, I went about to close with the land. We sounded every half hour on board, and the sounding reported for a long time a fine sand bottom, sometimes very pure and sometimes coarse yellow sand. We even had one at 28 fathoms which is absolutely similar to that encountered fairly ordinarily at the mouths of rivers and we all thought, from the appearance presented to us by the land, we would find one. Several persons who climbed to the top of the masts even thought they could perceive it and in consequence of their report, I decided to anchor in the open roadstead at twenty to twenty-one fathoms, if the bottom continued to be good.
In approaching the land, we saw two sand coves on which the sea appeared fairly calm and it was in front of the easternmost one that I anchored at 23 fathoms depth, fine sand mixed with a little mud, at most four miles from the coast. The Naturaliste being much to leeward, having well been able to distinguish our manoeuvre since it was still daylight, I was not anxious about what it would do to come join us and indeed at eight o'clock it came to anchor abreast of us.
As soon as I was at anchor, I sent my boat to sound all around the vessel and even at a considerable distance. All the soundings it took gave an excellent bottom and I was without anxiety for my anchor. This operation completed and not wishing to pass a night doing nothing, I had the dredge hauled out by my boat and (at) a distance of two hundred and fifty fathoms from the vessel. We were not very fortunate, however some rather curious things in sea-urchins, starfish and plants.
During the night, a boat was prepared to depart the next day before daybreak, to go recognize the country. I gave its command to Citizen Freycinet, all the scholars wanted to accompany him, but as the boat could hold in all only eight men, there were discontent and there will be more often in like occasions. The gardener Riedelé and the mineralogist Depuche were the only ones designated to go ashore. The one to give us an idea of the country, and the other to know the nature of the soil which presented to us a more agreeable appearance than the parts we had recognized up to then.
During the night of the tenth to the eleventh, the weather was fine and the winds from south-south-east to south-east moderate. However, about eleven o'clock, we had a strong gust which, making us drag on our anchor, very nearly made us run into the Naturaliste which, nevertheless, we did not touch, but it was very close.
