Anchorage on the Coast of New Holland at 33° 30' 55 seconds south latitude & 111° 56' 56" east longitude. Of the 11th Prairial of the 9th year & (31 May 1801)
On the eleventh, one hour before daylight, my small boat departed for the land under the command of Citizen Freycinet, and the persons designated the previous evening accompanied it. This officer was provided with the orders relating to the mission he had to fulfil and I am pleased to believe that he will execute it with exactitude.
At daylight, measures were taken to put the longboat to sea one (sic) which I wanted to send (sic) to recognize the lands which surrounded us and especially the cape which forms the entrance to the bay to the south, which I wanted to fix the position with exactitude. For this reason the astronomer Bernier and the geographer Boulanger were ordered to embark for this purpose. The command of this longboat was entrusted to Citizen Picquet to whom I gave a written order on what he was to do. At ten o'clock, the well-armed longboat, provided with all that was necessary, departed.
Citizen Hamelin having come on board, we agreed on the work we would occupy ourselves with our boats. But before he sent a boat ashore, I wanted to await the return of mine to know what reliance to place on the places which appeared to offer us easy landing.
At noon, we observed the latitude of the anchorage where we were: 33° 30' 55" and the longitude indicated by the timekeepers placed us at (no figures).
Shortly after, my boat arrived, and the persons who had accompanied M. Freycinet, as well as he, made to me the following reports:
Report of Citizen Freycinet, commander of the boat, on the occasion of our first landing on the Western Coast of New Holland.
"According to the instructions you transmitted to me yesterday evening of the 10th current, I departed in the morning in the small boat with Citizens Depuche and Riedelé to recognize the part of the coast of New Holland remaining to the south of our present anchorage.
"I arrived at seven o'clock in a small cove terminated by two fairly salient points whose reciprocal bearing is about N. NW and S. SE. They are distant from each other about one and a quarter leagues. The bottom of this cove is a white sand beach and although the landing at first appeared easy, I found fairly considerable surf. For this reason, I forbade the boatmen to leave their boat for an instant and when the naturalists and I were landed, I had the boat hauled offshore where it remained anchored on its grappling anchor.
"My first concern (was) to travel a little through the country to gain a general knowledge of it and of its inhabitants if there were any. I soon had certainty of the contrary and found no vestige of human industry. The quantity of wood which I perceived on the heights made me hope to discover some sources of fresh water, but my search in that regard was fruitless. The land, despite a great quantity of vegetable productions, appears too sandy to be fertile and this region seems to offer navigators no other resources than firewood, the most common tree is a species of eucalyptus. It rises only to mediocre height. One also finds in quantity a shrub which grows in clumps and which the form and odour of its leaves makes one take for laurel, but Citizen Riedelé told me that it was a species of (no name)
"Another tree, whose leaves fairly similar to that of vetiver, forming a bouquet which rises above a fairly thick trunk and colour of charcoal, gave me a species of pod of which I provide you a sample.
"On the heights which dominate the cove where I landed, are found several very considerable blocks of granite.
"I also perceived several large black birds but too far away to say anything about them. Our boat was followed by a troop of gulls whose familiarity surprised us. I believed I recognized on the sand tracks of quadrupeds and principally those of an animal with cloven hooves.
"After a walk of about one hour, I returned to the boat to take the soundings of the small cove as you had prescribed. My plan was to fix each of them by bearings taken from the point of N. NW and from one of the corvettes, these two points being to be known with great precision. The winds having freshened and the sea becoming more choppy, the movement of my small boat prevented me from continuing the already somewhat uncertain bearings since I was forced to take them with a boat compass.
"The soundings gave me at ½ cable and at two cables from the shore, the following soundings of which you will find the results appended:
"distances from the edge of the sea
"at ½ cable, from one and a half to three fathoms, fine sand and rocks
"at 1 cable, from three to seven fathoms, fine sand mixed with coral
"at 2 cables, from ten to fifteen fathoms, fine sand and clean bottom.
"I was unable to sound the cove from one point to the other, this work would have required more time than you had prescribed. Besides the wind continuing to freshen, I had to fear not being able to reach on board if I let myself fall off toward the coast. At the quarter of the point of N. NW to the point S. SE is an eminence whose point terminates in a small bar. It would be dangerous for longboats to land in this small place, the same as at one cable from there, at S ¼ SE. All along the coast at half a cable are scattered small underwater rocks, they are fairly apparent and easy to avoid.
"I think that, if the breeze is at all strong, one cannot land on this beach with large longboats without compromising them. But the anchorage at half a cable is fairly good. In all the part of the coast which is in view, the sea appeared to me to break with violence.
"At ten o'clock, the naturalists Depuche and Riedelé made their way to the boat. I immediately made course to return on board sounding every 7 minutes. The soundings increased gradually until about five cables from the coast. I have since constantly found twenty fathoms on a fine sand bottom.
Report of Citizen Picquet, commander of the longboat.
"According to the orders you gave me on the 11th current, at ten and a quarter o'clock (a blank), I took command of the well-armed longboat in which embarked the citizens Bernier, astronomer, and Boulanger, geographer, whom I was to land as close as possible to the western point of our present anchorage. But the coast which I followed at very small distance from W. SW to the west, presented to me no place to land, being bordered by reefs and sand beaches on which the sea breaks with violence.
"According to the request of the astronomer and the geographer, I placed myself at half a cable west of the point which they wished to determine. But the cloudy sky did not permit observations. Then I decided to return to the anchorage of the corvettes. The winds from east-south-east to south-east forced me to tack and the currents set me to the south. As I found myself unable to make the anchorage, the sea being rough, and finding no shelter on the coast because of the surf which the sea swell carries there, I tacked all night.
"Besides, the coast appeared to me sound at one mile distance. The different soundings which I took at one league to the east of the western point, were according to the following table:
"at 10 fathoms from the shore: two fathoms fine sand and rocks,
"at 50 fathoms: five fathoms same bottom,
"at 100 fathoms: fifteen fathoms sand,
"at 200 fathoms above fifteen fathoms, sand.
"The currents toward this point are very violent. I think them occasioned by the tides, and I observed that the ebb bore to the south-west and the flood to the north-east. The bearing at one league to the east-north-east of the lands of this point is E. SE and in the south-south (sic) by southwest insofar as one can observe with a boat compass.
"The lands appeared to me sandy, covered with trees in many parts of the shore, and toward the summits, bare. I remarked at a quarter league to the east of the western point a bar which breaks with force at the moment when one least expects it on a depth of 7 to 8 fathoms of water".
Report of the mineralogist Depuche.
"The land where we descended and which lies at SW ¼ south of the corvettes, forms a small demi-elliptical cove. The two points which form it appeared to me inaccessible because of the rocks which advance offshore and the breakers which result from them. Throughout its extent, it offers a beach of very fine white sand. The uniformity of this beach is interrupted from time to time by large greyish or reddish rocks which protrude from the sand where they seem as if implanted. The sea breaks against all these asperities, but with much less violence than against the two points. The bottom is strewn with rocks which appeared to me of the same nature and similarly situated. They are very apparent although covered by 6, 8, 10, 12 & 15 fathoms of water and more as one advances offshore. What makes them especially very sensitive is the contrast which arises from their darkened colour and the white sand which composes the bottom in all the other parts. This contrast affects the colour of the sea in such a manner that from nearby heights it would be easy not only to count the number of these rocks, but also to indicate precisely their form and the space they occupy. For the rest, none appeared dangerous to us and at two cables from the shore, they are at least at eight or ten fathoms depth.
"The sea breaks on the beach in such a manner that despite the fine weather which we enjoyed, it was necessary to wade into the water up to the waist to reach the shore. Here, in a few words, is the aspect of the country which we had before our eyes from the point of our landing, that is to say from the middle of the cove. We found first a very even and sandy beach which extends about fifty paces from the limit of ordinary tides insofar as I could judge. It is bordered by a small cliff, if I can give that name to a terrace of five to eight feet elevation and composed also of very fine white sand. This cliff appeared to me to extend throughout the cove and border everywhere the shore. It is precisely above that vegetation begins. It is at first not very active, but becomes more so at the end of two or three hundred paces as one advances into less sandy and higher ground. This terrace rises indeed with a gentle slope and leads to the foot of a hill which forms what one might call the first plane of the terrain. The hills which form the second are much more extended and much more arid. The first contain a fairly great quantity of trees of medium size, the shrubs and parasitic plants are in great number. Those on the contrary offered us only short heather, or plants which from a distance had the appearance of it, divided from place to place by some stunted trees.
"The hills which are found in the first plane terminate in a gentle and extended slope toward the middle of the cove from which results a small valley which opens on to the beach and penetrates into the interior of the country forming several sinuosities. This valley communicates with the shore in the same manner as that which you observed all along the coast which we were following on the ninth of Prairial, that is to say by a beach of very low sand. This beach contains no stream of water, nor any trace of momentary currents which ravines and valleys often produce. However the vegetation is more active on the banks of this valley than anywhere else, the trees more closely packed appeared to me covered with fine foliage and especially more elevated and better nourished.
"Before ending this topographical account, I would observe to you, Commander, that the cove of which I am speaking appeared to me to be the third of the bay where we were entering counting from the point which we doubled on the tenth, and that these three coves and another further to the east form together a fourth cove which includes the entire coast we have before our eyes.
"The place of our landing appeared to me remarkable for the fine granite which I perceived from all sides. That which composes the rocks of the edge of the sea is of very fine but sensible grain. These rocks are divided into layers more or less wide, each regular in its thickness. They extend to containing between them blades of a black and brilliant substance which I recognized as black mica scattered with grains of very attenuated quartz. One sees there also blades of transparent quartz (rock crystal in mass), they can be half an inch or an inch thick. The external surface of this granite has been rounded and polished by the perpetual action of the waves. Several are surmounted by a crust more or less thick of a calcareous substance entirely compartmented and filled with shells pulverized and petrified or simply encrusted. These crusts or deposits detach easily from the granite which served them, so to speak, as a gangue (illegible) and this without their surface being in any way altered. The rounded form presented by the granite, the very place where the matter rested, proves in an evident manner that the existence of this matter is much posterior to the first lands where the waves break on these shores. I believe it due to animals (a blank) so abundant in these waters.
"On most of the neighbouring heights, the rock shows itself bare. I visited several of these points and found everywhere granite or feldspath, quartz and mica dominated noticeably. The feldspath is sometimes in such quantity that one can scarcely distinguish the two other substances. I also encountered several pieces where quartz abounded noticeably.
"The granite is here, as on the edges of the sea, composed of almost straight and very characterized layers. I said that the first were separated by blades of black mica. This mica is pulverized and forms with the grains of quartz a particular granite of black colour. Others are mixed with transparent quartz. These are most often mixed by blades of crystallized feldspath, so that it is very common to find the entire surface of a large block of granite covered with fine crystals of this substance. All affect the primitive form which is peculiar to it. On one of the slopes forming the valley, I observed several layers of granite which jutted out vividly from the ground. Their inclination could be approximately 30 to 70 degrees, they had a width almost equal to their thickness, I can compare them better than to quadrangular prisms of basalt or well to the profile of a wall constructed of large blocks. The fissures which divided them into large sections were so regular and so equally spaced, the layers so sensitive and so numerous, that it is impossible not to convince oneself here of the truth which M. de Saussure was the first to recognize and which several naturalists still dispute, that granites are susceptible to forming layers and that granitic terrain can be, like secondary terrain, composed of a number more or less large of superposed beds, et cetera.
"Despite the efforts I made to determine the direction toward which all these granitic layers incline, I was unable to do so in a general manner. Most appeared to me to incline toward the NW. Others seemed to have an inclination entirely contrary. This was undoubtedly owing to the fissures perpendicular to the layers which were easy to confuse with the exterior layers. The solution of this kind of problem would have required more time than I had at my disposal.
"I also found on the entire slope of the hill which we travelled large blocks of limonous iron ore. All are of irregular shapes. They are at most half an inch in size. They are abundantly disseminated on the surface of the soil which itself appeared to me very ferruginous.
"Finally, if I sum up the different geological observations which I have just exposed, I would be led to the following remarks:
"1) the terrain where we descended offered me none of the products which belong to the domain of fire, the soil is therefore not volcanic.
"2) it offered me likewise none of the substances which are called secondary formation, it therefore does not belong to the sedimentary terrain.
"3) the primordial substances show themselves everywhere, it is therefore of primary formation.
"4) sand abounds there, iron ore limonous and ferruginous soil are found there, it has therefore been modified by alluvions. By judging by analogy the neighbouring points which one perceived from the cove and especially from the anchorage, particularly the two points which terminate the land we have before our eyes, we will conclude that the primitive rock and the alluvial terrain compose entirely this part of the great bay where we are entering.
Particular Remarks
"I saw black birds with large head and long white tail underneath, they had the beak curved in the manner of parrots, the same as the cry of these birds. I met a small grey bird the size of our French robins. Like the latter, it appeared to like the scrub, it was impossible for me to approach it closely. I killed a lizard of ordinary size and pleasantly striped on the back, it made its residence in a rock fissure.
"The country abounds in ants, they did not appear to be otherwise formed than those of Europe. One also finds there frequently masses of earth which must have been the work of some animals.
"Many sea birds of whitish colour flew by the hundreds above our boat and looked at us with attentive curiosity. The tail of these birds is forked and the two parts which compose it are noticeably separated.
"I remarked in several places burrows similar to those of our rabbits. Several appeared newly dug, I looked carefully to see if I could perceive some hole, but the loose soil offered none. The edges of the sea, however, offered us the imprints of a cloven hoof. One finds everywhere and in quantity droppings more or less fresh. They have the consistency and form of horse droppings. In their greatest dimension, they are scarcely an inch and even three-quarters of an inch.
"A species of tree which I can compare only to the vaquois of Île de France although its leaves are infinitely less wide, bears a resin of a red-yellow colour very pleasant. It spreads a bad odour in burning. This tree and several others of high timber and resinous seem to have experienced the action of fairly violent fire. Was it the natives or the heat of summer which kindled it?
"Finally, Commander, I saw nothing which could make me suspect that the region was inhabited by other living beings than animals.

1801-05-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and ESE. At midnight we were losing the land appreciably and the lead gave no bottom at 60 fathoms; we filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails. At 8 crowded sail to close the land, which bore from us S 5° E to N 72° E; Cape Leeuwin S 9° E. At 10.30 saw a thick smoke in the S 27° E. We ran along the coast until noon at 3 miles, when it appeared to take an ESE trend and form a gulf. At noon, being in 33° 22' 20" of latitude observed and in 112° 3' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 25' NW. We took the bearing of the southernmost land in sight S 38° W, and of the cape forming the SW entrance of the gulf S 85° E; the lead having given since 2 o'clock from 54 fathoms to 30, sand, rock and coral. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack; at 1 went onto the port tack and stood in for the land; the Naturaliste signalled us a danger in the N 22° 30' W. At 5 anchored in 23 fathoms, muddy sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 78° 45' W and a point S 14° E. At 7 the Naturaliste anchored near us. At 11 we dragged two thirds of a cable's length; the mizzen topsail, which had been kept on the mast, was furled and we brought up. The gulf in which we anchored was named Geographe Bay, and the SW point of the gulf, Cape Géographe.

1801-05-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At a quarter to one we took the bearing of a reef NW by W by compass, distant 2 leagues and a half. At the same moment Cape B S 25° W. At 7.30 we went about and stood to windward of Point O. At 4.30 sounded in 25 fathoms, sand and coral. At 4.30 went onto the starboard tack. At 5.15 the commander let us know by three lights that he was at anchor; he then bore from us S 14° E. We went about and stood on on the port tack. At six we went about again; at a quarter to seven, the commander bearing from us SW by W, we went onto the port tack and, steering for the Géographe, passed under her stern; he ordered us to anchor. At 7 [a figure struck out, illegible] we were anchored in 20 fathoms, muddy sand mixed with blackish gravel, and veered 100 fathoms of cable. Saw several fires on the coast. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 3° S; Point O WSW 2° 30' S; Point P south 7° 30' [one word illegible]. From 4 to 8 we struck the main topgallant mast and stopped the topsails with rope yarns. At 8 a.m. the Géographe had sent her boat ashore, and as ours was about to shove off the commander hailed us to send it only when his was back.
1801-05-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At five o'clock in the evening, being at anchor, the point forming the entrance of the bay of which we had become aware in the morning, remained at W ¼ NW at a distance of 4 leagues.
The lands most in view in the part of the South East to S ¼ SE 3° East
The cove across which we were at South 5° East
1801-05-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At 5 a.m. Citizen Freycinet left in the small boat to survey the country abreast of the anchorage; the gardener and the mineralogist went with him. The longboat and the large boat were put in the water. The first was sent off under the orders of Citizen Piquet to survey the coast and determine the position of Cape Géographe; the astronomer and the surveyor went in her. At noon Cape Géographe bore from us N 86° 15' W. The latitude observed 33° 28' 30" and the longitude by No. 27, 112° 1' 30". At 12.15 Citizen Freycinet was back; he had had great difficulty in landing and had not found a drop of drinkable water. In the evening the boats were hoisted in, and a light was kept at the masthead during the night to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea choppy and the wind in gusts. We sent a boat ashore which did not return until 5. At 7 p.m. the captain was back from his visit to the end of Point P, lying S 37° E. At 7 a.m. we received the order to get under way; at 9.30 we filled with the winds ESE, a fresh breeze. Bearings: Point N S 43° W; Point O S 2° W; Point P S 2° E; and the easternmost land east 2° S.
1801-06-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, we had knowledge of our boat, which for a reason I cannot fathom, remained out all night despite my express order to the officer commanding her to return before nightfall. As soon as she was at a small distance from us, we made ready to set sail and I informed the Naturaliste to do likewise, which she did.
When Citizen Picquet came aboard, he acquainted me with the cause of his delay, and as I have transcribed in full the written report he gave me of this expedition, which was not very successful, I shall say nothing of it here.
After setting sail, we ran on the north-north-east tack, the winds being from the east, a light breeze and the sea very fine.
When our anchor was weighed, we found on the flukes which had taken the bottom a species of black argillaceous mud mixed with much fine sand and especially with mica. Our cables suffered no sort of chafing and the sheathing itself was very intact, proof of the goodness of the bottom. However, it seemed to us that, although good, it must be somewhat hard. But once anchors have a little dragged, I think it is difficult for them to break free a second time. We made several balls from the matter drawn from the bottom, which we intended to dry to carry to France.
While we were under sail, running on the north-north-east tack, the lookouts, from the top of the masts, announced to us several times that they saw a chain of breakers extending far out to sea. I myself believed I could perceive them from below, and it seemed to me even that they were very low islands on which one could distinguish trees with the naked eye. Several of the officers went aloft to the topgallant yards at different times and all asserted that they were breakers on which the swell was even breaking with force. As for myself, I claimed to see trees there and, that, quite distinctly.
Be that as it may, we continued our course, the lead in hand, in order to see what it could be. I intended to send my boat, which was in tow, ahead to reconnoitre them, but I delayed until we were nearer.
In continuing our course, a succession of these same breakers appeared throughout the entire horizon, so that in order to reach the anchorage we had occupied two days before, it would have been necessary to pass over it.
This circumstance alone undeceived us and I saw clearly that what we perceived was nothing other than the effect of mirage and doubtless of the position of the sun and the tide. Nevertheless, there were many unbelievers aboard and several remained persuaded that it is a chain of breakers. But the truth is that they exist only in their imagination.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 33° 18' 41" and the longitude, deduced from the rate of our timekeepers, was for No. 35, 111° 56' 56" and for No. 27, 111° 56' 56".
After noon, we went about to run ashore, the wind was then very light and we were bearing only to the north. Supposing that the winds would not change, we had a fair tack towards the land. But they were so variable that we had little hope of advancing beyond our first anchorage.
In the afternoon, running towards the land and consequently to the south, the succession of breakers we had seen in the morning to the north appeared again, and the lookouts announced them in the same manner. The route seemed absolutely closed, and many people had difficulty conceiving how we had entered such a great bay without observing the dangers that surrounded it. But as I had observed the dangers as well as the others and the illusion had ceased for me, I continued my course without being disturbed and without paying attention to what was being said, so that at about four o'clock in the afternoon we passed under full sail through the middle of the reefs announced and on which we had twenty-eight fathoms of water, bottom of very fine grey sand. The winds then began to calm and we were still far from the coast which, in the place where we had our course, is found to be much lower than all those we had seen up to that moment.
At six o'clock, being in perfect calm and the current carrying us south-west, we anchored at about three leagues from the coast in twenty-three fathoms, bottom of very fine grey sand.
When we were at anchor, all our sails set, I had the drag cast and we took some curious objects which I preserve most carefully, so certain am I that they will be new and precious.
About an hour after we had cast anchor, the winds shifted to the south and a fine breeze sprang up. We much regretted that this breeze had not come earlier, but we consoled ourselves with the hope of having an interview on the morrow with the inhabitants of the country, for the fires we saw on the coast left us in no doubt that there were some very near the place of our anchorage.
At seven o'clock, the Naturaliste came to join us and anchored by our side. During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth, the weather was fine and the breeze moderate.

1801-06-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E, very variable. At 6.30 a.m. hoisted the topsails and hove short; hailed the Naturaliste to get under way at once. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet arrived; he had not been able to land at Cape Géographe nor anywhere near it; the currents had carried him offshore and he had beaten to windward all night without gaining. At 8 we got under way and lay to until 9, when we shaped our course N and N 22° E, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At noon in 33° 19' of latitude observed and in 112° 1' 30" of longitude by No. 27; Cape Géographe then bore from us S 45° W. At half past noon went close-hauled on the port tack, steering S 11° E. At 6 anchored in 23 fathoms, grey sand; saw a very large fire in the S 56° W which lasted 2 hours. The dredge brought up many objects of natural history. Est. lat. 33° 30' and est. long. 112° 13' at the anchorage.

1801-06-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. At 1.10 we went about, as did the commander, and we sounded in 25 fathoms, gravelly sand; at 4, 23 fathoms, the same bottom. Bearings taken at sunset: Point N W 21° 30' S; Point O W 44° 30' S; Point P south 5° 30' W; the end of the land to windward of us east 1° 30' N. At 6.30 saw a fire ashore which we took bearing SW by W. At 6.45 we were at anchor. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 18° 15' N; Point O W 28° 15' N; Point P W 61° 15' N; the easternmost end of the land E 18° 15' N. At 8.30 a.m. filled under all sail. At 10 a.m. went about and sounded in 18 fathoms, sand and shell; at 11, 20 fathoms; at 11.30 went onto the port tack, the same bottom and the same depth as at 11.

1801-06-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from ENE to south. At 6.45 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the longboat to survey part of the gulf. At 8 got under way and shaped our course SSW and SSE, close-hauled on the port tack. At 10 saw a very thick smoke in a wood near the shore. Our longboat made us signals of good anchorage near the land. At noon, being in 33° 33' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 55' of longitude by No. 27. Cape Géographe bore from us N 66° W and another point N 57° E. At noon went onto the starboard tack, heading north. At 2.30 went onto the port tack, heading S 22° 30' E. At 3.30 went onto the starboard tack, heading east. At 4 Citizen Bonnefoi arrived with the longboat. At 5, Cape Géographe N 82° W. At 8 anchored in 18 fathoms, coarse sand, in 33° 27' 40" of latitude by account and 112° 24' of longitude by account. The day's soundings were from 22 to 15 fathoms, grey muddy sand and red sand.

1801-06-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. We sounded every half hour in 18, 16, 16, 18, 19, 19 and 20 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. At 8.10 p.m. we let go the port anchor in 20 fathoms and veered 65 fathoms of cable; the lead brought up, alongside and all about, 20 fathoms of reddish sand mixed with gravel. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 4° 45' S, estimated distance 5 leagues; the end of the opposite land, which we shall call J, E 43° 30' N, estimated distance 10 leagues. At 9.15 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack.
1801-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, in the morning, we set sail with very fine weather and a breeze from the east variable towards the north. As I did not wish to leave this bay without knowing its depth, we tacked most of the day in order to try to gain ground to the east as much as possible.
We saw, from time to time, in the course of the morning, great clouds of smoke rising from the coast which was becoming much higher than that which we had coasted the day before. All the soundings taken in the morning constantly indicated a uniform and progressive depth, all times when we ran the tack towards land as well as that towards the open sea, and up to that moment, this coast is very sound and easy of access in all the extent we have traversed.
At noon, running the north tack, the latitude was observed as 33° 15' 55" and the longitude deduced from the timekeepers was for No. 27, 111° 56' 24" and 112° 6' 27" for No. 35. I cannot conceive how this easterly course, indicated by the timekeepers, was so inconsiderable in that the sight of land made us perfectly well aware that we had made progress on this wind more than they indicated. However, as the rate of our timekeepers had not varied and we could not doubt that the observations were not retarded, we multiplied them more than ever, and supposing that the evening observations gave more easterly course than those made in the morning, it appears that the mirage which had so often (made) us see breakers where there were none was the true cause of the error we perceived too clearly not to doubt it, and from that time we sought to prevent its effects.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, we went about towards the land and anchored after sunset in 12 fathoms of water at about two leagues from the coast.

1801-06-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to NE. At 8.15 a.m. got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, heading N 11° E. At noon in 33° 15' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 20" of longitude by No. 27, Cape Géographe bearing S 56° W and another point N 56° E (a). At 1 went onto the port tack, heading S 45° E. At 5.30 anchored in 12 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing S 79° W and point (a) N 45° E. Latitude observed 33° 27' 30", longitude by No. 27, 112° 7' 30" at the anchorage. The day's soundings were from 25 to 18 fathoms, coarse red sand. During the night several fires were seen in the bay.

1801-06-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. At 1.45 sounded in 23 fathoms, reddish sand mixed with glittering gravel; at 4, the same bottom and the same depth. Bearings taken at 4 on the 14th Prairial: Point N, forming the starboard end of the gulf, south 73° W; the port end of the same bight N 65° E, at 10 miles' distance; the end of the land stretching north, called the Paps, N 48° E. At 4.45 the lead brought up 16 fathoms, fine sand. At 6, 14 fathoms, and it kept shoaling from 13 to 14, the same bottom. At the same hour went onto the starboard tack, and shortly afterwards onto the port tack, standing in for the anchorage. At 6.30 we let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, fine sand mixed with broken shell; the soundings were the same all round the corvette from 6 until midnight. The currents setting us onto our cable, we laid the mizzen topsail aback. At midnight we saw a fire on the hill bearing from us S 6° W. Fine weather, smooth sea, and a light breeze.
1801-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the winds being very light from the east to east-north-east, I decided, at the request of Citizens Bernier and Boulanger, to remain at anchor to send them both ashore to take hour angles and (distances) of the sun from the moon. The weather was very fine and there was not a cloud. In consequence, I decided to accompany them and had the great boat prepared in order.
As on the previous day, my intention was not to remain in the anchorage, I had ordered that my boat, whose command I had entrusted to young Bougainville, depart at four o'clock in the morning and that she should proceed as far as she could to the north-east, visiting all the coves and creeks that might be found on her way.
At nine o'clock, we left the ship to go ashore. All the scientists, as one might imagine, wanted to be of the party, so that independently of the astronomer and the geographer, I had as travel companions Citizens Maugé, Riedelé, Depuche, and we set out. The small boat had departed at five o'clock in the morning and had taken with it Péron and Leschenault. They were to return at nine o'clock. But the midshipman who had command of her, having through a bad manoeuvre fallen far to leeward, had not yet landed when we left.
We found, going ashore, a strong current setting to the south, and it appeared to us then that there must be an ebb tide. We had to row and even with force for three long hours, and finally we arrived ashore in the middle of the cove which lay across from the ships. Until then, we had seen none of the natives of the country, but at the moment we landed, we saw one who was half in the water and engaged in fishing by spearing the fish with thrusts of his spear. He appeared, at first, to pay little attention to us and to occupy himself solely with his fishing. But when we had landed, at about a musket shot's distance from him, he came out of the water and gained, without too much hurrying, a sand dune which lay before him. I remarked only that despite his gait being assured, he looked often towards us, doubtless to see if we were following him.
We went, indeed, after him and approached him fairly near on the eminence where he had stopped. Citizen Depuche, who was ahead of all, showed him some glass-bead necklaces which I had provided. But as he kept advancing, he then began to cry out with terrible force, making signs for us to turn back, and as he directed them all towards the ships, we had no doubt as to what he meant to say. Nevertheless, as we kept advancing, he put himself into all sorts of attitudes, continuing his howls, and finally he picked up three sorts of lances or spears and went off precipitately without having made any offensive gesture towards us.
This man was of very black colour and naked from head to foot except for a skin or tree bark which covered his back. To judge by the colour of his beard, which was very long and grey, he must be a man far advanced in age. Although he had taken to flight, we followed him, but when we were at the top of the dune where he had first retired, he had already gained much ground ahead of us and was at the extremity of a plain which ended at the edge of a wood. Independently of the three spears he carried, he had in his hand a firebrand, which leads me to believe that as soon as they catch anything while fishing or otherwise, they cook it and eat it at once.
Having no longer hope of being able to catch up with him at the great distance at which he already was from us, I gave up the pursuit. But Citizen Depuche wanted to go further, accompanied by two men of the boat. He followed the route he had taken for about half a league and returned without having seen him again.
From the moment we abandoned the pursuit of this man whom we had no hope of catching up with, we occupied ourselves in examining the places where we were and the astronomer and geographer began their observations.
All the coast, as far as the eye could extend, is bordered by sand dunes, among which there are some which, not being covered with scrub, offer those great white patches one perceives at sea when prolonging the coast at a certain distance. All end at the sea by a fairly steep slope. But the side facing the land is much less rugged and covered everywhere with scrub and small trees of different species. Then one finds a plain of about a quarter of a league in extent which ends at the edge of a vast forest which offers a very pleasant prospect. Our gardener found its soil, although sandy, of very good quality and even very suitable for cultivation. In crossing the plain of which I have just spoken and in the extent of which there are, scattered here and there, several large full-grown trees which by their leaves resemble quite pine trees. We met several well-trodden paths and we followed them. They led us to large circular encampments where fires had very recently been made, which proved that the natives stop there sometimes, no doubt, to regale themselves with their fishing or hunting.
The traces of fire are so multiplied everywhere and the paths so well beaten that it appeared to me that this place is much frequented. The great woods which form the beginning of the (in the margin: forest appeared to us to be of the species (no name) but none of those in view were in flower. In crossing the plain, we met a fairly large quantity of quails and we (did not) have the skill to kill a single one. Our gardener made an ample collection of plants, and Maugé and I killed different species of very curious birds.
We believed we recognized, in this excursion, the traces of several quadrupeds without quite knowing what they could be. We collected their droppings which appeared to me to approach much those of the dog, and some indications recognized in the sand lead me to believe that the natives make use of them, for we saw very distinctly on the beach the tracks of men and of an animal which followed him and which we believe to be a dog.
After a walk of about three hours, we returned to our boat, and the helmsman as well as those who had remained to guard it told us that six savages had appeared at the point, and that after watching them for about a quarter of an hour, they had disappeared into the dunes and they had lost sight of them.
I noticed on the inner slope of the dune facing the sea three different marks of seaweed and broken shells which made me judge the height to which the sea must rise in different circumstances. As we were then at ebb tide, the first layer of seaweed still fresh clearly showed that the sea had not risen higher, and it was the time of the neap tides. A second layer of seaweed and broken shells like the first appeared six feet distant, and as the seaweed was dry, I think it indicated up to where the sea reaches in the great tides of the new and full moons. The third layer, finally, much higher and almost at the foot of the dunes, appeared to me the place where the sea rises in gales of wind when they pass from the north to the south-west by the west.
All the dunes appeared to me to be the work of the sea which carries the sand, and of the wind which accumulates it and carries it to a certain distance as the ages pass. The flat ground one encounters after passing the dunes did not appear to me any higher than the surface of the sea. The tide, according to my reckoning, must rise four feet at neap tide, and eight or nine in the great tides, and at least fifteen in gales of wind. One finds on the shore fragments of beautiful shells which we much regretted not having entire.
While we were travelling somewhat in the interior of the country, I had planted in the plain we were crossing, which is well sheltered from sea winds, corn, pips of pear, apple, peach, apricot trees and various other kinds of vegetables. If all these things turn out well, it will be, for the future, an increase of subsistence for the individuals who are found in this part of New Holland, whose existence appeared to me very miserable.
Among the plants we found, two are found in the environs of Paris, one a species of wild sorrel and (no name).
We brought back aboard some celery that we found very good in soup, as well as another plant called (no name).
Before embarking, persuaded that the natives would not fail to come and see what we had done at the place of our landing, I had a stick planted in the ground to which I attached an empty bottle, a bead necklace, some biscuit, a nail and some other trifles. May these objects not occasion disputes amongst them, and may he who finds them first remain their owner.
At six o'clock, the boat was back aboard, and I had it embarked at once in order to set sail the next day at daybreak.
At about seven-thirty, while we were at dinner, M. Hamelin came aboard with several of his officers who had gone ashore. One of them, M. Hérisson, informed me that having landed to the south of the ships, at about three leagues to leeward, he had penetrated inland and that chance had led him to the banks of a great river, or at any rate a lake, which he had followed for more than two leagues without seeing the end. He had met on (the) lake a great quantity of birds of different species unknown to him, but he could not kill any, being no hunter. M. Hérisson could not ascertain whether this lake or river, for he believes it is one, opens to the sea, in that he was too far from his boat to search for it, but at any rate, he assures us that it penetrates far into the interior of the country.
The report of M. Hérisson seemed to me too interesting not to have more certain information on the nature and usefulness of this lake or river if it is one, not to order a new visit, and although he told me the water was brackish and that in the vicinity he had found a kind of well dug by the natives where the water was very good. I decided to remain at anchor and ordered M. Hamelin to send, during the night, the same officer, and that I would also send my boat, whose command I gave to M. Le Bas. M. Hamelin having asked me to go himself to make this search, I granted him permission.
During the night of the 15th to the 16th, the weather was very fine and there was a light wind from the east to the north-east.
Report of Citizen Bougainville, Midshipman, commanding the Boat.
"On leaving here, I directed my course, according to your orders, to the NE ¼ N, as soon as I was at two cables' lengths from the ships. Then I began to sound, and from that moment until 7 hours 10 minutes, when I was already about six miles from the Géographe, the sounding constantly gave me 15, 14 & 13 fathoms, sometimes bottom of white sand, sometimes bottom of small red and grey gravels. At seven-thirty, I changed course and set my course for the land. The northernmost point in view remained at NE 5° east. The one most to the east and closest to me, to S. SW. I continued this tack until about a mile from the coast, and the depth decreased successively from 15 fathoms to 11 f. ½, always bottom of white or grey sand. At eight forty-five minutes, I again set course for the offing, and the depth increased gradually in the same proportion that it had followed while decreasing during the previous tack.
"From that hour until one forty-five minutes, I continued to tack back and forth in the hope of reaching the point which remained in the east to me and which, from the bearing of the lands, I believe to form the northernmost point of the great bay. One then discovers another bay much less considerable, but which appeared to me to extend far into the lands, and in the same manner as if the waters of a great river came to discharge into it.
"During this time I constantly continued to sound and the soundings gave me, as before, 14, 13, 12, 10 & 8 fathoms of water so long as I was at a certain distance from the land. But at about three cables' lengths from the shore, the nature of the bottom much varied. Here are the principal changes it underwent: 6, 5, 4, & 3, sometimes bottom of red and grey sand, sometimes bottom of rock and coral and broken shells.
"At 11 hours and a half, I perceived in the SW, at two miles distance, very thick smoke. The ships remained to me at the west and the point of land closest to me, to N. NE 5° E.
"The land then had the appearance of an island, one point of which formed an extremity and the point from which smoke came the south extremity. All the rest of the bay was below my horizon. One could perceive only near the ships, of which my reckoning placed me five leagues, a small portion of coast remaining in the W ¼ SW.
"At a quarter past noon, I thought I noticed that the sea was rising, and then the current set in the NE ¼N.
"At two o'clock, despairing of being able to double the eastern point before nightfall, although I was not then more than a mile and a half distant, I bore away to keep along the coast and approach the ships. By the reckoning I made of my wake, I think that this point is distant from the ships five and a half leagues. In bearing on it as well as the ships, I found it remained in the NE ¼ E.
"I continued to keep along the coast at about two cables' lengths from the shore, sounding every 10 minutes, and always found five and four fathoms, bottom of grey sand mixed with coral and sometimes small rocks, which was moreover easy to see from the transparency of the water.
"All this part of the coast offers easy landing, it is bordered by sand dunes not very high and covered with a species of very dry heather. One could perceive above them the tops of the great trees which are in the rear. If I except a black bird whose cry is rather similar to the cawing of the raven and several others of the gannet species, I saw nothing along the shore. Only I distinguished a great quantity of burrows of an animal smaller than the rabbit. I also believed I noticed, from the layers of seaweed that the sea leaves as it recedes, that it must rise there some ten feet. Towards three o'clock, we were obliged to move a little further from the shore because of a bank covered with rocks in several places and on which the sea was breaking with considerable force. This bank may be (a mile in width) by (a mile in length) (in the margin: to correct: this breaker is 2 miles long and 80 metres or half a cable's length wide) and is situated at three cables' lengths from the shore. When I recognized it, I was near four leagues from the ships, which remained to me in the W. NW, I had the easternmost point to the NE and the southernmost point to the SW.
"At 3 o'clock and a half, the winds refusing greatly, I feared being driven too far to leeward and manoeuvred to reach the ships.
"From the moment I left the land until I arrived aboard, I did not cease sounding, and the sounding gave me successively 5, 5 ½, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 11 ½, 12, 12 and a half fathoms, bottom of grey sand mixed with small red gravel.
Position at the anchorage, latitude observed at noon: 33° 26' 49" South
Longitude of the timekeepers 112° 21' 15, average of 4 sets of observations taken before and after noon. 112° 29' 4" from distances taken ashore. Latitude of the place of observation, 33° 30' 0"
1801-06-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from E. At 4 a.m. Citizen Bougainville left in the longboat to sound along the coast, and I in the small boat to have grass cut for our livestock; the zoologist and the botanist came with me. At 8.30 the commander and all the scientists went ashore in the large boat. At 4 p.m. I came aboard, Citizen Bougainville at 5.30 and the commander at 6. The latter had seen Aboriginal people, who would not communicate; I had seen no inhabitants but had seen their tracks, and those of a dog's paws. No one had found drinkable water.

1801-06-05.journal_anonyme: At 6 a.m. we sent off two boats to go ashore, one under the orders of Citizen Heirisson and the other under those of Citizen Freycinet. They found bare footprints, which makes us believe there are Aboriginal people here; they also found kangaroo tracks and celery like that of France. The weather fine, the sea smooth and the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. On the 16th at 4 a.m. our two boats were sent off in company with the longboat, which by the commander's order took four days' provisions.
1801-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth (5 June 1801), at three o'clock in the morning, I sent my boat, well armed and furnished with everything necessary, under the command of Citizen Ste Croix, my flag captain. M. Hamelin himself departed in his boat, accompanied by M. Hérisson, to visit the lake or river of which he had spoken the day before, in order to have more exact knowledge of the places he had designated for us. I had asked this officer to make me an exact and very detailed report of what he had seen and noticed the day before. I expected to receive it before his departure, and as he had not yet sent it to me, I think he did not have time to do it.
Be that as it may, my boat and two boats of the Naturaliste departed at the appointed hour. The winds were then from the north-east, a fine breeze. And as they were to proceed to the south of our anchorage, they must have reached the designated place early.
In the morning, the breeze was strong from N. NE and the sea became heavy, which left me not without anxiety for the fate of my boats, in that the swell must break on the coast. All the scientists who were aboard, with the exception of the astronomer, the geographer and Maugé who all had much work each in their own line, embarked in the boat, and I gave as assistant to M. Le Bas Citizen Ronsard, acting as ensign aboard.
I awaited their return with all the more impatience in that the weather being unsuitable for keeping boats on the coast, I feared that their eagerness to discover the place they were going to visit might lead them to commit some imprudence. However, I did not fail before their departure to recommend to all of them everything that the most strict precaution should make them consider.
At noon, we observed aboard 33° 26' 43" of south latitude, which differed by only six seconds from the latitude observed the day before. Thus, one can conclude from this that the latitude of our anchorage is sufficiently well determined. The longitude taken the day before ashore from distances of the sun from the moon was 112° 29' 4", and that of the timekeepers being 112° 8' 29", there was a difference to the east of 20' 35" with the timekeepers.
Ashore in the morning and evening, hour angles were taken whose result was found for the morning to be 112° 16' 9" and for the evening 112° 9' 20" (in the margin: Bernier). This difference between the two observations served to demonstrate that the effects of mirages had occasioned those we had encountered in the preceding days, and that the altitudes observed must have been affected in the same manner.
In the afternoon, the breeze calmed a little and the winds shifted to the north. The agitation of the sea was considerable and the ship pitched heavily, which did not diminish my anxieties about the situation in which the boats I had sent ashore might be, and whose return I awaited with the greatest impatience. A little before sunset, having become aware of two of our boats keeping along the coast to gain the windward, I judged they were returning aboard, but I had no knowledge of my boat, easy to distinguish by her sail plan. A fire was kept going all night at the head of the mizzen mast to indicate the ships' position to the boats. But it was labour in vain, nothing arrived. However, at about two o'clock in the night, the Naturaliste having extinguished her fire, we judged that hers had returned.
During the night, the sea remained rough and the winds were from north to north-north-east moderate, although good gusts passed from time to time.
Anchorage. Latitude observed at noon 33° 26' 38" South.
Longitude of the timekeepers.
Note.
The boat departed at four o'clock in the morning under the command of Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas to ascertain the location of the mouth of a river which was believed to have been discovered to the S. SE of our anchorage. All the naturalists accompanied her as well as Citizen Ronsard acting as ensign. This vessel was furnished with everything necessary for its safety and that of the individuals who were aboard. It also had provisions for three days, although it was to return the same day!
1801-06-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 3 a.m. the longboat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Le Bas; with several of the scientists he was to survey the country and try to communicate with the Aboriginal people. Struck the topgallant masts. During the night kept a light at the gaff to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-06.journal_anonyme: The winds having fallen light, we put the dinghy in the water to send the commander a letter the captain had left on board. In the afternoon the wind blew lightly from the east, the sea still with a heavy swell. At 7 p.m. the large boat was back; Citizen Saint-Cricq had seen many Aboriginal people who took flight at his approach. The day before, the commander had seen six Aboriginal men, five of whom fled at his approach; the sixth, an older man, came towards the commander with threatening gestures, pointing to his ship and giving him to understand that he was not looking for him and that he should withdraw from this land, which belonged to him. The commander, seeing that he could learn nothing from this man, took the opposite direction and went off into the woods with all those accompanying him.
1801-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth (6 June 1801), in the morning, we had no knowledge of our boats, however we noticed that one of the Naturaliste's boats had returned aboard that ship during the night. The wind being then too strong and the sea too heavy to send to find out what news it might bring, we had to wait for a more favourable moment.
In the morning, although the sky was very fine, the breeze from north-north-east to north became so strong that I found myself, at each gust, obliged to set sail. But as the bottom seemed very good since we were not dragging on our anchor despite my having only seventy fathoms of cable out, I continued to keep the position I had. Only I had the topgallant masts struck down. It was then impossible for our boats to return, but I was no less dissatisfied that they had not returned aboard the day before, having had the time necessary to clear up the doubt of the existence or not of a river flowing to the sea in our vicinity.
The breeze of yesterday having been less strong, we had observed that about two o'clock it had begun to calm, and I hoped the same would happen today, for if it continued until evening, I presume the sea would be too heavy to be able to hold to the anchor.
At noon, the latitude was again observed as 33° 26' 28" and the longitude of the timekeepers was for No. 27 (no figures) and that for No. 35 (no figures) from the morning observation, while that of the evening was (no figures) from the first and (no figures) from the second. The difference which the morning observations and those of the evening had been producing for some time was a problem difficult enough to solve. However, we remained convinced that it could, and even must, be caused by the state of the atmosphere, presumably more laden with vapour before the sun had passed the meridian than when it had passed.
In the evening, the breeze calmed as I had expected, and the sea became fine. I had the imperative signal hoisted to the boats to return aboard, and accompanied it with a cannon shot which was renewed every two hours. However, at sunset I had no knowledge that they were on their way to return aboard, although the horizon was very clear and I could perfectly distinguish the edges of the coast to six leagues distance, from south-west to north-east.
About four o'clock in the afternoon, the boat of the Naturaliste which had returned aboard the previous night, went to the Géographe, and the mineralogist who was in her and who had gone ashore the day before, reported to me that what one had taken for a river was nothing but a small lagoon into which the sea water entered. He assured me he had been to the mouth which is barred by means of sorts of wooden stakes which the natives of the country plant at its opening to catch the fish which the incoming tide brings into it. He had judged this place of so little consequence that he had not even wanted to wait for the return of his travel companions. He added to me that several of those who were ashore had communicated with the natives of the country, especially with a woman who was pregnant and about forty years old. From his report, it appears that our men caused her no fright and that she waited for them patiently in the place where she had stopped. It was not the same with a man who accompanied her and who took to flight. Different gifts were made to this woman which appeared very agreeable to her, and it was noticed that she valued a small mirror more than all the other things which were offered to her.
From the report which the mineralogist of the Naturaliste had just made to me, I had difficulty conceiving what motive could have caused the delay of my boat. The only reason which seemed plausible to me was to believe that M. Ste Croix Le Bas, to whose command I had entrusted her, had been seduced by the fine talk of the naturalists who were with him, and that, regardless of the precarious situation in which the ship found herself, he had been able, without foreseeing the consequences, to be influenced and grant them more time than he should. From this conviction, I resolved firmly that such a thing should not happen again, and whether these gentlemen be satisfied or not, little I care, but they shall not go ashore again unless the ship runs no risk of breaking free and they of being (stranded) on a desert and unknown coast.
After sunset, having perceived nothing at the horizon that announced their return, I ordered fires to be lit at all the masts and to continue firing the cannon every two hours. My small distance from the land leads me to believe they will become aware of this order to return aboard at once. And if he who commands the boat has judged from the sunset what the weather should be tomorrow, I do not doubt that all will be aboard by ten o'clock at the latest.
Dampier, in his Voyage to New Holland, observes that when the sun rises and sets with very bright red, the next day the breeze is ordinarily very strong. From nine o'clock in the morning until three o'clock in the afternoon, &c. Although we are not at the same latitude as Dampier was when he made this observation, his remark is no less true, and I have found until this moment that all times when the sun rose or set as he describes it, the winds were very strong the next day.
At nine-thirty in the night, although the wind had much calmed, M. Hamelin arrived aboard. He had been at sea in his small boat with four men for about twenty-two hours. During the height of the wind which was from eight o'clock in the morning until four o'clock in the afternoon, he had spent all (that) time at anchor on his grappling anchor at the risk of being a thousand times engulfed. The swell was breaking with such force that he could do nothing but constantly empty the water that entered. He informed me that my boat was stranded on the sand without knowing precisely how this accident had happened. This news was a thunderbolt to me, given the situation of those who had embarked in her. Before leaving his travel companions, M. Hamelin gave them all the arms and ammunition he had, so that they would be better able to defend themselves. They still had two days' provisions. We agreed together that, from four o'clock in the morning, his great boat and mine would leave to bring, to the place he indicated for me, what might be necessary to float the boat again & to bring back at least those who were ashore if we had to abandon her. Since ten o'clock, the winds had shifted to the east and the sky was fairly fine, but in the middle of the night, they shifted to the south-west and north and it began to blow a strong breeze again. It would be difficult to convey all the suffering I endured seeing that tomorrow I would be unable to give any help to the people in my boat and perhaps already at the mercy of the natives of the country who, seeing their distress, seemed to me should become enterprising.
Bearings of the land.
At four o'clock the point forming the entrance of the bay to the south to west 6 south
Another point the closest to us to north 56° east
The land most to the north in view to north 30° east
Bearings of the anchorage.
The westernmost point to W ¼ SW
The northernmost point to N 45° east
