Note.
The boat did not return to the ship. But at sunset, I perceived her under sail as well as the great boat of the Naturaliste. I know not what either of them was doing or what they were seeking, but I was inclined to believe they were tacking to reach the ship during the night.
1801-06-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE, a high sea. At 9 a.m. struck the topgallant masts. At 2 p.m. the wind fell. At 3 fired a gun and made the signal to recall the longboat. At 4.30 and at 6 fired a gun and showed a light at the gaff. At 7.45 Captain Hamelin came to tell the commander that our longboat had been cast on the shore, but that no one was lost. He himself, in his boat, had been obliged to pass the previous night at anchor offshore and had only reached his ship at nightfall.

1801-06-07.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from the east. At 7 p.m. the captain's boat was back and brought us the unhappy news that the Géographe's longboat was cast away on the coast. The captain wrote at once to the commander, who was in mortal anxiety; a boat was sent off with the letter. The commander, judging that the captain had not given him enough detail, decided to send for him aboard; the captain embarked at once in his boat and returned shortly afterwards.
1801-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
According to the weather during the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth, I changed my resolution as to how I should render assistance to our people who were ashore, and after having embarked in my great boat the master carpenter and six good rowers, I sent it at once to M. Hamelin's ship, to which I addressed the following letter:
The Commander of the Expedition &c. to Captain Hamelin
"At four o'clock in the morning, my boat shall be alongside your ship, and yours, which I invite you to have ready at the same hour, if the wind is manageable and moderate, will indicate to it the place where it should land.
"At daybreak, you will yourself set sail and go seek an anchorage abreast of the place where you know our people to be, in order to ensure their return. You will approach as close to land as possible without, however, compromising the safety of your ship. Observe only whether the tack you hold, should it put you to leeward of the anchorage you must take, not to go too far from it. By this precaution, it will always be easy for our boats to rejoin you.
"As soon as you are in position, I shall follow you."
Having then given to Citizen Bonnefoy acting as ensign, orders relating to the command of my boat and the course it should take, I had it brought alongside the Naturaliste to depart together with that ship's boat, and I wrote to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas, to whose command I had entrusted my boat two days before, the following letter:
The Commander of the Expedition to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas. 11 o'clock in the evening on the 17th prairial.
"I have just, citizen, been informed by the arrival of M. Hamelin of the lamentable accident experienced by the boat whose command I had entrusted to you. It seems to me that you had every means to prevent or avoid it if prudence and precaution had directed your conduct before and after landing.
"Be that as it may, as the moment is not suitable for making you the reproaches you seem to merit, I hope at least that you will not compromise the new assistance you are about to receive from the two ships, and that you will watch with more active precaution for the safety of the boats that will come to seek you as well as all those who accompanied you. I order you, if there is no means of saving my boat without running new risks, to abandon her and to distribute all those ashore between the boat of the Naturaliste and mine, and to reach as soon as possible the ship which will be (easiest) for you to join regarding your position.
"You will receive provisions and war munitions. I wish the former to arrive in time for you, and that you not find yourself in need of using the latter. Moreover, our boats are furnished with everything that may be necessary to float the boat again if possible, which nevertheless I am far from believing, since the critical position in which you find yourself has not enabled you to find the resources you needed. Greetings. N. B.
The boat, as I have said above, reached the Naturaliste at four o'clock in the morning, but the wind increased so greatly and the sea became so rough that it did not judge it proper to send them out.
Owing to this setback, I signalled at once to Captain Hamelin to execute the order I had given him. He replied that he would do so. At seven o'clock, that ship still not being under sail, I renewed to that ship the signal of execution; it then replied that it was impossible at that moment because the turnbuckle it had employed and then a tackle in three had broken.
This setback having decided me to set sail myself to keep along the entire coast, not knowing the place where I should land, I had a reef taken in each topsail, that is to say a second one, for there was already one. And at nine o'clock, I was under sail. The winds being then from north to N. NE, strong breeze, I had only my topsails serve, and having taken starboard tack, I approached the coast at three miles distance and kept along it, observing with the greatest attention if I perceived any signals or anyone walking on the shore. At eleven o'clock, being two leagues from the point I had left, I found a small sandbank on which the sea rose a little. I kept it at six fathoms distance at a mile off, it may be about that length, and seemed to run N. NE and S. SW. After passing it, I continued my course, constantly keeping the lead in hand and six fathoms of bottom, sometimes very fine sand, sometimes very coarse sand. I could also distinctly see, as if I had been ashore, all the objects that were on the sand. But I saw no one who could make me suspect that our people were in the vicinity. At eleven-thirty, several very thick smokes rose from behind the dunes which seemed to announce that there was someone there. I did not know quite which one to steer for, because several were already downwind of me. Nevertheless, I continued my course and headed for one that seemed to come directly from the shore. At noon, I had covered three leagues, I then became aware of two people on the shore, but as they withdrew at once into the dunes, I judged them to be natives of the country. However, it had seemed to me from the manner in which they moved that they were our people. A short time after, keeping along the coast, in six and seven fathoms, I saw four or five other people walking along the shore, who, from time to time, bent down to pick up something. The smoke I had headed for having dispersed, I again imagined it must be natives who did not wish to make their position known, and the men I had seen similarly made for the dunes and disappeared.
My anxieties about the fate of those ashore increasing more and more, I resolved to anchor in that same place to send it to be visited. Although it seemed to me that those I was seeking were not there, since instead of waiting for us and making some signals of recognition, they fled at our approach and did not reappear.
Having at noon dropped an anchor in seven fathoms of water, bottom of sand, I at once sent my great boat, whose management I entrusted to Citizen Bonnefoy with a strict order not to land if the landing was difficult, as it seemed it would be, indeed, from the weather that was prevailing. He had orders, after having examined that place, if he saw no debris of our boat, to keep along the coast until sunset and to return at once aboard. It seemed quite natural to think that if our gentlemen were in the vicinity, they would come, if not in their entirety to the boat, at least in part, and that finally they would show themselves.
My boat having departed, I kept my eyes constantly on the shore to see if I would perceive anyone, and I had the bitter pain, surely, of seeing it drop anchor without anyone appearing. Thinking then that it had surely become aware of my boat or some of its debris, I could not hold back my tears and retired to my cabin to reflect on the steps I should take further. It seemed to me then undoubitable that the natives of the country, having perceived the distress in which those ashore found themselves, had attacked them and made themselves masters of them. One will conceive better than I can describe all (that) is painful about the mere idea with which I was occupied, and so many circumstances combined served to confirm it. For I could not conceive that we had not been made any signals and that no one had shown themselves on the shore. Abandoned to these sad reflections and my heart filled with sorrow and sadness, I knew not what course to take, when, at about three-thirty, I was told that several people were seen on the edges of the shore who seemed to be conversing with the men of the boat. It was even added that several were believed to be recognized and that there was no doubt that this was part of those we were seeking. Having myself at once looked towards the shore, I saw, as did the others, several people who seemed to be conver(sing) with the men of the boat. But I was so convinced that it could not be those ashore, since they had made us no signals to make themselves known, that I persuaded myself it was natives trying to prevent our people from landing and that, no doubt, they were engaged in breaking up our boat, which several people believed they had recognized.
From that moment, I observed until nightfall and with the most scrupulous attention all the movements of my boat and of those ashore. It seemed to me that I was being shown a place easy for landing and that even it was going there. At four o'clock, I believed I saw it sending ashore a rope which I had provided, and various objects suitable for being able to float the boat again if it were capable. All these manoeuvres tranquillized me a little, and then I attributed to the carelessness and apathy of all those ashore the conduct they had held in not making themselves known. Nevertheless, I was far from being without anxiety still, and I awaited nightfall with the greatest impatience because I had agreed with the officer commanding the boat that he would fire one or two rockets to let me know he had met our people. At six o'clock, although it was very dark, no rocket had yet been fired. For fear it was an oversight on the part of the officer, I then burned several flares and finally at seven-thirty a rocket was fired in reply, which calmed my anxieties and drew me from the painful existence in which I had lived for three whole days without being able to find, even in moments of sleep, the rest which was so necessary for me.
At nine o'clock in the evening, my boat being back aboard, brought only Citizen Péron, who was more dead than alive, having been obliged to go into the water to embark, the boat being unable to reach the beach. Citizen Le Bas would not allow the other naturalists to embark on the pretext that he needed them to help him float the boat again, but I think it was rather so as to be in greater numbers and to impress the natives of the country more, should they become enterprising.
From the report of Citizen Bonnefoy who commanded my boat, he had arrived ashore and recognized the boat stranded in the sand before having perceived anyone. No doubt all were on the reverse of the dunes to be more sheltered from the wind. It appears that it will be very difficult to save the boat, which is so stranded in the sand that the sea covers it entirely. I count on making one last effort tomorrow and abandoning her if I cannot get her off.
About three o'clock in the afternoon, the Naturaliste set sail and came to anchor near us at a small distance. M. Hamelin reported to me that after making every effort in the morning to set sail, he had not been able to, and that in the afternoon, making fresh efforts, he had only been able to weigh his anchor because the flukes had separated from the stock and remained on the bottom, as did his cable and buoy. He plans to send for them tomorrow if the weather permits.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the weather was fairly fine, although in the evening it had an ill appearance. The winds were from east to east-north-east moderate, but the swell was so strong and so high that the ship rolled at anchor as if in a rough sea in calm.
Change of anchorage. Latitude observed south (no figures) Longitude of the timekeepers (no figures).
1801-06-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 4.15 the large boat was sent aboard the Naturaliste. At 7.30 took the second reef in the topsails, which were stopped with rope yarns, and signalled the Naturaliste to carry out the order received; she asked leave to slip her cable. We hailed her to send our boat back; an officer came to explain to the commander what prevented him from getting under way: in heaving round, his stoppers had parted several times and he had a man hurt. At 8.30 got under way; at 9 shaped our course and steered successively S 78° 45' E, S 67° 30' E, S 45° E, S 22° 30' E and south, the lead giving 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 and 8 fathoms, fine sand. At 11 several people were seen on the shore. At 11.30 we anchored in 8 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 85° W and another point N 34° E. Latitude observed 33° 33' 0", longitude by No. 27, 112° 13' 50" at the anchorage. At noon the wind and sea fell; the large boat was sent off with a hawser, provisions and stores for the longboat's crew. Fired two guns. At 3.30 the Naturaliste got under way and came and anchored near us. Captain Hamelin came aboard and informed the commander that after much effort to weigh his anchor it had come up with a fluke broken. At nightfall showed a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour. At 8 the large boat came back and brought Citizen Péron, one of the shipwrecked naturalists. During the night the longboat's crew made a fire on the shore.

1801-06-08.journal_anonyme: Blowing hard from NE, a very high sea. The Géographe's boat came aboard at 4 a.m. with orders to man our large boat and put into it all the gear needed to repair the stranded longboat; the bad weather prevented the two boats from shoving off. At 7 o'clock the commander gave written orders to get under way and anchor within the bay. We at once hove round at the capstan, but the heavy sea tried us greatly and the cable came in only with difficulty; at half past eight all the stoppers parted and the little cable we had got in ran out again, wounding one of our quartermasters severely. At 9 the Géographe was under sail and recalled her boat; one of our officers went aboard her for orders. At 2 p.m. we rigged a voyol to heave with more power at the capstan. At 3 we found the flukes had parted from the shank; we finished getting in the rest of the cable and catted the stump of the anchor. At 3.30 we shaped our course NW by N and anchored at 5 in 5 fathoms of water, fine sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable, the commander bearing from us SSE. The captain went aboard the Géographe. At 5.30 saw two fires in the SW. A fresh breeze from ENE. On the 19th at 4 a.m. our large boat left with the commander's boat to carry help to the stranded longboat.
1801-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth (8 June 1801), in the morning, the weather being fairly fine although the sea was still rough and swell. Despite the east-north-east winds which had resumed during the night, and north-east which was then prevailing, I had my boat depart, to whose command I gave Bougainville with a strict order not to risk her and to compromise her in the slightest matter. I also ordered the Naturaliste to send hers out with eight men. And my master carpenter was to take an exact knowledge of the boat and its position in order to decide whether we should persist in saving her.
By the same occasion, I wrote to M. Ste Croix Le Bas the following letter:
"The Commander of the Expedition &c. to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas,
"By the letter I addressed to you yesterday, and which I had little hope of getting to you, not knowing where to find you, I ordered you to return aboard or at least to have a part of those with you return there, and who surely are useless to you. I hold you personally responsible for this disobedience which causes me to prolong my stay at an insecure anchorage which I would not keep if I were less interested in your personal safety as well as that of all those with you.
"You should have judged from the appearance of the weather that it is probable it will not be long before becoming bad, and the barometer announces it only too well, since it fell six lines in yesterday's day.
"I send you for the last time my boat and that of the Naturaliste to transport all of you aboard. I am pleased to believe that you will no longer oppose the embarkation of anyone. The safety of the ships and of those aboard must not be preferred to the very uncertain saving of a boat which will be out of service for a long time, according to the reports that have been made to me of its present situation. Moreover, I am sending you the master carpenter who will judge better than anyone else.
"Greetings. N. B".
From the moment of the departure of my boat until its return aboard, I was in continual anxieties for fear it might suffer some damage which would prevent it from returning. I could see by means of my spyglass how considerable the undertow was ashore, and the people I was waiting for could not embark without putting themselves in the water up to the hips. Finally, at about noon, I saw that of the Naturaliste set sail and return. It arrived aboard about two o'clock with all the naturalists. All were soaked to the skin and numb with cold.
The officer commanding it announced to me that the boat was so stranded in the sand, and the sea so heavy on the shore that it was absolutely necessary, at least for the moment, to renounce trying to save her. As soon as I was informed of the accident which had befallen her and the manner in which the sea had cast her on the shore, I had considered her entirely lost, but as MM. Le Bas and Ronsard, perhaps to excuse their negligence, persisted in making me told that they would save her if I sent them everything they asked for, I sent them against my will in men and apparatus everything that was demanded of me.
During the evening, the ship was so much tossed about at the anchorage that I feared every moment some damage to my masting, although the topgallant masts were struck down. I fired the cannon every hour to make my boat and that of the Naturaliste return as quickly as possible, the latter of which I had sent out again, fearing mine could not hold all those ashore.
Finally, at about four o'clock, it arrived aboard with all my people, but to embark them all it had to abandon all other effects. So that, independently of my boat completely armed and rigged, I lost still all the assistance which had been asked of me in the hope of floating her again.
Almost all the objects which the naturalists had collected and assembled during their stay ashore suffered the same fate, and in this part Riedelé was treated more roughly than the others, for, independently of the boxes he had left ashore, the sea, as it rushed over the boat of the Naturaliste, had passed over his head and removed what he had enclosed of the most precious in a tin box.
As soon as M. Ste Croix Le Bas came aboard, he was not slow in coming to apologize for the event which had befallen him, persisting always in saying that it was no one's fault and that if the sea had not been so bad, he would have saved the boat. I listened to his apologies without reply, the situation in which he was being not suitable for making him the reproaches he deserves.
As soon as the boat was empty, I had it hoisted aboard, but all my anxieties were not yet at an end, since the Naturaliste still had two boats ashore, its great boat which I had had sent out so mine would be less burdened, and its small one which I had seen go ashore in the morning with one of its officers, no doubt to amuse themselves, since it made landing far from the place where our people were. At nightfall, both were still ashore and all the cannon shots fired to make them return aboard could not quicken their return.
At sunset, the weather had the most ominous appearance. Large black and hideous clouds surrounded our entire horizon from north to west, and there was no doubt that winds were coming from that quarter during the night. I was well resolved to set sail, even if I had to return the next day if the weather was fine, to that same place to send to fetch the blocks, grappling anchors, pulleys, cordage, masts, planking, pincers, jacks &c. that we had left there and which I much regretted. But on the other hand, I did not wish to leave until the Naturaliste's boats were back. At eight o'clock, they had not yet appeared, however, we were burning at every quarter of an hour aboard very brilliant flares to indicate the ship's position to them, and the Naturaliste from time to time sent up rockets.
Finally, between eight-thirty and nine o'clock, both arrived. M. Millius, who was in the small boat, told me that, having gone to the place where the boat was to see if he could be of some use, he had found no one, but seeing many of our effects on the beach he had tried to save some of them, and this attempt had cost the life of one of his rowers who was drowned, carried away by a wave. The fear of compromising his other rowers made him renounce making further attempts. But for this misfortune, I would at least have had, for consolation, in my misfortune, that no one had become a victim of the imprudence of two officers, but happiness was not made for me, and by a peculiar fatality, he who had least deserved to feel its effects became its victim.
As soon as M. Millius and his men had rested a little, I sent them back to their ship and had M. Hamelin notified that, according to the fall of the barometer which was no more than twenty-eight inches, and the appearance of the weather, I was about to set sail at once and invited him to do the same.
Hardly had the Naturaliste's boats cleared her side than I much regretted having sent them out, fearing still some new misfortunes, in that we suddenly came a strong gust of wind from the north, which could only cause these boats to drift to leeward of their ship, or at the very least, greatly delay their arrival aboard and increase their difficulties. The gust we had, fortunately, did not last long, as it ceased after a quarter of an hour. But it was nevertheless strong enough to make the Naturaliste drag, which was thrown a quarter of a league to leeward of us. This accident could not have come at a better moment so that her boats would not have easier arrival aboard.
At half past ten, I was under sail and the Naturaliste likewise. The winds were then almost calm and from the north-north-east quarter. We held the north-west tack to gain the middle of the bay where I meant to tack back and forth until the wind had decided and the sky cleared. From the moment we set sail until midnight, the winds were very light and we often had rain. But from that time until day, we had them from north-north-east fresh breeze, obliged to take the third reef in the topsails and even to furl them. As that part of the bay in which we were was perfectly well known to us, having crossed it sounding in all directions and knowing the nature of the soundings and their distances from the coast, I lay to under the main topsail, small jib and mizzen jib, under which sail plan the ship behaved very well and we passed thus the rest of the night, the Naturaliste at a small distance from us.
Report of the Master Carpenter concerning the boat.
"I consider, said the master on his return, your boat lost, because it is impossible to work on her, the sea being too agitated, and unless there is a calm of several days, she will not be at rest in the place where she is.
"This boat is entirely sunk and the sea covers her by more than two feet. She is moreover entirely full of sand and so stranded all around that she forms a bank of more than five feet circumference on which one can walk as on a platform. I do not think the boat has any damage. But unless there is a high tide when the sea recedes enough to leave her uncovered, it is useless to attempt to des(and) her. If before I had had to descend ashore all the objects that were asked for and which are lost for us, I had been able to see for myself, I would have spared you the extra loss of all the objects I left, being unable to re-embark them in the boat which was intended to transport everyone aboard".
Bearings of the land.
At noon the point forming the south entrance of the bay to west 5° north
The lands to the north most in view to the NE ¼ N
Note. I set sail to go opposite the place where Captain Hamelin had indicated that my boat was on the coast.
Note.
My large boat, entrusted to Citizen Bonnefoy, departed as soon as we were at anchor to see, along the coast, if he could discover the remains of my cutter or anything else which might indicate to him the place where all those who were inside had withdrawn. It returned on board at half past seven and brought me news of everyone.
1801-06-08.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to ESE. At 4 a.m. our large boat and the Naturaliste's were sent off with express orders to bring back all the men who were ashore and to abandon the longboat and the gear that had been sent to get her off. The barometer falling fast made us fear bad weather. In the afternoon the two large boats brought back all our people. The longboat was abandoned with a kedge anchor, hawser, tackles, arms and stores. At 8 a boat from the Naturaliste came aboard. Citizen Milius, who commanded her, told us that he came from the shore and had lost one of his boat's crew named Vasse: the sea being very high and breaking with force on the shore, the boat had been obliged to keep at some distance so as not to be swamped; each man had taken to the water to embark, hauling himself along by the boat's grapnel line; all succeeded except Vasse, who, being drunk, was carried away by a sea. At 9 got under way, as did the Naturaliste. The wind at noon; at 11 almost calm, with rain. The barometer still falling.

1801-06-09.journal_anonyme: The wind NE freshening a great deal; our large boat went aboard the Géographe carrying part of the people who had been ashore, and was sent off again to fetch the rest. Seeing that we could not get the longboat off, we abandoned her with all the gear we had landed, and sent up several rockets to mark our position for our two boats, being in great anxiety on their account. At 8 our small boat was back, telling us that the large one was following. At the same moment the ship dragged in a squall and we veered cable; but still driving fast towards the land, the captain decided to get under way. We hove round at once at the capstan, but the ship still casting towards the land, and the capstan meeting little resistance from the cable, we supposed the latter had parted or the anchor been damaged — which we verified at 10.30 p.m., for having then finished hauling the warp aboard we saw that the anchor had only one fluke left. As soon as it was catted we made sail with the winds SSE, variable and very light. Citizen Milius, first lieutenant, took charge of the working of the ship. At 7.30 a.m. a strong breeze, a high sea and the sky overcast.
1801-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 20th, in the morning, it continued to blow a fresh gale from north-north-east to north, the sky overcast and misty with rain. We had then to decide to make sail, and in consequence, I had the lower sails and the main topsail rigged, all reefs taken. the Naturaliste, of which we caught sight during a clearing, was found to be much to leeward of us. And as it was making sail, I presumed it was near the coast, which the mist hid from our view, but from which, according to the depth, we reckoned ourselves three leagues distant, in its part nearest to us.
During the morning, strong squalls passed and we worked to windward with considerable success despite the boards being short and we losing much in going about. Nevertheless, we worked well to windward to get out of the bay, and I would have done so immediately, if the Naturaliste did not (appear) to be too far leeward.
At noon, we had a small clearing and the weather seemed disposed to improve, although the barometer, which was below twenty-eight, announced that it would become worse. Our hope for fair weather was not of long duration, for at two o'clock, the sky had a worse appearance than ever, and the squalls were much stronger than in the morning.
About four o'clock, the Naturaliste had almost closed with us, and I had furled my mainsail, considering myself sufficiently to windward to stand off if the weather became worse, a thing which seemed to me quite likely, as it was already very bad. The evening passed as the morning, working to windward tack upon tack without having lost or gained much, but always in a position where we had nothing to fear.
At eight o'clock, seeing no sign of change, I determined to stand off and get out of the bay, for fear that if the wind shifted to north-west and the bad weather continued, it would be difficult for me to go south, the north-north-east board being unable to be long. The sea had become very heavy, and although the vessel was well supported with the sail I carried, it nevertheless experienced very rough and violent motions. At ten o'clock, the Naturaliste was close enough for us to distinguish it well; however, it appeared that the vessel did not see us, since it fired rockets twice in different places, no doubt to indicate its position. Since we had perfect knowledge of it, I replied only with a light that I had placed at the mizen gaff.
At midnight, perceiving that the current or the tide was driving me towards land, from the sounding and the nature of the bottom, I took the offshore course and got out of the bay for my own tranquility and that of the vessel. I made this signal to the Naturaliste, but I do not know if it saw it, having seen nothing that might lead me to suspect it.
During the rest of the night, it continued to blow a fresh gale. The squalls succeeded one another with great rapidity, and it was without question the worst weather we had had since our departure from France.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From ten o'clock to midnight: eight and ten fathoms, sandy bottom.
From midnight to four o'clock: 12 & 16, same bottom.
From four o'clock to eight: 23 & 25, bottom of small gravel.
From eight o'clock to noon: 15 to 20, fine sand.
The mist and rain did not permit us to take bearings.
Note. All the persons who had been ashore in the cutter returned on board at six o'clock in the evening; there remained ashore only two boats of the Naturaliste, which I was awaiting with great impatience to set sail. They arrived at nine o'clock, and the officer in charge informed me that one of its boat's crew had been drowned, having been swept away by a wave at the moment he was (embarking).
1801-06-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, almost calm. At midnight it began to freshen, and the wind blew hard in gusts, with a high sea and rain. At 3.30 lay to; at 5 filled and stood on. At noon, in a clear interval, took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 85° W, about 18 miles off. The Naturaliste to leeward, beating like ourselves to get out of the gulf; the wind from NE to north. At noon in 33° 25' 20" of latitude by account and in 112° 5' 50" of longitude. At 4, Cape Géographe S 82° W, about 12 miles off. At 7.30 the Naturaliste was in sight to leeward; at midnight she bore from us SSW at a short distance.

1801-06-10.journal_anonyme: At 1.30 p.m. we wore ship. At 2.30 we sighted the Géographe ahead and to windward of us standing on the opposite tack; at 3.30 wore ship. At 4.30 the commander bearing from us north. At 5.30, at 8 and at midnight wore ship. Bearings taken at 2.30 p.m.: the starboard point of the gulf on entering N 78° W, distant 10 miles. At 3.30 the same point N 86° W, distant 8 miles. Thick weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts.
1801-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, at daylight, we found ourselves out of the bay, the wind and weather being always the same. However, we found the sea somewhat less heavy, but the current or tide which was driving us south-east, seemed to have much greater velocity.
Although, sometimes, our horizon was fairly extensive, we had no knowledge of the Naturaliste, which, in all probability, had not come out of the bay or had run less far offshore. Nevertheless, I was without anxiety, convinced that by resuming the inshore course, I could not fail to find it.
At ten o'clock, the wind increasing always, I furled the mainsail and the small topsail and carried only the foresail, the main topsail with lower reef and the mizen staysail. Then I went about and stood towards the land, convinced that I was going to meet the Naturaliste. But at noon, we had not yet caught sight of it. We only saw, in the morning, several whales playing on the water, and one, in particular, to which a sword fish was waging a furious combat, which greatly amused us, spite the bad weather. At noon, having not got the sun, we had no meridional altitude, but according to our dead reckoning, we reckoned ourselves at 33° 30' of south latitude.
In the afternoon, the winds shifted to north-north-west, from where they blew as hard as they had done when they were at north-north-east, and with no appearance of any change. I held the inshore course until three o'clock, when being no more than three leagues from it, I wore round, the course offshore, having no more hope of finding the Naturaliste except at the river of Seals, which I had indicated to him as first rendezvous in case of separation.
During the evening of the 20th, the squalls were heavier and stronger than they had been, and the wind, warm. The weather was very bad and the barometer at 27.10 lines. We prepared ourselves, in the evening, to pass a bad night, but as the course I was making was taking me offshore, I did not believe I had much to fear.
At six o'clock, we had 50 fathoms of bottom, and the sounding indicated rocks. At seven o'clock, we had only forty-six, same bottom. This sudden decrease troubled me, since necessarily I ought to be moving away from the coast according to the course I was making. Thus, I ought to have been surprised to see the depth decrease, when it ought to have increased. Finally, at half past seven, having only thirty-five fathoms, bottom of rocks, my anxieties redoubled from fear of encountering some reef offshore, and I went about towards the land, sounding continually. During this course which I held for an hour, I passed from 35 to 27, grey sand (in the margin: reef of the Naturaliste). And then, recognising the sounding of the place where I was, I went about again and put the vessel to the test, for I had it carry its four main sails, three reefs in the topsails and the fore topgallant sail with the cape stay sail. A quarter of an hour after being on course, we had 28 fathoms, then 35, and then 45, grey sand, and at midnight no bottom at 70 fathoms. I then had the mainsail, the small topsail and the fore topgallant sail furled, and held the sail I had before.
I know not what to attribute this sudden change of bottom to, although, however, it seems to me more fitting to think that it comes from the direction of the land than from any other cause, and that the tides, the drift and the heavy sea will have made us hug the coast more closely than our dead reckoning carried us. For the rest, as we are violently drawn to south-south-east, and it will be necessary to work back to the north as soon as the winds are manageable and will permit it, we shall be in a position to verify this uncertainty. Nothing leads us to believe that there is a shoal in this part offshore from the coast, and although that was at first my opinion, I prefer to believe I prefer to believe (sic) that we had more drift and a stronger tide than we supposed from our dead reckoning.
During the rest of the night, we sounded often without finding bottom at 70 fathoms, and this came from the fact that the coast, then changing direction and bearing more to south-south-east, we were moving away from it. The weather continued to be very bad. The barometer, which, at the beginning of the night, had risen two lines, consequently to 28, descended again to 27.10, and seemed to us not destined to stop at that point. The sky having too bad an appearance.
If, as I suspect, the Naturaliste has remained in the bay, I fear that it will have suffered damage there, being obliged to continually make sail to hold its own against the sea and the tides which drive it towards the coast, and since all that we have seen of it offers no shelter when the winds are from north-north-east to south by the west, it is a very bad place when the winds blow hard from any of the points of that horizon.

From four o'clock to eight o'clock, 22, 25 & 26, fine grey sand.

Bearings of the land at noon.
Cape Discontent at north 5° east.
At four o'clock in the afternoon the point forming the south entrance of the bay at west 8° south, four leagues.
At midnight the point forming the south entrance of the bay at south-west.
At three o'clock the same point at south-south-west.
Note: at ten o'clock the Naturaliste remained to our south-south-west at a small distance. From that time on, it was not seen during the rest of the night.
1801-06-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard and variable from NE to NW in gusts, a high sea, with rain. At 1 we lost sight of the Naturaliste. At 3 the southern shores of the gulf bore from us S 45° W, and at 4, S 22° 30' W. At 10, being clear of the gulf, lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the storm staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon in 33° 46' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 40' of longitude by account. At 1 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 50° E and the point of the islet (seen on the 8th) S 41° E. At 9 filled and stood on under courses. From midnight to 8 a.m. the lead gave from 20 to 33 fathoms, grey sand; from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. no bottom at 80 fathoms; from 6 p.m. to midnight from 50 to 28 fathoms, rocky bottom.

1801-06-11.journal_anonyme: During the night the kedge anchor was carried away by a sea which parted both lashings. A very high sea, the wind still blowing hard. Given the weakness of our crew, both watches were kept on deck. At 8 a.m. Point N bore from us west. But the winds having headed us 2 points in a squall, we wore ship.
1801-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, the weather was even worse than the day before. We spent the day working to windward tack upon tack to hold our own against the sea, the wind and the currents. But despite all our efforts, we were being rapidly driven to the south-east, or, at all events, to the south-south-east. The winds, in the morning, shifted to north-west and varied to west-north-west accompanied by heavy rain and such strong squalls that I expected at any moment to lose some sails. The barometer was then at 27 inches, eight lines, and we had never seen it so low, so that the bad weather seemed to be coming to an end. The sea was so heavy that in the rolls, water came over the lee waist and we had all possible difficulty in saving ourselves from the falls which the rapidity of the vessel's motions occasioned for us. For my part, I sustained one from which I fear to feel the effects for a long time.
At noon, we were, according to our dead reckoning, at 34° 10', (in the margin: Cape Leeuwin), finding ourselves east and west of the point which we had previously taken for Cape Leeuwin, easy to recognise by the great white patch which the mountain forming the extremity of this point presents. We then believed we recognised that Cape Leeuwin ought to be found further to the south, since we then had in view a fairly large extent of coast which extended to the south-east, which we ought not to have seen if the point which we had first taken for the most westerly land had truly been so, since all the other lands to the east ought to have been hidden from us.
From this it follows that the most westerly point of the Leeuwin lands is much further south than the 34 degrees 10 minutes which most of our charts assign as its latitude. I put off to a more favourable time to assure myself of this fact.
During the evening, the winds remained at west-north-west, always in squalls, and often we had very heavy rain. My intention was, if they did not change, to hold the south course until midnight, to take then the one which would bring me back to the land. At the beginning of the night, the weather seemed disposed to improve. The barometer rose about a line and a half, but it was only to descend again to 27 inches 8 lines, as it had been almost all day.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, we held the south course until midnight, and then resumed the north course until four o'clock in the morning, when the sounding having given forty fathoms, bottom of rocks, we resumed the south course. We had, during the night, many flashes of lightning, rain, and often thunder.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.

1801-06-11.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from NNW to W; a high sea and rain. At midnight lay to again under the same canvas. At 8 the land stretched from N 22° 30' E to S 45° E. At noon in 34° 5' 20" of latitude by account and in 111° 44' 10" of longitude by account, Cape Géographe bearing from us N 15° E and Cape Leeuwin east, about 9 miles off. At 4, Cape Géographe N 11° E, Cape Leeuwin N 25° E and the point of the islet S 68° E. We have had no sight of the Naturaliste since the 21st at 1 a.m.

1801-06-12.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a very high sea, blowing a strong breeze from the WNW in gusts. Bearings at 2 p.m.: the middle of the two headlands E 5° S. At 4.30 took the bearing of the end of the land NNE 1° E, distant 10 leagues. Sent up rockets and showed a light every half hour to mark our position for the commander, whom we had lost.
1801-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, although the weather was much the same, the squalls and the squalls commenced, nevertheless, to be less frequent and less heavy. The sky was sometimes cloudy and fair, and we caught sight of the land without, however, being able to distinguish anything because it was too misty. I was then holding the south course, being firmly determined not to close with the land (except) when the weather should improve or the winds permit me to make direct course to the north-west.
During the whole morning, the sky was fairly fair, and at noon, we finally obtained a meridional altitude which placed us at 34° 39' 49" of south latitude, so that since our departure from the bay, we (were) carried more than twenty leagues to the south, despite the fact that by the different courses I had held, I had always tried to reduce the loss of way as much as possible.
During the evening, the hope of seeing the weather improve dissipated. The sky covered itself again with dark and thick clouds, and the squalls commenced with all all (sic) the force and activity of the previous days, which led me to continue the south course, although the winds ranged themselves in the west quarter.
At sunset, our conjectures regarding the portion of the lands which we had judged the day before to be the most westerly of those known as the Leeuwin lands, were verified, and we had full knowledge of the island where M. St Alloüarn must have anchored, but it is far from certain that it is, as he says, at 34° 17'. I believe, on the contrary, very close to 35°, since it is about ten leagues by our dead reckoning from the point where we observed 34° 10' and directly in the south-south-east. If, to-morrow, the weather is fair, it will be a fine opportunity to verify this fact.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth, the winds shifted to the west and varied to west-south-west, which obliged me to take the north-west course. We did not lack rain, thunder or lightning during the night. But although the squalls were heavy, they were nothing (in) comparison to those we had endured on the previous days. Moreover, they succeeded one another with much less rapidity, and the fairness of the sky, when they had passed, seemed to presage the end of the bad weather which the barometer refused to indicate to us, remaining constantly between 27.8 and 27.10.
While running the north-west course, we sounded every hour, but we never found bottom with 70 & 80 fathoms of line.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From noon to three o'clock, 45 & 35 fathoms, bottom of rocks.
From three o'clock to five o'clock, 37 & 50 fathoms, sand & coral.

From midnight to four o'clock in the morning, veered 70 fathoms, no bottom.

Note: there is an error in what I said this day regarding the position of the point of Leeuwin.

1801-06-12.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from WNW to WSW. A high sea, with light rain at intervals. At 8 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight, north; Cape Leeuwin N 11° E; the point of the islet N 79° E; and the islet S 79° E. At noon the land could no longer be seen. We were in 34° 37' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' of longitude by account. At nightfall the wind fell away a great deal.

1801-06-13.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from WNW. At 6 p.m. wore ship. A very high sea, the wind still blowing hard and in gusts, with much lightning from SSW round to NW.
1801-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, the weather cleared and we had a fine day. We took advantage of it to close with the land, from which our course and the tides had carried us considerably far. Although the sky had cleared, we nevertheless had, in the morning, some fairly strong squalls, but this did not prevent me from making sail and letting out a reef of the topsails.
When we had somewhat closed with the land, we obtained a perfect knowledge of the most westerly part known as the Leeuwin lands, and we also recognised the island where M. St Alloüarn must have anchored, but we did not see, and indeed they do not exist, the chain of islands which he claims extended to the south-east or south-south-east, nor the reefs which he says he took bearings of to the north-west of the anchorage where he was then. We ranged this part of the coast closely enough to be able to assert that he was mistaken.
The lands which are to the south-east and the east-south-east of the westernmost point of the Leeuwin land, can well, at a distance of seven to eight leagues, present themselves to the view as islands, and this is not the only part of this coast which presents the same effect. But if one approaches them, as we did at two or three leagues distance, one recognises perfectly that all that one believed ought to be islands, belong to the mainland to which they are joined by lower ground which cannot be seen except at a small distance.
For the rest, the most westerly part of the Leeuwin land is of a good height and can be seen easily ten leagues at sea. But the island which is separated from it by about two leagues, is much lower and can only be seen at a moderate distance.
As we were unable to obtain an observation at noon, the sun being enveloped in clouds, it was not very easy for us to determine exactly the latitude and longitude of this point. But from the observations we made afterwards, referred to those which took place when we arrived on this coast, (it) cannot give an error of more than three minutes in the latitude of this point, which we fix at 34° 17' and 111° 54' 0" of east longitude.
For the rest, as I propose to revisit this cape when I shall make my way in the coming summer to the land of Diemen, I hope to determine its latitude and longitude exactly.
In the afternoon, having closed with the land, we coasted it again and took at the different points which we had already seen, other bearings to better assure the first.
In the evening, the weather was fairly fair and the barometer rose to 28 inches, which was very agreeable to us, for for four days the bad weather had much inconvenienced us, and even more, our livestock, which we lost almost entirely. This loss was all the more keenly felt since we had employed all sorts of means to shelter it from the bad weather.
During the night, the weather was fairly fair and the winds from the west moderate. I held the north-west course to be in a position to re-enter the next day the bay from which the bad weather had driven me out, in order to finish taking its bearings.
In ascending from the point of Leeuwin to the bay, we remarked, for the second time, and it is perhaps a rather peculiar thing, that all this extent of coast which offers no shelter, even for a boat, is everywhere bordered by rocks
of granite on which the sea breaks with great noise, whilst in the bay of the Géographe, we see them only on the first point which forms its entrance, all the rest being only sand dunes.
It is also to be remarked that from the westernmost point of the Leeuwin lands to the one which forms the entrance of the bay of which I have just spoken, the bottom is constantly bad, either near the coast or offshore. While in the bay, we find everywhere a fine and good bottom on which we can anchor at whatever distance we wish from the coast.
Bearing of the Leeuwin lands to the south of the bay of the Géographe.
The most westerly point of the lands in this part at north-east one-quarter east.
The island of M. St Alloüarn at the east-north-east.
A white point which, at first, we had taken for Cape Leeuwin from the latitude which our charts assign to it: at north 7° east.
The lands visible most to the north of us at north 3° west.

From noon to four o'clock, 30, 45 & 35, bottom of rocks and coral.
From four to eight, 35, 33, 40, bottom of rocks and coral.

From midnight to four o'clock in the morning, 80 fathoms, no bottom.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock, 80 fathoms, no bottom.

1801-06-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze, variable from W to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted; at 7 filled and stood on, lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 8 the point of the islet N 15° E and another point N 22° 30' W. At noon in 34° 26' of latitude by account and in 111° 55' of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 3° W, Cape Leeuwin N 7° E, the point of the islet N 56° E and the islet N 68° E. At 4.45 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 28° E, 23 miles off; the White Mountain, which had at first been taken for Cape Leeuwin, east, 10 miles off; Cape Leeuwin S 50° E, 22 miles off. During the night carried little sail so as not to run past Cape Géographe. The topgallant masts were swayed up.

1801-06-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from WNW. At 3.30 went about, being only 5 or 6 leagues from the land, and steered close-hauled. At 5.30 hove to, being 15 to 18 miles from the coast, and sounded in 25 fathoms, fine sand. At 5.50 stood on again. At 7.15 the wind having hauled in a squall, went onto the port tack; at 7.45 the lead brought up 45 fathoms, fine sand. At 10.30 a.m. we passed over a weedy bottom in separate patches, easy to make out, which seemed to rise above the bottom from 14, 12, 13, 11 to 10 fathoms. At 10.30 we let go the anchor in 9 fathoms, clean grey sand. Bearings of the anchorage: the western point of Rottnest Island W half N; the SW point W 27° S; the west end of the island lying off the end of Rottnest S 9° E; an islet or rock lying east of that one S 25° E; the southernmost visible end of the mainland S 33° E.
1801-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, at daylight, the weather being fair and the winds from the west, fine breeze, we first set course to the north, but after having recognised that the currents, during the night, had carried us far offshore, as well as the course we had been holding, we steered for some time to the north-east and, finally, to the east to re-enter our great bay, from which we were distant about six leagues.
In the morning, we let out a second reef of the topsails and I had the fore topgallant sail rigged. I was rather annoyed at re-entering the bay with west winds on account of the difficulty I should have in getting out if they remained in that quarter and the weather became bad. But the hope that I might have during the night, the land breeze, as it had always occurred the first time I entered it, made me proceed.
At noon, being north and south of the point which forms its entrance, we observed the latitude of 33° 30' 32" south and the longitude indicated by the timekeepers was then 111° 27' 13". I expected to find the Naturaliste there, but having no knowledge of it, I think it will have made its way to Rottnest Island, which I had indicated to it as first rendezvous in case of separation.
At four o'clock, we were abreast of the place where I had advanced and we continued our bearings from this point, easy to recognise from the notes we had taken whilst we were at anchor there.
At sunset, the weather was fair and the barometer at 28 inches 2 lines, which tranquillised us somewhat. However, I kept at a certain distance from the coast and set myself close-hauled on the starboard tack, intending to spend the night working to windward, as the winds were not favourable for anchoring.
At eight o'clock, having no more than eighteen fathoms of water, I went about and set course to the south-west and south-west one-quarter west under the topsails and the foresail. I found the same depth until ten o'clock, when it began to increase, and at eleven I was at twenty fathoms, fine sandy bottom.
At the beginning of the night, we had several squalls with wind and rain, but they were of short duration. However, about half past ten, it began to blow fresh breeze, although the sky was fairly fair and clear, and all seemed to announce that the night would not be fine or pleasant to pass, having the land under the lee and at a very small distance.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth, the weather indeed became bad and we had squalls so strong that we had to take a second reef in the topsails. At midnight, we took the north course, which we continued until daylight, with the sounding line and giving never less than nineteen to twenty fathoms of water with different qualities of bottom.

1801-06-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to NW. At 7, having doubled Cape Géographe, we bore away east into the gulf to see whether the Naturaliste might be there. At noon in 33° 31' of latitude observed and in 111° 27' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 50' NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Géographe S 73° W and a NE point of the gulf N 55° E. At 5, having seen nothing in the gulf, we hauled to the wind on the port tack; at 6.30 went onto the starboard tack. During the night overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts, with squalls.

1801-06-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from WNW. We sent our large boat to survey Rottnest Island; she was back at 8 p.m. A national flag was planted on a high hill nearest the shore, in case he should pass that way when we were no longer at the anchorage. The winds variable from W to WNW.
1801-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, at daylight, we had a squall so heavy and rain that we had to take in our topsails and even strike them completely. This squall lasted about half an hour, after which the weather cleared and the sky became very clear, although misty. The winds remained always from the west and so strong that we were unable to let out the second reef of our topsails. However, as we had the land under the lee and at a small distance, we sent down our mainsail, changed the day before, as the one which was in place was no longer able to withstand fresh squalls, if, as there was too much appearance of it, we should have any more.
At eight o'clock, the fog which hid from us the view of most of the coast, having dissipated somewhat, we saw it distinctly extending behind us to the south-east and ahead of us to the north-east.
This coast appeared to us much less uniform than that of the bay of the Géographe, but we could distinctly see, behind the sand dunes which form its shore, two ranges of mountains much higher than anything we had seen until then, and we estimated that the range most advanced into the land could be about fifteen leagues from us.
We could not, during the whole day, take any bearing of the coast, which we extended sometimes to three leagues distance and often more, when we found ourselves abreast of some indentation. The wind was so little manageable during the whole day, that we sought only to work a little offshore rather than try to approach it.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 32° 38' 41" and the longitude indicated by the timekeepers was, for the same hour, for No. 27 of 111° 45' 20" and for No. 35 of 111° 48' 30".
According to the dead reckoning of the courses made, we found that the currents or tides had changed direction, since we had ten minutes difference to the north.
In the afternoon, the weather was no finer than it had been in the morning; on the contrary, the wind increased considerably and the squalls succeeded one another with more rapidity than ever, almost certain presage of a bad night. At four o'clock, we were obliged to furl our fore topgallant sail and carry only our main sails, two reefs in the topsails.
While extending from the coast, in the evening, we found ourselves abreast of a large bay, whose northern extremity terminates, no doubt, at the point which should form the entrance of the Swan river or the river of Swans, from which we were not more than five to six leagues distant according to the dead reckoning of the way made since noon and the observation of the latitude at that time. But
we had no hope of seeing it soon, since we had to return over our course as soon as the weather would permit, to visit the coast we had just passed without having been able to determine its bearing and its sinuosities.
At six o'clock in the evening, we went about on the other tack by going about, although the breeze was very strong. As we were heading south-west one-quarter south, I think that this course will lift us well off the coast, from which we shall always be able to judge the proximity by the sounding.
At half past seven, the sheet of our main topsail to windward parted. But as this sail was quickly gathered in, it was not damaged by the force of the wind.
During the rest of the night, the weather was continually by squalls and rain with very strong gusts from the north-west one-quarter west to west-south-west. We ran, during the night, two courses, the sounding indicating the times when it was necessary to change.

1801-06-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to W in gusts. At midnight went onto the port tack. At 8 we were about 18 miles from the land; it appeared to stretch away in the N 22° 30' E and to form a bight. At 11 a very conspicuous point bore from us east, about 12 miles off. At noon in 32° 36' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 45' 20" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. At 6 the land stretched from N 11° E to S 67° 30' E. Went onto the starboard tack. Squally weather, with rain.

1801-06-16.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze in gusts from W to W by N, blowing hard. Our large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq. At 8.30 p.m., the corvette dragging, we let go our sheet anchor with a range of 30 fathoms. At 9 a.m. the boat was back, not having been able to land because of the bad weather.
1801-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh in the morning, the winds the winds (sic) were from west-south-west, often variable to south-west. The sky, although very cloudy and overcast, was less rainy than the day before and even during the course of the morning, it became fairly fair. However, the weather not being suitable for approaching the land, we continued to hold the closest course on the south course until ten o'clock, when we took the north-west course to carry us further offshore from the coast until the weather permitted us to come to recognise it with more safety. When we went about, our distance from the land could be at most four leagues and we had then from 18 to 15 fathoms of water, sandy bottom, sometimes coral and even rocks.
The fog which covered most of the lands, made them too confused for us to take certain or recognisable bearings, which we could recognise upon our return to the same place, for which reason we confined ourselves to bearing the two extremities in sight both to the north and to the south and the middle of that which we had abreast of us.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 32° 42' 57" and that of the dead reckoning placed us at 32° 37' 47", which gave us a difference to the south, for the different courses made during the twenty-four hours, 10' 10". The longitude indicated by the timekeepers was, reduced to noon, of 111° 46' 14" for No. 27 and of 112° 57' for No. 35, whose daily motion was accelerating more and more compared to that of No. 27.
In the afternoon, the winds shifted to the west and we had almost a calm, which made us hope for a change in our favour, as since the new moon, the weather had been almost always bad, the winds, if not entirely contrary, at least little manageable. The barometer, moreover, had already risen to 28 inches 2 lines.
As the weather then was fair and we were making little way, we amused ourselves by dredging. The bottom being sandy and the depth not considerable since we had only from 18 to 20 fathoms of water. Among the different objects of natural history which we took in dredging, nothing was very curious except some sponges and several jellyfish. Among the latter, we took one of extreme beauty and undoubtedly entirely new to the curious. The dredge brought back several starfish new to us, and which will also be so to many others, several holothurians similar to those of which I give a drawing, and finally a prodigious quantity of shells of the species known as swallows. But they were all so small that we are persuaded that it is a variety of the species which is known, and that this one does not grow larger, as it would be quite extraordinary if among the thousands which we drew from the sea bottom and at different times, we had not found any larger ones.
The variety of colours of the sponges would make them very interesting if they retained the fine colours which they had when they came out of the water, but as they lose much, they do not present the same interest to those who will receive them as they gave us pleasure in taking them.
During the night of the 27th to the 28th, the weather was fair. We made some courses with the winds from the north and the north-north-east not to move away from the coast in order to take up early on the morrow the continuation of our work.

1801-06-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze and light from WSW to SW. At midnight went onto the port tack; at 4 onto the starboard. At 8 the land stretched from N 56° E to S 34° E. At 10.45 went onto the port tack, being about 4 miles from the coast, which appears to trend NNE and SSW. It is very low near the shore; inland, fairly high and well wooded mountains could be seen. At noon the northernmost land in sight bore N 34° E, 10 miles off, and the southernmost S 22° E, 21 miles off. At noon in 32° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 22' NW. The dredge was put over several times and brought up many objects of natural history. At 10, the breeze being from the north, went onto the starboard tack.

1801-06-17.journal_anonyme: Grey weather, the sky cloudy, blowing a strong breeze and in heavy gusts from WNW. At 6.30 a.m. the small boat was sent off to Rottnest with two days' provisions; the large boat took six days' provisions to go and examine the Swan River. At 8.30 a.m. the longboat was sent off with 2 days' provisions.
1801-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the weather being fair, the winds at north-north-east, fine breeze and the sea beautiful, I set course to the east as soon as daylight broke to close with the land, which the sounding placed me then about four leagues distant. The sky was so clear and serene at sunrise that we already regarded this day as one of the finest we had yet had since our arrival in these waters. We were then, far from foreseeing the almost sudden change which took place in the morning.
However that may be, at eight o'clock, being no more than a small distance and at most one league away, having only eight fathoms of water, sometimes good sandy bottom, sometimes sand and coral, and even sometimes hard coral without sand, we bore away to the south-south-east to extend along it in its whole length, determine all its points and finally complete our work in this part.
At half past nine, we had already covered nearly four leagues of coast at the distance of which I have just spoken. Many azimuths, angles and bearings had been taken and everything until then was going very well. We had no more than about four leagues of way to make to reach the point which forms the north entrance of the fine and large bay of the Géographe, when the men of the forecastle announced breakers ahead of us. As I was always on deck, I sighted them at once myself and I quickly bore away with the vessel, taking the tack to starboard. We passed at a mile and a half at most from these breakers on which the sea rolled with great force, which made it all the more remarkable.
We had scarcely moved away from them half a league when we had a squall of the most vigorous kind from the north-north-east, without our being able to see where it had come from. I set course to the west for some time to move away a little from the coast which I reckoned to close with again as soon as this squall had passed. But gradually, as the sky darkened, the mist, rain and strong wind succeeded the fine breeze we had had for part of the morning, and we had to hold the closest course to the port tack.
At noon, being unable to observe the latitude, all our work of the morning became useless, our hour angles, our azimuths &a were entirely lost, and all that remained of what we had done was an exact knowledge of the coast and some notes on the different views which were presented to us by the continuous chain of sand dunes by which it is everywhere bordered.
When we had knowledge of the reef of which I have just spoken, we were heading south one-quarter south-west and we had it right ahead of us. After moving it a little away, it remained at south 10° east. The position which we assign to it on the chart, although a little doubtful, can differ only by a mile or a mile and a half, either to the north or to the south, and as it is (comparable) to a dune all of sand and without other verdure than that which is found at the summit, it will be all the more easy to recognise when we return to seek it, as it is the most remarkable that one sees in all this part of the coast.
As far as I could judge of this reef, from the small distance at which we passed from it, it does not appear to me that it has more than a cable's length in length by half a length in width, and in all probability, there would be a passage between it and the land, at least, the tranquillity of the sea in that place gives reason to presume it. As it is the only known danger (in the margin: see the reef of the Naturaliste) that we have yet encountered on the Leeuwin lands, I have named it the Unique.
In the afternoon, the weather became so bad and the winds, which had first shifted to the north, then to north-north-west and to north-west, were so strong that it was necessary to take successively the three reefs in the topsails, furl our mainsail, the fore topgallant sail and finally the small topsail, and still in what remained of sails, the vessel had all that it could carry.
The rain was almost continuous all morning evening, so that having no more hope of closing with the land for this day, I continued to run offshore until six o'clock in the evening when I went about to the north, the winds being then at west-south-west and the sea very heavy. We had at that time thirty fathoms of water, sandy bottom, which should place us seven or eight leagues from the nearest coast.
During the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth, the weather continued to be by squalls and often rain. However, the squalls were less strong than they had been during the day, but the sea was none the less heavy and agitated. We continued during the night to sound every half hour as had been arranged since we were on the coast. The sounding never reported less than 23 fathoms and often more.

1801-06-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather until 10.30, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NE; afterwards overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from N to W. At 3 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 bore away east for the land. At 8 took the bearing of a very high mountain inland, S 35° E; we then bore away south and S 11° W and ran along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It runs roughly north and south and is very low; it is not so well wooded as in the gulf. I thought I could see that it was fringed with coral. The sea broke there violently. The lead gave from 8 to 13 fathoms, coral bottom. At 10.15 breakers were seen ahead in the S 10° E at a short distance; we at once hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. The wind freshened by degrees. At noon the land stretched from N 68° E to S 40° E. At noon in 32° 43' 57" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 26' NW. At 1 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail; at 6 lay to with the port side to the wind.

1801-06-18.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sky cloudy and a very high sea. We kept a light at the gaff all night to mark our position for the boats. At 10 a.m. the dinghy brought the news that the small boat was cast on the shore and could not be got off without the help of a large boat, her crew being short of water and having very little food. The sea being very high and the wind too strong for the dinghy to do the work of a large boat, we had to wait for the longboat's return — and she too, unknown to us, was then on shore and short of every kind of provision.
1801-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the weather was, at the least, quite as bad as it had been the day before, and we did not lack in the morning wind or rain. However, the sun appeared from time to time, and when the squalls and the gusts had passed, the sky remained fairly fair for a few moments.
As the winds had been fairly constantly from the west to west-north-west, we (held) always the north course, pulling as much as was possible for us towards the west, sounding every half hour without having ever had less than twenty-three fathoms of water and very often 25 and 28, sandy bottom and sometimes coarse gravels.
The vessel's canvas was not very suitable for working to windward, since we carried only the foresail, the main topsail and the mizen staysail, but it was all that the vessel could support, and even in the gusts it sometimes had too much.
During most of the morning, we had no sight of the land, but at noon, it showed itself very distinctly, and that with which we were nearest remained at north-east one-quarter east, four or five leagues distant and perhaps less, as one could distinctly see the white patch of the sand dunes which border the coast, which, in truth, appeared to me higher in this part than in any other.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 32° 16' 28" south and that of our course reckoned was of 32° 16' 23", so that the small difference which we found was attributed to the tides which, during twenty-four hours, having acted on our course in the contrary direction, had become null for us. This reasoning is perhaps not positive, but at least it is probable, since on the previous days, when the course had not been in the same quarter, there had always been fairly considerable differences, either to the north or to the south.
From the latitude observed at noon, we were not far distant from Rottnest Island, and I think even that we had good knowledge of it, because about two o'clock, we discovered a land which appeared isolated from all others, remaining to our north-east at a distance of six to seven leagues. This land appeared to us higher than those which we had seen until then, but the weather being too uncertain for approaching it more closely, I put on the other tack in order to be able to double easily before night, the point of a fairly deep bay which was abreast of us and whose northern extremity will no doubt terminate near Rottnest Island and perhaps form the entrance of the river of Swans.
Although we were then quite close to the coast which was abreast of us, the depth always increased from 25 to thirty fathoms, bottom of greyish sand and sometimes red.
The sea, in these waters, was extremely heavy and elevated, which was for me one more reason not to run further to the north in a time that had the worst appearance.
In the afternoon, the winds varied from west to west-south-west and the rain and the squalls and strong gusts recommenced anew. Nevertheless, as I wished to double before night, the nearest point to us and of which I have spoken above, I had the small topsail and the fore topgallant sail rigged, both with their lower reefs. But at five o'clock, I was obliged to furl the first by the violence of the squalls which we had at that time.
A little before night, we took bearings of the nearest lands to the east, and those which remained to our north at north-east, the estimated distance of the first was four leagues and for the others, eight.
After sunset, the weather was entirely bad, and in the strong gusts, the winds sometimes shifted as far as south-west, which made the course which I was then holding somewhat bad. Nevertheless, the sounding constantly reported 25 fathoms, sandy bottom.
I determined to continue it until I found no more than twenty.
At eight o'clock, the squalls became so frequent that one did not wait for the other. Most of them were very heavy and all announced a very bad night. The barometer, which, during the day, although the weather was not fair, had risen to 28.1 lines, descended in the evening to 27.11 and seemed to confirm the announcement which the state of the atmosphere had only too much indicated to us. Nevertheless, the sea was less heavy and elevated than we had had it all day.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth, the weather was extremely bad. It blew very hard until midnight, when the winds having shifted to south-east, rain commenced to fall abundantly, thunder and lightning accompanied it, and it seemed that the elements were in convulsion.
Independently of all the discomfort which such weather caused us, an event of another kind and much more disagreeable than rain, thunder and lightning came to increase our anxieties. At the change of watch at eight o'clock, the sounding regularly reported from 25 to 24 fathoms, fine bottom of grey sand, and it was the same as we had found whilst running to the north, but at half past eight, it gave no more than 21 fathoms, bottom of rocks. At nine o'clock, we also had 20 and a half fathoms same bottom, but at half past nine, we found ourselves all at once at twelve, always bottom of rocks, so that it was necessary at once to come about and take the north course, pulling as much as we were able towards the west. We moved away (very) promptly from a place which could have become very fatal to us if I had not been continually on deck and always with the sounding line in hand.
Half an hour, at most, after going about on the port tack, the depth increased by three fathoms, the other half hour after by three fathoms again, and finally at one o'clock we were again at 25 fathoms, fine sand.
In coming about, the bell was rung and all the crew were promptly on their feet, although it was in the midst of a squall, the manoeuvre was prompt and I felt pleasure in doing them justice on this occasion.
At eleven o'clock, the winds having shifted to south-south-east, calmed much and we had only to endure rain and storms.
