1801-06-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with thunder, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to south. At noon in 32° 16' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 39' 30" of longitude by No. 27. The land bore from us N 79° E at a great distance. At 2 filled and stood on, starboard tack, under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the storm staysail, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. (The Naturaliste, at anchor off Rottnest Island, sighted us at 2 in the S 22° 30' W, 24 miles off.) At 5 the north point in sight N 45° E and the south point N 79° E. At 9.30, having found ourselves on a shoal of reddish sand, we went onto the port tack and gave the course N 45° W, and at 10, N 67° 30' W. At 9.30 the lead had given 12 fathoms, and a quarter of an hour before, 25 to 21 fathoms, grey sand.

1801-06-19.journal_anonyme: The dinghy was sent off under the orders of Citizen Couture to join the large boat. At 2 p.m. the Géographe was sighted in the SSW under her topsails, 24 miles off; we lost sight of her 2 hours later. The winds from east to ESE.
1801-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 30th, in the morning, with the winds having returned to the south-west, it continued to blow with force, but at least the sky was cloudy and fine, and the squalls of the previous days had disappeared, if not entirely, at least they no longer followed each other with the same rapidity. The sea, however, was extremely rough, and the oscillating movements it caused to the vessel fatigued her greatly, as they did us all.
At eight o'clock, seeing no sign of any change in the weather, I resolved to make course to the north-west by north in order to reach a more suitable latitude for navigation and our work, reserving the right to return from north to south to resume the work I was abandoning should the weather become manageable.
On the 7th we had knowledge of land, and on the 8th we began to take bearings of it, either from a distance or at close quarters until the 29th in the evening. However, the bad weather had permitted us to accomplish very little that was good up to this epoch. And except for the coast from the western point of Leeuwin to the point which forms the entrance of the fine bay which I have named after the Géographe, all the rest was nothing but detached and sketchy pieces which the slightest fair weather would have enabled us to complete within two days had we been fortunate enough to have it. It was this expectation and the little that remained to be done which had decided me until then to remain exposed to all the bad weather we have experienced, which twice drove us out of the bay and caused us to drift south of the point Leeuwin. So that for twenty-three days we were merely tacking back and forth to get clear of the coast on which the winds repeatedly set us whenever we approached close enough to examine it properly.
The four anchorages we made in the bay furnished us with interesting details about the nature of the soil, the bearing of part of the coasts, the population it might contain, and the resources which navigators might find there for wood, fishing, and hunting. But they should not expect to find water in any manner whatsoever, and water they might obtain by filtration by digging in the earth would be but a very poor resource. For the rest, the anchorage in the bay of the Géographe is everywhere good and solid from thirty to ten fathoms. The nature of the bottom, though extremely variable, is none the less good, and the few madrepores occasionally encountered there are too soft to damage cables.
The regularity of the bottom throughout this entire bay is such that one can know very nearly what distance one is from the coast during the night. One ordinarily has ten fathoms at a small league from land and this is the place where the anchorage is least good. But by keeping at two leagues from the coast in fourteen to fifteen fathoms of water, one is perfectly safe there and the holding is firm. From league to league, going seaward, the bottom increases gradually, and at ten leagues from the most inland indentation, one finds 27 and 28 fathoms of very fine sand.
It is with regret that I quit a place which must be most delightful during the fine season and in which, while occupying ourselves with our geographical work, we were gathering by means of our dredge many objects of natural history and some of the newest for science. But as I am determined to return to retrace my steps at some time to complete the entire exploration of this coast, I shall always be in a position to derive the best advantage possible from it.
One will find in my detailed journal the various reports which have been made to me by all those who have landed several times. There will perhaps be little agreement in the manner of viewing things of each in particular, but nevertheless all are sufficiently consistent regarding the principal matters such as the nature of the soil, its productions, its resources, its population, and especially its constitution, which appears to leave no room for doubt.
In the morning of the 30th, having resolved, as I have said, to move up to the north, I directed the course to the north-east by north, the wind being at the south-west, a fresh breeze which did not permit me to venture setting the topgallant sail and shaking out a reef in my topsails on which for a long time all three had been taken. Nevertheless, we proceeded fairly well and the vessel, with the little canvas she carried, was still making two leagues and two and a half leagues per hour.
We could not get an hour angle in the morning, but at noon, the sun having appeared, we observed a latitude of 31 degrees 57 minutes south, which placed us, according to some of our charts, east and west of the island of Rottnest or of the Swan river, which I left with much reluctance, though this was merely a postponement.
During the evening, the breeze continued to be strong and the sea so elevated and rough that we had not seen it so high throughout the course we had made up to that moment. We sounded several times in the morning and evening without finding bottom at fifty nor at seventy fathoms.
After sunset, the wind calmed considerably and we occasionally had small squalls with rain without strong wind as had occurred on the previous days. At eight o'clock we set the cape tack sail and the topgallant sail, all reefs taken. The rest of the night was without incident and the weather was rather fine. The sea, however, was constantly bad and much fatigued us. In the course of the day, the barometer rose to 28 inches three lines, which caused us to judge that the bad weather was approaching its end.

From two o'clock to four, 70 fathoms, no bottom.
From four to eight, 70 fathoms, no bottom.
From eight o'clock to midnight, 80 fathoms, no bottom.
Bearings of the land at noon:
The land in view most to the east at north 38° east eight leagues distant.
The land most to the north in view at north 33° east.
Bearings of the land.
At five o'clock the land appeared from east 11° north to north 45° east at the estimated distance of 6 to 7 leagues, the sky being covered and having a very threatening appearance.
Particular remarks.
Our landfall at the cape or the point of the lands of Leeuwin was made in the most beautiful weather in the world, both during the night and during the day. The land and sea breezes appeared at first to have a uniform and regular progression. In the morning we usually had them from the east, variable to the north, and in the afternoon they almost invariably came from the south-east towards the south, and remained there through the greater part of the night. The breezes were then moderate and most pleasant. The sky was almost always fine and the night illuminated by the moon. Fair weather accompanied us even into the bay of the Géographe in which we preserved it for a few days more. But at the last quarter of the moon it changed entirely, and from the time we were forced to leave this bay it was bad for longer than we had had it fair, and scarcely had we a fine day from the sixteenth of the month of Prairial until the first of Messidor when I resolved to advance to the north.
The currents, during our time on this coast, changed direction twice. From the point Leeuwin to the cape of the Discontented, they carried us with force to the south towards the west and sometimes also towards the east. But from this cape going up to the north, they appeared to us to be directed more ordinarily to the north towards the west than in any other part.
The tides on the coast and within the bays are not too strong there and scarcely rise in neap tides above six feet, and in the new and full moons above eight or nine. When they rise higher, it must be from an accidental cause or the force of the north to south winds passing through the west.
All the coast we saw is without reef or dangers extending seaward, and those which are very close to land are too visible to avoid. All the shores of the sea are nothing but an uninterrupted succession of sand dunes more or less elevated, and some of which serve to take good landmarks.
From the point Leeuwin to the cape of the Discontented (word crossed out with a cross) the coast or the hills somewhat distant from it are not as well wooded as in the bay of the Géographe. Nowhere can one anchor without running the risk of having one's cable at least very much damaged if it is not cut, whereas inside the cape of the Géographe the anchorage is clear throughout the entire extent of the bay.
The declination of the magnetic needle was (no figures) to (no figures) north-west.
During our stay in the bay of the Géographe we found but few resources there. Fish were very rare, but whales, on the other hand, were very common. Only one or two sea turtles were seen. The land does not appear to provide much for the food of the natives, who seemed to draw it principally from the sea. Everywhere penetrated, no tree bearing fruit fit to eat was encountered, nor any leguminous plant. The only refreshment we found there was wild celery and a species of purslane but the latter was not as good as the other.
Shells, and especially those of the class of scallops are not rare there. The woods appeared to be of poor quality and little fit to be worked. Several offered a resin of which we have several samples and from which, without doubt, advantage could be taken. The nature of the soil was likewise judged to be unsuitable for sustained cultivation.
1801-06-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to SW. At 8 the land was seen at the limit of sight. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At noon in 31° 59' 10" of latitude observed and in 111° 6' 30" of longitude by account. The variation in Geographe Bay was 5° 25', the mean of a great number of observations I made there, all of which agreed within 5 minutes. The Naturaliste, which during the gale in the gulf had doubled the north point, had shaped her course for Rottnest Island, the first place of rendezvous, and had anchored there on the morning of the 25th.

1801-06-20.journal_anonyme: The winds from E to SSE freshened. The corvette dragging fast, we veered 90 fathoms of cable. At 4 p.m. let go the starboard anchor, allowing it to take up the range of 30 fathoms that had been made. Squally weather, the wind in gusts.
1801-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Messidor, in the morning, although the sky was very overcast and our horizon rather dark, we nevertheless had a fine breeze from the south-west variable to the south-south-west. The topgallant sail which had been furled in the night was trimmed anew and, at eight o'clock, despite the sea still being very rough and elevated, I ordered one of the three reefs in the topsails to be shaken out. I likewise directed the course to the north by north-west, finding myself far enough to the west to have nothing to fear from the Abrolhos which I wished to pass wide of.
In the morning the weather appeared to be settling in quite fair. We had some small squalls with rain and a little wind, but they were short-lived. The barometer, moreover, was rising considerably and was already at 28 inches 5 lines. As up to this moment it has not deceived us, I had great confidence in it. Nevertheless, I was surprised to see the sea constantly rough and bad, which made me believe that further south of our latitude the weather must not be very fine.
At noon we observed 30° 32' 28" of latitude and the longitude, indicated by the timekeepers, was for No. 27 of 109° 52' 6" and for No. 35 of 110° 7' 36". According to the dead reckoning of the course made during the 24 hours, there was a difference to the (no direction) of (no figures) and one to (no direction) of (no figures). This difference is perhaps rather the effect of the rough sea than that of the currents or the tides.
In the afternoon the weather was fine and the horizon very clear. But for the great swell which singularly fatigued the vessel and her rigging, we should have made passable progress to the north by north-west and perhaps we should have reached in the night the latitude of the Abrolhos which our charts place very differently one from another. According to the one used on M. d'Entrecasteaux's voyage, the southernmost part of this danger is at 29° 30' of south latitude, and according to a Dutch chart which appears to be carefully done, it is fixed at 27° 58'. So that not knowing to which of the two charts to give the preference, one must keep a careful watch and be continuously on guard.
At sunset we had an amplitude observation which gave 5° 8 north-west for the declination of the magnetic needle, but the movements of the vessel were so violent and rapid that it should be considered very doubtful.
At the change of watch at eight o'clock I ordered that we sound every two hours and pay out at least 70 fathoms of line in order to be able to perceive early any Abrolhos banks if they should chance to be met with on our course, a thing from which I am far from thinking probable since if the wind does not blow harder than it now does we shall scarcely be tomorrow at noon at the latitude which their position gives them as being their most southern.
During the night of the first to the 2nd the sky, though very overcast, was rather fine. We sounded at 10 o'clock, at midnight, at two o'clock, and at four o'clock in the morning, but found no bottom at one hundred ten fathoms at full depth, which enabled us to continue our course without having to alter and without anxiety.
1801-06-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSW. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' W. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 52' 6" of longitude by No. 27. At 10 and at midnight sounded without finding bottom at 110 fathoms. Water was put on an allowance of 1 bottle a day.

1801-06-21.journal_anonyme: At 8 a.m. the corvette Naturaliste got under way, and at the same moment one of the dinghies was sent off to Rottnest Island. The dinghy sent off the day before to Rottnest came aboard at 10 a.m. She brought the news that the longboat had been cast ashore on the 29th at 8.30 a.m.; a dinghy was sent off at once with six days' provisions and the tools needed to repair her. The sky overcast, a swell running, the winds blowing at intervals from the ENE.
1801-06-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 2nd of Messidor, in the morning, the sky was rather fine and clear. The winds shifted to the south, variable to the south-south-east, light breeze. We then shook out a second reef in our topsails and set our main sail and our stay-sails although the sea was still very elevated and rough.
In the course of the morning the sky, which was rather fine and clear at sunrise, suddenly became overcast and we immediately had a light gentle rain and much fog. At eight o'clock I had ordered the course to be steered to the north by north-east and we were making course in that direction, the breeze being then from the south-east to the east-south-east rather weak and continually decreasing.
At noon we had no observation for the latitude and that of the dead reckoning placed us only at 28° 58' south, that is still south of the Abrolhos banks according to the government chart, and precisely at the latitude of the southernmost part of this danger according to a Dutch chart which, as I have already observed, seemed to me rather carefully done and in which I had for that reason some confidence. For the rest, as our dead reckoning placed us far to the west of this danger, I had nothing to fear from encountering it while steering to the north by north-east.
In the afternoon the fog dispersed, but calm having succeeded it we made very little progress until sunset, when the winds having shifted to the east-south-east freshened a little. Our horizon from the east to the north-west passing through the north became very clear and far extended, so that all announced to us fair weather. The barometer in the morning, despite the rain and fog, had risen to 28 inches seven lines, which had scarcely happened to it since our departure, but in the afternoon it fell to 28 inches 5 and 28 inches 6 where it seemed to tend to fix itself.
At the beginning of the night I ordered that we sound again every two hours and I shall continue to take this precaution until we have passed the banks of which I have just spoken, from the uncertainty of their true position.
During the night of the 2nd to the 3rd the weather was very fine and clear. With winds from the east-south-east, fine breeze and even rather fresh since it obliged us to take a second reef in the topgallant sail. We sounded several times in the night without finding bottom at 70 and 80 fathoms. We continued to steer to the north by north-east although at midnight I estimated I had passed the Abrolhos banks, the sea having become very fine, we were no longer tormented as we had been on the previous days by the movements of the vessel.
1801-06-21.journal_breton_geographe: Misty weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW, SSW, S, SE, ESE and E, with light rain. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude by account and corrected, and in 109° 30' of longitude by account. Variation 5° 1' NW. At 10 sounded without finding bottom at 70 fathoms.

1801-06-22.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from the east. Everything Citizen Milius, lieutenant, asked for to repair the longboat was sent to him.
1801-06-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 3rd, in the morning, fair weather continued and the sky was obscured by no clouds. The winds were from the east-south-east slightly variable to the east but in the morning they were so weak that we advanced little.
As soon as it was light I ordered the course to be steered to the north-east by north and at sunrise land was sighted from the tops of the masts which leads me to believe that we have passed much closer to the Abrolhos banks than the dead reckoning of the course I had made indicated.
At ten o'clock we had perfect knowledge of the land from the deck. It presented itself to us under a very regular form and we were even somewhat astonished to see a considerable extent of coast offer us no point which could be remarked in preference to another. Only the coast seemed to us higher than all those we had previously seen and the mountains which form its elevation are much closer to the shore than at the coast of Leeuwin where they are truly situated quite far inland.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 27° 24' 16" south and the longitude according to the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 109° 48' 54" and for No. 35 of 110° 4' 53".
Starting from the latitude observed on the first of Messidor we found a difference to the south of 35 miles, occasioned without doubt by the currents supposing that the dead reckoning made according to the ordinary usage is good.
In the afternoon the calm continued until two o'clock but then we had a light breeze from the south which passing afterwards to the south-south-east increased as the sun descended towards the horizon. We took advantage of this breeze to close with the land of which a little before sunset we were at two and a half leagues or at most three leagues. We distinguished then perfectly all the coast from the east-south-east to the north. But the appearance far from being fine and agreeable like that of the coast of Leeuwin offered us everywhere nothing but a considerable elevation and on which no trees were to be seen but only a kind of grass or moss of a very dark often blackish colour. Everywhere on the slope facing the sea ravines could be distinguished occasioned without doubt by the drainage of rainwater. In several places the ground was bare and we judged from the colour that it must be sand.
The shores of the sea appeared to us likewise cut sheer and so steep-to that there must be deep water and even in quantity right up to the land.
For the rest I do not remember having seen any country which offered me a view as disagreeable as this part of the Lands of Concord. Seven or eight leagues of coast which we had time to examine well before nightfall have no other merit than being very safe and easy for navigation although they offer no shelter, even for a boat. What remains for us to see until the bay of the Sea Dogs of Dampier will perhaps be more interesting. But it is only too probable that all this coast is similar to itself and the part of the Lands of Leeuwin is infinitely better although the terrain is of sand as is this one.
After sunset and at the beginning of night I directed my course so as to follow the coast at a distance of three or four leagues. The winds being always from the south-south-east, fine breeze, and the sea fair. We steered successively to the north, to the north by north-west, to the north-north-west, to the north-west by north and finally to the north-west. At seven o'clock we sounded and found no bottom at fifty fathoms. As this coast appears to be of no interest for navigation still less for natural history I did not think I ought to stop at it especially as the plan the Dutch have made of it appeared to me
to be fairly well done. I have merely taken views of the coast which will give an idea of what it can be.
At eight o'clock I ordered course to be made to the north-west until midnight and that I would continue it until day if before that time a line of fifty fathoms did not bring up bottom.
During the night of the 3rd to the 4th we had no bottom at fifty fathoms up to that epoch but from nine o'clock to eleven o'clock we found it of fine sand at 55 and 53 fathoms and at one o'clock after midnight we had it at seventy-five fathoms rock bottom. In the rest of the night sounding was neglected and according to the reason given me by the officer it appears that this is my fault for not having told him that he must do it every hour as had been done until then when we were in the neighbourhood of the coast or when we did not wish to go too far from it.
However it is good to say that having stood watch myself until midnight I said to the officer who relieved me: you are in fifty-two fathoms of water you will continue the same course and at one o'clock when you sound if the bottom increases you will go off a quarter to windward and if on the contrary it decreases you will bear away a quarter. It seems to me that this order was not meant to say to sound only at one o'clock which would have been against our usual and long-established practices.
For the rest the night was without incident the weather was fine and the winds from the south-south-east a fine breeze and fair sea.

1801-06-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to south. At 7 the land was sighted; it stretched from N 45° E to east. The course was given N 33° 45' E. The sea was covered with weed. At noon in 27° 23' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 48' 54" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 27' 20" NW. The land from N 19° E to S 80° E. At 4 it stretched from N 11° E to S 34° E. We bore up N 45° W to run along the coast, which lies roughly NNW and SSE. It does not offer the same appearance as the Leeuwin land: it is very high and sheer. Not a tree is to be made out. At 9.30 shaped the course N 67° 30' W and carried little sail. At 9 the lead gave 55 fathoms and at 11, 52 fathoms, sandy bottom.

1801-06-23.journal_anonyme: At two in the afternoon the hand mill was set up aft on the port side. At 4 p.m. the large boat was back from her expedition; Citizen Heirisson brought a bottle of fresh water which he had got in the upper part of the Swan River. At 11 p.m. we put the repaired longboat in the water. The wind a fresh breeze from the east.
1801-06-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 4th at daybreak we had no knowledge of the land in that we continued up to that time to run to the NO ¼ west the vessel making 7 to 8 knots. However at four o'clock in the morning having asked the helmsman how much water had been found at this sounding, it was he who informed me that for an hour no plumb-line had been cast. I then gave the course to the NO ¼ north and at daybreak we held as close-hauled as possible with all sail set.
When I came on deck I asked the officer who was far from being at his post why he had not warned me that we could not see the land. His reply was that he had not received the order. It was moreover made with such bad grace that I turned my back on him and went to tell the master to rig the topgallant sails. When they were in position the sailors asked several times if they should shake them out; I told them yes. Then the watch officer, Citizen Picquet, for I must name him, told me that since I was commanding myself he would leave the watch. "You are perfectly free to do so" I replied "and even for the whole campaign if it pleases you". He withdrew and I continued his watch.
At ten o'clock the look-outs sighted the land and a little later we saw it ourselves from the deck. We continued to run towards it and at noon we were still about three leagues distant. By the latitude observed at the same epoch we recognised that it was the southern point of the island of Dirk Hartog. It lay then to the SE ¼ east of us. And we had observed 26° 1' 15" of south latitude the longitude of the timekeepers for the same moment was 109° 2' 48" for No. 27 and 109° 18' 29" for No. 35. The dead reckoning of the course travelled in twenty-four hours gave a difference of 17 minutes to the south.
In the evening we followed at a league's distance the western coast of the island of Dirk Hartog which offered to us throughout its whole extent an aspect that was arid disagreeable and sad and finally worse than the part of the Lands of Concord which we had seen the day before. The sea broke all along the coast with great force and often we saw it rise to the height of the cliffs which are cut sheer and straight as a wall without any noticeable slope to the eye. We cast the lead from time to time but never found bottom at 25 fathoms. It is true that the vessel was making much progress or at least appeared to be from the log. But the time it took us to pass from one point to another and the frequent tide-rips we encountered could only too well teach us that the current was extremely violent in this part and that it had its direction to the south-south-west.
All the vegetation we perceived on the island was reduced to some species of heath and grass of a very dark colour. Still this variety appeared quite rarely. The coast was in horizontal layers of sand and without doubt granite which we shall be better able to verify when we are in the bay of the Sea Dogs of Dampier.
At sunset we were abreast of the north-west point of this island. The land makes a bend to the north-east and seems afterwards to extend to the north as is very well represented by my Dutch chart. A little later we had knowledge of the Sterile islands which we approached as closely as the remaining daylight allowed.
During the night of the 4th to the 5th the weather was very fine and a fine breeze blew from the south-south-east. From the bearings taken at sunset and at four seven hours in the evening I directed my course to the north sounding every hour. At ten o'clock as the bottom decreased by six fathoms I bore to the north-north-west and at one o'clock having increased by five fathoms I resumed the course to the north until two o'clock when I resolved to run a little course to the south-west and at four o'clock until daybreak another to the east-north-east. As at two or three leagues at most from the Sterile islands we had fairly constantly found 52 fathoms
of water it seemed quite natural to me to maintain this same depth while making course to the north persuaded that the next day at daybreak I should find myself in sight of and near the part which forms the entrance of the bay. What we see tomorrow morning will show whether this reasoning is sound and whether the currents from which so far I have not been able to guard myself will always work against us contrary to our expectation.
During the night of the 4th to the 5th the weather was fine nevertheless the atmosphere was charged with humid vapours although there were few clouds which sometimes described a circle around the moon which was not at all pleasant to see.

At noon the same land extended from NE to SE five leagues estimated distance. It was the last of the Sterile islands or the one forming the entrance to the bay of the Sea Dogs.
Note: in the morning of the 4th Citizen Picquet who had withdrawn from his watch in the morning came to see me in my cabin where he explained to me how offended he had been by what I had ordered to be done in different manoeuvres without warning him by asking me permission to resume his service. I took this opportunity to warn him that any officer who abandoned his watch cut a poor figure and that besides I found him little fitted for a campaign such as the one I was making. This officer full of self-esteem thinks himself much more learned than he really is especially in practice. Although my intention was not for him to resume his service on board I nevertheless consented to his request and I hope another occasion does not present itself to remove all kind of command from him on board.

1801-06-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to south. At 1 shaped the course N 56° 15' W; at 5 shaped the course N 33° 45' W and crowded sail. At 7 the commander gave orders directly to the helmsman to steer N 22° 30' E, and had the yards trimmed, taking no notice of Citizen Piquet, the officer of the watch, who observed to him that he was useless on deck and that he would leave the watch if the commander wished; and on his orders he left it. At 9 the land was sighted; at noon it bore from us N 11° E to S 56° E. At noon in 26° 1' 35" of latitude observed and in 109° 2' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 20' NW. Bore up north and ran along the west coast of Dirk Hartog Island. We passed through tide rips whose direction was north and south and whose strength may have been 3 to 4 knots, for despite our apparent speed of 6 to 7 knots we doubled the land only very slowly. At 4 bore up N 22° 30' E, at 5 N 33° 45' E. At 5.15 took the bearing of the west point of Dirk Hartog S 22° 30' W and the north point S 78° E; the southernmost of the Dorre islands from N 30° E to N 40° E. At 6 set topsails, heading N 11° 15' E. At 7, Dorre Island from N 50° E to N 8° [E]. Bore up north and N 22° 30' W to draw off from it.

1801-06-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from ENE to NE and NNE. The longboat was put on her chocks. The large boat was sent off to help Citizen Saint-Cricq, to go to the island lying south of the anchorage.
1801-06-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 5th in the morning we had knowledge of the land from the south-east 5° east but it was only seen from the tops of the masts. The winds were then from the south-east fine breeze and we were holding as close-hauled as possible with the course to the east-north-east which should have brought us to close with it promptly but despite the fact that we had all sails set and the vessel was making according to the log four and three knots we could never get close enough to see it from the deck so much did the current prevent us from making headway.
In the morning the breeze calmed considerably and at noon the vessel could scarcely be steered. At the same epoch we observed the latitude which was 24° 18' 33" which placed us by the northern point of the most advanced of the Sterile islands consequently at the opening of the bay of the Sea Dogs into which I wished to enter. The little freshness there was then shifted to the north-east and we took the starboard tack immediately.
In the evening the calm continued and we advanced very little. However at five o'clock we began to see the land from below which lay to the east-north-east to the east. I continued until eight o'clock to hold as close-hauled as possible to starboard the winds varying from east to south-east very weak. At eight o'clock we took the starboard course making very little progress from the calm then prevailing. The bottom was 40 fathoms fine grey sand.
During the night I ordered that soundings be taken every hour according to custom and as I had stood the last watch on deck the watch officer was ordered to warn me if the bottom came to decrease my intention being to drop an anchor by the run if it were calm and we should be in thirty or thirty-five fathoms of water.
From eight o'clock until midnight the weather was rather fine and the moon illuminated the horizon very agreeably. But at that epoch it became covered with clouds and the moon until morning was constantly surrounded by an auréole which rendered its aspect disagreeable and seemed to indicate a change in weather and even winds which I feared to see shift to the north-west in that the sea although still fine was raised by a considerable swell coming from that part of the horizon extremely charged with dark thick clouds.
At two o'clock having perceived the land in the east-north-east quarter I set the course to the north. We were then in 40 fathoms fine very fine grey sand. The winds variable from east-south-east to east-north-east very weak we likewise diminished sail so as not to go too far north to keep ourselves at the opening of the bay where I wished to come to anchor.

1801-06-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from south to NE. At 2 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 4 went onto the starboard tack and crowded sail to close the land. At 8 the northernmost Dorre island S 50° E. At noon in 24° 18' of latitude observed and in 109° 3' 26" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 23' NW. At noon went onto the port tack; at 5 the land from N 68° E to N 85° E; at 8 went onto the starboard tack. Saw very large sharks.

1801-06-25.journal_anonyme: At 2 p.m. the dinghy was back; she was sent off again under the orders of the second petty officers. A strong breeze from NE to NNE.
1801-06-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 6th of Messidor at daybreak we held as close-hauled as possible in the north-east direction as much as the winds would permit in order to close with the coast and make its reconnaissance. According to my dead reckoning and making allowance for the progress the currents might have caused us by the previous day's calm I estimated myself to be at the northern extremity of the last of the Sterile islands consequently at the opening of the bay of the Sea Dogs into which I reckoned to enter the same day. But the weather had such a bad appearance that I cherished little hope of arriving there.
The entire horizon from the south-west to the north-west was so dark and charged with great black thick clouds that I had not yet seen a sky with so bad an appearance. The sun was likewise obscured by many clouds accumulated one upon another which rendered the atmosphere very disagreeable to the eye. Nevertheless the barometer which I consulted often descended slowly and seemed to remain at 28 inches 2 lines of 28 inches 3 and 5 which was its height the day before. As it had not yet deceived us I pleased myself to believe that the weather would become fair incessantly and that the east winds would soon cause the piles of clouds to disappear which nevertheless caused me some uneasiness.
Despite the bad appearance of the weather I resolved to close with the land and for that purpose I went about before the wind at nine o'clock with all sails set.
At a quarter to ten o'clock the breeze first increased a little and then the weather came in squalls with strong gusts and rain so that it appeared to me that the bad weather was determined and about to break out although the winds were still in the north-east to north-east by east quarter. In consequence of this fear which appeared to me only too well founded I went about before the wind and took the course of the offing in order to support it more easily should it come to declare itself.
After having changed course with the wind and gusts continually increasing I had the main sail furled and took all reefs in the topsails.
At eleven o'clock the rain the wind and the gusts ceased. The sky although no clearer nevertheless had a better appearance and I flattered myself that soon a fine sky would replace that which we had had in the morning.
At one o'clock we resumed the course towards the land which we continued until five o'clock in the evening when it was necessary to resume the offing course. The wind was then very uncertain and the sea although it was almost calm for us was driven by two very great swells one coming from the north-west and the other from the north-east. The sky became covered anew with clouds and fog. Although we were rather close to land when we went about the bearings which were taken were very unsatisfactory and we were all the less certain of our position in that we could not observe the sun at noon or know thereby if the currents had carried us in the direction which they had had up to then.
About six o'clock we perceived two great volumes of smoke on land and at nightfall we saw perfectly the fires which were causing it. As the Sterile islands are not inhabited it seemed to me that these fires were a little to the north of the point of mainland which forms the entrance to the bay and which lay to us then at the east 18° south.
During the night the winds were almost calm and the sky overcast and dark. We made little progress in sounding every half hour in order to know if the currents were carrying us on land or if we were going seaward as the course we were making should carry us and even the current for at that epoch it should according to my previous observations have had ebb tide. For the rest whether the tides carried us to land or to the offing we were sufficiently far from the coast to have nothing to fear from the effect which they could have.

1801-06-25.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to NE. At 2 a.m., having sighted the land in the N 68° E, headed north under topsails. At daybreak it stretched from S 45° E to S 79° E. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under all sail. At 9 went onto the port tack; the wind freshened. At 10, the wind a strong breeze, lay to on the starboard tack under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon the land S 67° 30' E, being in 23° 56' 40" of latitude by account and in 109° 15' 32" of longitude by account. At 1 lay to on the port tack. At 4.30 the land in sight from S 45° E to S 68° E, about 24 miles off. A very thick column of smoke in the S 72° E. At 5.30 filled and stood on on the starboard tack under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail.

1801-06-26.journal_anonyme: At 3.30 p.m. the large boat was back from her mission. At 10 a.m. fired three swivel guns and hoisted a flag at the masthead to recall the dinghy, which was ashore. A light breeze from W.
1801-06-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 7th in the morning the weather turned fair although the sky remained covered. The great heaps of clouds accumulated one upon another which we had seen the day before had disappeared and we had the hope that we could observe the meridian altitude at noon. The great swell from the NW had likewise disappeared so we took the course towards the land in order to close with it and make its proper reconnaissance. We accordingly shook out our reefs in the topsails and set all sails.
At sunrise knowledge of the coast was had which extended in relation to our position from the north-east to the east-south-east.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 23° 50' 45" which as I had suspected placed me north of the entrance to the bay. As we could not take an hour angle in the morning nor in the evening the sun having appeared only about noon we have not been able to fix the longitude of the cape or point upon which we were directing our course. However at four o'clock an hour angle was taken which although somewhat doubtful placed us then at 109° 23' 32" for No. 27 and 109° 38' 30" for No. 35.
In the afternoon we continued to make course towards the land all sails set the weather being very fine and the sea calm. We coasted fairly close to a large extent of the coast to the north of the entrance to the bay and we could distinctly perceive a long chain of reefs which although close to land offer no place for a boat to land. The view I give of this coast will show how arid and disagreeable it is to the eye.
At sunset the wind calmed considerably and not to be carried to the offing by the current or driven too far inshore I resolved to anchor as soon as I should have good holding ground of thirty to thirty-five fathoms which caused me to remain under canvas until seven three-quarters o'clock when having then thirty-four fathoms at a league and a half from land at most I dropped an anchor from the cat-head proposing to remain in the position I then had until the next morning at daybreak. We veered out eighty fathoms of cable and I thought myself very secure.
Nevertheless at half-past nine we were obliged to weigh our anchor the vessel in spite of the little wind that was blowing continuously drifting to the north-west. As I could not persuade myself that the anchor was badly placed it seemed quite natural to me to believe that the bottom was hard and that it had not been able to take but when it was hove up we found that the cable made a cross over the fluke of the anchor and we recognised the cause which was making us drift. It is rather difficult to conceive how this cross was made in anchoring for according to the master's report the anchor and cable were well cleared. However it seems to me that there was too much of the latter at the hawsehole and the anchor in falling must surely have become entangled in the slack of the cable.
During the night of the 7th to the 8th the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate. We spent it tacking back and forth so that at daybreak we found ourselves about the same place where we had dropped our anchor the day before.
Bearings of the land in the 24 hours of the 7th to the 8th of Messidor.
The lands in view most to the north to the north 10° east at sunset.
The lands closest to us abreast to the south 78° east. " " ".
The southernmost point in view to the south. " " ".
Bearings of the anchorage where we dropped our anchor:
The great cape which we believe forms the entrance to the bay to the north at the north 33° 45' east mainland. A point to the north 55° east. "".
The land most to the south in view to the south 45° east. "".
Bearings at four o'clock in the morning:
The lands most to the north in view to the NE two and a half leagues distance.
Bearings at seven o'clock in the morning:
The land most to the north in view to the north 25° east.
A point high and sheer to the north 65° east.
The lands to the south most in view to the east 80° south.
Bearings at noon:
The southern point of the Sterile islands to the south 51° west.
The point most to the north in view on the continent to the north 25° east.

Soundings and nature of the bottom during the 24 hours of the 7th to the 8th of Messidor.
From noon to four o'clock continuously 30 fathoms fine sand.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock in the evening from 33 to 31 same bottom.
From eight o'clock to midnight 35 fathoms white sand.
From midnight to four o'clock 35 33 30 same bottom.
From four to eight o'clock in the morning 30 and 31 fine sand.
From eight o'clock to noon 30 25 and 20 same bottom.
Note: the entrance to the bay of the Sea Dogs to the north is very recognisable. The lands forming the opening of the bay in this part are high and steep. The Dutch plan gives a very exact and very well done view of it. Of all the charts we have this is the most exact and best done. It appears that the Dutch have taken great care in making the bearing of all this coast on which they might well have views for whale fishing which is the only resource it can present.
These fish are in such great quantities there that one is often inconvenienced by them and boats sometimes run risks from the enormous masses of water they raise which appear to be reefs where the sea breaks furiously.
Lands of Concord. Bearings.
On the 6th at sunrise the lands extended from the east ¼ south-east to the south-east.
At noon the same lands remained at the east-south-east three leagues distance.
At four o'clock in the evening the lands of the continent showed themselves to the east 22° south.
A very thick volume of smoke was seen to the east 18° south.
1801-06-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to SE. At daybreak the land was sighted from the topgallant crosstrees; crowded sail to close it. At 9 went onto the port tack. At noon in 23° 47' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 30" of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 80° E and the southernmost S 12° E. We ran along the land to the north of the bay. At 5 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight N 40° E; a large cape, the nearest, forming the entrance to Shark Bay, S 57° E; the land in sight as far as south. At 7.45 anchored abreast of a cove in 34 fathoms, sandy bottom, the large cape bearing N 33° 45' E and the entrance of the cove from N 55° E to S 45° E. At 10 got under way, because we were dragging and the current was setting us onto the coast; our anchor had fouled its stock. Shaped our course N 11° 15' W, running along the coast at a short distance.

1801-06-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from W to WSW. The dinghy came aboard at 3 p.m. and brought back a sea snake. At 7.30 on the 8th the captain embarked in the large boat. The winds from the south drew round to the east.
1801-06-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, in the morning, we crowded sail to run into the bay. The weather was very fine and the sea smooth. We ran along the whole coast, which is high in this part, at a very small distance, in order to keep well to windward of the Barren Isles, which I expected to see at any moment. From eight o'clock until noon, it blew a fresh breeze from the eastward, and we were forced to shorten sail in order to sound more at our ease.
About eleven o'clock, the land to the north was already far from us, and nothing more could be seen but the summits of the highest hillocks, which seemed to form a chain of islands. This is doubtless the appearance presented by the whole of this coast, which has led many navigators who have not approached it closely enough to believe that there were many islands off the continent. But it is none the less true that from Cape Leeuwin to the north of Dirk Hartog Island, none exist except Rottnest Island and the islets in its neighbourhood. And the whole of the land lying between the former and Dirk Hartog Island is a continent which may be run along very closely throughout its whole extent.
After Dirk Hartog Island come the Barren Isles, of which it doubtless itself forms a part, for it has no advantage over those to the north of it except that of being a little higher. But the eye rests with no more pleasure on the one than on the other.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 24° 38' 1" and the longitude was found, by good observations, to be 109° 23' 32" for No. 25 (sic) and 109° 38' 30" for No. 25 (sic)
At the same moment, the southernmost point of the Barren Isles bore from us south 51° west, the northernmost land of the continent north 25° east, and the easternmost land in sight south 7° east.
At one o'clock the breeze began to lull, and at two we came to an anchor in 16 fathoms of water, a bottom of black and muddy sand. We paid out 70 fathoms of cable.
As soon as we were at anchor, I sent a boat ashore on the first of the Barren Isles to reconnoitre the coast and see whether landing there was easy. Citizen Riedelé embarked in it, and steered a course for a sandy cove which we had abeam.
During the evening the weather continued fine, and it fell almost a dead calm, so that the ship could never swing head to wind, the current being stronger and having a speed of one mile according to the log. It set to the north-west on the ebb.
When the boat had gone, I sent to sound at one and two cables' length around the ship. We found astern 19 fathoms, on the port side 18, on the starboard side 17, and ahead 17 fathoms, black and muddy sand such as we had had in the 20 fathoms.
The rest of the evening had nothing particular. I only informed the naturalists that if the report made on the boat's return should be favourable, I would go ashore the next day, and that those who wished to accompany me might make their preparations beforehand.
In the night of the eighth to the ninth, the winds were almost calm and variable from the east to the north-west. We continually heard the blowing of whales, and by means of the fine moonlight that prevailed, we could easily make out the places where they were disporting themselves.
At ten minutes past eight, the tide was slack, and shortly after the flood began.
About two o'clock in the night, the longboat returned on board, but as I had not rested for a long time and had retired to my cabin, I was not informed of its return.
Bearings of the anchorage.
The southernmost land of the Barren Isles in sight, west 43° south.
The northernmost point of the first of the Barren Isles, west 16° north
The northernmost point of the continent in sight, north 56° east.
1801-06-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SSE. At midnight steered north, running along the coast. At 4 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack; the large cape then bore from us N 45° E, 9 miles off. At 8 bore away south, S 11° 15' W and S 22° 30' W to enter Shark Bay. At 7 the large cape bore from us N 65° E. At 10 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the south. At noon in 24° 38' of latitude observed and in 109° 23' of longitude by No. 27. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island S 51° W, and the mainland from N 25° E to S 7° E. At 2.30 anchored in Shark Bay in 16 fathoms, muddy sand, the northern Dorre island bearing from N 74° W to S 47° W and the northernmost mainland N 56° E. The large boat, under the orders of Bonnefoi, was sent off to Dorre Island. At 4 the current ran 1 knot, the ebb making, its direction NW. At 8 a fire was seen on Dorre Island, lit by our boat's crew. At 8.15 the tide turned, the flood beginning. During the night a light was kept at the gaff.

1801-06-28.journal_anonyme: We made ready to get under way. On the 9th at 7 a.m. we got under way with the winds NE, a fresh breeze. At noon we sounded in 26 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. The weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky without cloud.
1801-06-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Anchorage in Dampier's Dogs' Marine Bay.
On the ninth, in the morning, Citizen Bonnefoy, to whom I had entrusted the command of my boat to go and reconnoitre the coast, having told me he had landed with great ease in two convenient coves, I had both the large and small boats immediately armed, in which all the naturalists embarked. The gardener who had accompanied Bonnefoy the previous day had brought back two bundles of different plants which he had gathered by moonlight and which had appeared to him all new. So that, although he had passed the greater part of the night, he wished to return again.
At eight o'clock, the two boats put off, I embarked in one and the other was entrusted to Citizen Picquet. We carried with us a seine and everything necessary for fishing and hunting. And we set out so confident that we should take a great quantity of fish that we neglected every sort of provisions except biscuit and water.
When we departed, the sky was fair and the wind calm. We were two hours in reaching land because all the oarsmen of the boats, who had not been selected, could not swim.
About eleven o'clock, the sky became covered with clouds, without that, for all that, it had bad appearance. I was the more vexed by this as it would prevent me from observing the latitude on shore and from taking hour angles there. But the others were pleased by it because this weather seemed to them more suitable for fishing, hunting and the excursions that each proposed to make.
Our first care, when the large boat was empty, was to place it on its grapnel in a place of safety and the small boat was arranged to haul out the seine.
The first two attempts that we made were not successful, for we took nothing at all. We then began to regret that we had not embarked something to accompany our biscuit but it was too late.
The gardener and the other naturalists advanced into the island to examine its productions. Maugé and I gave chase to the birds and each received orders to be returned to the shore by five o'clock at the latest to dine there and then return on board.
Our different excursions into the interior of the island produced for us twelve or fifteen species of new plants, two very fine lizards and seven birds, two of which are particularly remarkable for the beauty of their plumage. We also saw some kangaroos. I even shot one, but I presumably only frightened it, for after receiving the gunshot, it ran away as before.
The terrain forming the island on which we were is sand sometimes mixed with some rock platforms of fairly hard grain. The greater part of the shrubs growing on this barren land were in flower or ready to flower. The tallest that we encountered in all our excursions had not more than ten feet of height. Only one, on the summit of the hillock, could have fifteen to eighteen feet, but Nature, to punish it for rising so high, had condemned it to death for we found it in that state. The thickest trunk of all the shrubs that we encountered could have seven to eight inches of diameter. But this thickness is rarely seen in them.
Chance had made us land in the place of the island where vegetation was strongest for those who crossed it from north to south were quite vexed to have taken that trouble, for they encountered everywhere only arid sands and many rock platforms on which there was not even moss. What had decided us to undertake this excursion came from the fact that we believed we had recognised many traces of a fairly large cloven-footed animal and we hoped to see it by covering much ground, but we found nothing, only we saw some snakes of black colour and even fairly large.
On returning to the shore, we saw with pleasure that the boat crews had
taken about a hundred fish among which there were some very pretty ones from the variety of their colours. But in general, they were all of a small species and very much resembling that of sardines, which was indeed the name we gave them. The largest resembled the whiting of Europe well enough in form and taste. However, we believed we observed that this one had the head more elongated.
When the distribution had been made, we cooked our share for dinner and it was found that everything was very good. As there was little, I confined myself to eating oysters and crabs of which good provision had been made.
At low tide, we found on the reefs bordering the beach in different places, very fine sea-snails, some ordinary ears (?) and a fine Crown of Ethiopia with its fish which doubtless is not as in Europe and of which I give a drawing. We also gathered some fairly fine mussels and several other ordinary shells and especially barnacles of which the sailors made good cheer.
At five o'clock, everyone had returned except Citizen Péron who, having doubtless yielded to his ardour, had advanced too far to be back at the appointed time. While waiting for him, we sat down to dinner and we dined without him, for he did not return.
At six o'clock, the people I had sent to meet him returning without having caught sight of him, I returned on board in the large boat and left Citizen Picquet on shore with the small one to wait for him, giving him orders to come on board as soon as the moon should rise, the sky not having too fair an appearance.
At half past nine, we arrived on board by a very calm and very dark time and as we distinguished two great fires on shore, one especially very high on the dunes, we concluded that Citizen Péron was not yet back and that presumably he had lost his way in the island which, as I was told, he had the project of crossing.
On my return on board, I was informed that during the day more than six hundred pounds of good fish had been caught on the line independently of two or three dog-fish which everyone found very good to eat. This news pleased me the more as it made me forget the regret I had at not having taken fish for everyone with the seine.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth, the sky cleared and we had, about two o'clock, the winds at south-east strong breeze, which was not convenient for the return of the boat which had no water and very few other provisions.
Bearings of the anchorage.
The southernmost lands of the Sterile Islands in sight south 47° west
The northernmost point of the first of these two islands west 16° north
The northernmost lands in sight of the continent north 56° east
1801-06-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SSE. At midnight Bonnefoi came back with the large boat. At 7.30 a.m. the commander and all the naturalists went to Dorre Island in the two boats. Saw a great number of whales; fish were taken in abundance and some were salted. At nightfall our people lit a fire ashore; we showed a light at each masthead and burnt flares every half hour. At 9.30 the commander and the naturalists arrived in the large boat. The small one had stayed ashore under the orders of Citizen Piquet, to wait for the zoologist Péron, who had not appeared at the hour fixed for departure.

1801-06-29.journal_anonyme: The weather hazy and squally, with lightning in the west. At 2 p.m. the lead brought up 27 fathoms, grey sand, coral and gravel. The wind ESE, variable to SE. At 11.30 a current was observed setting from NNW to SSE.
1801-06-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, in the morning, it blew a strong breeze from the south-south-east and at sunrise, we did not yet see the boat return, proof that Citizen Péron had not closed with it during the night and that he had passed it somewhere on the island, not knowing where he was.
At last, by dint of looking, we caught sight of the boat under sail about ten o'clock, tacking to return on board where it arrived with considerable difficulty at one in the afternoon. Fortunately Citizen Péron was in it. After coming aboard, he presented himself to me in the most pitiful state, not having eaten for twenty-four hours, and exhausted with fatigue, having wandered almost all the night until, falling from weariness, he fell into a deep sleep at the foot of a bush until day when, having oriented himself, he returned to the shore where he found the people who were in pursuit of him.
As he is to make me a report of his adventure, I shall limit myself here to what I could say about it, but I promised him well that when he returned to shore, I would have him accompanied by someone who, not losing sight of him, would answer to me that he would be returned to the place of departure at the time which would be appointed.
As it was too late to set sail, we passed the rest of the day and all the night, which was fine, at anchor. The winds almost calm.
1801-06-29.journal_breton_geographe: Latitude observed at the anchorage 24° 46' 20"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 20' 40". Variation, the mean of 7 observations at the anchorage, 6° 1' 7" NW. The tides set NW and SE, and the sea rises 7½ feet. At half past noon the small boat arrived, bringing back Citizen Péron, who, having gone too far into the island, had lost himself there and passed the night in the scrub; at daybreak he had found our people. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S and SSE.

1801-06-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSE, variable to ENE and N. At eight in the evening the lead brought up 24 fathoms, sand and rock [several words illegible] every half hour. At midnight we hove to with the port side to the wind. At 7.45 went about onto the starboard tack. Bearings taken at noon: the northernmost peak NE by N; the one to the NE, NE 1° N; the southernmost NE 1° E.
1801-06-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, at sunrise, we set sail to come and reconnoitre the mainland coast to the east of the anchorage we were leaving. The winds were then at south-south-east very weak, variable to the south-east. We made course, close-hauled on the starboard tack and all sails set, sounding constantly. During the morning, we had from sixteen fathoms of sand bottom to thirteen, same bottom.
We saw, all morning, a great quantity of whales all around us which afforded great recreation aboard. They are so little wild in these waters that they came always close to the vessels and it would have been easy for us to shoot them with rifle fire if a ball could have killed them.
At noon, the observed latitude was 24° 40' 5" and the longitude, indicated by the timekeepers, was, for No. 27 of 109° 21' 23" and for No. 35 of 109° 31' 47". The land most to the north in sight then bore from us north 5° east and that most to the east, also in sight, at east 5° north. We had, then, thirteen fathoms of water, bottom of grey sand. But perceiving very white water ahead of us at about a league distance, I had a boat put to sea which I sent to sound ahead of the vessel with orders to stop when it found itself in good anchorage between nine and ten fathoms. I gave the command of it to Citizen Bonnefoy who executed this commission with great intelligence.
At one o'clock, being in perfect calm and having the beginning of the ebb tide, I had the anchor laid out in ten fathoms, bottom of grey sand and recalled the boat aboard.
As soon as we were at anchor and our sails furled, I had it depart again with Citizen Bougainville to go and reconnoitre the coast and seek a suitable place for disembarkation to send it to be visited. I very seriously recommended to M. Bougainville not to commit himself at night and to return aboard without landing if he had not time to reconnoitre before sunset a suitable place for disembarkation.
At two o'clock, the boat put off and MM. Depuche and Riedelé Bernier, having wished to embark in it, accompanied Citizen Bougainville.
During the night of the eleventh to the twelfth, the weather was very fine and the winds at south-east variable towards the south almost calm. At one o'clock at night, my boat returned and its commander having reported to me that he had approached the land in four fathoms of water and that he had not been able to approach nearer, because everywhere he had found the coast bordered by a reef on which the sea broke with great violence although it was calm. This reef, according to Citizen Bougainville and those who accompanied him, advances nearly a league into the sea and it would be useless to seek to land there, at least in the place where they landed and in the space of a league and a half of coast which he covered before nightfall and his return aboard.
Bearings of the lands at our second anchorage in Sea Dogs Bay.
The northernmost land in sight of the first of the Sterile Islands at west 11° 15' north.
The easternmost land of the continent in sight at east 22° 30' south.
The view which I give of the coast of the continent renders, as well as possible, the aspect which the coast presented to us, then, and the outlook is not agreeable.
Soundings from the first to the second anchorage.
Having departed from 16 fathoms, bottom of sand and mud, it was always diminishing gradually to 10 fathoms, same bottom. At eleven o'clock, I dispatched the small boat to sound ahead of the vessel at about a league distance from the place where we anchored, it having signalled to us only eight fathoms, I stopped, the winds being almost calm and the ebb tide contrary.
Bearings of the anchorage. Sea Dogs Bay
The northernmost lands of the first Sterile Island at west 15° 15' north
The (lands) most to the east of the continent which were in sight at east 22° 30' south
The lands of the continent in sight in the northern part from the east to the northeast by east
1801-06-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SW. At 7.30 got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, N 67° 30' E, east and S 67° 30' E, the small boat sounding ahead. Saw a turtle. At noon in 24° 44' 4" of latitude observed and in 109° 26' 8" of longitude by No. 27. At 1 anchored in 9 fathoms, fine sand, the north point of the northern Dorre island bearing N 79° W, the mainland S 67° 30' E about 12 miles off. At 2.15 the small boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Bougainville to survey the mainland. During the night a light was kept and a flare burnt every half hour to mark our position for the boat. Variation 5° 22' at the anchorage. At midnight she was back; it had been impossible for Citizen Bougainville to land because of the bar, which broke with force all along the coast and two cables from the shore.

1801-07-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds varying from N to NNW and W. At noon and at four o'clock went about. At 5 p.m. sounded every half hour in 27, 24, 23, 23, 24 and 25 fathoms, rock and coral bottom. We had a great deal of rain during the night. At 4 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Noon bearings: the end of the great southern cliff E 25° 15' S; the north end of the next great cliff E 7° 15' S, estimated distance 11 miles.
1801-07-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, being informed by the reports of the previous day that there was no possibility of landing in the place where I had anchored the day before, I got under way at daybreak to come and reconnoitre the island which is found in the middle of the bay and of which I flattered myself to have knowledge during the morning, if it continued to blow as it did when we set sail. But, about ten o'clock, the breeze which was then at the east variable to the east-south-east, began to calm and at noon, the vessel was moved only by the current which at that time was still in our favour.
We had, during all the morning, the spectacle of several whales playing on the waters and, although it was no longer new for us, everyone still saw it with as much pleasure as if it had been for the first time.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 25° 0' 21" and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us at the same time, by 109° 29' 50" on No. 27 and by 109° 43' 54" on No. 35.
From several series of distances of the sun to the moon taken during the morning, the average gave 109° 25' 43", so that our timekeepers seemed to differ only 11' 9" to the west, which requires for confirmation, a longer series of observations.
In the afternoon, although we were in perfect calm, we remained under sail until four o'clock in the hope that the offshore breeze might come to us. But the ebb tide being then against us, and the vessel drifting much to the north-east, we furled our sails and anchored in 13 fathoms, fine bottom of grey sand.
At sunset, we gained knowledge of a portion of the second of the Sterile Islands which then bore from us at west 5° north. We also saw throughout, a continuation of the same island bearing to the south-west. It is by error or want of knowledge of the places that the officer who was then on watch marked in his bearing of the sunset or of half past four, the time when we anchored, a small island, for none exists in this part.
During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth, the wind was calm until about ten o'clock at night when there came to us a small freshness from the south-east and which lasted the rest of the night during which the weather was very fine.
Soundings while we were under sail.
On getting under way in 10 fathoms of water, we diminished augmented the bottom (un)til noon when we were in 13 fathoms, sand and seaweed in long narrow leaves.
From noon to the moment we anchored, we maintained the bottom of 13 fathoms by which we let fall a bower anchor.
Note: While the time we were under sail in calm, the dredge was cast several times which brought us, in objects of natural history, several fine starfish of a new species, many shells named strombus and some scallops which had nothing particularly bright in their colours and which, nevertheless, are believed to be a new species.
Soundings and quality of bottom during the 24 hours.
During the evening, 11 1/2 fathoms, white sand mixed with broken shells.
Bearings of the lands
At noon, the mainland coasts extended for us from north 70° east to south 45° east.
Without date a table of the log, meteorology filled in between 1 and 4 o'clock
(according to the mention dated of the next table it is about the beginning of the log table from the 12th to the 13th messidor).
1801-07-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from NE to SE. At 6 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course S 11° 15' E, south, S 11° 15' W and S 67° 30' W, the lead giving from 10 to 13 fathoms, grey sand. At noon in 25° 0' of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 35" of longitude by No. 27. The mainland in sight N 70° E. At 4.15 we anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand, the southern Dorre island bearing from S 45° W to N 85° W. The mean variation of three observations was 4° 13' 42" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds a light breeze at WNW. At 1 the lookout reported breakers inshore and offshore; 20 minutes later they seemed to stretch a long way out to sea, and at the same moment we hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack. From noon to 4 the soundings varied from 21 to 27 fathoms, coral and white gravel mixed with broken shell. From 4.30 to 8 sounded every half hour in 28 fathoms, coral and gravel; 26, 26, 26, 25, rock and gravel bottom. At 4.30 a.m. went about and stood in on the shore tack; at 6 went about again.
1801-07-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth messidor, at daybreak, we set sail again to come and seek the island in the middle of the bay of which Dampier speaks. And as he says that he feared not to find sufficient water to pass to the east of it, I had my boat depart in advance to sound ahead with orders to moor its grapnel as soon as it found itself below eight fathoms of water by steering directly south which was the course I intended to follow.
As soon as the boat departed, we followed it under our small topsail and the flying topgallant sail in order to keep it always ahead of us. Until noon, it constantly signalled to us above ten fathoms of water, good anchorage and as we also sounded continuously aboard, we navigated a long time before decreasing by one fathom. However, at noon, we had only eleven and a half.
At ten o'clock, we gained knowledge from above the deck of this island in the middle of the bay which I expected to see the day before according to the Dutch map in which I had quite confidence although I had already convinced myself that in it they had placed the first of the Sterile Islands, that is to say the one most to the north, 19' more north than it actually is, as we had the opportunity to observe. I well thought that the placement of this first island should influence that which I was seeking and I equally expected to find it too far north, as it actually is since at noon, having observed 25° 18' 37" this placed us on the middle of the island, while at the same moment, it still bore from us at the east 19° south, in its southernmost part.
I reserve for a more particular examination of this bay to make known the errors which this map seems to me to be susceptible.
During the greater part of the morning, there had been a fine breeze from the east, but about noon, calm took us and at half past one, we had to anchor so as not to fall too far to leeward, the little freshness there was then being from the south-east.
I had given orders to my boat, if we anchored in sight of the island, to push to shore to well reconnoitre it and see if it would find a suitable place for disembarkation, my intention being to stop there to determine the rate of our timekeepers and establish our observatory. As we were moored nearly three leagues from the coast, the boat did not return before nightfall.
In the afternoon, there was a small breeze from the north-west which rose about three o'clock, but I did not think it prudent to approach nearer to land and wished to wait for the report of the boat.
During the night of the 13th to the 14th, the weather was fine, it continued to blow from the north-west, small breeze until about nine o'clock, when it passed to the north. During the night, I had two cannon shots fired in the hope that they could be heard from the Géographe if she should be found in the vicinity of the place where we were at anchor. Rockets were also launched but all was to no purpose, we received no answer to any of these signals. At nine o'clock, the boat returned aboard, having found no suitable place for disembarkation.

1801-07-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to E. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course south, the lead giving from 12 to 11 fathoms. At noon in 25° 19' 26" of latitude observed and in 109° 23' 5" of longitude by No. 27, the east point of the middle peninsula bearing S 71° E and the westernmost point in sight S 13° E. The small boat sounding ahead of us. At 1.30, being in a flat calm, we anchored in 11 fathoms, white sand, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 50° E and the westernmost point in sight S 5° E. At 7 and at 7.15 fired a gun to warn the Naturaliste should she be in the bay; showed a light at the gaff, burnt flares every quarter of an hour and sent up a rocket every half hour to give our position to the small boat, which arrived at 9. The mean variation of three observations was 3° 59' 20" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-03.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sea rather high, the winds varying from NW to N in strong gusts. At 6 p.m. went about onto the port tack. The wind still very violent, with lightning from every point of the horizon. At 10.30 wore onto the starboard tack. About six in the morning we lay to. Continual rain.
1801-07-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, at daybreak, we set sail with a fine breeze from the north-north-west, variable to the north. As the distance we had to cover was small, we only set our topsails. We had moreover the small boat which was proceeding ahead sounding although we continually did the same thing aboard.
At nine o'clock, being in nine fathoms, bottom of white sand mixed with broken shells, we anchored again at about a league and a half from shore. On our way to the anchorage, we skirted for about a league, the edge of a great sand bank on which the sea was very high. The boat which had reconnoitred it the day before had found 7, 6 & 5 fathoms of bottom in the place where it crossed it, but to judge from the surge of the sea, it appears that in approaching the island, it has much less bottom. I reserve, during our stay at the anchorage to have it visited better. According to the report of Bonnefoy who commanded the small boat, this bank extends directly to the east and may have a league and a half in that direction.
As soon as we were at anchor, the topgallant yards were struck down and my intention was to moor with two anchors for greater safety. But in the morning, the weather having changed, it took on a bad appearance, I deferred this operation in order to be more ready to set sail if it became bad.
However, I sent my boat ashore to reconnoitre the coast and seek easy disembarkation. It returned about eleven o'clock, with the bad news that it had not been able to land in any of the coves into which it had gone, the whole coast being bordered by a rock platform on which the sea broke heavily, the winds being at the north-north-west fairly strong.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 25° 30' 44" south, and shortly after, we perceived to the south of our anchorage, two other sand banks of which we had no knowledge on our way to it, so that we found ourselves in a very bad position, and from which I sought to extricate myself at once by setting sail. As there was then an ebb tide, the current caused us to drift to the opposite side from that which would have been most convenient for us and we were obliged to bear away luff for luff, when the anchor was weighed. This forced manoeuvre brought us very close to the bank which we were seeking to avoid and when the vessel had finished her evolution, we had only six fathoms of water and the sea very turbulent. We immediately forced sail to rise and stood on the tack towards the bank which remained to the east and of which we had gained knowledge in the morning. We approached it to eight fathoms and then, we let the helm go, but the vessel failed to go about. We trimmed the sails again and, after running a cable's length, we tried a second time to go about and we succeeded.
From two o'clock until sunset, we were constantly engaged in working between the banks which seemed to extend as we rose to windward. We always approached them to eight and seven fathoms and, then, we went about.
At sunset, the weather set in with squalls and rain. The winds which were at the north-west, passed to the west, strong gale, and it was not until nine o'clock that we found ourselves finally out of danger. The tack was bringing us, then, to the north, we soon had 11 and 12 fathoms and I passed the rest of the night maintaining this depth while waiting for day. Everyone was on watch, except the naturalists, the midshipmen and the naval officers who passed a very good night in their cabins and appearing only when their watch called them on deck, where they were quite useless. Although the barometer had fallen to 28 inches 1 line, the weather was not very bad and even during the night when the moon was somewhat high on the horizon, the rain ceased and the sky became clearer.
