1801-07-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to N. At 7.30 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course south under topsails, the small boat sounding ahead. At 9.30 we anchored in 9 fathoms, sand and shell, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 83° E, a fairly conspicuous hill S 25° E, the westernmost point in sight S 3° W. The topgallant masts were struck. Citizen Bonnefoi, who was sounding in the small boat, found off the east point of the peninsula a sandbank with only 2 fathoms on it; at the edge of the bank he found 6 fathoms, and the Géographe then bore from him S 22° 30' E, 9 miles off; the east point of the peninsula S 33° 45' E and the westernmost point in sight S 33° 45' W. The small boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey the coast and look for a place fit to set up our observatory. Latitude observed at the anchorage 25° 30' 27"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 25' 37". The wind freshening, at 1 o'clock Citizen Bonnefoi came back; he had not been able to land on the peninsula because the sea broke there with force. At 2 we got under way, casting to starboard towards the land although we had meant to cast to port. We at once bore away and went onto the starboard tack. This manoeuvre had brought us very close to the east point. At 2.30 went about onto the port tack. The wind a strong breeze from NNW to W; overcast and squally weather, the sea rather high. At 3, being very near the east point and the bank, we put the helm down and missed stays; we had only time to gather way and put about again, and fortunately we came round onto the starboard tack. Several people maintained that we had touched at the moment when the ship, being in stays, had gathered sternway. At 4 went onto the port tack; at 5.30 onto the starboard; at 6.30 onto the port; at 11.30 onto the starboard. During the night the wind blowing hard, the sea not very high, with rain. The soundings since getting under way have been from 6 to 11 fathoms.

1801-07-04.journal_anonyme: The wind showing no sign of changing, we kept under the same canvas throughout; squally weather, a high sea and continual rain, the wind WNW in strong gusts.
1801-07-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather cleared up, however the sea was very turbulent and a large swell from the north made us well aware that it must have blown a strong gale from that part of the horizon. We were then coasting along the lands which run to the south-south-east, on the mainland coast where they form a very great indentation. The colour of the water which was extremely white, announced to us that the bottom was not very considerable and we sometimes had only nine and eight fathoms.
Having no more hope of being able to establish our observatory to regulate the rate of our timekeepers except on the northernmost of the Sterile Islands, I decided to come and seek good anchorage there as much sheltered as would be possible from the winds of the north and north-west which are the most bad on this ungracious and sterile coast.
At noon, we gained knowledge of the northernmost of these islands, which then bore from us at west 23° south. The northern point of the great land then bore from us at north 22° east and this point appeared to us to be that which should form the entrance to the bay.
In the afternoon, the winds being at the west-south-west variable to the south-west, we were close-hauled in the starboard tack towards the north, when at one o'clock, we fell from 15 fathoms to six, although we were in the middle of the channel. We let the helm go at once, and at two o'clock, having ten fathoms of water, we sought to close with the land on which I wanted to come and establish the astronomers and naturalists.
During the evening, the winds passed to the south, so that having no hope of reaching the anchorage before nightfall, I went about at six o'clock in the evening, and passed the rest of the night which was quite fine, working from tack to tack.
At eleven o'clock, the officer who was on watch, having perceived considerable whiteness on the water remaining on the lee side, immediately took the port amures, but as he did not warn me, I can say nothing for or against what he believes to have
seen. But supposing he had perceived something, we were then in twenty-five fathoms of water, bottom of grey sand. The rest of the night had nothing particular, only the winds which we had in the southern part, passed to the south-east very weak and the sky fine.

In this position the southern part of the second (of the) Sterile Islands remains at the south-south-west at a distance of seven or eight leagues.
1801-07-04.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from W to SW. At 2 a.m. lay to with the port side to the wind under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At daybreak the wind fell. During the day the weather was fine and the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. At 6.45 filled and stood on, the course N 33° 45' E. At 7.15 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the west. At 8 shaped the course N 11° 15' E. At 9.30 the mainland was sighted to the east. At 10 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 10.30 little Koks Island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At noon in 24° 44' 43" of latitude observed and in 109° 25' 32" of longitude by No. 27. The north point of Koks Island S 67° 0' W and the mainland north (the northernmost point in sight). At 1, the bottom having shoaled from 15 fathoms to 6, we bore away N 11° 15' W; the depth increased gradually, and at 2.30 we lay close-hauled again on the port tack. At 6 went onto the starboard tack. At 11, the sea being thought to break on the lee bow, we went onto the port tack.

1801-07-05.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, blowing hard from the west. From 8 to midnight and from midnight to 4 a.m. we sounded every hour without being able to find bottom, running out 87 and 100 fathoms of line. The wind having drawn round to NNW and then to NNW, we trimmed the sails and bore away NE. The weather fine, a swell running.
1801-07-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the winds being at the south-east variable to the east, we steered for the northernmost of the Sterile Islands which then bore from us at the west-south-west, and at eight o'clock, we anchored in 13 fathoms of water, grey sand, having paid out 35 fathoms of cable.
As soon as we were at anchor and the sails furled, I immediately had both the large and small boats put out to carry ashore our instruments and our tents. I myself embarked in one of the two and we came to establish ourselves in a cove at about a league from our first anchorage.
Before departing, I gave orders that the vessel be moored south-east and north-west and that the topgallant sails be struck down and even to lower the masts if the wind should come. I also prescribed to Citizen Le Bas to whom I left the command of the vessel, to fish a cable on a watch cable on a third anchor and to keep it ready to moor if the wind should come.
The whole shipboard service having been arranged, I proceeded ashore and immediately had our two tents erected in which all the scholars and I lodged. The astronomical circle and the telescope were placed in suitable places for observations, but we could do nothing that same day, having had only the time necessary to prepare ourselves for the next day.
On leaving the vessel, I warned M. Freycinet that, the next day, he would depart in the large boat with the boatswain to go to the southern point of the second of the Sterile Islands to determine the latitude and to take hour angles and bearings there. I warned him to have the large boat armed so that nothing was wanting to it and to provision himself accordingly in consequence of the mission he would have to fulfil and which I should discuss with him the next day, in that he should come to our tents before setting out.
The weather was very fine, all day, nevertheless, we found the sea somewhat turbulent and the disembarkation not too easy in the cove which we had chosen and which appeared to us very sheltered, the two entrances being closed (by) two large rocks of about a hundred paces in length, at a musket shot distance from the shore and fifty paces wide forming two islands.
When the winds are from the north to the south-east passing through the west, this cove is very convenient, but when they are from the north to the south-east by the east and the breeze is somewhat strong, one must take to the water so as not to compromise
the boats. The sea breaking too much on the shore which is, however, only a fine sand beach.
During the night, the weather was calm and we had a cloudless sky which promised us good observations for the next day.
1801-07-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to E. At 3.30, the soundings having shoaled appreciably, we went onto the starboard tack; at 5.30 onto the port tack. The northern Dorre island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At 7 shaped our course S 45° W to stand in for the anchorage. At 8 anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand. At 9.30 the commander and all the naturalists landed on the northern Dorre island to camp there. The tents, the astronomical instruments and provisions were sent ashore. At 10.30 we moored NE and SW with a bower anchor, having 60 fathoms to starboard to the NE and 50 fathoms to port to the SW, Koks Island bearing N 30° W, the north point of the northern Dorre island N 50° W 10 miles off, the tents N 60° W 8 miles off, a large headland of Dorre Island S 22° 30' W. The topgallant masts were struck, the sheet anchor got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The two boats came back from the shore and were sent off again to the camp with effects for the commander; they came aboard during the night.

1801-07-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW. The amplitude at setting gave us 7° 15' of NW variation. At 8.30 p.m. went onto the port tack. Ran out 100 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 1 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 3 hove to on the other tack. Noon bearings: the white cliff E 4° 30' N, estimated distance 23 miles; the nearest peak E 5° 30' S, estimated distance 25 miles; the furthest E 10° 30' S, distance 28 miles.
1801-07-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, we were not deceived in our expectations: the weather was very fine and we made various observations with our astronomical circle to well assure ourselves of the rate of our timekeepers on which we had some doubts.
About eight o'clock, M. Freycinet and the boatswain came in the large boat to take my orders and execute the mission of which I had warned him the day before, before he came ashore. But as he had taken provisions for only two days and he needed them for four to well execute his mission, I deferred his departure until the next day, but not without displeasure at his lack of foresight and at that of the one who had dispatched him with so little provision.
Be that as it may, I employed the boat's crew to make wood which had to be fetched more than three-quarters of a league into the interior of the island, across the brushwood among which the march and transport were very painful. However, we managed by dint of work and effort to complete his load.
The lovers of pleasure, and I have a great number, set about hunting kangaroos and killed about twenty. Part of them was sent aboard and the rest was reserved for our consumption ashore.
In the afternoon, we cast the seine several times but without success for we took nothing at all. Fishing for shellfish was more successful, we gathered many crabs fairly good (sic) to eat, nerites of (?) of different species and especially many oysters, but small and very difficult to open. They had about the shape and taste of those eaten in the colonies whether of America or the Islands of France and Bourbon
Among the seabirds which were shot the first day, there were some of a pretty species. Some are known under the name of magpie of the sea having half the body black and white and the beak and feet a beautiful red. Maugé found that two eagles which were shot would be a new species since they appeared to live only on fish and shellfish of which good store was found in their bodies. We named it, for this reason, the fishing eagle.
The land birds were the same as those we had seen at our first anchorage on this coast.
In the evening, I had the two boats which were ashore depart for the vessel, and I recommended to M. Freycinet, the greatest exactitude in the mission which he had to execute and to take provisions for six days. This mission was not very complicated, it was confined to going to the southern point of the second and at the same time the largest of the Sterile Islands to determine its latitude with precision and to take various hour angles in order to calculate, afterwards, the longitude. I gave him my timekeeper for this purpose, on which he could rely.
We passed very cheerfully the night ashore and we were not incommoded by the dew nor the cold although the first was very abundant and the second quite keen during the night. The sky was cloudless, the winds at the south-east almost calm. However the thermometer fell to ten degrees from 19 at which it had been during the day, in the shade.
1801-07-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to SSW. At 5 a.m. the boats were sent off to the tents with bread and water. We worked on the rigging and the sails. At nightfall the boats came back loaded with firewood.

1801-07-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather with rain, the winds varying from NW by N to NW and WNW. At 2.45 went about. At 9 a.m. a very violent squall passed over with rain; sounded every half hour and ran out 60 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-07-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, the weather continued fine and we repeated our observations of the previous day with success. I shall give the data of the results when they shall have been calculated.
We perceived from shore, the departure of the large boat for the mission it had to execute. I had joined to M. Freycinet, the boatswain, a learned man on whom he could rely. This companion of his voyage did not appear very agreeable to him and he would have much preferred to embark his protégé, the midshipman Breton, one of the most useless of all those aboard.
During the course of the day, our gardener made an ample harvest of plants all beautiful and new. I shall make known on our departure from this island, the different species and numbers which he will have found there.
The other naturalists occupied themselves with fishing and hunting. Citizen Péron, whose extreme ardour drives him to undertake everything without reflection on the dangers to which he exposes himself, went to visit the western part of the island, and was, as is his habit, alone. He found, in his excursion, nothing of interest and so as not to have undertaken it in vain, he went to the seashore to gather shells.
He first amused himself at the expense of the crabs, and having left his shirt, he confined about fifty of them inside it. This complaisance on his part would have merited a happier fate than that which was reserved for him. For, having wished to go on some rock where the sea seemed to him to break only with moderation, he was knocked over by a wave which upset him and took from him most of the fine shells which he claims to have encountered. His fall occasioned him several injuries in different parts of his body which made him (take) the course of withdrawing. But instead of orienting himself to make course from west to east, he took that from north to south, so that for the second time, he completely lost his way and did not rejoin us until about nine o'clock in the evening, overwhelmed with fatigue and weariness, having been obliged to abandon on the way, his tin box, his shirt and his crabs.
Our hunters, during the day, waged a war to the death on kangaroos and killed nearly thirty.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the sky was very fine and the winds almost calm in the southern to south-south-east part.
1801-07-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE and calm. At 5 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp with water and provisions, and the large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to the southern Dorre island. At nightfall the small boat arrived loaded with wood.

1801-07-08.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sky overcast, a swell running. A light breeze from WSW to SW by W. The land in sight at a great distance. At midnight hove to and sounded several times without finding bottom. At 6 a.m. filled and stood on.
1801-07-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, in the morning, Citizens Boulanger and Maurouard set out to come and reconnoitre, by land, the southern point of the first of the Sterile Islands on which we had established ourselves. They departed at daybreak and their intention was to make a circuit of it. They took precautions accordingly.
Citizens Bernier, astronomer, Depuche, mineralogist, and I, also set out to come and take hour angles and altitudes of the sun at that of the north in order to fix its position in a certain and precise manner, for that which the Dutch map gives it, which I am using, is very defective and differs according to our previous observations, by nearly 20' in latitude. We had very fine weather, during this excursion which was only two hours to reach the most advanced land to the north of this island. After resting a little, we took at half past ten o'clock, an hour angle, and several angles of the point where we were, at the vessel.
Before and after the passage of the sun through the meridian, we had good altitudes, so that our journey was successful and that (we) will be able to determine, with exactness and
precision, the entrance of the bay.
Our work being finished and to our satisfaction, we visited the surroundings of this point at the extremity of which is found a small islet separated from the island by about a musket shot and to which, however, it is joined by a reef which does not entirely uncover but on which the sea breaks with great violence. This islet is at north 5° east of the point where we made our observations.
Before we set out to rejoin our tents, we placed in a well-sealed bottle and placed in a place, sheltered from the injuries of time, the following note:
"On the nineteenth messidor, Citizens Bernier astronomer,
"Depuche, mineralogist, and the commander-in-chief of
"the expedition came to this northern point of the island,
"to determine its latitude and longitude in order to
"fix in a precise manner the entrance of Sea Dogs
"Bay discovered by Dampier north of the Sterile Islands".
Signed Baudin, commander, Depuche mineralogist, Bernier astronomer.
On our return, we followed the seashore and amused ourselves fishing for shells. This fishing was not successful and we found only three or four species which we had already encountered.
In the evening, the weather had a very bad appearance in the part from the south to south-south-east. The whole horizon was charged with thick heavy clouds and it seemed to us that it should rain quite abundantly, at four or five leagues distance from our establishment.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth, the weather cleared up, the winds passed to the north-west and then to the west, almost calm on shore.
I had given orders to the master of the small boat which I met, to make wood in a cove (and) to return aboard before the bad weather which seemed it should make during the night. Although he promised me well to depart at once, he did not set out until after sunset. The south-east breeze which he was making at sea no longer permitting him to be able to return aboard, he was obliged to pass the night on his grapnel and to throw into the sea all the wood which he had gathered in the evening, which would not have happened if he had departed at the moment I gave him the order.
1801-07-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW. At 4 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp; she came back at 11 loaded with wood and left again at noon for the camp. At 4 the weather turned overcast, the breeze freshened and drew round to SSE, blowing strong, with a high sea. During the night kept a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour.

1801-07-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSW and SW. At 1 we sighted the Abrolhos at a middling distance. At 4.45 hove to; at the same hour the lead brought up 34 fathoms, fine sand; the depth and the bottom did not vary until 8. We filled for 10 minutes and then hove to again. At 4 the winds having drawn round to ESE we hove to on the starboard tack. At 6 filled and stood on.
1801-07-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, at sunrise, the sky being quite fine although it appeared to us that a good breeze blew from the south-east at sea, we saw under sail, our large and small boats returning to the vessel. The precipitation of M. Freycinet's return at first gave me a bad idea of the success of his mission because it did not appear to me possible that he had executed it well, in so short a time. However, I await the report he will make to me before judging.
During the day, we received no boats from the vessel and we were forced to restrict ourselves on our water ration in fear that the weather might not be fine the next day. We continued observations ashore with the astronomical circle and these were the last. My intention being to return aboard for fear of a change of weather at the new moon which was to occur the next day.
MM. Boulanger and Maurouard arrived about four o'clock in the afternoon from their excursion to the south of the island at the end of which they could not arrive, the distance according to their estimate being much greater than that given to it, from which it follows that this excursion was useless.
Our gardener continued his excursions into the interior of the island and despite its sterility, he brought back each day, new plants and specimens very curious. Maugé, for his part did not lack work, beautiful birds were provided to him and, the insects and shells occupied him when he had no more to work on.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first, the weather cleared up. The breeze calmed greatly and we had the hope of seeing arrive early the next day, our boats with our water provision which was beginning to be very short.
1801-07-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 10.30 Citizen Freycinet arrived in the large boat from the southern Dorre island, which he had left the day before at 4 o'clock at the beginning of the bad weather; he had spent the whole night lying to and at daybreak had shaped his course for the ship. At noon the small boat was seen anchored astern of us with a red flag at her mast; the large boat was at once sent off to carry her a line from the ship. At 2, suspecting that the large boat had let go the line, one of the yawls was sent to carry her the end; at 5 all three boats were aboard. The small boat had left the camp the day before loaded with wood; she had spent the night beating without being able to fetch the ship, and had been obliged to throw her wood overboard. At daybreak she had gained a little at the oars, but had been forced to anchor, her crew, who had neither drunk nor eaten, having no strength left.

1801-07-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light from SE to ESE. From 4 to 8 p.m. the lead brought up 29 to 30 fathoms, blackish sand. At 8 hove to with the port side to the wind, heading SW. At 2 we hove to on the other tack, and at 5.30 a.m. we filled and stood on.
1801-07-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, the weather being fine, we finally saw arrive one of our boats which departed from the vessel about seven o'clock, the time at which it should have been returned ashore. At eight o'clock, the large boat also arrived that is to say departed from the vessel, it arrived about nine o'clock. M. Freycinet came to make me a report of his journey which, as I had foreseen from the precipitation of his return, is, in little, nothing. Instead of bringing us good observations, he brought back a great quantity of kangaroos, for his platter. Although I had not told him to take his protégé, the Breton, he embarked him if not to help him, at least to afford him the pleasure of the hunt, which he acquitted himself very well of.
In the first boat which arrived to us, were found a number of hunters and several persons who were sick when it came to performing service aboard, but who found strength to run all day hunting in the greatest heat of the sun. Of this number, was young Bougainville who will soon be unable to continue.
I sent the large boat as soon as it arrived, to make wood and the small one returned to the vessel loaded with part of our baggage, for I seriously considered moving. I thought it could make two trips during the course of the day, but as in the second, all the useless ones who had been sent to us and who intended to stay the night ashore had to be embarked, that prevented it from performing the service to which I destined it. Citizen Péron was also dispatched to the vessel in order to have his wounds dressed. The astronomer Bernier returned there as well.
During the night, the weather continued fine and we passed part of it preparing for the next day, the embarking of all our effects.
1801-07-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE. At 5 a.m. the two boats were sent off to the camp with provisions and water. Our fishermen, who had taken nothing since we anchored, made a very good haul today. In the evening the two boats came back from the camp. Twelve lashes with a rope's end were given to the seaman Gimes for having threatened to throw Citizen Bougainville, midshipman in charge of the party in the large boat, into the sea.

1801-07-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from E to SSE and SE. At 8 p.m. hove to with the port side to the wind. From 4 to 8 the lead brought up 30 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell; 28, 28, 32 and 33, grey sand and gravel. At 2 a.m. filled and hove to again at 4. At 5 a.m. filled and stood on; at 7 a.m. and at 11 went about.
1801-07-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, in the morning, the weather being very fine and the winds almost calm in the north-east to east part, our two boats arrived. The large boat was at once dispatched to go and get wood of which we were beginning to be in want, because care was not taken to warn me when we were in the bay of the Géographe where there was every facility to get it. As it was known that we must go shortly to that of Sea Dogs, it is likely that it was judged to have enough, which actually happened, but we no longer then had the same facility to procure it, that which the islands produce being of bad quality and little suitable for consumption by the vessels.
As soon as our boats arrived, we struck one of our tents which was at once carried aboard as well as several other of our effects. When the large boat had made one trip of wood, it was employed in transporting us and all our ba(ggage), so that at sunset, we were all aboard as well as our effects.
I was all the more pressed to arrive there because the barometer and the hygrometer seemed to announce to us the end of the fine bad weather. The sky, during the night, truly covered over with clouds, in all parts of the horizon, and the winds, although still weak, fixed themselves in the west part variable to the north-west. The sea did not delay in becoming turbulent and agitated and one could perfectly hear the breakers in the western part of the island.
1801-07-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW. At daybreak the two boats were sent off to the camp. At 10 they came back loaded with effects and left again at once. At 2 the small boat arrived loaded with effects from the camp and went back at once. The topgallant masts were swayed up, the rigging set up and the repair of the sails continued. At 5 the commander and all the naturalists came back aboard in the two boats, which brought the tents, the astronomical instruments and the rest of the effects that were at the camp. The boats were hoisted in. On board 24° 50' 30" was observed at the anchorage, and 109° 12' 46" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 4° 33' NW, the mean of 5 observations. The tides set NNW and SSE and run at one knot and a half. At the camp 24° 47' 30" of latitude and 109° 2' 9" of longitude were observed. At the north point of the northern Dorre island 24° 45' 30" of latitude and 108° 59' 12" of longitude were observed.

1801-07-12.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, the sea smooth, a light breeze variable from N by NW to N and NNE. At 1 the lead brought up 27 fathoms, reddish sand and fine gravel. At 8.30 p.m., being 2 leagues and a half from the coast and standing in for it, we changed tacks.
1801-07-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the weather having a bad appearance, I had the watch cable struck and its anchor put in position. Then, we unmoored, and at half past eleven, we were under sail. The winds at north-north-east fine breeze, I reckoned we could get out of the bay before nightfall, or at least, position myself to pass through the middle of the channel, but as in the afternoon, they came to us from the north part, variable to north-north-west, we passed the evening working between the bay, the sounding line in hand.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth, we were not without anxiety occasioned not only by the bad weather which it made, but still more by the irregularity of the bottom. My intention was, according to the weather and the winds which reigned, to keep myself between twelve and eighteen fathoms of water to preserve roughly the middle of the bay, but it happened to us often to fall suddenly from eighteen and twenty fathoms to twelve and even below so that at any moment, we could meet some shoals which would have played us a very bad trick.
It appears to me that the bottoms and the soundings indicated on the Dutch map which I am using, are placed at random and that this map has good only the configuration and the direction of the lands which, except for the island in the middle of the bay, seemed to us very exact and well done to us. It appears demonstrated to me that in the middle of the entrance to the north of Sea Dogs Bay, there is a fairly extensive bank on which we advanced to six fathoms of water. If, then, the sea had been less turbulent, I would have had it visited by the boat, but when I found myself coming back from the island in the middle, there was no way to put a boat out and I scarcely saw the lands of the mainland coast which are not as low in this part as they appear on the map.
On making course, then, to the west to gain the second of the first of the Sterile Islands, on which I wanted to come and establish our observatory, I passed suddenly from 15 fathoms to eight and it was only in approaching the island that I found by the sounding line, a regular bottom of 15, 14, 13 and twelve fathoms, bottom on which I anchored, the lands bearing from me according to the bearing which I gave of them on the day of our anchorage.
Thus, according to what happened to us, I believe I passed over the two extremities of this bank and as no breakers appeared in the middle, perhaps the passage through it is practicable, but I do not guarantee it.
There are few places of this bay which we have not traversed at different times as may be judged from the courses placed on the plan which I give of it, and we had only to regret that we could not find a place to land on the mainland coast. Every time we found ourselves there, the winds were either at the north or at the north-west or at the west, so that the sea broke everywhere with great violence. The coast, although furnished with sand beaches which, from afar, announce easy disembarkation, is bordered by a rock platform which often advances nearly half a league into the sea.
1801-07-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At 6 a.m. the sheet anchor's cable was unbent and the anchor stowed. At 9 we unmoored; at 11.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W, the south point of the same island S 50° W, the large headland of Dorre Island S 33° W. At noon overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze. Beating to get out of Shark Bay. At 4.45 the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W. Continual rain during the night.

1801-07-13.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from N to NNE and NNW, squally weather, the sea rather high. At 4 wore onto the port tack. At 1.30 a.m. the lead brought up 50 fathoms, reddish sand. Calm about four o'clock, the sky dark with a great deal of rain falling; about 9 it freshened from the NNE.
1801-07-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, we awaited daylight with great impatience, believing that we would have a view of both shores or at least one of the two to fix our position and the course we had to make to get out to sea. The weather had a bad appearance and the sea was becoming rough. The barometer which, during the night, had fallen to 28, announced nothing good to us and it became prudent and pressing to make for the open sea to be in safety.
At daybreak, a large cloud came to develop over us and gave us such a great quantity of rain that it would have been easy to collect several barrels of it, but we were so occupied with sounding and maneuvering that the sailors scarcely had time to collect some to wash their linen. The winds, which, during the night, had been fairly constant at north-north-east became very variable and finally fixed at south-west around seven o'clock in the morning. Our horizon was so (narrowed) (in margin: here because) at daybreak scarcely extended it to a cannon shot and we were just as uncertain of the course we had to make to get out as if we had been in the depths of night. (in margin: here because)
However, as it was necessary to make a decision, I had the ship steered west when the winds permitted it to approach the first of the Sterile Islands whose sounding I knew. We cast the lead every five minutes. When I set my course west, I had fifteen fathoms and I followed this course until thirteen, then I steered north to regain the middle of the bay. At eight o'clock, I found myself again in fifteen fathoms. The time, still rainy, did not extend our horizon which was still very contracted. From north, I passed, until ten o'clock, to the course north-north-west and always in 15 fathoms. From ten o'clock to noon, I had the ship steered north-west, convinced that I was in the middle of the bay. Indeed the bottom increased gradually until eighteen fathoms and at noon we had thirty two, which put us absolutely outside, without our having had any knowledge of the lands.
Then I went to rest for there had been twenty six hours that I had been on deck without resting once. I observed at that time that none of the officers except the one on watch mounted the deck and the frequent tacks we made did not prevent them from sleeping deeply any more than (if) we had been in the most pleasant position. Before retiring, I ordered to continue the course north-west in order to make for the open sea and only to sound every hour.
Throughout the evening, the sky was dark, overcast and rainy. Only, although continuous, it was much less abundant.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to the south, we were in a calm until four o'clock when they came to us from the north-east, a fine breeze. We took the course north by drawing towards the west, under the foresail and the three topsails, two reefs in each. My intention (was) to get sufficiently far out to sea to withstand a squall if, as appearances seemed to announce, it took place. But I wanted, before leaving this shore, to come and take the latitude of the point which forms its entrance to the bay on the north side in order to know exactly its distance from the first of the Sterile Islands which the Dutch chart seemed to me to have crowded too much.
A little before sunset (sic), we had a clearing which allowed us to see, for a moment, the mainland coast which then remained to us from south to east at a considerable distance and about three leagues from us.
During the night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth, the weather was scarcely better than it had been during the day. I gave the course north for the night with orders to sound every hour and to go about at three o'clock in the morning if there appeared to be fine weather. But the weather was very inconstant and the winds variable, which obliged us to different maneuvers until the following day.
***(it is really page 264)
Bearings of the lands.
At four o'clock in the evening,
the most northerly point of the first of the Sterile Islands remained at north 40° west.
1801-07-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a flat calm, a light breeze from NNE, and from S to SSW at 7 a.m. At noon in 24° 31' 32" of latitude by account and in 108° 59' 46" of longitude by account. At 8 squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE. At 10.30 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail and the mizzen staysail. At 11.45 the wind shifted to W and hauled to NW and NNW.

1801-07-14.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, continual rain, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a light breeze variable from NNE, NNW to south. At 7.30 p.m. the lead brought up 37 fathoms, reddish sand. At the same hour the wind shifted to SSW. At 4 a.m. we hoisted a flag at the gaff in honour of the 14th of July. At 11 we sighted the land at a distance of 30 miles.
1801-07-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the weather appearing to be clearing, I sought to close with the land in order to find myself at midday, east and west of the cape which forms the entrance to the bay at north in that this point became important for determining its opening. The entrance by the first of the Sterile Islands being well established according to our observations made on shore.
At half past ten, we had reached the point I was seeking and then we lay to awaiting the passage of the sun to the meridian.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 24° 18' 58" south and the longitude, deduced from the rate of our timekeepers, was for No. 27 of 109° 9' 3" and for No. 35 of 109° 18' 58". The large cape which forms the entrance to the bay at north then remained at east 17° north, at a distance of two to three leagues. I did not approach it any closer in that the winds were at w-nw and the sky did not have too fine an appearance. Moreover, we had already traversed the whole of this coast so closely that it was not possible to go wrong according to the knowledge we had of it.
After the observation of the meridian height, having nothing more to do on this coast, I made course to come to recognize as promptly as possible, the north-west point of this same land and steered north with a fine and strong breeze of w-nw. The sea fairly fine and the sky appearing to want to rid itself of the clouds which rendered its appearance little pleasant.
During the evening, the weather continued to clear and at sunset, the winds shifted to west, variable to w-sw, which made us make good progress during the night. According to the observation of Dampier and the difference to the east which he had experienced in this same area, I had the ship steered n ¼ nw during the night which was fine.
We sounded every hour but we found no bottom at 60 fathoms.
Remarks during our last stay at the Sterile Islands.
According to the observations made on shore, the northern point of this island the first of these islands is at 24° 45' 30" south latitude and its longitude, taking the mean of the results given by our timekeepers, would be 109° 34' 44" east. The inclination of the magnetic needle was observed there as 49° for needle No. 2 and 54° for No. 4, on the 16 messidor. These observations repeated on the 18, gave for needle No. 2, 50° and for No. 4, 52° 15, so that the mean would be 51° 18' 45".
The declination observed on board was found for the position of the ship's anchorage as 7° 8' 18", the same observations made on shore gave only 5° 45' 15".
Although the sky was fine the first days of our encampment on shore, it was not possible to make any observation either at night or by day to determine by this means the true longitude of this island. The moon was then too close to the sun and there was no eclipse of Jupiter's satellites.
Moreover, our first gardener Ridelé to whom every moment is precious, found in this small island, seventy species of plants most of which will, without doubt, be unknown to botanists. The zoologist Maugé uniquely occupied with natural history and jealous of fulfilling his duties well, gathered ten species of birds which he believes to be new. The others hunted kangaroos and some lizards. Among the latter, we caught two which are without doubt, the same of which Dampier speaks under the name of guanos and which is truly very hideous. But we caught two of another species, very pretty in colour and very large. See the figure drawn from nature in the journal written out.
A remark which I have made and which is perhaps not without interest, is that all the animals we encountered, did not seem to us wicked. These lizards although so hideous, allowed themselves to be caught by hand without seeking to flee or to defend themselves. Two black snakes which we did not catch for fear, gave those who looked at them, all the time they wanted to consider them and did not hide until we approached them very closely. The kangaroos wounded and which we still caught alive, did not seek at all to bite and a small one which we caught, without doing it harm, at once began to lick the hand of the one who had caught it.
Among the shells, we found only four or five fairly fine species and only two which appeared to us unknown. Citizen Maugé collected ten sorts of insects most of which are in the class of dung beetles. We found only two species of butterflies, one of day and the other of night. And several caterpillars of the first were caught which is fairly beautiful seen from below and having much relation with the cabbage butterfly in Europe seen from above.
The fish which were caught on the line are, in general, of the perch species and only a fairly large quantity of a sort was caught which the sailors call Cape and which they say common and similar in the colonies. The fish known under the name of parrots are absolutely the same as those seen between the tropics. Moreover, I have had drawn in colour, those which appeared to me the rarest and most curious.
During our stay on shore, we constantly lived on crabs, oysters, nerites, (burgi), lobsters, fish and kangaroos. The sea dog, when young and small, appeared to me quite good and I preferred it to the kangaroo which was the delight of everyone.
The boats which came and went sometimes perceived in their courses some very large green turtles, but we did not have the skill to catch any. We met two dead on the shore whose head was the size of that of a sheep. Although I have seen very large ones at the Island of Ascension, they were far from approaching the volume which the two of which we encountered the remains should have had. There are also seen, on the coast, some whale bones, but they are small and offer nothing remarkable.
The greater part of the wood which we collected on the coast (was) no doubt brought there by the tides from the mainland, for we found much of it which had begun to burn. And moreover, the island does not produce any of this quality. Moreover, this bay offers few resources to navigators: not a drop of fresh water, very little wood and very difficult to obtain. Fishing alone, or the need to repair considerable damage could decide to go there. One lives well there, as long as the winds are from the west, east and south-east, even until south if they are moderate, but from all the other points of the horizon if it blows at all, the sea is very rough and landing is no longer practicable.
When I came to anchor on the mainland coast, the weather had been very fine for two days and the winds very moderate at north-east and east coming directly from over the land. I had reason to think that landing would be easy and yet the boats could not approach the coast closer than half a league, the sea breaking everywhere with a great crash.
During our stay in the Bay of Sea Dogs, the chief of navigation whom I had specially charged with the observation of the tides, made me the following report:
"On the 8 messidor at eight o'clock, the flood began. The same day at 20 hours, return of the flood.
"On the 9 at 12:45 minutes, commencement of the ebb. The same day at 13 hours return of the ebb.
"On the 9 at 8 hours 30 minutes, commencement of the flood. The same day at 19h 15' return of the flood.
"On the 10 at 12:45 minutes, commencement of the ebb. On the 10 at 13h 10' return of the ebb.
"On the 10 at 9h 20 minutes, commencement of the flood. The same day at 20h return of the flood.
"I observe that during the observations which lasted two days and a half, the waters (sensibly) remained at the same height although we are certain, by the rocks of the shore, that the sea there rises more than eight feet.
"The intervals between each tide are not equal because it is extremely difficult to know with precision, the moment when the sea is slack. The true interval between each tide should be 12h 24', it is here only 11h 43' which gives a difference of 41', but it seems that the number of observations is not large enough to make this inequality disappear".
***(it is really page 265)
Bearings of the lands.
Towards the end of the noon watch at four o'clock we had in a clearing knowledge of the mainland coast. It remained from south to east.
On the 25 at noon, the large cape which forms the entrance to the bay of the Sea Dogs at north remained at us at east 17° north at two or three leagues at most.
The other lands in going north were seen from east to north-east.
1801-07-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 6.30 filled and stood on, and at 6.45 shaped the course S 45° E, and at 8 east. At 9.30 the land was sighted in the N 79° E and we steered for it. At 10.30, being abreast of the large cape at the entrance to Shark Bay, we hove to with the port side to the wind. At noon in 24° 17' 16" of latitude observed and in 109° 9' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 3° 35'. The large cape bore from us N 73° E, and the land in sight as far as N 44° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course north. At 4 took the bearing of the large cape S 78° E, the southernmost land S 35° E. At 5.30 the course was given N 11° 15' W. The large cape then bore from us S 43° E, and the land in sight from S 32° E to S 64° E. At 10 p.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the fourth time, in 109° 10' of longitude.

1801-07-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, continual rain, a light breeze from NNW to SW. At 4 p.m. fired 21 guns in memory of the 14th of July, whose anniversary was celebrated. At 6.45 a squall got up in the SW with lightning and a little thunder; we steered NNW. At daybreak we sighted the land and made all sail to close it. At noon the lead brought up 47 fathoms, rocky bottom.
1801-07-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, the weather was fine and the winds at w-sw, fine breeze. We made course until noon to the north by drawing towards the east and having observed the latitude of 22° 17' 3", I had the ship steered north-east to close with the land of which we had knowledge in the evening at two o'clock, it remaining to us from east to south-east at eight leagues' distance.
The longitude indicated by the timekeepers put us at noon, according to No. 27 at 109° 6' 18" and according to No. 35 at 108° 57' 59".
In the evening, we continued to steer north-east, all canvas spread, until eight o'clock in the evening and then we lay across until midnight, course set to the east and from midnight to four o'clock in the morning, on the other tack course set to the west. We sounded during the night which was very fine, every hour, but found no bottom at 120 fathoms. I could have made course towards the land, but I feared to encounter unexpectedly, the banks of which Dampier speaks being at very much the same thing as the latitude which he gives them and being unable, moreover, to count on good keeping watch, I equally needed rest and I was suffering cruelly from a colic of the lower belly. A day more or less did not appear to me a great loss and I had no need to increase my anxieties.
***(it is really page 266)
Bearings of the lands.
On the twenty-fifth at sunset the lands at most northerly view remained at east 26° south.
Those the most southerly at east 58° south.
The middle of this coast at east 47° south.
1801-07-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SE. At 6.30 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 22° 17' 3" of latitude observed and in 109° 6' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 42' NW. The course was given N 45° E. At 4 the land was sighted from N 79° E to S 67° 30' E, as far as the eye could reach. At 8 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at midnight hove to on the port tack.

1801-07-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A light breeze from SW to SW by W. At 8 p.m. the lead brought up 58 fathoms, fine sand. From 9 to 10 and 11 ran out 70 fathoms without finding bottom. At daybreak sighted the land, which I take to be the entrance to Shark Bay.
1801-07-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at four o'clock in the morning, the weather being fine and the winds at south-east, fine breeze, we steered south to east-north-east by hauling as close to the wind as was possible to come to take knowledge of the land which, according to my dead reckoning, I counted to see at sunrise. It was indeed believed to be sighted and we continued this same course in that the look-outs claimed to see it at this point of sail. But after running until noon without discovering anything and having observed 21° 6' 27" south latitude, I went about and ran to the south, until four o'clock when the winds having failed us, we could not steer the ship, nor give it any movement.
The longitude indicated by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, put us according to No. 27 at 110° 16' 18" and according to No. 35 at 110° 4' 21".
During the day, as during the night, the lead was cast every hour and we found no bottom at 120 fathoms' depth.
About nine o'clock, we had a little freshness from west-south-west variable a little towards the south but in general, it was almost calm all night which was very fine despite the inconstancy of the wind. This calm was all the more disagreeable in that we had every reason to fear that the currents would cause us to drift much further offshore than I desired since at noon, we had 19' 21" more than the dead reckoning of the routes, during the 24 hours, indicated.
***(it is really page 267)
Bearings of the lands.
On the twenty-seventh at four o'clock in the afternoon,
the lands showed themselves from east by north-east to east-south-east.
The distance was too considerable to recognize it well.
1801-07-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE. At 4 filled and stood on, the course N 45° E; at 6.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 110° 18' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 33' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 13' 0" of longitude. At noon went onto the port tack; at 6 a flat calm. At 8, a light breeze from WSW, shaped the course S 25° E.

1801-07-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to SSW. We ran along Dirk Hartog Island and sounded in 45 fathoms, reddish sand. At 7.45 a.m. we let go the port anchor in 18 fathoms, fine muddy sand, and veered 60 fathoms of cable. At 8 a.m. we sent the small boat away to sound. At 9 it was back and we fired two guns. From 10 until midnight a current setting ESE held the ship almost broadside on.
1801-07-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 28, in the morning, the winds shifted to the south and at sunrise, they took strength and held, throughout the morning, at south-south-east. We steered to the east, all canvas spread, without having knowledge of any land, nor bottom at 120 fathoms.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 21° 4' 50" and according to dead reckoning, it should have been 21° 20', thus we had still 15' 10" difference to the north, despite that all the course according to dead reckoning carried us to the south. The longitude indicated by the timekeepers, was, for No. 27 of 110° 50' 48" and for No. 35 of 110° 35' 22". Two sets of distances put us at 112° 54' 4", which gave us a difference to the east so considerable that we judged them very doubtful although the weather was fine and suitable for such observations. However 2° 10' 59" of difference to the east did not allow us to have confidence in them.
In any case, I continued to make course to the east until four o'clock in the evening. A very light breeze from south-south-east which did not permit us to make much progress, at this time, the winds having shifted to south-west, always very faint, I took the tack to the south towards the east.
At sunset, having no knowledge of land and no bottom, I continued this same course until nine o'clock, when having found thirty fathoms, bottom of coarse gravel, I went about to the open sea.
During the night, from the twenty eighth to the 29, the winds were very faint and we spent it maintaining ourselves in 30 and fifty fathoms, the weather being very fine and the sea calm.
***(it is really page 268)
1801-07-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to SW. At daybreak shaped the course east and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 4' 58" of latitude observed and in 110° 54' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 46' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 47' 6" of longitude.

1801-07-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind very light from the south. On the 29th the weather was unsettled and calm; a breath from N by NE gave us hopes of getting under way, but the calm returned. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq to go to Dorre Island, and the dinghy to Dirk Hartog.
1801-07-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, at daybreak, we saw land in the south-east extending a little to the south-east by south. The sky, then, was dark and overcast having no fine appearance. However, it became fine in the course of the morning and, at nine o'clock, we recognized that the land which we had in view at a distance then of four leagues, was an islet of about a league and a half in extent remaining then at us, at east 12° north.
According to our charts and especially the Dutch one more detailed than the others, this should have been one of those placed to the east of the north-west point of the lands of Concord and we judged it so ourselves.
At ten o'clock, we sighted another island extending from east 53° south to east 21° south and shortly after a third remaining at south 10° west. We made course to range these islands seeking to close with the north-west point of the continent of which I flattered myself to soon have knowledge. The distance at which the Dutch chart places it, being not considerable. The second of these islets appeared to us larger than the other two and to have, according to our dead reckoning, three leagues in extent, which is absolutely contrary to the figure which the chart gives of it. Moreover, the terrain of the first two appeared to us very sandy and arid, the third alone, had a little verdure produced by plants of very low elevation. In doubling the first, we saw, at the point of the east, a reef on which the sea broke strongly although it was calm. The second also had one, but less extensive.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 21° 19' 27" south. Thus, according to the Dutch chart, we were still 15 minutes from the north-west point of the lands of Concord and we should have had knowledge of it, the weather being then very fine. But the calm having come, we lost the hope of taking knowledge of it before night. From sunrise until noon, we had successively had 51 fathoms down to 27, grey sand.
The longitude indicated by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, gave for No. 27, 111° 1' 34" and for No. 35, 110° 42' 59". From other sets of distances from the sun to the moon the difference found the day before was renewed again and we had doubts about the results indicated by the timekeepers. Distances 112° 26' 57".
In the afternoon, the calm continued or at least, the breeze was so faint that we advanced very little. At three o'clock, the winds which had, some time before, shifted to north-east, jumped to west-south-west, which made us take the course of nw.
During the night of the 29 to the 30, we tacked back and forth to keep our position putting off until the following day to take knowledge of the mainland coast. We had during the night from 46 to 75 fathoms' bottom, muddy sand.
***(it is really page 269)
Bearings of the lands.
On the twenty-ninth at daybreak, knowledge was had of the land extending from south-east to se ¼ south, at five leagues' distance. It was presumed that it was an island.
At half past nine o'clock this island remained at us at east 12° north.
At noon two others were observed, one at north 66° east and the other at south 10° west, these are the islands indicated in the Dutch chart.
1801-07-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WNW to WSW, from SE to NE and from WSW to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E. At 9 took the bearing of an islet N 78° E, 12 miles off. At noon it bore from us N 66° E, another from S 37° E to S 19° E, and another S 40° W. At noon in 21° 19' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 1' 32" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 53' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 26' 57" of longitude. At 3 the last islet bore from us S 67° 30' W.

1801-07-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to NNW, running under the fore topsail, mizzen topsail and jibs. At 1.30 let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, sand and fine gravel, and veered 35 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the NW point of Dirk Hartog Island W 13° N; the southernmost visible end of the same island S 9° E; the middle of Dorre Island N 17° W. While running in we sounded and found 15 and 13 fathoms, sand and gravel. At 9.30 p.m. the large boat was back. The dinghy returned at 10.30 a.m.
1801-07-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 30, at sunrise, we again had knowledge of the islands seen the day before, but they were only perceived from the top of the masts. The most easterly remained at us then, from south to south-east. The calm having continued until eight o'clock, the winds shifted to the east, fine breeze. We took
advantage of it both to close with the land and to recognize well the position of the islands which we had in view.
At eight o'clock, the first of the three, seen the day before, remained at east 25° south, the second at south 62° east, the third at west 43° south. A land ahead of us which we judged should be the continent at west 22° 30' south.
We continued, throughout the morning, to make course towards the land most in view of us which, truly, was the continent. But in ranging the islands at a distance of two leagues to two and a half leagues, we were surprised to see a much greater number than the Dutch chart bears. Which leads me to believe that those who surveyed the chart of the continent in this part as well as the islands which are found there, had not advanced as far to the east as we. We were equally surprised to find no bottom at a distance so little considerable from land in 50 and 60 fathoms, whilst, when we were further to the east, we found it in 30 up to near six leagues' distance from the coast.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 21° 31' 30" south, which corresponds fairly well with that which the Dutch chart gives to the north-west point of New Holland. And I believe that it is placed there with much more exactness than on all the other charts. The islets and islands appeared to us also to be better placed than on Robertson's chart and the French chart drawn at the depot, which place them, I believe, too far to the east as may be judged by the following bearing:
Bearing at noon after the observation of the meridian height.
The land taken for the continent or the north-west point of the coast at west 37° south.
The land to the west the most in view of the same coast at west 43° south.
Three sand islets from east 71° south to east 28° south.
An island of little extent on which appeared only very little vegetation at east 25° south.
Another island where vegetation was more animated at east 6° south.
(Sketch of which it would be good to take a copy)
The three other islands perceived in the morning were then out of sight.
After noon, the weather still being fine although the sky already had very bad appearance, we continued to follow along the firm coast the north-west point of which remained at us at one o'clock at east 77° south, and that more west at south 13° west. We could then distinguish very well the reef marked in our charts at the north-west point. My intention was to come to anchor in the place where the English and Dutch charts indicate good anchorage and I was going to make course accordingly, when the winds suddenly shifted with force to the west and then to west-north-west, which obliged me to run to the open sea.
At five o'clock, the weather became bad and the barometer, which had fallen to 28 inches two lines since noon, obliged me to take precautions for the night and against bad weather. We thus took an additional reef in each topsail and unrigged our topgallant sails. As our foresail was in bad condition and incapable of resisting a squall, I had it changed and we at once bent a new one. While we were occupied with this work, the weather became bad, the sky covered itself at all points of the horizon and we had abundant rain until six o'clock. The winds were then, at w-nw and I was making south 43° west.
Unable to resolve myself to leave this coast without having visited it and to clear up a doubt which had arisen, I decided to move away only sufficiently from the coast to be able to withstand without fear, bad weather, if it took place. I passed the night tacking back and forth at seven or eight leagues offshore, having no bottom at one hundred twenty fathoms.
During the night of the 30 to the first, the weather was not fine and we had fairly often strong squalls from west-south-west, some of which were heavy enough to make us furl the storm topsail and reef our topsails shortly after in which there were however two reefs already taken.
When, before the bad weather, we were ranging the part of the firm coast which, in this place runs east and west, we lost sight of the land at the point where, once arrived at the western point one could see further, another land directing itself from west towards south which will without doubt join another part of very high lands which remained at us to the south-west and which is represented in the Dutch chart as the highest lands of the continent. Several persons claimed that the land which we had just passed was an island and that it was wrongly that it was taken for the firm coast. Despite appearances, I did not share this opinion. But, without pronouncing on the question, I put off until the time when the weather would be manageable to clear up the fact. It appears to me moreover, impossible that the Dutch who followed all this coast very closely would not have perceived this island, if indeed it is one, which I am far from believing. I think that what we saw, is only the opening of some deep bay or perhaps even the entrance to what they call the William River. Moreover I hope that soon this conjecture will be verified.
***(it is really page 270)
Bearings of the lands.
On the 30 in the morning, the land was seen again from the top of the masts from the s-se to the south.
At noon, one of the islands seen the day before remained at east 25° south.
A second at south 62° east.
The portion of land taken for the continent extended only from west 37° south
until west 45° south. But we were still too far away from this
part to make sure if it was not a third island.
1801-07-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather in the forenoon and overcast in the afternoon. The wind from WSW, SW, ESE, E, ENE, N, NE, NNE and WSW. At noon in 21° 32' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 30' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 9' NW. An island S 65° E, another S 62° E, another from S 47° W to S 53° W; it is this last that the commander took for the entrance to the Willem River, and off which he hove to on the 3rd Thermidor [22 July 1801] in the afternoon. The wind a strong breeze, with rain, squalls and gusts.

1801-07-20.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from SW to W. The sky cloudy with light rain at intervals. At 7 p.m. the corvette dragging, we veered to 80 fathoms of cable; the tide set NW, as observed at 8.30 and at 9. At noon the currents had the same set.
1801-07-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of thermidor, at four o'clock in the morning, we made course since midnight on the tack of north 65° west, the weather still menacing and very unsuitable for approaching the land. We nevertheless had knowledge of it at daybreak, it remaining at us at south 45° west. But it was only seen from the top of the masts. We continued this same tack until eight o'clock, and then we took that and then we took that (sic) of south 22° 30' west maintaining our same canvas that is to say under our topsails and the foresail. The sea was beginning to become rough, the swell hollow, which did not announce the return of fine weather. However, the barometer seemed to announce it to us since it had already risen above 28 inches.
At ten o'clock, we had knowledge of the land and at noon, it remained at us in the following bearing:
The part of coast taken for the continent at south-west at 15 miles' distance.
A part of the islands seen the day before from south to south-east 5° east.
We had no observation of latitude that day and at noon, we went about. We sounded at the same moment, and (it) there was no bottom at 120 fathoms.
In the afternoon, we steered to the west by drawing towards the north as much as was possible for us, but the winds being variable from south-west to west-south-west, the course took as much to the north as to the south, so that on this tack, it was worth scarcely more than the west. The sky continued to be very cloudy with bad appearance. However, there were several clearings which seemed to announce the return of fine weather and the barometer also began to rise.
At four o'clock in the evening, we sighted the land again from the top of the masts and it remained then in the part of the south but the distance was too considerable to be able to distinguish what it could be.
At eight o'clock we took the starboard tack and at midnight, we went about until four o'clock in order to maintain ourselves, if possible, in the position where we were at sunset.
During the night of the first to the 2, the sky was fairly fine and we had the winds from south-south-east to south-east, strong breeze. The sea had become very swell. We sounded every hour during the night without finding bottom at one hundred fathoms.
The sunset, according to the remarks of Dampier, announced to us a strong breeze for the following day, and I wished that it would not take place in order to approach the coast.
***(it is really page 271)
Bearings of the lands.
On the first of thermidor at noon, the lands of the continent remained at south 50° west at 15 miles.
one of the islands of the day before at se.
1801-07-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SE. At noon in 21° 26' 22" of latitude by account and in 109° 55' of longitude by account. Variation 2° 53' NW. An island south, another from S 34° E to S 50° E. The mainland S 50° W, about 15 miles off. At 4 the land could be seen from aloft to the south.

1801-07-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. We observed a current setting strongly ESE. At 7 a.m. we weighed the starboard anchor, and when it was up we found the shank broken 2½ feet above the flukes. Let go the starboard anchor. At 9 a.m. sent off a boat under the orders of the chief quartermaster to go to Dirk Hartog and observe the tides.
1801-07-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 2, in the morning, it continued to blow strong breeze from south-east by east to south-east and at sunrise, it increased further. At the same moment, we saw the land which (we) judged to be still that which forms the north-west part of the lands of Concord. We were then passably far from the shore and it appeared to us difficult to be able to approach it if the breeze continued in the same direction and with the same force.
At four o'clock in the morning, we did not go about, the lead having not given bottom at one hundred fathoms. As the land extended from south-east to south by south-west, the tack which we held was the best to close with it and indeed, we had a perfect view of it from the deck at seven o'clock. Only, it appeared to us, by the point of sail at which it remained at us, that for two days, the currents or tides had carried us greatly to the north-west.
At eight o'clock, we went about and we made course to the east towards the north, to approach ourselves further of the point which we wished to recognize when we took the other tack, which I counted to do as soon as the observation of the meridian height.
At noon, the latitude was found to be 21° 28' 28", positively the same as the Dutch chart gives to this much desired point. The mean of the longitude of the timekeepers was 110° 20' 48" and we were about six leagues under the wind of the point which then remained at us at south 5° east. It appears, according to this bearing, that the land which we had in view, was not the point which we sought to close with, for it could not remain at us to the south if the latitude is well determined. The lands the most in view in the part of the west remained also at us at south 15° west.
After the observation, the winds being at south-south-east variable to the east strong breeze, we changed tacks and held as close in the tack to the south towards the west until six o'clock in the evening.
This tack brought us a little closer to the coast of which at four o'clock, the dead reckoning of the distance put us at five leagues. The coast showed itself then, from south 34° east to south 8° west. The lands were extremely high and elevated as may be seen in the figure which I give of it and we recognized in no way, in the aspect which it presented to us, the north-west point of which we had passed so close two days before, despite that our latitude was very nearly the same.
At sunset, we made new bearings and the lands in view remained at us at the points of sail hereafter:
The land to the east drawing to the south at east 27° south.
The most elevated part of the same land which was in its middle at south 22° east.
The extremity in view, of the lands the most to the south at south.
According to this bearing and the position of the ship, we continued the same tack until six o'clock, the time at which we went about. The winds were then, at south-south-east variable towards the east and the sea a little swell. In the soundings taken during the night, from sixty to one hundred twenty fathoms, we had no bottom.
The course, for the night, was set as close to the wind as possible on each tack which were changed at midnight and at four o'clock. During the night, the weather was fine and clear and the breeze fairly fresh from south-south-east.
***(it is really page 272)
Bearings of the lands.
On the 2 at sunset, the lands the most to the east drawing to the south remained at south 67° east.
The part of the same land the most elevated and which was also its middle at south 22° east.
The surplus of the lands in view bore directly to the south.
[2V p. 270***]
***(it is really page 272) blank
***(it is really page 273)
Bearings of the western point of the lands of Concord.
On the 3 at noon, the point forming the north-west extremity of the lands of Concord at east 56° 30' south.
The reef which joins this point at east 55° south.
The eastern point forming the entrance to the William River at east 87° 30' south.
The western point of the same river at south 1° west.
The lands which extend to the south of the William River at south 18° west.
To the north and to the east of the north-west point one saw one of the islets recognized some days
before remaining at east 55° south, a second at east 15° south.
These two islets were only seen from the top of the masts.

1801-07-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At daybreak the mainland was sighted from S 11° 15' W to S 33° 45' E; at 8 it could be seen from S 10° E to S 65° E. At noon in 21° 28' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 20' 48" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 47' NW. The land from S 5° E to S 15° W.

1801-07-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NE to ESE. On the morning of the 3rd we laid out the port anchor, the currents setting ESE.
1801-07-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 3 of thermidor, in the morning, we closed with the land, the winds being at south-south-east, fine breeze, and we came to seek this north-west point of the continent after which we had been running for several days. At half past nine, it was almost abreast of us at a league and a half distance and at ten o'clock, we lay to awaiting the passage of the sun to the meridian and to observe the latitude. During this time, we took several angles and azimuths and at noon, we observed the latitude of the ship as 21° 33' 5" south and this point then remained at us at east 56° 30' south which would fix the latitude at 21° 36'. That is to say little difference with that which the Dutch chart gives it starting from the reef of the firm land and not from the reef which extends a little offshore from this point and on which one saw the sea break in an extraordinary manner by the height to which the sea rose in spreading over the rocks which were found there.
I would have greatly desired to be able to gain the anchorage which the charts indicate, but as I was under the wind and the current and drift carried me to the nw, there was no appearance of gaining it by tacking all the more so as the breeze having greatly freshened, it would have been necessary to reef the topsails. The coast, moreover, appeared to me little easy for landing and although the winds came from over the land, the sea broke all along the shore with enough force that a boat could not approach it.
At noon, we observed all the most remarkable points and they remained at us at the points of sail hereafter. The longitude of the timekeepers was 110° 35' 1" for No. 27 and 110° 2' 5" for No. 35.
The point forming the north-west extremity of the lands of Concord at east 56° 30' south.
The reef which joins this point at east 55° south.
The eastern point, forming the entrance to the William River at east 87° 30' south.
The western point of the same river at south 1° west.
The land which extends to the south of the William River at south 18° west.
To the north and to the east of the north-west point,
one saw one of the islets perceived some days before which remained at east 55° south
and another at east 15° south.
These two islets were only seen from the top of the masts and form part of those which we had skirted some days before and of which I have given the position with regard to the point of the mainland.
According to the observed latitude, our bearings and the position of the ship, it appears certain that the English and French charts place this point too far to the north.
The French chart places it at 21° 30' south.
The Arrowsmith chart at 21° 20'.
The Robertson chart at 21° 5'.
And the Dutch chart at 21° 35'.
Everything leads us to believe that the Dutch chart, which we have often found to be at fault, for latitudes, is exact for that of this part. The configuration of the land is also very well detailed in it and when one confronts it with that of the land, one cannot fail to recognize it.
I also think that the islands to the east of this point, are placed too far to the east, not excepting the Dutch chart. After having completed all our observations, we made course to the ne, all canvas
, all canvas spread and we soon lost sight of the land as well as the bottom.
When we came to lie across north and south of the point of which I have just spoken, we had first found bottom in 35 fathoms, sand and rock. Then we found it at 40, brown sand. The drift, while we lay to, having carried us to the nw, we found it at noon in 55 fathoms, muddy sand.
From the north-west point until the entrance to the William River, the land presents itself in the form of an island from which one distinguishes perfectly the two extremities and it is for this reason that those who do not know that there is a river there, still think that it is an island which joins, it is true, to the other point by a reef on which we saw the sea break with as much force as on the north-west reef and I believe that, in the calmest weather, a boat could not pass there.
One sees, by the bearing of the two lands which form this entrance, how little considerable the opening is since at the small distance at which we were, it is only 3° 30' by the compass.
I think that our observations on the bearing and placement of this point on the chart, of our course since our making land on the Leeuwin coast, will be satisfactory and that they will serve, by and by, as a basis for the bearing of all this coast, which the Dutch appear to have visited with care and on which, without doubt, they would have established themselves if it had offered them the resources which they counted on finding there. But a country which has neither fresh water, nor port for the safety of ships, could not suit them. As by and by, it will suit no one to seek to establish themselves there at least in this part.
1801-07-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. At 5.45 the high land of the mainland from S 5° W to S 34° W; the island taken for the entrance to the Willem River from S 27° E to S 57° E and from S 62° E to S 78° E. At 10 hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At noon in 21° 33' 5" of latitude observed and in 110° 35' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 16' NW. The high land of the mainland S 48° W.
