Willem Island from S 18° W to S 1° W and from S 2° E to S 33° E. The east point, which bore from us S 33° E at 6 miles, is surrounded by reefs stretching as far as S 35° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course N 45° E. At 8 Citizen Le Bas was to take the watch, but the commander, who had had some difficulty with him that morning, forbade Bonnefoi to have him woken and took his watch himself. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. The commander hove to at noon under the lee of an island which he took for the entrance to the Willem River. From the deck two islands could be seen, one from S 33° E to S 2° E and the other from S 1° W to S 18° W; and the space between these two islands, from S 2° E to S 1° W, is what he took for the river's mouth. But from the topgallant crosstrees I saw, as did several other people, the two islands joined by a chain of reefs awash, on which the sea broke. I saw land as far as the eye could reach to the south, an islet in the S 35° E and another in the S 75° E.

1801-07-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. In the afternoon weighed the starboard anchor and let go the port one, veering a range of 80 fathoms. At 11.15 p.m. the current turned back towards the ESE.
1801-07-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
After having taken a new departure on leaving the north-west point of the Lands of Concord, I gave the course north-east and we followed this point of sail by a fine breeze from south-south-east variable to south-east.
On the 3, at sunset, we reduced canvas although we had lost bottom at sixty fathoms and that one had perceived no land at the horizon.
During the night of the 3 to the 4, the weather was fine, the winds in the same direction and we followed the same course. But at this time, the lead having brought up 56 fathoms, bottom of coarse sand, I had her laid to until daybreak continuing to sound in order to know in which direction we would be carried by the drift of the ship or the currents if they were stronger.
According to the soundings until six o'clock on the 4 in the morning, it appears that they carried us to the east since the bottom decreased and that the drift of the ship should throw it to the north-west, we had then fifty fathoms bottom of fine grey sand.
On the 4, at daybreak we resumed the course north-east. The winds being at east-south-east, fine breeze. And at sunrise one sighted a land to the south-east from the top of the masts, which, at eight o'clock, seemed to extend to the east by south-east, I presumed according to the course which we had made, that this should be the continuity of New Holland and not the Rosemary Islands which, according to the latitude which Dampier gives them and even our charts, although it is not the same, could not remain at us at this point of sail. I also thought that if as Dampier says, there is a chain of islands which extends to the continent, I could not fail to encounter some one in following the course north-east and before having passed 20° latitude. It is why I did not change it. The winds moreover would have taken us away from it rather than brought us closer.
At eight o'clock, the lead brought up no more than 37 fathoms of bottom and I expected to see land incessantly. But at nine o'clock, it was 46 and at ten o'clock 50 which made us lose the hope of encountering it as promptly as I would have desired.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 20° 6' 47" which put us at very nearly that which the charts give to the Rosemary Islands. The longitude indicated by the timekeepers put us at 111° 29' 45" at No. 27 and at 110° 53' 39" at No. 35.
According to the course which we made on leaving the north-west point of the continent, I believe myself founded to think that the chain of islands of which Dampier speaks does not extend as he says, as far to the east and to the south of these Rosemary Islands and that the openings which may be found there, if indeed islands are found to the south of the Rosemary Islands, are much wider than he announces since one could pass in the channels which they form without having knowledge of the lands which may be found to the north as to the south.
In the evening of the 4, we found the sea swell and were even obliged to furl our topgallant sails to ease the mast. The course was always on the tack of the north by drawing to the east as much as the wind permitted.
At sunset, we had no bottom at 76 fathoms but at eight o'clock we found it at 82, grey sand.
During the night, the weather was fine and we lost bottom. The winds were much the same.
1801-07-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E as far as the eye could reach. At 6.30 filled and stood on under all sail, the course N 45° E. At noon in 20° 6' 8" of latitude observed and in 119° 29' 4" of longitude by No. 27. At 5 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. Variation 2° 21' NW.

1801-07-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and bright. A light breeze from WSW to N and NE. At 4.30 p.m. slack water; at 5 it set east.
1801-07-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 5 in the morning, the weather continued fine and about six o'clock, the winds shifted to east-south-east varying towards the south. We continued the tack of the north by the east until ten o'clock and I took, then, that of the south, all canvas spread.
We had some time after sunrise, a visit from several red-beaked and red-tailed boobies. It was the first time, since our arrival, on this coast that we encountered this species of bird. Although one sees some occasionally at the making land of the Islands of France and Bourbon, we had not encountered any similar, since our departure.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 19° 8' 48" and the longitude of our timekeepers reduced to the same hour was for No. 27 of 112° 21' 12" and for No. 37 (sic) of 111° 41' 48". The daily delay which, for some time, this timekeeper had experienced, gave us well many doubts about the goodness of its results.
In the evening of the 5, we continued the tack of the south until half past five in the evening when, the course taking too much to the west, we took the starboard tack. The breeze had then greatly diminished and there was appearance of calm for the night. However, we were mistaken, for we had a fine breeze from the land from south-south-east to south-east which made us advance to the east.
At eight o'clock, we cast the lead and found bottom in 90 fathoms grey sand. At ten o'clock, we found it not at one hundred fathoms nor in the rest of the night which was very fine and clear, no cloud hiding the brightness of the moon from us.
1801-07-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. Saw tropic birds. At noon in 19° 8' 35" of latitude observed and in 112° 21' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 59' NW.

1801-07-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from WSW to SE by way of south. The chief quartermaster, coming to report to the captain on his observations of the tides, brought back a pewter plate found on Dirk Hartog Island bearing a Dutch inscription; the captain had another placed beside it and planted a national flag. Shortly afterwards he embarked in his boat.
1801-07-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 6, the weather continued fine in the morning, and the winds shifted from se to east-north-east slight breeze. I expected to see it increase as the sun rose higher on the horizon, but my conjecture did not prove correct for it blew little and at noon we were almost in a calm.
At half past seven, we went about and took the tack of the south, all canvas spread seeking to approach the land.
At noon, the observed latitude was 19° 14' 7" south and the longitude according to the timekeepers put us at 112° 49' 4" at No. 27 and at 112° 4' 47" at No. 35. That observed by five sets of distances from the sun to the moon gave 1° 40' more to the east.
Shortly after the observation of the meridian height, the winds shifted to south-west and south-south-west which made us take the starboard tack on the course to the south towards the east. The breeze was very faint at first, so we made little progress, but at sunset it increased and we advanced a little, the lead in hand.
At eight o'clock, finding no bottom at 60 fathoms, we continued our course. At midnight, we found it in eighty fathoms, bottom of mud, and we were then almost in a calm the winds at south variable at south by south-west.
At one o'clock, bottom was found of mud at 72 fathoms. It was the first time we had found any of this quality. At three o'clock, it was the same but at 80 fathoms and at five o'clock we found 87.
Moreover, the night was very fine and the sea calm. We had only to complain of the calm, because I presumed that the currents would carry us to the nw.
1801-07-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine, warm weather, the wind a light breeze from E to south. At noon in 19° 14' 10" of latitude observed and in 112° 49' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 31' NW.

1801-07-26.journal_anonyme: A hazy sky, a choppy sea, a fresh breeze from SW to W. Burnt priming to show our position to the small boat. At 2 a.m. it was back.
1801-07-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 7th, calm prevailed until nine o'clock in the morning, but the winds then shifted to the south-west and we enjoyed a fresh breeze from that quarter all day long. We took advantage of it to close with the land, which I hoped to make out before nightfall, and to make good progress; I did not take soundings during the day.
At noon, the observed latitude was 19° 30' 17" and the longitude by the timekeepers was 113° 46' 40" for No. 27 and 112° 57' 35" for No. 35. The dead reckoning for the course run in the 24 hours showed six minutes south more than the observation.
During the evening, the winds shifted from the south-west to the west-south-west and we continued making south.
After sunset, having made out no land, I sounded and we obtained 32 fathoms, a bottom of grey and red sand mixed with small broken shells. We then furled the mainsail and at seven o'clock, finding no more than 29 fathoms, we did the same with the topgallant sails and staysails. At eight o'clock, the depth was 28 fathoms despite having made little progress during this last hour.
Since my intention was to come to anchor in twenty fathoms if I should find good holding, I continued making south and even south-south-west, the winds having shifted to the west. But at midnight, we still had twenty-five fathoms, calm having prevented us from making headway. Nevertheless, I furled the foresail and (we) continued our course under the topsails. The sounding from midnight to four o'clock was between 24 and 23 fathoms, always good holding.
We had seen, in the evening and shortly before sunset, a great quantity of whales which appeared to us much larger than those we had seen off the lands of Concord. It was a warning that we were in water of middling depth, for it did not appear usual to us to encounter them in 50 and 60 fathoms, and according to our observations, they hold more generally in twenty fathoms and below than above.
Throughout the night, the sky was very fine and without cloud. The clearness of the moon gave us a horizon of at least three leagues' extent, yet we (did not) perceive the land despite the shallowness of the waters.
1801-07-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light and a fresh breeze from south to W. From 10 until noon we crossed several tide rips whose direction seemed to be NNE and SSW. At noon in 19° 30' 0" of latitude observed and in 113° 51' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 54' NW.

1801-07-27.journal_anonyme: Squally weather with rain, a light air from NNE to north.
1801-07-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 8th, shortly before five o'clock in the morning, being in 21 fathoms, we made out the land, which bore to us on the port bow. We set our course to the north to await daylight and as soon as it began, we distinguished it much better.
At six o'clock we resumed our southerly course and at sunrise the land we had in sight presented itself to us under the form of an island, the southern part toward the west being much higher than the southern part toward the east. From the masthead one could see in the distance other lands that stretched as far as the eye could reach, which we judged to be the continent, although we could not yet distinguish the lower lands which seemed to join together all the elevations we perceived on the land, and which at first glance appeared to be as many islands as there were hillocks.
Be that as it may, we continued our course southward, but the bottom diminished so rapidly that, before we had gone more than a league, there were only fifteen fathoms. Nevertheless, we did not alter course, but at nine o'clock, finding no more than nine fathoms to nine fathoms and 1/2, I came to anchor in good holding of red and grey sand, because opinions were divided regarding the land we had in sight, which was at least four leagues from us. Some maintained it was an island and others, the land of the continent.
Since on all our charts, there is only that of the depot where an island is marked on the coast where we found ourselves at the latitude of our dead reckoning, which placed us at 20° 17' south, I thought it proper to verify this fact. In consequence, I had my large boat lowered and gave its command to Citizen Ronsard to go and reconnoitre it and take soundings on the route he would make to reach the part that appeared to us the most easterly.
The boat, well equipped, left the ship at nine o'clock and made course to the south with a fresh breeze from the west. After its departure, I also sent the small boat to take soundings to the east, and I remained at anchor to await the return of these two boats.
At noon the observed latitude was 20° 20' 0" south and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us at 114° 5' 31" for No. 27 and 113° 15' 24" for No. 35, in that this timekeeper was losing daily on the advance that it (had) gained over the other.
After the observation of the meridian altitude, the small boat I had sent to take soundings to the east of the ship, not paying attention that the wind and current were favourable to it, drifted far beyond the limit I had set for it, which was one league at the most, so that it was obliged to let go its grapnel but made distress signals; and not knowing what it could be, I immediately set sail to go to meet it. On the course we made to join it we had not less than 9 and 10 fathoms, a bottom of sand mixed with red gravel.
At two o'clock we came to anchor again, having joined and taken on board our small boat, which I feared would not arrive either during the day or even during the night, the breeze having increased considerably and being truly too strong for it, if I had not gone to meet it.
Not long before sunset, we perceived in the north 55° east, a very considerable eddy which several persons believed to be nothing other than a tidal race. But I do not share this opinion and I am persuaded on the contrary that it is a shoal in which there remains not much water at low water. I am all the more inclined to believe what I put forward as certain, since every time the sea has presented the same effect to us and we have continued in the same course, to be sure with the lead in hand, the bottom has diminished suddenly and in less than ten minutes we passed from 14 and 15 fathoms to 9½ and 10, which obliged us to change course immediately.
After sunset, having had no report of my large boat and the breeze continuing to be strong, I did not expect its return until the morrow, hoping only that it would die away during the night.
However, as the wind was fair and they had provisions for only one day, it might be that it tried to return on board, and in order to indicate to it the new position of the ship, of which perhaps they had not learned of the departure, I gave orders to fire flares every hour. During the night of the 8th to the 9th, the weather was very fine and clear, but the breeze always very strong from the west and the sea rough. Since we were anchored in good holding with sixty fathoms of cable, the ship lay firm on her anchor and we were not obliged to veer a greater scope. Around two o'clock, it began to moderate and the sea became fine. The sailors, at the change of tide, occupied themselves in fishing, but their attempts were not successful for they caught nothing.
Bearings from our first anchorage on the north coast of New Holland.
The western point of a land having the appearance of an island at south 38° west
The eastern point of the same land at south 20° west
The lands presumed to be those of the continent extending from south 5° west to south 30° east
This land presented to us the aspect that the drawing I had made of it gives, and the anchorage where we were in 9 fathoms of water placed us five leagues from the nearest coast to us.
On the lands which we are inclined to believe are those of the continent several hillocks rather high could be distinguished in the distance, and one could not see the low lands which joined them one to the other.
1801-07-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 4.45 a.m., having sighted land to the south, we bore up for it and made it out to be an island. At 8 its east point bore from us south and the west point S 10° W, 15 miles off; the mainland could be seen as far as S 45° E. At 8.45 we anchored in 10 fathoms, red sand, the west point of the island bearing S 11° 30' W and the east point S 7° 30'. The mainland being very low, only its highest points could be seen from the deck, and they looked like so many islands. The nearest to the east point of the island bore from us S 6° E, the second S 16° E, the third S 24° E and the fourth S 29° E. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Ronsard to survey the island; the small boat, although deep with water, left at 9.30 to sound 3 miles to the east. The current was then running 1.3 knots. At noon 20° 19' 59" of latitude and 114° 5' 53" of longitude by No. 27 were observed. The small boat was seen anchored 6 miles to the east with a signal at her mast, which made us think she needed help; and having no boat to send her, we went to her with the ship. We got under way at 1 and bore up for the boat; at 2 we anchored very near her and she came aboard (variation 1° 21' NW at the anchorage). Citizen Baudin, midshipman, who was in charge of her, told us that after sounding 3 miles to the east of the ship (as ordered) he had tried to come back aboard, but that the current had carried him away and he had been obliged to anchor and set all his crew to baling out the boat, which they could never get free of water. We lay anchored in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, the west point of the island bearing S 21° W and the east point S 17° W; a rise of the mainland south, another S 9° E, another S 20° E. In the N 51° E the sea formed an eddy that seemed caused by a shoal. During the night a rocket was sent up every hour.

1801-07-28.journal_anonyme: Misty and squally weather, light rain at intervals. A fresh breeze from SW. At noon the tide began to turn to the westward.
1801-07-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 9th, in the morning, the weather was fine and the breeze light, although still from the west-south-west. The sea was also calm and at sunrise, I expected to see my large boat on its way back on board. But having had no report of it, I feared it had been stranded and that this was the cause of its delay.
However, at seven o'clock, it was perceived from the masthead, which was found to be far to the west of the place where we were at anchor. At nine o'clock, it was on board and Citizen Ronsard, who commanded it, having had no knowledge of our change of anchorage, had departed from the land at moonrise, relying on the breeze that was blowing to be on board before midnight. But having searched for us in vain according to the bearing he had taken of our first position and finding himself in a depth greater than that of the anchorage where we were at his departure, decided to tack during the night in order to find us better at daylight. He had no knowledge of all the flares we had fired during the night.
As soon as he arrived, we set sail and sailed along the coast until seven o'clock in the evening, keeping ourselves in ten, eleven, and sometimes twelve fathoms of water, but in general the bottom was very uneven.
At noon, the observed latitude was 20° 20' 13" and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us according to No. 27 at 114° 8' 51" and according to No. 35 at 113° 14' 21". The weather was then very fine and the wind almost calm. In the morning, we had had it from south-south-east to south, but in the afternoon, it returned to the west with a fresh breeze and we made some progress, having our course to the land which then bore to us east-south-east.
Around five o'clock, I perceived ahead of us an eddy like those we had encountered before. I immediately gave orders to steer two points to windward to leave it to starboard, but as we approached it with the lead in hand, the bottom which was twelve fathoms suddenly passed to eight and a half. I immediately bore away to the north-east and the bottom increased as rapidly as it had diminished. We passed at a mile's distance from this shoal and the sea broke upon it as on a reef.
At sunset, I had a view of the lands we had in sight taken and one will see in the figure I have made of it how low they are in this part. We had then no more than ten fathoms of water, yet they were scarcely seen from the deck. The effect that the sight of this coast produced on me has truly presented to me what must be called low and submerged lands. And although Dampier says they are of middling height at low water, I believe that had he seen those we are sailing along, he would have explained himself differently. For the rest, as I hope to find myself soon in the place where he landed, we shall be able to verify whether what remains for us to see is more pleasant than what we have just passed.
We saw, during the evening, four or five large clouds of smoke in different places on the coast; thus there is no doubt that this part is inhabited. But the fires that produced them appeared to us somewhat advanced into the land.
At seven o'clock in the evening, the weather being fine and the breeze moderate, I determined to come to anchor until daylight. I preferred this course to that of remaining under sail a little offshore to pass the night, which would have taken me too far from the land and which the winds from the east-south-east or at least from the south-east to which I had to expect would not have allowed me to close with easily. The bottom was then nine fathoms and a half, coarse sand mixed with very small red, brown and black stones with some fragments of small broken shells.
Bearings from our second anchorage on the north-west coast of New Holland.
The easternmost point of the lands in sight at east 30° south
The southernmost land also in sight at south 22° 30' west
The middle of the lands abeam to us at east 74° south
The bottom was nine fathoms and a half, coarse gravels and sand.
Since soundings were taken every hour during the night to know if the sea rose and fell in the anchorage we occupied, it was noticed that it diminished by two fathoms and rose by as much.

Report of Citizen Ronsard acting as Ensign and commanding the large boat for the reconnaissance of the land

"Citizen Commander,

"In departing the day before yesterday in accordance with your orders to reconnoitre the nearest land to the anchorage, I directed my course to S ¼ S.W. sounding at each mile of progress according to dead reckoning. I found constantly a bottom of sand or gravel in eleven fathoms and a half of water, up to three leagues from the ship. Then, the bottom diminished imperceptibly and at four leagues, I had no more than ten fathoms. I found the same water for the space of a league. The bottom was also of the same nature with the exception of one sounding which gave me black mud. At noon, I estimated myself more than five leagues from the ship and at a league and a half distance from the land. I then had eight fathoms of water, a bottom of fine sand. The western point of the land on which I was steering bore to me south 20° west and the lands of the continent toward the east at great distance, extending to the south.

"As we advanced, low lands were discovered toward the east, which seemed to form small islands, which is all the more certain that when we were more inside, the lands of the continent could be seen at a great distance to the south and south-south-east. The bottom then diminished, and I found no more than three fathoms. The sea being calm and finding myself abeam of a small sandy cove, I directed myself toward this place all the more willingly since the landing appeared easy and even convenient to me. Although my desire was to advance more to the south in order to assure myself,

"as you had recommended to me, whether the land across from which the ship was anchored was an island or joined to the continent by some lower lands, I nevertheless decided to let go the grapnel in this cove which appeared to me (sic) so convenient for the safety of the boat. When I had entered it, it seemed to me by the marks that the tide had left that it could have fallen eight feet and I ran the boat aground on a very even sandy beach where (it) was in complete safety. The guard was entrusted to two men and I arranged the rest to draw the best possible use from it and at the same time the greatest utility. Two were assigned to travel the edges of the sea to collect shells if there were any, and two others were ordered to advance some distance into the country to collect plants, observing them to always choose among those they might encounter, those which would have flowers or at least fruits.

"As for myself, accompanied by M. Fortin, I occupied myself more particularly with the nautical observations with which you were good enough to charge me and in consequence, I made my route by land to the east-south-east, causing myself to be followed by a man to carry the collections of natural history that circumstances might make me encounter. On my route, I encountered two springs of fresh water which, according to my dead reckoning, could furnish about three barrels a day and perhaps more. Thus, one can get water and wood on this land although the vegetation is not abundant.

"Arrived on the summit of the most elevated rocks of the eastern part, I had the conviction that this land is an island separated from the continent by an arm of sea of about seven or eight miles, and as the tide was almost low when I found myself at this point, I was able to see distinctly in the middle of the channel the banks that are in the interval of sea which (sic) makes it an island. If, in the approaches to these banks, there is water there, this place could offer a good anchorage.

"The low lands to the east which form the second of the islands is separated from this (sic) where I was and which is high about four or five miles (sic). But it forms a striking contrast with that where I landed in that there is only sands covered with little vegetation, while that where I was is high and steep and full of rocks. At the western point of this island there is a bank which extends quite far in the same direction.

"I estimate that high tide took place on land at noon. At the end of the ebb, it appeared to me to have risen 20 feet and in the full of the flood it had risen only four feet from the mark of the highest tides.

"The currents on land appeared to us to have their direction from east to west, but they did not appear to us to have great force as we approached the coast.

"The soil of the island is for the greater part a heap of basalt prisms piled one upon another. Often and particularly on the summit of the peaks, they rest on one of their smallest faces. Some of these rocks dominate others to such a height that at a distance one would take them for tree trunks; elsewhere they represent the aspect of sloping walls. In the valleys, they are heaped without symmetry and appear to have fallen from the neighbouring hills. For the rest, all these lavas have very sharp ridges, except those which are beaten by the sea and those which one encounters in sorts of gullies or ravines where it appears that the water from rains has rolled as a torrent. Their external surfaces are covered with an oxide of iron which gives to the entire island a reddish-brown colour so that the parts which are

"detached by the waters seem to furnish food to the vegetation found then mixed with a little sand which, no doubt, the winds have carried there. Each of these deposits in the middle of the rocks forms a sort of garden very pleasant to the view and allow the escape of a most pleasant odour. It is in similar places that I collected the plants I brought back, taking care to choose what seemed to me able to interest botany (sic).

"I saw on this land no trace of inhabitants, however one would perhaps be inclined to believe that the natives of the continent sometimes go there since I encountered there some tree trunks at the foot of which fires must have been made. Another observation can also confirm this conjecture in that I found in different places, fragments of lava broken freshly without it being apparent that they had been broken by the impact of some other masses which time or wind might have caused to collapse. These breaks had the colour of basalt without decomposition.

"The only living beings that we encountered are a kangaroo of the large species and another quadruped of the size of a large dog of a tawny colour having a large tail well furnished with hair and pendant. I saw it too far away to be able to give a more correct idea of it and when I pursued it, I was not able (to) cut off its retreat or oblige it to pass closer to me. An eagle, a raven and several seagulls as well as two species of small ground birds showed themselves to us.

"We also encountered a snake as large as the arm, having more than five feet in length, grey and covered with scales, a multitude of very large locusts, flies similar to those of France, ants of the large and small species and several butterflies black with white spots.

"The edges of the sea furnished different species of shells of which I brought back a sample.

"At night, having cleared up the point of geography for which I had been sent, I prepared myself to return on board as soon as the boat would be afloat and at ten o'clock we embarked. In setting off, I made course to N ¼ N.W. On land, the sea was calm, but when we were offshore, it became rough and heavy. After having made course for about five hours and finding myself in eighteen fathoms of water, which placed me far offshore from the ship, I came about in order to maintain myself until daylight in a lesser depth. But at sunrise, not perceiving the ship, I made course to return to the anchorage I had left and it was in returning to land that we made out the ship, I immediately took the shortest course to rejoin it".

Report of the chief of the helm, Fortin, employed in the same expedition as M. Ronsard.

(no written or numerical mention)
1801-07-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW to WNW. At 10.30 Citizen Ronsard arrived in the large boat; he had walked over the island and found very good water there. It is well wooded and landing is easy; he brought back many shells, among them two of the kind called the admiral, which led the commander to name this island, and another small sandy one 2 miles from it which we cannot see from the ship because it is awash, the Admiral Islands. At 10.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon in 20° 20' 13" of latitude observed and in 114° 10' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 50' NW. At 1 bore away S 67° 30' E towards a very thick column of smoke. At 4 took the bearing of the Admiral Islands from S 33° W to S 67° 30' W, the mainland stretching from S 15° W to S 67° 30' E. Several columns of smoke could be seen at different points of the mainland, the most conspicuous being the one we were steering for. At 4.45, the water having shoaled, we bore up gradually as far as N 56° 15' E. At 5 an eddy formed by a shoal was seen abeam at two cables. At 5.30 took the bearing of the Admiral Island S 34° W, the sandy Admiral island S 5° W, the mainland in sight from south to S 50° E. At 7.30 we anchored in 10 fathoms, grey sand, the mainland bearing from S 24° W to S 57° E (this bearing was taken the next day at daybreak). At the anchorage the currents set east and west and run 1.5 [knots].

1801-07-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from SE to SSE falling away a great deal. Two men were sent to Dirk Hartog with 15 days' provisions to make signals to the Géographe should she appear on the coast. About 8 in the evening the captain held a council on what course to take in the separation we found ourselves in; it was decided that we should wait as long as the quantity of water we had on board would allow, which was down to 70 casks.
1801-07-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 10th, as soon as we had well recognised and taken bearings of the land from the masthead, for it could scarcely be distinguished from the deck, we set sail in the intention of sailing along the coast. But the winds, at sunrise, having shifted from south-south-east to south-east, we lost it from sight all the more quickly in that it could not be distinguished, according to me, more than three leagues distance.
At nine o'clock, the breeze having become strong, we were forced to take a second reef in the topsails and continued thereafter our course, the lead in hand, steering close-hauled. The soundings throughout the morning were fairly regular from 10 to 15 fathoms, a bottom of sand and coarse gravels mixed with small broken shells.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 20° 0' 33" and the longitude according to our timekeepers was 115° 6' 0" for No. 27 and 114° 7' 57" for No. 35. It is difficult to account for the daily loss that this timekeeper has experienced since our departure from Seals Bay, unless one believes that one of the two has experienced some severe shocks in lowering it to the shore, which, however, is not likely, according to the precautions that were taken to keep it sheltered from this accident.
In the afternoon, the winds varied until the east and the breeze having moderated, we loosened the reefs which it had obliged us to take in the morning.
At sunset, we had no knowledge of the lands, which is all the less surprising in that we then had 23 fathoms of water.
During the night of the 10th to the 11th, the winds returned to south-south-east and we continued to keep the wind to close with the land. But as the breeze was very light, we made little progress. The bottom on which we passed during the night was found to be from 25 to 30 fathoms, grey sand and sometimes mixed with coarse gravels and small flat stones of different colours.
1801-07-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SSE. At 6.30 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 11.30 took the bearing of a column of smoke S 5° E, no land being in sight. At noon in 20° 0' 30" of latitude observed and in 114° 46' 0" of longitude by No. 27.

1801-07-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene. Winds from ENE to NW, almost calm. Saw several meteors in the NE.
1801-07-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 11th, at eight o'clock, we had the sea breeze and it was much more moderate than the day before. We went about on the southerly tack, having then 35 fathoms of water and wishing to close with the land, from which the direction of the wind that had blown the day before had carried us a little too far offshore.
At noon, we were already at 21 fathoms, but without knowledge of any land. The latitude had been observed at 19° 40' 52".
In the afternoon the winds varied from the east toward the north and for two hours, the soundings were very irregular between twenty and eleven fathoms which made me fear we were in the neighbourhood of some shoal. However, as I wished to make out the land which could not be very far away since one perceived, for half an hour past, several smokes in different points of the horizon.
At two o'clock, the lookouts which had announced to us for half an hour, the land to windward of us and of which we then had knowledge from the deck, warned us that there was ahead of it at a rather great distance, a shoal on which the sea broke much. Several persons went to the masthead to reconnoitre it and as their report confirmed the report that had been made, I immediately had every man go to his post to be ready to go about quickly if the case required it. And I continued my course as if there had been no danger, only with the precaution of sounding often. But the bottom always holding between eleven and fourteen fathoms, I wished to penetrate further. But it was repeated to me several times that we were approaching much the breakers that were to windward of us, which made me take the course of putting on the other tack.
Then the land which we had in sight was taken, and which appeared to us under the form of an isolated point which touches the great land which we could not discover, although several persons, especially those who saw only islands, asserted that it was one. If the fact is true, it would be passably far from the continent and would have its inhabitants, for one could distinctly see several fires on it.
The northerly tack took us away from the land and although the wind was very light we could scarcely see it at sunset from the masthead, then bearing to us south-east by east.
During the night of the 11th to the 12th, the winds were very variable until eleven o'clock and almost calm. They then shifted to west-north-west and we steered on the northerly tack toward the east, maintaining ourselves between twenty and twenty-five fathoms. At midnight, we steered north-east on the same depths. We then had a moment of concern about what the weather might be the next day. The sky had become covered with clouds and the barometer had suddenly fallen a line and a half. The hygrometer, however, varied little and Citizen Péron observed that if there was bad weather, it would be more rather thundery than rainy.
1801-07-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to N. At noon in 19° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 115° 10' 27" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 1° 39' NW. At noon a very low land was sighted in the S 75° E, having the look of a sandy island. The sea broke on it with force, especially at its southern part, where a chain of breakers began and stretched away to the south. This islet cannot be far from the mainland, for from the topgallant crosstrees I saw a smoke in the distance. At 5 the sandy islet (seen from the crosstrees) bore S 56° E. At 8 calm; at 9 a fresh breeze from WNW, the course was given N 22° 30' E and at 10, N 33° 45' E.

1801-07-31.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW in strong gusts. At 4.30 the tide began to turn.
1801-07-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 12th, at daylight the sky had rather bad appearance, the whole horizon in the part from west to north being laden with large and thick clouds. However, that of the part from west to south being very clear and the winds having this direction, it seemed to us that we would have fine weather, which indeed happened for the winds having freshened from south to south-south-west and south-west, they made the clouds disappear and at ten o'clock the sky was perfectly fine.
At sunrise although we were at 31 fathoms of water, we nevertheless had knowledge of the land from the masthead. It presented itself under the form of a rather elevated hillock bearing to us south 5° west. I do not doubt that this land is some elevation in the interior of the continent despite its resemblance to an island for we have so often been deceived by a similar appearance that one can never be too wary of it.
At six o'clock, I had the course steered east-north-east but as soundings were taken every half hour, seeing that the bottom increased instead of diminishing as I had expected, we steered east and I continued this course until noon, always surprised to see the bottom increase while I expected to see it diminish very rapidly, as had happened to us the previous days.
During the forenoon, there was a fresh breeze from south to south-south-west and we made a good course to the east.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 19° 18' 41" and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us at No. 27 by 116° 12' 18" and at No. 35 by 115° 14' 7".
As this latitude placed us at a fairly great distance from land and the sounding confirmed it, I had the course held as close as possible to south-south-east, the winds being then south-west, in order to come to make out the land before nightfall and see whether this part of the coast was more approachable than those we had seen before this time.
At two o'clock and a half, we began to have knowledge of several smokes rising from different points of the coast, but one could not, for all that, see the land from the topgallant-sail yard. We continued to make course all sail set until sunset without having knowledge of it from the deck, but it was distinguished well enough from the masthead. We had then eleven and twelve fathoms of
(water) and the two extremities of the land in sight bore to us, the first at east 55° south, the second at south 33° west and the middle of these lands to the south. It was not possible to take a view of them in that they appeared absolutely level with the sea with no elevation that could be remarked.
However, as I had resolved to approach the land as much as it would be possible, I continued to make course to the south but at six o'clock having passed suddenly from eleven fathoms to eight and a half, I came about to seaward, this course having appeared to me the most prudent.
During the night of the 12th to the 13th, the winds were, at first from south-west fairly moderate but they shifted successively to south and at midnight, we had them from south-south-east strong breeze, which obliged us to take a second reef in the topsails. At this time, the sounding gave 32 fathoms, which made me take the course, in order not to go too far from the coast, to heave-to under port tack until daylight, sounding every hour, in order to know whether the current was taking us to the land or the drift offshore as I supposed.
For the rest, it blew a strong breeze at the rising of the moon and it was a bad presage for what the weather might be the next day.
1801-07-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to south. At midnight the course was given N 45° E, and at 4, N 56° 15' E. At 6 took the bearing of the sandy islet S 5° W. The course was given east. At noon in 19° 17' 51" of latitude observed and in 116° 8' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 56' NW. At half past noon lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 3.30 a column of smoke was seen in the S 45° E, no land being in sight. At 5.30 it was seen stretching from S 35° E to S 33° W, and a large column of smoke S 57° W. At 6, having only 9 fathoms, went onto the port tack. At midnight hove to with the port side to the wind; a strong breeze.

1801-08-01.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a fresh breeze from S by E, SSE and ESE. At noon we got under way under topsails. We sounded and found from 6 to 9 fathoms, sand, coral and broken shell. At 3 let go the starboard anchor in 9 fathoms. Bearings of the anchorage: the visible NW end of Dirk Hartog W 6° S; the SE end of the same island W 39° S; the middle of the island within the bay E 12° S.
1801-08-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 13th, in the morning, it continued to blow a very strong breeze as I had expected. At daylight, we found ourselves fairly far from the coast since the bottom was 36 fathoms, so I had the course steered close-hauled to close with it, the winds being from the south-east varying to south-south-east. After sunrise, they became so strong that it was necessary to take the third reef in the fore-topsails and the flying topgallant sail, but around eleven o'clock, it began to weaken. The sea had become rough and although the course should have brought us nearer to the land, the sounding which at noon was 39 fathoms, made it sufficiently clear to us that the currents and the drift of the ship were taking us away from it by carrying us in the north and perhaps even in the north-west.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 19° 10' 12" and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us according to No. 27 at 116° 24' 31" and according to No. 35 at 115° 22' 16". Several distances of the sun to the moon were taken in the morning, the results of which gave (no figures), from which it resulted a difference with the timekeepers of (no figures)
In the afternoon, we continued to make course close-hauled forcing sail according to the winds that were then blowing. The breeze had already begun to be less strong, but it was not until sunset that we could loosen a reef of our topsails and that was not of much use to us for shortly after, the calm was so profound that the ship could scarcely steer. However, the sea was still heavy and it was not until eight o'clock in the evening that we found it more calm, the bottom was then 45 fathoms.
According to the observations made the day before and on this same day to know the declination of the magnetic needle, we found it to be (no figures) to the north-east which did not accord, according to our longitude, with the observations of the navigators who preceded us. But this remark has nothing surprising in it in that its change since those times has necessarily had to bring about a change in that of the declination.
During the night of the 13th to the 14th, the calm lasted until ten o'clock,
and then, we had the land breeze which, light at first, was nevertheless fairly strong when it shifted to south-south-west. Nevertheless, we continued to make course to the east, the lead in hand, and with little sail, having the hope of not being far from the land for the next day. However, as the sounding was constantly between thirty-eight and forty fathoms, it seemed to me that we (should not) be as close to the coast as we presumed, although at sunset, one had perceived several smokes coming from the land without having had knowledge of it.
1801-08-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course given east. At noon in 19° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 116° 22' 9" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 15' NW.

1801-08-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a clear sky. A light breeze S, SE, SSE and ESE. At 10 the tide turned to the SE.
1801-08-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 14th, after sunrise, the winds varied from south-south-east to S.E. by south and the breeze was strong enough during the morning to prevent us from loosening a reef in our topsails which had two reefs taken in. The sea was even fairly rough, and we had forty-two fathoms of water, which clearly demonstrated to us that the course had taken more to the north than the dead reckoning we had made of it.
Throughout the forenoon, we made course to the east as much as the wind permitted and it was not without astonishment that we saw the bottom increase while it seemed to us, according to the bearing that the charts give to the land, that it should diminish. The part where the winds held not allowing us to go on the other tack, we continued running east by drawing a little to the north.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 18° 48' 29" and the longitude by the timekeepers reduced to the same time placed us at No. 27 by 117° 7' 45" and at No. 35 by 115° 55' 29". The distances taken of the sun to the moon the day before, having been found bad by the difficulty that had been encountered in taking them, we renewed them in the forenoon and the result was that we found ourselves at 119° 7' 36" which gave an enormous difference with the timekeepers since at No. 27 there was found a difference of 1° 59' 34" west and at No. 35 3° 11' 53" also to the west. What can be the cause of such great difference in timekeepers whose rate had varied so little before our departure from Seals Bay, the astronomer Bernier persisting in saying that they have absolutely experienced no shock nor tremor either in putting them on shore or at the moment when they were brought back on board?
Around two o'clock in the afternoon, the breeze began to moderate a little but nevertheless much less than it had done the previous days, which made me keep the reefs in the topsails.
At four o'clock, we had 34 fathoms, but at sunset, we had no knowledge of land which led me to continue the same course. At eight o'clock, the bottom was thirty fathoms and since some of our charts indicate, at the latitude where we estimated this same sounding almost all land, it seemed to me that it would not be prudent to continue long the same course so that at eight o'clock and a half, I put on the other tack, the drift being to take me in the north and consequently move me away from the coast.
During the night of the 14th to the 15th, the winds were from south-south-east and sometimes variable to south, strong breeze, the sea, nevertheless fairly fine. At midnight, the breeze, far from increasing or diminishing as was ordinary, did nothing but increase so that it was necessary to take the second reef in the small topsail. During the rest of the night, the winds blew with the same force and everything announced to us a strong breeze for the next day. The sounding which, at eight o'clock, was 29 fathoms, increased during the night and until the next day at daylight, by 6 fathoms so that we found ourselves at sunrise at 35.
1801-08-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to south. At noon in 18° 44' 17" of latitude observed and in 117° 8' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 42' NW. The lunar distances gave 118° 35' of longitude. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds SSE to SE, almost calm. At 2 p.m. the large boat took 15 days' provisions to go and survey Shark Bay.
1801-08-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 15th, having no more than thirty-five fathoms of water at sunrise, we made as much sail as the wind, which was very strong in the part from the south-east to south-south-east, would allow us to carry and I always kept the hope of seeing the land soon.
At ten o'clock, the bottom passed suddenly from 35 fathoms to 39, which led me to believe that we were moving away from it instead of approaching it. But at noon, having had it again at thirty-five, I changed my opinion. It was unfortunate that the winds did not permit us to make some progress to the south to approach it more promptly. However, I always kept the hope of having knowledge of it before nightfall, if, nevertheless, the direction that our charts give it was good.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 18° 6' 34" and the longitude of our timekeepers, the results of which since the last observation by distances of the sun to the moon had given us 2 and 3 degrees of difference, seemed to us very uncertain. However, as it was not necessary to give it up entirely we found ourselves according to No. 27 at 118° 5' 34" and according to No. 35 at 116° 79' 54".
In the afternoon, we continued to make course to the east, taking as little to the north as was possible. The sounding constantly reported 35 fathoms, and it was not until sunset that the bottom began a little to diminish. We had at this time no knowledge of the lands, nor even any index which might make us suspect that we were near them. We indeed saw some black and white gannets which, at sunset, were taking their direction to the south, no doubt to go on land, but it was not possible for us to calculate what distance they might have to go to reach it.
After sunset, the breeze began to diminish and the winds having slightly shifted toward the south, we were able to steer to the east by south-east. At eight o'clock, the bottom was 30 fathoms and I continued the same course until the moment we should arrive at 25 fathoms, giving orders to warn me as soon as we should reach it.
At eight o'clock and a half, although we had had no knowledge of the land during the night, I perceived a brightness on the horizon under the lee of the ship which appeared to me to be occasioned only by a fire on land. I immediately had a man go up in the lookout in the masthead and who, without going higher, had a perfect knowledge of the fire in the place where I had indicated to him to look. However, the bottom being still considerable enough for us to have nothing to fear, I continued the same course until nine o'clock, but then distinctly seeing the fire which was on land from the deck, and having no more than 23 fathoms of water, I had the course put on the other tack and we steered to the south until one o'clock in the night, when the breeze having shifted to the east-south-east very strong, I heaved-to under starboard tack so that the drift would take us in the north.
During the rest of the night, the sky was very fine and clear, but we endured from time to time very strong gusts from the south-east to east-south-east, direction which the winds took. The sounding increased gradually and from one o'clock in the night until five o'clock the next day, we passed from 28 to 35 fathoms of water, fine sand mixed with small broken shells.
1801-08-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course east. At noon in 18° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 118° 3' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 2' NW. At 8.30, having sighted a fire ahead, we went onto the port tack. At 9 the fire bore from us N 50° E; it could no longer be seen at 10.30. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky a little cloudy. A light breeze from ESE to SSE and south. At 2.15 p.m. the corvette made sail until 6 p.m., when we anchored in 8 fathoms, sandy bottom. On the 16th at 11 a.m. a thick smoke was seen on the mainland which had risen all at once. The captain, wondering what could have caused this kind of eruption, sent off the small boat under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq.
1801-08-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 16th, in the morning, it continued to blow a very strong breeze from the part of the south-east to east-south-east. At sunrise, the lookouts did not perceive the land and I do not know why, for at seven o'clock fifteen minutes, we had perfect knowledge of it and the distance that we had made since sunrise until that time was not considerable enough not (sic) to have seen it earlier.
Be that as it may, when we saw the land from the masthead, it bore to us east 36° south. One could equally see from the south to south by south-east very thick smoke which no doubt came from the fires that we had perceived the day before. The bottom was then 35 fathoms.
At nine o'clock we had perfect knowledge of the land from the deck and it appeared to us much higher than all those we had had until then, that is to say since we had been sailing along the coast of the north-west. I flattered myself that this disposition of the land would allow us to approach it quite closely to recognise it well in that I presumed that the waters would be deeper than we found them in the places where it is low and submerged and which had not allowed us to approach it. However, at noon, we had no more than fourteen fathoms, whilst an hour before we had found twenty.
The meridian altitude at the same time placed us at 17° 28' 26" and the longitude of our timekeepers was found to be at No. 27 of 118° 26' 13" and at No. 28 (sic) of 117° 5' 54".
We made, in the forenoon, all our efforts to take some series of distances of the sun to the moon but the breeze was so fresh that we could not succeed in it by the agitation that our instruments experienced despite all our precautions to secure them. According to the bearing that was taken at noon, the land extended from north 57° east to south 52° east.
As the land bore to us to the lee of the course on which we were steering, I had the course steered north-east and we soon perceived lands trending still more to the north. From noon until four o'clock, the sounding constantly reported from 15 to 12 fathoms fine sand bottom and small broken shells, but then it passed to ten fathoms and even to 9, which made us successively haul up two points to maintain ourselves in ten fathoms. The breeze had much moderated and we carried our topgallant sails although with two reefs in the topsails.
The land that we sailed along in the afternoon, at a distance of at most four leagues is very recognisable and of an appearance much less wild than all those we had seen since we had been in this part of the coast. One could distinguish behind the edge of the sea, two elevations fairly considerable and covered with verdure, the first, that is to say the summit of the dunes was equally covered with plants or shrubs which made the prospect pleasant. The terrain which reached down to the edge of the sea had two very distinct colours, in some places it was fairly bright red and in others very white sand which seemed to announce an easy landing. My intention at first was not to come to anchor, but the calm having come on after sunset, I anchored in nine fathoms and a half good holding, with the fear however of being obliged to set sail during the night if the breeze should come to be as strong as it had been the previous days.
During the evening, we saw along the whole coast, a great quantity of fires but several were so considerable that they did not appear to us to be the place where the natives lived. It was very probably a conflagration in some parts of the woods for the smoke was so considerable that the air was obscured by it.
During the night of the 16th to the 17th, the weather was fine and the breeze almost calm until about two o'clock in the night, when it began to freshen from the part of the south-east, but it was moderate. Although at anchor, I had given orders to sound exactly every hour in order to know whether the flood or ebb of the waters was sensible in the place we occupied. We were astonished not only not to perceive it, but also to recognise that the current had little activity, since despite the light wind that was blowing, we remained constantly swinging at our anchor head to wind, which we had not experienced at our other anchorages, although the breeze there had been much stronger.
Bearings of the anchorage.
The lands most to the north in sight at north 57° east
The lands most to the south also in sight at south 5° east
The middle of the lands, that is to say those which were abeam of us at south 68° east.
The soundings from noon until the moment when we came to anchor were fairly regular from 15 fathoms to nine and a half.
1801-08-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 1.30 the previous day's fire was sighted in the N 33° E. It disappeared at 4. At 6 filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 7.15 the land was sighted from the crosstrees from east to N 68° E. At 10 it could be seen from the deck; it appeared fairly high, in the S 56° E. At noon in 17° 28' 16" of latitude observed and in 118° 26' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 14' NW. The land from S 64° E to N 68° E, with several columns of smoke at different points of the coast. At 1 bore away N 45° E and ran along the coast, on which we saw a countless number of fires and smokes. At 4 bore away N 22° 30' E. The northernmost land in sight N 54° E; low, wooded land which appeared to form a bight S 85° E; a great white cliff S 53° E; a white headland S 22° E. At 6 anchored in 9 fathoms, coarse sand and broken shell, the land bearing from S 5° E to N 57° E. An immense fire burned all night in the N 68° E.

1801-08-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from SW to W and N. At 2 p.m. got under way under topsails and staysails. At 5 anchored in 5 fathoms, fine sand. At 9 p.m. the small boat was back and reported that the smoke we had seen came from the fires of the Aboriginal people, gathered to the number of 9, men and women together.
1801-08-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 17th, in the morning, I intended to send a boat on shore to reconnoitre the coast and visit the country, but before sending it, I was glad to assure myself of the weather after sunrise since the manner in which it had set the day before, and the appearance it had in the morning at its rising, seemed to announce to us a strong breeze for the day.
This prognostication was not deceiving for hardly had it risen five or six degrees above the horizon when it began to freshen strong breeze which decided me to set sail at once. As soon as we were under sail, I directed my course to approach the land a little more, wishing to sail along it in eight or nine fathoms in order to well recognise a point cut sheer and which had the appearance of a cape from which the land should take another direction. But after an hour's course, having passed suddenly from nine fathoms and a half and even from eleven to seven, I had the course steered to the north in the hope of finding deeper water and it was not without astonishment that I saw it diminish to six and even five fathoms, although we were sensibly moving away from the land. From eight o'clock until nine, we hauled up successively from the north until the west, always always (sic) on a bottom of six fathoms and six fathoms and a half and it was not until that time that the bottom began to increase.
At nine o'clock and a half, being at fifteen fathoms, I again set the course to the north having, at this point of sailing, several lands to windward of us which had the appearance of several islands. We made course to approach them until ten o'clock, but finding no more than eight fathoms, I had to bear away again to the north-west to put ourselves in deeper water. We then had the certainty that the lands in sight were a succession of islands which very probably are joined one to another by reefs or sand banks on which there is very little water since one could see in several places the sea rising to a great height. The two first islets, that is to say those which we had doubled, are of little extent and can scarcely be perceived at more than three leagues' distance. Two others which are to the north of these, are more considerable and may have two leagues' extent from north to south, but at the northern point of the first, one sees a reef which advances much to the north and on which the sea breaks. We were then making course to the north-west and the bottom was from eight to fifteen fathoms. When we had doubled these two islands and the reef which is at the last, we saw no more lands than to the north-east and at a great distance and I then resumed the course to the north-north-east, keeping as close-hauled as possible. But the bottom having suddenly passed from 15 to 9 fathoms, it appeared to me that we were on the edge of a bank. Which is all the more confirmed in that the lookouts which I had sent to the masthead announced to us that they (could) distinctly perceive it by the change of colour of the waters, and that it extended to leeward of us. However, as we were at a great distance from land since it could scarcely be seen, I continued the same course, the lead in hand. But it was not for long for a quarter of an hour after, we found no more than six and a half fathoms, which obliged me again to bear away to the north-west by west to have more water. We continued this course until noon without having a very rapid increase. However, then, we had eleven fathoms and sometimes twelve.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 16° 53' 30" and the longitude according to the timekeepers, was for No. 27 of 118° 28' 3" and for No. 35 of 116° 47' 54".
After noon, being at fifteen fathoms, I made course from north-west by west to north, coming about by quarter of an hour intervals to go round at my ease the northern part of the bank of which we had had knowledge. At two o'clock, the bottom began to diminish again and we fell again to seven and a half fathoms although then, we were steering to the NNW. We had to bear away again and steer to the north-west. This same bottom of seven fathoms to eight lasted nearly half an hour and finally it passed to 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 from two o'clock and a half to three o'clock. From three o'clock until three o'clock and a half, making course to the north-north-west, we passed suddenly from 15 to 18 fathoms and from 18 to 20. Although the wind was very light, the sea was a little agitated and I concluded from it that we were entirely delivered from this bank on which with a fairly strong breeze, the sea had been very calm and smooth.
At four o'clock, we lay to the closest to the wind all sail set, to try not to move too far from the continent. The bottom was then 22 fathoms.
At sunset, there was no appearance of land and we had the course put to the north toward the east as much as was possible.
During the night of the 17th to the 18th, the breeze was very light or to speak more correctly, we remained almost in calm until eleven o'clock in the evening, when we had a little freshness from the south-south-east. The bottom was then 27 fathoms. At midnight, it was 23 and we were steering to the north-east by north. This diminution made me think that we were not very far from the coast. But at one o'clock, the sounding reported 30 fathoms, and at two o'clock, 35. We then steered to the north-east and I followed this same course until daylight, all sail set, no longer finding the bottom at 35 fathoms. The breeze had then increased and we were making fairly good progress, with the winds from the south-east.

Note: At seven o'clock and a half in the morning, M. Picquet who, being on watch and wholly occupied in tormenting the helmsmen because he found that the clock was not going fast enough for his impatience, caused me all the more irritation as the noise he was making prevented me from working in my cabin where I was occupied at that moment. As we were making course on the land, the lead in hand, the helmsman charged with that employment repeated to him several times: M. Picquet, 9 fathoms 1/2, M. Picquet, 9 fathoms 1/2, M. Picquet, 9 fathoms 1/2, without his paying the least attention. I then raised my voice and I said to him in turn: M. Picquet it is to the sounding that you must attend and not to the clock. His self-esteem, no doubt offended by my remark, made him advance with a movement of vivacity quite reprehensible to the entrance of my cabin, which I am careful to keep open either day or night when he is on watch, and said to me in his own terms: by God Sir, you are quite ridiculous to find it wrong that I look after the clock. My reply was that I found only him impertinent and ridiculous on board and in order that he no longer have occasion to put himself in the case of punishing him in the way he would have deserved, I removed the command of a watch from him while awaiting that I might be able to get rid of him altogether.
The verbal order that I was giving him not having seemed to him sufficient, he asked me for one in writing, in consequence I addressed to him the following letter:

"The Commander of the expedition to Citizen Picquet,

"Your repeated impertinences, your conduct in the service and your discourteous replies, every time I have represented to you your duties, having finally exhausted my patience, I warn you that you will command no more watches on board.

"The safety of the ship and of all persons on it requires me to take this precaution. I have only to regret that I did not take it earlier". N.B.

In order not to disrupt the order of service, I took his watch which I continued until our arrival at Timor. The aspirant who was doing it with him, was placed with M. Freycinet, and I kept with me the one who was doing it with him.
1801-08-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At 6 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet, officer of the watch, having the glass set and asking the chief quartermaster whether note had been taken of the time elapsed since getting under way, the commander, who was in bed, called out to him from his cabin that he was tiresome, that it was a question of the lead and not of the glass, and that if the watch wearied him he might leave it, and that he would take it himself; and he did take it. At noon in 16° 53' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 36' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 42' NW. Took the bearing of a sandy islet S 89° E and the north point of the land in sight N 74° E; at a short distance from that point a bank could be seen stretching far away to the N 22° 30' W, on which the sea broke. Since 8 a.m. the bottom has been very uneven. We were no doubt on the edge of a bank whose direction is at first N by NW, then runs NW, and then takes a northerly direction again. We tried to keep near the course N 45° E but were always obliged to bear away. At 1 we lost sight of the land; at 7 calm. From 8 to 11 the course made good was N by NW; from 11 to noon NW; from noon to 3.30 NW by N; and from 3.30 to midnight N and NE by N. Commander Baudin gave me orders to take the watch in Citizen Piquet's place, and I kept it until Timor.

1801-08-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to SSW and south.
1801-08-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, at sunrise, we had no knowledge of the land which, nevertheless, we were not far distant from according to the course we had steered during the night, supposing, however, that the bearing our charts gave to it was exact, which appeared very doubtful, for having steered east-north-east for almost the whole morning with a fine breeze from south-east to south-south-east, we had no knowledge of it at noon, nor during the rest of the day.
The observed latitude was 16° 1' 27" and the longitude deduced from the timekeepers placed us at No. 27 by 118° 59' 0" and at No. 35 by 117° 26' 29".
In the evening, the wind was slight and we had observed for several days that as soon as the sun had passed the meridian, the wind calmed by degrees, and at the moment of its setting, it blew so little that the ship could scarcely steer.
We had throughout the day the company of a great quantity of birds, such as boobies, gulls, frigatebirds. Only, one remarked more particularly a flight of ducks which made two or three times the round of the vessel. Whales appeared only in small number, but much larger than all those we had seen hitherto.
From sunrise to sunset, the sounding varied from 40 fathoms to 30, with different bottoms suitable for anchorage.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the weather was fine and the wind calm until midnight. As I happened to be on watch then, having taken that of M. Picquet, I had the drag cast several times which, apart from what it brought back to us of several fine objects of natural history, also served to make known to us the direction of the currents which were then carrying us to the north-west. Although we kept the course east during the calm, the tide was so strong that the drag had the effect of a kedge anchor upon the vessel, coming straight ahead, and it was in that direction that we hauled it on board.
At midnight, the winds passed to the south and then to the south-south-west, fine breeze. We passed the rest of the night making way under our topsails and always with the lead in hand so as not to be surprised by too sudden a decrease in the depth.
1801-08-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to E. At 2 a.m. the course was given N 45° E and at 5.30 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 16° 0' 14" of latitude observed and in 118° 59' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 29' NW. At 7 calm; the dredge was put over and brought up many objects of natural history.

1801-08-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south to SSE. At 4 a.m. the longboat was put in the water together with the small boat and the dinghy, and most of the gear was embarked in them for the camp set up ashore to repair the longboat.
1801-08-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, in the morning, it continued to blow a fine breeze from the south-south-east. We made course to the east, all sails set, without having knowledge of land, which did not fail to surprise me for I believed myself much nearer although the sounding was still at 50 fathoms. It was therefore necessary to crowd on sail to come and reconnoitre it and that is what we did by continuing course to the east.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 40' 57" and the longitude according to the timekeepers was for No. 27, 119° 46' 7" and for No. 35, 118° 13' 59".
Shortly after, the look-outs announced land a little under the wind to us and we soon, ourselves, perceived it from the deck. It presented itself first in the form of an island of moderate and very regular elevation, but we were not long in seeing the low lands which accompanied it at both extremities and we were convinced, by the extent which we perceived, that it was the continent. My intention being to anchor on this coast, I continued to make course towards an indentation which lay before us and in the middle of which we found a very strong current which prevented us from advancing and made us drift towards the part of the land which remained to us in the north, a little towards the west. The sounding was then 20 to 25 fathoms but the bottom so bad that there was too much risk in anchoring there. I therefore took the course of returning on my steps, but I had to make course to the west and even, to the west-south-west, in order to be able to double several banks which we perceived and of which we had had no knowledge hitherto. The breeze was very slight but the current carried us to the north-west. We fortunately moved away from the land by drifting past a bank of considerable extent on which, notwithstanding the calm, the sea broke strongly.
A little before sunset, we saw at the surface of the water several sand banks from which the sea had just receded and it is there, without doubt, that M. Saint Aloüarn intended to designate, on his chart by the quantity of points found there and which appear to form as many islands. It is possible that there may be found between these banks and the firm coast, a channel through which one could pass, but I think that it is not vessels like ours which should seek them. This supposition may be all the better founded in that one could see distinctly between the great land and the banks which had just become uncovered a considerable extent of water where the sea appeared tranquil.
At sunset, we found ourselves already somewhat offshore and the sounding was 25 to thirty fathoms, but the bottom so bad that we had to give up anchoring for the night, unless forced to do so by some unforeseen circumstance. It was then calm and the current seemed to be setting to the south with considerable velocity.
From six o'clock until ten o'clock, we made very little way with the help of our sails, and the bottom decreased enough to cause us anxiety about the direction in which the return of the tide might carry us. In consequence I had a chain secured to the second anchor so as to be able to use it if necessary. This precaution proved unnecessary for this time, for the breeze coming to us a little earlier than usual, we moved away by the help of our sails. During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth, the sky was very fine and the winds were from the south. We kept close-hauled on the port tack, with little sail, sounding continuously. We were astonished to see that in going offshore, the bottom was found to be always coral and rocks, all the more so as it was the first time we had encountered this nature on the coast.
1801-08-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At midnight the course was given east. At noon in 15° 40' 41" of latitude observed and in 119° 46' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 36' NW. Land was sighted to the north; at 3 went onto the port tack. At 4 it bore from us from north to N 45° E, and at 5.30 from N 22° W to N 52° E. Calm at 5, the current setting us in the N 45° W; at 9.30 a light breeze. We could not anchor at nightfall, the bottom being coral.

1801-08-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds almost calm, the horizon loaded.
1801-08-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, in the morning, being hove to for four hours, we ran to the north-east until eight o'clock, and then I ordered course steered to east-north-east to close with the land of which we had knowledge at sunrise and which lay from east 16° south to east 26° south. As we approached it, we were convinced that it was the same part of the coast we had reconnoitred the day before.
From eight o'clock until noon, we had a fairly fine breeze from the south and we were making course east-north-east when the look-outs, from the tops of the masts, announced a sand bank on which the sea broke heavily. Nevertheless, as we had no bottom at 30 fathoms, I did not change course until we distinctly perceived from the deck the bank and the breakers which had been reported to us. To double this reef, we were obliged to bear away until north, we passed it at about one league distance without having bottom at 25 fathoms. After doubling it, we came successively to the wind to resume the course which should bring us to close with the coast. The danger we had just passed presented itself in the form of a small island of very white sand, sufficiently elevated in its middle to be seen by day at two leagues distance, but it is covered by the sea at its northern and southern extremities by shoals on which the sea rolls with force and which extend half a league in the same direction.
In the east of this bank, we perceived land which we judged to be that of the continent at a distance of about five leagues, appearing to extend particularly from east, drawing towards the north. At ten o'clock, losing sight of them, we kept rather closer to the wind to bring them nearer but at half past ten, we had knowledge of a second sand bank covered by the sea and which we passed three-quarters of a league distant without having bottom at 45 fathoms. A third remaining on our starboard quarter obliged us to bear away again and at half past eleven, the sea appearing clear to us, we put the course north-east by east and east-north-east.
According to what had happened to us from yesterday noon until this day at the same hour, it appears that the coast is scarcely practicable from 16° forty minutes of latitude until the 15° 17' which was that which we observed at noon.
