According to the longitude of our timekeepers we found ourselves at No. 27, 119° 46' 7" and according to No. 35, 118° 13' 59". The bottom was at 45 fathoms, sand and coral.
In the afternoon, the breeze calmed as it had done on the preceding days, so that making very little way, we had no knowledge of the land at sunset. Notwithstanding the little wind there was, we took in sail at eight o'clock, and continued the same course on our topsails only until five o'clock the next day, sounding every hour.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st, the weather was fine and the sky humid. The hygrometer had held for several days at 95° and sometimes above, whilst the barometer remained fairly constantly at 28 inches 2 lines. The march of the hygrometer seemed to announce a change of weather for the new moon and I expected it all the more so as, since we had been on the coasts of New Holland, its renewal had brought about some.
The winds were very slight and variable during the night, from west to south-west and the sounding was found to be between 35 and 40 fathoms, sand and coral, which made the bottom little suitable for anchorage. During the day and part of the night, the drag was cast several times and apart from some branches of coral, it also brought back fragments of pieces of the same nature and several fine fan-shaped sponges, as well as fine medusae very difficult to preserve whole in spite of all the different procedures we employed to achieve it.
1801-08-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 4 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E, crowding sail. At 7 the same land as the day before was sighted from aloft, from S 64° E to S 74° E. At 8.30, having sighted ahead at a short distance a sandbank awash, we bore up north. Having cleared it we resumed our course, and then saw in the S 45° E low land on which the sea broke furiously; at 10 we lost sight of it. At 10.30 a sandbank was seen abeam to windward (S 22° 30' E) 2 miles off. At noon in 15° 17' 40" of latitude observed and in 119° 56' 35" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 34' NW. At 1 the course was given N 78° 45' E. We passed close to a shoal of fish over which there was a very great number of birds; from a distance it might have been taken for a sandbank with the sea breaking on it. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty, a light breeze from SSE, SSW and SE. At 1 a.m. the tide turned to the NW.
1801-08-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, at half past five in the morning, the weather being very fine and the sea calm, we set all sails, having a small breeze from the south, variable to south-south-east, making course east by north-east until sunrise and at seven o'clock, I ordered the course set to the east to come and reconnoitre the land of which we had knowledge at eight hours less ten minutes. It lay from east 22° south to east 50° south.
During the morning, the breeze increased somewhat, but it was so slight that the current made us progress more than the wind.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 8' 30" and the longitude of the timekeepers was for No. 27, 120° 49' 40" and for No. 35, 119° 9' 39".
The northernmost land in view lay from the deck at south 75 east, an island at south 50° east and the southernmost lands at south 22° 30' east.
In the morning, the nature of the bottom changed entirely and instead of finding it sand and coral, as we had for some time, it was of grey marl into which the lead sank entirely. We cast the drag on this bottom, which was the first of this quality we had found, but it brought back only mud of which we made some balls for samples. They soon, being dried in the sun, acquired much consistency. The mineralogist Depuche believes it to be, by the fineness of its grain, much superior to that employed in the pottery manufactured in France.
In the afternoon, the breeze calmed entirely and the currents, according to our dead reckoning, seemed to carry us to the NW at one mile per hour. We had, the whole evening, the sight of a great quantity of birds of the species of boobies and gulls. We also crossed several tidal races which appeared very rapid to us and which caused us to cast the sounding several times from fear of finding ourselves on some banks.
At sunset, we had in view a long succession of islands behind which one could perceive the continent but which lay at too considerable a distance to give it a certain bearing. All the islands which we had in view appeared to offer some openings where perhaps one would find shelter and it was for that reason I decided not to move away from them during the night, so as to be able to visit them the next day. The breeze having freshened somewhat after sunset, we continued to coast along the land until eight o'clock and then put the course offshore under our topsails.
Bearings at sunset.
The chain of islands and islets which we had in view extended from east 3° north to east 60° south.
A portion of land of considerable height which we judged must form part of the continent, lay from east 87° south to east 42° south to east 87° south.
During the night of the 21st to the 22nd, we had either calm or very inconstant winds during its duration. At midnight, one thought to see a fire at east 33° 15' south, but without having certainty, it was judged to be such, according to a fairly brilliant gleam which one thought to see on the horizon.
The sounding which was cast hourly, was very regular and we never had less than 35 fathoms, always bottom of marl into which the lead entered to the extreme upper end of its elevation which was 15 inches.
About two o'clock, the officer on watch having warned me that it was beginning to freshen from the south, I ordered to heave to on the starboard tack while waiting for daylight and continuing to sound.
1801-08-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm and a light breeze from W to SSW. At 5.45 filled and stood on N 78° 45' E under all sail. At 7 the course was given east; at 8 the mainland was sighted from S 40° to S 68° E. At 10 a flat calm; until noon the current set us S 67° 30' E. At noon in 15° 8' 10" of latitude observed and in 120° 44' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 44' NW, the mainland bearing from S 22° E to S 75° E and an island S 50° E. From noon to 3 the current set us N 45° W. At 3, a light breeze, shaped the course east. At 5.45 took the bearing of the northernmost part of the mainland in sight N 87° E; a sandy islet A S 85° E; the nearest land (of the mainland) S 63° E; an islet S 30° E; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 3° E. At 7.30 a dull roar was heard, caused by a tide rip which we crossed. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack.

1801-08-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy and the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE.
1801-08-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, at daybreak, we found ourselves only about one league from the coast and it was not without astonishment that I found myself so near land with 35 to 36 fathoms of water, for my dead reckoning placed me at nearly four leagues distance. I can only attribute it to the rapidity of the current which must have carried us in the south-east direction with great velocity. But in sounding every hour, the decrease in the bottom should have made me aware of it, at least that was how I believed I could prevent these effects.
The islet, across which we found ourselves, was a rock of about half a league extent, very elevated in its middle, and its two extremities terminating in a low point which extended southward about a good league offshore, and to the north by low land which joined it to another, more considerable island. All these parts were seen very well at sunrise, but as there was then flood, they soon became covered by the sea, so that around the island there was no longer seen but a succession of very extensive breakers on which the sea, in spite of the calm, broke strongly. If the flood had not carried us to the north, and even rather vigorously, we should have been obliged to anchor so as not to fall upon them and to wait in that position for the wind to permit us to double them. We passed about a small league offshore from this danger, having 36 fathoms, fine bottom of marl. Bearings at sunrise:
The most visible islet, to the east.
A succession of islets more or less large from east 10° south to east 63° south.
A portion of land presumed to form part of the continent, from east 29° south to south 5° west.
All the islands and rocks which border the continent in this part are far distant from it and appear to offer passages for small boats only at high tide, notwithstanding that several offer great openings. It is, moreover, easy to judge from the colour of the water which is very white, that there must be very little in most of the channels which these islands form.
According to our observations, we had therefore to give up anchoring in this part of the coast. In consequence with the help of the currents, for it was almost calm the whole morning, we moved somewhat away from the coast and continued along the lands which lay to the east, drawing a little to the north.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 14° 59' 43" and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us at No. 27 by 121° 6' 42" and at No. 35 by 119° 25' 5". The point plotted on Robertson's chart which I use because the scale is larger than on the others, was still in error in that it shows the land much further west than it actually is, according to the march of the timekeepers as well as by the observations of distances.
The islet across which we found ourselves at sunrise is particularly remarkable for its white colour in its most elevated parts and brown going to the sea when seen at two or three (leagues) distance, finding itself then at the surface of the water, it presents itself then as a shoal on which the sea breaks with violence.
In the afternoon, we had very variable winds little suited to advance us and one could say that it was rather calm than wind. The freshnesses which they sometimes gave us came sometimes from the south, from the south-west and even from the NW.
At sunset, a large rock which we had doubled, presented to us a form so particular that I made an isolated sketch of it which will make it recognised by all those who, subsequently, shall have occasion to see it. Whether one comes from the south or the north, it presents itself in the form of a barn very regular, but in doubling it, it takes absolutely that of an
inverted bowl and displays to the view all its regularity.
Bearings at sunset.
A succession of the islets seen previously lay from east to south.
And that, so particular by its form, was the southernmost under the appearance of a barn whilst when (we) sketched it under the form of an inverted bowl it lay south 20° east.
After sunset, we had a small breeze from west to WNW until about eight or nine o'clock in the evening. As we had not seen land to the north in drawing towards the east, at sunset I ordered course to NE ¼ E until that moment, and at eight o'clock, we put the course north-east by north to move away from the coast and have drift for the night. The calm having taken us again between nine and ten o'clock, we made very little way. I gave order to the officer who took the watch at eight o'clock to sound every hour, when the bottom would be above 30 fathoms and every half hour when it would be below, not wishing to approach the land further than 25 fathoms.
At nine o'clock, having the bottom which I had prescribed, one went about immediately and we carried to WNW, course which could not fail to carry us offshore. Nevertheless, before the calm had taken us, we were still only (at) 28 fathoms and at midnight at 26. As I took the watch at that time, I had a kedge anchor dropped and veered 40 fathoms. The bottom having appeared to us very good and clean.
In furling the sails, one distinctly perceived the land from the yards and when one warned me that it lay south-east, I soon had knowledge of it from the deck. Although we had nothing certain about the hour of the tides in these waters, I thought that we had the beginning of the ebb and so as to know whether the water set in our anchorage, I regularly had the sounding lead cast every hour.
At midnight, we had 26 fathoms bottom by which I had ordered the anchor dropped.
At one o'clock we had 25 and, successively until six o'clock, the bottom decreased so that at that time we had only 20 and even less, so that we recognised that the sea had fallen for us six fathoms and no doubt more ashore.
The log, which was also cast every hour, gave three degrees knots of velocity. The first two hours it was one and a quarter knots, the second two of nearly two knots and the last two of a little more than one knot. The vessel kept everted to the current from south-south-west to south-south-east.
1801-08-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm, and a light and very variable breeze. At midnight a fire was sighted in the S 57° E. At 2 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 5.30 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E. Islet A then bore from us S 5° E; at 8 it bore south, and off its west point there were breakers stretching as far as S 12° W; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 34° W; a fairly conspicuous point of the mainland S 11° E; the northernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 50° E; an islet S 85° E; another east. From 8 until noon a flat calm, the currents setting us S 67° 30' E about 4 miles. At noon in 14° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 121° 5' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 20' NE. Islet A bore from us S 35° W, a second S 40° E, a third S 44° E, a fourth S 46° E, a fifth S 80° E and a sixth S 88° E. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack (heading NE by N). At 8.30 went onto the starboard tack (heading SW by W). At 10.30 onto the port tack (heading NW). At midnight, being in a flat calm, we let go a kedge anchor in 24 fathoms, soft mud. Bearings taken at the anchorage (on the 23rd at sunrise): we were near a chain of islands stretching from S 36° W to S 71° E; island B, the nearest, bore from us S 51° E, 4 miles off. Latitude observed at the anchorage 14° 47' 40"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 121° 25' 0"; the variation NE at the anchorage 0° 7' 20".

1801-08-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze in gusts from S, SSE and SE.
1801-08-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, having recognised our position, we found ourselves anchored across a great quantity of islands, and the nearest to us was at a distance of a good league. The others extended from east 42° north to the south. Most appeared to form sufficiently considerable openings so that the hope of finding, among so many islands, good shelter for vessels, decided me to send them to reconnoitre, especially in the part which appeared to me best suited to my views.
I therefore had the boat immediately put to sea and I entrusted the command to Citizen Bonnefoy. The naturalists Depuche, Riedelé, and Maugé embarked with him and at seven o'clock, they departed. They first directed their course to the nearest land we had in view across from us and arrived within gun-shot of land, they still had twenty fathoms bottom of the same nature as that on which we were anchored but it was impossible for them to land, the whole coast being bordered by reefs on which the swell rose to a great height. They then changed course to enter the indentation which I had designated to them, but scarcely had they doubled the southern point of the first island, when they saw it joined to the second by a chain of rocks.
at the surface of the water on which the sea was already beginning to mount. Nevertheless, they coasted it to its middle, in the hope of finding some gaps through which they could penetrate. But their search was fruitless and they returned on board, some much annoyed at not having been able to reach land and the others at having fruitlessly and in the strongest heat of the sun, sought in vain, a place suitable for landing.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 14° 47' 50" and the longitude according to the timekeepers placed us at No. 27 by 121° 24' 54" and at No. 38 by 119° 34' 59".
This point of arrival plotted on Robertson's chart had made us pass over a part of the lands which he places at this latitude on his chart, so that it was again demonstrated to us either that our longitude deduced from the timekeepers and from lunar observations was false or that he places them much further to the east than the west where they actually lie.
We took from this anchorage several bearings and supposing the march of the timekeepers passable or the observations from distances good, one will be able to correct the chart for this part of which the latitude, moreover, is exact since it is the result of a great quantity of observations made in fine weather and at leisure.
The boat then being returned and hoisted in, we set sail to seek a place more favourable for landing. During the evening, we coasted a long succession of islands and islets more or less considerable. But the largest of all these islands did not appear to us to be more than two leagues extent from one end to the other. They are generally of considerable elevation and appear to be joined under water by shoals on most of which the sea rolls to a great elevation, which is without doubt occasioned by the violence of the currents for the winds were so slight that in a place where there would be none, these shoals would be very dangerous even to boats which sought to penetrate into the openings which they appear to show between them.
In the afternoon, the breeze was very slight and we were making course from north towards east, prolonging at two leagues distance, the islands of which we had knowledge, when the look-out from the top of the masts announced a breaker ahead of us. We approached it, with the lead in hand, until we could distinguish it from the deck and we recognised that it lay nearly NE SW. The bottom was then 30 fathoms. Nevertheless, we steered north for some time, but seeing that the bottom increased, we came successively to the wind and resumed the course north-east by north. We passed four or five miles distance from this reef.
At sunset, the land remaining from east 3° south to east 21° north, this latter part appeared to us to be the continental lands, appearing to us behind the islands, see the sketch which I give of it.
After sunset, I continued to make course to the east, taking from the north with a very slight breeze until ten o'clock and then, I dropped a kedge anchor at 38 fathoms bottom of clay and sand.
During the night, we measured every hour, the velocity of the current by the log. At half past ten it was paying out one and a half knots and was directing into the south-south-east. At midnight, it was paying out only one and a half knots in the same direction. The bottom was then 24 and a half fathoms so that it had fallen in two hours by 3 and a half fathoms, having anchored at single anchors on this bottom taken at single anchors after the vessel had swung on its anchor.
We occupied ourselves, during the rest of the night, with fishing but with the exception of some jaw-fish or rather, small-bearded fish, we took nothing else. This poor success was attributed to the force of the current which hindered the fishing lines.
1801-08-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to WNW. At 2 a.m. the current set N by NE and ran 1.5 knots. At 7.15 the tide turned. At 7.30 the large boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey island B, the nearest. At 9.30 he came back without having been able to land, the sea breaking on every part of the island. At noon we got under way, the course N 33° 45' E. At 4 the course was given N 22° 30' E. At 4.30, having sighted in the N 56° E and N 68° E a breaker lying roughly NW and SE and 5 miles off, we steered north; but the water deepening, we resumed N 22° 30' E. At 5 took the bearing of an islet S 87° E, a second S 88° E, an island N 85° E to east, a third islet N 83° E, a fourth N 80° E, a fifth N 78° E, a sixth N 77° E, a large island from N 74° E to N 69° E. At 8 saw a fire in the S 22° 30' E. At 10, being becalmed, we let go a kedge anchor in 38 fathoms, muddy sand. At 10.30 the current ran 5.5 knots setting S 22° 30' E [sic]. At midnight it ran 0.5 in the same direction.

1801-08-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE.
1801-08-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, we found ourselves still anchored opposite a chain of islands of which I counted seven, extending from east 10° south to east 69° south. The middle of the island nearest to us lay to the east 45° 30' south at a distance of about two leagues. This island, as well as those in the vicinity, are high and steep but surrounded by reefs which do not permit landing and which we could distinguish perfectly from the deck. I think well, as Dampier remarks, that one could land in some parts of these islands when the sea is high and one can strand one's boat on the sand awaiting the return of the tide to return. The naturalists would well have wished that I had done the same. But apart from the fact that I have no boat to compromise, this land, as well as all those which we had passed for several days, did not appear to me suitable for research in natural history and especially as regards botany for one saw only a few trees scattered at distances, of moderate elevation and of even poorer vegetation.
At seven o'clock, we set sail with a very slight breeze from the south-west, which I hoped would become stronger in the morning. We steered first to the north-east and then, we took the course more to the east to come and reconnoitre a large land which showed itself in the east by north-east and which then extended to the east-north-east. The lands, at the distance at which we then found ourselves, had the appearance of three islands with a fairly great opening between each of them.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 14° 16' 58 and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us by 121° 50' 32" at No. 27 and 119° 58' 13" at No. 35. This point, like the previous one, plotted on Robertson's chart, (in the margin: still causes us to pass) over the extremity of the land which he shows as the northernmost in this part of the chart. We recognised then, perfectly, that the lands on which we had the course, were truly three islands and the continent behind. It appears to me that these three islands are not badly placed in the bad chart of M. St Aloüarn and I believe that, truly, he had knowledge of them although from a distance for, if he had approached them at a distance of three leagues, he would not have failed to perceive all the dangers which one finds more than a league offshore and on which the sea breaks and rolls enough to cause one to tremble if one found oneself engaged in them. The first of these three islands lay then at a distance of three and a half to four leagues, remaining to the east 23° south.
At half past two in the afternoon, we found ourselves to have doubled the reef which defends the approach to these islands. It extended from the south 16° east to the west 60° south. There is good reason to believe that a part of the rocks which form its bar must be uncovered in great tides but moreover, as the sea breaks strongly there, even in calms, it will always be easy for vessels which navigate in these waters to have knowledge of it.
After doubling the danger of which I have just spoken, we came to the wind but it was not for long for the look-outs from the top of the masts soon announced another breaker to the east-north-east. Shortly after, we had knowledge of it from the deck and we were obliged to bear away to the north-east to double it. This one having much less (extent) than that which we had just passed and at the distance at which we doubled it which was not more than three-quarters of a league, there was, as at the other, 35 fathoms of water, bottom of sand and clay.
From four o'clock until eight, we continued to make course, with the lead in hand, but as the depth of the water did not announce the approach of the dangers which one could encounter at every step along these islands, I ordered the anchor dropped on a good bottom at 35 fathoms.
In the night of the 24th to the 25th, we had flat calm. The log was cast every hour,
so as to know, if possible, the force and direction of the currents. From half past eight until eleven o'clock, its velocity was one and a third knots per hour according to the log, but much greater judging by dead reckoning. Its direction went to the south-south-west and the vessel was constantly everted with the course north-north-east. At half past eleven, the tide was slack and at midnight the vessel everted with the course north north south-south-west, the current then taking to the north-north-east and the moment of the return of the tide on the coast.
The sea set much less in this latter anchorage than in the others, which no doubt comes from the greater depth of the bottom on which we were held. The difference in the sounding was not, for the flood as for the ebb, but two and a half fathoms. Consequently, much less considerable than in the places where we had found it five fathoms and even five and a half.
1801-08-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SW to NW. At half past midnight the tide turned and set NNE, its speed increasing to 1.5 knots. At 5 it was 0.9, to the north. At 7 it was slack water; we got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, and at 8 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 14° 15' 12" of latitude observed and in 121° 50' 32" of longitude by No. 27. At noon a reef was sighted between the land and us, stretching NW and SE. At 3.30, having sighted from aloft breakers ahead (N 67° 30' E), the course was given N 45° E. At 4.15, having sighted breakers from N 67° 30' E to N 85° E, we steered N 33° 45' E. At 5.30 resumed the course N 45° E. At 5.45 took the bearing of the land [illegible] of the mainland east; an islet S 19° E; the offshore breaker of that islet S 22° 30' E; the west end of a second islet S 11° E and the west end of a third S 5° W. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings at the anchorage: the breakers from N 87° E to S 75° E; the land [illegible] of the mainland S 79° E; the three islets taken at 5.45 appeared to form only one, whose ends bore from us, one S 9° E and the other S 11° W. Calm during the night. From 8 to 9 the current set S 22° 30' W and ran 1 knot; from 9 until midnight it set south.

1801-08-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and serene, a fresh breeze from ESE to south.
1801-08-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, having recognised the position of the anchorage where we had stopped the evening before, at eight o'clock in the evening, we made the following bearings:
The easternmost land relatively to the position of the vessel at east 11° south
A long chain of breakers from the north 57° east to the east 15° south
A high land in the form of an island to the east 32° south
Another island, in appearance, to the east 38° south
A third very high island to the east 81° south
A fairly extensive breaker at the south 5° west
And a fourth very high island at the south 5° west.
As soon as the sun rose, we prepared to set sail with a small breeze from the south, variable to south-south-east. After our anchor was weighed, we made course east thirty-two degrees north, to come and reconnoitre a land which was announced to us by the look-outs from the top of the masts to lie ahead of us. We had in the morning, very fine weather, but the breeze was slight.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 14° 2' 6" and the longitude of the timekeepers was for No. 27, 122° 12' 4" and for No. 35, 120° 15' 37".
The point plotted on Robertson's chart had made us pass over all the lands shown furthest to the north by the charts and nevertheless we were well certain that we had not yet reached the latitude of those which the look-outs announced to us were ahead of us.
The little progress which we had made in the morning had little changed our position relatively to the bearings of the lands. Those however the most ahead of us lay from east 5° north to the south 57° west. In this extent, there were several islands and islets and a portion of coast which we judged to be that of the continent, until we had proof to the contrary.
It will no doubt be difficult for all those who shall see the log-book of the vessel to understand anything from all the bearings which are entered. I employed all sorts of means and representations from the beginning to engage the officers to pay attention to this work but all that I could say was useless and as they all believed themselves very learned, it was not possible for me to persuade them to make them in the manner which I would have desired. Also it is for that reason that I formed in my manner one of the quartermasters to whom I recognised much intelligence to make them directly for me and I hope that one will (not) find the confusion which is found in all those of the others.
In the afternoon, we continued to advance to the east, drawing a little to the north, as much as the wind could permit it but its slight force did not permit us to make great progress until eight o'clock when I anchored at 35 fathoms, bottom of sand and clay. I estimated myself then across from the land which must be the northernmost in this part of the coast. But I could not distinguish at the distance at which I found myself at sunset, whether it was firm coast or an island, although it presented under this latter aspect. But as it was much lower than all those which we had passed hitherto, it is possible that it was joined to the continent by some still lower land, which I put off to the next day to verify.
During the night of the 25th to the 26th, we cast, as usual, the log every hour to know the velocity and direction of the currents. As we anchored at the beginning of the ebb, the vessel kept to the current with course NNE and its velocity until midnight was one and a third knots, then it decreased noticeably (to) 9/10 of a knot which it came abeam to veer with course south-south-west, gaining progressively the same velocity. In the flood as in the ebb, the sea descended and mounted in the place where we were anchored, by only two fathoms.
During the night, it was perfectly calm, but the atmosphere was very humid and the hygrometer rose to 98°, the barometer held between 28 p 2 l and 28 p 5.
We had seen in the morning, several sea snakes much longer and thicker than those which we had encountered hitherto although they were spotted in the same manner. The whales had absolutely abandoned us and even for a long time and we saw only a few birds of the species of boobies and gulls.
1801-08-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to NW. At 7.45 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° 15' E; a breaker was sighted between the land and us. At noon took the bearing of the east point of a land supposed to be the mainland S 73° E; the middle of an island S 68° E; the breaker seen in the morning S 34° E; an islet S 6° W; an island from S 15° W to S 8° E; a second islet S 26° W. In the distance two hummocks could be seen, one S 45° E and the other S 48°, supposed to belong to the mainland. At noon in 14° 2' 6" of latitude observed and in 122° 12' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 14' NE. Shaped the course N 73° E at 4. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy sand. Calm during the night. From 8 to 11 the current set SSW and ran 1.3 knots; from 11 until midnight it ran only 0.9 knots.

1801-08-14.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon the currents set to the SE.
1801-08-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, at sunrise, we took a bearing and a view of our anchorage from the stern, recognising that the land which we counted upon to end the continent in the north-west in this part, was still an island of four or five leagues extent but, in effect, the northernmost land which we had yet encountered. The following bearing gave us the direction of the lands in the following manner:
The easternmost point of a long and flat island at east 19° south
An isolated peak at east 40° south
High land having the appearance of an island at east 45° south
Another island at east 47° south
Two isolated peaks which may be found perhaps on the great land at east 55° south
A very high land in the distance under the appearance of an island at east 64° south
The land in view furthest to the south at east 69° south
As our horizon was very extensive and we had sight of no land from the east towards the north, I thought that the island, across which we were anchored, must end it in that part. Also as soon as we were under sail, I ordered course steered east by south-east. But as soon as we had doubled the western point of the island of which I have just spoken, we perceived ahead of us a very extensive reef on which the sea broke heavily and which, to double it at a small league distance, obliged us to steer more to the north and even for some time to the north-east. As soon as we had passed it, I resumed the course to the east convinced that I would not be long (in) having knowledge of the continental lands which must lie in that direction. We indeed had knowledge of it about ten o'clock in the morning, and the bottom was still the same as that found at the moment when we doubled the reef of which I have spoken, that is to say thirty-three fathoms. Shortly after, there were only thirty, and we continued our same course, convinced that we would not be long (in) encountering the continental lands, regarding myself as relieved of all these long succession of islands, islets and reefs which had prevented me from approaching them. I was much deceived in my expectation for, at eleven o'clock, the look-outs announced to us that they saw ahead of us and even under the lee, a long succession of breakers which extended as far as the eye could see. Nevertheless, we continued to run to the east to recognise the land which we had seen, but we soon encountered the reef which had been announced to us, so that we had to bear away to the north-east by north-east to prolong it from the east-north-east. We were forced to carry to the north-east without being able yet to double it. From north-east, we came to the north-north-east and finally to the north. We would no doubt have got out of it on this course if the wind had not failed us, but the calm having taken us about two o'clock and the flood carrying us with great velocity on the reefs which were then abeam of us, we were obliged to drop a kedge anchor at thirty-two fathoms, bottom of sand and clay. As it was perfectly calm, we only eased off our sails without furling them so as to be more ready to profit by the breeze if it came to appear, in the rest of the evening.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 13° 52' 16" south and the longitude of our timekeepers placed us according to No. 27 (at) 122° 36' 55" and according to No. 35 at 120° 21' 33". A succession of distances taken by the astronomer Bernier gave 123° 19' which placed it to the east of No. 27 in which we had more confidence than in No. 35 of 0° 42' 5". I had also taken that day a sextuple distance the result of which placed me at 121° 12' 41" so that I found myself with Citizen Bernier, a difference to the west of 1° 16' 19" and with No. 27 of 0° 34' 16".
At four o'clock in the afternoon, the time at which we anchored, we made the following bearing:
The visible extremity of the reef which seemed to extend to the north-east at east 28° north
An islet appearing to hold to the reef at east 5° south. The continuation of the same reef extending to the south at east 45° south
Fairly high land presumed to hold to the continent at east 75° south. All these points and the latitude and longitude of the vessel being unable to agree or relate with any of the charts of which I am possessed, I am possessed that New Holland is there traced only on conjecture. However, it was easy to recognise that that of the depot, although imperfect, was the least bad in that it gives fairly well the configuration of the land of which the north-west point of this part is truly formed by a long flat island having in its eastern part, a great reef on which the sea breaks strongly and which we had recognised and doubled in the morning. It was according to the indication of this same chart that I steered to the east, drawing to the south as much as it was possible for me according to the winds which were then blowing, that I had knowledge of the second reef which it indicates and which I coasted a part of until the moment when the calm obliged me to anchor. I believed only to recognise for this moment, that it was not placed far enough to the north, but I put off to the next day to verify exactly its position.
During the night of the 26th to the 27th, the weather was fine and the wind calm. The velocity of the current was found to be one and a half knots from four o'clock until six and carrying in the N. NE. Then it took its direction to the south-west with the same velocity. The water was at the same height in the flood as in the ebb or at least we perceived no sensible decrease, since during the time which we were anchored.
1801-08-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze and calm, from S to SW. At midnight it was slack water; from midnight to 2 the current ran 0.5 knots and from 2 to 4, 1.5 knots to the NNE. At 6.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 78° 45' E. At 8 took the bearing of an islet D south; several hummocks supposed to belong to the mainland from S 7° E to S 24° E; an island C, off whose east point there is a reef, from S 29° E to S 40° E. At 8.30, having sighted a shoal ahead, we steered N 56° 15' E. At 10 the course was given east. At 11 a chain of breakers was sighted stretching from south to east; we bore up N 67° 30' E and then N 56° 15' E. At noon took the bearing of island C from S 47° W to S 38° W; islet D S 31° W; the hummocks of the mainland from S 23° W to S 3° W; the mainland in sight from S 57° E to S 68° E; the chain of breakers stretched from S 8° E to N 58° E, with a sandy islet in the middle of the breakers N 85° E. At noon in 13° 52' 16" of latitude observed and in 122° 36' 52" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 5' NE. The lunar distances gave 123° 19' of longitude. Shortly after noon the chain of breakers was seen to stretch as far as ahead of us (N 56° 15' E); we steered N 22° 30' E and then N 22° 30' W. At 2.30, being in a flat calm with the tide setting us onto the breakers, we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom, island C bearing from S 25° W to S 22° W and the sandy islet of the breakers S 62° E. At 6 the current ran 1.1 knots to the NNE. At 7.30 it was slack water; it turned shortly afterwards and set SSW. At 10 the current ran 1 knot, and at midnight 0.3 knots.

1801-08-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At 2 p.m. the large boat was back from her mission.
1801-08-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at daybreak, we prepared to set sail and at sunrise, we were greatly astonished to see across from us a great sand bank at the surface of the water, occupying the whole extent which we had borne the day before and on which the sea broke with such force (in the margin: that it rose to a prodigious height). One could distinctly distinguish several elevations, on this bank, formed by rocks of different forms and which, at high tide serve to make known the danger from further off as had happened to us.
As soon as our anchor was weighed, we set all our sails, making course to NE ¼ of north to move away from the bank of which we had knowledge. From north-east by north, we came successively to NE ¼ east with the precaution of keeping a sharp look-out and sounding every half hour. The bottom was constantly 29 and 30 fathoms until half past eight o'clock, the time at which we found ourselves in a very considerable tidal race. I at first paid little attention to it because, ten minutes before encountering it, we had 30 fathoms of water. Nevertheless, I had the lead cast and it was not without astonishment that I (in the margin: found) myself at 20 fathoms. Five minutes after, there were only 15. And at fifty minutes past eight, there were only eleven. I took the tack to the port immediately and I believe it was greatly time for, perhaps, in running ten minutes more, we were aground although at a very great distance from the lands since one could scarcely distinguish it from the top of the masts. Be that as it may, in making course to the north-west, we soon found 15 fathoms and soon after, 20 and 25. As soon as we were in deep water and entirely out of (in the margin: this danger), in that which the colour of the water indicated to us as well as the sounding, we coasted its edges (in the margin: of the bank) which were perfectly well delineated. One then steered to the north believing one had no more danger to fear. As I was constantly occupied in looking all around the vessel with my telescope, I perceived straight ahead of us, and at half gunshot distance, a very white mark at the surface of the water. I immediately ordered course to the NE, not doubting that it was a danger which I had perceived. The sounding was immediately cast which brought back 23 fathoms, and before one had no bottom at 35. I had the quartermaster mount on the topsail yard to examine what it could be. As soon as he was there, he announced to us that it was two small mounds of sand which we passed most fortunately without a greater decrease in depth at pistol shot distance. After passing them, we lost bottom at 35 fathoms. This danger is at the latitude of 13° 28' south and according to our timekeepers, at 122° 35' of longitude. Its extent is not more than 15 to 20 feet in circumference and consequently much more dangerous if one encounters it.
In continuing to steer to the north a little towards the east, we soon had knowledge of the continuation of the bank from which we had got out in the morning. But in this place it broke with force and described an arc so considerable that in order to be able to double it, it was necessary to again make course with the tack to port and steer to the west-north-west until eleven o'clock, when its most visible part lay by our starboard quarter. This caused us to carry to the north-west. A portion of the bank was dry and in its south-eastern part, relatively to us, it appeared to offer a passage which I wanted to go and reconnoitre when it was announced to us for the third time, new breakers, to port of us so that we had to again take the course to the west-north-west. Nevertheless, we always had above 30 fathoms of bottom at two gunshots from the reefs.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 13° 34' 59" and the longitude of our timekeepers placed us at No. 27 by 122° 35' 18" and at No. 35 by 120° 30' 45". The average result of three successions of
distances of the moon to the sun taken by the astronomer Bernier, gave 123° 31' 58" for the longitude of the vessel which plotted on No. 27, in which, as I have already observed, (in the margin: I had more confidence), placed it 0° 56' 40" further to the east than did this timekeeper.
It did not appear to me doubtful that the bank shown on the chart of the Hydrographic Office, was not that of which we had already coasted a great part, but it also appeared certain that its northern extremity, is shown much too far to the south, since according to the latitude observed at noon of 13° 34' 59" it placed still a point in sight to the north-north-east at a league and a half distance, without being able to affirm whether it was its extremity or not. The calm which ensued before we could double it, left us with doubts on this subject, and the ebb which soon took us moved us away from it so much that it was not possible to take more exact knowledge of it for the moment. The winds having also passed to the north-east in the evening, obliged us only to bear away under the lee to the NNW, and at five o'clock we went about to take an anchorage along the edges of this bank, the bottom having been as much as 44 fathoms on the NNW tack.
At seven o'clock in the evening, finding ourselves at 32 fathoms and in calm, we anchored for the night a kedge anchor on a bottom of a different nature to those which we had found for several days and which was of mud and coarse sand of different colours and small shells, whole and broken.
In the tides of the night, the strongest of the current was one and a half knots and the sea, in the flood as in the ebb, set about two fathoms at the anchorage. Besides, the sky was very humid and the wind almost perfectly calm, if one excepted a few small squalls of an instant coming from the south or south-south-west.
1801-08-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from S to SSE. At 1.15 the tide turned, the currents then setting NNE and running more than 1.2 knots. At 6.30 we got under way and steered N 56° 15' E and N 45° E. At 8.30 the colour of the sea showed a shoal; we had 29 fathoms, and a moment later only 20. We bore away and the bottom shoaled to 15 fathoms and then, at 11, to 11; we then hauled to the wind on the port tack. The water deepened and we came round to the north. At 9.30 two white patches like two small banks were sighted ahead (to the north). We steered N 11° 15' E to pass between them and the great bank. At 10.30 breakers were sighted stretching from N 33° 45' E to N 78° 45' E; we steered N 56° 15' W to weather them. At noon a point of the great bank bore from us N 50° E, 6 miles off, being in 13° 34' 18" of latitude observed and in 122° 35' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 26' NE. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At half past noon the point of the bank supposed to be the northernmost bore from us N 22° 30' E. At 7 we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 8.30 we swung to the flood, which set SW and ran 1.4 knots.

1801-08-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SE.
1801-08-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, from four-thirty in the morning, we prepared to set sail in the hope that the breeze would rise with the sun. But the flat calm having continued, we were forced to remain at anchor to await the breeze so that the currents would not carry us on a course opposite to the one I wished to follow.
About ten o'clock, a light breeze rose from south-south-east towards east-south-east which I judged to be the beginning of the breeze. In consequence we raised our anchor and set sail but without advancing much for the calm continued. From the moment we got under way until noon, the depth remained between 33 and thirty-five fathoms sand and coarse gravel mixed with some fine coral which the dredge brought back.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 25' 1" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at No. 27 by 122° 39' 28" and at No. 35 by 120° 30' 39".
Three series of distances taken by the astronomer Bernier, reduced to noon, gave as mean result for the longitude of the ship, 123° 22' 1". So that the observations by distances came within a degree of the rate of the timekeepers from those made, the other moon, which had differed from them by one degree forty-two minutes. The astronomer Bernier thinks that this great approach may be occasioned by the calculation of the tables which he does not believe to be accurate, having observed no change in the rate of the timekeepers.
In the afternoon, the weather was very fine but the calm continued. As the current was then bearing us to the south-south-west, we thought we perceived, on our starboard side, the sea breaking and we accordingly set our course to the north-east to move away from that place. From noon until six o'clock, the depth passed from 35 fathoms to 50 (no bottom found), which made me believe that we were free of all the banks in the middle of which we had been engaged for two or three days. At seven o'clock the breeze
having veered to north-east variable towards east, we made our course north 28° west. At eight o'clock we sounded although we had made little way and we were greatly surprised to find ourselves in 29 fathoms, sand and gravel bottom. I then had the course altered to west-north-west, but the depth having suddenly diminished successively, and in a very short time so that it was no more than nineteen fathoms, sand and coarse gravel. I anchored to await daylight. I had then taken the course of south-south-east and the depth had increased by four fathoms.
During the night, although there was a fair breeze blowing, the vessel having swung on the current with heading to the north-east at the turn of tide, the heading was maintained to the south-west which makes me think that all the banks and shoals which we had encountered had changed the direction of the tides which before were north-north-east and south-south-west. The speed of the current was a knot and a half at its strongest and the sea rose and fell by nearly four fathoms at the place where we were at anchor.
During the night, the weather was fine but the air so damp that the watch were greatly troubled by it.
1801-08-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSE to NE. At 1 we swung to the ebb, setting NE and running 0.7; at 4 it ran 1.3 knots. At 8 it was slack water; at 9.30 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° E. At noon in 13° 24' 49" of latitude observed and in 122° 39' 28" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 36' NE. At 1 a flat calm; at 5.30 the breeze freshened from NE and we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack, the lead giving no bottom at 50 fathoms. At 8, having found 29 fathoms, we bore away N 67° 30' W and N 78° 45' W. The water shoaling further, we hauled to the wind on the port tack, and at 9.30 we anchored in 24 fathoms, sandy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 10 the current set SW and ran 0.7 knots. At 2 slack water; the current then set NE and ran 1.3 knots.

1801-08-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, the rising sun announced a strong breeze for the morning and we hastened for that reason to set sail. When our anchor was weighed, I ordered the course to the north-east persuaded that we would gain depth of water since the day before it had diminished as we made course to north-north-west, north-west, west, west-south-west and south-west and south, while it had increased as soon as the course took an easterly direction. This conjecture was verified because, hardly had we made half a league to the north-east when we found thirty fathoms and shortly after, forty. There is reason to believe that our last anchorage was at the eastern extremity of the part of the bank recognised on the previous days and which since, I have found marked and indicated in the English chart published in 1787 by Robertson, the only one which mentions it and gives it the extent that it can have.
In weighing our anchor, we lost our buoy and part of its warp, it appears that it became entangled with some coral rock which cut it in two as perfectly as one would have done with a hatchet. Nevertheless, our cable had not at all suffered while we were at anchor.
In the morning, the breeze which had been announced to us by the rising sun came on and we were obliged to take two reefs in the topsails to avoid compromising our course. The sea became promptly rough and the vessel was greatly troubled by it. The greater part of the scholars had seasickness.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 13° 1' 31" but there was no hour angle for the rate of the timekeepers.
I expected that the breeze would diminish after the passage of the sun through the meridian, but it was not so. It continued until the setting of the sun with the same strength. I held, until eight o'clock in the evening, the course to the north, drawing towards the east as much as possible and to not stray too far from the coast, I took that to the south towards the east until three o'clock in the morning when I went about to that of the north.
During the night of the 29th to the 30th, the weather was fine and clear, only it continued to blow a strong breeze from east-south-east to south-south-east. At midnight we lost the bottom at 54 fathoms.
1801-08-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to E. At 6 a.m., the wind having freshened a great deal, we began to heave round, the ship dragging. At 6.45 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack; we lost our buoy and buoy rope. At noon in 13° 0' 54" of latitude observed and in 122° 47' 40" of longitude by account. At 8 went onto the port tack. At noon no bottom at 40 fathoms. From noon until midnight we had from 45 to 55 fathoms.

1801-08-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky. Wind SE, a light breeze. At 3.45 p.m. sent off [the boat] under the orders of Citizen Ransonnet with 2 days' provisions to fetch the 2 men who had been stationed on Dirk Hartog.
1801-08-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, in the morning, it continued to blow fresh from the part of the part (sic) of the east-south-east. We held as close to the wind as possible in the course to the north towards the east under the foresail and our topsails, two reefs taken, and the vessel had as much as it could bear. We sustained, during the morning, some damage in our sails which the wind tore in different places.
The latitude observed at noon was 12° 20' 34". There was not, this day, any hour angle for the rate of the timekeepers, the wind and the heavy sea not permitting that any could be taken.
In the afternoon, the breeze although a little less strong, did not permit us to increase the sails and I was surprised to find the sea as rough and troubled as we encountered it. The cause must doubtless be attributed to the reflux of the tides which, acting contrary to the wind, must have occasioned the heavy swell by which we were more than once wetted.
During the night of the 30th to the first, it blew in squalls, however we found the sea a little less rough than it had been during the day.
From eight o'clock to midnight, the sounding reported from 50 to 45 fathoms, muddy sand, and from midnight to four o'clock the next morning, from 46 to 42, coarse gravel. At eight o'clock the next morning, we had 45, muddy sand. During all night, we were surrounded by gannets, gulls and other sea birds whose repeated and continual cries made me fear to be still in the vicinity of some dangers, which made me redouble my attention that a good watch be kept, but we perceived nothing.
1801-08-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to E. At 3 went onto the starboard tack under the foresail, both topsails double-reefed, the fore staysail, the mizzen and its staysail. At noon in 12° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 123° 2' 46" of longitude by account. The lead gave from 40 to 43 fathoms.

1801-08-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth, the winds a light breeze from ESE to north. The large boat was back on the 30th. She was sent off again to fetch the rest of the gear.
1801-08-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first, the winds were constantly from south-east by east to east-south-east, strong breeze, and the sea a little less rough than on the preceding days. I was informed in the morning, by the Frigate Captain or to say it better, he announced to me again that we had no more than three or four days of wood and at most twenty days of water at the ordinary ration. The naturalists, on the other hand, who for more than a month had lacked fresh provisions, sighed after the port of call of Timor, and although they said nothing about it to me, they were talking about it in such a manner that their conversation reached me. I myself felt the necessity of not persisting, in the state I was in, to come to recognise the north cape of the land of Van Diemen. The lack of a boat or of any other craft capable of proceeding ahead of the vessel was becoming for me increasingly indispensable, either to recognise the coast closely, or to send it to investigate, in such a way that seeing I could do nothing, I decided to make course to the north-west to gain the anchorage that everyone desired with the greatest impatience.
This news had such an effect on several of the sick who were on board, that several found enough strength to get upon the deck in order to assure themselves if it (was) true.
At ten o'clock, I therefore gave the course to the north-west which was followed until noon. The latitude observed then being 10° 59' 53", I had the course set to the north-west. According to the longitude indicated by the timekeepers reduced to the same hour, No. 27 placed us at 123° 44' 40" and No. 35 at 121° 23' 47". The distances were, as I observed at the time they were taken, 42' more to the east.
In the afternoon, we found it very disagreeable that the wind continued to blow fresh and although the sea was still heavy and rough, we nevertheless loosened a reef in our topsails, and in the evening we set the topgallant sails.
During all the day, the sky had bad appearance and it was obscured by heavy clouds which announced to us, if not bad weather, at least rain.
After the setting of the sun, the weather had no better appearance. However, we continued the same course until eight o'clock in the evening when, estimating myself, according to the distance made on the log, to be at 10° 25' of south latitude, I had the sails reduced for the night, by giving the course to the west-north-west.
At two o'clock in the night, the sky being very dark and obscure, I had the vessel put under heave-to to await daylight.
1801-08-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to ESE. At 10 a.m. the commander decided to shape our course for Timor; we headed north, making sail. At noon in 10° 59' 57" of latitude observed and in 123° 37' 52" of longitude by account. During the night overcast weather; we sounded several times without finding bottom at 120 fathoms. At noon the course was given N 45° W and at 9, N 67° 30' W.

1801-08-20.journal_anonyme: Throughout the 24 hours fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NW, W and SW. Calm at the close of the day.
1801-08-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, at five o'clock in the morning, we set all sails and even our studding sails to come to recognise the land of which I hoped to have knowledge before noon if the longitude indicated by our No. 27, in which I had sufficient confidence, should prove to be good. But I was deceived in my expectation for we had no knowledge of it. It is true that the horizon was not very extensive and the sky had an even worse appearance than the day before.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 10° 21' 53" and the longitude of the timekeepers was for No. 27 of 121° 34' 31" and for No. 35 of 119° 13' 56" so that this point laid down on Robertson's chart of which I made use on account of the scale which is larger than the others, placed me over the south-west point of Timor. The same point laid down on the other charts which have been given to me, placed me at so little distance from it that if the longitude of this island was well placed, I must have had knowledge of it. But as nothing was perceived, there is every appearance that No. 27 is not much better than No. 35. We shall see in the course of the evening, if the breeze continues, if the distances will be more accurate and analogous to the position that the knowledge of the times gives to this island.
In the afternoon, the weather was very dark and misty so that our horizon had very little extent. However, about three o'clock, we perceived through the mist which hid the view of land from us, the high mountains of the island of Timor.
A little before the setting of the sun, the horizon having become clearer, we had a very pleasant view of it and until six o'clock, we approached the coast to about a league and a half or at most two leagues distance. As none of us knew this coast, we were in uncertainty whether a low point which lay three leagues to the west was that of the south-west of the island. Had we been able to see the island of Roti, our doubts would have ceased. But the horizon was too limited in that quarter and we did not estimate it at more than four leagues. I therefore resolved to tack throughout the night in sight of the island of Timor in order not to fall to leeward of the strait of Semau into which I intended to pass in order to obtain an exact knowledge of it.
During the night of the second to the third, the weather was very variable and the winds from the east to east-north-east were moderate.
Bearings of the land at sunset:
The westernmost land in view, at west 10° north.
The easternmost land in view, at north 56° east.
The land abeam of us at north 42° west, distance of about 2 leagues.
1801-08-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the port tack; at 5 filled and stood on, the course S 78° 45' W; at 10 it was given west. At noon in 10° 21' 42" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 31" of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, in a clear interval, the high land of Timor was sighted from N 11° E to N 68° W. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack, the land stretching from N 36° E to N 80° W, 6 miles off. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.

1801-08-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NE, SW, south and SE. Calm from 8 until noon.
1801-08-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, in the morning, as soon as it began to grow light, I approached the coast at a distance of a mile and a half in order not to miss the entrance to the strait of Semau of which it appeared to me that one can have knowledge only at a small distance from that of Timor. As the longitude of the timekeepers and even those of the distances were defective, supposing that that of the south-west point of this island was well placed on the charts, I thought it proper to assure myself of the depth of all the bays, and it was for this reason that we often had to bear away to the west-south-west and south-west to double all the points which we encountered before arriving at the last one. The whole coast which we often skirted at a distance less than that of which I have just spoken, is not equally sound everywhere, and one encounters quite often shoals easily in truth to be recognised by the colour of the water. Thus they are not dangerous and within cannon shot of these dangers, one does not find bottom at 30 fathoms.
Several points have equally a small chain of breakers which extend sometimes more than a mile offshore and on which the sea breaks heavily. But in general, the fifteen leagues of coast which we made to arrive at the south-west point of the island of Timor, is very sound and easy to recognise when, once, one has had knowledge of it. See the different views in the journal.
It was not until ten o'clock that we had knowledge of the island of Roti of which the furthest extent in view remained to us then at south-west by west. We continued our course with a very strong breeze from the east and we finally arrived, about half past eleven, at the western extremity of Timor. As we doubled the point and the reef which borders it a good mile offshore, I had the course laid close to the wind and the winds served us as desired for shortly after, they passed to the south-east which much facilitated our entrance into this strait. The breeze was then so fresh that we could not carry the topgallant sails.
At the entrance of the strait we made the following bearings:
The south-west point of Timor at east 66° south.
The south point of the island of Semau at west 22° south.
The middle of the northern part of the island of Roti at south 2° east.
As soon as we were in the strait, I sought to close with the coast of Timor in the hope of finding there abreast of the sandy bays which are met with there, some places suitable for anchorage, although the plans which we have of this part indicate everywhere a very considerable depth. We did not find it at first at 50 fathoms in the middle of the strait, but as we approached the coast of Timor, we found it first at forty and, two or three soundings after at 28, the quality of the bottom was different at each cast of the lead. Some gave coarse gravel and these were the first, others fine black sand and mud, and others sand mixed with some small fragments of coral. I then resolved to anchor in this anchorage in order to send to recognise what remained for us to do in the way to double the point which I believe to be that of Coupang and of which I estimated myself still two leagues away. At the same moment, the wind failed us all at once and in order not to be carried by the current onto a sandbank which was lying athwart our course at a mile distance, we let go a sheet anchor in 28 fathoms, bottom of fine sand mixed as I have said above with some small fragments of broken coral but too weak to give any concern for the cable.
As soon as our sails were furled, I immediately had the gig lowered and gave the command of her to M. Freycinet in order that he might recognise the point of Coupang and the course which must be held after doubling it to enter into the bay of that name.
He had also orders to push forward to the establishment of the Dutch, that is to say to the fort of Concorde if it was not too far distant, in consequence I gave him, for the Governor of that establishment, the following letter:
"Sir,
"I have the honour to inform you that having been sent by the French Government on a voyage of discoveries and public utility, I have found myself forced to abandon the coasts of New Holland where I could not obtain the water and other refreshments necessary for its continuation.
"I hope that by virtue of the passports of your nation of which I am the bearer, and which I reserve to communicate to you at our first meeting, you will be willing to assist us in everything that may depend upon you.
"The officer bearing my letter is charged with praying you to send us a pilot, none of us being acquainted with the place of anchorage of the roads of Coupang. I am &a …"
At two o'clock, the boat left the ship, well equipped and the ensign Bougainville accompanied M. Freycinet. I had embarked in the boat, a Malay and a Hollander to serve as interpreter.
The anchorage which we occupied on the north-south-west coast of the island of Timor was extremely pleasant to look upon. We were surrounded by land and as if enclosed in a circle of which the island of Roti formed the end but at a considerable distance. The lands, in all their outline, except however at the point which I presume to be that of Coupang, are of good height and covered with trees from the shores of the sea to the upper extremity. On our port side, the island of Semau offered the same appearance and we had to the east, the island which is found abreast of the bay which is there marked.
However, notwithstanding the beauty of the place, we saw there only a bad hut and two or three inhabitants occupied in fishing at low tide.
Notwithstanding that Dampier who passed through this strait, says that the tides are not strong there, we found there, however, a current quite rapid, the flood setting north-east and the ebb south-west. When we entered this strait, the tide was still flood and to judge by the tide mark on shore, it must rise to a good height. We were greatly astonished at four o'clock in the evening, to see ahead of us and a little on the starboard, a sandbank appear and of which we had had no previous knowledge, the calm doubtless preventing the sea from breaking on it. Its extent appeared to us to be not considerable and I deferred to the next day to send to sound it.
In the afternoon, we took many cross bearings to have a plan of this part and I give a particular drawing of the place where we are anchored so much did it appear to me particularly pleasant.
After the setting of the sun, we had a light breeze from the north which lasted about two hours, then the winds passed to the south-east and calm. The night was very humid and without the slightest wind.
Bearings of the anchorage.
1801-08-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to ESE. At 2 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 we bore away west and ran along the southern side of Timor at a short distance. At 10 Roti Island was sighted in the S 56° W. At 11.30, being off the mouth of Semau Strait, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and ran in; Roti then bore from us south. At noon took the bearing of the south point of Semau S 70° W, the northern part of Roti S 2° E, the south point of Timor with its reefs S 24° E. At 12.45, the breeze having fallen and the tide setting us out (to the south), we anchored in 28 fathoms, muddy sand, the south point of Timor bearing S 15° W, the end of the reefs off that point S 25° W, the south point of Semau S 49° W, a small island off Semau from N 45° W to N 29° W. At 1 the large boat was sent off to Kupang, the Dutch settlement on Timor; we did not know whether the settlement might be in English hands, and the boat carried an Anglo-French flag of truce. Citizen Freycinet, who commanded her, was to inform the governor of our arrival in the strait and of the stay we meant to make at Kupang.

1801-08-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty. A light breeze variable from SE to south, SSE and SSW. A fresh breeze. At 7 p.m. Citizen Ransonnet, acting ensign, went to take charge of the camp; and the next morning at 5 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, and I embarked in the large boat to go and survey the north of the bay. Our starboard anchor being foul, we weighed it, after which we let it go in 6 fathoms, sand and weed. Bearings of the anchorage: the north point E 19° N; the south point S 10° E; the camp S 23° 30' S.
1801-08-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the morning, I flattered myself that my boat would be on board before daylight and that at the rising of the sun, we could weigh our anchor to gain the anchorage of the bay of Coupang into which I intended to go with the assistance of my gig and pinnace supposing that no pilot should be sent to us which I had requested.
About seven o'clock, not seeing my boat appear, I determined to send one of my smallest boats ashore with the geographer Boulanger to take new bearings on shore and to sound the bank of which I spoke yesterday. As we were only at a quarter league from the place where this boat had orders to land, I could defend her in case of need with the artillery of the vessel which I had prepared for that purpose. But this precaution was unnecessary for we had no need of it at all and the crew of the boat disembarked without the least difficulty although they encountered some Indians with whom we saw them in conference. As soon as the citizens Boulanger and Maurouard had made their bearings, they followed the Indians into the interior of the country and we lost sight of them.
On their return on board, about noon, we were informed that they had been well received by the natives of the country and that they had advanced about half a league into its interior where they had found about thirty men assembled in different houses, all armed with muskets, calling themselves in the service of the Dutch company.
The sounding at a musket shot from the shore, was from two to three fathoms, then it increased to the same distance from five to eleven bad bottom. From the latter to the vessel, the bottom increased suddenly from twenty to thirty and was not found very good. At the edges of the bank of which I spoke, there was four and five fathoms of water, then great depth. A vessel at anchor with a chain would appear to me sufficiently well in safety in the place where we were.
At half past ten, we had knowledge of our boat forcing sail to join us, but as the wind was light and the tide was against her, she did not arrive on board until about two o'clock in the afternoon, bringing us a pilot sent by the Governor.
Monsieur Freycinet who had the command of her, reported to me that the flag of truce which he carried, caused at first much concern and yet he lowered it as soon as the fortress had hoisted the Dutch flag. He informed us also that the English had made themselves masters of the fortress, the year before, but that they were compelled to evacuate it in one night, not having (been able to) conciliate the friendship of the people of the country whose asylum and rights they violated in the most shameful manner, which occasioned on their part, a war in which they lost many men without having obtained any fruit from this conquest. One may well expect that they devastated the country as much as they could. Also the town is, for the greater part, destroyed and what iron could not reach, has become the prey of the flames. They did not fail to blow up the fortress which, however, is absolutely restored by the activity of the Dutch and the assistance which has been furnished to them by the different sovereigns with whom they live in good intelligence.
As soon as the pilot arrived, who turned out to be French and from Bayonne, we set sail and manoeuvred to stand in for the coast of Semau in order to move away from a danger which is found at the point of Coupang and which extends nearly a quarter of a league into the sea. We were anchored at a little league inside this point and after doubling it, we still had three more leagues to make to gain the anchorage of the bay.
The best course to follow, when the wind allows it, is to keep the middle of the channel. But if it is necessary to tack, one should have the greatest attention not to approach too closely the projecting points of the land, either on the side of Timor or on the side of Semau, in that all have reefs which extend far enough offshore and which are perceived from a considerable distance, by day, by the change of colour of the waters. For the rest, the channel appeared to me very convenient and although the bottom is considerable there, one can, in case of calm, anchor with a kedge there by fifty or sixty fathoms in waiting for the breeze, but if one anchors there with a sheet anchor by a less depth, it is good to have chains, otherwise one runs the risk of having one's cable damaged as happened to us.
Another inconvenience which prevents the Dutch from using this channel, comes from the fact that the winds are very variable there and one finds oneself, for this reason, sometimes embarrassed there. This happened to us also for at less than a mile from the coast, we were once becalmed all at once, and obliged to go on the other tack holding all the sails on the mast not to go ahead. But when the wind blows, one runs no risk and there is good tacking, the narrowest part of the channel appeared to me to have three-quarters of a league at most.
As soon as we came clear of the bay of Coupang, the winds having shifted to the east, a fresh breeze, we tacked back and forth to gain the anchorage and as it was a fine clear moonlight and as our pilot appeared to me sufficiently good, we continued to make sail, with the care not to approach too closely a small island situated in the middle of the bay which the Dutch call the Turtle Island. In passing before the fort at the setting of the sun, we assured our flag by a powder gun and the fort replied in the same manner. Finally, at nine o'clock, we anchored in 28 fathoms, good muddy bottom, within musket shot of a Dutch brigantine which was on the roads. After we had assured our flag, the Governor sent on board to ask me not to salute, making it known to me that not only had he very little powder remaining, but also that some inconvenience would result in that the natives of the interior of the country had orders to come armed into the town whenever they heard more than three cannon shots. I did in this regard what appeared to me to be agreeable to the Governor and we did not salute.
Bearings of the anchorage in the bay of Coupang:
The westernmost point in view of the island of Timor at west 28° south.
The fort of Concorde at west 81° south.
The north point of Timor at east 88° north.
The northernmost extent in view of the island of Semau at north 71° west.
The two extremities of the small island of the Turtles from north 10° 30' west to north 16° 30' west. Distance from land about a mile and a half.
1801-08-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. At 8 the surveyor landed on Timor with his instruments, abreast of the anchorage; he came back at half past noon. He had been very well received by fishermen living on the strait, who told him that Kupang was in Dutch hands. At 1 Citizen Freycinet arrived from Kupang; he had been very well received by the governor, who was sending us a pilot, a Frenchman in the Company's service, to take us to Kupang. We got under way at once; the cable was found chafed. At 6, after doubling the last point of the strait, the wind shifted to the east; we missed stays, boxed her round to the south and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. We fired a gun, to which Fort Concordia answered with one. We made several boards to gain the anchorage, where at 9.30 we let go the anchor in 24 fathoms, muddy bottom; the topgallant masts were struck at once. Bearings at the anchorage, being moored: Turtle Island from N 11° W to N 17° W; the north end of Semau N 71° W; the west point of Timor S 62° W; Fort Concordia S 9° W; the northernmost point of Timor in sight N 2° E.

1801-08-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from S, NE, SW and SSW.
1801-08-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the (fifth), at eight o'clock in the morning, I prepared to pay a visit to the Governor and I landed at nine o'clock, not only to compliment him, but also to take knowledge of the resources of the country and to obtain a lodging there for our scorbutic patients of whom two had it to the highest degree. Before quitting the vessel, I wrote to citizen Picquet whose duties had been suspended since the period of which I have made mention in the course of time. This officer who does not even deserve the name, has not ceased to behave badly on board and any other, less patient and less a friend of peace and tranquillity, would have treated him very differently from me.
To citizen Picquet,
I inform you, citizen, that you must occupy yourself, in the shortest time possible, in seeking lodging on shore in which you will await the arrival of the Naturaliste, no longer being part of my staff.
At that time, if it still suits Captain Hamelin to receive you, he will employ you as he deems fit to your personal merit and your talents.
