Besides, I invite you to behave on shore in such a manner as not to give to the inhabitants of the country, as many subjects of discontent as you have caused me to experience since the moment I had the complaisance to receive you on board the Géographe.
You will be given the rations of the ship, in conformity with the distribution which will be made during the stay of the vessel on this road.
As soon as citizen Picquet had received this letter, he presented himself in a fury and on entering my cabin, foaming with rage, he began thus: "damned Sir, I find you very amusing to write to me in such a manner". This beginning and the state in which he was, made such an impression upon me that I ordered him immediately, without speaking another word, to withdraw at once from my presence and I closed my door as soon as he had passed it. Such an example of insubordination must not go unpunished and from that moment, I resolved to have him placed in the Dutch fortress, contenting myself with keeping him on board until I should have made, with the Governor, arrangements in consequence.
This indecent scene having detained me on board longer than I had intended, it was ten o'clock when I landed accompanied by citizen Bonnefoy, midshipman of the Navy, acting as ensign. As the pilot was in the boat and the tide was high, we entered the river and landed near the fortress. The Governor and his secretary came to receive us with much politeness and afterwards conducted us to his house.
After the first compliments, I presented him with the passports of the Company and the letter which accompanied them. He immediately took them up for reading and asked me to entrust them to him for one or two days to make a copy which he said he was obliged to send to Batavia for his personal responsibility. I did not think I should refuse his request and I entrusted them to him.
We then spoke of our particular needs, of the house to put our sick in and of another, particular one, for the lodging of the naturalists, which was found very promptly. The Governor had the politeness to tell me that as soon as my boat had departed, he had provided a lodging for me and that
he would conduct me to it after dinner. The conversation then becoming general, I enquired about the resources of the country which, according to the account which the Governor gave me, should not be considerable whilst the pilot whom he sent on board spoke to us in quite another manner.
Having represented to him the necessity I was under of building a boat in replacement of the one I had lost, he observed to me that the thing would be possible but that, however, there would be some difficulties in obtaining wood suitable for this object, in that it would be necessary to go choose and cut it at about three leagues from the bay. Nevertheless, he promised me to give me conductors and even men to assist us in this work.
At one o'clock, we sat down to table. The dinner was good, served neatly and even with elegance. The Governor had doubtless invited the principal people of his establishment since there were three more persons present who were his secretary, the physician, both Dutch, and the commander of the militia or of the people of the Malay country.
After dinner, according to custom, it was necessary to smoke the pipe and wait until the sun was less ardent to go out and at this period, he showed me the different lodgings which he had intended for us. First, he conducted me to a superb house which, transported into a European colony, would appear there with grace. It belonged to the wife of a Governor who died in the country, who willingly withdrew to her estate to cede it to me during the duration of our stay. The second was less elegant, but equally convenient, it was rented for eight piastres a month and intended for the naturalists. The third being destined to serve as a hospital was spacious, well aired and property of the Company. The English had much degraded it as well as the church which is near it, but they were occupied in preparing the part which our people were to occupy.
We then made a walk until the setting of the sun and I took leave of the Governor and his company to retire on board, not thinking to establish myself on shore until the next day.
During the day, the Governor sent on board as a present, a small ox, a pig, a sheep and different fruits of the country, apologising that he could not do better and even he added to me that they lacked the most necessary things by the want of communication with Batavia. In the conversation, he told me what I already knew of the conduct of the English after the surrender of the fortress and he only informed me of the capture of all their other establishments in the Moluccas by that nation.
At eight o'clock, I retired on board and found the vessel moored as I had given orders. The night had nothing particular, the sky was very fine and the wind which had been from the north, strong breeze, during the day, calmed as soon as the sun had set.
In my conversation with the Governor, I forgot to inform him of the intention I had of placing citizen Picquet under arrest in the fortress until the arrival of the Naturaliste.
1801-08-23.journal_breton_geographe: At 9.30 a.m. the commander landed, accompanied by Citizen Bonnefoi. His boat came back with lemons, limes and oranges sent by the governor; we were given leave to communicate with the shore. Several canoes brought poultry and fruit to sell. In the afternoon we moored east and west with a bower anchor; a prau brought us a buffalo, two sheep and firewood, of which we were short. In the evening the commander came back aboard.

1801-08-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the air thick. A fresh breeze variable from SSW, SSE and south. At 5.15 a.m. the camp's dinghy came to fetch the caulkers to work on the longboat.
1801-08-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, in the morning, all the naturalists who wished to land were ordered to be ready at eight o'clock and to embark their effects in the boats of the vessel.
As I was preparing to leave, M. Picquet came to me again to ask me to go on shore to seek lodging in conformity with the letter I had addressed to him the day before. I replied to him that he had no need to take this trouble and that I was going to occupy myself with it and that I would have him informed when it was prepared. He withdrew making very expressive gestures to which, however, I appeared to pay no attention, in order to avoid coming to unfortunate extremities.
As soon as we landed, I conducted those of the naturalists who were in the boat with me to their lodging, of which they took possession and I went to mine to do the same by having my effects transported there. We were so near one another that one could speak easily by the window without having the trouble of going out.
The sick were likewise established on shore, in the morning and before noon, everything was in order at the hospital.
As I had no kitchen established, I went without ceremony to ask dinner from the Governor and I brought with me, M. Boulanger our geographer. The Governor received us as well as the day before and gave us a very good dinner.
The rest of the day had nothing particular and we spent it putting our affairs in order and establishing ourselves in such a way as no longer to incommode anyone.
In the evening at eight o'clock, the Governor sent to inform me that he had just been informed that there had appeared a three-masted vessel at the entrance of the strait of Semau, that this vessel had made a signal which was judged to be to request a pilot, but that its flag could not be distinguished. He added to me that he had given orders for a pilot to be sent to it the next day and that in consequence, he was sending back at once the one who had brought him this news. We were all the more pleased with this information because we thought it could only be the Naturaliste about whose fate I had great concerns.
1801-08-24.journal_breton_geographe: In the morning he landed with all the naturalists, to live ashore. The sails were unbent, the topgallant masts got down and the running rigging unrove. A hospital was set up in the town, where the surgeon-major and all the sick went. All our empty casks were sent ashore.

1801-08-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and SSW.
1801-08-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, about eight o'clock in the morning, I received a visit from the Governor and his clerk. I gave him the list of fresh provisions which we needed per decade, as well as those which I intended to embark at departure. I also informed him how pressed we were to begin our boat promptly and he gave immediate orders to a Frenchman established in this country for thirty years, to conduct us to the place where suitable wood should be found in order to mark the trees to be felled afterwards. Citizen Ronsard, engineer, and the master carpenter were charged with this corvée in which our first gardener Riedelé asked to be included in order to know the productions of the district where we were to go. His request was granted and it was arranged that we should set out the next day, at break of day.
After breakfast, the Governor withdrew to his house renewing to us that he would do everything possible to procure for us the things of which we might have need.
I was far from suspecting, at the moment when he withdrew, the new scene which was about to take place, but scarcely had there been a quarter of an hour since he left when M. Picquet presented himself asking to speak to me in private. He was in uniform and had his sabre at his side. Not being able to suspect his intentions, I passed with him into the drawing room, for at the moment when he arrived, I was under the gallery occupied, with citizen Boulanger, in copying a particular plan of the island of Timor which the Governor had lent to us.
When we were in the drawing room, M. Picquet approached me and said: "Sir, as we are no longer here on board, I hope that you will be willing to give me satisfaction for the manner in which you have treated me and I have come on shore expressly for that purpose". He had until then held his hat in his hand, but having finished his discourse, he put it on his head to await my reply.
I considered him for more than two minutes with a severe look without saying anything to him and I admit that I did not believe myself capable of so much patience. My silence, which he took for a new affront, rendered him furious and he asked me why I did not reply to him, adding that he was well worth it. I replied to him then with all the moderation possible that if I had not yet replied to him in the manner I ought, it was from fear of having misunderstood what he had said to me and that to remove my doubts on that subject, I begged him to be willing to repeat himself. There is doubtless no one who, after such conduct, would not have recognised the crime of which he was rendering himself guilty and would not have withdrawn, covered with shame and contempt for himself. But M. Picquet, far from having remorse, replied to me then: "damned, if you have not understood me, follow me, and putting his hand on his sabre, if you dare approach me, you will see the use I will make of it". His discourse did not prevent me from changing place, but it was to pass into the gallery and I commanded the first one I met to go fetch me four musketeers from the fort to have him conducted to prison. This order, to which, doubtless, he was not expecting, made him shudder with rage and led him for two or three minutes to deliver himself to all manner of invectives and then, he disappeared like a flash. Monsieur Ronsard whom he met wanted to accost him and speak to him, but he merely said to him that he was going on board. As Monsieur Ronsard knew nothing of what had passed, he came to the house and I informed him of M. Picquet's conduct. It was then that he told me he had met him and that from his distraught appearance, he had well judged that there must have been a scene rather violent.
Knowing that M. Picquet was back on board, I then wrote the following letter to M. le Bas:
"I am pleased to believe, citizen, that the intentions of M. Picquet were not known to you when you permitted him to land, and in order to inform you of it, I am well pleased to make known to you that he presented himself at my house, not to make me apologies for his past conduct, but only to indulge in invectives and finally to propose to me to draw the sword with him. &a &a...
"When the French Government hears this news it will doubtless blame me for not having had him shot on the spot to serve as an example, but I resolve to endure the reproach, not on account of him who deserves no consideration, but for his family whom I know to be respectable.
"For the rest, from fear of being obliged, after having suffered so much, to come to extremities which are repugnant to my character, you will have him confined on board, until further order from me, and at the least if he behaves badly there, you will confine him in his cabin with a sentry at his door and give me notice of it immediately.
"I believe the Naturaliste signalled in the strait of Semau". NB
As it was then approaching noon, I countermanded the guard which I had sent for and deferred to the evening to entertain the Dutch Governor about what I had to say to him concerning this officer and the course to which I had decided to hold myself.
The scandalous scene of M. Picquet was not long in spreading through the town and it was even announced on board before my letter arrived there. About two o'clock in the afternoon, I received the following reply from M. le Bas:
"Commandant,
"It was a question of a visit to be made to the Governor by M. Picquet when this officer asked me to go on shore.
"You will do me justice in believing that the intentions which he has manifested at your house were not known to me. I am too much a partisan of subordination and discipline to suffer that one departs from it and whoever it may be on board, I swear to you, has not applauded his conduct. I have made known your orders to him and he will conform to them.
In the afternoon, I paid a visit to the Governor, accompanied by a person of the country who was acting as interpreter. In the conversation which I had with him, I begged him to be willing to receive in the fortress, the officer whose conduct I had made known to him in order not to be obliged to make him undergo the penalty imposed by the general law of all nations against one who behaves in the manner in which Monsieur Picquet has done. He made no difficulty in complying with my request, only, he begged me to make it to him in writing so that he could make a formal report of it to the Council of Batavia.
As this Commandant proposed to send out in 25 or 30 days, a brigantine which was on the roads to Batavia, I also proposed to him to have him sent in this colony whence I would take with the Governor of Batavia the suitable arrangements for his passage for his return to Europe where he is to go to account for his conduct. All my requests were granted with the only observation to make them in writing.
After having settled our matters, we arranged that I would address my letter to him the next day, but that he would in advance have prepared the lodging which he was destining for him in the fortress where he would be confined until the departure of the ship for Batavia.
The rest of the day had nothing particular. The scene of the morning was only the news of all the day and a great subject of astonishment for the Dutch.
1801-08-25.journal_breton_geographe: The topmasts were struck and the lower yards lowered; the sheet anchor was got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The crew had fresh meat and fish.

1801-08-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the sky cloudless. A fresh breeze from SW and SSW.
1801-08-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, in the morning, I did not fail to write to the Governor the following letter as we had arranged the evening before. It was conceived in these terms:
M. the Governor,
It is in the name of the French Republic that I address myself to you to ask that you will have the complaisance to receive in the fortress one of the officers who formed part of my staff although he was not on the corvette which I commanded at the departure from France. But it is no longer possible for me to keep him any longer on board, given his bad conduct. As it seems to me useless to enter into details on this subject, I have only to beg you to have him confined in the fort, until the departure of the vessel which you are in the intention of sending shortly to Batavia. I shall satisfy all the expenses which his detention and his departure may occasion upon the demand which you will make of it.
The letter which I beg you to have transmitted to the Governor General at Batavia, will put you in a position to judge of the means which I employ to facilitate his return to Europe where he is to appear to account for his conduct.
This officer has the rank of ensign which I leave to him and is named Picquet. He is about 22 or 23 years of age and mad or furious by character. He will be conducted, tomorrow, to the fort or rather if it is possible. Signed N. B.
The same day, I gave a dinner to the Governor, to his secretary and to the surgeon who are the three principal persons of the establishment. All the scholars and naturalists were there, so that all were not satisfied because I had not presented them in body, at the moment of my arrival.
In the middle of dinner, we learned very pleasant news and an orderly came to announce to the Governor that knowledge had been had at the entrance of the strait of Semau of a large vessel which had made some signals as is the practice in requesting a pilot. We did not doubt but that it was the Naturaliste and in consequence, we urged him to send out a pilot, which he promised us to do. This was the second time we had this information and, as one always flatters oneself with seeing arrive what one desires, we thought that this vessel which had not appeared the evening before as we had expected, had found winds which had prevented it from being able to gain the entrance of this strait, but that doubtless, it would be more fortunate this time.
As, on separating in the evening, it was agreed that M. Picquet would be placed in the fortress, the next day, I wrote to citizen le Bas, the following letter:
The Commandant &a:
I inform you that tomorrow morning, M. Picquet will land with all his effects to occupy the apartment which I have had prepared for him.
I have likewise provided for his sustenance and his departure to Batavia as well as for his return to Europe, where he will arrive long before us.
You will be pleased to inform him on my part, to be ready for the moment when I shall arrive on board which will be about eight o'clock if you will have the complaisance to send me the boat. You will give orders to the master gunner that the naval troops be in uniform and their arms loaded with ball.
Signed N. B.
About eight o'clock in the evening, a new notice from the Governor made known to me that several cannon shots had been heard in the north of the island of Semau and that there was appearance that the vessel which had seemed to wish to enter the strait had changed its mind and preferred to come by the ordinary passage. I immediately gave orders to citizen le Bas to send out the next day at break of day, the gig and to give the command of it to citizen Bonnefoy to go in discovery in that direction.
During the night, nothing particular passed. The weather was very fine and the winds almost calm from the east to east-south-east quarter.
1801-08-26.journal_breton_geographe: Work was interrupted, the crew being unwell, which was put down to the water. The carpenters were sent ashore with their tools and planking to build us a longboat there under Citizen Ronsard's direction. A canoe brought us firewood. Some of the local people reported that a three-masted ship had anchored at the entrance to Semau Strait, from which she had got under way, and that they had heard gunfire to the west of Semau.

1801-08-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A fresh breeze from SSW.
1801-08-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 9th, from four o'clock in the morning, the large boat commanded by Citizen Bonnefoy left the ship and directed its course according to the instructions I had given.
At eight o'clock, I went on board and found everything prepared as I had ordered the day before. After having conversed with M. Le Bas, I had M. Picquet told to have his effects embarked and that the guard would conduct him to the Dutch fortress where he would be confined until the departure of the vessel which the Governor proposed to dispatch as soon as possible to Batavia. I allowed this officer, who does not deserve the name, to retain his rank of ensign at the solicitation of the other officers while warning him, nevertheless, that if he abused it to misbehave with the people of the country that the Governor of this establishment would be authorised by a letter from me to take it from him. He had the fortress for a prison so long as he would behave well there. He was not taken to the fort by the guard as I had planned, and yet I gave my officers this mark of indulgence. At nine o'clock, he left the ship.
Shortly after, I went ashore myself to attend to my affairs and to provide for the departure of those who were destined to go to seek the wood which the carpenters had chosen to construct our boat, which I was eager to see begin.
In the afternoon, Citizen Bonnefoy came to report to me on the journey he had made in the boat. After having doubled the North point of the island of Semau, he had coasted along the western part until its southern extremity while visiting the different coves he encountered, but he had knowledge of no vessel either at anchor or under sail, so it appears that the vessel which had been seen the day before was a passing vessel having no intention of calling at this establishment. I informed the Governor of the report which had just been made to me. And that of the people of the strait which he received almost at the same time proved to be in conformity with what I was telling him.
He also announced to me the reception of Citizen Piquet in the fort and the request he had made of him for his sword to restore it to him when he would leave.
1801-08-27.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the large boat to try to discover whether this ship might be the Naturaliste. At 9 the commander came aboard; the detachment took up arms (loaded and with bayonets fixed) and he gave orders to take Citizen Piquet, ensign, to Fort Concordia with his effects, and to send him his provisions. Citizen Freycinet obtained leave to take him there alone. He was received ashore by the Dutch guard and taken to the fort, where the sergeant commanding the fort asked him for his sword. After this business the commander went back ashore. At 2.30 Citizen Bonnefoi came back in the large boat; he had coasted the western side of Semau without discovering anything.

1801-08-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW. At 5.30 a.m. a Malay named Sodomson, shipped at Mauritius, died of putrid fever.
1801-08-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
The tenth had nothing remarkable. As it was a decadi, no work was done on board and half the crew received permission to go ashore on the condition of not spreading themselves about the countryside.
I delivered to the Commandant of the fort during the day a note of all the articles of exchange we had on board, informing him that I had no other money to give him for our expenses during our stay at Timor.
Our sick ashore were already beginning to feel the beneficial effects of the change in diet, and I neglected nothing for their prompt recovery.
On board, almost the entire crew was incommoded by the water. I believe the cause is to be attributed to the fact that it was taken at high tide, and that in order to have less trouble, they did not advance far enough up the river. In order to avoid the unfortunate consequences that might result, and also to relieve the crew in this work, which is always laborious in hot countries, I resolved to have it done by the people of the country.
1801-08-28.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; a large part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-08-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to SW. At 3 the longboat came loaded with wood and went back ashore at once.
1801-08-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
The eleventh, we began to put our water barrels ashore and to empty those in the hold which were filled with seawater. The crew who carried them down to the bank of the river had also brought about twenty galley barrels for the ship's daily consumption, but after filling them, having not had the forethought to leave someone to guard them, they went further away under the pretext of bathing, so that during their absence, seven of them were stolen. I made my complaints to the Governor who promised me to do his best to discover the thieves. He warned me that in future we must place our barrels at the fortress, that he would have them filled and answer for them. And that if we proceeded otherwise, we would run the risk of losing them.
On board, we reset the topmasts and sent up the topgallant masts. Part of the crew was employed with the seine, and the catch was not bad. We took, besides various species of fish, two turtles.
The Governor, who is the only one who engages in any trade with foreigners, procured for us a wild buffalo weighing about two hundred pounds every two days, so that both on board and ashore, we enjoyed good meat. But we lacked vegetables and other refreshments, much better than meat. All provisions increased in price for us, and although we witnessed what he charged the people of the country, we were obliged to pay double.
1801-08-29.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. A working party was set up ashore to fill our casks; at low water we watered in the Kupang river.

1801-08-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE.
1801-08-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twelfth, we continued on board the necessary work to put the vessel in a condition to receive water, timber, and other things of which we might have need.
I again gave dinner to the Governor, his secretary, and the commander of the militia of the country, who is here a person of importance.
Since our arrival, the Dutch Governor had treated us very well, and not a day had passed on which he had not made us some present of pork, venison, vegetables, and mutton, the original breed of which appeared to me to come from the Cape of India, or at least to resemble greatly those of that country.
In the afternoon, we went to pay a visit to the lady who had ceded to me the fine house in which I was lodged, and who, for that reason, had withdrawn to one of her estates, at about three quarters of a league from the town.
I was far from expecting the reception we received, which was truly made to astonish strangers. More than one hundred slaves of both sexes, well dressed, formed two groups at the ends of the veranda under which we were received. The lady of the house, Timorese in origin, advancing to the staircase, came politely to receive us and begged us to enter. Her bearing was noble and her manners easy.
After the first compliments, I had her thanked through my interpreter for the graciousness she had shown in ceding to me her house, for which she would not receive any compensation. And having expressed to her how sorry I was for the inconvenience that her removal must have caused her, she replied obligingly that she was always pleased when an opportunity presented itself to be of service to foreigners, and especially to Frenchmen.
Tea and coffee were then served to those who wished to take them, and these beverages were accompanied by a multitude of sweets prepared at her home and served alternately by a score of young girls neatly dressed, and for the most part pretty. Those who tasted these delicacies assured us they would not be made better in Paris. It appears the Governor had announced us, and that this lady wished to display herself before us in all her splendour. All the dishes were of silver, finely wrought, and the luxury yielded nothing to elegance.
The sight which the whole presented was truly fine, and if I could have foreseen it, I would have brought with me the draughtsman, who, without doubt, would have made a fine picture of it. We remained at this lady's home about an hour and a half, and as night was falling, I informed the Governor who had accompanied us that I was at his orders and that we would leave when he thought fit. He replied that the approach of night need not worry me, in that we would see there as clearly as in full daylight to return. We remained therefore another half hour, and at six o'clock and a half, we prepared to depart. This lady, seeing our preparations for departure, had word sent to me that, knowing we were collecting shells, she had some which she begged me to accept, regretting greatly that they were not more beautiful. She then had presented to me by one of her women a basket in which were found a very fine conch, two vessels, and pretty bobbins. I thanked her much for this kindness, and we took leave of her, asking her permission to come from time to time to see her during our stay in the island.
The Governor was quite right in telling me that we would see there as clearly as in full daylight, for a great quantity of torches were immediately lit. Some were large wax torches, and others made with the wood called chandelle wood and coated with a kind of resin, so that the whole emitted much light, even at a great distance. The slaves bearing the wax torches were in front at fifteen paces from us, and the others at the same distance behind.
Our departure from this house was no less brilliant than had been our arrival, and the whole resembled perfectly a decoration from the Opera in Paris. The route we took to return was different from the path we had taken to go there, and we returned by the seashore.
I was informed on the way that this lady had been the wife of a Dutch Governor who, in dying, had left her all his property, although he had no child with her. She is named (a white) and is perhaps fifty years old. She is given thirty thousand readale of income, a thousand slaves at her disposal distributed over three fine estates, well built and well maintained. The four finest houses of the town belong to her, and although she suffered much loss when the English took the fortress, she still passes for the wealthiest person in the country.
On going inland to her home, we met a herd of more than two hundred head of cattle, well maintained. But the oxen as well as the heifers are of a very small breed and appear to me to be of the Manila breed. She has likewise numerous flocks of sheep and goats and much poultry. In short, it appears that this dwelling lacks nothing, for there are found there fine ponds in which one sees swimming a great number of carp and many other freshwater fish.
The Governor took us to see a spring whose volume is very considerable, and it is from this same place that different channels have been made which conduct it to the dwelling we have just left.
Upon our arrival in town, the Governor escorted us back to our lodging, and we wished each other good evening, thanking him much for the pleasant enjoyment he had afforded us.

1801-08-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE.
1801-08-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
The thirteenth, we continued our work as usual. Two members of the crew entered the hospital, one affected with a discharge of blood and the other with a fever whose character we are still ignorant of.
Our carpenters, who had left to seek timber suitable for the construction of our longboat, arrived. They were absent longer than I had presumed, because not only were they obliged to cut it themselves, but also to carry it to the boat. The people the Governor had provided, being unwilling to help them at all. Be that as it may, I had it carried at once to the shipyard we had chosen, and we will finally apply ourselves without interruption to this work.
At dinner, I was much astonished to learn that several of the naturalists had taken offence that I had not taken them all with me to pay a visit to the lady at whose home I had gone the day before. I had only taken Citizen Ronsard, whom I chanced to meet, and Messrs. Bernier and Maugé. The account which these would have given to the others concerning the manner in which we were received would doubtless have created jealousy and occasioned remarks. I do not believe myself obliged to have eight or ten people in my suite when I wish to pay a visit to someone, but it is true that if I could have foreseen what happened to us, I would have willingly given them this satisfaction without, however, believing that it was a duty on my part.
In the evening, the boats put ashore a fairly large quantity of water containers, and I had them conducted to the fortress, or at least under the inspection of the guard of the castle, in order to prevent them from being stolen or damaged, for the people are very fond of the iron hoops which are upon them, and make no scruple of removing them when they find the opportunity.

1801-09-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and east. The large boat came in from her mission to the north of the bay. She brought eight enormous turtles, which gave us great pleasure.
1801-09-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fourteenth, an imprudence committed by someone from the ship occasioned complaints from the Governor. People to whom M. Le Bas had allowed, without my orders, to go ashore to hunt, spread themselves about the countryside, and their hunting not having been successful, they no doubt wished to compensate themselves by firing at domesticated pigeons. I am ignorant whether they killed any, but several lead shot wounded a girl who was in the neighbourhood. Her parents did not fail to bring her to the Dutch Governor to establish the fact, and this came near to making us quarrel with the people of the country. However, I got off with making some presents and promising that it would not happen again.
In consequence, I wrote to Citizen Le Bas a letter forbidding anyone from the ship to come ashore with firearms without a written permission from me and signed by me. This prohibition occasioned murmurs and even remarks. But I paid little heed to them.
We passed the day occupied with our affairs, and on board we heaved up the anchors to inspect the cables, for we had been warned that this precaution was necessary although we were on a bottom of mud, in that experience had proved that coral rocks are sometimes encountered which cut them.
1801-09-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fish were taken with the seine and distributed to the crew; the watering continues.

1801-09-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW. During the night the winds drew round from south to WSW, almost calm.
1801-09-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fifteenth, I experienced a rather violent attack of fever which seized me all at once and which obliged me to keep my chamber. I do not know to what to attribute the cause, for, having risen in the morning between four and a half o'clock and five o'clock, as was my custom, I felt very well.
Nothing new happened during the day. But at about eight o'clock in the evening, I was informed that sixteen hoops had been stolen from our water containers, which I had nevertheless had placed under the inspection of the guard of the castle. I immediately made complaints to the Governor, who replied that he had already warned us that this might happen to us, and that we had been wrong not to have put them inside the fortress as he had told us. He added, nevertheless, that he would make all diligence to find them if it were possible.
The fever which had seized me in the morning at about seven o'clock, left me in the afternoon, and I had a fairly good night.
1801-09-02.journal_breton_geographe: Part of the crew went ashore to walk about. Fish and a small turtle were taken with the seine.

1801-09-03.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky overcast, the winds very light and variable from WSW, SW and W. We set up our shrouds, stowed our anchors and hoisted in the longboat and the other boats.
1801-09-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
The sixteenth, I found myself as well as usual, and the fever did not appear at all during the day, nor during the night. It was not the same with the master of the household, who appeared likely to suffer a serious illness, and who, to prevent or cure it, was placed in the care of the faculty.
I received in the morning a visit from the Governor, to whom I gave breakfast, as well as to his secretary. He then asked to speak to me in private, and having summoned an interpreter, we passed into my chamber. He warned me then that five men of my crew had presented themselves at his home the day before to request their discharge, wishing to go to Batavia. These five men came from a Prussian vessel which was at the Île de France, and whom the Captain had put in prison for reasons unknown to me. These men were sent on board the corvette the day before departure by order of the two administrations of the Île de France, and at their own request in writing, no doubt, rather to get themselves out of prison than with the intention of making the voyage. Be that as it may, not wishing to grant these five men, who were very necessary to me, their discharge, I contented myself with telling the Governor that they could nevertheless obtain their leave if they succeeded in having themselves replaced by five other Europeans and good sailors like them. According to the instances of the Governor to obtain their discharge, I am led to believe that he was the most interested party, and that he desired to have them to employ on his brigantine which was to depart shortly for Batavia.
During the day, we embarked several cords of wood. We set up the keel, the stem, and the sternpost of the longboat, whose length and other proportions were somewhat stronger than those we had lost.
1801-09-03.journal_breton_geographe: The coopers went to repair our casks and put on hoops that had been stolen. Fish and a small turtle were taken.

1801-09-04.journal_anonyme: A high sea, misty and squally weather and a cloudy sky. A fresh breeze from W to SW in strong gusts. At 10.20 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course W by N.
1801-09-04.journal_baudin_autographe: The seventeenth, the work continued on board as well as on shore, but the work proceeded slowly because I could not procure any relief for the crew for the transport of the objects which had to be either embarked or put ashore. It was never possible for me to persuade the people of the country to help us, either by paying them by the day or by giving them some of our articles of exchange. Idleness and sloth are their greatest enjoyment, and as they have few needs, they scarcely think of procuring themselves some comforts by work when the opportunity presents itself. Slaves only are forced by their masters to work, but this does not extend to hiring them to foreigners.
1801-09-04.journal_breton_geographe: A prau brought us 2 cords of wood.

1801-09-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to south. Soundings from midnight to 4: from 1 to 2, 65 and 66 fathoms, fine reddish sand; at 3 and at 4, 80 and 85 fathoms. At noon on the 18th we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn.
1801-09-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth our occupations were much the same as the day before, however we took on board some forty casks of water and that was the heaviest part of our work. The Governor had them brought on board by his slaves or those belonging to the Company, but they would never lend us a hand to hoist them aboard, nor even wait until they were empty to carry them back.
Pages 49 to 77 are blank
DEPARTURE FROM COUPANG, BAY OF TIMOR, FOR VAN DIEMEN'S LAND, SOUTH OF NEW HOLLAND
1801-09-05.journal_breton_geographe: In the evening Citizen Le Bas, who until now had borne the whole duty alone, entered in the ship's log that, all the midshipmen except one (Bonnefoi) reporting themselves sick, Citizens Freycinet, Bonnefoi and myself were left with the duty.

1801-09-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea and the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom; from 2 to 4 the same.
1801-09-06.journal_breton_geographe: I went to the hospital ashore for the itch. At 9 p.m. a canoe brought a letter from the commander to Citizen Le Bas, telling him that there were two English frigates and three small vessels anchored in Semau Strait, which was causing much alarm ashore; he ordered him to send Citizen Freycinet at daybreak to reconnoitre them.

1801-09-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea with a little swell, a fresh breeze from ESE to SE. From 10 until midnight sounded without finding bottom. At 10 set the studdingsails and staysails.
1801-09-07.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Freycinet, carrying our passports and a letter from the commander to the English commodore, left for Semau Strait; he was back at 2 and had seen no ship at all. Work was suspended, but no one went ashore; we rested on board. Canoes brought us water.

1801-09-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE. At 3.30 a.m. ran out 87 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 4 a.m. the breeze got up from the SE.
1801-09-08.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. 95 sacks of wheat were sent to the hospital to be dried and winnowed by the convalescents.

1801-09-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south; we sounded without finding bottom. At sunrise we set the studdingsails.
1801-09-09.journal_breton_geographe: Having tasted the water the canoes were bringing us, we found it brackish and sent it back.

1801-09-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds very light and variable from SSE to SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-09-10.journal_breton_geographe: The two topmasts were swayed up and the lower yards hoisted. Our boats and some canoes continue to water for us.

1801-09-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SSE to SE. Ran out 90 fathoms of line without finding bottom.

1801-09-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE, south and ESE. Sounded all night without finding bottom.
1801-09-12.journal_breton_geographe: The mizzen topgallant mast was swayed up.

1801-09-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. The sky cloudy and dark. A strong breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught a tern.

1801-09-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSE, ESE and east. Sounded without finding bottom.
1801-09-14.journal_breton_geographe: The topgallant masts were got up.

1801-09-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught two boobies. At 9.15 a.m. sighted land N 5° E. Noon bearings: the westernmost visible end N 18° E; a remarkable peak N 22° E, distance 8 miles; the northernmost visible end N 32° E.

1801-09-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from east to SE and ESE. At 3.10 lost sight of the land. At 9 a.m. bore away for Savu Island; running along the southern side of this island, we saw on the shore several local people and a few huts. Noon bearings: the south point of Savu S 5° W; the visible end of this island N 70° E; the middle of this part of the island S 36° W.

1801-09-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE, south and SE. Sounded all night without finding bottom. From the 30th [Fructidor] to the 1st complementary day [Year 9, 17-18 September 1801]. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light and variable from S by W, S by E, SE and E by S. Saw several fires on the coast.
1801-09-17.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-09-18.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order.

1801-09-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky, a light breeze variable from E to NW, south and SE. At 3 went about onto the port tack.

1801-09-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3.15 p.m. the breeze got up from the SSE. At 8 it drew round to SE by E, making us run 7 knots. At 2 took a reef in the mizzen topsail. Bearings at 10: the visible south point of the land east 30° S, about 30 miles off; the north point east, estimated distance from the furthest land [sentence incomplete].

1801-09-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind variable from WNW, SE, SW, NW. During the night we sounded without finding bottom. Lay to from 4 until 5.15, when we filled and stood on. At 6.15 hove to to put the large boat in the water. She left under the orders of Citizen Freycinet, carrying the national flag and pendant; we hoisted our colours and put a signal flag at the foremast head. Shortly afterwards we sighted a boat ahead of us which seemed to have come from the ship in sight, which we recognised to our satisfaction as the Géographe.
1801-09-21.journal_breton_geographe: At daybreak a three-masted ship was sighted beating in towards Kupang; bets were at once laid that it was the Naturaliste. The commander sent orders to make the private signal, and shortly afterwards we recognised the Naturaliste, which also made the private signal. Our boat was sent off to her with some refreshments. At 1 she anchored near us to the NW, two cables off. She saluted us with 5 guns, which we returned, and at once dressed ship. We sent her fresh water and our boat to help her moor.

1801-09-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from SSW to SE and to east and south. At 1 we anchored in 28 fathoms forward and 26 fathoms aft. In the afternoon the two skiffs and the longboat were put in the water to moor us. At 9 a.m. on the 5th we were moored, the western anchor with a range of 50 fathoms to port, the eastern anchor with a range of 100 fathoms to starboard. Bearings of the anchorage: the middle of the fort of Kupang south, distance 1 mile; the south point of Timor S 65° W, 5 miles; the north point N 7° E, 21 miles; the middle of Sandy Island N 11° W, 5 miles.
1801-09-22.journal_breton_geographe: The ship's outside, the masts and the yards were painted. A little fish was taken with the seine.

1801-11-12.journal_anonyme: Hardly had we arrived at Kupang than we set about overhauling the rigging; the orlop deck was taken up, we watered and fresh provisions were embarked. The town of Kupang is defended by a poor fort, and more surely by the courage of the Malays. The English took Kupang during this war, but the men left to garrison the fort were massacred by the Malays and Timor returned into Dutch hands. During our stay the nights and mornings were calm; about 11 the breeze often got up very strong, the winds being then NW and NNW. They fell away at the close of the day and drew round to east and SE. On the 1st Brumaire [Year 10, 23 October 1801] we sighted a frigate standing in for Kupang Bay. Commander Baudin sent a boat aboard her under the orders of a midshipman carrying our passports; on our boat's return we learnt that the frigate sighted was the Virginie, which had come to attack us. As soon as the English frigate's captain had seen our passports, he filled and beat out of the bay. During our stay we lost two men from dysentery. The Géographe lost 5, among them Citizen Riedlé, the gardener-botanist, a man full of zeal for his calling; he was given the same funeral honours as would have been paid to the head of the expedition. He was buried beside Mr Nelson, Captain Bligh's gardener-botanist, who also died at Timor. We lost 9 men by desertion.
1801-11-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the evening we unmoored; the cable was found chafed about 20 fathoms from the bend. The second anchor was weighed and let go again at once. The small boat and the yawl were hoisted in.

1801-11-13.journal_anonyme: At five in the morning we got under way with a light breeze from SE. At noon we took the compass bearing of the NW point of Semau W 29° S, 5 miles off, and the NW end of Sandy Island E 11° N, distance 8 [miles].
1801-11-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-second, from four o'clock in the morning, we prepared for departure, although it was my fever day. I was too impatient to leave a country where illnesses had treated us so badly to defer my departure to the next day; in consequence, I made signal to the Naturaliste to set sail, and I did the same myself. The winds were then from the east to the south-east, very light. But I flattered myself that the land breeze would be felt at sunrise, and that by this means we could double the small island of (the) Tortue and its great reef before the arrival of the sea breeze. This hope did not come to pass, for at about eight o'clock, we were in a calm. But as there was then an ebb tide, it contributed much to carry us out of the pass, to the north of Semau.
According to the information I obtained during my stay at Timor, it appears that both large and small vessels should prefer this passage to any other, in that it is much more convenient than that which is found to the north of the island of Tortue and the south side of Coupang Bay. The windward work is more extensive and the banks fewer in number.
At about eleven o'clock, the winds having shifted to north-west, a fine breeze, we bore towards the coast of Semau, which we could not double, which obliged us to tack for some time, but in the afternoon they shifted to west-south-west, and we gained the offing by passing at about three leagues from the island of Tortue, whose reef which is found to the west of this land extends near two leagues offshore. Bearings of the land at noon:
The fort of Concordia bearing south 45° east.
The island of Tortue bearing west 18° south.
The north coast of Semau bearing west 36° south.
In the afternoon, the winds having held fairly constantly in the south-west quarter, variable towards the west, we were obliged to keep the larboard tack towards the north, and we continued it until the middle of the night, when we took the starboard tack towards the south.
At sunset, the land bore us as follows:
A part of the north coast of the island of Rottie bearing south 5° east.
The lands of the same island most in sight bearing south 10° east.
The north coast of Semau bearing south 16° east.
A part of the north coast of Timor in sight bearing north 25° west.
During the night from the 22nd to the 23rd, the winds were light and very inconstant. We had a fairly fine sky, although very humid, and the sea was calm. According to our observations, the current appeared to carry us in the north-west during the duration of the flood as well as during that of the ebb.
At midnight, we made signal to the Naturaliste to go about, and we also changed our tacks to bear towards the south, my intention being to make the passage between the island of Rottie and that of Savu, if the winds were not too contrary.
1801-11-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE, SE, E, NE, NNW, WNW, W, WSW and SW. At 4 a.m. the topgallant masts were rigged and the topsails hoisted, stopped with rope yarns. At 5 got under way with the Géographe and shaped our course N 33° 45' W, N 56° 15' W and N 67° 30' W to leave the bay. At 11, the wind having hauled to the NW, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At noon, the commander having gone onto the port tack, we followed his movement. The NW point of Semau then bore from us S 61° W, 5 miles off, and the NW point of Turtle Island N 79° E, 8 miles off. At 4, Roti Island from S 84° W to S 88° W, and Batu Island N 45° E. The captain cancelled the distribution of hens made on the 20th; he gave 100 to the officers, 50 to the chief petty officers, 30 to the second petty officers, 20 to the petty officers, and the rest to the sick.

1801-11-14.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WNW to SW, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, the course NNW. At 4 a.m. we steered S by E, with a great deal of thunder and lightning. At noon took the bearing of the island of Roti S 46° 30' W.
1801-11-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-third, in the morning, after recognizing and taking bearings of the land, we were rather astonished to find ourselves scarcely more advanced than the evening before, and although it had blown but little during the night, I nevertheless expected that the current would have carried us tolerably far towards the west.
Bearings in the morning at sunrise:
A part of the north coast of Semau bearing east 27° north.
The lands most in sight of the same island bearing east 10° south.
The north part of Rottie bearing south 30° east.
During the morning, the winds were very variable from the south to the east, and often calm. We held as much as possible on the westerly course by standing south as much as possible. At about eight o'clock, the Naturaliste having closed with us, we spoke to her, and I was informed that most of her sick were entering into convalescence, but that two were in danger. Our situation was much the same. Those affected with dysentery were much better, but I had continual anxieties for our second gardener, whom a malignant fever had reduced to such a state of weakness and drowsiness that his recovery was very doubtful.
As this day was not a bad one for me, I was tolerably well, nevertheless I often experienced numbness in the legs which only too well informed me that I was not yet out of trouble.
At noon we observed the latitude of 9° 58' south, and the estimated longitude according to the routes travelled since departure was 121° 13' east.
At the same time, the lands most in sight of the island of Rottie extended towards the south-south-east, at a great distance.
In the afternoon, the calm continued until about three o'clock, when the winds having shifted to west-south-west, variable towards the south, increased somewhat. We then lost sight of land and directed our course as close-hauled as possible, but we saw with regret that we were strongly carried towards the north-west by violent tidal currents which came to us from the south to the south-east.
(Reproduce the sketch which is in the margin)
During the night from the 23rd to the 24th, the sky was again overcast and very humid. I do not know if this state of the atmosphere contributed to the discomfort which all our sick experienced, but the fact is that they were worse than usual. I myself felt it, and had a restless night, during which we were often becalmed, although sometimes a breeze came to us from the east, which would have been very pleasant for us if it had blown.
Note: During the day, I had the water consumption regulated so that what happened to us might not occur again, as we had nearly experienced it during our last voyage. Those concerning tea and coffee were also fixed, as well as for sugar, for if the ordinary course had been followed, there would have been nothing left for us at the end of three months, although we have on board as much as we need for nine.
1801-11-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8 took the bearing of the SW end of Semau S 78° E, the part of Timor in sight N 69° E. At 9 we passed under the commander's stern; he gave us the course south. Variation 0° 58' NW. At noon, being in 10° 3' 30" of latitude, we took the bearing of Dorr Island S 46° E, 18 miles off by the observed latitude and the bearing. The longitude was 120° 45'. It is from there that I took my point of departure. Savary, boatswain's mate, died of dysentery. It was signalled to the commander.

1801-11-15.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WSW to SW, the weather fine, the sky clear and the sea smooth. At noon a man named Savary died, which was announced to the commander by the agreed signal.
1801-11-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-fourth, in the morning, the winds continued to be extremely variable, and the sky became stormy in several parts of the horizon. A little before sunrise, we had several heavy showers of rain, but without wind. At daybreak, the sky became very overcast. We saw several waterspouts form, and although the air currents in the atmosphere were different, at least judging by the opposite movement of the clouds, they all had the same inclination. These phenomena occurred at different times and lasted no more than three to four minutes, after which they dispersed.
At the doctor's visit, all our sick were found to be tolerably well, except our garden boy Riedelé Sautier, who was in agony, having been attacked by tetanus during the night. All the remedies in use in such circumstances were administered to him at once, but they were useless, and about noon, he died. Apart from the regrets which his loss caused me with regard to his personal qualities, I saw with great sorrow that the part of our voyage concerning botany would be very incomplete, since I had had the misfortune to lose the two people who were engaged in it with zeal and assiduity.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 9° 39' 9" south, which gave us a great difference to the north from our reckoning. According to an hour angle taken in the afternoon, the longitude of the ship was found to be 120° 38', starting from 121° 47' for that of Timor. Although we took about two hundred distances during our stay at Coupang to determine with accuracy that of this place, we did not yet know the results, in that they have not been calculated.
In the afternoon, the weather became fine and the horizon, which had been thick and misty all morning, became clear. The winds also shifted to south-south-east, and we approached as much as possible the route from south to west.
During the night from the 24th to the 25th, they held in the same quarter, but they were so light that we advanced little. The tidal currents which we crossed during these twenty-four hours, appeared to us stronger than those which we had experienced in the preceding days, and had the same direction.
1801-11-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to ESE. At noon in 9° 38' 32" of latitude observed and in 120° 15' 46" of longitude by the watches. The variation 1° 5' 40" NW. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-11-16.journal_anonyme: The winds from south to SSE and ESE, the course SW and SSW, fine weather, smooth sea, the air rather thick and the winds light. At noon we sighted the land of Savu; we took the bearing of a very conspicuous headland SSE.
1801-11-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-fifth, in the morning, the sky was very overcast and almost always charged with stormy vapours which made one fear some squalls. However, the winds were very light from the south to the east, which gave us the means to advance a little towards the south.
At noon, the observed latitude was 10° 0' 44" south, and the longitude according to the rate of No. 35 was 119° 50'. That by the reckoning was 120° 18'.
During the time of the observation of the meridian height, we perceived a land in the south extending 12° towards the east. This land was the island of Savu, on which the Dutch sent a sergeant during our stay at Timor. The functions which this man exercises in the country during the six months of stay which he makes there, are reduced to causing the Company to be paid the tribute which it has imposed on the inhabitants in the alliance which it has made with them. It consists in rice, raw wax, honey, and some slaves, as well as some sandalwood. In exchange for these objects, the Company gives some handkerchiefs and cloths manufactured in Java.
The private trade between this island and Timor, although of little consequence in itself, is nevertheless fairly active. As the inhabitants of Savu are navigators, and those of Timor seldom leave their homes, they bring them painted cloths of different colours for the clothing of men and women, which are generally preferred for the elegance of the design and the fineness to those manufactured in Timor. Fish oil, coconuts, mats made of fan palms, and dried fish compose the greater part of their cargo, on the value of which the Company draws a duty of ten per cent, and reserves the price which may suit it.
In the afternoon, the winds having drawn closer to the east, we were able to approach the land a little, and we prolonged the south-west part of Savu at a fairly great distance. At about four o'clock, we had a perfect view of the island which is found at the south-west point, and by its beam. This island is high and well wooded, and appeared to us to be inhabited. The channel which is found between it and Savu may have four or five leagues of width and apparently offers a good passage to vessels which would keep fairly close to the coast of Savu to take advantage of it.
Bearings at sunset:
The point most in sight of the east part of Savu bearing east 54° south.
A low point belonging to the small island of which I have spoken bearing south 10° east. A fairly remarkable hillock of the same land bearing west 88° south. The part most to the south and west of the lands in sight bearing west 75° south.
According to this bearing, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course for the night, south-south-west, supposing that the winds would permit us to make it.
During the night from the 25th to the 26th, the winds were very variable and unequal, and the sky overcast and stormy. We had some small squalls of brief duration, and the winds held fairly constantly from the east to the south-east, sometimes a fine breeze, sometimes light.
During the night, several fires were perceived on the small island to the south-west of Savu; thus there is no doubt that it is inhabited, and indeed it appeared to us by its agreeable aspect to deserve to be inhabited.
1801-11-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. The commander signalled the death of a man (Sautier, gardener). At noon sighted Savu Island in the S 22° 30' E, being in 10° 4' 13" of latitude observed and in 119° 53' 3" of longitude by the watches. At 8.30 observed 1° 5' 30" of NW variation. At 1 the course was signalled S 11° 15' W. At 6 took the bearing of Savu from S 17° E to S 67° E and Benjuar Island from south to S 9° W. At midnight Benjuar Island bore from us S 22° 30' E. There was a fire on it.

1801-11-17.journal_anonyme: The wind varying from SE by E to south, a light breeze. At 1 the commander signalled the course S by W. At 4 took the bearing of the NW end of Savu S 10° E; the SE end E 41° S; Benjuar Island S 7° W.
1801-11-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-sixth, as soon as the moon set, the weather became fine, and we had the beginning of a fine breeze from the south-east, which appeared to be about to increase at sunrise.
Bearings of the land at the same time:
The lands in sight of the island Savu bearing east 16° north.
The north point of the small island near Savu bearing east 12° north.
The south point of the same island bearing south 89° east.
A small islet ahead of us bearing south 28° west.
The bearings, as reported above on all our charts, offered only poor results, and it does not appear to me doubtful that most of the lands, with the exception of Savu, are not poorly placed there.
On Robertson Arrowsmith's map, the island which is found to the south-west of Savu, there bears the name of Bonjour Island, and it is the only map which gives it a name. His Nouvelle Island, which comes next, is placed much too far to the west and south.
On Robertson's map, the island at the south-west point of Savu is fairly well placed, but the other is placed much further west-south-south-west than it actually is, and one would be the victim of the error of his map, especially at night, for the distance which he gives for the channel is more than half less than he announces it.
It is the same on the French map published in 1791. That in manuscript of the voyage of M. d'Entrecasteaux is the most exact of all for the subject of which I speak.
A reflection which the sight and the bearing of the lands suggested to me is perhaps not without foundation. It appears to me that the island named by Arrowsmith, Bonjour Island, is the small Savu. Its proximity to the great island of the same name, its inhabitants, its extent, and its agreeable aspect, appear to confirm this opinion. The other island marked on the maps as Nouvelle Savu is not distant from that of which I have just spoken, only by eight or nine leagues at most. It is rather a barren rock than anything else, and about two leagues in extent. We coasted this island in its northern part at three quarters of a league distance. Everywhere we discovered nothing but rocks heaped one upon another which appeared to be the work of some convulsion of nature. A few clumps of trees form all its ornament. The coast, except for some coves of very white sand, is formed of rocks cut perpendicularly, and the sea broke upon them everywhere with fury, although we were under the lee of it.
At eight o'clock, we had doubled this rock, and at noon, it bore us north 30° east.
The latitude observed then was 11° 2' 23" south, and the longitude on No. 35 was 119° 14' 27"; the reckoning placed us at 119° 50'.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine but the breeze was weak. We made the course as near the south as possible, regulating ourselves on the rate of the Naturaliste, which caused us to lose much headway.
At sunset, I had the displeasure of learning of the death of one named Corroyer, one of our best sailors and helmsman. We all regretted him, as he was very steady and very active. He had only fallen ill with dysentery a few days before our departure, and although treated by the doctors from the beginning, they could not save him.
The night from the 26th to the 27th had nothing particular. The weather was fine, but the winds shifted to the south, taking the west, which made them very unfavourable to the course we had to make.
1801-11-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 4, Benjuar Island from S 68° E to S 85° E, 5 miles off. At 6.30 New Savu was sighted in the S 30° W. At noon it bore from us N 30° E, 15 miles off, being in 11° 2' 10" of latitude observed and in 119° 18' 39" of longitude by account.

1801-11-18.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from SE, south and SSW. Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light air. The commander signalled us the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-seventh, in the morning, having passed the day before all the known islands which are found to the south and west of Timor, I signalled to the Naturaliste that we would make course to the south-south-west by compass if the winds permitted.
In the morning, the breeze was very light from the south. In return, we had very fine weather and the sea calm, although driven by a heavy swell from the south-west without our being able to divine the cause.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 11° 34' 28" south, and the longitude deduced from the rate of No. 35 was 118° 13' 39", while the reckoning placed us at 119° 33' 12", which gave for the timekeeper a difference west of 1° 19' 33" since the departure from Timor. It appears likely that such a difference, in so short a time, must be attributed to a strong current which carried us towards the west and the north, as we had observed in the beds of the tides which we encountered in doubling the islands, whose direction extended from the south-east to the north-west.
In the afternoon, the winds varied from the south to the south-south-east and made our course a little better, but it was not for long, for at sunset, they came back to the south.
During the night from the 27th to the 28th, we found the sea more swell than it had been during the day, and the vessel pitched much. The humidity was considerable during the night, and our sick, although sheltered, were incommoded by it. I myself, although convalescent, suffered much from it and experienced such weakness in the legs that I could not support myself on my feet. I also experienced some cramps, but they were not of long duration.
1801-11-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to SSW. At 1 hove to to wait for the Géographe. At 1.45 she had closed; we filled and stood on. At 8, 0° 49' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 36' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 29' 3" of longitude by account. The cables were unbent and the anchors secured in their stowage.

1801-11-19.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from S, SSE to SW, almost calm, the weather fine, the sea smooth. The commander signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-eighth, the weather continued fine, but the winds were so variable that we advanced little on a good course. The sea, always swell from the south to the south-west, did not announce any near change in the winds. However, I flattered myself that at full moon, we would experience one which would make the course better. Being persuaded that the winds, if they did not come from the south to the east, would at least come to us from the west to the south. The sequel will verify this conjecture.
Our sick in the morning experienced much relief from what they had suffered during the night. Nevertheless, two were in great danger, and the opinion of the doctors was that they could not recover. Citizen Maugé, who was also affected with dysentery, did not look well, and I was not without anxiety on his account, especially as I feared that those we had lost of the same disease would make some impression on him which could only delay his recovery.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 11° 30' 51" and the longitude of No. 35 placed us at 116° 59' 36". That of the reckoning was only 118° 45', which further increased the difference west of the timekeeper.
In the afternoon, the winds varied from the south to the south-south-east, and the sea, although fine, remained always swell. We continued the port tack from the west to the south, keeping the wind as close-hauled as possible, but the slow pace of the Naturaliste and the drift of that vessel when close-hauled, prevented us from taking advantage of the little benefit we could derive from it.
During the night from the 28th to the 29th, the winds came back to the south towards the west; the breeze was very light, or to speak truly, we had almost calm for the greater part of the night. The vessel was long surrounded by fish; we could only harpoon a porpoise, which we nevertheless lost at the moment it was being hauled on board, the harpoon having broken.
1801-11-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. The commander signalled us the death of a man (Corroyer). At 7.45, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 33' 12" of latitude observed and in 117° 29' 15" of longitude by account.

1801-11-20.journal_anonyme: Winds from S, SW and WSW. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, a fresh breeze.
1801-11-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-ninth, in the morning, the winds having shifted to the south-west, variable towards the west, we took the starboard tack on the course from south to the east. The breeze was light and the sea always swell.
In the morning, general quarters was called. The ship was cleaned and perfumed in all its parts, and our carpenters, after this first work was finished, were ordered to complete the work which remained to be done on the longboat.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 11° 34' 22" and the longitude on No. 35 was found to be 116° 17' 48". That of the reckoning placed us at 118° 5', which gave constantly less headway to the west than the timekeeper indicated.
In the evening, the breeze was very variable and light, and we continued our same course to rise in the west. It is by inadvertence that I said above that in the morning we took the tack from south to the east.
At about four o'clock in the evening, we lost one named Poussin, a good sailor and attached to the service of the hold. It is all too likely that all those affected with dysentery will have the same fate, and the characteristics of this terrible disease are so frightening that for one who is seized by it, one believes oneself already dead, which only contributes to aggravating the disease of those who have it. Fevers, although bad, are not as fatal to us, and since our departure from Timor, we have lost but one man of this illness.
During the night from the 29th to the 30th, the weather was fine, and the sky less humid than usual. Nevertheless, I had a very bad night. The sleeplessness which I experienced was complete, and the weakness in the legs greater than in the preceding days. My situation seemed to announce a new relapse. We continued to make course as close to the wind as possible, gaining towards the west as much as we could.
1801-11-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. At noon in 11° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 116° 47' 51" of longitude by account.

1801-11-21.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from W to SW, the sea and the weather fine, the breeze pleasant.
1801-11-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The thirtieth, the winds having at last shifted to the south-west, sometimes varying towards the west, we changed tacks to run south, standing towards the east to rise in latitude. The Naturaliste was ordered to do the same, and we continued to keep the wind as close-hauled as possible until it permitted us to bear away to the south-south-west, which is the course I intend to hold if they become favourable before we become too far to the south.
At noon, we observed 12° 19' 0" of latitude, and the longitude of our No. 35 placed us at 117° 11' 28". That of the reckoning was 118° 33' 12", which gave a difference of 0° 24' 34" to the east by the timekeeper more than the estimated course. What can be the cause of this great difference, and all opposite in these twenty-four hours to those which we had observed until then?
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine, the breeze light and variable as usual.
During this day, finding myself tolerably well, despite the discomfort I had experienced the day before, I went, jointly with the doctor, to visit our sick. This was but the second of this kind since our departure, in that my health had not permitted me to make more.
I found Citizens Maugé and Depuche tolerably well but not entirely out of danger. The master sailmaker much incommoded with a pain in the liver, but having the apparent symptoms of bad health. All the fever patients were in full convalescence and would soon be out of danger. But our cannoneer Masson was in agony from the sequel of dysentery and without hope of recovery. I ordered some changes in the berth of the sick for their greater comfort, and saw that we would soon cease to lose men.
The night from the 30th to the 1st frimaire had nothing new; the winds were light and variable as usual, and we made very little headway.
1801-11-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from SSW to W. At noon in 12° 20' 50" of latitude observed and in 117° 22' 45" of longitude by account. At 4, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation.

1801-11-22.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from W to WSW and WNW, the weather fine, a swell running from the SW and a fresh breeze.
1801-11-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The first of frimaire, in the morning, the winds were extremely light after sunrise. However, they drew nearer to the west than they had yet done, which gave us hope that they might vary from the west towards the north as we drew nearer to the coasts of New Holland.
In the morning, one named Mantel, cannoneer and mason by trade, died from the sequel of a dysentery which had caused him to languish for a long time. Three days before his death, he had wanted to throw himself into the sea, and he would have perished at that time without the promptness with which we saved him. When he was back on board, he told us with great sang-froid: You render me a very bad service, for I know well that I cannot recover from my disease, and thus you only prolong my sufferings by a few more days.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 13° 00' 41" and the longitude on No. 35 gave 117° 6' 22". We were astonished to see by the timekeeper a few minutes of headway to the west, while according to the reckoning of the course, it gave 14' 8" to the east. This difference appeared to indicate a near change in the direction of the currents which until then had carried us to the east, according to the results of the same timekeeper. The longitude by the reckoning was 118° 48' 18".
In the afternoon, the winds were about the same as those we had had during the morning, only the breeze was a little fresher. We continued to steer south, taking the west as much as possible. As we had seen during the day several flocks of birds of the species of gulls, I presumed that we might be in the neighbourhood of the rocks and sand banks of which Dampier speaks. In consequence, I ordered good watch to be kept, but we perceived nothing which could confirm my conjecture, and if they exist in these waters, it appears likely that we were to windward of them, for the swell which we had had from the south-west for several days had lost nothing of its force. At eight o'clock in the evening, being by our reckoning at 13° 22' of south latitude, we began to approach that which Dampier indicates for the banks and rocks of which he speaks in his first voyage to the Australian lands. But as the weather was very clear and fine, and our night horizon had at least two leagues of extent, we continued our course with the precaution of keeping good watch. All night, the sky being fine, we sailed without anxiety, making nevertheless only such headway as was necessary not to be at 13° 50' before daybreak.
1801-11-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 8, 1° 46' 20" of NW variation. Saw a tropic bird. At noon in 13° 5' 10" of latitude observed and in 117° 42' 51" of longitude by account. We shifted our suit of sails.

1801-11-23.journal_anonyme: The winds from W to WSW, a fresh breeze. The commander signalled the course SW by S; he also signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
