Historical events & Remarks.
The second, we had continuation of fine weather, and it would be difficult to meet with a finer one than that which we have had since our departure from Coupang, with the exception, however, of the winds which were often light and contrary to the course which I proposed to hold to double the most western point of New Holland.
At sunrise, the winds varied a little from the west towards the north, and the breeze was stronger than usual. We were at this time at a short distance from the latitude of the rocks seen by Dampier, which he places at 13° 50' of south latitude. But we saw no sign which could make us suspect that these dangers are placed in the waters we have crossed. According to our longitude, we must have passed them at about thirty-five leagues, according to the position which Robertson gives them on his map of 1791.
At eight o'clock, we spoke to the Naturaliste. Captain Hamelin gave me news of his sick, numbering twelve, but all in full convalescence. This vessel was much more fortunate than we, in that it had lost but one man since the departure from Timor, whilst we have lost four. We agreed to make course towards the south-west by south, if the winds permitted, in order to carry ourselves a little more to the west, so as to be able to double the western point of New Holland, as I have remarked above.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 56' 57" south, and the longitude of No. 35 placed us at 117° 16' 13". That of the reckoning was much higher and placed us at 118° 58' 42". The distance which we reckoned we had made to the south in 24 hours proved less considerable than we had thought, and the course reduced gave 0° 17' 17" more to the south than the observation. This difference can only be attributed to some current which carried us to the north, for as from morning we no longer experienced the heavy swell from the south-west which we had encountered in the preceding days.
In the afternoon, the breeze was fairly fine although less strong than in the morning, and the winds drew nearer to the west by the south. At sunset, we were almost in a calm, the vessel scarcely under command.
During the night from the 2nd to the 3rd, the sky was extremely fine and pleasant, but the calm lasted long, and it was not until the middle of the night that the breeze rose a little from the west, variable, sometimes towards the south and sometimes towards the north.
1801-11-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. We spoke the commander, who gave us the course S 33° 45' should the wind draw aft. He signalled us the death of a man (Mantel). At noon in 14° 2' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 55' 33" of longitude by account, and in 117° 35' 0" of longitude by the watches. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds. At 5.45, 2° 3' 20" of NW variation.

1801-11-24.journal_anonyme: The winds varied from NW, W and WSW. At 9 we began to lie our course. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-11-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, although the barometer had begun to fall from daybreak, the weather remained very fine and clear and we had, in the morning, a pleasant breeze from west-south-west until about the time of the sun's passing the meridian, when it shifted further to the south. The Naturaliste being found very far leeward, we bore away towards her and closed with her. This vessel appeared to drift much more during this passage than in the previous one, which perhaps arose from the change it made in its stowage during our stay at Coupang.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 14° 52' 54" south and the longitude from No. 35 put us at 117° 42' 52", whilst dead reckoning put us at 119° 20' 48". The difference between the observation and dead reckoning continued to be north and we had 10' 48" more to the south by dead reckoning.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine. I found myself, on this day, in better health than I had been since our departure and I held myself fairly steady on my legs, which until then had served only to give me evidence of my great weakness. Our other sick were also much better and especially Citizen Maugé and Citizen Depuche attacked by dysentery. Among the crew, two men left the sick quarters, but two others entered it who had contracted fever, I knew not how.
The barometer, which during much of the day had stood at 28 and sometimes even below, made us fear bad weather. However, nothing seemed to announce it, the sky being very fine and almost without cloud. The tranquillity of the sea was the same, a proof that no squalls had passed in the vicinity, for it would have been more agitated than we found it.
During the night of the third to the fourth, the sky remained fine and clear. However the hygrometer was at 98° which indicated great humidity in the air, the effects of which the watch felt particularly. After the rising of the moon which was about half-past ten, it became less considerable, and everyone found themselves better for it. The winds, during the night, shifted from the west quarter towards the north and our course became better for it, we could at times steer south-west by south and make some headway on that quarter of the wind.
1801-11-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to SSW. At noon in 14° 55' 35" of latitude observed and in 117° 46' 0" of longitude by the watches. At 5, 1° 48' 0" of NW variation. Saw a shark. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 45° W.

1801-11-25.journal_anonyme: Winds SW, WSW and SSW, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky serene throughout the twenty-four hours. At 8 a.m. a topman named Fanfan died of dysentery.
1801-11-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 118° 03' 55"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 14' 8" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 12' 53" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, after sunrise, the breeze which had been during part of the night from the west quarter towards the north continued in the same direction and increased a little as the sun rose to the meridian. As we found ourselves already far advanced to the south, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to the south-west and we steered to that quarter of the wind when we could make it.
In the morning, several distances of the sun to the moon were taken, the mean result of which put us at 118° 3' 55" reduced at noon. The longitude indicated by No. 35 differed, at the same time, by 14' 8" to the west and dead reckoning put us 1° 12' 53" further to the east than the distances. The meridian altitude was 15° 37' 19", which also gave a difference with that of the course run of 8' 47" less to the south. As the differences had been more or less considerable since the departure from Coupang, it is not doubtful that the currents then had their direction to the north. A greater quantity of observations by distances, if the weather remains fine, will put us in a position to judge whether they set from the east or to the west.
About ten in the morning, the Naturaliste, by means of a signal agreed between her and me, announced to me that she had just lost a man dead of dysentery. All our sick on board were much better and I hope I shall have no more to regret the loss of anyone and especially of Citizen Maugé and Citizen Depuche suffering from this fatal disease.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine, but the breeze fell much and the winds shifted again from the west to the south. The tranquillity of the sea announced calm and we had it indeed after sunset. At the same time, the sky which throughout the day had been perfectly clear and fine suddenly became covered with clouds. In the north-west quarter, it did not have a fine appearance. We were persuaded that the winds would come to us from that point of the horizon and perhaps even the bad weather which seemed to be announced by the barometer, which continued to fall, but it was not so. Little by little the clouds dispersed despite the great calm that then prevailed and at the rising of the moon the sky became as clear as it had been during the day. About midnight we had a light breeze from the west which was strong enough to make the ship answer to the helm. It increased a little as the moon rose above the horizon.
1801-11-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SSW. At 7.30, 0° 57' 26" of NW variation. Hubert, known as Fanfan, died of a disease of the liver. At noon in 15° 38' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 58' of longitude by the watches.

1801-11-26.journal_anonyme: Winds W to SW and SSW, a light breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The winds varied from W to WNW and WSW. At 8 a.m. a man named Ivan died of dysentery.
1801-11-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 118° 14' 27"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 9' 17" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 18' 21" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, after having passed part of the night in calm, we had a slight breeze from south-west to west which, little by little, shifted from west to north. At sunrise, I bore directly down on the Naturaliste to speak to Captain Hamelin. This vessel was about two leagues leeward and was sailing large, so that I could not understand the course she was making. After joining her, I asked the reason why she was not being close-hauled, as I had signalled. Captain Hamelin sent me word that his vessel steered very badly and that although he had always the helm to leeward, it obeyed it not at all. As this vessel had never appeared to us to have (sic) such bad qualities, I represented to him that it was absolutely necessary to change something in its stowage and to place it more forward or aft, as he might think fit. He promised me that he would attend to it, which he must necessarily do, for it is not possible to sail together if he does not remedy it. I estimate that since our departure from Timor he has caused us to fall leeward of more than forty leagues. For three times a day, and often twice in the night, we are obliged to bear away on her to avoid a separation which might become fatal to one or the other.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 16° 9' 15" south and the longitude indicated by No. 35 put us at 118° 5' 10". A series of several distances of the sun to the moon taken in the morning gave us 118° 14' 27" which differed only by 0° 9' 17" to the east more than by the timekeeper. The difference in dead reckoning was much more considerable since we found ourselves carried to the east by 1° 18' 21". By the observation of the meridian altitude, the currents always set to the north towards the east, but they appeared to us to have less force, the differences always becoming smaller as we advanced to the south. That of this day was 0° 11' 27".
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine, but the winds fell away considerably and shifted from west to south. At four o'clock, the Naturaliste signalled to us that she had lost a man which made since our departure from Timor eight men on the two vessels, of which seven by dysentery.
At sunset, or at least a short time after, the winds having shifted to south-south-west very light, we changed tacks and took the course west to north. The night of the 5th to the 6th was very fine and the winds variable from south-south-west to south-west very light. The sky was fine and the humidity sufficiently abundant to be uncomfortable. As the Naturaliste was always much leeward, signals were made to her several times by fires and we closed with her.
1801-11-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SW. Le Bouru died of dysentery. At 8.30, 0° 32' 20" of NW variation. We spoke the commander, who urged the captain to use every means to keep the ship from making so much leeway, having been told that she was always very slack; he answered that this was not surprising, as she was too much by the head. At noon in 16° 14' 24" of latitude observed and in 118° 6' 0" of longitude by the watches, and in 118° 11' 0" of longitude by lunar distances.

1801-11-27.journal_anonyme: Winds WSW to SW, very light throughout the 24 hours.
1801-11-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 117° 29' 8"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 4' 4" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 2° 0' 20" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, the winds continued from the south-west, varying a little towards the south. The breeze was very light until the rising of the sun, when it increased a little. But about nine o'clock, it fell again and we made very little progress.
We saw in the morning several flocks of birds of considerable size of a kind of gull. They were in large flocks on the water, which led us to believe they were occupied in feeding. Despite all our attention to discover what could attract them to the place where they were found, we saw nothing.
We occupied ourselves, before noon, in making an inventory of the objects and effects belonging to Citizen Riedelé, our gardener who died at Coupang. Among his papers we found something in the form of a will containing his last wishes concerning what regards him, which he charged me with personally. I caused all his collections and papers to be gathered to deliver them to the Museum, which, on learning the news of his death, will regret him no less than I do.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 58' 57" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 117° 27' 8", which differed from the timekeeper only by 0° 4' 4". It would be difficult, from the distance covered according to dead reckoning or the time we have had, to explain how we could have advanced to the west by 0° 45' 19", and this difficulty can only be resolved by admitting a very violent current nearly in this direction, in that the difference to the north is not considerable enough for it to have deviated much, which the observation of tomorrow will be able to verify.
In the afternoon, the weather remained very fine and the sky perfectly clear until sunset. The winds held constantly in the same direction they had adopted for a long time, but they were very light. We took towards the end of the day a very fine dolphin, which was all the more pleasant to us as it was the first delicate fish caught at sea since our departure from France.
The night of the sixth to the seventh was fine and the winds light from the south-west. We continued to steer close-hauled on the north-west tack.
1801-11-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.30, 1° 47' 10" of NW variation. At noon in 15° 59' 51" of latitude observed and in 117° 49' 30" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 1° 54' 50" of NW variation.

1801-11-28.journal_anonyme: Winds SW and S by W; at 9 they drew round to NW and held there all night. Fine weather. A light breeze.
1801-11-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 116° 53' 7"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 11' 19" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 39' 17" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, we had a pleasant breeze but the winds were constantly from the south-west quarter, varying a little towards the south, which did not make them better for the course we should make. According to all that has been published on the monsoons and on the general winds, we had reason to be astonished at finding them so different from what they should have been, for, supposing we were still in the regions proper to the monsoons, we should have found winds from the west variable towards the north and if we had passed the line assigned to them, we should have had them from the south-east. There is no doubt that we were in one of these two regions and nevertheless we had none of those announced to us as certain. It is therefore true that the seasons are not so certain as is believed, at least far from the coasts, and what has happened to us is the proof of it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 24' 3" south and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 116° 41' 48". Three series of distances taken in the morning gave, reduced to noon, 116° 53' 7", from which resulted a difference of 0° 11' 19" more to the east than the timekeeper.
Within the 24 hours, we experienced a singularity rather particular. The day when the vessel made little progress, the results of the timekeeper as well as the distances gave us a difference of 40 minutes to the west and the dead reckoning of the distance covered gave not more than 10 minutes. Today, the rate of the same timekeeper and the distances observed gave us 31' 57" of distance to the west whilst by the course we made, the difference was 60 minutes or one degree. These two differences in opposite senses nevertheless present a difficult problem to be resolved and the course of our navigation will be able to make it known.
During the evening, the weather continued fine and the breeze fell as the sun approached the horizon. The winds also shifted more to the south, they even took a little from the east, which led us to hope to have them soon from the south-east as we should have found them long ago.
All our sick, with the exception of the master sailmaker, were doing very well and the physician regards them as out of danger. As for what concerns me, although in good bodily health for several days, there remains always in my legs a great weakness which fatigues me.
Part of the night of the seventh to the eighth passed in calm or at least with very little wind and when the winds gained a little force, they came to us again from the south-west quarter.
1801-11-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At noon in 15° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 116° 55' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-11-29.journal_anonyme: The winds S by W to south; during the night they were SSW, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-11-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 115° 52' 51"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 9' 51" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 25' 33" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, the winds followed the same course as usual, that is to say that in the morning they varied from the south-west towards the west, whilst at noon they began to vary from the south-west towards the south. I confess that I understood nothing of the direction of these winds which were so contrary to what is told us about the regularity of their changes in the regions affected by the monsoons and their constancy from the south-east in those of the general winds. If the winds we encounter were produced by an accidental cause, it seems to me that their course would not have been so regular nor so long, for the cause which produced them should not have remained so long in the same state.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 14° 43' 45" and the longitude of our No. 35, the only one we have left, put us at 115° 43' 30". The distances taken in the morning gave 115° 52' 51" which changed the difference indicated by the timekeeper which until then had been to the east and which today is found to be 9' 51" to the east.
From what had happened to us the two preceding days, we expected a great difference either to the east or to the west with the course run according to dead reckoning, nevertheless it was little considerable to our great astonishment for we found only 13' more than the observation. Thus, what can one reasonably judge from the differences in opposite senses which we experienced on the sixth and seventh?
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine and the winds, as I have already observed, shifted towards the south as the sun approached the horizon. Its force likewise diminished in proportion and after sunset we were almost in calm until the middle of the night, when a breeze a little stronger began to make itself felt, taking from the south towards the west.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth, nothing new happened. We were often obliged to bear away on the Naturaliste which always fell much to leeward. This vessel sails much worse than it had done previously.
All our sick are much better and even the sailmaker, who was the most afflicted of all. I regard Maugé as out of danger and Mr. Depuche is far advanced in his convalescence. It is moreover high time that all these dysenteries cease, for they have treated us very ill.
1801-11-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 7.45, 1° 42' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 14° 46' 24" of latitude observed and in 115° 54' 24" of longitude by account.

1801-11-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Observations by distances of the sun to the moon reduced at noon 115° 15' 4"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 0' 38" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 31' 20" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, the breeze was very light before the rising of the sun. And it was not until about eight o'clock that it began to freshen. The winds having shifted to the south-west and even to the west-south-west, we changed tacks to take the course to the south-east and we continued it until one o'clock in the afternoon when their inconstancy obliged us to resume it on the other tack.
In the morning, there was a pleasant breeze and sometimes we were obliged to reef the topgallant sails. The sky was then cloudy although fine and the sea fine.
At noon, the observed latitude was found to be 14° 56' 22" south and the longitude from No. 35 was 115° 15' 42", which gave 0° 0' 38" difference to the east for the timekeeper. It appeared to us that the estimated course of the 24 hours had been less affected by the currents since the differences which resulted from the observations were less considerable. That of the meridian altitude was however 15' 17" more to the south but that in longitude was only 5' 24" to the west.
During the evening, the weather turned fine again, that is to say all the clouds which the sun had brought us before its passage at the meridian dispersed and the sky became very clear. The winds then shifted to south-south-west and even to south by south-west and fell until sunset, when they took a little more force. At this time, we were obliged to sail large for a while to come up with the Naturaliste. It was rare since our departure from Timor that we had not been obliged to make this maneuver three or four times in 24 hours.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth, the winds held to the south and to the south by south-south-west. The breeze was quite pleasant and if we had been alone, we should have profited well from it.
From eight o'clock in the evening until four o'clock in the morning of the tenth, the sky, although very clear and brilliant with the light of the stars, gave us much humidity. The decks and upper works of the ship were wet with it, as if water had been thrown upon them, and one could very well distinguish on the ropes the humid vapours which attached themselves to them.
The sick, except the sailmaker, are always doing better and better and I flatter myself that in the course of the next ten days most will be out of the hospital.
1801-11-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.15, 2° 40' 40" of NW variation. Saw tropic birds and flying fish. At noon in 14° 53' 38" of latitude observed and in 115° 17' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-12-01.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, a fresh breeze; at 11 they drew round to SE and we lay our course SW. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-12-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, the winds continued from south by south-west to south and even came to south by south-east in the morning. But it was not for long, for they resumed before the end of the day their ordinary course. The breeze was however pleasant and sometimes accompanied by strong squalls. The sky, very clear at the rising of the sun, gradually covered itself with clouds of white colour which one could see forming at the horizon and, as it rose, they increased in number, so that at ten o'clock it was very cloudy although fine. This phenomenon had been occurring only for two or three days. Until now it has not been of long duration, for by five o'clock in the evening at the latest all the clouds had disappeared in the same manner in which they had appeared in the morning.
About seven o'clock, Captain Hamelin made me a signal to ask that I send a boat to him. The weather being then fine and the breeze still light, his request was acceded to and we bore away towards him to come up with him. When I hove-to within musket-shot of this vessel, the boat was sent and Mr. Freycinet the Younger handed me two letters, one from Mr. Hamelin and the other from Messrs. Millius and Saint Criq.
By the letter from Mr. Hamelin, I was informed that he had lost, since our departure, three men dead of dysentery, that he still had ten sick, of the number of which was Citizen Le Villain of Havre who had great difficulty in recovering and about whom there were even fears. The nine others were less ill and out of danger. By a great number of distances observed on board this vessel, the longitude was 115° 18' 28", reduced to the noon of the ninth, and that of their timekeeper was 115° 28' 6", which gave them for its rate 0° 10' 12" to the east. Thus their longitude observed by distances differed from ours only by 0° 3' 24" east and that of the timekeepers by 12' 24".
That from Messrs. Millius and Saint Criq, these two officers asked me to receive, to share with the officers, half of a calf which the Governor had given them at Timor and which they had preserved until this day. By the return of the boat which I sent immediately, I made known to Captain Hamelin the result of our observations and the situation in which our sick were. To Messrs. Millius and Saint Criq (I sent) (in the margin: thanks).
After the departure of the boat, we continued our course under easy sail until the Naturaliste was able to follow us, which was not long in happening.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 14° 53' 13" and we were surprised to have made no progress to the south, in that the course of the 24 hours seemed to indicate it, also after having reduced it we found we had made only 3' to the south.
In the afternoon, the sky, as I have already observed, cleared of the clouds that had appeared in the morning and the wind fell. The sea, which had become rough by the breeze, became fine and the winds shifted from the south towards the west. Before night we came up with the Naturaliste. We had during its duration fine weather, a fine sea, light wind and much humidity.
1801-12-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 8, 1° 22' 30" of NW variation. At 6 we asked the commander leave to communicate; he having granted it, we lay under topsails to wait for the Géographe, which was to windward at a great distance and was bearing down on us. At 7 hove to; our boat carried half a bullock, which Citizens Milius and Saint-Cricq were sending to the commander and the officers of the Géographe. At 8.30 we filled and stood on. At noon in 15° 0' 24" of latitude observed and in 114° 16' 12" of longitude by account. Saw tropic birds. At 4, 2° 8' 50" of NW variation. On the evening of the 10th I received orders to take Citizen Milius's watch, he having been ill for several days.

1801-12-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SSE and south; during the day they drew round to S, SSW and SW. Fine weather, a swell running.
1801-12-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, we did not have, after the rising of the sun, nor as it rose above the horizon, the clouds we had observed in its course the two preceding days. The sky was fine all day, but the breeze was light. Nevertheless, the winds varied from the south towards the east which gave us reason to hope we should soon have them from the south-east, although the swell came to us always from the south-west rather strong and high.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 3' 3" south and the longitude deduced from the rate of No. 35 was 113° 21' 5". The currents during these 24 hours had borne us only 0° 5' to the north, thus the difference was much less considerable than we had had until this time.
In the afternoon, the winds were about in the same quarter as in the morning, but we observed at sunset that they did not follow their accustomed course, in shifting from the south to the south-west, which was infinitely agreeable to us.
As we were all on the quarterdeck between five and six o'clock in the evening making conversation, it fell upon the great humidity there was at night. I then asked Citizen Péron who was charged with this part of our observations if he continued to make them in his bed, because he spoke of them, if he had observed them on the deck or in some other part of the ship. The scholar, from our arrival at Timor, had thrown himself passionately into shells and even with fury although he had no knowledge in this kind. A snail, a nerite, etc. was a treasure to him, so that to gather them in profusion he employed all his time to it and neglected by this means other works which he would have filled much better than the one he has just undertaken and which according to his principles he will doubtless pursue.
Be that as it may about the future, as it is here only a matter of what happened yesterday, he well saw that I wanted to jest with him, but to get out of it he told me that as his mother was no longer having children and as he was the whole hope of the family, he did not want to kill himself making observations at night and that besides he had done enough of them on this part in getting us to Timor. I observed to him that despite the goodness of his observations, the sun was not in this part of the hemisphere when we coasted along the coasts of New Holland and that consequently it was good to have observations made at different times. His answers of excuse and little suited for a scholar astonished me and in order that the conversation should have no further continuation, I contented myself with saying to him, "you are well the master of working or not, but at least you will not object to having others pursue the work which you would not formerly have wished to let them do." I therefore asked him to hand me the hygrometer of which I had made him the depositary.
The night of the eleventh to the twelfth had nothing particular. The wind blew in squalls from the south-south-west to the south-south-east and we found the swell rather strong and high.
1801-12-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 7.30, 1° 9' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 8' 49" of latitude observed and in 113° 16' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-03.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE to south, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The currents appeared to set strongly to the north.
1801-12-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, we had fine weather, a pleasant breeze and winds from the south variable towards the east, but the sea was a little rough and driven by a swell from the south rather high which made us drift much to the north.
During the morning, the carpenters worked on the masting of our boat which had been finished in the preceding days of putting in order, for as I have already remarked, we had embarked it at Timor very imperfect, the sickness of our carpenters having singularly delayed the works.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 00' 55" south and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 112° 5' 42". We were astonished to have gained nothing to the south by the course of the 24 hours which by reduction announced to us 15° 16' 57".
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine and there was a pleasant breeze even after sunset, which was not usual. At six o'clock, we steered towards the Naturaliste to come up with her. At half-past seven, she was abeam of us at half a mile distance. This vessel, despite the changes that Captain Hamelin made in its stowage, continues to sail very badly and to drift much. According to the course it makes daily, it appears that in order to steer tolerably and make some progress, it needs two full quarters of canvas.
During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth, the sky was very fine until midnight, but then it became very cloudy. The breeze also fell and the winds shifted from the south towards the west. The sea was then very rough and very swelling. The humidity was considerable and uncomfortable.
During the evening, I had been with the physician to visit all our sick. It seemed to me that with the exception of the sailmaker who is attacked with a liver disease, all the others were doing fairly well. Citizens Maugé and Depuche are always doing better and better and although they are not yet entirely cured, they are nevertheless regarded as absolutely out of danger. Our hydrographer Boulanger is also beginning to recover and the fever which he had brought as well as I from Timor has not appeared for six days.
As for what concerns me, I find myself well and my strength is beginning to return.
1801-12-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 1' 46" of latitude observed and in 112° 9' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-04.journal_anonyme: Throughout the twenty-four hours the winds varied from south to SSE. A strong breeze, a high sea, the weather clear enough.
1801-12-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we had the appearance of a change of weather and perhaps also of wind, which we greatly desired not to be carried too far off shore from the western point of New Holland. If the winds had permitted us, as at the beginning of our departure, to bear us to the south, my intention was to search for the Rosemary Islands of which Dampier speaks and which I believe to be much more to the east than they are placed on our charts. But according to all appearance, we shall have to abandon this project at least for the present.
During the morning, the winds which during the night had been fairly constantly from the south-south-east, returned to the south at the rising of the sun and varied sometimes towards the east and sometimes towards the west. We found the sea very swelling all day.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 12' 24", that of the dead reckoning for the distance run being 15° 14' 59". This gave us apparently little difference to the west and we could not verify the fact by the rate of our timekeeper in that it was not possible to have an hour angle, so cloudy was the sky in the morning as in the evening. By our estimated longitude we found ourselves only at 112° 28' 0" but we knew by the latest observations to be much too far to the east.
In the course of the evening, the sky was not fine and I even feared bad weather for the night and the barometer seemed also to announce it. Nevertheless we had none. It was dark and humid and the breeze moderate from the south-south-east. The heavy swell which had prevailed for some time caused the Naturaliste to drift considerably so that not to lose her, it was almost always necessary to have her sailing large and to bear away often.
1801-12-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 15° 15' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 4' 0" of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze in gusts.

1801-12-05.journal_anonyme: Winds S by E to south, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a heavy swell running. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-12-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the fourteenth, although the sky was still very cloudy, the weather nevertheless had a less threatening appearance than the previous day, but the sea was even more swelling than usual and I would not be surprised if some strong squalls had passed in the southern part of New Holland.
In the morning we had the winds from the south, variable to south by south-east, moderate. We held on board a sale of the effects of Citizen Riedelé, who died at Timor on the 29th of Vendémiaire. The impossibility of being able to preserve them on board during the time we have to remain at sea decided me to take this course, which is moreover in accordance with the ordinances and with his intentions according to the writing which he addressed to me.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 15° 44' 6" and the longitude indicated by our No. 35 reduced to the same hour put us at 109° 11' 23" which gave a distance to the west in 48 hours of 2° 54' 42" whilst by dead reckoning we found only 2° 34' 18". We thus had a difference to the west of 20 minutes (sic for 20') more than our dead reckoning.
During the evening, the weather seemed to be turning fine and the greater part of the clouds dispersed. The sale of the objects and effects was continued, of which everything was sold very dear. I bought for my own account part of his books which in memory of him I shall preserve preciously.
According to the physician's report, it appears that Citizen Depuche is not yet entirely out of danger and that his dysentery might have unfortunate consequences. Citizen Maugé, without being entirely free of it, is doing very well and undoubtedly will recover soon. The sickness of the master sailmaker degenerates into dropsy and offers little hope of his recovery. All the others are infinitely better.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth, the weather was fairly fine although cloudy. The winds deviated little from the south and the breeze was moderate.
1801-12-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 41' 21" of latitude observed and in 109° 51' 54" of longitude by account.

1801-12-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather seemed to be turning fine. The clouds dispersed for the greater part and the sky became clear.
In the morning there was a fairly pleasant breeze but in squalls and the winds were from the south by south-east, variable to the south. The heavy swell which we had had for several days began to fall.
At noon, the observed latitude was 16° 4' 2" south and we had for the first time since our departure from Timor a small difference to the south of about two minutes. By the timekeeper No. 35 our longitude was 107° 39' 20" which gave us 21' difference to the west more than the distance covered by dead reckoning.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine. We came up with the Naturaliste which was more than two leagues to leeward and at four o'clock, having approached her within hailing distance, I asked him for news of his sick and if he had made to his vessel the changes which he had announced to me.
To the first of these questions, he replied to me that all his sick were doing very well and especially Mr. Le Villain who had been long in danger from the consequences of dysentery.
To the second, he made known to me that he had indeed changed the stowage of his hold, but that his vessel did not hold the wind better for it. Only he found an advantage in the sailing in that he recognised having more speed than before.
During the night of the fifteenth to the sixteenth, the winds were about the same as we had had them during the course of the day and the breeze was moderate. We nevertheless did not have a fine sky and all points of the horizon loaded themselves with clouds. There was nevertheless little variation in the movement of the barometer which held constantly at 28 inches 1 line. The humidity was also less considerable than the preceding days.
1801-12-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At 8.30, 3° 19' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 16° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-07.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, a fresh breeze in gusts, fine weather, a swell running. Saw tropic birds.
1801-12-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the sky although cloudy was nevertheless fairly fine and we had a pleasant breeze from south by south-east to south and sometimes to south by south-west. We continued the course close-hauled with canvas conformable to that of the Naturaliste or at least to its sailing. This vessel had lost much to windward during the night and we had to bear away towards her to come up with her. At eleven o'clock, he furled his topgallant sails and took them down. There was then a good breeze and the sea was beginning to get rough although it was still tolerably fine, but the sky had bad appearance for the evening and night.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 16° 24' 9" south and the longitude deduced from No. 35 put us at 106° 10' 57", which gave for 24 hours 1° 28' 23" of distance to the west. By the dead reckoning of the course run, we found only 0° 3' 53" difference to the east and 0° 2' 40" to the south.
In the evening, there was a strong breeze and the sea became rough. At two o'clock, we took a second reef in the topsails and furled our staysails.
Citizen Depuche found himself more troubled this day with his dysentery than he had been previously and I fear some unfortunate accident for him in that the remedies seem to have no effect on him, at least in appearance, for he is extremely weak and languid.
Citizen Maugé is always doing better and better and although he still passes a little blood, he feels well and has good appetite.
The other sick, with the exception of the sailmaker, will not be long from now in leaving the hospital.
The sale of all the effects belonging to those we had lost both at Coupang and elsewhere, that is to say at sea since our departure from Timor, was completed in this day.
During the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth, the weather was not bad as it had the appearance of being, but the sky remained loaded with many clouds. The winds before sunset had shifted to the south-east. I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to south-south-west, but this vessel not being able to keep close-hauled, steered to the south-west and obliged to follow her, we lost all the advantage which the change offered us.
1801-12-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SE. At noon in 16° 28' 43" of latitude observed and in 106° 59' 30" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-12-08.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, SE and SE by S, a strong breeze, a high sea, the sky cloudy. The commander signalled the course SSW.
1801-12-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventeenth, the winds from the south-east appeared to be settling and we hoped to see them continue on this quarter of the wind and even to have them more towards the east if they should vary. As there had been a strong breeze the previous day, the sea was a little rough and swelling and continued to become more so during the rest of the day, the breeze becoming again very strong when the sun had risen above the horizon.
The sky which we had had cloudy for several days was still so this day. Our horizon was little extended and dull, of a whitish colour, similar to that which is commonly met with between the coast of Africa and the Cape Verde Islands.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 17° 24' 52" south and the longitude deduced from dead reckoning was 107° 12' 20". Having had no hour angle, we had not that which our No. 35 could indicate. The difference between the reduced course and the meridian observation gave 0° 3' 16" to the south.
In the afternoon, there continued to be a good breeze. The heavy swell that there was then fatigued somewhat the spars and I had the topgallant sails taken down.
At five o'clock, we bore away towards the Naturaliste to come up with her, although she was very far to leeward, we overtook her before night.
During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth, the winds were the same and the breeze decreased little in force, but the Naturaliste having furled her main topgallant sail and her staysails, we furled the main sail.
The humidity indicated by the hygrometer during the night was less considerable than appearances announced it, for on seeing the little elevation of the clouds, it seemed there was more. The barometer also rose to 28 inches 2 lines, which had not happened to it for a long time.
1801-12-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 17° 27' 0" of latitude observed and in 105° 47' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-09.journal_anonyme: The winds SE, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a high sea, the ship pitching heavily. Saw several petrels and some flying fish.
1801-12-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, the winds continued from the south-east, strong breeze. Nevertheless, the Naturaliste carried her main topgallant sail, which did not give me too much pleasure. I did not signal to him to reduce it in that we had agreed together that he should never make any signal to compromise his spars on the pretext of wanting to follow me and that I much preferred to wait for him. At the same time when he had all sails set except her fore topgallant sail, I had for all my canvas the foresail, two reefs in all the topsails and the mizzen. And even with so little canvas spread, I gave a fairly strong heel. He on the contrary did not appear incommoded by it. It is true that it was not the first time he made us know that his ship heeled with difficulty.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 18° 34' 6" south and the longitude deduced from the dead reckoning of the course put us at 106° 15' 44". The little extent of the horizon, in the morning as in the evening, did not permit us to take an hour angle.
In the afternoon, the winds were the same as we had had them in the morning. At two o'clock, we began to come up with the Naturaliste, the weather having bad appearance. This vessel, despite all her canvas, had nevertheless fallen nearly two leagues to leeward. At five, we had her abeam of us at half a cannon shot.
According to our previous observations, we were beginning to approach on the chart the place where the Triads are placed and perhaps tomorrow in the morning we shall have knowledge of them, if they have been well determined by the Dutch, although I doubt it. We saw nothing moreover in the evening, nor at sunset, which could lead us to believe that we should see them the next day.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the breeze was a little less strong than it had been during the day, but it was scarcely but after the setting of the moon that it began to fall. The sky did not become finer for it, it became on the contrary more cloudy and one could scarcely distinguish from time to time some stars, and they were moreover of a rather pale colour.
1801-12-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 18° 37' 18" of latitude observed and in 104° 44' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-10.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SE by S, a strong breeze and in gusts, the weather overcast and misty. At 6.30 a.m. the main jib split.
1801-12-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the nineteenth, the weather was as on the preceding days very cloudy with bad appearance, the sea always a little rough and swelling. The winds held to the south-east, strong breeze, varying sometimes to south-east by south.
At daybreak, our estimated latitude put us at nearly the latitude where the Dutch chart places the Triads and according to the observed longitude, we should pass near them to see them. Nevertheless we had knowledge of nothing which could lead us to suspect that we had passed so near as the point marked on the charts indicates.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 19° 46' 18" and the longitude from No. 35 was found to be 102° 5' 2". We had difference with the estimated course of 0° 6' 24" to the south and 0° 7' 15" to the west.
In the afternoon, the sky seemed to be turning fine in becoming clearer in several points of the horizon. But this fine spell did not last long for at sunset it was more cloudy than ever. The air was then very cold and we were obliged to take woollen clothing, at least the greater part of us.
The sick who remained with us were not the better for it either and despite the attention paid to closing the portholes early, several complained of pains which they were not accustomed to experiencing. Citizens Maugé and Depuche are recovering day by day, nevertheless this latter is always weak and languid.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth, the weather was passable although very cloudy, the winds held in the south-east quarter moderate, nevertheless the night was cold without being very humid.
1801-12-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 8, 3° 56' 20" of NW variation. The flying jib boom was rigged in. At noon in 19° 46' 40" of latitude observed and in 103° 37' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-11.journal_anonyme: The winds SE to ESE, a strong breeze, the weather fine, a high sea and the sky cloudy.
1801-12-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, in the morning, the weather seemed to be turning altogether fine. The clouds with which for several days the sky was laden dispersed for the greater part as the winds from the south-east gained in force and as the sun rose above the horizon. The sea also became calmer and everything seemed to announce fine weather for the future. Nevertheless we changed nothing in our canvas and even the Naturaliste with all sails spread had difficulty following us.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 21° 7' 49" which gave us a great difference to the south from our dead reckoning which put us only at 20° 49' 41" so that we did not well know what reason to attribute this difference to. The most general opinion nevertheless was that having had to pass near the Triads, whether they be placed according to the observations of the Dutch or the Danes, we could have met a current between these islands or rocks which set more to the south than if we had passed them at a distance. This reasoning, however equivocal it appeared to me, is perhaps not without foundation. But be that as it may, we nevertheless had 0° 28' 8" difference to the south. The longitude indicated by No. 35 put us at 101° 10' 26".
Several distances of the sun to the moon were taken in the afternoon but the results were so different from what was expected that no account was taken of them.
On board the Naturaliste, 100° 3' was observed.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine and the breeze from the south-east, little variable and fairly pleasant. The sky became very fine, all the clouds having for the greater part disappeared.
After sunset, we likewise had fine weather but the breeze fell a little. I signalled to the Naturaliste that we should take the course to the south if the winds permitted it.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first, the heavy swell which we had had the preceding days diminished and the sea became fine. The sky remained fine during the night and although there was little wind, the air was cold.
1801-12-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. Spoiled coconuts were served out to the crew. At noon in 21° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 102° 49' 24" of longitude by account, and in 100° 52' 40" of longitude by lunar distances. The commander signalled the course S 11° 15' W.

1801-12-12.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SE, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. At noon the commander signalled the course S by W.
1801-12-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, the weather continued fine and there was a pleasant breeze from south-east by east to east-south-east. We could have steered directly to the south but for the Naturaliste. But as this vessel was sailing large, we also bore away with all sail, but it drifted not the less for that and went scarcely faster although the sea was fine and although it had spread all the canvas it could carry.
At noon we observed the latitude of 22° 31' 10" and the longitude from No. 35 was 100° 28' 10" which gave us a difference west of 14' from the estimated course, although the two latitudes compared with each other gave only 3' 3" difference.
In the afternoon we tried to take distances of the sun to the moon, but clouds which rose at this time did not permit us to do it. Nevertheless the weather was fine except for this inconvenience.
During the evening the winds were fairly constantly from the east-south-east, pleasant breeze, and we much regretted not to profit better from it than we did for the reasons of which I have spoken above.
At sunset, not seeing great appearance of breeze for the night, we loosened a reef in our main topsail in order to encourage our companion of the voyage not to reduce sail.
About midnight, our master sailmaker died. He had fallen sick a few days before our departure from Timor, but not of dysentery. He complained only of some pains in the belly and in the liver. It was thought at first that his disease would be nothing and that he would soon be recovered, but instead of that he grew always worse since we put to sea and it was recognised some time afterwards that the seat of the disease was truly in the liver. Remedies were accordingly administered to him which were judged to be suitable for him, but they were without effect. He gradually became dropsical and no longer gave hope of being able to save him.
The sky although cloudy was fine during the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second and the winds held to SE by E light breeze.
1801-12-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to E. At 7.15, 4° 0' 0" of NW variation. Saw a pintado petrel. At noon in 22° 12' 34" of latitude by account and in 100° 26' 46" of longitude by account. At 4.15, 3° 33' 30" of NW variation.

1801-12-13.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to E by S, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, and cloudy during the night.
1801-12-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude observed by distances of the sun to the moon 99° 27' 28"
Difference from the timekeeper 0° 22' 7" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning 3° 52' 16" to the east
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-second, the breeze was light in the morning and the winds the same as the previous day. But the sky was very fine and few clouds at the horizon. We remarked that for two or three days, as we began to approach the sun, the air was infinitely more pleasant and less humid, but that at night the cold was sharp and penetrating. The watch were obliged to change their clothing and to take winter clothes not to be incommoded.
At noon, the observed latitude was 24° 3" south but somewhat doubtful in that we were under the sun. Nevertheless the error could not be very considerable. That of dead reckoning put us at 23° 52' 7".
The longitude indicated by No. 35 was found to be 99° 49' 35" and that by distances of sun to moon was 99° 27' 28" so that it resulted that the observations compared with each other gave between them a difference of 22' 7" of which the timekeeper was to the east. The same observations compared with dead reckoning gave 3° 52' 16" of which we found ourselves to be to the east.
On board the Naturaliste they signalled to us for the longitude observed by distances 99° 42'. In the afternoon, the weather continued fine but the winds shifted a little towards the south and even came to south-south-east. The breeze was also stronger and little regular.
An inventory and sale of the effects which had belonged to our master sailmaker was made so that they might not be taken or lost and that his family might have the proceeds. The loss of this man grieved me all the more in that he was extremely temperate, industrious and orderly and understood his trade very well and I was very satisfied with him. Independently of the qualities which were peculiar to him, he was a good seaman and always the first on the yards when it was necessary.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, we had a very cloudy sky, strong squalls from the south-east and nevertheless fairly fine weather. We changed nothing in our canvas except to wait for the Naturaliste, which happened often.
1801-12-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 8.15, 4° 33' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 24° 3' 37" of latitude observed and in 100° 1' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-14.journal_anonyme: The winds SE by E to SSE and SE, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy.
1801-12-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, there appeared to be a change in the weather in that the sky which had been fair and very clear for several days became very overcast and laden with thick clouds, which more often than not prevented us from seeing the sun. The sea was also less fair and we encountered a heavy swell from the south which seemed to take a little of the west.
However, though the sky was very laden with clouds, the barometer which we frequently consulted varied little in its motion and announced nothing ill to us.
In the morning, we brought up on deck part of our spare rigging to examine it and give it some air. We had observed on the previous day a leak of water that communicated from above the second deck into the cockpit, which made us fear that some piece might be damaged. But we saw with pleasure that the rigging of the mainmast which was brought up first, as the most doubtful, had suffered no harm. I noted only that what (that) we were doing this day would not have been done when the sky was very fair and the sun very hot.
At noon, we were able to observe the latitude which was found to be 25° 30' 30" south. The longitude of No. 35 placed us at 98° 39' 2" which gave again a difference to the west fairly considerable since we found we had made 11' 33" more than our dead reckoning gave us. The difference in the two latitudes was also 11' 52".
During the evening, the sky became even much more overcast and thick than it had been in the morning. Nevertheless, the clouds were of a fine light grey and offered nothing disagreeable to the eye or alarming for the night. But the swell from the south had considerably increased and as we were taking it almost ahead, the ship pitched much and was tolerably troubled. We then had for our whole canvas our major sails, one reef in the main topsail, two in the mizzen topsail and two in the mizzen topgallant sail. I had difficulty seeing that the Naturaliste was carrying her topgallant sails for fear of seeing the masts come down.
During the night of the 23rd to the 24th, the sky remained as it had been at sunset, very overcast. We saw neither the moon nor the stars, but we had no bad weather either. The winds were fairly constantly from the south-east, moderate.
1801-12-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 7.15, 5° 18' 20" of NW variation. Saw a petrel. At noon in 25° 36' 38" of latitude observed and in 99° 5' 10" of longitude by account. At 4.30, 6° 45' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-15.journal_anonyme: A light breeze SE to SE by S. Overcast weather, the sea smooth, the night damp. At noon the winds varied from SE by S to E by S.
1801-12-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the sky remained dark and overcast as it had been the previous day and even more so, for we saw hardly any sun throughout the whole day. The heavy swell which we had had the previous day was, however, less strong and the sea became fairly fair. The winds, which in the morning had been variable now towards the south, now towards the east, came round to the east-south-east but were little constant there and changed often.
We had no hour angle during the morning, but a few minutes before noon, the sun showed itself for an instant and we observed the latitude which was found to be 26° 37' 18" which gave, with that of our dead reckoning, a difference to the south of 11' 8". The distance to the west appeared to us to have been 0° 46' 18".
At about one o'clock in the afternoon, the Naturaliste made us a signal to ask us to send our surgeon to her. We then diminished sail to allow this vessel to approach more closely and when she was on our beam at a short distance, we both hove to. I did not have a boat lowered into the sea, which decided her to send us hers. But when it had cleared the ship, it was taking on so much water that it had scarcely time to return on board.
Captain Hamelin then asked me to send him mine, but it was in the same case and could not hold on the water either. I then took the course of passing under the stern of this vessel and I hove to so close under her lee that we were almost yard-arm to yard-arm. Her boat then came on board without danger and the officer who was in it handed me a letter from this Captain by which he asked me to be willing to send him our surgeon and even Citizen Péron who is also one for a consultation on the medicines to be administered to Mr. Le Villain, assistant naturalist, who was very ill and even in danger from the effects of a dysentery to which had joined an intermittent fever of the most violent kind.
Our two surgeons departed at once and went on board. Following the report which they made to me on their return, it is to be feared that Citizen Le Villain will not survive the force of his illness and it appeared to me that they had little hope of being able to get him out of his troubles.
At four o'clock, we resumed our course with our usual canvas and the Naturaliste, after having put her boat on her channels to have it caulked, did the same. I intend to have the same repair done to mine as soon as the weather permits.
During the night of the 24th to the 25th, the weather was always very overcast. The moon although advanced, could not disperse the clouds, but we had no strong winds and only a few small gusts which passed from time to time.
1801-12-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 26° 34' 12" of latitude observed and in 98° 19' 28" of longitude by account. At 2, at the request of the ship's surgeon, the captain asked the commander to send us his surgeon; the commander having consented, we hove to and sent a boat aboard the Géographe. She brought Citizens L'Haridon and Péron, who consulted with our surgeons on the illness of Citizen Levillain, the zoologist. At 4 they returned to their ship, and at 4.15 we filled and stood on.

1801-12-16.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SSE, a fresh breeze, misty weather, the sky overcast. At 2 a boat was sent to the Géographe to fetch the surgeon-major.
1801-12-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, the winds were extremely variable and, scarcely in the whole day, were they for an hour continuously in the same point of the compass although they departed little from the south-east whether their inconstancy turned towards the east or towards the south. The sea, although fair, was always driven by a strong swell from the south to south-south-west which seemed to indicate to us that we would have them from that quarter. The sky was overcast as on the other days past, but the clouds were no longer as thick and of so dark a colour. The sun even showed itself fairly fair at different times in the morning, and we were able to observe it.
At noon, the latitude was found to be 27° 41' 50" which gave little difference with our dead reckoning, but it was not (not) the same with the distance made to the west, for the timekeeper placed us at 96° 43' 50" which gave in forty-eight hours 1° 55' 12" while according to our dead reckoning, we had only made 1° 24' 18".
In the afternoon, the sky became fair and at sunset, there remained in the air only very few clouds. But the breeze had calmed much. Six of our sick came out this day from the hospital and were returned to work but I exempted them still for some time from standing watch during the night.
Citizen Maugé is entirely recovered and is currently in very good health. Mr. Depuche, our mineralogist, is still languishing and has great difficulty taking on strength. Our surgeon maintains that he does not have dysentery and that his illness is the same of which Dampier was attacked for so long in his first voyage.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth, the sky was very fair and clear but the winds very light and also variable in much the same way as they had been during the day. We made course close-hauled under our usual canvas with the Naturaliste at a short distance under our lee and hoping to soon gain the regions of the variable winds which will allow us to regain promptly the ground lost that the trade winds have obliged us to make to the west.
1801-12-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 27° 38' 16" of latitude observed and in 97° 41' 58" of longitude by account.

1801-12-17.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SSE and ESE. A light breeze, the sky overcast, the weather misty.
1801-12-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, the sky continued to be fair in the morning and the winds always inconstant and light. From the south-east, they passed to the south-south-east and even more to the south when the sun approached the meridian. The sea was then fairly fair although driven for several days by a strong swell from the south to south-south-west. The barometer which, in the previous night, had risen to 28 inches five lines, announced to us only fair weather, but we lacked the good wind.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 28° 25' 24" and that of our dead reckoning gave us 28° 33' 11". It was the first time that it had given us a difference to the south, for, until this moment, the observation had been greater than the dead reckoning. This doubtless comes from the distance which was badly estimated.
Following the rate of our No. 35, the longitude reduced to noon was 96° 27' 6" which gave, in twenty-four hours, 0° 16' 44" of distance to the west and the reduction of the estimated course following usage gave 0° 35' 16". Thus, the dead reckoning was in excess of 0° 18' 42".
After the observation of the meridian height, the winds being at the south, we changed our sails and took the weather tacks on the starboard in order to bear to the east as much as it would be possible for us and shorten thereby our passage which the distance made to the west could not fail to render long if we did not encounter soon some good breezes from that quarter.
Throughout the whole evening, the breeze was very light but the winds passed to the south by south-west which led us to believe that we (were) not far distant from being in the variable winds. Towards the end of the day, the sky became very fair and clear, all the clouds having disappeared shortly after sunset.
I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to the south-east by east until such time as the winds would permit us to make good distance bearing more to the south.
During the night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh, the sky remained fair until two o'clock in the morning, but then, it became covered with clouds and turned to squalls. The winds were then at the south-south (sic) varying sometimes to the south-west by south. We had, during the squalls, some strong gusts which however did not force the Naturaliste, which was at a short distance from us, to close her topgallant sails, for she carried them throughout the night.
1801-12-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. At 8.15, 6° 46' 0" of NW variation; 7° 51' 40" at 5.15 in the evening. At noon in 28° 22' 53" of latitude observed and in 97° 1' 16" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E. At 1.30 he cancelled the previous signal and signalled the course S 67° 30' E; at 3.15 he made the signal to steer a point to windward of the course signalled.

1801-12-18.journal_anonyme: Winds south, a fresh breeze. At half past noon went about and headed ESE. In the afternoon the winds varied from SSW to SW and we steered SE by E. In the forenoon the winds freshened and the topgallant masts were struck.
1801-12-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, the sky had a very bad appearance. The squalls, which had begun in the previous night, became more frequent and heavier. The sea was also beginning to grow. The winds were at the south-south-west variable to the south-west by south, fresh breeze, and the vessel was making good distance to the south-east by east, under the major sails one reef in each topsail. The barometer which, until the day, had held at 28 inches four lines, descended suddenly or at least in very little time to 28 inches 1.5 lines, which did not promise us fair weather.
The Naturaliste having closed and ungeared her topgallant sails, we took a second reef in our topsails and furled our staysails in order that she could follow us. But we were exempt from taking down our topgallant sails for they had always been down since our departure from Timor.
Despite the sky having retained its bad appearance the greater part of the morning, it seemed, nevertheless, to want to turn fair. About eleven o'clock, the misty clouds which covered the sun which had not yet appeared, parted and at noon we were able to observe the latitude which was found to be 29° 1' south. That of our dead reckoning gave 29° 3' 59". This placed us positively on the parallel of the lookout marked on our charts as a bank of rocks at the water's edge. It is that it remained to us at about thirty leagues distance to the east. But whether it exists or not, we (did not) see anything in the day which could make us suspect that we could have it in our vicinity. As at the course which we are making, we ought to pass fairly close to it, perhaps we will tomorrow have some appearance of its existence.
From an hour angle taken in the afternoon, the longitude of the timekeeper No. 35 placed us at 98° 40' 12" which gave distance to the west for the 24 hours, the course being reduced to noon, 2° 13' 6". The dead reckoning gave 2° 22' 2" and a difference of 10' 56" too much to the east by dead reckoning.
At sunset, the sky was fairly fair and without bad appearance for the night, but the breeze had calmed much and we had to fear that the winds would not come to us from the south. The sea was rough throughout the night and the vessel laboured much. The winds were the same indeed, but very light.
1801-12-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to south. At noon in 29° 10' 35" of latitude by account and in 99° 20' 46" of longitude by account.

1801-12-19.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, blowing hard. Dark weather, the sky cloudy. In the forenoon the winds varied from S by W to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-12-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the good wind of the previous day calmed much, and we found the sea extremely rough and disagreeable. The movements of the vessel were so violent throughout the whole day that I feared experiencing some damage to my masting. The Naturaliste had some in her sails and signalled them to us about ten o'clock. As we were at a short distance from each other and she found herself ahead of us, she luffed so that we were obliged to avoid her by putting all our aft sails on the mast.
At the course which we were making, as I observed yesterday, we had to pass fairly close to the lookout marked on our charts, but we had absolutely no knowledge of anything which would announce to us its proximity. There were seen, throughout the whole day, two birds of the species of those which are called wind-tail and it is to be believed that in the vicinity of this danger there must be found there a fairly great quantity of them.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 29° 26' 46" south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 104° 12' 38". We had no hour angle to have that of our timekeeper.
In the afternoon, the calm continued and the winds were from the south by south-west to the south. The vessel was still more troubled than it had been in the morning and I had difficulty conceiving how the Naturaliste could carry her topgallant sails high. It is true that the small elevation of her masts put her more able to withstand the shock that they occasioned to her by the beating of her sails in the rolling and it is by a reason entirely opposite that I was anxious for mine when a similar thing happened.
Two men well recovered from dysentery and out of the sick-berth for several days, re-entered it having been attacked anew. The surgeon's opinion is that not only will they have eaten too much, but that moreover they have also made some excess with their comrades to make up for the diet to which they had been constrained during their illness.
During the night of the 28th to the 29th, the sky was fairly fair although covered with misty clouds which greatly shortened our horizon. In spite of the brightness of the moon. The winds came back indeed to the south-west and even to the south-west but so light that the vessel did not labour the less, the sea being always very deep and long.
1801-12-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. The topmast backstays were set up. At noon in 29° 20' 41" of latitude observed and in 101° 3' 52" of longitude by account.

1801-12-20.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE, a light breeze. The weather fine, the sea smooth. During the night the winds varied from SSW to SW by S. The course SE by E.
1801-12-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, the sea was still very rough and disagreeable a great part of the morning, but we had a small breeze from the south-west which rendered the movements of the corvette less precipitous. However, we preferred to rig our studdingsails to follow the Naturaliste, which carried all it could put outside, rather than to rig our topgallant sails.
The sky although very nebulous was fairly fair throughout the day and there was appearance of good breeze for the evening.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 29° 54' 22" south. That of our dead reckoning was only 29° 48' 40" which gave us 0° 5' 42" more to the south than we reckoned, according to the distance estimated.
The longitude at No. 35 was 101° 2' 8" for the distance of two days, which carried us to the east by 2° 21' 56", the dead reckoning gave 0° 20' 40" in excess.
In the evening, the sea began to be nevertheless rough, but more tranquil. The different swells, by which it had been agitated the previous day, merged in one and we rigged our main topgallant sail. The winds, until after sunset, had been favourable to us and the breeze pretty, but about eight o'clock, they passed to the south-south-west variable to the south and obliged us to keep close-hauled.
The night of the 29th to the 30th, although dark and the sky very nebulous, had nothing particular. The winds remained about as they were and we continued the same course.
About eight o'clock in the evening, there spread in the part of the aft deck, a smell of burning and smoke fairly thick, without knowing whence it could come or what could be its cause. I had the citizen Freycinet called at once (and told him) to go and see ahead what this could be. His reply was that he had given the order to the master gunner. Little satisfied with this carelessness in such a case, I transported myself to that spot at once myself, and made a general inspection of the kitchens, of the oven and of the forge which had been used during the day. I found all in order and without the least indication that the smoke which had spread came from that part of the vessel. Having then descended into the powder magazine to see if anything would be discovered, I saw nothing either but I felt a smell of burning which I could not define.
Having given order that all lights be extinguished at once in the cabins of the officers and naturalists, which greatly displeased the most part of them, the smell dissipated little by little without however having discovered whence it came. Until this moment, I had granted that one could have light until ten o'clock, to please everyone. The pretext which was put forward to obtain it was always the work, the reflections and the habit which had been contracted of doing much better that which one had to get written at night than during the day. I should without doubt have, at that epoch, not permitted (to have any) which was done for the general safety for from that moment, the fear that someone would set fire in his cabin was not one of my least anxieties, having been too often witness to the little precaution that each one employed to put themselves sheltered from this accident.
1801-12-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 29° 34' 29" of latitude by account and in 102° 12' 16" of longitude by account. All night the Géographe was astern at a great distance. At 5.45, 8° 0' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-21.journal_anonyme: The winds SW to WSW, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, heading SE by E.
1801-12-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, the sky had a very bad appearance and seemed to forebode a few squalls. The winds, in the morning, were very variable from south by west a quarter west to south-west a quarter west, but we got off, for this time, with only the fright, for about eight o'clock the sky began to clear up and became brighter. The breeze also freshened a little and we set our topgallant sails to take advantage of the wind, which was fair, and to give chase to the Naturaliste, which, as it happened, found herself a good way ahead of us. The sea, then, was fairly smooth (and) had very little left of the heavy swell which had made itself felt in the days before and had greatly fatigued us.
At noon we observed the latitude to be 30° 16' 7" south, and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us at 102° 23' 10". We could not conceive how, after having made all the way reckoned by the log to the south-east by east, and even a few degrees more to the south, we found ourselves so little advanced in latitude.
