The difference we had in these twenty-four hours is the most considerable there has been up to now, since according to the dead reckoning of the courses and the way made good, we made ourselves out to be at 30° 51' 44" of south latitude and 103° 4' 8" of longitude, whereas by the observations we found only 30° 16' 7" for the latitude and 102° 23' 10" for the longitude, so that the difference between the observations and the dead reckoning was 0° 35' 34" to the north and 41' 58" to the west. We are all the more ignorant of the cause which may have given rise to this difference in that we have noticed nothing to which it can be attributed.
As soon as the observation of the sun for its meridian altitude was finished, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course to the south-east, if the wind should allow it.
During the greater part of the evening, the sky was fairly fine and the breeze pleasant, but about six o'clock it became overcast and cloudy, with strong squalls from time to time. We took in our topgallant sails, having closed with and passed the Naturaliste.
After sunset, the wind freshened considerably, and so that our companion should not be obliged to make too much sail to follow us during the night, I had a second reef taken in the topsails and remained under our principal sails. The night, without being fine, was nevertheless not very bad; strong squalls passed over, but they were not of long duration. The sea, however, was beginning to grow rough and uncomfortable.

1801-12-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 2 a.m., having lost sight of the Géographe, we shortened sail to wait for her. At daybreak she closed and we crowded sail. At noon in 30° 18' 37" of latitude observed and in 104° 9' 52" of longitude by account. At noon the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 4.15, 6° 55' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-22.journal_anonyme: The winds SW by S until midnight, when they drew round to south and SSE, a strong breeze. The commander signalled the course SE.
1801-12-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Nivôse, the sky was hardly fairer than it had been the previous night but the winds although stronger, were also much more disagreeable to us. Their varieties from the south towards the east were also not suitable to our course so that we had to steer close-hauled, as close as it was possible. The sea being already a little rough and fearing some squalls, I had the topgallant sails ungeared and tightened a little the backstays of our lower masts which, by the agitation which they experienced on the 28th and 29th of Frimaire, found themselves to have some slack.
The Naturaliste went along as usual under the lee, for as soon as the sea becomes rough, this vessel sails very badly close-hauled.
At noon, we did not see the sun and the latitude according to the estimate of our routes, was found to be 30° 22' 50". The distance made to the east referred to the last result of our timekeeper No. 35, placed us at 104° 26' 10" supposing that the difference experienced the previous day was not sensible for this day.
We learned with sorrow, in the course of the morning that Citizen Maugé who, for more than ten days, was entirely recovered, was going to be attacked anew with an illness of which he believed himself entirely rid. At the moment when he came to my place for dinner, not having seen him in the morning, the change which I remarked in his face made me ask him if he did not feel as well as usual. To which he replied that no, having suffered much all night from pains in the lower belly. He attributed the cause to boiled prunes of which, for some time, he had been in the habit of using. He ate little this time and retired early to his cabin, finding the cold a little too sharp.
During the evening, the weather remained the same as in the morning, and the winds always variable in the same quarter. But the breeze was more steady and the gusts less frequently followed. Only the sea was more agitated.
At sunset, we closed with the Naturaliste at about two leagues under the lee to not lose her during the night which, despite bad appearances, was fair by a sky as nebulous as the one we had. We had nothing to complain of but the cold to which the most part of us were very sensitive, which is usual when one passes suddenly from a very hot climate to a mild one.
1801-12-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 30° 31' 1" of latitude by account and in 106° 14' 22" of longitude by account. At 8 a main topmast backstay parted and was replaced for the time being by a lee backstay. At 9 Citizen Levillain died.

1801-12-23.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from south to SSW. At 8 the main topmast backstay parted close to the crosstrees. Citizen Levillain, the zoologist, died of a bloody flux.
1801-12-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, the winds continued to be very contrary to us since they came to us from the south and from the south by south-east and we had need to make distance to the south. The heavy sea and the drift of the vessel caused our course to take north, but still it was better for us to hold in the eastern tack because at least we gained on one side while losing on the other, instead that on the western tack, we would have lost on both sides.
About six o'clock in the morning, Captain Hamelin made known to me by a particular signal that Citizen Le Villain, embarked as assistant naturalist, no longer existed. He had been attacked during his stay at Timor, with a dysentery of which one had managed to cure him. But as soon as he found himself in good health on board where he had retired early, he had no more regard for the diet which he was urged to maintain and he ate of everything indifferently with excess. He soon experienced pains in the belly and colic which, having degenerated into diarrhoea, occasioned to him a short time after, a relapse and a second dysentery much more difficult to cure than the first and of which, despite all the resources of medicine and others, he died.
This young man who had already made a campaign with me for natural history, had talents and would have been, without doubt, thereafter, strong in this field, if premature death had not taken him from us. He was moreover, of a gentle character, affable and of good society. His comrades will without doubt regret him in all these respects when they learn the end of his career which I do not make known to them at this moment in that Citizens Depuche and Maugé are not well. Citizen Maugé, especially, gives me much anxiety in that he was perfectly recovered and it appears that having eaten too much will be the cause of a second relapse.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 30° 3' 58" south which carried us about 13 minutes to the north of our last observation. The longitude indicated by No. 35 placed us at 107° 4' 23" so that in forty-eight hours, we had advanced to the east by 4° 31' 13" while by dead reckoning, we found only 3° 53' 0" which gave more to the timekeeper 0° 48' 13", a difference nearly equal to that experienced on the 30th of Frimaire by the observation of the sun at noon.
During the evening, the winds were no better than they had been in the morning. But the sky was less laden and seemed to want to turn fair, especially in the north-west quarter, the horizon being very clear. We hoped that the winds could shift there at sunset, but in this we were greatly mistaken, for they ranged more to the south and it blew such a fresh breeze that, to not tire our masting, and oblige the Naturaliste to make too much canvas, we took a third reef in the main topsail and furled the main sail.
The breeze was stiff during the night from the south to the south-south-east, but the weather fair and the sky fairly clear. We continued the eastern tack, bringing us still at eighty leagues from the lands of New Holland nearest to us.
1801-12-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSW to SSE. At daybreak the main topmast backstay was set up again. At noon in 30° 1' 38" of latitude observed and in 107° 58' 16" of longitude by account.

1801-12-24.journal_anonyme: A high sea, the weather overcast, the wind a strong breeze from south to SE and SSE. At 8 a.m. wore ship.
1801-12-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, after sunrise, the winds continuing to blow from the south-south-east quarter, fresh breeze, and seeming to want to fix themselves there, we continued the eastern tack until eight o'clock, when we wore round before the wind, the sea being too agitated and rough to endeavour to go about. The Naturaliste did the same and we ran to the south-west. Scarcely were we oriented in the tack which we had just taken, when the winds varied from the south-east towards the east, which rendered our course so much the better as we made little distance to the west, at least according to our dead reckoning.
During the morning, the sky was fairly fair and the weather clear, but the sea remained strongly rough and agitated, appearing to have been raised by several different winds.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 30° 8' 26", which surprised us much, for according to our dead reckoning, we expected to find distance to the north. The difference of the estimated latitude from that observed was considerable since we made ourselves by our dead reckoning at 29° 40' 42" which gave to the south 0° 27' 44" on which we were not expecting.
The longitude indicated by No. 35 placed us at 108° 4' 57" and gave only 7' 54" of difference in the distance estimated to the west.
In the evening, the winds were in the same quarter and the sky remained fair although more overcast. The breeze was, also, more moderate and the sea began to fall. After sunset, we loosened a reef from our main topsail and followed the Naturaliste, under our major sails with two reefs in each.
During the night of the third to the fourth, we had the same wind as during the day, only it was moderate and the sky much more overcast. We continued the same course under the same canvas. The sea became fair and we were no more incommoded by the heavy swell of the days past.
Citizen Maugé who had made the relapse of which I spoke yesterday, did not pass too well through the day and complained of feeling very sharp pains in the lower belly. His face had become sad and my fears for the sequel of his illness did not fail to increase.
Citizen Depuche, for his part, found himself a little better and seemed to enter into full convalescence. The other sick also experienced a change for the better.
1801-12-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 30° 9' 28" of latitude observed and in 109° 0' 28" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 6° 57' 0" of NW variation. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.

1801-12-25.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a strong breeze from SE. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.
1801-12-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, at daybreak, the Naturaliste finding herself at about two leagues under the lee to us, we were obliged to bear away to close with her. I have difficulty conceiving in which direction the wind this vessel had to steer during the night. For having lost sight of her at midnight, we carried full sail until three o'clock without having knowledge of her. We resumed, then, the course of close-hauled to not find ourselves too much ahead of her, waiting for the day to join her. We had, in the morning, the winds from the south-east variable until the south by south-east, light breeze, the sea having become very fair. The sky remained overcast and damp as it had been in the night and we saw the sun rarely. However at noon, one could observe the latitude and it was found to be 31° 28' 58" south, that of our dead reckoning gave 31° 36' 52".
As we had no hour angle, we were obliged to refer to our dead reckoning for the distance made to the west and which was found to be (no figures).
In the afternoon, the winds were extremely variable from the south by south-east to the south by south-west and the sky did not have fair appearance. At sunset especially, it seemed to indicate to us bad weather and the barometer also began to fall. Clouds very dark and very extensive appeared as if fixed to the horizon from the south to the south-west and did not begin to rise until about ten o'clock. All the atmosphere became then very dark and bad weather seemed inevitable. But we were prepared to receive it having only our major sails and two reefs in our topsails. The Naturaliste which was a little aft, still carried her topgallant sails. Nevertheless, the sea was fair and no swell nor heavy sea made itself felt, which gave us the hope that all would dissipate in mist as that had already happened several times.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth, despite that all the appearances promised us bad weather and that the fall of the barometer seemed to confirm it, we had none however. The sky was extremely dark and overcast with winds from the south by south-east to the south, very moderate. I remained on deck until ten o'clock, but then the clouds which had frightened us, developed and instead of winds, gave us only much humidity. The rising of the moon which entered its last quarter, changed nothing, and the humidity continued during the rest of the night.
1801-12-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At noon in 31° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 108° 4' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-26.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 5 went about. At 9.30 a.m. the course was signalled S 45° E.
1801-12-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, the sky remained dark, overcast and laden with thick clouds at all points of the horizon. I do not recall, having ever encountered, in the climates where I have passed in the winter, having ever had an atmosphere so long laden with vapours of an appearance as disagreeable as the one we are traversing, at this moment. Since our exit from the trade winds, we have had it almost always similar. At first, little accustomed to navigating under a sky so nebulous, we (we) expected at each moment some squall from the appearances, for in any other climate, similar clouds would not develop without occasioning some.
The winds having passed from the south to the south-south-west, we changed tack at four o'clock in the morning and took the south-east tack. In the morning, the breeze was good, accompanied from time to time by some gusts and fog, but all of it was of little duration. Nevertheless, the sea was beginning to grow rough.
At noon, having no height of the sun from observation, that which the dead reckoning gave to it placed us at 32° 2' 28" of latitude. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper since the last observation, placed us at 106° 40' 41".
In the evening, the weather was a little clearer and less laden than in the morning. The sun showed itself even at several times but of a pale colour and under the form as one sees it in Europe during the bad days of the winter. At its setting, the sky covered itself, as usual and the winds approached the south. The sea was beginning to become deep and agitated. Before nightfall, we closed with the Naturaliste, which had fallen much under the lee and I signalled to her that I would make course to the south-south-east, if the winds became good.
During the day, Citizen Maugé who had been attacked anew with a dysenteric flux, had an indigestion which tired him much and was only relieved by the remedies which were given him to take towards the end of the day.
The night of the fifth to the sixth had nothing particular and was absolutely similar to the previous ones that is to say that the sky was constantly overcast, laden with humid and cold vapours, without bad weather. The winds held themselves for the most part to the south, moderate, without the sea becoming more agitated than it was at sunset, only the swells were longer and less numerous.
1801-12-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSW. At 9.30 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 11 we had a squall in which the middle staysail was split; in hauling it down it was shifted. At noon in 31° 55' 2" of latitude by account and in 107° 42' 10" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E.

1801-12-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE. At 5.30 p.m. the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E in case the winds should draw aft.
1801-12-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, the winds were the same as the preceding days and it was (not) without displeasure that we found them so contrary to our course, for since our exit from the trade winds, they had been favourable to us only two days. Finally, with patience and forced resignation, one must hope that they will change if not before the end of this month, at least at the beginning of the next. And perhaps then we will have a sky which will let us perceive that we are in the summer of this hemisphere.
During the morning, we saw sometimes the sun, but at intervals so short that one could not take an hour angle. Nevertheless at noon, we observed the latitude which was found to be 31° 42' 15" while that of our dead reckoning placed us at 32° 5' 16", so that we found ourselves to have a difference to the north in forty-eight hours of 23 minutes one second, occasioned without doubt by a change of direction in the currents which, until then, had given us differences to the south.
In the afternoon, the sky, although overcast and dark, had better appearance than usual, but this was not for long, for at sunset, it covered itself anew with large dark and thick clouds. The winds which, sometimes, had varied from the south to the south by south-west, passed to the south-south-east, light breeze and seemed to want to fix themselves there for the night. At eight o'clock, having closed with the Naturaliste which was under the lee, I signalled to her to wear round and we took the south-west tack to try to regain to the south what we had lost in the two preceding days and put ourselves in a position to double the western point of the lands of Leeuwin.
The night of the sixth to the seventh was (not) fair. As to the brightness of the sky scarcely did we see from time to time, a few stars and even the moon when she had risen above the horizon. But we had no, moreover, bad weather although it was for us as announced by an extremely long and deep swell from the south.
Citizen Maugé found himself much better in this day than the previous day and experienced great relief in the pains which he felt in the lower belly after having expelled by the effect of a medicine, a great quantity of corrupted water which was without doubt the principal cause of his ill. At least the surgeons judged it thus.
Citizen Depuche is about in the same state without a well sensible change and our geographer still has the fever and strong colic. The other sick are in good train for a prompt recovery.
1801-12-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 39' 10" of latitude observed and in 109° 13' 4" of longitude by account. Saw albatrosses and petrels.

1801-12-28.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from south to SSE. At 8.15 the commander, after closing us, went about, and we did the same.
1801-12-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, we continued the south-west tack as much as the winds could allow us, but their variety and their inconstancy made us gain so little distance to the south that this day became as nothing for our navigation.
In the course of the morning, the weather seemed to want to turn fair and although the sky was still very nebulous, we had the view of the sun during a part of the day. It was the first time that a similar thing had happened to us since we had left the regions of the trade winds.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 31° 50' 22" and the longitude indicated by No. 35 was found to be 108° 19'. On board the Naturaliste one counted 108° 48'. The rate of the timekeeper compared with the estimate of our course since forty-eight hours, gave us distance made to the east of 1° 38' 19" while the other gave us 2° 18' 24" which made a difference of 0° 40' 5" for the distance estimated. From the differences in the latitudes, the currents seemed to direct themselves towards the north to the east.
During the evening, the weather continued to be fairly fair until evening, but about an hour before sunset, the sky became dark and very nebulous as usual, and even the clouds were of a colour still more dark than ordinary, which was not of too good omen for the night. However, it was not bad, and even there blew very little and that no doubt contributed to making fall the heavy swell which we had from the south, in that it diminished much and tired us less.
Citizens Depuche and Maugé passed the day fairly well. This latter especially did not feel the effects of the pains which he had experienced the preceding days. And his dysenteric flux appears to have ceased.
On the request of the officers of the General Staff, the sharing of the tea which remained on board was done during the evening, consisting of ten pounds. Four were first, set aside for the sick present or to come, the surplus was shared into two equal portions of which one was intended for the crew and the other for them.
I have difficulty conceiving how those who do not regard any expense when it is a matter of pleasures or fancies, have not provided themselves with a box of tea rather than having recourse to that embarked for the use of the sailors.
1801-12-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 49' 38" of latitude observed and in 108° 57' 40" of longitude by account.

1801-12-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south to SE. At 9 squally weather with fairly violent gusts; the dinghy was put on the gratings to be repaired. At 7.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-12-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, the winds were almost calm the greater part of the day and the sky nebulous with a little very fine rain or rather a thick mist sometimes. All the points of the horizon offered to the sight large dark clouds driven by a high wind in different directions. When a few of these clouds passed on our side, they seemed to bring us thunder and winds, and nevertheless, they gave us only light gusts accompanied by a little soft rain or a thick fog.
All the morning passed in changing our sails from one tack to the other without, almost, making any distance. But we were compensated for it by the capture which we made of a dozen of those beautiful blue snails which we had encountered in doubling Cape Good Hope and of which I have given the drawing in my written journal. The sea although rough, was calm which facilitated for us the means to perceive them. One also took advantage of the little wind which there was to tighten our shrouds of the topsail and topgallant sails which needed it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 32° 0' 39" south, but we judged it faulty in that the horizon was too dark and of little extent.
In the afternoon, the sky became fair and, about four o'clock, there came to us a little breeze from the south towards the west which permitted us to steer some time to the south-east and to the south-east by east. But after sunset, the winds passed again to the south and to the south by south-west very light. We then loosened a reef from our topsails to close with the Naturaliste which I had let pass ahead.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth, the sky was covered but fair, we had a light breeze from the south-east, we continued the south-east tack drawing more to the south when the variety of the wind facilitated for us the means. At ten o'clock we passed the Naturaliste which found herself a little to the windward to us.
There (happened) this same day, some little difficulties discontent at the table of the General Staff and of the naturalists which occasioned complaints. Those who had given rise to it came into my cabin and I made them friendly the representations which I judged convenient to stifle early, these little dissensions which ordinarily finish by falling out seriously with each other. From the report which was made to me by the two parties, it seemed to me that both had some faults. Be that as it may, I hope that this will not happen again and that I will not be obliged to take the party which I have announced if one does not want to agree and live in good intelligence.
1801-12-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. Saw albatrosses. At noon in 31° 59' 56" of latitude observed and in 108° 23' 58" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW.

1801-12-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, calm until 3, when the breeze got up from the south, variable to SW and SSE by way of south. Obs. lat. 32° 12' 22".
1801-12-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, the winds varied from the south towards the east and the breeze was light. The sky, although very nebulous at sunrise, became fair against its ordinary character, which made us hope that the winds would perhaps range themselves in the east quarter towards the north and that we could repair the time lost in making a good course, but it was not so and (they) fixed themselves at the south-south-east.
At daybreak, the Naturaliste finding herself very far from us, we were obliged to lower our main sail and our staysails to wait for her. This would not have happened if, during the night, the officers who were on watch on board this vessel, had answered the signals which we made to her to know her position.
As there was calm in the morning, we took some more snails similar to those of which I spoke yesterday, but we found them less beautiful.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 32° 11' 7". We had no hour angle or to say better, one did not take any and I do not know why for the sky was fair enough for that.
After the observation of the meridian height, the winds seeming fixed at the south-south-east, I signalled to wear round and we changed our tacks. By this means, the Naturaliste found herself ahead of us and at a fairly great distance, but we had soon joined her, being to the windward of her.
During the evening, it blew a good breeze and we made a fair distance to the south-west. The winds varied a few times a quarter more to the south, but it was only in gusts which were not long.
The night had nothing particular, only the sky covered itself with clouds which did not have bad appearance and which gave a little wind when their direction made them pass above us.
At nine o'clock in the evening, the Naturaliste beginning to remain aft, we furled all our staysails and took a second reef in the mizzen topsail.
1801-12-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SE. At noon in 32° 12' 23" of latitude observed and in 109° 20' 46" of longitude by account. At 6, 6° 47' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to east. At half past noon went onto the port tack and made all sail.
1801-12-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the tenth, in the morning, we experienced some favourable changes in the variety of winds, in that they shifted from south-east to east-south-east and even to east by south. It was the first time since we quit the general winds that they had taken so much to the east. We continued to make course as far to the south as was possible to us in order to gain latitude, since we could not make a direct course. The sky was very overcast during the morning and showed itself only in very short intervals.

At about ten o'clock, M. Freycinet, head of the officers' mess, came to tell me that it was impossible for them to live on the ordinary ration as granted by the regulations to everyone. According to the account he showed me, in the ten-day period they had consumed all that was due to them for a month. I observed to M. Freycinet how he would place us in difficulty if we continued at this rate, telling him that in six months the officers' table would, by itself, have consumed all the provisions that were on board, and that my duty prescribed to me imperatively that I should show as much care for the sailors, who were men of labour and toil, as for officers who appear on deck only four hours a day. As there remained to them only very little fresh meat, I took advantage of this occasion to show him the abuse that had been made of what had been embarked at Timor, and the fresh provisions were sufficient for six months if one had used them with moderation.

I moreover remarked to him that rather than twelve persons at their table, including the naturalists, there were found only seven, since three from our departure who had been ill had been constantly maintained at my table, and that independently of that, I was accustomed to invite two other persons when my dinner was adequate. That then I was equal in number to them, that I had embarked much less provisions and that what remained to me would last yet longer, by the order I had established, and that he should do the same. The various observations he made to me in the name of all decided me to grant them one-third more of what was due to them to content them. But it is nonetheless true that seven persons consume entirely the ration of twelve and I do not know if the supplement that will be given to them will be sufficient.

At noon, the observed latitude was 33° 13' 32" south and the timekeeper's longitude indicated 107° 43' 26" east of Paris. Whence it results that, to advance ourselves a little to the south, we had lost, in the last three days in different courses, 0° 35' 34" of distance to the east. According to the dead reckoning of our courses made, it was found to be 0° 41' 48", which in the three days gave only a difference of 0° 6' 14" from the observations.

During the evening, the winds, which at about eleven o'clock in the morning had shifted to east by south, were not long in returning to south-east, and after sunset they took even more to the south and were very variable throughout the night. The breeze was likewise irregular and the wind in little squalls. This night was, for us, the darkest we had yet had without, nevertheless, appearing to bring bad weather. We did not see a single star shine despite the clouds not having much thickness.

At about four o'clock in the evening, having come alongside the Naturaliste, Captain Hamelin asked me if he could hold the sale of the effects of the dead. I replied to him yes. M. Hamelin also informed me that his convalescents had much difficulty recovering and that they were lingering in their recuperation. The longitude of his (sic) timekeepers differed little from ours.
1801-12-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 33° 15' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-01.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze. The effects of the late Le Bourgeois and Savary were sold.
1802-01-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the eleventh, in the morning, we had, contrary to what was usual, a fine sky and the appearance of a fine day, but the winds were not more favourable to us than in the preceding days and kept, as was usual, from south-east to south or south-south-east, or from south-west to south when they changed direction. The weather was cold during the morning and although the breeze was weak the atmosphere gave us more coolness than the sun gave us warmth. We were nevertheless in the height of summer.

At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 8' 7" and the timekeeper's longitude put us at 106° 50' 43". The difference that we found between the dead reckoning and the observation during these twenty four hours was 0° 17' 28" to the west and 0° 3' 57" to the north.

In the afternoon, the sky continued to be fine and the sea calm without being disturbed by any swell which would announce an imminent change to us. However, from noon until two o'clock, the winds passed successively to south and from there to south-west and even we had them, for an instant, at west-south-west. From the beginning, we went about in order to steer to the east, and as they became favourable to us, we adjusted our course from east towards south. The Naturaliste made the same manoeuvre and I signalled to her the course south-east by compass. This vessel apparently did not see our signal although she was not very far away and we kept her high until after sunset without her having responded.

At about seven o'clock in the evening, the winds began to draw towards the south. The sky became cloudy and dark, nevertheless the night was fine and the wind was light.

During the day, we saw various species of petrels about the size of a duck with the back grey, the belly white, as well as the neck and head of a dark brown tending to black which made the white patch on the neck highly recognizable. It was the first time that we had seen such birds.
1802-01-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. The effects of the late Bourgeois and Savary were sold. At noon in 34° 0' 0" of latitude observed and in 107° 50' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south. At 1.30 changed tacks. The effects of Citizen Levillain were sold.
1802-01-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, the winds were all day in the southern quarter towards the east. There was little wind and the weather was very fine. However, the little freshness there was seemed to us colder than the heat of the sun was hot. We took advantage of this fine day to air part of our spare rigging, which appeared to the boatswain to need it.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 34° 4' 58" south and the longitude given by our timekeeper was 107° 40' 15". The difference between the dead reckoning course and the observation gave a difference of 7' 44" to the north and 11' 58" to the west.
During the evening, the wind dropped a great deal and the sky, which was very fine at sunset, gave us no sign of wind for the night, which indeed passed almost in calm. Despite the beauty of the sky, we were very surprised at the movement of the barometer, which from 28 inches three lines, where it had risen the previous day, was by noon no more than 28 in. 1.5, and we had never had such fine weather. At sunset ………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………..
According to the doctor's report, our sick were much better and Citizens Maugé and Depuche were again entering convalescence. However, this improvement announced by the doctor did not show on their faces, for both had them singularly drawn and livid, which did not seem to me a good omen. Citizen Maugé especially gave me great concern, and although his dysentery had stopped for the second time, he was far from appearing to me out of danger.
Two men of the crew also left the sick berth and the others did not appear likely to remain there much longer.
1802-01-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. The mizzen topgallant mast was wedged and its shrouds and backstays set up. The effects of the late Levillain were sold. At noon in 34° 4' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 51' 10" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30 he was to leeward at a great distance. We supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flags giving the course; so we bore away S 67° 30' E, and east, and closed him.

1802-01-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from south to SSW and W. At 1.45 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30, being far to leeward, we supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flag that gave the course; we at once bore away S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the thirteenth, at sunrise we had all the appearance of a fine day, the sky being fine and entirely cleared of those thick and dark clouds which had accompanied us for so long. But the fine sky which it was so pleasant to us to see occasioned calm for us until about eight o'clock, when the winds having shifted from south by south-west to west, there came a little breeze which permitted us to make course south-east in order to place ourselves in good time at the latitude of the western lands of Leeuwin, of which I intended to take knowledge if the weather remained fine.

At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 7' 31" south and that of the dead reckoning put us at 34° 11' 4", so that the difference to the north was not considerable since it was found to be only 3' 33". The longitude of the timekeeper put us at 108° 29' 29" and by the estimated course to the east we found a difference of 7' 9".

In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to north-west and west, there began to blow a fine breeze and we crowded on sail in order to take advantage of it. The sky, during the evening, was fine but gradually it became covered with clouds and grew dark. The barometer, which had spontaneously descended to 28 inches despite the fine weather, seemed to announce to us some squalls which we should have expected on the new moon. However, the sea was reasonably fine and as we were not experiencing those great swells which announce bad weather to come and even that which has passed in the waters where we were, it seemed to us that we should have nothing to fear as to the present state of the sky, which nevertheless was not fine at about eight o'clock in the evening, and at that time the sea was already beginning to be a little disturbed.

During the night of the thirteenth to the fourteenth, the winds varied from west to west by north-west. It blew fresh and in squalls. We even had a little rain but, more usually, murky clouds which gave us fairly strong squalls. At ten o'clock, we took a second reef in our topsails and furled all our smaller sails to be more prepared in case of need. I also had the stern light lit for the rest of the night so that the Naturaliste, which was astern, could adjust her sails accordingly. The sea was beginning to grow heavy and we should have expected some squalls, but as the wind appeared likely to be favourable to us, we were not averse to seeing it build, provided, however, that it was not to excess.
1802-01-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 6 a flat calm; at 8 the breeze got up from WNW and blew from WNW to W, a fresh breeze. At noon in 34° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 109° 54' 46" of longitude by account. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E for 8 o'clock. At 11 we had a slight squall with rain; the fore studdingsail boom broke as the studdingsails were taken in.

1802-01-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from W to WNW; set the studdingsails and royals. The commander signalled the course for 8 o'clock as S 33° 45' E. At 4 a.m. overcast weather, a strong breeze and a high sea.
1802-01-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
[3V p. 185 Historical events & Remarks.

On the fourteenth, the winds were variable from west to west by north-west and a fresh breeze blew. At four o'clock in the morning, reckoning myself at thirty five degrees south latitude and at no great distance from the western lands of New Holland, I set course to east by south-east in the hope that I might gain knowledge of it during the day if the breeze, or rather to say the strong wind that we had, continued. Although the sea was beginning to grow very heavy we changed nothing in our sail which, however, appeared to fatigue our masts in the great rolls that the waves occasioned to the vessel.

In the morning, we saw many petrels with white belly and dark grey back as well as several albatrosses of medium size. The small petrels known by the name of storm petrels also kept us company and remained in great quantity in the eddy occasioned by the ship's wake. Despite all the means that we employed, we were unable to catch any, they did not even seek to take the bait that we offered them.

At noon, we observed the latitude of 35° 14' 54" which put us a little south of the lands of Leeuwin, and if the longitude of our timekeeper had been exact, we should have had knowledge of the land since it put us at 111° 30' 57". It is true that the horizon extended no more than five or six leagues, the sky although fine being charged with vapours.

According to the dead reckoning of the course made, our latitude was found to be 35° 39' 43, so that we had a considerable difference to the north from the observation. As it was found to be 24' 49" and as we had never found one so great, it seemed to us that a strong current had powerfully carried us to the north, and this conjecture appeared all the better founded in that in the correction of the course estimated eastward there was found only seven minutes of difference from that which the timekeeper indicated for the twenty four hours.

During the evening, a fresh wind continued to blow from west by north-west to north-west. The sky was reasonably fine until about three o'clock, but then it became covered with clouds, and we had sometimes strong squalls. The barometer below 28 inches gave us no promise of a fine night. We prepared accordingly, and at six o'clock, no longer having hope of sighting the land, from the state of the horizon, I set course to south-east.

From the signs of which we had knowledge, there is every appearance that we should have seen it if the weather had been finer. I am even persuaded that we were on soundings on soundings (sic) in that several whales showed themselves near the vessel and that in these waters we have remarked that they seldom keep far from the coasts. As the weather was not convenient for sounding, I continued my course.

During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth, we had continually squalls and strong gales, sometimes with rain, sometimes without. As the wind was very good for us to make up a little of the lost time, we all endured the discomfort that ensues from it, but we were less troubled by it than by the heavy sea which fatigued us greatly and even more the vessel.
1802-01-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to WSW. A high sea. Two large pieces of wood passed alongside. At noon in 35° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 112° 44' 16" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. Saw a whale. During the night the wind in gusts, with rain and frequent squalls.

1802-01-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to WSW. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. In the forenoon the weather cleared.
1802-01-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather was much the same as the day before but the winds shifted to west by south-west which made us fear to see them soon take the southern part and grow calm. For that is their usual progress, at least by this meridian. They have it thus around the meridian of Madagascar. They had, however, lost nothing of their force at west-south-west and they compelled us, on the contrary, to take the third reef in the lower topsail which I was pleased to have changed the day before, for fear of seeing it carried away by some squall. The sea was, then, very heavy and we perceived by the seams of our strakes (?) of which the caulking was found to be coming out, that the vessel had much more fatigued than we had judged.

At noon, the latitude was observed, although doubtful on account of the great elevation of the sea which rendered the horizon difficult, of 36° 31' 27". That of the dead reckoning of the course made in the twenty four hours gave us 36° 54' 39". So that the same difference, experienced the day before, was renewed and we had one to the north of 0° 23' 12". That of the distance made to the east compared with that indicated by the timekeeper was but 59 seconds, proof that the difference does not come from the estimate and that a strong current directing to the north is encountered in these waters.

In the afternoon, the winds followed the course that we had presumed they would take, and shifted to south-west without abating. But the sky had a worse appearance than when they had been from west towards north. The clouds were darker and thicker and the rain, when it fell, very cold. We bent our storm staysail in case of need. The barometer, still holding at 27 inches 10 lines, announced nothing favourable to us and the state of the atmosphere seemed to confirm it.

However, at about six o'clock, the sky became fairly fine and the horizon clear in the south-west to north-west part, the winds even drew towards the west and the sea appeared less disturbed to us. We even set our main sail. The weather was squally until midnight and a little before that hour, we received a squall which obliged us to furl the main sail and let fly the sheet to scud two or three points further off the wind until it had passed. Then, the winds shifted to west-south-west by west and came as far as south-south-west and abated, which greatly incommoded us, the sea tossing us in all directions and causing fear of having damage to the masts or to the sails by the violent movements that the light wind caused them, in the great rolling.
1802-01-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea. The wind a strong breeze from W to SW, with rain. At noon in 36° 28' 23" of latitude observed and in 115° 56' 58" of longitude by account.

1802-01-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze and in gusts. At 1 lowered and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. As soon as it was repaired we took the 2 reefs and sheeted home. At daybreak the weather turned fine; we rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail.
1802-01-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the sixteenth, in the morning, we had the winds from west-south-west to north-west by north-west and a moderate breeze, but the sea being heavy and the swell deep, the vessel fatigued much as did her masts. However, to follow the Naturaliste which was carrying all sail and her studding sails, forced me to set more sail than I would have wished for fear of causing some damage. Nevertheless, as the weather then was fine, I had a reef let out in each topsail and rigged the studding sails as well as the topgallant sails. The sea appeared to be growing calm although always very agitated.

At noon, we observed the latitude of 37° 38' 40" south and that of the dead reckoning gave us 37° 57' 37", consequently a northern difference of 18' 57". The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 117° 25' 53" and the course to the east according to the dead reckoning of 2° 45' which gave a difference from that indicated by the timekeeper of only 3' 27". Thus, it appears almost beyond doubt that the direction of the currents is to the north with fairly great velocity which, perhaps, will continue to diminish as we proceed south of the Lands of Night.

In the afternoon, the appearance of continuing fine weather vanished, the sky became covered with great black and thick clouds and grew very dark. The winds shifted to west where they held fairly constant and a good breeze blew. As the vessel was fatiguing too much with all her sail and, moreover, the weather had very bad appearance, I had the studding sails and topgallant sails furled in order that the Naturaliste, which, contrary to custom was ahead, should do the same, which she executed.

During all the day, we had the company of a fairly great quantity of albatrosses of the great species and of the two two (sic) varieties that are known in this kind of bird. We also saw several petrels of mediocre size.

The night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth was very dark and without bad weather. Very thick and damp clouds often passed over us which gave us a little rain of short duration and without strong wind or squalls. The sea fell much, but there was always a deep and rolling swell which occasioned to us rolling movements all the more unpleasant because we were running before the wind.
1802-01-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to NW. Saw albatrosses, petrels, bonito and weed. At noon in 37° 40' 15" of latitude observed and in 118° 41' 40" of longitude by account. At 4 the Géographe was far astern and was not crowding sail; we shortened ours. At 7.15 hove to on the port tack, and at 8 filled and stood on.

1802-01-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from NW to W. At 7.15 hove to to wait. At 8, having closed, we filled and stood on.
1802-01-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the seventeenth, in the morning, the winds which had been for the greater part of the night at north-west, shifted after a strong squall of rain, to west by south-west and successively to south-west continuing to blow a good breeze.

During most of the morning, we did not lack rain, but at about eleven o'clock, the sky became clear from west to north and we were not long in having sight of the sun whose warmth was very pleasant to us in that the cold made itself keenly felt. The hygrometer, despite the rain, remained at 90° and it had rarely happened to it since our departure to indicate this degree of saturation.

We had, all morning, the company of many petrels of the species which sailors do not like to have in that most are persuaded that its presence is of bad omen. As they were in great number in the ship's wake, it appears likely that this species is more abundant in these seas than in others where one encounters them only rarely and only when the weather is bad.

At noon, the latitude was observed to be 39° 20' 46" and that of the dead reckoning was found to be 39° 28' 29" which gave a northern difference of only 7' 43", a sum much less considerable than those of the preceding days. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 120° 22' 30" and the distance made to the east according to the dead reckoning was 3° 0' and that of the timekeeper 2° 56' 27".

In the afternoon, the sky was fairly fine and the winds shifted from south-west towards west, without the breeze losing anything of its force. I continued the course south-east not only to get south of the Strait of Bass in order to find weaker currents but also to have a longer course if the winds should subsequently shift to south, which appeared to me fairly probable.

I do not know if one should attribute to the state of the atmosphere charged for several days with much vapour, the discomfort that generally all our sick were experiencing, but it is nonetheless true that for three or four days, their convalescence far from consolidating seemed on the contrary to be destined to be longer.

During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth, the weather, without being very fine, was not bad and the squalls that came to us gave more fog than rain and wind.
1802-01-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W. At 2.30 the main topsail tie and lift parted; all was repaired by 3.30. At noon in 39° 18' 41" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 34" of longitude by account. At 5.30, 5° 40' 40" of NW variation. Rain during the night.

1802-01-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from NW; all sail set, studdingsails and royals.
1802-01-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the eighteenth, in the morning, we had the winds from the western part variable sometimes at west-south-west and continuation of good breeze, but the sky which had been fairly fine became covered with clouds and we had abundantly rain, hail and strong squalls for nearly two hours in succession. The sea was also beginning to become very heavy and rolling but as we were running almost before the wind we set our topgallant sails, the Naturaliste having all sail set and her studding sails.

We saw, during the day, many birds of different species and which, for the most part, were unknown to us. That which was most noticeable was a species of sea snipe, having absolutely the flight as swift and jerky as that of land but it did not have the long beak. On our first arrival on the coast of New Holland, we had well distinguished birds similar in size and flight, but those which we had in sight, that day, did not have the same colour in plumage, and the tail seemed to us to be less tapered than that of which I spoke at the time. The whole upper part of the body of these was a dark brown and the underside of the belly, very white. The head and neck of an ashen grey which was noticeable. The albatrosses appeared to us also less large than those which are encountered in the waters of the Cape of Good Hope.

We also saw several patches of seaweed of the species known by the name of fucus giganteus.

At noon, the latitude was observed to be 41° 9' 32" south. That of the dead reckoning was 41° 17' 40" which again gave a northern difference of 8' 8". The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 123° 42' 7" which gave a course to the east during the twenty four hours of 3° 19' 37", the dead reckoning gave 3° 24' 0".

In the afternoon, the winds continued to hold in the western part to west-south-west and the sky took a very bad appearance for the night. The barometer which held constantly at 27 inches 8 & 9 lines, also did not promise that it would be fine, which caused us to prepare accordingly. Before sunset, the topgallant sails were taken in and I had two reefs taken in each topsail. The Naturaliste also furled her studding sails and her other light sails.

During the night, of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, a fresh wind blew in strong squalls, we furled our main sail and made way under our topsails and foresail continuing to steer to east-south-east, the course which I had taken and signalled, as soon as the observation of the sun's altitude at noon.
1802-01-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW, with rain. At 2.30, in a squall, the main topsail sheet parted; by 3.30 the damage was repaired. At noon in 41° 8' 14" of latitude observed and in 124° 16' 40" of longitude by account. The commander signalled the course S 67° 30' E.

1802-01-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from W to WSW. At noon the course was signalled S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the nineteenth, we had the winds at west-south-west, good breeze, until about eight o'clock, when they returned to west. The sky was very overcast in the morning and the horizon hazy. We had sometimes fairly strong squalls accompanied by a little rain, but they were not of long duration. The birds which had accompanied us the day before, reappeared again, however the number of them was less considerable.

During the morning, we saw almost no sun, but around noon, it showed itself for an instant and we were able to observe its height which, although doubtful, put us at 42° 0' 10". That found by the dead reckoning of the course made gave 42° 0' 8" which leads me to believe that the observation was not good, given the little difference that resulted from it. The distance made to the east reported from the longitude of the day before put us at (no figures).

In the afternoon, the sky remained dark as it had been in the morning, and the horizon continued to extend but little. Nevertheless, the winds were more regular and less variable. The sea, always heavy, fatigued us greatly by the rolling movements that it occasioned to the vessel and the discomfort was only compensated by the good course that we were making and which enabled us to make up for the lost time before we could proceed south and east of the lands of Leeuwin.

Our sick were greatly incommoded by this weather which, nevertheless, was very advantageous to us.

Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, was the one who felt most the effects of it in that it occasioned him a continual vomiting which forced him to remain several days in succession in his berth. It was the same for Citizen Maugé who, unable to support himself against the rolling, remained continually shut up in his cabin.

The night of the nineteenth to the twentieth had nothing particular. The winds were much the same. Although it was darker than any of those we had had up to that point, there was no bad weather and very few of those strong squalls which had almost always followed us. The sea also appeared less agitated and the waves were longer without breaking one upon the other as usual.

One of our foreign sailors, taken at the Island of France, was punished in the middle of the night and received twenty five strokes of rope's ends, for having drawn his knife against the second mate who was making him return to his post.
1802-01-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to WNW. Saw a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 42° 7' 2" of latitude by account and in 128° 5' 28" of longitude by account. During the night the wind blowing hard in gusts, with rain; kept the topsails reefed. In the night of the 9th [Nivôse, 30 December 1801] I had a high fever which forced me to keep my bed all through the 10th [Nivôse, 31 December 1801]; on the 11th [Nivôse, 1 January 1802] I was a little better, and a purge and an emetic set me up. It was not until the 14th [Nivôse, 4 January 1802] that the surgeon-major allowed me to resume my watch. I was still weak, but within 4 days I was in as good health as before my illness.

1802-01-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast and fresh weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from W to WNW and SW. Saw a whale and some seaweed.
1802-01-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the twentieth, the winds continued to be very favourable to us and the sky was fairly fine all the day, but we found the sea so agitated and the swell so great, high and rolling, that it was not possible for us to increase sail. The rolling movements were even so violent and numerous that I feared at every instant to have damage to the masts or to the rigging. However, the Naturaliste, to keep up with us, was carrying her studding sails and her topgallant sails without it appearing that this incommoded her in any manner.

We had, as on the preceding days, the company of several birds of the species of which I have already spoken, but it was much less in number. We also saw two whales at no great distance from the vessel and which followed us for more than two hours. It was a recreation for us to see them try their pace with ours. Sometimes we passed them, but when it took their fancy to give us chase, they had soon overtaken us.

At noon, the latitude was observed to be 43° 2' 32". That of the dead reckoning was 43° 0' 16" so that the little difference that had been found for two or three days between the dead reckoning and the observation made us see that we no longer had the strong current which had sometimes given us great differences to the north.

The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 132° 14' 16" which, since the last observed hour angle gave, in forty eight hours, 8° 32' 48" of distance to the east. By the dead reckoning of the route, we found we had made 8° 52' 0" which gave a difference of 17' 51" more. Thus the dead reckoning of the course made was fairly good.

In the afternoon, the sky appeared to want to become fine and became fairly clear. We did all we could to take azimuths in order to know the declination of the needle, but the movements of the vessel were so numerous that it was very difficult for us to have any confidence in the results that the calculation of these observations gave us. However, it appeared to us that the declination must have changed and be north-east instead of north-west, which nevertheless should not be regarded as certain from what I have just said about the difficulties of obtaining reliable results by the compass.

During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first, we had very fine weather until the setting of the moon. The winds towards the end of the day had shifted to west by north-west and appeared in the night to want to become fixed at north-west. This direction on their part was very pleasant to us in that it put an end to the great swaying which tormented us all the day. But also, the sky became dark and hazy, which gave us an horizon very much limited. Moreover, a fine breeze blew and we continued to steer east by south-east, the course which I had signalled to the Naturaliste after the observation of the meridian altitude.
1802-01-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to WNW. Saw a whale and a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 40° 57' 53" of latitude observed and in 132° 8' 16" of longitude by account. At 2 the commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E. In the course of the day the five courses and topsails were shifted. Variation 2° 38' NE.

1802-01-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NW. We shifted the foresail and the main topsail. The commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E.
1802-01-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the twenty-first, the winds remained at north-west, strong breeze. It was very fine weather for us. Therefore we took ample advantage of it to approach the land of Diemen which we all had great desire to know. The sky, however, had not good appearance during the morning, in that it was almost always charged with vapours and fogs which gave us sometimes a little soft rain. Nevertheless, we saw sometimes the sun and at noon, we were able to take its height which was found to be forty three degrees fifty minutes, so that the course was found to have taken more to the south than I had thought.

Although the weather was very hazy and the clouds were driven with great speed, the sea did not seem to announce bad weather, whilst the barometer and hygrometer warned us to the contrary. The former had descended to 27 inches 8⅕ lines with appearance of falling further and the latter had risen to 96° of humidity, which had not happened to it for a long time.

We could not take an hour angle during the day to know exactly the distance made to the east during these twenty four hours, but the dead reckoning of our route gave us 4° 37' 0", which put us at 136° 51' 16". Consequently, at about one hundred and ten leagues from the south-west cape of the Land of Diemen.

After the observation of the meridian altitude, I set course to east by north-east to bring ourselves a little to the north and we continued for the rest of the day to steer at this wind point, making good progress. But at about two o'clock, the wind increased to such a degree as to oblige the Naturaliste to furl her topgallant sails, and us, in order not to leave her too far astern, to take a third reef in our topsails. The sea was still tolerably fine, but if the wind continues with the same force, it will not be long before it becomes very heavy. During the whole evening, the sky was dark and charged with a thick fog which infinitely limited our horizon.

At six o'clock and a half, we received a very violent squall accompanied by much rain which made the winds shift to west. A little time after, the sky appeared to want to become fine for the night, which indeed happened for it was tolerably fine and even fairly clear. We changed nothing in our course and passed it under our ordinary sail, always making good progress.
1802-01-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW, with rain. The sails unbent were examined and condemned, except the foresail. At noon in 43° 38' 29" of latitude by account and in 136° 36' 16" of longitude by account.

1802-01-12.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, rain at intervals, a high sea and a strong breeze from NW to W. At 6.30 the commander made the signal to bend our cables.
1802-01-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the twenty-second, in the morning, the weather was fairly fine and the winds at west a fine breeze. The sea being always tolerably heavy and rolling, we rolled much, the vessel not having the side heeled to the wind.

At about eight o'clock, I signalled to the Naturaliste to slip her cables and we did the same in the morning. At ten o'clock, we received a strong squall mingled with wind, rain and hail. It lasted more than half an hour and made me fear a change in the weather. But as it passed, the sky became fine again and even we had it clearer than it had been until then.

We saw, in the course of the morning, several companies of birds flying in flocks, but they kept at too great a distance from the vessel for us to be able to judge if they were familiar to us or not.

At noon, the observed latitude was 43° 33' 14" and that of the dead reckoning 43° 32' which gave little difference. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper put us at 140° 51' 25" which gave a distance to the east since the last observation of 8° 37' 16", whilst the dead reckoning gave us 9° 50'. The difference, in forty eight hours, was very considerable, since we found ourselves 1° 12' 41" more to the west than we reckoned.

In the afternoon, the weather continued fine. We saw, during the evening, several schools of porpoises which came to play around the vessel but which did not remain there long. We did not harpoon any, because the ship was going too fast.

At sunset, Captain Hamelin asked me if I intended to make sail all the night. I replied to him that that would depend on the weather we should have, but that when I put the ship to, if the case should occur, I would signal him by lighting my stern light and that he should regulate himself accordingly.

At eight o'clock, having no knowledge of land of which I still reckoned myself about twelve or fifteen leagues, we continued to make course to east by north-east until about ten o'clock. But the weather then became so bad that I decided to put the ship to, the course south towards the west.

During the rest of the night, the weather was very bad, we had continually rain, hail and very strong squalls. One may even say that it was the worst from the state of the atmosphere that we had had up to that moment.
1802-01-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to W, with rain. At 6.30 the commander signalled us to bend our cables, which we did, and got the anchors ready to let go. In a squall the fore studdingsail boom broke; it was at once replaced by one from the main yard. At noon in 43° 31' 30" of latitude observed and in 141° 2' 40" of longitude by account. At 5, 6° 22' 30" of NE variation. At 10 the commander having hove to on the starboard tack, we did the same, after lowering the topsails on the caps.

1802-01-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW to W and SW. During the night the commander having hove to, we did the same. At 3.45 we sighted the land in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander. We closed the coast and ran along it. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30', distance 9.5 miles; the Mewstone S 85° E, distance 5 miles; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 46° E, distance 4 miles.
1802-01-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the Land of Diemen:
At eight o'clock in the morning, the south-west cape at north 10° west, 2½ leagues
The Maatsuiker Islands at east-north-east, 3 leagues
The Mewstone to the east
At noon the Mewstone at south 68° west
The land nearest to us at north 61° west
The south cape at north 49° 45' east
The northernmost lands in sight from north to 54° east
The Scully Islands at east 45° south

Historical events & Remarks.

VIEW OF THE WESTERN COAST OF THE ISLAND OF DIEMEN

On the twenty-third, at daybreak, we had knowledge of the land which remained to us from north-north-east to east-north-east. But it was so covered with fog that we could distinguish its form with difficulty. Our dead reckoning put us about eight leagues from it. The part of coast which we had in sight was high and would no doubt have offered us a pleasant aspect, if the weather had been clearer. Nevertheless, we crowded on sail to approach it more closely and at eight o'clock, having come alongside it, we took the south-west cape of the Land of the Island of Diemen at north 10° west at about two and a half to three leagues distance. The Maatsuiker Islands of Tasman then remained to us to the east-north-east, three leagues according to our dead reckoning, and the Mewstone of Furneaux to the east.

Our position being well determined, we made course to double this last rock, which we passed to the south at a very small distance, and we steered then more to the north to close with the land. The weather, although in squalls, was fairly fine during the morning and as a good breeze blew, we reached about noon the most southern cape of the land of which I have just spoken. As we coasted along quite near all that part of the coast comprised between these two capes, I had all the views of it taken and I hope that they will not be without interest.

At noon, the Mewstone of which we still had knowledge remained to us at south 68° west. The land nearest to us at north 61° west and the south cape at north 49° 45' east. The northernmost lands in sight were visible from north to 54° east.

My intention being to enter the Bay of the Search in order to take shelter there from the bad weather with which we were threatened, I rallied the Naturaliste and gave him orders to proceed ahead under easy canvas, the weather not permitting us to put boats out to guide us to the anchorage. But the plan which M. d'Entrecasteaux gives of it appearing to us made with the greatest care, we (sic) gave it all confidence and followed it.

However, as the Naturaliste had orders to sound continually while making course and was about a mile and a half from us who were steering in his waters and sounding also without finding bottom at fifteen fathoms, we were very surprised to see him arrive suddenly and take at once starboard tack closing with the wind to the best. We then had the Sterile Islands in sight at a small distance. We at once imitated the Naturaliste's manoeuvre and took, like him, starboard tack to double to windward the Green Islands. The weather then had the worst appearance and the squalls were so strong that, although we had only the topsails and foresail, the vessel had as much sail as she could carry.

After having risen to windward of the Sterile Islands and having doubled them, the Naturaliste bore away to double the channel. On my part, I had a second reef taken in the topsails and was still undecided if I should enter by giving up the anchorage of the Search which it was no longer possible to gain. The weather was always bad and the land so hidden by rain that one could hardly distinguish it. But at about two o'clock, the squalls and the rain which hid it from our view, as well as from the Naturaliste's, found me in the middle of the channel and closer to the Island of Entrecasteaux than to the mainland. Then I decided to enter the channel. The Naturaliste being about two leagues ahead. We therefore entered the narrow channel to gain the anchorage of the Great Bay which I had indicated to the Naturaliste in case of separation.

In coasting along the Island of Entrecasteaux, we saw at its northern extremity a band of fifteen to twenty natives who came to the seashore to see us pass. They stood for some time collected together, appearing to make signs which we could not quite understand. But as we were making great progress, we soon lost sight of them. The lead until then had not brought us bottom at twenty fathoms. After having doubled the Island of Partridges, we perceived the Naturaliste at anchor and came to place ourselves near him, in the place marked on the plan of the Great Bay by twenty three fathoms with mud bottom.

It is doubtless difficult to see anything better made than the plan which Citizen Beaupré, geographical engineer of this expedition, gives of it, and one may be assured that he has left nothing to be done for those who may succeed him and who will come to recognize this part of the strait.

As soon as we were established on our anchor, Captain Hamelin came on board and he informed me of the motives which had prevented him from entering the Bay of the Search. A bank of rocks which was before him, being at five fathoms depth, had made him fear to run aground in trying to pass one side or the other. In consequence, he preferred to direct his course to windward of the Green or Sterile Islands in order to arrive and enter the channel.

We agreed together that, from the next day, his cutter would proceed to the Port of Hope and visit it in order to assure ourselves that the English had made no establishment there and if there were any convenient places to procure water. Mine was destined to go to recognize the Huon River and the Port of Swans.

Towards the end of the day, we saw several fires in different parts of this Great Bay in which one finds oneself as in a basin although a strong wind blew from south to south-west. The sea was calm there and it must never be agitated no matter whence the winds come. The prospect of this anchorage is extremely agreeable, a thing of which one may judge by the view which I give of it.

We decided also, M. Hamelin and I, that the next day we would go to visit the coast and the natives, if however they would consent to be approached. We also had great interest in seeing if in this anchorage there were any good places to cast a fishing net.

During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth, the weather was continually bad and rainy. Very strong squalls passed over us, but we did not drag our anchor having only to hold against the force of the wind and no swell. We had sixty fathoms of cable out.
1802-01-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 3.45 the land was sighted in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander at once. At 4 we signalled it again. At 4.30 filled and stood on and closed the land, which we made out to be the SW cape of Van Diemen's Land. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30' W, 10 miles off; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 56° E, 4 miles off; and the Mewstone S 85° E, 5 miles off. At noon took the bearing of the South Cape N 48° E, 4 miles off, and the Mewstone S 67° 30' W. Latitude by account 43° 33' 6", the same by the bearing 43° 44' 0"; longitude by account 143° 50' 22", the same by the bearing 144° 30' 0". Running very close along Van Diemen's Land and shaping our course to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel. At half past noon we spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. Several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 breakers were sighted ahead at a short distance (these breakers are marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart and lie between the south point of Anse des Ormiers and the Sterile Islands). The captain, who took them for canoes of the Aboriginal people coming aboard, said "let her come to port"; and I, who had the watch, repeated his order and had it carried out by the helmsman, who kept hauling his tiller to port. But a few minutes later, being already almost in the wash of the breakers, everyone having cried out that we were on the breakers, we hauled smartly to the wind on the starboard tack and weathered the Sterile Islands handsomely. The commander, who was keeping astern at some distance, followed our movement. At 3.15, being a little offshore, we bore away for Cape Bruny. The commander, who at that moment was taking in reefs, held his wind a while longer and at last shaped his course as we had. Having reached the mouth of the channel, we ran in; and after doubling Pointe Labillardière and the NE point of Partridge Island, we hauled to the wind to gain the anchorage of the Grande Anse in Bruny Island. At 4.15 we let go the anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud, under Partridge Island, Huon Island bearing S 88° E, Lahaye Island N 51° W, and the north point of Partridge Island N 82° W. At 4.45 the commander anchored S 30° E of us, two cables off. We asked his leave to put the boats in the water and to send one aboard him, which he granted. The boats were put in the water and we sent for the Géographe's doctors to see Citizen Milius, who was still ill. I went with the captain aboard the Géographe and had the pleasure of embracing my friends. The dinghy went fishing under Partridge Island and came back without having taken anything.

1802-01-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, standing in to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel and running very close along the land. At noon spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. We crowded sail; several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 we sighted several lines of breakers ahead. We at once hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack to weather the Sterile Islands; the Géographe followed our movement. At 3.45 we bore away for Cape Bruny; having reached the mouth of the channel we ran in and made for the anchorage of Grande Anse. At 4.15 we let go the starboard anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud. Bearings of the anchorage: the point of Partridge Island S 82° W; Lahaye Island N 54° W; Huon Island S 88° E. At 5 a.m. the longboat was sent off to look for a watering place.
1802-01-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.

On the twenty-fourth, early in the morning, our boats departed, as we had agreed the day before and I gave in writing to M. Freycinet the following instructions:

At the anchorage of the Great Bay, Channel of Entrecasteaux.

To Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant of the Ship,

"I entrust to you, citizen, the command of my cutter to go to visit several places, which, although already well determined in the reconnaissance made of them by General d'Entrecasteaux, may offer us different objects of curiosity and natural history.

"In consequence of this resolution, Citizens Péron and Guichenot will accompany you on this excursion as well as Messieurs Barbe and Lesueur. I invite you therefore to facilitate the means for them to render the duty they are about to perform with you as useful as will be possible to you.
