"Leaving the ship, you will direct your course towards the Huon River and after entering its mouth, you will land at the Port of Swans where you will remain some time in order to procure for us birds of that species.

"I think that two days will be sufficient for the excursion you are about to make. Thus, you will only take provisions for that space of time.

"I do not need to recommend to you an always active vigilance for the safety of the cutter and of all those who accompany you. But if you encounter natives, which is very probable, it is absolutely forbidden to you to commit any hostility towards them unless the safety of someone in particular or of all in general depends on it. The inhabitants of this country are, from what is known of their character, not wicked, unless one provokes them. It is therefore by benefits and gifts that you should predispose them in our favour.

"You will not forget to see if there is some convenient place to procure water and to make soundings and bearings of the places where you land." Signed N. B.

At the departure of M. Freycinet, I had delivered to him mirrors, beads, snuff-boxes, axes, knives &c &c and recommended to him economy and impartiality in the distributions he might make of them.

At about eight o'clock, I embarked in my great boat, accompanied by Citizens Laridon, surgeon, and Bernier, astronomer, to go on shore. The small boat in which were Messrs. Ronsard, Bougainville and Petit, draughtsman, was also of the party. Passing astern of the Naturaliste, Captain Hamelin joined us.

It was not without difficulty that we succeeded in reaching the land, in that a strong wind blew from the south-west and a strong current carried us considerably to the south-east. However, after rowing with force for about an hour and a half, we disembarked on the Island of Partridges of which we were only one mile distant, from the anchorage of the ships. After disembarking, we wished to traverse the island in its breadth, but we were not long in being obliged to regain the seashore, so difficult and encumbered by grass and brush we found the path. The woods of this island are of fine growth and high. Most are of the species of eucalyptus, but we encountered only few plants in flower. When we had succeeded in regaining the seashore, we followed the shore, walking continually on rocks at the foot of which the sea was beating, and of the nature of granite. We found a ball of granite fairly curious for its shape, having absolutely the form and size of a twelve-pound shot. A little time after, we perceived three persons from the Naturaliste, it was Monsieur Leschenault and two men of the crew of that vessel who had landed before us. They were in the middle of four natives and all were walking together. Although they came towards us, we quickened our pace to accost them sooner. The natives who had followed them until then, intimidated no doubt by the number, retired into the wood and we lost sight of them.

M. Leschenault informed us that having been to the end of the island, they had crossed by wading the small channel which separates it from that of Entrecasteaux and they came directly to him making many gestures which announced confidence and without any design to harm and that, moreover, they were without any kind of arms. As soon as they had approached, M. Leschenault took their hand, caressed them and gave them some gifts. Confidence was quickly established with them and from then on, they accompanied this naturalist everywhere he went sometimes speaking to each other, sometimes singing. One of them, who was wearing a necklace of fairly well polished shells, made him a present of it.

Having left Monsieur Leschenault to continue his course, we continued ours in order to go to recognize a sand beach which appeared to us suitable to cast a fishing net. The natives who had kept to the wood reappeared then and came to accost us without the least suspicion. We took their hand and caressed them as M. Leschenault had done and gave them also some trifles as gifts. There were only three, the others had taken another route but they were not long in coming to rejoin their companions and to make us great signs of friendship. Some of us who were eating biscuit gave a piece to each of those who were around us, but they made little account of it as well as of bread.

We could understand nothing of the long speeches they made to us, but their signs were much more intelligible and we understood perfectly that they were telling us to follow them to join their companions who were on the other side of the water. We therefore walked together until the end of the island, but we did not think it proper to accompany them further in that it was necessary to put ourselves into the water up to the middle of the body to cross the channel which separates this from the great one. Most of the objects that we had appeared to tempt them greatly, and they would have had great pleasure in seeing us give them our clothes. These men were naked from head to foot. Only one had a piece of skin which covered part of his shoulders and loins. Their colour is much less dark than that of the negroes of Africa. And perhaps it is because they do not find themselves dark enough that they paint different parts of the face with charcoal. All were tattooed from the shoulder to about six inches below. The lines were circular and some lengthwise. For the rest, they had nothing disagreeable in their face. Their physiognomy was merry and even gay, the look lively, the nose a little flat, the mouth large, fine white teeth well arranged, without any defect if, however, their great width is not one. Their stature did not appear to us below five feet two inches nor above five feet six. The proportions of the body well taken but the legs weak and thin with little calf. They could have been from twenty five to forty years old.

After they had left us to join their companions, we retraced our steps, having recognized that one could cast a fishing net conveniently in that place and perhaps even with advantage, the bottom being not considerable and of fine sand. A second band of six or seven natives who had also communicated with our people remaining in charge of the boats were returning with the gifts that had been made to them and which they were carrying at the neck. One had placed a jacket that a sailor had given him, a piece of flag cloth &c &c.

Among those who made up this latter band, two were remarkable for the elegance of their costume, one who had the skin of a kangaroo or some other animal, had the shoulders and breast covered up to the navel. His head seemed to us covered with a kind of cap in the form of a wig which we long thought was made of seaweed. But having examined it more closely, we recognized that it was his hair which, divided into small bands five to six lines wide and about an inch long and fastened by grease and reddish-brown earth formed a cap around his head which every movement he made agitated in different ways. The other, who was quite naked had only his head shaved and a cord of hair which went round it.

We brought back from this excursion many mussels of which the form differs from ours, some limpets not very curious and several abalone shells as well as different species of nerites. We collected three or four shells that are not known to us but of a very small size.

As we had not brought anything to dine on shore, we all embarked at four o'clock to go on board.

I forgot to remark that when we wished to try to pass to the other side of the island by crossing through the woods, we encountered trees of prodigious size and most of them were burnt up to seven or eight feet high, the fire had been directed with symmetry and the space that had been hollowed out by means of fire could easily contain eight to ten persons. All the openings were without exception sheltered from the south to the north by the west. One also encounters in the wood several of these great trees that the winds have knocked down and their direction always had the head of the tree pointing to the north, undeniable proof that the winds from south-west, west and north-west are more violent from this part than from any other point of the compass.

The birds seemed to gather there in great number, several had a very pleasant song. However, parrots and macaws seem to be the dominant species. I do not know why this island has been named the Island of Partridges, for we saw none. Although we had travelled over a fairly considerable extent, we only killed a thrush and a parrot.

Judging of the heights of the tide by the mark left by the sea, it must rise to four or five feet when it is at its greatest height.

The night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth was like the preceding ones. A strong wind blew from south to south-south-west, in strong squalls mingled with rain.
1802-01-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to WSW, with squalls and rain. At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat to water in Port Espérance or in the Huon River; Citizens Freycinet, lieutenant, Faure, surveyor, and Bailly, mineralogist, took the opportunity to come along. At 8 the captain and some of the officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island and communicated with the Aboriginal people. The dinghy went fishing and took nothing. In the evening all the boats (except the longboat) came back aboard. An inclination of 68° 36' 0" was observed in the Grande Anse.

At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat, manned with 7 men and provisioned for 2 days, to water in Port Espérance; and should I be unable to water there, I was to go to the Huon River. Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly came with me. The weather was overcast and squally with rain; a good breeze from the south carried me to Port Espérance in very little time. I closed the south point and ran along the coast within a boathook's length. I went into the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream; the longboat touched, and having got off without difficulty, I landed on the starboard point with Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly. We made for the stream; it was dry, with only brackish water in a few holes. Having re-embarked, I crossed the harbour to look for another stream marked on the chart abreast of the first. I tried to land thereabouts, but it was impossible (the shore being foul, and the longboat touching on a muddy sand bottom at some distance from the beach). I ran along the shore and saw a trickle of water running over the sand; seeing no convenience for watering there, I decided to go to the Huon River. The wind was a strong breeze in puffs and very variable; I beat for 3 hours between Lahaye Island and the north point. At last I put the men to the oars, and having doubled the north point with great difficulty, I made sail and shaped my course for the Huon River. I closed and ran along the right bank. At sunset, finding myself abreast of Port des Cygnes, I went in after doubling the second point to starboard. I sighted the Géographe's longboat in a cove; I bore up for her and landed beside her. I learnt that when the longboat had come alongside the shore, several Aboriginal people had run up with cries of joy, that the eldest (probably the head of the family) had thrown his arms round the neck of Citizen Freycinet the elder, commanding the longboat, and that they had taken him to their huts.

After searching the cove without finding water, I came back to the boats, where I found Freycinet the elder and 6 Aboriginal people: 2 men, a young woman and 3 little boys. The elder of the men had a short, curly beard; their hair was woolly and smeared with a kind of red grease. The two men and the woman, who must have had hair on their private parts, had shaved it. The woman had her face smeared with black; and to show us how she blackened it she rubbed both hands on a burnt tree, puffed out her cheeks and drew her hands over them from her ears to her nose and eyes. She then wanted to do as much to each of us. They each had a kangaroo skin which covered their shoulders only. The men did not appear to us jealous; they let us caress the young woman, who seemed to take some pleasure in it. We loaded them with presents; they took everything eagerly and, without examining it, handed it to the woman, who stowed it in her kangaroo skin. Several times I tried to make them look in a mirror and held it before their eyes, but they at once turned away sharply. I also tried to show them the use of knives by cutting wood in front of them; they paid no attention and threw themselves on the knife to get it, and as soon as they had it they gave it to the woman. The only thing that held their attention was a tricolour plume I had on my hat; I gave it to the younger of the men, who at once put it in his hair, and the elder seemed vexed that I had not given it to him. Before we arrived they had stolen a bottle of brandy from the Géographe's longboat and hidden it in a hollow tree, where the boat's crew, who had seen them do it, recovered it. When we re-embarked, all of them (except the eldest) got into my longboat; but we had scarcely shoved off when the eldest called them, and they took to the water. They made signs to us as long as we could see them.

I passed the night, with the Géographe's longboat, in a very fine cove next to the last. At daybreak the Freycinets and I went round it on foot, hoping to find fresh water there. We found several streams, which we went up; the water was drinkable only too far from their mouths for the ships to water there, though we filled a few breakers. After our round we re-embarked. Freycinet the elder sounded the cove, and I shaped my course for the head of the harbour, running along the land within a boathook's length. Having reached it, I ran along the shore to port, and seeing no stream I resolved to return aboard, having only two meals' provisions left. I gave the order to steer out of the harbour. A short distance from where we had passed the night I met the Géographe's longboat standing for the head of the harbour. Freycinet the elder hailed me and asked what I was about; I answered that I was going back aboard. He told me he was going to dine at the head of the harbour on a swan he had just shot. Whereupon Freycinet the younger, without warning me, gave the coxswain orders to steer for the head of the harbour; we set our sails and chased swans. Right at the head of the harbour the water shoaled suddenly and we grounded on soft mud. We rowed, poled, got off, and grounded again. Citizen Freycinet had taken the tiller and I had taken an oar. We had been rowing some minutes when I gave the order to pole; Citizen Freycinet appeared displeased and spoke harshly to me. The boat's crew did not know which of the two to obey. I observed to Citizen Freycinet that the captain, having entrusted the longboat to me, had thought me capable of handling her and that I answered for her. He said no more; I repeated the order I had given, and shortly afterwards the longboat was afloat. I had her anchored to give the crew a moment's rest and let them dine. I then had it out with Citizen Freycinet, and the longboat being out of all danger, I offered to hand over the command of her to him. He took it. We landed near the Géographe's people and dined there. In the evening we left in company with the Géographe's boat, and on the 26th [Nivôse, 16 January 1802] at 5 a.m. we arrived aboard. I reported to the captain what had passed. He blamed Citizen Freycinet's conduct and told me I had been wrong to give up the command of the longboat to him.

1802-01-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and a strong breeze from S to SSW. All the boats were back except the longboat.
1802-01-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-fifth, in the morning, despite the breeze still being very strong and winds from the south varying to the south-west, the large and small boats commanded by Citizens Bonnefoy and Ransonnet departed to go fishing and received orders to proceed to the place designated to them. As I was very convinced that the natives who were in the neighbourhood would not fail to go and find them, I had them given some trifles to maintain good understanding. This being the only means to employ in such circumstances, I even recommended to each of these officers to give them a little of our catch if it was abundant, and yet to always remain on their guard.
Citizen Maugé, although still very ill, wished to go ashore and indeed he went, despite all the representations I made to him about his situation and the dangers to which he would be exposed by the inclemency of the air and the state of the atmosphere charged with moist and unhealthy vapours for people even in good health. However, none of these considerations could detain him. Without regard for the consequences that might result, he set out. The astronomer Bernier
also departed to observe the latitude of this cove, the declination of the magnetic needle and its inclination. From the manner in which the natives had behaved the previous day, I was content to place two sailors with their arms in the large boat, this means of defence appearing sufficient to me for the safety of all those who departed.
After the departure of my two boats, Captain Hamelin went down to the place where they were to seine; I had agreed the previous day to be there also, but the weather which appeared rainy had such a bad appearance that I preferred to remain on board to put in order various things I had to do.
At one o'clock, one of the boats returned with very few fish of the species of plaice and rays, and the catch was very little abundant. The small boat could not return at the same moment because it had run aground. The large boat also had the same fate from the little attention of the officer commanding it. While those were occupied with the fishing, the natives of the country assembled in great numbers at the place our people had chosen to haul the seine ashore. Men, women and children and Europeans all were mingled and without mistrust of each other and without fear. The boat which had remained aground being alone ashore, there were only six of our men there and the natives, all told, were more than fifty. A great fire was lit and all having gathered around it, they were asked to sit, which they did immediately, and the best of understanding reigned between them and the boatmen. This occasion was taken to draw several of them, whose portraits will be found in the journal. But we could not succeed in obtaining those of the women and children, in that they could not remain a moment in the same place, like the children, but for the men, they were more docile and we easily succeeded in capturing the character of their features well.
At three o'clock, the small boat being back, I blamed Citizen Bonnefoy strongly for having run aground, he threw the blame on the guardians of the boat, which is always the custom, for officers never wish to be at fault. However, this imprudence was the cause that Acting-Ensign Maurouard, whom I had attached to the astronomer, received a spear thrust at the very moment when preparations were being made to embark. He was struck in the lateral part of the neck on the right and traversed it entirely in a horizontal direction, appearing to have run only under the skin. This spear was undoubtedly vigorously thrown, for it passed through a double woollen waistcoat, and it is unknown whence it came. The wound did not appear dangerous to the physicians and they hoped that he would soon be cured of it. It appeared to me, however, considerable enough that I did not have the same opinion.
It is difficult enough to be able to guess what might have caused the beginning of hostility, for from the reports that each made to me in particular, it appears that the best of understanding reigned constantly between the two parties. A quarter of an hour before embarking, all the natives had indeed disappeared, but as they departed laden with presents and very joyful, one was far from suspecting anything of it.
As soon as the spear thrust was launched, Citizens Bonnefoy and Maurouard, who were armed with muskets, mounted an elevation to see if they would discover anything, and indeed saw seven or eight of the natives armed with spears, but who made no movement upon perceiving them. Orders were given to everyone to proceed on board the boat, which was then afloat, and they themselves then came to embark without having been (pursued) in any manner.
The more I reflected upon this unexpected accident to find its cause, the less
it was easy for me to find it, and unless the detail of which I am about to speak gave rise to it, one would without doubt have to attribute it to perfidy and to the little fear that those who were still ashore had inspired in them.
While everyone was gathered around the fire, awaiting the return of the tide, Citizen Maurouard, strong and vigorous, wished to exercise his strength with the one of the natives whom he judged the strongest of the band. He first began by grasping his wrist in the manner in which young men do it in Europe, making a sign to his opponent to oppose him with as much resistance as possible, which he understood very well, but he could not resist the opposition offered by Maurouard. After this first success, the two athletes seized each other by the body in order to see which of the two would throw the other. Maurouard was again the victor and threw the other to the ground. As this scene took place on the sand, the fall could not be dangerous for either of them. Everything moreover passed off in laughter and the vanquished appeared more pleased with his fall than the victor with his triumph.
However, it seems probable to me that the natives, seeing their companion vanquished by strength, would have sought afterwards to make known that they were not vanquished by skill and cunning, and that it is perhaps what gave rise to the spear which had been thrown, since it was the only one that left. It is not however to be presumed that they wished us to answer with a musket shot, for they are very much afraid of that weapon, only when one touches it.
If one is to believe several persons' word, the women took different forms and means to attract some of them aside, and the signs they made them were too expressive to be mistaken about their intentions. Some boatmen of the Naturaliste even affirmed that, having followed some of them, they had completely satisfied their curiosity, but not their desires.
It was remarked, for the second time, that the natives would neither eat nor drink anything of what our people brought ashore with them, but those who, at the beginning of their arrival, were in the boat of the Naturaliste stole everything that came under their hand, even to the keys of the benches. A child of about fifteen to eighteen years of age had received for his share a marline-spike which he had put around his body by means of the rope attached to it. Although he had taken the precaution of hiding the iron under his kangaroo skin, it was discovered by the rope. The marline-spike was taken from him, which made him weep much. Then one of the elders of the band struck him rather roughly while speaking to him very quickly, and he ceased his lamentations. As we could not hear what was being said to him, we could not know whether he was reproaching him for the theft he had made or whether he was blaming him for not having been more clever, which is all too likely from the desire they show to seize everything we had. They took, in our boat, an empty bottle which was left to them.
One of our sailors having exchanged with one of them his jacket for a kangaroo skin, at once put it around his neck and withdrew aside. His first care was to cut off all the buttons, and then he abandoned the jacket which the sailor took back on embarking. Another to whom a long cloth pair of trousers had been given was so embarrassed in it that he had all the trouble in the world to reach a tree about twenty-five paces from him. He quickly rid himself of this cumbersome garment there and did not even wish to take the buttons, which they appeared to be very fond of.
Citizen Bonnefoy exchanged with a woman his necklace for a small mirror. The medallion of this necklace was an English penny and a metal button. But one could
not know at what time she had received it. Looking at herself in the mirror that had just been given to her, she made all sorts of grimaces, the repetition of which appeared to amuse her greatly, and then she withdrew aside with a child she was nursing to smear herself with charcoal, and then came to show herself in her new attire, so true is it that in all the countries of the world, women neglect no means to please or seduce.
At sunset, the sky having cleared up greatly, the winds calmed and we had the appearance of change. Only, we had reason to fear seeing the winds pass to the north, taking from the east. For I was resolved to change position as soon as the return of my boats, which I expected at the latest in the night. M. Hamelin, who came on board in the evening, was informed of this disposition.
During the night, the winds passed to the north, as the appearances had announced to us, and the breeze was very light. The boat arrived at about two o'clock in the morning, and as I had warned that I be informed when it appeared, I received these gentlemen and saw with regret that their expedition had not had the success I had expected of it.
1802-01-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to W. The captain and the officers landed on Bruny Island and came back aboard at noon.

1802-01-16.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the wind fell away a great deal. In the afternoon the breeze varied from SSW to W, N and NNE. At 6.30 a.m. the longboat was back, not having been able to find a convenient place to water.
1802-01-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-sixth, in the morning, the winds being from the north varying to the north-north-east, there was no way to set sail. So that this day would not be entirely lost, I had the carpenters go ashore to cut wood and make the replacements of which we might have need in this matter.
As there had been little order the previous day among the people who had been fishing, and as soon as anyone was ashore, they would go wherever they wished without permission and according to their whim, I judged it convenient to remedy this inconvenience, and to prevent it in the future, I gave to M. Ronsard, who was charged with this task, the following instruction:
"The Commandant et cetera,
"To Citizen Ronsard, lieutenant of the ship at sea on board the Géographe.
"You will take, citizen, the command of the boat to proceed to the same place where we went together the day before yesterday. The object of your mission is to have it filled with firewood and to return immediately on board. The facility you will find in this work means it should be neither long nor difficult, and so that it may be completed more promptly, you will employ everyone on it. While the carpenters cut it, the others will transport it on board, and under no pretext, be it for fishing, hunting or otherwise, will you suffer anyone to stray out of your sight.
"The Acting-Ensign Baudin who accompanies you will supervise the sailors for the transport of the wood, whilst you and the two gunners I give you will protect the workers, should the natives wish to trouble you. The purpose of the task you are about to undertake is therefore to attend solely to this work and to return on board as soon as it is completed, or even sooner if I give you the signal.
"I hope that you will place the boat in a position so as not to fear that it will run aground".
Signed N. B.
After the departure of the boat, I asked M. Hamelin, who was on board, to send his to the same place and for the same purpose, and I then invited him to have Citizen Faure, geographer, embarked in his boat to go to sound
in all directions the cove of our anchorage, which does not appear to have been sounded when General d'Entrecasteaux had it surveyed.
Several of the naturalists also went ashore to make researches relating to their knowledge, but as I had visited this place the previous day, it seemed to me they would find nothing of great importance there.
In the afternoon, we had a very strong squall with rain in abundance and thunder without stint. This squall lasted a good hour and our workers ashore must have been greatly inconvenienced by it. I learned with sorrow that M. Depuche, who is only just entering convalescence, was there, having proceeded there in a boat of the Naturaliste. This mineralogist, little reasonable in this circumstance, has undoubtedly not reflected upon the unfortunate accidents which might be the consequence of his imprudence. His action, which he wishes to call zealous, and which to me appears to merit a quite different appellation, has decided me to allow him to do in the future whatever may please him according to his way of reasoning. The little account he makes of our advice regarding what concerns his life relieves me of the necessity of continuing them.
A little before sunset, all the boats were back on board their respective vessels, and I warned Captain Hamelin that we would set sail the following day, if the weather permitted, so as to advance as far as possible in the channel to gain the port of the north-west, where I reckoned to remain to replace my water.
The night of the 27th to the 28th (sic) had nothing particular, the winds were always in the west to north-west quarter with strong gusts and often rain.
It had been remarked during the day that the natives were no longer in our neighbourhood, for no one was seen and not even any of their fires. Captain Hamelin, who had proceeded to the northern extremity of this cove to sound its contour, met there about thirty of them who, seeing his boat approach the coast, believed, no doubt, that he wished to disembark there, and seemed to wish to oppose it. All were armed with spears, and so that they should not lack this weapon, several could be distinguished carrying large bundles of them. One of them who walked ahead had in his hand a burning firebrand by means of which he set fire to everything wherever they passed. Which, I believe, is quite their custom when they wish to warn or begin war amongst themselves.
1802-01-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW. At 5 a.m. I came back aboard with the longboat without having been able to water, either in Port Espérance or in Port des Cygnes. In the latter I had a dispute with Citizen Freycinet and handed over the command of the longboat to him (see my report to the captain). At 8 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, was sent off in the large boat to sound the inner part of the Grande Anse. Our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went for firewood on Partridge Island; the sick were sent there to walk about a little. I took the opportunity to go shooting on the island. At 4 p.m. the weather turned overcast and stormy and the wind freshened from the WNW. Our longboat being loaded, we made haste to leave so as to reach the ship before the storm broke; but we were scarcely halfway when the wind came on to blow hard, with a high sea, thunder, lightning and pouring rain. We did not take in an inch of sail; two cables from the ship the foremast broke off level with the collar, and before the grapnel and its rope could be got ready we drove and anchored in the ship's wake. At 6, the breeze having fallen a great deal, we came aboard. Citizen Faure came back in the large boat at nightfall. The draught was taken: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 10 feet 10 inches, difference 1 foot 1 inch. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman of the Géographe, in charge of a party in a boat, received a spear wound in the shoulder on Bruny Island.

1802-01-17.journal_anonyme: The weather, fine enough at first, turned overcast; the wind freshened from the WNW and the storm broke at 4.30 with a great deal of rain. At 5 a.m. the commander made the signal to get under way; at 8.30 we were under sail, and at 10 and at noon we were abreast of Pointe Riche, forming the southern entrance to Isthmus Bay.
1802-01-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-seventh, at five o'clock in the morning, the winds being from the west, fine breeze, we prepared to get under way. I made the same signal to the Naturaliste and we went about after trimming and hoisting our topsails. We reckoned to be soon under sail, but we did not succeed in setting them until half-past seven o'clock, for the anchorage we occupied held so well that we had infinite trouble in weighing our anchor. And we could not accomplish this until after we had already had to set up tackle on the cable. When our anchor was quite high and clear of the water, there was found on it more than a thousand pounds weight of black firm mud, which the water current had neither washed away nor loosened from the anchor.
The Naturaliste experienced the same difficulty. It appears that with good cables, one would be perfectly safe in this anchorage, even with very strong winds.
As soon as we were under sail, we closed with the shore to port so as to keep the wind to enter the channel as far as would be possible. Despite the confidence we ought to have had in the plan of Citizen Beaupré, we always had the soundings at hand and found everywhere those he indicates. It is, as I have already observed, difficult to execute work more exact and more detailed than that of this strait, and with such a plan, one could traverse it by day or night, should the winds permit a direct course.
When we had traversed the large and small coves, as well as a part of the bay of the Isthmus, we came to recognise the small island which is found at no great distance from Cape Legrand. We were obliged to tack to double it, but it was impossible for us to pass Cape Legrand, so we anchored at no great distance from this cape, in nine fathoms of water, bottom of sand and very black mud, at about one mile from a point of the cove which was a little ahead of us and which appeared rather deep. There was found in the northern part of this bay a small island much less large than Green Island and all covered with trees of which the chart makes no mention, no doubt on account of its little importance.
In the passage we made to gain the anchorage we now occupy here, the winds were very inconstant and seemed to follow the direction of the mountains. When there were any gaps from which they could escape, very strong gusts passed, and the next instant we were in a flat calm.
The view is extremely pleasant throughout the entire channel. The mountains are there covered with wood from the sea's edge to their summits, and the different shades of verdure render the landscape very beautiful. One will be able to judge of it from the perspective it affords.
At about three o'clock in the afternoon, I went ashore accompanied by Citizens Bonnefoy and Guichenot. During the three and a half hours we spent there, we made quite a long excursion in the country, without meeting any of the natives. We found there several traces of their sojourns and a single hut, if indeed one can give that name to the shelters they are accustomed to make to put themselves under cover from the wind or rain. From this little excursion we brought back some plants to dry, a very pretty little quadruped that no one knows, and four species of different birds. We saw some quails, two or three ring-doves, and many parrots and parakeets which it was not possible to approach, nor two kangaroos.
The sea-shore offered us nothing of interest in shells or in marine plants. The species that were found there were little abundant and similar to those which we had collected in the Great Cove.
The night had nothing particular and the winds passed to the north-west, which (rendered) them entirely contrary to the course we had to make the following day. We had sometimes rain but the squalls were not long.
1802-01-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to N. At 5 the commander made the signal to get under way. At 9.30 got under way and shaped our course up the channel. We had great difficulty weighing our anchor; we broke a messenger and then rigged a voyol. At noon, being abreast of Isthmus Bay, the wind headed us; we beat until 2.30 without being able to weather Green Island. The commander then having anchored east of Green Island, we anchored in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand, Pointe Legrand bearing N 3° W, the Géographe and the middle of Green Island N 22° E, Pointe Riche S 33° E, and Satellite Island from S 15° W to S 22° W. Citizen Faure went to sound the channel; he saw a seal on Green Island. Several officers and naturalists landed on Van Diemen's Land abreast of the anchorage.

1802-01-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze with strong gusts at intervals from W to NW. Being near Green Island, we anchored on the opposite side of the channel in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand. Satellite Island bore from us S 15° W to S 22° W; Pointe Riche S 33° E; the middle of Green Island N 22° E; Pointe Legrand N 3° W. Pointe Legrand bore from us N 22° E, past Green Island.
1802-01-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-eighth, in the morning, it was impossible to set sail, the winds being north-west and very variable. We had, in the morning, some quite violent squalls. Nevertheless, I ordered Citizen Bernier to be taken to Cape Legrand to obtain its latitude by means of an artificial horizon and to observe the declination of the needle there. After his departure, the cutter equally conveyed to shore Citizen Péron and Mr. Freycinet, one of my officers. We had seen, during the night, no fire that might inform us in what place the natives might be found.
In the afternoon, the (sky was) very cloudy and had a very bad appearance. (Large) squalls from north-west to west made themselves felt, and one, more more (sic)particularly than the others, since it put us adrift despite our anchor being on good ground and we having out seventy fathoms of cable. Being unable to keep the vessel steady by letting out more cable, we were obliged to moor a second anchor with sixty fathoms and we held firm. But we had lost more than half a league in drifting, which made our sailing quite difficult, if the winds did not change direction.
Around four o'clock in the afternoon, the sky, which had been until then very rainy, appeared to be inclined to clear up. The Naturaliste, which was at anchor in the southern part of Green Island and which, like us, had been set adrift by the squalls which had passed, took advantage of the winds which had come from the west, a fresh breeze, and easily rounded Cape Legrand; but our position not being as advantageous as his, we could not do the same and had to resolve to pass the night where we were.
According to the observations of Citizen Bernier taken before and after noon, Cape Legrand would be found at the latitude of (no figures)
The declination of the needle was observed to be (no figures)
Before the night, which appeared to be likely to be passable, I had the anchor weighed which the squalls had obliged me to moor in the evening. We also passed our preventers in case it became necessary to brace up the upper masts.
Citizen Péron brought back little from his excursion and I knew in advance that the shore did not produce much in shells or marine animals. The botanical products were the same as those we had already encountered, but our hunters were more successful and supplied us with five or six species of birds.
The night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth had nothing particular, the sky was quite fine and the wind calm save for a few cats' paws. No fire was seen in our entire horizon.
1802-01-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to NW in gusts, with rain. Despite the bad weather we ran out a warp towards Pointe Legrand and hauled in on it, being obliged to let go the bower anchor in heavy gusts. At 5 the wind hauled to the W and drew round to WSW. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port; at 7 doubled Pointe Legrand and at 7.45 Pointe Gicquel. At 8 we anchored at the entrance of the North West Port, Pointe Legrand bearing S 12° W, Pointe Gicquel S 25° W, Pointe Pierson N 36° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.

1802-01-19.journal_anonyme: In the roads of the North West Port, Van Diemen's Land. We warped in towards the anchorage; at 3.30 the breeze got up and we hoisted our topsails, but having dragged our kedge anchor we let go a bower. At 6 p.m. we got under way and anchored at the entrance to the North West Port. Bearings: Pointe Legrand S 12° W; Pointe Gicquel S 25° W; Pointe Pierson N 36° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.
1802-01-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-ninth, we had the winds from the north, very light. Although they were contrary to the course which we needed to make to reach the North-West port where I intended to stop, I ordered the sails to be set from four o'clock in the morning to take a better position than the one we occupied. We succeeded, by tacking from side to side, in rounding Cape Legrand, and we would have continued to advance further into the channel if the winds had not failed us. At ten o'clock, being in a flat calm and the current contrary, we anchored on the larboard shore, in eleven fathoms of water, muddy bottom. The Naturaliste was at about the same position but about a league ahead of us. After anchoring, we let out twenty-five fathoms of cable and we kept our topsails hoisted to be ready to sail if the wind should permit it during the day.
The sky was very fine throughout the morning, and the sun very hot. It was truly summer weather, and this day became for us the most agreeable we had had for a long time.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, a small breeze from the north-west springing up, we set sail again. Although the current was contrary to us, I hoped to be able to approach the entrance of the port before nightfall. We tacked accordingly, but with little success. We were even carried by the current into the bight of the bay which is found in the western part of Entrecasteaux Island, and we approached the land near enough to fear we should be obliged to anchor there, which would have been indispensable if, around four o'clock in the evening, the direction of the current had not changed. We were then able to extricate ourselves from this bight, and around six o'clock we succeeded in gaining the Naturaliste, alongside which we anchored. A short time after, Captain Hamelin, who had arrived the previous day at the entrance of this port, informed me that he had had it explored by his boats, that the plan of it was very accurate, but that in the ravines one had not found the rivers which are indicated upon it. This news was all the more disagreeable to me as I had chosen this place only on the certainty I had that fresh water should be found there, and even in abundance.
As we were in essential need of replacing that which we had consumed since our departure from Timor, not knowing whether in the other parts of the coast which we had to visit we should have the means of obtaining it, I resolved to send to explore the North River. The various streams which the plan indicates seemed to us likely to furnish some. The large boat of the Naturaliste, the best of all our boats, was ordered to undertake this duty which was to last two days. And Mr. Breton received orders to depart the next day at daybreak.
The place where we were was very well inhabited. Fires could be seen at every point of the coast and in abundance. However, several boats of the Naturaliste which approached them could not communicate with the natives. They fled at their approach, and it was never possible to join them. We also saw several of them cross in canoes from the mainland to Entrecasteaux Island. One of these canoes in which there were four men advanced within musket shot of the Naturaliste without wishing to approach her further, notwithstanding all the invitations we made to them by presenting them with various objects to induce them to come alongside. We could not well make out whether their oars were paddles or sticks, but they paddled in the same manner as if they had been paddles.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth, the sky was fairly fine, nevertheless there passed some fairly strong squalls from the north-west. We were at anchor in thirteen fathoms on a good muddy bottom.
Bearings of our fourth anchorage in Entrecasteaux Channel:
(no mention of bearings)
1802-01-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW. A dog was heard barking ashore. The Aboriginal people lit many fires at different points of the coast. Officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island to try to communicate with them, but they fled at their approach. The longboat, with a working party, went for firewood to Pointe Gicquel. Two catamarans were seen crossing the channel from Pointe Pierson to Pointe de la Sortie, in one of them four Aboriginal people and in the other six. The captain dredged all the afternoon and took a considerable quantity of scallops. The longboat came back at nightfall loaded with wood. At 6 the Géographe anchored near us.

1802-01-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, winds from N to NNW, a light breeze. The longboat went for wood. The large boat was sent off to the North River.
1802-01-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
The thirtieth, our boats departed the day before at daybreak, as I had agreed with Captain Hamelin the day before. His boat went to the North River like ours, and I gave the command of mine to Citizen Ronsard with the following instruction:
"The Commander to Citizen Ronsard, Lieutenant of the Ship,
"At daybreak you will have the large boat fitted out and will take its command to proceed to the head of the North-West port explored by Mr. d'Entrecasteaux.
"As Mr. Hamelin has had the whole circuit of this port surveyed, he has ascertained that no water is to be found there in this season. Thus you will have nothing to search for in this part. But you will do all you can to obtain swans and that is the sole object of your mission. The plan which has been given to us of this port is, moreover, so accurate that it leaves nothing to be desired for geographical details.
"You will take with you Citizen Barbe and Midshipman Baudin, and you will ship provisions for two days although I do not think you will need them for so long. You will not forget to provide yourself with some glass beads and other trifles to make presents of them to the natives if you should meet with any. Remember well, above all, that you are forbidden to commit any hostility against them, unless the safety of the persons who accompany you should be in jeopardy." Signed N.B.
At the departure of the boats, the weather was very fine, the sky clear, and a fine breeze from the north-west. But in the course of the morning the winds shifted to the south-west, accompanied by rain and very strong squalls. The Naturaliste was set adrift, and in order that the Géographe should not be, I had a second anchor veered out, as much to moderate the gyrations of the vessel which the current caused to rotate in every direction, as to hold better against the force of the wind.
A small tent was also erected on shore for the astronomer in order to be able to observe the eclipse, if possible.
When all was completed, I sent to cast the seine in a pretty little sandy cove about a mile from the ship and which appeared to me very convenient for this purpose. It was situated on the starboard shore, that is, in the northern part of Bruny Island.
We saw fires at different points of the coast throughout the day, but at a fairly great distance from us. The natives did not show themselves in either of the two parts of the coast which we visited. Nevertheless, one penetrated quite far into the interior, especially on the larboard shore.
In the afternoon, the weather, although unfavourable, was finer than it had been in the morning. Our gardener brought back several species of trees and shrubs which were planted to increase those which we had collected elsewhere, and he left in exchange for what he had taken all sorts of stone fruits and vegetable seeds which were placed in the most suitable spots for their rapid growth.
The catch was not abundant, but the little fish that were obtained were of very good quality, as were the lobsters. The birds which were brought back were similar to those we already had. It was only observed that the crows which we had not yet seen were similar to those of Europe, both for their plumage and for their cawing and even their habits. Among the fish, there is a small one quite peculiar in its anterior fins, in that they have a perfect resemblance to hands, and which it uses to fasten itself to the rocks when out of water.
During the night of the thirtieth to the first of Ventôse (sic), the sky cleared and the winds returned to the north-west, varying towards the west. Only a few squalls passed, and of little consequence.
About midnight I heard a boat being hailed. I thought it was my boat returning from the mission with which I had charged it, but I was mistaken; it was simply officers of the ship who, having spent part of the day on board the Naturaliste, were returning at so unseasonable an hour.
Citizen Maugé, who since his relapse had been growing steadily worse and who, despite his condition and my representations, had insisted on going ashore as if he had been in good health, found himself on this day much worse than usual, and I began to fear that his illness might become very serious and that he might not recover from it. The report which the physician has just made to me at this moment is, unfortunately, only too much in accordance with my opinion and my fears.
Citizen Depuche, who regards his excursions as acts of zeal whereas they are nothing but rash, is in worse health than usual, and perhaps he will meet the same end as the others if he continues to pay as little heed as he has done hitherto to the advice which friendship and duty have caused me to give him and which he treats as whim and desire to thwart him.
The other patients are in fairly good condition, with the exception of one of our sailors who is always very weak and languid.
1802-01-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW, with heavy gusts and rain. At 5 the longboat, with a working party, went for wood. At 6 I was sent off in the large boat to go up the North River to look for a watering place for the ships; I was armed with two blunderbusses and four muskets and had 4 days' provisions. At 2 p.m. the ship dragged, veered cable and then let go a second anchor. The yards were sent down and the topgallant masts struck. The longboat came back loaded with wood.

1802-01-21.journal_anonyme: Squally weather. A fresh breeze from WNW with strong gusts and rain. At 2 we dragged and veered 12 fathoms of cable; shortly afterwards let go the port anchor.
1802-01-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first, in the morning, I again dispatched my gig under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy to make a second time the circuit of the North-West port to search for the fresh-water stream indicated on the plan which I had before me. I could not believe that none existed, as had been declared to me by Citizen Hérisson, who had been the first charged with this reconnaissance.
Captain Hamelin, for his part, also departed in his gig to examine very closely the whole larboard shore, even abreast of Green Island, in order to ascertain the existence or otherwise of any one of the rivers which the English had marked in this part on the inaccurate plan which Arrowsmith had given of the channel discovered by Mr. d'Entrecasteaux.
After the departure of these two boats, the astronomer prepared himself for his observation of the next day which was to take place between half past nine in the morning, (sic) Jupiter being to pass over the sun.
The others on board were busy emptying the water from the hold and preparing our water barrels, for I was always persuaded that we should find a place suitable to fill them in the vicinity of our anchorage.
In the morning, the sky was fairly fine and we took advantage of it to send ashore some of our sick in order that they might have a change of air. We saw, as on the preceding days, many places where fires were lit, but we saw none of the natives show themselves on the edge of the shore.
In the afternoon, the sky was finer than it had been in the morning. The winds shifted to west-north-west, varying to north-west with strong squalls and then a flat calm.
About three o'clock, my gig returned on board with the bad news of having found only dry ravines everywhere it had penetrated. A short time after, the boat which had gone to the net also returned and brought enough fish to give to the whole crew. There were especially many little rays very agreeably shaded.
At six o'clock, Citizen Ronsard also returned from hunting swans where he had been since the day before. He brought back two birds of this species, four small ducks or teals, and some land birds similar to those we already had. But he had at last found the fresh-water stream which the others had long and vainly sought. This officer reported to me that in truth it would not be very easy to obtain the quantity of water which each ship needed, but that by clearing a little the entrance of the river obstructed by trees which the torrents, which must occur during winter or the rainy season, had carried there. This news was infinitely pleasant to me in this respect, but it only served to prove to me how little one should rely on the vigilance and accuracy of a search entrusted often to an officer who sees only his speedy return on board when he is charged with a mission which is not agreeable to him.
Captain Hamelin, returning from his excursion, also reported to me having found a small fresh-water stream at a small distance from our anchorage, but it was only a small trickle of water and scarcely suitable for taking in water for two vessels like ours. He perceived, from the signs which he met with, that some European vessels had stopped there and had taken in water, since he saw that several large trees which prevented the boats from approaching the shore had been sawed, others cut with hatchets.
After consulting each other on what remained for us to do, we agreed to enter further into the North-West port and to choose preferably the place found by Mr. Ronsard and indicated on the plan which we had of this port. In consequence, we unmoored immediately with the intention of sailing the next day or of warping if the wind was calm.
The place recognised by Captain Hamelin must be the one which the English had named on Arrowsmith's plan, Annas River, a very unsuitable name for a stream so inconsiderable.
During the night of the first to the second, the sky was fairly fine after the rising of the moon and the cats' paws which passed from time to time were not strong.
1802-01-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW in gusts, with light rain at intervals. At daybreak the captain left in the longboat to look for a watering place. The two anchors were weighed and one let go in 30 fathoms, mud and shell, Pointe Legrand bearing S 13° W, Pointe Gicquel S 61° W, and Pointe de la Sortie N 45° E. At 9 p.m. the captain came back with the longboat; he had not found a watering place, but he brought back a great quantity of oysters, which were distributed to the crew.

1802-01-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WNW to W in strong gusts. The wind having fallen, the commander gave us orders to warp in. At 10 the large boat came back from her mission to the North River; she found there a very convenient watering place.
1802-01-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
The second, from four o'clock in the morning, I again sent Citizen Ronsard to go to make a more exact reconnaissance of the place of which he had spoken to me. As he had recognised the channel at different places and there were several banks which dry out fairly widely at low water, he was ordered to wait until it had retired in order to plant beacons there so that our boats might not run aground in proceeding there.
As soon as the boat departed, the wind being absolutely calm, I ordered a warp to be veered out of five hundred to six hundred fathoms and we hauled upon it after having weighed our bower anchor. During this work we had some cats' paws of short duration, but our lines held fast.
The astronomers had been put on shore from four o'clock in the morning, and I hoped they could easily observe the passage of Jupiter over the sun, the weather being fine at the time when it was to take place.
Having hauled ourselves the length of our warp, we dropped a bower anchor in order to veer out another. But the winds having shifted to the north-east, we immediately took advantage to set sail and by means of our staysails forward and aft we entered this port, but not so far in as I would have wished, in that the calm and the ebb which had just occurred obliged us to drop anchor in the place where we were and which was a good league away from that which we had just left.
The Naturaliste, which was not under way when the wind came for us, was obliged to veer out a second warp, but around five o'clock in the evening a second breeze from the north-east springing up, he had it weighed by his gig and made use of his sails. As it lasted longer than the one we had had at about two o'clock in the afternoon, he entered about half a league further in than we did.
Captain Hamelin coming on board in the evening, we agreed to send the next morning our two large boats on an expedition to make the reconnaissance of which I shall give the detail in tomorrow's entry.
On Citizen Ronsard's return, he informed me that he had marked the whole channel at low water, but that he had observed that the sea had risen much less than the day before. It appeared, according to what he told me, that the boats would not be able to float at low water at the mouth of the river, although there were five to six feet of water in the place where they could land. I put off until the next day to assure myself by myself of what might be, having the intention of going ashore as soon as the boats which I wished to send for an expedition of eight or ten days should have departed. Citizen Ronsard brought back a pelican of very great beauty for the length of its bill and the distribution of its plumage. Its size appeared to us more considerable than those which were known to us, and we did not doubt but that it was a superb specimen for the cabinet of natural history.
On the return of the astronomers, I learned with regret that they had not been able to observe the eclipse,
which had caused me to remain two days at the anchorage which I had just left. They did not attribute the cause to the weather, since the sun was very clear, but to their astronomical telescopes, which they did not find strong enough. It is a fine opportunity lost for the accuracy of the lunar tables.
The night of the second to the third had nothing particular. We saw distinctly several fires in our vicinity and we hoped that the next day it would perhaps be possible to communicate with the natives.
In the expedition which Captain Hamelin had made, he had met two who were crossing in their poor canoe from the great island to that of Entrecasteaux. As soon as they were on shore, they dragged the canoe into the woods and, according to their custom, set fire all along the shore where they passed. It is doubtless from fear that one might perceive on the grass the path which they had taken.
1802-01-22.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNE. By the commander's order we warped into the head of the port. At 5.30 p.m. we got under way with a light breeze from NE and stood into the port. At 6.15 we anchored in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom [corner torn], Pointe Gicquel bearing S 22° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 84° E.

At 10 a.m. I came in from my errand; before coming alongside, the captain ordered me to go and report my mission to the commander. I informed him that I had found a very convenient watering place; he told me that for the present it was of no use to us, because Citizen Ronsard had found a river at the head of the port where we should water. I came back aboard and gave him the following report:

By your orders I left the ship on the 30th Nivôse [20 January 1802] at 6 a.m. in the large boat, armed and provisioned for four days. I was to go up the North River to see what facility there might be for watering the corvettes, and to be back aboard on the morning of the 2nd Pluviôse [22 January 1802]. The weather was fine enough and the wind a fresh breeze from the north; I was obliged to beat at the river's mouth. The weather turned squally and the wind blew hard in gusts from the north with rain. I was reduced to carrying only the foresail and mainsail, both reefed; yet by taking advantage of the wind's small shifts (and probably helped by the tide) I reached by nightfall the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream (on the left bank at the foot of the plateau). I made the boat fast in a little creek to starboard and went with three armed men towards the stream, where I found very good water. The tide was then low; I came back to the boat, and having embarked, I went in with the first of the flood to the head of the cove, hugging the land to starboard close enough to touch the oars on shore, finding 3 fathoms, 2½, 2, 1½ and 1 fathom, where I landed 200 paces from the watering place, afloat; and there I had my breakers filled, and a tierce I had with me. I sounded the cove: I had 5 fathoms in the middle and on the starboard side; the port side is low and muddy. This watering place is very convenient; there is anchorage for the corvettes abreast of the cove in 10 and 15 fathoms, and even in the cove in 5 fathoms. The longboats can come alongside the bank at low water and load there. The only labour would be to roll the casks from the watering place to the boats, over 200 paces of dry, level ground.

I passed the night in this cove, and on the 1st Pluviôse [21 January 1802] at daybreak I left it to go up the river. I had to beat the whole way with a fresh breeze. Having got about 3 miles beyond the place where D'Entrecasteaux's boats had been, and having found from that point 5 fathoms down to 2½, I met a very violent current at a point which hid the river's course from me. Yet the tide was low, for several branches partly sunk in the mud, with shells on them, showed how far the tide rose. I rowed in the middle of the river, along the right bank, along the left bank, without being able to stem the current. I landed on the left bank near the point I had not been able to double, and after walking some time along the river I saw that beyond the point it ran NW and then appeared to divide into two arms, one running N and the other WSW. However much I wished to find the river's source, I thought I ought to stop my survey there: you had fixed the 2nd for my return, and besides my mission was fulfilled, since I had found a watering place. I went down the river and passed the night at the same place as the night before (the Watering Cove). I shot several swans there, and sounded the cove more carefully. At daybreak I left it and reached the ship at 10 a.m. Going down the river I sounded it and found from 10 to 20 fathoms.

On the strength of the report I had made to him, the commander sent off his large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to go up the river. He was favoured by the wind, which he had aft the whole way; the first evening he slept 3 miles above the place where I had been stopped, and met no violent current. He examined the arms I had seen: the WSW one was the river's course, the other only a very large inlet. He went up the river as far as it was navigable by boat and on foot, about 9 miles, without seeing its source.

During our stay in the North West Port the sick were put ashore every fine day; they were given 2 armed men to guard them, and these two men cut firewood for us.

1802-01-23.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from N to NW and NE. At 5.30, being at the end of the warp and the breeze freshening, we got under way under fore-and-aft sails and let go the anchor in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 22° E; Cape de la Sortie E 6° N. We moored east and west.
1802-01-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-third, in the morning, the weather being very fine and the winds almost calm, I dispatched my large boat, of which I gave the command to Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant of the Ship, with the following instruction:
"North-West Port, Entrecasteaux Channel,
"The Commander to Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant of the Ship
"Tomorrow, at daybreak, you will take command of the large boat to go to reconnoitre in detail the North River.
"According to the report which has been made to me, this river which divides into two parts at a small distance from the place where stopped the boats of the Recherche and the Espérance, merits serious attention and it is for this reason that I confide to you the care of this work. In consequence, you will ascend it as far as it will be possible for you to advance, and if, as Midshipman Le Breton declares to me (who was sent there by Captain Hamelin), it divides into two parts, you will choose that which will appear to you the most advantageous or the most navigable and even you will visit both of them if you can contrive to do so.
"You will doubtless find a strong current in the place where the division takes place which has been announced to me and of which I have just spoken to you, but that should not cause you to abandon this reconnaissance unless the want of water oblige you to do so. This current, which is rapid in the middle, will surely be much less rapid on one of the two sides.
"You will embark with you Citizen Péron and a midshipman of whom I leave you the choice. You will take provisions for your men for eight to ten days and a tent to shelter you if you should be obliged to remain on shore or in some parts of the coast.
"Although the boat of the Naturaliste has not communicated with any of the natives, perhaps you will be more fortunate and in this hope you must furnish yourself with some trifles to make presents to them. I do not repeat to you what I have already said on the manner in which you should conduct yourself towards them, persuaded that you have not forgotten it." Signed N.B.
After the departure of this boat, I invited Captain Hamelin to come on board and when he was arrived, I agreed with him that his boat should make a somewhat longer expedition and that he would send it well armed to visit Frederick Henry Bay of Tasman and to see if in the communication which it appears to have with that of Marion, there was a practicable passage for our corvettes. If Citizen Boulanger had been more advanced in his convalescence, I would have asked him to make this expedition, but being not yet strong enough,
Citizen Faure, engineer of the Géographe, went alone. The mineralogist Bailly, to whom it was proposed to join this party, preferred to stay, finding it too long or too difficult.
The boat of the Naturaliste departed at six o'clock in the morning. Ours had pushed off at four. By this means, I hoped they would not join, which would not be a misfortune for their meeting could only harm or delay the mission which each is to fulfil, as had already happened.
Our boats had also been sent off early in the morning to carry our barrels on shore and fill them. And departing at eight o'clock from the ship in my small boat, I expected to find each at work when I should arrive. But in this I was greatly mistaken, for having rounded a point which hid it from my view, I recognised her occupied in the pursuit of swans instead of being in the place where she had been ordered to go. It was not without displeasure that I saw the manoeuvre which she was making, especially as she no longer had time to arrive with the high tide as I had calculated. Citizen Freycinet Ransonet, midshipman to whom I had given the command, doubtless did not believe that I was observing him so closely. Be that as it may, I went straight on shore to the appointed place and I had time to visit the river and the surrounding country before she arrived. As the tide had already fallen considerably, she could not pass through the channel which I had had marked, she ran aground, but it was not for long, for she refloated, the bottom being very soft mud, and gained the larboard shore where that of Captain Hamelin was. When she had cast her grappling iron, I went on board her and gave orders that a float be made of all the barrels to haul them onto a small island which was situated opposite the mouth of the river in order to have them filled at low tide. Mr. Ransonnet was very surprised to see me and doubtless very little pleased with what I said to him regarding his conduct in this expedition. Captain Hamelin gave the same order to his men and in an hour all our casks were arranged to be filled as soon as the moment should be favourable.
The small island of which I have just spoken appeared to me very fit to establish our observatory and I decided that the next day all our instruments would be transported there, that is to say, those of which we could have need.
When I visited the country adjacent to the stream, we recognised that the low ground which surrounds it is a fairly extensive plain cut by different channels into which the sea rises at every tide, the water being as salt as that in the middle of the bay. This plain, when cultivated, after having given a drain to the waters, would be very fertile for the soil is excellent. That of the mountains which surround it at about a cannon shot is equally good and this place appeared to me convenient for a settlement.
In the excursion we made into the interior, we skirted for nearly four leagues the fresh-water stream where we were to take in water. Its bed is very winding and of considerable width. It appeared to us to have its source at the plateau mountain. We saw, in this excursion, a kangaroo of the large species and the citizen shot at it with a ball at a good distance but did him no harm. As he had seen it near he assured us it was the size of a mill. The land birds appeared to us very rare, we saw only some parakeets and a partridge or quail of ordinary size. We were more fortunate with regard to plant collecting: the gardener collected several to plant and I a considerable number for the herbarium.
This place was formerly inhabited by a family of natives and we encountered eight of their huts which had not been abandoned long, for the eucalyptus bark of which they were formed was still fresh. There was found a cord made of tree bark fibre and a poor vessel of very hard wood which was probably used by them for drinking. Almost all the large trees which we saw were greatly damaged by fire and most ready to fall
at the slightest squall from the north-west which might occur.
Returning to our boats, I killed a serpent of about two feet in length. It appeared to me to have nothing remarkable. The spots on its skin were ash-grey varied with white points, the underneath entirely white. It made no gesture which could make me suspect it to be venomous. When I killed it, it had half its body in a hole and was seeking to lodge itself entirely there. In trying to withdraw it after it was dead, it divided into two.
At three o'clock, we embarked again to return on board, leaving our boats occupied in taking in water. We had the winds from the south very light and the tide against us, which greatly delayed us. I skirted the whole starboard shore and saw nothing particular.
The night of the third to the fourth passed in calm and was fairly fine, one of our boats which had gone to fish with a line saw several natives on the edge of the sea at a short distance, also fishing with torches.
1802-01-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: The weather was fine and the wind a light breeze from N to NW. At 6 a.m. the large boat, with 15 days' provisions, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey the North Bay and the passage marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island. At 7 our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went to water at the head of the port. We moored east and west with a kedge anchor. Draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 2 inches, difference 0 feet 9 inches. The observatory was set up on a small islet at the head of the port, at the mouth of the river.

1802-01-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds east, variable to SE, almost calm. During the night a very thick fog kept us from making out the coast; during the night the winds went right round the compass and varied from [one word illegible] WNW, W and WSW, a strong breeze. Citizen Saint-Cricq embarked in the dinghy with his instruments to go to the observatory set up at the head of the North West Port.
1802-01-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, we experienced in the morning so strong a breeze from west-south-west to west, that we were set adrift three or four times by the force of the squalls. We could not even hold with two anchors and we were forced to put out a third to steady us. This squall lasted until three o'clock in the afternoon, the weather being hazy and fine, after which calm set in and lasted all night.
Nothing of note occurred aboard on this day. Only the observatory was established ashore and the instruments were carried there.
Our cutter, which I expected at the evening tide, did not come, doubtless through the negligence of the officer who commands it, who was perhaps out hunting at the moment when he ought to have departed, as he was at the moment when he ought to have arrived.
Aboard, we set about preparing the interior of the ship and inspecting our sails, some of which were found to be damaged, although they were enclosed and suspended in their cases. There had been some leaks along the seams of the deck which we should not have discovered so soon without this inspection.
The boat which went fishing from four o'clock in the afternoon until nine in the evening, brought back sufficient fish to give to all the crew. The largest were of the species of rays and dogfish, the others were flounders, perches and a kind of mullets which we judged by experience to be the best of all.
1802-01-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SW in gusts; it fell away at nightfall.

1802-01-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze in gusts from WSW, south, SW and W. At 7.30 a working party of 6 men was sent ashore to stay there and fill the casks.
1802-01-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, at five o'clock in the morning, we finally saw our boats return, which would perhaps still be ashore if they had had provisions, for I had only put on board supplies for two days. They brought fifteen or eighteen barrels which were immediately transferred into our storage casks. I sent them out again at eight o'clock, under the command of Citizen Ronsard who had been tasked with marking the narrow and difficult channel that leads to the river or rather to the stream and who even claimed to be able to conduct the boats to its mouth at sea.
I also embarked in my small canoe to go to the observatory and see how it had been established. I saw with regret and even with displeasure that this place was going to become the tavern of the two vessels, a place of continual communication, for five boats made their way there while I was there, or at least the persons they transported, as those who conducted them. In an island that was no more than twenty-five to thirty feet long by fifteen in its greatest width, there were seven or eight different kitchens and I was informed that the day before, we had nearly
been burned there entirely with the tents and instruments because the different fires from one kitchen to another having communicated with each other, it had caught the grass. Fortunately, the winds were from the land, for otherwise, everything would have been lost.
Everything that I saw made me depart hastily from a place that would only serve to delay our operations and prolong our stay in this roadstead.
Citizen Depuche, whom until this time I had cared for and treated as if he had belonged to me, left the ship (with) weapons and baggage to go establish himself ashore. The physician apprised me of the remarks he had made to him to persuade him not to take a step so rash and ill-considered, but all was in vain and he became so stubborn as to become angry with the physician and with those who tried to make him aware of the unfortunate consequences that could result from this folly, his health not being sufficiently well restored to indulge the whims of his mind.
The fear that I would not approve his conduct no doubt prevented him from informing me of his decision, for he left without telling me anything.
During the time I remained ashore, I made with the physician and the gardener a long excursion along the banks of the river and into the interior of the country. We saw very little that was new and brought back but few things, whether in plants or seeds, or objects of natural history. This part of the coast being not very rich in variety of species.
In going and returning aboard, we saw no swans nor pelicans, which I attributed to the great quantity of gunshots that had been fired for the past three days. The persons who were destined to protect the boats in case of need, imitating the conduct of the officer who commanded them, scattered into the woods as soon as they arrived ashore and would not return except when pressed by hunger or having no more ammunition. As I was a witness to what took place at the second voyage of the boat, I decided no longer to give to the persons who would find themselves there in the future any firearms and would limit their defence to that of a sabre, a decision that Captain Hamelin had already taken.
During this day, the weather was fine and the breeze light. At night, we had a dead calm and a clear sky, the winds or the freshness in the north-easterly quarter.
1802-01-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from W to NW. At 6 a.m. the longboat came in loaded with water. She left again at 7.15 with a working party of 7 men commanded by a midshipman, who are to stay at the watering place to fill the casks, roll them down and raft them, so that the longboat may find them ready and have only to take them in.

1802-01-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind east, a fresh breeze. Calm all the afternoon. From 4 to 10 the breeze got up from NE to ENE, freshening a great deal; at noon it was blowing hard from that quarter.
1802-01-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, our boats did not appear at the turning of the tide, which made me fear that they were still aground, at least mine, for it was in that position the day before when I embarked to return aboard.
