Citizen Ronsard, not wishing to follow that of the Naturaliste out of attachment for the channel he had marked out, ran aground there whilst the other remained afloat in the same place where they had been able to penetrate the first time and which is within gun-shot of the mouth of the fresh-water stream at sea.
In the course of the morning, I saw to the buckets of living plants that we had gathered and planted since our entry into the channel. The number, at that point, was not considerable since it amounted only to some forty shrubs. It was surely not for want of search and expeditions into the interior of the country that it was not above the quantity I have just named, and it is only to the little variety of species to be found there that it must be attributed.
One of our canoes was equally dispatched for fishing and its voyage was not successful for it returned at sunset without having caught anything. At the same time, we received news of our large canoe, absent for three days and returning from the mission which I had entrusted to Citizen Freycinet. I was greatly surprised to see it return so promptly, and I began to fear that he had executed it poorly. I make no mention here of what Citizen Freycinet reported to me inasmuch as I shall give in writing the report which he is engaged in making to me of what he saw and encountered.
Citizen Péron who accompanied him was not successful in these searches for objects of natural history and reported so few things that they are not worth mentioning.
From ten o'clock in the morning until sunset, the winds were from east to north-east by squalls and strong breeze, the sky being fine although very hazy and laden with vapours. At night, we had calm and fine weather. Our water boats not having appeared, we hoped that they would come during the night, especially as it had been observed that the sea was rising much more at this time than at any other.
1802-01-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE to ENE. At 9 p.m. a musket shot was thought to have been heard ashore to the NE; the yawl was at once sent away armed, and found no one.

1802-01-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A strong breeze from ENE to NNE. The longboat went watering.
1802-01-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, at daylight, we perceived our boats returning aboard with their cargo. The wind was absolutely calm and the ebb tide facilitated their return. At half past six, they were aboard and unloaded immediately. My intention was that they should depart again immediately. But at the moment when they were about to push off, there came to us a squall so strong from north to north-north-west that we were obliged to hold them fast. And they could not set out until about eight o'clock.
During the morning, the sky was very overcast and hazy. We saw the sun only at very short intervals and the clouds were so low and so thick that there was every appearance that we were going to have some strong squalls. I was all the more vexed that our boats had departed inasmuch as the barometer confirmed by its sudden lowering the state of the atmosphere. Both were obliged to seek shelter by the force of the wind. Mine awkwardly made for the starboard shore, where it was not sheltered from the winds which had shifted to north-west whilst that of the Naturaliste came to take shelter on the port shore.
Nevertheless, about noon, although it was still blowing in strong squalls, the sky became clearer and appeared to be improving. We saw our boats set sail to go to the head of the port where they would be sheltered for the night if the weather became bad again.
In the morning, we also passed over our cables which had twisted one over the other in the change of winds, in order to have them in a condition to be able to give a greater reach if the case required it, and we also rigged the lifts of the top masts in order to be all ready to strike if we were forced.
In the afternoon, the winds shifted to the west, it continued to blow a strong breeze but nevertheless, it was much less strong than it had been in the morning. The carpenters were sent ashore to cut trees suitable to make us planks of which we were beginning to have great need. The masters also requested one of the small boats to go fishing. It was granted to them in the belief that we shall have calm for the night and even from sunset, as it has almost always happened to us since we have been in this port.
From sunset until ten o'clock, it continued to blow in strong squalls, but at that time, calm succeeded it and we had very fine weather the rest of the night.
The boat that I had sent fishing took advantage of it to return aboard. We had caught a fair amount of fish.
1802-01-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 4.15 a.m. the longboat came in. She weighed the kedge anchor and carried it SW of the bower, so that we are now moored NE and SW. Overcast weather; the breeze freshened and blew strong in gusts from NW to W. At 6.30 (on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802]) the mooring hawser parted; we veered cable to 150 fathoms. The longboat weighed the kedge anchor; not being able to get the end of the hawser, which was foul of the flukes of the bower anchor, we unbent it and put a buoy on the end. The longboat left for the watering place. At 9 a second anchor was let go.

1802-01-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from WNW to NW in heavy gusts. It fell away about four o'clock. The longboat came aboard with her load of water. She left again at once for the watering place.
1802-01-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, at four o'clock in the morning, I was rather surprised to learn that our boat had returned aboard with its complete load of water. The diligence that Citizen Bonnefoy showed in this circumstance served only to demonstrate to me that those who, until that moment had been charged with this task, had been more occupied with their pleasure than with their duty and I did not fail to make it known to them by having them observe the difference that resulted from it.
If there had been an occasion fit to excuse the delay in the return of the boat, it was, no doubt, that in which Citizen Bonnefoy found himself, for the strong wind and even the bad weather had lasted all day and part of the night. Nevertheless, he accomplished, in four hours of calm, what the others had not been able to do in forty-eight hours of fine weather.
As soon as it was unloaded, it set out again under the command of First-class Midshipman Maurouard.
The weather was fine in the morning, and at sunrise the winds shifted to north-west, light breeze. I went ashore with our carpenters to examine the trees which they were to have felled the day before and which I intended to have made into planks of which, as I have already observed, we were beginning to have great need.
Hardly had we arrived, when it began to blow with full force from the west to west-north-west. As, at my departure there was no surveying officer, although it was past seven o'clock, I gave to the boatswain who was on watch the necessary orders for the safety of the vessel, if the weather became bad.
During the morning, I made an inspection of the trees which had been felled the day before. They were fine on the outside and of fine appearance, but all had their heartwood damaged. We also cut down several more which, having no fault perceptible to the eye, appeared to me to be more sound. But I was mistaken for they were still more defective than those which the carpenters had selected. As it was becoming useless to fell a greater number, we stopped there, limiting ourselves to taking those which were the best and the most suitable for the use we intended to make of them. After having them sawed into sections of ten to twelve feet long, we had them brought down to the edge of the sea by rolling them from the summit of the mountain which was very steep. However, several became stuck in holes from which we had quite (difficulty) getting them out.
At three o'clock in the afternoon, we returned to the edge of the sea to return aboard, but the breeze was so strong that we had to wait wait (sic) for a lull which took place about four o'clock and of which we took advantage forthwith, for the sky had a very bad appearance for the night. We had intended to bring back some of our trees in tow but we were forced to abandon that idea for fear of being set adrift. We had observed before embarking that it had been no less windy aboard than ashore, since the lower yards had been taken in and the topgallant masts struck. Nevertheless, the ship did not appear to us to have dragged on its anchors.
At five o'clock, I returned aboard, quite drenched by the waves which the agitation of the sea had caused to enter into our canoe. It was high time we arrived there for, hardly had we got there when it began to blow with full force. From this excursion I brought back some flowering plants that no one had yet found and several species of seeds, in the number of which there is indigo, which appeared to us singular at such a latitude, moreover, this plant is here quite common.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth, the winds were from the west in gusts and strong squalls. But less violent than during the day.
1802-01-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NW. At 3.30 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once. A little rain.

1802-01-29.journal_anonyme: Rainy weather, the sea smooth, a strong breeze in [one word illegible] puffs from NW, WSW, WNW and W. The longboat came in with her load of water. She was sent off again at once.
1802-01-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
The ninth, our boat returned on board at the same hour as it had come the day before. But she did not bring back, as usual, her full cargo.
The midshipman who commanded her reported to me that the sea having risen considerably that day, the water had been found to be of poor quality and that he had preferred to return on board with the tide rather than wait for it to be low to complete it.
She returned for the same purpose as soon as she was unloaded. At the same time I received a letter from the astronomer Bernier who complained that he and his comrades had no provisions. Although he had invited several times those who had gone on shore and returned on board to have some sent to them. I sent his letter to the officer in charge of the provisions in order to remedy this inconvenience.
A short time after the departure of the boat, the wind increased considerably and we had about as strong squalls as the day before. She worked to windward for a long time with little success, but at last, having gained the larboard shore, she decided to man her oars and proceeded by rowing. The boat of the Naturaliste did the same.
During the morning, the squalls were often accompanied by rain and sometimes we had it quite abundantly. Nevertheless, I sent the small boat to the seine, having nothing better to do and the strong wind not allowing us to go to seek our spare masts.
In the afternoon, the weather was more pleasant than it had been in the morning and the breeze calmed much at three o'clock. At six, our boat returned from fishing. The second mate to whom I had given the command reported to me that they had had an interview with the natives who, to the number of seven, had assembled around them. At the moment when they became aware of it, they were dining in the shelter of a rock and it was by bursts of laughter that they announced their presence, long before they were perceived or that one suspected their arrival. All were armed with a spear and one of them carried a bundle quite large and in which, according to the estimate that was made of it, judging by their ordinary size, there could be about a hundred. As our men were not armed nor in a state of defence, they first thought of re-embarking in order to avoid any surprise, but as the natives had stopped at a certain distance from them to examine their movements, one of our fishermen who carried two bottles in one of which there was still a little rum showed them to them by making signs to invite them to come to take them. Immediately, they laid down their weapons, of which they entrusted the guard to the one who was carrying in addition the bundle of which I have just spoken, and advanced cheerfully towards them, testifying by gestures and cries of joy that they had no evil intention.
Our fishermen, seeing them in these happy dispositions, all returned to the place where they had lit their fire and the natives followed them there without the slightest mistrust. They then continued their meal consisting of fish which they had caught and what, as a precaution, they had brought from the ship. Provisions were offered to the natives who had mingled with them to share what remained, but they refused to take anything, nor even taste the liquor which remained in the bottles, but they showed great desire to have them. They did not fail to give them to them with some rum which they made no use of and which they even poured on the ground, very pleased to possess the vessels.
After the first gift, the familiarity between them and our men became so great and confidence was so well established on both sides, that they began to dance all together. But this exercise tiring them too much or not amusing them much, they were soon tired of it,
and preferred to occupy themselves with things more suitable to their taste. Everyone having sat down again, their attention fixed on the pockets and the metal buttons which were found on some of the waistcoats of our men. Several did not need to be asked to search in them for what might suit them, whilst others announced by unequivocal signs the satisfaction the satisfaction (sic) which they would have to receive buttons. Several were cut off which were distributed to them and they showed great satisfaction.
After about two hours of staying together, they thought of re-embarking to seek a more convenient place for fishing and they parted the best of friends. The embarking was not troubled in any way and the natives continued to give them great signs of joy and contentment. No women or children were seen in this interview, but as a fairly thick smoke was perceived on the two-thirds of the mountain at the foot of which they were, they did not doubt that they were in this place.
The boat was, at that time, in the last cove which terminates Bruny Island of Entrecasteaux to the north and they even thought they recognised among the seven natives who came to mingle with our men two of those with whom we had communicated during our stay at the Great Cove.
The fishing, although not very abundant, was sufficient to give to everyone. The fish that were caught, with the exception of one, were of the same species of those of which I have already spoken. The bizarre and extraordinary form of this latter can be seen in the journal where are the objects of curiosity and natural history.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth, the wind blew in strong squalls accompanied by heavy rains which, in general, were of short duration.
1802-01-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW. At 4 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at 6. The carpenters went to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-01-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, blowing hard in heavy gusts from W to WSW and WNW. In the forenoon they drew round to SE and SSE, almost calm. We were busy stowing the sheet anchor.
1802-01-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
The tenth, in the morning, our boat not having returned as usual, I took advantage of the calm which was then to send to fetch the boards which we had cut as well as the spars for our use.
I had prepared the day before the reply which I made to Citizen Bernier to the letter which he had addressed to me and of which I join here the copy:
"The Commander to
"Citizen Bernier, astronomer,
"It was not possible for me, Citizen, to take advantage yesterday of the departure of the boat to reply to the letter which you had the honour of writing to me the seventh of this month. It is not that it did not reach me in time, but those who could give me information on its contents, not having risen according to the custom of the ship until between eight and nine o'clock in the morning, I feared to interrupt the sleep free from care and anxiety of which they were enjoying although the weather and circumstances were not favourable to authorise it.
"Be that as it may, according to the information which I procured, it appears that with the exception of oil, and perhaps also of vinegar, you should not have lacked anything. However, your letter announces to me quite the contrary, since you appear to lack everything. I ask you therefore, for the future, to let me know what you need in order that I may have it reach you. I only recommend you not to wait until the last moment to send me the note the note.
"No one was able to tell me what you mean by ordinary rations of the ship, and you may be, moreover, assured that no one has extraordinary ones, not even for water, given the difficulty of procuring it as easily as I would have wished,
"I am obliged to say to Mr. de St Croix, whom I urgently ask, when he kills some rare and precious birds, to send them to us. We will keep only the feathers and the wing tips. The remainder, that is to say the body, will be scrupulously returned to the destination which he shall have announced. We indeed have a wood-pigeon similar to that which he sent yesterday on board the Naturaliste. And as it is a bird as rare as precious for natural history, it would have been infinitely important to preserve a part of the specimen to replace that of the same kind which we were fortunate to procure.
"Many things to all those who are with you." Signed N.B.
At nine o'clock, our large boat returned with the boards and spars which it had gone to fetch. While they were being embarked, Mr. Hamelin came on board and a short time after, I departed in his boat to go to the place where the natives were that our men had seen the day before. The care which they had taken to maintain several fires all night did not allow us to doubt that they were in this place. I took with me the draughtsman and the physician.
About ten o'clock, we saw a canoe in which there were four or five men which departed from the northern point of Entrecasteaux Island to go to that of Pierson. They stood upright to paddle and appeared to us to go very fast, for we soon lost sight of them. A short time after, we arrived on shore. Seven of the natives, among whom there was a child of twelve to fifteen years, showed themselves on the slope of the hill opposite our landing. They were without arms, but very attentive to all our movements. In approaching them, we made them several signs of friendship to invite them to wait for us, for they were advancing as we approached them. It seemed to us quite astonishing to see them so mistrustful, whereas the day before they had not made the least difficulty to mingle with our men.
As I had furnished myself with some gifts, I made shine before their eyes one or two glass bead necklaces which attracted their attention. One of them having made me a sign to give it to him, I made him one so that he would come to take them. Before determining to do so, he consulted the others who, to all appearances, having approved his resolution, he advanced with an air of confidence which proved to us that he was without suspicion, although he had a stone in his hand. As soon as we had joined him, we heaped caresses upon him which entirely reassured him and I gave him some glass beads which he examined with pleasure. His companions, witnesses to what had just taken place, were not long in arriving and were also well received. We had then six with us, but the youngest always kept apart and nothing could tempt him. After having walked together, they addressed several speeches to us which they accompanied with gestures and we could not doubt that they did not see us unwillingly, since they invited us to re-embark. Among the different words which they pronounced, that of kaouékaouré was often repeated very often and even with a tone of command. It means in the language of the Negroes of Mozambique on the coast of Africa, go away, but I cannot say if it has the same meaning among those of the land of Diemen.
Be that as it may, we paid little heed to their kaouékaouré and their signs and we advanced into the interior to botanise. They followed us for some time, but as we were making our way to approach a place from which came a fairly thick smoke, they made so much noise that we judged it must be the place where their women and children were whom they did not want us to approach. As I was most in advance, that one of the natives who was near us, without arms, made me turn about by clearly showing me that we must not go in that direction. As I wished to preserve the good understanding which prevailed between us, I changed direction by telling the others to do the same and they appeared very satisfied. Then they abandoned us and appeared to make their way towards our boat which was at some distance from the shore and which they could not reach by wading.
During the excursion we made in the wood we found but few things in plants and I brought back but one new species of the class of heaths and indigo seed. We saw but one kangaroo of the small species and very few birds. Most of the trees were burnt as everywhere else and the ground more sandy than all those which we had encountered hitherto.
About two o'clock, according to the altitude of the sun, we returned on our steps to return on board. In approaching the shore, we met three of the natives to whom we had made gifts in the morning. It appeared to us that they had followed us at a fairly great distance and we were astonished to see them armed, each with two or three spears. Nevertheless, we approached them in going to meet them. Their kaouékaouré recommenced as we advanced towards them and they always kept at a fairly great distance. Annoyed at not being able to join them, we took the course of sitting down all on a fallen tree across our path, waiting to see which direction they would take. Seeing us in this position, they also stopped to examine us by speaking to each other. They were then fifty paces from us. The gestures which we made to them to approach further were well understood and whether to obtain the new objects which we presented to them or some other motive, they went to lay down their spears behind trees and joined us, having but one or two stones in their hand. Being all together, they made us a sign to put aside my gun which a sailor sitting near me was holding. On our part, we made them understand to throw their stones, which they did immediately. Having invited them to sit, they did not need much persuasion and soon they became as familiar as if we had been very accustomed to see ourselves united. Everything which we had in our hand or on us appeared to suit them and they made an inspection of our pockets, but with our consent. Having left nothing after the inspection of the pockets, they went to that of our clothes, and to please them in everything, we showed them our breasts, which they appeared very curious about. However, they only showed astonishment at that of the physician, which, having no hair, excited great exclamations in them and greater bursts of laughter. After having satisfied themselves in this part, they went to the legs and several had the complaisance to comply with this whim of theirs. They would have liked to see something else, but we did not think it proper to show them. Among the three natives who were sitting beside us, two had on their legs two considerable wounds still fresh. The third had a dislocation in one of the fingers of the right hand. All three were aged from forty to forty-five years and rather poorly built, especially in the lower part of the body. Their features painted with powdered charcoal and over which they had applied red ochre which we had given them had nothing disagreeable. It was on the contrary well marked and characteristic. The forehead being very prominent made them appear to have eyes very sunken and even small at a certain distance. The cheekbones were very prominent, the mouth large, the teeth large, fine, white and well arranged. The eyes lively
but the look anxious and always on the watch. At the slightest movement which we made, they were instantly on their feet and especially if the gun was touched, of which they certainly knew the effect and of which they had great fear. It does not appear to me doubtful that in other circumstances some of them have had bitter experience of it.
During nearly two hours which our interview with these three natives lasted, we had all the time to consider them at our leisure. We pronounced to them different words which they repeated very distinctly and I was even astonished at the little difficulty it caused them. However those in which there were 'r' or 's' were not as easy for them.
Captain Hamelin wishing to make an exchange of their spears with some other things, made them the proposal by signs which were well understood, and it was agreed that they would give a spear for a uniform button. The agreement being settled, one of them went to fetch one and delivered it on receiving the agreed price. The two others did the same and delivered them in the same manner, being careful not to relinquish them until they were paid in advance. As two had been brought, one wished to see if by not paying them until after receiving it he would consent to give it, but he carefully avoided it and even refused to deliver it after obtaining payment for it. But as, according to the custom which had been established, one held the spear at one end when one gave the button, he was obliged to release it and this did not appear to please him.
The transaction being completed, the natives kept at some distance from us, as if they had been afraid that we should use against them the weapons which they had just sold us. However, seeing that we were making our way to return to our boats, they followed us again. Citizen Petit, who had drawn one of them, found the drawing which he had made taken from his hand. But, as agile as the one who had snatched it from him, he retook it and we continued to make our way to the edge of the sea. We had scarcely arrived there when the three natives with whom we had been on such good terms and whom we had heaped with gifts began to gather stones and soon sent them to us. Several reached our boats, although at a great distance, and fortunately did not wound anyone. I was not as fortunate as the others, for one fairly large, having struck me at the moment when I was bending down to examine a shell valve, slightly wounded me in the hip. I at once aimed at the one who had hurled it at me and this movement frightened him so much that he bent down and ran as fast as he could, although he was well beyond the range of my gun.
The fear that they might charge again at the moment of our embarking made me take the course of advancing again towards them while everyone would be embarking. Captain Hamelin followed me. We saw the natives at a considerable distance, calling to each other by loud cries to which answers came from afar. We then returned to embark, persuaded that they would not be long in appearing in considerable numbers. This actually happened, for a short time after, we saw twelve or fifteen of them appear on the edge of the shore, from which we were fairly distant to be unable to distinguish what they were carrying. They were directing their course to the south-west. As the wind was favourable, we put our helm towards them in drawing nearer to the coast. Then, seeing that we were approaching them much more swiftly than they were walking, although they had doubled their pace, they divided into several bands and entered the wood where we soon lost sight of them.
During our return on board, we sought to explain their hostile conduct at the moment of our separation. We could find no cause for it but in the regret of having exchanged their spears with us, which perhaps by this means they thought to obtain.
Captain Hamelin dined on board and spent the rest of the evening there. Our boats did not appear, to our great astonishment, which made us fear that the water had not risen enough to float our float of full barrels.
Throughout this day, the weather was very fine and the wind light from the east-south-east. It was the same during the night which passed in calm.
1802-01-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from WSW to SE. The carpenters went back to cut wood. The commander and the captain communicated with the Aboriginal people on Bruny Island and handed out trinkets to them; at the moment they were embarking they received a volley of stones, which wounded no one. The commander alone had the misfortune to take one on the back, which did him no harm. It was the same group that had wounded Citizen Maurouard with a spear.

1802-01-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SE to east and SSE. The captain communicated with the Aboriginal people of Bruny Island. The winds drew round to SW, NW, NNE and ENE, a light breeze. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-01-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
The eleventh, in the morning, we did not yet see our boats return and I gave orders that a boat be fitted out to go to inquire of the cause of their delay.
The crews having provisions but for one day, it appeared to me fairly difficult to explain why they had not returned even when empty.
Several persons of the ship, always ingenious for tormenting themselves or for troubling others, came to inform me of their fears about the fate of those who were on shore, in that they were poorly armed. They did not wish to take the trouble to reflect that there were more than forty persons in the same place and that by numbers alone, they had no need of arms. An observation so natural could not, however, reassure them and their fears, on seeing the boats come of which we became aware about seven and a half o'clock, did not cease until they were on board and they had examined and counted everyone. I could not help laughing at such ridiculous weakness in those who had put themselves forward for their representations. And I made use of this occasion to announce to them all the danger which they were exposing themselves to in consuming in part hunting provisions the ammunition which I gave them for their own defence and which their extravagance had caused me to suppress.
Something far more disagreeable to me than all which had been said to me about the fate of the men occupied in taking in water came to complete the ill humour with which I was affected by the delay of our boats. It was the quality of the water which had been brought and which had to be thrown into the sea. The master of the boat declared to me that the fault was with Midshipman Le Brun who was commanding this boat, in that he would not wait until the tide was low enough to have the barrels filled. For proof of what he said, he had me taste a barrel of water made an hour and a half after our barrels were filled and which proved to be very good. It resulted from this conduct that we have just lost two days for nothing. All the excuse which the midshipman gave me was that the Naturaliste, in whose boat there was an officer, had done the same and that it was according to his conduct that he had regulated his own. I think, from that, that if this officer had the fancy to set fire to his boat, he would have done the same to imitate him.
What had just happened had also taken place on the previous voyage, so that to see if things would go better by entrusting the boat only to the master, I took the course of sending him alone as soon as we should need to examine our cables which it was essential to weigh for fear that the anchors, which were all three forward, should damage our cables during the swinging. During the morning, this work was undertaken which was not finished until one o'clock in the afternoon.
At about three o'clock, the boat departed for its destination and I gave to the master who was commanding it the orders which I judged suitable so that he would discharge well his commission, by flattering his self-esteem and by this means I hope that we shall not be obliged to throw away the water which he will send us.
Having not much to do on board, I sent the small boat to fish with a line
with seven men. This method had been fairly successful for us every time it had been used. The weather moreover was very fine and likely to procure us something. As the part of coast which he had chosen, as being the best, was in the same place where we had been attacked with stones the day before, and several smokes announced to us the presence of the natives, it was expressly forbidden to them to go on shore anywhere and to return on board before nine o'clock.
They returned in fact at that time and our fishermen informed us that they had seen a great number of natives which they estimated at forty persons, including women and children. The latter were in considerable numbers. All having made their way to the edge of the sea opposite the boat, did not cease inviting by signs our men to go on shore and not having succeeded in this, they began to dance and to perform all sorts of antics. From the boat, an empty bottle was shown to them, it was known that they liked this vessel much by the care which they had taken of those which had previously been given to them. They invited our men by very expressive signs to give it to them, which they did by throwing it into the water at a small distance from the boat. One of the women of the group and according to the fishermen it was not the oldest, immediately stripped off the kangaroo skin which covered her back and having set out swimming, came to take it with great manifestations of joy when she returned to the shore. The dances and invitations for our men to come to share them recommenced, but they did not comply. On departing for the shore, it was made known to them that they would return the next day and they appeared very satisfied.
Throughout the day, the weather was very fine and the winds from east to south-east, light breeze. At sunset, they shifted to the west where they remained all night during which there were some strong cats' paws but of short duration.
1802-01-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNE, S and WSW. The carpenters went to cut wood. At 7 the longboat came in from the watering place and went back there at 11.

1802-02-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the winds very light from ENE, east, NW and SW. At noon squally weather and the winds a strong breeze from SW to NW. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-02-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twelfth, in the morning, the sky was very fine although with winds from the west variable to west-south-west, which was not usual. I sent to inform Captain Hamelin to send me one of his boats with five or six men and that I would furnish as many to go to fish with the seine.
In the meantime, our boats arrived with their full cargo of good water. Not only did they make more diligence than usual, but moreover the water which they brought us was of the best quality possible, which confirmed me in the opinion of the uselessness of putting any of those who, by duty, should have been present.
At nine o'clock, we departed from the ship for fishing, wishing to see for myself in what manner the natives would conduct themselves, especially according to the report which had been made to me the day before. The weather was, at our departure, very fine and the breeze from the west not strong. On our arrival on shore, we met no one. But we had scarcely had time to cast the seine when the natives appeared, making great exclamations which announced their contentment to see us. They were sixteen in number, but there were but four men. The rest consisted of two women and children of different ages, the oldest did not appear to be more than twelve years and the youngest five, except an infant at the breast of about three months.
The men did not need much persuasion to come to us. But the children were not at first as confident. None had in hand neither weapons nor stones. I distributed to each some glass beads which appeared to give them much pleasure. Then, making them understand that I wished also to give to the children, they called them and approached us, but not without fear. One of the youngest, who had not dared follow the others, was unsuccessfully called several times by his father, which caused him to go to fetch him and he
brought him to us as if by force. We soon reassured him by our caresses accompanied by small gifts as well as his comrades, so that at the end of half an hour, they were as familiarized with us as if we had been old acquaintances.
As I wished to have the drawing of the women and some children, I told them to sit, which they did with much complaisance. But as they were preparing to draw in the seine, it was no longer possible to prevent them from running to it, either from the novelty to them of this way of fishing or for some other motive which I cannot explain.
The joy of the children and even of the men was at its height when they saw the fish which was caught in the seine. The exclamations and capers made known to us sufficiently how pleased they were. We offered them to share our catch, but they refused to accept anything, by making us understand that they did not eat fish, but only shellfish and crustaceans.
The seine was veered out for the third time and while the boat carried it offshore to give it the necessary circuit, we went to sit down again at the feet of the slope of the hill opposite which we were. The natives followed us there and we all sat together on the grass. I always had beside me two men who observed all my movements because I was the only one who had a firearm. If I happened to pass it from right to left, their anxiety was immediately shown and it was sufficient to change its position to see how much they feared the effect of a gun.
The children, becoming more and more familiar, played with our men in the best of humours. They had a very amiable cheerfulness. Their features were also very pleasant, not being disfigured by dirt or the black and red colours which the men and women used to adorn themselves. We exercised with them in running, in capers and different other games which amused the natives much. We took advantage of this moment of gaiety to complete the drawings which had been sketched at the time of their arrival.
When the seine was drawn in, all went to it as at the first time, and especially the children, who hauled with good will on the ropes, by imitating and repeating very intelligibly all which our men said. I was truly astonished at the fact that children who, at first sight, had appeared so fearful and so timid, had become so tame in so little time, to the point they had reached. When our men would not dance, play or run with them, they tormented them until they had done what they wanted. Another circumstance not less extraordinary and scarcely easy to explain is that the men who were with us were the same as those who, a day before, had attacked us with stones at the moment of our departure. They recognised us perfectly by making us understand that they had already seen us. However, they were in the midst of us and at our discretion. Someone wished to remind them of what they had done to us in this circumstance, but I opposed it in order that they should not believe that we held any resentment for it.
The fishing which we made during our stay on shore was not abundant and we took scarcely more than what was necessary for the consumption of one day on board each ship. When it was finished, one prepared to make the pot for the dinner of our men. As soon as it was ready and the rations were distributed, we invited the natives to take part in it, but none would accept anything and they appeared greatly astonished to see that fish was being eaten.
We were expecting every moment three of our men who had advanced to the north of the cove where we were. They were not long in returning, having announced on landing
that I would return on board at three o'clock. When we saw them gather again, they were accompanied by a dozen natives whom we recognised as they approached us to be women. They were not long in informing us of the manner in which they had met them, as they were returning from fishing, loaded with a great quantity of lobsters and abalone which they had doubtless taken in the rocks which were at the extremity of the northern point of this island. These women first showed some fear of this meeting and immediately fled into the wood where they went to deposit and hide the product of their fishing. They were followed by making signs of friendship to them and by showing them the gifts one wished to give them. It appears that the hope of obtaining a bottle caused them to stop and to wait for our gentlemen, who soon joined them. As they saw that one did not seek to take their catch, confidence was soon established. First one began by sitting, and the fair ones, wishing doubtless to please the new company by which they found themselves surrounded, smeared their faces with powdered charcoal softened with their saliva and then made such entreaties to their admirers that they let themselves be done the same, so that when they returned, they could no longer be recognised but by their clothing. One of them having withdrawn into the wood with Mr. Hérisson will perhaps have completely satisfied her curiosity, for they were very curious to see not only the breast of our officers and scholars, but also if they resembled the men of the country in form or faculties.
This extra company caused us to stay an hour and a half longer on shore to examine them better. But they kept more aloof and as soon as one wished to approach them, they withdrew. I think that the presence of the men, who were doubtless their husbands, was the principal cause of their reserve, for they had shown much less when they found themselves at a distance. It does not appear doubtful that it is not the same family. Among the women, there were two daughters who were not yet of marriageable age. They were absolutely naked, but each woman wore on her shoulders a kangaroo skin which only served to cover their shoulders and a small part of their breasts.
At the moment when I announced that we were going to depart, two of the men went up on the slope of the mountain where the children and women followed them. They each took a bundle of spears, either to be on their guard or to attack us. A third was not long in following them, so that we were accompanied only to our boats by only a man and a child of about nine years. Both followed Captain Hamelin and sought at the moment when he was embarking to snatch his sword. We did not doubt that those who had provided themselves with spears had not taken this course but to protect his retreat if he had achieved his purpose and one had run after him. This, however, is but a conjecture, for Captain Hamelin, who was suspicious of the stroke, had taken precautions to prevent it.
Our embarking, by this means, was in no way troubled and we all arrived on board at five and a half o'clock.
The physician declared to me immediately on my arrival that Citizen Maugé had been very indisposed during the day and he was beginning to fear that he would not be able to save him, his illness having the most sinister characteristics. This news greatly afflicted me and caused me to fear that what I had long foreseen should come to pass.
During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth, the weather was very fine and the winds shifted to the north almost calm. Our boat did not return from its mission at this tide, having perhaps been sent from the ship too late to be able to take advantage of it.
1802-02-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SW to W. At 7.15 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place. She went to fetch firewood cut by the two men guarding the sick; at 1 she brought in her load and left at 3 for the watering place. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 10 feet 8 inches, difference 1 foot 0 inches.

1802-02-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze variable from WNW to W. The longboat left for the watering place. The forenoon was almost calm; the carpenters worked on the starboard hawse bolsters.
1802-02-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we had the finest weather in the world, the sea and wind were absolutely calm. As we had not much to do, the small boat was sent out fishing and headed for the same place where we ourselves had been, the day before. I entrusted its command to the master.
At nine o'clock, M. Freycinet wished to go ashore, to the same place, with Citizen Péron. I remarked to them that by rising earlier than usual for days of pleasure, they could have taken advantage of the boat that had departed between seven or eight o'clock, which would have been much more suitable. Nevertheless, I had a boat armed for these two gentlemen and invited them to send it back to me as soon as they had arrived. Officers of the Naturaliste were called by a signal agreed upon the day before, who were to be of this party, and finally, at half past ten, they set out.
Captain Hamelin, who from the morning had been dredging to gather oysters, returned at five o'clock in the evening with a good supply of this shellfish and several other species for natural history. Citizens Depuche and Bailly, mineralogists, had embarked with him. By one of the most extraordinary peculiarities, M. Bailly having gone ashore to examine some stones that had caught his attention, started a kangaroo of the size of a large lamb. He had no gun to shoot it with, but, suddenly recovering from the fright it had given him, he hurled his hammer at it and had the good fortune to break one of its legs and captured it.
This animal walks absolutely on its hind feet without making any use of those in front, which appear to serve it only for scratching the earth and making the hole in which it lodges itself. The one that Citizen Bailly captured and painted from nature is perhaps a variety of those we have seen, for it does not resemble them at all in the colour of its fur, nor those I saw at the Museum in Paris. It was a female.
In the afternoon, we got word of the boat of the Naturaliste which was returning from the expedition I had sent it on to assure myself positively whether there exists a passage from Frederick Henry Bay to Marion Bay, as our charts seem to indicate, since they represent Abel Tasman's Island as separated by a small channel from the mainland of Van Diemen's Land.
According to the report of the geographer Faure, whom I sent there expressly, it appears that it is by error that Abel Tasman's Land is made an island. It joins Van Diemen's Land by an isthmus which, at no time, the sea can cover, and which is about ninety paces in length and of width about as much. Citizen Faure traversed it entirely and in all directions. One can see in the plan that he drew up, not only that of Frederick Henry Bay, but also the isthmus which joins the alleged island of Tasman to that of Van Diemen's Land, from which, certainly, it is not separated by any channels (sic).
This expedition was not useless for geography since it corrects an error, but it was of little advantage for natural history. However, some beautiful whelks were brought back from it, of which only one was whole and had its animal.
Our boat also returned from fishing, at sunset, and brought us a fairly large quantity of fish. A part was taken on board the Naturaliste.
As I was only waiting for the return of Captain Hamelin's boat to set sail from this port, I gave (order) that the next day, we hoisted from daybreak, the lower yards and our topgallant masts which the force of the south-west wind had made us lower. During the night, the weather was fine though misty, our boats did not appear.
[3V p. 233 A] Copy of original documents which might serve to give some clarification on the conduct of Citizen Millius, Captain of Frigate, under the orders of Cit. Hamelin commanding the Naturaliste. (documents included here, but written by another hand. The reason for which they are in this place is neither explicit, nor explicated)
First document,
Letter from Cit Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Citizen Commander,
The lieutenant of the line P. Millius, is an excellent officer, good manoeuvrer, good observer, and deserves the rank of Captain of Frigate (sic), I expect it for him from your justice.
Please, I pray you, in your letters to the Minister of the Navy, recall to him all my staff and notably Captain Millius, officer of the highest merit.
Greetings and highest consideration.
Signed, Cn Hamelin.
This letter is dated from Île de France on 27 Vendémiaire.
[3V p. 233 B] Second document,
Letter from Cn Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Cit. Comdt,
I request the rank of captain of frigate for lieutenant of the line P. Millius. This officer, advantageously known at Brest, at Rochefort, ports where he served, has been in his grade for a long time.
He was a full lieutenant on the frigate La Fraternité which I commanded in the 5th year. Already he had navigated as a lieutenant of the line on the Révolution. Since that time, he has not ceased to go to sea, and all the chiefs who have known him unite in granting him eminent talents (especially for manoeuvring, which his zeal alone equals).
To recommend the advancement of Citizen Millius to you is to invoke from you an act of justice.
Greetings and highest consideration.
Signed Cn. Hamelin
This letter is written in Coupang, island of Timor, on the 5th complementary day in year 9.
[3V p. 233 C] Third document,
Letter from Captain Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition at the moment when he sets sail from Port Jackson on the West coast of New Holland.
Citizen Comdt
I leave here Citizen Millius, too ill to be able to re-embark.
(Note) this letter contains many other things foreign to this matter
Signed Cdt. Hamelin.
It must be observed that the illness of Citizen Millius was so grave that the doctors had several times assembled to pronounce upon his condition, which was regarded as desperate. The certificates with which Cit. Millius is provided testify to this.
Thus with the unfavourable sequel that M. Baudin attributed to this officer is a wickedness
[3V p. 233 D] Another letter from Captain Hamelin which evidently proves that Citizen Millius, although still very ill, wished to resume his service on board the Naturaliste during the second port of call at Port Jackson.
The Capt Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Citizen Comdt,
The present state of the health of Cn Millius is, in my eyes, too little satisfactory for me to believe him recovered. (He) requests that he resume and continue for a long time his service at sea.
His bilious temperament and his severe relapses are too well known to me to expose myself again to continual anxieties on board regarding his welfare.
Signed Cn Hamelin
[3V p. 233 E] 5th document.
Letter from Capt. Hamelin
to Cit. Millius, captain of frigate.
Citizen,
According to the reports of the English doctors, Thomson, Harris, and Milchalon, informed by Citizen Bellefin, our chief health officer, on the poor health which you have enjoyed for a very long time and particularly on the present state of illness, and according to your wish, I consent to your disembarkation from the corvette the Naturaliste.
I wish you a speedy recovery and a happy voyage.
Friendly greetings.
Signed Cn Hamelin.
1802-02-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. The carpenters worked at shifting the hawse bolsters. Fish were taken and distributed to the crew. Citizen Faure came in at 4.30 in the large boat. He had surveyed the North Bay and had found no passage between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island, which is joined to the land by a spit of sand; he had found fresh water in many places. The captain brought back many fish and oysters, which were distributed.

1802-02-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE to NE and WNW. At 4 the large boat came back from her duty; she found that Marion Bay does not communicate with Frederick Hendrik Bay, only a narrow spit of sand separating them, so that Abel Tasman Island is no more than a peninsula; and she was unable to communicate with the Aboriginal people.
1802-02-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, at dawn the winds were perfectly calm and the air so foggy that we could scarcely distinguish the land nearest to us, though we were not more than a mile distant from it. Nevertheless our boats arrived about eight o'clock and the master told me that the cause of his delay was that the sea having risen very little the previous day, they had not been able to fill their barrels, not having sufficient water to convey them ashore.
As soon as they were unloaded, I sent them immediately to fetch some twenty barrels that remained there. And shortly after I dispatched the great cutter to take aboard the tents and astronomical instruments that had been brought ashore. By the same occasion, I addressed to M. Bernier, our astronomer, the following note:
"I send you, Citizen, the great cutter to take all the effects that are ashore as well as the astronomical instruments that you have conveyed there. As you will doubtless have been warned this morning early of this measure by the Naturaliste's boat, you will surely occasion no delay in the return of the one I send you, which I expect this evening as also yourself. Signed N. B."
"P. S. Although it is not necessary to tell you that M. de Criq should take advantage of this same occasion, I beg you, however, to inform him of it."
During the morning, the fog cleared a little and we had a light breeze from the north-east. Captain Hamelin came on board and left shortly after with Citizen Ronsard, a keen lover of hunting. Having nothing much to do on board, I sent a party of the crew fishing with the seine.
In the afternoon, the atmosphere continued to be laden with fog and the winds always from the north-east, very faint. The carpenters were occupied in squaring and sawing into planks the tree trunks that we had felled ashore.
On the return of my fishing boat, we found the catch quite abundant, even more considerable than any we had made hitherto, we took enough for two full days for both vessels.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth, the great cutter returned on board with all the astronomical instruments and the surplus of everything that had been conveyed ashore. The winds were perfectly calm and the sky very foggy.
The natives were witnesses to the fishing we had done and behaved in a very peaceful and friendly manner towards our people. Of everything given to them, nothing appeared more agreeable to them than a few empty bottles.
1802-02-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At daybreak swayed up the topgallant masts. The longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once, empty, to fetch the remaining casks and bring back the party stationed at the watering place. We sent to fetch from the shore the pieces of timber the carpenters had cut. The astronomical instruments came back aboard.

1802-02-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE, NE, NNE, N and NW. The observatory was struck, as was the camp set up ashore for watering.
1802-02-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, about nine o'clock in the morning, our boats returned on board with the surplus of water casks that were ashore, which completed the supplies for our hold. It was not possible to set sail that day. The little breeze there was came from the north-east, variable to the east. The atmosphere was moreover so laden with fog that we could scarcely distinguish the land nearest to us.
I had not thought it necessary to speak until this moment of what was passing on board the Naturaliste between Captain Hamelin and Citizen Millius, his first officer, especially as I had never heard anything but good from the latter by his Captain. Although I was informed in a very exact and detailed manner that the two lived but poorly together. Citizen Millius, to whom had been granted much more authority than was fitting, had become so accustomed to it that he had permitted himself several times some exemplary corrections upon the crew, persuaded that he ought not even to account for them to his Captain. The latter, after having borne it improperly at first, wished to remedy the innovations
that might occur in future and made known to him, on this subject, his intentions. They were ill received and became, subsequently, the source of all the disagreements that one and the other experienced from the misunderstanding that has reigned between them for a very long time. Had Captain Hamelin informed me during our stay at Timor of what was passing, I would have gladly availed myself of the letter that Citizen Millius then addressed to me to grant him the discharge he sought on account of illness, and in truth he was ill at that time. But knowing nothing as yet, I was the first to urge Citizen Millius to continue the voyage, representing to him that his advancement depended upon it and that he ought not to harbour a chimerical fear for his situation, seeing his illness which I found far less serious than my own. Finally I did so much and on several occasions, for he came to see me often on the same subject, that I succeeded in deciding him to continue the voyage. Perhaps he made this decision only in the hope that I would give him the place of M. Le Bas. Which was far from my intention, not wishing to have an officer who believed himself more able than myself, although perhaps he was less so.
From our departure from Timor to our arrival at the North-West port, Citizen Millius was always treated as a sick man and performed no service except a few acts of authority. Captain Hamelin found this wrong and made friendly reproaches to him, inviting him not to place him in the case of making known that he alone commanded on board &a.
I shall not report the two improper scenes that this officer made publicly before his Captain, persuaded that M. Hamelin will have taken account of them in his journal and that I would have punished him severely if he had lodged a complaint with me. But Citizen Millius having come to find me to urge me to receive him on board in his capacity of Frigate Captain which he had obtained only at the instance of M. Hamelin, I eluded giving him a positive answer, confining myself to telling him that I would see whether the thing could be done without disturbing the order of service that I had established. I hoped by my silence, easily explained, to make known to him that the thing was not possible. But as I was informed that he had packed his trunks and was awaiting nothing more than his order for discharge, complaining greatly that I had not already given him an answer, I addressed to him the following letter:
"The Commander &a to Citizen Millius, Frigate Captain on board the Naturaliste, under the orders of Captain Hamelin,
"Citizen, following the request you made to me these past days, to be placed on the Géographe, I announce to you with regret that the thing is more difficult than I would have imagined. I could receive you there only by acting with authority, which would occasion an infinity of discontent and would in this way trouble the tranquillity that still reigns on board.
"I desire to have hereafter a more favourable opportunity to make known to you how much pleasure I would take in doing what might be agreeable to you." Signed N. B."
Captain Hamelin having come to dine on board, I communicated to him the letter I had addressed to M. Millius and profited by this occasion to make known to him how much he had been wrong not to have informed me of the conduct of M. Millius towards him. He excused himself on different pretexts which did not appear to me to be able to exculpate him from this want of confidence.
Moreover, all that I had already learned indirectly of the character of M. Millius and of his pretensions were, for me, a powerful motive to persist in not receiving him on board and, evil against evil, I prefer to leave things as they are than to bring trouble and disorder on board by receiving him.
In the afternoon, the weather having continued foggy and the winds weak from the east to the south-east, we saw no appearance of being able to get under way before nightfall. All our boats, with the exception of (the) cutter which I wished to keep in tow, were hoisted on board, but I did not think it advisable to remove the anchors.
The night of the fifteenth to the sixteenth passed in calm with a sky always very foggy.
Citizen Bernier reported to me that some twenty natives, men, women and children, had come to visit them on the island where they were established and to which one could proceed at low water. Two were allowed to enter under the tent to examine its contents. The beds alone appeared to fix their attention. During their stay with our people, the two goats and a sheep that we had put ashore to recover a little amused them more than anything else. They often addressed them and invited them several times to eat.
Although they had behaved peacefully, the sailors of the boats nonetheless had cause to complain of them in that they stole three bottles in which there was arak. It was much less to drink the liquor than to obtain the vessel, as we ourselves knew.
These natives were likewise among those we had during our stay at the Grande Anse, or at least several were believed to be recognised. When they left the tents, they entered the water above their waist to make their way to the main land. One alone, however, embarked in one of our small boats without the slightest distrust and was conducted there by our people. It was not remarked that any of them appeared to have any authority over the others. The men were absolutely naked, holding in accordance with a custom fairly ordinary, their foreskin in hand. Only the women had a kangaroo skin over their shoulder.
1802-02-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. The starboard anchor was weighed and 100 fathoms of the port cable hauled in. At noon the longboat came in from the watering place with the rest of the casks full, the working party and the effects from the camp. She was hoisted in, as was the large boat.

1802-02-05.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from east to south and SSE. At half past noon the longboat was back. On the 16th at 4 a.m. hove short, sheeted home and hoisted the topsails; the misty and almost calm weather prevented us from getting under way, and we lowered and furled the topsails and veered 6 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, at daybreak we removed the anchors in order to set sail as soon as the weather should clear. The little breeze there was then was from the westward. We hoped that at sunrise the fog would disperse and the breeze would gain strength. In consequence, we remained apeak on a bow anchor.
It was not without difficulty that we managed to weigh our sheet anchors. They were found to be so covered with mud that after breaking our hawser, we were obliged to put up a large tackle on the starboard cable; even then we had considerable trouble in getting them to slip.
During the morning, the winds having shifted to the east, light breeze and afterwards to the north-east, we lost hope of being able to get under way. The sky was, moreover, so foggy that it would have been difficult to set sail even had the winds been favourable. Having nothing better to do, I had the examination and inspection of the objects of curiosity and natural history collected or gathered by M. Le Villain until the time of his death continued in my presence. Captain Hamelin having had them conveyed on board. The things that were delivered to us had so little merit that I found myself obliged to write to the Commander of the Naturaliste the following letter:
"The Commander to Captain Hamelin
"Citizen,
"I inform you that after having made an inventory and general inspection of the objects of curiosity and natural history collected and gathered by M. Le Villain, we were much astonished to find only things of little value, very common and without merit. We knew of him,
however, a fair number of shells that Citizen Maugé, chief naturalist, had taken the trouble to preserve and which he had placed in a particular box enclosed in the cases where were and still are the things of little value that were left there.
"As the cases were well closed and immediately afterwards, it does not appear to us doubtful that since his death, someone on board has presumed, without your knowledge, to open them and to remove the objects which belonged unquestionably to the Government.
"I invite you therefore to make a scrupulous search to recover what is missing and to make known to me the authors of such a delinquency.
"I have also just been informed that when the various articles belonging to him were sold, several of those which had been obtained by purchase or by gift were included therein. This disposition is absolutely contrary to the ordinances which authorise only the sale of linen or of that which is liable to spoil. If these articles are not of this number, you will be kind enough to claim them from those who purchased them, to draw up an inventory of which you will send me a duplicate signed by you and to keep them at the disposal of his family to dispose of as they see fit. It is said that there were some gold articles which also passed into sale.
"Among the birds, no trace was found of those stuffed at Île de France and it is asserted that they were publicly sold. They are in the case of objects belonging to the Government."
"Your fellow-citizen. . Signed N. B."
During the course of the day, the winds having continued to vary from the south-east to the north-east, it was not possible for us to get under way. At sunset, we could not refrain from remarking the brilliant colour of its disc, which was of the most vivid red that one could imagine. Between the fifteenth and eighteenth degrees North and sometimes even by a latitude further South, I had on several occasions seen a similar phenomenon on the coast of New Holland, but in those instances the sky was ordinarily clear and serene, instead of which in this one, the whole atmosphere was laden with fog as humid as it was thick. This appearance was almost always the presage and even the announcement of some squalls for the following day and perhaps we should feel their effect.
At the commencement of the night, Captain Hamelin addressed to me by his boat several small pine boxes and cases containing various objects of natural history which had been sold as his effects. These objects being the property of the Government since we knew, beyond doubt, that they had been collected by different persons during the ports of call we made until the death of this assistant naturalist. I claimed them in his name to return them to him. All were examined with care upon their arrival on board and are at present deposited in cases made expressly with a mark which certifies that they were gathered and collected during the voyage.
The sky having been tolerably fine and the wind calm for the greater part of the night, I remained on our bow anchor. But about three o'clock in the morning, there came to us a gust of wind from the north which brought with it a suffocating heat. As this wind came to us from the bottom of the bay, the cause of this sudden heat appeared to me to be attributable to the burning of the mountains which lie there and which, since our arrival, have been continuously on fire. The first squall we received put us adrift and, being unable to bring up with a hundred fathoms of rope out, we were obliged to let go a sheet anchor while awaiting daylight, to see what the weather, which from then had a very bad appearance, would do.
The barometer had suddenly fallen to 27 inches 7 lines from 28 inches 1 line at which it was a little before the squall. The thermometer which I had exposed to the open air after having experienced myself the sudden heat that had occurred, rose to 18 degrees in less than a quarter of an hour. On taking it from my cabin, it was at twelve and a half.
1802-02-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. At 4.15 a.m., having a light air from the south, we hove short, hoisted and sheeted home the topsails; but a flat calm coming on, we furled the topsails and lay at long stay. We had caught the end of the hawser that parted on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802] and kept it aboard.

1802-02-06.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sea smooth, a flat calm. The breeze got up from the NNE and drew round, freshening, to NW, W and SW. The corvette dragging fast towards the land, we struck our topgallant masts. The Aboriginal people lit fires round the shores of the port.
1802-02-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, at daybreak, the weather instead of clearing became worse, and what the sunset had announced to us the previous day was verified during the morning. The squalls from the north-west to the west became so violent that we were obliged to pay out a hundred and twenty fathoms of our cable to avoid drifting too much onto the starboard shore, from which we found ourselves no more than a mile distant.
After sunrise, the winds shifted to the west and increased further in strength. The sky became dark, laden with vapours and we had rain cold enough for us to feel it. Having little more to drift by, given the small distance at which we were from the land, I had a second sheet anchor let go to port by way of precaution and paid out thirty-five fathoms of cable. It served not only to hold us more firmly but also to moderate the vessel's turning. We weighed the bow anchor with the cutter.
About eight o'clock, seeing no appearance of change in the state of the sky, I had the topgallant masts struck down and laid on deck, for they were quite useless to us and had been used very little during the voyage. We put in place poles which served us just as well without our topsail masts being overloaded with useless weight in this circumstance. This country, moreover, appeared to me but little suited to topgallant masts for since we have been here, it has happened to us to have sometimes two days of fair weather but never three.
Be that as it may, from ten o'clock to noon, the sky became tolerably fine and clear. The heavy clouds which had alarmed us in the morning dispersed and the squalls although very frequent were less violent and less lasting. I wished to avail myself of this interval to set sail. We accordingly hove up our port anchor, but something having gone wrong through the strength of the wind, I stopped this work and resolved to wait for the wind to become more manageable. My position, moreover, was not the most favourable, so it appeared to me much more prudent to defer for a day or two, if necessary, than to expose myself to being cast upon the shore.
About noon, the winds shifted to the south, a fresh breeze and varied during the course of the day and evening to the south-south-east. I was then the less displeased at not having got under way since it had appeared to me from the direction of the clouds that they would not remain long from the west or south-west as we had had them in the morning.
Throughout the day, we saw considerable fires at no great distance from the shore. They increased so much by the violence of the wind that at noon the whole port side was ablaze. That of starboard, although considerable, was less so. There is no doubt that it is the natives who are the cause of these great conflagrations for the direction of the wind would not have given them the ones we successively saw them take. It is not perhaps solely for the pleasure of destroying that they thus set fire to their forests and it is reasonable to suppose they have a purpose of utility in it. According to this reasoning, it might perhaps be occasioned only with the intention of destroying the grasses and other brushwood which make their progress difficult and troublesome or for the hunting of some quadrupeds known in the neighbourhood.
After sunset, the breeze calmed considerably, the winds shifted first to the east and afterwards to the north, perfectly calm. The sky, although damp, was fairly fine during the night and we had constantly before our view all the havoc which the fire was making in the depths and surroundings of the North-West port. The little wind there was when they shifted to the north was probably the cause which prevented us from feeling as on the previous day the heat of the burning of the land.
1802-02-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm; the heat was stifling. At 2.30 a.m. a light breeze got up from NNE, drew round to NW and W, freshening, and at last to SW, a strong breeze with violent gusts. At 5 we had dragged and veered cable, and slipped the hawser with a buoy whose lashing gave way. At 6 the topgallant masts were got down. At 7.30 we dragged and let go a second anchor, the wind blowing hard from WSW to SSW. The Aboriginal people lit many fires round the shores of the port; we saw five of them on the nearest shore, each with a brand in his hand, setting fire everywhere. At nightfall the wind fell away, and it was calm during the night.

1802-02-07.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze in gusts from SW, SSE and south; it fell away in the afternoon. We made attempts to get under way, but a calm coming on we let go a bower anchor.
1802-02-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, at half past three in the morning, word was brought to me that the winds were from the north-west, light breeze, and the sky fine. I gave orders that the bell be immediately rung and that we proceed without delay to weigh our port anchor, as we still had two out. As soon as it was apeak, we hove up the starboard anchor. The weather was still fair and the winds from the same quarter. But about an hour before sunrise, a very dense fog which did not allow us to see the shore, of which we were but a mile distant, came to obscure the air. As I thought it would be quickly dispersed by the sun, we hove apeak and we held ourselves ready as soon as it disappeared to set sail although the wind, which was from the north-west, was very light. The Naturaliste did the same and hauled in her topsails.
At seven o'clock breakfast was served to the crew, still in the hope that the sky would become clearer and we saw with regret that the fog became increasingly considerable.
About eight o'clock, we were perfectly calm without the slightest appearance of breeze in any quarter of the horizon. However, about ten o'clock, we had a little wind from the south-east variable to the east. There was then no longer any possibility of getting under way and we were compelled to lower our topsails and pay out thirty fathoms of cable to avoid dragging. Captain Hamelin's boat having come on board, he asked me to send a party fishing since there was no appearance the winds would change during the rest of the day. I sent one also with the seine and we went ashore on the starboard shore.
The excursion we made into the interior of the country, although fairly considerable, produced nothing interesting to us. I brought back nothing but a new and rather pretty bird, as well as a plant with mature seeds which no one until that moment had yet encountered.
Citizens Depuche and Péron having requested to be put ashore to go and speak with the natives of the country in order to increase the vocabulary they had begun, I gave orders that one of our light boats be given to them, and they departed. I remarked to them, nevertheless, that their hope would be disappointed and that they would find no one, being persuaded that the natives had changed their dwelling place, having seen no smoke in the place where they had settled upon their arrival. Although they were persuaded to the contrary, the event proved to them that my remark was not as wanting in judgment as they thought, since on their return they reported to me that they had found no one.
The fishing done by our boat was passable. Among the fish that were caught, there were three of what Anderson names the elephant fish. This name was doubtless given to it by this naturalist only on account of the proboscis which hangs at the extremity of its snout. The description which he gives of it did not appear to our naturalists to be exact. One of these three fish bore beneath the belly two things quite extraordinary which I shall do my best to preserve the material of which they are made, appearing sufficiently solid to warrant this hope: it is believed that this is an envelope in which is enclosed the reproduction of this fish. This conjecture is all the more plausible since it was a female, which dragged them after her having them attached by a ligament to the opening of the matrix. There were also taken with the seine two fine shells of the whelk species.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the winds were perfectly calm and the sky very overcast with little appearance of fair weather for the following day.
1802-02-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather. At 4.15 a.m., a breeze from NNW, we weighed both anchors in turn and got under way under topsails. We hauled in 50 fathoms of the hawser, which had stayed foul of the anchor's flukes, and took the draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 7 inches, difference 4 inches. At 7.30 a flat calm; anchored and lay at long stay with the topsails hoisted. The breeze got up from the south and veered as far as east. At nightfall the commander signalled us to follow his movements; accordingly we lowered the topsails and veered cable.

1802-02-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather; throughout the twenty-four hours a very light breeze variable from south to ESE and SE. In the forenoon the commander having squared his yards, we did the same.
1802-02-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, we remained perfectly calm until about nine o'clock in the morning. The sky although very dark was tolerably fine. At that time, there came to us a light breeze from the south-east which gradually varied towards the east and, about noon, the winds having increased a little, settled in that quarter of the horizon.
Seeing no appearance of being able to get under way during the evening, I sent two boats fishing, one with the seine and the other with lines. The latter was much more successful than the small cutter, for it caught sufficient fish to distribute to the crew. What the other brought back was scarcely worth speaking of.
During the evening, the winds remained from the east, a nice breeze, but at the commencement of the night the sky had so bad an appearance that we paid out twenty fathoms more of cable than we had had during the day to be more secure on our anchor.
