However, despite the appearance of the sky, there was no bad weather, and the greater part of the night passed in calm.
Citizen Maugé was very ill during this day and it is all too probable that we shall unfortunately lose him soon, for he wastes away before one's eyes every day and his belly becomes more and more swollen. About four o'clock in the afternoon, he sent for me and spoke to me of his situation. I did all in my power to encourage him to be patient, especially as for some days past he had become very anxious and even difficult. He asked me to assemble for the following day, if we did not depart, the two physicians of the Naturaliste to consult together on the continuation of his treatment for the future course of his illness. I promised to do all that he desired in this regard and was not even willing to defer to the following day the assembly which he requested, but he insisted that it be put off until that time.
1802-02-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to NE. Fish were taken and distributed.

1802-02-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a little misty; shipped the winter spar. A fresh breeze from E by S to NE. The dinghy brought back fish and went straight back to the fishing.
1802-02-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, the weather was so foggy that at daybreak we could scarcely perceive the land and even the Naturaliste which was quite near us. We hoped that the sun at its rising, or in mounting the horizon, might perhaps disperse it and the winds become favourable. In consequence, we hove to long a-peak in order to profit by it at once if they should be favourable to us.
At nine o'clock, the fog being as thick as at daybreak and the wind perfectly calm, I warned our chief physician of the desire of Citizen Maugé that he consult with the others on the situation and the best means to be employed to help him through it. M. Laridon confirmed what he had already told me regarding the little hope he had of seeing this naturalist recover and wrote to Citizens Bellefin and Colas to urge them to come on board as soon as possible.
The letter was carried at once and at eleven o'clock both arrived on board. According to the consultation which they held together, the illness of Citizen Maugé was regarded as fatal and, not being curable by the aid of medicine, so that if he does recover its cause will rather be attributable to the unknown course of nature than to the remedies which shall be employed by the medical profession.
About noon, I went ashore with Captain Hamelin and we remained there about three hours. My intention was to obtain some butterflies of the country. But this excursion was not successful, all those I caught were of the same
species and not pleasing to the eye.
Three of our boats were employed in fishing and all three were successful, fish was caught for two days, independent of a fairly large quantity which was given to the Naturaliste.
During the course of the evening, the winds were very light from the east to the east-south-east and we had rain. The sky remained so overcast and foggy throughout the day that we saw the sun appear only at two very short intervals.
The night of the twentieth to the twenty-first passed in calm, the sky always very dark and foggy.
1802-02-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. At 4 p.m. the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. She was back at 8.15 and was hoisted in, together with a catamaran she had found adrift in the channel.

1802-02-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 4 the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. At 8 p.m. she was back; she was hoisted in, together with a catamaran belonging to the Aboriginal people which they had found adrift in the middle of the channel. From the 21st to the 22nd [Pluviôse, Year 10, 10-11 February 1802]. Overcast, misty weather, fine rain throughout the twenty-four hours, a flat calm.
1802-02-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, there was no better appearance of being able to get under way than on the previous days. The sky was extremely overcast, the wind calm from the east-north-east and the state of the atmosphere very thick. Before deciding to allow the boats to go fishing, I waited until about eleven o'clock in the hope that if the winds made up their minds they might shift to the south by taking from the west. But it was in vain for, when the breeze began to freshen a little, they remained from the east without any hope of seeing them vary.
During the evening, the winds were from the south-south-east, light breeze and at the commencement of the night we had the regret of seeing no appearance of change in the state of the atmosphere which became laden with thick fog. The wind fell entirely calm.
Captain Hamelin's boat returning from fishing brought on board a canoe, the only mark of industry that we have recognised until this day among the inhabitants of this part of the coast. I believe that the term of raft or floating buoy would suit much better than that of canoe, the assemblage of bundles of tree bark which they lash together and which they use to pass from one land to another. The sticks which they use to put it in motion have, likewise, no resemblance to the paddles in use in canoes, see the drawing which I give of them. These buoys pointed at both ends may have two or three inches deep inside and have, over canoes, the advantage of not being able to capsize, their displacement being considerable. The rowers stand or sit on their heels upon them.
1802-02-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a flat calm. Fish were distributed to the crew. Rain during the night.

1802-02-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, the fog continued all day and the wind was absolutely calm, the little breeze which made itself felt from time to time came to us from the south-south-east. The sky was so dark throughout the day and the air so thick that the edges of the coast could scarcely be distinguished. We saw with regret that this day was still lost to us, having no means of employing it usefully. The environs of the port and other parts of the strait had been so well explored by the naturalists that they appeared likely to find there only things of which they were already in possession. On the other hand, the hope that the wind might change at any moment did not permit me to send boats too far away. For if at first we had been able to foresee what happened to us, I would not have failed to send to visit the place where the garden of M. La Hay was established, it is the only part of the strait which we have not visited.
During the evening, the weather remaining as before, boats were sent fishing and it was fairly successful and abundant, although done with lines.
The night passed in calm, the sky even more foggy than is customary.

1802-02-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, the sky continued to be extremely foggy and thick, the winds from the south to the south-south-east almost calm. We remained hove to in the hope that they would shift to the south towards the west, but this expectation was unsuccessful for, about ten o'clock, the little breeze there was fell entirely calm and did not return to us from the south towards the east until the afternoon.
I then decided to send a boat fishing with the seine and another with lines. The fishing was fairly abundant and independent of the fish, we caught a hundred crabs of the species of spider crabs.
On the evening, the sky appeared to be clearing, the fog dispersed a (sic) little and the night which passed in calm was fairly fine. From it we augured a change in our favour for the following day.

1802-02-13.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather. A light breeze from south and SE, with fine rain until four in the morning. The dinghy left for the fishing.
1802-02-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, we were deceived in our expectation. The sky was to be sure finer than is customary and we sometimes saw the sun which had not happened to us for a long time. But the little wind there was came from the south variable to the south-east. Notwithstanding the little appearance there was of getting under way during the day, I was not willing to send any boat out to go fishing, but I sent my cutter which was not hoisted on board and which I intended to keep in tow, with the dredge.
At noon, it returned and brought us back only a single beautiful shell which, although dead, compensated us a little for our (stay) at anchor, so beautiful and precious did it appear to us. None of us know it, nor anything that (approaches) it.
During the day, Citizen Maugé appeared to me more ill than usual. As I went to see him every two hours, I found him such drowsiness and such great weakness that he had difficulty moving and truly I despaired of his recovery, although the physicians had assured me for a long time that they regarded it as impossible. It appeared to me that the patient himself was affected by it, for he spoke to me only of his approaching death, so long as I was with him and (of the) regrets of his friends whose counsel he had despised in undertaking this voyage despite them. I at once called the physician of the Naturaliste and a new consultation was held. The results were the same as the first time they had assembled, that is to say that the illness was fatal and that he could recover from it only through an extraordinary cause. This new opinion made such an impression upon me that I passed the day very ill at ease. I had always had hope until this moment, and the situation alone of Citizen Maugé made me lose it rather than anything the physicians said to me, despite all their knowledge.
At sunset, calm came on and lasted the greater part of the night. The sky nevertheless was fairly fine until two o'clock in the morning, when the winds having shifted to the north variable towards the east, it became cloudy and overcast.
1802-02-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to ESE. Latitude of the observatory, North West Port: 43° 1' 1"; longitude 145° 5' 0"; variation NE 10° 25' 0".

1802-02-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from east to ESE. At 4.30, the breeze being from the NW, we hove round on the cables, and at 5 hoisted the topsails; at 5.30 got under way and made all sail, ranging along Van Diemen's Land. After doubling the east point of the North West Port the winds headed us; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter, and on the 10th board we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 44° E; Pointe Pierson N 15° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E.
1802-02-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, at daybreak, the winds varied from north to north-north-west. The desire we had to leave caused us to set sail at once. The breeze although very light, permitted us with the aid of the ebb tide to make about a league, but at that time the winds shifted to the north-east and even to the east which was absolutely contrary to our course. We then began to tack and this manœuvre lasted until ten o'clock with very little success. The winds were so inconstant that we had them sometimes from the north, sometimes from the east and even at times from the south-west, but all these puffs were the affair of a moment, perfect calm immediately succeeded them; at ten o'clock, the tide being strong enough to cause us to drift with great speed towards the shore of Bruny Island we were obliged to anchor within musket shot of the land. The Naturaliste at the same time fortunately found itself on the main shore and anchored at about two-thirds of the channel.
As the position in which I found myself was not good to keep, I had a rope hauled out to the north-north-east but the current having caused our cutter to drift to the south-west, it was not advantageous to us, however it put us in a position to withdraw a little from the shore.
In the afternoon, the winds being from the east variable towards the north, we hauled out a second rope which made us gain approximately the middle of the channel. And we remained on a bow anchor in twenty fathoms of water, good bottom.
At sunset, the sky which had been fine during the day became dark and the wind fell calm. I sent two boats fishing at four o'clock in the afternoon, having nothing better to do.
According to the surgeon's report, Citizen Maugé was much worse than usual and I had no difficulty in convincing myself of it by my own observations, in the different visits I made to him during the day.
The night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth passed in calm, the sky fairly fine.
1802-02-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from NNW. At 5.30 we got under way and shaped our course to leave the port, hugging the eastern shore of the port, after doubling its east point. The wind headed us, drawing round to NE and ENE; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter. At 9, on the tenth board, we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, Pointe Gicquel bearing S 44° W, Pointe Pierson N 15° E, and Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E. The breeze varied from east to west by way of north.

1802-02-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to east. During the night the wind drew round to W, a fresh breeze; stopped the topsails with rope yarns. The winds hauled to the SW and drew round to south; the topsails were lowered.
1802-02-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, the sky was foggy and overcast until sunrise. From daybreak we hove apeak and hoisted our topsails, the winds then being from the north-north-west and very weak. We waited to get under way for them to gain some strength to overcome the current which was against us. But they were not long in shifting to the south and when the sun dispersed the fog about seven o'clock they shifted to the south-east and east.
We were then obliged to pay out cable and lower our topsails. During the rest of the day there blew a fresh breeze from the east. The astronomer went to take the latitude (of) the point which forms the entrance to the port on Bruny Island. The small cutter and another boat departed for fishing and the cutter for dredging. None of these boats were successful. During the day communication was held with the natives who behaved very peacefully. It is true that they were in small numbers.
During the night, it was calm as usual.
1802-02-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to NE by way of east; a little rain.

1802-02-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from ENE to NE. At 5 a.m. loosed the topsails and got under way on the starboard tack, the winds a light breeze from NNW to NE. Being under Van Diemen's Land we were taken aback and went onto the port tack; at 6.30 we let go the anchor.
1802-02-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at three o'clock in the morning, there came a light breeze from the north which decided me (to) have the bell rung at once to be ready to set sail at daybreak. The weather was fine and the sky clear which made me believe that the winds might be favourable to us. As soon as we were under way, we made way, but scarcely had we made half a league when the wind fell entirely calm and the ship would not steer. We were obliged to drop anchor, all sails set.
At seven o'clock, the breeze from the north-north-east to the north-east came on. It was necessary to furl the sails and pay out cable. The weather was fine during the rest of the day, the astronomers were put ashore to make observations and two boats were ordered to go fishing.
About seven o'clock, there came a light breeze from the south-west, we at once set
sail so impatient was I to leave the strait where I believe it is not prudent to enter when one has no time to lose by reason of the difficulty of being able to leave it. As soon as we were apeak, calm came on, we had to hold on and wait, despite ourselves, for a more favourable moment. Finally it arrived, and during the night we managed to double Pierson Point. The vessels anchored at about a league outside the points. By this means we had no more such fear of the variability of the winds since, unless we had them directly from the south-east, we had hope of getting out by tacking. During the night the weather and sky being fine, soundings were sent around the vessel at half a league, the bottom was found to be 12 to 14 fathoms, mud. About two o'clock, the breeze came on from the south-east and the winds in fairly strong puffs. Towards the end of the night, calm replaced it.
1802-02-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze from NE to NNW. At 5 a.m. we got under way on the starboard tack; being close in with Van Diemen's Land, we were taken aback and went onto the port tack. At 6.30, the commander having anchored, we did the same. The rigging was set up. The wind, a fresh breeze from NNW, hauled to N, NNW, NW, W and SW. At 6 a flat calm. At 6.15 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander signalled us to get under way at once. At 7.15 we were under sail, shaping our course to leave the channel. At 8, after doubling Pointe de la Sortie, we anchored in 14 fathoms, the south end of Willaumez Island bearing east, Pointe de la Sortie S 22° W and Pointe Pierson S 50° W. Calm during the night.

1802-02-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE, N, NNW, NW, W and SW. It fell calm; at 6 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander made the signal to get under way; at 7 we were under sail and shaped our course to leave the channel. After doubling Pointe de la Sortie we let go the anchor; at 10.30, the breeze having settled in the SE, we got under way under our fore-and-aft sails; shortly afterwards we sheeted home the topsails and took in the courses, a fresh breeze from SE. At noon took the bearing of Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W; Pointe de la Direction N 4° 30' E; and Cape Trobriand S 1° E.
1802-02-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, about eight o'clock in the morning, the breeze having come on from the east variable to east-south-east, we set sail in fine weather, the current with us and with hope of doubling Direction Cape and even Villiaume Island before the return of the tide which was to occur about one o'clock or half past one in the afternoon. We made several tacks between the cape and Bruny Island, with the hand lead, and at noon we doubled at a quarter of a league's distance the rocks which are at the point of this last island, no bottom at fifteen fathoms.
During the evening, we continued to tack between Cape Raoul on the Tasman Peninsula and Cape Trobriant on Bruny Island. The tacks were then long, nevertheless we made little progress, the current being against us. The winds were then from the south-east and the sky very damp. After sunset, the breeze fell much and the tide swept us along, bearing us rapidly towards one or the other shore according to the tack we were on. At the commencement of the night, Cape Raoul lay from us south 85° east, and Cape Trobriant, south 16° west.
From sunset until about two o'clock in the morning, the little wind there was proved almost calm and very variable, we made but little progress except through the aid of the tide which was then favourable to us. The sky became so laden with clouds and fogs that we often lost sight of the land although we were not far from it, sounding between 28 and 36 fathoms.
At one o'clock, the winds having shifted to west-south-west and then to south-south-west, a fresh breeze, we made way to double Cape Raoul, leaving the Naturaliste far behind us.
1802-02-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At 9.15 a.m. we got under way and beat between Bruny Island and the northern peninsula to weather the Tasman Peninsula and reach Maria Island. At noon Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W, Pointe de la Direction N 5° E, Cape Trobriand S 1° E. At 4, Pointe de la Sortie N 73° W, Pointe de la Direction N 59° W, Cape Trobriand S 9° W, Cape Cannelé S 6° W. At 11.30 a flat calm.

1802-02-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. During the night sounded every half hour and found from 28 to 40 fathoms. We rigged the topgallant masts after cutting off their poles. A fresh breeze from SE, south and SSW.
1802-02-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, before daybreak, we had doubled Cape Raoul in misty weather, though fair enough. The winds were then from the south-west, a fine breeze, and the sea was also raised by a heavy swell from the north-south. At seven o'clock, we doubled Cape Trobriant Pillar and the little island of Tasman, then directing our course to pass between the rocks of Hyppolite and the mainland. As we proceeded along this whole coast at three-quarters of a league at most from the shore, and often less, we took bearings and observations everywhere. This part of the coast is sparsely wooded compared to that of the strait, but in return it offers a great quantity of sites of the greatest interest.
As the whole stretch of coast between Cape Pillar and Cape Frederick Henry had no name, we gave one to each of the points or capes where our bearings began and ended.
The high lands forming Cape Pillar are generally arid and sparsely wooded, but a little to the north of this cape, vegetation presents itself in an agreeable view, varied by the shades of colour. I named Point of the Organists the first point found to the north of Cape Pillar and abeam of the rocks of Hyppolite.
In crossing the channel that separated them from the mainland, we found no bottom at 30 fathoms, and the current was setting north at a considerable rate. The government chart indicates only two (rocks), yet there are three, well distinct and separated from one another. The largest of the three lies more to the east than the other two, and I believe that by working to windward one could pass between the first and second, (although) the gap is but narrow. This first rock is elevated, and coming from the south it (presents) itself in the form of a range mark.
After doubling them, we continued to coast along the mainland at half a league and three-quarters of a league from the shore. We named Petite Point that which forms the northern entrance of the first indent in the form of a bay marked on the government chart. The view (of) the whole of this part is very agreeable. The lands are high, elevated and well wooded. The indent offers a beach of very remarkable white sand, and the sea appeared to us quite calm. This cove could offer shelter only for small boats, at least, so I judged it from its want of shelter from the north to the south by the east. This point is low and even.
From Petite Point to Cape of the Peaks, the lands are high and of fine appearance. The summit and slope of the mountains are extremely steep on the seaward side, and offer no suitable place for landing except in the great cove found in this part. Here, as in the other, there is a fine beach of white sand, and the sea quite smooth close to the shore.
From Cape of the Peaks to Cape Frederick Henry, the lands are higher than anywhere else and well wooded. This cape is very remarkable for the prominent points resembling steeples that are found there and which give it a very particular aspect. The interval separating it from Cape Frederick Henry offers neither anchorage nor shelter, and the sea breaks everywhere with force.
According to the course we steered from Cape Pillar (in the margin: to Cape Frederick Henry), it seems to me that the coast does not trend far enough to the west, and the two capes should be different from that which was given them. One will be able to judge better from the plan which we are about to draw up of this part of the coast.
As Cape Frederick Henry forms the entrance to the bay to which the name of Bay of Marion has been given, we crossed it without visiting it, having the intention to have it examined scrupulously during the sojourn I planned to make at Marion Island. For I am persuaded that there is an error in the government charts regarding the placing of the bay, which Tasman named Bay of Frederick Henry.
About four o'clock in the afternoon, we came to anchor in nine fathoms of sand, roughly east-west of Oyster Bay. The Naturaliste, which had fallen astern being unable to double Cape Raoul, arrived about five o'clock. This vessel passed outside the rocks of Hyppolite.
Citizen Maugé, during this day, was much worse than usual, and according to the doctor's report, there was no appearance that he could pass the night. Although I should have expected this sad news from one moment to the next, it made such an impression on me that I fell ill from it.
Bearing from our anchorage to Maria Island. The southernmost point of this island in view, south 28° east. Two rocks a little way offshore on which the sea breaks, south 24° 30' (26° 30'). The entrance to Oyster Bay north 60° east & north 7° east.
(No entry for the Thirtieth of Pluviôse)
1802-02-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N, SW, S, SSE. At midnight the course was given S 45° E. Cape Trobriand then bore from us S 34° W, 3 miles off. At 4 it bore S 68° W; the wind having headed us, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 8 the course was given S 78° 45' E. Cape Raoul bore from us N 8° E, Cape Pillar N 58° E and Little Tasman Island N 70° E. We bore up by degrees to N 11° 15' W. At 10.15 doubled Tasman Island. At 11.15 doubled the great Hippolyte Rock. At noon, in 43° 8' 30" of latitude observed, it bore from us S 8° W. The topgallant masts were rigged, their poles having been cut off, and the topgallant sails bent. At 3.30 we ran into the channel separating Maria Island from Van Diemen's Land. At 4.15 anchored near the Géographe in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, an islet in the channel bearing N 19° W, the northernmost point of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 6° W, the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 4° E, the SW point of the same island S 29° E, the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 9° E, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E, Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W. During the night the wind a strong breeze from E to NNE. A little fish was taken.

1802-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 3 we ran into the channel that separates Van Diemen's Land from Maria Island; at 4.15 we anchored in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the westernmost visible end of Maria Island N 4° E; Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E; the south end of the same island S 29° E; Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W; the southernmost visible cape of the Tasman Peninsula S 9° E.
1802-02-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNW. At 3.30 the large boat, provisioned for 10 days, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure to survey the Schouten Islands. At 6 the captain left for Frederick Hendrik Bay. I landed on Maria Island abreast of the anchorage with our botanist and the second surgeon, and, shooting as we went, reached the head of Oyster Bay. I looked there for the watering place marked on Cox's chart and found none; I saw only a pool of brackish water and the bed of a stream where there might be fresh water in the rainy season. At spring tides the sea rose into the pool, for there was a channel traced in the sand and marine plants round its edges. In the evening, coming back, we found a grave near a hut of the Aboriginal people; we turned over the earth and our surgeon recognised among the ashes and charcoal human bones that were partly burnt. The grave was covered with grass and small pieces of bark held down by two spears whose ends were driven into the ground, the whole covered with large sheets of bark that we had difficulty in moving. We put everything back as we had found it and came back aboard. In our walk we saw no Aboriginal people; we found several huts, in one of which they had slept not long before, for the grass was still fresh and there were crayfish shells recently grilled. We found fresh water in several holes. At 5 p.m. the weather turned overcast and it freshened. The topgallant masts were struck and a light shown at the gaff for the captain's boat. At 11 the wind drew round to SE, a strong breeze.

1802-02-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind light from NNW. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened from the north; veered 30 fathoms of cable and struck the topgallant masts. The dinghy went fishing; the longboat was sent off with 3 days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Freycinet. From the 1st to the 2nd [Ventôse, Year 10, 20-21 February 1802]. Overcast and misty weather, the wind ESE, a fresh breeze. The dinghy came back from the fishing with a great many fish and crayfish. At 6 a.m. the commander cockbilled his yards and put his pendant and his ensign at half mast on account of the death of the zoologist Maugé; we did the same. At 9 the body of the deceased was carried ashore and buried; all the officers of both ships attended his funeral.
1802-02-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Ventôse, early in the morning, I gave orders to Captain Hamelin to send his large boat to reconnoitre the island of Schouten and the others to the north, to which Tasman gave different names. The officer in command of it was ordered to visit the channel that separates them from the mainland, and Citizen Faure was to draw up an exact plan of it as well as of the whole coast. Provisions for eight days were embarked for everyone, this period seeming to me sufficient for this expedition.
For my part, I sent Citizen Boulanger to circumnavigate Maria Island and draw up the plan of this island. Citizen Péron was employed in this expedition.
After the departure of these two boats, I came myself to reconnoitre Oyster Bay; despite all my searching, I found not the place indicated by Cox as that where water and firewood could be obtained. The circuit of this bay which I made on foot afforded me the knowledge of only two places on its circumference which had the appearance of a watering-place in the rainy or winter season. But we encountered (two) channels fairly wide although but shallow in which the sea rises at high tide. We made the complete circuit of them, and all the water we found in different holes was salt and even corrupted, having no outlet and being renewed only at spring tides or by bad weather.
The first channel may be from one hundred and fifty to two hundred paces, following the different courses it takes. We saw there remains of wood cut with saw and axe, which leaves no doubt that it is the place of which Cox meant to speak. This channel is approximately at the quarter of the bay on the south side.
The second channel is found approximately at the three-quarters point of its course on the north side. Its mouth to the sea is extremely narrow and is seen only when one reaches it. Then it widens gradually, and as one advances into the interior. Following its different windings, it resembles exactly a small river of considerable width (sic). It is not doubtful that the channel has been carved by rainwaters, and that in the damp season it is increased by the waters flowing from the mountains in the neighbourhood. But at this moment it is filled only with sea-water, quite as salt at its inland extremity as at its mouth to the sea. As it was late when we made this discovery, we (decided) to go to its extremity, and we retraced our steps after following it for more than a quarter of a league, putting off until the following day to see how far it extended. The ground forming both shores is flat and covered with beach ridges. Between these two arms of the sea there is but very little width for crossing the island. The narrowest place is not more than a hundred paces, and the widest one, two hundred in a straight line. One then sees a great part of the eastern coast of this island and a second bay, in which there is a bar on which the sea breaks to a great height, and the noise made by four waves rolling one upon another makes the view very agreeable, but landing impossible, except at the extremities of the points which form it.
On proceeding to the northern point of Oyster Bay, we saw about twenty natives on the edge of the beach, men, women and children. Most were armed with a spear made like those of the Entrecasteaux channel. They made no offensive gesture at our landing, only they moved away a little from the shore. The signs of friendship which we made to them, after landing, seemed to reassure them, and the presents which soon followed these demonstrations established confidence between them and us.
All sitting together pell-mell, we examined them with attention, and they did the same of us. The women and children held themselves, nonetheless, a little apart, and did not appear to us as gay as those of Bruny Island, which no doubt comes from their having had less opportunity to see ships and the strangers in them. The children especially appeared very timid and fearful. Despite the invitations of their father and mother to come and take what we offered them, they dared not approach us, and we were obliged to throw it to them, and after picking it up, they withdrew very quickly.
The adults, both men and women, were absolutely naked. The latter, like those of Bruny Channel, wore on the shoulder a kangaroo skin. The men were better made than those we had already met. Although tattooed like the others, the bands on their arms were more numerous, except that they appeared to us a little less wide; they had thin legs and a somewhat protuberant belly. The physiognomy of the women is not pleasing. They are generally ill-formed and of moderate height. Some of the men had their faces smeared with charcoal. Their habits and manner of life appeared to us similar to those of the people of the strait. Before parting at sunset, we exchanged some trifles with them for their spears. This exchange took place very amicably on both sides. We took leave of them, giving them to understand that we should return the following day.
Captain Hamelin went to visit Marion Bay, and I await his return to know what remains for us to do in this part.
(two lines struck out)
1802-02-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 1 a.m. the captain came in in his boat. At 10 a.m., on the commander's signal, the longboat was put in the water. At 11 she was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to survey the coast from Cape des Sarcelles to the northernmost point in sight from the anchorage. Many crayfish were taken and a meal of them distributed to the crew. At 2 the carpenters went to Maria Island to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-02-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, according to the report of M. Hamelin, who believed he had completely reconnoitred Bay of Frederick Henry, I caused my boat to be armed and gave command of it to M. Freycinet with the following order:
The Commanding Officer to Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant of the Navy
According to the report just made to me by Captain Hamelin, there is no doubt that Bay of Frederick Henry is placed in the southern part of that which the new charts name Bay of Marion, and that it is in the eastern part of the Peninsula of Tasman, and not in the western part as indicated by the government chart.
In order to fix the doubtful opinion which this geographical point has presented, you will take the command of the boat, and you will proceed directly to the cape which we have just named Cape of the Teal. You will observe the latitude there, and you will endeavour by hour angles to determine its longitude.
From this cape, you will proceed directly along the whole of the mainland coast, as close to the shore as you can. All the coves which you encounter must be visited scrupulously in order to assure yourself whether there is any opening there. On your arrival at the entrance to Bay of Frederick Henry, you will go with caution in that the banks of sand marked on the plan which Valentin gives us of it exist, and that they dry at low water. If there were not sufficient water to go round this bay with the boat, you will do so by land, but in either case it must be completed entirely. You must apply the greatest exactness in all your bearings and multiply them as much as will be possible, for the perfection of the plan of this bay and its depth.
Should bad weather during your absence force me to set sail, you will find me at Cape Frederick Henry. Citizens Bernier, Depuche, and Barbe are appointed to accompany you.
You will not permit that anything be disposed of in any manner, nor under any pretext, of the munitions of war destined to ensure your defence and the safety of the boat. Signed N. B.
Immediately after the departure of this boat, Captain Hamelin's boat was ordered to proceed to Cape of the Teal, which forms the entrance of the channel between Maria Island and the mainland, and to follow the whole coast going northward in order to obtain its plan as well as that of the coves found there.
The other boats were sent fishing and to Oyster Bay. But none were successful. Those of the men of science who landed communicated with the natives and brought back nothing new to us.
Citizen Maugé was dying throughout the day, and expired at eleven o'clock at night.

1802-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from NE to SE. The dinghy carried the sick ashore. At 3 squared our yards, following the commander's example. The dinghy came back from the fishing and brought a great quantity of crayfish.
1802-02-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, as soon as it was daylight, I gave orders that the yards should be topped and the colours struck to half-mast to announce to Captain Hamelin the loss we had sustained. I also sent him a note inviting him to encourage those of his officers and men of science who would wish to attend the funeral of our unfortunate companion to leave the ship when our boat set out.
At nine o'clock, I embarked for the burial of a man whose death and last words penetrated me with sorrow, for a few moments before he died he said to me, "it is for having been too attached to you that I am dying, and that I have spurned the advice of my friends, but at least remember me in reward for the sacrifice I have made to you".
On leaving the ship, a salute was fired from all our artillery, when we were halfway between the ship and the shore a second took place, and on landing on the beach a third. The body of this naturalist was buried between two casuarinas and two eucalyptus trees, and on one of the latter a plate of lead was placed with the following inscription engraved upon it:
Here was buried Citizen René Maugé, zoologist in the expedition of Discovery
under the command of Captain Baudin,
The expedition has suffered an irreparable loss in the death of Citizen Maugé. This naturalist had not the title of man of science, but he did more, alone, than all the men of science together. Entirely occupied with his work, he thought only of fulfilling his duty well, and never was I in the situation of having to remonstrate with him on this subject.
It is most painful for me to see that Citizen Riedelé and he, the two only true friends I have had on board, have become the victims of the friendship they bore me, the sole motive which determined each of them to undertake this campaign which became so fatal to them.
After completing the burial of Citizen Maugé, at which I was accompanied by Captain Hamelin, several of his officers and men of science, I went to reconnoitre a ravine discovered by the carpenters of the Naturaliste, and in which we were assured there was no lack of fresh water. A beaten path, used by the natives, soon conducted us there, but we were surprised, from what we had been told, to find in a pool only a little stagnant water of an extremely insipid taste. All that could be obtained in the course of the day was three barrels of galley water, independent of the consumption of those on shore. This stream must, nevertheless, be considerable in times of heavy rain.
Several natives had gathered about our people and even put the carpenters to flight after much importuning them. They even made some attempts to take away their axes. One of them, and he was the youngest, was taken by force into the wood. They contented themselves with examining him from head to foot without, however, doing him any harm, nor even taking his axe when the ceremony was over. When we arrived, the natives withdrew, and we had much difficulty in gathering them round us. However, by spending time and making friendly signs we succeeded. They all carried a spear and a kind of club, very roughly made and little capable of doing much harm, which was thrown at a short distance.
When we had succeeded in gathering them together, we recognised them as the same we had met the day before and on the day of our arrival. Confidence was soon re-established, and the rest of the day passed quietly with them.
Citizen Ronsard, who had been ordered to ascertain whether the arm of the sea which want of daylight had not permitted us to ascend entirely was considerable or whether it communicated with some reservoir of fresh water, assured us that he had made the complete circuit of it and that from one end to the other the water was salt.
The natives of Marion Island know, as well as those of Entrecasteaux Strait, the effect of our firearms, but they had not so much fear of them, and the noise produced (by) the explosion made but little impression on them. They asked M. Ronsard to shoot some birds which they were to pick up themselves and which were given to them. They were not long in plucking them, and having grilled them a little at our men's fire, they ate them with good appetite without wasting anything, that is, entrails and all.
At four o'clock, I returned on board with Captain Hamelin, leaving everyone on shore and two boats to bring them back when they should think fit. The large boat returned the same day, and the geographer Boulanger is about to occupy himself in drawing the plan of the island of which he has just completed the circuit.
Citizen Péron, having discovered a tomb, brought back several human bones and even some portions of flesh which fire had not consumed. Citizen Leschenault found another also, so that it does not appear doubtful that the practice of burning the dead is used by the inhabitants of this island and of the mainland coast. The tomb, of which I give a detailed drawing, and (from) what we have seen and done with the greatest order and care, they are infinitely superior to all that are known of them, and one may say that they are more anxious to preserve and transmit the memory of their dead parents or friends than to think of their own preservation.
Citizen Péron, who has visited a tomb at his leisure, will give us a more exact description of it than what I could say, from the report made to me, and the drawings of Citizen Petit will supply what may be wanting.
During the night the sky was misty and rainy. The winds from the south-east with strong gusts. We paid out the scope of fifty fathoms, which had been reduced to thirty during the day which was fine.
1802-02-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW to SE and to N. Many crayfish were taken and given to the crew. At 5 p.m. Citizen Freycinet came in with the longboat; as she was making a great deal of water she was hoisted in at once to be repaired. Light rain during the night.

1802-02-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SE to N. At 5 the longboat came in from her expedition; she had surveyed from Cape des Sarcelles as far as the northernmost point of the Van Diemen's Land anchorage. She was making a great deal of water; she was hoisted in and put on the gratings to be repaired.
1802-02-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, early in the morning, Captain Hamelin having come to me, we embarked in my boat to visit a small island to the north of our anchorage, which is situated approximately in the middle of the channel between the mainland and Maria Island. We arrived there at nine o'clock. As it is surrounded all around by large rocks awash and many pebbles, landing is not easy. However, we went ashore and visited it entirely. There are no trees or shrubs upon it, yet the soil covering the nucleus of granite rocks of which it is formed is good and fit for vegetation. Everywhere we saw a kind of grass, long and very fine, which would no doubt make good pasture for cattle. The whole surface of this island, oval in shape, is flat and may be about three hundred paces from east to west and one hundred and eighty from north to south. Everywhere on it we see fragments of oyster shells, mussels, &a, calcined, which testify that the natives stop there when crossing from one land to another. It was for (this) reason that I named this island, Island of Rest.
From its centre we took bearings on the lands in the following directions:
The most prominent point to the north of the island of Diemen, north 3° east
The middle of a small islet in Oyster Bay, north 65° east
The south-west point of Maria Island, south 35° east
Cape Frederick Henry, south 18° east
The lands of the indent of the bay
Cape of the Teal, south 3° west
A rock awash in the western part of the Island of Rest, at two cable lengths offshore, north 65° west
As this island and the shores of the coast produced nothing for natural history, we crossed the channel and went to Oyster Bay and landed on a low point found in this part. There we saw three canoes of the natives, absolutely like the one seen in the strait, in shape. But they were made of bundles of reeds, arranged in the same manner as those made from tree bark, and smaller. We found there several large spears which we took, and which appeared to us more suitable for fishing than for any other use on account of their great length.
During our stay on shore, we saw no natives, as they were in the other part of the bay with several of our men who were there. At four o'clock, we returned on board.
The boats which had been sent fishing in the morning, brought back few fish but a fairly large quantity of lobsters so that each man had one. The whole of this coast in general is sparsely stocked with fish, at least to judge from the unsuccessful attempts we made to catch some.
During the day, the sky was very overcast and the winds from the east to south-east, with a light breeze. During the night they shifted to the north and brought us rain.
1802-02-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a flat calm and continual rain. The dinghy went to Oyster Bay for oysters and brought back a full load.

1802-02-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm, continual rain. The dinghy came in loaded with oysters. At 7.45, having dragged in a squall, we veered 80 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, Captain Hamelin informed me that his boat had returned, telling me that he would hand me for examination the plan which the officer who had had command of it had surveyed and was occupied in drawing up. A small river of brackish fresh water had been discovered in this part of the coast, but to which the boats could not approach.
Throughout the morning, the weather was rainy and misty and the winds from the north with a light breeze. Three boats were, nevertheless, sent fishing.
The evening was no finer than the morning had been, and the men of science who had landed in the hope of seeing the natives returned without having met them. The fishing of our boats was no more abundant than in lobster and oysters, the dredge brought back nothing of value for natural history.
During the night we had winds from the south with gusts and more often calm. The rain was continual and heavy.
(in another hand)
1802-02-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 5 the dinghy left for Oyster Bay. At 7 the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 7.45 we dragged and veered cable. At noon the wind blowing hard from SSW, a high sea. At nightfall the wind and sea went down a great deal. A light was kept at the gaff on account of the dinghy.

1802-02-25.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from WSW. At sunset the wind and sea went down a great deal. Kept a light at the gaff all night to show our position to the dinghy. At 6.30 a.m. the captain embarked in his boat to go and meet her. At 10.30 a.m. the dinghy came in loaded with oysters.
1802-02-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, the winds continued from the south and the sky had a very bad appearance. About eight o'clock, we had a strong squall and much rain. The force of the wind caused us to drag on our anchor; we paid out 70 fathoms of cable without the ship dragging, which obliged us to anchor a second anchor. At ten o'clock, the sky became clearer and the sun appeared for a few moments but not for long. The rain commenced again and the rest of the morning was far from fine.
In the afternoon, the rain was continual and heavy, the winds varied from south to south-south-west, the sea became heavy. In the morning, the barometer had fallen to 27 8 (inches) and everything announced to us some squalls. However, a little before night, it rose to 28 inches and the rain ceased. Nevertheless, as a precaution we paid out one hundred fathoms of our main scope and seventy of the other.
During the night the wind fell entirely and the sky became clear and fine.
1802-02-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 10.30 the dinghy came back loaded with oysters. The breeze from N to NNW.

1802-02-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to NNW. At 2 furled all sail. The dinghy went fishing. In the forenoon weighed the port anchor to inspect it; as soon as it was up we let it go again in 13 fathoms, fine sand. Obs. lat. taken ashore while at anchor 42° 42' 10"; long. 145° 54' 0".
1802-02-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, in the morning we had the finest weather in the world and the wind calm. As soon as it was daylight, we weighed our anchors and let fall that of the starboard which, as I believed, was not found to be fouled. After this manoeuvre, the boats were sent fishing and the men of science went on shore, as did the gardener.
During the morning, we dried our sails, and the clothes of the crew were hung out to air.
We had no news of our boat and I could not conceive the cause of its delay.
The weather remained fine in the evening and we had a light breeze from the north-east. The swell occasioned by the heavy wind of the previous day had not entirely subsided and the ship rolled considerably.
At noon, the latitude of the anchorage was observed to be 42° 42' 30". In the evening, the weather remained fine and the same was true during the night. At sunset, we heard news of our boat returning from its mission, which gave me infinite pleasure. I think that the work which it was to undertake will be exact, the time employed on it having been sufficient to do it to complete satisfaction.
Our men of science, in their excursions, did not see the natives.
1802-02-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNW. The anchor was weighed and another let go in 13 fathoms, fine sand. The sick went ashore. At 11.30 Citizen Faure came in in the large boat. He had examined the supposed Schouten Islands and found only one and several small islets; what was taken for the Schouten Islands is only a very high peninsula joined to the land by a very low neck. The masts were swayed up and the topgallant sails bent. On the commander's signal the large boat was hoisted in. At nightfall the sick came back aboard. During the night the breeze from SW. Latitude of the anchorage 42° 38' 30"; longitude 145° 17' 17"; variation on Maria Island 11° 37' 0" NE.

1802-02-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, at daybreak, the cutter arrived on board. According to the verbal report made to me by the officer (In the margin this note: Citizen Freycinét of the Naturaliste: it is the only place which presents some resources and is the sole port of call in bad weather, but the channel leading to it needs to be better known.) who had been in command of it, I was entirely convinced that Frédéric Henry Bay was incorrectly placed on the hydrographic office chart as on the newly drawn English chart. And I could not conceive how it had been placed in the eastern part of Tasman Peninsula. Unless that peninsula was truly an island, but as we are now well certain to the contrary, the plan which Valentin gives of it, although inaccurate in detail, leaves no doubt that the bay which was named Marion Bay is the same one in which Tasman anchored on leaving Tempest Bay and that he visited the blind arm indicated on his chart.

Moreover, I refer to the report of M. Freycinét and his chart for fuller details.

No natives were seen during this excursion, but we encountered everywhere traces of the residence which they sometimes make there.

At about eight o'clock, I went ashore in Captain Hamelin's boat and we returned on board at one o'clock in the afternoon, having caught sight of his large boat returning from visiting the islands spoken of by Tasman, Furneaux and others, situated on the chart to the north of Maria Island.

This boat, in which I had caused Citizen Faure, geographical engineer, to embark, had orders to proceed up along the islands as far as 42° latitude and to return along the channels which they should form between themselves and the land of Diemen.

Citizen Faure took eight days to complete this mission; he actually proceeded as far as the 42nd degree, continually hoping to find some openings which would allow him to circumnavigate these islands, and it was not without astonishment that he saw that there existed only two, inconsiderable ones, that of Schouten and a rock which forms a second having about one mile of extent.

Having returned on his steps, he passed between Schouten Island and the rock of which I have just spoken and penetrated into a large channel which is found between the two lands, the eastern part of which presents islands. Arrived at its northern extremity, he found there a deep bay and several coves which offer shelter for a good anchorage but no opening to the sea, nor to the north either; see his chart and his route.

It appears, from circumstantial details given by M. Faure that Tasman and Furneaux passed at too considerable a distance from the land to recognise it well, and that, perceiving isolated hillocks, they made islands of them, being unable to have knowledge of the low-lying lands which unite them to one another. This error is often repeated at sea at a somewhat considerable distance, but the boat hugged this entire coast too closely to have been mistaken about it.

Having nothing more to do at Maria Island, nor in the neighbourhood, I gave orders to Captain Hamelin to hold himself ready to set sail on the following morning, to proceed to the strait which separates the land of Diemen from New Holland.

We had reason to regret during this port of call that we could not find any place suitable for a water supply. It is not that fresh water is lacking there; on the contrary, we found it in different parts of the great coast and even of Maria Island, except at the place indicated by the English; but it is impossible to obtain it with boats.

All the coast, from Cape Frédéric Hendrik as far as that which we named Cape (no name) is high, well-wooded and can easily be seen for ten to twelve leagues when the horizon is not thick, which is not usual in these waters. See the views which I had taken of it.

In the afternoon, the cutter was embarked and everything was prepared to set sail on the following morning, with the intention of proceeding to the southern point of Schouten Island by running through the channel of Maria Island, if the winds would permit it, for it has too little width and depth to tack in it with a large vessel.

During the night, the wind was calm and the sky very fine.

Particular Remarks during our sojourn in the channel

of Bruny d'Entrecasteaux, southern part of the land of Diemen,

and on our port of call at Maria Island.

The channel discovered and recognised in the voyage of rear-admiral d'Entrecasteaux is, without contradiction, of great utility for navigation, since it offers a multitude of ports either for vessels which would have damage to repair, or for those which sought only refreshments and a little rest. The only inconvenience which it presents is the difficulty of obtaining fresh water to replace that which would have been consumed in proceeding to it. Nevertheless, we found several streams which it would be easy to conduct to the sea if we were provided with all that is necessary to give them an outlet.

The place named the Port of Swans which I had carefully visited is, of the whole channel, that which appears the most suitable to establish a European colony.

The natives with whom we communicated in this port, and those of the great cove where we were at anchor, appeared to us of a gentle and peaceful character. They are generally of good height, but not too well made. Their physiognomy offers a particular character and all have an air of resemblance which seems to announce that the population is not considerable. At least on Bruny Island on which was the greatest number which we saw together. We counted them, once, fifty-five, men, women and children, all together. Although they have almost all thin legs and weak arms, they nevertheless appear strong and vigorous. All, without exception, have the mouth very wide, the teeth large, complete and well-arranged. They appeared to the learned, to have been filed, but I believe that this is an error in that the upper jaw falling well perpendicularly on the lower, they have the appearance of being molars rather than incisors. Their (eyes) although sunken, are lively and their gaze uneasy, a cause which may perhaps be produced by the difference which men so different from them must have inspired in them. Their belly is large, their hair curly, but much less thick than that of Africans and not so long. The arms, shoulders and above the navel are tattooed in a rather regular manner. This tattooing is done in a manner rather difficult to understand, in that the marks are raised above the skin. I leave it to our learned men to give the reason, but it appears to me that they employ neither fire nor any sharp instrument to achieve it, because the scars would be sunk into the skin instead of being well more raised than it. Tattooing, among these peoples, appears to be practised only at a determined epoch, for children, even of twelve to fifteen years, had no mark. Although their noses are flattened, they resemble in nothing that of the negroes of Africa. Some, indeed, have it long and well-proportioned. Among the children, one was distinguished who might well have some European for a father; his skin was of a light brown colour while the ordinary colour of those of these
islanders is much more like that of the Caraïbes of America than of the Africans of the Guinea coast.

Although we saw several, the shoulders and breast covered with a skin of kangaroo, they are more generally naked, as for the men. But all the women that we saw wore skins which appear rather designed to form kinds of sacks, in which they put what is given to them or what they gather as they walk.

The men have rather a singular habit which greatly amused our sailors, that of almost always holding the extremity of their foreskin in their hand; thus it is very much elongated. These peoples, although savage and wandering, did not appear to me to be subject to making war among themselves, or, at least, they bore no scar on the body which could give rise to suspicion that they did so frequently. The only ones which we saw them have were occasioned by fire. They appear also to be subject to a kind of yaws, for several had ulcers on their legs. We saw on their face or on their body no mark of smallpox. They are perhaps also fortunate enough not to know the great.

Their huts are the most miserable of all those which one could imagine. A piece of wood in the form of an arc forms the whole framework, which is covered with some bark of the eucalyptus which they remove from these trees. All the marks of industry which we saw in them consist of their spears and a club-head which is not very dangerous. The vessels of which they make use to drink is (sic) made of a kind of seaweed of which the leaf is very large and thick. They employ it likewise in the form of a shoe when they have sore feet. The baskets, of which the women make use for fishing, is not without merit, by the long labour which it must cost them. Thus do they attach great value to it and only exchange it with regret. The canoes of which they make use to communicate from one place to another are rather kinds of buoys than anything else and resemble these boats only in the form which is pointed at both ends, and more raised than the rest. The one which we found on the shore had 14 feet in length from one point to the other extremity. It was formed by three bundles of eucalyptus bark rolled one upon the other and of the shape of a yard, that is to say thicker in the middle than at the extremities. These three bundles were joined together by ties of the same bark, which renders their joining rather easy, but unsuitable for the use which can be made of it. The length from inside to inside of this frail boat was nine feet one inch, its width from outside to outside was two feet nine inches and its depth two feet two inches. We had seen them several times pass from one land to the other in the channel, in the number of three and four persons. We did not see that they made use of paddles, but of long sticks which they made perform the functions. They are ordinarily bent when they make this kind of bark-raft go, and we only saw them venture in it in very calm and fine weather.

These peoples appear to draw their principal subsistence from the sea bottom and feed more particularly on shells than on anything else. They did not appear to us to set great store by fish and we could not succeed in making them accept any, whether that taken alive in the seine, or that which our people prepared for their dinner and which they saw them eat with good appetite. They made likewise very little account of our biscuit and fresh bread. At the beginning, they received it and, at our imitation, they made as if to eat it, but as soon as we moved away from them a little, they threw it aside. Some drank a little arrack but in small quantity. The bottle which contained it seemed to give them more pleasure than what was in it.

Among the different objects which we distributed to them in beads, trinkets &a, the buttons of our clothes appeared to please them more than anything else.

Several entered our boats, perhaps with the design of taking what they could find suitable to them, and indeed made a clean sweep of several things, but we experienced no resistance on their part in making them return what we did not wish them to take away. Some boatmen having stripped themselves of their jackets, to make them presents, they accepted them without allowing them to be put on them. To show the use they were to make of them, the jackets were later found at the foot of a tree. Only, they had removed the buttons which were of mother-of-pearl and not of metal.

At our first meeting, the natives of Bruny Island which we encountered came to us with simple demonstrations of friendship, or in the hope of obtaining some presents from us. They presented themselves without arms, received our caresses with pleasure and what we distributed to them with great demonstrations of joy. They imitated easily and with gestures repeated several French words distinctly and followed us in our course over the country and on the shore of the sea. Although we were armed with rifles and sabres, they have a perfect knowledge of both of these weapons and appear to dread their effects, of which, without doubt, some of their number have been the victim.

The day before our departure from the great cove, Citizen Maurouard, first-class midshipman since our departure from Timor, received, at the moment when he least expected it, a thrust of a spear which passed a little above his shoulder and made him a rather deep wound. It is rather difficult to say why it was thrown at him, for we had spent the whole morning with them, their women and their children in the best understanding.

Leaving the Great Cove, I proceeded to the North-West port where I hoped to obtain fresh water with more ease than anywhere else, given the difficulties of having our barrels transported to the places where it was found and which were known to us. We anchored a little inside the entrance of this port and made a rather long stay there to obtain only one hundred barrels of water of little agreeable flavour although potable. The stream which supplied it flows into the sea, but the quantity of banks and the small quantity of water found there prevent the cutters and other boats from approaching it. One is obliged to make an empty scow to take them to the water point and to bring them back full in the same manner, which renders this work long and painful for the crews and occasions a considerable loss of time. It was on an island opposite the mouth of this stream that our observatory was established. On our arrival at this port, we saw many fires and smoke which indicated to us that it was passably inhabited. Nevertheless, we were several days without seeing any of the natives. Nevertheless, on the third day of our arrival, some were seen on the cove of Bruny Island which faces Gicquel Point. I proceeded immediately to shore to observe them and to make them some presents if we could communicate with them. At the approach of the boat, they withdrew into the woods. But, appearing to pay them no attention I amused myself on the shores of the sea in gathering some shells. Soon, they showed themselves again and little by little, they approached near enough to be able to speak. I engaged them by signs and by the sight of some glass beads, to join me. They were four in number, each having a spear in their hand and I my rifle. We were at some length inviting each other to join together and seeing that they did not change position, I went to them. They waited for me very quietly, received my presents with pleasure,

and we began a conversation of gestures and by some words. Captain Hamelin in whose boat I had embarked, having rejoined me with two of his men, we all sat down on the grass. We had all the time to examine at our leisure the natives who differ in no way from those of the Great Cove. On parting to return on board, at about three o'clock in the afternoon, we gave them to understand that we would return the following day to the same place promising them new presents if they would be found there. But whether our return was not agreeable to them, or some other motive, they assailed us with a shower of stones thrown very adroitly and even from far off. When we embarked, several passed over the boat with still much speed, and one wounded me rather severely in the left hip. Although they were out of the range of my rifle, I took aim and this movement having sufficed to disperse them all, I was not obliged to let them hear the explosion. Before separating, Captain Hamelin and I had taken the precaution of exchanging for buttons of the Navy of which they made much account. A button marked with an anchor was the price of a spear. This exchange was made in good faith and without deceit.

Despite what had happened to us, we went ashore the following day but in greater numbers. We found the natives in the same place which we had indicated to them. The company, however, was more numerous in that their women and their children were there. I gave to all, glass beads, some buttons and other trifles. We were astonished to see the same men who had thrown stones at us the day before, give themselves to us without the least mark of distrust and this alone proves to me either that they are not wicked by nature or that they judged us incapable of doing them harm. As soon as we were all assembled, we told them to sit which they did immediately by inviting us to do likewise. Our people were mixed pell-mell with their women and their children, but I had beside me two men solely occupied in examining all my movements and above all my rifle. If it happened that I passed it from left to right or from right to left, they appeared immediately uneasy and were ready to get up to go away. Nevertheless, it was not difficult to reassure them and confidence was soon restored. The children, who at our approach had appeared very fearful and timid, were soon familiarised and played at all sorts of games with our people. They exercised themselves in running, in jumping with one of them, but they were not brilliant in any of these exercises. The women were not beautiful and their kangaroo skins did not serve to diminish the impression which their faces made on us.

We made, during this interview, several throws of the seine and took a fair quantity of fish. The men and children gave with great demonstrations of joy, a hand to haul the seine to shore, but they constantly refused to share with us the fish which was taken there by making signs that they did not eat any. These fish were principally of the species of rays and flounders and of very good flavour. None of us shared the opinion of M. Anderson on that which he named the elephant fish, more known under the name of antarctic chimera, and which he says is one of the best of those which were taken during his stay in Adventure Bay. It is on the contrary, according to us, the worst of all those which we took at the outlet of the strait and in the bay. We dined all on shore, seated in the middle of the natives, without being able to decide them to take anything, but they received with much pleasure the empty bottles which we gave them. I do not know if they feared that we would give them back to them at the moment of departure, but as soon as one was given to them, they passed it to their women who went to hide it in the woods and came back afterwards to take their places among us.

I made a present to one of them (of) a small mirror which did not produce the effect which I expected,

for after having looked at herself in it for an instant, she (passed) it to another who made no use of it. The ladies as well as the men had their faces differently besmeared, either with crushed charcoal, or with a kind of ochre of a dark red. They painted likewise several of our learned men who lent themselves willingly to this whim on their part. This ceremony amused the spectators greatly and occasioned great outbursts of laughter from the natives.

We gathered during this day a rather great quantity of words which are not found in the vocabulary of La Billardière.

Our separation, before sunset had nothing particular about it and was much more amicable than that of the day before.

Each day that we remained in the strait, waiting for the wind to permit us to leave it, we saw them and conversed with them on the shore of the sea or a little in the interior of the country, but they never offered to let us see their encampment and when we asked them to conduct us there they answered: I do not understand you.

I give in my journal several drawings of the figure and the clothing of these peoples as well as a model of their huts and their canoes.

The quality of the soil, in this southern part of the great island of Diemen is everywhere suitable for cultivation and its goodness would answer for the success of the crops if active and industrious people devoted themselves to it. Eucalyptus and casuarina are the dominant trees. As several people have already given descriptions of them, I will not speak of them. The plants, in general, are not much varied there, insects very rare and kangaroos uncommon and difficult to hunt. The woods are full of three or four kinds of parakeets and of two species of crows of which we have a good stock for the natural history cabinet. The mosquitoes are not as numerous or as troublesome as in America, but there is found there a large fly very troublesome, extremely multiplied and of which the sting is painful. The small birds are not abundant and with the exception of a species of swallows which perch on the trees, the others are only seen from time to time.

The sea-birds are more abundant, but more difficult to approach than those of land. We could only procure among the latter two swans and a superb black and white pelican.
