During our sojourn at the NW port, we had a few fine days, but in general, the sky was overcast and often very misty. The winds reigned more from the north to the south by the east than from the north to the south by the west, but we had sometimes from this latter quarter such strong gusts and squalls that two sheet anchors and more than one hundred fathoms of cable scarcely sufficed to keep us off. The sea, however, was never much agitated and the holding very good. The winds from east to south are weak and bring much mist. Those from the south-west often give rain and those from the west to the north, fine weather.

Of Maria Island and the bay called Marion Bay.

On leaving the Entrecasteaux channel, we were obliged to double Cape Raoul at close-hauled, the winds having been constantly from the south-east, varying to the east, having passed in the night to the south-west and to the south, we found ourselves in the neighbourhood of Cape Pillar and doubled in the morning the small island of Tasman. Directing afterwards the course to the north, a little towards the west, we skirted very closely the eastern part of the great island of Diemen, passing in the middle of the channel which is found between it and the rocks of Hyppolite. All this coast, of which I give views of points in succession, offers a very pleasant aspect and the most picturesque which one could encounter.

Cape Pillar is little wooded and is composed only of granite rocks piled one upon the other of very irregular forms. It is the same with the small island of Tasman.

From Cape of the Organists to that of Frédéric Henry, the coast is generally elevated and bold; one can skirt it with a fair wind at small cannon shot without anything to fear. The large rocks which are sometimes seen beyond the points have nothing dangerous about them, everywhere there is much water. This part is as well wooded as that of the Entrecasteaux channel and the verdure has appeared more pleasant to us. This perhaps comes from the fact that the natives, frequenting it less, the trees are not there half burned as everywhere else. Eucalyptus and casuarina appeared to dominate everywhere.

The channel which is found between Cape Frédéric Henry and Maria Island is fine and deep. One does not begin to find bottom at 30 and 25 fathoms until after one has doubled the south-west point of this island. Then it decreases promptly and one finds only eight and nine fathoms at the opening of Oyster Bay. It was off this bay that we anchored, the second day of our leaving the Entrecasteaux channel.

From the first day that we arrived on shore, we communicated with the natives who inhabit this island. They were twenty-three in number, men, women and children. They received us in a friendly manner and without the least distrust. All had, nevertheless, a spear and were on the defensive, but the presents which I made to them, soon reassured them and a mutual confidence was soon established between them and us.

The natives appeared to us much stronger and more robust than those of the Entrecasteaux channel or of Bruny Island. They are in general taller and better made. Perhaps they have more means of subsistence or less difficulty in procuring it. But their women are not more agreeable than the others, and their children more fearful and less confident than those of Bruny Island. There is no doubt that it is the same people, as much because of their language as because of their habits. The same manner of covering themselves with kangaroo skins, of building their huts and of feeding themselves is common to them with the exception that these eat birds which we offered and which the others would not receive. They made no more account than their comrades of our biscuit, bread and arrack, but they had the same desire for our bottles, for glass beads, kaki buttons, however they hesitated long before exchanging their spears.

Their canoes although of the same form are not bundles of tree bark, it is reeds which replace them and arranged in the same manner.

One of the most remarkable things which we discovered by means of a happy chance, is the manner in which they bury their dead. I give a drawing of their tombs, but it is not doubtful that they burn the dead and that they preserve only the ashes and the bones which the fire has not destroyed in order to keep them with care. The two which we found and which were excavated, offered us a sight which surprised us greatly. It was first necessary to dismantle a kind of hut in the form of a sugarloaf. The eucalyptus barks which formed it, rested on four branches of tree bent in a semicircle and fixed in the ground by the extremities. Above these four hoops forming about the bottom of a basket, were found two or three layers of fine grass of a kind of grass very common on this island and which must be good pasture for livestock. After having lifted this grass, we found a heap of ashes among which were found several bones of human body and even some portions of flesh which fire had not yet consumed. At the extremity of the heap of ashes was found a small conduit which is, very likely, that in which they place the corpse to which they render the honours of burial. We were all the more delighted at this meeting because no traveller has told us anything on this subject, at least that has come to my knowledge.

Citizen Péron, in his capacity as Observer of Man, will no doubt give a very circumstantial detail of the form of this tomb as well as of his ideas on the cause of this usage among these peoples, a usage very different from that which is practised in the islands of the South Sea.

During our sojourn on this island, we augmented our small vocabulary not a little with new words collected with care. The natives of this country did not appear to us to have been often visited by Europeans and we did not find in them, as in those of Bruny Island, any object received from them. We (in the margin: still on the chart of M. Freycinét) managed to learn from them the place where they go to obtain fresh water and it is surely not in the place indicated by M. Cox on the chart which he drew of this island. The two streams which they showed us, empty into the sea in East Bay in the middle of which is found a terrible bar if the winds be from the north to the south by the east. Our firearms did not make as much impression on the natives as on those of Bruny Island. The noise of the explosion caused them only an instant of surprise and they showed astonishment only in seeing the blood flow from the birds which they asked us to kill and which they ate immediately without drawing them, being content to leave them in the fire until the feather was well burned which was not long.

During our sojourn at Maria Island, Captain Hamelin's boat had orders to proceed as far as the 42nd degree of latitude to recognise the islands drawn on the chart of M. Flinders, according to Furneaux. It met only that named Schouten Island by Tasman, and another smaller which one could name the Island of the Seals in that it is covered with them. The channel which separates these two islands is narrow, but deep. The lands of the north are joined to the great island of Diemen and form a deep bay on each side of which are different coves which offer good shelter.

The cutter of the Naturaliste was equally sent to visit all the coast the coast (sic) from Cape of the Teal to the southern point of Schouten Island where the work of the boat was to begin.

I sent mine to recognise and to visit with the most scrupulous attention Marion Bay. For, from what I knew of Tasman's voyage, it appeared to me impossible to believe that the bay which he named Frédéric Henry was that placed on the hydrographic office chart, being already well assured that the land which was named Tasman Island is a peninsula joined to the continent by an isthmus, inconsiderable truly, but not badly elevated and fairly well wooded. The report of the officer who had

command of it confirmed this conjecture well demonstrated by the chart which I had drawn up of this part of the coast, beginning from Cape of the Teal as far as that of Marion Bay.

My large boat was employed in making the circuit of Maria Island to verify that of M. Cox.

We were not fortunate with regard to fishing at this port of call. The fish which we took there was truly very good but not abundant. It was not the same with oysters and a kind of lobster, for every day we took more than the crew could consume. The oysters were of good quality but the lobsters far superior to those eaten in Europe by the delicacy and lightness of their flesh. It appears that the natives make their principal resource of these two things for their food, for everywhere one encounters heaps of debris which announce the great consumption which they make of them.

We bought from the natives of this island very large spears which we had not seen until that moment. They gave us to understand that they served them for the hunting of kangaroo. They made not great proof of skill in throwing those of which they ordinarily made use. A single one struck the target at which one was aiming at a distance of fifteen to twenty paces.

They showed us likewise the manner in which they sharpen them. It is firstly with a stone which they use as we would a piece of glass and to give it polish, they employ an oyster shell which they have made sharp.

Our gardener gave one of them a pruning-knife showing him how he should use it. He made the same use of it as he did of his stone and returned it to him when he employed his oyster shell for the perfection of his work.

These peoples do not appear to have any knowledge of iron and of its utility. They made not the least account of the nails which we wished to give them and returned them to us as a useless thing.

The son of the master carpenter of the Naturaliste having been taken off by force into the wood, they contented themselves with visiting him from head to foot, without doing him any harm. And after having satisfied their curiosity, they left him free to rejoin his comrades. This young man carried with him a large axe which tempted them not at all despite that they had examined with much attention the manner in which he made use of it.

One of the novices of the Géographe was likewise visited by these peoples and in the presence of Citizen Péron. The natives found him in such happy dispositions that they testified much joy and satisfaction.

DEPARTURE FROM MARIA ISLAND FOR BANKS STRAIT

On the eighth, at eight o'clock in the morning, we set sail to leave by the south of the channel of Maria Island with a light breeze from the north very weak. I would have much wished that the winds would have permitted me to pass to the north of the island to clear by the channel which is found between it and Schouten Island, but the thing was not possible.

Scarcely had we proceeded half a league when we found ourselves in a dead calm, but as the ebb tide was still making itself felt we let ourselves drift to the south, hoping that the flood tide would give us a little wind. Nevertheless, we prepared a warp anchor for anchoring in case it was necessary to use it.

At eleven o'clock, a light breeze from the south-east began to make itself felt and as we doubled the south-west point of Maria Island, they took strength and their direction more to the east. The course which we were then holding conducted us into Marion Bay, but we did not enter it before because as soon as the south point of Maria Island was doubled, the winds varied from the north-east to the north-north-east, a fine breeze so that we passed at a rather great distance from Cape Frédéric Henry. The course to the north towards the east was continued until midnight through very fine weather, but having the winds absolutely contrary to the course which it was necessary for us to make in order to proceed to the forty-second degree of latitude where were terminated the reconnaissances of this part of the coast made by Citizen Faure, geographical engineer on board the Naturaliste.

When one enters the channel of Maria Island to come to anchor abreast of Oyster Bay, one does not begin to find bottom at 28 or 30 fathoms until one is within the south-west point of this island. The lands in this part are high, elevated, well-wooded and of a pleasant aspect.

The indentation of Oyster Bay is rather deep and offers a fine beach of white sand, but there is found there very little water and vessels of the draught of ours would not be safe in this bay if they came to drift on their anchors by winds from the west or the south-west and it would be extremely difficult to leave it by tacking. Opposite the north point of this bay, there is found a small island of the shape of an A as I have already noted. It is in the channel which it forms between Maria Island and itself that one must pass to leave by the north. This route can only be undertaken with winds which can permit of keeping in the middle of the channel. Otherwise one would run the risk of finding oneself engaged in it and perhaps even of running aground. If one had to tack and the vessel failed to go about, the distance from one land to the other is three-quarters of a league or a league at most.

The lands opposite to Maria Island are high and well-wooded, there are found different coves rather deep but not suitable to offer shelter for because the winds from the north to the east blow full into them rendering the sea very agitated especially when they are in opposition to the direction of the current. The port which (in the left margin: Citizen Freycinét of the Naturaliste found is the only place which presents some resources and a port of call in bad weather, but the channel which leads to it needs to be better known).

During our sojourn at this anchorage, we saw no smoke over all this extent of coast, proof that it is inhabited only in certain circumstances.
1802-02-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from SSW which hauled to south and east and settled at NNE. At 9 got under way and shaped our course S 22° 30' E to double the SW point of Maria Island. At 10.30 the air drew round to SSE; we were taken aback and lay close-hauled on the port tack, standing for Cape des Sarcelles. The breeze freshened, drawing aft as far as north. At noon, being in 42° 44' 4" of latitude, we took the bearing of the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 38° E, the islet in the channel N 20° W, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 6° W, and the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 6° E. At 4, Schouten Island N 6° W, Maria Island from N 27° W to N 61° W, Tasman Island S 20° W. At 6, the NE point of Maria Island N 45° W, Tasman Island S 43°, Cape Pillar S 47° W. At 10, not seeing the Géographe, we showed a light at the foremast head; it stayed there until 11.45 without her answering.

1802-02-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NNE to N and NW. Took the bearing of the middle of Schouten Island N 6° W; the visible north part of Maria Island N 27° W; the south point of the same island N 61° W; Little Tasman Island S 20° E. At 9 p.m. sounded without finding bottom at 80 fathoms.
1802-02-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the lands.
At six o'clock in the evening, the lands to the south closest to Cape Pillar, south 43° west
The most easterly point of Maria Island, north 42° west
The lands most in view to the north, north 22° 30' east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, we ran the tack from north-west from midnight until eight o'clock in the morning, in order to close with the land to follow it closely, should a fair wind declare itself. But it was not so, and after sunrise, they set between the north and north-west, diminishing in force as the sun rose on the horizon.
At daylight, we had knowledge of the land, but from the position of Maria Island, relatively to us. We recognised that the currents had carried us much to the south since our departure. At eight o'clock, we tacked to seaward, steering as close to the wind as possible in the direction of east towards the north.
During the morning, the sky, although fine, was charged with humid vapours which sometimes gave us mist and calm.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 43° 4' 31", which confirmed that the currents had carried us much more to the south than the dead reckoning of the course we had made indicated. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper put us at 146° 14' 37". Although we had perfect knowledge of the lands, we found ourselves at too considerable a distance from them to make useful bearings of them.
In the afternoon, we continued to make course to the east towards the north. The wind, which had greatly calmed, recovered its force, and the breeze was fine, but it was from the north and too contrary to the course which we had to make for us to be satisfied. The sea became heavy, and at sunset the sky became covered with a fairly thick mist.
According to several azimuths taken on board in the morning, the declination of the needle was found to be 11° 30' north-east. But this observation appears to me doubtful, not believing it to be so considerable.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth, the weather was not fine. We received several strong gusts which caused us to take in the topsails, and we took another reef in them. The rain was sometimes heavy and the mist continual. We did not change course during the night. The winds did not render it better on one tack than on the other.
1802-02-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to NW. At midnight the Géographe was sighted. At noon in 42° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 146° 33' 0" of longitude by the watches. Took the bearing of the NE point of Maria Island N 41° W and Tasman Island S 47° W. At 5.15, 10° 58' 40" of NE variation; at 6.30, 11° 19' 10" the same. Fine rain and thick mist during the night.

1802-03-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from north. At 10.30 p.m. we lost sight of the commander; kept a light all night. At 1.45 a.m. we sighted him ahead and at very little distance; crowded sail to close him. At 8 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, the winds were constantly from the north to the north-east throughout the morning, and the sky extremely humid and misty. The sea, which had been fairly rough at night, was now agitated only by a slight swell coming from the north-east. The breeze had also greatly diminished.
At eight o'clock, we took the tack to the north-west to close with the land, although the weather was more suitable for moving away from it than for reconnoitring it. But on the other hand, I did not wish to find myself too far to seaward when the wind became fair, which might happen at any moment.
At noon, we had no observation, the sky on the contrary became more misty than it had yet been, and we had a considerable amount of rain.
According to the dead reckoning of the courses made, we found ourselves at 42° 54' of south latitude and at the 147th degree of longitude to the east of Paris.
In the afternoon, the weather appeared to be clearing. The rain ceased about four o'clock in the evening, and the mist dispersed at sunset. Although our horizon was then fairly extensive, we had no knowledge of land, which made me fear that the currents had carried us much more to the south-east than we thought, especially as this had happened to us on the first day of our departure.
At eight o'clock, we went about to pass the night to seaward. The Naturaliste did the same. The sky was then fine, but the rapid movement of the hygrometer towards very great humidity was not long (in) proving to us that the fine weather would not be of long duration. The barometer, however, held fairly high not to fear rough weather, which did not appear to be as near us as the hygrometer announced.
At midnight, the winds being from the north varying north-north-west, strong breeze and in gusts, the sky became covered with thick mist which allowed us scarcely to see one another. This thick fog lasted about half an hour and became afterwards less dense. But our horizon was scarcely extended more than a quarter of a league. From time to time, the Naturaliste was sighted, a little to leeward and at a good distance so as not to separate.
1802-03-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Misty and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW and NNE. At noon in 42° 39' 38" of latitude observed and in 147° 49' 54" of longitude by account. At 5, 10° 11' 0" of NE variation.

1802-03-02.journal_anonyme: Misty and rainy weather, a fresh breeze from north. At 8.15, after missing stays twice, wore onto the port tack. At 6.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Declination by azimuths 12° 33' 10 NE
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, the winds were the same as the previous days, that is, absolutely contrary to our course. At six o'clock, we tacked to bear on the land. The sea was beginning to become heavy, and the breeze uneven. The humidity and mist of the night had somewhat dispersed. The state of the sky promised us good observations in the morning and at noon. But none of these fine hopes were realised. The mist returned about ten o'clock, and did not let the sun be seen for the rest of the day.
At noon, according to our dead reckoning, we found ourselves at 41° 58' of south latitude and at 146° 39' of east longitude. The hygrometer was then at 98° 30 and it did not appear that it would stop there. The barometer had also fallen somewhat, but not in a way to announce bad weather.
In the afternoon, we continued to run towards the land until six o'clock in the evening. Our horizon extended to about a league, and this appeared to me sufficient not to fear encountering it unexpectedly. We had no knowledge of it in this tack. Although the Naturaliste was fairly close to us, it often happened that we could not see one another, which decided me to make the signal to her to go about by firing gun shots.
During the evening, we saw passing along the side a large quantity of large molluscs, like those which we had often seen stranded on the shores of the coast. We also encountered many masses of seaweed. All these signs led us to believe that we were not far distant from the coast, and that in the course of the next day, I might have knowledge of it, if the weather permitted us to approach it.
During the night, the sky was fairly fine although a thick mist surrounded the horizon, the winds varied from north to north-north-west, moderate, and we made course in the easterly tack with few sails, the Naturaliste in our wake at a little distance. The sea had become fine although we still felt a heavy swell from the north-east.
During the day, the decks and between-decks of the ship had been perfumed in all its parts to renew the bad air which the great humidity must have introduced there.
1802-03-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Very misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NNE. At noon in 42° 17' 41" of latitude observed and in 147° 36' 30" of longitude by account. In the afternoon the bell was rung every quarter of an hour and swivel guns fired. The 12th [Ventôse, 3 March 1802]. Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 8.15, 9° 28' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 41° 50' 20" of latitude observed and in 147° 33' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 a flat calm; at 3.15 the breeze got up from the SE. We lay under topsails with the yards square, making short boards to starboard and port to wait for the commander, who had signalled no course. At 7.15, being within hail, he ordered us to lie close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails until midnight; from midnight to 4 to steer S 22° 30' W; and that then, if the weather allowed, we should bear away west to close the land. Should he lie to, he was to warn us by a swivel gun. From 8 until midnight the commander showed us a light every half hour.

1802-03-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from north. A smooth sea, a very thick fog; rang the bell to make ourselves heard by the commander. At 6.30 changed tacks on the commander's signal.
1802-03-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, there was no appearance of change in the wind, which still held in the direction of the north-east to the north-west, and the sky extremely misty. At four o'clock, we had taken the north-west tack to close with the land during the day, should the sky become a little clear. The breeze was very light in the morning and we often lost sight of the Naturaliste although it was only at a very short distance from us.
At noon, we had a dead calm, the ship scarcely steering. According to our dead reckoning, we made ourselves at 41° 47' 58" of south latitude and at 146° 34' of east longitude.
In the afternoon, the winds passed to the south-east, fine breeze, but the sky became no clearer. We steered to the north by compass and made fairly good progress until eight o'clock. The Naturaliste, which I had come up with about half-past seven, was warned that at eight o'clock we would take the starboard tack until midnight, and that we should make course to the wind's eye under topsails. That at midnight we would take the port tack under the same canvas until daylight, and that then we should bear away to the west to come and reconnoitre the land, should the weather be clear and suitable for approaching it. I also warned him that in the case that we should heave to or lie to the wind, this manoeuvre should be indicated to him by two gun shots.
The estimated latitude of this ship was the same for him as for us, but he made himself much more to the east.
From eight o'clock until eleven we had sight of this ship by means of the lights which we showed each other hour by hour, but then we lost sight of him entirely. The mist having become too thick.
A little before midnight, the winds passed to the east, fine breeze. We missed stays and came back on the same tack until the time indicated to change. At midnight we put the port tack and made course to the south-south-east. The winds varied little during the rest of the night, but the sky was so misty and humid that one could scarcely see from the bow to the stern of the ship. The winds were light and we made little progress during the four hours.

1802-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 4 went onto the starboard tack to close the commander; he ordered us to keep close-hauled on the starboard tack until midnight, and from midnight to 4 to steer SSW. Overcast weather during the night and the wind a strong breeze in puffs. At 6.30 we lost sight of the commander.
1802-03-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Eclipse of the sun at 2 hours 13 minutes 49 seconds for the commencement. Its end was not visible to us, the sky being too covered by clouds.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the thirteenth, the winds were in the direction of the east and always very variable, or to say it better, we had almost calm in the morning and a sky constantly misty. We had no news of the Naturaliste in the morning, nor during the various clearings which took place in the course of the day. I was beginning to fear that Captain Hamelin, to whom I had said the day before that we would make course to the south-south-west, had not taken this warning to the letter and that he had only attended to the fact that the winds were then to the south-east. But as I could not fail to meet him on the coast which we were to close with as soon as the weather cleared and became bright, I was not at all concerned.
At noon, the sun showed itself a little. We observed its altitude which was found to be 41° 30' 30". This result, although very doubtful, agreed fairly well with our dead reckoning which put us at 41° 28' 40".
After noon, we had much to regret that the state of the sky did not permit us to observe completely the commencement and end of an eclipse of the sun which took place. It commenced at two hours thirteen minutes forty-nine seconds and was very long. We saw this eclipse until nearly half-past three, but the sky having entirely covered itself, we could not know the hour at which it terminated. This eclipse was not central for us in that we were too far advanced to the east. During its duration, the sky became fairly dark. This spectacle would have been very pleasing on a fine day.
In the evening, the weather appeared to be clearing and the horizon was fairly extensive. As we thought we had sighted the Naturaliste, two rockets were thrown at the beginning of the night which were not seen, supposing we had seen it, for there was no answer to them.
During the night, we made two tacks. The sky became nebulous and better for us than we had had it since our departure from Maria Island. The breeze was very uneven and the winds variable from south-east towards the east.
1802-03-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a light breeze from ESE to SSE. At midnight went onto the port tack, the course S 22° 30' W. The commander, on the same tack, then bore from us N 11° W; at 12.15 we lost sight of him to the north. We sent up several rockets without his answering. At 4 shaped the course west. At 6.15 the Géographe was sighted in the S 45° E, and at 6.30 further south. We then shaped the course S 22° 30' W; having lost sight of her again, we resumed the course west. The mist very thick; we fired several swivel guns without answer. At noon in 41° 29' 52" of latitude observed and in 147° 11' 0" of longitude by account. At 3, in a clear interval, we saw an eclipse of the sun for about 2 minutes. At 6.15 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack under topsails. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, almost calm from the SSW. At 1 the breeze got up from the ESE and freshened steadily. At 6 sighted the land in the west, and at 6.30 sighted the commander in the ENE. We fired three swivel guns to make ourselves seen.
1802-03-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the fourteenth, in the morning, the horizon was fairly fine, although the weather was overcast and in squalls. At seven o'clock, it became clearer and we had knowledge of the land to the west. Shortly after, we sighted the Naturaliste which we came up with. We continued to steer towards the land, steering as close to the wind as possible, my intention being to commence an exact reconnoissance of it from the 42nd degree of latitude, the point where the geographer Faure had stopped, when I sent him to ascertain whether the channel marked on the charts was navigable.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 41° 33' 36", but we had no hour angle to ascertain the longitude indicated by the timekeepers.
During the evening, we tacked back and forth to gain ground to the south, and I hoped that with the wind which might arise during the night, we should reach for the following day the latitude from which I calculated to commence our work. This hope was not realised. A little before sunset, we fell into a calm, which lasted the greater part of the night, which was fine and the sky clear. We were about a league and a half from the coast when the calm commenced, but as there was always a little breeze from time to time, we steered to the south-east when the ship had a little way.
At seven o'clock, the depth was forty-eight fathoms, sand, broken shells and small fragments of coral, nevertheless very suitable for anchorage in case of need. At eight o'clock, the depth was the same.
In the watch from eight o'clock to midnight, it decreased by five fathoms and we never had more until day. We sounded every hour, for fear of being carried to the coast by the currents or the tide.
All the lands which we saw during the day, both to the south and to the north of Cape St Patrick, are very high, well wooded, and of an agreeable aspect. I (took) no views of it at this time, preferring to give them ascending from south to north. The whole coast in this part appears very sound, and one can, no doubt, when the wind blows, approach it more closely than we were, although one could distinctly see the beach which appeared to be rocks at an angle.
1802-03-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to E. At 2 went onto the port tack, the course S 67° 30' W. At daybreak crowded sail and shaped the course N 56° 15' W. At 6 land was sighted to the west, and at 6.30 the Géographe in the ENE; we fired swivel guns so that she might see us. At noon in 41° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' of longitude by account. The land in sight from S 4° W to N 33° W. At 7 a flat calm; the Géographe, out of sight, did not answer the lights we showed.

1802-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE to east and NE. At 4 took the bearing of the southernmost visible end S 8° E; the northernmost visible end N 16° W. At 4 went about onto the starboard tack. At 9 a.m. we came up with the commander, who told us he was going to send a boat to the coast; he ordered us to keep close-hauled. At 10.15 the commander hove to and put his boat in the water. We then lay close-hauled on the port tack.
1802-03-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ when it had passed, and a gun shot was fired every half hour. Despite all these precautions, we did not see it arrive during the night.
At nine o'clock, Captain Hamelin having passed astern, I requested him to repeat the signals which we should make so that a greater number might be better perceived or heard. All was useless.
It would be difficult to explain why this ship came down on us and broke our jib boom. It had passed to leeward all sails set, having considerable way. Apparently the officer of the watch wanted to double us to windward by a clever manoeuvre, in his fashion. And having misjudged the distance, he put our hawse in the main shrouds. Fortunately we managed to get round in time so as not to run foul of one another.
From the Fourteenth to the Fifteenth
On the fifteenth, in the morning, we had the winds from the north-east, light breeze and almost calm. We found ourselves, at daylight, about two small leagues from the land, by 43 fathoms, bottom of sand and broken shells. We made course to the south-south-west-east and to the south-east to prolong the coast until the day permitted us to distinguish it well.
At sunrise, we closed with it to assure ourselves of its direction and the contours which it may have in this part. The lands there are very high and present to the view several planes of well-wooded mountains and of an agreeable aspect. As we made ourselves by our dead reckoning at the 42nd degree of latitude, I wished to assure myself of the existence or not of the islands seen by Captain Furneaux. I was well (in the margin: persuaded) by what he said himself of this land, that he had seen it only from a considerable distance, since he gives it as low land, but that was not enough for the existence of these islands. Despite the report of Citizen Faure, geographer on board the Naturaliste, whom I had sent expressly to visit them, I continued the course to the south to about 42° 12' without meeting any. It is true that although I prolonged this coast much nearer than any navigator has done, I was for a moment deceived by the appearances, but I was not long in seeing, as I advanced to the south, that (what) I believed to be an island was nothing other than a very high mountain which advances seaward and terminates in it by a sudden abatement in its southern part. But on the north side, it joins the great land or rather to another mountain by a very low tongue of land, although entirely covered with trees. From this, it is not surprising that it presented itself in the form of an island to Captain Furneaux, if he only passed two leagues offshore from it, since we who were much nearer the coast than he was, were for a moment in doubt as to what it could be.
In the morning, the weather being very fine and clear and the breeze moderate, I caused my large boat to be launched, of which I gave command to the midshipman of the first class Maurouard. Our geographer, Citizen Boulanger, who unfortunately has very short sight, being unable to make bearings and take angles unless he has his nose on the land, embarked in it to approach the coast more closely than can be done with a large ship. I recommended to him very expressly before his departure to return on board before night and to place himself in such a way relative to us as not to lose sight of us. All these precautions were useless. At noon, it was no longer visible. He will, no doubt, have run so much towards the land that he will not have stopped until he had no more means of approaching it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 42° 10' 44" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us (at) 146° 9' 21". We tacked then to close with our boat and ran to land until we were near enough to be unable to approach it more closely and without having knowledge of it. At four o'clock, we tacked to gain a little height, and at five, resumed the land tack. The breeze was then a little strong, and I was much sorry that my boat was absent, having no knowledge of it. From six to eight o'clock we made two more tacks and were no more fortunate. It did not appear.
As it was agreed that it should be back before night, I decided to lie to under topsails. The breeze was then less strong and the sky fine. We lit fires to indicate our position to it, and every hour we launched a rocket $$$ (see page 14)
1802-03-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to N. At 3.30 the commander was sighted in the S by SE. At 5, 7° 10' 42" of NE variation; at 8, 7° 35' 0" the same. At 9.45 we spoke the commander; he told us he was going to send his large boat to the coast and that meanwhile we should stand off and on. At noon in 42° 10' 9" of latitude observed and in 146° 49' 36" of longitude by account. The north end of Maria Island S 20° W, the north end of Schouten Island S 38° W, the Schouten isthmus S 81° W. At 5 p.m., in going about, when the after sails were shifted, the main topgallant brace not having been let go, the yard broke in the middle. At 8 the Géographe showed a light at her masthead; she then bore from us N 56° E on the port bow. At 8.15 she sent up a rocket; we were to windward of her and very close; she still had her light and was lying to. We bore away before the wind and hauled to the wind to leeward of her under all sail. She was ordering us to repeat the signals she would make for her boat, which had not yet returned. As we ran alongside her — fortunately she got off with her spritsail yard and we with our crossjack yard, both of which broke. At 11 our damage was repaired. We sent up rockets and fired a swivel gun to imitate the commander, whom we lost sight of at 10 in the S 56° W.

1802-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, the sea smooth, keeping the same tack as the commander. At 8.15 he sent up a rocket; we were ahead of him. He was then lying to; we bore away to pass under his lee. The commander ordered us to repeat what they should do at the same instant; his spritsail yard fouled our main shrouds, and his jib boom caught our crossjack yard and broke it. We set about repairing the damage.
1802-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, having remained awake all night at a small distance from the coast in hope of seeing my boat arrive, and making signals to it every half hour, as I have already said, to indicate my position, I came up with the land at a mile and a half at most from the shore and often less, in order to meet it. To accomplish this more surely, I commenced an exact search at the very point where it had landed, ascending afterwards to the north. I thought that the fair wind which it had had the day before might have determined Citizen Boulanger to infringe the positive order I had given him the day before to be back before night. The fine weather continued and the favourable appearance that it would continue the whole of this day, did not, however, diminish my anxieties, fearing that in wanting to land to pass the night, his boat might have suffered some damage.
After having gained the large cape which I named Cape Pelé, in that it is absolutely destitute of vegetation, I came to reconnoitre, very closely, that which the English have named Cape St Patrick, in prolonging the coast at the distance of which I have just spoken, and we saw absolutely nothing that could lead us to suspect it was in this part.
At noon, we observed 42° 4' 45" of latitude and the longitude indicated by our timekeeper No. 35 put us at 146° 4' 28". The weather being always fine and the sea fine, with winds from the north to the north-north-west and north-west, I did not tack until it was no longer possible to approach the coast more closely, taking care to make the offshore tacks very short and in such a manner that the boat could never lose sight of the ship, if it were in the vicinity. In the land tack which was longer than usual, evening than morning, in that the winds passed to the west-north-west, we fired the cannon every quarter hour and the mountains repeated them so much that they should be heard almost at the extremities of the island. Nevertheless, I had the mortification of seeing the sun set without seeing anything. I was then halfway between Sainte Helen Point and Cape St Patrick. About eight o'clock, having sighted a fire which appeared to me very near the coast, I did not doubt that it was our men indicating to us by this means their position, especially as it was very well maintained throughout the night. Accordingly, I gave orders that we should not lose sight of it, which caused us to lie to under our topsails, now on one tack, now on the other. It appears, nevertheless, that the currents carried us to the east, for the depth which was 55 fathoms at eight o'clock in the evening had passed to 75, sand and broken shells mixed with some madrepores.
For a moment we had the fear of bad weather, for a very dark cloud from the south direction brought us a gust so heavy that we were forced to furl our topsails and to lie to under the fore staysail and mizzen staysail. As this squall came to us from over the land, I was not at all concerned for the boat, not supposing it to be at sea then. The strong wind lasted until midnight, after which it calmed, and the sea, which was beginning to become heavy, was soon improved, as was the sky, which remained very clear for the rest of the night.
I was very uncomfortable during the day, and the anxieties which the absence of my boat gave me were not likely to restore me.
1802-03-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNW to NNE. At daybreak the commander was sighted. At 8 the Schouten isthmus S 64° W. At noon in 42° 3' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 42" of longitude by account. At 5.30 the commander fired several guns; he then bore from us N 40° W at a great distance. At 5.45 the Schouten isthmus S 57° W and Maria Island S 24°. At 7 a flat calm, the weather overcast in the S 45° E with the look of wind. At 8 it blew hard from the SE; shaped our course north. At 10 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the wind blowing hard with a high sea. During the night we fired a swivel gun and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. Changed tacks several times. At 9.15 fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the commander. At 5 the land in the west; at 7 p.m. the commander was not to be seen. Took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 5° E; Eddystone Rock W; the northern end of Van Diemen's Land N 28° W; the southernmost of the Furneaux Islands N 11° E.
1802-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, the winds were variable from the south-west to the south, moderate at first, and very light in the morning. As soon as it was daylight, we tried to approach the coast and to come and reconnoitre the fire which we had sighted the day before, and which, as we had judged, was found very near the edge of the sea. If the winds had not been suitable and very favourable for the return of ours, I should have thought, as everyone on board believed, that it was truly that of our men. But not seeing them return, I had an opinion quite contrary, not wishing even to believe in the reasons which were put forward to authorise their delay, for everyone said then that, in all appearance the boat was lost, but that at least the men were on shore, since they made it so well known by the way their fire was maintained. However probable all these reasonings were, they changed nothing in my way of thinking.
Finally, between noon and one o'clock, being no longer at more than a small league's distance from this fire which fixed the attention of everyone, I hove to to cause the boat to be launched. I gave command of it to Citizen Bonnefoy, with orders to go and reconnoitre this fire and to examine what it might be. The boat was provided with eight days' provisions and what might be necessary to float the boat or repair it if necessary. Citizen Bonnefoy had orders, if he met no one, nor any sign of the passage of our men, to make course to visit a large sandy cove into which I had not dared enter the day before, although I had approached it closely enough to distinguish anyone on shore if there had been people on the beach.
Immediately after Citizen Bonnefoy's departure, all our eyes were turned upon him and we observed all his movements. He was seen approaching the coast, examining the fire, and then directing his course to the south, clear proof that he had met nothing. When he was abreast of us, we set sail and followed him with the ship. He went round the whole of the cove of which I have just spoken, found everywhere a fine sandy beach, easy landing, and no sign which could lead him to believe that our boat was in this indent. From this cove, he doubled at pistol-shot distance Cape Blanc and returned on board at seven o'clock, seven and a half hours, with the sad news that he had seen nothing. The boat was immediately embarked, and it was time, for the wind increased considerably and the sea became rough.
During the night, it blew a fresh breeze from the north to the south-west. We kept a little way off the coast and put off until the following day the continuation of our search, ascending to the north. The depth at half-past ten was 70 fathoms and at midnight, 75, bottom of coral.
I was bedridden almost the whole of this day by intestinal colic which caused me such suffering that I found no relief in all the remedies which were given me.
Before night, a signal of rallying had been made to the Naturaliste, but whether it did not perceive it or whether it feared to run foul of us a second time, it was not long before we lost sight of it, making a course opposite to ours. I scarcely know how to interpret this manoeuvre.
1802-03-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to W by way of S, E and N. At midnight shaped the course north. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze. We had no sight of the Géographe. At 8.45, 7° 46' 30" of NE variation, shaping our course for Banks Strait and running along the coast. At noon in 41° 11' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 29' 6" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands N 11° W, Eddystone Rock west, and Van Diemen's Land from S 5° E to N 28° W. At 3.45 a ship was sighted in the S 68° E which was thought to be the Géographe. We bore away for her and were not long in making her out to be an English schooner lying to. At 6.15 we hove to to windward of her and showed our colours; she at once filled and crowded sail. We did the same and steered for her. Having soon come up with her, we hailed her that we were a ship of discovery and a friend. She then hove to again, and so did we. I went aboard her with Citizen Milius and we came back aboard at 7.30. We filled and stood on and the schooner held her course. She was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before, bound for Maria Island to fish and to hunt seals and kangaroos. She was manned with 14 men and a boy. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. At noon fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the Géographe, which was thought to be in sight to the south. At 3.45 we sighted a ship in the ESE which we took for the Géographe; we bore away for her and were not long in recognising her for a schooner. We hoisted our colours and Citizen Milius went aboard; she was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before; she was fur sealing.
1802-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ (continued from page 21) that a few more searches be made. We all presume that it would only be possible to the south to have some information about it. The present statement is signed by all.
Although I was of an opinion entirely opposed to that of everyone, being unable to persuade myself that the boat was south of Cape Pelé, since it should formally make course to the north, I conformed to the wish which everyone expressed that we should return to the south, and I maneuvred during the night accordingly.
Historical events & Remarks.
The day of the eighteenth was employed entirely in the search for our boat. We prolonged for the third time the whole coast which we had already visited, but we advanced to the north of the island more than we had yet done, persuaded that our boat, favoured by the winds and the fine weather which it had had for three days, had wished to take advantage of it and make progress. We did not keep more than two miles from the coast the whole day, and despite this we saw nothing. I did not know what to think myself about the fate of my boat and those who were in it. However, the weather which it had had could not make me believe that the boat had been submerged, unless it had found itself far out to sea in the night of the 16th to the 17th, when a squall of four hours' duration obliged us to lie to.
At noon, the sky, although fine, was too misty for us to permit us to take the altitude of the sun; but by the knowledge which our previous courses had given us of the coast, we made ourselves at sunset between Eddystone Point and that of Sainte Hélène, that is to say at about 41° 25' of south latitude.
Wishing to take nothing upon myself for the new searches to be made for our men and the boat, I addressed the following order to Citizen Freycinet, who is the most senior of the ship's officers:
"Citizen, this evening at eight o'clock and sooner if possible, you will assemble the Officers and the naturalists in the great cabin in order to know whether, despite all the searches, unfortunately useless, which we have made since three days to find our boat on a mission for geographical operations, there is anyone who retains the hope that it could be met by returning to the south.
"A process-verbal shall be drawn up of the opinions and answers which each shall sign".
The first masters were ordered to do the same, and here is the result of this proceeding.
"To-day, eighteenth Ventôse in the 10th year of the French Republic at half-past seven in the evening, according to the order of the Commander of the expedition of discoveries, Citizen Henri Freycinet, lieutenant of the navy on board the corvette the Géographe, has assembled the Officers and the naturalists embarked on this ship, to know whether, according to the searches made to find the large boat lost three days ago in a geographical expedition, it is more convenient to continue searching for it to the north of Sainte Hélène Point or to return to the southern part where the boat separated from the ship &a. Citizen Freycinet gave knowledge of the facts brought to the log book of the ship relative to the winds which have prevailed since the departure of the boat and the manoeuvres made to facilitate the return of this boat. After a serious examination of all these circumstances, the Officers and the naturalists have concluded that they all retain some hope of finding the boat in the fairly considerable indent (in the margin on the left: which forms) the northern point of the island of Schouten. They declare furthermore that they do not think it necessary to make new searches from Cape Pelé to Sainte Hélène Point, the whole of this part having been visited scrupulously by our boat and the corvette. The Officers and the naturalists have signed the present declaration".
Opinion of the First Masters.
The masters having consulted together relative to the boat, although having no great hope about it, would find it fairly urgent, if the winds permit $$$ (continued page 20)
1802-03-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SW. At noon in 40° 22' 39" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' 54" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 68° W to S 68° W. At 4.30 the wind shifted from W to SE and veered to ESE and SSW; the sea driven from the west and breaking against the SE wind made us appear ringed with breakers. At 5.45 we saw a waterspout. At 6 the Furneaux Islands bore from N 33° W to N 66° W, and Van Diemen's Land from S 22° W to S 66° W.

1802-03-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW, south and SE. At 4 took the bearing of the northern end of the Furneaux Islands N 40° W, the southern end N 55° W. At 4.30 the winds having shifted to SE we went onto the port tack. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 15° E; the northern end N 70° [illegible]; the southern end of the Furneaux Islands N 18° W, the northern end N 14° E. At 9 we sighted a ship at anchor between Swan Island and the land of the Furneaux Islands. At 10 hove to and put the large boat in the water to go aboard the ship sighted.
1802-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, at daylight, we prepared to close with the land to continue the searches relating to our boat. A sail was sighted ahead of us which, at first, we judged to be the Naturaliste, but we were not long in perceiving that we had been mistaken; the ship in question was rigged as a schooner. As I presumed it must be some boat from Port Jackson, and perhaps employed in the reconnaissance of this coast, I bore away towards it, and at seven o'clock, having come up with it at half a pistol shot distance, I hailed it.
I was then informed that it was indeed an English schooner proceeding to Maria Island or the neighbourhood to fish for seals. Being very glad to profit by this occasion to obtain assistance for my boat, should we happen to have knowledge of it, I caused a boat to be launched and sent an officer on board to ask the captain to have the kindness to come and speak to me. At quarter-past seven, he arrived accompanied no doubt by his mate. I informed him of the accident which had befallen me and proposed to him, on paying him what he should ask, to remain two or three days with me, so as to leave no cove, however small it might be, without properly reconnoitring it. I could not persuade him to accept my proposals, and he excused himself on the ground that the fishing season was too far advanced, but that I might be assured that he would not fail to make searches on his side in case the events had decided our men to return to this place.
The captain of this schooner also gave us some information on different good anchorages found in the Furneaux Islands, and especially that which the English have named Preservation Island, where it is, according to them, easy to make water and wood. They also told us that between Eddystone Point and Swan Island, there is a very extensive reef which extends more than four or five miles offshore, which is not marked on the new chart of M. Flinders, and which they assure exists. On asking them if they had need of anything, they asked me to give them a chart of the strait and a half-hour clock, having broken theirs.
The Naturaliste had also met this boat and had warned it that probably we would speak to it. Captain Hamelin was letting me know that he was going to anchor in the strait, and it is probably this rather particular idea which led him to separate from us without having informed me of it. At eight o'clock, I caused these two men to be returned to their ship, promising them a good reward if they brought my men to Port Jackson.
We then closed with the land, but the winds being from south by south-west and south-south-west, we made little progress to the south.
At noon, the latitude observed was 41° 36' 29" and the longitude indicated by the timekeeper put us at 146° 57' 10".
In the afternoon, the winds having passed to the south and south-south-east, we approached the land fairly closely to be in a position the following day to prolong it at a very little distance. The night was fine and we passed it hove to.
1802-03-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to NE. At 8 took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 15° E to N 76° W, Swan Island N 56° W, and the Furneaux Islands from N 18° W to N 14° E, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. A ship was sighted at anchor under Swan Island; shortly afterwards we made her out to be an English brig. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Milius to go aboard her. At noon in 40° 44' 58" of latitude observed and in 146° 14' 12" of longitude, the north point of Swan Island bearing N 75° W. At 12.15 a boat we had taken for the brig's came aboard. What was our astonishment! It was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th [Ventôse, 6 March 1802] at 10.15 a.m. abreast of the Schouten Peninsula. This boat had tried to come back aboard the Géographe on the evening of the 15th, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land and run along it as far as Swan Island, where very fortunately she had found the English brig, who gave them provisions of which they were short. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman commanding the boat, had at once made for Banks Strait, knowing that the ships were to pass that way. At 1.45 we anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, the north point of Swan Island bearing S 61° E, the SW point of the same island (past Hunting Islet) S 35° E, the westernmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight S 48° W, the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 38° W, their east end N 27° W. At 3.30 Citizen Milius came back from the brig, which was the Harrington, Captain Campbell, of Port Jackson, bound on a sealing and fishing voyage. At 7.30 the Harrington passed alongside; Captain Campbell promised ours to come and dine with him the next day.

1802-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm, a light air from NE to NNE. At 12.15 the boat we had taken for the brig's boat came aboard; it was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th at 10.30 a.m. This boat had tried to close us, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land. They had run along it as far as Swan Island, where they found the English brig, who gave them the provisions they lacked. At 10.45 anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, and veered 150 fathoms of cable. Bearings: the northern end of Swan Island S 61° E; its SW end (past a hunting islet) S 35° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 48° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 38° W; their eastern end N 27° W. At 3 Mr Milius was back in the large boat; she was the Harrington of Port Jackson, Captain Campbell.
1802-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ (continued from page 25) According to the statement of the officers, naturalists and masters, I changed course to ascend to the north, gaining ground to the east as much as the winds permitted.
The weather was fairly fine in the evening, but we found the sea very heavy, driven by a swell from the north which did not announce the early return of fair wind.
During the night, the sky was fairly fine, but the winds in squalls and strong gusts.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, the weather was fine and the winds being from north-north-west, we had weather to our wish to prolong the coast, of which we often kept less than a mile distance and without seeing anything except some smoke on the tops of the mountains. From Cape Pelé going to Cape Blanc, the ground is extremely arid and sparsely wooded. The mountains in the whole of this part are only heaps of rocks on which appears very little vegetation. They terminate abruptly at the sea, and in passing as near as we did, one sees several large rocks detached from them, and at the foot of which there appears to be plenty of water. The searches which we made in this part gave us no information on what we desired.
At noon, the latitude observed was 42° 16' 26" and the longitude 146° 3' 55". The island of Schouten then lay south 2° west, and Maria Island was seen in the distance further to the south.
Having assembled again the Officers, the naturalists and the masters to know if they desired that we should advance further to the south, they addressed to me the process-verbals of which here is a copy:
"To-day 20 Ventôse in the 10th year of the French Republic, at noon, by order of the Commander of the expedition of discoveries, Citizen Freycinet, lieutenant of the navy on board the corvette the Géographe, has convoked the Officers and the naturalists to determine to what point to the south the search for our large boat should be pursued.
"The Officers and naturalists declare that it would be at least useless to run further to the south than the southern point of the island of Schouten, on the height of which the Géographe now finds itself. The manner in which our boat and the corvette have visited the coast from Cape Sainte Hélène to this place, joined to the consideration of the facts brought to the log book of the ship, leaves the utmost moral certainty that the boat could not have passed the two points between which our searches extended, and that it has, unhappily, perished at sea.
"At sea, on the eastern coast of the island of Anthony van Diemen, the same day and year as above. "Follow the names of the Officers and naturalists.
"The first masters having assembled for the second time, by the authority of the Commander, to consider whether there is occasion to adopt new means to enable us to discover traces or signs of the course which our boat may have taken. Seeing the rigorous searches which have been made both with the ship and with the boat. Considering the number of days which have elapsed since its disappearance and the great closeness with which we have approached the land in covering a space of more than 25 leagues, both before and after the point where the boat was to go. Seeing, finally, the impossibility that the boat could have reached the limit where we now find ourselves. We have unanimously thought that a longer search would henceforth be useless in these waters, and that a new loss of time would be unfavourable to the expedition, persuaded that our hope, if we are still permitted to retain any, can only be fulfilled by ascending to the north. &a". Signed by the masters &a.
1802-03-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NNW. At daybreak the large boat was sent off to Point Portland under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, who was to make observations there. At 8 the brig Harrington, which lay anchored 2 miles west of us, got under way and shaped her course S 67° 30' W. At 7 p.m. the large boat came in from Point Portland.

1802-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW and NNE. Began painting the ship's outside. The large boat came back from Cape Portland. The Géographe's boat was put in the water to go and survey from Eddystone Rock as far as Swan Island.
1802-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, the winds were very inconsistent throughout the day, but always from the north to the west and not favourable to the course which I wished to make to come and reconnoitre Sainte Hélène Point and then ascend the coast to the entrance of Bass Strait. At eight o'clock, we took the west tack with winds from north-north-west. The breeze was then light and the sea very rough with an overcast sky. However, at noon, we observed the latitude which was found to be 42° 11' 11". The longitude of the timekeeper put us at 147° 7' 49", much further south than our dead reckoning made it.
In the afternoon, we continued to hold the west tack towards the north. The sky became dark and even misty, the breeze fairly strong, and the sea always disturbed and heavy.
We had already noticed several times that whenever the breeze had any strength, the sea quickly became rough, but it also calmed quickly as soon as it ceased. We attributed the cause to the currents, which, being opposed to the direction of the winds, occasioned the effect.
For four days, I had been very uncomfortable and found little relief in the remedies which the doctors gave me. My trouble was occasioned by colic in the lower belly which tormented me continually and which the unfortunate event which had happened to our boat was not calculated to remove. The more I reflected upon this event, the less I could convince myself that anything unfortunate had befallen it if it had kept to the coast, and I still hope to find it somewhere at the entrance of the strait. It is true that the men in it will not have lacked miseries from want of provisions and perhaps water, but finally, if they have not lacked courage, they will still be in existence.
At eight o'clock, the winds being from the north-west, we took for the night the north tack towards the east, all reefs in the topsails, the breeze being in gusts and the sea bad. The sky, nevertheless, was fairly fine and even clear from time to time.
1802-03-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 8 a.m. the Géographe's boat was sent off with Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger to survey the coast from Eddystone Rock to Swan Island; she had 5 days' provisions. The dinghy went fishing to the Furneaux Islands. The corvette was painted. At 9 Citizen Saint-Cricq went to make observations on Swan Island; I landed there with my gun, as did several officers and naturalists. We sent the boat back, and she carried Citizen Milius to Hunting Islet. At nightfall she came to fetch us from Swan Island and took us to the islet; we killed a seal there, which we left. We loaded the boat with geese, penguins and other birds that we took in burrows under the grass; we came back aboard at 2 a.m. (on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802]).

1802-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 6 the large boat was back from Swan Island; we went on painting the ship's outside. At 2 everyone came in in the large boat with a very good bag. At 4.45 slack water; at 5.15 the ebb, and at 11.30 the flood.
1802-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, the weather was fine during the morning, the breeze calmed much and the sea became fine. The winds appeared to wish to become fixed at north-west, and as we made little progress, I continued the north tack towards the east.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 41° 34' 7" and the longitude 147° 21' 27". I certainly did not make myself so far to the east by dead reckoning. However, I did not change course in the evening and ran the same tack until eight o'clock in the evening. The sky, which had been fine all the morning, began to become misty after the sun's passage to the meridian, and became so towards the end of the day that our horizon extended at most to half a league. As every time the weather had become misty, we had had it for several days in succession, I began to fear that the same would happen to us this time. But at the beginning of the night, we had the pleasure of seeing it disperse, and it was not until after moonset that it began again. The hygrometer announced this change to us for it was advancing rapidly towards humidity. The barometer had also fallen much. We had had it since the day before below 28 inches, and this was not a good sign, for it has always happened to us to have some squalls when it fell below 28.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, the winds, after having been light and very variable from north-north-east to west-south-west passing through the north, suddenly jumped to south-south-west, and caused us to miss stays. It was then two o'clock in the morning, so we took the south tack towards the east which we continued until day. The sky was very misty and the humidity so abundant that all those who were on watch were as much incommoded by it as if there had been heavy and continual rain. It appears that misty weather is very common in these waters, for we have often had it for several days in succession since our entry into Entrecasteaux Channel until now. But I do not believe it is unhealthy, or at least no one has yet felt any bad effects from it.
1802-03-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a flat calm. The dinghy came in from the Furneaux Islands with a little fish and loaded with young seals. I was put ashore on Hunting Islet with three men and two days' provisions to kill seals; I had my gun and was well supplied with powder and shot. It was a pleasure party for me. At 8.30 p.m. the large boat was sent off to Port Kent (in the Furneaux Islands) with Citizen Faure, surveyor, and several naturalists. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 38' 50"; longitude 145° 51' 0". NE variation on the 19th [Ventôse, 10 March 1802] at 4.15 p.m., 10° 6' 0"; on the 20th [Ventôse, 11 March 1802] at 8.45 a.m., 9° 12' 0"; the same day at 5.30 p.m., 10° 4' 30"; at 6.30 p.m., 10° 35' 0"; on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 23' 20". The flood sets west and the ebb east. The greatest rate of the current is 2.8 knots. Citizen Milius proposed that I should go to Hunting Islet to kill seals. I accepted with pleasure, took 3 men with me and 2 days' provisions, and had myself landed on the west side of the islet. The weather was superb and I promised myself much amusement from the trip.

1802-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. The dinghy came back from the fishing with few fish. The large boat landed Citizen Breton with three men. At 8.30 she left for Port King in the Furneaux Islands with Mr Faure, the surveyor, and Bailly, the mineralogist.
1802-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the winds which, during the night, had jumped to south-south-west, passed to the south at daylight, and from south to east-south-east, but they soon returned to south-south-east and appeared to wish to become fixed there. We then made course towards the west to approach the coast, although the sky was still very misty.
At eight o'clock, the weather had such a bad appearance that, not judging it prudent to continue this course, I preferred to lie to, waiting for a more favourable change. The breeze was very strong all the morning. The sky became also a little clearer. We sometimes saw the sun, but not at the moment when it would have been most necessary for us to observe its meridian altitude.
At noon, we made ourselves, according to our dead reckoning, at 41° 22' 19" of south latitude, and the estimated longitude put us at 147° 5', at about 15 or 16 leagues from the coast.
We continued to lie to until 4 o'clock in the afternoon, when, seeing the barometer rise to 28 inches 2 lines, despite the appearance of bad weather, we set the topsails and foremast staysail, again steering to the west. Our horizon could extend to three leagues.
From noon until five o'clock, the weather was fairly fine, the breeze moderate, and the sea rough. We continued to make course to the west until six o'clock, when, having taken good knowledge of the land, we took the north-east tack to hold a little way off the coast, of which the dead reckoning put us at about six leagues.
During the night, the winds were from east-south-east to east-south-east, and were often in gusts followed by calm, especially towards the end of the night. The weather also turned to rain, and we had a considerable amount of it until morning. We sounded several times during the night without finding bottom at 70 and eighty fathoms. We carried few sails in hope that the weather would clear for the following day to enter the strait if there was occasion.
1802-03-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
At 1 a.m. the wind blew a strong breeze from ESE. The topgallant masts were struck; the weather overcast at noon. The cable, having to bear the force of the wind and the flood tide, chafed badly; at 3.30 it parted. Another anchor was let go at once and the parted cable hauled in. We dragged until 5, when the cable held. The wind blowing hard in gusts; at 6.15 the cable parted. We at once lay to under the fore staysail, the storm staysail, the mizzen and its staysail, and hauled in the parted cable. At 9 took the bearing of a fire in the S 22° 30' E. During the night squally weather, with thunder, lightning and pouring rain.

At daybreak, each of us having armed himself with a handspike, we went hunting. We killed several enormous seals which we found asleep on the grass. We skinned them for the hides and took only the livers and kidneys, which we ate and which I found excellent. In the forenoon we took birds in their burrows, and this, with the kidneys, gave us a passable dinner. The weather had turned overcast and seemed likely to grow bad; the sea broke terribly on the east side of the islet. In landing I had taken the ship's bearing past a point at noon; I saw her much further west. I supposed she had dragged; shortly afterwards the mist hid her and I saw her no more. The wind blew hard from the east. At the close of day, being at the south part of the islet, I saw a boat doubling the south point of Swan Island and landing on its SW side; I had no doubt it was the Géographe's boat, which had left the ship on the 21st to survey from Eddystone to Swan Island. The night was horrible, with pouring rain and thunder, the sky on fire; and having no shelter we were soaked through. The bad weather, with the anxiety our situation caused me, made me pass a dreadful night.

1802-03-15.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from east to ESE, a swell running. The cable chafing extremely, at 3.45 it parted; the starboard cable was at once bent round the mast and at 4 the anchor was let go. We had doubled the turn round the bitts and clapped on breaking stoppers at intervals. The turns came off the bitts and the cable ran out to the end with 4 or 5 fathoms lashed to it; we let go the bend at the foot of the mast and took a turn round the bitts, having first bent a spare brace to serve as a buoy rope on the buoy. We hauled in the port cable, which had parted near the bend; we dragged until 5, when the cable [one word illegible] end on, the wind still blowing hard. At 6.15 the starboard cable parted and we lay to on the starboard tack.
1802-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, we again saw the land, which I found much nearer to me than my dead reckoning made it. As it was very misty and the weather was far from fine, it appeared to me that I was at four leagues at most from it. The winds being from east varying to east-south-east, I resumed the north-east tack to gain the open sea, carrying full sail.
Throughout the morning, we had continual rain on us and often thunder over our heads. Everything seemed to announce the approach of some vigorous squalls, and nevertheless, the barometer held constantly at 28 3.5, so it appeared to us, according to its movement, that the present weather was only a storm which would not be of long duration. But whatever may be for the future, as I found myself too near the land for strong south-east winds, I tried to get away from it.
At noon, the winds having passed to the east-north-east, we took the south-east tack under our major sails, all reefs in the topsails.
According to our dead reckoning, we made ourselves at 41° 1' 19" of south latitude.
In the afternoon, it continued to blow a fresh breeze from the east-north-east. The rain, although continual, was less heavy, and the sky, although dark, less loaded with vapours. The barometer constantly at 28 3 experienced no change.
At eight o'clock, we took the north-east tack which we followed until the following day. During the night, the winds varied from east-north-east to east-south-east. The sky again covered itself with dark and thick clouds. Rain and squalls commenced again and the weather was fairly bad.
For five days, I had been much uncomfortable from the colic of which I have spoken, and it was only from this moment that I began to experience some relief from the remedies which were administered to me. The doctors feared that I had some serious illness, and I myself had the same opinion. But according to the state in which I find myself to-day, it appears that I shall not be long in being entirely recovered.
1802-03-15.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea. At 6 a.m. the Furneaux Islands were sighted in the N 45° E. A cable and an iron chain were bent to the mooring anchor. At noon in 40° 27' 26" of latitude by account and in 145° 29' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 land was sighted in the N 22° 30' E. At 6 rain, mist and thunder; the wind fell a little and the sea went down a great deal. We sounded exactly every half hour and found from 21 to 39 fathoms, coral bottom.

At daybreak we went hunting again and killed several more seals, which did us good, for we had no provisions left. I had the meat taken and smoked, not knowing to what we might be reduced. The rain was useful to us: every hollow in the rocks was filled with water, which I found drinkable. I had a breaker I had with me filled, and several bottles that had held brandy and vinegar, and urged my three men not to touch them but to go and drink from the hollows as I did. In a clear interval I saw the Furneaux Islands and did not see the ship. I no longer doubted that the bad weather had forced her to get under way. I went at once to the south part of the islet, and having seen the boat in the same place as the day before, I put my handkerchief on the end of an English oar (a) that was on the beach and planted it in the rocks. Shortly afterwards I saw several people run from the boat behind some rocks, almost certain that my signal had been seen. I left it there and went to reassure my men. About 4 o'clock Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger came in the Géographe's boat to fetch us and took us to Swan Island. We shared the little provisions they had left; they had dug a well which gave us very good water; I had my gun, which gave us game. There was a great quantity of geese, which were our chief food while we waited for the Naturaliste.
