On the morning of the 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1802] a boat was seen coming from the Furneaux Islands and standing for Hunting Islet; we made her a signal with a handkerchief and a musket shot, and she came and joined us. It was our large boat, which had left the ship on the evening of the 22nd for Port King, where she had ridden out the bad weather. Captain Hamelin had told midshipman Brèvedent that should he not find the ship at the same anchorage, he was to come and fetch me from Hunting Islet and then make for Waterhouse, where we should wait for him, or he for us. Accordingly we left Swan Island, 25 people in the two boats, and shaped our course for Waterhouse, where we arrived at nightfall and slept.

1802-03-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard [illegible] from the ESE [illegible], a high sea. At 2 sighted the land in the N 22° 30' E; at [illegible] the wind fell away. Rain, mist and thunder; the weather having turned [illegible] we set our courses. On the [illegible] tack.
1802-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the winds were from east-south-east, more moderate than on the previous days. The sky also became clearer during the day, and the rain was only at intervals and not heavy. At four o'clock, we had taken the south tack and continued it until noon, when, having observed the latitude, although doubtful, we found ourselves at 41° 20' 42". The estimated longitude put us at 147° 27', but it was all the worse in that in the morning we had had good knowledge of land, despite the horizon being of moderate extent and even not too clear in this part. When we saw the land, it lay to our west, extending to the north and south.
As the observed latitude put us much to the south of the entrance to the strait, I steered to the north-north-east until four o'clock. The weather still had too bad an appearance to take the course to the west, and for this reason, I preferred to hold myself well away from the shore until it cleared.
About four o'clock in the afternoon, the breeze strengthened much. The sky became laden with vapours, the rain commenced again, and squalls were frequent. The winds also passed to the east.
Despite the little appearance of a near change in the weather, the barometer absolutely wished to reassure us by rising to fine. We had it at noon at 28 inches 4.8, which had not happened to it for a long time. When the rain and wind commenced again before sunset, it held itself at the same height, and I believed it to be greatly in fault. It was not the same with the hygrometer, which was advancing rapidly towards great humidity, having passed successively from 95 to 98.
During the night, the weather was very inconstant. We had it sometimes fine, but most often overcast, humid and rainy. The squalls, although frequent, were, however, much less heavy than those which we had received on the previous days. Towards the end of the night, it appeared to wish to become quite fine. We made two tacks, one to the south and the other to the north-east, under the foremast staysail and our topsails all reefed.
My health, during this day, began to become better, and I was able to leave my cabin, suffering much less than I had been until then.
1802-03-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 2.30 a.m. we had a heavy squall, after which the wind fell away by degrees. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE; land was sighted to windward and the topgallant masts swayed up. At 9 filled and stood on. At noon the land from S 22° W to S 45° E, being in 40° 40' 22" of latitude observed and in 145° 0' 30" of longitude by account. At 4, Flat Island S 55° E. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened; during the night the wind a strong breeze.

1802-03-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from east to ESE. [Illegible.] At 2.30 went about; took the bearing then of the westernmost visible end of the land S 35° W; the easternmost visible end S 68° E; Flat Island S 79° E.
1802-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
at noon at 40° 48' 6"
The point to the south of Van Diemen's Land in view remained to the south 10° west
The northernmost point in view to the south 25° west
The southernmost of the Furneaux Islands to the north 56° west
The northernmost point in view of the same islands to the north 45 west
At four o'clock
The western extremity of the Furneaux Islands in view to the north 60° west
The easternmost extremity to the north 14° east
An isolated rock followed by breakers to the north 10° west
A part of Van Diemen's Land to the south 12° east
The lands of the same island to the north-west 33° 45' south
(in the margin) At five o'clock, we had
Cape Portland to the south 38° west
The little Swan Island to the south 9° east
The Island of Preservation to the north 36° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, in the morning, the sky being fine and the winds from the east-north-east, a fair breeze, I resolved to bear away to enter the Strait of Banks. The barometer, which had always remained very high, seemed to promise us a continuation of fine weather; in consequence I gave the course west-north-west by compass, persuaded that we were further south than our dead reckoning made us out to be, having not seen the sun for several days.
At six o'clock land had been sighted in the west-south-west, but it was too hazy to be able to distinguish what it could be. From the moment I resolved to bear away, we continued on the course of west-north-west, and at noon we observed a latitude of 40° 48' 6", which placed us precisely on that which the English chart gives for the entrance of the Strait. We had then a perfect knowledge of the Furneaux Islands, which terminate its opening to the north. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 146° 20' 42", and little different from the distance we judged ourselves to be from the land, according to our dead reckoning by eye.
In the afternoon, we gradually altered the course somewhat more to the west, and we did not pass at more than one league from the various rocks that are to the south of the first island, and on which the sea breaks heavily, which makes them easy to avoid.
At four o'clock, the sky began to become obscured. Again, the whole horizon became covered with dark and thick clouds and already had the most threatening appearance. As we were well advanced, there was nothing to be gained by retracing our steps. So we continued on our course as if the weather had been very fine.
The westernmost extremity in view of the Furneaux Islands remained to the north 60° west
And the easternmost extremity to the north 14° east
An isolated rock on which the sea broke heavily to the north 10° west
The southernmost lands of Van Diemen's Land remained to the south 12° east
And those most to the north relatively to our position to the west 35° 45' south The Furneaux Islands, at the entrance of the Strait, appear devoid of trees and even of verdure. At least, one sees very little there. But further within, they are well wooded and of an agreeable aspect. Their elevation is considerable and in fine weather, one must be able to see them easily at 12 & 15 leagues. The lands on the shore of Van Diemen's Land, in this part, are low, and the mountains one perceives are far inland.
At five o'clock, we had knowledge of Cape Portland, which remained to us to the south 36° west. The little Swan Island to the south 9° 30' east, and the island we judged to be that of (the) Preservation to the north 36° west.
We put the bow to the west at six o'clock and at eight, to the west by south-west to keep ourselves in the middle of the channel during the night, my intention being to stop at the island which the English have named Water House. The depth we found in crossing the channel was 30 to 35 fathoms, not very suitable for anchorage. At eight o'clock, it was only 24, mixed with sand, coral and small flat stones. The sky had then such a threatening appearance that we took a second reef in the topsails and loosened our foresail, making way until eleven o'clock. The depth had increased by 4 fathoms and was hardly any better for it. However, one could anchor there in case of necessity. We found the current very strong in passing the Strait.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) and its direction seemed parallel to our course, that is to say, to run to the west. From midnight to daylight, the weather was so bad with the rain and the heavy squalls that we endured, that I resolved to lie-to on the wind, two hours on each tack. The depth ran from 28 to 34 fathoms in the northerly heading and from 34 to 30 in that to the south.
1802-03-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 10.30 the Furneaux Islands were sighted N 50° E. At noon in 40° 41' 40" of latitude observed and in 145° 28' 6" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from us N 60° E, Rocky Islet S 10° E, the land from S 7° W to S 65° E.

1802-03-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from east. At 6.30 took the bearing of Waterhouse Island from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7 we [illegible] the large boat, which was standing towards us; at 7.15 went about and bore down on her; at 7.45 hove to with the lee side to the wind. At 8 the large boat came in with everyone aboard.
1802-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At eight o'clock in the morning, the lands which form the indentation of Cape Portland, for we could not see its extremity, remained to the east 12° N
The south-western point of Water House to the east 6° N
And the little islet of which I have spoken to the south 7 west
The lands of Van Diemen's Island in view to the south 10° west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, the weather became less bad than it had been during the night. The rain ceased at the setting of the moon, but the sky remained dark and covered. At daylight, the mist which deprived us of the sight of land having dispersed, we saw it distinctly and we found ourselves opposite a small flat island and very uniform, which is, without doubt, that which the English have indicated on their chart by a point. However, it appeared to us considerable enough to merit being given another form. According to my dead reckoning, it could have, at least, half a league from east to west. It offers no particular point which could distinguish it and is extremely uniform throughout its whole surface. It appeared to us steep-to and without danger, at least in its northern band. At about a league's distance, the depth was 36 fathoms, not suitable for anchorage.
From the bearing of this island and that of Water House, which is distant from it by four, we recognized our position and saw with regret that we were much to leeward of it.
At eight o'clock, we took the northern tack towards the east. A fair breeze was blowing and the weather was manageable although the sky always had a threatening appearance. The depth, until noon, was increasing and, at that time, it was 38 fathoms. In the morning, we took advantage of the little wind there was to change our foresail and the main topsail, incapable of resisting the first squalls that would come.
At noon, the sun having appeared when we least expected it, we observed 40° 37' 44"; this observation is nevertheless doubtful, the mist rendering the horizon as little clear as it was extensive. Immediately after noon, the sky became covered again, we entirely lost the sight of the lands until six o'clock, when we took bearings of those most to the east, in the south-east, those most to the west, to the south 30 west, and the islet seen in the morning, to the south 11° 15 west.
At four o'clock, we had taken the southern tack towards the east, and at seven o'clock, being in 35 fathoms at two leagues to windward of our islet, we took that of the north towards the east, which we followed until eleven o'clock.
From eight o'clock until eleven, the breeze from the east to the east-south-east was very strong. We had such heavy squalls that we had to take the third reef in the topsails. But about two o'clock, the weather became fine and became clear. The breeze became very weak and the current appeared to carry us towards the west with considerable rapidity.
1802-03-18.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 6.30, Waterhouse from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7.15, standing on the north board, a boat was seen making for the ship; we at once went about and bore up for her. At 7.45 we hove to to wait for her. At 8 I came aboard in our large boat with Citizen Leschenault, midshipman Brèvedent in charge of the party, and 2 of the boat's crew. The Géographe's boat and a large part of our people had stayed at Waterhouse, thinking the ship was going to anchor there. The boat was hoisted in at once and we put the ensign at half mast and fired a swivel gun to call the Géographe's boat. At 8 Waterhouse bore from us S 16° E to S 44° E. At 9 filled and stood on. At 9.30 hove to; the Géographe's boat came in, having again left several people behind — among others Bailly the mineralogist, who wanted to stay at Waterhouse because, he said, the ship was to anchor there. The captain sent the boat off at once to bring back the rest of the people, sending word to the obstinate mineralogist that if he did not come back at once he would leave him ashore. Filled and stood on. At noon in 40° 48' 30" of latitude observed and in 145° 52' 48" of longitude by account. At 2.15 hove to; the boat came back with the rest of the people and was hoisted in at once. At 3 filled and stood on. At 4, Waterhouse from S 2° E to S 14° E. During the night squally weather with light rain, the wind a strong breeze, with lightning.

At daybreak the Naturaliste was seen standing for the island. I proposed going aboard at once, but everyone said she was going to come to the anchorage and that we must wait for her. At 6 she took the north board. I embarked in our boat with 4 men and reached the ship at 8.

1802-03-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to [illegible]. At noon took the bearing of the northern end of Swan Island S 62° E; its southern end S 49° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 46° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 45° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 20° W.
1802-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six o'clock in the morning,
The easternmost lands to the south-east
The westernmost lands to the south by south-west
The middle of the little Sterile Island to the south by south-west.
At eight o'clock
The lands in view to the west to the south 40° west
The lands most in view to the east to the south 75° east
The little Sterile Island to the south 15° west
At noon
The northernmost land in view of the Furneaux Islands to the north 54° east
Cape Portland to the north 88 east
The northern point of Water House to the south 59° east
The little Sterile Island to the south 59° 30' west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, the weather was very fine in the morning, but at sunrise, a calm took us and we made very little progress until ten o'clock, when a little breeze came to us from the north-west by west. We found ourselves equally very little advanced to the east by the two tacks that we had made during the night since at daylight, the little Sterile Island was found only a little to leeward of us, at about a league and a half at most.
As my intention was to visit the island which the English have named Water House, I took advantage of the little strength of breeze that we had then, and closed with the coast to take knowledge of it by the sight of the channel which it must form with the great land. For, otherwise, it would not be possible to distinguish it from the rest of the coast with which it must blend for as little as one is distant from it. At eleven o'clock, having recognized it, we steered to the west. I traced the whole of its western part in the hope of encountering the Naturaliste to which I had indicated it as a rendezvous, in case of separation before our entry into the Strait. The more I reflected on the motives which could have decided Captain Hamelin to leave me on the eastern coast of Diemen, the less I could conceive the reason, and I am even more astonished not to have encountered him at the indicated place. For having made almost the circuit of this last island, I had no knowledge of him. Perhaps I shall be more fortunate at Port Dalrymple since he made it known to me by the master of the English schooner to whom I spoke myself that he was proceeding into the Strait and would anchor where he could, so that it will perhaps be very difficult to encounter him.
At noon, we observed a latitude of 40° 44' 11" and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us at 145° 5' 12", about 0° 19' 0" further west than the position of Water House which remained to us then to the south 59' east at the distance of a league. This island is of good height in its northern part and much lower in that of the south. It is, in general, little wooded and the trees found there are not of great elevation and only on the side of the east. The whole western part is dry and arid. One distinguishes there several large black rocks which contrast perfectly with the colour of the ground which is yellowish. This island did not appear to me to merit the name that it bears, for it seems to offer no appearance of finding water there, and I am persuaded that it was named Water House only because the English who visited it will have had much rain, which is not rare with winds from the east and south-east, for every time we have had them from that quarter, we have not been without it. The depth, when we left it, was 16 fathoms, sand.
Whatever it may be, not encountering the Naturaliste there, I did not stop there and took the port tack as soon as I was assured that either he had not been there or at least that he had departed. The winds were then variable from the west to the west-south-west and the breeze somewhat strong; it continued in the same manner until the setting of the sun. The sea was already beginning to grow rough, the sky became more and more cloudy and the barometer continued to fall, so that I was well pleased to stand off to seaward.
During the evening, although a strong breeze was blowing, we held all sails set to take knowledge, before the night, of the islands in the northern part forming the continuation of the small Furneaux archipelago, but at the setting of the sun, the sea having become very rough and the wind in squalls, we took a second reef in the topsails. The islands remained to us then in the position indicated by the bearing.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) As the weather was fine and the strong breeze had dispersed all the clouds, we were not sorry to have it so violent in that it left us the faculty to observe at our ease, the commencement and the end of a lunar eclipse visible to us, which we observed with precision. I shall give the results in the day of tomorrow, when the calculations shall be terminated.
1802-03-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At 10.30, being roughly at the place where the two anchors had been lost, we hove to and filled several times to try to make out their buoys. At noon took the bearing of the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 20° W, their east end N 54° E, the north end of Swan Island S 62° E and its south-west end S 49° E. (a) This oar was found by us when we landed on the islet for the first time (on the 21st [Ventôse, 12 March 1802]); it had been picked up to be carried aboard and was fortunately forgotten, for there was not a piece of wood on the islet but what the sea brought. At 2, having been unable to make out our buoys, the captain decided to go and look for the Géographe to the south; we made sail to leave the strait. At 4 Swan Island bore from us N 57° W to N 61° W. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly 5 digits; it ended about 10.30. During the night overcast weather, with rain.

1802-03-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, lying to on the starboard tack, a fresh breeze from W to south and SE. At 2 we were at the place where we had lost our two anchors; we hoped to make out the buoys, and not seeing them we bore away to go in search of the Géographe. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly five digits; it ended at 10.30.
1802-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At six o'clock:
The northern extremity in view of the Furneaux Islands to the north 30° west
At ten o'clock, at night:
One of the Furneaux Islands in view to the north 56° east
At midnight:
The same island to the north 28° east
We thought we saw other lands to the north of this island.
At five o'clock in the morning,
The northernmost Furneaux Island in view to the north 7° east
From this point to the south 17° west one saw a long succession of high lands divided into several clumps which appeared to be as many separate islands.
At noon,
The same lands extended (in the left margin: from the north) 42° 30' east to south 20° west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, the winds having greatly calmed, we set about tacking with all sails set, by the beam of the Furneaux Islands whose dead reckoning placed the lands abeam of us at about six leagues. At eight o'clock, we made a general bearing of the lands in view.
As this group of islands appeared to us much more considerable than the number indicated, by this latitude, does not present on the English chart, which doubtless comes from the fact that the distance at which we were from them prevented us from seeing the low lands which unite most of them to one another. I give moreover a very exact view of the aspect which the land presents by the latitude of 40° 21 minutes and the longitude 144° 57' 48" according to our timekeepers.
From the lunar eclipse observed the day before, our No. 35 was found to have a difference of only 0° 1' 28" 5"' to the west of the longitude indicated by the Nautical Almanac, which indicated 11h 6m 0s for the time of the middle of the eclipse and which was for us at 1h 48m 46 s 9 thirds.
One has reduced the time to the meridian of Greenwich because, in the Ephemeris published in Paris one has, by oversight, transcribed the time of the phases of the moon, without reducing them to the meridian of Paris.
The shadow entered between Heraclides and Aristarchus; it exited in the greatest phase opposite Aristotle. In the greatest phase, it extended from Grimaldi to the Sea of Crises.
As in the morning the wind blew very little, we held the northern tack with winds from the west-south-west variable sometimes to the south-west. But at noon, they passed to the west and we took the southern tack to come and recognize Port Dalrymple. We saw that day many porpoises, spouters and two whales of mediocre size. The birds showed themselves in so small a number that one is led to believe that all these islands are not very fish-bearing, at least judging from this conjecture.
In the evening, the winds continued to be very weak and the tranquility of the sea announced to us a calm. The depth was in 42 fathoms, sand and shells. It was the most considerable that we have had up to this moment in the Strait, but it is far from being everywhere of the same nature. The southern tack that we had taken at noon was not long, for the calm and the little wind that there was obliged me to head north-west, the winds being west-south-west.
From eight o'clock until midnight, the weather was fine and the winds suitable to carry us to the west, which we did. But from midnight until daylight, it became covered with clouds, became rainy and took the most threatening appearance for the day. We lay-to on the wind from midnight until four o'clock, to avoid making too much way to the west, wishing to recognize Port Dalrymple. We had then two reefs in the topsails and the wind which was from the north was always increasing. However, the barometer was still at 27 inches 10 lines and the hygrometer between 94 & 95.
1802-03-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to W by way of NE. At noon in 41° 29' 33" of latitude observed and in 146° 37' 30" of longitude by account. Van Diemen's Land still in sight. At 10.30 the weather turned overcast. At midnight hove to. During the night we burnt priming and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-21.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the wind a light breeze from NE to W and NW. The sea smooth. At 4 the land in sight from N 24° W to S 5° E. We hove to during the night. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of Maria Island from S 54° W to S 41° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 25° W; the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon took the bearing of the south end of Schouten Island N 68° W, 8 miles off.
1802-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Note + Bearings of the land.
At six o'clock in the morning
The land, although very obscured, showed itself from the south-south-east to the north-east.
At seven o'clock, we obtained knowledge of the rock which the English have named the Pyramid
At eight o'clock we had it to the west at three-quarters of a league distance
The group of the Kent Islands to the north by north-west
And the largest of the Furneaux Islands to the east by north-east
At noon, the easternmost point of the Kent Islands was to our great satisfaction to the east-south-east.
(in the margin) Furneaux Islands
At four o'clock in the afternoon
The northernmost islet in view to the north 10° east
Cape Franklin to the north 60° east
The southernmost land in view to the south 19° 30 east
At the end of the day, the land was seen from north 29° east, to south 10° east.
That which was nearest the corvette remained to the north 87° east.
Note: All the bearings should be referred to the log table of the 30th ventose to the first germinal.
Historical events & Remarks
On the thirtieth, we had very bad weather throughout the morning. The sky was constantly dark, laden with clouds and full of vapours which gave us continuous rain, heavy squalls and a heavy sea. The breeze, which was still from the north, became so strong that we had to take the third reef in our topsails and even to furl our flying topgallant sail which was carried away by a bad manœuvre of the officer of the watch. As soon as the debris had been gathered up, I had the main topsail furled for fear the same should happen to it, and the foresail, using the trysail in its place. So that we remained as if hove-to under the small foresail, the trysail, the main topsail to the lowest reef and the mizzen stay-sail. The vessel behaved very well under this sail arrangement but although she made two and a half knots and sometimes three knots, we had to keep the helm fully to starboard, otherwise she would make great bearings away if we raised it.
The winds, in the morning, varied from the north to the west-north-west without bringing any change in the weather, but I was well pleased to see them take this direction because it facilitated for us the means to draw away from the coast of Diemen upon which we found ourselves a little too far to leeward for weather so unmanageable.
At eight o'clock, we wore ship and then held close-hauled under the same sail arrangement, heading north. When we wore ship, the depth was 45 fathoms and at noon, although we had made about three leagues to the north according to our dead reckoning, it had not yet increased. According to our dead reckoning, we placed ourselves at the same time at 40° 34' 15" of latitude and 145° 27' 18" of longitude.
During the evening the weather was less rainy than it had been in the morning but the wind succeeded to the rain, for it was much stronger. We saw the sun occasionally and had the hope that at its setting, the sky might become fine. At two o'clock the lead reported forty-six fathoms and at four o'clock, 45. At this time, the wind had considerably increased. Nothing in the air announcing a change for the night, I prepared myself to withstand the equinox gale which there was no way to avoid. We began by hauling in the boom of the bowsprit and lowering the mizzen gaff. Next, we took a reef in our lower sails in case the proximity of the land upon which the drift and the current were carrying us, obliged us to have recourse to it, (with another handwriting, the following interjections hé ! hé ! hô ! hô !).
At eight o'clock, the depth being still 45 fathoms, but the wind more violent, it seemed to me that we had lost nothing or at least little, so that I remained under the same sail arrangement until a sensible diminution, not being able to go on the other tack in that it had become too bad.
From eight o'clock to midnight, the sea was extremely bad, we received several waves aboard which, in truth, discomforted us little. But a more pressing danger was felt. The depth diminished successively from 45 to 41 fathoms and, from midnight to one o'clock, we passed from 41 to 35. As there was no longer time to lose, I had the bell rung so that everyone kept on deck and we hauled our lower sails, not without difficulty. But finally, we achieved it. The corvette certainly had all that she could bear and more than once, we had the gunwale in the water. The winds were then from the south-west and we were steering north 57 west, which, with the drift and the declination of the compass needle, did not prevent our (course) from taking much to the east. When we were oriented, they doubled
(In the left margin perpendicularly) and tripled all the sheets and tacks, but that did not prevent our small foresail from being carried away as well as the trysail which fortunately suffered no damage being under the lee of the main sail. During the watch from midnight to four o'clock, I did not wish soundings to be taken for the greater tranquility of everyone. For if the depth had been found to be always diminishing, most would perhaps have believed themselves lost without resources.
1802-03-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from N to WNW, a high sea. At 5 lay to. At 8 Maria Island from S 41° W to S 54° W and the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon in 42° 18' 45" of latitude by account and in 146° 33' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-03-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze in gusts from NW to W and SW. A high sea; the middle of Schouten Island bore from us N 84° W. At 10 blowing hard in gusts, a very high sea, the weather overcast.
1802-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Note + :
(in the left margin) : + the bearing should be referred to the log table of the first to the two Germinal.
Bearing of the land.
At four o'clock in the afternoon :
The northern extremity of the largest of the Furneaux Islands to the south
At six o'clock :
The land extended from south 70° west to south 30° west
At nine o'clock in the evening, we thought we saw land to the south-west but whether we saw it or not, the depth being no more than twenty fathoms, and the sea still heavy, we steered to the east-north-east to move away from the coast.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of germinal, as soon as it was daylight, we perceived the land to leeward of us, remaining to us remaining to us (sic) from south-east to north-east by north. It was with great pleasure that I found myself at a reasonable distance, that is to say at about four leagues according to my dead reckoning. We continued to hold close-hauled under our lower sails and, at sunrise, I had the topsails serve, all (reefs) taken to better carry us to windward in the wind which was always violent and in squalls. The sky, nevertheless, was fine although very cloudy.
At seven o'clock, having had good knowledge of the rock which the English have named the Pyramid, we doubled it at about three-quarters of a league distance, and when we had it to the west, the group of the Kent Islands remained to us to the north by north-west. Our position then, being well determined, I resolved to make way to exit the Strait in order to come to shelter ourselves a little from the wind and the sea on the eastern coast of the Furneaux Islands, seeing no appearance of change in the weather.
After having doubled the Pyramid, we did not delay in perceiving the second rock which the English chart indicates to the south and to the west of the Kent Islands. We doubled it at the same distance as the first in order to pass through the channel which it forms with the islands. The passage is fine, but the sea there was extremely heavy and the current rapid, for we were making at the log eleven and twelve knots. If the weather had been more manageable, I would have sounded all this channel, but there was no way to engage in that owing to the weather. I would also have passed through that which separates the Kent Islands among themselves where, perhaps, there are some good anchorages, despite the little appearance that they offer to view, and we ranged them quite close, both in the west and in the east to perceive the greatest part of the creeks which are found there.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 39° 22' 44", which corresponds roughly to that which the plan gives to these islands of which we could be at three minutes to the north. As there was no hour angle, we do not know if their longitude corresponds to that which we could have observed.
All the islands appeared to me to offer little resources to navigators. They seem even to be nothing but peaks of mountains on which there is very little vegetation, although one sees from time to time some isolated trees separated from one another. The Pyramid is only an arid rock and the little island in front of the group of Kent is not of another nature. But there is, at the northern extremity of this last, two rocks which advance passably far to seaward and which resemble two little haystacks. The English chart makes no mention of them.
As soon as the Kent Islands were passed, we made way to recognize the northern point of the Furneaux Islands and at four o'clock, we obtained the sight of the two islets which are found there. At six o'clock, they remained to us to the south 70° west.
From this bearing, we made way to follow the land in its eastern part, being in 40 fathoms depth, but whether the current carried us more to land than we thought, or whether there is little water in this part, at eight o'clock there was no more than 32 fathoms. At the same hour, we had taken the north-west tack to not go too far to the south. But at nine o'clock, having no more than twenty fathoms and always strong winds, I had us bear away to the east-north-east to
(In the left margin perpendicularly) move away from the coast of which we had knowledge. We lost the bottom promptly and at midnight, we lay-to, heading north-west. During the night, it continued to blow a strong breeze and with very heavy squalls. The sky was, however, fine and the clouds although numerous, announced nothing similar to us to what we experienced. The sea although sheltered from the islands was almost as heavy as that we had before.
1802-03-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from W to SW, a high sea and rain. At 8 the land in sight from S 45° W to S 68° W, 30 miles off. At noon in 41° 51' 0" of latitude observed and in 147° 15' 24" of longitude by account.

1802-03-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze W to SW in gusts, light rain at intervals. At 7.15 a.m. went about.
1802-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, the weather was fine, but the sea always very heavy and swell and the wind in heavy squalls. We continued to hove-to on the same tack waiting for it to become manageable which the barometer seemed to announce to us in that at four o'clock in the morning, it was at 27 inches 7 lines and appearing to rise further, during the day, which indeed took place for at noon, it was already at 28 p 1l 5,l, and the squalls were beginning to become much less strong and frequent.
The latitude was observed of 39° 6' 34" and the longitude of our timekeeper placed us at 146° 50' 47" so that we found ourselves much further east than we thought.
From the appearance that there was that the weather was going to become fine, we replaced our lower yards at their places and we loosened the reefs which had been taken in their sails and which had served us so well to carry us away from the coast. Despite the regret that I had for the absence of the Naturaliste, I was well pleased that in this circumstance, it was distant from us, presuming it in a better position than was ours, when the bad weather commenced.
The equinox, as it appears from the weather we have just had, is no less to be feared in these seas than in those of Europe. And the vessels which, at this time, find themselves to the west of the Furneaux Islands were well advised to keep to the offing until it is past, for if they are not good close-hauled sailors, they run the risk of being driven down upon these islands by the currents which are very rapid there, in such a manner as to find themselves greatly embarrassed as has happened to us ourselves.
In the afternoon, the weather became altogether fine, the sky became clear and the wind calmed little by little. At five o'clock, we had our main topsail serve to not be too discomforted by the movements of the vessel occasioned by the effect of the waves which were still very strong. At eight o'clock, we set the foresail and the small topsail and we had the ship steered on the northern tack towards the west. We continued this same course during the night, with winds from the west variable to the west-south-west. The weather was fine and the breeze very moderate, sometimes even weak. We sounded several times without finding bottom at 110 fathoms.
1802-03-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SSW to WNW in gusts, a high sea and rain. At noon in 42° 1' 3" of latitude observed and in 148° 3' 34" of longitude by account. The weather cleared and the wind and sea went down. At 1.30 we filled and stood on under courses. At 4 fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze.

1802-03-24.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, blowing hard from SW. At 1 the wind and sea went down; our main topsail having split, a new one was bent. About 8 p.m. the winds drew round to NW and freshened.
1802-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, the sky was extremely fine and clear and the sea beautiful. There remained neither in the air nor on the water any trace of the weather that had prevailed for three days. We repaired, during the morning the little damage that we had sustained in some of our standing rigging and the mizzen gaff was replaced at its post. At six o'clock, we loosened a reef in the topsails and at eight o'clock we set all sails except the main sail in which there were some repairs to make.
From the rising of the sun until eight o'clock in the morning, we were surrounded by an immense quantity of spouters which came to play and amuse us by their manoeuvres and their leaps. Then they disappeared directing themselves to the west at half a league from the vessel. They agitated the sea in such a manner that if we had not known what it was, one could have believed that there was a bank at the surface of the water in the place that they occupied.
All the clothing and hammocks of the sailors were put in the air to remove the damp that they had contracted for several days. We also cleaned and perfumed the vessel in all its parts.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 38° 26' 41" and our longitude placed us at 146° 9' 1" at about six or seven leagues from the coast of New Holland of which, nevertheless, we had no knowledge, without doubt because the lands in this part are low as announced by the English chart which we were using.
During the evening, the weather continued fine, and the winds showed themselves very little from the north-north-west but the winds passed suddenly from the west-north-north-west to the west and to the south-west. We went about to change our tacks and we continued to run to the north until eight o'clock in the evening, being in eighty-five fathoms of depth, fine grey sand, we took the course to the south a little to the east.
From six o'clock in the evening, one saw the sea grow visibly and become excessively rough, which was not a good sign for the weather that might come during the night, against which one took precautions in advance by taking a second reef in the topsails. Which was not a labour lost lost (sic), for after eight o'clock, the wind became very violent and the sea very heavy. At the rising of the moon, the squalls were so frequent and the gusts so strong that we were obliged to furl successively the small topsail and the flying topgallant sail. At ten o'clock we did the same with the foresail and we lay-to under the main topsail after having taken all its reefs.
During the rest of the night, it continued to blow a very fresh gale and we endured sometimes squalls extremely heavy. They were ordinarily accompanied by abundant and cold rain which made them still more disagreeable. The sea had become very heavy and was beginning to become as bad as the preceding days. However, we hoped that it would not last, the barometer holding at 28 inches 2 lines. At midnight, the depth was eighty fathoms and at two o'clock, we could find it no more at one hundred ten.
1802-03-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind freshening and blowing strong in gusts at 3 a.m. from NNW to WSW. At noon in 42° 14' 26" of latitude observed and in 147° 7' 0" of longitude by account. At 1.45 land was sighted to the west; at 6 Maria Island bore from us from S 58° W to S 65° W and the south end of Schouten Island S 88° W.

1802-03-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, blowing hard from NW to W and SW in heavy gusts, a high sea. At 1 the land sighted in the west stretched from N 45° W to S 55° W. Saw a fire on Schouten Island. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 58° W to S 65° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 45° W.
1802-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, the wind increased more and more and the gusts or rather, the squalls were so strong that I feared more than once to lose my main topsail, which nevertheless I was obliged to keep set by the force of the wind, so that the vessel was less tormented by the sea which had become very heavy. This second gale appeared to me to be the continuation of that of the equinox, despite the small interval that there was between one and the other.
We continued to hove-to during the morning, heading south, which did not fail to throw us much to the east. But I preferred, nevertheless, this course to that of the north which would have carried me about as much there.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 38° 56' 17" and the longitude was 146° 43' 31". The squalls for about two hours began to become less strong and less frequent. The barometer seemed equally to announce to us the speedy return of fine weather, having risen to 28 inches 4 lines, which did not happen to it often as I have observed several times. But on the other hand, the sea remained heavy and rough which made me take the course to continue on the southern tack rather than to make more sail to carry me into that of the north. However, at six o'clock, the weather having become fine with all the appearance of a moderate breeze for the night, we went about and we had the foresail serve, which did not prevent the drift, which was always very considerable from the great agitation of the sea.
During the night, the sky became clear. We continued the north-west tack, under the same sail arrangement, that is to say with the foresail, the main topsail, the small foresail and the mizzen stay-sail. At midnight, we sounded 70 fathoms without finding bottom and from midnight to four o'clock, we did not find it either by 110. Which confirmed me in the opinion that I had, that we were more to the east than our dead reckoning made, and even the longitude indicated by the timekeeper, the hour angle taken, not having been taken by weather convenient for such observations.
1802-03-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW. At 4 a.m. Maria Island bore from us S 75° W. At 8, Schouten Island from N 87° W to S 86° W and Maria Island from S 60° W to S 49° W. At noon in 42° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 55' 13" of longitude by account. At 6, Maria Island from S 56° W to S 61° W and the islet south of Schouten Island N 89° W. During the night squally weather, with rain.

1802-03-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a strong breeze from SW. A high sea; during the night overcast and squally weather and we reefed the topsails several times. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 78° W to W; Schouten Island from N 67° W to N 64° W.
1802-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning the sky was not as fine as it had been in the night, but the wind had fallen greatly and the sea was passably fine. We set all sails to enter the Strait before the night, if it was possible or at least to close with the land if we could not achieve it.
In the morning, the winds became more favourable to us by permitting us to make course west by compass. And if they had not been as weak as they were until noon, we would have had the hope of seeing the land before the night. We made, this day, the sale of some of the effects of Citizen Maugé who died during our stay at María Island. These objects consisted of wine, arrack, pickles and other provisions of the mouth embarked by him both on departure from Europe, and during our stay at the Isle of France.
At noon the estimated latitude was 38° 35' 1" and the longitude was 146° 24' 27" although the weather was then very fine, the sun was found enveloped in clouds which did not permit us to bring it to the horizon.
In the afternoon, we had the winds from the part of the east to the north-east, fair breeze. We made course of the west towards the south to not elevate ourselves too much to the north, hoping that it would be possible to see the land before the setting of the sun, although our dead reckoning placed us at a considerable distance from it. But we had no knowledge of it. After the setting of the sun, the winds varied from the east towards the south and during the night, from the east towards the north. The weather was fine and clear and the breeze quite fresh.
At seven-three-quarters, I gave order to the officer of the watch to have soundings taken, which he executed. And at eight o'clock, he reported to me that having cast out 90 fathoms to the plumb, he had not found bottom at this depth. I was astonished, for I expected to have it by a sounding much less considerable. We continued until nine o'clock the course of the west towards the south and at that time I came myself on deck to have soundings taken. We found ourselves, then, in 43 fathoms. Surprised at not having found bottom by 90, an hour before, I made inquiries about the manner in which the lead had been cast and I was informed that in order to have done it sooner, they had contented themselves with launching the vessel a little into the wind, but that it was making three knots at least when the line was thrown. I expressed, to the officer who was on watch when that occurred, my dissatisfaction with his manoeuvre in making known to him the danger to which it exposed us especially during the night.
I then regulated the sail arrangement under the topsails in which I had a second reef taken and we made, during the rest of the night, tacks of about three leagues now to the north, now to the south. As we sounded every hour, we never found less than 41 fathoms, nor more than 47, bottom of sand and suitable for anchorage.
1802-03-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to SSE, with light rain at intervals. At 10.30, 9° 50' of NW variation. At noon in 42° 39' 2" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 25" of longitude by the watches; by account 146° 58' 24" of longitude. At 6, Schouten Island from N 37° W to N 41° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 78° W. At 11 calm, the weather overcast.

1802-03-27.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a light breeze from SSW to south, with light rain at intervals. About 3 a.m. the winds hauled to the east and freshened. In the forenoon saw whales. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W; Schouten Island from N 26° W to N 39° W; Tasman Island S 30° W.
1802-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land.
At five o'clock in the morning we perceived the lands of the continent of New Holland extending from north to north-east by north
At ten o'clock, we saw others in the south-west, presumed to be the group of the Kent Islands
At noon, the same lands remained to the south 24° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, at daylight, we obtained knowledge of the coast of New Holland and I was surprised to see lands passably elevated, but nevertheless not as high and mountainous as those of Van Diemen's Island or the Furneaux Islands. The ground appeared to us uniform and cut in several places, as if they had been separate islands. The English chart does not seem to announce that this land can be seen at the distance at which we found ourselves from it, which, according to my dead reckoning could be six or seven leagues.
From the commencement of the day when the land was bearing from north to north-east by east, we continued to steer north drawing to the west to follow and better recognize it. But apparently it forms a considerable indentation in the place where we found it, for at eight o'clock, we could see it only from the top of the masts.
Persuaded that I was much further north than the entrance to the Strait since I had no knowledge of the Furneaux Islands, although the horizon was clear and extensive in that part, I had the course set to the south-west to find ourselves by 39° of south latitude at noon if a good breeze continued to blow. We did not sound in the morning to not lose time, wishing to enter the Strait before the night, if it was possible.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 39° 9' 2" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 145° 19' 56". At the same moment, we bore on a high land which remained to us to the south 24° west. We were for some time uncertain whether it was not the group of the Kent Islands, but this uncertainty was not of long duration, in that having steered south to well recognize them, we passed through the channel which they form with the Furneaux Islands. This channel has not yet been visited, or if it has been attended to since the chart which the English gave of the great Strait which separates Van Diemen's Land from the Furneaux Islands and from the southern part of New Holland, there will be several changes to make to it. Several islands and islets which are found at the middle of the channel to the south of the group of Kent, are not placed there.
A rock which, at first, presents itself under the form of that of the Pyramid, can mislead navigators by a horizon little extensive, which is not rare in these quarters. But as one approaches it, it takes an entirely different form, resembling a brioche. It is entirely devoid of verdure at its base and at the summit is white. When the two extremities of the group of Kent remain one to the north 6° east, and the other to the north 16° 30' east, the rock is to the north 51° east and little things excepted, in the middle of the channel, nevertheless, a little nearer to the group of Kent than to the Furneaux Islands. Another rock, more extensive, is seen to the north 59° east, and the Pyramid to the south 10° east;
To the west of the Kent Islands, is the rock of which the chart makes mention, but then, one sees to the north 66° west, an elevated islet of which it gives no knowledge and which cannot be one of those placed to the south of Wilson's Point by the little distance at which it is found from the little island of which I have just spoken.
The group of Kent and the lands of the environs, appeared to us placed too far to the east, at least by our observations and the routes which we followed in skirting the islands in their southern parts.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) After the bearing, we continued the course of the west towards the south until midnight, at which time, we took a second reef in the topsails and we lay-to to wait for daylight. We sounded often during the night. The first sounding gave 47 fathoms and the last 52, fine grey sand mixed. The weather was fine and a good breeze blew from the east-north-east to the north-east by east. The sea although fine was a little swell.
1802-03-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NE. At noon in 42° 45' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 39' 7" of longitude by account, Schouten Island bearing from us N 26° W to N 39° W, Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W and Tasman Island S 30° W. Saw a whale. At 6 took the bearing of the high land (the supposed Schouten Islands) forming Schouten Island and the Schouten Peninsula, from N 18° W to N 38°; Maria Island from N 73° W to S 80° W; and the southernmost end of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 30° W.

1802-03-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N and NE, the sea smooth. At 6.30 a.m. the winds drew round to NW. Having been taken aback, we boxed her round. At noon took the bearing of the NE end of Maria Island N 46° W.
1802-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land.
At four o'clock,
the easternmost land of the group of Kent remained to the west 31° N,
An isolated islet which is found almost in the middle of the channel to the south of the group, to the east 15° south,
And the islet which is found in the western part of the group, to the west 16° south.,
We had also knowledge of the Pyramid and we saw on the horizon, a high and little extended land which remained to the west 4° south.
At six o'clock,
The rock in the middle of the channel between the group of Kent and the Furneaux Islands, remained to the north 51° west,
Another rock more considerable and nearer to the Furneaux Islands than to the group, to the north 59° east,
The Pyramid to the south 10° east,
The extremities of the group of Kent, one to the north 6° east, the other to the north 16° 30' east,
The islet to the west of the group to the north 37° west,
(In the left margin perpendicularly)
A second islet to the west of that one which does not appear marked on the chart, was seen to the north 66° west,
The opening of the channel of the Kent Islands to the north 2° east.
At six o'clock in the evening,
The second islet of which I have just spoken to the north 73° west,
And the Pyramid to the south 63° east.
At eight o'clock in the morning, one saw a part of those which are indicated to the south of the Promontory from the north 25° east, until the north 27 east.
At noon, these islets were bearing on the wind quarters as follows:
The middle of a large rock to the south 85° 30' east,
Two others less large than this first one to the south 28° east, and to the south 76° east,
Three rocks or islets to the north of the first rock, to the north 25° east, to the north 36° east, and to the north 45° 35' east,
The lands of the Promontory to the north 21° 50' west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, at daylight, we saw again the islet which, the evening before had been bearing to the north 73° west, but we had no knowledge of the Kent Islands nor the Pyramid, which made me think that the islet which we had in view was rather one of those situated to the south of the Promontory than that of the evening before despite its perfect resemblance.
We continued to make course to the north to come to recognize (in the left margin: the lands) continental and, especially, the Promontory, in order to assure ourselves if its position was well determined.
At noon, we had the sun above the land, nevertheless, the result of the observations made both before and behind to have its passage at the meridian, gave for the latitude of the vessel 39° 30' 5". Thus the error produced by some instruments must be found compensated by those that the others could have had. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper placed us at 143° 56' 58".
It would result from the observations that and our little distance from the land that the Promontory would be more north than it should be and too far to the east. Which confirmed our conjectures on the Kent Islands of which, nevertheless, the latitude appeared to us well determined.
At the same time of noon, we made the following bearings. Namely:
The middle of a large islet or rather of a very elevated rock remained to us to the south 55° 30' east
Two other rocks less large than that one to the south 78° 15' east and to the south 74° 20' east.
Three others to the north of the first were bearing, one to the north 27° east, another to the north 36° 10' east and the third to the north 46° 35' east.
The top of an islet forming the eastern extremity of the land remained to the north 17° 50' east.
Other islets were seen from the north 5° 15' west until the north 16° west and the westernmost land in view was to the north 21° 50' west.
It was difficult, amid so many islets or rocks more or less large, to distinguish with certainty the lands at the end of the Promontory, although one saw very well the whole of those which must form it
From noon to three o'clock in the afternoon, we continued to steer north 22° 30' west and then, we had perfect knowledge of the southern extremity of the Promontory having passed at a very small distance, all the lands and islands which hid it from our view. We took, then, a second bearing which gave us:
Wilson's Promontory to the east 7° north
The western point of the land most in view to the north 29° 30' west
The islets extended then from the north 67° west until the south 71° east. In the number, are included the islets which are found to the west and to the north of the Promontory. There were fifteen in view, in this moment. Which gives me occasion to think that the chart does not indicate as many as there should be, since we had so great a number in view in this moment that it is to be believed that the distance traveled since morning must have put several out of view.
The lands of the Promontory are very high and mountainous composed of two and sometimes three ranges of mountains which succeed one another. Those nearest the sea-shore, terminate there by a steep slope which announces much water in the channels which they form with the islands. The aspect of them is pleasant only in the distance for the most part are arid and the rock which forms them is seen bare in several places. The interior or the second and third range is better wooded. Finally, this coast presents dangers only those which are visible. The depth of the water at a league at the most from the islets is above 30 fathoms.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) At six o'clock in the evening, the western point which forms the bay indicated to the north-west of the Promontory, remained to the north 33° west. At this extremity, one saw the sea break, but little to seaward. During the night, the weather was fine and the breeze moderate. We kept a reasonable distance from the land to follow it the next day.
1802-03-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8 Tasman Island bore from us S 30° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 65° W. At noon in 42° 55' 8" of latitude observed and in 146° 38' 25" of longitude by account. The wind having drawn aft, we steered N 33° 45' W and N 11° 15' W. Saw many tuna and porpoises. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Pillar S 18° W, Maria Island from west to N 51° W. At 9.30 hove to abreast of Schouten Island. Light fine rain.

1802-03-29.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind a light breeze from SW, south and SSE. Saw a considerable quantity of tuna and porpoises. At 9.30 p.m. hove to under the main topsail. At midnight, being very near Schouten Island, we filled and stood on; at 1 hove to again until 5, when we filled and ran along the coast at a distance of 2 miles. It is clear and well wooded but offers no shelter from the winds off the sea. At noon took the bearing of the middle of a low stretch of land having the look of an island S 19° W; the land from S 10° E to N 19° W.
1802-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land:
At six o'clock in the evening,
The western extremity which forms the first bay to the north-west of the Promontory, to the north 33° west,
One of the islets to the south-east of the Promontory, to the east 18° 30' south.
At eight o'clock in the morning,
The islet to the south-east of the Promontory, to the east 21° 40' south,
The western extremity of the bay of the day before, to the west,
The westernmost lands in view, to the north 29° west,
Those of the Promontory, to the east 12° 45' north.
At noon,
The point of the lands most eastern in view, to the south 68° east,
The land to the north 74° 45' west,
A land which we thought to be the island which forms the Port of the West and which it was not, to the north 38° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, at daylight, we made course to come to recognize the second bay to the north-west of the Promontory with a little wind from the south-east to the east. The lands of the Promontory were seen to the east and the bay point which forms the entrance the western extremity of the second bay remained to us to the west. This bay appeared to us to form an indentation much more considerable than the English chart seems to indicate. It contains moreover, an infinity of creeks more or less large formed by points advanced which could merit the name of capes, according to the manner in which they are found placed. The lands of this second bay are of good height at the two extremities of each point. But most of the ground which forms the outline of it, is low and divided sometimes by elevations which resemble islands. The sea-shores are formed by sand dunes which offer to the view several white patches. In the interior of the lands, one sees in a considerable distance, a long succession of mountains of moderate height at least relatively to the distance at which we found ourselves from them. Nevertheless they appeared to us well wooded. Their direction extended from the north-east to the south-west.
At noon, we observed a latitude of 38° 47' 19" and the longitude of our No. 35 placed us at 142° 58' 4". There is no doubt that either this latitude and even that of the day before are defective or that (sic) the chart which the English give of it has neither the position, nor the configuration that the coast should have in this part. Without having ranged close to the land as much as the course which they appear to have made indicates, we have followed its borders at a league at the most and often less, which put us in a position to see several reefs and islets of which their plan makes no mention. Several of these rocks even obliged us to haul up to the wind to be able to double them.
In the afternoon we continued to follow the land, we passed very close to a large point advanced which was believed to be the island which forms the Port of the West, because its eastern part forms an indentation which seemed to indicate a channel. But after having doubled it, we could not doubt that there was neither island, nor port in this place, having followed the whole of the western part at three-quarters of a league. After having assured ourselves that the Port of the West could not be in these environs, we made course of the north towards the west to take knowledge of the lands of this bay which are generally low and sandy. Seeing nothing which could make us suspect that the Port of the West was in this part, we believed we had passed it relying on the longitude of the timekeeper which, indeed, placed it to us in the north towards the east. Nevertheless, I could not hold to this idea because we had, since Wilson's Promontory, followed the land close enough to have no knowledge of it if it had been found on the route which we followed.
In continuing to make course of the north towards the west, we saw ahead of us, high lands which were without doubt some mountains of the interior of the country, being still too far to distinguish the borders of the shore. But as the night was coming on, we limited to the position where the vessel found itself then, our work of this day. At the setting of the sun, the lands most in view to the west, remained to the west 2° south and those most to the east to the south 20° east.
During the night, we held the southern tack towards the west with little sail. The lead which was cast every hour, never reported more than 49 fathoms, nor less than 47.
1802-03-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At midnight, being too near Schouten Island, we filled to draw off and hove to again at 1. We sent up a rocket every hour. At 5 filled and stood on, running along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It is clear and well wooded. At 8.45, 8° 31' of NE variation. At noon in 41° 44' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 49" of longitude by account. At 3 we were abreast of a small well-wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 50" of latitude. It is the only place on the coast we have run along where a ship can shelter from the winds off the sea. According to Citizen Maurouard there is good anchorage between the land and the island, and it can be entered by either the north or the south passage. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack.

1802-03-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to SSE and south. At 3 we took the bearing, to the west of us, of a small and fairly well wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 51" of south latitude. It is the only place on the east coast of Van Diemen's Land where a ship can take refuge. It lies a short distance from the land, and one may run in by either the south or the north passage. At noon took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 18° W to S 86° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 54° W to N 18° W.
1802-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land
At daylight, the land extended relatively to our position from the south 20° east until the west 2° south. In this interval, one saw a large indentation in which no land appeared and which we were to visit.
At eleven o'clock, having arrived in the above indentation, the entrance of the Port of the West remained to us to the east 6° north and the western extremity of the land to the west 30° south.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, at daylight, we had a fair breeze from the east variable to the east-north-east. We took advantage of it to make course, all sails set, steering to the north-north-east to come to recognize a large indentation which remained to us in this quarter and in which no land was seen. Although our last bearing, taken the evening before at the setting of the sun, was well known to us, I did not wish to make course on the lands which we had in view to leeward of us, without having recognized what the part could be in which no land was seen.
The course from north to north-north-east which we followed until eleven o'clock in the morning, making good distance, finally led us into the large indentation of which I have just spoken. As the land is extremely low in all this part, we had good knowledge of the shore only when we were at a league and a half at the most distance from it. While we were skirting the coast, we saw an opening which appeared to us to be undoubtedly the place which the English have named the Port of (Western in another hand) the West. The bearings which I had made at this time referred to the chart, accorded well with the dead reckoning of our course and the distance traveled the day before. So I remain persuaded that this place is truly that of the Port of the West. But I persist in saying that all the coast placed to the east in the plan, has been poorly seen until the western point of the first bay.
At noon, we observed a latitude of 38° 32' 13" and the longitude indicated by the timekeeper placed us at (no figures)
To exit from the indentation into which we had entered, we had to make course to the south-west by west and to the south-west. We followed by this means, a long succession of high mountains of which the first range terminates abruptly to the sea. The change which we perceived in the colour of the water, made us several times, cast the lead. But as we did not find bottom at thirty fathoms, we attributed the cause to the effects of the sun.
At eleven o'clock, when I took the bearing of the place which I am persuaded is the Port of the West, the land most in view to the west remained to me to the west 30° south, and the middle of the channel which can have a league of width, was to the east 56° south.
At three o'clock in the afternoon, continuing to follow the coast, steering to the south-west and south-west by west, we arrived at the cape which appeared to us to form the extremity of the land in view to the west. And when we had it in this quarter, the lands which we saw further to the west extended remained, then, to the west 22° 30' south, so that it would result that the cape is at 38° 48' of south latitude and the distance to travel 30 miles and one third. All this part of the coast is high, well wooded and of an agreeable aspect. One sees there small creeks of white sand little consequent where, and sometimes the sea breaks, but all to shore. I named the cape which appeared to me to be the most to the south since Wilson's Promontory, the Cape of Representations, over (some) disputes which were (made) to me by the Staff at that very moment.
During the rest of the day, we continued the course to the south-west following the coast at a small distance. It was of an agreeable aspect and without any danger which was not apparent. The bearings were pushed as far forward as it was possible and we stopped at the point which I named the Point of the Platform, in order to begin again the next day at the same place. At eight o'clock, we took the southern tack to put ourselves a little offshore from the coast.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) During the night, the weather was fine and the sea beautiful. At eight o'clock, we had bottom at 45 fathoms of poor quality. At midnight, it was 54 of the same nature. From midnight to 3 o'clock, it was found from 54 to 51 and at four o'clock, we had only 30, which made us resume the southern tack until daylight. When the bottom was found at 30 fathoms, the land was seen in the north-east.
1802-03-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to NW by way of east. At 2 a.m. hove to; at 5 filled and stood in to close the land. At 8.30, 9° 54' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 49' 17" of latitude observed and in 146° 50' 25" of longitude by account, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. At 5.30 the air having come from the west, we steered offshore; shortly afterwards it came back to ESE. We hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 6 Swan Island S 81° W. At midnight calm; lay to.

1802-03-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds east, almost calm. At 1 a.m. hove to under the main topsail. At 3 filled and stood on, and at 4 hove to again in the same way. We got a kedge anchor ready to let go. At noon took the bearing of the middle of Swan Island S 75° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 65° W to north.
1802-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land
At four o'clock,
the easternmost point of the lands in view remained to the north 16° east,
the Cape of Representations to the north 89° west,
The land extended to all view in the west of this cape.
At eight o'clock in the evening,
a point which appeared to us in the evening to form the extremity of the land to the south, remained to us to the west at about a league and a half.
At noon,
a cape which I named the Cape of the Marshal remained to the east
and the land ahead of us, extended until the west by north-west forming a coast filled with cliffs cut perpendicularly to the sea.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, at daylight, we closed with the land to accost the Point of the Platform from which we were at four leagues, at the most, to the south. At seven o'clock, being well assured of our position of the day before, we continued our work with the hope of making a good day, for a fair breeze was blowing from the east to the east-north-east and we steered to the north, all sails set. The coast which we followed from seven o'clock until noon, is high and mountainous, of an aspect which for a glance as varied and agreeable as that of the day before being almost entirely wooded to the edge of the sea, with the exception, however, of some large white patches which we saw in different places and which could serve as points of recognition. The direction of the coast, from the Cape of the Platform to that which we doubled at noon, was from (no figures).
I named the last cape, the Cape of the Marshal in that one sees upon it an eminence at the edge of the sea, two cavities which have absolutely the form of a horseshoe.
At ten o'clock, we were for a moment in a calm. The winds or at least, a little breeze which came to us from the part of the west, made us take the south-west tack, but it was not for long for at eleven o'clock, the eastern breeze returned to us and a fair fresh breeze was blowing.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 38° 52' 15" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 140° 38' 4".
During the evening, we continued to follow the coast which changes, here, in nature and aspect. Although the ground at the sea-shore is high and steep, it appears arid until the range of mountains which are seen in the interior and which are well wooded. In the morning, we had perceived smoke to the west of this land, which indicated to us that it was inhabited in this part for it is the first we had seen since our departure from the Promontory. We saw the same fire again in the afternoon, on the top of an elevation at the edge of the sea, but it was not very considerable.
All the coast which we followed appeared to me unapproachable and not even offer shelter for a boat. Although it is divided into several creeks more or less large which would seem to announce an easy landing, the sea breaks all along the shore. It is what we positively assured ourselves of by the little distance we were from it.
I gave the name of Cape of the Cliffs to that which one encounters first after having doubled the Cape of the Marshal from which it is found distant eight and a half leagues. The course to make to go there is north 23° west. Little things excepted, the same as that from the Point of the Platform to this first cape. But the distance of it is not as considerable, being only 19 and a half miles. After having passed the Point of the Cliffs, one encounters a large indentation which offers nothing of interest to the view and of a very sad aspect. We followed it along its whole extent and to exit from it, we had to make distance to the south, after which the coast extends in the west and west by south-west, as far as the view can extend. It is at this last point that we finished our bearings after the setting of the sun.
At seven o'clock, we headed to the closest, the cape to the south to move away from the coast during the night and at eight o'clock, the lead reported 29 fathoms of bottom, being according to our dead reckoning at two good leagues at that time.. During the night, the weather was fine and the breeze weak. We made about four leagues in the southern tack and we then lay becalmed drifting to the north-west. The lead increased regularly until 46 fathoms, coarse gravel and rotten shells.
1802-03-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm with very variable light airs. At 5 filled and stood west with a light breeze from SE. At 8 the north point of Swan Island bore from us S 69° W. At 9.30, 10° 6' 40" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 26" of latitude observed and in 146° 41' 31" of longitude by account, Swan Island (its middle) bearing from us S 75° W. At 2.30, the breeze from the west, we made several boards until 6.30, when we fell into a flat calm. At 7.15 we let go a kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage taken at daybreak: Swan Island (its middle) S 19° E, and the Furneaux Islands from N 42° E to N 28° W.

1802-04-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NW to west. A calm coming on, at 7.15 we let go the kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, and veered 50 fathoms of hawser. At 6.30 a.m. got under way under topsails and made all sail. At noon took the bearing of the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 5° W; the eastern end N 50° E; the north end of Swan Island N 88° E; Waterhouse Island from S 48° W to S 59° W.
1802-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land.
At six o'clock in the evening,
The land most in view to the east, remained to the south 71° east.,
The westernmost land in view to the north 65° west,
And that nearest to the vessel to the north 48° east, distance of a league from this last one.
At six o'clock in the morning,
The easternmost land in view, was to the north 45° east,
That most to the west, to the north 22° 30' west,
One saw in the interior of the lands, an elevated peak remaining to the north 56° 15' east
At noon,
The Lark Island in its northern part, remained to the north 41° west,
and in its southern part, to the north 69° west,
One saw from this point, lands to all view, in the west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, we found ourselves a little too far from the coast which obliged us to trim starboard tacks to approach it more closely, the winds being then from the north-east, good breeze. After having recognized the point where we had stopped the day before, we followed the coast to recognize a land quite elevated which remained to us a little to leeward and which appeared to me very far advanced relatively to a cape which showed itself to the west-north-west of our position. As a good breeze was blowing, we easily and promptly closed with this land which we recognized to be an island of about a good league from the continent and offering between it and it, an easy passage. This island, which is very flat and uniform, was the first we had encountered since our departure from the Promontory, for its distance from the firm coast. My intention being to pass through the channel which it presented, we hauled up as much as necessary to enter it. But at the same moment that we were going to double it, the wind failed us, suddenly, and we were carried much nearer than I would have desired, of a long succession of breakers of which all its eastern part is surrounded.
