Our position was, then, all the more disagreeable in that the bottom, which was still 27 fathoms although at a small league from the coast, was not at all suitable for anchorage.
At noon, we observed a latitude of 38° 27' 32" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 139° 39' 54". A little while after, a small freshness from the south-east came to us which we took advantage of well quickly to move away from this island coast which we doubled in its southern part at a league distance. This island is entirely devoid of trees and seems to be covered only by a kind of heath very little elevated and did not appear to offer the least resource. Its recognition is easy and its latitude well determined since it remained to us to the east when we observed 38° 27' 32" of latitude. Its southern extremity, is more elevated than that of the north and the sea breaks with even more force than in its eastern part. The coast of the continent which is opposite to it is formed of dunes interspersed with large white patches and the edge of the coast sandy.
In the afternoon, the winds passed to the east, fair breeze, and we continued our course to know the depth (with another hand: the extent) of a large indentation which remained to us to the north. Before leaving this island, I named it the Lark Island, because we took one which came to rest on board, when we were abeam of it.
In making course to the north in the indentation which we had before us, we perceived a second island also a little offshore from the continent and of which the channel appeared equally easy, but not wishing to abandon the recognition which we wished to make of this large bay, we continued to make course to the north-west until we had assured ourselves that it offered nothing of interest. Then, we changed tacks and took the closest on the southern-south-west side to double the second island of which I have just spoken before the night which was beginning to approach. This second island is only an arid rock followed by two others which do not appear separated at a certain distance, but which are all joined together by a reef at the surface of the water. This island was named the Dragon Island, by the perfect resemblance both to the east and to the west which it has with the fabulous animal to which this name has been given. The lands of the continent are high, cut perpendicularly to the sea and a little wooded, but the approach is difficult from a long succession of breakers whose noise is heard from a considerable distance.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) At seven o'clock, our bearings ended at the point of a large cape easy to know for the next day. Although at a league and a half at the most from the lands, the bottom was 45 fathoms and very bad for anchorage. From eight o'clock to midnight, in the southern tack towards the east, it passed to 85 and in that of the west towards the north, from 85 to 55, same quality. Besides, the weather was fine and the sea calm. The (winds) varied from the east towards the south as from the east towards the north. (One saw) fires in different parts of the coast.
1802-04-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to ENE. At 6.30 a.m. got under way and shaped our course for Waterhouse. At 8, the Furneaux Islands from N 32° W to N 56° E, Swan Island from S 64° E to S 51° E and Cape Portland S 19° W. At 8.15, 9° 54' of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 42" of latitude observed and in 146° 15' 49" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands from N 5° W to N 50° E, the north end of Swan Island N 88° E, Waterhouse from S 48° W to S 59° W. At 1 both large boats were sent off under the orders of Citizens Heirisson and Maurouard to go round Waterhouse and look for any orders the commander might have left there. At 5.45 we let go a kedge anchor in 23 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 16° E to N 56° E, the easternmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 78° E, the north point of Waterhouse S 87° E, its SW point S 23° E, Flat Island S 66° W.

1802-04-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE. Our large boat and the Géographe's boat were put in the water to go round Waterhouse and look for any instructions the commander might have left there. At 5.45 let go a kedge anchor in 20 fathoms, grey sand mixed with broken shell, and veered 60 fathoms of hawser. Bearings of the anchorage: the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 16° E; the eastern end N 56° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 78° E; the westernmost end S 52° W; the north end of Waterhouse S 87° E; the south end S 23° E; Flat Island S 66° E. At 10 a.m. both large boats came back without having found anything to show that the commander had been there.
1802-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At five and a half o'clock in the evening, a second islet offshore from the coast which I named the Dragon Island remained to the north 3° west, distance a league.
At seven o'clock, the lands most in view ahead of us remained to the west 20° north
At six o'clock in the morning, the Dragon Island was to the east 28° north
At noon, the lands most in view to the east, remained to the south 70° east
Those most to the west, to the north 45° west
A large white patch formed by a sand dune and distant from us by a good league, remained to the north 75° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we found ourselves in a very advantageous position to begin, at the rising of the sun, our bearings. The fair breeze which was blowing then, from the north-east to the north-north-east gave us even the hope of pushing them forward enough during the day. But we were deceived in our expectation by the calm and small breezes from the north to the north-west which did not permit us to advance much and which, even, moved us away which moves us from the land from which we were, at the most, at a league when it came to us. The coast which we had in view in the morning, was high and passably wooded in the interior of the country. Next, there succeeded to it a sandy and arid ground, terminated at the edge of the sea by dunes which offered everywhere large white patches and few points of recognition. There was, still, by our beam, a large indentation whose western extremity, in view, seemed to terminate to the north-west.
For several days, it had been remarked that in the morning, the winds came to us quite regularly from the north-north-east to the north-east and that a good breeze blew until about nine or ten o'clock, and that then, it diminished noticeably so that at noon, we found ourselves in a calm. Between noon and two o'clock, the winds passed from the east to the south-east and a fair breeze was blowing. If this progress was regular for them in this season, it would be a great advantage for us, but a longer series of observations is needed in that regard, to say what is the case.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 38° 17' 57".
In the evening, we continued to follow the coast which is, here, all uniform with the exception of some peaks of mountains seen in the interior of the country. The sea-shores are continual dunes at the foot of which the sea breaks with such force that it would be impossible to land there. About three and a half hours, making course to the north-west with a fair breeze from the south-east, having penetrated into an indentation no less considerable than that of the day before, although the opening of it was not as large, we saw at the moment when we were sailing in the greatest security, a breaker right ahead of us which the sun had hidden from our sight. We were not, then, more than two miles from it so that we had only the time necessary to trim port tacks steering to the south-south-west and the south-west to double it. Perhaps the channel which is found between this danger and the great land is practicable but I do not guarantee it, having left it on starboard in doubling it. Its extent is not considerable, not being more than a mile in its greatest length. After having passed it, we steered to the west by south-west and to the west to close with the westernmost land which we then had in view. By the beam of the danger of which I have just spoken, I did not have soundings taken in order not to discourage anyone if the bottom was little considerable. A louis of gratification was granted to the one named Ciré, sailor topman who saw it first and gave us notice.
In approaching the land again, we saw a third islet which was distant from it by a small distance and which we subsequently recognized to be joined to it by a reef on which the sea rose to a great height. I gave this islet the name of the Camel Island because it had roughly the form of this animal. It is easy to recognize by an elevated peak, inclined to the north-west. Our bearings of the day ended at a point a little more advanced which we had ahead of this islet. Other lands were also seen to the west 22° 30' north.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) At eight o'clock, we took as usual, the southern tack which was continued until midnight by fine weather. We sounded at the same time, to set the southern course and found bottom in 23 fathoms not suitable for anchorage. To our great astonishment, bottom was not found at nine o'clock at 45 and at ten o'clock, it was eighty-two, at midnight, ninety, when we took the northern tack.
1802-04-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SE. At 10 both boats came in from Waterhouse, where they had found nothing to show that the commander had been there. The sick were sent to Waterhouse; the seamen known as shooters were sent there to shoot for the crew. At half past noon the large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to Port Dalrymple. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 11 feet 5 inches, difference 3 inches. At 11 p.m. the sick and the shooters came back aboard; the shooting was not as good as might have been expected.

1802-04-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze varying from NNE to ESE. Our large boat was sent off to Port Dalrymple.
1802-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land.
At four o'clock,
bearing the eastern extremity of the land to the south 72° 30' east,
The middle of the breakers perceived in the bottom of the bay to the north 11° 30' west
The western extremity of the land to the north 85 west
At daylight, the land was seen from the north to the north-east but at too great a distance to distinguish its form. We saw in this land, during the morning no points recognized the day before.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we found ourselves in a position altogether different from that which I expected to have. This event was without doubt, produced by two causes, but all different from one another. The first was by the fault or carelessness of the officer who had the watch from midnight to four o'clock, for not having informed me that at one o'clock, he had not found bottom at 115 fathoms. And the second must be attributed to the force of the currents which, apparently, carried us to the west with greater speed than usual, since we found ourselves to have far passed the point of bearing which should serve us for recognition for our work in this day.
Whatever it may be, we had good knowledge of the land at daylight, but it presented itself to us in a form so different from what we had seen up to then, that we recognized absolutely nothing of what we had perceived the day before. As the winds were, then, variable from the north to the north-west and they were the same throughout the morning, I did not change tack until the afternoon in order to have a horizon extended enough to not have the sun above the land which, in the place where we found ourselves is very low and terminated at the sea by sand dunes of mediocre elevation, filled with white patches illuminated sometimes by the sun which makes them appear from a considerable distance.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 37° 52' 20" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 137° 37' 40". Consequently, much further west than the dead reckoning of the routes traveled up to this day, despite their little difference with the heights observed since the departure from the Promontory.
Throughout the entire evening, we followed a coast very low and very uniform, on which one saw, for all elevation only sand dunes more or less high ones than the others. Although we were four and five leagues from the coast, the depth of the water was quite considerable and we had fifty fathoms of water at this distance. The bottom was somewhat coarse sand and reddish, it appeared suitable for anchorage. It was the first of this nature that we had yet encountered on the coast. We continued to make course to the east taking some south to come to take knowledge of the last bearing that we had made not wishing, as much as will be possible, to leave any gap in all this coast.
About four o'clock in the afternoon, the sky became very cloudy and there was appearance of change in the weather. Nevertheless, the winds which we had had to the west, the greatest part of the day, passed to the north-east, but the breeze was very weak and we advanced little. A heavy swell from the south-west was also making itself felt and I greatly feared some gusts from this point of the horizon all the more so that the thermo barometer was beginning to fall and the hygrometer advancing towards humidity.
At eight o'clock, we made course somewhat more to the south and we spent the night tacking back and forth in the hope of recognizing for the next day the point which we were seeking to regain. The wind which was very weak and variable gave us, nevertheless little hope of achieving it.
During the night, the noise which the surge of the swell made on the coast was heard so well that if the lead had not indicated to us that we were passably far offshore, we would not have estimated ourselves at more than a league.
1802-04-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from ESE to north. At 10.30 I went with Citizen Milius and several others to shoot on Van Diemen's Land. The dinghy, which had been fishing at Waterhouse, brought back a little fish. At nightfall a light was shown at the gaff and priming burnt every half hour.

1802-04-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze variable from east to north. We kept a light at the gaff until the arrival of our boat, which was back at 1 a.m.
1802-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At six o'clock in the evening,
the two extremities of the land in view remained one to the north
68° east, and the other to the north 25° east.
At eight o'clock in the morning,
one saw the land from the north until the east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, the winds, in the morning, were from the north variable towards the east, and so weak that the vessel had difficulty steering. We were at about four leagues from the coast which we continued to follow to gain a large point judged, at the distance at which we found ourselves, to be that which we had been seeking since yesterday. The weather was very fine, throughout the morning, and the clouds which had been piled one upon the other, had disappeared. But the swell was always the same. The barometer which, the day before, had constantly remained at 28 inches 5 lines, was rising a little and we had it, then, at 28 inches 6 lines.
Throughout the morning, the noise which the sea made on the edge of the coast or on the reefs which are found a little offshore, was heard. We distinguished them perfectly from the deck and one saw the sea rise to a very great height. At nine o'clock, being in a calm, I had the lead cast. The bottom was found in 23 fathoms and the quality of a kind of white slime or decomposition of marl of the same colour, and very hard to the lead.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 37° 56' 15" and the longitude, indicated by the timekeeper, was 138° 5' 49".
We had then very fine weather, but the wind so calm that the vessel scarcely steered. It was a great regret for us not to be able to take advantage, for lack of wind, of the fine weather which had prevailed for five or six days, all the more so that the bad season was approaching by great strides.
About two o'clock, having well recognized the points fixed by our last bearings, we made course to continue our work following the coast at a distance so little considerable that we often had only fifteen fathoms of bottom, being at less than a league distance. The land, in this part was the lowest we had yet had. One could well see in the interior of the country, some peaks of mediocre height, but they were few in number. The whole edge of the shore, is a succession of sand dunes, the most part, arid and without verdure. One could distinguish ahead of the beach, a continual succession of rocks which advance into the sea at a small distance and on which the wave breaks with extraordinary force. It was the cause of the continual noise which we heard.
At the setting of the sun, knowledge was obtained of a sand bank quite extended situated at the extremity of the land most in view to the west. At the moment when it was bearing for the first time, it remained to the west-north-west by compass and when the day began to end, one thought one perceived that it extended until the west-south-west. As we were then, a little more distant from the land which makes here, quite a large cove, the bottom had increased by six fathoms, in the space of an hour and a half. Having taken the southern-south-west tack to move away from the coast and the dangers which may be found there, we put off until the next day the recognition of this bank, if the weather permitted it. One saw during the day, several fires in the interior of the country, but none on the edges of the sea.
During the night, the winds were, for the most part of the time, calm. Nevertheless, although the vessel appeared not to be going forward, the bottom increased continually and rapidly since at eleven o'clock, we did not find it at 110 fathoms. In the northern tack which we followed from midnight until daylight, we did not have it either at this depth.
1802-04-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to WNW. At 1.15 we came in from Van Diemen's Land, where we had spent the 13th [Germinal, 3 April 1802]. We saw many kangaroos there; we were able to fire at only one, which we missed. We found good water and a watering place on the shore where it would be very easy to water in fine weather, because the boat could come alongside the rocks and fill the casks with a hose. Geese and other birds were killed and distributed. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 45' 34"; longitude 145° 37' 00". NE variation on the 12th [Germinal, 2 April 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 22' 00"; the same day at 4.30 p.m., 10° 08' 40"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 12' 30"; on the 14th [Germinal, 4 April 1802] at 4 p.m., 10° 48' 20"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 13' 30"; on the 15th [Germinal, 5 April 1802] at 6.15 a.m., 9° 30' 40". The tides were scarcely perceptible; the flood sets SW and the ebb NE. The greatest rate of the current was 1.0 knot.

1802-04-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from north to WNW. Calm for the rest of the day. At 7.30 the breeze got up from the ENE. We fired a gun to call the dinghy and hoisted our topsails; at 11 the dinghy being back, she was hoisted in.
1802-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon,
One saw, in a break which lasted only a moment, the land from the north until the north-east.
At noon,
The westernmost land in view remained to the north 22° 30' west,
That most to the south to the south 63° 30' east,
The eastern point of an islet on the coast nearest to the vessel was seen to the north 77° 30' east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the winds continued to be very weak and variable from the south towards the west, but the rain ceased and the sky appeared to want to become fine. At daylight, we had knowledge of the land, but at a distance too considerable to well recognize the place where we were and the point where our bearings had ended. We made course to the north towards the east to close with the land in order to assure ourselves positively of the place where we had stopped and which we recognized about eight o'clock in the morning. After having well assured ourselves of our position, we resumed the course to the north towards the west following the coast at a league at the most distance. In this place, it is all composed of arid sand dunes and little pleasant to the view. In the interior of the country, one sees ground quite elevated and well wooded.
In the morning, we followed a very large cove forming quite a considerable indentation in its north-east part. This indentation is terminated by an advanced cape at the extremity of which is found a little island which advances into the sea about half a league. Its south-east part is low and very little wide, but that of the north is more elevated and is seen from a considerable distance. This island is surrounded by breakers all around its circumference, consequently little approachable. It is the same with all the coast which is defended by a reef and a succession of rocks more or less elevated which do not permit landing there.
After having doubled this island, the course took much more to the north than it had done up to that moment and to continue to follow the coast, we steered for quite a long time to the north-north-west, not changing course except to move away from some breakers which sometimes extend offshore.
At noon, we saw not the sun, although the weather was quite fine. According to our dead reckoning, we placed ourselves at 37° 27'.
About three o'clock, we had knowledge of an underwater reef which is found near half a league from the coast. We perceived it a little late, for it was already by our beam when knowledge was obtained from the deck. We took, at once, port tacks with winds from the south-south-east to move away from it a little. Nevertheless, we did not pass at more than a mile from it in ten fathoms of water, bottom hard and of rocks.
After having put, successively, back to the course of north-north-west, we came to recognize another cape which remained to us to the north by north-west and seemed to terminate the coast in this quarter. This cape is formed by a jutting point cut perpendicularly to the sea. Ahead, are found three small rocks, one of which is particularly remarkable when coming from the east in that it is cut in two and forms an embrasure as that of a fortress could be. The coast forms still here, a large indentation and appears to be directed to the north by north-west. The lands are no longer as low, nor formed by sand dunes, as we had had them during more than half the day.
Our bearings ended after the setting of the sun at a succession of islets and rocks which do not touch the coast, of which, nevertheless, they are little distant. In the evening, the breeze from the south-south-east became fresh and we greatly regretted to see it come at a moment when we could not take advantage of it, being obliged to stand off for the night.
(In the left margin perpendicularly) During the night, a fair breeze blew from the south-east to the south-east by south. We held, with little sail, the southern-south-west tack until midnight and then, we took that of the east-north (sic) and the north-east, the winds having become variable and very weak. The various soundings which were taken, gave 30 fathoms at two leagues from lands and 64 when we changed tacks. This depth was the highest that we attained and which, according to our dead reckoning, should have placed us at five leagues at the most from the coast. In general, the sounding was very irregular in the first tack.
1802-04-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to south. The boats were hoisted in. At 10.30 hoisted the topsails and fired a swivel gun to call the yawl, which was fishing; at noon she came in and was hoisted in. At 1.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 67° 30' W for Port Dalrymple, where we were to pick up our large boat. At 6 the middle of Waterhouse bore from us N 76° E, 5 miles off, and Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. At 8 a flat calm. During the night overcast weather with continual light rain.

1802-04-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to ESE. At 1.30 got under way and made all sail, studdingsails to port. It fell calm all at once. At 6.30 took the bearing of the middle of Waterhouse Island N 76° E, about 5 miles off; Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. The breeze having freshened, made all sail. At 2, being very close to Flat Island, within a mile, and unable to weather it, we wore ship and made sail to work to windward.
1802-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon,
the middle of an islet of which I have made mention, remained to the north 5° east
and the two extremities of the land in view extended from the north 3° west until the south 56° east.
At daylight,
one saw the land from the north to the north-north-east
At noon,
the rocks and shallows which had made us change course remained to the east 21° 30' north
and the land in view to the east 10° north.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, we closed with the land with winds from the east, small breeze and at eight o'clock, we perfectly recognized all our bearing points of the day before. But we found ourselves a little more distant from the coast than we expected, although during the night, we had maintained ourselves between 64 and 45 fathoms of bottom. The sky, in the morning was dark and covered, the horizon hazy, which made the portion of coast in view, as if divided into an infinity of small islands. But the mist having dispersed, all the coast, from the north-north-west until the east, showed itself in its whole extent. It is, here, as I observed it yesterday, elevated, covered with trees and cut perpendicularly at the edge of the sea where the shore is not a succession of arid and sterile sand dunes as that which we had followed the greatest part of the day. At about the middle of the cove which the coast makes here, are two islets or rocks longer than elevated which make it recognizable by their forms, being divided by openings resembling those of a fortress on which cannons would have been placed. The sea breaks around these rocks and at each of the points, but these breakers do not advance offshore.
At nine and a half o'clock, following the coast at the distance of a league, I had soundings taken. I thought that we could have fifteen fathoms of water at this distance, but only ten were found, we would have continued the course which we were then making if the bottom had not fallen to 8 and even to six fathoms, without any indication announcing such a sudden diminution. But in working to put ourselves a little more offshore, we were very astonished to see a rock at the surface of the water of which we had until then, had no knowledge and which the lookouts, even, had not seen. To double it, we were obliged to steer to the south-west without the bottom increasing noticeably. This rock, on which the sea breaks strongly, is surrounded by reefs and seems to join to the great land by a chain of breakers which leaves no hope of a passage although the channel which is found between it and the land is more than a league in width. To the north of this rock, one sees two others smaller and a breaker which extends in the north-north-west. We passed at about a league and a half from this danger in 15 fathoms of water, skirting it in its western part. It will be prudent for navigators who succeed us to be wary of it by its distance from the firm coast. As soon as we were a little to the north of it, we sought to close with the land and the bottom diminished promptly, for we passed in half an hour from 15 fathoms to twelve. Nevertheless, we made very astonished of the east-north-east to penetrate into a large bay of which we saw no end of the lands in this quarter of the wind. We advanced into it until in eight and nine fathoms of water before having knowledge of it and we skirted it at this same depth. The land, in this part, is very low, forms several creeks not very considerable which terminate at the sea by sand dunes of mediocre height or to speak better, very low.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 37° 1' 47" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 136° 59' 12" which gave us a difference of 3° with that of the dead reckoning since the departure from the Promontory.
After the setting of the sun, and our bearings of the day finished, we took the southern-south-west tack to the south-west with a strong breeze from the south-south-east to the south-east. During the night, a strong breeze was blowing. We made little sail to avoid going
(In the left margin perpendicularly) too far from the coast while maintaining ourselves between twenty-five and thirty-five fathoms with a beautiful sand bottom. It would have been possible to anchor there if the breeze had been less strong. From midnight to four o'clock, we lay becalmed but the drift and the current threw us much to the west, the bottom always increasing which decided me to take the north-east tack to regain bottom between twenty and 25 fathoms before daylight.
1802-04-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze and calm. At 8 a.m. Flat Island bore from us S 19° W, 4 miles off. At 11.30 the breeze allowed us to shape our course S 45° W. At noon in 40° 49' 34" of latitude by account and in 145° 15' 36" of longitude by account, Flat Island bearing from us S 81° E to S 88° E, 3 miles off. At 6 it bore N 56° E and Rocky Islet S 55° W.

1802-04-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light air from N to south by way of east. At 5 a light breeze got up from the WSW. We lay close-hauled on the port tack. During the night a fresh breeze from south to SSE and SE. At midnight hove to with the main topsail to the mast; at 2 filled and set the courses. At 9.30 a.m., being abreast of Port Dalrymple and seeing our boat, we clewed up our courses and fired a swivel gun. At 10 wore onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail. The large boat came in and was hoisted in at once; at 11 filled and made all sail, studdingsails to starboard.
1802-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearing of the land:
At six o'clock,
the two extremities of the land in view, remained one to the south 46° east,
and the other to the north 23° west.
At daylight,
one saw the land from the east-north-east until the north.
At noon, it extended in the north-west as far as the view could extend.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, at daylight, we closed with the coast for the continuation of our work, but it was only about ten o'clock, that we could begin them in that we found ourselves more offshore than the bottom which we had during the night, seemed to indicate. We steered to approach it at a small league distance to the north-east which still made us penetrate into a large deep cove of as little interest as those which we had visited up to then. To exit from it, we had to pass successively from the north-east to the north-west by west. All the coast which we followed from yesterday, is composed only of sand dunes which inspire only sadness and regrets. Independent of the bad and disagreeable aspect which it offers to the view, the sea breaks all along the shore with extraordinary force and two or three swells which it makes before arriving there, indicates that there is in this part, a shallows which must advance at least half a mile offshore.
The lookouts, from the top of the masts, and the curious who wished to climb there, reported that the interior of the country, as far as their sight could penetrate, was nothing but arid sands on which there was no vegetation.
The coast which we explored this day, had nevertheless an advantage which we found not at all in that of the day before, it is that the water was deeper there and the bottom regular. Although at a small league from shore, we never had less than 16 fathoms of water when we doubled the points of the small creeks which are found there, and 19 to 20, when they were passed or even before arriving at them.
At noon, the latitude was observed of 36° 1' 10", and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 137° 9' 40".
In the afternoon, we continued to follow a coast all sandy and formed of dunes of the same nature. But, about three o'clock, we began to discover high lands which appeared to us to be of an agreeable aspect. A little while after, we saw a vessel which we thought, at first, to be the Naturaliste, for we were far from believing that there were other European vessels in these quarters, and in the season in which we found ourselves. Nevertheless, we were greatly mistaken for, as we approached her, we recognized by her masts and her capacity that it was not she. Finally, at five o'clock, being able to distinguish each other perfectly, this vessel made a signal to us which we did not understand and consequently to which we did not respond. Then, she hoisted English colours and reduced sail. On our side, we hoisted national colours and I headed to the closest to accost her. As she hailed us first, the question was asked what vessel we were. My response was: French. The question was then asked if it was Captain Baudin who commanded. I was very surprised, not only by the question but also to hear myself named. Having answered that yes, the English vessel lay to. Seeing it make dispositions to send a boat alongside, I also lay to to wait for it. The English Captain, M. Flinders that same who (in the left margin: discovered the strait which should bear his name and which), very improperly, has been named Banks Strait, came aboard, congratulated himself greatly on the pleasant meeting he was making, but was very reserved, about all the rest. As soon as I learned his name, I made him my compliments on the pleasure which I experienced in making his acquaintance. &a.
I communicated to him all that
(In the left margin perpendicularly) all that we had put in order up to this moment concerning our geographic work. As it was already late, M. Flinders told me that if I wished to run an offshore tack during the night and a second to shore to wait for daylight, he would return to my aboard the next day, and would give me different notions about the portion of coast which he had visited from Cape Leeuwin until here. I was very pleased with his proposal and we agreed to keep together during the night which was very fine.
1802-04-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to E. At 1, Rocky Islet S 11° E, 1 mile off. At 8 it bore from us S 85° E. At 9, being abreast of Port Dalrymple, we fired a swivel gun to call our boat, which was sighted at 9.30 under the land. At 10 hove to; she came in and was hoisted in. At 11 filled and stood on, the course north. At noon in 40° 56' 16" of latitude by account and in 144° 42' 6" of longitude by account. At 6 hove to with the port side to the wind.

1802-04-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, light rain, a fresh breeze from SE to east and ESE, freshening. At 7 sighted the land in the N 10° E. At noon took the bearing of island (A) S 66° E; a low island (G) N 70° E; another, a sugarloaf, N 58° E; (M) N 50° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a very conspicuous white rock, pierced in its western part, N 7° E. Wilson's Promontory, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations, lies in 39° 10' 54" of south latitude and 147° 37' 31" of east longitude. Islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of east longitude.

and the other to the north 23° west.

At noon, it extended in the north-west as far as the view could extend.

1802-04-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 5 a.m. we filled and stood on, the course N 11° 15' W. At 7.15 a very high islet (A) was sighted in the N 10° E. At 10.25 it bore from us east (true); a neighbouring islet D N 86° E; another S 85° E (B). At noon in 39° 16' 28" of latitude observed and in 144° 32' 0" of longitude. Took the bearing of a very conspicuous white rock, pierced on its west side, N 7° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a rock M N 50° E; a very high islet P N 58° E; another, C, low, N 70° E; islet A S 66° E. From this bearing and that of 10.25, islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of longitude. At 12.45 we hove to and put the Géographe's boat in the water; she was provisioned for 15 days and left at 1.30 under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, accompanied by Citizen Boulanger, surveyor, to fix the promontory and survey the coast as far as Western Port. At 1.45 we filled and stood in for the promontory. At 3.15, being very near it, we bore away N 65° 15' W and ran along the islets at its end. At 4.30, 8° 45' 30" of NE variation; at 5.45, 8° 29' 0" the same. At 6 took the bearing of a very conspicuous cape N 45° E and another, A, N 33° W, half a mile off. Between these two capes there is a large bight. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 50" of longitude. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; the wind a strong breeze, the weather overcast, with light rain. At midnight filled on the port tack, the land in sight to the NE.

1802-04-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to SE and NE. The Géographe's boat was put in the water with fifteen days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, lieutenant, and Boulanger, the surveyor, to determine the position of the promontory. At 9 p.m. went onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail; the lead brought up 40 fathoms, rocky bottom. At 6 filled and made sail. At noon took the bearing of cape (B) N 41° E; Western Island N 46° W, about 10 miles off.
1802-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
The land extended from south-east 85° east to the west.
At noon,
It stretched from north 72° east to south 72° west.
A small islet fairly near to us then lay at north 25° west.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the nineteenth, in the morning, Mr. Flinders, making his preparations to return to his ship, as he had informed me the previous day, I hove to again in order to wait for him. At six-thirty, he arrived, accompanied by the same person who had come the day before. As he was much less reserved in this second visit than he had been the day before, he informed me that his vessel was named the Investigator and that he had sailed from Europe about eight months after me. He also told me that he had begun his reconnaissance of the coasts of New Holland at Cape Leeuwin, had visited the islands of St Peter and St Francis, as well as the whole coast as far as the place where we met each other. He also communicated to me the plan of a port he had discovered in an island of which we were only fifteen to twenty leagues distant and which he had named Kangaroo Island, on account of the great number he had found in that place. This island, according to his account, is long, high, extensive and offers a good passage between it and the continent. He had remained there six weeks, and consequently had time to examine it thoroughly.
Before we separated, Mr. Flinders gave me several charts published by Arrowsmith since our departure. As I informed him of the accident that had befallen my boat, asking him to give it the assistance he could if he happened to encounter it, he informed me that a similar misfortune had occurred to him at his Kangaroo Island, where he had lost eight men and a boat. The second vessel that accompanied him was also separated from him in the equinox gale which I received partly in the Strait of Bass and the end beyond. Mr. Flinders told me on parting that he was going to steer for the strait and endeavour to reconnoitre a land which is said to exist between the Hunter Islands and the port which they have named the Western Port. At eight o'clock in the morning we separated, wishing each other a good voyage.
During the rest of the day, the wind was light. We were even sometimes in calm, at the mercy of the current which carried us towards the coast of which we were then only a league distant. After examining my bearings of the previous day, we coasted along the high land which we had seen a little before sunset. The coast, in this place, had an aspect that, if not very pleasant to the eye, was at least preferable to that of the sandy dunes which we had just left.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 36', but very uncertain, and at three o'clock, we sighted the island and the islets of which Mr. Flinders had spoken to me. I set course to run through the channel which separates this island from the continent, but the light wind which prevailed did not allow me to enter before nightfall, and at five o'clock I came about to stand out to sea.
In coasting along the mainland during the day, we discovered three small islands or rocks which are at so small a distance from it that, in order to see them, it was necessary to coast as close as we did. In calm, one could anchor there in 24 or 21 fathoms, the bottom being sand and suitable for anchorage, a thing fairly rare from the Promontory until now.
At sunset, Mr. Flinders's vessel could still be seen running on the south-west tack.
During the night, the winds were fairly fresh from the south to south-south-east until midnight, but then they fell calm, and shortly after, we made the land tack.
1802-04-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from N to S by way of east. At 3.30 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on. At 7.30 Cape A bore from us east, 11 miles off. At noon in 38° 46' 0" of latitude observed and in 143° 55' 6" of longitude by account, a cape B bearing N 41° E and Western Island N 46° W, 10 miles off. At noon the large boat and the small boat were put in the water and provisioned for 10 days. At 1.45 they left under the orders of Citizen Milius, accompanied by Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey Western Port. At 4.15, 9° 16' 0" of NE variation; at 5.15, 9° 14' 30" of variation; at 5.45, 38° 48' 19" of latitude observed. At 4 the promontory S 70° E, cape B N 55° E, Western Island from N 27° W to N 32° W, the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 61° W. At 5.30 the promontory S 75° E, Western Island N 14° W.

1802-04-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE. The large boat and the small boat were put in the water, one under the orders of Citizen Milius, frigate captain, and the other under those of Citizen Brèvedent, midshipman; they left to survey Western Port. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 48" of east longitude.
1802-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
Two small islands or rocks of which we were at some distance, lay one at south 50° west, and the other at south 57° west.
The westernmost land in sight of the continent, lay at north 71° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, in the morning, having ascertained all our points from the previous day, we shaped course for two islets placed to the east of Kangaroo Island. The first is merely a heap of rocks elevated enough to be perceived five or six leagues from sea. It appears sound and we never had less than 16 fathoms at a league's distance. It is not the same for the second rock, which has, in its south-east part, a long reef on which the sea breaks heavily and rises to a considerable height. As I am drawing a view of these two islets, I will not enlarge further on this subject. The latitude of the first appeared to me to be about 35° 42'. As the one which lies to the south-east of it is not far distant, it is not possible that navigators should be unaware of both together.
The channel which separates the two islets from the mainland is beautiful, deep and commodious. It is the same for the channel which they form with the eastern coast of Kangaroo Island.
We were greatly hindered, in the afternoon, by the light winds which were nearly calm. But the current served us fairly well, though it carried us towards the mainland, moving to the north-west. We passed near a projecting point whence it appeared afterwards to run north-north-west at a small league in 18 fathoms of water. The land here is of considerable height and very varied in appearance, but leaving regret at not being able to land, the beach terminating sheer to the sea. One occasionally finds, however, small sandy creeks where the sea also breaks at the edge of the shore.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 39' 51" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 135° 42' 10".
In the evening, we steered to approach the eastern part of Kangaroo Island which we had in sight and upon which Mr. Flinders had given me some details. We had, at sunset, a light breeze from the east which, though very slight, facilitated our approach. The bottom was very uneven in the course we made to reach it and the weakness of the breeze induced me to anchor about nine o'clock in the evening, in twenty-six fathoms, sandy bottom. But whether it was too hard or otherwise, our anchor did not hold and we were forced to make sail again. While our anchor was at the bottom, we perceived that the current was very strong and that its direction was indeed north-west since we were dragging our anchor to leeward. The rest of the night was spent tacking, making alternate tacks, awaiting daylight to continue surveying the principal points which will be able to determine the position of this island relative to the mainland. The channel which it forms with Cape Etoile is about four and a half to five leagues at most.
During the night, the weather had a very bad appearance for the following day. The sky became covered with clouds in the northern quarter and we sometimes had rain without wind.
1802-04-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from WNW to S, and calm. At 8.45, 8° 34' 50" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 58' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 43' 12" of longitude by account. At 4 Western Island N 8° W, 14 miles off. At 4.30, 9° 54' 20" of NE variation. At 6, Western Island from N 6° W to N 15° W, 8 miles off.

1802-04-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south and to the west. At 4 took the bearing of Western Island N 8° W, about 14 miles off. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the other tack; at 7 a.m. filled and stood on. At noon Western Island N 47° W; Cape Bon N 75° W.
1802-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon,
The two extremities of the mainland lay one at north 70° east and the other at north 56° west.
The land most in sight from Kangaroo Island from south 29° west to south 78° west.
The middle of the two double islets in the evening was (south) 46° east for one, and S. 36° east for the other.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, in the morning, running on the tack in the channel which it forms with Kangaroo Island, we suddenly saw on the edge of the coast from which we were then not far distant, a very bright light such as is ordinarily carried by those who go fishing by the seashore during the night. At first light, we saw it much more clearly and someone even thought they could distinguish the person carrying it. It could indeed be, for we saw it moved in different directions and it was not a fixed fire, having it sometimes ahead and sometimes behind the first bearing we had made of it. When day broke, it disappeared.
Until sunrise, the winds were very light and inconstant, but then they settled in the north and a fresh breeze blew until noon. We coasted along a considerable stretch of the eastern coast of Kangaroo Island and visited several fairly deep coves where, in the good season, that is to say in summer, there are good anchorages and shelter from the north-west to the south passing through the west. But from every other point of the horizon, the sea must be rough there since we found it so in moderate northerly winds. The soundings, all along the coast, are fairly regular. They are ten fathoms at a league and a half from the coast, and seven and six at a small distance. The interior of the country offers a fairly pleasant appearance and although most of the trees had lost their leaves, there remained still enough green vegetation for the view to be pleasant. I coasted very close to the land, not only to have exact bearings of it but also in the hope of recognizing the port which they (margin note: that the English) say they found there and in which Mr. Flinders told me he had remained six week to make the reconnaissance of this part of the coast. It appears, until this point, that I have misunderstood or misheard the latitude he gave me for it, for the land does not appear to us until this point to extend as far north as I think I heard him say.
In the morning, we were obliged to go about to double a projecting point which the winds did not allow us to double without moving away from it somewhat.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 40'. There was no hour angle.
During the evening, we continued to coast along at some distance with a fair breeze and after sunset, we bore away to the north-east to close with the mainland. During the night, the winds were light and inconstant. We endeavoured to maintain ourselves in 20 fathoms and we had succeeded when at midnight we suddenly fell into 15 fathoms and shortly after into 12. We then perceived low, level land on which the sea broke fairly heavily to be heard distinctly. We did not know what land it could be, which led us to decide to bear away successively until south-east, when we found the bottom of 20 fathoms again. The rest of the night was spent tacking in short boards in order not to move too far away from the land which we had perceived during the night so as to recognize it the next day. When we sighted it, we were steering north-east and its two extremities in sight lay one at north 15° east and the other at south 85° west.
1802-04-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to W. At half past midnight hove to; at 7 filled and stood on. At 7.30, 8° 6' 20" of NE variation. At 8, Western Island N 48° W. At noon in 38° 55' 26" of latitude observed and in 143° 50' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island N 27° W, cape B N 75° E. At 6, the middle of Western Island N 10° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to SSW and NW. At 6 took the bearing of the middle of Western Island N 10° W, about 9 miles off. At noon we had it bearing from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off.
1802-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
The extremities of the mainland in sight lay one at south 70° east, and the other and the other (sic) at north 25° east.
That of Kangaroo Island extended from south 33° east to south 68° west.
At two o'clock at night,
Land was sighted, and we took its bearing from north 15° east to south 85° west.
At eight o'clock in the morning,
The middle of the land sighted during the night lay at north 15° west,
And the mainland extended from south 67° east to south 33° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, we saw again the land which we had sighted during the night. It appeared to us very low and such as we had judged it, but much more extensive. Its two extremities extended from south 67° 30' east to south 63° 30' west. It seemed to us that it must be an island which lay to the north 45° west at its middle. (Left-margin note: it is the southern part of the lands which separate the two gulfs).
We also sighted a part of Kangaroo Island whose two extremities in sight extended from south 33° 30' west to south 67° 30' east. As we also had in sight the high lands of the continent at a distance of five to six leagues, I preferred to shape course on our latest bearings rather than delay at this island, being moreover persuaded that I would see it again in continuing along the mainland which makes, here, a very great indentation.
During the morning, the wind blew a fairly fresh breeze, but from the north, which was not very favourable for the course we would have to make after having coasted close enough to the land to recognize it well.
Calm having set in about eleven o'clock, and the currents carrying us with speed into a great bay across our path, we were obliged to go about to move out to sea as soon as the breeze should come in.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 27' 0" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 135° 33' 6".
During the evening, we had a light breeze from the north to north-north-west by means of which we moved out a little from the coast, but it was very slight and of short duration. However, we had moved away by nearly a league and a half from the coast, and the bottom was then 20 fathoms, suitable for anchorage. The small stretch of coast which we made during this day is high and very mountainous. We observed no danger that was not visible. Most of the mountains were bare of trees, others had some which had lost their leaves and the greater part offered only barren ground covered with dried herbs having the colour of straw.
At sunset, the winds or rather the breeze shifted to the south-west, we shaped course to the north-north-east on the land which lay ahead in that direction, estimating ourselves at eight leagues in order to approach it during the night so as not to lose time the next day. The land extending much to the north in this part, we hoped to find, in the gulf which it appeared to indicate, some port, for it is most surprising that we have not yet found one in all the extent of coast which we have visited.
During the night, the weather was fairly fine until about two o'clock. But then it began to rain and with strong squalls which obliged us to take a second reef in our topsails. We ran during the night different tacks in order to keep in sight of the coast which, from the manner in which we had seen it terminate at the sea, appeared to offer no danger.
1802-04-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8, Western Island N 4° W, 9 miles off. At 10.30, 7° 24' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 143° 35' 30" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off. At 4, cape B N 83° E, and Western Island from N 16° W to N 25° W. The Géographe's boat was sighted standing towards us; at 4.30 hove to. Citizen Saint-Cricq came in from his errand; the boat was hoisted in and at 5 we filled and stood on. At 6, Western Island from N 30° W to N 38° W and cape B N 86° E. During the night overcast and stormy weather.

1802-04-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At half past noon hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 3 filled with the winds south to SSE and SSW. The Géographe's boat was sighted; we hove to and at 4 she was hoisted in. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4 hove to on the other tack. At noon Western Island N 35° W, about 8 miles off.
1802-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock, the westernmost point of the continent in sight lay at south 12° west,
The westernmost point of Kangaroo Island at south 29° west,
The easternmost point of the same island at north 25° east.
At noon the two extremities of Kangaroo Island extended relative to our position from south 78° 30' east to south 26° west,
The land nearest to the ship at north 24° 30' east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, we had the winds from the east-south-east, strong and in squalls. However the sky did not have a bad appearance and appeared to be clearing during the day, which indeed happened, as soon as they had shifted to the south. We took advantage of it to advance to the north along a land of the continent which took that direction. As it continued to blow a strong breeze during the morning, we made good progress and explored the coast at a distance of a small league from the land and sometimes less. The bottom was found along the coast from 16 to 20 fathoms, suitable for anchorage, being sand although somewhat hard. This part of the same coast had very few trees and nevertheless offered several fairly picturesque views. We discovered no shelter there for vessels and only a cove of some considerable size whose edge of the beach appeared to be very white sand. The other coves were cut sheer at the sea and appeared to offer no landing place, although they were sheltered from the wind, the sea broke on the shore as if the wave had passed over a sand bar.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 12' 0" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 135° 47' 22".
In the afternoon, we sighted, after having passed the chain of mountains of which this coast is formed, very low land which began at the extremity of a point which advanced into the sea by a very gradual slope. We thought at first that it was only a tongue of land which could not be of great extent. But as we approached it, this tongue of land which we had thought must be of little consequence extended more and more to the north, trending somewhat to the east. We followed it in all its extent until four o'clock in the afternoon, the water being always decreasing, we thought we had reached the head of the gulf. The sounding then showed 7 and 8 fathoms, sandy bottom. As we also had land in sight to the west we no longer doubted that we found ourselves deep in a gulf whose width was not known to us. We began, about five o'clock, to give a westerly direction to the course we were making. We sounded continuously, finding always seven and eight fathoms. But at sunset, we suddenly fell into five fathoms and even less. We immediately bore away by hauling close on the south-west tack. But we were nearly half an hour before seeing it increase by half a fathom. At last, we passed successively from 5 to 6, 7, 8 and 16 fathoms. But it soon decreased again, which decided me to tack, making alternate tacks, to endeavour if it were possible to maintain myself between fifteen and twenty fathoms, being at eight o'clock in the evening in 18. The crew was forbidden to go to bed before ten o'clock, the time when I thought myself relieved of all anxiety for the night, if the bottom continued to increase. At nine o'clock, having found eighteen fathoms of water, it was permitted to those who were not on watch to retire. But it was not for long, for at half-past nine, we suddenly fell into eleven fathoms, and they were immediately recalled to go about with greater ease. During the rest of the night, everyone was on watch. We made different tacks, taking as turning points the soundings which decreased from the strongest we had found, on one tack as on the other. By this means we maintained ourselves between 15 and 20 fathoms, having had the good fortune to have fair weather, otherwise we might perhaps have found ourselves in great difficulty.
(Written vertically in the left margin) I named this gulf the Gulf of the Bad on account of the fatigue which it occasioned to all the crew. The winds were very variable during the night. We expected that the south-south-west tack which we took several times would carry us to sea, but (nothing) came of it and served only to show us the land to leeward of us, and the bottom was decreasing as rapidly on that as on the eastern tack.
1802-04-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SW. At 2 hove to; at 7.30 filled and stood on. At 8, Western Island from N 38° W to N 47° W and cape B S 88° E; hove to. At 10.15 filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 37' 20" of latitude by account and in 143° 37' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 35° W, 8 miles off. At 4 it bore N 45° W, 15 miles off, and at 6.15 N 38° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a strong breeze from SSW to south and SW. We beat all night abreast of Western Port. At 4 hove to; at 6 filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off; Cape de la Roche N 89° E.
1802-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the lands which seemed to us to form the southern extremity of the second part of the gulf, lay west by south-west. And we had in sight a part of Kangaroo Island extending extending (sic) from south-south-east to south-west by west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, we found ourselves surrounded by lands except for the south-west quarter which appeared clear and offered a good passage. We had in sight the two coasts which formed the gulf which we had not perceived the day before, owing to the proximity at which we had coasted the starboard coast, namely that on the port side. The difference between these two coasts is very different one from the other. That on the starboard, as I have already observed, is formed by a chain of high mountains and without much verdure, while that opposite to it is a flat and level coast on which one sees only two or three elevations formed by sand dunes which can serve as landmarks. These dunes, which begin at the edge of the sea, are well wooded and before seeing the land, one perceives them at the horizon's edge, rising gradually until one has approached near enough to discover the lands which support them.
As we had visited all the starboard coast of this gulf, I wished equally to know that on the port side. This led me to steer to the south-west in south-east winds, a fair breeze. In approaching it, we first discovered a very extensive bank making a great circuit which advanced at least a league and a half to sea. We partly went around it by taking soundings which left us nothing to fear. This danger is easy to recognize by the colour of the water which appears a very light green there. After passing it, we closed with the coast. The bottom then decreased from 24 fathoms to 7 and a half, which prevented me from approaching it more closely, unwilling to run the same risks as the day before. I ordered to go about, steering to the east-north-east, but we had scarcely made two miles when the bottom, which had somewhat increased, suddenly fell to five fathoms. I bore away to the north-east, steering to regain the place where I was to the south-west. We quickly found 7 and 8 fathoms again, and the lookouts then reported to us that they saw to the south-west a sand bank half exposed, whose northern extremity, to judge by the colour of the water, extended as far as the port quarter and lay to the north-north-east of us. The course which we made to the north-east seems to confirm what they reported to us, for we were nearly an hour in 8 and 10 fathoms, and as long in 11 and 12. Although the breeze was light, we made fair progress. The bottom then passing from 12 to 25 fathoms in a short time, we once more hoped to be clear of the shallows, and shaped course to close with the mountainous coast to the starboard of which the depths were known to us. The weather in the morning, although misty and with light squalls, was fair, but the winds very variable.
At noon, we had no latitude observations, the sky having become covered with clouds. I was sorry to give up the port coast of this gulf, which, moreover, offers no advantage to navigators, but I cannot say with certainty if this coast is not formed of several islands, which I suspect to be very likely, although I am not certain of it.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to the south-east, a fair breeze, we endeavoured to close with the coast which was known to us in order to examine Mr. Flinders's Kangaroo Island. At five o'clock, being at the opening of the entrance to the gulf which we were leaving, we kept close-hauled on the south-by-west tack in order to come alongside the island during the night which was fair and with a moderate breeze. The soundings were very regular between 26 and 20 fathoms. The bottom was sometimes suitable for anchorage, being sand and coarse gravel, and sometimes bad, of coral or hard.
1802-04-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SW. At 4 hove to and at 6 filled and stood on. At 8, 8° 8' 50" of NE variation. Cape B N 38° E and Western Island N 37° W, 12 miles off. At noon in 38° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 143° 31' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off, and cape B N 89° E; the breeze light. At 4 a flat calm, Western Island from N 38° W to N 43° W.

1802-04-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to SE by way of south. At 11.30 hove to on the port tack, Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off.
1802-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
(No mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, having come alongside during the night the northern part of the coast of Kangaroo Island which we had left on the 21st in the evening to make for the mainland, we recognized our last bearings on this island, and after having observed them well at a small distance from the coast, we coasted it making course to the west until about ten o'clock in the morning, when it appeared to us to be heading a little towards the south. The weather was fine all the morning and a fair breeze blew from the east.
The lookouts, from the tops of the masts, continually announced to us that we had on our starboard a very low land which was appearing as we advanced to the west, but we had no knowledge of it from the deck. However, we saw, to the north, several fires which assured us of the truth of what they reported.
As I did not expect to encounter off the mainland an island so extensive from east to west which appeared to be the one in sight, I was astonished not to see its end, for as we doubled each point, another immediately appeared to succeed it. All the coast which we coasted, in the morning as in the afternoon, was high and steep. At the edge of the sea, at intervals, one saw small coves of little depth but offering no shelter from the western side between north and south-east. The bottom was fairly constant and we never had less than twenty fathoms and often twenty-five at a small league from the coast. The appearance of this island is pleasant and very varied. Although it was not entirely wooded, it had the advantage of delighting us much more than everything we had seen before.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 30' 35" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 134° 46' 34".
In the afternoon, we were told of several islands to leeward of us. I thought it could be some considerable elevation on the mainland whose lower extremities were not visible. But at three o'clock, we passed a small island very high on which we had no doubt. But I do not think the other lands announced as islands and of which we had knowledge from the deck are such, although they had the appearance of islands.
We continued, during the evening, to coast the northern part of Kangaroo Island and we did not see its end until sunset. Despite a good breeze blowing, we made slow progress and a strong current which appeared to us to be flowing east and west seemed much to retard our progress.
During the night, we made several tacks from the small island seen in the evening to that of Kangaroo Island and at two o'clock we shaped course to the north to close with the mainland on which I wished to be near to visit it the next day. The weather was fine all night and a moderate breeze, from east-north-east to east-south-east.
1802-04-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to ENE. At 8, Western Island N 16° W, 9 miles off. At 9, 6° 19' of NE variation. At 11.30 hove to and at noon filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 34' 34" of latitude by account and in 143° 24' 42" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off. At 4 the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 57° W, Western Island N 31° E, and cape B N 55° E. During the night the wind a strong breeze. Wilson's Promontory lies in 39° 10' 54" of latitude and 144° 37' 31" of longitude. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude.

1802-04-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to east and to NE by way of north. At noon filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off; the western end of the mainland N 62° W.
1802-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
On the 26th at noon, the group of islands which we had recognized in the morning extended from north 30° east to west 35° south. That to the east forming the channel by which we had entered to close with the mainland, was at south 48° east, and that to the west at south 78° west.
The mainland was visible from south 68° east to north 74° 45' east.
At six o'clock, the islet to the east forming the channel through which we had passed, was at south 42° east, that to the west at west 24° north. The mainland was visible from north 69° east to to (sic) south 58° east. To be verified.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, at daybreak, we perceived land at several points of the horizon and at sunrise we recognized that most of them were islets and rocks, separated one from another by channels which, to judge by their distance, appeared fairly convenient. Four of these islets and rocks lay to the north to us, taking towards east, and five towards west taking from north. Another portion of land which we judged by its extent to be part of the mainland lay to the north-west. As I wished to close with the mainland, I ordered to steer through the middle of a channel about three leagues wide. The waters there appeared deeper than elsewhere and we found them so, for the sounding never showed less than 26 fathoms and sometimes much more. The view which I give of this channel and of the islets and rocks which form it will make them easy to recognize.
In the morning, the winds were very light and variable. As the current was favourable to us, we crossed the channel while closing with the mainland which is, here, of very dismal appearance. Two high points which one easily distinguished, were formed by brown rocks of a very dismal colour and the middle of the land between them formed dunes of white sand, the greater part deprived of all manner of vegetation. Starting from the eastern point of the mainland of which I have just spoken, a reef was discovered at the water's edge situated about the middle of the channel which is found between the mainland and the islet to the east of the channel forming that through which we had passed. As it was very extensive, it is to be presumed that it leaves no passage between it and the mainland. The sea was also seen breaking on the portion of coast which we judged to be part of the continent and several fires were seen rising from the interior of the country. The calm and the light breeze which came to us from the north to north-north-west forced us to go about and return by the same channel through which we had entered (awaiting the wind to permit us to fix the course which we should have to make).
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 15' 6" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 134° 11' 29".
The southernmost land of the continent of which we found ourselves then only about a league and a half distant at most, lay to the south 68° east and extended to the north 74° 45' east.
The islet forming to the east the channel through which we had passed was at south 48° east. During the greater part of the evening we were in calm, presenting our bow to the west towards the south. But about four o'clock, a light breeze from south to south-south-west coming to us, we resumed the course to the north towards the west in order to close with the mainland.
By the bearing taken at six o'clock, the southernmost point of the mainland relative to our position lay to the south 59° east and the lands were seen to extend to the north-north-east. The islet to the east forming the channel through which we had passed was at south 42° east, and that to the west at west 25° north.
During the night which was very fine, we made little sail steering to the north towards the east. We did not lose sight of the land and the bottom constantly maintained 32 fathoms.
1802-04-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to NE. At 8, Western Island N 6° E, 9 miles off. At 8.45, 6° 28' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 44' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 33' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off, and the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 62° W. At 4, Western Island from N 11° W to N 24° W. At 4.30, 8° 1' 40" of NE variation.

1802-04-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and the wind a strong breeze from east to NE and to NW by way of north. At 3 p.m. bore away for Western Island; at 5 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. From the bearing of the promontory, which lay a mile north of us, I concluded its latitude to be 39° 10' 26".
1802-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six o'clock in the morning and evening, the mainland extended from north-east by north to south-south-east.
At noon, they were visible from east 23° south to east 78° north. The middle of what was in sight formed a large bay of low land lying at east 20° north.
At sunset, the northernmost land in sight was at north 22° 30' east, and the southernmost also in sight lay at east 75° south. The two extremities of the island which we had just doubled were, one at east 61° south and the other at north-east 12° south. The middle of the islet of which I have spoken at east 3° south.
At noon, the mainland extended from north 45° east to south 40° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, having made course all night to the north towards the east with little sail and without losing sight of the land, we found ourselves abreast of a very great and no less deep bay. One could scarcely distinguish from the deck the continuation of the land in several indentations, but from the tops, one perceived it very well.
As the winds were then from the south and very variable, we held close-hauled steering to the east and even more to the south. But the breeze was so light during all the morning that we made little progress. From the direction which the land appeared to be taking, it was very likely that if we were not in a new gulf, we found ourselves at least in a very deep indentation towards the east since we did not see the land terminate in that quarter.
At daybreak, we had no knowledge of the islands seen the day before. In spite of the little progress we made during the day, the bottom did not cease to decrease much and even rapidly. At ten o'clock we were in thirty and a half fathoms and half an hour later we had only 25. From 25, it passed to 17, at which time the ship having missed stays, we found 21 fathoms when the evolution to put her on the same tack was completed. The winds being then at east-north-east obliged us to bear away to the north, which at noon put us back in 25 fathoms, not having made more than a league since the moment when we found 17.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 34° 42' 46" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 134° 37' 40".
As we had still much to do on the coast of New Holland and as we had not more than two months' water remaining, I judged it proper to begin to reduce the ration early, that is to say that instead of giving two and a half bottles per man, we gave only two. This was certainly not a considerable reduction since we still gave more than was prescribed by the regulations in long voyages. However, this caused some discontent, not among the sailors, but in another quarter. Be that as it may, this changed nothing in the determination I had taken on this subject, being convinced that one can very well do without taking tea and coffee twice a day. So, whether contented or not, I was the first to conform to it in good grace.
During the evening, the winds having resumed from east towards the south, we closed with the coast, but the breeze was so light that we made little progress. All the lands which we had in sight during this day are low and offer few remarkable points. The edge of the sea is formed sometimes of sand dunes and sometimes by cliffs cut sheer where one sees only crevasses between the sinuosities which they form.
At five o'clock in the afternoon, we saw two islands very close to the continent. The first, that is the one most to the south, could be a league and a half in extent from south-south-west to north-north-east, and the second is only a rock of about half a league having, like the first, a reef at each of its extremities on which the sea breaks heavily. We passed by these two islands at a distance of a league in 9, 10, 11 and 12 fathoms and from the continent at three leagues.
(Written vertically in the left margin) During the night, the weather was very fine. We made course from north towards the east until eight o'clock, when having reduced sail, we ran a tack to seaward until midnight, when we hove to in 17 fathoms. The drift or the current having carried us to 20 fathoms, we resumed the course to the north towards the east to close with the coast which then could not be far away.
1802-04-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SW by way of north. At 8.30, 6° 26' of NE variation. At noon in 38° 42' 17" of latitude observed and in 143° 51' 24" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. At 3.30, having sighted our two boats, we hove to; at 4 the large one, with Citizen Milius, came in and was hoisted in at once. At 4, Western Island N 34° W, 9 miles off. At 5.15 the small boat came in and was hoisted in. At 6, Western Island N 43° W. At 8 we filled and stood on, the course S 45° E. The weather turned overcast with light rain; at midnight we hove to.

1802-04-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW. The two boats came in at 5.15 and were hoisted in at once. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4.30 filled and wore onto the starboard tack, and shaped our course to leave the strait.
1802-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
The mainland extended from north 50° east to south 37° east,
A land to leeward, was visible from north 38° west to north 46° west.
At two o'clock,
A reef was perceived ahead of us.
At three o'clock,
It lay to the north 71° east at a distance of a league at most.
At sunset, we being at a small distance from the indentation of the gulf, the lands to the west lay for us from west 20° north to west 80° north and those to the east extended for us from south 34° east to north 64° east.
