Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, we found ourselves distant from the land about four leagues and in 17 fathoms, sandy bottom. At eight o'clock, we had closed with it in 15 fathoms, same bottom. And during the rest of the morning, we coasted it at a distance of two leagues. The winds which were then almost calm did not allow us to approach it more closely.
All the coast which we had in sight during the morning was in general of medium height. One saw, however, at intervals, elevations more considerable than the greater part of the coast to which they were joined by lower and well-wooded lands, to judge at least by the sight, for one could distinguish the tops of the trees without having knowledge of the water's edge.
The sounding was fairly uniform from the beginning of the day until noon, remaining almost always between twenty and sixteen fathoms.
At noon, we observed the latitude to be 34° 11' 38" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 134° 47' 27".
During the morning, we had sighted a land to leeward of us fairly high which lay to the north-west of us. The sight of this land, which was fairly extensive, gave rise to several conjectures on board. Some asserted, without knowing very well why, that it must be the beginning of the islands of St Peter and St Francis, although the latitude was very different. Others thought they saw in this isolated land a very extensive island of which no one before us had had knowledge, etc.
My opinion, which I kept to myself, was that we could very well be in a second gulf much more advanced to the north than that which we had just passed. However, as the swell appeared to me too strong to be so far into the land, I did not quite know what to make of it.
Be that as it may, we continued to make course to the north taking somewhat to the east, coasting the coast which opened in the direction of north by north-east, and as we advanced the bottom decreased proportionally. But between one and two o'clock in the afternoon, it suddenly passed from 15 to 12 fathoms and, in half an hour, from 12 to 9. Then, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us breakers ahead of us and a little to port of the ship. We were not long in recognizing them well from the deck, which made me take port tack, convinced that I would not find a passage between them and the mainland of the eastern quarter.
After having hauled our closest, the course west-north-west, we continued to steer in that direction while coasting in eight fathoms of water the reef of which I have spoken and which appeared to us to be the top of a sand bank at the water's edge. For no rock was seen rising above the level of the sea. But the sea broke strongly. The extent of this danger is not very considerable and appeared to us not to have more than half a league where the wave broke.
At three o'clock, beginning to move away from it, I ordered a bearing to be taken and it then lay to the north 71° east, which from the course steered since noon would place its latitude at 34° 8' 54" and the longitude of (no figures).
The light wind which blew having shifted to the south, we steered until four to the west and as the bottom was then 13 fathoms, we resumed the course to the north-north-west in order to see if the land which we had to port joined that to the east as I suspected. At sunset, being still at too great a distance from the western coast to recognize it well, we resumed the course to the north towards the east until eight o'clock, when we changed tack to pass the night tacking.
(Written vertically in the left margin) From eight o'clock in the evening until midnight, the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate, but at that time, the winds having shifted to the west-north-west, it became so strong that we could carry only the foresail and our topsails with all reefs taken. The rest of the night was anything but pleasant and the movement of the barometer was not calculated to reassure us, deep as we were in the presumed gulf, if the weather should become bad and the winds shift to the south-west.
1802-04-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from SW to SSW. At 4 we filled and stood on, the land from N 22° E to S 79° E. At 8, cape A N 28° W, the promontory S 84° E, islet P S 70° E. At noon, cape A N 34° W, the promontory S 77°, 6 miles off, islet P S 68° E. By this bearing we were in 39° 8' 45" of latitude and 144° 30' 18" of longitude. At 6, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 71° E, the 2 islets C S 86° E, islet P S 81° E, islet A S 57° E. At midnight the promontory N 85° E, 15 miles off.

1802-04-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a flat calm. At 1.30 the breeze got up from the SW. Made all sail. At 7 p.m. clewed up and furled the topgallant sails and struck the main topgallant mast to repair it. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the north, the promontory bearing N 85° E, 5 leagues off; we wore onto the port tack and passed between the islets and rocks of the promontory. At noon took the bearing of two rocks, one N 42° E, the other N 78° W, half a mile off; the promontory N [illegible], 9 miles off; the sugarloaf N 88° W; islet A S 25° E; rock D S 57° E; an island H N 70° E.
1802-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
On the twenty-ninth at daybreak, the eastern lands were visible from east-north-east to east-south-east at a distance of six leagues. The horizon to the west was too hazy to perceive the coast in that quarter.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, I expected that the weather would clear and that during the day we could explore the part of coast which we had seen the day before. But instead of that, the sky, which had been fairly fine during the night, became damp and hazy, with very bad appearance for the rest of the day.
At seven o'clock, the land was perceived from the tops of the masts from east-north-east to north-north-west, which proved only too well that we were in a gulf as I had always thought from the shallowness of the waters and their progressive decrease when we made course towards the west or towards the east in crossing the width which it forms from one coast to the other.
As the weather had too bad an appearance to think of recognizing the western part of this gulf, I endeavoured to move to the south as much as possible to be in a more advantageous position. The winds in the morning varied from north-west to south-west and were frequently accompanied by squalls and strong gusts.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 34° 42' 31", but uncertain. There was no hour angle. At the same time, we saw from the tops of the masts a land in the south-east by south which we recognized in the evening as the land we had already seen on entering the gulf.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, the wind increasing constantly and accompanied by strong gusts, we wore round and shaped course to the north-west towards the west in order to move away from the coast for greater safety during the night which appeared to be likely to be very trying for us. At two o'clock, the wind increasing constantly and the sea becoming heavier, we had to furl the flying topgallant sail and shortly after the fore topsail. Although we had no canvas left but the foresail, the main topsail with all reefs taken, and the mizzen staysail, the ship in the gusts had as much as she could carry. We continued the north-west by west tack until eight o'clock in the evening when, having 23 fathoms of water, we made it our point of departure for the tacking through the night during which the weather was very bad and the squalls even heavier than those we had had during the day. Several times, we were obliged to furl our main topsail despite the little canvas which remained to it. The tacks were of four hours and we managed to maintain ourselves between 20 and 24 fathoms of water by tacking over a bottom which never exceeded 30 fathoms, decreasing to the west as to the east, once it had been reached.
This night was very trying for the crew and for me, in that we spent it constantly on deck. All the officers except those who changed watches spent it just as calmly in their beds as if the ship had been in the greatest security. As it was not the first time it had happened to them, even in a more critical position than that in which we found ourselves, I was not at all astonished at it and left them quite undisturbed, a course which I have decided to take every time such an occasion presents itself.
The sheet of our small jib and the halyard failed twice during the night, but this sail was only slightly damaged. The squalls which gave us rain were very cold and sometimes the water resembled half-melted snow, which led us to conclude that the winter must not be very pleasant in these climates.
Scholars are however of a contrary opinion because they have seen parakeets in D'Entrecasteaux Channel.
1802-04-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NE. At 1.30 we hove to, and at 3 filled and stood on. At 4 the promontory N 68° E. At 5 shaped our course to double the promontory, hauling to the wind on the port tack. At 8, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 78° E 1 mile off, the 2 islets C S 82°, islet P S 75° E and islet A S 56° E. At 8.55 the white rock bore abeam, true north, 3 cables off. At 9.50 the promontory bore abeam, true north, 1 mile off. We passed among the islets and rocks of the promontory, leaving to port the white rock, the islets C and rock M, and to starboard islet A, islet D, islet P and so on. At noon in 39° 14' 20" of latitude observed and in 144° 58' 0" of longitude by account, the promontory bearing N 63° W, the islets C one N 42° W and the other N 78° W, half a mile off, islet P N 88° W, islet A S 25° E, islet D S 75° E, and an island H N 70° E. At 4 took the bearing of the northernmost end of the mainland in sight N 76° W, the promontory N 76° W, islet P S 85° W and islet D S 16° E. At 4.30, 7° 26' 20" of NE variation. At 5.30 the promontory N 80° W, the middle of island H N 66° E, another island S 68° E. At 8 the wind drew round to the west, freshening; we shaped the course N 56° 15' E. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, a high sea, with rain.

1802-04-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NE to W, SW and NW. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, the weather overcast and squally, a high sea, a great deal of rain. At 6 a.m. land was sighted to windward; at 8 it stretched from N 23° E to N 45° W. The wind still a strong breeze. At noon the land from N 22° W to N 70° E.
1802-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak, the lands of the eastern coast of the gulf were visible to the east-north-east.
At noon, being nearer to the coast, they extended from north 22° east to south 45° east. We thought we perceived an islet at south 12° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, we experienced very little change in the weather. It continued to blow strongly all day. The greater part of the squalls were rainy and in gusts. However, they were less violent than the day before since we could set the fore topsail, the flying topgallant sail and the storm staysail.
As I wished to ascertain with accuracy our distance from the eastern coast of the gulf which I will call so until I have proof to the contrary, we went about at four o'clock in the morning to shape course to the south-east, for the winds were then to the south-south-west and appeared to be setting in that direction.
At daybreak, the land appeared to the lookouts from the tops of the masts in the east-north-east, but it was visible to us only about ten o'clock. We recognized that it was a portion of coast seen the day before.
From four o'clock until half-past eleven, we were on a bottom from 24 to 17 fathoms and we maintained this last for more than three hours without any perceptible decrease. But then we passed from 17 to 10 fathoms, still being three leagues from the land, which made us go about to shape course to the west, always with a heavy sea and strong winds with rain and squalls of short duration, now more and now less violent.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 34° 38' 30". There was no hour angle.
From noon until eight o'clock in the evening, we held the west by south tack, my intention being to close with the western coast of the gulf so as to exit from it the next day by that part if the weather was manageable and the winds favourable. As the squalls had become less frequent, we had for a moment the hope of seeing the weather soon clear and the barometer seemed to announce it, for it rose a little. But after sunset, our hopes vanished. The gusts and the strong squalls recommenced again and did not cease except in small intervals.
The night was in general bad. We always had regular soundings on both tacks which we ran and were almost always between 22 and 24 fathoms, hard and rocky bottom.
From eight o'clock until midnight, we ran the east by south tack and from midnight until daybreak, the west by south tack. The sky was constantly thick, loaded with dark clouds, most often rainy and accompanied by strong gusts. We maintained the same canvas of the day without adding anything to it. The position in which I found myself not making me believe it necessary to strain the ship's masts.
1802-04-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At 6 the land was sighted; at 8 it stretched from N 22° E to N 45° E, and at noon from N 22° W to N 70° E. At noon in 37° 57' 40" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 12" of longitude by account. At 4, Cape Howe N 32° E and the southernmost end of the mainland in sight S 76° E. At 5.30, Cape Howe N 20° E; the land in sight during the night.

1802-04-21.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze from NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Howe N 32° E; the visible end of the land S 76° W. At 4.30 the weather cleared. At noon land in sight from N 45° W to S 61° W. At noon we found the same latitude, the same longitude and the same variation that Cook found. We were also at the same distance from the land and in the same month.
1802-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak, the lands extended from east to south forming a circuit whose middle lay to the south-east. The part comprised between south-east and south appeared to be broken by lands higher than we judged to be the islets which we had seen on entering the gulf.
At half-past five in the evening, the western lands extended from west by north-west to south-west.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the first of Floréal, the weather was hardly better than the preceding days. We had rain, squalls and wind all the morning. Nevertheless, it was less violent than it had been up to that time and the strong squalls which it brought were also less violent and passed sooner than they had been accustomed to do, but on the other hand, they succeeded one another with more rapidity. We found in the morning the sea more heavy with swell than usual, but the wave less large. The sounding always reported a regular bottom on one tack as on the other and the bottom was sometimes (sic) of coarse sand and rocks mixed with coral and madrépores.
At six o'clock, running the west by south tack since midnight, we had knowledge of land ahead of us. To windward and to leeward, it extended from south 50° west to north 5° west. Several of the portions comprised in the interval above appeared to form several islands, which, most likely it may be. But the lands to the north of west were recognized as those of the mainland and consequently that other part of the gulf which we had had little knowledge of, owing to the contrary winds and the bad weather which had prevailed for several days.
At half-past six in the morning, we took the east by south tack not to run too far to leeward of the islets which we thought we had seen in the morning and which are most likely those which lay to the west of us when we entered the gulf by the channel of which I have made mention. We continued this tack until noon, having knowledge of the eastern lands and the islet forming the channel through which we had entered. We thought we recognized from the tops of the masts this islet by its form and elevation. As my intention was to exit the gulf by a different route from that which had led me into it, I resumed the west tack to be more able to profit from the first fine weather which might present itself.
At noon, we saw the sun for a moment and we observed its height to be 34° 40' 27". This latitude, although I suspect it to be uncertain, always appears to me preferable to that of the dead reckoning in a place where the currents are strong and of changing direction.
During the evening, we had for a moment the hope of seeing the weather clear but it was of short duration, for after sunset it became worse than it had been until then. During the night, the squalls were so abundant and so strong that they forced us several times to furl our topsails, although they were at the lowest reef. In any other position than that in which I found myself, I certainly would not have carried them. At six o'clock, the time when we went about, we had the land in sight from west-south-west to north-west, at a distance of three leagues at most, the bottom being 19 fathoms very mixed with sand, coral and rocks. We made two tacks during the night in order to maintain ourselves about the middle of the channel.
1802-04-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather with frequent squalls, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W, a high sea. At noon in 36° 18' 4" of latitude observed and in 148° 48' 42" of longitude by account. At 4, the Pigeon House N 18° W and Mount Dromedary S 54° W. During the night the wind blew hard. At 4.30 p.m., 9° 50' 50" of NE variation.

1802-04-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from SW to W and NW. At 4 a.m. Mount Dromedary bore from us S 54° W, the Pigeon House N 18° W. At 5.30 blowing hard from the west, a high sea. At 3.15 a.m. the wind having fallen a little, set the mizzen topsail. At daybreak the land as far as the eye could see in the west (from aloft); at 5 it stretched from W to N 45° W. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
On the second at seven o'clock in the morning, the eastern lands were visible, although hazy, from south-south-east to east at a distance of four leagues.
The haze did not permit a precise bearing at sunset, only lands were seen at south 5° west and others at south 50° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, holding the east by south tack, we had knowledge about seven o'clock of the same eastern lands which we had seen the day before. But as they lay more to the south than when we had last observed them, we were convinced that we had drifted considerably to the north, which did not make our position better.
The weather continuing always to have bad appearance, without any hope of change, I ordered to take the west by north tack, the winds then being at south-south-west and when we were hauled close-hauled on the port tack, we took a reef in the foresail and in the mainsail which we set again as soon as this operation was completed, so that we made course under our four principal sails with all reefs taken. The ship appeared to handle well under this canvas and made much less leeway than before. The squalls and gusts which we received did not make her heel more than usual, but in truth they were less strong than during the night.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 34° 38' 27" and the timekeeper longitude which we had not been able to have for three days placed us at 134° 6' 26".
From the latitude observation, we found ourselves more to the north than the day before, which confirmed to us that the course or rather the turns before the wind had carried us to the north.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, the winds appearing to be about to shift to the south-west, we took advantage of the interval which there usually was between the squalls to go about on the course to the south towards the east. The ship, despite the heavy sea, made a very good evolution with the canvas she carried, having only taken the precaution of running out the foresail sheet early and choking the forebraces, a manoeuvre which infinitely displeased the learned naval officers who accompanied me and who, no doubt, would have failed in the evolution had they attempted it otherwise. We could see, when we went about, the western lands and the bottom was 23 fathoms. The distance at which I estimated ourselves from them was three and a half to four leagues.
During the evening, the winds became manageable, the squalls less violent and the sea became fine. We augured from this a speedy change in our favour, although the barometer had not yet announced anything to us about it.
At six o'clock in the evening, having run all the evening the east by south tack, we went about to seaward at a distance of two leagues from the eastern coast which we recognized perfectly to be the southern extremity of the gulf in which we had entered. During the night, the sky was fine and the squalls moderate. Those which gave rain or wind were not of long duration and in general the weather was fairly fine and even very fine if one wished to compare it to that which we had experienced for three days.
The sounding during the night was not very different from that which we were accustomed to have, only it was noted that the depth was somewhat greater and the bottom of fine grey sand, whereas it had almost always been unsuitable for anchorage or very bad.
1802-04-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW. At daybreak the land was sighted as far as the eye could reach to the west. At 8.15, 10° 6' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 28' 38" of latitude observed and in 149° 44' 0" of longitude by account. At 5.45, Cape St George S 80° W.

1802-04-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from NW to NNW. At 5 p.m. Cape St George S 82° W. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. Furled the main topgallant sail and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. At noon the land in sight from S 15° W to N 45° W.
1802-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, the winds and the weather became more manageable, we took advantage of it to endeavour to gain ground to the west in order to recognize the lands in that part of the gulf, but we were unable to accomplish this.
At ten o'clock, making course to the west somewhat towards the south, we were forced to go about suddenly to avoid a shallow bank at whose edge we found ourselves in 20 fathoms of water. The lookouts had announced to us long since a tongue of breakers which blocked our passage to the west extending from west-north-west to south-south-west. When we went about, we had good knowledge of this danger from the deck but we were still more than a league distant and the bottom was 28 and 29 fathoms. As the sea was not breaking on the shallow bank which was ahead of this chain of rocks, we had a narrow escape from running aground upon it. Fortunately the ship did not fail to go about and most likely we should have been in great difficulty if the evolution had failed. We also had in sight a great part of the lands forming the opposite part of the eastern coast of the gulf, as well as the five islets and rocks which we had seen on the 26th Germinal, but we had to give up the attempt to find a passage in the channels which they form and some of which appeared to me navigable. The current, the winds and their positions not even allowing us to approach them at a great distance. Although I had already lost four days trying to recognize them, I decided to exit this group of islands by the same channel through which I had entered in order to be in a position to withstand the bad weather if it should occur again.
At noon, we observed the latitude to be 34° 50' 28" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 133° 58' 28".
In the afternoon, the weather appeared to be about to clear. The squalls, the rain and the gusts disappeared entirely and the sky was fairly fine all the evening. The reef which we had encountered in the morning and the shallow bank which is in front of it appeared to us to extend from the mainland to an island about three leagues in extent which lay to the west 22° 30' south of us. All the tacks which we made between the eastern lands of the gulf and this danger could only be of two hours and of two and a half to three leagues at most.
During all the night, we made the same manoeuvre keeping as close as possible to the island forming the channel through which we had entered and through which also I wished to exit the next day. We had very fine weather all night and a moderate breeze. The moonlight allowing us always to have good knowledge of the coast.
All the crew was on watch in order to be more ready for the turns of the tack.
1802-04-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to W. At noon in 35° 11' 26" of latitude observed and in 148° 41' 42" of longitude by account. The land from N 34° W to S 45° W. At 8 a.m., 10° 40' 10" of NE variation. At 3.15 we had a heavy squall from the west. During the night squally weather, the wind a strong breeze. The land has been in sight throughout.

1802-04-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; went about onto the starboard tack. A strong breeze from SW to W and SSW. At 4.30 the middle of the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W. At 5 p.m. we heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we supposed it was in honour of St George's day. At 7.30 p.m. the weather turned overcast and the wind blew hard; we stayed under our courses. At 6.30 hove to and put the large boat in the water; Mr Milius was about to embark in her to go up to Port Jackson, but rain came on and the boat was veered astern. At 8 a.m., having seen a boat standing towards us, we hove to; the pilot came aboard and we at once beat to windward. At 11.45, under North Head, having missed stays, we wore ship; in this last movement our large boat, which was in tow, capsized and the painter parted. Our small boat, together with the English boat, was sent to save the boat's crew and to take the swamped boat in tow to carry her ashore.
1802-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, in the morning, having spent all the night tacking, we found ourselves positively at the opening of the channel through which we had entered the gulf. As a fair breeze then blew from south-south-east shifting to south-east, we took advantage of it to exit the group of islands and rocks by which we had been surrounded for several days. We passed at a small distance from the island which lay to leeward of us and whose eastern and southern extremity is much higher than its northern and western extremity. As I have already spoken of this island and its form and as I give a view of it and of the two rocks at its southern part, I will not enlarge further on this subject.
When we had doubled it, we endeavoured to close with the western coast of the great island of Kangaroo Island which we were beginning to have knowledge of, but the wind having failed us, we made little progress.
We took in the morning new bearings of the islands and islets which are found on this part of the coast which offered us no anchorage while we were engaged in recognizing it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 35° 23' 40" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 133° 49' 31".
During the evening, the breeze was very light and the sky fine although the horizon was not very extensive. We hauled up our lower yards and loosened all the reefs in our sails, convinced that the weather was about to clear. In the case that it should become bad, we were at least in a position to fear nothing and very different from that in which we were during the three days of bad weather which we had just passed.
At sunset, we furled our mainsail and at eight o'clock, we changed our tack and shaped course close-hauled starboard tack until midnight, when we took the south by east tack until daybreak.
During the night, the sky was fine and the breeze moderate. We also found the sea fine, being not far distant from Kangaroo Island whose extremities in sight after sunset lay to us from south 40° east to south 83° east. The lands, or to be more precise, the islands which lay to the north towards the west, lay to us from north-west to west-south-west.
We had during the two tacks which we made during the night, soundings of 50, 60 and 78 fathoms.
1802-04-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 11 we showed our colours and the flag of truce. At noon in 33° 47' 23" of latitude observed and in 148° 50' 36" of longitude by account. Signals were seen on the south point of the entrance to Port Jackson, which bore from us S 65° W to S 68° W, and the land from N 26° W to S 56° W. At 4 the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W, and at 5.30 N 62° W. We heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we thought it was in honour of King George's birthday. At nightfall a fire was lit at the entrance to Port Jackson; at 6 it bore from us S 59° W, at 8 S 54° W, at 10 S 85° W, at midnight N 79° W. During the night the wind blew hard, the weather overcast, with rain and thunder.

1802-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, having in sight a small archipelago of islands and islets, the first was observed at north 23° west, the 2nd at north 12° west, the 3rd at north 17° east, two rocks dependent on them at north 18° 15' east, the 4th at north 78° east, the 5th at east 7° south and the 6th at east 7° south.
At sunset, other islands were seen whose extremities extended from west by north-west to north-west by north.
Those passed during the day, being one beyond the other, their northernmost extremity was observed at north 6° west, 18 miles distance, and the easternmost part at east, 25 miles.
(In the margin: Two small islands near the coast were visible to the north-west, and the one furthest offshore at north 10° west.)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, we made course to the north taking somewhat to the west to close with the lands which lay ahead in that direction in order to recognize them, renouncing, on account of the advanced season and the direction of the wind, to visit the southern part of the great island of Kangaroo Island whose lands in sight lay to us from north 60° east to south 66° east.
Although the sky did not have a fine appearance in the morning, we nevertheless had fine weather and a fair breeze from east-south-east shifting to east-north-east, but we found the sea somewhat heavy with swell and fairly agitated, a cause which we attributed to the speed of the currents which appeared to us to be opposed to the direction of the wind.
During the morning, we had knowledge of the five islands to the east of the channel through which we had entered the gulf and of which we had visited the northern part. Three of these islands are surrounded by reefs in their southern part and the sea broke heavily at a considerable distance from the shore. All are barren and sterile, having no appearance of vegetation, and one can hardly consider them as anything but rocks placed at a certain distance from the mainland, of which one perceives the lands at a distance. We passed at a small distance from this group of islands and islets whose position can be well determined by all the various bearings which were taken of them. All different in their extent, although the largest did not appear to me to have more than two leagues in extent from east to west.
At noon, we observed the latitude to be 35° 19' 3" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 133° 20' 34".
During the evening, the weather continued fine and the breeze held. We coasted sometimes the mainland and sometimes islands which are at a small distance from it. I do not know if one would find a good passage between these islands and the mainland, but the channels which they form either between themselves or with the mainland did not appear to me to have opening enough to enter into, and especially not in the season we are in. These latter islands are more extensive than those passed in the morning and almost all have at their extremity reefs which extend quite far to seaward. That especially which we doubled at sunset has one on which the sea broke extraordinarily and we had knowledge of it more than two leagues away. To double it, we were obliged to steer for some time to the west-south-west, making progress to the north-west.
At sunset, we saw several lands still having the appearance of islands although I believe they are not. The westernmost land in sight lay to us west by south-west, forming a great indentation to the north-north-west in which no land was visible. We deferred to the next day to recognize what it could be and at six o'clock, we took the south tack to tack through the night.
1802-04-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SSE. At 6.15 we hove to and put the large boat in the water. Citizen Milius and I were to embark in her to go to Sydney and inform the English governor of our arrival and the object of our voyage; but the weather appeared so bad to Citizen Milius that the boat was veered astern. At 8, having sighted a boat standing towards us, we hove to to wait for her. At 8.15 she came aboard and brought us an English pilot; he at once made sail to gain the port. At 9 a swivel gun was fired to confirm our colours. At 11.45, under North Head, we missed stays and wore ship. In this last movement the large boat (which was in tow and under sail) capsized and her tow rope parted. The pilot's boat and our small boat at once went to save the boat's crew and to take the boat in tow and beach her. At 3.30 we anchored at the entrance to the port in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, North Head bearing N 67° E, South Head S 52° E, Camp Cove S 16° E, Bradleys Head S 36° W and Middle Head N 65° W. At 4.45 Citizen Milius and I left in the Géographe's boat for Sydney. Squally and very overcast weather, with pouring rain, the wind from WSW to SW.

1802-04-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SW to SSE. At 1.45, the wind having drawn aft, we bore away for the entrance to the port and shortened sail by degrees. At 3.30, having doubled South Head very close, we let go the anchor at the mouth of the channel in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, and veered 60 fathoms of cable, South Head bearing S 52° E; Camp Cove S 16° E; Bradleys Head S 36° W; Georges Head S 48° W; Middle Head N 65° W; North Head N 67° E by compass. As soon as the sails were furled, the Géographe's large boat was put in the water and left for Sydney Town; the wind a strong breeze, squally weather and rain. At anchor at the entrance to Port Jackson.
1802-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, in the morning, we found ourselves about at the same place where we had ended the reconnaissance of the coast visited on the fifth. But we recognized that all the land summits of which we had had knowledge the evening before at sunset were only a small archipelago of islets and rocks more or less large. As they appeared to have navigable channels, especially with the winds we had, I decided to pass between them and the mainland and we were fortunate enough to have chosen by chance the best passage. For we saw in passing the one to which I gave preference over the others, several reefs which seem to indicate they are not convenient.
As I give a detailed view of these rocks and islets, it will be easy to recognize the channel which should be taken in preference to the others. All these islets and rocks are entirely deprived of vegetation, or at least, one sees there only some dried bushes. But the waters there are deep and we never had less than twenty-four fathoms in the channel in which we entered.
The mainland, as will be seen in the views which have been made of it, is hardly more pleasant in appearance than the islands. The edge of the coast is, like everywhere else, cut sheer at the sea and a reef guards the approach to the shore which is formed only of a heap of rocks piled up one upon the other in several places. And sand dunes without verdure extending as far as the view can penetrate into the interior of lands which are sometimes high and sometimes low, but in general of good height. One also sees in the interior of the country several high mountains whose chain is not very extensive.
At noon, we found ourselves by our position to have the sun on the land to the north as well as to the south, which prevented us from observing its passage at the meridian. We were then almost in calm, but the breeze from south to south-west having come in, we exited this archipelago where it would not have been convenient to pass the night with contrary winds.
During the evening, we doubled a point of the mainland at the end of which the land takes a sudden direction to the north-north-east about three leagues and in the form of a very deep bay which we visited as much as the wind could permit, the winds being then from east to east-south-east. As this bay is found between a chain of mountains, I thought to find good shelter there for the night, but the winds did not permit us to reach its greatest indentation. Besides, it offers nothing particular, the edges of the shore are only barren sands and the mountains which form its extremities are only enormous masses of rocks piled one upon the other. What appeared most remarkable in this place was the direction of an isolated mountain extending from east to west while all the others were from south-east to north-west.
At sunset, we took the offshore tack, having perceived nothing to the west which could give us concern during the night. As we had land on all sides, I moved away a little from the mainland and passed the night hove-to making alternate tacks.
1802-04-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW. A meal of provisions was sent to the crews of the large and small boats by a fishing boat. The governor sent vegetables. I came back aboard with an English officer to invite the captain to dine with Colonel Paterson, the lieutenant-governor (Governor King was at Parramatta); he excused himself on account of the bad weather, and I went back to Sydney with the officer. The topgallant masts were got down. An orderly brought the captain a letter announcing the governor's arrival at Sydney. At nightfall a small fishing boat brought Citizen Moreau, who had been in the small boat. He had been obliged to have the small boat in which he came carried by hand from the beach where the boats lay to the inside of the harbour. He asked the captain to send provisions to the boats' crews, who were without; and this contemptible man, who counts every mouthful of his crew's food and would feed them on grass if he could, ordered that only one meal be sent them, saying that if more were sent the rogues would not come back aboard and would rather stay ashore idling. Citizen Moreau observed to him that it was impossible for the boats to come back with him in them, that they had tried several times to return aboard and had always been forced to put back on account of the sea and the wind; that the wretched boats' crews, who had had only one meal since the morning before, would have died of hunger had not one of the English boatmen lent him money to buy them a little fish; that they were soaked and had neither shelter nor a change of clothes; that one of them was injured; and that they would therefore be better aboard if they could get there. None of these truths made any impression on this hard and barbarous man: only one meal of provisions was sent to the boats' crews.

1802-04-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the winds a strong breeze from south to SSW. Almost continual rain. At 3 a [boat] came aboard to invite the captain, on Colonel Paterson's behalf, to dine with him; but the bad weather prevented him from accepting the invitation. The topgallant masts were struck and the topmasts got down. An orderly brought packets to the captain to announce the governor's arrival at Sydney Town (he was in the country when we arrived at Port Jackson). A fishing boat brought me back on board.
1802-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, we found ourselves much to leeward of the land observed and recognized the evening before. I attributed the cause to the currents which had carried us to the north-west, for the little progress which we made during the night should have been compensated since we must have drifted as much on one tack as on the other, according to the regular hours at which we changed tacks.
But, be that as it may, as soon as it was daybreak, we hauled close-hauled by a light breeze from the east which only lasted until about ten o'clock in the morning, when it was replaced by a calm which prevented us from having as good a day as I had hoped for.
During the morning, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us that we had on our port several islands and islets to leeward and they counted as many as nine. We had knowledge of three from the deck before noon, but we did not see the others. The weather was very fine during the morning and we succeeded, despite the weakness of the wind, in closing with the coast at a distance of two leagues. The lands in this part are not uniform, neither in elevation nor in appearance, but all terminate sheer at the sea and the waters there are deep. We had 40 fathoms at a league and a half's distance. There are found in this area two or three fairly deep bays and the shore which terminates them in their indentation is very low and deprived of vegetation.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 55' 20" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 132° 15' 17".
From noon until two o'clock, we were in a dead calm and the ship held her course with difficulty. But then a light breeze came to us from the south-west, shifting to the south, with which we approached to a league's distance from the coast which we then coasted until sunset. Its direction was from north towards the west, which led us to believe that we would not be long in having knowledge of the islands of St Francis and St Peter. Perhaps all those which we have passed in the last two days are part of this archipelago. The four or five leagues of coast which we made in the afternoon are of good height but of a very particular appearance. The edge of the shore is formed of a long succession of cliffs cut sheer where the rock appears bare and of yellow colour when lit by the sun, and of a very dark brown in the parts not facing it. The interior of the country appears as barren as the edges of the sea. However, we saw a fire at a considerable distance from the coast.
At sunset, we had knowledge of all the islands which the lookouts had announced to us in the morning, several were of a very particular form as will be seen in the drawing which I give of them.
We also perceived ahead of us two larger islands than those which lay to leeward and which appeared to offer a good channel between them and the mainland. As night was falling and it was not prudent to engage further than we were, we hauled port tack to tack during the night. But about seven o'clock, the wind (Written vertically in the left margin) being almost calm with little hope of having wind during the night, I decided to anchor a bower in 33 fathoms, the bottom being very fine sand, without any mixture of coral or madrépores. We had not often encountered such a bottom. By this means we passed the night tranquilly during which the weather was fine and the breeze moderate.
1802-04-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south, with continual rain. The longboat was put in the water. Citizen Milius and I came back aboard. A warp was run out.

1802-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south to SSW and SW, continual rain. At 3 our boat left for Sydney Town. We ran out a warp and hove round on the cable, but the wind having freshened we left off the work with 45 fathoms of cable out. At 5 a.m. weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser; being at long stay we let go the bower anchor. The captain embarked in his boat with the officers and scientists to go and pay a visit to the governor. At 11.30 our large and small boats came aboard undamaged; only a seaman named Happeday had his shoulder crushed in the wreck of the large boat.
1802-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, at first light, we weighed with winds from the north towards the west, which obliged us to spend the day, or at least a great part of it, tacking in the channel which exists between the mainland and the islands near which we had anchored. As it was dark when we anchored, we had knowledge only of the nearest islet and which is also the highest. Its middle lay at west 22° north of us.
At sunrise, we recognized the islands which surrounded us and which were five in number, more or less distant from one another, but all had a barren aspect and seem to offer neither shelter nor resources to navigators who may frequent these waters.
Among these five islands, there is one which is very flat and fairly long, forming a fairly deep bay terminated by a sandy beach. But I do not know if the channels which separate it from the others are navigable, as I did not penetrate into them. As for that which is between the mainland and these islands, it is about four leagues wide and the water is deep, we finding never less than 28 fathoms and that was only for a moment, for we generally had between 33 and 30.
During the morning, Citizen Freycinet came to observe to me that as most of our helmsmen were sick and unable to perform their duty, it was absolutely necessary to choose from the rest of the crew men who could replace them. He added that to remedy this inconvenience, he asked to be authorized to have the master carpenter and the second caulker steer. I observed to him that in such circumstances, it was less orders that were needed than a simple request made with good grace, since the two men had a profession so opposed to that for which he wished to employ them. My reply, no doubt, was not agreeable to him, for he replied that such a step towards people as inferior to him could not be made by an officer like him, et cetera, et cetera.
I then decided to give a written order which would be entered on the slate which the officers keep so that all the aspirants, both first and second class, should perform during their watch an hour and a half, which was certainly not hard work for them and could only contribute to their instruction. However, it resulted in an effect quite contrary to what I had expected, for all these gentlemen regarded it as a disgrace and schemed to be excused from it. Mr. Bougainville, who was the senior, flatly refused to go and used the pretext that he was ill to cover his disobedience. Mr. Brun claimed that by the regulations he was exempt of right. The aspirant Baudin was the only one who showed good will, which brought him much raillery from his comrades. All expected that I would punish them differently, but they were quite mistaken, and I merely forbade them all manner of duty on board, telling them that I would get along without them for steering just as well as I had done without them for other things.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 47' 35" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 132° 10' 54".
(Written vertically in the left margin) We had in sight the five islands of the morning and the top of some rocks seen the day before. In the afternoon, the winds having suddenly calmed, came to us from the north-west. We endeavoured to close with the mainland, but at night, having made little progress, we could not well distinguish the outlines which it appeared to have. We recognized only an island and a rock far offshore which we passed during the night while keeping close to the island opposite which we had anchored the day before.
1802-04-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The governor sent us vegetables. At 7 the captain, accompanied by the officers and naturalists, went to pay a visit to the governor; they were back at 2. At 11.30 a.m. our two boats came in. Only one man, Happedey, had a dislocated shoulder. From 5 a.m. until 4 p.m. we warped.

1802-04-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW, SW and WSW, with light rain until 4. At 1 weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser. At 2 the captain and all those with him came back from Sydney Town. At 4 weighed the kedge anchor and let go the bower, which proved to be foul, and hove round on the hawser. When we were at long stay on the hawser we ran out a warp and catted the bower anchor. At 9.15 weighed the kedge anchor, on which we were up and down, and hove round on the warp. A sloop bound for Tahiti sailed from Port Jackson.
1802-04-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, having made some progress to the north and to the west during the night without losing sight of the land, we continued to coast it and to take its bearings which could fix its position. The sky, although misty during the morning, was fairly fine, but the winds were not favourable to us, being variable from north-north-north-east (sic) to north-north-west.
The lands which we had in sight were, for the most part, of good height and divided by others more low. But all offered only a sad and disagreeable appearance, being for the most part barren and without vegetation, or at least, having no sort of verdure then, which led us to believe that in the fine season they might be different from what we saw them.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 36' 54" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 131° 10' 57". If we suppose it correct, there remained nothing for us but to advance to the north to have knowledge of the islands of St Peter and St Francis, but the wind did not permit us.
After the observation of the sun, we went about to avoid moving away from the coast. The winds, moreover, which shifted while calming to the north towards the west, drew us a little nearer to it, although during the rest of the day they were weak and very inconstant.
Before sunset, the sky became covered with clouds and had very bad appearance. The movement of the barometer seemed also to announce some squalls to us, for it was falling very rapidly and was no more than 28 inches 2 lines, whereas it had stood at 28 inches 6 lines the day before. The hygrometer followed much the same course.
The winds from the north, whether towards the east or towards the west, were warm and kept the thermometer much higher than when we had them from the south, either by the east or by the west.
During the night, the winds, after having gone around several points of the compass, shifted to the south and finally fixed at south-east. The breeze was very light until midnight, when it began to freshen. We made course to the north to close with the coast from which we found ourselves then fairly distant, taking care to sound every hour. The bottom which it reported was never below 35 fathoms nor above 46 which was that from which we had departed at eight o'clock in the evening. Besides, the night had nothing particular, we occasionally had light rain of short duration and the sky, although dark and heavily laden in the south-west, did not give for this moment the bad weather which I expected and which I believe will not fail to occur at the renewal of the moon.
1802-04-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. We warped from 4 a.m. until 9.30. The Nautilus, a private vessel fitted out as a letter of marque and bound for Tahiti, left the port. At noon Captain Scott of the sloop Porpoise came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the sloop Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern. We saluted her with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". The governor and the civil and military officers of Sydney came aboard, where they stayed until 2. The captain, the officers and the naturalists went to Sydney to the dinner given by the governor. We warped as soon as they had left. At 3.15, being under Bradleys Point, we got under way with a light breeze from NNW. At 5 we anchored in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and at once moored NNW and SSE with a kedge anchor, in Neutral Bay, near Rock Island.

1802-04-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm at noon. Captain Scott, commanding the sloop Porpoise, came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the brig Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern; he was greeted with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". He came aboard at once with the civil and military officers of Sydney Town. He left at 2 and was followed by the captain and his officers. At 2.30 ran out a warp; the kedge anchor was weighed at once and, the tide carrying us in, towed by the longboat and the large boat, a light air came on and we set our fore-and-aft sails. At 5 we let go the anchor in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and veered 40 fathoms of cable. The longboat carried out a kedge anchor and we moored NNW and SSE with 90 fathoms of cable out.
1802-04-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(No mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, having closed with the mainland during the night, we lay-to under the topsails from five o'clock until day was sufficiently advanced to recognize the coast and our position. The noise made by the surf on the shore announced to us that we were not very far from it, although the sounding showed 35 fathoms.
At sunrise, we found ourselves abreast of a fairly deep indentation. However, one could perfectly distinguish the lands which are of moderate elevation, but the points which form its extremities are infinitely higher both to the north and to the south.
From the one which forms the northern entrance of this bay, runs a reef which is very extensive in the direction of the south-east and on which the sea breaks heavily. Although it appeared to us to close the passage of the entrance to this indentation, it is possible it may be navigable. The winds which were then from east to east-north-east did not permit us to ascertain. We passed at a good league's distance from the reef of which I have spoken, having found not less than 35 fathoms.
At seven o'clock, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us an island to leeward which we soon perceived from the deck. It appeared to us to be of good height and to offer an easy channel between it and the mainland coast. We saw in its southern part a fairly extensive reef on which the sea rose to a great height. As it appeared far offshore, it was judged that it did not belong to this island.
During the morning, the winds were very light and variable. As they shifted to the north-east, we lost the hope of entering the channel which this island forms with the mainland. We found the sea very heavy with swell and a long swell from the south-south-west which led us to believe that we no longer had land in that quarter of the horizon.
At noon, we had no latitude from observation, the sky being dark and overcast. That of the dead reckoning placed us at 32° 51' 36".
After doubling the small island of which I have spoken above and the reefs which are at its two extremities, we approached the mainland which is here very low. It appears to me that if we had passed in the channel which the island forms with the advanced point opposite to it, it would not have been easy to pass between it and the mainland, so close it appeared to us to be to it. The mainland is so low in this part of the coast that one can hardly see it two leagues from the deck and we had knowledge long before of several fires which rose from different parts, without the lookouts from the tops of the masts having any view of the coast.
A little before sunset, we were much surprised to see that we still had lands to leeward extending even to the south-west by west. For we did not expect, from our estimated latitude and our position on the chart, to see them extend as far to the south as they did. The barometer being no more than 28 inches and believing the bad weather about to make itself felt, I lay-to for the night in order not to involve myself among unknown lands or islands, should it come on. During the night, the sky was very dark and the breeze light until about three o'clock, but then it increased gradually and became fresh without squalls. We sounded regularly every hour and we had constantly from 35 to 38 fathoms of water.
(Written vertically in the left margin)
1802-04-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At 2.30 a.m. the captain, the officers and the naturalists came aboard. The mainsail and main topsail, which needed repair, were unbent. The longboat made one trip for water. A large English three-master came in, loaded with whale oil.

1802-05-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm; hoisted in our large boat. At 4 a three-master came into the port from the whale fishery. The longboat went watering.
1802-05-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
($$ continued from page 127) even closer than we had done while standing back to the north. At six o'clock, the rock of which I have spoken, and the island, the westernmost, showed themselves again, and we made of them our point of departure for the course to be kept during the night. The number of islands in this group is far more considerable than the charts indicate, and as I intend to go round them on their western sides, I hope I shall be able to determine it.
During the night, the winds were very unsteady and the breeze moderate. We kept the course from the west toward the south as far as the winds allowed, the bottom being regular from 35 to 43 fathoms.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, a little before daybreak, being hove to in 37 fathoms of water, we suddenly passed to 30, and this within the space of half an hour. This unexpected change surprised us all the more in that during the night the bottom had been very regular, increasing fathom by fathom only at intervals of time fixed by the clock. Half an hour later, having found forty fathoms, we continued hove to until daylight. At that time, we got sight of the land to windward of us at about four leagues' distance. It presented itself in the form of a small island of little extent, but I remained persuaded that it was a point of the mainland, and the same that had been sighted the evening before to the south-west and south-west by west.
Be that as it may, the winds being at north-north-east, variable to the north, a strong breeze, we made our course on the starboard tack, hauling as close to the wind as we possibly could, but we could not close with the land near enough to see those of the evening before, which are, as I have observed, very low. As we rounded those we had in sight, the lookouts reported another to us, further to the north, which likewise seemed to them to be an island, seeing nothing in the recess of its direction relative to that which we were leaving. Only, they could make out a reef which appeared to be in the middle of these two lands. The winds not allowing us to go and reconnoitre anything, for the moment, as to what this stretch might be, we continued the board from west toward north until ten o'clock, when the winds having shifted to north-north-west, we took that of north-east.
Throughout the whole morning, the sky was dark and overcast, the breeze fresh and the sea somewhat rough. The long swell from south-south-west to south-west that we had encountered the evening before had almost entirely disappeared.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 32° 47' 16". There was no hour angle for the longitude of the timekeeper. At the moment of the observation, the land bore from us from west 76° 15' north to north 3° 45' east. Another was also seen further to the west, in the form of an islet, and in the interval separating these two lands, several rocks awash, on which the sea broke heavily, seemed to indicate that the channel they form between the land and themselves is not convenient. As we were then keeping the board from north toward east, with a pleasant breeze from the north-west, we soon closed with the land we had had in sight since morning, which, by its difference from that seen the evening before, appeared to me not to form part of the mainland. This conjecture was soon verified, for as we advanced to the north, it was recognised that this could only be the beginning of the group of islands and islets known by the name of St Francis. Following them along their eastern parts, we counted eleven in sight, including from the one that appeared to us the westernmost to the one that could be seen furthest to the north. We entered the channel which separates this group of islands from those named St Peter, of which we likewise got sight, but too far to the east to be well made out. The St Francis islands are generally of little extent. The largest of those we saw during the evening is no more than three leagues from north to south, and the others much less. All are barren, devoid of vegetation, and seem to offer navigators no resources whatsoever. Most of the channels which
($$ in the left margin, perpendicular) separate them from one another are obstructed with reefs which must make the passage difficult, supposing them to be practicable at all. Only two seemed to us to offer a good one, and I would have attempted it had the wind not been contrary to us. As we ran along seven of these islands at a short distance, it was easy for us to judge them well. At three o'clock, being unable to round the one that lay ahead of us, we went about and retraced our steps, coasting along them ($$ see the end, page 126)
1802-05-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The sick were sent to the hospital at Sydney. The longboat made two trips for water. A notice was read to the crew by which Captain Hamelin warns the inhabitants of the colony that he will not be answerable for debts contracted by his crew. During the night the wind a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The establishment of the port at Sydney Cove is 8 o'clock; the tide rises there 7 feet 6 English inches.

1802-05-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm. The longboat went for water and wood; the sick were carried to the hospital; the cables were got out of the hold to come at the bar iron. During our stay at Port Jackson we watered, fresh provisions were embarked and we got wood. On the 13th [Floréal, Year 10, 3 May 1802] tents were set up ashore for the observatory. A Frenchman authorised by the governor was shipped aboard and came on board. At 5.30 p.m. on the 19th [Floréal, Year 10, 9 May 1802] the ship Investigator came into the port, having left England 10 months before and coming from the SW coast, where she had met the Géographe in 35° 41' south and 126° 49' east longitude. On the 20th [Floréal, Year 10, 10 May 1802] at 5 an English longboat brought us an anchor. At 7 a.m. on the 21st [Floréal, Year 10, 11 May 1802] an English ship brought the news of the preliminaries of peace. The winds were constantly from WNW to WSW and sometimes from the east. We embarked as provisions [one word illegible], potatoes, [one word illegible] and wheat [two words illegible]. At 7 we made ready to get under way. At 10.15 we were under sail.
1802-05-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we made our course to the north to close with the group of the St Francis islands, which it was my intention to go round on its western side in order to reconnoitre the mainland coast from the point at which General d'Entrecasteaux had stopped. But about eight o'clock, the lookouts having reported land to us in the west, we saw shortly after, and not without astonishment, that it was the same land we had left the evening before, and from which we found ourselves more than six leagues to leeward, whereas the course that had been kept during the night ought, if not to have set us to the east of it, at least not to have carried us as far from it as we found ourselves.
It does not seem doubtful that we experienced, during the previous night, a strong current which carried us to the east much more than we could have supposed.
Throughout the whole morning, we made our course to the north to explore the lands we had ahead of us, and which were not known to us. These are, no doubt, the two islands which the depot chart mentions and which it places to the east of the St Francis islands. These two islands, which we approached very closely, are indeed shown on this chart, but their latitude did not appear correct to us. For at the moment when we observed the passage of the sun over the meridian, the ship's latitude being 32° 31' 3", we were not more than a league distant from the southernmost, which is placed at 32° on the chart. The longitude of the timekeeper, reduced to the same time, placed us at 130° 58' 14". A similar error had appeared to us the evening before as to the placement of the southernmost of the St Francis islands.
At noon, being unable to round the north point of the island off which we found ourselves, we went about. It then bore from us N. by NE, and the second island was at NE by N. The channel which separates them from one another is of little extent, and I do not know whether the passage through it is easy. Throughout the whole day, we were surprised to find the sea very rough and as agitated as if the weather had been bad. Although there was little wind, and the long swell we found came to us directly from under the lee of the lands which bore from us from south-west by west to north, we could attribute the cause of it only to the strength of the currents. The two islands of which I have just spoken are of good height and just as barren and sterile as those seen previously, so no one will be astonished that they were given the name of two saints who had taken vows of poverty.
I greatly regretted not being able to enter the channel formed by these two islands with the group of the St Francis islands, in order to gain knowledge of the mainland in that part. At two o'clock, we wanted to try to work into it by going about, wind (ahead), but the sea was so rough that we could not manage it. Although there was a pleasant breeze blowing at that time, we could never keep the ship close-hauled, although the helm was always kept to leeward. I decided, then, to continue the board to the south-west so as to gain to windward of the islands, the west winds and the currents leaving me no hope of penetrating into their channels from the east. During the night, the winds were very variable from north-west to west-south-west, where they settled. We had rain at times and a great deal of dampness, the sounding was carried between 38 and 42 fathoms.
1802-05-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The longboat made one trip for water. An observatory was set up on Green Point.

1802-05-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, having made our course all night from south toward west as far as the winds would allow us, we again got sight of the St Francis islands, the southernmost of which in view bore north-north-east, but they could only be seen from the mast-heads. As my intention was, as I have already stated, to go round these islands by the west, the winds not allowing me to attempt it by the east, we steered a (little) more to the west of north than to the north. We had, throughout the whole morning, an extraordinarily strong and high swell, which led us to believe either that it had blown very hard from that quarter of the south-west, or that we should shortly have some squalls from that point of the horizon. However, as the barometer, which in the days past had fallen as low as 27 inches 5 lines, was beginning to rise again, and as we had it, this day, at 27 8, we hoped to get off with only the fright, the sky, moreover, being tolerably fine.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 1' 39", and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 130° 40' 19". This latitude placed us further south than I had expected. We made our course north-north-west until eight o'clock in the evening.
Citizen Chle Baudin was made this day Midshipman of the first class, and I addressed to him the following letters:
"It is with great pleasure, citizen, that I have seen you, since our departure from Timor, exercise yourself in "all the tasks which can form a good officer of the Navy, and without practical knowledge of which one "does not deserve to be one.
"I hope that, in making you Midshipman of the first class, by virtue of the powers granted to me for that "purpose by the Government, you will continue to deserve, by modest, industrious and active conduct, "the advancement which it allows me to give to those who conduct themselves well. And that far from "believing, as your comrades think, that this is an exemption from personal duty and particular "instruction, you will make yourself useful on board in whatever manner it may be, and that I shall judge "fit or proper to employ you." Signed N. B.
To this letter I added the following:
"You will find enclosed with this letter, citizen, that which appoints you Midshipman of the first class, "a rank which I did not think I ought to grant you at Timor, but which your conduct, since our departure "from that port of call, now causes you to obtain. You must not doubt how agreeable it is to me to be able "to advance you, and you must be persuaded that the pleasure I feel in doing so is equal to the pain I feel "at having done so for those who have abused it. I invite you, then, always to conduct yourself in an "exemplary manner and to take no account of the indiscreet and thoughtless remarks which your comrades "have made or may still make. Think of yourself alone and deserve advancement. Reflect on the "satisfaction which your family will feel at it, and those who solicited your embarkation on this "expedition. You and Citizen Bonnefoy will probably be the only Midshipmen who will not have "disappointed the Government's expectations, so let that be one more motive for the conduct you have "to keep up until the end of the campaign. The likeness of your name to mine makes me speak to you as "if you were my son, but be well convinced that this consideration, were it to exist, could not lead me "to grant you what I should believe you had not deserved. Your advancement "depends, then, on you alone, and if, being Midshipman of the
(in the left margin, perpendicular) "first class, you were to go, like so many others, to "persuade yourself that there remains nothing more for you to learn, you would in that case cause me, "not only to repent of what I had done for you, but also to ask the Government that the rank "you obtain and that which awaits you be regarded as undeserved." Signed N. B.
1802-05-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to SW. The mainsail was bent and the turns of the cables taken off. We sent for 124 lb of bread from Mr Palmer's house. The longboat made two trips for water.

1802-05-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, at daybreak, the flat calm which had prevailed during the night having made us fall a good deal to leeward of the St Francis islands, which we had been fairly close to the evening before at sunset, we sought to close with them again by standing to the north as far as the winds allowed us. But, although they had shifted from north toward east, from eight o'clock in the morning, the breeze was so faint that we saw them only at a very great distance. We had, nevertheless, a perfect view of the rocks and breakers and breakers (sic) to the east west of these islands, as well as of the one which is found the most distant in that quarter, and of which I have already spoken in making mention of the others. During the morning, we had the same bottom as the previous night, at 40 fathoms, but at noon we found none at 50 fathoms.
At the same time, the latitude was observed to be 32° 46' 12", and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 130° 21' 8". The lands in sight of the group of the St Francis islands then bore from us north 23° 45' east, and the island which is found furthest to the west, shown on the chart, bore due north. The reef which lies about halfway across the channel could no longer be seen, nor the one which is found furthest to the south of the group.
The heavy swell we had had the previous day began to be less trying for us, and the sky having turned fine, we hoped that the fine weather was about to return, although the rise of the barometer was not so prompt as the state of the atmosphere seemed to foretell.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to north-east and even further to the east, we made our course to the north to draw nearer to the mainland coast, in order to go round the islands by their western parts, but we advanced little, owing to the weakness of the wind. At eight o'clock, the sounding giving a bottom of 38 fathoms and the wind being very faint, we hove to and thus passed the night, during which the winds were very variable and unsteady. There were at times squalls which gave us more rain than wind. The sea, although disturbed by a very heavy swell from the south-west, did not forebode bad weather and seemed rather to be the aftermath of a gale that had passed than the herald of an approaching squall
1802-05-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to W. Sent for bread. The cables that had been got out of the hold were found gnawed by rats in several places.

1802-05-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, judging myself sufficiently to the west to round the St Francis islands conveniently, we took our course, crowding sail, to close with the mainland in that quarter, in order afterwards to go round the islands, returning toward the east, persuaded that I should find, in the channels which separate them from the mainland, some good passages.
At eight o'clock, we got sight of the land to the north, and at ten o'clock we found ourselves in a deep bay, the two extremities of which could be seen from the west to the south-east, passing through the north.
We stood into the recess which lay directly ahead of us, hauling close to the wind and with a rather fresh breeze. In entering this great bight, we had no sight of the islands which lay to leeward of us.
I was astonished to find this part of the mainland much further south than the chart of General d'Entrecasteaux's voyage indicates, for when we went about, the estimated latitude was only 32° 12' 28", and our distance from the coast three leagues. There then lay before us a small islet of little consequence for its extent, and on which the sea broke heavily.
At ten o'clock, being fairly close to the coast, we went about, wind ahead, to come and get sight of the entrance of this bight at its western part. And during the manoeuvre, there suddenly fell upon us a squall so strong that our topmasts were for a moment endangered. After having brought the wind into the sails, we were obliged to take in our topsails and the fore topgallant sail, so violent was the wind. But as we were in a recess and it came to us over the land, the sea was smooth. I persuaded myself at first that this very strong squall would only be momentary, all the more as the sky was fine, but as we opened up the western point of this bight, we found the sea so rough and agitated that there could be no doubt it came from afar, and that, in all likelihood, we were going to weather some squalls. The barometer, on the other hand, had fallen to 28 inches.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 32° 21' 57". There was no hour angle.
In the afternoon, making our course to the south toward the west to stand off the islands, from which we could not have been far, the wind did nothing but increase, and ended by becoming so violent that, had I not been obliged to make way to raise ourselves from the coast, I should have lain to. Although we had for sail only the foresail and the mainsail, the ship was fatigued by it, and often gave a very heavy lurch.
At four o'clock, we got sight of the westernmost island of the St Francis group. We did not pass it at more than a league and a half distance. The sea broke in a frightful manner the whole length of the coast. The other islands were not long in showing themselves. We carried as much sail as possible to bring ourselves to the south. The heavy sea, the wind, the leeway and the ship's sail were not favourable to the course that had to be made, yet we rounded them during the night, never having less than 43 to 45 fathoms of water, fine sand.
As I feared a shift of wind more than the land, I spent the whole night on deck, none of the officers who are on board knowing what it is to
(in the left margin, perpendicular) find oneself in such a circumstance, in which the most skilful seamen are often at a loss. I had, as usual, for company whoever happened to be on watch. The others passed the night very quietly in their cabins. The shift of wind that I feared did not take place, but the night was none the less bad, and the squalls violent.
1802-05-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to NW. Sent for bread. An Englishman came to fetch a gallon of brandy in payment for the notices printed at Sydney.

1802-05-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the winds, although still in the quarter from west to west-south-west, were less violent than during the night. About eight o'clock, they shifted to south-west, and we were able to set our topsails with all their reefs. Although the sea was still extremely rough and heavy, we continued to keep the board from south toward east until noon, when we took that from west to north so as not to draw too far from the coast.
In the morning, the lookouts at the mast-heads told us they had sight of the land to the north-east, and believed they recognised some of the islets we had seen in the preceding days.
At noon, the latitude was 32° 23' 44", which gave us nearly a degree to the south in the 24 hours that had just passed. There was, this day, no hour angle. The bottom was, then, 42 fathoms.
During the evening, the sky was very dark, without, however, having a bad appearance. The strength of the wind diminished by degrees, and at sunset it was very moderate.
