At eight o'clock, the bottom being no more than 35 fathoms, we wore round and made our course from south toward east until four o'clock, when we resumed the course from west toward north.
During the night, we had a few (squalls), but of as little duration as consequence. The sky, though overcast, was very dry, and the barometer rising, I was pleased to believe that the fine weather was about to return and that we should be able to finish what remained for us to do on this coast.
Everyone was longing for a port of call, and in fact we all needed one. There was no longer any wood from one day to the next; we were reduced to expedients to procure some, and our stock of water could not last much longer. I felt, as everyone did, these privations, but the desire to fulfil the Government's intentions made them more bearable to me than to the others. Scurvy, which was beginning to make progress among several members of the crew, was what pained me the most, but I nevertheless persisted in my resolution to go round the St Peter islands by passing to the west, a thing which was neither long nor difficult, provided the weather turned fine.
One of our scientists, whom I do not name, was attacked by a most peculiar illness: the fear of dying seized him, and he persuaded himself that his career was at an end.
1802-05-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to WSW. Sent for bread; took the turns off the cables. The longboat carried 128 bars of iron to Sydney and brought back 60 sacks of wheat.

1802-05-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, we made our course to gain to the west, in order to come and reconnoitre the point at which General d'Entrecasteaux had stopped, so as afterwards to come back by the east to reconnoitre the part of the mainland included between that point and the one where we had stopped to the west of the St Francis and St Peter islands. The winds, which for eight days had been constantly variable from north-west to south-west, by squalls or very violent, had not allowed us to finish our work in the same manner in which we had begun it.
During the day, the breeze was very faint, the sky overcast, and the sea less bad than in the preceding days, although disturbed by a long swell from west to south-west. We had the bottom fairly constantly between 36 and 40 fathoms of water, but in the evening it increased, and we passed successively from 40 to 45 and even 50, to fall back afterwards to 45. These inequalities that we found in the soundings during the evening were the first of this kind that we had met with at so great a depth of water.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 11' 42"; there was no hour angle for the longitude of the timekeeper.
In the afternoon, the sky remained overcast and even very heavy in the quarter of the south-west to the west, so that we still had the fear of weathering some squall from that point of the horizon. But we got off with only the fright, for the night was fairly fine and the breeze very faint. We continued to make our course to the west under easy sail, my intention being to stand to the north the next day, if the winds remained the same and the weather was favourable for coming to reconnoitre the land.
In the morning, I received complaints from the crew about the poor quality of the salt meat that had just been served out, and which was indeed not good. It came, however, from a cask that was whole and well conditioned. I gave orders that it be set aside so that another might be opened, which proved even worse than the first. We therefore had recourse to a third, which at last proved very good. As there remained to us only one more of that kind, it was put off until the next day to ascertain the condition it might be in.
The biscuit we were using was likewise not very excellent, and had for a long time been crumbling into dust, being all riddled with worms and eaten by moths.
1802-05-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW. Sent for bread. The longboat brought from Sydney 40 sacks of wheat, pumpkins and potatoes. The topgallant masts were got up.

1802-05-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, in the morning, we made our course to the north, a little toward the west, to close with the mainland, finding myself sufficiently advanced to the west to take up the coast again at the point where General d'Entrecasteaux appears to have left it. Although the weather did not have a fine appearance, we had at least the winds favourable for returning to the south, should it turn bad. In the morning, the lookouts at the mast-heads reported to us the land and some breakers at a fairly great distance offshore, bearing from us north-east by east. As the wind came to us directly from that point of the horizon, we could not get sight of it from the deck, and the mainland was not visible there until about noon. The sky was then so overcast and dark that one (sic) could scarcely see to work or read in one's cabin. The barometer was, nevertheless, at 28 inches 4 lines, which did not forebode any fresh squalls for us.
In the evening, we continued to make our course for the coast, and we did not have long to wait to get a good sight of it. It presented itself to us at first in a fairly regular form and of middling height, but as we drew nearer to it, it was recognised as being like most of those we had seen previously, that is to say cut sheer down to the sea's edge, forming various bights more or less deep, but all of little consequence. We also made out two islets and a rock which lie at a fairly great distance from the coast, enough to suggest that one might easily pass between them and the mainland, although the sea breaks heavily in the vicinity. The two islets and the rock are fairly remarkable, which is why I think that General d'Entrecasteaux did not advance far enough to the east to have had sight of them, or if he did reconnoitre the point where we now find ourselves, which I believe to be the one where he stopped, some other circumstance must have hidden it from his view.
Be that as it may, we made various bearings of this part of the coast, which will link up with those we shall make on returning to the east as soon as the wind allows. At six o'clock, we set our course to the south to draw a little away from the coast, and I intended to spend the night there, lying to, but the weather began to turn very bad, with the wind coming in squalls. The barometer having fallen three lines in less than four hours' time, I no longer doubted the very imminent arrival of some squalls, and I was not deceived in my expectation, for the night was extremely bad. Serious reflections on the position in which I found myself: the weakness of my crew, which was no more than 30 men for working the ship, the pressing need we had of firewood, the shortness of the day, and a host of other particular reasons decided me to abandon the coast so as to make first for d'Entrecasteaux Channel, where the anchorage is good. And from there, to Port Jackson, where I have always kept the hope that the boat believed lost may have been able to arrive. The change of course was not long in becoming known, and everyone showed their satisfaction at it, and indeed we all had great need
(in the left margin, perpendicular) of a little rest.
1802-05-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SSE. Sent ashore for bread and vegetables. The main topsail was bent.

1802-05-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, we continued our course to the south, with strong north winds which would not have failed to carry us far offshore had I persisted any longer in remaining on the ungrateful coast of New Holland. Three squalls that I had already weathered within the space of ten days had continually thwarted the desire I had of visiting, in their whole extent, the islands of St Francis and of St Peter, which, to judge by what we have seen of them, are scarcely worth the trouble we took to succeed in it. However, I remain persuaded that, on examining them well, there must be found there some shelter for navigators who will frequent this part. But it is absolutely necessary, to carry out this work with any appearance of success, to be there in the middle of summer, when the days are long and the weather manageable. This is also what I intend to do next season. The southern part of the great island of Kangaroos may also prove very interesting, and although Mr Flinders told me he had remained there six weeks, it appears to me, from the sketch he traced of it in my cabin, that he has not visited the whole of it.
During the day of the nineteenth, the weather was, if not very bad, since we always had the wind astern or on the quarter, at least troublesome for the rain and dampness. Our sick, and especially the scorbutic, who already numbered 14, were greatly inconvenienced by it, and in several of them, sores broke out which had not yet appeared. The physicians found this effect of dampness to be of a quite remarkable nature among seafaring men.
Throughout the whole night from the nineteenth to the twentieth, the entire horizon was ablaze; the lightning was so frequent that the sight was dazzled by it, and often even discomforted. We hardly knew what the weather was going to become, but we were agreeably deceived to find that it would be no worse than it already was, and that the rain would get the better of the wind.
1802-05-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from W to WSW. The longboat made one trip for water. Sent ashore for vegetables and 106 lb of bread. At 5.30 p.m. the English ship Investigator came in, Captain Flinders, 10 months out from England and bound on a voyage of discovery. He had met and spoken the Géographe on the SW coast in 35° 41' of latitude and 126° 49' of longitude.

1802-05-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by two sequences of distances of the sun to the moon 129° 42' 41"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 35 129° 15' 51"
Difference West of the timekeeper to the observation 0° 26' 50"
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twentieth, the weather continued to be dark and laden with vapours. The humidity was even greater than the day before and the entire morning was spent in rain. Several claps of thunder were heard in the distance but did not reach us. The wind gradually decreasing announced a change at hand and although the barometer was still very low, we hoped it would be in our favour. The sea, however, was always heavy with swell and driven by a swell from the south-west which fatigued us greatly.
About ten o'clock, we caught a land bird, very pretty, which came to rest on board. It would be fairly difficult to explain how it found itself so far to sea, for we do not presume there are lands in our vicinity from the course and the distance we have made to the south since our departure from the mainland.
At noon, there was no observation, but we bore away to south by south-east, finding myself far enough to the south not to fear encountering during the night any of the islets which we knew remained in that quarter of the horizon and which we had observed on coming from the east.
During the evening, the weather appeared to be about to clear. The entire horizon from north to south-east passing through east became clear and the view extended fairly far. However, the winds, although very variable, remained from the north towards the west, only the breeze was very light, which caused the heavy swell from the south-west to fatigue us greatly by the large oscillations which it occasioned to the ship.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st, the weather was fairly fine and towards the end the winds shifted from the north towards the east, without increasing in strength. We continued the course of south by south-east with the same canvas which I had ordered for the night, which was the mainsail furled and two reefs in each topsail.
1802-05-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. Sent for 105 lb of bread. A great many articles of trade were carried to the captain's lodging, and pumpkins and cabbages brought back. An English longboat brought us an anchor and 162 gallons of brandy. At 7 an English ship came in bringing news of the general peace.

1802-05-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, the sky which had been fairly fine during the night became laden again with humid vapours and we had from time to time squalls followed by small gusts but of short duration, this did not prevent us from loosing a reef in our topsails, especially as the sea was calmer. The winds, which were then very variable from the north taking from the east, appeared to wish to fix at north-east, but it was only for a moment, for they returned soon to north-north-west, variable as far as west-north-west, almost calm. The sky, which had been dark and covered the greater part of the morning, cleared and at noon we observed the latitude of (no figures), the longitude indicated by the timekeeper placed us at (no figures).
During the afternoon, the weather continued fine. We steered to the south-east by south, but the breeze was so light that we made very little progress.
From the report which the doctor made to me, our sick were worse than usual and he could only attribute to the great humidity which had reigned for several days this unfortunate event, especially with regard to those who were attacked by scurvy. We redoubled cares and attention for them and I hope that if we arrive soon in D'Entrecasteaux Channel, rest and good food will be able to set them right.
At sunset, the weather was altogether fine and the horizon clear at all points, so that we had hope for a fine night lit by the moon which was already fairly advanced, but it was almost calm and we were making very little progress.
During the night of the twenty-first to the 22nd, the breeze continued to be very light and the weather fine. The winds varied from north by north-west, but but (sic) they were not strong enough to support and defend the ship against the agitation which the strong swell occasioned to it, which did not abandon us.
1802-05-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to NNE. An English boat brought us 296 pumpkins and 2800 lb of potatoes. The anchor received yesterday was stocked. Rain during the night. The 22nd [Floréal, 12 May 1802]. Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from E. Sent for 400 lb of bread and took the turns off the cables. A great many articles of trade were carried to the captain's lodging. At 8.30 p.m. an English ship came in from the whale fishery on the coast of New Zealand.

1802-05-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, during the day, the weather was fairly fine and a fair breeze blew from north-north-west shifting to west-north-west, but we found the sea always heavy, with swell and very agitated, however we increased canvas continuing to steer to the south-east by south, for I was convinced that we would not be long in having winds from the south to south-west.
During the morning, we saw a fairly large quantity of birds among which were found the Cape petrel which we had lost sight of for a long time. The others were albatrosses and a species of small grey and white petrel of which I have already spoken.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 38° 26' 3" and the timekeeper longitude placed us at 131° 5' 56".
During the evening, the sky although fairly fine became covered with clouds at several points of the horizon, it appeared to announce wind and rain for the night.
At sunset, it became hazy and humid. Our sick felt it keenly and several said they felt insupportable pains, without however their condition having appeared to increase, according to the doctors' report.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, a good breeze blew, but we had a heavy sea, a constantly covered sky and sometimes small squalls but of little consequence. We saw no sign in this day of speedy change in the weather and it appeared to us that the end of autumn in these climates is not very pleasant.

1802-05-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
[Official document: Reply from Citizen Hamelin to Citizen Millius's request to resume service on board the Naturaliste.
Citizen,
I transmit to Commander Baudin your request of this day to resume your service on board under the pretext of recovery.
I have the honour to observe to you that you have often experienced similar improvements to which relapses have always succeeded which, in interrupting your service have cost me several months of anxiety.
Salutations
Signed: the Captain of the Frigate
C. Hamelin
All original documents with certificates from the doctors are in the hands of the Captain of the Frigate Millius.]
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the weather although always covered and humid, was all the more bearable for those in good health because the wind was good and the breeze fresh. We continued to steer to the south-east by south to put ourselves in good time in the latitude of the south-western cape which I wished to come to recognize just as I had done on my first entry into the strait. As I expected to see the winds shortly shift from the north-west to the south and to the south-west, I was glad to make them favourable to the course which remained for me to make to gain the strait.
During the morning, the sky was constantly the same, that is to say almost always covered and laden with humid vapours which were not a good augury for the future. However, at noon we had a latitude, somewhat doubtful in truth, but which nevertheless gave us 40° 37' 16" and the timekeeper longitude was found to be 133° 4' 14".
During the afternoon, the weather was the same as that we found in the morning and the winds remained constantly at north-north-west, good breeze which was infinitely agreeable to us although we could not take full advantage of it by carrying a great deal of canvas because the sea was too heavy and agitated and the movements which it caused to the ship were lively and violent.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth, we found the sea so bad that we were obliged to furl our mainsail which, being often backed by the elevation of the swell, gave sudden jerks making us fear it might be torn. The same was done with the brigantine. Besides, the rest of the night had nothing particular and the weather was not bad.
1802-05-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to NE, with rain. An Englishman with an order from the captain came to fetch 90 bottles of arrack. Sent for pumpkins at the captain's lodging. The three Black men, Charlot, Jean and Jasmin, were discharged by the captain's order.

1802-05-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, a strong squall accompanied by gusts shifted the winds to the west-south-west and they became from that moment very variable and gradually calmed. A short time later, they returned to the north taking from the east without increasing in strength, but they gave us such abundant rain that it was continuous all the morning with appearance of not finishing as soon as we could have desired.
At noon, there was no observation and the dead reckoning of the course covered in twenty-four hours placed us at the latitude of 41° 49' 2". The longitude also estimated was 134° 54' 16". We then steered to the south-east having very little ground to make to the south in reason of that which remained for us to cover in longitude.
During the afternoon, the weather continued with rain and although it was less abundant than it had been in the morning, it was none the less continuous and uncomfortable especially for our sick, numbering twenty at this time, for the infirmary increased every day and a speedy port of call became more and more indispensable.
I expected that the heavy rain which had occurred all day would change the state of the sea, especially as the breeze was very moderate, but it remained constantly heavy and elevated, so that the ship and its masts fatigued all the more, the wind not being strong enough to support it.
Towards the end of the day, we saw little appearance of change in the weather for the night. However, the rain seemed about to cease in that different points of the horizon were no longer so laden with vapours. We had fairly fine weather until midnight and even almost calm, but from midnight, the winds having shifted to the south-east, the breeze became so strong that we were obliged to furl the greater part of our sails to keep only the foresail and the main topsail until we should know what would become of a wind which from the outset announced itself with so much strength and impetus.
1802-05-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to ENE. The longboat made one trip for water and one for wood. At daybreak a working party of fifteen men had been sent to cut wood.

1802-05-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, although the winds had entirely changed during the night, the rain continued for some time more, but finally it ceased about eight o'clock in the morning, and the sky became fairly fine although misty. The winds which were at the south-east were not very variable and the breeze no less strong than it had been during the night. We experienced in the morning a sudden change in the temperatures of the atmosphere. The air became dry and even cold. The thermometer suddenly fell to eight degrees, which had not happened to it even at our departure from Le Havre where it was at 9°. This change which we did not expect so soon was keenly felt by most of those on board and each one began to use his winter clothes. I was not the last to do the same.
At noon, we had no observed latitude. That of the dead reckoning placed us at 42° 45' 17" and our longitude was found to be 134° 32' 16" having made progress to the west during these twenty-four hours.
As the wind was found absolutely contrary to our course, I made no change to the canvas and continued the south tack taking the least to the west which was possible. We saw during the day the same species of birds which we had encountered two days before, but in much greater number. We had the good fortune to catch on a line a variety of albatross which was not known to us and which we found very beautiful. This bird, it appears, is very voracious and more than twenty took the bait which we threw to them. But as their strength was considerable, we could not have hauled them on board before they had broken our lines and more often still the hooks by which they were held, so that we had only one.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth, the wind calmed greatly from the start and we passed even a part of it in calm without the ship being able to steer. This gave us hope of a change of wind and we had it indeed, for they shifted to the south-south-east and made passable the course which we had to make.
The heavy swell and the long and elevated wave which we had constantly had since our departure from the coasts of New Holland ceased to be felt from the time when we encountered the winds at the south-east.
1802-05-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to N. Sent a working party of 15 men to cut wood. The draught was taken: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 11 feet 7 inches, difference 1 inch. The longboat made one trip for wood.

1802-05-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, the weather was fairly fine in the morning, but the winds were very variable and light compared to the preceding days. We found the sea no less agitated by a heavy swell from the south and south-east which made the sea uncomfortable although it appeared fairly calm.
At noon, we observed the latitude to be 43° 21' 38", the timekeeper longitude placed us at 134° 26' 17".
During the evening, the weather differed little from that we had in the morning and it was even much more agreeable than we had found it for several days, however, cold enough to make us blow on our hands. Our sick found great relief in it and the pains which they had felt up to then were much less vivid. I hope that the refreshments which I shall be able to procure for them in the channel or elsewhere will completely restore them if the weather is fine.
During the night of the 26th to the 27th, the sky became covered with clouds several times, but in general it was fine and the winds very variable from the south towards the east. We even had them at the north-east, but it was only for a moment.
We had during the day and even during the night the company of a fairly large number of petrels which the moonlight served to facilitate their view of the ship which they appeared to follow.
1802-05-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. Sent the working party of 15 men for wood; sent ashore for cabbages. The longboat made one trip for wood. At 10 p.m. the rain stopped, the weather cleared, the wind fell and drew round to the west. Citizen Milius stayed at Port Jackson on account of illness. Three Black men were discharged; a seaman named Horsfall (the one who escaped from the Virginie at Timor and came aboard by swimming) deserted. Two Frenchmen, convicts, were shipped.

1802-05-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The day of the twenty-seventh had nothing particular and as the weather was fine, our sick found themselves even better than the day before, positive proof that great humidity is if not the cause of scurvy, at least greatly accelerates the disposition one can have for this disease.
Although we were extremely short of firewood to burn since we had been reduced to consuming all that was bad in planks, barrels, etc. A little fire was made in their quarters to draw out as much moisture as was possible, but what we could give them was so little that it would not have been of great use.
At noon, although the weather was then fairly fine, we could not observe the sun's passage at the meridian, having the sky covered with clouds. From our dead reckoning, the latitude was found to be 43° 11' 40".
During the evening, the weather continued fine and the sea became fairly calm. The swell, although it still existed, had so much lost its strength that we were little inconvenienced by it.
From the morning, the winds having shifted to the south towards the west, we took advantage of it to advance to the east in order to reach the D'Entrecasteaux Channel as soon as possible and supply ourselves there with what we might be lacking. During the evening, we had them at the south-west, good fresh and made good use of them.
The night of the 27th to the 28th was accompanied by some squalls and even rain, but the wind which was good for us prevented paying great attention to it, and we kept all sails set.
1802-05-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to WNW. The longboat made one trip for water and wood. The observatory was struck. It was verified that our mill could give 9 lb of flour in 1½ hours from 15 lb of wheat. At 8 a cooper named Bouteiller was brought aboard in the large boat, wounded by a dagger thrust given him by midshipman Desgouhières, who was in charge of the party. Bouteiller and the other boat's crew were drinking in a tavern at Sydney; the midshipman went there and ordered them aboard the boat. Bouteiller, drunk, answered him insolently and came at him to strike him; he drew his dagger and Bouteiller took a thrust in the lower belly which the surgeon judged mortal.

1802-05-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, the weather was much less agreeable than the two preceding days, and our scorbutic patients had announced this change to us from the evening before by the renewal of their pains. The barometer and the hygrometer indicated the same, for the former was falling rapidly and the latter was advancing towards humidity.
During the morning, the sky was rainy and covered with a thick fog which penetrated so strongly into the interior of the ship that no part of it was excepted.
We had no observation for latitude at noon and one might even say we had lacked them for a long time, for those which we obtained before appeared to me very doubtful for accuracy. When the sun was fine, the horizon was so shortened or laden with vapours that they always appeared uncertain to me, although not everyone is of the same opinion. That of the dead reckoning placing us at 43° 43'. I continued to hold the course to the east, taking a little to the south so that an unexpected error should not expose us to some danger.
We found during the day the sea agitated and somewhat (no adjective) but it was unavoidable with the weather we had, nevertheless we continued to increase canvas to lose as little time as possible and reach a port of call of which we had absolute need.
In the afternoon, I ordered to steer east not to go too far to the south and this course was continued during the night although our little distance from the land according to our dead reckoning and even the results of the timekeeper indicated we should show more prudence. But as the night had fine moments and as occasionally our horizon was fairly extensive by the favour of the moon, we continued our course with the same security as if I had found myself far to seaward.
1802-05-18.journal_breton_naturaliste:
At midnight the weather turned overcast and the wind freshened. At 1 it was blowing hard in gusts, with thunder and rain; at 3 the weather cleared and the rain stopped. Cries were heard which were at first thought to come from Garden Island; but then believing them to be those of a drowning man, a boat was at once sent, which found about half a cable off a man trying to reach the ship by swimming. Questioned as to who he was and what he wanted, he said he was a soldier and had deserted to come aboard. He was taken at once aboard the Lady Nelson, which lay anchored near us. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW. At 5 the pilot came to take us out; the longboat went to weigh the kedge anchor, but the buoy rope having parted she came back aboard and was hoisted in, as were the other boats. At 8 the bower anchor was weighed, and at 10.15 we got under way from the kedge and shaped our course out of the port. At 11.30, after doubling North and South Head, we hove to and sent back the pilot, then filled and stood on; the anchors were secured in their stowage. Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from WSW to south, with rain; lay to under the foresail, both topsails close-reefed, the storm staysail, the fore staysail, the mizzen and its staysail.

During our stay at Port Jackson Captain Hamelin behaved in a manner unworthy of a French officer. Mr Palmer, the colony's commissary, had offered to supply him with everything he might need; he took only bread for the stay and wheat for the voyage. The governor supplied him with 162 gallons of brandy from the government stores and an anchor, which he paid for with bar iron. He had a great many articles of trade carried to his lodging at Sydney, and there he bartered them himself for potatoes and pumpkins that the inhabitants brought. This traffic, shameful in an officer — and above all in an officer commanding a ship and representing the French government — gave rise to difficulties between Captain Hamelin and the wretched convicts who were bartering their vegetables for tools, and Harris the justice of the peace had to restore peace between them. Captain Hamelin had so good a reputation at Sydney that one day, dining in town, a lady asked me whether he sold women's shoes.

1802-05-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from WSW, SSW and south; the wind came on to blow hard. At daybreak a man not belonging to the crew was found; he said he was an English soldier and had come aboard by swimming during the night of the 27th to the 28th [Floréal, Year 10, 17-18 May 1802].
1802-05-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the sky remained overcast, misty and rainy, and for our part, we continued our course as if it had been the finest weather in the world, without changing anything in our sails.
At eight o'clock, we caught sight of land in a break in the clouds and I recognised that we found ourselves a little further north than the south-west cape of Van Diemen's Land, being at much the same position as when I had first had sight of it. Since these lands were well known to me, I accordingly set my course for what remained to be done to enter the strait. Only, I feared that the shortness of daylight might not be sufficient to achieve this, having been unable to see the rocks named Mewstone to the east except about noon.
The breeze was then strong from the west-north-west and we made good progress. I continued, nevertheless, to carry as much canvas as was necessary so as not to compromise the masts. But in the evening, it became so strong that notwithstanding the desire I had to arrive before nightfall, I found myself obliged to take a second reef in the topsails.
At four o'clock, we caught sight of Tasman's White Rocks, but we were still to the west of them, as also of the entrance to the strait, which deprived me of all hope of being able to enter before nightfall, which showed no fair signs.
At sunset, which did not long delay after this moment, we suddenly fell not into dead calm, but at least into an atmosphere so variable that scarcely had we trimmed on one tack when we had to go onto another. This variability of the wind, no doubt occasioned by the different positions of the long and numerous succession of mountains which form this part of the coast, kept us in continual activity for two hours and was not pleasant for us, especially as the depth of the water, though at a small distance from the coast, was considerable and the bottom foul. But at length, about eight o'clock, the wind set towards the south with very fresh breezes, which obliged us to take the third reef in the topsails and to close-reef our mainsail (sic).
We took advantage of the first squalls that presented themselves to make some progress to the east by standing to the north in order to pass the night off Bruny Island, of which we had obtained good bearings. By this means, I extricated myself from difficulty with respect to Tasman's White Rocks, on which the current or other circumstances might have caused us to drift had the calm and the violent gusts lasted any longer.
After moonrise, which occurred about ten-thirty, the winds increased considerably, the sea became very heavy and rough, and notwithstanding the violent squalls we experienced, I made towards Bruny Island where I hove to until midnight, when, finding myself too close to the land, I stood a little to the south and then to the east where I remained until daylight.
1802-05-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SSW to S. At 3 a.m. Bouteiller died of his wound. At daybreak a stranger was discovered; he said he was an English soldier and had come aboard on the 28th about 3 a.m. The topgallant masts were got down. The weather cleared, the wind fell and was a light breeze from S to ESE. At noon in 34° 20' 23" of latitude observed and in 149° 36' 24" of longitude by account. At 2 we filled and stood on; at 4 the land from N 12° W to S 29° W.

1802-05-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a strong breeze from south, SE, W and NW. At noon the land from N 28° W to S 48° W.
1802-05-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the anchorage, Bay of Adventure:
The south point of the entrance to the bay or Cape Cannelé south 33° east
Cape Too Billant north 10° east
The middle of the isthmus north 30° west
The south point of Tasman Island north 64° east
Historical events & Remarks.
The twentieth. The thirtieth, in the morning, being off Bruny Island at about three leagues' distance, the land was scarcely visible, so misty and vaporous was it. Since we found ourselves a little to the east of it, I lost all hope of being able to enter the strait. Not only were the winds too violent to recover the distance we had lost, but the weather was so unsuitable that it would have been the height of imprudence to attempt it. The necessity and want of firewood caused me then to take the course of attempting to gain the anchorage of the Bay of Adventure, and I was fortunate enough to achieve this by coasting along the shore from Borelle Islands to this bay almost at musket shot, seeing at times the summits of the mountains but not the shores of the coast. Within Borelle Islands, I was surprised to find the sea so rough as what we encountered, which made me suspect that the east or south-east winds had much prevailed along this coast.
About eight o'clock, the weather having cleared a little, it was then easy for me to recognise the Bay of Adventure according to the plan given by the geographers of the expedition of General d'Entrecasteaux, so that we were already very near it when the weather gave me hope of being able to anchor there, which indeed took place at half-past eight. I do not recollect having seen a more picturesque view than that presented by Cape Cannelé, a name which is (sic) very appropriate to it.
As soon as we were at anchor, the launch and all those on board capable of wielding an axe were sent ashore to get firewood for us.
Two other boats were likewise sent there, one to carry the learned men and others, and the other for fishing. Our sick, who were much interested in this, waited with great impatience for the return of the latter, and the hope they had of regaling themselves during the day was not realised, for it did not return until very late, but at least with a sufficiently abundant catch for everyone to benefit from it, although there were only four people with lines.
Our launch and our learned men brought back (sic) about four cords of wood; the learned men little of novelty, but the names of several people of the Recherche engraved on the bark of the trees.
Everything was arranged so that, during the night, a second trip for firewood should be made if the weather cleared.
Citizen [Péron]—who is always making or believes himself to be making new discoveries—claimed to have found a river which no one had seen before him since none of the travellers who have visited this part more thoroughly than we did make mention of it. But be that as it may, water there was plentiful and all the gullies abounded in it. It appears that it had already rained abundantly in this part of the coast. The vegetation there was so vigorous that all the trees were covered with foliage of the finest green, infinitely more pleasant to the eye than when we entered the strait (for the first time) in the midst of the fine season.
The fish we caught were of the same species as those we already knew. The gardener, who is not one of the learned men, nevertheless managed to find four new plants which we had not encountered elsewhere.
The physician Laridon believed he had determined the question regarding quadrupeds, and brought back bones that were charred, which, in my opinion, belonged to some seals or other marine animal which may have served as food for the natives. If they are from a terrestrial animal, which is not probable, it must have been larger than an elephant.
At midnight, the launch departed from the ship under the command of Citizen Ronsard, both to get firewood and to see whether the water, which according to everyone was very plentiful in different places, was equally convenient to take on board by means of our launch.
During the night, the weather cleared and the winds shifted to north-north-west, light breeze.
1802-05-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NW, SW to SE. At 10, 10° 19' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 25' 24" of latitude observed and in 149° 17' 36" of longitude by account. The land from N 28° W to N 48° W.

1802-05-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from W to S and SE. At daybreak sighted the land; at noon it stretched from N 29° W to S 51° W.
1802-05-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
The first of Prairial, the weather was extremely fine throughout the day. However, we did not derive all the advantage from it despite the precaution I had taken to ensure that not a moment was lost. My launch, which I had sent in the middle of the night the previous day, did not return until about three o'clock in the afternoon, whereas it should have been on board at ten o'clock in the morning. The small boat which should have arrived before it did not land until after the launch, and might still have been ashore if I had not recalled it by firing the cannon.
All these delays and the movement of the barometer, which was continuously falling and which, at noon, stood at 28 inches, determined me to change my intention and to take the course of getting under way as soon as we were ready for it. We therefore set about, as soon as the launch was unloaded, hoisting it on board, as well as all the other boats. This work was lengthy, and scarcely had we finished it by six o'clock in the evening, at a season when darkness falls from five o'clock and even before.
I should have wished to be able to get under way immediately, but the exhaustion in which my crew found itself caused me, in any case, to defer until the next day. And since the sky had a fair appearance, I even exempted them from keeping watch.
The midshipman Le Brun, whom, at the instigation of Captain Hamelin, I had made a first-class midshipman, and whose insubordinate conduct, following the advice of the son of M. Bougainville, who conducts himself as badly as possible, was put in the brig for the night for having treated with the utmost indecency the master gunner who remonstrated with him about the dangers to which he was exposing us all by lighting his pipe at the bitt lantern with a paper tube which, without further consequence, he threw on deck after using it.
Since the young man, although full of strength and vigour, had for a month done no duty on board, I demoted him to second-class midshipman, the rank in which he had been embarked at the Île de France.
Citizen Bougainville, who had done no more duty than he since the same period, retained his rank, but I hope that my remarks to the Minister of the Navy will inform him how little he is fitted to make a good officer, and still less to serve in that capacity.
The night of the first to the second was much fairer than the movement of the barometer had led us to expect. I was all the more pleased as the rest of the crew, who truly had need of it, was not interrupted. The winds varied from north to north-west and even to west, but the breeze was moderate and without gusts, which, I believe, is not usual in these waters during this season.
1802-05-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to south. At daybreak the land was sighted; at noon it bore from us N 29° W to S 51° W, being in 34° 56' 40" of latitude observed and in 149° 9' 30" of longitude by account.

1802-05-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to S by E. At 12.15 went onto the starboard tack. At 10 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-05-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the small Tasman Island remained at north 55° east
Cape Pillar at north 40° east
Cape Batral (Balsah, Baltra ?) at north 33° west
Cape Cannelé at south 76° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The second. From five o'clock in the morning, the weather being very fine and the winds from the west varying towards the north, we prepared ourselves to get under way. We first set about securing in position our second sheet anchor, which as a precaution had been made ready to drop if needed. This work completed, we weighed the one that was at the bottom and got under way, which did not take place until about seven o'clock, although we had set about it early enough to be ready before that time.
During the morning, we had a fair breeze and fine weather. It continued thus in the afternoon, so that by nightfall we had rounded Cape Pillar and had perfect sight of Hippolyte Rocks as well as of Cape Frederick Henry and of Maria Island. But the winds beginning to decrease, we had all the more reason to fear them from the north, as we were beginning to have a fairly heavy swell from that quarter of the horizon, which, moreover, was very clear and extensive.
During the night, we were not disappointed in our expectations, for the winds were constantly from the north-west, sometimes varying towards the north. We endeavoured in vain to close with the land so as to begin the geographical work on this part of the coast the next day. We were unable to succeed notwithstanding that we sailed as close to the wind as was possible for us.
Had I not been greatly indisposed and obliged to keep to my cabin when we coasted along this shore in every way trying to recover our boat, this work would not have remained undone, and notwithstanding the unfortunate event that had just befallen us, I should have taken advantage of it for bearings which, perhaps, we shall not be able to take as close, if the wind does not favour us in the present circumstances as much as it did then.
During the night, the sky was tolerably fine, and the sea, though heavy, troubled us but little.
1802-05-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a pleasant breeze from SSE to E. At noon in 35° 25' 4" of latitude by account and in 149° 12' 6" of longitude by account.

1802-05-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from SE. The sea smooth. At 6 p.m. went onto the starboard tack; at 6 a.m. onto the port tack.
1802-05-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon
Cape Pillar remained at east 23° north,
and Cape Frederick Henry at east 69° 44' 5" north
At noon,
the middle of Maria Island at south 89° west,
Cape Pelé at south 87° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The third, in the morning, the sky, though very misty and overcast, was tolerably fine. The lands seen the day before remained to us in daylight at the following compass points, or to speak more correctly, they extended from north 76° 15' west to south 62° west. We were too far distant to give to each, with certainty, the different names which are indicated in the journal.
Since the winds were constantly from the north towards the west, we continued to hold the same tack towards the east and north, sailing close to the wind as closely as possible. The sky having cleared during the morning, we obtained the sun at noon, and the latitude was observed to be 42° 43' 0". The longitude by the timekeeper placed us, for the moment of observation, at 146° 17' 6".
The heavy swell from the north having greatly diminished, we hoped to shortly have the winds from another quarter of the horizon.
Throughout the evening, they were nevertheless the same and varied very little. But during the night, they shifted and began to become very variable, although remaining still from the north pulling towards the west. Their strength alone decreased gradually.
I was informed during the day by the physician that several of our sick were worse than usual, although the weather was mild and not very humid. I was the more surprised since it had seemed to me that the circumstances should hasten their recovery rather than increase their illness. According to the advice I had just received, I sought to know the cause, and I succeeded in discovering the reason which is that, following the example of gluttons, they had eaten so much of fish that most of them had indigestion. Those who had not been previously attacked by dysentery got off with suffering a little from stomach ache, which they experienced. But those who had already had it and who had not recovered from it were attacked by it again, and it is very doubtful that they will recover from it.
My cook, without being in the worst case, but who had been ill for three months and consequently on a restricted diet, indulged so much that he had an indigestion which caused him to end his life on the very day of our departure.
1802-05-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a pleasant breeze from ESE to south. At noon in 35° 32' 58" of latitude by account and in 149° 23' 0" of longitude by account. At 8 the wind freshened by degrees.

1802-05-24.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, the sea smooth enough, a fresh breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. The wind freshened steadily and blew hard, with a high sea. At midnight took all the reefs in the main topsail; the fore topsail split while we were taking in the reefs. During the night the port cathead was carried away by a sea. The fore topsail was repaired and the port cathead was made good.
1802-05-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
The southernmost point visible of Van Diemen's Land at south 21° west
Cape Pelé at south 38° 30' west
The northernmost land visible at north 37° 30' west
Historical events & Remarks.
The fourth. Towards the end of the night of the third, the winds having shifted to the south-west, we steered a course to the north until daylight. At that time, we had good sight of the land, but at too great a distance to establish the true position of the vessel, which, according to the dead reckoning of the distance traveled, should have been abeam or a little further north than Schouten Island.
To settle the matter, we steered to the west bearing a little to the north, believing that I should recognize the coast perfectly as we approached it, and especially when we should be only a short distance from it. Since the sky was very overcast, there was hardly any prospect of obtaining the sun's meridian altitude at noon. And indeed we did not get it. Everyone, however, and especially the learned men, claimed to recognize the cape that I had named Cape Pelé, and I was the only one not to recognize either this cape or the appearance of the neighbouring lands which lie both to the north and to the south of it. This surprised me all the more since I believed and still believe I have memory quite as good as theirs, without having their wit.
Be that as it may, I steered for an elevated piece of land which seemed to me to be the cape I was seeking, but after approaching it, I went about to stand to the south, having satisfied myself that it was not. It would have been easy to begin taking bearings at the place where I was and to profit by the wind which was most favourable to us, but I preferred to come and recognize the cape that I had seen the first time and which proves by its position the non-existence of the islands indicated by Captain Furneaux, rather than leave it behind.
This error on my part pleased more than one person on board and was not a little in persuading everyone that they were better able to command the vessel than myself.
Since I had entirely forgotten that I was in my bed, ill, at the time that we were on this part of the coast, it was no longer difficult for me to understand why I did not recognize lands that I had never seen.
During the evening, the breeze fell greatly and became variable. We made two tacks until nightfall, which were not very successful, and we gained little to windward, finding that I had passed Cape Pelé which I hope to gain during the night in order to begin at daylight the bearing of all this coast to the entrance of Banks Strait.
During the night, the winds were absolutely calm and the vessel remained for several hours in succession without headway, at most we made three leagues.
1802-05-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind blowing hard from S to SSW. At midnight, the fore topsail having been split while reefing it, we lay to. The port cathead was carried away by a sea. At 6, the wind having fallen, we filled and stood on. The cathead and the fore topsail were repaired. At noon in 36° 8' 40" of latitude by account and in 150° 9' 54" of longitude by account.

1802-05-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. A high sea. Continual rain. At 6 wore onto the port tack; at 9.45 wore onto the starboard tack; at 11 set the mizzen topsail.
1802-05-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
(end of page 175) of us, I had not been able to receive it.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 42° 9' 4" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us at 145° 21' 44".
In the evening, we continued to steer to the south and at three o'clock in the afternoon, having completed our work to the south of Schouten Island, we laid the vessel close to the wind on the larboard tack to work our way to the east and north as much as possible.
Historical events & Remarks.
The fifth. In the morning, the calm that we had had during the night continued until about seven o'clock. But then a light breeze came to us from the north-west which, having successively shifted to the north, gained a little strength as the sun rose above the horizon. We took advantage of it to close with the land, which we approached at a distance of one league, and from that moment began our geographical work while steering a course from north to south.
According to our bearings of the day before and the observations taken on shore, the current had carried us to the north two leagues beyond our dead reckoning. Since I was ill at the time when we first coasted this shore, I was not a little surprised that the principal points had not been observed and that more notice had not been taken of it than if we had been far offshore. Nevertheless, they boasted of having passed it much closer than I did, and even without taking the trouble to take soundings.
Be that as it may, having very favourable winds for proceeding to the south, I took advantage of it and had all the work of this section, which extended to the southernmost point of Schouten Island and the rocks and islets belonging to it, carried out by Citizen Ronsard and the astronomer Bernier.
I have difficulty in understanding how Captain Furneaux could place on the chart of this coast the three fairly large islands mentioned in his map. Unless he meant to speak of some large rocks which are altogether on shore and to which the name of islands, however small one may suppose them, cannot apply. According to what he says, that they are low lands, I am therefore justified in believing that he saw this coast only from afar, and even from very far off. For certainly, it is high and very high. I am therefore not at all surprised that he saw islands at the latitude which he indicates, since it is precisely one of the most elevated places on the coast, so that he took the summits of mountains, which he could not see the low lands connecting to one another, for islands.
We, who this last time have traversed all this coast from the latitude of 42° 8' to 42° 30', were at first deceived like him, but the error was only temporary, having made sure that what appeared to be islands was nothing else than mountains separated from one another by low lands which form bays more or less deep.
Between Schouten Island and the mainland, there is a channel which appears navigable and may offer some places of refuge if needed. But neither the weather nor the season was suitable for venturing into it, which prevented me from exploring it. Besides, the launch which, during our stay at Maria Island, was sent there for the purpose with the hydrographer Faure, will no doubt make known the resources it can offer to navigators. According to the verbal report which he gave me, he did not, any more than we, encounter the islands placed on Captain Furneaux's chart. But he found a deep inlet which extends considerably to the north. Since his plan was not completed at the moment when the Naturaliste separated (see end of previous page).
1802-05-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 36° 9' 16" of latitude by account and in 149° 29' 48" of longitude by account.

1802-05-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW. Shook out the reefs of the topsails. At 10 a light breeze got up from N by E; rigged out the studdingsails to starboard.
1802-05-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
The sixth. In the morning, having got a little to windward to the east during the night, we endeavoured to close with the land by going about to continue our bearings, but the winds being still from the northerly quarter towards the west, the sky overcast and the weather squally, this day was entirely lost. We had sight of the land, but we found ourselves too far distant to be able to distinguish which part we were near. Especially as at noon we had no observation from the sun's meridian altitude.
During the morning, one of the helmsmen who had been suspected of having stolen fish-hooks was so offended at this suspicion that he raised an infernal din. I was unable to make him be silent, notwithstanding repeated orders that I gave him, and the moment I had returned to my cabin, he began again. Annoyed at all this uproar, I gave orders that he be given twelve blows with a rope's end, which was about to be carried out when, to escape it, he threw himself into the sea. Although the weather was not very favourable, at the same moment we set all our sails and lowered the small boat. Since he was an excellent swimmer, it was not difficult to recover him. My intention was to have him given twenty blows with a cane when he arrived, but the physicians having found him in no condition to receive them, the matter was postponed.
In the evening, we continued to steer for the land, which was very misty, and at six o'clock, being no longer but at three leagues' distance, we came about off shore, carrying little sail in order not to go too far off, the winds being still variable from the west towards the north and the sea heavy and rough. During the night, the breeze was light, which was much the same to us, provided we had good winds the next day.
1802-05-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. At noon in 36° 40' 29" of latitude observed and in 150° 3' 54" of longitude by account. The wind a light breeze from N to WNW. The topmast studdingsail booms were rigged in.

1802-05-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, a light breeze from NW, from south to SW.
1802-05-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
The seventh. The winds being the same as the day before, or at least nearly so, we lost all hope of being able to close with the land in a manner to recognize it properly for the continuation of the geographical work that remained to be done. Since the weather was still squally with a most threatening appearance and we sometimes had very violent squalls, we continued on the northern tack in order to get far enough to windward in this quarter to work off the shore while standing to the south, the winds showing no sign of changing as soon as we could have wished. We had no observation at noon for the latitude, but we could not fail to observe that the currents had carried us to the east beyond our dead reckoning, having no sight of the land although our horizon was sometimes very extensive.
During the morning, someone, though I know not who, having made representations to the physician Laridon that it was he who was the cause that I kept the sea so long because he did not give me knowledge of the situation of our sick nor of their number, he brought me a long list on this subject, of which I certainly had no need, knowing the number as well as he. If it had been in my power to diminish the ills they had, I should certainly have done so, but being unable to decide to abandon a coast which had been neglected in having bearings taken of it, whilst we were searching for our boat and which had been traversed in every direction at that time, I invited him to tell those who had put him up to making representations to me that our stay at sea was a consequence of their negligence and that they had only themselves to blame if it should result.
I do not know if the physician carried out his commission, but I nonetheless continued to work to windward until it pleased the winds to be favourable to us. Besides, so little remained to be done that we needed only a day or two of fine and good weather to complete this work. But it is true that these two circumstances appear rare in this season.
During the night, the winds were the same and nothing announced an early change.
1802-05-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to SSW. At noon in 37° 37' 80" of latitude observed and in 150° 2' 0" of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze in gusts. At 11.30 the wind was blowing in heavy gusts; I had the watch and woke the captain to ask leave to take the second reef in the topsails, which I had just lowered to half mast. He refused at first, telling me it was not blowing (he was in his bed, well covered, the curtains drawn). I then proposed shaking out the reef; and he told me to take the second reef.

1802-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. The wind having freshened, we took all the reefs in the topsails. At 4 a.m. the weather cleared; at 10 overcast weather, a fresh breeze in gusts.
1802-05-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The eighth. The winds shifted to the south-west and did not thereby improve our position. We had them during the morning in strong squalls and gusts that obliged us to close-reef our mainsail and to keep all reefs in our topsails.
Since everyone knew that my intention was to put into Port Jackson, although I had communicated it to no one, the officers as well as the naturalists and learned men were displeased that I was not taking advantage of the fair wind to set that course. This was much the same to me, since I had made up my mind and wished to wait a while longer before abandoning this coast rather than be obliged to return a third time.
Throughout the day, we held the coastal tack and had no sight of the land at sunset, although our horizon was then very extensive.
From an observation we had at noon, although a little doubtful, we found ourselves north of the 41st degree, which determined me to take the southern tack which I held all the night, which was fine and even pleasant for the season we were in. But the sea, which was heavy and rough, fatigued us considerably.
From the distance we covered in the day to close with the land of which our dead reckoning led us to believe we were much nearer than we actually were, I no longer doubted that the direction of the currents carried us rather strongly to the east. But since we had to work to the south, I was forced to set that course and consequently to go further from the coast since it ran to the east by the wind direction.
The weather, which had become very dry, made me fear on the other hand that we should experience fresh difficulties if the winds should shift to the north when we were to the south, as had already happened since we began the work on this part of the coast.
1802-05-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather with frequent squalls, the wind blowing hard from W to SSW. At midnight, in taking in reefs in the main topsail, it was torn from its bolt-rope; we unbent it at once. At noon in 39° 17' 15" of latitude observed and in 150° 43' 42" of longitude by account. The repaired main topsail was bent. At 8 p.m., when Citizen Freycinet went for the captain's orders, he charged him not to shorten sail, and not to do as I had done, who, being drunk the evening before, had asked leave to take in reefs.

1802-05-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from SW. At daybreak the port cathead was found carried away and was repaired at once. At 10 the wind a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea rather high.
1802-05-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
The ninth. The winds being constantly south-west with little variation, we continued the southern tack. The state of the atmosphere, though tolerably fine, seemed to announce an early change. The part of the horizon between south and east became clouded, and the south-west breeze became very light. I expected from moment to moment to have them from the south, but this hope was not realised and the day was spent in fruitless waiting.
At noon we had a good observation of latitude and in the morning several hour angles had been taken. We found ourselves by the sun's meridian altitude at 41° 15' 20" of latitude, and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us at 147° 11' 8". Not being far enough south to change course, we continued the south-south-east tack, but the wind was so light that we made very little progress.
Two more men entered the sick-bay this day and our sailmaker was suddenly attacked by a flux which had all the appearance of dysentery; the physicians could not discover the cause.
Twenty men in the sick-bay out of a total of 75, including the learned men and others, did not cease to greatly reduce the number of men available for the working of the ship. It had long been impossible for us to go about on either tack without bringing all hands on deck, and this also forced me to make longer tacks than would have been necessary in other circumstances.
After sunset, the wind having fallen completely, and the horizon in the south being very confused, I no longer doubted that the winds would come from that quarter in the night and would soon put us in a position to abandon this coast to seek the rest of which we had all had need after nine months of continuous stay at sea.
During the night of the 9th to the 10th, the winds did not shift to the south as I had expected from the state of the atmosphere in that quarter. They were extremely variable from the south-west quarter and often calm, without the vessel being able to steer.
1802-05-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SW to SSW. At daybreak the port cathead was found carried away and was repaired. Fine weather, the wind falling by degrees. At noon in 40° 53' 36" of latitude observed and in 151° 54' 54" of longitude by account. At 6 a flat calm. At 3.45, 9° 51' 50" of NE variation.

1802-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a light breeze from SW to NW by way of west. At 6.30 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack.
1802-05-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The tenth. In the morning, the winds or rather the little freshness that was felt before daylight came to us from the north to north-west. We took advantage of it to close with the land by steering to the west, and when the breeze became a little fresher, we steered to the south-west, all sails set, to close with it, for I was eager to complete the geographical work of this coast for fear of encountering some squall that would drive us far from it altogether, in the season we were in.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 31° 41' 3" (sic). There was no hour angle. The weather, which was dark and laden with vapours and sometimes rainy, promised no fine days ahead, but since the barometer was at 28 inches two lines, I hoped it might yet clear.
In the afternoon, the horizon having cleared, the winds shifted to the west, variable to the south-west, which obliged us to work to windward again in order to close with the land. The various tacks we made during the evening advanced us but little, and we had no sight of the land before nightfall, which we spent as we had the evening in working to windward. The weather was fine, dry and even cold. Despite this, our sick benefited but little from it and complained even more than ever.
Since we had almost no fresh provisions left and fortunately for them, I had saved what little remained since my last illness, I had them given one of the three pigs I had left and of which I had deprived myself so as to be available for anyone who should become ill. They received enough for three meals and the rest was salted to serve them later.
Two more men entered the sick-bay this day, complaining of severe pains without showing any apparent symptoms of illness. Among them was the baker, who was very useful to those who were already afflicted, so that the supply of fresh bread to the sick suddenly failed.
1802-05-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from NW to W. At noon in 41° 8' 11" of latitude observed and in 151° 33' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-05-31.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea [one word erased, illegible], a light breeze from NW to W and SW. At 6 p.m. went onto the port tack.
1802-05-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Latitude observed 41° 21' 7" south
According to the dead reckoning 41° 22' 43"
Longitude estimated 146° 19' east
Rhumb north 62° 49' west
Distance 37.2 miles
Variation observed 8° 6' north-east.
C. Baudin.
Historical events & Remarks.
The eleventh. The weather remained fine, but the winds were constantly from the west south-west quarter, which was not at all convenient for us. Running the northern tack towards the west to try to close with the land, of which we had not yet had sight although we should not have been far distant.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 41° 21' 33" and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us at 146° 39' 30". But we had recognized that it was losing, so that we found ourselves only the further distant from the coast.
In the afternoon, the sky became clouded with clouds, became sometimes dark and even rainy. But from the movement of the barometer, this did not appear to have any consequence, which is why we endeavoured to close with the land.
During the night, we found the sea very heavy from the south-east. The winds were then from the east to north-east quarter, very variable and almost calm.
At noon, we thought we caught sight of the land to the west, and certainly we should have had good sight of it if the horizon had not been so clouded in that quarter.
In the evening, a general cleaning of the ship was carried out, and it was not without need, for it had been neglected since our departure from the Bay of Adventure. When it was finished, the vessel was perfumed in all its parts, as well as the sick-bay.
Most of them complained loudly that I wished to let them die at sea by not seeking to put into a place where they might obtain some relief. So much so that, regardless of the personal privations I was making to give them fresh meat which I might have consumed, they regarded me as the principal cause of their illnesses for keeping the sea too long. The officers and the learned men murmured no less and blamed, if not directly me, at least the physician, telling him at every moment that he was deceiving me about their situation, number and appearance, saying they would all die.
Since I did not see it in the same way as all these gentlemen, I continued to keep the sea rather than be obliged to return a fourth time to this coast which, through their fault, was not finished at the time when, unfortunately, I found myself ill so as not to have taken advantage of an opportunity as favourable as that which presented itself then, since it had been traversed three times from north to south and from south to north.
1802-05-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to south. At 10.15, 12° 16' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 41° 54' 9" of latitude observed and in 151° 16' 36" of longitude by account. At 3.30, 10° 53' 40" of NE variation.

1802-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW to south and SW. At 6 and 9 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twelfth. We had the winds from the north-east, fair breeze, but often misty skies and rain. However, when the squalls had passed, the weather was tolerably fine. We steered for the land, all sails set.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 41° 22' 53" and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us at 145° 46' 9", which proved it had a difference to the east, since we had no more than a very uncertain sight of the land, given the state of the sky and the horizon which was not very extensive. However, at two o'clock in the afternoon, the sky having cleared, we saw it distinctly, although still very distant.
During the evening, although the weather was not of the most convenient and we often had squalls and rain, we came within a league and a half, or at most, of the distance, my intention being to pass the night working to windward in this position so as to be able to continue the bearing of the coast from the next day by standing to the south to reach the point where we had already begun. But during the night, the weather became so bad that we had to make sail to get a little offshore. The rain was so abundant and continuous that we were greatly inconvenienced by it. The sky was so black and dark that we bumped into one another when we had to manoeuvre without seeing each other, and often we mistook one manoeuvre for another. If we had been absolutely short of water, it would undoubtedly have been a fine opportunity to collect it, and I am persuaded that within a quarter of an hour one could have filled a cask. This weather lasted all the night without the least interruption, and since the barometer did not fall below 28 inches five lines, in such bad weather, I remained persuaded that it would not last long and that we might have a change in our favour for the next day. During the night, we steered to the south taking as much east as was possible when the winds permitted so as not to find ourselves too far afloat on the coast should they not become favourable for the next day.
1802-06-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 41° 55' 27" of latitude observed and in 150° 44' 36" of longitude by account. At 3.15, 11° 57' 20" of NE variation; a flat calm. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the ENE and we shaped the course S 45° W.

1802-06-02.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SSW, almost calm. At 4 a flat calm. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the ENE; rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail. Shook out all the reefs.
1802-06-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The thirteenth. I was much deceived in my expectation. The weather was infinitely worse than the day before and the rain equally continuous and abundant. I had the lead cast several times during the night without finding bottom at 78 and 65 fathoms, which led me to believe that I was at least three leagues from the coast, but it was at most.
The weather not permitting us to carry much canvas, we were successively obliged to furl the fore-topgallant sail, the fore-topsail, and to take all reefs in the mainsail, which, with the state of the sea, did not fail to greatly increase the drift and make the course very bad. For I feared, if there was no change, that we should not be able to double Schouten Island, and it was hardly possible to go about with the north-east winds very variable, now towards the east, now towards the north, and never from the east towards the south.
According to our dead reckoning, we were at noon at 41° 42' 5" and our longitude, equally estimated, was 146° 15' 7", but very doubtful, from the weather we had had. During the morning, thunder and hail did not fail us. I greatly regretted that our lightning-conductors were not in place, but since our topgallant masts had been unrigged, they were, for the moment, useless to us. This storm lasted from ten in the morning until noon and, as it remained long very close to the vessel, there was to be feared that it would cause us some damage in our masts if the consequences should be more unfortunate to us.
During the evening, the rain was less continuous; the winds remained always from the east to east-north-east in squalls and strong gusts. Which, to my great regret, obliged us to constantly hold the southern tack towards the east and made me always fear that we should not be able to double Schouten Island which projects a little more to the east than the eastern coast of Van Diemen's Land.
During the night, I set as much sail as possible to support myself against the drift and not to be driven upon the coast, which gave me considerable anxiety although the course I had made before should have worked me a little off the coast. We cast the lead several times without finding bottom and I believed myself out of danger.
1802-06-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind freshening by degrees to a strong breeze, a very high sea. At 11.30 the course was given S 33° 45' W. At noon in 42° 29' 9" of latitude by account and in 149° 36' 6" of longitude by account. The wind was from NE to E.

1802-06-03.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from NE to east and ESE. At 8 a.m. took in the studdingsails and lowered the main jib to half mast.
1802-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The fourteenth. In the morning, at six o'clock, I cast the lead again, estimating myself to be abeam of Schouten Island or at least nearly so. Having had no bottom at four o'clock, at 70 and 80 fathoms, I did not expect to find it and believed myself far enough offshore to have nothing more to fear from the bad weather which continued always without the least sign of change, so taken up was the entire horizon. But against my expectation, we found bottom at 55 fathoms, rocks and large stones. This news was certainly not agreeable to me, and yet I had to make little of it so as not to cast dismay throughout the vessel. However, as I had the bell rung to bring all hands on deck, I ordered that the vessel go about at once to put on the other tack. The few men there were to manoeuvre made this evolution long and it lasted more than half an hour. Fortunately for us the winds served us as we wished on this occasion, in that they shifted to the east-south-east and made the other tack quite good for us notwithstanding the drift which was three-quarters although we had close-hauled our mainsail to have less of it. Since we knew this coast well enough to know that one must be very close to it to find 55 fathoms, I am persuaded that we were not, when we went about, more than a league or a league and a quarter from it.
During the morning and for the rest of the day, we forced the vessel to try to work to the east in that there was no longer any doubt that the weather we had had for three days was the beginning of a gale and it was necessary to put ourselves in a position to support it without adding to other fears that which is the most disagreeable of all, and which is to be driven upon the coast.
At noon, our estimated latitude placed us at 42° 21' 41" and according to our dead reckoning, we could be four leagues from the coast.
