In the evening, there was no sign of change in the weather. The squalls, on the contrary, became stronger and more continuous than they had been. We did not reduce sail. Our masts, which we had tested more than once, did not, it is true, give us great anxiety. But the most fortunate thing for us, notwithstanding the bad weather, was to see the winds range to the south-east and thus put us in a position to stand offshore to be without fear.
During the night, the weather was truly bad and it was even the roughest that we had had up to then. The winds shifted to the south-south-east without diminishing in force. The sea became extremely heavy and we were often inconvenienced by it. The thunder had disappeared during the evening and we did not hear it rumble during the night.
1802-06-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from ENE to SE. At noon in 44° 54' 39" of latitude by account and in 146° 14' 54" of longitude by account. At noon shaped the course S 45° W and at 3.30 S 56° 15' W. The 15th [Prairial, 4 June 1802]. Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSW. At 3 a.m. the course was given S 67° 30' W, and at noon S 78° 45' W. At noon in 45° 39' 52" of latitude observed, in 141° 43' 48" of longitude by account and 142° 40' 0" of longitude by the watches. At 3.30, 8° 13' 40" of NE variation. The wind falling away at the close of day.

1802-06-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze, a high sea. At 3.30 shaped our course S 56° 15' W. From SE to SSE.
1802-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The fifteenth. The weather was absolutely the same as the day before, and if it was not worse as to the wind, the squalls and the gusts, at least the sea was very heavy. A long hollow and elevated wave seemed to threaten us at every moment to engulf us, and I constantly feared to see some break on board when they came to break against the side of the vessel. We were quits for the fright on this day, and we lost only our lee bulwark which was carried away by one that entered by the bow of the vessel. The fastenings of our anchors which were secured in such a way as to have nothing to fear from this quarter were so shaken that it wanted little for them to have been overturned, which would have inconvenienced us all the more as they were in the cathead. We had to set about promptly to secure them again and this with ten men from the two watches who were all that remained in good health of the rest of the crew.
At noon, the observed latitude placed us at 41° 18' 27" and the longitude at 147° 33' 15". There was then no appearance of change in the weather, and the movement of the barometer did not indicate that it should be soon. We had taken reefs in the lower sails to relieve our masts. But in close-hauling the foresail, it was torn. We put the fore-topsail and the fore-topmast staysail in its place. The vessel behaved very well under this canvas and the mainsail.
During the night, the squalls and the gusts were more continuous and even stronger than they had been during the day. But we had the good fortune of having nothing to change in the arrangement of our sails for it would have been impossible to do so, having only four men able to remain on deck including the officer of the watch. This decided me to run before the wind and seek Port Jackson, being no longer able to keep the sea.
It is much against my will that I was obliged to renounce completing the full reconnaissance of the eastern coast of Van Diemen's Land. But it is none the less true that it is solely the fault of the officers who, not knowing that one must not lose a moment at sea, neglected to do it while we were searching for our boat, under the pretext that Citizen Boulanger was occupied with it and that they did not wish to compete with him on this subject. All this would not have happened if, at that unfortunate period, I had not been greatly indisposed, and we should be in a very different position from that in which we find ourselves.

1802-06-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running; the wind, at first a strong breeze, fell away as it hauled from south to SW. At noon the course was set S 78° 45' W.
1802-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The sixteenth. In the morning, we had some hope of change in the weather. It was announced to us by the barometer which seemed about to rise. However, there was still a strong breeze and squalls, but as we were running before the wind with the winds from the south, they seemed to us less violent and more bearable.
As soon as it was daylight, we set about changing the foresail and with the few people there were able to work, it was bent to the yard by ten o'clock. A reef was taken in it and it was set. The sea was still heavy, the swell hollow and deep, but the ship making good progress, we had little to fear.
During the morning, we occasionally saw the sun, and at noon we were even able to observe the latitude, which was found to be 38° 41' 3", whereas the dead reckoning placed us only at 39° 3' 51". It is true that the observed latitude was a little doubtful, but it cannot differ as much as that given by the dead reckoning from the course travelled.
In the afternoon, the weather continued squally with gusts, but less strong than usual. The sky also became misty and less laden. We continued to steer to the north-north-east to double the western eastern point that terminates the land of New Holland and which the English have named Cape Kamhaw.
Towards evening, the breeze fell greatly although the squalls were still frequent. We had no doubt of a change in our favour, especially as the winds began to range to the south towards the west.
During the night, we doubled the point I have just mentioned and continued the same course until midnight when we took that of north a quarter north-east so as not to make too much easting.
The sea, though more calm, was still very heavy and rough. And as we had the wind nearly astern, the vessel rolled greatly. We consoled ourselves with the certainty we had that the weather would be finer and more favourable for the next day. We had all had need of it, and especially the crew to dry their clothes which for six days had been so soaked as no longer to serve them.
1802-06-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to W. At 10.30, 9° 20' 10" of NE variation. At noon in 44° 53' 33" of latitude observed and in 140° 26' 54" of longitude by account. At 3 the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts during the night. I had the watch from 8 until midnight; and fearing to draw some rudeness from the captain, I kept the topsails hoisted throughout my watch, at the risk of seeing the topmasts come down at every pitch. The ship laboured a great deal and made 2 inches of water an hour, whereas at Port Jackson she made none. The captain, in spite of all he had been told at Sydney (Governor King said to him as he left, "I hope to see you back here within a month"), was determined to go looking for southerly winds to the south.

1802-06-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from W to SW. At 12.15 wore onto the starboard tack. At 8 blowing hard in gusts. A very high sea.
1802-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The seventeenth. We were not disappointed in our expectation. The weather was fine though with small squalls and rain now and then, but it was not abundant and of short duration. As soon as it was daylight, we steered to the north-west to close with the land which by my dead reckoning was at twenty-five leagues at the latitude where I then was. The sea was no longer agitated except by the aftermath of the wind which had prevailed, and the swell had greatly diminished. We were able to let out a reef in our topsails. And so as not to lose time, we kept the reefs in the lower sails for it would have taken the greater part of the day to get our lower yards to their posts with the few men I had; moreover I doubt if we should have succeeded, at least judging by the time it took to let out a reef in the topsails and hoist them.
This day was entirely taken up in cleaning the inside of the vessel which the great number of sick that I had had put in a sad state.
Those who were well dried some of their clothing, and if the weather continues fine on the day following this, they will be in a position to use them.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 36° 37' 43", but a little doubtful in that at the moment of the sun's meridian passage a squall deprived us of the sight. Departing from this latitude, an hour angle taken in the evening gave for the longitude by the timekeeper 150° 29' 30". But according to our subsequent observations, we should be further east by about one degree.
During the evening, the weather continued fine and always accompanied by some squalls of little consequence. We followed the north-west course until eight o'clock when we took that of north for the night.
During the night of the 17th to the 18th, we continued to steer north to work up promptly to the latitude of Port Jackson where I expected to find the winds more manageable and accompanied by fewer squalls than those we had had for several days.
1802-06-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from SSW to WNW. At 4.15, in wearing ship, the foresail was torn from its bolt-rope. We lay to and bent another foresail. The wind fell and was a fresh breeze at 10; filled and stood on. At noon in 46° 9' 23" of latitude observed and in 140° 12' 48" of longitude by account. In the evening the captain gave orders to serve 6 ounces of boiled wheat for the crew's breakfast and as much for supper, and 6 ounces of beef or 4 ounces of salt pork with half a pound of bread for dinner. On the morning of the 18th at breakfast the crew would not eat the boiled wheat and gave it to the pigs; they asked that bread be made for them instead from the flour and bran, and the captain granted it.

1802-06-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to W and NW. At 8 went about onto the starboard tack. In the forenoon Mabulot, gunner, received 15 lashes with a rope's end for striking the second gunner's mate. On the evening of the 17th the rations were reduced as is known. For breakfast 6 ounces of boiled wheat were served, and for dinner half a pound of bread, 6 ounces of beef and four ounces of salt pork. This measure did not take effect until the morning of the 18th.
1802-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The eighteenth. At daybreak, we left the northerly course to steer more to the west so as to see the land of which I flattered myself to have good sight before nightfall. The weather, which was tolerably fine in the morning and the sky fairly clear, changed suddenly. The rain, the squalls and the gusts recommenced as vigorously as before. Nevertheless, we continued to steer for the land until five o'clock, when the weather showing all signs of becoming very bad for the night, I changed my intention to go a little offshore.
At noon, in a break in the clouds, we were able to observe the sun's altitude which placed us at 34° 21' 40", so that we had only about ten leagues left to make to the north to be at the latitude of Port Jackson.
A little before sunset, the wind became so violent and the squalls so continuous that we were obliged to close-reef the fore-topsail and the fore-topgallant sail as well as our mainsail. We also took the third reef in the main-topsail.
I was vexed, from the threatening appearance of the sky, to have run so close to the shore during the day in that it would become very difficult to work off the coast if the wind should continue. Although we were heading north-east, the drift was so considerable that notwithstanding the variation was in our favour, the course barely made good was north.
Nevertheless, as during the night we had no sight of land with an horizon estimated to have four leagues' extent, I believed myself in complete safety. The barometer which, moreover, had not fallen during the day, led me to think that this squall would not last long.
During the night of the 18th to the 19th, the weather was absolutely bad and the squalls and gusts very violent. It was hardly possible for us to carry our mainsail notwithstanding all reefs, if we had been able to use it. In a short time, the sea became as heavy as in the gale we had experienced two days before this new squall.
A man named Racine, master of the hold, died during the night from the effects of scurvy with which he had long been afflicted. I much fear we shall lose many more attacked by this cruel disease in its third degree if the weather does not change soon.
1802-06-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to N. At 10, 9° 20' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 46° 25' 34" of latitude observed and in 138° 56' 12" of longitude by account. At nightfall the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts. A very high sea; the pitching very hard, and because of the sea and the canvas carried it strained the ship extremely.

1802-06-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea and the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NNW. The wind freshened steadily; by midnight it was blowing hard. The fore staysail halliard parted and the main topsail split.
1802-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The nineteenth. The weather was even worse than the day before. The squalls, the gusts and the heavy wind reigned all day without the least interruption. The sea, becoming very heavy, caused us such considerable drift that had we been near the coast it would have been difficult for us to work off it. Especially as the two tacks were worthless, the winds being from the east-south-east variable to the east.
We were surrounded all day by checkerboard petrels, other petrels, and other birds of ill omen. But as I estimated myself at least fifteen leagues from the coast, I was without anxiety. The barometer, moreover, falling little, I hoped that from moment to moment this squall would cease.
At noon, the estimated latitude placed us at 33° 41' 34" and according to the last observation of longitude, ours was 150° 26' 48". But we made little of it, knowing that the timekeeper was running slow by nearly a degree and a half.
During the evening, and especially towards the end of the day, the weather seemed about to change and clear up. In several parts of the horizon, the sky was clear and the view extended tolerably far. We had no sight of land at sunset.
The hope of seeing the weather clear up was not of long duration. About seven o'clock in the evening, the misty squalls, sometimes rainy, and the gusts, recommenced as vigorously as before and lasted the greater part of the night. At eight o'clock, we took the north-north-east tack with east winds which, having shifted to east-south-east, allowed us to steer north and even a little to windward.
Our sick, during this day, and especially the scorbutic patients, found themselves worse than usual and their pains were more acute. However, the weather was less humid than in the past. Was it the approach of the coast or the warning of some coming squalls which caused them this greater discomfort? This is what the physicians could not decide and still less understand.
1802-06-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from N to WSW, a high sea. At 4.15 the fore staysail halliard parted and the sail was split; we unbent it. At 10 the main topsail split and was repaired. At noon in 46° 51' 10" of latitude by account and in 135° 29' 10" of longitude by account. In a gust the mainsail tack parted, and for all the speed with which it was clewed up the sail was split and had to be unbent. At 1 the captain assembled the officers to have their opinion on what remained to be done in the situation we were in. There were only 37 days' provisions left aboard, and could we hope, on half rations, to be at Mauritius within 74 days? It was decided to put back to Port Jackson. Accordingly at 2.15 we bore away N 67° 30' E, and at 4, N 56° 15' E. At 6 the weather cleared and the wind fell.

1802-06-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea, from W to WSW and WNW. In the gusts the [one word illegible] of the mainsail parted, and for all the speed with which it was clewed up, the sail was torn from its bolt-rope; we unbent it at once. At 1 the captain held a council on what remained for us to do in the situation we were in: there were only 37 days' provisions left on board, and could we hope to reach Mauritius in 74 days on half rations? It was decided to put back to Port Jackson. After taking the second reef in the main topsail we wore onto the starboard tack and headed N 67° 30' E.
1802-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twentieth. The weather, though no finer than the preceding days, was nevertheless more pleasant and less bad. The winds having shifted to the south-east, the squalls were less frequent and the sky clearer. Although there was a very strong breeze, I had the fore-topsail and the fore-topgallant sail set, steering to the south-west to close with the land so as to be able to lodge for the winter at the first opportunity that should present itself.
Throughout the morning, it blew strongly, but as we were running with the wind a little on the beam the gusts seemed less severe than those we had endured the preceding days, although they seemed to me nearly the same except only that the sky was infinitely finer. The barometer, which since the middle of the night had been continuously falling, seemed to announce that the fine weather would not last long and even to be on our guard since it was no more than 28 inches one line, 28 feet 4, a height at which it had remained during the height of this last squall.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 49' 47", which placed us nearly at the latitude of Port Jackson, and the timekeeper gave for longitude 149° 33' 12". This result, with the difference to the west which we supposed it to have according to our previous observations, placed us about 25 leagues from the coast.
Throughout the evening, we steered west a few degrees south and made good progress. The sky was tolerably fine when the squalls had passed, but the sea singularly agitated and rough.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st, the winds were favourable to us and the sea manageable. The gusts, although good, were less rough than they had been during the day, and the weather seemed likely to be finer for the next day.
We held during the night the course to the east towards the south so as not to be carried too far north either by the current or by the drift which the state of the sea caused to the vessel.
1802-06-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from WSW to NW. At noon in 45° 55' 28" of latitude by account and in 138° 30' 54" of longitude by account. The mainsail and the fore staysail were bent.

1802-06-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a light breeze from WSW and south. A new mainsail was bent.
1802-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-first. The hope we had had during the night of seeing the weather clear up was soon dispelled. At daybreak, the sky became covered again with dark and heavy clouds. The squalls, the squalls accompanied by rain resumed and lasted the greater part of the morning and prevented us from carrying sail.
Our sick found themselves greatly inconvenienced on this day, and two more entered the sick-bay, attacked by scurvy. So that our force for working the vessel was so diminished that we could do nothing without being obliged to bring both watches on deck, which did not fail to fatigue extremely those to whom there remained any strength.
At noon, we had no observed latitude and that of the dead reckoning placed us at 33° 55' 28", so that we needed only a day of fine weather and fair wind to reach the port.
In the afternoon, the weather having cleared a little, we sighted the land. It lay to us from west-south-west to north-west a quarter north, if indeed it was land, for we had not any assured certainty of it and it might very well be that what we took for land was nothing else than a bar of mist.
Although the weather was dark and humid, and the breeze more moderate, the squalls were none the less frequent and the sea always driven by a swell strongly elevated from the south to south-south-west.
The night of the 21st to the 22nd had nothing particular except that the squalls became less frequent with the south winds variable towards the west. The sky was even fairly clear at times and we finally counted on seeing the bad weather soon cease although the movement of the barometer was slow to rise above 28 inches.
We made only two tacks in the 24 hours. The weakness of the crew did not permit us to multiply them too much so as to leave them some moments more for the rest of which they had the greatest need.
1802-06-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the breeze light from SW to E. At noon in 44° 38' 14" of latitude observed and in 139° 14' of longitude by the watches. At 3.45, 8° 40' 50" of NE variation.

1802-06-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, light rain, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to east and NE. At 8.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.
1802-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 3 hours 15' the part of land which could be perceived in the mist, remained from west-south-west to north-west a quarter north.
At noon, the land visible extended from south-west to north-west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-second. The weather was not as fine as it had seemed likely to become on the 21st. Nevertheless, we continued the western tack to come and recognize the land. Our estimated latitude placing us at that of Port Jackson. The weather, at daybreak, was calm and with small squalls, but it became misty and the horizon not very extensive.
At half-past seven, we had good sight of the land and closed with it at about two leagues' distance. The manner in which the shore was presented on which the sea broke greatly, made me perceive that we were probably north of the latitude of the port and this fear was but too confirmed by the observation of the sun's meridian passage, for our latitude was found to be 33° 26' 49" whereas that according to our dead reckoning was 34° 0' 4". We had taken the south-east tack some time before the observation so as not to have the sun over the land in order to be more certain of our true position.
After the observation of the sun at noon, we continued to steer to the south-east by a very strong breeze from the south a quarter south-west to south-south-west. But we could not increase sail, the wind being too strong and the sea too rough. However, our officers who are learned men thought the breeze was fine and the sea fine. I think that if they had been in command, they would have set the topgallant sails to confirm their talent to the high opinion they have of their knowledge. As for myself, who was guided only by my own in wondering that he could not gain to windward, I kept the reefs in the lower sails and all those in the topsails, not even wishing them to set the mainsail which it would not have been possible to furl during the day and still less during the night if the squalls of the preceding days had returned.
In the afternoon, we truly had the appearance of seeing the weather clear up. Although there was little variation in the wind, this hope was not confirmed by the barometer which remained in the same state as it had been during the gusts. However, the night being very fine and the sky clear, everything seemed to announce to us that we were at the end of the bad weather.
1802-06-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather. A breeze from NNE to ESE, and calm. At noon in 44° 43' 44" of latitude by account and in 139° 37' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-06-12.journal_anonyme: The weather, overcast at first, cleared; the sea smooth. A light breeze from ESE to SE.
1802-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five o'clock 15', in a clear space we saw the land to the W.S.W.
At noon, it extended from S.W. ¼ W to N.W. ¼ N.

Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, having gone about at midnight, we continued to make our way westward with moderate south-south-west winds and fair weather. We did not see the land at the beginning of the day, but when the sun had dispersed the fog that deprived us of the view of it, a great expanse of coast extending from west-south-west to north-north-west came into sight as we drew near. During the morning, we recognised our points of observation from the previous day, and by all appearances we had gained little ground to the south, although dead reckoning told us otherwise.
Throughout the morning, the sky was very fair, the breeze moderate, but the winds constantly from the south-south-west, much against the course we had to make to reach the latitude of Port Jackson, which everyone was longing for.
At noon, we observed the altitude of the sun of 33° 25' 7" and it was not without regret and astonishment that we found ourselves so little advanced as on the previous day. We had just lost an entire day to no purpose, whilst we had not an hour to spare to satisfy everyone and relieve our sick.
The lands to the north of Port Jackson are very high and can be perceived from far off when the weather is fair and clear. The greatest elevations do not end in an abrupt and steep slope at the water's edge as in several other parts of the coast of New Holland. They have, on the contrary, land of moderate height at the edge of the coast, and the mountains appear to extend far into the interior of the country. To the north, or at least at no great distance from Broken Bay, one sees three mountains, of which the most distant commands all the others when they come together. This indication alone will be able to make known to navigators who, like ourselves, shall be several days without being able to observe the latitude, that they are to the north of the port, and that they must advance to the south if they seek to make port of call there.
During the afternoon, the weather being quite fair, we hauled up our lower yards and shook out the reefs in the mainsails. We resumed the course to the south towards the east, the winds having shifted to the south-west.
Throughout the night, the weather remained fair and the sky constantly clear. We made what southing we could, endeavouring to regain the latitude of Port Jackson from which the winds, the drift, and the currents had driven us.
1802-06-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to ENE. At 10, 7° 12' 40" of NE variation. At noon in 44° 27' 34" of latitude observed and in 139° 50' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-06-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east. At 5.45 went onto the port tack. At 8.30 a.m. onto the starboard tack.
1802-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the northern extremity of the land in sight, remained to the north 66° W,
the southern extremity to the south 61° W.

Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, having had the finest weather possible during the night of the twenty-third, the atmosphere changed all at once, the sky became showery with squalls and the winds gusty, so that we were obliged to take a second reef in our topsails. The sea, though still fair, was driven by a heavy swell from the south which announced to us that we should soon have the winds from that quarter. But as, according to the dead reckoning of the distance covered in the twenty-four hours of the previous day, I found myself reasonably far to the south of Port Jackson, it was rather indifferent to me whether they should blow from that direction.
At eight o'clock, we took the tack to the west towards the north to close with the land, of which I flattered myself we should have sight before nightfall. At about ten o'clock, the sky, which from the morning had taken on such a bad appearance, became (fair) as suddenly as it had changed some hours before, but there continued to blow a strong breeze.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 34° 4' 46" which placed us, far from being as far south as the dead reckoning of the course we had made would have indicated. This circumstance, joined to previous observations, leads me to believe that in this season there exists on this coast a rapid current which appears to be directed towards the north-east.
During the afternoon, the weather continuing fair, we followed the tack to the west towards the north, the winds being very variable from south-west to south-south-west. In the evening, they moderated a little and we were able to shake out the reef taken in the morning in the topsails. Although we had made a reasonable distance from eight o'clock in the morning until sunset, we did not have sight of land, nevertheless it could not be far away.
The weather was so fair at sunset that we continued on the western course without reducing sail, and at ten o'clock we had a perfect sight of it, finding ourselves according to our dead reckoning about three leagues away. The winds, which then shifted to the west-south-west, obliged us to bear away to the south, which I was very pleased with at the moment, being well persuaded from the course we had just made that we must once again be to the north of Port Jackson.
1802-06-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ENE to SE. At noon in 44° 47' 10" of latitude observed and in 140° 1' 0" of longitude by the watches.

1802-06-14.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SE. At 8.30 p.m. and at 2 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the weather was very fair but the winds almost always contrary to the direct course we should have needed to make to reach Port Jackson. So many hindrances, in constant opposition to our desire to arrive speedily, put everyone in a bad humour, and the gaiety, often noisy, that ordinarily prevailed was replaced by an excess of melancholy which was not pleasant for those who know how to bear their troubles with patience and submit to events.
As we had had sight of the land during the night, we changed tack at daybreak to close with the coast, from which we found ourselves seven or eight leagues away at sunrise.
The lands we had in sight during the morning are generally high and the mountains offer few points of recognition at that distance. Nevertheless, we well recognised that these lands were new to us and had no resemblance to those we had seen when we were further to the north.
At noon, the latitude (was) observed to be 33° 48' 22", which placed us still to the north of Port Jackson, although the dead reckoning of the courses made would have placed us to the south. Until noon, there had blown a light breeze from the south-west to the south-south-west and sometimes from the south-west to the west-south-west. But calm having followed, the vessel could no longer steer and we lay across the swell for the rest of the evening and even the greater part of the night, although the sky was very cloudy and all the part of the horizon from south-east to south-west was very dark.
During the night, we sounded twice. At midnight, we had bottom at 75 fathoms and at two o'clock at 70, proof that the current and the the (sic) sea were carrying us towards the shore since the depth was decreasing.
At three o'clock, a squall, or rather a violent storm, brought us much rain, very large hail, lightning so bright we could scarcely see, and thunder to our satisfaction. This storm lasted an hour and a half without ceasing; it was more unbearable from the rain and hail than from the wind which, nevertheless, gave rather strong gusts to oblige us to haul down our topsails. As it made almost the circuit of the horizon, it obliged us to perform various maneuvers, always slow in such circumstances, and unpleasant when one lacks hands for their execution. The force of the squall having passed, we took the reefs in the topsails, the sky having a very bad appearance.
1802-06-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to NE, with rain. At noon in 44° 18' 9" of latitude observed and in 140° 37' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-06-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from east to SE. In the forenoon it freshened and blew in gusts.
1802-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 4 o'clock 45" (sic),
the lands extended from north 17° west to south 59° west.
At noon,
Broken Bay remained to the north 20° west
The northern point of Botany Bay to the south 65° west.

Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, after the storm which we had experienced towards the end of the night had passed, thunder continued to be heard in the distance, but the whole part of the horizon comprised between the south and the north-west through the west became clear and promised us fair weather for the day. It was indeed so, but the winds were so light, so fickle, and so variable that when they had force enough to make the vessel move, we were obliged constantly to work the sails to change them from one tack to the other.
From the land reconnaissance we made at daybreak, it was easy for us to perceive that, if we had not lost way to the north-east, we had at least gained very little to the south-west, which was confirmed by the observation of the sun at noon, which gave us 0' difference from the previous day, the latitude being 33° 45' 53". At this time, our distance from the coast was six or seven leagues, and it was not (without) regret that one (found oneself) so close to the port without being able to enter it.
During the evening, the calm continued until half past seven. Various parts of the horizon became charged with dark and stormy clouds. Thunder was heard in the distance, and at eight o'clock, one of these storms fell upon us. It was much less violent than the one we received the previous day and lasted only half an hour. As it came from the south-west, we took a second reef in the topsails and went about to seaward, so that it would not drive us too much towards the shore, from which we were three leagues away (in another hand: ?) and in 75 fathoms of hard bottom.
During the night, the sky cleared and the storms disappeared. We heard thunder often rumbling, but in the direction of the coast, and although the light breeze that blew came from the south-west to the west-south-west, they dissipated without reaching us. The various tacks that the variability of the winds obliged us to make served only to take us away from the land which we not only did not see again during the night, despite the fair horizon, but also lost the bottom which we did not find at a hundred fathoms.
1802-06-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 43° 31' 52" of latitude observed and in 142° 22' 6" of longitude by account.

1802-06-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At 6 p.m. and at 6 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, the weather continued fair and the winds shifted to the south-west, somewhat variable to the west, and there blew a good breeze during the morning which we spent beating to windward.
It was not without astonishment that, when the day was far enough advanced for us to recognise the land, we saw that the currents had carried us to the north-east six or seven leagues, which was all the more unpleasant for us because the winds had shifted to the south-west and we had to run again to the south-south-east to regain our latitude.
So many hindrances, and so continuous, served only to increase the sadness that reigned on board, and each man, not bearing his troubles with patience, prepared new torments for himself by the displeasure of not being able to be set ashore according to his desires.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 33° 30' 42" which confirmed the remarks made on the occasion of sighting the land in the morning. We had held the coastal tack until then, which brought us almost to the entrance of Broken Bay (the two words Broken Bay written in another hand).
After the observation of the sun, we took the offshore tack to steer once more to the south, and I decided to continue it as long as possible so as to see whether, since there was no sign of the wind changing, I would be more fortunate in subsequently closing with the coast from the south.
During the evening and part of the night, the breeze was light. Nevertheless, we found the sea agitated and even heavy with swell. About seven o'clock, we had a storm which gave us some rain and little wind. It was not of long duration.
As soon as it had passed, the winds became variable from south-west to west-south-west, which rendered them fit for the course we had to make to the south, but absolutely contrary for closing with the coast. We had fair weather all night and a fresh breeze.
1802-06-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 43° 47' 10" of latitude observed and in 142° 52' 24" of longitude by account. At 4 the land was sighted to the east.

1802-06-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SSE to south. At 4 sighted Van Diemen's Land in the east. At 4.45 p.m. and at 4.30 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the breeze, always variable from west-south-west to south-west, became so strong that we had to furl our mainsail and take a second reef in the topsails. While we were occupied with this manoeuvre, we discovered a sail ahead and coming towards us. As soon as the reefs were taken, we went about to go to meet her. As we drew near, we thought we recognised Mr. Flinders' vessel and she had indeed the appearance of it. But when we were no more than a small distance away, I judged her to be a vessel newly departed from the port and bound for whaling, from the quantity of boats with which she was surrounded.
As this vessel was running on the opposite tack, we joined company with her promptly. She hoisted English colours and we replied with ours. As she passed our stern, she told me she came from Port Jackson and was bound for whaling. I asked her for news of Mr. Flinders, whom she informed me had arrived at the port. She also informed me that the Naturaliste had made port of call there. As she told me she had something to say to me and was about to lower her boat, we discontinued the conversation until her arrival.
1802-06-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to S, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 44° 2' 51" of latitude observed and in 142° 44' 0" of longitude by account.

1802-06-18.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SE. At 5 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same.
1802-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
[Day missing from the Soviche edition, transcribed by eye from the BnF typescript copy (SG MS4-33), view 501. The manuscript narrative stops on 28 Prairial; the copy notes: "The historical events and remarks stop here; the astronomical observations etc. continue as follows."]
From the 28th to the 29th Prairial (18 June 1802).
Course north 27° east. Distance run 44 3/10 miles. South latitude by reckoning 33° 42' 45", observed 33° 31' 49". East longitude by chronometer no. 35, estimated 148° 28' 42". Hygrometer 87°. Barometer 27 inches 0 lines 11. Thermometer 10°.
1802-06-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 44° 12' of latitude observed and in 143° 32' of longitude by the watches. Saw several whales. At 3 the land was sighted from north to N 22° E, about 24 miles off. At 8 shaped the course SE.

1802-06-19.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a swell running, a light breeze from south, SW and SSE. At 3 Van Diemen's Land was sighted; it stretched from north to N 22° 30' E. At 4.15 p.m. and at 8.30 changed tacks.
1802-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 29th to the 30th Prairial (19 June 1802).
Course south 35° east. Distance run 40 miles. South latitude by reckoning 34° 4' 13", observed 33° 52' 33". East longitude by reckoning 148° 11' 6". Hygrometer 87°. Barometer 28 inches 1 line. Thermometer 11°.
1802-06-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to W. At 8 the course was given east; at 9.30, N 78° 45' E; and at noon, N 67° 30' E. At noon in 44° 41' 33" of latitude observed and in 144° 43' of longitude by account. At 6 the course was given N 45° E, and at midnight N 22° 30' E.

1802-06-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SW. At noon the course was set N 67° E. At 6.30 land was sighted in various quarters from N 67° 30' W as far as S 67° 30' W. At 8 it stretched from N 64° W to S 85° W. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island N 86° W.
1802-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 30th Prairial to the 1st Messidor (20 June 1802).
Course south 43° west. Distance run 24 6/10 miles. South latitude by reckoning 34° 11' 9", observed 33° 54' 53". East longitude by reckoning 147° 50' 54". Hygrometer 86°. Barometer 28 inches 3 lines. Thermometer 11°.
1802-06-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 6 the course was given north, and at noon N 11° 15' W. At 6.30 the land was sighted from N 68° W to S 68° W. At noon in 42° 51' 16" of latitude observed and in 146° 56' 24" of longitude by account, the middle of Maria Island bearing from us N 86° W. At 4 it bore S 65° W, and the high land of Schouten Island and Peninsula from S 80° W to N 77° W.

1802-06-21.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth. A fresh breeze from W to WNW. At noon the course was set N 11° 15' W. At 4 took the bearing of the middle of Maria Island S 65° W and the high land of the Schouten islands and peninsulas from S 80° W to N 77° W. At daybreak the land was sighted a long way off from the crosstrees; it stretched from N 34° W to S 22° W. At noon in sight in the west at a very great distance.
1802-06-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW to WSW. At daybreak the land was sighted as far as the eye could reach. At noon in 40° 32' of latitude observed and in 147° 11' 36" of longitude by account. The land in sight to the west as far as the eye could reach. At 3, 11° 4' 10" of NE variation. At 8 the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts.

1802-06-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from W to WSW and SW. At 8 p.m. it freshened and blew in gusts. At 6 a.m. the land in sight in the NW. At 8 it stretched as far as N 15° 15' E. The course was given north and then N 11° 15' E. At noon the land from N 15° W to S 44° W.
1802-06-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SW. At 6.30 the land was sighted in the N 45° W; at 8 it stretched as far as N 11° 15' E. The course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 37° 35' 40" of latitude observed and in 147° 38' 0" of longitude by account. The land from N 15° W to S 44° W, 5 miles off. The wind fell and was a fresh breeze. At 6.30 a fire was seen abeam.

1802-06-23.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW. At 4 the land from N 16° W to S 4° W. At 6.30 saw a fire abeam. At 8 a.m. the land from N 20° W to S 21° W. At noon took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 5° W, the Pigeon House S 86°, and the end of the land S 39° W. Almost calm. The corvette was painted.
1802-06-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WSW to S. At noon in 35° 24' 55" of latitude observed and in 148° 7' 6" of longitude by account. Long Nose Point bore from us N 5° W, the Pigeon House S 68° W, the southernmost end of the land in sight S 39° W. The corvette was painted. At 2 almost calm; the air varied from S to N by way of east, and at 4 settled in the north. It freshened from NNE to NNW. At 4 took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 6° W, the middle of the entrance to Jervis Bay N 18° W, the Pigeon House S 67° W.

1802-06-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3 a light air from the north drew round at once to the east and we wore onto the port tack. At 4 took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 6° W, the middle of Jervis Bay N 18° W, the Pigeon House S 67° W, the southernmost visible end of the land S 27° W. At 2 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack. The wind drew round to the north and freshened. At 9.15 a.m. sighted a ship abeam standing on the opposite tack. The cables were bent. Obs. lat. 34° 59' 27"; est. long. 148° 38' 42".
1802-06-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to N. At daybreak a ship was sighted in the NNW. At 9.15 she was abeam; we showed our colours and she did not answer. At 9.30, 13° 13' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 59' 27" of latitude observed and in 148° 38' 42" of longitude by account. The land from W to N 65° W. The cables were bent and the anchors got ready to let go.

1802-06-25.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from north. At 2 p.m. and at 6.15 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same. At 11 very high land was sighted from N 56° W to W. Obs. lat. 34° 20' 22"; est. long. 148° 16' 36". Var. 13° 13' 20" NE.
1802-06-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NW. At 11 the land was sighted from N 56° W to W. At noon in 34° 20' 22" of latitude observed and in 148° 16' 36" of longitude by account. Continual rain during the night.

1802-06-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from N, NW, SW and south. At 1, at 6 and at 9 changed tacks. At 2 a.m., at 5 and at 9 changed tacks. At 8 the land in sight but very hazy. Est. lat. 34° 1' 28"; est. long. 148° 27' 30".
1802-06-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to SSE. At 8 the land was in sight but very hazy. At noon in 34° 1' 28" of latitude by account and in 148° 27' 30" of longitude by account. At 6 a ship's light was thought to be seen in the S 22° W at a short distance.

1802-06-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 4 and at 8 p.m. changed tacks; at 1.30 the same. At 7 sighted the land from N 45° W to S 45° W. Got the port anchor ready to let go. At 10.15 hove to with the main topsail to the wind, the land at a short distance. Obs. lat. 34° 23' 33"; est. long. 148° 15' 12".
1802-06-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At 7 the land was sighted from N 45° W to S 45° W. At 10.15 we hove to to wait for the noon altitude; our reckoning put us abreast of Port Jackson, which could not be seen. At noon, having found 34° 23' 33" of latitude, we filled and stood on and ran along the coast a mile off. At 4 the captain gave the order for every man to his station to go to the anchorage. We showed our colours and fired a swivel gun. At 5, being off the mouth of Port Jackson and able to run in, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 5.30 the lighthouse of the port bore from us S 85° W, 2 miles off. At 6.30 and at 7 the lighthouse light S 68° W, and at 11 S 74° W. The weather turned overcast and the wind freshened; at 9 went onto the port tack.

1802-06-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south, SE and ESE. At noon filled and stood in to close the land; after coming very near it we ran along it at a mile's distance. At 5 p.m., being off the mouth of Port Jackson, we lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the lighthouse light bearing S 85° W. At 9 went onto the port tack. At 4 a.m. hove to; at 8 filled and stood on. At 9.30 a.m. we shaped our course to run into the port, and at 11.30 we anchored between Middle Head and South Head. Lat. 34° 3' 9"; long. 148° 26' 12". The latitude determined at the observatory was 33° 51' 10" and the longitude 149° 5'. Var. 9° 40' 0" NE. We found the commander there, arrived 10 days before; he had three quarters of his crew in hospital. The captain went aboard the commander and from there ashore, which was his place of residence.
1802-06-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE. At midnight went onto the starboard tack; at 3 back onto the port tack. At 4 hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 7 filled and stood west for the land. At 7.30 hove to again with the port side to the wind. At 8 filled and stood on close-hauled on the port tack and made sail. At 9.30 the entrance to Port Jackson was sighted S 22° W; we shaped our course to run in. At 11.30 we anchored between South Head and Middle Head, North Head bearing N 65° E, South Head S 87° E, Camp Cove S 25° E, Bradleys Head S 25° W and Middle Head N 37° W. As soon as we were anchored the pilot came aboard and wanted to make us get under way to take us to Neutral Bay, but the captain would not. The pilot told us that the Géographe had been at Port Jackson since the 1st Messidor [20 June 1802]; that she had arrived with her crew in their cots, and that Governor King had sent him men and boats to warp her to Neutral Bay. The captain at once sent off the Géographe's boat, with her people and an officer of ours, to inform the commander of our arrival.

1802-11-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Year 11 of the French Republic.
The twenty-sixth. At daybreak, with everyone on board, everything was prepared for getting under way. The winds were then from the west very light, but persuaded that they would increase as the sun rose above the horizon, we set sail, having moreover the tide with us.
To get our anchor apeak, we had to use the heavy tackle so envasated was it found. The efforts made to heave it with the cable were not only fruitless but also harmful, for the cable was broken.
During the night that preceded our departure, a general search was made through the vessel to ensure there was no one hidden. We had all the more reason to believe we would find no one since on the preceding days nine men and a woman had been put ashore who had taken refuge there. However, we found still twelve more who were also sent back.
At five o'clock, being under sail and in calm, we let drift awaiting the breeze which did not declare itself until about seven o'clock in the morning. The winds came first from the northerly quarter and a few minutes later shifted to north-east. The Naturaliste, which found herself ahead and to leeward of the reef which is in the middle of the passage, being unable to double it was obliged to let drop a sheet anchor, which led me to take the course of doing the same, although it would have been easy for me to get out of the port by taking advantage of the position I was in. The Casuarina, which was following us, did not anchor for the moment and amused herself by working to windward in the vicinity of the vessel.
The American ship, the Fanny, which is sailing with us to go to Batavia by passing through Bass Strait, imitated our manoeuvre and anchored.
Having no longer hope of getting to sea that day, I sent the Casuarina to carry the astronomer Bernier to the south point of the entrance of the port so that he might determine its latitude with precision. In this interval, we found still three men hidden in our launch. I notified the port captain and the secretary of Government, who came on board after we had anchored. The first claimed the three men, but I did not deem it fitting to give them to him, merely telling him that I would act towards them as I had done towards the twelve that I had put ashore during the night. He appeared satisfied with this reply and we parted good friends.
About nine o'clock in the morning, I sent my boat to put these three men ashore under the guard of the master gunner. I was far from believing that an attempt would be made to take them from us by force, for if I could have suspected it I should have been on guard against such an attempt. Nevertheless, at the moment when they were about to be landed, the port captain's boat came alongside mine, and the men it carried being armed, obliged the men of my boat who were not armed to deliver these three men to them, whom they conducted on board the American ship the Fanny where the port captain then was.
As soon as this dishonest proceeding became known to me, I at once sent an officer to ask the port captain by what order his men or he himself had just seized one of my boats. I added that the Governor's orders concerning deserters, if there were any, were as well known to me as to himself, and that in consequence I would myself go to complain of his conduct in this circumstance and demand the satisfaction I should think proper.
The officer sent on board the American, not having found the port captain there, was informed that he was fishing in the cove opposite to which we were anchored and went to speak to him. After discharging his commission, he returned on board. And the port captain, accompanied by the secretary of Government, having followed very close behind, also arrived. I then represented to the port captain how thoughtless his conduct was in regard to what had just happened and I assured him most positively that if the Casuarina had been on board, I should have ordered him to drive away his boat and even to sink her if he had persisted, notwithstanding my prohibition, in trying to take from my boat the men I was putting ashore.
At these words, the port captain gave me his word of honour that he had nothing to do with this affair and had given no order on the subject. He offered me all the satisfaction I could desire, but I would accept none, preferring to have an interview on this subject with the Governor himself.
The port captain and the secretary of Government having withdrawn, I made signal to the Casuarina to pass astern and went to Sydney on board this vessel.
In the interview I had with M. Governor King regarding what had happened, he publicly blamed the conduct that had been held on this occasion and as proof of disapproval, he granted pardon for this time to all those who had deserted although their departure and their names were known before they were taken in my boat. I think that the port captain, on his return, will receive a lesson that will make him more circumspect in the future.
About eleven o'clock in the evening, a young English woman named Mary Bickaith presented herself on board dressed as a man. I had known her during my stay at Port Jackson and more than once she had begged me to obtain from Governor King that she might return to England as attached to M. Thomson. I had promised to interest myself for her and indeed I spoke of it to the Governor who would not have refused this request if it had not been contrary to the general instructions concerning the transported. But he told me that if she wished to leave, no search would be made regarding her. She was therefore embarked on board the Naturaliste the day before departure, but being unable to reappear in England without authentic permission from the Governor, I have taken her on board to place her somewhere in the Moluccas where her youth and age will soon have made her noticed and find a happy lot. This young lady belongs to well-born people in England and came to accompany her mother who was condemned to end her days at Port Jackson for having taken a piece of muslin from a merchant's shop where she had made some other purchases. The daughter preferred to accompany her mother in her exile rather than be sent to a convent, the only education offered to her to compensate for the loss of her mother. She is seventeen years old and interesting more by her conduct than by her prettiness.

1802-11-18.journal_anonyme: On the 26th Brumaire we lay anchored at the mouth of the port, where we had anchored. At 4.30 we hoisted our topsails and got under way, as did the commander. At 6.30, being outside the heads, the pilot left us and we steered out to sea. The winds south to S by W, a strong breeze. At 12.10 the commander made the signal to change tacks, which we did at once. Lat. 34° 1' 24"; long. 149° 19' 30".
1802-11-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock, having dismissed the pilot,
The northernmost extremity of the land in sight in this part, remained at north 3° west.
The south point of the entrance of Port Jackson at north 51° west,
The north point of the entrance of the same port at north 15° west,
The north point of the entrance of Botany Bay at south 34° west.
Historical events & remarks.
The twenty-seventh. In the morning, the weather being fine and the winds from the westerly quarter very light, we nevertheless set sail in the hope that they would increase at sunrise and that we might get out of the port. The Naturaliste, the Casuarina, and the Fanny, an American ship, did the same, and all four we directed our course to pass north of the reef which is found in the middle of the passage of the entrance to this port. Scarcely had we doubled it than the winds shifted to the south-west and south, strong breeze, so that we no longer had hope of a fine day for the rest of the day. For when the winds are from this quarter, they ordinarily blow in strong gusts with squalls and accompanied by rains, mists and thunder.
At eight o'clock, being quite clear of the port, we dismissed our pilots and held as close to the wind on the starboard tack. In the morning, we unrigged our topgallant mast as a useless burden to carry in the campaign in which we found ourselves.
In this first tack, we did not take a high opinion of the sailing of the Casuarina which did not answer our expectation. It is true that the sea was a little rough for so small a vessel, but the little canvas we had relative to her which carried all her sails did not prevent her from falling far behind. The ship the Fanny, whose sailing we had been told was remarkable, could not follow the Naturaliste with equal sails.
At noon, the observed latitude was so uncertain that we did not take it into account. The sky began from then on to become covered with clouds with very threatening appearance and thunder was heard although still in the distance.
In the afternoon, we took the coastal tack so as not to lose sight of the coast. The winds were already very fresh and we had all two reefs in our topsails. On this tack, we closed with the Casuarina which should find the weather very bad. Nevertheless, this small vessel behaved very well and shipped but little water. The tack we ran on the shore was only two hours, when we resumed that of the open sea by going about before the wind. When we changed course, the land in sight seemed to extend from north-north-west to west-south-west.
At four o'clock, we experienced a very violent storm. The lightning and the thunder followed one another with such rapidity that the sight was fatigued by the former and the head dizzy from the latter. There is no doubt that the thunder fell very close to us, and I regard myself as very fortunate that none of the vessels was struck by it. This storm lasted nearly two hours, extending from the south-west to the north-north-east.
At sunset, the rain having ceased and the storm having moved away, we could still hear it rumble for a long time, but we had nothing more to fear from it. During the night, the breeze was very uneven, the winds varied from south to south-south-east. The sky remained dark and overcast with little appearance of a fine day for the next day. The sea was very heavy and the vessel fatigued greatly, being obliged to carry little sail so as not to lose sight of the other vessels which were directing their course on our stern lantern.
1802-11-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather. At 4 a.m. Captain Hamelin took aboard the Géographe the girl he had brought aboard on the 25th. At 5.30 we got under way with the division. The wind a light breeze from the south. At 6.30, being clear of the port, the pilot left us. At 8 the wind freshened and was a strong breeze from S to SSE, the weather squally, with thunder and rain. At noon in 31° 1' 44" of latitude and 149° 19' 30" of longitude, carrying little sail on account of the Casuarina. In the afternoon, being near the vane, I had a strong electric shock; Brue and Bougainville, who were near me, felt the same shock. At nightfall, seeing no ship of the division, we lay to and showed a light.

1802-11-19.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea and a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 3 changed tacks; at 8 hoisted a light at the gaff which we kept all the watch. At 4.25 and 5.30 changed tacks. We were at first standing in to close the commander; at 7.50, he having gone about, we did the same. The land in sight from W to SW. Obs. lat. 34° 20'; long. 149° 54' 30".
1802-11-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock, the land in sight seemed to extend from west-north-west to west-south-west.
Historical events & remarks.
The twenty-eighth. The weather was scarcely more fine or convenient than the day before. The winds which during the night had varied from south to south-south-east, shifted in the morning from south-south-east to south-east, but they were so light that the vessel scarcely steered. The sea which was none the less heavy and rough, agitated us in all directions, and I feared for some time that we should have damage to our masts in that the new shrouds of our lower rigging had given much slack as a result of the first rolling which the vessel had experienced since our departure. In the morning, we held the southern tack towards the west so as not to get the land too far.
At noon, the sky being overcast, we had no observation of latitude.
During the evening, the Naturaliste and the Casuarina having closed with us, we spoke to each. The captain of the Casuarina let us know that he had fatigued greatly the last night and that his vessel had made as much as five inches of water per hour, but that was for the most part from the upper parts. At the moment when he spoke to us, it was no more than one inch in the same interval of time. I particularly recommended him to keep as close to me as possible, and not to fatigue his masts by overloading with sails when the weather was not fine, that I would always regulate myself on his sailing.
About four o'clock, the winds having shifted to the east-south-east, we had hope of having them shortly from the north-east followed by fine weather. For during our stay at Port Jackson we had seen them almost always make this change in the atmosphere. But it did not take place on this occasion, for the sky remained dark and overcast. The sea, nevertheless, became more calm and seemed to announce to us an early change.
During the night, which without being fine, was not nearly as bad as the preceding one, we made various manoeuvres so as not to get far from the other vessels and directed our course to the south when the winds permitted us to work that way.
We observed during the day that a strong current seemed to carry us violently to the south-west, which seemed to us all the more certain since when we ran the coastal tack we needed about half the time to approach the land as it had taken to move away from it.
This observation may be useful to navigators who will frequent this coast, for if during the night, one should regulate in the neighbourhood of the land, with the tacks equally long on each side, one would risk being much sooner ashore than one would have judged.
1802-11-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to E. At 4 a.m. the division was sighted and we filled and stood on. At noon the land from S 45° W to W, being in 34° 20' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 54' 30" of longitude by account. At 3 we passed under the commander's stern; he gave us the course south.

1802-11-20.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the sea less swelly, a fresh breeze from east to NE and north. At 3 passed under the Géographe's stern; she ordered us to steer south. At 4 and at 5 laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the Géographe and the Casuarina. At 6 sighted a sail in the SW; at 7 she was made out to be a schooner. The Géographe hove to and sent a boat aboard her, the distance from the land about six leagues. Obs. lat. 36° 3'; long. 149° 43' 58".
1802-11-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 6 hours 45 minutes the land in sight extended from south-west to north-west.
At noon, the lands in sight remained from north 15° west to south 45° west.
Historical events & remarks.
The twenty-ninth. In the morning, the winds seeming to want to settle in the northerly quarter towards the east, we steered to the south-south-west regulating ourselves on the sailing of the other vessels which at daybreak were all found at but little distance from us. Since the Casuarina sailed the least well of all, she prevented us from profiting as much from the fair wind as we should have done in other circumstances. But it was essential to preserve this small vessel for the utility it will be to us hereafter.
At half-past seven, having sighted a schooner ahead of us, we chased her and having joined her, we recognized that it was the same one we had already encountered at sea when my boat went astray on the coast of Van Diemen's Land. Having laid to, I sent a boat on board to see if the captain who had just again returned from the seal hunt would have some curiosity objects to give me. For at his departure from Port Jackson he had promised to bring me all he could procure.
About seven o'clock, the captain of this schooner came on board and presented me only with a wombat of extraordinary size. We learned that the schooner the Enterprise commanded by Captain Le Corre, which had put in at Port Jackson, was lost and that the captain and five men had had the misfortune of being drowned in this wreck which took place on islands named the Two Sisters situated at the north point of the Furneaux Islands. One of the interested parties in this schooner was going to Port Jackson to freight a vessel which could go to collect the debris they had saved from this wreck. Part of the crew had remained on the island with provisions and was occupied in the seal hunt until the return of this interested party in the expedition and probably the author of the voyage. According to his report, it appears that this event took place as a result of a gale while at anchor in the Bad Bay which is found to the east of this island. We all regretted the loss of Captain Le Corre whom we had known at Port Jackson and whose society was very agreeable.
At eight o'clock, we separated from this schooner which continued her course for Port Jackson and we, ours to seek the entrance of Bass Strait.
At noon we had only a very doubtful observation and on which it was impossible to rely.
In the afternoon, it continued to blow a strong breeze from the north-north-east and at four o'clock we had perfect sight of the mountain which the English have named Dromedary Mountain, very recognizable from its shape. It remained to us at north 58° west. It is one of the best points of recognition that the whole coast can offer from the Promontory to Port Jackson.
During the evening, it continued to blow a fair breeze, but at sunset it diminished greatly. The vessels were notified that the course for the night would be to the south. They all passed astern when I laid to under the wind to await the Casuarina which was astern.
During the night, the winds were very variable and returned to the south-west which obliged us to hold as close as possible on the course of south-south-east. Although the sky had a very threatening appearance, we passed it without very strong squalls and received only some squalls of rain which were not of long duration.
1802-11-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from E to NNW. At 6 a.m. a ship was sighted in the S 45° W, and at 7 she was made out to be an English schooner; the Géographe communicated with her. At noon the land 18 miles off, in 36° 3' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 43' 54" of longitude by account. Sailing under topsails.

1802-11-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from N to SW. We kept the topsails on the caps to wait for the ships; at 6.50 lay to to wait for the commander. The land ahead of us and the Géographe at a middling distance. Lat. 37° 28' 0", long. 149° 29' 58". From the 30th [Brumaire] to the 1st Frimaire [Year 11, 21-22 November 1802]. Overcast weather, the horizon thick, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SW. At 1.55 changed tacks and hove to under the main topsail; at 3 filled and stood on. At 6 and at 7 changed tacks; the commander in the SW at a good distance. Obs. lat. 38° 24', est. long. 150° 24' 28".
1802-11-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock, the land visible extended from north to south as far as the eye could see.
Dromedary Mountain remained at north 58° west.
At two o'clock in the night, we thought we saw land to the west.
Historical events & remarks.
The thirtieth. The winds having returned to the south-west, very variable, they gave us again dark and overcast weather, with a fairly threatening appearance for the rest of the day. We steered in the morning as close as possible on the western tack towards the north to come and recognize the land which in this part is high and mountainous and can be seen from a great distance when the weather is fine and clear.
At noon, we had no observation for the meridian altitude and I even observed that since our departure from Port Jackson, we have had only once a good one. The currents in these waters appear so violent that it would be very essential to have fine weather when in them so as to prevent great errors in the dead reckoning in the course we believe we have followed.
According to the dead reckoning we were at 37° 27' 54" and our longitude estimated since the last observation at No. 35 placed us at 148° 32' 30".
About three and a half o'clock, finding ourselves fairly close to the coast, we took the southern tack towards the east by going about. We then had in sight a chain of very high mountains the two visible extremities of which extended for us from south 50° west to north 50° west.
At sunset, the same extent of land was seen from south 69° west to north 88° west. The coast was too misty to get an exact view of it. However, we thought we observed that the high mountains that we had in sight did not terminate at the sea shore but were in the interior and preceded by other mountains much less elevated which terminated at the shore.
After sunset, we hove to to await the Casuarina and the other vessels which were astern. We also took the third reef in our topsails so that they should not be obliged to carry too much sail for the night. The weather moreover had a very threatening appearance and we had to fear some squalls.
The night of the 30th to the 1st Brumaire had nothing nevertheless disagreeable except very great humidity followed by very dark weather. We heard thunder rumble at times but it did not approach us and remained at a great distance. The sea was also not convenient, and the vessel was violently agitated by the swell notwithstanding that there was a fair breeze from the south-west variable towards the west.
During the night, we frequently made signals to our vessels in company to know their positions and to indicate ours to them.
1802-11-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to SSW. At noon the land 13 miles off, in 37° 28' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 29' 54" of longitude by account.

1802-11-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the extremities of the land, although very misty, were seen from south 50° west to north 50° west.
At sunset,
they extended from south 60° west to north 80° west.
Historical events & remarks.
The first Brumaire year 11, the winds remained from the south-west varying towards the west. They were in squalls and squalls, the sea always very heavy. In the morning, we made various manoeuvres so as not to separate from our vessels. Although the weather was not fine, we nevertheless set about to tighten our main mast shrouds which had taken so much slack from their new rigging that I was continually in fear of damage. We began first by tightening those of the lee side in order to do the same operation to the others when we changed tack.
We continued the southern course until noon when, estimating ourselves at the latitude of 38° 15' and the longitude of 148° 54' 52", we put about to the other tack, having run before the wind to close with the Casuarina which found herself greatly inconvenienced by the bad weather we had since our departure.
During the evening, we did to our starboard shrouds the same operation that we had done in the morning to those of the port side, and by this means our masts found themselves out of danger. The weather we had in the afternoon was scarcely suitable for this operation, for we often had rain and strong gusts.
In the evening, the weather seemed to change and want to clear up. The winds shifted to the south about three o'clock in the afternoon and calmed greatly. Little by little the heavy clouds that enveloped the whole horizon dispersed so that the view could extend fairly far in the space between the west and the south-east passing by the south. We closed with the Casuarina at sunset to whom I spoke to recommend him to keep as close to us as possible. The captain of this small vessel informed us that he had been obliged to unship his topgallant mast, one of the bars that cross the slings having broken in the oscillations of the vessel. Besides, he was making no more water than usual and only from the upper parts, which is all the less surprising since the planking of this part having been used green, must necessarily have made the caulking little solid for the first time.
At sunset, the man who was in the look-out thought he saw land to the west, but I think he was mistaken and that we were too far south for him to see it, especially since in the position we were in, the land must be very low, at least our charts announce it so.
During the night, the weather was fairly fine and the sea improved. We continued the southern tack towards the west until midnight and then we took that of the south towards the east. At this time, the winds had become very variable and almost calm. They were the same for the rest of the night.
1802-11-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to south. At noon in 38° 24' 0" of latitude observed and in 150° 24' 24" of longitude by account. Almost calm since noon.

1802-11-23.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, a high sea, from W to south and SW. At noon and at midnight changed tacks; at 5.30 a.m. wore ship. Obs. lat. 38° 40' 24", long. 148° 58' 12".
1802-11-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At sunset, we thought we saw the land from the top of the masts to the west, but the weather was not fine enough to have certainty that it was.
Historical events & remarks.
The second Brumaire. In the morning, the weather continued fine, but the breeze was very light, variable and inconstant. The winds were for some time to the south and varied afterwards to the east quarter. At daybreak, we had taken the southern tack bearing to the west. The sea having become fine and the sky very clear in the east, we had hope of a fine day and fair wind. This hope was verified for the weather was fine, but the breeze too weak to our desire.
At noon, we had an observation of latitude which placed us at 38° 39' 7", and our longitude according to the running of No. 35 was found to be 147° 59' 18". This position compared with that of our dead reckoning gave us a difference of 0° 10' 45" in latitude and one of 0° 29' 27" in longitude. The error occasioned by these two differences was attributed to currents, although this supposition seems false to me since according to the direction supposed for them it should have been to the south and west, whereas it was found to be to the north and west, the estimated latitude being 38° 28' 22" and the longitude 148° 28' 34".
In the afternoon, the winds shifted to the east and did not increase. We continued to steer south-west a quarter west to come and recognize the entrance of the strait north of the Kent Islands, my intention being to enter the channel which they form with the Promontory and the other islands which depend on it.
At six o'clock, the weather continuing fine and the breeze still light, I laid to to await the Casuarina which was much astern. I took advantage of this loss of time to send a boat on board the Naturaliste and had the captain Hamelin remit to him what remained of my packets for the Minister of the Navy as well as various letters for my particular acquaintances.
The captain of the American ship, the Fanny, having also come on board, I informed him of the loss of the schooner, the Enterprise, Captain Le Corre as well as the misfortune the captain had in being drowned and five of his men. The American supercargo, M. Cornwell, had had the good fortune to escape.
At seven o'clock, he returned on board and the Casuarina having joined us, we resumed the south-west a quarter west course.
During the night, we continued the same course, still having much distance to make to the west before being at the place where the Kent Islands are situated, being in the middle of the channel which separates the Furneaux Islands from the coast of New Holland. The breeze during the night was no stronger than it had been during the day and the weather, although very dark and overcast, was fairly fine except for great humidity which sometimes inconvenienced the men on watch.
1802-11-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm and a light breeze from ESE to ENE. The course S 56° 15' W, following the commander's, he having signalled none. At noon in 38° 40' 24" of latitude observed and in 149° 58' 48" of longitude by account. At 5, the commander having hove to, the division did the same; a boat from the Géographe brought us packets for the government and a wombat. She told us of the loss of the Surprise, a French schooner, and of an English sloop on the Sisters. The commander had learnt of it from the English schooner he had communicated with on the 29th [Brumaire, 20 November 1802]. Only 5 men of the Surprise were saved, none of them French. We handed over to the boat our flags and the signal book. At 7 we filled and stood on.

1802-11-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from ESE to ENE and NE.
