The commander having hove to, we did the same; a boat came from the Géographe bringing us the packets to hand to the captain. At 7 we filled and stood on; the wind having freshened we shortened sail so as not to run past the commander. At noon the course was shaped west. Obs. lat. 39° 23' 42", est. long. 148° 32' 42".
1802-11-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock in the morning, in a clear spell, we thought we made out the high lands of the Furneaux islands, to the west-south-west. But the weather was too hazy for this to appear certain.
Historical events & remarks.
On the third, the weather was very dark and overcast, the winds were variable from east to north-east, a light breeze, and we found the sea smooth. We continued the course south-west by west until noon, when, having observed the latitude of 39° 33' 42", we changed it to stand to west by north-west, so as not to go further south and to compensate for the effect of the currents.
About eight o'clock, having made signal to the Naturaliste to steer in our waters, the Casuarina was also brought under our stern, to give her fresh bread, which they received with all the more pleasure as it had been several days that they had eaten nothing but biscuit and cheese, not having been able to cook in the time of the heavy sea.
According to the dead reckoning of the course made in the twenty-four hours, the estimated latitude proved to be only 39° 16' 10", which gave, with the observation, a difference of 0° 17' 32", by which the currents had carried us to the south. There was no hour angle in the course of the day, and it was only by chance that the sun showed itself at the moment of its passage over the meridian. According to our dead reckoning, corrected by the previous day's observation, we made ourselves out to be at (no figures).
In the afternoon, the sky continued to be dark and overcast, without, however, having any bad appearance. The breeze from the north-east was a little stronger than in the morning, and the sea entirely smooth. We saw a great quantity of birds of the white gannet kind, and many white and grey gulls. We also had the company of a whale which followed us for some time. It was of good size, but not of the species that gives spermaceti, in that it blew the water vertically and not horizontally, as is claimed by those who follow that fishery, and who, by their own account, have no other means of recognising it.
After sunset, all the ships having closed up together, we took the board from south toward east, being almost becalmed, with very dark and stormy weather, hearing thunder rumbling in several points of the horizon. From eight o'clock until eleven o'clock, the calm occasioned us various manoeuvres. At that time we sounded, and it was not without astonishment that we found ourselves in 28 fathoms, bottom of white sand and rotten shells. As, by our dead reckoning, we could only be in the vicinity of the Furneaux islands, onto which the currents must have carried us according to the course we had made since noon, we brought her close-hauled on the northern board, with winds from east-north-east, very variable. We took care to sound every half hour, and we saw with pleasure that the bottom increased imperceptibly. We passed, within an hour's time, from 28 to 31 fathoms, and the bottom was then no longer so clean, being mixed with coral. As the breeze was still, at that time, very faint, and the currents might carry us onto the coast, I had an anchor cleared for mooring, and the whole crew was on watch, with the exception of the officers, who passed the night, according to their custom, in their beds. There appeared on deck only whoever was on watch, waiting impatiently for it to be over so as to do like the others.
From midnight to four o'clock, we had several shifts of wind which kept us manoeuvring a great deal. The winds passed from west to south south south-west (sic) to south and to east, following the direction of the storms by which we were surrounded. We had, in the intervals, a little wind, and let out the reefs of our topsails so as to profit by it. At three o'clock in the night, the bottom was thirty-four fathoms, and we continued our course to the north, all sail out, with the exception of our topgallant sails, which were not bent.
The Casuarina kept close to us the whole night and imitated our manoeuvres.
1802-11-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to ESE. At noon in 39° 23' 42" of latitude observed and in 148° 33' 18" of longitude by account. In the afternoon overcast and rainy weather, with squalls; from 8 to 10 lay to.

1802-11-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE, falling away entirely calm. At 9 we went onto the port tack; at midnight back onto the starboard tack. During the night the wind shifted rapidly from NNE to W. The commander not being in sight, we kept a light at the foremast head; at 3.30 we sighted him ahead of us. Est. lat. 38° 52' 12", est. long. 147° 23'.
1802-11-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five o'clock in the morning, we thought we had sight of the Furneaux islands to the west and west-south-west, but the horizon was not clear enough for us to be sure that we saw the land. The sounding was then 35 fathoms.
Historical events & remarks.
On the fourth, at daybreak, the weather was fairly fine to the W, but the whole horizon, between the east and the north, passing through the south, was so laden with haze that the view did not extend beyond two leagues. The thunder, which rumbled continually in the southern quarter, forewarned us of the arrival of some storm. And we were not long in having a very violent one from that quarter. The one we received lasted about two hours and was accompanied by abundant rain. The claps of thunder and the flashes of lightning were very frequent. Lightning struck very near us, although we had not foreseen it, but it produced exactly the effect of the whistling of a cannon ball passing at a short distance from the ships. When the worst of this storm had passed, the weather seemed to want to turn fine, but this appearance was not of long duration; the squalls began again shortly after, and throughout the rest of the day we had a great many more of them than we could have wished.
Making then but little sail, so as to wait for the consort ships, which were astern of us, they closed with us about nine o'clock. Captain Hamelin hailed me to ask to go and reconnoitre the land. I asked him what he thought of the weather we were having, observing to him that it scarcely seemed to me suitable for entering the strait, but as he observed to me that he saw no objection to passing through it, and that we were losing a fair wind, I told him he might chase ahead, that I would follow him, which we both did at once, and were followed by the Casuarina and the American ship.
At noon, we had no observation of latitude; that of our dead reckoning placed us at 38° 54' 42", and the longitude, likewise reckoned, was 145° 12' 28".
During the evening, the sky had a very bad appearance, and the thunder rumbled on every side, though at a distance. The winds, which had been at east, shifted to north-east and varied at times toward the north. The breeze was unsteady and often came in strong squalls, following the direction of the gusts that the wind brought us. We sounded only once in the morning, so as not to lose time, and we had 40 fathoms of water. It was then seven o'clock in the morning, and we were still making our course to the north. We did not bear away to the west until after having spoken with Captain Hamelin, and it was about nine o'clock.
At five o'clock in the evening, the weather having cleared a little in the southern quarter, we caught sight of the summit of the high mountains of the Furneaux islands, which showed itself above the haze with which the land was surrounded. It seemed to me that I recognised the mountain the English have named the Three Patriarchs, from the appearance the peaks present to the view. We continued to make our course to the west until six o'clock, and then closed with the ships. The Naturaliste, which had chased ahead to get sight of the Kent group, did not see them at all. I informed her that we should spend the night tacking, standing four hours to the north and four hours to the south. At eight o'clock, the winds jumped to the north, varying to north-north-west. The weather was then stormy and rainy. At nine o'clock the winds jumped all at once to south-south-west and blew suddenly with such violence that the ship was laid over on her side and gave a fairly heavy lurch. As she was quite a while without answering her helm, we were obliged to slack away in a body the sheets of the main topsail and of the fore topgallant sail. The mizzen sail was the sail that troubled us the most. However, the ship came up and righted herself. The topsails and the foresail having been clewed up and then furled, we lay to under the small jib and the mizzen staysail, and thus passed the night, sounding every hour, with the facility of being able to draw off whenever we should judge it fitting.
From south-west, the winds shifted to west and blew with violence. The sky became clear, and as the wind did nothing but increase, we had no doubt that it would continue so for some time. We lay to the whole night, catching sight from time to time of the lights of the ships. The soundings were very regular, from 31 to 34 fathoms. The order was to go about whenever we should have less than 28.
1802-11-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to NNE; at 3 a.m. it shifted to the west and hauled to the south, then east, and at last N and WNW. At noon in 38° 52' 12" of latitude by account and in 147° 43' 48" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands in the S 11° 15' W. Four English convicts were discovered hidden in the hold. At 9 the wind shifted to the west, blowing hard in gusts; we lay to and lost sight of the division.

1802-11-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from ENE to N, W and WNW. At 4 p.m. 4 convicts were found in the hold, where they had hidden themselves. At 8 the winds, drawing round to north and WNW, came on to blow hard; at midnight wore onto the port tack. At daybreak sighted a ship in the WSW. At 9 went onto the starboard tack, the land NW 5° N. Obs. lat. 38° 42' 55", est. long. 147° 0' 52".
1802-11-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock in the morning, the land of which we got sight, and which I presume to be that of Wilsons Promontory, extended from the west to the north-west. The sounding was then 35 fathoms.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, the squall which had begun the evening before, in the night, lasted the whole day without the least interruption. The sea was not long in becoming very rough, and we were fairly well tormented by the violent motions of the ship. The sky was, nevertheless, fine, and there was no appearance that this weather would last very long.
At daybreak, we caught sight of the ship the Fanny, which bore from us to the south, at a great distance. The Naturaliste was seen from the mast-heads to the east by south-east, but we had no sight at all of the Casuarina, about which I was uneasy, fearing that she might have suffered some damage in her masting from the suddenness with which the heavy wind had set in. At the same time, we also got sight of the land, in the western quarter. But we could not tell whether it was that of the Kent group of islands or that of the Promontory, the latitude by which we then reckoned ourselves being too uncertain for anything positive to be said on the subject.
During the morning, we continued lying to under the small jib and the mizzen staysail. The wind was so strong that the ship had enough with these two sails alone, so as not to render her motions too violent. We sounded the whole morning every two hours, and we had a fairly regular bottom between thirty and thirty-four fathoms.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 39° 8' 30", and the estimated longitude placed us at 145° 4' 28". Although the sky was fine and the horizon extensive, the wind was so strong that this observation must not be regarded as very good, in that it was extremely difficult to (keep) the instruments in the position that would have best suited them. But in any case, I do not think that the error which may have resulted from it is above four to five minutes, either to the north or to the south.
The estimated latitude was 38° 57', and even more doubtful than the one we had observed.
During the evening, the winds varied a little from south-west toward north. The sea had become very rough, and although there was no appearance of a calm, I expected nevertheless that one would take place after sunset. We continued still lying to on the course from SW to south, making about south-east corrected for leeway. The soundings, from noon until eight o'clock in the evening, kept imperceptibly increasing throughout. At noon we were in 35 fathoms, and surrounded by a great quantity of birds of every kind.
During the evening, the winds continued a strong gale from the quarter of west-north-west, the sea growing ever rougher. However, about five o'clock in the evening, they were less violent and seemed to want to abate, the squalls being then less heavy and less prolonged than they had been during the day. The horizon, though still hazy, cleared from time to time. We continued the board to the south until midnight, when we took that to the north, having 34 fathoms of water when we went about, and the winds at west, variable to west-south-west.
During the night, the sky was fine and the wind fell off a great deal; we changed nothing in our sail, with the exception of the storm staysail, which we set. From midnight to eight o'clock in the morning, the bottom increased in the same proportion that it had decreased while lying to on the southern course, and we had 45 fathoms when we took the course to the south.
1802-11-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from WNW to WSW. At daybreak a ship of the division was sighted, which was lost sight of shortly afterwards. At 9 the land was sighted in the N 40° W. At noon in 38° 42' 55" of latitude observed and in 147° 43' 0" of longitude by account.

1802-11-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, blowing hard from WNW, W and NW. We had no sight of the ships of the division. At 7 p.m. and at midnight changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 3' 0", est. long. 147° 24' 34".
1802-11-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At sunset, we thought we made out a land to the NW and one to the S.SW. This report must be regarded as very doubtful.
One of the three ships that had been lost sight of was sighted to the north.
Historical events & Remarks &c.
On the sixth, the weather was fairly fine throughout the whole morning. The sea, which during the night had fallen a great deal, became smoother still, and nothing gave sign that the weather would turn as bad again as we had had it the evening before.
About five o'clock, running the board to the south, we got sight of the Naturaliste, the Casuarina and the Fanny, which we had lost sight of the evening before. None of these ships appeared to us to have suffered in her masting from the sudden change that had been occasioned by the strong squall which had come on at the moment when it was least expected, in the night from the fourth to the fifth.
At eight o'clock, we had closed with these three ships, which were to leeward of us, and we continued to run in company on the board from south toward west, having at times the winds at west-north-west, variable toward the north, a light breeze. The sounding, during the morning's run, kept gradually increasing, and we had forty fathoms at noon. At the same time, the observed latitude was 39° 8' 15", and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 placed us at 146° 6' 11". According to these data, laid down on the English chart of the strait, it followed that the northern part of the Kent islands bore from us south 64° west, the Two Sisters, north of the Furneaux islands, south 25° west, the islands of the Promontory south 86° west, and the Promontory south 87° west. As the islets that lie to the south of them
The great difference found between the dead reckoning and the observation, both for the latitude and for the longitude, does not seem to me to be entirely attributable to the current, but rather to a poor estimate of the ship's course, which had made much more to the north and to the east than had been supposed while we were lying to. Be that as it may, we had a difference in latitude of 0° 26' 37", and in longitude one of 0° 35' 31". The dead reckoning placing us at 39° 34' 52" of latitude and 145° 30' 40" of longitude.
During the evening, the sky, which had been fairly fine and clear in the morning, became very dark and confused. It remained so until about four o'clock in the evening, when the winds shifted to the west, freshening in a manner that made us fear a return of the bad weather. The rain and mist which then came on made us take in our mainsail, the mizzen sail and the fore topgallant sail. At five o'clock, the wind still increasing, it became necessary to take the third reef in the topsails and to wait to see what would be the outcome of the bad appearance that was threatening. At four o'clock, we had no more than thirty-five fathoms, having decreased by five since noon, when we were steering to the south toward the west, the point of sailing on which the Furneaux islands were to lie from us, of which I should have been very glad to get sight before nightfall. At six o'clock, having no more than thirty fathoms of water, we should most certainly have got sight of the land had the horizon been less confused. The view extended, at most, a league and a half offshore of the ship. I put off going about for some time longer, in the hope that the weather would clear a little, which indeed happened about seven o'clock. And we saw perfectly the Two Sisters, islets to the north of the Furneaux islands. They bore from us south 25° west. As the noon fix had given us, we reckoned ourselves at three or four leagues' distance from them. As the Naturaliste was near us, I told her to go about, wind astern, to run the board to the north during the night. The other ships imitated our manoeuvre. During the night, the weather was very unsteady, bad, and in squalls, the winds variable from west toward south. We took in our fore topsail and often set the main one against the mast, so as not to draw away from the other ships. We sounded every hour, and the bottom kept ever increasing.
1802-11-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to NW. At daybreak the division was sighted and closed; we had filled at 5. At noon in 39° 3' 0" of latitude observed and in 148° 6' 42" of longitude by account. At 6 the Furneaux Islands from S 19° W to S 30° W. At 5 we lay to.

1802-11-28.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather. The commander very close astern of us. The wind a strong breeze from WSW to WNW and SW. At 6 saw the land from S 19° W to S 30° W; at 6.30 changed tacks, and at 8 a.m. the same. Obs. lat. 38° 50' 19", est. long. 147° 44' 4".
1802-11-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock, sighted the land from the deck to the south-south-west.
At seven o'clock, took a bearing of the middle of the Two Sisters, north of the Furneaux islands, south 20° west, distance twelve miles.
Observations, Historical events & remarks.
On the seventh, the weather, without being fine, was (less) bad than we had had it in the night of the sixth, though cloudy and with squalls. The gusts were less heavy. The sea, however, was still hollow and rough; we ran the board to the north until eight o'clock, when we took that to the south. At two o'clock in the previous night, we had lost the bottom at 45 fathoms, and in the morning's soundings it could no longer be found, either at 60 or at seventy fathoms, which leads me to believe that the course had trended much more from west to east than had been reckoned, or that the direction of the currents had changed.
The whole morning, the sky, although tolerably fine, did not fail to give us a few squalls, but in general they were of little consequence and of short duration.
At noon, we observed the latitude to be 38° 57' 48", and the longitude by No. 35 proved to be 146° 21' 19". This, against our expectation, gave us way made to the east, although we ought to have had none on this point of sailing, according to the various courses we had followed. The difference between the dead reckoning and the observation was 0° 11' 20" for the latitude and 0° 12' 32" for the longitude. The difference by the observation was to the north, and to the east for the longitude.
In the afternoon, we continued to run the board to the south, in the hope of regaining the bottom we had lost, but it was to no purpose, for we did not succeed in it, either during the day or even during the night. Nevertheless, we resumed the board to the north at midnight, so as to find ourselves the next day at very nearly the same latitude as the evening before.
During the evening, the sky cleared itself of all the clouds that had confused it during (the day), which gave us hope of a coming change in our favour. As the quarter from east to south was very clear, it seemed to us that we should not be long in having the winds from that point of the horizon. But this conjecture was not confirmed; they remained fairly constantly at west, varying at times toward south, a light breeze. The sea also began to grow smoother.
At eight o'clock, we were astonished to see that Venus found herself so close to the moon. As it seemed to us that she must be eclipsed before her setting, we kept watch to observe her and followed her until ten o'clock. The eclipse did not take place, but Venus passed so close to the shaded edge of the moon that she seemed to touch it, so slight was the interval separating the one from the other. The weather was fairly fine during the night, in the middle of which we took our course to the north under little sail.
1802-11-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SW. At noon in 38° 50' 19" of latitude observed and in 148° 26' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-11-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth enough, a strong breeze from WSW to W. At midnight changed tacks. Obs. lat. 38° 51' 10", long. 147° 54'.
1802-11-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
The 8th, the weather was very fine and the sea had considerably improved. But the winds were not favourable, and we had to continue tacking now on one tack, now on the other. We continued, in the morning, the northerly tack that we had been on since midnight. We took advantage, from the morning, of the fine weather that prevailed to make a general sweep and to perfume the decks and between-decks. All our sails were, likewise, dried.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 38° 50' 2" and the longitude from No. 35 placed us at 146° 34' 19", which gave us thirteen minutes of easting and confirmed to us that the strong westerly to southerly winds that we (had) encountered in the days past had changed the direction of the currents that all navigators who have frequented these waters before us assert to run in a south-westerly direction.
In the afternoon, the weather being very fine and the sea calm, we made a signal to the Casuarina to pass astern to receive fresh bread which we sent her by means of a whip. Citizen Freycinet informed us that, during the bad weather, she was making eight inches of water per hour but that this came only from the upper parts of his vessel which needed to be caulked again. She was not making more than an inch of water when the sea was fine.
Since the weather had almost always been bad and the sea rough since our departure from Port Jackson, we had hardly been able until that moment to attend to the accommodation of the crew, who lay indiscriminately in whatever place they could find and especially in the between-decks, which occasioned much difficulty in finding them at night, when there was a need for everyone to be on deck. To remedy this inconvenience for the future, all the hammocks were slung beneath the gangways following ordinary usage, with express prohibition to anyone whatsoever to change their place.
At sunset, or at least shortly before, Captain Hamelin passed astern and, having hailed me, informed me that a man named Claine, formerly a master gunner aboard the Géographe and who was being sent to France for trial, the Council of Justice having declared itself incompetent to pronounce on the declaration of the jury, had just struck the officer of the watch. In asking me what punishment I wished to inflict on him, my reply was to have him given fifty lashes without prejudice to the sentence he would have to undergo on his arrival.
After sunset, the breeze increased somewhat but constantly from the westerly quarter, varying a little towards the south. As clouds were beginning to form from the south to south-south-east, we hoped soon to have winds from that quarter and continued our course to the south under the topsails and foresail, having furled our mainsail which was of no use to us and which we had only kept set to dry and air it.
During the night of the 8th to the 9th, the winds, although variable, did not change. We had from time to time some squalls and after moonset, the sky became damp, the horizon misty and thick with little appearance of fine weather for the following day.
1802-11-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WSW to W. At 9 filled and stood on under courses. At noon in 38° 51' 10" of latitude observed and in 148° 35' 42" of longitude by account. At 3 Citizen Moreau, officer of the watch, laid a complaint against Barbier (one of the prisoners for theft) who had struck him. The captain sentenced him to 50 lashes with a rope's end. At 5 we spoke the commander, who, on the captain's complaint against Barbier, also sentenced him to 50 lashes. Despite this order the captain did not have them given, though Citizen Moreau asked for it.

1802-11-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a light breeze from WSW which freshened as it drew round to WNW. At 5 spoke the Géographe. Obs. lat. 39° 35' 0", est. long. 147° 43' 54".
1802-11-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the northern extremity of the two islands named the Sisters bore west 16° south.
The middle of the islet east of the Patriarchs bore south 8° west.
Note: By two series of lunar distances, the longitude was found to be 146° 10' 36", which gave a difference, with the timekeeper, of 7' 24" further west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The 9th, during the watch from four to eight o'clock in the morning, the Naturaliste being very close to us under our lee, wanted to pass to windward of us; the officer of the watch, attempting to pass ahead of us, nearly threw our bowsprit overboard by a manoeuvre as ignorant as it was thoughtless. I was then in my cabin and had no knowledge of it. But when I came on deck, the officer of the watch informed me of what had nearly happened. I then approached that vessel which was again under our lee and hailed her to know who was the officer of the watch who had executed such a manoeuvre. I was informed that it was Citizen Hérisson and I was consequently not surprised, for although he believes himself very learned as a sailor, he scarcely knows how to trim his sails and in no way how to extricate himself from a difficult situation when he has got himself into one. I requested Captain Hamelin to tell him that if such a manoeuvre occurred a second time, he would no longer command the watch. Although he was on watch, his inattention to keeping his vessel properly steered was the cause that he ran aboard us again and struck us on the side, across our main shrouds. Fortunately the sea was fine and the wind light, for otherwise we would have suffered much damage. No damage resulted except to one of my boats, which was partly stove in but which nonetheless offered sufficient resistance to throw the ship off and by that means we were promptly separated.
During the morning we had an overcast sky, some squalls with a little rain and little appearance of fine weather.
At ten o'clock we sighted land, from west by south-west to south. We recognised it as Furneaux Islands and the Two Sisters which we had seen in the days past. We continued the south-westerly tack, with winds from west-north-west, to close with the land.
At noon, although showing squalls, the weather having cleared, we observed the latitude of 39° 37' 49" and the longitude from No. 35 placed us at 146° 17' 58". At the same moment, the islands named the Two Sisters bore west 5° south and the islet situated east of about the middle of the largest of the Furneaux Islands bore south 8° west. This bearing, laid on the chart and corrected for variation, gave but three minutes eastward difference with the timekeeper's longitude, which proves that this land is correctly placed. At noon the soundings showed 27 fathoms, soft bottom and suitable for anchorage. After taking the bearing, we took the northern tack, seeing no improvement in the weather but on the contrary all the signs of some new squall.
During the evening, sailing north-west, the sky cleared a little but the winds varied little from south-west to south. At four o'clock, the Two Sisters bore south 51° 30' west.
At sunset, the weather appeared to be clearing, the horizon having cleared of all the dark clouds which rendered the sight disagreeable and the outlook unfavourable. The wind likewise abated considerably although it did not change direction. We continued, during the night, the northern tack which we had taken at noon and it was not until midnight that (we) took the southern tack.
Note: For several days we had been constantly experiencing considerable northerly differences, so that it seems scarcely doubtful that the currents are bound to follow the direction of the winds when they blow for a long time from the same quarter, rather than a constant direction as had been represented to us. In making for Port Jackson we had already experienced the same effect.
1802-11-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to WSW. At noon in 39° 35' 0" of latitude observed and in 148° 20' 42" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands from S 12° W to S 65° W.

1802-12-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from WSW. At 6 passed under the Géographe's stern and laid the mizzen topsail to the mast. At 6 took the bearing of the northernmost end of the [one word illegible] S 45° W; the south end of the Furneaux Islands S 7° W. Obs. lat. 39° 24' 21", long. 147° 34' 54". From the 10th to the 11th [Frimaire, Year 11, 1-2 December 1802]. Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to WNW. At 4 changed tacks. At 6 took the bearing of the land from S 2° W to S 33° W. The Géographe in the NW by N, very close. At 3.45 a.m. changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 17' 45", est. long. 146° 36' 54".
1802-12-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock, the southern extremity of the Furneaux Islands in sight, bore south 30° west.
The Two Sisters north of these same islands, bore south 51° west and south 59° west.
At sunset, the land extended from south 15° west to south 50° west.
At daylight, the land was seen from south-south-west to south-west.
At noon, the land in sight extended from south 5° west to south 69° west, 39 fathoms, no bottom found.
Longitude by two series of distances 146° 16' 20".
Historical events & Remarks.
The 10th, we had very fine weather all the morning, and a light breeze from west-north-west to west-south-west. At daylight, the land of the Furneaux Islands, from which we were sufficiently distant, was seen from south-south-west to south-west. The wind was very light all day, and as we ardently desired to see it change, we flattered ourselves that the calm which the sea announced to us would bring what we so greatly wished; nevertheless this did not occur for the day.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 39° 33' 42" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 146° 25' 18". At the same moment, the land in sight remained from south 5° west to south 60° west. We were then making a course to the south with winds from west-north-west. The bottom was lost at 39 fathoms.
Two English prisoners who had hidden themselves in the vessel were found while stowing the between-decks. When questioned on the motif which had led them to hide aboard, they replied that it was to recover their liberty. I informed them that they would be put on King Island like the four who were aboard the Naturaliste and the three who had been found on the Fanny. There is no doubt that the desertions had been favoured by members of the crew, for since fourteen days we had been at sea, these deserters had lacked neither water nor provisions.
During the evening, the weather continued to be very fine and the sky extremely clear. We made a course over the middle of the Furneaux Islands until four o'clock in the afternoon, when we took the northern tack.
At sunset, the land remained from south 74° west to south 29° west.
The night of the 10th to the 11th was very fine. We passed it almost in calm, and none of us doubted that it was a portent of an easterly wind for the following day. When we took the northern tack, the sounding was 32 fathoms. At eight o'clock 32 and at midnight 37 fathoms. Although the greater part of the night had passed in calm, we nevertheless had from time to time some indications that we would have fine wind on the following day, in that sometimes the light breeze that came to us was from the north-east quarter.
1802-12-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW to WSW. At daybreak the Furneaux Islands from S 16° W to S 25° W, 8 miles off. At noon their southernmost end in sight S 8° W and the northernmost of the Sisters S 50° W, being in 39° 24' 21" of latitude observed and in 148° 12' 0" of longitude by account. At 11 a flat calm.

1802-12-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock in the evening, the northernmost of the Two Sisters remained south 74° west, and the Furneaux Islands were seen from south 68° 30' west to south 29° west.
At five o'clock in the morning, the Furneaux Islands were seen from south 10° west to south 57° west.
At noon, the Kent group was south 80° west. A small island further south, south 36° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The 11th, in the morning, we were not deceived in our expectation. Winds came to us from the north-east quarter, variable towards the east. The breeze was feeble at first and increased but little during the course of the morning. As the Naturaliste was near us, I told her to make all sail and I did the same myself. Setting our topgallant sails, we steered west, standing a little south, in order to recognise as soon as possible the Kent group which dead reckoning and bearings placed ten leagues to the westward.
At daylight the Furneaux Islands including the Two Sisters remained from south 11° west to south 57° west.
During the morning, the weather was very fine and the sea calm. The breeze increased little. Around eleven o'clock, we caught sight of the Kent group islands. And at noon, having observed the latitude of 39° 28' 40", this group was bearing south 80° west. A small island, in the south of this group, bore south 36° west. The sounding showed 33 fathoms, soft bottom although little suitable for anchorage.
The longitude from No. 35 placed us at 146° 44'.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine. We crowded on sail to double the Kent islands before night, and by that means to enter the strait. But the breeze was so feeble that we could not accomplish it. We had, the Naturaliste and I, left the Casuarina and the Fanny astern, which we nevertheless always kept in sight. My intention was to await them after being within the islands as soon as I should have doubled them.
At nine o'clock in the evening, having good knowledge of the northern point of these islands which we passed at half a league distance, we made course to double them. But the calm having taken hold of us, and the vessel scarcely steerable at certain intervals, it was not until midnight that the northern cape of this part remained to the south and at 37 fathoms depth at not more than two leagues distance, for the land was seen perfectly even after moonset.
During the night, the winds were very variable from east to south and from south to south-west. We often had (fear) of being obliged to return on our steps. At different times, the sky was misty and very overcast, and we received from time to time some sudden gusts after which a flat calm succeeded them. Nevertheless, the sky became fine again and the light breeze that we had was from the south to south-south-east, or to speak more accurately, for the greater part of the night it was calm. We kept our stern lantern constantly lit to serve as an indication to the vessels which were behind us and which must have had knowledge of it.
1802-12-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm until 4, when the breeze got up from ENE to NE; we ran into Bass Strait. At noon in 39° 17' 45" of latitude observed and in 147° 28' 0" of longitude by account. The northernmost end of the Furneaux Islands in sight S 16° E, the Sisters S 10° W, the Kent Group S 80° W, 24 miles off. The Casuarina and the Fanny out of sight astern. Almost calm during the night.

1802-12-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NE, NNW, north, south and SW. We steered to weather the Kent Group to the north. At 7 a.m. spoke the Géographe. Bearings taken at noon: Wilson's Promontory N 23° W; two islets, one S 27° E, the other N 73° E. Obs. lat. 39° 25' 50", est. long. 145° 30' 54".
1802-12-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land: (in the margin: lunar distances 4° 2' 55")
At four o'clock, the Kent group extended from south 73° west to south 87° west. The northern extremity of the Sisters south 70° east. The part of the Furneaux Islands in sight, from south 51° east to south 26° east. The rock, the Brioche at about the middle of the channel between the Furneaux and Kent islands, south 14° east, and a large islet at the opening of this same channel south 22° 30' west.
At midnight, the western extremity of the Kent Islands was south 2° west and the lands to the east in sight, south 22° east.
At five o'clock in the morning, the middle of the Kent group was east 5° north, an islet which is to the west of it, south 40° east. The islets placed to the west and north of the Kent group having been taken for bearings to establish their geographical position, I do not speak of them here.
Historical events & Remarks.
The 12th, having passed the greater part of the night in calm, we found ourselves surrounded by islands and islets. I was the more surprised at this situation in that, having already exited the Strait of Bass by passing to the north of the Kent group, I had seen none of them. Although they are little distant from it and at one or two minutes at the same latitude, to extricate ourselves from this labyrinth, we set course south-south-west with a very feeble breeze from south-east variable to east. We passed easily those most to the east and north and we would have similarly rounded the others easily if the winds (had) held to the same point of the horizon from which we had them in the morning. But after sunrise, they shifted first to the south and afterwards to south-south-west and south-west by west. As I did not wish to exit the channel, I determined to traverse the channels which these islets form between themselves. The passage which they presented to the view appeared good and even convenient. The one which we chose proved such, since we never had less than thirty fathoms and often more, at a league from the coast. Although these channels are not wide, I am as it were persuaded that one can, without danger, navigate them, judging only by the elevation and form of the rocks which compose them.
The new English map of Mr. Flinders makes no mention of them although the course he made seems to indicate that he should have seen them. I am the less surprised at this in that I did not see them myself although I must have passed very close to them in doubling the Kent Islands to the north to exit the strait. As I am taking exact bearings of them, I will give their position in a separate chart.
At daylight, we obtained good knowledge of the Casuarina and the Fanny, but they were quite plainly to the east. My position not allowing me to await them, the Naturaliste and I made sail to extricate ourselves from the archipelago in which we were engaged and which is situated about six leagues to the west of the Kent group. We passed through the channel which is formed by the islet which I named the Sight Post and the one which bears the name of the Two Brothers. And after doubling them, we continued our course from south towards west as far as the winds permitted but without hope of being able to double the Cone Islet, a large and remarkable rock of which I give the view and position in my chart of the Promontory at Port Bass.
As we approached this islet, we obtained knowledge of a reef flush with the water, which is the more dangerous when one is tacking in these waters, in that it has little extent, but as the sea broke upon it quite strongly, we were warned of it in good time. The necessary bearings were taken to ensure its position for the safety of navigators.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 39° 24' 45" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 144° 25' 56". As the weather was fine, the western tack towards the north was continued following the wind, but at half past one, finding ourselves sufficiently to windward to double the Sight Post to the north, we took the southern tack towards the west. We effectively doubled the large rock and the two others which are to the west of it and some minutes to the south. The Naturaliste continuing the northern tack. I hoisted a signal of caution to her so that when she came to the southern tack, she should take heed of the reef of which I have just spoken and which we passed at not more than three quarters of a league distance.
During the evening, we continued the southern tack towards the west when the winds permitted and followed it until midnight when we took the northern tack. During the night, although the sky was very cloudy with squalls and bad appearance, we had fairly fine weather and experienced only a few small squalls of little importance. The Naturaliste carried her tack so far that she did not close with us although we constantly had the topgallant sail on the mast.
1802-12-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from N to W by way of E and south. At 8 the promontory N 36° W, islet A west, islet D S 75° W, islet B S 70° W, the Kent Group S 80° E, islet P N 80° W. The Casuarina out of sight, as was the Fanny. At noon in 39° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 146° 8' 0" of longitude by account, and in 144° 42' 43" of longitude from the bearing of the promontory N 23° W and the observed latitude. At 1.45 the jib boom broke; it was not blowing, and we learnt that it had been sprung for several days. At 12.45 a breaker was seen west of islet P which is not marked on the chart and which we had not seen in Germinal and Floréal of Year 10; it lies in [blank] of latitude and [blank] of longitude. At 6 the promontory N 22° W, islet A N 45° E, islet D N 56° E and islet B N 68° E. During the night the Géographe out of sight.

1802-12-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from W to WSW, freshening. At 1.55 the jib boom broke and was rigged in at once. At 12.45 took the bearing of a breaker not marked on the chart, W 22° S, estimated distance 6 miles. At 10 p.m., at 1 a.m. and at 4 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 49' 27", est. long. 145° 23' 12".
1802-12-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock the middle of the lands of the Promontory remained north 15° 15' west.
At six o'clock, the same lands remained north 16° west.
At eight o'clock in the morning, we had them in the same direction extending a little to the east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The 13th, the weather was not fine, nevertheless at daylight we obtained knowledge of the Naturaliste much to windward of us. We also caught sight of the American vessel the Fanny sailing on the northern tack, but we did not see the Casuarina and I do not know why for she was sailing as well as the Fanny. The sky had a very bad appearance all the morning and the breeze unequal from the south-west to south-west quarter. As the sea was fine, we were easily persuaded that this wind would not be of long duration. We continued the northern tack until five o'clock, at which time we took the southern tack, the winds then being at south-west, they shifted to west during the morning.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 39° 47' 51" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 144° 15' 16". We had then no more dangers to fear, at least of those which are known. The lands of the Promontory which we still had in sight at six o'clock in the morning to the west, disappeared for us. The horizon not being fine.
In the afternoon, the clouds which had rendered it disagreeable for us in the morning, dispersed and everything seemed to announce to us a fine day for the following day. The wind abated as the sun descended to the horizon and we remained persuaded that if it calmed entirely during the night, we would have winds from the east and north-east for the following day.
The American vessel crowded on sail all day to close with us. And at sunset, she was not more than about a league and a half from us and to windward.
During the night, the weather was fine. We changed nothing to our sail and I gave order that if the winds did not change, one should go about at midnight to take the northern tack. This order was executed but about three o'clock in the morning, the breeze having entirely calmed, the winds shifted to the south-east and we made course to the west, setting all sail.
1802-12-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to WSW. At daybreak the commander was sighted and closed. At noon in 39° 49' 27" of latitude observed and in 144° 44' 43" of longitude from the bearing of islet A N 5° E, islets D and B in line N 12° E. A new jib boom was rigged. At 10 the Fanny closed us and passed under our stern.

1802-12-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze from W to SSW, varying to SSE and NE. Rigged a new jib boom. At 8 and at 8.45 changed tacks; at 1 a.m. wore ship. The commander a short distance ahead of us. Obs. lat. 40° 9' 10", est. long. 144° 40' 0".
1802-12-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mentions)
Historical events & Remarks.
The 14th, the winds which had shifted to the south-east, were at first very feeble, but after sunrise, coming to the north and then to the east-north-east, they gathered strength and we had during the morning a fine breeze. We steered west, all sail set, to come in search of King Island whose position both in latitude and longitude is still very doubtful and uncertain according to the diversity of opinions of English fishermen who have frequented these waters. The chart which Mr. Mercy gave of it when he commanded Lady Nelson is, I think, what is most known on this part up to this moment. Inasmuch as it appears he had stayed there fairly long although he had not made the tour of it.
As there was a fine breeze during the morning, the American vessel could not follow the Naturaliste who carried all the sail she could set. But I did not judge it proper to wait for her in that she would have time to close with us during the night, having the intention to pass it tacking with little sail.
At noon, the latitude was observed to be 40° 10' 42" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 143° 38' 0". This position referred to what we knew of King Island placed us about twenty leagues to the west, some degrees north.
As this longitude and the latitude observed should give us knowledge of some of the Hunter Islands, I continued the course to the west, persuaded that I would be able to obtain knowledge of them at sunset, if the weather continued fine.
In the evening, the breeze was fresher than we had had it in the morning and we made good progress to the west. Someone coming to complain that he had lost a watch for three days, a general search was made of all chests and bags. It did not serve to recover the watch, but it contributed to the recovery of various articles of exchange which had been abstracted and hidden in different parts of the vessel. The authors of these thefts could not be discovered, which is very fortunate for them for they would have been punished in a manner to prevent that similar ones should occur in future.
At sunset, the weather was still fine, but the horizon became charged with such a great quantity of vapours that it greatly reduced its extent, which was probably the cause for which we did not see land neither to the west nor to the south. Captain Hamelin, having come alongside me, asked me if I wished to despatch him, but I observed to him that the navigation of the strait not being well known, it seemed to me prudent to have good knowledge of the land before we said farewell. After sunset, we continued the course to the west until nine o'clock, but then we took the northern tack towards the east, as close-hauled as we could. The sky at that time was overcast with bad appearance. The sounding which at nine o'clock in the evening was 35 fathoms, was no more than 29 at midnight and at one o'clock it was 25, which decided me to change course towards the east. The sky became more and more confused and the weather set with squalls with strong gusts and rain during the rest of the night. In running the southern tack, the sounding was always increasing and at five o'clock in the morning, we again had 35 fathoms.
1802-12-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to SSE, calm, and a strong breeze from NE to E. The Fanny left us and shaped her course for Batavia. At noon in 40° 9' 10" of latitude observed and in 144° 1' 30" of longitude by account. At 9 the commander having hauled close to the wind, we followed his movement.

1802-12-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from ENE to east. The commander very close. At 4.25 a.m. changed tacks. At 7 a.m. the commander hoisted the national flag, clewed up his foresail and lowered his topsails on the caps; at 7.30 he gave orders to make sail. At 9 the winds having shifted to the SW, from which they blew very strong, we at once went onto the starboard tack. At 10 sighted an island to the south and went about at once. At 11 we took the bearing of King Island, 10 miles off, from NW by W to north. Obs. lat. 40° 15' 22", est. long. 143° 0' 0".
1802-12-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the lookouts having got sight of King Island in the morning, the land in view bore from us from west to north-west by west, at a distance of four to five leagues.
At two o'clock, the point which forms the south entrance of the place the English have named Seal Bay was borne W. NW, three leagues.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, we had the winds at east, accompanied by rain and very strong squalls. We were then running the board to the south, and I intended to keep it up for some time so as to gain a little offing, in order the more surely to weather the heavy weather which there was every appearance we were going to have. The Naturaliste being a good deal to leeward of us, I had her stood down for, to close with her, and when I had come sufficiently near her, I hoisted the national colours to her, so that she might make her course for France, but whether the haze did not allow her to distinguish the colours of this flag, or whether she did not understand this signal, she hove to, believing that I wished to speak to her. This manoeuvre obliged me to close with her, and then I invited her to continue her course, so as to take advantage, if not of fine weather, for it was indeed very bad then, at least of not losing the fair wind for standing to the west. After this explanation, we wished each other reciprocally a good voyage and good health, and she bore away. This moment of parting caused me extreme distress, and I felt on this account a tightening of the heart which made me withdraw into my cabin. I truly loved Captain Hamelin for his particular qualities, and when one has run, in company, the same dangers for two years, it was natural to feel the impression that the moment of his departure made upon me.
The breeze was very strong when Captain Hamelin left, and to keep her in sight longer, I took the board to the north toward the west. But scarcely had we both brought ourselves close-hauled when the winds shifted to west-south-west, varying toward south-west, which made her take the board to the south, while I made that to the north-west, which promptly parted us from one another.
About ten o'clock, we had a sudden shift of wind which brought them round to south-west. The sky then became clear and seemed to want to turn fine. So that at eleven o'clock we had a good sight of King Island, which bore from us from west to north-west by west; at noon, the latitude was observed to be 40° 10'. We continued the course close-hauled to close with it and gain the anchorage of Elephant Bay, if possible, during the evening. The breeze was very strong, and we carried the reefs in the topsails. We also had the sea rough and heavy, but also the hope of finding it smooth on drawing near the land.
About two o'clock, we were astonished to see the Naturaliste again, running the coastal board as we were. When she had closed with us, I made her the signal to close, in that the winds not being suitable for making way, it was better that she should remain at anchor, all the more as I still had letters to give her.
When we had closed with the land, we ran along it to gain the anchorage, and having made out Elephant Bay, which is, properly speaking, only a bight open to all the winds from south-south-west to north-north-west, passing through the east, we there let go a bower anchor in 14 fathoms, bottom of sand, having no shelter except from winds from south-west to north-west by way of the west.
Shortly after, the Casuarina, which we had lost sight of for several days, appeared and came to anchor beside us. In the evening, Captain Hamelin came on board, and we talked together of his approaching departure. I invited him to remain the next day, should the winds not be fair, and undertook to have his water, consumed since departure, replaced for him, if it were possible to procure some easily the next day. The night was fine, and the wind fell entirely calm after sunset.
Stay at King Island.
1802-12-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to SW by way of NW. At 7.30 the commander having hove to, we ran alongside him and hove to. He wished us a good voyage and ordered the captain to make sail; we at once filled and stood west, crowding sail. At 9, the wind hauling to the west, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and shifted the mainsail. At 10, having sighted an island to the south 4 miles off, we went onto the port tack. At 11.30 another island was sighted to the west 6 miles off, and King Island from north to N 56° W. At noon in 40° 15' 22" of latitude observed and in 142° 21' 30" of longitude by account. At 12.15 we bore away north to round King Island, which bore from us as far as N 11° 15' W. At 1.30 the Géographe was sighted to the north, holding her wind to close the land. When we had come a little nearer her she made us a signal which we could not understand, having no signal book left; she then made the signal to close and fired a gun, and we closed her. The commander ordered us to follow him to the anchorage. At 4.30 we anchored under the coast near the Géographe, King Island bearing from S 19° W to N 44° W. Shortly afterwards the Casuarina was sighted under the land and came and anchored near us. Five English convicts were sent aboard the Géographe, and we gave her our large boat.

1802-12-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a strong breeze from SW to south and SSE. We bent a new mainsail. King Island was in sight as far as N by NW; we then hauled to the wind to round it. The Géographe, which was to leeward and close-hauled, was closed; she made us a signal we did not understand, then fired a gun and hoisted the signal to close, and we came to the anchorage north of King Island, as did she. The large boat put aboard her the five convicts found on board during the passage; we gave our large boat to the commander. Obs. lat. 39° 53' 0", long. 142° 54' 48".
1802-12-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Sixteenth (7 December 1802). On the sixteenth, in the morning, we put our boats into the water. I despatched Citizen Freycinet, commanding the Casuarina, to proceed to the Hunter islands, at the western part of the north point of Van Diemen's Land, in order to determine their latitude in an exact manner, to make the plan of the harbours that may be found among the islands, and to fix their respective positions. This knowledge is all the more necessary for the safety of navigators, in that they form the entrance of the strait to the south of King Island. Citizens Freycinet and Boulanger were each entrusted with the following instructions:
The Commander &c. to Citizen Freycinet:
"As soon as Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, has come on board, you will get under sail "to proceed to the Hunter islands, of which the French Government wishes the geography to be made with "all the exactness of which this work is capable.
"In order to accomplish this as completely as possible, you will facilitate the work for Citizen Boulanger "by every means at your disposal, taking care, nevertheless, not to endanger, among "these islands, the safety of the ship you command, should there be too much risk in venturing among them.
"You will employ, in this work, as little time as possible, and will contrive to be back "in this same place within a fortnight. As the Géographe's position is not too secure at "this anchorage in winds from north to south passing through the east, this will not prevent you from "waiting for me here, should you not find me here at the time of your return, in that I shall come back "here again to rejoin you, should the winds oblige me to leave during your absence.
"The English who reside ashore will let you know the place to which I shall have taken the ship, should there be, in "the exploration about to be made of the island, a harbour where the ship might be in safety." Farewell, N. B.
The Commander &c. to Citizen Boulanger:
"The usefulness which must result, for the perfection of geography and the safety of navigators, from "a good knowledge of the position of the Hunter islands, which form the entrance of Bass Strait to the south of "King Island, has decided me to invite you to undertake this work. And in order to enable you to carry it out in "a manner that will leave you nothing to be desired, I have decided that the Casuarina, commanded by Citizen Freycinet, "shall convey you to the places you are to reconnoitre.
"This officer will facilitate for you every means at his disposal for the execution of the work "with which you are charged. Thus there remains nothing for me to recommend to you but to do it as promptly as "possible, so as not to delay too much our departure for other work no less interesting. As I am "persuaded that a fortnight will be more than sufficient for you, I shall expect you at that time and even "before, at this place, or should I be absent from it, you will be informed on your return of the manner in which "we are to rejoin one another." Farewell, N. B.
After having despatched Citizens Freycinet and Boulanger, I had my longboat prepared, the command of which I entrusted to Midshipman of the first class Baudin, and charged Citizen Faure, formerly geographer on board the Naturaliste and who was presently with me, with making the entire circuit of King Island, beginning from the north. There was put on board the boat, for ten days, provisions and everything
that was necessary for the geography of this coast.
Instructions given to Midshipman Baudin:
"I entrust to you, citizen, the command of my longboat, to convey Citizen Faure, "geographer, around King Island, beginning from the north. You will take care to stop at all the "points that Citizen Faure shall judge to deserve particular attention.
"When you are in the southern part of King Island, you must navigate with caution, in that "it is said several reefs and rocks awash are met with there, which it is prudent to pass with "caution. You will employ, on this excursion, only as little time as possible, and will come "to rejoin me at the same place from which you set out. Should I not be there, and had bad weather forced me to "put to sea, I shall not fail to return to this place, and as soon as you get sight of the "ship, you will go on board." Farewell, N. B.
To Citizen Faure, geographer:
"Citizen Boulanger having been sent on the mission for the reconnaissance of the Hunter islands, I have "reserved, citizen, the entire work of King Island for you, and you are personally charged with it.
"In order to give you every facility for doing so, I place at your disposal my longboat, of which "I entrust the command to Midshipman of the 1st class Baudin. He has orders to convey you around the island "and to set you down at the places where you wish to land. I cannot too strongly recommend to you the greatest "exactness in the work with which you are charged. You will yourself feel all the "consequence of it for the safety of navigators, since this island forms, to the west, the entrance of Bass Strait and Banks Strait, "which are known to you." Farewell. N. B.
As soon as this boat had departed, I sent off, in another, Citizen Ronsard, to examine, at some distance from us to the north, a place which seemed to me more convenient for the safety of the ship, in that an islet, which lies about a league off the land, appears to afford shelter when the winds are at south.
For the rest of the day, the weather was (fine), and the wind, almost calm, was in the southern quarter, variable to south-south-west. Captain Hamelin came to dine on board, and we agreed that if my launch, which had gone to seek a place suitable for watering, came back only laden, I would send it to him.
During this day, we found that the currents were very strong, but that they were only those of a regular tide, since they changed every six hours. We measured, on this first day, their speed at various times during the flood as during the ebb, and found by means of the log that their greatest speed was one mile three quarters.
It would be difficult to say why the name of bay has been given to the place we occupy, for it is positively only a bight without depth that could have led to its being so named. The two others, which lie to the north and to the south of this one, are no better, although the one to the south likewise bears the name of bay.
During the night, the wind was calm, the boats came back on board, but the launch brought back no water, the places it had frequented on this first expedition not being suitable for procuring any. On shore, the sea was found very rough and landing difficult.
Stay at King Island.
1802-12-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to south. At daybreak the midshipmen went to walk about on King Island in the small boat, manned by themselves. The dinghy, with the petty officers, went fishing. The commander sent a zoological case and a wombat. At nightfall the small boat came back from King Island. We began setting up the rigging and worked at it all night. At the anchorage, in 39° 50' 17" of latitude and 142° 16' 18" of longitude by account, the currents set N and S at a rate of 1.7 knots (maximum). The Casuarina got under way for the Hunter Islands; a boat of the Géographe went round King Island.

1802-12-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a strong breeze from the south falling away at nightfall. The tide, which until 2 had set south at 1.7 knots, began at 3 to set north.
1802-12-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Seventeenth of Frimaire (8 December 1802). On the seventeenth, in the morning, having learned of the return of my launch and of one of my boats, which I had sent both to make water and to communicate with the English who were on shore, occupied with sealing and with a species of seal they have named sea elephant, I was informed by the officers who were in these two boats that water was very difficult to procure at the place where they had landed, but that the people who inhabited the country had shown them another place which was more convenient, promising to go there the next day and to make a fire there to point it out to us. According to this arrangement, we waited constantly throughout the whole day for the signal that was to be made to us, and yet we saw nothing.
In the morning, the weather was fine, and the breeze light from south to south-south-west, as we had had it the evening before. The Naturaliste having to leave the next day, I went on board her with Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, to examine the state of the plants. We found them all in good condition, as were the live quadrupeds and birds. Only, we had had the misfortune to lose the last kangaroo remaining to us. Its death occurred following an injury that came to its thigh. But I have no doubt that all that remains will arrive safely.
After dinner, I took leave of Captain Hamelin and wished him a good voyage. I believe it is proper to observe that I had the pleasure of seeing only one of his officers, and even then I believe he would not have appeared had Captain Hamelin not invited him to dine with us. On leaving, I had them thanked for their politeness, having it said to them that I was quite glad not to have farewells to make to them.
In the evening, we got sight of a schooner making for the anchorage, which came, by every appearance, from Port Jackson. She anchored about eight o'clock, astern of the Naturaliste. As soon as I arrived on board, I sent to Citizen Depuche two sheep, twelve fowls and a pig from my own provisions, to contribute, along with Captain Hamelin's assistance, to his having fresh provisions for as long as possible during the crossing, his health being disordered.
I saw with infinite regret that the officers of that ship had preferred to spend, on frivolous and useless expenses, the money I had given them for keeping their table, having no other provisions than twelve pigs which they had had salted even before departure. Had I been able to foresee such an abuse, I would have done, in their regard, what I did with those who are with me and who wished to imitate them, but it was too late by the time I was informed of part of the conduct of some of those of the Naturaliste.
About nine o'clock, the winds having shifted to south toward east, Captain Hamelin got under sail and directed his course to pass to the north of King Island. The weather being very fine, I hope he will have cleared the strait early and that he will be favoured in making the longitude of the lands of Leeuwin.
1802-12-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. We finished setting up the rigging. The dinghy came back and brought few fish but many penguins, which were distributed to the crew. The commander came to dine aboard. On leaving he said to the captain: "I am spared taking leave of your officers; they have not had the civility to come and salute me." At 6 p.m. a sail was sighted in the east, which was made out to be an English schooner. At 7.30 she anchored near us and her captain came aboard. She was the Cumberland and had left Port Jackson 4 days after us. She was coming to King Island to take off the convicts we had, and was then to go and examine Frederick Hendrik Bay and the North River, where the English intended to form a settlement. She told us that the day after our departure from Port Jackson the Lady Nelson had arrived there, having left the Investigator in 20° of south latitude after bad weather in which he had lost 3 anchors and she all of hers (she had made one of wood). At 8.30 we got under way and shaped our course N 22° 30' E; at midnight the course was given north. An immense fire could be seen on the island at Elephant Bay. Since Port Jackson a wombat, both kangaroos and some birds had died; one of the dogs was injured.

1802-12-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SSE. The rigging was set up and the dinghy hoisted in; the topsails were stopped with rope yarns. The commander came to dine aboard and left at 6. At the same hour a sail was sighted in the east: it was a schooner which had left Port Jackson four days after us. At eight in the evening we got under way and shaped our course. We set about stowing the anchors. At 3 a.m., in sight of the northern coast of the anchorage, we took the bearing of the visible part of King Island, which stretched from S by SE to SSW. King Island at noon SE; the mainland NNW, distant 24 miles. Obs. lat. 39° 19' 55", long. 142° 18' 42".
1802-12-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Eighteenth of Frimaire (9 December 1802). On the eighteenth, in the morning, I had put ashore by my boat eight men who had hidden themselves, both on board the Géographe and on the Naturaliste, when we were on the point of leaving Port Jackson. They were given a bag of bread and some clothing. They were put ashore with the other Englishmen who are on the island, and who were very little pleased at their arrival, fearing that they might behave badly toward them. On leaving the ship, they came to beg me to give each of them a knife, but fearing that they might
make ill use of it, I would not grant their request, on which they insisted a great deal.
About nine o'clock, a boat came on board, having set out from the schooner that had arrived the evening before. At the moment when those who were in it came on board the Géographe, I was at work in my cabin, and it was not without surprise that I saw introduced an officer of the English Navy, accompanied by a geographer I had known at Port Jackson. After having reciprocally complimented one another on our meeting, I proposed to them to breakfast with us, which they accepted. It was then that Mr Robbins, who commanded this schooner, handed me a letter from Mr King, Governor of Port Jackson, and, shortly after, his instructions as to what he had to do. Having taken cognisance of Mr King's letter, I read his instructions, which, in all likelihood, are not entirely known to me, for he will not have shown me everything. But the contents of Mr King's letter gave me sufficient enlightenment to see the motive of his voyage, which had no other purpose than to observe us. I append here the translation of Governor King's letter:
"To the Commander of the Expedition &c.:
"You will doubtless be surprised to see a ship so near you. You knew my "intentions to make a settlement to the south, but this has been hastened by the reports that have been "communicated to me as soon as you departed. These reports are that the French wish to make a settlement in "the vicinity of Storm Bay, or in the part called Frederick Henry Bay. It is added that "these are the orders you have from the French Republic. This is what I was informed of by Colonel "Paterson, after your departure, he himself having been forewarned by a person from your ship.
"You will readily conceive that had such information been known to me before your "departure, I would have asked you for an explanation of it. But I knew nothing of it, and at present I do not "even believe it, and think it a rumour lightly ventured, of which, nevertheless, I have judged it fitting to "inform you, in case the Cumberland should come to meet with you. The commander of that ship is furnished "with my orders, and he is instructed to communicate them to you.
"My family and I wish you all that you could desire, and we shall long remember "the pleasure we have had in your company. We beg you to remember us to all your officers, and "to Captain Hamelin."
Signed, Governor King.
If this letter is not transcribed literally, it is very nearly what it contains. As I reserve to myself the right to answer Governor King in very few words on this subject, I was very reserved with these gentlemen who were on board, and contented myself with saying that I fully expected that after our departure, several stories would be made up that our presence prevented.
The English claim to Van Diemen's Land was strongly asserted in the instructions of the Captain of the schooner, but it was founded only on the taking of possession by Captain Phillip, the limits of which are set out in what we have known from the very beginning of the present settlement. It does not, therefore, seem doubtful to me that Governor King feared, from what he may have been told, that I might set someone down on this land to occupy it first, and that it was for this security's sake
Stay at King Island
that he was led to despatch a ship to observe us. I was only sorry that the Naturaliste had still been found there, because he entrusted her with fresh packets for the English Government, in which, no doubt, he gives an account of the step he has just taken, as well as of what he believes he has learned. The Naturaliste having left before the Governor's letter reached me, I have not been able to send it in the original to the French Government.
After we had parted, these gentlemen went ashore to see how their countrymen's work stood, and to take a view of the country. I informed them beforehand that we dined every day at four o'clock, and that they would be welcome, whenever they should wish to come and share it. They were also informed that I had put ashore eight deserters, in accordance with the promise I had made to Governor King not to carry them off, should any be found on board.
The rest of the evening had nothing particular about it. We occupied ourselves setting up the tent for the observatory on Elephant Islet, and made ready to transport all the naturalists ashore the next day. During the night, the winds were at south and calm.
The Eighteenth of Frimaire. (9 December 1802) On the eighteenth, the boats having returned the evening before from the shore, having found a place suitable for watering, the launch was despatched there with its rig of empty casks. The longboat also set out to transport the scientists, their science and their baggage, for these gentlemen never travel except with pomp and magnificence. The cooks and their utensils, the pots, the saucepans and the stewpots so encumbered the boat that not all of it could be stowed, and part of it had to be put in the launch. All this paraphernalia put me in such ill humour that I withdrew into my cabin, quite displeased that they had not all gone off on the Naturaliste.
At nine o'clock, I sent a boat on board the Cumberland with an officer, to return to these gentlemen the visit they had paid me. On its return, I was informed that during the night they had lost an anchor, their cable having been cut, no doubt, by some coral. Their intention, as I was told, was to ask me for another, but I have none that would suit her. And even had I one, it would not be prudent for me to strip myself of it, for the Casuarina might, from one moment to the next, have need of it.
At three o'clock in the afternoon, the Cumberland's boat came on board with the Captain and Mr Grimes, engineer and surveyor, who was with him. We dined together. The conversation had nothing particular about it, and there was no question whatsoever of the motive of their voyage. But they observed to me that, having been despatched in the greatest haste, they lacked a great many things, and that it had even been forgotten to give them a little gunpowder. They likewise had only one set of sails, all worn out, and no canvas to mend them with in case of need, and consequently neither thread nor needles. As they then made me a request for several other items, I invited them to make it in writing, promising to give them everything I could do without, without inconvenience. They told me they would not fail to send me this request the next day. At seven o'clock we parted, and I had them conveyed in one of my boats to their ship. The weather was fine throughout the day and during the night, with winds from south to south-east.
1802-12-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ESE to SSW. At 3.30, being abreast of the northern part of King Island, the course was given N 45° W; at 8 it was given S 78° 45' W. King Island bore from us S 11° E to S 22° W. At noon in 39° 19' 55" of latitude observed and in 141° 42' 24" of longitude by account. King Island S 45° E and the mainland N 22° W, 24 miles off; at 6 N 22° E, as far as the eye could reach.

1802-12-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south to SW. At 6 the land of New Holland could still be seen in the NNE as far as the eye could reach. Obs. lat. 39° 1' 5", long. 140° 30' 48".
1802-12-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Nineteenth of Frimaire (10 December 1802). On the nineteenth, we continued to work at replacing our water. The tents and all the great paraphernalia of the naturalists had been landed the evening before, so that I found myself rid of them until the moment of re-embarkation. There remains on board only Mr Bailly, mineralogist, and I scarcely know why. I had planned to go ashore in the morning, to return in the evening. But about eight o'clock, the wind having increased, I changed my resolution, fearing to be obliged to get under sail. Although the breeze was fresh and the weather seemed to be turning bad, it nevertheless turned fine again during the day. When the time of the flood tide had passed, they fell calm, and the sea, which had been fairly disturbed by the tidal current, likewise subsided.
During the day, the schooner Cumberland got under sail and drew nearer to the coast. I could well have done the same, for the greater convenience of our boats, but I preferred to remain at the place where I found myself, being better prepared for getting under way in winds from east or south-east.
At the beginning of the night, the launch came back on board with its load of water, that is to say having filled about sixteen casks that served us as ground tier.
During the night, there was nothing particular, and the breeze fell calm about nine o'clock, as it had been since we have been at this anchorage.
1802-12-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to SSE. At noon in 39° 3' of latitude by account and in 139° 54' of longitude by account.
