At 6 an island was sighted in the N 3° E. At 8 the course was given S 67° 30' W. At 9.30 we sounded without finding bottom at 120 fathoms.

1802-12-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds variable from SW, SSE and east. At 6 took the bearing of an island N 3° E. At 9.30 p.m. sounded without finding bottom. Obs. lat. 38° 39' 56", est. long. 137° 31'.
1802-12-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Twentieth of Frimaire (11 December 1802). On the twentieth, the wind being almost calm and the weather very fine, we weighed our anchor, being persuaded that it must be fouled with its own cable, from the swinging the ship had done at every change of tide. When we were apeak, we let go the port one and weighed the other. As the cable came in on board, it was noticed that it was much chafed at about twenty fathoms from the clinch. We were all the more vexed at this, as it was a new cable going into the water for the first time. When our anchor was awash, we found it not only fouled, as we had suspected, but we also saw that the shackle was broken, which surprised us greatly. We set to work at once to bring it on board to change it, far from expecting that it was going to become useless to us once it was presented in the manner suitable for this work. It was only then that it was noticed that the eye which fits over the anchor's bill was entirely unsoldered and no longer held to anything. This discovery obliged us to condemn it and to bring up another from the hold.
It does not seem doubtful that the nature of the bottom, which the sounding indicates everywhere as fine sand, is mixed with patches of coral. And our cable would undoubtedly have been cut had we not examined it in time. It was ordered to be veered to about thirty fathoms from the clinch, so that a like accident should not befall it in future. The work of which I have just spoken occupied our people almost the whole day.
The Cumberland sent me, in the morning, a boat on board with the note of what she stood in greatest need of. Her request was filled in full, and there were sent to her the following articles: a sounding lead, a line of sixty fathoms, a piece of canvas of one hundred and eight English yards, a pound of sail twine, six needles, six padlock hasps and their staples. The Captain also sent to ask me to make an anchor shackle. His being broken, he asked me for a boat to go and drag for the one he had lost. The weather not being suitable for this last piece of work, it was put off to another time, as was his anchor stock, not having sent the proportions.
There were also given to him thirty twelve-pound charges of powder, having nothing on board with which to fire a musket shot. During the night, the sky was overcast, the weather rainy and the breeze very unsteady from the eastern quarter. The launch brought back on board its load of water.
1802-12-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to E. At 4 the course given west. At noon in 38° 40' of latitude observed and in 138° 17' of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze.

1802-12-12.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sea getting up a little as the easterly breeze held; the pump sucked at 15 inches. Est. lat. 38° 26' 33", est. long. 134° 14' 0".
1802-12-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind very unsteady from E to N. At noon in 38° 12' of latitude by account and in 135° 23' of longitude by account.

1802-12-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind very unsteady and very variable from east to N and NW. From midnight to 4 a very thick fog. Obs. lat. 38° 41' 17", est. long. 132° 32'.
1802-12-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock in the evening, the rock, or rather the islet which the English have named the Elephants, bore to the west-north-west, at an estimated distance of two leagues.
The land was too hazy for one to be able to distinguish the northern and southern extremities from the sight of King Island.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, in the morning, we embarked the water that our cutter had brought in during the night. My intention was to send it back immediately for a third voyage, but the weather had such a bad appearance that, fearing it might become seriously bad, I preferred to have it brought on board if I was obliged to set sail so that it was safer. I used the same precaution with regard to our three other boats which were alongside.
We occupied ourselves, in the course of the morning, with preparing our watch cable, work which could not be done the previous day.
During the evening, the sea began to become rough and I wanted to set sail, but as we had observed that, since our arrival on this coast, the wind had always calmed after sunset, I thought that the same would happen for the coming night and I kept my position.
The schooner the Cumberland had set sail to get closer to the bottom of the cove and fetch water and wood.
At about three and a half o'clock, I was warned that we were dragging, the ship having come across. But we soon found that (we) were being carried away by the current, our cable being broken. We immediately got under way, going down on the port side and took the southern course towards the east by easterly winds which then changed to east-north-east. As we had a good buoy on our anchor, I was not worried, being well persuaded that I would find it as soon as the weather permitted me to return to the anchorage. What had just happened to us confirmed me even more that the place where we were at anchor, though clean by the indication of the plumb, is nothing of the sort and that there is a great quantity of corals or rocks covered superficially by very fine sand.
At five o'clock, being reasonably far from the coast, we went about to take the northern course and at eight o'clock, being about abeam of the rock or large islet which the English have named the Elephant. We took its bearing at west-north-west at a distance of two leagues according to our dead reckoning which may be in error in that the haze which covered the land did not permit us to do better. After this bearing, we continued the northern course towards the east as much as the winds permitted. The depth was then eleven fathoms and I was very surprised that it was not greater at such a distance from the coast. However, we continued the same course, sounding frequently. This course led us into a tidal eddy where the sea was strongly agitated and choppy. I immediately had the lead thrown and we found only six and a half fathoms. We continued the same course, sounding constantly. We then found eight, nine and fifteen without having made a distance that suggested we should be increasing so rapidly.
For several days, I had observed that to the north-east of our anchorage, a large swell would rise from time to time which sometimes seemed to me to break. The day I dined on board the Naturaliste which was further to the east than us, I saw it even better and had it observed by Captain Hamelin; men were sent aloft who, after observing for a long time, said they could see nothing. But I remained no less persuaded that there must be shallow water in that place and I
engaged him to pay all the more attention to it when he set sail, since the danger, if there was one, lay on the course he had to take.
I remain therefore, persuaded from what I observed of our anchorage and the shallow water we found when passing that place, that it is prudent to be wary of it and I believe there is even less water to the east of the place where we found only six and a half fathoms. My intention is indeed to send someone to reconnoitre that place as soon as the weather permits to know for certain what is the case.
From fifteen fathoms we passed to 18 and to 22 and at two o'clock in the morning, we were at fifty.
The night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second was for us one of the worst we had passed since our departure. The rain was abundant and almost continuous. The winds turned at different times all round the horizon and obliged us to constantly work our sails. Lightning and thunder claps were so numerous that one might say that for more than four hours in succession they had no interruption until the next day. As I spent the night on deck, my sight was so much affected that in the end I could not distinguish any object.
The Twenty-second (13 December 1802), at daylight, the weather was hardly any better than the day before. We went about at four o'clock in the morning to take the southern course towards the east in order to keep ourselves at the latitude of the island, being far enough to the east to withstand a blow of weather if it should come to pass as the appearance of the atmosphere and the movement of the barometer which was below 27 (sic) inches seemed to announce. However, as the sea had greatly abated, we flattered ourselves that we would get off with a fright, and that during the day the sky would clear up. These sudden changes had already taken place several times. What we had foreseen or rather wished for, came to pass, for about eight o'clock, the wind began to calm and having shifted to the north, it dispersed both the clouds and the haze which surrounded our horizon.
At eleven o'clock, steering south 87° west, we sighted the land which was then bearing from west to west-south-west.
At noon, we observed 39° 50' 27" of south latitude. As the astronomer and the timekeepers were ashore, we had no hour angle for the longitude.
In the afternoon, we continued to make progress towards the land. We soon sighted the islet on which our astronomer Bernier was, and shortly after, we saw at anchor the schooner the Cumberland which greatly surprised us for the weather of the day before did not allow us to believe that she could have remained at anchor. So one might well say that the Captain who commanded her was more fortunate than prudent. Perhaps also he could not get under way in easterly winds without running the risk of running ashore, being entirely at the bottom of the cove and about one mile from the shore. Be that as it may, his position decided me to approach closer to the coast in the hope that the bottom would be better, so I came to anchor in ten fathoms of water still however on a sandy bottom which should not be of good holding. But I thought that the rocks of the bottom must be covered with a thicker layer than by fourteen fathoms which was our first anchorage.
As soon as the vessel was moored and our sails furled, we launched the boats and I immediately sent the officers Bonnefoy and Ransonnet, one in my cutter and the other in my large canoe, to reconnoitre and search for the buoy of the anchor whose cable had been cut by the bottom. As we had good bearings of it, it could not be lost.
Each of them was given a signal flag so they would let us know when they found it. Immediately after their departure, I had our large anchor prepared at anchorage and had the cable which would serve it prepared in case of need.
During the rest of the evening, the weather was very fine and the sea calm, which helped greatly in allowing us to recover our anchor which I should have been very sorry to lose.
At seven o'clock, we sighted the canoe which I had sent under the orders of M. Faure. As it was returning from the south, there was no doubt that it had completely gone round the island.
Half an hour later, we saw our cutter strike its sails which led us to conjecture that it was moored to our buoy, which it signalled to us shortly after.
On the arrival of M. Faure and the midshipman who commanded the canoe, I was informed of the cruise they had just made, but as both of them are to make a written report to me, I will speak of it on another occasion.
At midnight, our cutter returned on board but without being able to raise our anchor. The same officers who had been charged with this task were ordered to set out again the next day at daybreak and not to return on board without bringing it back. During the night, the weather was fine and the winds were north-westerly and moderate.
1802-12-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to SSW by way of west. At noon in 38° 41' of latitude observed and in 133° 59' of longitude by account.

1802-12-14.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a fresh breeze from WSW, SSE and ESE by way of south. At 8 changed tacks; we worked at setting up the main yard slings. Est. lat. 38° 53' 6", long. 131° 46'.
1802-12-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings from the anchorage:
The point to the south of the cove at south 22° east
The north point at north 23° west
The islet at north 8° east
The tents of the Naturaliste at south 18° west
The establishment of the English fishermen at north 46° west
The schooner the Cumberland abeam of us at one mile. The distance from the ship to the shore: 3 miles.
(continued from page 279) He dined with our scholars, which he had just done not seeming to me to be an act of politeness. I do not know if those were his orders, but it confirmed me that he had been sent to observe us rather than to deliver to me the insignificant letter which the Governor King had addressed to me on this occasion.
After my return on board, our cutter and the two canoes brought back our anchor which they had had considerable trouble raising. The precaution had been taken of dropping a shackle before trying to extract it from the bottom, and this measure was very prudent for the cable parted twice. As soon as it was on board, it was put in place and secured immediately.
At four o'clock, the English schooner set sail and sent us another canoe on board to ask me to give him the iron rings I had promised him for his anchor, if they were ready. M. Robbins made known to me by this occasion that he was going to seek the anchorage which was to the north-west of the island from what he had heard about it from our scholars to whom the men of the canoe had spoken. His four rings were handed to him and he continued his way. The winds were then east very light, but as the flood tide favoured him, he moved away from the shore before nightfall. At sunset, the wind continued to freshen, but as the sea had little movement, I thought that it was only a passing breeze and which would not fail to calm at the beginning of the night, as had happened every day since we had been on this coast. Nevertheless, so as not to be hampered if I had to get under way, I had three of my boats put on board, leaving out only my cutter which I wanted to moor to our cable if I had to set sail.
From eight o'clock to ten, the sky was very dark and the winds still east but moderate. A few stronger gusts passed occasionally and ceased as soon as the cloud which had caused it had passed the ship. The rain, nevertheless, was continuous, but without lightning or thunder and the sea was always calm.
Despite such little appearance of bad weather, the wind increased about ten o'clock and it began with fairly strong gusts which succeeded one another continuously. I began then to fear that I could not remain at anchor. Being unable to count on the bottom, I immediately rang the bell to bring everyone on deck and be ready to slip our cable by the end if the ship should drag. Despite this (precaution),
the crew was extremely slow to appear and it was necessary more than once to send below to make them come up. I had already given orders that our cutter be moored to the buoy of the anchor, but it was so long before this was put into execution that the ship was set adrift before it could be done.
As the current was against us, it was carrying us rapidly towards the shore and we had only seven fathoms of water when we had raised our topsails. Fortunately for us, the winds shifted to the north-east for otherwise we should have had trouble getting ourselves out of the bad position in which we found ourselves.
It is certain that the crew showed themselves very badly in this occasion and whether it was the fear of the rain which was abundant or whether they were ignorant of the danger in which we were, they were very slow to come up on deck. Once the ship was out of danger, which was not long, when the sails were up, we occupied ourselves with our cutter which there was no longer any means of embarking both because the sea had already become bad and for lack of space to stow it, the other boats having been put in the place it was to occupy. We were therefore obliged to pay it out astern and tow it by means of a strong line which was secured to the rail. As it appeared to be safe in this position, we continued to make way to get ourselves a little offshore.
During the rest of the night, the weather was very bad. And to have it as we had encountered the day before, there was nothing lacking but thunder and lightning, which did not occur this time.
About two o'clock, thinking ourselves far enough offshore to have nothing to fear, we took a third reef in the topsails, but as we were sounding every half hour, we were very surprised to find only ten fathoms of water whereas I thought I had at least twenty-five from the distance I estimated I had made to the east-south-east. We continued then to sound constantly and in less than half an hour we passed to eight and seven, which decided me to bear away immediately to the south-east, persuaded that the flood tide had carried us to the north-east and made us get near the shoal of which I have already spoken. On the south-east course, the bottom increased noticeably, we passed from seven to fifteen. Then we close-hauled again and shortly after we found only twelve and then eleven. But as I believed myself at the eastern extremity of the shoal and that I believed myself no longer to be in the west, we continued the same course sounding always so as not to be surprised if it should continue to diminish. From twelve, we came to fifteen and almost immediately to twenty. When we were at twenty-five, having nothing more to fear, I gave orders that we continue the same tack, sounding only from two hours to two hours. I then withdrew to my cabin to change, being wet to the bone. The rain continued the rest of the night and the wind was strong with heavy gusts. As they were drawing from the part of the north, we hoped that fine weather would not be long in appearing.
Of 23 Frimaire (14 December 1802). On the twenty-third the cutter and the large canoe departed at four o'clock in the morning as ordered the day before. At five o'clock both were on the buoy, and we saw from the ship that efforts were being made to raise it. At seven o'clock, a second canoe was sent to the island where our observatory was to bring back four men I had put there to cut hay. It returned on board at ten o'clock, and I immediately sent it for reinforcement to the men who had gone to raise my anchor, which we knew was then afloat. But as the winds and tide were contrary, the cutter could not return.
About nine o'clock, the Captain of the English schooner the Cumberland, M. Robben, came on board, asking me to have four iron rings prepared for one of his anchors which had broken. The one which belonged to him having been broken, I gave orders that they should be prepared for him and he then went ashore. As the weather was very fine in the morning, I decided to go ashore. It was the first time I had left the ship since our arrival on this coast, but I was pleased to see what our scholars who had been there for several days were doing and how they were spending their time. I arrived ashore about noon. I found there the Captain of the English schooner and this did not surprise me since he had told me he was going there. But on the other hand, I was quite surprised to see an English flag positively in the place where our tents were set up. I thought at first, from the way it was placed, that it was a flag standing upright. But having caught sight of a soldier in red uniform with a bayonet in his hand, I asked what it could be. Our scholars then told me that about an hour before, M. Robbins, who had come ashore to dine with them, had placed it in the manner I saw it and that they did not know what it meant, unless it was to let us know that the island belonged to him. I did not think it right to enter into any explanation on this subject, since it is certain that they were the fishermen who discovered and frequented this island before us. But if the property belongs to whoever went round it first, it is certain that it was the French.
At two o'clock, the weather not having a good appearance, although there was a calm, I returned on board and left M. Robbins and his flag quite alone and undisturbed. (continued page 280)
1802-12-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather with rain, the wind a light breeze from SSW to NE. At 4 the course given N 67° 30' W; a sail was sighted in the S 34° E. At noon in 38° 49' of latitude by account and in 133° 12' of longitude by account. At 2 the wind freshened and was a strong breeze from S to SW.

1802-12-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, continual rain during the watch. The wind light until 2, then a strong breeze from south to SW. Obs. lat. 37° 40' 42", long. 129° 27'.
1802-12-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, when daylight began to appear, it was noticed that our cutter which we had been towing all night was ready to sink. I was warned and immediately gave orders to the officer of the watch to bring her across and haul her on board so as to put her on the tackles and then on board, no matter where. While this manoeuvre was being executed which, however, was not long, she sank and capsized almost immediately. I thought we should be content with the loss of the objects which were in her. But it was not so, for when we tried to haul her on board, the rail to which the line was secured was separated from the cutter and there is reason to believe that the entire bow was broken. As she was floating on the water, I gave orders that we go about to approach her and not lose sight of her. But this was useless for, at the same moment, the blocks which supported and served as guides for the strops of the rudder bar, having failed, the ship could not complete her evolution by wearing round and came again on the port tack. A squall of the most violent kind followed all these misfortunes so that we were obliged to heave to and to furl with all speed our foresail and our topsails to remain under the storm jib and the mizzen. We immediately occupied ourselves with the repair of the damage to the rudder bar of which we were soon in a position to make use.
After sunrise, the wind increased to such a point that we were very glad to have heaved to early for we should infallibly have lost some sails in furling them. The force of the wind carried from the extremity of the waves such a great quantity of vapour that it seemed that it was raining continuously around the ship although the sky was fairly clear. This gale lasted without much interruption until noon, when the winds having shifted from north-north-west to west, calmed a little and allowed us to set our foresail and the small topsail, keeping the course north towards the west, no longer having hope of finding our cutter except by a happy chance.
In the afternoon, the winds shifted from west to south-west and they were very unequal accompanied sometimes by rain, squalls and strong gusts. The sky nevertheless seemed to want to clear up and we had it fairly fine at sunset.
During the night, the weather was hardly different from what it had been during the evening, the winds shifted little from west by south-west, but they were nonetheless often accompanied by gales, rain and gusts. Nothing was changed in the sails and at midnight, being by thirty-nine fathoms depth, we took the southern course which was continued until daylight.
1802-12-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW, with squalls; struck the topgallant masts. At noon in 37° 41' of latitude observed and in 131° 51' of longitude by account.

1802-12-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the wind falling away from SW, W, NW and WSW. At 4 it freshened and the sky clouded over, with a high sea. Obs. lat. 37° 17' 33", long. 128° 45'.
1802-12-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the weather continued with squalls and strong gusts. However, it seemed from the state of the atmosphere that we should soon have a change in our favour. The sea, although still very rough and agitated, was beginning to abate and the gales became, each time one came to us, less severe. The winds which had constantly blown from west by south-west, shifted to west by north-north-west about eleven o'clock and the sky cleared, although the barometer was still low, that is to say below 27 inches.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 39° 28' 12" and I was surprised to find myself so far north. According to the dead reckoning of the various courses we had made, we did not expect to be more than 39° 39' 34", so we found ourselves with a difference of 0° 11' 24" more north than we reckoned. This error since departure was attributed to the currents which we knew were very strong and irregular in their directions.
During the evening, the weather being fine, we took the southern course to regain the latitude of the island. The wind having greatly calmed, we loosened a reef in the topsails and set more sail.
At noon, the lead reported forty fathoms. At four o'clock, it was only (no figures) and at eight, (no figures). We then resumed the northern course which was continued until midnight and we came back again to the southern one.
At sunset, we did not see the land from which we were no doubt further to the east than the dead reckoning indicated. The entire horizon in the western part was heavily overcast and announced some new gale for the night. In order to withstand them quietly and without fatigue, I took the precaution of taking a third reef in the topsails and furling the other sails which we had set during the evening. The precaution I took was not entirely useless for during the night the weather became bad, rainy and there were strong gusts which succeeded one another with some rapidity. The sea did not become however very great which led me to believe that we were abeam of the island and not too far offshore. In the contrary case it would have been, like the previous days, strongly agitated, great and rough.
1802-12-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather with frequent squalls, the wind a strong breeze from NW to N. At noon in 37° 18' of latitude observed and in 131° 18' of longitude by account. At 1, in a squall, the fore staysail was torn from its stay; it was shifted. At 2 we took the lower reef in the topsails, and at 6 lay to.

1802-12-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather with frequent squalls, a strong breeze from SW. Took all the reefs in the topsails.
1802-12-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, the weather was constantly rainy throughout the morning and accompanied by very violent squalls with strong gusts. We were obliged to furl our flying topgallant and take a third reef in our topsails. The sea was no less disagreeable than the weather and several times we received waves on board.
At noon, we reckoned ourselves to be at 39° 50' 6" of latitude by our dead reckoning, but I think we were more south. Our longitude also placed us at 142° 29' 6", undoubtedly further west than we truly are, having had to drift greatly to the east according to the wind and sea we have constantly had since we left the anchorage. The barometer which was at 27° 6' did not announce a very imminent change.
In the morning in a clear spell, the lookouts from the tops of the masts thought they caught sight of land in the south-west by south. It is possible, but I doubt it. At ten o'clock, having had clear weather for an hour and a fairly extended horizon, we did not see the land in the south-west by south which we had been told of in the morning, but we distinctly made out in the south-east by south two islands and an isolated rock which appeared to be further to the west. I do not doubt that it was the islands which are near King Island and of which the Naturaliste had had knowledge. I was disposed to go and reconnoitre them in order not to lose our time needlessly in tacking, but the rain and haze having begun again and the gusts being even more violent, I could not execute this plan. We were even obliged to furl our small topsail, so heavy and well-conditioned were the gales we were continuously receiving.
The bottom was then thirty-three fathoms and we were on the northern course.
In the afternoon, seeing no appearance of change in the weather, we prepared ourselves for the night which presented itself under a very unpromising aspect. The horizon, in all its parts, was charged with thick stormy vapours which announced nothing but bad weather for the approaching night and the darkness of the sky made it longer than usual. For at seven and a half o'clock, one could no longer see. However, although the weather was very bad and the gusts in the squalls violent, we passed it better than I had expected. Although the entire horizon was lit up by continuous lightning, not a single clap of thunder was heard and all the clouds dissolved into rain. Several gave us fairly thick hail whose reception was not pleasant. Nevertheless, we found ourselves fortunate not to have been more ill-treated.
1802-12-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to WSW. At 9 we filled and stood on, the wind less strong. At noon in 35° 54' of latitude by account and in 131° 0' of longitude by account.

1802-12-18.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the wind a fresh breeze; the wind less fresh at 5.30 and at 9 p.m. Changed tacks. The main topgallant sail and main topsail were repaired, and we took the opportunity to set up the main topmast stay. Obs. lat. 35° 45' 24", long. 128° 23' 6".
1802-12-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, the weather, without being as bad as the day before, was hardly any better. The winds which had shifted to west-north-west, varied little and blew with force and in gusts within the squalls which often gave us hail although much smaller in volume than that of the previous night. At midnight, we took the southern course which was continued until eight o'clock in the morning when we came on to the northern one, by wearing round.
In the morning, the sky became fairly clear, but one squall followed immediately after another. However, at noon, we were able to observe the altitude of the sun which was found to be 39° 17' 30". According to our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves to be at 39° 26' 12" which gave us an error of 0° 8' 42" further north than we reckoned. Our longitude by dead reckoning was 142° 47' 26".
During the evening, the weather which had been fairly clear in the morning became covered again with clouds and haze. At noon, we took the southern course and about three o'clock, we sighted in the east by north-east a two-masted vessel. As it might be that this was the Casuarina, returning from the Hunter Islands, I gave orders that we reconnoitre her. Accordingly, we bore away towards her and soon joined her. We then saw that it was not her, but the English schooner the Cumberland which had left the anchorage on the same day. When we recognised her at a mile's distance, we resumed the southern course. This vessel was hove to under her mainsail with all reefs taken, she showed her flag when we had passed her and we replied without stopping. At five o'clock, we lost sight of her.
During the night of the 27th to the 28th, the weather was as we had had for four days, that is to say bad, rainy and in squalls with well-conditioned gales. Nevertheless, the sea appeared to us to be less bad. At eight o'clock, we took the northern course which was continued until four o'clock in the morning when we headed to the southern one, without the weather becoming better or announcing any change. The barometer only, still between 27° 7' and 27° 8' and although the thermometer was fairly high, this did not prevent us from often having hail in the squalls.
1802-12-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 6 we shook out the reefs and rigged the topgallant masts. At noon in 35° 45' of latitude observed and in 130° 55' of longitude by account.

1802-12-19.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea. A fresh breeze from WSW to SW. The main topsail and main topgallant sail being repaired and the backstays and stay set up, we set both sails. At 11 changed tacks. Est. lat. 36° 12' 10", long. 128° 54' 54".
1802-12-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the sky was very dark and hazy, several squalls gave us abundant rain, but as the gusts were much less strong than those of the night before, we believed that the bad weather was about to cease and that we should have a change in our favour during the day. The sea which was beginning also to be less great, contributed to making us believe in this change which each of us desired for it had been long enough that we were agitated and tormented by the bad weather.
During the morning, the sky indeed cleared and the horizon became clear and extended although the winds were still from the west, this did not however prevent us from undergoing from time to time fairly good gusts mingled with rain and hail, but it was very little in comparison to the past.
At noon, we observed the latitude as 39° 42' 51" and we reckoned ourselves at 143° 1' 4" of longitude. We were then on the southern course, and after the observation, we changed it to take the northern one. Scarcely were we headed when we caught sight of a large islet to the north-east. This sight surprised us at first, not believing we had land in our vicinity. We continued the northern course to find out what it was and, as the wind was then much less strong, we loosened a reef in the topsails and set the flying topgallant. As we advanced to the north, we sighted a second islet, and shortly after the coast of New Holland. We could no longer doubt that the drift, the currents and the strong wind had thrown us much further to the west than the east our dead reckoning made it and we positively assured ourselves by closing with the coast that the lands which we had in sight were those of Wilson Promontory, the first islet being that of the Cone and the second that which we had named the Aim Point. After we had assured ourselves of our position, we continued the route north towards the west, the winds having shifted to west-south-west. We also sighted the English schooner the Cumberland which was still further to the east than us and which was running the southern course.
The weather was fairly fine until about three o'clock in the afternoon, but at that time it became bad again. The sky became charged with thick clouds which gave us strong gusts and violent squalls, mingled with rain and hail. Although the weather had very bad appearance, we changed nothing in our sails in order to rise to windward of the land and the islets so that the southern course which I intended to take during the night became better. At seven o'clock in the evening, having had a clear spell, we took a final bearing of the Cone islet which was then bearing north 56° east at an estimated distance of seven or eight leagues.
From seven o'clock until ten o'clock at night, we continued to make way to the north, steering to the west as much as possible when the winds permitted, but despite this, the course was worth hardly more than north so strong was the wind and bad the sea. We were even obliged to take a third reef in the topsails before coming about to the south.
All night the weather was very bad and the violent squalls were always accompanied by rain and hail.
1802-12-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW. At noon in 36° 54' of latitude observed and in 131° 32' of longitude by account. Fine weather and the wind a fresh breeze in the afternoon.

1802-12-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky clear, the horizon thick, a swell running, a fresh breeze from SW. Est. lat. 36° 7' 10", long. 127° 34' 54".
1802-12-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At two o'clock in the afternoon,
the land of the Promontory was sighted with the southernmost bearing at north 28° east
The Cone islet was at north 40° east
And the Aim Point at north 73° east
At five o'clock,
The same Cone islet was at north 45° east
At six o'clock,
It was at north 40° east
And the land of the Promontory at north 20° east
At seven o'clock,
We saw the Cone islet again at north 56° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, we had the same weather as the day before and the squalls were even more frequent. The rain and hail succeeded one another with such rapidity that I believe that the worst winter's day in Europe is finer than this one was. The sea, which had become very great, greatly incommoded us, and we then received some waves. One of the seamen was knocked down and received a fall which will perhaps oblige him to remain long in his hammock.
As we had some clear spells in the intervals of the squalls, we had an observation of the sun at noon, and although it is doubtful, it is surely better than what our dead reckoning would have given us. This observation placed us at 40° 27' 5" and according to the bearing of the lands seen the day before, our estimated longitude placed us at 144° 12' instead of 142° 58' 38" which we had reckoned since our departure from King Island.
In the afternoon, the weather continued with squalls, strong gusts and rain. We received some so vigorous that they obliged us to furl our flying topgallant, for fear of losing the sail or breaking the mast. The winds, towards evening, having shifted more towards the south by passing to south-west, we continued the north-westerly course which I intended to follow until midnight if they remained in the same quarter. At sunset, the horizon from the south to the north being very extended, we had knowledge of no land in the vicinity.
During the night, the squalls and rain continued without interruption. When they had passed the sky was fairly fine, but the interval which they put between them was so small that one had hardly time to perceive it. Only, they sometimes caused the winds to shift as far as south-south-west which made me not take the southern course as I had intended, had they not permitted us to steer to the north-west. Moreover, we sounded several times during the night, without finding bottom at forty and forty-five fathoms, proof that we were fairly far from the coast and that the course we had made since noon had carried us fairly far some way to the west, despite the great sea, the drift and the current.
1802-12-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to W. At noon in 36° 7' of latitude by account and in 130° 14' of longitude by account. At 3 a flat calm; at 7 the breeze got up from the NE and drew round to NNE, a fresh breeze. The course was given S 67° 30' W.

1802-12-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm until 7, when the wind made; at 9 it blew a fresh breeze after drawing round to NNE. At 6 a.m. the wind, falling away more and more, drew round to WNW. Est. lat. 34° 54' 4", long. 125° 48' 24".
1802-12-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock in the morning,
The Cone islet remained at north 82° east.
At noon,
The lands of the southern extremity of Wilson Promontory were visible at north 85° east
And the lands in sight furthest to the north extended to north 22° 15' west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, in the morning, the weather at last seemed to want to clear up, although we still had from time to time some squalls with rain. They were not comparable to those we had had during the night, and still less with the previous days. As we had been on the north-westerly course all night, one expected to see the land at daylight, and indeed we should have recognised it had the horizon from the north to the east not been heavily overcast. But at six o'clock, the clouds which had hidden it from us having partly dispersed, we had sight of the Cone islet which was then at north 82° east at eight or ten leagues distance according to our dead reckoning.
About seven o'clock, the wind having greatly calmed, we set the flying topgallant. Shortly after, we hauled in the mainsail and about ten o'clock we loosened a reef in our topsails.
During the rest of the morning, the sky became completely fine. The clouds and squalls disappeared entirely and everything seemed to announce to us the return of fine weather, although the winds changed little. The barometer whose movements rarely deceived us was rising rapidly which had not happened for a long time.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 39° 4' 28". We then had good knowledge of the western coast of the Promontory and according to the bearing we took of it, our longitude was found to be 143° 31' 0", not far from Port of Bass.
In the afternoon, we continued the north-westerly course with very variable winds from south-west to west-south-west and the sky always fine, keeping the coast at seven or eight leagues distance. We continued this same course until four o'clock when we took the southern course.
At sunset, the sky which during the greater part of the day had been fine and clear, became covered again with clouds, but they did not have the appearance of those which carry gales and hail, so the sky was only dark and hazy and the wind almost calm until the next day when we had northeasterly winds. During the night, we sounded several times without finding bottom at forty-five fathoms.
1802-12-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE; it fell away at 6 and drew round to WNW at 7. Almost calm with continual rain; at 8 the breeze freshened and drew round to NNE, a fresh breeze. At noon in 36° 50' of latitude by account and in 128° 28' of longitude by account. At 2 the wind fell and drew round to the west and then to SSW, a strong breeze; the weather overcast and squally.

1802-12-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather; at 3 squally weather, the wind from W to SSW, a fresh breeze. Obs. lat. 36° 19' 43", est. long. 124° 7' 24".
1802-12-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon,
The lands of the Promontory were visible at south 78° east
And the lands furthest to the west, at north 16° west.
At four o'clock in the morning,
the Cone islet was seen at north 88° east, and the lands of the continent at north 24° east.
At six o'clock,
the Cone remained to the east at 7 or 8 leagues distance.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Nivôse, in the morning, the winds having shifted to the north-east, a light breeze, we made course to the south-west to go and seek King Island and recover the anchor and cable we had left there. I also expected to find the Casuarina there, which should have been back from her cruise according to the time I had fixed for her.
Throughout the morning we had a hazy sky and almost continuous light rain. In daylight, when the sky was less dark, we had sight of the lands of the Promontory. And at six o'clock, we took a bearing, in a momentary clear spell, of the Cone islet which was then to the east at 7 or 8 leagues distance. We attributed to the currents which, during the calm of the past night, must have carried us to the east, the knowledge we had in the morning of the lands which our dead reckoning had placed out of sight.
At noon, we had no observation of latitude. According to our dead reckoning it should have been 39° 31' 34", according to the reduction of the different courses we had made and the longitude of 142° 59'. But according to the bearing of the lands, we should have been no more than 38° 58' of latitude and 143° 48' 36" of longitude, which was very different from our dead reckoning.
In the afternoon, the weather was the same as in the morning, but a fine breeze from the north-east to the east-north-east blew and we made good way until six o'clock when we had sight of the land of King Island which remained to the west. We were astonished to encounter this island so soon when we still expected to be ten or twelve leagues from it, a distance to which our horizon could not extend on account of the quality of the atmosphere. But the land was too recognisable to be mistaken. Nevertheless, several persons claimed that what we saw could be nothing but the lands of the continent or some new islands placed to the north-west of King Island. Ridiculous as this assertion was, several remained convinced of it. Be that as it may, I continued to keep along the coast of King Island until eight o'clock in the evening and then I took the northern course which was followed for the greater part of the night, that is to say until four o'clock in the morning, although we were persuaded that we were running into the Great Bay where Port Philip is situated.
During the night, the weather was fairly fine and the winds from the east to the east-south-east very unequal, we sounded every hour and we had almost regularly a depth of twenty-seven fathoms without the slightest change.
1802-12-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 36° 20' of latitude by account and in 126° 48' of longitude by account.

1802-12-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea with a little swell, a fresh breeze from south to SE which drew round to NE. Obs. lat. 36° 39' 52", est. long. 123° 12' 20".
1802-12-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five o'clock in the afternoon,
King Island was sighted remaining in the west-south-west,
At eight o'clock in the morning,
its two extremities in sight remained from south 50° west to south 85° west.
At noon, being at anchor, the bearings of the anchorage were taken as follows:
The Elephants Rock islet at north 8° east.
The lands of the watering place at south 36° west.
The establishment of the fishermen at north 12° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, the weather being fine and the horizon very extended, we again saw King Island which remained in the west-south-west at an estimated distance of eight to nine leagues. As the winds were from the east-south-east to the south-east, I had not the desire to return to the anchorage despite the desire and need I had to find my anchor and cable. However, I decided to go there in order to assure myself at least whether the Casuarina which, according to her orders, should have been back, was there waiting for me. Our scholars, whom I had left ashore, were also lacking in bodily nourishment, for we saw no molluscs nor even seals which are there in great numbers. All these reasons therefore made me, again, run the chance of seeing the weather change or resuming the sea. I therefore gave orders to steer towards our old anchorage, so as to be better able to recover our anchor with the ship, having no longer a cutter to go and seek it.
At precisely noon, having reached the bearings which were to serve as our mark, we anchored in eight and a half fathoms and at very little distance from our buoy. But as the anchor did not bring the ship up immediately, the current caused us to drift from it by about half a league to the south. As soon as our sails were furled, we launched our three canoes. One was intended to go and fetch the astronomer from the islet where our observatory was established, the second was sent ashore to immediately dislodge our scholars and bring them on board without the least delay, the third, finally, went to moor on our buoy which it found only a short time before sunset. As soon as it was on it, we got under way with the ship and went to anchor so as to raise it with the ship. During this interval, the canoes returned from their missions and our astronomer, his baggage, his instruments and his person were embarked. The canoe sent for the other scholars was not so fortunate and came back without being able to land, so heavy was the sea and the bar. I shall have occasion to speak elsewhere of the difficulties this cove presents for landing, even when the weather is fine and the winds are from the west, which is why I shall say nothing of it for now.
The rest of the day and the greater part of the night was spent pursuing our anchor which we finally succeeded in drawing from the bottom as well as our cable which was found to be but little damaged. It was two and a half o'clock in the morning when everything was on board. This long delay was caused by the difficulty we had in passing a shackle on account of the violence of the current. Moreover, the night was very fine and the breeze from the south was moderate although fairly strong gusts occasionally passed.
I was very sorry not to find the Casuarina at this anchorage and I was not without anxiety about the accidents which might have befallen her if she had been engaged among the islands at the time when the gale began.
1802-12-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SE to NW by way of east. At noon in 36° 40' of latitude observed and in 125° 54' of longitude by account. From 9 to 10.30 we passed through immense shoals of fish spawn.

1802-12-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the wind almost calm and very variable. At 8 p.m. it freshened. From 9 p.m. until 10.30 we were surrounded by a great quantity of fish spawn. Obs. lat. 37° 25' 29", est. long. 121° 54' 20".
1802-12-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Staying at anchor. King Island.
On the third, the wind being almost calm and the sky very fine, I sent off at daybreak a canoe to go and fetch our scholars and their baggage and their specimens. I was persuaded that the fine weather of the night must have allayed the sea and that it would be easy to embark them. I was not deceived in my expectation. They all arrived about nine o'clock, with the exception of M. Péron who, seeing only molluscs at every step he took, had amused himself by missing the first canoe, no doubt counting on returning in the second which I had sent with the carpenters and the engineer Ronsard to go and cut wood suitable for the construction of the new cutter which I wanted to have built partly on board, so that there was only to set it up when we had a favourable opportunity.
In the morning, the master who presides over the establishment of the English fishermen in this cove came on board to be replenished with provisions which he had supplied to our scholars during my absence, and by this means I learned that they had not suffered more from hunger than we had, which gave me great pleasure. I gave this fisherman who is called Cooper, fifty pounds of biscuits, a large bottle of rum, twenty pounds of sugar, three pounds of tea and six bottles of red wine. I also bought from these people some emus or ducks, a male kangaroo much prized and three wombats. They spent part of the morning on board.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted from south-south-west to south-south-east, the breeze freshened considerably and the fishermen told me that I should expect to have a strong breeze for the night. My intention was indeed not to spend it at anchor, but what they told me made me hasten my departure. I at once called my canoe by a gun shot and had the topsails hoisted when the English fishermen left us. I gave M. Cooper the reply which I was making to M. King, Governor at Port Jackson for the letter which he had sent me by the Cumberland. As soon as my canoe arrived, we embarked it and set sail, it was then six o'clock in the evening.
During the night, the weather was not fine, but we had a very moderate breeze from south-south-east. I directed my course so as to gain knowledge the next day during the day of the Hunter Islands where I hoped to find the Casuarina in the channel which separates them from King Island, unable to conceive how, despite my verbal and written orders, she was not back, I having fixed the time when she should do so and having, for three days, had favourable winds.
1802-12-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 37° 25' of latitude observed and in 124° 34' of longitude by account.

1802-12-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, the wind a light breeze. In the forenoon set up the main topgallant mast. Saw weed. Obs. lat. 38° 24' 36", est. long. 120° 52' 20".
1802-12-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock in the evening,
The northern extremity of King Island remained at north 10° west,
the islet at north 32° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, in the morning, the winds having shifted during the night to the east-north-east, brought us very thick haze which lasted without much interruption throughout the day. Although the breeze was very moderate, we nevertheless found the sea very rough and driven by a swell from the south-west which seemed to announce to us that we should soon have the wind from that quarter.
At noon, there was no observation of latitude, that of dead reckoning placed us at 40° 12' 32" and we reckoned 142° 46' 42" of longitude.
This day, we began to work on the frame of our new cutter which I will have continued without interruption so as only to have to set it up in the first suitable place that may present itself. The carpenters charged with this work were exempted from keeping the night watch on the condition that they would work all day.
In the afternoon, the weather continued to be very hazy, the winds shifted to the east and were very variable, sometimes towards the north, sometimes towards the south. We often had calm and from time to time small gusts. We were sailing close-hauled, port tack. At five and a half o'clock, the haze having dispersed for a moment, we had sight of a small island of little extent but high. This land was taken at six o'clock, from south 20° west to south 40° west. As the current was carrying us with force to the south towards the east, we passed very near it. At seven o'clock, we had knowledge from on deck of a fairly extensive reef which remained at south 42° east. This reef served to make us know the island which is that which the English have named Albatross Island. As our position was not very pleasant in that it was almost calm and the ship could hardly be steered, we prepared an anchor to anchor in case of need. The breeze then coming from north-north-east to east-north-east, we went about and saw Albatross Island for a second time of which we were at two leagues at the most at thirty-one fathoms depth, bottom of coarse reddish sand. During the duration of the calm which took place until ten o'clock in the evening, we sounded every hour so as to ascertain whether the current was carrying us towards the shore or offshore, but we saw with pleasure that the bottom was increasing.
At ten o'clock, the winds coming to us from the west, variable to west-south-west, we took the northern course which we followed until four o'clock in the morning. During the night, the wind was light, we had constantly haze and great moisture with little wind.
1802-12-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to SW. At noon in 38° 25' of latitude observed and in 123° 32' of longitude by account. At 8 a flat calm; at midnight it freshened from the north.

1802-12-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather. At 1.15 changed tacks. At 4 a.m. overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze. Saw kelp pass alongside. Obs. lat. 38° 38' 17", long. 119° 35' 26".
1802-12-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At five and a half o'clock,
having had sight of land through the haze, we took its bearing,
at six o'clock, from south 28° west to south 40° west.
We also had sight of the shallow reef on which the sea broke heavily, remaining at SE by E.
The land in sight was Albatross Island and the reef which is to its east.
At daylight, we had sight of the Three Mandrils Island which we came to examine.
Historical events & remarks.
On the fifth, at daybreak, we went about to go and seek the Hunter Islands and range about their vicinity in order to see if we might not gain sight of the Casuarina whose delay surprised me more and more. Making course to the south-south-east, we had sight of land in good time and we saw clearly that it was not that of the previous day, although according to the dead reckoning of our course we should have been little distance from it. As we approached it, we recognised that this must be Three Mandrils Island, which was verified afterwards.
We had during the morning the finest weather in the world and a fine breeze from the south-west. It was, without question, the finest day we had had since our departure from Port Jackson.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 40° 18' 52" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 143° 0' 31". This longitude was found to be the same as that which is indicated in the English chart, or at least the difference is so little considerable that it merits no observation. About ten o'clock in the morning, we had had sight of the lands of Diemen and no doubt of those which bear the name of Cape Round which must have been given from the form it presents to view. As I wished to assure myself whether the Casuarina was not inside this island and at the anchorage indicated by M. Flinders, we continued to keep along the coast of Three Mandrils Island at small distance, and we were on the verge of doubling its eastern point when the winds refused us, which obliged us to take the north-westerly course.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted from south-west variable to south-south-west, I expected to be able easily enough to get away from the land to gain sight of the islands to the west of this one and which we had in view, but the flood tide which came on carried us with such speed to the north that we saw them only from a great distance and could hardly make them out from the deck. However, from the tops of the masts one could see very well Albatross Island and the reef which is marked on the chart.
At five o'clock, being about midway across the distance which forms the channel which lies between King Island and Three Mandrils Island, we had sight of this first one which was plainly visible. We continued to steer close to the wind approaching King Island and at seven o'clock we saw on the horizon in the wind a large islet shaped like a mandrel which was taken at south 6° west.
There is appearance that this islet is one of those which are to the south of King Island and of which Captain Hamelin had had sight. As I had sent the Casuarina to examine them and moreover the night was falling, I continued to make way towards King Island until nine o'clock in the evening when I went about to make some way to the south. During the night, the weather was very fine and we passed part of it in calm.
1802-12-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NW. At midnight the course west. At noon in 38° 39' of latitude observed and in 122° 16' of longitude by account.

1802-12-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy. A strong breeze in gusts and squally. At 1 a.m. wore onto the port tack; at 5 changed tacks. At 11 a.m. we had a squall which forced us to reef the topsails and let the main sheet fly. Est. lat. 39° 13' 41", est. long. 118° 50' 56".
1802-12-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the visible part of the Hunter Islands remained from south 44° east to south 27° east.
At seven o'clock,
the two extremities in sight of King Island remained from west 5° south to west 34° north.
An islet was visible then at south 6° west at an estimated distance of eight leagues.
At noon,
abeam of the middle of Elephant Bay, waiting for the Casuarina.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the winds were from the east variable to east-north-east, light breeze. We made course to approach King Island and come again to anchor in Elephant Cove. My intention was, if I did not find the Casuarina there, to leave her two or three barrels of biscuit which she might need and to continue immediately on my course to Kangaroo Island, indicating to her the place where she would find me on this coast.
As the breeze was very light throughout the morning, we advanced slowly and it was near eleven o'clock when we were at the entrance of this cove. Shortly after, there appeared to us at the northern extremity of this cove a small vessel under sail which we soon recognised to be the Casuarina.
As soon as we were assured that it was her, we made the rendezvous signal to her which she replied to. But as the current was contrary to her, she was carried with speed to the south which greatly delayed our meeting which could not take place until about four o'clock in the afternoon. As soon as we were alongside each other, I had a canoe put to sea to go and take our geographer who was on board and addressed to Citizen Freycinet the following letter:
The Commander and cetera… to Citizen Freycinet on board the Casuarina,
"We are going to make course for Kangaroo Island situated in its eastern part at 35° 39' 50" of "south latitude and 142° 13' 3" 135° 58' of east longitude. This island is easy to recognise from its "extent from east to west which is about 30 leagues and the latitude which I indicate to you is that of the "northern and eastern part. There are some islets to the east of this island which one must be wary of when "approaching it. But as they are high, one always perceives them in time to avoid them. It is on the eastern coast that "I intend to seek an anchorage and where I indicate to you a rendezvous in case of separation in the short "passage to be made to reach it.
"The continental lands in this part are high, very healthy and must be approached in preference to the "islets although they are equally very steep. It is from the northern and eastern part of this island that "the two gulfs of which you have heard commence and which are found on the continent".
Your fellow citizen, N. B.
By the return of the canoe which carried this letter and brought back Citizen Boulanger, I was informed that M. Freycinet needed water having been obliged to empty his casks to refloat her in the two groundings which he made while visiting the Hunter Islands and a great bay of Diemen Land, whilst wishing to assure himself of the existence or not of a river of which he thought he had recognised the signs. Some water was sent to her immediately and we continued our course to pass to the south of King Island. As we saw several lands to the south of this island at the beginning of the night, I did not wish to enter the channel in order to examine them the next day. Accordingly, we spent the night tacking about with very variable winds from the east sometimes to the north-east and sometimes to the south-east. The breeze was fresh during the night and the sky very hazy. At eleven o'clock, we lost sight of the Casuarina, despite all our attention to preserve it.
1802-12-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from WNW to WSW, with rain and hail. At noon in 39° 9' of latitude by account and in 120° 49' of longitude by account. At 1.30 struck the topgallant masts and lay to.

1802-12-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the horizon thick, with light hail at intervals. The sea rather high. The lee sheet of the main topsail being about to give way, we clewed the sail up. At 1.30 a.m. furled the topsails and hoisted the mizzen staysail; the weather overcast and squally with hail at intervals. At 4 wore ship; at 6 filled and stood on, taking two reefs in each topsail. The weather having cleared, we set the mizzen and the main jib and shook out one reef in each topsail. Obs. lat. 39° 18' 30", obs. long. 119° 20' 0".
1802-12-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
abeam of Elephant Cove, waiting for the Casuarina.
At seven o'clock,
the lands of the south-east of King Island remained at north 18° west.
A small islet was visible at south 5° west.
From the tops of the masts, other lands were perceived to the south-south-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, the sky was so hazy that our horizon extended hardly half a league. The wind blew fresh. We had no sight of the Casuarina and unless she was very near us, it would hardly have been possible to see her. At six o'clock, seeing no appearance of change in the weather and wishing to profit by the good wind to make my way to Kangaroo Island, I had the course set to the west and we entered the strait passing to the south of King Island and also to the south, according to my dead reckoning, of the islands which are in this channel. At nine and a half o'clock, the haze still being very thick and one could not see, I had the ship brought across and sounded in order to know by this means whether we were advanced into the channel or in the vicinity of some land which we did not know. The sounding was thirty-six fathoms and I was surprised not to find it greater. When we resumed course, I had the course set to the west-south-west so as not to go further north, being persuaded that there was nothing to fear in making the course take to the south which I was making in our position. At ten o'clock, we saw not without astonishment the sky suddenly clear and become fine. We at once had sight of King Island which remained at north to north 40° west at seven or eight leagues distance. We then resumed the north-westerly course steering to the north and made good way. From the tops of the masts, we saw no land from the south-east to the south-west.
In the morning, Citizen Boulanger who had been sent to the Hunter Islands informed me of what he had done concerning the mission with which I had charged him, but as he and Citizen Freycinet are to make a detailed and written report to me, I will speak of it on another occasion. He also told me that they had arrived at Elephant Cove the day before and that the Casuarina had lost an anchor having no cable on its buoy on its anchor. He assured me that the Casuarina had not suffered at all in the two groundings which she made, but that this vessel leaked a great deal through her upper works when the sea was rough.
In the afternoon, the weather became overcast and did not look fine for the rest of the day. The good wind which we had had all morning, successively shifted to the north and ended by passing to the west, which made us take the southern course. At noon, the latitude was observed as 40° 14' 31" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 141° 38' 27". We had recognised before this time that King Island was placed much too far to the east the west in the position which the English give to her. Its shape is also very different from that which they announce.
In running the southern course, we had sight of the Casuarina to the north-east. We went about to close with her and the winds having shifted to the south-west, when we joined her, we made course in the north-westerly tack.
At sunset, the wind began to blow fresh. We took two reefs in the topsails and during the night, which was passably fine, did all that was necessary to keep this vessel in sight. We found the sea so strongly rough that the vessel was greatly incommoded by it. We sounded at eight o'clock and at midnight without finding bottom at seventy fathoms.
1802-12-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At 6 filled and stood on. The weather cleared and the wind fell. At noon in 39° 20' of latitude observed, 119° 20' of longitude observed and 121° 31' of longitude by account.

1802-12-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, a swell running. Bent the storm staysail and the repaired main staysail. At 7 p.m. went onto the starboard tack. Saw kelp pass alongside. Obs. lat. 39° 23' 42", obs. long. 118° 15' 0".
1802-12-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the morning, the lands of the western part of King Island were visible in the north-east at great distance.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth (written in another hand: Nivôse), at four o'clock in the morning, we resumed the north-westerly course in that at midnight, the Casuarina not replying to our signals, we judged her to be astern and making very little way on account of the great swell which existed then and which we had all this day. We closed with her effectually at this course. The winds in the morning shifted from west-south-west to south-south-west and became favourable to our (sic) course. We made the most of them as much as was possible for us, but we advanced little, the breeze being very light.
I was in the morning of very ill humour on learning that five of the men whom I had put ashore on King Island had returned on board. As this caused me extraordinary consumption. I ordered that they should be fed at the expense of the boatswain's crew who had been sent ashore for the service of the vessel, being persuaded that it was they who had provided them with the means to return on board by embarking them in their canoes. This order was revoked this same day, having had proof to the contrary and being assured that they had been brought back by the boats of the fishermen who came several times on board under the pretence of selling us emus, wombats and kangaroos which I indeed bought from them.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 39° 59' 52" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 141° 7' 29". At daylight, we thought we had sight of King Island in the north-east, which is very doubtful although the horizon was very extended and the thing possible.
In the afternoon, the weather continued fine and the sea was always extremely rough, which announced that there had passed not long before some blow from the south-west. The winds shifted to the south and towards evening they passed to the south-east.
During the night, the breeze was fresh and we made good way steering from noon to north 67° 30' west, which course we followed until the next day. As this course brought us little near the land, we did not sound during the night.
1802-12-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NNW. At noon in 39° 24' of latitude observed and in 118° 15' of longitude observed.

1802-12-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze. At 5 a.m. continual rain and the look of squalls. Est. lat. 39° 52' 30", est. long. 115° 50' 38".
1802-12-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and we had a fine breeze from the south-east which we made use of to advance to the north and west. The slow progress of the Casuarina relative to us caused us to lose a great deal of time and distance waiting for her, but this small vessel was too necessary for me to discover the two gulfs which I did not wish to leave incomplete, not to wait for her. We had all day a very great swell from the south-west which fatigued us greatly, and more than once I feared damage to my masts so lively and numerous were the movements of the vessel.
At noon, we observed the latitude as 38° 51' 1" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 137° 55' 29". This point plotted on the English chart placed us at a small distance from the land. And to assure myself before night, I had the course set to the north, but we had no sight of it and I am persuaded that the chart which they have drawn of the part of coast we were extending along is as defective for the latitudes as for the longitudes. We were already certain of the second of these errors from their positions of King Island which is thirty minutes further to the west than it should be. And we are currently also convinced that the latitude which they have indicated for the island which I named Lark Island is more south by eleven minutes than it should be. That which we observed in very fine weather on this island cannot be doubtful since we had it to the east at not more than one league distance when we observed 38° 27' 32". It is probable that their chart is drawn according to the dead reckoning of the routes which they have travelled rather than on astronomical observations or bearings taken at small distance from the coast.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock, having made course to the north to gain sight of the land, we nevertheless did not see it and had the English chart been accurate, we should certainly have gained sight of it. At the same time, I had the lead cast, that is to say at eight o'clock, and we found bottom at fifty fathoms. Although the wind was very good to make way during the night, I did not wish to advance further into the west and still less to the north, in consequence I preferred to take the south-south-west course with little sail, putting off until the next day to close with the land if the winds continued to be favourable to us. We signalled the Casuarina to imitate our manoeuvre and we had her in sight all night. At ten o'clock and at midnight, we no longer found bottom at seventy fathoms.
1802-12-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind from N to WNW. At noon in 39° 39' of latitude by account and in 116° 8' of longitude by account.

1802-12-31.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth enough, a fresh breeze; about 9 it freshened. At 4 blowing hard; from 4.30 until 5 clewed up the main topsail by degrees to take the second reef and sheeted home again at once. Obs. lat. 41° 16' 35", est. long. 114° 43' 44".
1802-12-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, we had a very dark sky and great moisture. Nevertheless, the winds varied little and held fairly constantly in the south-east quarter, varying sometimes towards the east and sometimes towards the south. The breeze during the morning was light and we advanced little.
At daylight, we took the course north-north-west to close with the land. About eight o'clock, the weather became fine and we then had a fairly extended horizon, without gaining sight of land.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 37° 47' 10" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 137° 47' 2". We perceived shortly after, the land in the north-east, from the tops of the masts, and we soon saw from the deck the sand dunes which form this part of the coast, which made us steer somewhat more towards the west. Regarding as useless to plunge again into deep coves which offer neither interest nor particular remarks. We saw nevertheless passing our beam several smokes which announced the presence of some inhabitants.
In the afternoon, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us land in the west by south-west. We were very astonished at this warning, having perceived none in that quarter when we visited this coast for the first time. The sky then was not fine and the horizon charged with vapours. When the bearing of the announced land was indicated, each person thought to recognise it and I was deceived like others, for I was persuaded and even longer than the others that it was indeed land. I consequently had the course set immediately to the west and set all sails to gain good knowledge of it before nightfall so as to be able to visit it the next day, since the capes, the points and various other peculiarities of this land could be seen very well and were covered from time to time with haze to show themselves again in the same form which they had appeared in the beginning. Finally, night came always making course to the west and keeping up the hope of recognising by means of the sounding during the night the land which we were persuaded we had seen. This hope vanished for after having made course to the west until midnight without finding bottom, I was undeceived of the error in which I was and remain persuaded that it was only a band of haze which we had seen long fixed on the horizon and not land of which surely we should have gained sight on our first visit to this coast.
During the night, the winds which about eight o'clock in the evening had come to the south-south-west, shifted to the south-south-east very light, we continued as I have said the course to the west until midnight when having lost all hope, we took the north-westerly course which was continued until daylight. The sky was very dark and damp and the sea calm.
1802-12-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from NNW to W. At 7 lay to. The port anchor was stowed and its cable unbent. At noon in 41° 17' of latitude observed and in 114° 47' of longitude by account. At 1.30 filled and stood on.

1803-01-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a high sea, a strong breeze in gusts. At 1.35 wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 39° 47' 50", obs. long. 113° 50' 0".
1803-01-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At four o'clock,
the land in sight extended from north 13° east to south 88° east.
At seven o'clock,
it was visible from north 10° east to north 67° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, the sky although dark and overcast was passably fine. We had winds from the south variable towards the east, very light. In the morning, we made course to the north to gain sight of the coast of New Holland and then prolong it to attack Kangaroo Island by its eastern part. The weather became fine during the morning, the clouds dispersed. At this time we thought we saw the land from the tops of the masts, but we had no sight of it from the deck.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 36° 49' 16" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 136° 39' 15". We found in the reckoned latitude a considerable difference with that of the observation, which we attributed to the speed and direction of the currents which had carried us to the north far beyond our reckoning.
In the afternoon, the breeze was light and the winds always variable in the south towards the east. We continued the course to the north until about eight o'clock in the evening, without having any sight of land, of which nevertheless we must not have been very far distant.
At ten o'clock at night, the officer of the watch having received orders to sound every hour since we were making course north towards the west, found bottom at thirty-three fathoms, which made me steer close-hauled in the southern course towards the west, knowing that one is very close to the coast in this part with such a sounding. This officer, who believes himself more experienced than the others, did not warn me that we were on bottom, but as I was not asleep, I had heard the report which the boatswain who had sounded made to him. As the order was to warn me in such circumstances, I had him called and asked him by what reason he had not warned me that we were on bottom and at thirty-three fathoms. His reply was that he reserved to give me an account of his watch at midnight.
