Continuing the same course, I replied to him, you would certainly have announced to me that the ship was on the shore, for your knowledge does not yet reach to remembering that in the place where we are, the lead goes but little offshore. He wished then to enter into some details to prove to me that he was right, but I ended the conversation by ordering him to go about immediately in the southern course and not to fail a second time to execute the orders which he should receive.
The rest of the night had nothing particular, only we had a damp sky and a horizon little extended.
1803-01-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At noon in 39° 48' of latitude observed and in 113° 22' of longitude observed.

1803-01-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running and the wind a fresh breeze. The weather having cleared, we made more sail. In the forenoon unbent the starboard anchor and stowed it. Obs. lat. 38° 29' 52", obs. long. 112° 45' 54".
1803-01-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At daylight, we identified Kangaroo Island remaining in the north-north-west.
At noon, the extremities of this island in sight extended from north 68° east to south 50° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we had exact knowledge of the continental lands of New Holland, as well as those of the south-east part of Kangaroo Island. We found ourselves at daylight about three leagues from land, having perfect sight of the channel, that of Cape Atoile and the point inside of which I had anchored during our first reconnaissance of this coast.
As I had lost my cutter in the manner in which I spoke of it at the time this accident happened to me, and as the one being built on board was still only little advanced, I decided to make the geography of the southern part of this island with the ship. Accordingly, I gave orders to M. Freycinet who commands the Casuarina to follow us coasting the land as closely as possible and to visit all the indentations which would appear susceptible of offering something of interest. According to these arrangements, we approached the south-east point of Kangaroo Island and began our bearings at (no figures) hours in the morning starting from this point.
During the morning, the weather was fine and the breeze moderate but the winds were from the south which should not much advance the work of this day if, as we had reason to believe, the coast was directed in that quarter.
During the morning, the lands which we extended along are fairly high and terminate at the sea by a slope which is not extremely steep. All the ground is sandy and destitute of trees. One sees only from time to time some tufts of low heather which make all the ornament of this place. It falls far short of having the pleasant aspect of that which is opposite to the north.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 35° 52' 6" and the longitude by No. 35 placed us at 135° 41' 42".
During the afternoon, we entered a great bay which at the beginning had appeared by its direction to promise us a fortunate encounter and a shelter against the winds from the south-west to the north, but we found only a sandy coast little elevated in this part and destitute of all vegetation. To extend our tack we coasted the shore at two miles and often less. It is healthy and presents no danger, except on land where landing did not appear practicable with the southerly winds which then prevailed. The current appeared to us very violent all along this coast having its direction to the north-east. I think we were then at the moment of flood tide.
At two o'clock, we ran a short course offshore to rise from the coast of which we were no more than a mile and a half at the most. At three and a half o'clock, having resumed the shore course, we approached the eastern coast of this great bay whose wind direction did not permit us to double the point or southern cape.
The night was passed tacking about with winds from the same quarter and fine weather. We made about ten leagues of coast in this day without having found anything interesting on it, except that one of the highest mountains of this part presents to view a summit entirely of sand and on which one sees here and there some clumps of greenery. It is a very good reconnaissance for those whom chance may lead to this coast.
1803-01-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from W to WNW. The starboard anchor was stowed and its cable unbent. At noon in 38° 30' of latitude observed and in 112° 46' of longitude observed. A flat calm at 10.

1803-01-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At seven o'clock, the lands in sight of Kangaroo Island extended from SW by W to north 70° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we resumed the geographic work of the southern outlet of Kangaroo Island which we had begun the day before. After exactly verifying our last bearings, we coasted the shore to double an advanced point which hid the other lands to the west. When we had doubled it, we had sight of the rock offshore at about a league and a half from the coast on which the sea broke in an extraordinary manner. Not knowing if there was a passage between this islet and the great coast, I sailed close to the wind to pass to its south, but I was obliged to make a course offshore, not being able to double it.
The channel which separates it from the great coast appears fine and convenient to judge from appearances. As the Casuarina passed inside, she may be able to tell us what may be the depth of water, if indeed she sounded, which is very doubtful.
After doubling this rock to the south, we closed with the coast again and continued our work. During the morning, the weather was fine and there sometimes blew a fine breeze. In order to profit from it, we rigged our topgallant sails which we immediately set.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 36° 5' 53" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 135° 14' 50". According to the latitude observed this day and that which we already knew at the northern part of this island, it was not difficult for us to judge that it had little width from north to south and that it was, so to speak, only a narrow tongue of land compared to its length.
In the afternoon, we found the sea very rough and agitated in several ways, which made our progress slow. Nevertheless, we made a fair distance to the west with the hope of rounding this island in its western part before night.
About three o'clock, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us that they saw two fairly large islets ahead of us and a great reef to windward on which the sea broke with as much force as on that which we had doubled in the morning. We did not long in having sight of the reef and the islets from the deck. We were astonished to find such a danger so far offshore and isolated, which led me to believe that it might well be joined by a series of rocks under water to the two islets of which we had knowledge and with which it seemed to have the same direction. I judged it suitable to pass to its south, accordingly we steered close to the wind. In approaching this danger, we recognised that it was a cluster of rocks just awash whose extent from east to west might have a mile and a half of length. We passed it very close in doubling it. The channel with the islets appears good, but I do not advise engaging in it, for supposing the water to be deep, one would be greatly embarrassed if overtaken by calm.
The two islets which I have just mentioned are found precisely at the western part of this island which from this point, at once takes its direction to the north-west, as will be seen from the chart.
At sunset, the lookouts from the tops of the masts announced to us land in the west and several islets to the south-west, but I doubt the existence of either since the horizon was then charged with much vapour. However, to assure myself, I made way in the quarters indicated during the night, persuaded that the sounding would announce this land to me if it existed. At eight o'clock, we were at not more than one league from the north-west coast of Kangaroo Island and we took the south-west course having fifty-two fathoms of bottom. At nine o'clock we no longer found it at seventy, nor at midnight at one hundred fathoms, which confirmed to me that there was no land in the announced area. However, as several persons assure they saw it clearly, I will return to seek it when the work on the gulfs is finished. The rest of the night had nothing particular.
1803-01-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW; at 11 a flat calm. Saw porpoises. At noon in 38° 3' of latitude observed and in 112° 33' of longitude observed. The mainsail and the mizzen topsail were shifted and the topgallant masts rigged. At 7 the breeze got up from the ENE; the course was given N 67° 30' W.

1803-01-04.journal_anonyme: A flat calm, fine weather, a swell running. The mainsail and mizzen topsail were shifted and the storm staysail repaired. At ten the breeze got up and we made all sail. At 2 a.m. Obs. lat. 38° 7' 5", obs. long. 111° 48' 20".
1803-01-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At sunset, we thought we had sight of land in the west and of two or three islets in the south-west.
At noon, the extremities in sight of Kangaroo Island remained from SW by W to E by SE.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, early, we had completed our geographic work of the whole of Kangaroo Island so that if the English have over us the advantage of having arrived there a few days earlier, we have also over them that of having made the complete circumnavigation and of having determined its geographic position in a manner which leaves nothing to be desired for the safety of navigation.
All the land to the south of this island is composed only of sand, dunes and rock plateaus. The aspect of it is sad and disagreeable to view. Two fairly deep bays and an infinite number of coves more or less large all sandy or of rocks are all that was offered to our sight. But we found not a single place where landing appeared practicable so strongly did the sea break all along the beach. It is true that the winds were then from the southern quarter and the swell was very considerable. This island did not allow us to see the least elevated tree and only heather or other plants very little elevated. It is possible that the back of the elevations may be furnished with them, but it is what we cannot assure. The coast is elevated in certain parts and fairly low in others.
At noon, we observed the latitude as 35° 39' 55" and the longitude by timekeeper was 134° 27' 17". We were then coasting the shore very closely, my intention being to come and anchor in a great bay to the north which I had noticed the first time we explored this coast and in the bottom of which there might be some good anchorage judging from the different ways in which the points closed with each other.
During the evening, we had sight of the islets which are found to the south of the western extremity of the first gulf into which we had entered and which we left to port having had sight at sunset of the continental lands of this part which, as I observed at the time, are low.
During the evening, we lost sight of the Casuarina but I made little account of it, persuaded that she would join us during the night or by tacking on the coast to go up it with south-easterly winds.
After sunset, the breeze became strong and the sky had very bad appearance. But as the wind came to us from over the land, we found the sea fine. So as not to make too much distance and facilitate the means for the Casuarina to rejoin us, we took two reefs in the topsails and spent the night, which had strong gusts, making course to the east in order to go to the place where I intended to anchor the next day if the weather was fine.
As we sounded every hour during the night, the bottom which was twenty-five fathoms at eight o'clock, decreased gradually until midnight when we had no more than eighteen. We maintained this depth the rest of the night, so we did not change course. We sometimes had a hazy and very damp sky with little appearance of fine weather for the next day.
1803-01-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNE to WSW. At noon in 38° 7' of latitude observed and in 111° 48' of longitude observed. At 9 the weather overcast, the wind freshened. The 15th [Nivôse, 5 January 1803]. Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SSW; the main topmast and topgallant mast were set up. At noon in 37° 8' of latitude observed and in 110° 36' of longitude observed. At 7 the course given N 56° 15' W.

1803-01-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth. At 10 p.m. wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 37° 8' 5", obs. long. 110° 30' 50".
1803-01-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of land:
At seven o'clock,
The western extremity in sight of Kangaroo Island remained at south 53° west and extended to south 74° east.
An islet at north 66° west.
The continental lands in sight from NW 56° W to N 10° E
At noon,
part of Kangaroo Island from S 25° E to S 55° W.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, we had sight of part of the lands which form the western coast of the first gulf, which did not fail to astonish us in that by the course we should not have had sight of it, all the more so as these lands are generally low and even. We saw thereby that the currents had carried us much further north than our dead reckoning, a thing which had happened to us the first time we visited this gulf. The land in sight extended from the NNW to the NNE.
We did not see the Casuarina which we thought we had sighted during the night and to which we put a light to reply to that which we thought we saw from her.
During the morning, the weather was fairly fine, but we had winds from the south-east quarter and little suitable to the course we had to make, which obliged us when we had closed with the land to make small tacks to examine it again, but we saw only the same things as the first time.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 35° 26' 48" and the longitude by timekeeper placed us at 135° 30' 47".
In the afternoon, we continued to tack from tack to tack with a fine breeze from south-south-east variable to the south. The weather although fine was somewhat hazy so our horizon had little extent.
After sunset we took the southern course towards the east to pass the night at a small distance from the coast. As the weather was very fine and the haze dispersed, we had good knowledge in the middle of the night of the continental lands which form the eastern entrance of the first gulf.
We had had no sight of the Casuarina all day and I was very surprised not to see her arrive all the more so as we had made little distance. The tacks we ran not having been very advantageous and hindered by the currents which appeared to carry us strongly to the north-west.
The sounding during the twenty-four hours was between eighteen and fifteen fathoms, bottoms varied sometimes of pure sand, sometimes of sand and broken shells and other times of sand mixed with a little mud and weed. These different bottoms appeared to us suitable for anchorage in case of necessity, but having shelter only from winds from south-east to south-south-west, by the south.

1803-01-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze, a high sea. The storm staysail, gnawed by rats, was put out to dry and unbent for repair. Obs. lat. 35° 9', obs. long. 108° 46' 56".
1803-01-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Latitude of anchorage 35° 45' 16"
Longitude by No. 35 135° 39' 39".
STAYING AT Kangaroo Island
On the sixteenth, in the morning, we took port tack to close with the coast, my intention being to anchor in the first bay which is opposite the entrance of the second gulf. The first time I visited this coast, this bay and even that which follows it had appeared to me to offer some good shelters from the north-east to the west by the south. But the weather at that time did not permit me to visit it carefully in the same way as that which is to the west of it which is much deeper but where there is little water at the entrance, at a fairly great distance from land having found only five to six fathoms, sandy bottom.
Having entered the first bay of which I have just spoken, we anchored inside in eight fathoms of water, bottom of sand and seaweed, which led me to believe we should find good holding. We at once moored with a small stream anchor so that the current would not cause us to drag on our cable as had happened to us several times.
As soon as the vessel was moored, the boats were launched and I sent people to visit the coast to learn its outline and especially to see if there would not be fresh water in the various ravines which we had in view and which appeared to flow to the sea. Citizens Bonnefoy and Ransonnet each had command of a canoe for this exploration with orders to begin one from the western side of the bay and the other from the eastern side so as to meet in the indentation which it presented to the south. Citizen Ransonnet who was in the western part received orders to make a great fire on an advanced point to indicate to the Casuarina that we were in this bay if she should appear in the night.
A third canoe left about eleven o'clock with the carpenters to cut wood suitable for the construction of our cutter of which we had made the greater part of the frames since our departure from King Island.
At sunset, all the boats having returned on board, I was informed that in the bottom of the bay a small harbour was found which at first appeared convenient because the canoes had entered it at high water. But when it retreated it left uncovered a considerable quantity of sandbanks which were separated from each other only by channels of very little width and in which there was no more than two or three fathoms of water. The channel through which one must pass had three or four at high tide but was not the less obstructed by sandbanks. The short time which the boats had to visit this place not allowing them to give exact details, I put off to the next day sending to examine it again. The carpenters and those intended for the search for water did not find a drop and the first could not even find it in the proportions of which we had need. More than fifty trees which were felled were all found rotten to the heart. They also brought back having seen such a great quantity of kangaroos of the large species that they compared them to flocks of sheep and no more wild.
1803-01-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and the wind a light breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 35° 11' of latitude observed and in 108° 47' of longitude observed.

1803-01-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze. Lowered the gaff to take off an eyebolt and make a new span, the old one having parted in the morning; it was in place at 6 p.m. Obs. lat. 34° 40' 10", est. long. 107° 40' 26".
1803-01-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventeenth (7 January 1803). On the seventeenth, early in the morning, I sent my large canoe under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy and had it accompanied by the engineer geographer Faure with orders to make an exact visit of the harbour which was discovered the day before and to draw its chart. This canoe was provided with provisions for two to three days with orders to return to get them from the ship if the details of this harbour required more time than I had fixed.
About nine o'clock, we had sight of the Casuarina which made course to go to the anchorage which we occupied. As soon as she had sight of us, the Captain of this vessel came on board shortly after to submit to me a statement of his needs which did not consist of few things. Before examining his request, I had him given an anchor, a rope and a hawser so that he might at once moor with two anchors. The caulkers were also sent to his ship to cover her upper works which caused her to leak greatly.
In the morning we had a strong breeze from the north-west which, having made the sea somewhat agitated and choppy, did not permit us to be able to work on board this vessel. As the canoe which was sent ashore the previous day in search of some fresh water stream had brought back a kangaroo of the large species, the greater part of it was distributed to the crews.
In the afternoon we were entirely occupied working for the Casuarina. The forge especially had much to do to repair one of her anchors of which the iron ring was broken. It was also necessary to make new for her rings for her topsail masts, change their bars and an infinity of other works which the facility of having us engaged M. Freycinet to ask of us. This vessel also lacked water having emptied her casks when she grounded in the bay which she wanted to explore on the coast of Diemen, to the south of the Hunter Islands. I had delivered to her four barrels of water assuring her well that I would not give her any more, being unable to expose myself to lack it myself for the pleasure of giving her some.
At the beginning of the night, the sky had bad appearance which decided me to pay out cable up to eighty fathoms for greater safety. This precaution was not useless for we had fairly strong gusts and were often on the verge of anchoring a second anchor. Nevertheless the vessel held firm which confirmed me that the holding was not bad although a small mooring anchor had not held with one hundred twenty fathoms of cable.
1803-01-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to ENE. At noon in 34° 40' of latitude observed and in 107° 40' of longitude by account. The course given N 33° 45' W.

1803-01-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At 6 a.m. the mizzen topsail tie parted at the collar and was at once refitted. At 8 clewed up and furled the mizzen topsail and rove the top rope to lower the mast and refit the masthead rigging. Est. lat. 33° 30' 35", est. long. 106° 27' 50".
1803-01-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighteenth (8 January 1803). On the eighteenth, the weather was hardly finer than the day before which caused me to remove our topgallant masts. In the morning, the canoe which I had sent to visit and draw the chart of the harbour found at the bottom of the bay returned on board. The officer who commanded it and Citizen Faure told me that the work was finished which greatly surprised me all the more since according to the first information which had been given me the work should be long and even difficult. I expressed to these gentlemen my fears about the promptness and forced diligence which they appeared to have shown but they assured me no less that they had seen everything and examined everything and that this indentation was less a harbour than a cluster of sandbanks and shoals most of which were uncovered at low water. Despite all their searches, they found no water and only several streams of salt water which were lost in marshes.
As Citizen Faure is to give me a detailed chart of this place, I shall not speak of it at greater length before having received it.
During the day work was continued for the Casuarina in order to put her in condition to fulfil the mission which I intended to entrust to her.
In the evening the weather continued to be in squalls accompanied by rain and fairly strong gusts and the winds shifted from south-west to west-south-west but during the night it was not as disagreeable as we had it during the day.
1803-01-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ESE to SSE. The mizzen topmast head rigging was refitted. At noon in 33° 29' of latitude by account and in 106° 28' of longitude by account.

1803-01-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea very smooth. Swayed up and set up the mizzen topgallant mast; at 4 p.m. the sail was set. Est. lat. 32° 5' 5", est. long. 104° 59' 20".
1803-01-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 19th (9 January 1803). On the nineteenth I sent off one of my canoes again under the command of Citizen Ransonnet to go and examine a second bay to the west of that where we are and much deeper. He had orders to round it entirely and examine with care all its extent so as to assure ourselves whether it did not contain some fresh water stream and some trees for the vessels. The canoe was provided for three days of provisions and everything that was necessary to survey this bay. I did not embark a geographer thinking that Citizen Ransonnet would acquit himself as well as those who are on board.
After sending off this canoe, I went ashore to visit a ravine in the neighbourhood of our anchorage and in which I counted to find water from the freshness which the plants had in this part of the coast. My intention also was to make a well in the earth if I did not find running water. That is why I took people with me and all that was necessary for this work. As soon as we were disembarked I went to visit the place of which I have just spoken and found in this ravine only the greatest dryness. We made five large holes in the earth which were of no utility for at less than two feet of depth we found the rock which forms no doubt the nucleus of this island.
The botanist Leschenault and the garden boy who had come ashore with me as well as Citizen Péron occupied themselves with their work and when they had rejoined us with little success in their excursions, we thought to return on board, having for all our fortune a living kangaroo which our dog caught shortly before we left. On leaving I left two English to land to kill kangaroos by lying in wait at night as they are accustomed to do.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the weather was passably bad with winds from the south-west. We had been well moored during the day with two anchors one to the north-east and the other to the south-west.
1803-01-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SSE to SE. Saw flying fish. At noon in 32° 4' of latitude by account and in 104° 59' of longitude by account.

1803-01-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze. A swell from the SW. Made all sail. Obs. lat. 30° 35' 32", est. long. 103° 40' 50".
1803-01-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
"The Commandant to Citizen Freycinet aboard the Casuarina,
"As soon as your vessel shall be repaired, you will set sail and make directly course to reconnoitre the western coast of the first gulf opposite which we are at anchor and whose high lands which you have in view to the east-north-east, form the eastern side. We penetrated into this gulf as far as latitude 34° 38' and we then had perfect knowledge of the lands from north to north-north-west, but we found then the waters so shallow that it was not possible for me to approach near enough to the coast to visit it well.
"The shallow draft of your vessel will all the more facilitate the work which remains to be done for Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, and who accompanies you, in that it is not considerable and will not require much time, in that you must by no means occupy yourself with the eastern coast, which has been well explored with the vessel.
"You will, therefore, make course directly to the north on departing, to gain as quickly as possible the extremity of this gulf and descend it, then, by coasting the western coast. You will not go ashore below two fathoms of water. This order is imperative and you will be personally responsible to the Government for the events which may befall you if you do not heed it. The western coast of this first gulf appeared to us generally not very elevated and composed in several places of sand dunes. You must examine it with caution and sound often to avoid running aground on the banks which may be found there, for I am assured that there are several shoals there.
"At the southern extremity of this first gulf, the coast forms an advanced cape, and the entrance of a second gulf presents itself. You will then have knowledge of several islands and islets to the south and west. They offer different channels which are practicable with prudence. You will leave these islets to the south, without wasting time to reconnoitre them, their respective positions having been determined by us. When you shall be in the second gulf, you will do as for the first, that is to say you will immediately take the northern direction to gain its extremity without occupying yourself with the eastern coast which is known to us. We were only able to reach latitude 34° 11' in going up the eastern coast. I think it extends further to the north and it is this which you must ascertain. The point where we stopped and which we would have taken up if bad weather had not prevented us, is easy to recognise, being remarkable by a reef flush with the water, not far from the coast and on which the sea breaks much. According to the estimate of the course which we made from noon until three o'clock in the afternoon and the bearing which was then taken of this danger, its latitude would be thirty four degrees eight minutes. It appeared to us to be the summit of a sand bank which uncovers and breaks strongly at low tide. We had eight fathoms of water, sandy bottom, at about a league distance.
"The eastern coast of this second gulf is not very elevated and formed by sand dunes more or less high, but in the indentation of the north-north-east where we did not penetrate, we see high lands which I suspect to be mountain peaks in the interior of the country. When you shall be at the bottom of this gulf, if however you can get there without danger, and without having less than two fathoms of water, you will begin to coast the west in returning to the south, having made bearings of the eastern part beginning from the reef of which I have spoken to you. The lands to the west appeared to us very high and perhaps you will find something interesting there. In approaching the southern extremity of this same coast, there should be found a small port in which Mr. Flinders stayed fairly long. You will examine this port and Mr. Boulanger will draw up its plan.
"If you have an opportunity to be able to replace your water, you will not fail to do it observing nevertheless not to spend more time than necessary. Fifteen or eighteen days, supposing the hindrances of the season, are more than sufficient for the work which you have to do. I will wait for you here until that time, but I warn you that if you are not back at the latest within twenty days, counting from your departure, I will set sail to proceed to the islands Saint Peter and Saint François where I have many things to do. The impossibility of being able to replace my water does not permit me to wait longer for you. As the Government has not asked me for the topography of some ungracious and sterile parts of New Holland, but only knowledge of the coast, you will go ashore only in the place where you will have certainty of being able to get water with facility. If you encounter some large openings, you will retrace your steps before visiting them so that I may conduct the vessel to them. The same will be the case if what we have judged to be gulfs, were two islands.
"The route which I have indicated to you in the present instruction is no doubt the shortest, nevertheless, you must modify or change it according to the winds which you find for I suppose them equally good for going north as for returning south. You may therefore take that which will be most suitable to the winds which you encounter, whether you begin with the first or the second of these two gulfs.
"As I am determined to set sail if you are not back at the time which I have fixed, you will return here to assure yourself if I have departed before making course for the islands Saint Peter and Saint François where I count to proceed. This group of islands is at latitude 32° 31' south and longitude 131° 25'. I will make all efforts to take knowledge of the continent to the north, which it was not possible for me to gain the first time I visited the southern part of these islands. They are not inhabited. If you see any smoke there, it will surely be us who will have set fire to indicate to you that we are in the neighbourhood or that we have passed there. If, as I fear, I could not get water in this part of the coast, I would proceed to King George's Port of which you have a plan in the atlas of Vancouver's voyage. From King George's Port, I will make course for Geographer's Bay, Leeuwin coast.
"If you do not find us here, you will leave at once for the islands Saint Peter and Saint François making course to the west by this same latitude if the winds permit in order to get yourself promptly out of all the islets, rocks and reefs which are found on a route which would take too much to the north and which we know as well as the continental coast. You will not take my small boat, this boat would undoubtedly be lost if I left it with you. Besides, it is absolutely useless to you. It would only retard your progress or compromise your vessel which will set sail this night or tomorrow morning at the latest. On your return, you will give me a written report of your work and your remarks".
Your fellow citizen. Signed N. B.
"The Commandant to Citizen Boulanger, engineer geographer,
"I invite you, as soon as the Casuarina shall be repaired, to go on board this vessel to do the geography of the two western coasts of the gulfs in the neighbourhood of which we are now. When we explored the eastern part of these same gulfs, the lack of water for the size of the vessel and other circumstances no less unfavourable, did not permit us to occupy ourselves with this work which is too interesting for knowledge of the coast to be abandoned and it is for this reason that I urge you to do it with all the accuracy that shall be possible for you.
"Citizen Freycinet has orders to make directly course to the north to take knowledge of the exact depth of the first although I am persuaded that we have seen it ourselves being at 34° 38' of latitude, coasting at not great distance, the eastern coast on which you will not stop. But it is not the same for those of the west which it is necessary that you make entirely. The lands in this part are generally low and the waters, even at a fairly great distance, have little depth.
"The work of this first gulf completed, you will pass into the second continuing to coast the continental coast without stopping at the islets and rocks which will remain to your south and west, their respective positions being known to us. When you shall be in this second gulf, Citizen Freycinet has orders to do as for the first, that is to say he will take the northern direction to know its depth and will then visit the western coast which, very different from the one opposite to it, is high and mountainous, if however the plains of mountains, of which we have had knowledge, are not found in the interior of the country. We penetrated into this gulf as far as latitude 34° 11', but we were not yet in its greatest depth and the bad weather which came to us at that time, did not permit us to return there.
"According to all probabilities and even supposing the hindrances of the season, fifteen or eighteen days are more than sufficient for the work which you have to do in that you must by no means occupy yourself with the eastern coast of these two gulfs which we have recognised ourselves in a manner sufficient for the perfection of geography.
"The islands and islets which are to the south and west of the entrance of the second gulf, must also not detain you but it is enjoined on Citizen Freycinet to seek a port which should be found at the western extremity of the second gulf, and in which it is said that Mr. Flinders stayed. You will draw up a plan of it if possible, this place of call needing to be known. According to the information given to me, there should be found opposite the entrance of this port, an island which ensures its safety from winds from south-east to north-east.
"I announce to Citizen Freycinet the time fixed at which I will depart from here, and as the time which I count to stay here is more considerable than that which you need, I do not doubt that you will be back before the time which I have fixed. Nevertheless, if it were otherwise, I give him orders to come join me at the islands Saint Peter and Saint François at latitude 32° 31' and longitude 131° 25'. These islands are easy to recognise and of easy access. I will make all my efforts to take knowledge of the continent to the north of this group of islands which I was not able to reach when I was in these waters. If I could not get water in this part of the coast, I would proceed to King George's Port for the replacements which I need. As it has a plan of this port in the atlas of Vancouver's voyage, he will find it easily. I observe to you only that it is said that its latitude is more south by 10 minutes. Moreover, by coasting the coast in this part, he will no doubt have knowledge of it.
"Although I have prescribed to Citizen Freycinet the route which he must take in that I believe it the best, he must nevertheless conform to that which the winds which he may encounter would require him to make: whether he begins with the first or the second of these gulfs. My wish is only to shorten as much as possible the time of his absence, the situation in which we are not permitting us to waste time uselessly. He also has orders, if he encountered some large openings at the extremity of the gulfs or if what we took for gulfs were islands, to retrace his steps without going round them so that I may conduct the vessel. It is expressly recommended to him not to go ashore and never to go below two fathoms of water so as not again to compromise, as has happened to him, his vessel nor the safety of those who accompany him. The Government has not asked me for the topography of some ungracious and sterile parts of New Holland but only knowledge of the coast or of great openings which it might offer. I hope that you will be willing to confine yourself within these same limits and finish as quickly as possible the work with which you are charged which would be the work of four or five days if the winds were favourable to you". "Your fellow citizen. Signed N. B".
During the day of the twentieth we continued to put the Casuarina in state to depart. The carpenters aboard were employed to go cut wood for the construction of our shallop which was being made aboard and a second boat visited several small bays to the east of our anchorage to see if fresh water streams could not be found there.
At sunset, the Casuarina being ready, Mr. Boulanger went on board and the vessel set sail about ten o'clock at night with very fine weather and a fine breeze from the south variable sometimes towards the east.
1803-01-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. At noon in 30° 36' of latitude observed and in 103° 41' of longitude by account.

1803-01-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and sky, the sea smooth, almost calm. At 4.30 the topman on his rounds reported that the main topsail tie was about to part; we at once secured the topsail and shifted the main topsail tie, which was doubled. Obs. lat. 29° 50' 19", long. 102° 50' 50".
1803-01-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 21st (January 11, 1803). The twenty-first, the weather continued fine and we had all day a fine breeze from the south-east. In the morning, we passed our cables and the crew was employed in various other works relative to the vessel. During the day, a fairly large quantity of mackerel of medium size were caught on the line. The small boat, which had been sent to fish on a point to the east of our anchorage, was less fortunate than we. It brought back only about fifty fish all of the same species and known under the name of parrots. Those who hunted kangaroos were not badly treated, they brought in five of the large species of which the total weight could be about two hundred and fifty to three hundred pounds.
About four o'clock in the afternoon, Citizen Ransonnet returned from the mission with which he had been charged without having found anything very interesting and not a single drop of water. He saw in this course many cassowaries and kangaroos, two of the latter were taken alive but we preferred to cut their throats rather than bring them on board. As a plan of the bay which he surveyed is to be made, I will give the details when his work is handed to me.
During the night, the weather was fine and the winds from the south-east.
1803-01-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 29° 50' of latitude observed and in 102° 58' of longitude by account. At 7 a flat calm.

1803-01-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds very light. At 5 the topman on his rounds at the mainmast reported that the main topsail sheet was chafed where it bears on the yardarm block. Obs. lat. 29° 56' 10", est. long. 102° 37' 30".
1803-01-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 22nd (January 12, 1803). The twenty-second, at daylight, two boats were sent to fish with the seine. Citizens Leschenault and Péron were of the party. The same day, the astronomical circle was taken on shore but I did not wish to establish a tent there, in that the apparatus which accompanies it is so considerable that it usually takes a whole day to bring all back on board, which is not convenient in an anchorage like that which we occupy, where one must always be ready to depart and often by cutting or veering cables.
It was agreed that the astronomer Bernier would go ashore in the morning at eight o'clock and would return between three and four o'clock in the afternoon. Our timekeepers, of which the rate had been well determined at King Island, should not need great correction.
At noon, one of the fishing boats being back, brought nothing at all. According to the report, it is the great quantity of seals found on the beach where it went, that the cause is attributed to.
The small boat which had remained to bring back Messrs. Leschenault and Péron did not arrive on board until four o'clock in the afternoon. The first was not fortunate in his course and brought back only two or three plants which he did not know, but Citizen Péron was very joyful to have gathered three or four molluscs, two small lizards and a half dozen sea ears which the sailors have filled their chests with. During the evening, the breeze was light and the winds in the south-east quarter by gusts. The night had nothing particular except that it was very damp although with very fine sky.
1803-01-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a flat calm until 9, when the breeze got up from NW to N. At noon in 29° 56' of latitude observed and in 102° 45' of longitude by account.

1803-01-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth. Freshened the nip of the main topsail sheet to starboard. At 2.15 the winds having shifted to the SW, we went onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 29° 32' 5", est. long. 101° 17' 32".
1803-01-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 23rd (January 13, 1803). The twenty-third, I sent at the morning a boat under the command of Aspirant Baudin to visit the bay in which we had anchored the first time we had knowledge of this island and in which we did not stay because our anchor did not hold. As this bay is found in the eastern part of the island, he spent the day out and on his return, I was informed that we could get some water there by digging wells. The boat's crew had procured some by this means and had found inside the beach a muddy ground in which they had procured some fairly good water. I put off until the next day to assure myself more positively of what was the case.
Another boat was occupied during the day in getting wood, and brought us two loads. A third boat was given to the master to go get oysters in Pelican Bay.
At sunset, the boats being back on board, the one which had been sent for water returned with two small casks only which were the product of the first, then two others were dug beside this first and I hope that the three together will furnish our consumption during our stay here. It is only unfortunate that we must go far to fetch it.
The master's boat returned laden with oysters which were distributed to all the crew. It also brought a fairly large quantity of pelican eggs and about thirty birds of the same name taken from their nests.
During the night, the weather was fine, the sky damp as usual, and the winds absolutely calm.
1803-01-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather. At 2.15 the breeze from WNW shifted to SW; shaped the course N 56° 15' W. The breeze freshened as it hauled to the south and was a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 29° 35' of latitude observed and in 101° 25' of longitude by account. The course given N 33° 45' W.

1803-01-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze; set the studdingsails to starboard. Obs. lat. 27° 39' 11", obs. long. 98° 34'.
1803-01-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
The 24th (January 14, 1803), we put our shallop on the stocks on board the vessel itself. The keel was presented, the stem and sternpost set, and during the rest of the day, all the timbers which had been prepared in advance were put in place.
The boats were sent, as usual, to get water and wood and I sent in the first one of our hunters to procure some particular birds which we were told had red tails and grey bodies, being of the size of the cockatoo which they were said to resemble in beak. The weather was fine all day. We had only a light breeze from the south variable to south-south-west.
At night, the boats returned on board with little water and even fewer objects of curiosity. The red-tailed birds which had been announced to us, turned out to be nothing more than black cockatoos with red patches in the tail feathers and absolutely similar to those which we had procured at Port Jackson. The best which there was were two pigeons with golden wings which were in very good condition.
The night had nothing particular and was fine, although very damp.
1803-01-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 27° 39' of latitude observed, 98° 34' of longitude observed and 99° 43' of longitude by account. At 6 the course given N 45° W.

1803-01-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze. The sea smooth enough. Obs. lat. 26° 22' 40", est. long. 97° 54' 14".
1803-01-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 26° 23' of latitude observed and in 96° 53' of longitude by account.

1803-01-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. Took in the studdingsails and set the staysails. Obs. lat. 25° 20' 46", est. long. 96° 26' 14".
1803-01-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 26th (January 16, 1803). The twenty-sixth, our works were the same as those of the day before and the boats had the same destinations. On board we occupied ourselves with the part of the rigging which needed repair and our lower shrouds as well as our topsail shrouds were set up and the vessel put in state to take to sea, as soon as we wished.
In the afternoon, the sky which had been very fine in the morning, became dark and stormy with appearance of bad weather during the night. The barometer had also fallen much which warned us to be on our guard. At sunset, thunder began to rumble and we had some fairly strong blows. Nevertheless, little by little the weather became fine and we were quit for the fright. During the night, the winds were very variable and in gusts from the north to the east.
(no entry for the 25th Nivôse, we will continue with the days given by Nicolas Baudin).
1803-01-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 25° 21' of latitude observed and in 95° 25' of longitude by account.

1803-01-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth, a light breeze. One of the fore topsail tie blocks having broken, we secured the yard to repair the damage. At noon the course NW by W. Obs. lat. 23° 59' 23", obs. long. 94° 24' 38".
1803-01-17.journal_baudin_autographe: From the 27th (January 17, 1803), the twenty (sic), we had all day a strong breeze from west to south-west which made the sea rough and swell, nevertheless, our large boat was sent to carry ashore the carpenters who had pieces of timber to cut for the bow of our shallop. It made two voyages in the day, although the weather was scarcely suitable for work like that with which it was charged. The boat intended to get water did not return on board because of the strength of the wind. We had for the greater part of the day lightning in different parts of the horizon but we did not hear thunder rumble. In the evening, the weather became fine and the breeze calmed entirely during the night which was fine.
1803-01-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 23° 59' of latitude observed and in 94° 25' of longitude observed. The course given N 56° 15' W. Saw tropic birds. At 10 crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the sixth time.

1803-01-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze. Saw many flying fish. At 10 p.m. on the 27th crossed the Tropic of Capricorn. Obs. lat. 22° 49' 34", obs. long. 90° 1' 0".
1803-01-18.journal_baudin_autographe: From the 28th (January 18, 1803). The twenty-eighth, the winds were south-south-east moderate. We continued ordinary works that is to say we got water and wood either for burning or for the construction of our shallop of which the wales were put in place. The night had nothing particular. The wind was almost calm and the sky fine.
1803-01-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. Saw flying fish, bonito and tropic birds. At noon in 22° 50' of latitude observed and in 90° 1' of longitude observed.

1803-01-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. In the forenoon put the small boat on the gratings to repair her. Obs. lat. 21° 24' 21", est. long. 90° 19' 56".
1803-01-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
From the 29th (January 19, 1803). The twenty-ninth, the weather continued fine, which pleased me all the more in that the Casuarina having been constantly favoured by the winds, I expected to see her arrive presently, if she conformed to the instruction which I gave her, which, in my opinion, is very doubtful in that the officers always believe themselves more knowledgeable than those under whose orders they serve.
We got little water in this day, the wells filling only very slowly. The other boat was employed in transporting wood to burn. During the night, fine weather and fine breeze from the north-east.
1803-01-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a good breeze from SE to ESE. At 6 the course given N 45° W. At noon in 21° 24' of latitude observed and in 87° 57' of longitude by account. At 3 the course given N 67° 30' W, and at 6 N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze. At 3 shaped the course WNW. The main topgallant halliard having [given way], it was refitted at once. Est. lat. 20° 48' 9", est. long. 87° 31' 56".
1803-01-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the thirtieth, the weather being fine, I had put ashore, at the place where the watering is done, a cock and two hens. I likewise left on this beach a boar and a sow to multiply there and be able afterwards to prove useful to the navigators who frequent the waters (of) this island during the summer, so as to offer good refreshments to the vessels that may wish to stop there. And the anchorage seems to me tolerably good to lie in safety, provided the winds are not forced from north-east to north-west by the north. For then the sea runs very high and rough there, but one has the resource of being able to get under way easily and to return when the bad weather has passed.
The hunters who were ashore took, in the course of the day, with the help of our dogs, twelve great kangaroos of various sizes. Seven of this number were taken alive and put in pens on board to be kept. Among those we hope to carry to our own country are three females that have young ones and that may perhaps come through well. I shall try, before setting out, to complete a score of them alive, so as to have a better hope of preserving some of them during the crossing.
During the night the weather was dark and we sometimes had violent squalls from the east-north-east.
1803-01-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from ESE to E. At noon in 20° 47' of latitude by account and in 85° 9' of longitude by account. In the 24 hours the main topsail tie, the main topgallant halliard and two studdingsail halliards parted.

1803-01-21.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, a good breeze. The topmast studdingsail halliard having parted, the sail was [recovered] and set again a moment later. At 9.45 the main topsail tie and the port topmast halliard parted; we at once took in the studdingsails, furled the main topgallant sail and clewed up the main topsail. At 1.30 we swayed and hoisted the main topsail and main topgallant sail. Obs. lat. 20° 32', est. long. 84° 51' 56".
1803-01-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the First of Pluviôse (21 January 1803). On the first of Pluviôse, the winds were at north-west and squally in the morning. The sky likewise had a bad appearance, being very dark and laden with clouds, but the whole cleared away in the afternoon, when the winds shifted to south-south-west.
The longboat, which I had sent off the evening before with two days' provisions under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy, to go and cut us some spars fit for the masting of our boats, returned on board at about seven in the morning, bringing us a few logs that were barely fit to make gratings' battens. As this was the second time that Citizen Bonnefoy had acquitted himself very badly of the commissions with which he was charged, not liking to leave the ship in which he finds himself, in keeping with his tastes of having nothing to do, I resolved to employ him no more. I had also embarked Citizen Le Sueur in this boat, to procure us some live emus, there being many in the neighbourhood of the place to which the boat had gone, but they would not give him the time necessary to hunt them with the dogs he had embarked expressly for that purpose.
The rest of the day was spent on the work of our launch and various other tasks on board. During the night the weather was fine and the winds at south, moderate, though from time to time some strong gusts passed.
1803-01-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from E. At noon in 20° 32' of latitude observed and in 82° 29' of longitude by account.

1803-01-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fine breeze. At 7 furled the fore topgallant sail and took in the studdingsails. Obs. lat. 20° 15' 50", est. long. 84° 51' 56".
1803-01-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Second (22 January 1803). On the second, at six in the morning, I went ashore, accompanied by the carpenters, to try to cut wood fit to make us planking, of which we were beginning to have need for the continuation of our launch, which then had her wales in place and one strake below.
We had not, up to this moment, found any straight wood fit for the purpose along the shore, the casuarina, which might have replaced the eucalyptus, being constantly rotten at the heart. More than sixty trees of this latter species were felled without our being able to find a single one fit for use. All that this painful expedition procured us was some twenty pieces suitable for turning into knees and a few crooks, but we brought back only two pieces of straight wood, of which one is very doubtful.
As I kept constantly beside the carpenters to press on the work, I very nearly was crushed by the fall of a tree which, falling in a direction different from that we had judged it would take, knocked me over in its fall, and I found myself so entangled in the branches that it took a long time to get me out. I got off with a few injuries to the head and other parts of the body. This fall made me spend the night ashore, where I rested perfectly well, though very ill at ease. We had, during the day, very fine weather and, in the night, a light breeze from the east which made the air very dry and even cold.
1803-01-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to ESE. At noon in 20° 16' of latitude observed and in 79° 26' of longitude by account. The course given N 84° 22' 30" W (west half north).

1803-01-23.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze. The dinghy was got up on deck and, being judged past repair by the master carpenter, was thrown overboard. Obs. lat. 20° 5' 39", est. long. 78° 16' 26".
1803-01-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Third of Pluviôse (23 January 1803). On the third, in the morning, I came back on board with the wood that could not all be carried the evening before. I also brought with me three live kangaroos, which were put into pens like the others and of which I take the greatest care. There was one female and two males. These three animals were taken by our dogs without being hurt. One of them thought to save itself by throwing itself into the water, but it fell into our power after having made a fine resistance.
The rest of the day was spent on the work on board, and all the carpenters resumed that of the launch, putting off till the morrow the search for wood in another place where, perhaps, we shall be more fortunate. During the night the sky was very dark and overcast and the winds at south-east, very light.
Of the Third of Pluviôse (23 January 1803) On the third, at sunrise, the carpenters were again sent ashore to look for wood fit for planking. A second boat set out in the morning to go and observe the latitude at the entrance of Port des Pélicans, situated at the bottom of the bay before which we lie. It was the master of the helmsmen (in another hand: !) who was charged with this task, most of the ship's officers having no instruments, and those who have them regarding it as beneath their dignity.
I sent off a third boat when it returned from watering, to help with the transport of the wood the carpenters would cut. Two of our hunters went to spend the day ashore to try to procure us some new birds of which I was told there was knowledge.
During the day these two boats could make but one trip, and our hunters sent us three live kangaroos which, like the others, were put into the pens made from two cabins that were taken apart to lodge them. We had, the whole (day), a pleasant breeze from the east-south-east. In the night it held at east, almost calm.
1803-01-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Dark weather, the wind a strong breeze from ESE to E. The dinghy, having been judged unfit for service, was broken up and thrown overboard. The jib boom was rigged in and the topmasts and topgallant masts set up. At noon in 20° 6' of latitude observed and in 75° 53' of longitude by account. The course given west.

1803-01-24.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and a strong breeze, a high sea. We set up the topmast backstays and the topgallant shrouds and backstays. Est. lat. 20° 16' 9", est. long. 74° 28' 26".
1803-01-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fourth of Pluviôse (24 January 1803). On the fourth, the work on board was the same as the day before. We continued cutting wood for the planking and we set up our saws on board to rip it to thickness. We had no one who had followed this trade, which did not fail to make the work difficult for those employed on it. As in such a circumstance an example had to be given, I sawed part of the first piece with the purser's clerk, Boivin. Citizen Ronsard relieved me, but the other officers took good care to show themselves. Though none of them knows the first piece of timber that goes into a vessel, there is not one who has gone near the launch since she has been on the stocks. These works, they say, are made for the common people; a naval officer need only know how to trim his ship and rest when his watch is over.
In the evening the carpenters returned on board and our hunters too, not having been fortunate in their excursions. The night had nothing particular about it; the sky was overcast and the horizon hazy, with winds from the east in strong gusts.
1803-01-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from E. The fore topgallant mast was struck; the main topsail tie and a studdingsail halliard parted. At noon in 20° 16' of latitude by account and in 72° 5' of longitude by account.

1803-01-25.journal_anonyme: Dark, overcast weather, with light rain almost throughout. At 9 the main topsail tie having parted, took in the studdingsails and lowered the main topsail on the cap. Obs. lat. 20° 41' 36", est. long. 70° 16' 56".
1803-01-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fifth of Pluviôse (25 January 1803). On the fifth, seeing the Casuarina not return, absent for a fortnight, I began to fear either that she had not carried out the orders I had given her on leaving, or that some unfortunate accident had befallen her. However, the continual fine weather that has prevailed since the time of her departure makes this latter conjecture much less probable than the former.
Be that as it may, I shall wait until the time I have fixed, but if she does not appear within the four days remaining to complete it, I shall continue on my course without troubling myself further about it.
We finished, during this day, the embarking of the wood for our launch, at which I was well pleased. On board, the work of making it into planks continued, and those charged with this task carried it out much better than the day before. We made, as usual, our consumption of water for the day. We had calm both day and night, and very great heat at both these times.
1803-01-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast, rainy and squally weather. The wind blowing hard from E in gusts, the sea extremely high, the ship labouring a great deal. At noon the course given N 78° 45' W, in 20° 42' of latitude observed and in 67° 54' of longitude by account. On taking the watch at noon the captain ordered me to take in nothing until something carried away. We were under the foresail, topsails hoisted, main topgallant sail and studdingsails to starboard and port, forward and aft. The mainmast was labouring a great deal. At 2, in a squall, the main topgallant sheet and the studdingsail halliards or tacks having parted, I had the topgallant sail furled and the studdingsails taken in. We took the lower reef in the main topsail and the second in the fore, struck the main topgallant mast and the gaff, and set up the main topmast and topgallant mast. From 6 until midnight the wind blew very hard in gusts and the sea was higher than at any other time of the voyage, and would have forced us to run before it had it not been our course. We ran 12.5 knots, which is the greatest speed the ship has yet made. The rolling was very heavy; several people were hurt. I was thrown from starboard to port against the gunwale and lay stunned; I had a bad bruise on the right knee, where an abscess formed which kept me from walking — though it did not keep me from standing my watch.

1803-01-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts. Shortened sail and lowered the gaff. Obs. lat. 21° 8' 59", obs. long. 68° 10'.
1803-01-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 6th of Pluviôse (26 January 1803). On the sixth, we had a very cloudy sky and the winds at north-east, a pleasant breeze. Our occupations of the day were, as usual, the replenishing of our water consumption and the work on our launch, which was beginning to advance and to take a good shape.
I sent men to hunt kangaroo, but we were not fortunate. Only one was taken alive and brought on board, along with three others strangled by the dogs.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind calm.
1803-01-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from ENE to NNE. We shook out the reefs of the topsails, rigged the topgallant masts and the gaff and ran out the jib boom. At noon in 20° 9' of latitude observed, 68° 10' of longitude observed and 64° 2' of longitude by account. The course given N 67° 30' W. Saw a frigate bird. During the night overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts with frequent lulls.

1803-01-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze, a swell running. Crowded sail, hoisted the gaff and ran out the boom. Saw a frigate bird wheeling above our masts. Overcast weather, a strong breeze and continual rain. Obs. lat. 20° 20' 34", est. long. 67° 2' 0".
1803-01-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 7th (27 January 1803). On the seventh, the weather was much the same as the day before, and the sky had a fairly bad appearance, so as to make us fear some squall, the horizon being laden with storms in several quarters. But the breeze from the north-east, variable towards the north, which set in during the morning, dispersed the clouds that were piling up one upon another, and the weather turned fine again.
The work on the launch was continued, and those charged with making us planks for the planking acquitted themselves very well.
During the night the sky again became overcast with clouds and grew stormy. We had, from time to time, some squalls from the south and at times rain.
1803-01-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from N to ENE. At noon in 20° 20' of latitude observed and in 66° 40' of longitude observed. The course given N 78° 45' W. The cables were bent. At midnight the course given N 84° 22' 30" W (west half north).

1803-01-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth. Saw tropic birds. In the afternoon bent our cables. Obs. lat. 20° 28' 8", est. long. 63° 49' 0".
1803-01-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
As I counted on setting sail as soon as the time which I had prescribed to the Casuarina for being back was expired, I began to have white casuarina branches embarked for the food of our kangaroos which were doing very well. We already had fifteen, two of which had died which had been too seriously wounded by the dogs to recover.
During the night, the wind was calm and the sky fine.
1803-01-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, with rain at intervals. A good breeze from E to N. Saw tropic birds. At noon in 20° 28' of latitude observed and in 63° 11' of longitude by account. The course given N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, rain at intervals, a fresh breeze. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 20° 26' 42", est. long. 60° 58'.
1803-01-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daybreak we put our launch on her side to paint her bottom, work that could not easily be done at sea, on account of our other boats which would have hampered us too much. We had time, in the course of the day, to put on four strakes, which was sufficient for the port side, which was to be planked first. The caulkers worked the greater part of the night by torchlight to caulk the part that had (been) planked during the day.
In the evening the boats, being back on board, brought us another live kangaroo, which was put with the others. Citizen Bernier was also sent ashore to continue taking distances.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind almost calm.
1803-01-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to E. At 8 the course given N 67° 3' W. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds. At noon in 20° 27' of latitude observed and in 60° 20' of longitude by account. At 4 the course given N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 20° 23' 19", obs. long. 58° 37' 0".
1803-01-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 10th of Pluviôse (30 January 1803). On the tenth, in the morning, we changed our launch to the other side, and during the day the same operation as the day before was performed on her. The work was pushed on as much as possible, and in the evening we set her permanently on her stocks, the caulkers having also finished theirs.
During the day we had very fine weather and a pleasant breeze from the south-south-east. I gave up entirely the hope of seeing the Casuarina arrive, and could conceive no better reason for so long an absence on her part.
Be that as it may, being resolved to sail, the ship was prepared accordingly. Our topgallant masts, which had been struck, were sent up again and the yards crossed.
A little before sunset, a band of several kangaroos having appeared on the edge of the shore, abreast of the ship, I at once sent men to hunt them in the hope of taking some of them alive. I was not disappointed in my expectation, for at nine o'clock the boat, being back, brought us three fine ones, though one of them was badly wounded.
During the night, fire broke out on board above the galleys and pierced the deck. It was noticed in time to be put out at once. The officer who was on watch was placed under arrest for not having warned me of this accident, which, fortunately, had no further consequences.
1803-01-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from E to ENE. At 8 the course given N 67° 30' W. At noon in 20° 23' of latitude observed and in 58° 37' of longitude observed. At 6 the course given N 78° 45' W. Saw many tropic birds and tropic gulls.

1803-01-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. Saw many tropic birds and tropic gulls. Obs. lat. 20° 14' 4", est. long. 55° 54'. Departure from Mauritius.
1803-01-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 11th (31 January 1803). On the eleventh, I ought to have made sail, the twenty days allowed at the longest, which I had prescribed to the Casuarina, having expired. However, I spent one more day at anchor in the hope of seeing her arrive, but it was to no purpose that I lost the twenty-four hours.
The weather was very fine during the morning, and we had a pleasant breeze from south-south-east to south-south-west, of which I much regretted not having taken advantage.
The boat charged with providing for our consumption of water brought us, on its return, two pretty live emus which they took with the help of the dogs. Despite all our attempts, we had not, until then, been able to get near them, although the places they frequent were known to us. This fortunate capture made me regret less the loss of the day I had just spent waiting for the Casuarina.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind calm.
1803-01-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to ESE. At 8 the course given N 67° 30' E. At noon in 20° 14' of latitude observed and in 55° 53' of longitude by account. During the night we lay close-hauled and hove to.

1803-02-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth of Pluviôse, from four o'clock in the morning, we made our preparations to get under way as soon as the breeze should set in, as we had been accustomed to have it most of the time we remained at this anchorage. We began by taking in our three boats, and then we weighed with the ship our sheet anchor and hove short on the other. The crew was then given breakfast. After which, having hoisted our topsails to the masthead, we tripped the anchor and made sail, abandoning the Casuarina to her good fortune, as it had pleased her to abandon us to ours.
My intention being to come and reconnoitre a land which the lookouts (sic) had reported to us, in the western part of Île Borda, I steered west and south. Once I was outside the bay in which we had anchored, I ran along, for the third time, the whole of the north coast of this island, again identifying all the points that have served us in drawing up the chart of it, which seems to me to leave nothing to be desired.
In the afternoon the winds were at south, variable to south-south-east, but the breeze freshened so much that we were obliged that we were obliged (sic) to take two reefs in the topsails and to furl all our staysails. Although the wind came to us over the land, the sea did not fail to be rough and disturbed.
At two o'clock we sighted the Casuarina, standing on the eastern tack. I expected that as soon as she perceived us she would put herself on the same tack as us and follow us. Accordingly, when we were no more than a cannon-shot from one another, I had the mainsail brailed up and furled so that she might have less difficulty in following us. But this troubled her very little, and she continued to stand to the east, so much so that at half past three we lost sight of her. It is doubtless difficult to explain this manoeuvre on the part of Citizen Freycinet, and no doubt he will make it known to us at our first meeting.
As I wished to get clear of the islands and rocks that lie to the north of Île Borda, I continued on my course, preferring to wait for the Casuarina at the extremity of this island rather than lose time running after her by beating up to the east. For it was not to be presumed that she would hold this tack for long, if indeed her intention was to rejoin us, which I am very far from believing.
At eight o'clock, being at the western part of this island, I carried little sail during the night and kept always in sight of the coast, having the poop lantern lit so that the Casuarina might have knowledge of us, should it please her not to go to the anchorage or to any other place.
During the night the sky was dark and damp; we had at times some squalls of rain, but they were of little consequence and of short duration. The breeze fell entirely calm and the winds varied from south-south-east to north-east.
1803-02-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from ENE to NE. At daybreak we shaped our course and sighted Mauritius. During the night we stood off and on.

1803-02-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock the western point of Île Borda bore south 22° west, at a distance of two miles.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, at daybreak, having no knowledge of the Casuarina, I resolved to stand a little to the east in the hope of meeting her. But at eight o'clock, not wishing to go in for the fourth time from the western point of Île Borda, I resolved to steer south to try to fall in with the land which had been reported to us when we ran up this part of the coast coming from the south. During the morning, and indeed the whole day, the weather was little suited to this search, being dark, hazy, and often rainy. But as there were, from time to time, a few clear spells, we sometimes had a fairly extensive horizon, without perceiving anything that could make us suspect we had any land in the neighbourhood.
At noon we had no observed latitude. That by dead reckoning placed us in 36° 5' 7", and the longitude was 134° 21' 10".
In the afternoon the wind fell off a good deal, and the haze was almost continual, with a few intervals excepted. We continued steering south, edging a little to the west, until night, without having any indication of the approach of land. As at this time I lost hope of falling in with it, and as we were well to the south of the place where it had been said to lie, and of which note was made at that time, I had the course altered further to the west during the night.
If, however, there does exist a land to the west of Île Borda, it can only be a few insignificant islets that leave a quite clear channel between them and the western coast of Île Borda. My opinion is that none exists, although several persons claim to have seen it.
During the night the weather was very damp from the haze and the light rain we had at intervals. The winds, on the other hand, were extremely variable and often calm, (they) ranged over different points of the compass. Soundings were taken several times, as a precaution, without finding bottom at ninety fathoms. We had besides a strong swell from south to south-west, which indicated to us plainly enough that we had no land to fear in this quarter.
1803-02-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 4 a.m. we shaped our course for the North West Port; at 9.30 doubled Coin de Mire. At 1.30 p.m. we anchored inside the Deux Frères and warped in under Île aux Tonneliers, where we made fast with four moorings.

1803-02-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth the sky remained as hazy as on the preceding days, and the rain, though not very heavy, did not fail to inconvenience us a great deal. We continued to steer west, without rising much to the north, wishing to make sure that there did not exist, in this latitude, any land that might trouble the navigators who, in future, will frequent these waters, as being the shortest course they have to make to return to Europe. During the morning the breeze was light, and we had the winds at south, variable to south-south-east.
At noon we had no observation of latitude, and by our dead reckoning we made ourselves to be in 36° 21' 27" and 133° 26' 47" of longitude. The barometer, which kept always below 27 28°, did not announce to us the speedy return of the disagreeable weather we had had since our departure from Île Borda.
In the afternoon we had our course altered a little to the north, and we continued it thus until the middle of the night, when the winds having passed the winds having (sic) passed to south-west, variable to west-south-west, obliged us to keep close-hauled on the course to the north-north-west.
As we had for a long time been experiencing a fairly strong swell from the south-west, we had reason to fear seeing the winds settle for some time in that quarter, or even bring us some squalls.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth the weather was far from fine. The winds from west-south-west blew at times in strong gusts, giving us very cold rain. They obliged us, in the middle of the night, to take two reefs in our topsails.
As, since our departure from Île Borda, work had been going on unceasingly on our launch, I flattered myself that she might be fit to serve us at the Îles St Pierre and St François, where I should surely have occasion to anchor, being persuaded that among these islands there must be found some good shelter, and perhaps also a useful port of call for the navigators who will succeed us.
1803-02-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the morning I went to the hospital for the abscess on my knee. The port's caulkers worked on the ship. We watered.

1803-02-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather seemed as though it wished to turn fine, and the barometer, in a very short interval, rose from 27 p 10 l to 28 p 2 l, which was for us a good omen. The winds varied from south-south-west to south, and sometimes even to south-south-east. We had, nevertheless, still a very heavy sea from the south-west, though otherwise the sea was fine.
At daybreak we found two of our kangaroos dead in their pens. I had no doubt that it was the bad weather that had caused us to lose them, for they were quite soaked by the rain and the continual haze we had had for three days, notwithstanding that the greatest care had been taken to cover their pens well with good tarpaulins.
