This accident decided me to keep them no longer on the gangways where they were lodged. But to find them another convenient place, it was necessary to make two persons discontented, or at least one, for he showed it to me in no uncertain manner, reproaching me that if he was on board it was indeed my fault, since I had not been willing to let him leave on the Naturaliste, in accordance with the written request he made me at Port Jackson, etc. "You are right," I said to him by way of answer, "but I would have taken good care not to urge you not to dishonour yourself, had I been able to foresee that you were capable of preferring your comforts and a few passing conveniences to the greater success of the expedition and to what may be useful to our country." I nonetheless took the cabin of M. Leschenault, our botanist, and that of M. Ransonnet, which I needed to lodge the seven kangaroos that were exposed to all the inclemencies of the weather on our gangways.
At noon the latitude by observation, which had been wanting for three days, placed us in 34° 55' 27", and the longitude by the reckoning was found to be 131° 27' 50". So as not to go further west, I had the ship steered north-north-west in order to close with the mainland, a little to the east of the place where I had ceased to see it, having in that quarter a landmark that could not be mistaken, there being an islet of a particular shape, which is the last one met with coming from the east when making for the Îles St Pierre. It is for this reason that I gave it, at that time, the name of Postillon.
During the rest of the day, the sky, though very cloudy, was tolerably fine, and the winds very variable from south-south-west to south, but the barometer still rising, we remained convinced that very shortly we should have fine weather, although the sea was still very rough from the south-west.
At eight o'clock in the evening we hauled close on the course to the south towards the west, which we continued until midnight, and at that time and at that time (sic), that to the south-east until daybreak, so as not to close with the land, from which I did not reckon myself at any great distance, and also for fear that the islets we had in our course might extend further south than those whose positions we already had assured.

1803-02-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak,
the islets seen the day before bore east by north at a distance of two leagues.
At eight o'clock,
we had knowledge of the mainland to the east ¼ south-east; it was seen only from the mastheads.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the sixteenth, at daybreak we steered north in order to close with the land during the day. The weather was fine and the sea fine, but the swell was so considerable that we were obliged to keep the reefs in our topsails, so much was our masting strained by the sharp and continual rolling it caused the ship.
About six o'clock the lookouts reported to us that they saw several islets to the east by north. We were not long in perceiving them from below, and at eight o'clock we recognised them perfectly to be the same ones of which we already had knowledge and had fixed the position. We continued, during the morning, to steer north so as to close with the land at the islet of Postillon, from which point I must do everything possible not to lose sight of the mainland again until I have rounded to the north the Îles St Pierre and St François.
At noon we observed the latitude of 36° 33' 33° 36' 33", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 131° 36' 13".
During the evening the weather continued fine, and at sunset the breeze freshened a great deal. At six o'clock the islets seen in the morning bore from from (sic) north-east to east-north-east at a fairly great distance. We continued to steer north until eight o'clock, when we took the tack to the south towards the west, which we held until the next day, carrying little sail.
The weather was fine during (the evening); the winds varied from south-east to south-south-east and fell calm a short time after moonrise.
At eight o'clock we were in 40 fathoms of water, and we kept this depth until daybreak, when it was found to be 45 fathoms.
One of the islets we had in view almost the whole day is easy to recognise by its shape, having the appearance of a haystack at a distance of eight or ten leagues, but when one comes nearer to it, one sees a lower land joining it, which has the appearance of a saddle. The other islets are much lower and are seen only when the one of the Meulot de Foin presents itself in the form of a saddle. Those which lie more to the north-east are not seen, or are seen only, when one has rounded the one I have just spoken of.

1803-02-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
we had knowledge of three islets to the north-east, which we recognised at sunset,
to be the same ones we had seen on our first run along the coast, having passed to the east of them to follow the mainland.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, in the morning, we closed with the mainland, steering north-east. It seemed to us that the currents had carried us a good deal to the east during the night, for at daybreak we found ourselves no more than three leagues from the islets seen the day before. The sky, which was then overcast, turned fine again, and we had all morning a pleasant breeze from south-east to south-south-east, making good way. The heavy swell, which had not left us since our departure from Île Borda, became much less strong, and we found the sea fine.
At noon the latitude was observed at 32° 43' 35", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 131° 43' 47".
As we had then closed with the mainland and well identified our islet of Postillon, we began from this point new bearings of the coast, so as to continue them, if it were possible for us, as far as the 128th degree of longitude, which, together with what General d'Entrecasteaux has done, will give an exact knowledge of the whole southern coast of New Holland.
After having rounded to the north the islet of Postillon, we followed the coast closely, tracing its various windings. The breeze was very strong in the evening, and we advanced fairly rapidly until evening, five o'clock, when, finding ourselves abreast of the Îles St Pierre, we tacked out to sea so as not not (sic) to engage ourselves during the night among islands whose position and number are little certain, all the more since we counted three of them, whereas the chart makes mention of only two.
Both to the north-west and to the south-east of the islet of Postillon, the shores are reefs that extend in these two directions to nearly a mile offshore and on which the sea breaks a great deal. The channel they form with the mainland appears, nevertheless, practicable, but it is more prudent to pass south of them in order to close with the coast.
The night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth was spent tacking, all the reefs taken in the topsails, in sight of the Îles St Pierre. The breeze was fresh and the sky, though cloudy, was nevertheless fine. The lead was never below 34 fathoms, and at midnight, when we tacked onto the course to the east towards the north, it was 37, sand and broken shells.
The lands we saw in the afternoon are of middling height and often divided into lower parts that are only distinguished on approach. They offer little that is pleasant to the eye, appearing to be but very little wooded and without any tall timber.

1803-02-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock in the evening,
the eastern part of the St Pierre islands bore north 50° west,
an islet was seen to the north 25° west.
The most easterly point of the continental land bore north 87° east.
On the 18th at 7 o'clock in the morning, we found ourselves we found ourselves (sic) about a league and a half from the coast of the most easterly of the St Pierre islands.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, being at two leagues' distance from the most easterly of the St Pierre islands, we closed with the continental point at which our bearings of the previous day had ended. The coast in this part forms a great indentation in the shape of a wide bay which extends to the north-east by north. We stood into it to learn its depth and see whether there might not be found some port where ships could lie in safety. As the weather was fine and the breeze fresh, we advanced fairly rapidly, keeping the lead continually in hand. When we found no more than eleven fathoms of water, we fell, in less than a quarter of an hour, to six, which obliged us to bear away and even to change tacks to gain the other cape which forms the entrance to this bay on the west. We were still nearly two leagues from the north-east indentation, but it could be plainly made out that it offered neither cuts nor openings that could lead one to believe that anything of interest was to be found there.
This shortage of water having obliged us to stand a little further out, we sighted a long reef awash on which the sea rose to a great height and which appeared to us to be more than a league in extent. We then had fifteen fathoms of water, and being unable to pass between the mainland and it, we were compelled to close with the eastern part of the St Pierre islands and to pass between these islands and the reef, keeping, at a mile and a half at most, along the third, which the chart makes no mention of. The channel between this island and the reef is a good league wide and the bottom 15 to 18 fathoms, sand mixed with broken shells.
Having rounded it, we saw several other islands to the west and to the east which we judged must form part of the St François islands. In the channels which separate the islands from one another there are several reefs awash on which the sea breaks strongly, but which can be passed fairly close without anything to fear, the water being deep. We were often obliged to luff for some and bear away for others. At last, steering north towards east to close with the land, we rounded two islands which lie very close to the mainland, and when we were to the north of the first, we had sight of a great bay even deeper than the one passed that morning. It seemed to me that we ought to find good shelter there, and I decided to look for an anchorage there by working round their western sides. This conjecture proved true, for when we had them to the south-east, we found the sea there very calm. We then shortened sail and, continuing to steer north, in eleven and twelve fathoms of water, we advanced as far as six fathoms, where I came to anchor a league and a half from the coast on a bottom of grey sand mixed with broken shells and weed. The land of the indentation still bore more than two leagues from us to the east-south-east, but before penetrating it with the ship, it was necessary to make certain whether there was (water) enough to enter as well as to get out again.
As soon as our sails were furled, two boats were sent out at once to sound around the ship and in different directions.
I was informed on their return that the bottom of this bay was in no way practicable, even for a small vessel. At about a mile from the ship there was no more than five fathoms of water. Half a mile further, four, and almost immediately, three and two. Further in, nothing was to be seen but shoals and a continual succession of sandbanks which are partly uncovered at low water.
The boat which had orders to head north-west gave us a moment of joy and satisfaction by telling us that it had made the discovery of a fine port in which there were four rivers, and that in the one it had entered there were four fathoms of water and three further in. That in truth the water there was salt but that in all likelihood it would end by becoming fresh the further one went in. This was for us all the more agreeable in that it made up for our regret at having found nothing, up to that moment, on this coast that could compensate for our pains and be of use to navigators.
The small boat which I had also sent to the island opposite which we were at anchor, and in which Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, embarked to survey the country and its produce, did not return until nightfall, having remained aground at low water more than two miles from the coast.
According to the gardener's report, this island is formed of nothing but sand, on which grow various shrubs of little height. He brought back from this excursion only a few plants with seeds, having found none in flower. Among them is one which has quite the habit of the olive tree and whose fruit resembles it in miniature, though the seed it contains is quite different. A large fire was lit on this island to serve as a mark of recognition for the Casuarina, should she come to pass in these waters.
As it blew a strong breeze all day all day (sic), and we had only thirty fathoms of cable out, twenty more were paid out, and despite the strong squalls from the south-south-east, we held fast on our anchor, proof that the bottom was not bad and the holding good.
1803-02-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: General Magallon came to visit the ship.

1803-02-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
The 19th Pluviôse (8 February 1803). On the nineteenth, at daybreak, having no hope of being able to work further into the bay, I sent off two boats to go round it entirely. As we had the sun to the north as to the south and consequently little means of observing the latitude on board, Citizen Bernier embarked in the one which began its course to the east and the command of which I gave to Citizen Bonnefoy, with the instruction annexed hereto:
"To Citizen Bonnefoy, ensign of the ship &c,
"Tomorrow at daybreak, you will take command of the large longboat and will put Citizen Bernier ashore in the deepest indentation of the bay within which we are at anchor, and which bears from you east and east by south-east by compass.
"To get there, you will first steer for the point which bears from you east and east by south-east by compass from our anchorage, in order to make certain whether, as is claimed, the land which we have to the south-east is an island. When you have gained certainty as to what it is, you will continue your course
"to reach the indentation of which I have spoken to you.
"Immediately after Citizen Bernier has finished his observation, you will follow the coast and give the greatest attention to examining and charting its contour. Should any openings be met with, you will visit them, and should they prove too deep, you will make note of them and of their direction before retracing your steps. As it is probable that the part of the coast you are to explore is frequented by the natives, since we have on several occasions perceived smoke there, you will take care to avoid any dispute with them, and will try, on the contrary, to make them understand, by gestures of friendship or the sight of the presents I intend for them, how peaceable your intentions are.
"In all likelihood, you will be absent one or two days before having gone round the circuit made by the bay in which we lie, so you will take the greatest care not to let your boat run aground.
"You will keep note of the time of the turn of the tides and of their greatest rise, observing on the edge of the shore the lines of demarcation which may make this known to you.
"I hope that the desire to return on board will not make you show too much haste in fulfilling the mission with which you are charged, and that you will acquit yourself of it in a manner leaving no doubt about the places you are going to visit. Your boat will be provided with three days' provisions, and in every circumstance you will avoid making use, against the natives, of the arms which are embarked for the safety of all those who accompany you." Signed N. B.
In the second boat which I sent out to go round by the north, and of which Citizen Ransonnet had the command, I had Citizen Faure, geographical engineer, embark to examine in detail the port that had been reported to us and to survey its plan.
Copy of the instruction given to Citizen Ransonnet.
"Tomorrow, 19 Pluviôse, at daybreak, you will take command of one of our large boats and will proceed to the place that the second master of the helm, Martin, will point out to you.
"According to the imperfect survey which he has given me of the port he has come upon, this place appears to deserve closer examination, which is also why Citizen Faure accompanies you, in order to survey its plan as exactly as shall be possible. As this place appears frequented by the natives, you must visit it with prudence and not compromise yourself by letting your boat run aground. You will avoid every kind of engagement with them. Should they come to meet you, in order not to be obliged to make use of the arms which I place at your disposal, you will try, on the contrary, to induce them to approach you, by offering to their view the presents I intend for them, and will employ every gesture of friendship used in such cases, to make them understand how peaceable and friendly your intentions are.
"I hope that the desire to fulfil your mission well will make you take the time necessary for it, and that you will not return on board until the work is finished. You will provide yourself with provisions for three days." Signed N. B.
When the two boats had been sent off, I sent out the small one with the dredge, which brought us back nothing curious or of interest. .
It appears that the bottom on which we lie is little frequented by fish, for not a single one was taken with the line. The scarcity of sea birds frequenting this bay likewise indicated to us that they are not common here.
Throughout the whole day it blew a strong breeze from the south-south-east to the south, and during the night it was even fresher than during the day. The ship, nevertheless, held fast on her anchor, though it is true she had no strain to sustain against the sea. The direction of the current observed on board came to us from the south on the flood and from the east-north-east on the ebb. Its speed was about a mile an hour at two-thirds of the tide.
1803-02-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: We were ready to put to sea. Two men deserted, two were left in hospital, and we took 10 from La Cayenne, of whom 3 were unfit for service. Citizen Depuche, mineralogist, stayed at Mauritius, being unable to bear the passage to France. Citizens Le Bas, frigate captain (whom we had left wounded at Timor) and Lucas, ensign, came aboard as passengers. We took 120 pots of brandy in place of the same quantity lost on the passage from Port Jackson; 300 lb of rice, 150 lb of beans, 65 lb of coffee, 3 lb of tea and 25 sacks of maize for the voyage to France.

1803-02-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
The 20th Pluviôse (9 February 1803). On the twentieth, the weather continued fine and the winds still in the south, variable to the south-south-east, a strong breeze. We occupied ourselves on board with finishing the work on our launch, which was completed that day, together with her masting, her sails and her rigging. By this means we found ourselves able to make use of her at the first moment the occasion should present itself, and I hope that the fate of this third one will be happier than that of the other two.
In the morning I sent the small boat ashore to procure grass for our kangaroos, which are all in very good condition and have good appetites. But that which was brought back did not suit them at all, and none would eat it. As they are beginning to grow accustomed to maize, I hope soon to be able to wean them entirely from this food.
In the afternoon we had sight of our two boats making their return. That of Citizen Bonnefoy arrived first. According to the verbal report he made me, the bottom of this bay offers no resource, lacking water everywhere and able to be frequented scarcely even by small craft. They could not approach the land closer than a mile. And in order to put Citizen Bernier ashore, the boat had to be run aground. According to his observation, the latitude of the place where he landed would be 32° 24' and the longitude 131° 27' 45". But he regards these observations as very doubtful, owing to the great elevation of the sun in relation to an artificial horizon which he was obliged to use. Moreover, in the whole circuit made by the bay, no opening was met with that could give reason to suspect that there was any river or stream flowing to the sea. It even appears that in the rainy season, the water is absorbed by the sand before it can take any direction. The whole interior of the country appeared to them sandy and covered with a kind of heath of little height, without any timber trees. A branch of shrub was brought back whose fruits had an agreeable taste, on which the crew of the boat regaled themselves thoroughly. Perhaps the written report which I am awaiting from Citizen Bonnefoy will teach me something more interesting.
On the arrival of Citizen Freycinet and Mr Faure, the port which had been reported to us was indeed found to exist, but the lack of water renders it impracticable for a ship of our size, and even well below that, there being at high water among the banks found there only three
fathoms of water. The rivers likewise are nothing but arms of the sea which lose themselves in marshes. The isthmus which forms the entrance of this port on the south is no more than ninety to a hundred paces wide and is nothing other than a heap of sand covered with shrubs of little height. In this port were taken some fish of the trevally kind, on which the sailors regaled themselves, as well as on the same fruits that the other boat had come upon.
From atop the isthmus a fire was seen in the interior of the country, and someone even claimed to have seen natives on the beach, but at a great distance. I am awaiting the written report of Citizen Ransonnet and the detailed plan of Mr Faure.
Mr Bonnefoy's boat likewise saw some smoke in the interior of the country but had no sight of the natives, of whom, however, some traces were thought to be noticed.
During the night the weather was very cloudy and the breeze still strong. I should have liked to be able to get under sail the following day, but as I had been told that a kind of kangaroo of quite a different colour from that which we knew, and some very peculiar birds, had been seen on the island, I decided to remain one day more, for the natural history of the country, which it is proper to make known.
1803-02-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: The ship swung. I left the hospital and came back aboard in the evening. On reaching Mauritius the only animals left alive were 3 cassowaries, 3 wombats, 2 swans, the goose from Bass Strait, the 2 dogs and a few birds. We took aboard 2 Bengal does, 2 guinea fowl and 1 four-horned sheep.

1803-02-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
The 21st Pluviôse (10 February 1803). On the twenty-first, in the morning, the weather being as on the preceding days, I sent off the large boat and all our hunters with the dogs, to try to bring us back something new. As it was a party of pleasure, all the naturalists, who until then had remained quietly on board for fear of not being comfortable in a boat that might be one or two nights ashore, asked to go along. They were taken there. I wish them to enjoy themselves well and to return content with their outing, even if they should not be content with what may be found.
Citizen Péron is the only one who embarked in the boat commanded by Mr Bonnefoy, but the short stay he made ashore did not render his pains very useful (added above the line, and in another hand: "I had embarked despite you. The specimens I gathered in the excursion in question were very interesting and numerous. Read my zoological commentaries" by Péron?)
During the morning we hoisted in two of our boats and everything was made ready to depart tomorrow, if the winds are favourable to us.
The breeze was very strong during the day and I was astonished to see the ship hold so fast on her anchor. It is true that we then had seventy fathoms of cable out.
At sunset, the boat which had taken the naturalists and our hunters ashore returned on board. The former brought back several new plants and the latter some birds we had not yet seen, two live short-tailed opossums, three dead, and two kangaroo rats which appeared to us different from those we knew, at least in the colour of their fur.
The boat was hoisted in at once and the ship made ready to get under sail the following day.
Departure from the Baie des Saints
1803-02-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 10 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course to pass north of Réunion, which was sighted during the night.

1803-02-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, smooth sea. At 4 took the bearing of Morne Brabant south 30° east, estimated distance 19 miles. We rounded Réunion by the north, which brought us calms. Longitude and latitude from the bearing: 21° 8'; long. 52° 35' 0".
1803-02-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
(end of page 359) at the very moment when the ship, which was making six knots, was about to run onto it. We were fortunate enough to avoid it by bracing up as sharply as possible close-hauled; I do not believe we passed it at more than half musket-shot, and from the western extremity of the reef of which I have just spoken, at a mile and a half at most.
At these islands we ended our bearings of the south and south-west coast of New Holland, and I have no doubt that the chart we shall give of it, joined to that published of d'Entrecasteaux's voyage, will give an exact knowledge of this whole part so long unknown to Europeans.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, the winds being south-east by east, a strong breeze, we made our dispositions to get under way. As we had seventy fathoms of cable out, we had a good deal of trouble in heaving short, the moment at which I expected to start dragging, if indeed that did not happen sooner. But I was disappointed in my expectation, for it was a long time before we could break out the anchor.
As soon as it was catted, we made sail on the topsails, two reefs taken in, and the foresail. I reckoned on being able easily to range along the west coast of the bay from which we were coming out, but scarcely had we made a mile and a half in approaching it than the bottom, which before had been eight fathoms, fell suddenly to five, which obliged us to stand a little further out until we were clear of the points which form its entrance. Having then no bottom at ten fathoms, we followed the mainland closely, tracing all its windings. The land, in this part, is all sandy and dune-like, most often without the least vegetation. What was a little shaded was covered only by a few shrubs of little height.
In coasting along, we left to the south the northern part of the St François islands and the reefs of rock which are found at their extremities or in the channels which separate them from one another.
At noon the latitude observed was 32° 2' 56" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 130° 21' 13". This latitude placed us (no figures) minutes to the north of our anchorage in the Baie des Saints.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze, and we took advantage of it to push our bearings as far forward as possible in order to finish the 129th degree of longitude before night, if possible. In continuing along the mainland coast, which in this last part is fairly elevated on the second range of mountains seen in the interior of the country, we sighted several islands lying fairly close to the coast, which are nothing other than rocks isolated from one another, on which the sea breaks strongly. At each extremity of the points or capes that we rounded, the sea was so hollow and the swell so high that it made the ship yaw off 20 to 25 degrees. And I believe it would be very difficult to work up from this coast were it necessary to beat to windward with winds from the south-west to the south-east. We attributed the effect of this great swell to the currents, there being no bottom at 25 fathoms.
At five o'clock we sighted four islets and a great reef lying in the direction of our course. We continued to steer for them to examine them, and we soon saw that (in the margin: it was those) which we had already sighted when we sought, before this last occasion, to make out the mainland to the north of the St Pierre and St François islands, coming from the west. The four islets and the reef which lies a little to the west of them are not good to frequent, although we passed very close to them. It very nearly happened that the sun, so beneficial and so useful to navigation, became the cause of our loss, in that it hid from us the sight of a small flat rock awash of which we had knowledge (continued, previous page 358)

1803-02-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm, a swell running. Clewed up the courses and lay under topsails. At noon went onto the port tack. Est. lat. 22° 1' 42", long. 51° 33' 24".
1803-02-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, having steered, during the night, to the south-west to draw away from the coast, my intention being to reach King George's port as soon as possible without examining the islands of the Archipelago of the Recherche. We continued in the morning to steer south 32° 30' west, until noon, when we took that of south-west. It seemed to me that this course was useful for the safety of the navigation, since it should enable us to make certain whether there did not exist some islets or reef among those made known by General d'Entrecasteaux.
We had, all day, a good breeze from the east and fine weather, but we found the sea strongly swollen and agitated. All morning a very great quantity of birds of the petrel and albatross kind were seen. They disappeared in the evening.
At noon the latitude was observed at 33° 52' 12" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 put us at 128° 37' 5".
During the evening the weather continued fine and the winds varied from east-south-east to south-east. When I consider the winds we have met since our departure from King Island, I truly find it hard to understand how the English could have persuaded themselves that only strong westerly and south-westerly winds are met with on the course I had to make. This opinion, which I was far from sharing, citing to them the winds I had met the year before, could not draw them out of the error in which they are, and I do not know on what authority, since none of their ships leaving Port Jackson for Europe will for a long time yet prefer the route by Cape Horn to that of Bass Strait, which is without question the better in this season.
During the night the weather continued fine and we had a pleasant breeze from the east-south-east, with the help of which we made good progress to the west, drawing a little to the south.

1803-02-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, the winds from SE to east, a fresh breeze. Shifted the mizzen topsail tie. Est. lat. 24° 12' 54", est. long. 49° 39' 24".
1803-02-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, the winds continued very favourable to us and we took advantage of it. We had, as on the previous day, a good breeze from the east to east-south-east, and the sea still swollen. In the morning we passed through a fairly considerable tide-race which came upon us from the south-west and lasted nearly half an hour. The noise made by the waves striking against one another closely resembled the noise made by waves rolling on a sandy beach.
In the morning, the work on our boats, on which the gunwales had to be changed, was finished.
At noon the latitude was observed at 34° 9' 31" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 134° 58' 23" (124° 58' 5" on the page of astronomical observations, which corresponds better to the course followed to the west.)
The weather continued fine in the evening and we brought the course to less southing, but at sunset the sky had a very bad appearance. The whole horizon became covered with thick clouds and the barometer fell a great deal. There was every appearance of bad weather for the night; nevertheless, we did not shorten sail, so as to take advantage of the good wind for as long as it should last.
After sunset the sky was very dark and the night very obscure. We saw several storms forming in the north-east, from which came much lightning, but the sound of the thunder did not reach us. There were only, at times, a few squalls of little duration and consequence. The winds, which towards the end of the day had settled in the east, varied little from it, and we had only disagreeable weather, for which we were amply compensated by the good progress we made, which brought us swiftly nearer to the islands of the Archipelago of the Recherche.
We lost this day one of the kangaroos taken on Opossum Island in the Baie des Saints. Its death was the result of the wounds it had received from the dogs, in addition to a shot of small shot. This species, as I have already observed, is much the same as those of Shark Bay in size, and differs only in the colour of the fur, which is redder.

1803-02-14.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from NE to ENE. Shifted the [one word illegible] of the main brace, and one of the fore topsail tie blocks. Obs. lat. 26° 11' 46", est. long. 47° 51' 24".
1803-02-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, we (sic) in the morning, we had the winds in the east, variable towards the north, and the breeze slackened a little. The sky was constantly overcast, dark and hazy, so that we did not see the sun the whole day. We steered west to gain as soon as possible the longitude of King George's port, so as to make the south-west winds favourable to us, should they come to declare themselves, as there was appearance of by the state of the atmosphere and the movement of the barometer.
According to our dead reckoning, we found ourselves at noon at the latitude of 35° 47' 55" and our longitude was 121° 41' 5".
During the evening the weather was the same as we had had in the morning, but the winds came back from the east towards the south, and were extremely variable. We continued to steer west until eight o'clock in the evening, when we steered west by south-west, during the night, so as not to make any northing.
As I reckoned myself to be in the vicinity of the Archipelago of the Recherche, I had the lead cast at midnight to learn whether the bottom extended far to the south of these islands. We did not find it at 120 fathoms straight down. No change was made to the sail, and we kept under way the whole night, which had a very bad appearance without, however, bringing any change in the weather, but much inconstancy in the winds, which did nothing but shift between east and south. We saw during the night several storms forming in the north-east, which produced much lightning for us, and the thunder was heard rumbling in the distance only twice. A few squalls that we had gave us more rain than wind and were not of long duration. The haze alone accompanied us constantly.

1803-02-15.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, continual rain. At 2 the fore topgallant sheet having parted, the sail was furled. Est. lat. 28° 25' 46", est. long. 44° 56' 24".
1803-02-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-sixth, in the morning, despite the little appearance of fair weather for the day, we endeavoured to close with the coast by steering west-north-west, with winds from east-south-east which, in the morning, varied to south-south-west, a fresh breeze. The heavy swell which had accompanied us for so long had begun to disappear and the sea had become smooth.
In the morning, the wind having much abated and shifted to south-south-west, we feared we should soon have them from that quarter and accompanied by some squalls, the barometer having fallen below 28 inches.
By our dead reckoning, we made ourselves at noon at 35° 58' 0" south latitude and the estimated longitude placed us at 119° 8' 5". This position laid down upon the chart, placing us approximately sixty leagues to the west-north-west of King George's Sound, we steered north-west by west in the evening and continued on this course until eight o'clock in the evening, when, seeing no appearance of change in the weather, we took that of west by south-west for the night, although we had found no bottom at eight o'clock by 120 fathoms.
During the day, we saw a considerable number of brown albatrosses and several species of petrels amongst which were found several of those that sailors have named storm-petrels. But as the barometer was beginning to rise, their appearance was not for us a bad omen.
The night had nothing particular save a thick and continuous mist which, however, began to disperse after moonrise. The sky, nevertheless, remained very overcast and our horizon was not more than half a league in extent. We sounded twice during the night without finding bottom at 120 fathoms.
Following various remarks I made during the day on the surface of the sea which was smooth, I thought I could perceive that the direction of the current set toward the south inasmuch as the ridges that formed on the surface of the sea-waves came constantly from the north, a direction altogether opposed to the winds which we had during the day.

1803-02-16.journal_anonyme: Rainy and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE which shifted to WSW. Went onto the starboard tack; at 3.30 a.m. it shifted to NW. Obs. lat. 29° 39' 4", est. long. 44° 19' 36".
1803-02-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
The twenty-seventh, we continued to make our way west, steering north so as to close with the coast to windward of the anchorage of King George's Sound. We had in this day the same weather as the days before, that is to say a fresh breeze from the south variable sometimes towards the east. The sea, always driven by a strong swell from south to south-west, announced to us that we should not be long before having winds from that quarter, which made it desirable to gain the anchorage I wished to occupy as soon as possible.
At noon, we had no observation of latitude and that of the dead reckoning to which we had, for a long time, been obliged to rely placed us at (no figures) and the longitude was (no figures).
It had rarely happened to us to have been so long without being able to observe the passage of the sun at the meridian, and we greatly regretted that this disadvantage should come upon us at a time when we had the greatest need of it.
However, we continued our course and at two o'clock, we had a view of a very elevated coast on which could be distinguished different mountain peaks which, at the distance at which we found ourselves, appeared to form several islands. After having closed with the coast so as to see it well, we recognised that the nearest land to us which then lay to the north (in the margin in N. B.'s writing: 5° to the east) was the island which General d'Entrecasteaux named the Pelée Island. Mount Gardener of Vancouver lay north 56° west. As it was then too late to be able to enter the port before nightfall, we took as close to the wind as we could on the south-west tack, but their inconstancy obliged us, shortly after, to take that of the east.
During the night, the winds were light and variable, and often indeed we had calm accompanied by mist and rain without any appearance of bad weather although the barometer had much fallen and did not appear to be inclined to rise. In order not to be carried too far to the east, we lay to for some time, the main topsail set on the mast.

1803-02-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a little rain. Lowered the main topsail on the cap to refit its sheet, which had parted. Est. lat. 29° 48' 34", est. long. 43° 37' 36".
1803-02-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At two o'clock,
we obtained sight of the land and at sunset after having closed with it, Mount Gardener remained to us at north 56° west
And Pelée Island at north a quarter east
The 28th at noon, the entrance of the port was at north 85° west
And we moored to anchor in the bay by 17 fathoms of water, sandy and muddy bottom.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-eighth, in the morning, we found ourselves to have been more to the east than our dead reckoning made us, which obliged us to close with the land again which we then coasted at a small distance. After having doubled the western part of Pelée Island, and well recognised the channel which separates it from the mainland, we saw, between its distance from Mount Gardener, several inlets which seemed to announce that there might be some good shelters there. I did not go to visit them with the ship but I took the resolution to have them examined in detail by one of my boats as soon as we should be in a place of safety. I also had the officer to whom I destined this task observe the places which seemed to me to merit preference over the others. And we continued our course.
During the morning, the breeze was sometimes very light and despite our small distance from the anchorage, we feared more than once not to reach it before nightfall. However, the wind having somewhat increased, at sunset we made our way there, passing between the Seal Island and the mainland in order to moor abreast of the cove in which is found the water source of which Vancouver speaks. At eight o'clock, estimating ourselves to be opposite it, we let drop a sheet anchor by seventeen fathoms muddy sandy bottom and we immediately took a second anchor, the weather not having a good appearance. We also unrigged the topgallant sails for the night, and everything was arranged for the greatest safety of the ship.
During the night, we had calm and the sky very overcast and misty.
Stay in King George's Bay.

1803-02-18.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SW to south. The sea rather high. The weather overcast. On the morning of the 29th the mizzen shrouds were set up.
1803-02-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Twenty-Ninth (18 February 1803), at daybreak, we sent our boats to sea. One was, straightway, to recognise the water source, and the other occupied in establishing our observatory which was placed on an island rather pleasant which lay to us at north-west by north of the ship.
The boat for the water source being returned, I was informed that it was very good and easy to procure. We found there ten barrels belonging to the Casuarina which we knew should be in one of the two ports and which had informed us that it had arrived before us by a flag placed on the summit of the Seal Island. We had announced our arrival to it the previous day by a cannon shot fired in the night and to which it had replied with several rockets which had informed us that it was in Princess Charlotte Harbour.
About eight o'clock, we obtained sight of the boat of that ship and shortly after, arrived Citizen Freycinet who commands it. Having asked him why he had not closed with me when we met on Île Borda, he replied that he had not been able to join me and that besides I should wait for him. I then represented to him the poor manoeuvre which he had made and which sailors will be able to judge, but he remained nonetheless convinced that his had been better than ours and that it was the only one that had caused the separation of which I complained. As I had indicated to him the Isles Saint Peter and Saint Francis,
as first rendezvous, I asked him again whether it was by my fault that he had not gone there, he replied equally that yes, inasmuch as they were not found at the latitude and longitude which I had indicated to him. Despite that we came to seek them precisely at the same place, he objected to me moreover that having very little water, he had believed it more prudent to come to this port than to continue to seek me with the uncertainty of knowing whether he would meet me. Finally, he ended by telling me that his ship having need of several repairs, he needed caulkers and carpenters and that he had run aground on the sand to make these works easier.
The details which Citizen Freycinet had just given me were not proper to excuse his conduct and to show him how little I was satisfied with it, I said to him as sole answer that I was going to send to his ship a caulker and a carpenter, and that he could dispose of them as he saw fit. Immediately after, I embarked in my boat and came myself to visit the water source to ascertain whether it was as easy and convenient as had been announced. After having examined it, I found it indeed to be so and straightway I had our tents established there, of which one was destined for the sick that we had then to the number of four and the other for the naturalists.
I also had a large reservoir made for the washing of the crew's clothing and hammocks, wishing to take advantage of this opportunity to have them washed.
About noon, we had a strong squall from the west to west-south-west which obliged us to let out our mooring cable. Nevertheless, we were set adrift twice by the force of the wind and obliged by precaution for the night to prepare our main anchor which was put in moorings. The sky had such a bad appearance and the mountains were so laden with vapours that there was every appearance that we were going to receive some squalls. The barometer which was below 28 announced them also. And they were not long in arriving for in the night, rain, hail and wind distressed us in every way. At eight o'clock in the evening, we moored the main anchor and the ship held fast at her post. We had also struck down the topgallant masts.

1803-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running and a fresh breeze. At 3.30 the fore topgallant brace having parted at the masthead, we took in the studdingsail and clewed up the topgallant sail to repair the damage. Est. lat. 30° 14' 28", est. long. 38° 34' 42".
1803-02-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
The thirtieth (19 February 1803), the weather was less bad than the previous day without that, on that account, the sky had cleared. The winds varied from west-south-west to west and north-west. As the boats could come and go, we transported ashore our empty barrels which were to serve to make our water. We constructed a kind of conduit which by the means of our sounding pipes was to conduct the water as far as our boat barrels without the trouble of unloading them which would have been very convenient for us. But the pipes were found so little suitable that we had to return to the ordinary way in that they lost all the water before it reached the boat. We made in this day only one trip which procured us only twenty-eight barrels.
In the morning, we raised the anchor of the evening moored at the beginning of the night of the 29th to the 30th and it was prepared to be again in case of need. As the flukes which had taken the bottom were found laden with a large quantity of muddy sand, we recognised perfectly the quality of the bottom which was found, according to our opinion, too soft for the hold to be very good, despite that the anchors should penetrate well into it to render it solid.
In the afternoon, the weather seemed to want to turn fair and although strong squalls passed frequently, the heavy dark clouds had disappeared.
The night had nothing particular, it was interspersed with wind, squalls and calm.

1803-02-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from the east; at noon almost calm. Obs. lat. 31° 22' 57", est. long. 36° 2' 12".
1803-02-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the First Ventôse (20 February 1803). The first of Ventôse, I despatched two boats, one for six days' absence and the other for ten. That to which I gave the command to Citizen Ransonnet, with ten days' provisions, was to visit the part of the coast which lies between Mount Gardener of Vancouver and Pelée Island of d'Entrecasteaux. Citizen Ransonnet was bearer of the order and instructions as follows:
"I confide to you, Citizen, the command of my large boat to explore the part of coast comprised between Mount Gardener of Vancouver and Pelée Island of d'Entrecasteaux. It seemed to me that it was all the more useful to know it in detail in that it presents to view different sinuosities which can present resources or shelter against bad weather to navigators who, later, may frequent these waters.
"General d'Entrecasteaux and Vancouver saw only from afar the coast which you are going to visit closely and with scrupulous attention. You will penetrate into all the inlets which are found there and examine each of them in detail. If, as I am inclined to believe, you meet with some port there, you will make a plan of it, take soundings and determine with the greatest exactitude that will be possible for you, the points which form its entrances.
"As you have only eight or ten leagues of coast to explore, eight or ten days should be more than sufficient for this work. This is why you must be back at that time. You shall make no course to the east of the eastern point of Pelée Island and you shall confine yourself to the reconnaissance of the inlet which is found to its north.
"Have the greatest attention to the preservation of your boat and avoid with prudence all occasions that could compromise its safety". Greetings, Signed N. B.
In the second boat where I placed the midshipman of the Navy Baudin, I gave him for instruction the following:
"You are going to take, Citizen, the command of the large boat of the tender in which the geographer Faure must embark. You will make the entire tour of the bay and of the two ports in which we find ourselves, beginning with that which is to the north-west of our moorings as far as Mount Gardener. Citizen Faure being charged with making the plans of them, you will conduct him to the places which he may indicate to you or which shall appear to merit particular attention. You will not forget to take soundings of all the places where you pass and especially of the entrances of each port. It should be found in that which bears the name of Oyster Harbour, a bar on which there is only three fathoms of water, you will verify whether these data are correct or not.
"Have the greatest attention to the preservation of your boat and avoid with care, everything which could compromise its safety. You shall not delay aboard the Casuarina run aground in Princess Charlotte Harbour in order not to waste your time in unnecessary visits. Your boat will be provided with six days' provisions, but you will return, if it is possible before having consumed them, for I do not think that the work of Citizen Faure should require so much time".
After having despatched the two boats of which I have just spoken, it was ordered, to half of the crew, to send their clothing and hammocks ashore to be washed in the reservoirs which I had had made for this use. Four men of the crew were specially charged with this work. In the evening, we began the embarking of our water and we put aboard 25 barrels. The small boat which was sent to fish on Vancouver's Marine Cattle Island brought back only eight or ten fish of the parrot species for form, but very good to eat. No sea cattle were found there, which leads me to believe that they have a particular season in the year during which they frequent these waters.
During the night, the weather was tolerably fine and the breeze light and variable from south-west toward east.

1803-02-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the breeze light from ENE. Obs. lat. 31° 59' 20", est. long. 33° 40' 54".
1803-02-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 2nd Ventôse (21 February 1803). The second, the weather being fair, I left the ship at five o'clock and a half in the morning, in order to see for myself the harbours of Princess Charlotte and of Oysters. I made use, to make this visit, of my private boat which can contain only five men including him who steers it which (allowed) me to be myself its conductor.
Upon leaving the ship, I gave order to the officer who was on guard to raise our north-west anchor which had dragged in the squall which we had received the day after our arrival and to lay it again again (sic) in this direction of wind.
I went first to the island on which our observatory is placed and visited Citizen Bernier. This island bears no name in the plan of Vancouver although it is pleasant and better wooded than the others. After having spent two hours with Citizen Bernier, I went to Princess Charlotte Harbour following the edges of the coast. The entrance of this port which can have a mile of opening, is convenient and easy, but for a ship like ours, one would need to have the wind across the yardarm, the tacking being hardly practicable in the passage. One should, by preference, range the port side of the entrance, that of starboard having much less water.
Within this port, I perceived the Casuarina run aground at the bottom and I went aboard. This ship was completely in disorder and singularly unclean. The Captain who commands it replied to me that it was a necessary consequence of the situation in which he found himself. Most of the sailors were hunting or fishing. I remained only half an hour aboard this ship and gave order to Citizen Freycinet to come to the anchorage which I occupied in two days so that I would have put aboard him, the water and (the) wood of which he had need.
Princess Charlotte Harbour seemed to me convenient and offering a good place of shelter for ships which, beaten by the tempest, would have need of urgent repairs, but the water although it does not lack there, is less good and less easy to procure than in the place where we are. Neither is found anywhere in the whole circuit of the harbour, but two or three places where there are some clumps of trees fit to be used for ships of a certain size. The transport becomes difficult by the extent of the bank which forms the circuit of the bay and which uncovers in the high tides approximately one mile and a half offshore. The Casuarina, at this distance, had not more than one foot of water at low tide.
After having examined this harbour I went to that of Oysters, continuing to follow the coast which, on the outside, is of a much more agreeable aspect than all those I had seen until then. The great beach of sand which closes the inlet of the bay, is formed by low and sandy land. But in the interior, the mountains are elevated and well wooded with large trees to judge by view. Arrived at the entrance of the harbour formed to the north by a sandy point advanced and to the south by rather high lands, we steered into the middle of the channel to sound it and found the bottom between twelve and thirteen feet at low tide, so that I do not think there should be found more than fourteen or fifteen at high tide.
The port offers to view, a convenient and well-closed place, but we were not long in perceiving that it did not lack banks and that to frequent it, one must know them well. After having run aground two or three times and refloated ourselves, we came to land in the place where our large boat was and where was Citizen Faure whom I had charged with a more detailed reconnaissance than the one which I was making myself.
As it was beginning to be late when I arrived, we spent the rest of the day and the night in that place having only care to keep our boats afloat during the night in order to be able, the next day, to make the tour of the harbour and to visit all its parts. The large boat which had visited the island which Vancouver named the Island of the Garden, were much astonished not to find any of the seeds which he had deposited and only two or three bushes of greenery. The rest of the island which is not very considerable, was covered with a kind of very fine grass of yellowish colour. It appears that this quantity of grass will have hindered the reproduction of the seeds which he had deposited or more likely still that the large quantity of ants which were found there will have destroyed them as they came up.
Before sunset, we went up a rather elevated mountain from which we saw perfectly the interior of the country and all the lakes which are found there. Their positions will be placed on the particular plan which we shall give of this harbour.
A little before sunset, we saw at two different times, some of the natives who, the moment they perceived us although at a great distance, took to flight and (took) refuge in the woods. From the mountains where we were, we had seen very thick smoke, but at too great a distance to think of going there.

1803-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. From midnight to 4 stormy and squally weather, the sky overcast in the west with much lightning in the NW. The winds at 5 having shifted to NW, we trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack and made all sail. At 9.30 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Est. lat. 32° 36' 2", est. long. 31° 16' 54".
1803-02-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 3rd Ventôse (22 February 1803). The third, from five o'clock in the morning, we made our arrangements to go to visit the bottom of the port and to recognise the oyster banks of which Vancouver speaks. As the sea was low and we found ourselves in the tides of the new moon, we saw all the banks with which this harbour is filled and which (led) me to say to say (sic) that it is little suited for ships even of medium size. The main channel contains from six to seven fathoms of water but it has very little extent and if the force of the winds which sometimes blow in squalls and with violence especially when they are from south-west to north-west, should make it drift on its anchors, it would evidently run aground on the extremity of the banks which form it. It is true that it would not cause damage, the bottom being of sand and grass. But the hull would be no less fatigued in that it would only run aground partially. The other channels which divide the banks have only the water which is necessary for a boat, and still it is often found run aground as this happened several times to our large boat, and to mine, which drew half as much water.
At last, we reached the inlet of the harbour and we kept abreast of a bank where we took a considerable number of oysters lodged on a grassy bottom at one and a half and two feet of water. They were found of a good taste and very large. While the sailors occupied themselves with this fishery which lasted three-quarters of an hour, citizens Faure and Bailly were put ashore to visit two lagoons which we had recognised from the elevation on which we had climbed the previous day. And we made our way to an opening which had all the appearance of a river and the passage of which we sought for a long time among the banks. Before finding it, the large boat ran aground several times, which gave me a considerable advance over it, and after several turnings, I succeeded in meeting a channel where I found first, two fathoms of water and then, eight feet. This channel led me to a river of salt water or rather to an arm of the sea which advances deeply into the country making an infinity of sinuosities in different directions.
At the first point which forms its entrance, I met citizens Faure and Bailly whom I embarked notwithstanding the little space I had in my boat. And we went up together, the arm of the sea in which we found ourselves. The lagoons which they had visited, contain only salt water which the high sea introduces there by different small streams which run out to the sea. At one o'clock in the afternoon, having gone approximately one league and a half by water into the interior of the country, we stopped to dine opposite a small stream which communicated with the river and in which we judged there should be fresh water. Having landed, we went to visit it and found indeed, a small quantity which although not very pleasant to the taste, seemed very good to us in that we were in want of it.
In visiting the environs of the stream of which I have just spoken, we found two rather particular and interesting monuments, raised by the natives of the country, if one (could not) know the motive. The first was placed seven or eight feet from the stream in a place devoid of grass having three feet in circumference and surrounded by well-pointed spears painted red on the side of the point. There were, in all, eleven. Parallel to this trophy, on the other side of the stream, was found a similar one for the form and number of spears, but they seemed to defend the passage of the left bank to the right, as those of the left seemed to defend it to those of the right. Several people having thought that these spears had been painted red with blood, we took one to examine it more closely and we recognised that this colour had been given to them with resin of the eucalyptus.
Each endeavoured to guess what these monuments could be and we reasoned about them (in) various ways. According to my opinion, I think that these are two tombs in which rest two warriors of different tribes who have been placed there either after a particular combat between them or as a result of a more general action and which still seem to mistrust each other after death. I would not permit that one should disturb these tombs nor that one should take away the spears which form their ornament, in order that if any European arrives in these places, he might draw the conclusions which his imagination might suggest to him, but I placed on each of them two medals and some glass beads. Maize was also sown in the environs and some other gardening seeds.
Immediately after our dinner, we re-embarked to continue to go up the river in which I intended to penetrate fairly far to find fresh water. But, scarcely had we gone a mile further on, than we found little water and the passage closed by dams made in the manner of locks by the natives of the country. These dams were closed, at the extremities of the river, in the middle of which was found an island by natural rocks depending on each bank. But in the places where none were found and hollowed by the currents, the natives had introduced stones which arranged with art and symmetry one beside the other, give proof that they are not without intelligence. Until this time we had not found less than six feet of water and it was with much regret that we found ourselves stopped in the middle of our course. Citizens Faure and Bailly having been put ashore to observe (the) further course of the river, reported that it appeared obstructed only in the place where we (ourselves) found ourselves, and that, beyond the two dams which we had in view, it seemed as deep and navigable as we had found it until then. Upon this, arrived the large boat which, after having refloated itself, had followed us from afar. I decided, by means of this help, to have my boat transported over the dams and this operation was done much more easily than I had thought. When it had passed, we re-embarked anew and went up still another three-quarters of a mile, when six new dams and all more elevated one above the other above the water, closed entirely the passages to us and obliged us to turn back. The water was always salt and the current had half a knot of speed. We went ashore in discovery as the first time, and we still saw nothing that closed the river on the other side of these dams, but as the circuits which it makes are very numerous, the view did not extend far.
We remarked that the latest were still made with more intelligence than the first. Several could be distinguished of which the widest opening was on the side of the rising tide and that of the falling tide was so narrowed that it appeared quite difficult that the fish which the sea had been able easily to make enter would get out (an illegible word)
Obliged to turn back, we transported our boat anew over the dams which we had made it cross and thought of our return, the night beginning to approach.
The banks of the extent of river which we travelled are very agreeable to the eye. The land is high and well supplied with large trees. I collected different species of seeds and some plants in flower which are not known to me. We saw everywhere traces of fires and signs that the natives frequent these waters from time to time. But in the places where they had assembled easy to know by the places where they had established their fires, we found not the slightest sign of what had been able to serve their nourishment.
We collected several of their spears which were found against the trees as if they had been put in reserve. These instruments of war were crudely made and far less well proportioned than at Port Jackson. We saw, at the foot of a high mountain range whose direction extends from north to south in the interior of the country, many fires separated one from the other which made us think that the natives were, for that moment, in the environs, but they were too far from us to think of making our way there by crossing an unknown country and destitute of provisions. We gave up visiting them.
At sunset, after having descended the river by the same way which we had gone until the place where we could penetrate. We came to pass the night inside the port which we could not reach until about ten o'clock in the evening, after having run aground several times. The large boat to which the same thing happened, did not join us until the middle of the night and with considerable difficulty.
From what I have seen in the course which I have just made, I believe I can say that Oyster Harbour can hardly be frequented except by small ships. It is not worth at all, that of Princess Charlotte although the view of it be much more agreeable. We saw in the lagoons and in the bottom of the port only a few ducks, some teals, some cormorants and some gulls, but all these birds were so wild that one could only approach them at very great distances. We perceived not a single black swan.
During our stay, the boats took fish in abundance and very good. So we did well with it. The sea dogs which are abundant, caused us to lose many lines and hooks. The land birds are not common. I shot only a teal of a new species and a pigeon with golden wings.
The sand banks of Oyster Bay which uncover are filled with worm tubes which must be very harmful to ships that are not sheathed with copper. Whole shells are very rare there notwithstanding that many broken ones are found on the shore. We collected very few even so, of the genus of clams.
No. 5
From the Fourth Ventôse Year Ten until the
Seventeenth Thermidor of the same year
(reproduce the first page of the volume)
Continuation of our stay in King George's port.

1803-02-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A strong breeze. At 4.30 the main jib halliard block having broken, the sail was hauled down; set up the fore topgallant stay, shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 32° 54' 33", est. long. 29° 3' 24".
1803-02-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fourth Ventôse, at daybreak, I made my arrangements to return aboard and left to Citizen Faure the entire reconnaissance of the port and of the coast which terminates at Mount Gardener. From five o'clock in the morning, I set out. As I intended to stop at the observatory to be informed of the results of the eclipse of the sun which took place the third for us, a little before sunrise I was much astonished not to find Citizen Bernier established in the place where I had had his tent set up. But having obtained knowledge of him on the mainland opposite to the island where he was in the beginning, I went there and was informed that fire having broken out in the environs, he had been obliged to move away hastily and that he considered himself very fortunate that the instruments and the tent had not been attacked by it, in that, in less than a quarter of an hour, the greater part of the island had been set ablaze by the fire. This fire was occasioned by the fire of the kitchen which was being made in the environs.
The end of the eclipse of the sun was not visible for us, the sun having shown itself only about eight o'clock in the morning.
Citizen Bernier gave me notice of the arrival of the American brig on the anchorage. The very day that I departed from the ship, I had indeed obtained sight of this vessel but I thought it was the Casuarina and paid it little attention.
I spent part of the day with Citizen Bernier and visited the environs where I encountered some rather pretty plants.
In the afternoon the American Captain having been informed by his men that I was at this tent, came to see me. He informed me that he had departed from New York at the end of last month of September and that he was sent on a sealing voyage which, until that moment, had not been lucky for him in that he had been able to procure in the different places where he had landed only three or four hundred skins and that he had twenty thousand to collect before thinking of making his way to China. He had decided to come to this port on the information given by Vancouver who, in the season when he was there, saw many. As this vessel came from the east, he told me he had spoken to the boat commanded by Citizen Ransonnet whom I had, as I have already said, sent to recognise the part of coast comprised between Mount Gardener and Pelée Island.
I invited the Captain to dinner for the next day and after we had parted, I went aboard.
Nothing particular had happened during my absence, the water was so found that I was only waiting for the return
of the Casuarina and of Citizen Ransonnet to fix the day of my departure
The weather, although with squalls, followed by some gusts, during the night, had been generally fair without the ship having shifted.
According to the report of the physician, the sick who had been put ashore to the number of four, were much better.

1803-02-24.journal_anonyme: Obs. lat. 34° 6' 48", est. long. 25°. Fine weather, a light breeze, the sea smooth, the sky cloudy. At daybreak sighted land stretching from N 33° W to N 22° E. Noon bearings: the easternmost end of the land NE by N; the westernmost end WNW 5° W; the nearest land N by NW, distant 12 miles.
1803-02-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fifth (24 February 1803) The fifth, the Casuarina finally left the port of Princess Charlotte and came to anchor opposite the water source where we were making her water and ours. I sent a boat to her side in order to know whether she was ready (to) receive her water and Citizen Freycinet coming by the same boat aboard, informed me informed me (sic) that he also lacked wood and that he had not made any in Princess Charlotte Harbour despite that he had been there nearly fifteen days wandering about and doing nothing. But it is more probable that he did not know the quantity that had been made for him since according to the report that the carpenter who I had sent to work aboard made to me, his hold in which there were only three or four barrels, was so full that in order to make a place where the crew could lodge, at night, it was necessary to put a considerable quantity upon the deck.
Be that as it may, we agreed that I would have some cut for him ashore opposite the water source although he claimed he had none. But as I had seen it myself, I knew what to believe.
This officer remained complaisingly aboard until eight o'clock in the evening when it was necessary that one of my boats (be sent to sea) to conduct him aboard and to return.
The American Captain whom I had invited to dinner came aboard about two o'clock in the afternoon. Before sitting down to table, he asked me to give him, if it was possible, a chart of the coast of New Holland, having no information that could guide him in the routes which he was going to make for the search of the places which seals frequent nor for the direction of the coast or of the dangers which are found there. I gave him two of the charts of Citizen Beautemps Beaupré and one of the straits of Bass and Banks by Citizen Flinders, as well as particular observations on the entrance of Ports Phillip and Bass and on the position of King Island. I recommended to him very particularly, if he put into port at Île Borda, to prevent his men from shooting the pigs and the pigs (sic) and poultry which I had deposited on this island for the future utility of navigators who will frequent it. He promised me that no (harm) would be done to them if he landed in this part of which I indicated to him the best anchorage as well as the place where he could find a considerable number of seals. After dinner, he withdrew to his ship for the preparations for his departure as soon as the return of his boats which were fishing.
During the night of the fifth to the sixth, the weather was very bad. The winds varied from west to south-west with very strong gusts accompanied by much rain and almost continual. It was only toward the end of the night that the squalls ceased which, surely, would have set us adrift if they had continued longer.
1803-02-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak the land of Natal was sighted to the north; it was in sight all day.

1803-02-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from the east, the course west. Obs. lat. 35° 46' 22", est. long. 21° 5' 30".
1803-02-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Sixth Pluviôse (sic) (25 February 1803). The sixth, the weather being tolerably fair, I had the cutter armed to take aboard the Casuarina, the water and the wood which I had had cut the previous day. To hasten this work, I embarked myself in the cutter and undertook a task which would have much displeased my officers if I had charged them with it.
The wind having considerably increased when we were offshore of the ship, we were set adrift. The cutter not having enough ballast, we nearly filled twice or three times and we were obliged to gain the shore much to leeward in order to empty the water and unship our mast in order to reach the water source by oars. We were unable to arrive there before one o'clock in the afternoon, although we had departed at seven o'clock in the morning.
As Citizen Freycinet had been warned by me, from the previous day, of the work which he had to do during this day, I had presumed that he would be found ashore to hasten it, all the more as I had seen his boat go there several times, but I was informed that he could not come, having that day a grand dinner and great company. This conduct made me angry and I remained, the whole day, charged with the task and with the supervision of the crew of the cutter. Seven men of the Casuarina who had been put ashore, from the morning, without anyone to lead them, had decamped into the mountains or to fishing so that they appeared only at night, and that the cutter was unable to complete, in the evening, the work which there was, being obliged to employ everyone in going to cut and fetch, at the foot of the slope, the wood which had been cut there. I bore not without grumbling all these inconveniences and I returned aboard at night in my boat having given order to the crew of the cutter to sleep ashore in order to be better prepared to do what remained for the next day.
Upon my arrival at the tents, I found there only Citizen Guichenot, always occupied with his plants and his collections. I was informed that Citizen Leschenault, botanist, had gone to visit Citizen Bernier and that the second surgeon and Citizen the Observer of Mankind, Péron, had gone to dinner aboard the Casuarina. In the evening, the one and the other returned but Citizen Freycinet did not appear and he did well for I was disposed to give him a good scolding to teach him his duty and not to waste his time in pleasure when one has pressing work.
According to the report of the gardener, he had collected during his stay
ashore, more than one hundred and fifty different species of plants and completed sixty and eight pots of living ones. This was work and not wit.
I hope that citizens Péron and Leschenault will have composed sixty pages of writing which, by a contrary reason, will be wit and not work.
Upon my return aboard which arrived very opportunely, the winds from south-west took up again and gave us squalls and rain which lasted all the night.

1803-02-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds falling away gradually. At 2 the winds shifted to NW; trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 2 went about onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 35° 30' 59", est. long. 19° 50' 48".
1803-02-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventh (26 February 1803). The seventh, the boats were employed, from daybreak, in transporting both to the observatory and to the tents of the scholars, the provisions which had been lacking for them for two days, according to the reports which they made to me. Aboard, I was assured the contrary so that it is difficult to know who is right or wrong. Be that as it may, as I had seen myself that they were lacking in everything, I had given them what was necessary.
About ten o'clock, the Lieutenant of the Ship Freycinet came to ask me for a boat to go ashore. I gave it to him as well as to the surgeon Laridon who was of the party. But I was much astonished to see it directed to aboard the Casuarina where it remained until noon and having taken aboard the Captain, it went to shore. I learned afterwards that the land was returning, that day, the banquet of the previous day, and without knowing in advance I would have contributed myself to make it brilliant by some delicacies which I had sent to the scholars in the boat which departed in the morning.
The cutter which had taken the wood and made water for the Casuarina brought us from aboard only two empty barrels for the replacements in provisions which were asked of me, so that it will be necessary to waste another day to go fetch the others in supposing, however, that they have not been thrown overboard or consumed in another manner, which would be very disagreeable, having none aboard, neither barrel nor cask which could replace it.
A boat which was sent fishing on Black Head point, returned at sunset with very fine fish and in quantity sufficient for two meals for the whole crew. There were many large snappers of which one, in particular, had a head so peculiar that I had it destined (no continuation). This fish weighed 15 pounds. Another approaching the tuna without being of the species, weighed 37 pounds and will doubtless be good to eat. We took several perches and breams which will be no less good.
While the boat was occupied with fishing, three natives armed with spears passed over the mountains who observed some time our men and then continued their route which was directed toward the south-west.
The night had nothing particular. The winds were from the south-east to east almost calm.

1803-02-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds variable from W to SW and WNW. At 7.30 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Sighted two ships standing on the opposite tack. Est. lat. 35° 21' 41", est. long. 19° 42' 48".
1803-02-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighth Ventôse (27 February 1803). The eighth, in the morning, the weather being fair and the winds from east-south-east, a fresh breeze, citizens Boulanger, Faure and Bailly asked me for a boat to go ashore, having the project of taking different angles from some mountains for the construction of the port of which Citizen Faure had made the bearings. I had put at their disposal, the large boat in which they should return at sunset.
