The cutter was, equally, despatched to go take ashore, the wood which I had had cut for the Casuarina which, as had been foreseen, could not embark and which I took for myself, not wishing to have taken the trouble of having it cut uselessly although I had no need for it. The small boat was despatched for fishing in the same place where it had been the previous day.
About eight o'clock, the American ship, the Union, Captain Penleton of New York, set under sail and tacked with rather little success during all the morning, among the islands which form its entrance.
At nine o'clock, not seeing the Captain of the Casuarina arrive, I put one of the orderlies to sea, and addressed him the following letter:
"To Citizen Freycinet, aboard the Casuarina,
"Citizen, if it had pleased you to stay, yesterday, aboard the Casuarina to occupy yourself with "the fitting out of this ship or if, as you should have, you had gone ashore the day before yesterday, to "share with me, the task which I did entirely for you, I would not be obliged to make reproaches to you "on a conduct so little considered on your part, on the slowness which it puts in your works, on "the loss of time which results from it and finally on the state of intoxication in which were found the "crew of the cutter in returning from your ship.
"On the other hand, your pleasures which always take preference over your duties have not "allowed you to occupy yourself seriously with your replacements in provisions, for your state of "requests makes no mention at all of what remains for you aboard and which must greatly restrict it "according to what you have already received.
"For more convenience for you, you surely imagined that I was provided with barrels, barrelling "or casks which must be necessary for you for what I could give you. And it is no doubt this which is the "cause that you sent me only two empty barrels. But you will learn today that I have none neither even "of casks, of which I can dispose. Thus, if you have burned or thrown yours overboard, you will make "such other subsequent arrangements as it may please you. You will therefore be good enough, at the "receipt of this letter, to send me a general state, not of what you desire to have, but of what "remains for you aboard, for I will give you only what I can spare you". Your fellow citizen. N. B.
A little while after, Citizen Freycinet having come aboard, handed to me himself the note which I had had asked of him. He received, in this visit, a rebuke of which I hope he will remember both for the good of the service and for himself.
About three o'clock in the afternoon, we obtained sight of the return of the boat of Citizen Ransonnet which returned aboard where it arrived about six o'clock in the evening. According to the verbal report which he made to me, he has discovered three ports very convenient for ships of medium size in that there is found only three and a half and four fathoms of water at most. He also had occasion to communicate with the natives of the country who showed themselves little wild and were the first to give the example of their good dispositions since they began by laying aside their arms before approaching the crew of the boat who did the same and then mingled with them. We made ourselves understood the best possible by signs and the greater part of the day was passed with them in very good understanding. Only, they would not permit that one should be on the side where they had had their women withdraw to the number of three. On their side, they were five. They made no difficulty in drinking and eating all that was presented to them and regaled themselves abundantly with the sailors' cooking. As one had forgotten to put in the boat, the presents which I usually destined for the natives when we could communicate with them, they received from our men only the buttons of their clothes of which they made much account, handkerchiefs and some bad jackets which did not please them as much. I refer to the written report which Citizen Ransonnet must make to me for further details.
After sunset, citizens Boulanger, Faure and Bailly returned aboard and I had notice given to the tents of the naturalists, that one should be prepared to come aboard the next day.
In the night, the winds varied from east to north-east and the breeze was moderate although with a very cloudy sky.

1803-02-28.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from W to WSW. Two three-masters in sight to leeward. At 9.30 a.m. wore ship. Obs. lat. 35° 55' 29", est. long. 20° 16' 56". From the 9th to the 10th [Ventôse, Year 11, 28 February - 1 March 1803]. Fine weather, a light breeze from SW. The ship in sight steering for us. At 5 hoisted our colours to make ourselves known. At 5.30, being abeam, we hove to, as did she, and her captain came aboard. At 6 filled and stood on. Obs. lat. 35° 35' 19", est. long. 19° 46' 56".
1803-02-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Ninth Ventôse (28 February 1803). The ninth, from the morning, the cutter and the large boat were despatched to go raise the tents and bring back everyone aboard, as well as everything that was ashore. Aboard, we restored our main anchor to its place and we arranged the ship to receive our boats.
The large boat arrived at nine o'clock and the cutter at half past ten. The four sick who had passed this stay ashore, returned according to me, much worse than when they were taken there but according to the surgeon, much better in health despite the continual moisture which had not abandoned them and the little supervision that was had of their conduct and of their regime which, surely, was not a diet.
As soon as the arrival of the cutter, we embarked the living plants collected by Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, to the number of seventy species.
They were placed in different places of the ship and in my cabin in order to delay still for some (time) the lamentations which I would have to hear when it is absolutely necessary to take the cabins of those who still occupy some, in order to place the other objects of natural history which we may collect during the rest of the campaign.
As I was determined to set under sail the next day, whether the winds were fair or contrary, I prepared for the Captain of the Casuarina, the following instruction. He came aboard himself under the pretext of asking for it, but I replied to him that as I did not want everyone to have knowledge of what I had to tell him, I would send it to him when (I) judged it necessary and that besides, he should be ready to set sail for the next day & a.
"To Citizen Freycinet, commanding the schooner the Casuarina,
"Citizen, you have already been warned by the last instruction which I gave you at "Île Borda, that on leaving King George's port, I will go to Géographe Bay to finish what "remains to be done in geography in this part of the coast.
"I intend, before entering this bay, to put into port for one day only at Saint Alouarn Island "to determine in a precise manner, the latitude and longitude which I believe very doubtful according "to those which the French and English charts assign to it.
"If the winds are favourable to me and the weather fair, I would stay perhaps three or four days at "Rottnest Island and will go from there, to the anchorage of Dirk Hartog to take some tortoises before going further to the north. I observe to you, nevertheless, that these two latter stays are more probable "than certain.
"Whether they take place or not, I will stop for some time at the north-west point of "New Holland in order to assure myself positively whether the place which the Dutch have named the "William River, is not an island, as I suspect. If we should be separated at sea in the journey which there "is to make to go there, this point will be a means of rallying and the only one which I can indicate to "you.
"The winds from east and north-east which I expect to encounter in going up to the north will "make the route which remains for me to make on the north coast, too uncertain for me to be able to "prescribe other rendezvous to you. Besides, not wishing to put into port in any place frequented by "Europeans, it is therefore but too probable that if we have not rejoined each other at the north-west "point, we will not meet again. In consequence, after having cruised ten entire days between the north-"west point and the William River, you will make your way directly for the Isle of France. This point "is, according to the observations which we have made there, at 21° 36' south latitude and 110° 35' "east longitude. It is surrounded by reefs to the north which extend fairly far offshore and to the north of "these reefs one begins to see some of the islets which depend on it.
"As the entrance of the William River is found to the south of the latitude which I have just "given you, you will not go to the north of this meridian in the cruise which you will make if we were "separated. But after the time, which I have fixed, has expired, you will make, as I have already "prescribed for you, your way for the Isle of France while keeping yourself in the waters of the "general winds of the south-east and in conformity with the instruction of Citizen D'après.
"Upon your arrival in the port, you will hand over to the Administrators of the Government, "your ship to be employed in the service of the colony if they judge it necessary. I think you will "retain the command until my return in order to employ your time usefully. But if that does not suit "you, you are master to make your way to France by the first opportunity of which you will like to "(take) advantage.
"You will have the complaisance to hand over to the Administrators of the colony of the Isle "of France, the letter which I give you for them and to communicate to them the article of this "instruction which concerns the employment of your ship.
"It is therefore, henceforth, on you alone, that it will depend whether you accompany me or "not. I have never neglected to do everything which has been necessary to prevent the two "separations which have already taken place and which you could easily have avoided, either by the "manoeuvre, or in the execution of the orders which I gave you. Thus, you will have personally to "answer to the Government, for the expenses occasioned for the fitting out of your ship since they will "have become burdensome for the State and useless for the expedition".
"Your fellow citizen". NB.
"To the General Administrators of the Islands of France and Reunion,
"Citizens,
"The schooner of the Republic, the Casuarina, which I had built at Port Jackson in "replacement of the Naturaliste despatched for France, completely laden with the objects of natural "history which we have collected during our stay on the coast of New Holland, besides having been "separated from me in the journey from King George's port to the William River, I have given order "to Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant of the Ship, who commands it, to go to the Isle of France and to "hand over to you this ship to be employed in the service of the colony, if you judge it suitable. I "think that this officer will be quite pleased to retain the command until the period of my return. It "is why I pray you to be good enough to permit him to keep it. As I intend to go as soon as possible "to the Gulf of Carpentaria to complete entirely the instructions of the Government, I cannot assure you what will be the precise period of my arrival at the Isle of France, however I think that it will take place in eight or ten months at the latest.
"I will not enter for the moment into the detail of what we have done and discovered. But "I hope that the Government will be satisfied and the public pleased.
"Greetings & respects". N. B.
These two letters were sealed separately and sent by a midshipman of the Navy to Citizen Freycinet. On the envelope which contained them, there was for address: it is expressly forbidden to Citizen Freycinet, Captain of the Casuarina, to open this package before the ships are outside King George's Bay.
In the afternoon, we embarked the cutter and two of our boats, the third having been reserved to go fetch the instruments of astronomy, the tent and Citizen Bernier who had asked me to send for him only about three o'clock in the afternoon. He arrived aboard at sunset and at the moment when we were raising one of our anchors.
I completed, in this stay, five months of provisions aboard the Casuarina. So that if this ship should find itself separated from me in such a manner as not to be able to rejoin me at the rendezvous which I have indicated to it, it will always be furnished with all that may be necessary for it to make its way easily to the Isle of France.
We had, during all the day, a very strong breeze from the east wind which was not a good omen for the next day. But, as during the night, it had the custom of calming, we hoped that, by going about it early to set under sail, that we would have time to leave the bay with the light land breeze which, for the usual, took place from four o'clock in the morning until sunrise, when they passed to the north-east and then to the east strong breeze.
This stay was very agreeable for the crew and nevertheless harmful to some of them who made bad use of it by excessive consumptions of fresh fish. Every day, we took by the line, along the side, so great a quantity of mackerel that, independently of the forced consumptions which were made, was so considerable that we salted several barrels. A quantity no less great was dried and to be truthful, each made abundant provision of it for the sea. We were, in this, much more fortunate than Vancouver who, according to his report, encountered very few in the season when (he) made the reconnaissance of this port.
We (did not) attempt to fish with a seine, in that it would have been losing time. The bottom too steep not seeming to suit the fish all the more as the bottom is of very white sand and destitute of seaweed. However,
the men who were ashore took a ray with pointed sticks in the manner of the natives of the country.
The botanists were very content with the collections which they made. According to what Citizen Leschenault told me, it appears that he collected there approximately two hundred new species of plants which were not known to him, and as many varieties in the species. The gardener Guichenot is no less less (sic) satisfied and even richer still.
I think that Citizen Péron will also have a volume on worms and molluscs and one or two casks of broken shells. For in several places on the beach, one can collect them with a shovel. This must serve him, as he claims, to prove the epoch when New Holland must have come out of the depths of the sea.
As for me, I observed there that the tides are very irregular. Several times, the sea was twice high and low in six hours, which I had never yet seen anywhere. The tides of the day were generally not strong, and those of the night very great. In the day, it did not seem to me to rise above three feet whilst in the nights, it rose more than once to seven and eight. It is true that we were then in the renewal of the moon.
The winds, during our stay, were very variable. We had them from all points of the compass. But it appears that those from the east and west are the dominant and even the strongest, in that we always had them violent from these two points of the horizon. Those from west to south-west, are ordinarily accompanied by rains and mists. Those from east to south-east are, on the contrary, clear and the sky fair, but they bring into the bay a very strong swell which does not contribute to the safety of the ships.
Observations made ashore:
Latitude of the place of the observatory: (no figures)
Longitude of the same place: ( " " " )
Declination of the needle: ( " " " )
Inclination of the needle: ( " " " )
1803-02-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: We communicated with an American bound for the whale fishery in Delagoa Bay.

1803-03-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
At nine o'clock in the morning,
the Eclipse Islets remained to us at south 80° west,
Cape Howe at north 75° west.
Blad Head at north 15° west
and Mount Gardener at north 5° east.
At noon,
Blad Head was at north 35° 25° west
and the Eclipse Islets at north 55° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
Departure from King George's Bay
The tenth (1st March 1803), about four o'clock and a half, the weather having a fine appearance and the land breeze having announced itself by a light freshness from the north, variable to north-west, we made arrangements to set under sail and went about. We then hoisted the topsails and we set sail, all canvas spread, exiting by the south of the Seal Island. As we had made our way to the anchorage by the same passage which, nevertheless, appeared to us much more convenient to the north of this islet in that it is much more convenient and of easy tacking in case of opposition from the winds. We passed at approximately (half) a mile from this islet which is safe and around which the waters are deep. We had the bottom only once by nine fathoms and we lost it almost immediately by fourteen and fifteen. The course which we made to exit, was east-north-east and east by south-east.
At eight o'clock, we found ourselves sufficiently offshore to no longer fear the east and south-east winds, if they should occur and as I expected.
In doubling Black Head, we obtained sight of the reef indicated in Vancouver's particular plan, but it seemed to me that he places it much nearer to the coast than it really is.
The winds which we had from the north-west, passed successively to the south-west. And the appearance of a fine day announced by the sunrise and a fair sky, dissipated altogether. A thick mist deprived us almost entirely of the sight of land, although we were very near it. The direction of the winds having obliged us to take a course to the south-east, we followed it until noon when the sky having become clearer, we went about toward the land.
At nine o'clock, the Eclipse Islets remaining to us at south 80° west, Cape Howe at north 75° west and Mount Gardener at north 5° east, we took our starting point from this bearing.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 35° 21' 58" and our longitude starting from the bearing was, according to our dead reckoning, 115° 58' 24".
The tack from north toward west which we had taken at noon was continued until five o'clock, when not being able to double the Eclipse Islets, we resumed that from south toward west, the winds having shifted to west. A very high swell which came to us from that point of the horizon, did not announce good winds to us and the state of the atmosphere indicated bad weather. We saw, in the evening, several fires which proved to us that this part of the coast was tolerably inhabited for that moment. At eight o'clock, we made course to the south.
During the night, the winds were variable from west to west-south-west and the weather with squalls with strong gusts and rain especially after moonset. We continued the tack from south toward west.
1803-03-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: We sounded and had 102 fathoms, sandy bottom. Two sharks were taken.

1803-03-02.journal_anonyme: A flat calm. At 2 a light breeze got up from the east. At daybreak sighted five ships ahead of us and to windward. At 11 a.m. the lookout thought he saw land in the WNW. Obs. lat. 35° 31' 7", est. long. 18° 15' 26".
1803-03-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock in the evening,
Mount Gardener remained to the north 17° east.
Cape Chauve at north 10° west,
the Eclipse Islets at north 38° west
and the continental lands most to the west in view at north 56° west.
At daybreak,
we saw the land from the north to the north-north-west.
At noon,
Mount Gardener was observed at north 62° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The eleventh, in the morning, the weather was tolerably fair. At daybreak, we closed with the Casuarina which we had lost sight of during the night. And, after having joined it, we oriented in the course from west toward north, the winds being variable from south-west to south.
In the morning, the sky covered with clouds and had a very bad appearance. A very heavy swell from the south-west seemed to announce some squalls from that quarter, although on the other hand the barometer had begun to rise. The land was seen from the north to the north-north-west, but too obscurely to recognise the points well.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 31' 34" and as there was no hour angle, we made ourselves, according to our dead reckoning, by the longitude of 115° 54' 41". At that time, the sky having cleared, we obtained sight of Mount Gardener which was observed at north 62° east.
In the afternoon, we continued the tack from west toward north to close with the land. The sky no longer had, then, the bad appearance of the morning and our fears of bad weather to come dissipated. Nevertheless, the sea was no less very heavy with swell although there was little wind.
At sunset, we observed the lands as announced at the end of the log table and we took the tack to the south, for the night.
The coast which we had in view in the morning and even during all the day, is generally of good height and can easily be seen at ten and twelve leagues at sea when the weather is fair. The edges of the sea appear elevated and cut perpendicularly, offering from time to time some islets of little consequence which are not far from the shore. The elevations in the form of mountains which are seen at the edge of the sea, show themselves most often as islands, in that at four and five leagues' distance one does not see the low lands which join them one to the other.
In the night and especially after moonset, the winds were very variable and unequal. The sky was now clear and now dark, but we had neither squalls, nor gusts, as on the previous night.
1803-03-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak five ships were sighted shaping their course to double the Cape. At 11.30 land was thought to be seen in the N 68° W. The ship makes 4 inches of water an hour.

1803-03-03.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW. At 5 a.m. went about. The main topmast backstay having parted near the trestletrees, new masthead rigging was made up on the masthead with the same rope. Obs. lat. 36° 12' 20", est. long. 17° 51' 32".
1803-03-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
Mount Gardener remained to the north 52° east.
Cape Chauve at north 44° east.
The Eclipse Islets at north 21° east,
The continental lands most in view in the west at north 61° west.
At sunset,
Cape Chauve was observed at north 72° east,
The Eclipse Islets at north 85° east,
Cape Howe at north 42° west,
The continental lands, in view, at north 52° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twelfth, we had a continuation of the wind from west to south-west which was little suited to the course we had to make and which began strongly to displease us from the fear that it would not change until the new moon which was to take place the seventeenth. At sea, when the fair wind declares itself and the ship makes good progress, one easily persuades oneself, and even with pleasure, that it will last as long as one has need of it. But if it changes sooner than one had supposed, one sees nothing but particular and decided opposition. This was absolutely the case in which we found ourselves since our departure from King George's port, for most of us thought that the winds from west to south by the south-west must not abandon us until we should have attained the waters of the south-east winds about 28° south latitude. It would be difficult to explain what could give rise to such reasoning, for those who made it could establish it only on their particular ideas and not on experience since all were on their first voyage.
Be that as it may, it is nonetheless true that we were thwarted by the fact and that since our departure from the last port of call, the winds had constantly maintained themselves in the quarter which our prophets had announced.
During the morning, we had a tolerably fair sky and the coast was distinguished perfectly although we were rather far offshore.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 35° 27' 30" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 31 placed us at 115° 36' 30" which gave us but little progress toward the west, although according to our dead reckoning, the currents appeared to carry us toward the north-west with a rate of 18 miles in 24 hours. This observation is absolutely contrary to what Vancouver says who found currents which constantly carried him toward the south-east. But I attribute this to the periods of the seasons during which he frequented this coast which, according to me, are precisely those of the winds from south-west to north-west by the west while we were in those of the winds from south-east to north-east by the east as it is easy to convince oneself from those which we encountered.
This day having passed as the previous ones in tacking to elevate ourselves toward the west as much as possible. We found ourselves in the evening in sight of land and as we always bore away for the night, we observed at sunset, Cape Chauve at north 72° east, the middle of the Eclipse Islets at north 85° east and Cape Howe at north 42° west, the continental lands most in view in the west extended to north 52° west.
During the night, the night, the sky was very cloudy and the sea heavy with swell. We had, since ten o'clock in the morning, a long swell from the south-west which made the wave elevated and hollow. Nevertheless, the night was not bad although the sky was constantly laden with vapours and damp.

1803-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light air, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from WSW. At 2 the winds having shifted to NW, went onto the starboard tack. Obs. lat. 36° 8' 21", est. long. 17° 57' 6".
1803-03-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daybreak, the Eclipse Islets were seen in the north 65° east.
The lands to the west most in view at north 50° west.
Historical events & Remarks & a.
The thirteenth, in the morning, the winds varied from south-west to south and from south toward east but the breeze was so light that we made little progress toward the west. The sky, always overcast and misty, was hardly more favourable to us, however, we were still near enough to land to be able to recognise it.
At sunrise or to be more precise, when day was somewhat advanced, we saw again the Eclipse Islets of which the middle remained to us at north 65° east. We made course all morning, as much toward the west as was possible in conforming to the variability of the winds.
At noon, the sun having appeared, the latitude was observed at 35° 14' 0" and according to our dead reckoning, the longitude was found to be 115° 9' 54".
The sea, although somewhat less heavy than the previous day, was nevertheless always hollow and with a swell very long which seemed to come from afar.
In the afternoon, we had some squalls and rain, but they were neither of long duration, nor violent. The winds passed again to the south-west which made our prophets so accredited that one often went to consult them to know whether they would last much longer. Their opinion in that regard is not known to me.
At eight o'clock in the evening, we took, as was customary, the tack to the south which took somewhat to the east. During the night, there was almost calm. We sounded we sounded (sic) twice, only. The first cast of the lead brought 57 fathoms and the second 55. We went about at eleven o'clock the wind being almost calm.
During the day, we saw, all along the coast, so great a number of fires, that there is every appearance that this part was tolerably inhabited. We counted seventeen, all somewhat distant from each other and which in no way resembled those great conflagrations which we had often remarked, but which appeared on the contrary to be particular fires which were not of long duration and disappeared all before the end of the day.
The view of the coast was approximately similar to that which we had had since our departure from King George's Bay, that is to say divided by portions of high and low lands which seemed to us quite well wooded.

1803-03-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from NW. At 9 p.m. wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 36° 3' 17", est. long. 16° 12' 14".
1803-03-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock in the evening,
the two extremities of the continental lands in view were observed, one at north 85° east and the other at north 61° west.
At noon of the next day
they were seen from east a quarter north-east to west north-west.
Historical events and Remarks.
The fourteenth, the weather was hardly more fair than the previous days. However, the winds which, although very light had passed from south-south-east to north-east, seemed to announce a change in our favour, although the sky was very overcast and often misty. This change arrived in fact, in the morning for, gradually, the mist and clouds having dissipated, we had from time to time, a fair sky which permitted us to distinguish the coast well. The part across which we found ourselves, was extremely jagged and offered to view different openings which seemed to announce some good shelters for ships. This appearance well visible was confirmed by the lookouts from the tops of the masts who claimed to see great openings through which the water penetrated beyond the reach of their sight into the interior of the lands.
According to the proximity that General d'Entrecasteaux, Vancouver and more recently still Citizen Flinders have visited this coast, I was founded to believe that the water which one saw in the interior of the country was lagoons which did not communicate with the sea since all these navigators left no interruption on the coast of which they were much nearer than us, according to the trace of their route. Nevertheless, I much regretted being in calm and not being able to close with it.
At noon, we had no observation of latitude. That of our dead reckoning placed us at 35° 15' 45" and the longitude, also estimated, was 114° 45' 0".
From noon to four o'clock, the weather turned wholly fair. And about two o'clock, there arose a light breeze from the south-west by means of which we were able to steer the ship. Not being able to resist the desire which I had to assure myself whether this part of the coast did not offer, according to appearance, some ports which could be a resource for navigators and which had escaped the sight of those who had frequented it before us, I made signal to the Casuarina to pass under my stern and gave him order to go to recognise the openings which were abreast of us announcing that I would await his return in tacking back and forth in sight of the coast. He was enjoined not to stop in these openings if the weather remained fair and only to observe the entrances which they could form and to return at once to report to me. I agreed with the Captain of this schooner that if the weather became bad and I should be obliged to abandon the coast, that I would await him at the anchorage of Rottnest Island which I indicated to him as a place of rendezvous in that case only. The extent of coast which Citizen Freycinet had to see was at most, four or five leagues and should not require much time. He set out at once and directed himself to the point by which I had said to begin and which I believe to be the western part of Cape Nuyts.
During the night, the weather was very fair and the breeze moderate. We spent it in tacking in order to close with the land ourselves the next day if the wind would permit us to move away in case of need.

1803-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW, south and SSE. Worked at getting the bower anchors to the fore hatchway. Obs. lat. 34° 58' 10", est. long. 14° 45' 20".
1803-03-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset,
The continental lands in view extended from north 75° east to north 60° west.
At noon,
the point which lies between Cape Nuyts and Cape Leeuwin remained at north 68° west as well as the islet which depends on it.
Historical events & Remarks.
The fifteenth, in the morning, the weather continued fair and we had a very fine breeze from south-east to north. We closed with the land at a league and a half distance and tacked constantly back and forth all morning and a great part of the afternoon, in hopes of meeting the Casuarina. The course which we had held the previous night having put us three or four leagues to windward, I found myself in a position so much the more advantageous that it could not prolong the coast however near it might be, without obtaining sight of it. All the more so that the tacks were never more than two hours on one side as on the other until four o'clock in the evening. However, we did not see it, which leads me to believe that it will have found some convenient and good place to serve as a refuge for ships which accidents could oblige to seek shelter on this part of the coast.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 35° 9' 47" and the longitude of our timekeeper placed us at 114° 51' 3", which hardly agreed with that which the chart of Citizen Beautemps Beaupré gives to Cape or Point Nuyts.
In the afternoon, the sky continued to be fair and we always had the coast in sight at a small distance. But about two o'clock, there suddenly arose such thick mist that we (had) no longer sight of it. Nevertheless, persuaded that the weather which had not a bad appearance would turn fair at moonrise, we continued to run the same tacks which we had held in the morning. At sunset, seeing no appearance of change, we took a reef in each topsail and bore away for fear of bad weather, the barometer falling rapidly. The tack from south toward east which we had taken was continued until ten o'clock in the evening, when we took that to the north, the winds being from the east, a fine breeze, variable to east-north-east.
During the night, the weather was tolerably fair, but we had no sight of land although the horizon appeared to us quite extended. We sounded every two hours without finding bottom at 50 and 60 fathoms. The sea was somewhat agitated all night which we attributed rather to currents than to the force of the wind which was moderate.
1803-03-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: The anchors (all but one) were struck below; and on the 18th [Ventôse, 9 March 1803] the jib boom and spritsail yard were rigged in to ease the ship forward.

1803-03-07.journal_anonyme: The sea smooth, the weather very fine and the winds variable from SE, south, SSW and south. Obs. lat. 33° 30' 20", est. long. 13° 1' 20".
1803-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset,
we barely saw the land although we were not more than three leagues from it, so misty was it.
At daybreak, we perceived the land to the north, the horizon very misty.
At noon, we saw it also through the mist, estimated distance three leagues.
Of the 16th. Historical events & Remarks.
The sixteenth, at daybreak, running the land tack, we expected to see the see (sic) land and even quite near us, but the horizon was found so misty that we perceived it scarcely at an estimated distance of about three leagues. As day broke, the breeze became more and more light and the greater part of the morning passed in calm.
In different passing clearings which occurred, we saw from time to time the land and believed we recognised the point where the Casuarina should have begun the reconnaissance which I had ordered it to make. As we had no sight of this ship during the day, nor the day before, when the weather had been fair, I had no doubt that it had made some good discoveries, but that instead of coming to inform us, as I had expressly ordered, it had stopped there, caring little whether I was waiting for it or not.
These reflections which I was not making for the first time, made me ill-humoured and I was entirely convinced after all that I had already said to this Captain, that he made very little account of the orders which I gave him. Persuaded besides that he was only seeking an occasion for separation to go to the Isle of France, I took the resolution to put order to it at our first meeting. For this reason, I (decided) to cruise on this coast until the weather permitted me to recognise the coast myself with the ship.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 35° 18' 56" and the longitude of our timekeeper placed us at 114° 53' 41". So that we (ourselves) found ourselves a little more south and a little more west than the previous day.
In the morning, the mist dissipated only in very short intervals which did not even leave us time to recognise the land well. And during the evening, the sky became so dark that we lost hope of seeing it turn fair. The barometer which, for the past twenty-four hours, had fallen nearly four lines, did not announce to us either, the change which I desired. Nevertheless, as the sea did not announce to us bad weather, I continued to keep tacking back and forth regulating each tack to four hours' run.
During the day, the lead brought 48 to 45 fathoms and at eight o'clock it was 65.
The night had nothing particular and was even more agreeable than we should have expected it, according to the appearances at the end of the day. The winds were variable from east to east-north-east and the breeze little steady. We manoeuvred as during the day in order not to move away from the coast, hoping that the Casuarina might appear perhaps the next day.

1803-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SSW to SW. In the forenoon shifted the foresail. Obs. lat. 30° 56' 7", est. long. 10° 53' 26".
1803-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
The continental lands were seen from north-north-west to east-north.
The part of the coast which the Casuarina had gone to recognise (remained) to us from east-north-east to north-east a quarter north.
At noon,
we had Point Nuyts at north 78° east
and the two rocks marked on the chart of the reconnaissance made by d'Entrecasteaux at north 45° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The seventeenth, the winds passed from south-south-east to south, a strong breeze. We closed with the land in the very place where I had sent the Casuarina. But having no sight of it, I decided to continue my course. It was quite enough to have wasted two days uselessly waiting for it for a reconnaissance which was the work of three hours, having expressly ordered it to come and report to me whether the openings which I had indicated to it, were not the entrance to some ports, forbidding it to stop there if the weather was fair.
This officer, insubordinate by principle, has been unable until now to execute a commission nor even to comply with the orders which I gave him. For this reason, if he meets me at Rottnest Island which I indicated to him as a place of rendezvous, there is every likelihood that I will remove him from this command to try whether another will better comply with the orders which circumstances will cause me to give him.
At nine o'clock, we therefore took the course north 70° west and extended along the coast at a small distance, with a very good wind but an unpleasant sky.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 35° 4' 40" and the longitude of No. 35 placed us at 114° 3' 58". Point Nuyts then remained to us at north 78° east and the two rocks of which the chart of Citizen Beautemps Beaupré makes mention, at north 45° east.
In the afternoon, there continued to blow a fair breeze from south-south-east to south-east. We found the sea heavy and with swell. We extended along the coast at approximately a league and a half to two leagues distance. The lands in the interior are, as I have already observed, of good height and the edges of the sea, formed in great part by dunes of sand before which, there are sometimes some rocks which lie on the shore.
At sunset, Cape Leeuwin was observed at north 30° west. We had no sight of Saint Alouarn Island.
During the night which was dark and damp, we took the tack to the south until one o'clock, when we went about in order to find ourselves at Cape Leeuwin the next day at daybreak. Although the sky was fair during the night, we spent it quietly with two reefs in our topsails only we found the sea somewhat heavy and very rough with swell.

1803-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south and SE. The course NNW. In the forenoon rigged in the jib boom and spritsail yard. Obs. lat. 29° 20' 44", long. 9° 11' 23".
1803-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock Cape Leeuwin was observed at north 30° west,
At eight o'clock in the evening, it remained to us at north 5° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The eighteenth, in the morning, we recognised Cape Leeuwin and when day broke, we obtained sight of Saint Alouarn Island which we had uselessly sought when we visited this coast, for the first time. From which we concluded that the point which we had taken for Cape Leeuwin, was not the one to which this name applies, at least according to the chart of the geographer Beautemps Beaupré.
In the morning, we commenced new work on all this coast, that which had been done previously having been judged bad.
As I must account to the Government for the loss of this time, I must tell it that all our scholars were so little versed in the part which concerned each of them in particular, that they could make themselves useful only at the end of the campaign, supposing that they would work to acquire the necessary knowledge and especially the habit of such work which, with all the theory in the world, will always be incomplete when one does it for the first time and one has not exercised one's eye to judge either the distance of a coast or the depth of a cove. This is precisely the case in which our present and future geographers found themselves. At a league 3 & 4 leagues from land, all the coast appeared to them straight and on the same plane. As practice must have, since that time, taught them to judge better, it is probable that the work which they are doing now, will have merit and that their plans will be well made.
After having doubled Saint Alouarn Island, we coasted the land going up toward the north at a distance of a league at most. We were sailing then, in the greatest security and yet, we were very near our loss. At seven o'clock 30 minutes, having cast my eyes to leeward of us, I perceived a reef awash which broke greatly and scarcely (had) we time to avoid it by coming suddenly to the wind. The ship was then running 7 to eight miles, so that it obeyed promptly to its helm. Fortunately for us that this reef was found very steep otherwise the campaign was finished. In coming to the wind, the stern of the ship did not pass half a pistol shot from the rock. No one had had sight of this reef, of which nonetheless nothing would have hidden from us the view long before if one had paid attention to it.
Those who were on watch were confined for three days and the rest of the crew severely reprimanded. Punishment doubtless quite mild in comparison with the fatal consequences from which we barely escaped becoming the victim.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 33° 48' 24" and the longitude of our timekeeper placed us at 112° 50' 49". According to the observations made in the morning of Cape Leeuwin and of Saint Alouarn Island, it would follow that this island would be at 34° 27' 18" and by the longitude of 113° 1' 54", as Cape Leeuwin, at 34° 25' 51" and 112° 58' 0", which differs considerably from the position where this island and this point are placed in the depot chart.
During the evening, the weather was (blank) and we elevated ourselves as far as the south point which forms the entrance of the great Géographe Bay into which we were to enter the next day for the third time. During the night, the weather was fair and the breeze moderate, we made sail until midnight and lay to until daybreak.

1803-03-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from SSE to south. Stowed the jib boom and spritsail yard among the spare spars. Obs. lat. 27° 51' 20", est. long. 7° 1' 53".
1803-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon 22 minutes, the south point of the entrance of the bay was observed at south 46° west
and the lands in view, the most east, at north 67° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The nineteenth, in the morning, making course north 34° east, we were much astonished to perceive to leeward of us a fairly extended chain of reefs on which the sea broke with force. At six o'clock, we distinguished three which seemed to form a triangle in the direction from north to south. This danger was at approximately two miles from us and remained to us from north-west to north-west by west. As we had sounded every hour during the night and at five o'clock in the morning, the bottom was still at 25 fathoms, we were far from believing that we were so near a reef of which we had had no sight the year before, ( In the margin and in different writing: "it is the reef of the Naturaliste seen in Year 9"), although the bad weather had obliged us to tack in all directions, at the entrance of this bay. Be that as it may, we continued to keep as close to the wind as possible on the tack from north toward east, to gain the windward side and then went about to come to begin our work at the south point which forms the entrance of this bay.
When we obtained sight, for the first time, of this bay, the winds obliged us, as on this occasion, to bear away toward the north. The Naturaliste, after having run about two hours, signalled to us that the course which it was making, did not appear good to follow according to the report of the lookouts who claimed to see reefs, but as he himself mounted the topgallant yards, and saw nothing, he had doubts but not certainty. Today, it is demonstrated that the lookouts saw indeed this reef which he would have done well to go and recognise at the time. Its position will be well determined on our chart of this part of the coast, by all the observations which we have made of it.
In the afternoon, we passed near our first anchorage on this coast. We saw there many more fires than at the first time (in the margin and in different writing: "unfortunate Vasse") as well as on the part of coast which is found to the south of this point of the bay. We coasted it until evening at a small distance but the weather was so dirty and misty that one had difficulty in well recognising the different points which one observed being often enveloped in mist when one needed to see them. Nevertheless, we could take enough of them recognisable for the construction of the chart.
At seven o'clock, although the sky was very confused, it had no fair appearance, we moored a sheet anchor on a bottom of nine fathoms, sand and seaweed. We passed the night there, very quietly during which the weather turned fair, after moonrise.
The crew took, during the night, very fine fish and some of which weighed as much as twenty-five pounds. They were very good to eat, none of us know to what species to refer them, however, Citizen Péron believes they are of that (blank).

1803-03-11.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sea smooth, a pleasant breeze from south, SSW and SE. Bent the old foresail, repaired. Obs. lat. 26° 32' 3", est. long. 5° 9' 35".
1803-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock 45 minutes,
the point which forms the south entrance of Géographe Bay remained west 10° north, bearing doubtful by the mist.
Bearing of the anchorage.
The apparent point of the entrance of a small bay which I was sending to visit at south 9° east.
The south extremity of the lands to the west, at south 24 hours° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twentieth, at daybreak, we set under sail with a light breeze from south variable to south-south-east. My intention was to stop in Misfortune Cove in order to know what could have become of the objects of our lost cutter and to know whether the natives had seized them. But the misty weather of the previous evening, not having permitted us to recognise the coast well enough to know at what distance we could be from it, I could not guess that chance had made us precisely anchor in the same place. We therefore set sail to go to seek it further toward the north-east. And it was only after we had advanced about three leagues in this direction of wind, that we perfectly recognised the anchorage from which we had departed to go in search of our men, but it was then too late to turn back with winds blowing positively from the point of the horizon where we had to head. Rather than lose a day in tacking and, perhaps uselessly, I preferred to continue my course and to take advantage of the fair wind which we had to gain the bottom of the bay to the east which I did not believe far distant. We therefore continued to make our course, following all the sinuosities of the coast which is formed only by coves of little depth and without the slightest shelter against the winds from north to south-east by west.
At eleven o'clock three-quarters, being abreast of an opening which seemed to promise the entrance of a port, I had the anchor dropped to send it to visit. Citizen Bonnefoy was charged with this expedition with order to see what it could be. He departed from the ship at half past noon, to return before sunset.
At noon, the latitude of our anchorage was observed at 33° 15' 20" and the longitude of our timekeeper placed us at 113° 26' 33". Which gave us 0° 30' 6" difference in longitude since the observation of the previous noon. According to the direction of wind where the land remained to us whose extremity in sight was observed at (no figures), there is every appearance that we were entirely in the greatest depth of this bay, to the east. All the coast is nothing but a succession of sand dunes behind which one sees a mountain plain in the land, whose direction extends from north-west to south-east, and which are tolerably elevated.
At five o'clock, the boat being returned aboard, I was informed by Citizen Bonnefoy that the place which had offered us the appearance of a port, was indeed one, but it could suit only small ships which draw only eight to nine feet of water, still it would be necessary to know the channel well. He discovered, also, several lagoons of salt water which he did not believe he should visit in order to conform to the orders which I had given him, to be back at sunset. I refer for further details to the plan which he made of this place and to his report.
In the evening, the winds passed to the south-west and the sea became heavy. But as the weather was fair, I thought that the breeze would calm at sunset. For this reason I remained at anchor. We brought from land, some new plants
(in the margin vertically) and branches of casuarina for our kangaroos.
During the night, the weather turned wholly fair and the strong breeze which we had had in the evening, began to calm. The winds which, in the course which they had followed, had come as far as west, returned little by little to south-east passing through south. We took some fish but in less quantity than the previous night.

1803-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from south, SSE, SE and east. Overcast and damp weather. Obs. lat. 25° 36' 3", est. long. 3° 33' 30".
1803-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock, we took the bearing of the entrance into which the boat had gone, at south 15° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-first, at sunrise, we were under sail, making our course to run along the coast and to complete, if it were possible, the work of it in the course of the day, as concerns the recess which the land makes here to the east, since at noon our longitude was 113° 25' 53" and our latitude 32° 48' 0". Which placed us, in this position, to the east of the south point which forms the entrance of Géographe Bay by 0° 27' 53". But as in the previous courses we had been 0° 5' 2" further to the east, it follows that the greatest recess which the land makes to the east, must be placed at 113° 3' and by the latitude of (no figures).
This eastern longitude, compared with that given by the depot chart, to the island of Rottnest placed at 112° 8' 0", gave us therefore 35 minutes of way to make to the west in order to be clear of the land and entirely out of the bay.
In the morning, we ran along the coast, at a very small distance in order to take exact bearings. From the moment we set under sail until eleven o'clock, the bottom was constantly between nine and ten fathoms, sand and weed. But then it began to diminish and became uneven between seven and eight. We stood a little offshore but not enough, however, to avoid a shoal over the extremity of which we passed in four fathoms of water, the bottom having suddenly increased. As the sea was smooth, it was perfectly distinguishable. We first luffed up, but finding no increase and the sea appearing whiter than to leeward, we bore away again and steered, following with the eye, a direction which seemed to promise more water. By this means we avoided running aground on the west point of this shoal where was the greatest whiteness that we had remarked. And when we had passed it, we came again to the wind. The depth then increased noticeably, and in less than half an hour we passed from 4 to 15. As we were on this shoal at noon, its latitude is 32° 48' 0" and our longitude 113° 25' 52".
After having passed the shoal, we closed with the land again for the continuation of our bearings and we were a second time obliged to stand offshore, having passed suddenly from 11 to 12, to 7, which put us tolerably far out. Nevertheless, the windings of the coast and its points were plainly distinguished. Several recesses were perceived, but as they did not seem to me to offer anything of interest, I did not go to reconnoitre them particularly. The breeze, moreover, had become very fresh from south-west winds and it freshened so much toward four o'clock that it was necessary to take a reef in the topsails.
As we were advancing rapidly to the north, without seeing on the coast any indication which might make us suspect that it continued to the west, and as we were drawing nearer and nearer to the latitude of Rottnest Island, I began to distrust the position which our chart gave it, and it was not without reason for, at sunset, we had perfect sight of it and were convinced that its longitude had been badly determined.
Night coming on,
(in the margin vertically) it was deferred to verify whether our reasonings were correct or not. During the night, the sea was very heavy until about two o'clock in the morning, when the winds, having gone round to south-east, calmed. We made only two tacks and we kept ourselves at three leagues from the coast, not going in toward land under 30 fathoms.

1803-03-13.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, the winds very light, from ESE to south by way of north and west. Obs. lat. 24° 41' 57", est. long. 2° 15' 0".
1803-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
we recognised Rottnest Island, whose extremities in sight remained, one at north 22° east and the other at north 65° east.
The next day, at eight o'clock,
The west point of this island remained at south 12° west, and the easternmost land in sight, at south 27 east.
A rock or small islet very close to the island, was seen at south 30° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-second, at daylight, we found ourselves at about three leagues from the coast and were confirmed that it was positively Rottnest Island. As the weather was very fine and the sea smooth, being to the north of the island, I made my course to reach the anchorage in order to wait there for the Casuarina, for which I had appointed it as a rendezvous should bad weather occur while she had gone to reconnoitre the part of the coast which I had indicated to her and on which there was reason to believe she had stopped. But about seven o'clock, we sighted this vessel which was at anchor and which, having perceived us, set under sail. This unexpected meeting made me decide to pass beyond this place, which had moreover been visited by the Naturaliste and was not worth my stopping there. All that can be said of it, according to the report of Captain Hamelin and his officers who stayed there long enough, is that the anchorage is very bad and unsteady there. The winds from south-west to north-west blow full into it and the sea, in these circumstances, is very heavy there. The Swan River, which was ascended eighteen or twenty leagues, offers no resource. Fresh water is sometimes found there in streams which lose themselves in it, but they are of little consequence.
After having hove to in order to wait for the Casuarina, I had a boat put to sea and sent to fetch Citizen Freycinet. In the conversation which I had with him, I did not communicate to him the resolution which I had taken to remove from him the command of this schooner, and confined myself to asking him why he had again so poorly carried out the orders which I had given him. His disobedience having occasioned a fresh separation and the loss of two days which I spent waiting for him. Citizen Freycinet answered me that he had himself been very astonished at this fresh separation, in that he had been only five hours visiting the coast which I had assigned to him, and that immediately he had made his course to rejoin me, but that his separation must be attributed solely to the mist which came on in the afternoon and to the weather of the following day, which seemed to me fairly just.
Be that as it may, I gave him orders to follow me, and we steered north until noon and afterwards north-north-west until nightfall.
At noon, the observed latitude had been 31° 35' 12" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 113° 16' 15".
Throughout the whole day we had very fine weather and a pretty breeze from south-south-east to south-south-west, but we could scarcely take advantage of it for, in order to conform to the sailing of the Casuarina, it was necessary to carry only our topsails on the tone and two reefs in each.
At eight o'clock in the evening, being in only 27 fathoms of water, bottom of sand, rocks and coral, we made our course to the north-west for the night, during which it continued to blow a pretty breeze.

1803-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky overcast, a light breeze from SE, SSE and ESE. Obs. lat. 23° 34' 12", est. long. 0° 40' east.
1803-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset, the lands of la Concorde in sight extended from the north of the compass as far as east-south-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-third, in the morning, we resumed our course to the north-north-west in the hope of being able to pass, in the course of the day, the latitude of the Abrolhos, and perhaps even to sight them, although the course we were making put them to the west at a fairly great distance. But as the position given to this danger is placed differently in the charts, I think that Captain Hamelin, who had sight of it when proceeding from Rottnest Island to the bay of the Sea Dogs, will have determined their position in a certain manner. That is why it was fairly indifferent to me whether I sighted them or not.
In the morning it blew a pretty breeze and we profited from it no more than the day before, in order to conform to the sailing of the Casuarina, which I did not wish to lose sight of.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 29° 51' 34" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 111° 44' 44". We were astonished at not having more way to the north and no longer had hope of passing the Abrolhos before nightfall, since according to the Dutch chart which places them at 28° 58' 0" latitude, we still had to make 0° 23' 54" to the north directly in this quarter of wind.
During the evening, the weather became very cloudy but the breeze was none the worse for it. We found, nevertheless, the sea rougher and more agitated than the preceding days, which we attributed to the approach of this danger, whose extent, from north to south, is fairly considerable.
During the day, a tropicbird was seen, which seemed to us fairly extraordinary at the latitude at which we were, this species of bird not being accustomed to stray far from the tropics. The others which we saw in fairly great quantity, were shearwaters, petrels and gulls similar to those met with everywhere.
At eight o'clock, being nearly at the latitude of the southernmost point of the Abrolhos, we hove to in order to sound and remained there three quarters of an hour, to give the Casuarina time to close with us. Having found no bottom at 90 fathoms, we again took our course to the north-north-west. At midnight, we sounded a second time without finding bottom at 60, proof that we were far enough to the west of this danger to have nothing to fear from it. We continued our course to the north-north-west until the following day at daybreak, when we made it head from north toward east to close with the land, having the design of entering the bay of the Sea Dogs by the pass into which Dampier went, in order to take some turtles there for the refreshment of my crew.
1803-03-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: We crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the 8th time. From noon this day the crew had no more liquor.

1803-03-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from east to south and SE. Variation NW 18° 27' 47". Obs. lat. 22° 41' 34", est. long. W 0° 29' 30".
1803-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-fourth, in the morning, reckoning ourselves to the north of the Abrolhos, we resumed our course from north toward east so as not to draw too far away from the coast. We had, during the day, a pretty breeze from south-south-east to east-south-east of which we profited no more than the preceding days, being obliged to carry only very little sail in order to wait for the Casuarina.
In the morning we saw several tropicbirds and many other sea birds. We also had sight of some flying fish, which had not happened to us for a long time. A bonito of middling size was taken, the only fish of this species that we (had) seen since the beginning of the campaign.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 28° 1' 33" and the longitude of the timekeeper placed us at 111° 6' 45".
In the afternoon, the winds varied from south-east to south, a strong breeze. And although we had our topsails on the tone, two reefs taken, we were sometimes making between seven and eight knots so that the Casuarina could not follow us, with all sails out.
At four o'clock in the evening, we had sight of the land, from the mastheads. Only, it remained to us, then, from east as far as north-east as far as the eye could reach. We continued our course from north toward east until eight o'clock in the evening, when, being in 62 fathoms, we took, for the night, that from north toward west. It blew a strong breeze during the night, and we found the sea heavy as well as strongly agitated. The sounding, during the night, was between sixty-two and eighty-five fathoms.
During the day, one of our kangaroos and one of the emus died. It was the second time that this accident had happened to us. And we imputed the cause of it to the great movements of the vessel of the vessel (sic) which, having only little sail in order to keep with the Casuarina, was agitated in every way by the action of the sea, which was neither comfortable nor fair. These animals were stuffed in order to preserve their remains.

1803-03-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NE to NW, W and WNW. Obs. lat. 22° 9' 14", obs. long. W 4° 0'.
1803-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
At five o'clock in the evening,
the land was seen from the mastheads, extending from north-east as far as east.
At daybreak,
it was seen from north by east as far as south-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
The twenty-fifth, at daybreak, we had perfect sight of the land, although we had steered the whole night at north 22° 30' west. This made us suspect that we had made more way than our dead reckoning had until then given us. This conjecture was not long in being verified, for having brought our course more to the east in order to close with the land, we recognised, about ten o'clock, that we had passed beyond the middle of the island of Dirk Hartog.
We continued to run along this coast and at noon, being at the opening which separates it from the Sterile islands, we entered the channel, keeping fairly close along the island of Dirk Hartog in order to pass to the east of the shoal of which the charts make mention and which was discovered by Dampier.
At noon, we observed 25° 34' 21" south latitude and timekeeper No. 35 placed us at 110° 39' 56" longitude. This latitude, laid down on the Dutch chart, agreed but little with that which it gives to the north point of this island, which it places at 25° 22'. But we made little account of it, having been convinced on other occasions that it carries the whole coast further north than it ought to be. The difference of 0° 15' 21", including therein our distance from the coast, which we kept at four miles, was very nearly the same the same (sic) as that which we had found for the northernmost of the Sterile islands, when we established our observatory there.
At one o'clock, making our course east toward south in order to enter the bay, we had sight of the shoal of which Dampier speaks and on which the sea breaks from time to time. We doubled this shoal at about four miles' distance without finding bottom at 18 and 20 fathoms.
According to the bearing which I had taken at a quarter past two in the afternoon, it follows that when the point of the first of the Sterile islands, that is to say the southernmost, remains at north of the world and the north point of the island of Dirk Hartog at south-west by west true or corrected for the variation, the shoal or breaker remains at north-north-east, at a distance of about four miles.
When we (had) entirely doubled the island of Dirk Hartog, steering east toward south, we began to find the bottom, first at eighteen fathoms and shortly after at 15, then it became very irregular and decreased from 15 to seven to return afterwards to ten and eleven and from this last number to 8 and 7. We advanced, still making our course to the south-east under little sail and sounding continually. And a little before sunset, we had sight of the north point of the land which Dampier has named Middle Island, but which we now know to be a peninsula, according to the plan which the Naturaliste has made of this part of the bay, which she has had all the time to examine by the long stay she made there.
After sunset, not judging it prudent to go further forward, I came to anchor for the night in 7 fathoms of water, fine and clean sand, where we held fast although the breeze was fairly strong, but there was no sea.

1803-03-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze variable from WSW to SSE and SE by S. Obs. lat. 20° 33' 18", est. long. 5° 42'.
1803-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-sixth, at daybreak, I had two boats put to sea and gave the command of them to the first and second quartermasters of the helm, with orders to go sound ahead of the vessel, keeping one to larboard and the other to starboard. When they had left, and about half a league to windward and to leeward, we set under sail to draw nearer to the island where I have the design of remaining five or six days, as much to take some turtles there as to have examined whether the outlet from the bay by the north-east is practicable, which the navigators who have preceded us have not sought to know. As we found ourselves in a position ill suited, when I first made the north-west part of this peninsula, it was not possible for me to attempt it by going out, as I had intended, by the south part of the Dorre islands, in that I had entered by the north.
In the course we made to approach the land, the bottom held fairly long between 6 and seven fathoms of water. But, as we drew nearer, it passed to five fathoms and we were still at about two leagues from the coast. Fearing to see it diminish further by going more ahead, I came to anchor and made signal to the Casuarina to do likewise. On the return of the boats, which had run different tacks in every direction, I was assured that at a league from land there were everywhere 6 and seven fathoms, bottom of sand and weed, and that the spot where we were, which was not more than a musket shot in extent, was the only one where there were but five fathoms. Nevertheless, I kept the anchorage and did not think of changing it until our departure.
At nine o'clock two boats were despatched to go and fish for turtle. I gave the command of them to Ensign Ransonnet, with the following instruction:
"To Citizen Ransonnet &c.:
"You are going to take, citizen, the command of the two large boats to proceed to Turtle Island in order to procure yourself as great a quantity as you possibly can, my stay in this bay having no other object than that.
"As soon as the boat has its load, you will return at once on board. Although it is provided with six days' provisions, you will make every effort to be back before having consumed them.
"If the turtles are difficult to take, you will not permit any to be killed ashore for the use of the boats' crews, and will reserve them all for the general consumption on board.
"You will complete the loading of the large bastringue boat as soon as it arrives, so that it may return at once and without waiting for you. You will take care to have gathered the objects of curiosity or natural history that chance may cause you to meet with and will hand them all to me on your arrival on board.
"As the coxswain of your boat, Lefevre, knows the place where the turtles keep and has already been employed in this fishing in the time of the Naturaliste, he will conduct you to the place where there is the most hope of finding some." N. B.
After the departure of these craft, I despatched two others for line fishing and to seek an easy landing place. Four men were embarked in the one and three in the other, with orders to be back on board after sunset.
During the day, we occupied ourselves in changing some of our sails which needed fairly considerable repair.
On the return of the boats I was very astonished to learn that they had not been able to land, because a band of natives, whose number was put at more than a hundred, had opposed their landing and appeared strongly determined not to permit it. All were armed with spears, clubs and shields. As long as they were in sight of our people, who prudently kept out of range of their weapons, they were in continual agitation, running here and there and brandishing their spears.
It is probable that the fright they caused our people troubled them so much that they could not properly judge the number, some putting it as high as two hundred and the least frightened at thirty or forty, but all agreed in saying that (they were) very tall men, strong and vigorous, wearing a long black beard which came down onto their chests.
As I did not believe this part of the coast inhabited, the pousse-pied and the small boat were not provided with arms for their personal safety. This news and these details, which I hardly expected, made me take the resolution to make acquaintance with this people if it were possible. And to accomplish this, I gave orders that the longboat be prepared for the next day and that it be put to sea at daybreak.
During the day, I sent to fetch Citizen Freycinet, commanding the Casuarina, and gave him orders to set under sail for the next morning, prescribing him to make his course directly to the north, as far as twenty-four degrees of latitude, and afterwards to tack back and forth to return to the anchorage where we were. By this means I wished to ascertain whether the course to leave the bay by the north and gain the open sea was practicable, or whether the shoals which I suspect exist between the southernmost of the Dorre islands and the north point of the peninsula where we are, leave a channel that can be crossed without danger.
During the night, we had a fairly pretty breeze from south-south-west and the sea smooth. The sky was very damp and the horizon laden with vapours, although the stars were very bright.

1803-03-18.journal_anonyme: The sky overcast, the horizon thick, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 17° 58' 50", est. long. 6° 56' 36". Var. 17° 29' 20" NW.
1803-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at daybreak, the Casuarina got under sail to carry out the mission I had given her the previous day, which was, as I have already said, to go and make certain whether there was a practicable passage between the northern point of the Peninsula of Dampier and the islands of Dorre.
For our part, we put our launch to sea to go and make a landing, and I gave the command of it to Citizen Ronsard, with the instruction below:
"To Citizen Ronsard, Lieutenant of the ship,
"You are going to take, citizen, the command of the launch and the small boat, and you will go and land in the place that the second mate Le Beau will point out to you.
"According to the details he has given me, it appears that the extremity of this peninsula is fairly inhabited and that several families of natives are established there. The object of your mission is to make acquaintance with them, employing every means that may contribute to it, whether by the gestures customary in such cases, or by the sight of the presents you are bringing them.
"If one were to rely on all that has been told us by the men I had sent fishing, not only would the natives they saw be extraordinary men, but also little disposed to let you land. You must therefore conduct yourself with prudence and be continually on your guard.
"Take care above all not to make use of your arms until you have tried to make your landing without resorting to this means, for you must be persuaded that a few shots fired with powder alone will disperse them in such a way that you will no longer have occasion to meet them.
"You will leave armed men to guard the launch, and you will not advance too far into the interior of the country with those who accompany you, so as to be better able to protect it should circumstances require it, or should you be obliged to re-embark to avoid coming to extremities unfortunate for the natives.
"You will return on board this evening, together with all those who accompany you, to the number of 15 persons, not counting those who are in the small boat." Signed N. B.
When our launch approached the coast, we followed it with our eyes, observing all its movements. We saw it drop its grapnel, furl its sails, and all those who were in it go ashore without their appearing to us to meet the least difficulty. As several of those who had landed were seen walking on the shore, at a
fairly great distance from one another, it was conjectured that the natives, having seen that we were numerous, might have withdrawn, and that perhaps they would not even be met with.
Be that as it may, I was very impatient to see my launch return, which was not to come back until evening, and the wait for its return made this day very long for me, although I employed it entirely on geographical work for the construction of our charts.
At last, at six o'clock, it arrived, together with all those who had accompanied Citizen Ronsard. According to this officer's report, no one was encountered although a fairly great extent of ground had been traversed. Twelve or fifteen huts, much better made, however, than those met with until then, composed the village where this tribe lived. In some of them was found fire still lit but no household utensil, proof that the natives had abandoned them only after our departure. Among these dwellings, some were thought to be plainly recognised as belonging to the heads of the family, in that they were much larger and made with far more symmetry. Intending to send someone to make a drawing of them, I reserve making their shapes known when they are better known to me than from the report that has been made to me. No water was found in the vicinity of this village, which seemed to me very astonishing.
This part of the peninsula is entirely devoid of large trees. Nothing is found there but sparse bushes, and the soil is sandy in some places, of a red ochreous earth in others, which appears little suited to vegetation.
Our botanists brought back from this excursion only three or four new plants. Citizen Péron, a basket full of broken shells, and the hunters, four species of birds which had nothing particular about them.
Our small boat, which had spent its time fishing, was more fortunate than all the others, having having (sic) a full load of good and fine fish, most of which were of those the sailors call big-backs, and of which I had a drawing made.
As we rested a fairly long time in the huts of the natives, some presents were left there on leaving, consisting of glass beads, metal buttons, a small mirror, and a snuffbox with a negro's portrait on it. Perhaps, if any of them, having observed us during the day, comes to see what has been done in their dwelling, the sight of these presents may induce them to place more trust in us.
During the night the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate from south-south-west to south-east. Towards two o'clock it passed to the east, almost calm.

1803-03-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from ESE to SE. At daybreak sighted Saint Helena bearing NE by compass. Obs. lat. 15° 46' 25", est. long. 8° 13' 36". Var. 14° 19' 40" NW.
1803-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, I again sent my launch ashore under the command of Ensign of the ship Bonnefoy. The purpose of this second trip was not only to try to make acquaintance with the natives but also to employ the crew in making salt by boiling sea water in large cauldrons which were prepared expressly for this operation. As the fishing was abundant, I wanted to salt the fish that was its produce and which could not be kept for twenty-four hours, on account of the great heat. As our supply of salt was beginning to diminish considerably, it was necessary to have recourse to this expedient, all the more since there remained on board, for the ship's consumption, only enough for four to five months.
The launch had orders to spend the night ashore and not to return until the following evening.
I sent on this occasion the draughtsman to make a drawing of the natives' village and of the shape of their huts. The gardener Guichenot was also of the party, to gather plants for us. Among the naturalists, Citizen Péron was the only one who went ashore, the others not finding that the country deserved to be examined with more care than they had already given it in the small extent they had been able to see or traverse.
In the morning, the winds, which had passed to the east, returned, as usual, to the south-south-west, and the breeze was very moderate.
In the afternoon, the small boat had orders to go fishing and to spend the night there, so as to be back on board the following day before the heat of the day, for the preservation of the fish it might take. On board, we occupied ourselves with various works relating to the ship, awaiting only the return of the Casuarina and of the two boats which were turtle-fishing, in order to get under sail.
