During the night, nothing new occurred. We had constantly in view the fire around which our people were gathered, and no movement was seen on their part that could give rise to concern. The south-south-west breeze lasted all night and was fairly fresh, but we had a great deal of humidity although there was not a single cloud in the whole sky.
1803-03-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak Saint Helena was sighted in the N 45° E; at noon it bore from us S 43° E to S 58° E. The day after our departure from Mauritius a man was found who had hidden himself aboard at sailing.

1803-03-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, and squally at the end of the watch. At noon the course was shaped NNW. Obs. lat. 13° 50' 21", est. long. 10° 9'.
1803-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, our small boat returned from fishing, as had been agreed, and brought back such a great quantity of fish that, after distributing it abundantly to the whole crew, we did not know what to do with the rest. A great quantity of it was prepared, sprinkled with salt, and exposed to the sun to dry.
One of the punts, which had set out from morning to go fishing for crabs, shellfish and oysters, returned at noon with a second load of fish, so abundant was it. But it found neither crabs nor shellfish, only a few oysters shaped like a cock's comb. It was decided to cook the fish it had brought, so as to be able to keep it for the following day.
During the day the weather was very fine and the winds from the south to south-west by south, a light breeze.
At sunset I was astonished to see that on board the launch no preparation was being made to come on board, but as the officer I had embarked in her had express orders to be back before nightfall, I presumed that not everyone having yet come in, he had been delayed by the absence of one of them, among whom was undoubtedly Citizen Péron.
Be that as it may, at eight o'clock in the evening, seeing again the same fires that had been kept up the previous evening, I gave orders for a gun to be fired to recall this boat on board. At ten o'clock in the evening, not seeing it return, a second was fired, which had no more success. So that I lost hope of making, the following day, the tour I had planned to carry out myself in the south-western part of this peninsula. As the absence of my launch was formal disobedience to the orders that the officer commanding her had received from me, I have had 30 francs charged to his account for the two gun-shots with powder that he obliged me to expend to recall him.
The rest of the night had nothing particular about it; it blew little, or rather it passed in calm, with a very damp sky, often hazy.

1803-03-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 12° 5' 52", est. long. 11° 29' 0".
1803-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, in the morning, when the day was far enough advanced to make out and distinguish objects ashore, the launch was at last seen under sail, but as there was little wind, she had fallen a good deal to leeward, carried away by the ebb tide, which was bearing her to the north-west.
The weather was very fine until eight o'clock, but then there suddenly arose so thick a fog that we lost sight of both the land and the launch. This fog lasted until eleven o'clock, after which the weather turned fine again.
At half past one, the launch having returned and been made fast alongside, the officer commanding her informed me that he was bringing back six hundred pounds of very fine salt which had been gathered in a salt-water pond that at present was almost dry. After the information about what he had had to do ashore, I asked him why he had not conformed to the orders I had given him to return by sunset the following day. He then informed me that he had found himself in a very awkward position through the absence of Citizens Péron, Guichenot and Petit,
who, having left him in the morning without telling him anything of their plans, did not appear in the afternoon, but that as they had set out without water and without provisions, he had presumed that they could not be far from the meeting place, unless they had lost their way. He added that at four o'clock, not seeing them come in, he immediately sent off four armed men, who searched for them in different directions until nightfall and returned without having met them. Citizen Bonnefoy, fearing my reproaches at not bringing everyone back, and knowing well that he would be blamed for not having returned, preferred to spend the night waiting still longer. And at last, about nine o'clock in the evening, the three absent persons reappeared, worn out with fatigue, exhausted by hunger and thirst. Two of them lay down twelve or fifteen paces from the tent, and it was necessary to carry them there to bring them in.
From fuller details I was informed that Citizen Péron, the most thoughtless and improvident of all those on board, had persuaded the other two to cross the island from east to west, assuring them that it was at most a league in width, that he had made certain of this by examining the chart, and that consequently they had much more time than they needed to make the excursion he proposed. To decide them still further, he promised Citizen Guichenot an ample collection of new plants which they would not fail to meet with, and Citizen Petit much variety in his amusements, which was very agreeable to him. At last, all having followed Citizen Péron and adopted his plan, they set out. They began first by climbing a fairly high elevation, from which the ship was distinctly visible. This same height, on which stood a fairly tall tree, was taken as a landmark, and they were to come back to it again on their return. It was therefore from this point that they took their bearings to make the league of ground which was the width they had to cross.
After having walked about four hours together without the least interruption and in the full heat of the sun, the gardener Guichenot said to Citizen Péron: "but the league you announced to us is growing very long, and I think it is time to think of returning, for we must have as much ground to cover to rejoin the launch as we have covered since our departure." Citizen Péron well felt the justness of this reasoning, but got himself out of the difficulty by saying: "we have not kept enough to the left, that is what will have lengthened our march; let us now take this direction and we shall very soon reach our goal." He was followed like an experienced guide, and while they were advancing, several natives appeared armed with spears. They were at first afraid of them, having for their whole defence only a poor musket which they had borrowed from the provisions clerk and which was incapable of firing, as they found out. The natives continuing to pursue them, they conceived that it was more convenient to impose upon them by an assured bearing than to flee before them, and
from then on, they decided to go to meet them.
The natives, in their turn, stopped, but seeing that the others still advanced, they did on their side what ours had done on theirs. However, their advance was less hurried, and our men approached them closely enough to make each other out clearly. They began first by signalling to our three frightened men to follow them, which the latter took good care not to attempt. As the two parties were stopped facing one another, all the natives except one withdrew to one side. It was thought this was the chief. This would doubtless have been the moment to approach him too, but as no move was made to do so, the chief, apparently, advanced a few paces, made great gestures signalling to them to go away, and spoke very loudly. He was exactly obeyed, for our wandering travellers, not finding themselves in sufficient force, left them to resume the route which was to lead them to the seashore, on the other side of the island, where they at last arrived one o'clock after noon.
The finest opportunity that had presented itself for holding communication with the natives was missed on this occasion. And the draughtsman whom I had sent off expressly to draw those we might approach did nothing but a perspective view of the village where lived those we had met at our first landing on the island.
Having abandoned the natives, they set about searching for shells and brought back several absolutely similar to those found and brought back in abundance by the Naturaliste. This reflection alone should have sufficed to make them think of returning. But the leader of the party, the citizen who, up to this moment, had caused us nothing but trouble and worry whenever he was put ashore with no one to watch over and guide him, preferred to lose the time remaining to him roaming the seashore rather than turn back. So that they did not set out to return until with the certainty of being unable to be back before the time fixed for departure, even supposing they took the most direct route. Be that as it may, our travellers thought, rather late in truth, of returning, having neither water nor provisions. The night that came on increased their difficulty so much that they lost their way and went completely astray. Chance alone served them better in this circumstance than their bearings had done, for they found themselves on the opposite shore at the very moment when their reckoning of the distance covered still placed them three leagues away from it.
Citizen Péron having come to announce his return to me, he told me he was in a state unable to give me an account, and asked me to grant him, before making his report to me, the long rest of which he doubtless had very great need, since he could scarcely speak or hold himself up.
The rest of the day had nothing particular about it. The gardener Guichenot did not find a single plant and was made ill by fatigue,
for having good-naturedly carried the whole way a weight of twenty-five to thirty pounds of poor shells, gathered with as much pleasure as care by Citizen Péron, whom it was necessary to carry himself in order to bring him to the tent.
This is the third escapade of this kind that this learned naturalist has given us, but it will also be the last, for he will not go ashore again except when I myself am in the boat that takes him, and the limits I shall set for his excursions will not be extensive enough to delay the boat's departure, nor for him to be able to go far astray.
During the night the weather was fine and nothing particular occurred. We had the winds at south-south-west and the sky fine, though more clouded than usual.

1803-03-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. Est. lat. 10° 46' 22", est. long. 12° 34'. Var. 14° 1' 30" NW.
1803-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first Germinal, I sent off at daybreak my launch to go and fetch plants for our kangaroos, as she had not brought me back the day before those I had told her to fill up with, most of the men detailed for this work having been employed in the search for Citizen Péron and his company.
The small boat was likewise sent out fishing.
At ten o'clock we saw with pleasure Citizen Ransonnet returning from his mission, and if he brings us back a good number of turtles, we shall not have to regret the six days I had sacrificed in advance for this port of call, although it has procured us few objects for natural history.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, the boats were back on board, but we were disappointed in our expectation, for they had only six turtles each, among which there were only three of a weight of about two hundred and fifty to three hundred pounds, the other nine being of 25 to forty pounds.
According to Citizen Ransonnet's report, they were very difficult to take. And to procure them, the crews of the boats were obliged to take them in the water and to advance onto the banks where they lay, up to as much as four feet of water, which made the fishing very difficult and even dangerous, since a man named Lefevre was attacked by a large shark, which he was able to overcome and beat off only after stunning it and spearing it with harpoon-thrusts. These turtles, at least the smaller ones, were put into cut-down tubs with orders to take good care of them until we should be in need of them for our use.
Little was brought back in the way of natural history objects from this excursion, only some common shells, and as we already had many of these, they were nevertheless well paid for by our naturalists and scientists, who bought them from the sailors in payment of rum, so much so that in the evening sixteen persons were brawling in every part of the ship and I myself was obliged to strike several of them to obtain quiet. This was not the first time that a similar disorder had occurred. I had thought to remedy it by forbidding anything to be paid for with rum, but every prohibition is null for scientists such as ours, who believe themselves independent. I gave a particular order to the provisions clerk that he was henceforth not to issue a single drop of rum without an order signed by me, on pain of being suspended from his duties.
In the afternoon, the breeze was so strong from the south-west that I lost hope of seeing my launch arrive before nightfall. The Casuarina, which we had sighted from ten o'clock in the morning, had likewise fallen so far to leeward that we did not see her again until about four o'clock in the evening, and she did not reach the anchorage until about five o'clock.
As my intention was to get under way early the following day, I was very greatly put out by this circumstance, being unable to bring on board the four boats I had out until the launch had been placed there.
According to Mr Freycinet's report, it appears that the exit from Shark Bay by the north, passing between the Bernier and Dorre islands and the peninsula that Dampier did not know, is fairly difficult, and that one must be continually on one's guard, or else know the channel that lies between the banks which run out in different directions from these two pieces of land. It has often happened to the Casuarina to fall suddenly from eight fathoms to four, and from four to two or three, without knowing too well whether she should seek more water on the southern course or on the northern. As I had not foreseen all these difficulties, although I had myself become entangled among some of these banks in coming to seek the peninsula, which, like Dampier, I had taken for an island, I had not given him time to examine them well and to fix their position, which would require lengthy work and small boats to cross them in every direction.
Citizen Freycinet's report decided me to leave the bay by the same place where I had entered it, and I gave him orders to get under sail as soon as he should see us make our dispositions to get under way. I also very strongly recommended that he keep close to us during the night, on the new course we were going to make, as the only means of avoiding a separation.
During the night, the breeze was very strong; nevertheless, we did not need to pay out any cable, although we had only forty fathoms out. At half past eleven the launch arrived, but as a great part of her crew was drunk, thanks be rendered to the officers and naturalists, I put off embarking her until the following morning.
Particular remarks on the extent of coast
comprised between Cape Leeuwin and
the entrance of Shark Bay, discovered by Dampier.
The survey we have just made of the whole part of the coast named Leeuwin's Land, much more satisfactory than that made the first time we visited these waters, leaves nothing more to be desired; the direction and the various contours of the land will henceforth be well known, as will the two dangers which navigators who may frequent it will have to avoid, and which, at first, had escaped our notice.
It results, then, from our latest observations, made with all the more care because the weather and the winds served us generally rather well, that from Point Leeuwin as far as Rottnest Island, there is to be found no place that can offer a sure shelter against winds from north-east to south-west by the west, throughout the whole extent of this depth. And that indeed one can anchor only in the place we have named the Baie du Géographe, where the bottom is clean and suitable for anchoring. But this bay is good only in the fine season and when the breezes from north-east to south-east are moderate there. Even then, landing is not always easy there. Moreover, the coast is sound and can be ranged closely along its whole extent. It presents no dangers other than those marked on our charts, and whose position, being well determined, makes it easy to guard against them.
Although I did not anchor at Rottnest Island, this place, according to the report of Captain Hamelin and what I myself have seen of it, does not appear to me any more capable of sheltering a ship from bad weather than those places I have just spoken of, and all these places offer only a passing refuge, and only in fine weather in the fine season.
One thing that rather surprised us during this last period in which we have explored this coast is that we did not meet with a single living whale, and only three dead ones, whereas the first time we visited it, they were there in such great numbers that we were often inconvenienced by them. This difference doubtless comes from the season, which in all likelihood does not suit them. For it is a fact that we did not see a single one. Moreover, a longer series of observations on this subject would be needed to be able to say exactly what the case is. But it does not seem doubtful to me that ships intended for this fishery, arriving at the same time of year that we first came here, would promptly make their cargo and with much success. We never saw a single seal there.
Setting out from Rottnest Island, where some seals are found, we did not follow the coast to reach Shark Bay, since it has been well seen and represented by the Dutch, whose chart needs only the corrections occasioned by the imperfections of the instruments still in use when they made their survey of it. It was only after rounding the Abrolhos that we closed with it again.
My first entry into Shark Bay was made by the north, as I judged it easier to be able to penetrate as far as the inner reach by means of the west and south-west winds, which seemed to have continued to prevail and dominate up to that time. But the shallowness of the waters at low water, and the various sandbanks, not having allowed me to pass to the north or to the west of the land which seems to form an island in the middle of the channel, and which I believed indeed to be one, according to the report of the Dutch and of Dampier, I was obliged to turn back and to leave by the same place I had entered. This last time, having entered by the same passage as Dampier, I came to anchor in the northern part of this peninsula. And having had the channel examined which separates it from the southernmost of the Bernier and Dorre islands, I made certain that it is practicable and that one can leave by steering north. But that the passage between the sandbanks found there is not practicable for a large ship unless it be better known. The bank which lies between Dirk Hartog Island and the southernmost of the Bernier and Dorre islands is all the less dangerous in that the sea breaks strongly on it and it can be seen from more than a league off. It is only after rounding this bank in working up towards the east that the bottom decreases rapidly; one finds from 13 down to nine fathoms in the two-thirds of the distance to be made to reach the north point of the peninsula, and the course is south-east with the ebb, in order to guard against the effect of the current which sets to the north-west. On the flood, I think that by steering east one would get there in a straight line. At about two-thirds of the channel, the soundings are very irregular, between eight, seven, six and five fathoms, and we had them in this manner in making for the anchorage, by this last set of soundings, at about two leagues from the land, the nearest to the ship bearing east. But had we advanced a quarter of a league further, we should have had five and a half, six, and even seven fathoms, closer to the shore.
This anchorage appeared to us the surest and most convenient of all we made on the coast of New Holland. We had there a constantly smooth sea, and yet fairly strong breezes from south-south-west to south-west, without the ship ever dragging, although we had only forty fathoms of cable out. We found fishing very abundant in this place, and the natives little sociable, for it was not possible to approach them despite all our attempts to succeed in it. They even abandoned the village in which they were gathered on our arrival, and if those met with since in the eastern part of the island are not the same, there is every reason to believe that we never saw them again.
In the indentation which Shark Bay makes to the south-east, there is an infinity infinity (sic) of places offering shelters as sure as they are convenient for merchant ships of medium size and drawing no more than twelve feet of water. They would be so sheltered there from every wind that they would have nothing to fear. This place might perhaps deserve to be inhabited, were it regarded as a place suitable for the whale fishery, the only trade on this coast that can offer an advantage not to be neglected. I am persuaded that it was for reasons of policy that the Dutch did not give us a more accurate plan of it than that indicated by their charts.
As Captain Hamelin has thoroughly surveyed the whole of this part, and it has been carefully done, judging by the details of the plan he gave of it, I did not linger there, all the more since it would have required too long a stay for me to have it examined afresh. I had entered this bay only to procure turtles, and in this I was not very fortunate, since, as I have already observed, we took only twelve, owing to the season being contrary, it not being the time for laying, and we were obliged to take, in the water on the eastern banks, those that were brought back. But they are none the less abundant there for that, and in more favourable seasons an advantageous use could be made of them for trade. I do not know whether the shell is fit for trade, but this may be judged from the samples I am bringing to Europe.
Although fresh water was not found in the small searches that were made, it is not to be presumed that this part of the bay contains none, and even a fairly considerable quantity, if one looks at the signs which indicate that some must be found there.
I had always regarded as very extraordinary, and I would even say improbable, a fact reported by Dampier, who says he found in a shark's stomach part of a hippopotamus's head, but from the dead animal found, on Turtle Island, by the men of the boat who had gone there to fish, it hardly seems doubtful that the teeth they brought back, and which they handed over to me, belonged to a similar species. According to the information given to me, this animal might have been six feet long. It was dead and half rotten. Its head, according to their estimate, might have been a third of the size of its body; its tail was about two feet long. Its mouth, large and well open, was furnished with teeth similar to those of which I give the sample, but they did not count the number of them. As this animal was on the seashore and half buried in sand, they saw neither feet nor fins, for they took it for a fish. Its skin was a
dark grey, thick and rough to the touch, having some marks of hair of the same colour, but in small quantity. As the odour it gave off was not very pleasant, they did not attempt to turn it upside down to find out how it was made, and whether it had feet or fins.
However imperfect the description given to me of this animal may be, I believed I recognised a perfect resemblance to the hippopotamus, which is well known to me, having killed several in the river of Quitangonha in the vicinity of Quirimba on the coast of Africa. The arrangement of its teeth in particular seemed to me absolutely similar, and the scientists of Europe will judge, after having seen them, whether this conjecture is true or false.
The encounter with a fine specimen of this animal in these waters seems to indicate that there must be, in the vicinity of the places it frequents, some fresh-water lagoons where it goes to drink, for everyone knows that it makes use of them and that, although amphibious, it comes ashore every night and even sometimes during the day to graze and drink.
The men who were in the fishing boats swam across two or three arms of the sea which run into Turtle Island, of which they made the circuit, but which, according to the distance they say they covered, would appear to be larger than shown on the chart given of it by Citizen Faure, who was sent expressly to visit it and who saw nothing of it.
As I also do not know whether the shell of the turtle that can be fished in this bay is fit for trade, I have particularly recommended that the plates be kept, so that the Government may have it examined. This would be one more resource, if it proves good, for navigators who might undertake the whale fishery trade in these waters and in the Baie du Géographe. And, should it prove otherwise, it would still always be a resource for refreshing their crews.
Astronomical Observations
Latitude of the ship's anchorage 25° 30' 50"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 31 111° 27' 26"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 35 111° 12' 24" mean 111° 29' 59" (sic)
(In reality 111° 19' 59)
Longitude corrected for the error of the timekeepers 111° 0' 0"
Latitude of the north point of the peninsula observed ashore: 25° 29' 45", longitude 111° 7' 35"
Declination of the magnetic needle 5° 33' 59", mean term of 11 observations.
Note: during the stay at anchor and ashore, it was observed that the tides were very irregular and that their strength and duration depended much more on the winds and their directions than on the general laws of the ebb and flow of the sea. When the winds were from the south-west, they rose very high and fell little; with winds from the east, it was quite the contrary.

1803-03-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A pleasant breeze from SSE and ESE. Obs. lat. 9° 16' 30", est. long. 13° 44' 48".
1803-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
the north point of Dirk Hartog Island bore south 44° west.
The middle of the breaker which lies in the channel bore north 44° east.
The western point of Dorre Island bore north 20° east.
At the same time a reef was seen, on which the sea broke heavily, on the eastern coast of Dirk Hartog Island, bearing south 3° east.
Historical events & Remarks &c.
On the second, 23 March, about an hour before daybreak, we made our dispositions to hoist in our launch and the four other boats we had to bring on board. The work could not be finished until seven o'clock. Immediately after, we loosed the topsails in preparation for getting under way, and we weighed our anchor, which was catted at half past seven. In leaving the anchorage off the Peninsula of Dampier, we made much the same course to leave the bay as we had made to enter it. As the lead was cast continually on this course, just as had been done on the other, we found, with little difference, the same bottom. However, I thought I noticed that the soundings were more regular than we had found them on entering. The bottom, out at sea half a league from our anchorage, was 7, 8, 9, 8, 7, 9, until in sight of the reef which lies in the middle of the channel between the north point of Dirk Hartog Island and the south point of the first of the Bernier and Dorre islands. From the sighting of this danger, bearing then north-north-west, and on which the sea breaks heavily, which renders it less to be feared, the bottom begins to increase, and one passes rapidly from 9 fathoms to 10, 11, 12 & 15, after which no bottom is found with the hand lead if the ship is making headway and doing four knots.
We passed the reef of which I have just spoken, at about the same distance as we had passed it on entering, that is to say at three or four miles at most.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 25° 25' 53" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35, reduced to the same time, put us at 110° 34' 42".
Having rounded the reef, we successively brought the course further to the north until, having rounded the south point of the first of the Bernier and Dorre islands, we were able to steer directly north to continue along its coast on its western side.
However, as we had nothing to do on this coast, and as I feared the calm of the night, I kept out to sea, and so as not to be delayed, I directed my course to come and make out the north-west point as promptly as would be possible for me.
During the evening the weather continued fine and it blew a good breeze from south by south-west to south. During the evening little sail was carried, so as to conform to the Casuarina's progress.
During the night we had a sky far less fine than usual. The atmosphere became laden with vapours and we had a great deal of humidity. The lead, which at eight o'clock had given forty-five fathoms, was ninety at midnight and eighty-five at four o'clock in the morning, bottom of small gravel.

1803-03-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 7° 57' 31", est. long. 14° 42' 18". Var. 12° 26' NW.
1803-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock in the evening, the Bernier and Dorre islands were to be seen from
south-east to north-east by east.
At six o'clock, the point of the northernmost of them was thought to bear north-north-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, 24 March 1803, we steered north 22° 30' east, which is the direction the coast takes after rounding the point which forms the northern entrance of Shark Bay, to the north of the second of the Bernier and Dorre islands. We did not see the land during the day, which is perhaps due to the current having carried us further to the west than our reckoning of the course made showed. This conjecture appears to be confirmed by the result given by the timekeeper at noon, since it gave us 29 minutes 57 seconds of distance to the west, whereas the reckoning of the course gave only 20' 27". Moreover, as the land is very low in this part and the depth considerable at a short distance from the seashore, we were not astonished at not seeing it and at having a great deal of water.
During the morning, the weather, though fine, was not as pleasant as we had had it on the preceding days. Many clouds in the atmosphere often enveloped the sun without the heat being any less strong for it, since the thermometer rose to 24° at noon. We had not had it at so great an elevation for a long time.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 23° 20' 50" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 110° 4' 45".
The north-north-east course was continued in the evening, which made us continue along the coast, of which, nevertheless, we had no sight. We had, all day, the sight of many tropicbirds and white gulls with red beaks and feet. An eagle also came to perch on our topgallant crosstrees, and we should have taken it alive had not the man who was to catch it been afraid of it when he went to seize it.
At eight o'clock, not having found (the bottom) at a hundred fathoms, the north-north-east course was continued. Soundings were taken at midnight and at four o'clock without more success, which made me fear being further out from the coast than I thought.
During the night the sky continued to be very cloudy and damp, but the breeze was moderate and the sea less agitated than during the day. Little sail was carried on account of the Casuarina, which nevertheless had often to be waited for.

1803-03-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SSE. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 6° 11' 59", est. long. 15° 48' 18".
1803-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, 25 March 1803, in the morning, persuaded that we could not be far from the coast and that we should close with it easily before noon, in the vicinity of the Rivière Guillaume, I brought the course much more to the east than I had done until then. But despite this, having had no sight of the land, I could plainly perceive that there was an error in the course I had kept, but I did not know to what to attribute it.
At noon, the latitude having been observed at 21° 16' 50" and the longitude by No. 35, which I had always used, put us at 111° 20' 18". I was as astonished to find myself to the north of the north point as at having passed it in longitude without having noticed it. From this, the error was evident, and as it now only remained to find it, I accordingly asked Citizen Bernier to come by, and asked him how it happened that he had placed the longitude of the north-west point of New Holland at 110° 16' 40".
Citizen Bernier then observed to me, rightly, that the longitude I had taken was that given by the timekeeper at that time, but he added: "if you had taken what the correction of this timekeeper has produced, it is quite different, since it puts it at 111° 50' 40"." I had nothing to reply to his observation and acknowledged my error. But as I wished to sight this point a second time before standing further to the north and to the west east, I had her brought close-hauled, on the course south towards east, which was continued until ten o'clock at night, and then I ran an offshore board, not thinking it prudent to advance further in the darkness, although at that time the lead had brought up no bottom at eighty fathoms.
During the night, the breeze was strong, and we took a second reef in the topsails to relieve the Casuarina, which was carrying a press of sail to keep up with us. The sky, which had had a fairly bad appearance during the day, became clearer and almost all the clouds disappeared. But the breeze was none the less strong for that, and did not begin to slacken until about two o'clock in the morning, at which time we resumed the inshore board, which was followed until daylight. Soundings were taken at four o'clock without finding bottom; we could not, however, have been very far from the coast at that time.

1803-03-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SSE. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 4° 8' 16", est. long. 16° 41' 6".
1803-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
the north-west point of New Holland was borne south 3° east.
The mainland was then to be seen as far as south 12° west.
To the south-east, several islets were made out from the mastheads, between which and the north-west point breakers could be distinguished.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, 26 March 1803, at the beginning of the day, we sighted the land, which extended from south-south-west to south-east by south, and according to my dead reckoning, we might be six or seven leagues from it. It is doubtless by error that the officer who was on watch at that time judged that its elevation had nothing remarkable about it, for if he knew that of the lands neighbouring this part he would have spoken of it quite differently. I would say, then, I who know it, that it is very remarkable, and may even serve as a landmark in case of need, for a coast that can be made out at six or seven leagues at sea cannot be considered, in the vicinity of New Holland and in the part where we are, as a low land deserving little attention.
In the morning, we continued to hold close-hauled on the course to the east, drawing a little to the south, so as to make out clearly the north-west point, which we sighted about ten o'clock in the morning.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 21° 31' 3" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 put us at 111° 51' 37". This figure, compared with the reckoning of the course we had made in the twenty-four hours, gave a difference of 24 minutes 41 seconds from the reckoning, so that it placed us further east, proof either that the course was badly reckoned, or that the currents carried us to the west-north-west, since there were also five minutes' difference in the observation of the latitude.
Having rounded the north-west point, we continued along it at a fairly great distance. Although in sight of the islets marked on the Dutch chart, six were counted in the morning. But a little before sunset we saw a seventh, of which this chart makes no mention, and which was borne east 11° 30' north.
As my intention was to steer east, taking to the north only as much as should be necessary to run along the coast, of which I had resolved to take note in this part, I made no way during the night and spent it beating to windward. At six o'clock, the bottom was 24 fathoms, and at half past seven we tried to anchor, but the weather did not permit it, the winds having blown strongly from south-south-west to south.
In running the board to the west towards the north, we soon lost the bottom, but in that to the south-east, we found it at 65 and 53 fathoms.

1803-03-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from SSE, the course north. The sea very phosphorescent. Est. lat. 1° 53' 46", est. long. 17° 9' 12".
1803-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset, the islets seen in the evening bore east 11° south as far as SE.
At eight o'clock in the morning, the land in sight extended from NE ¼ N to SE ¼ E.
At noon, the same land was to be seen from N 67°30' E as far as south 5° east.
We then had a chain of islands and islets extending from south 5° east as far as south 22° 30' east. The islets and islands seemed to join one another by reefs.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, 27 March 1803, at daylight, we sighted the land, but only from the mastheads, and it was not until eight o'clock that we could take its bearing from the deck. Its direction then was from north-east by north to south-east by east, and its distance from the ship about three leagues. We were then steering east towards south, in order to make out, if it were possible for us, the part of the coast that lay furthest to windward, so as afterwards to bear up to run along that which remained to us from east towards north. But at six o'clock, the colour of the water, which was all white, told us that we were coming onto a bank. The lead was cast at the same moment and the bottom was twenty-two fathoms (in an insert: no bottom, see the officers' log), I wished to continue on our course, when the lookouts warned me that, from the agitation of the sea, at about half a league's distance ahead of us, it did not seem probable to them that there was water there, and that if we continued, we should not fail soon to run aground. I saw for myself the agitation they spoke of, and I confess I was frightened by it. I ordered the helm put over at once to starboard, the sea appearing calmer there, and we passed without sounding, for it was no longer time to have recourse to that means, within musket-shot of this place, which it seems to me very prudent to avoid, although I saw no apparent danger there other than what may be concluded from an extraordinary agitation of the sea, visible only in this part. Having passed this danger, which I truly believe to be one, we bore up as far as north 22° 30' east, so as to run at a good distance along the coast, which did not appear at all sound to approach too closely. We then sighted several banks to the north-east and to the north, and we found ourselves very fortunate not to have become entangled in them. We passed one of these banks at about half a league at most.
In the morning, we ran along part of the mainland coast, which we closed with once out of danger. The land we had in sight was of moderate height, but so uniform that it offered few remarkable points. After following it for about three leagues, the course we were making, which was from north 34° east to north 44° east, brought us onto a second bank of great extent, onto which we ran, although the change in the colour of the water had told us of it long before we reached it. But as the land we had in sight in this part formed a great indentation, in the depth of which none was to be seen, I wished to make certain whether these were not the two extremities of two islands, or whether the opening we saw did not lead into some entrance that might offer a good port. The lead gave 19 fathoms at the edge of this bank. We continued to advance onto it, so much so that we then sighted a reef, on which the sea broke heavily, and which was no more than a league from us. Disappointed in our expectation, we quickly sought to draw away
from this place. But to accomplish it, it was necessary to steer from north 30° west to north 60° west. Several persons believed that the ship was touching bottom, in that in the place where the ship was passing, the sand appeared to mix with the water, but I am not of this opinion, and as it was necessary to get clear on the course we were making, having no better one to take, I did not wish soundings to be taken, so that too discouraging a decrease in the depth should not dishearten the crew.
Once clear of this second danger, we began to bear away, and at noon we were able, without fear, to steer north.
At the same time, the latitude was observed at 20° 31' 52" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 put us at 112° 57' 28". The lands we then had in sight, at a great distance, extended from north 67° 30' east as far as south 5° east.
In the afternoon we wished to close with the coast, having no bottom at 25 fathoms, but the lookouts at the mastheads soon told us that we were running onto a fresh danger, in that they saw, ahead of us and as far as under the lee of our course, a long line of reefs on which the sea broke heavily. Before thinking of changing course, I sent the master of the helm up to the crosstrees to make certain what it might be. His report having confirmed the lookouts' warning, it was indeed necessary to decide on a change of course, and in order to round this reef at a league and a half at most, we were obliged to steer north-west for quite a long time. At two o'clock it was plainly made out from the deck, and at three o'clock it bore east 15° north, at its northernmost part.
For this last danger we did what we had done for the others, that is to say we successively took the course from north towards east as we brought it round from east towards south. At four o'clock it was scarcely to be seen.
If one is to rely on what the lookouts say and on the opinion of those who went to examine these breakers, they think it is a sandbank which must cover at high tide and which has a very great extent from north to south, and someone claimed to have distinguished summits of rocks above the water in the middle of the bank. But although I examined this reef like the others, I saw nothing of the kind there. I only saw that it does not break uniformly throughout its whole extent, and that there are places where the water appears deeper, having perceived neither swell nor breakers there. Moreover, even should the reef offer some passage between it and the coast, from which it lies more than three leagues out, it would be better to seek to hug the coast, leaving it to port, than to try to close with it by passing through the cuts that might perhaps be found there.
From half past four until eight o'clock, we tried to close with the land; the bottom being then 28 fathoms, we steered first north-north-east and passed from 28 to 35 fathoms, sand and small gravel. We then put the helm to north-east and the bottom increased a further five fathoms. As night was coming on, we steered only north-east by east until eight o'clock in the evening, and then we hauled close-hauled on the port tack, to spend the night beating to windward.
During the day it had blown a pleasant breeze from south to south-south-west, and it was much less strong than it had been for three days. The sea, nevertheless, was fairly swollen, which led us to believe that the strong breezes we had met with had prevailed for a long time, but that perhaps they were about to cease.
We saw, all day, a considerable quantity of sea birds of every kind, especially on the banks we passed over. A few dolphins were also seen, and a single sea-snake with a broad, flat tail. This was the first we had seen on this second visit to the north-west coast of New Holland.
During the night the weather was fine and the breeze very moderate. We held the board to the west towards the north until six o'clock at night, and then took that to the south-east with winds from south south-south-west (sic). As the order was to sound every two hours, on the offshore board, fixed at four leagues, we passed from 42 fathoms to sixty-five, and on the inshore one from 65 to 45. The bottom increased and decreased in the same progression on the one course as on the other.

1803-03-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky overcast, the sea smooth, the winds SSE, a fresh breeze. Obs. lat. 0° 3' 55" north, long. W 17° 32' 42".
1803-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
At three quarters past two,
the north extremity of the reef was abeam of us, visible from the deck.
At four o'clock it was borne south 65° east.
At noon,
the lands most in view to the north and south were to be seen from south 70° east to south 66° west.
In the morning the reef of the previous day had been seen from the mastheads in the S.W.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, 28 March 1803, at daylight, we sighted the land, which was borne to the south-south-east at a great distance. It presents itself in the form of an island of about four to five leagues in extent, and more. It has its two extremities higher than in the middle (?), which made the lookouts believe they were seeing a succession of dunes. I thought it must rather be some part of the mainland, higher than the coast generally is, and that we should see the coast only on advancing to the south-east. The bottom was then forty-two fathoms. There was also seen, in the southern part towards the west, the reef we had coasted the day before. At seven o'clock, the land sighted at daylight became visible from the deck, and in its appearance as in its shape, it resembled perfectly an island isolated from all other land.
During the whole morning, we continued the board to the south-east, believing that from one moment to the next we should see the land, and yet not making it out ahead of us, having in view only that which was abeam of us. The bottom, until ten o'clock, was regular between 42 and 40 fathoms, but at noon it was no more than 32. This great depth of water at four leagues at most from the land we had in sight would seem to confirm that it was an island, for on the mainland coast this depth is not ordinarily found.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 20° 16' 55" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 113° 16' 16". We continued to steer south-east until two o'clock, when the winds having drawn further round to the west, we brought her as much to the south as was possible. Despite this, at sunset we had no land in sight.
From noon to four o'clock, the lead passed from 32 fathoms to 24, and from seven to eight o'clock from 24 to 16. So sudden a decrease, and so little proportionate to the distance we had made in this space of time, decided me to stand out to sea at once, and we took the board to the north towards the west until ten o'clock, when we steered north-north-east. The lead then increased rapidly and we passed successively from 16 fathoms to 36. And without our changing course, it decreased in the same manner.
We had, throughout the whole day, very fine weather and a pleasant breeze which varied as far as west-south-west. During the night the weather was no less fine, but the breeze was fresher; ever since we had been to the east of the north-west point, we had always had, during the night, winds much stronger than during the day. Yet when we visited this coast for the first time, we had found quite the contrary; perhaps the cause of this might be attributed to the season, which was not the same.
1803-03-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 11.30 a.m. we crossed the Line in 17° 32' of longitude.

1803-03-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from south to SSE. Est. lat. 1° 23' 31" north, est. long. 17° 55' 24".
1803-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daylight,
the land was seen from south by south-east as far as south-east,
and at seven o'clock,
the charting of the coast was begun, which was nothing but a succession of islands and islets of greater or lesser size, preceded by several rocks in front of them,
the lands seen in the distance were presumed to be those of the mainland.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the eighth, 29 March 1803, the weather continued fine. At sunrise we sighted, from the mastheads, the land which extended from south by south-east as far as south-east. We steered close-hauled to close with it. And at seven o'clock, it was distinctly to be seen from the deck. It presented itself to us in an extremely peculiar shape, full of cuts, so that we could not tell whether this land was a barrier of islands in front of the mainland, or the mainland itself, which presented so peculiar a shape. However, when we were no more than two leagues' distance from it, we could no longer doubt that the land we were running along was a great number of islands linked one within another, forming among them all the cuts we had noticed. These islands formed three ranges, one behind the other, and behind them all could be seen a coast very even in its shape, which we judged must be the mainland. The depth of water, at two leagues from the coast, was considerable, and we had, until noon, from 30 down to 28 fathoms of water.
At the same time, the latitude was observed at 20° 25' 2" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 114° 7' 46".
During the evening we continued to run along the land at the same distance we had done in the morning, and we passed abeam of a fairly great extent of islands and islets. The largest of them all did not appear to us to be more than three leagues from east to west. There were, in front of these islands and islets, several detached rocks and banks which often obliged us to change course to avoid them. The banks which extended fairly far out to sea were easily distinguished by the colour of the water, which was all white. Some of the channels we saw between these islets are perhaps practicable, and in this latter case, good shelters should be found there, provided the bottom is suitable for anchoring.
It is difficult to conceive why the geographers of every nation who have given us the plan of this part of the coast make no mention of it whatever, and have represented the mainland there without offering any difficulty in making it out. What we have seen proves only too well that they worked either from false recollections, or that, being unable to detail them, it was easier for them to suppress all the islands and make a mainland of them. But the fact is that in front of it there must be found a great number of islands, in every sort of direction. We took on board as many bearings as possible of this whole part of the coast, but as these islands merged so much one with another, I believe it still imperfect, despite every care having been taken with it. If what Dampier tells us in speaking of his Rosemary Islands is true, I shall not hesitate to believe that the place where we are is the one where he anchored within one of the channels formed by these islands, which are generally high, and such as he depicts them. In the position he was in, he must indeed have seen only islands, and we ourselves, without having crossed to the south of them, saw nothing but islands the whole day.
(in the margin, vertically) However, the latitude of 20° 26' cannot suit them, since they are evidently further south. After sunset, not wishing to draw away from the coast, I anchored in 18 fathoms, bottom of sand and coarse gravel. Seventy fathoms of cable were paid out and the ship remained fast on her anchor, although the breeze was very fresh. The speed of the current was one knot, but the fall of the water, neither on the ebb nor on the flood, was perceptible to us.

1803-03-30.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, calm; lay under topsails. At 5 trimmed on the starboard tack. Calm all night; at 7 a.m. a light breeze got up from the west. We at once went onto the port tack and made all sail. Est. lat. 1° 49' 25", obs. long. 19° 47' W.
1803-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock,
the west point of the largest island bore south 85° west,
And at six o'clock,
an archipelago of islands and islets was borne from north 78° west as far as south 22° east.
At eight o'clock in the morning,
the succession of the same lands was to be seen from north 77° west as far as south 7° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, 30 March 1803, as soon as day began to break, we made ready to get under sail, and at sunrise we got under way. We steered first east, drawing to the south, but we soon began to lose depth rapidly. From 18 fathoms we passed, in half an hour, to 15; a quarter of an hour after, we had no more than 12, then eight, and finally six and a half, which obliged us to stand a little further out to sea.
During the morning the breeze was very light, and the winds at south-south-west, variable; the bottom varied between eight and eleven fathoms, and we passed several of the islands abeam of which we had spent the night at anchor. In advancing to the east, we discovered others, but further apart from one another. To the south of these islands, the land, seen only from the mastheads, seemed to form a great bay or indentation to the south-south (sic), but the entrance of which was barred by shoals, onto which we advanced only as far as 6 fathoms and a half. It was judged that the lands seen to the south-south-east must form part of the mainland, in that no interruption sufficiently noticeable was to be seen there to make one believe these lands were still islands. At eleven o'clock the calm took us. But an hour after, we had a light breeze from the north, by means of which we were able to make a little headway to the east.
At noon, we observed the latitude at 20° 28' 40" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 114° 58' 45". It follows, then, that the island we had abeam of us was the one to which we had given, on the previous voyage, the name of Île des Amiraux. This island is, moreover, very remarkable for its shape and elevation, and seems to end, on the east, the great number of islands we had coasted along for two days.
A little to the east of the Île des Amiraux, some more high lands are still to be seen, and fairly elevated peaks, which seem to form another range of islands further south than that of the Amiraux. But we know that these peaks are part of the mainland and join with lower lands, continually decreasing in elevation, so that the coast, which I suppose to be part of the mainland, becomes so low that it can scarcely be seen from three leagues.
After sunset, we came to anchor, but as we then had only 7 to eight fathoms at about two leagues from the land, I did not wish to do so until I should have a bottom of ten fathoms. In order to reach this promptly, I had the ship steered north-east, but contrary to my expectation, we passed from 8 to 7. The helm was then put to north-east. We sailed more than half an hour in 6 fathoms. At seven o'clock, the two extremities of the points forming the northern ends of the bank we were passing over were plainly made out. The bottom, in this part, was five fathoms and a half for a moment, but afterwards we found 7, 8, 9, 10, and came to anchor. During the night we had the winds at west, a pleasant breeze, and the sky was fine.

1803-03-31.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to W. At 3 trimmed close-hauled on the port tack. Obs. lat. 2° 38' 27", est. long. 19° 56'.
1803-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
the Île des Amiraux, seen in Thermidor of Year Nine, bore from south 47° west to south 41° west.
The east extremity of the land most in view, at N 58° east.
At the moment of getting under way,
a dry sandbank was seen to the south 6° east.
A smoke borne from the land at eight o'clock, south 45° east,
bore at noon south 20° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, 31 March 1803, in the morning, we got under sail at sunrise. At the same hour, those I had sent as lookouts reported that the land was to be seen from south-east by east as far as south, but they added that at about three miles from us to the south, they saw an uncovered sandbank. This was doubtless the one over which we had passed, and whose two points, forming the northern extremity, had appeared to us to have very little water, the sea there being all white.
The winds, which at the moment of getting under way were at south-south-west, passed, after sunrise, to south-east, and varied in the course of the morning to east-south-east. The breeze was fairly strong until about eleven o'clock, after which it slackened imperceptibly, veering more towards the north. The bottom increased as we advanced on the course from east towards north, and at noon it was already 20 fathoms.
At the same time, the latitude was observed at 20° 4' 22" and the longitude of No. 35 was 115° 40' 35". Throughout the whole morning, several columns of smoke were seen rising at points of the horizon comprised between east and south-east. But the land was not seen for all that, which, as I have already observed several times, is visible in this part only at eight and ten fathoms of water.
About two o'clock in the afternoon, the winds appearing to want to go round the compass by way of the north, we tacked onto the course to the south-east and followed the direction they took, drawing nearer to the east. At four o'clock, the land was sighted, but as night was beginning to draw near and there was no likelihood of our being close enough to it before sunset to make it out well, we bore up to close with the Casuarina, and at seven o'clock, being in no more than eight fathoms of water, we anchored on a very fine bottom of sand and mud.
As there had been several disputes during the day among the officers, who did not, on leaving their watch, hand over the orders I had given them, I decided, to prevent this happening again in future, to prescribe in writing what each was to do when the ship was at anchor during the night and under sail during the day. What I enjoined upon them on this subject is transcribed in the log book.
During the night, the breeze was weak and more often calm. The winds held in the west-north-west to west-south-west until about seven four o'clock in the morning, when they passed to south and south-east. At seven o'clock they were at south-east, a good breeze.
The observations made to learn the rise or fall of the waters gave a difference of one fathom on the flood. The current was scarcely perceptible. A few sharks and small perch were taken during the night, whose colour was very pretty to see.
1803-03-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak a ship was sighted in the N 45° E. At 6.30 p.m. another was sighted to the east.

1803-04-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm until 11 p.m. Saw several ships. At 6 a light breeze from SSW; at 2 it drew round to NW. Est. lat. 2° 49' 9", est. long. 19° 55'.
1803-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, 1 April 1803, the winds having passed to south-east shortly after we had got under sail, did not allow us to make out very well the land we had in sight, all the more since it was very low and even, offering no points more remarkable than one another. From the mastheads, this land was seen to extend from east as far as south-west. At six o'clock, we lost sight of it entirely and perceived only various columns of smoke rising in different directions. On losing sight of the land, the bottom increased rapidly, and at noon we had eighteen fathoms, bottom of small red gravel.
I very much regretted that the winds, in the morning, had carried us as far from the land as they had done, since I feared we should not see it again before sunset, the breeze from west to north-west being ordinarily weak and slow to declare itself in the evening.
At noon, we observed the latitude at 19° 51' and the longitude of No. 35 was 115° 58' 13".
In the afternoon, the breeze from west to south-west or to north-west did not occur as we had had it on the preceding days, so that we entirely lost hope of seeing the land before sunset, nor even at that time. The winds having, nevertheless, varied from east to NE and to N.N.E., we steered south, drawing to the east, but the breeze was so weak that we made very little headway. As there was every appearance of a great calm for the night, we anchored at nine o'clock in the evening in 15 fathoms, bottom of sand and broken shells. The winds, at this same time, had passed to the west, and they were fairly fresh for the rest of the night.
The speed of the current, during the night, appeared to be eight-tenths of a mile, its direction being to the west. Neither the fall nor the rise of the waters was perceptible.
As the heat was extremely strong during the day, I had given orders that a kind of beverage be prepared for the men of the crew, and that a ration of it be distributed to each of them at ten o'clock in the morning and at two o'clock in the afternoon. This beverage was composed of lemon juice and syrup mixed in water. This occasioned a greater consumption of water than usual, but I experienced for myself how much they needed it.
The boat which had been sounding around the ship, having passed near the Casuarina, two sick men were sent to me on board, one attacked by a beginning of bloody flux and the other injured by a fall.
1803-04-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Saw tide rips running E and W. At 5 p.m. saw a sail in the S 68° W.

1803-04-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to west. At 10, the breeze having freshened from the NE, went onto the starboard tack. Est. lat. 3° 20' 21", long. 20° 18' 48".
1803-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, 2 April 1803, at sunrise, we got under sail, and I was rather surprised not to have sight of the land which I reckoned to be at a short distance. We steered south 68° east until eight o'clock, when it was reported to us, bearing east 11° south and visible at that time only from the mastheads.
At nine o'clock, the same land that had been reported to us, together with a long chain of reefs lying to the west and to the north of it, became visible from the deck, and we soon perceived that this land was known to us, having seen it the first time we approached this coast. I did not then think it was an island, and had persuaded myself that it was only an advanced point of the mainland, the lands of which were seen to the south-east. But the Casuarina having passed through the channel that lies between it and the mainland, this error is corrected. This island is no more than two leagues in extent from south-east to north-west, and has nothing remarkable but a great uniformity throughout its extent, ending in a low point at each extremity. Its width is not very considerable, and in ranging close along the island on its eastern side, one finds fairly regularly nine and eight fathoms of water. It may be four to five leagues distant from the mainland, which is of little elevation in this part.
In rounding this island we passed at a good league from the reef lying to the north of it, which is very extensive. It appears to be formed by a sandbank on which, here and there, fairly high rocks of different shapes are to be seen. The sea does not break equally everywhere over the whole extent of this bank, but in certain places it rises to such a height that it can easily be perceived at about two leagues. The bottom was not more than (no figure) fathoms when we ran along it, and part of the mainland was sighted, offering the same aspect as that we had previously passed.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 19° 49' 13" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 116° 23' 48".
In the afternoon, the winds were very weak, and we had them variable from W.SW to N.NW until sunset. In seeking to close with the land after having passed the long reef of which I have just spoken, we sighted the second danger on which the sea was breaking, but it was of little extent and we rounded it easily. It is likely that this whole part of the coast is little approachable and that the bottom there is extremely uneven. In the watch from noon to four o'clock, we sailed between ten and fifteen fathoms, but at this time we suddenly fell to five and a half, which did not last long. After which the lead brought up 9 and 10 fathoms, but this was not for long, and we passed again to 8, 7, 6, 5. I reckoned on being able to get clear of the bank we found ourselves on by steering north, but it was quite the contrary, for after increasing a little, it decreased again, and we passed from eight to 4 and to 3 almost at the same moment. I then had all sail backed and we wore round, sternway on,
which promptly brought us back to four and five fathoms. We continued for some time on the south-south-west board, still with the lead in hand and a sharp lookout, and in less than half an hour we had eleven fathoms. I reckoned on being able to anchor at this depth, but the bottom being only rocks and large coral, it was necessary to give this up and seek a better place. We therefore continued on the south-south-west board, since the water had been continually increasing, although on this course, which could not be long, we were running onto the land. After having made about half a mile from the last sounding, which had been eleven fathoms, the bottom passed from eleven to eight and from eight to seven, still rocks and coral. We then wore round to work up to the north, without finding any increase, and on the contrary the water kept decreasing. The winds being from the west to north-west, it was not possible for us to get clear of the dangers among which we found ourselves by the course that had brought us there. So that I sought to extricate us by steering successively more to the east whenever the bottom decreased in going towards the north. On the various courses we made, we increased as far as nine fathoms and fell again to three. We then bore away from east to south-east and to south and even to south-south-south-west, which brought us back to 9 and 10 fathoms for some time. On the south-south-west course, the land was sighted, from which it was necessary to draw away again, and in order to try every means of getting out of our difficult position, we steered north-east by east as long as we had 9 and 10 fathoms. At last, the lead, which until then had always brought up a bottom of rocks and coral, brought up one of fine sand fit for anchoring. But within the space of one or two minutes, we passed from nine to six, which decided me to anchor, all sail still set, the breeze having but little strength. It was then about ten o'clock.
The position in which we found ourselves was such that it was scarcely possible to keep account of the various courses we made on this bank, nor of the duration of each, and that which we have deduced from them is more the subject of reflection after the danger had passed than of observation made at moments when we expected to see the ship run aground.
Be that as it may, we were, in the interval from seven o'clock to ten o'clock, carried twice into three fathoms of water, and had we not anchored as hastily as we did, we should have fallen into it a third time, as will be seen from the soundings taken by the boats at about a cable and a half from the ship.
As on this occasion the Casuarina was near us, I ordered her to steer east-north-east about a league and a half and to sound continually, so as to make certain whether an outlet remained to us in this quarter, and to signal it to us by a light in the most conspicuous place on her ship. When she had left, I
had a boat put to sea and gave the command of it to the master of the helm, with orders to go and sound at two cables from the ship and to make the round of it within that circumference, observing above all to keep within musket-shot of the ship. This concerned a place which, by the light of the moon, appeared to me to contain much less water than we had at the anchorage, judging by the swell the sea seemed to have there.
On his return, I was informed that this place did indeed contain only three fathoms of water, but that it had very little extent, and that one passed suddenly from three to four and to five. To the east of the ship, he found no more than five to six fathoms; to the north, four to five; to the west, 6 to 7; and to the south, 4 for a fairly great distance. The north-east part appeared to him the clearest of all, for the extent to which he had advanced, the bottom there being more regular, between five and six fathoms. The bottom was everywhere of fine sand.
At one o'clock, the Casuarina having returned, told me that she had not found the extremity of this bank on the east-north-east course I had prescribed for her, but that she had never found the bottom below five fathoms. She observed to me that she had passed several times from five to eleven fathoms and from twelve fathoms to five, and that one must expect to find only these same irregularities in seeking to get out by this course. However little satisfying her report was, I was at least glad to know that there was water for the ship and that the bottom was not bad.
From the information I had just received, I decided to spend the night at anchor, at the risk of seeing the ship run aground should the tide be very strong; I knew at least that no harm would come to her and that the rising tide would refloat her, whereas by changing position I might take up a much worse one.
During the night, the weather was fine. We had the winds at NW variable to W.NW, and the breeze did not oblige us to pay out cable, having only 25 fathoms veered. They passed at midnight to south, and the weather remained very fine. Soundings were taken regularly every hour without any decrease being perceived in the depth of water. The current was likewise very weak, being found to have only 4 tenths of a knot of speed. By this means we were much more fortunate than I had hoped.

1803-04-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from N and NNE. At 7 a.m. a light breeze from NNW. Obs. lat. 3° 29' 2", est. long. 20° 22' 30".
1803-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, 3 April 1803, in the morning, we waited for sunrise to get under sail, so as to make out, by the colour of the water, which was the best course we had to take to get ourselves out of the banks in which we found ourselves entangled. For, from what had happened to us the day before, we supposed there were two, one to the north of the ship and the other to the east.
At daybreak, we first sighted the land, which bore from south-south-west to south by south-east, at an estimated distance of three leagues. But at sunrise, a portion of the bank over which we had sailed the previous night was recognised, which was dry, and which was not estimated, at its greatest distance, to be more than two miles from the ship. No rock was seen on this uncovered portion, only a reddish sand almost level with the sea.
We then got under way, and as soon as we were under sail, we steered north 67° west. But at this time, having run about a mile and a quarter, Mr Freycinet, who had been keeping a lookout, reported to me that he had plainly made out the direction of the bank, and that it made a great circuit, running from south towards east-north-east as far as the eye could reach. This warning made us take a little more to the north, and we made, on this new course, about two miles, finding 7 to 11 fathoms of water. We then steered north-east to follow its direction, which we believed we could make out from the deck, but we passed rapidly from eleven to 7 and from 7 to 5. As another portion of this bank lay to leeward of us, to the north, we bore away only a point and a half, and made made (sic) about two more miles on this course. After which, the water having progressively increased to 10 fathoms, we believed ourselves entirely clear of it, so that we brought our course more to the east as we went forward.
From eight o'clock to noon, we steered east to close with the land, from which the morning's course had taken us far enough to lose sight of it; the bottom held between 12 and 14 fathoms.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 19° 41' 28" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 put us at 117° 3' 26", which gave us a difference of 12' more to the east than our dead reckoning. The land was still to be seen from the mastheads. At this time, it is true that the wind was so weak during these four hours that we made more headway by the help of the current than with our sails. We saw pass, all morning, alongside, a great quantity of sea-plants of every kind, many black and white snakes, and others striped with white and yellow. Some had a flat and broad tail, three or four fingers wide, and the others quite round. Those of this latter kind were much smaller than the others and were no more than two feet long, whereas the others were at least three and a half, and were of
the thickness of an arm.
From noon until three o'clock, we were almost in a flat calm, the ship scarcely answering her helm. In this interval, the bottom varied from 14 to 12 fathoms. We then had a light freshening from west-north-west and we steered east. The bottom having decreased from 12 to 10, although quite far out and almost out of sight of land, since it could scarcely be seen from the mastheads. This worried me a little, and I gave orders to steer more to the north. On this course, we passed from eight fathoms to seven, so that there was every appearance that we were running onto some fresh danger, of which, however, no perceptible sign was apparent on the surface of the water, which was as smooth as in a basin. We had scarcely made a mile and a half on the course north 68° east, when we saw the sea all white before us. We at once hauled close-hauled to come up to windward of the line indicated by the colour of the water, and in the short interval it took the ship to come up to the wind, the bottom increased decreased to four fathoms, and it could be plainly seen alongside; it was sand and weed with no appearance of rocks. As we had but little distance to cover to find this line, we continued our course, but from four fathoms we passed to three. The lookouts having claimed that there was more water on the starboard side than on the port side, we bore away a little, but this was only for an instant, for, finding only 14 feet of water, we immediately luffed again and passed to four fathoms, five minutes after to six, and suddenly to ten, having crossed the line on which the bank was plainly outlined, and which chance made us cross at its narrowest part. Its direction appeared to us to be from north 80° east to west-south-west.
By an unexpected stroke of good fortune, we did not touch on this bank in 14 feet, but had there been the least swell, there is no doubt that we should have struck, and perhaps in a manner that would have caused damage to our masts.
Everything that had happened to us since we had been in this part of the coast, and everything we have seen for ourselves of it, leads me to say that the geographers who have sought to trace the direction of the coasts, and even their details, would have done much better to suppress their work than to lead navigators into error, or to expose them to certain loss, should they place in their charts a trust that these are far from deserving. Everything they have done is defective and purely systematic. The latitudes as well as the longitudes are defective in them, and I believe it is for their own convenience that they have altered them, for it is impossible that they should be the result of any observations by navigators who have frequented these waters. For they would not have failed to meet with some one of the many dangers found here.
Having passed the new bank of which I have just spoken, we soon passed from three fathoms to fifteen and from fifteen to twenty. At this depth of water, we brought the course more to the east and continued to carry sail until eight o'clock in the evening, when, being in 25 fathoms and on a good bottom, I came to anchor. My intention being to try to see, the following morning, the land, from which I could not be very far.
As soon as the Casuarina had anchored beside us, I sent a boat aboard that ship to ask Citizen Freycinet to come and speak with me. When he arrived, I asked him whether he had sighted the bank over which we had passed. His answer was yes, and that he had likewise crossed it, but that he had never found less than six fathoms of water, and that it was for this reason that he had not signalled it to us.
According to what Citizen Freycinet told us, who was about a league to windward of us, it appears that we happened to cross this bank at its highest part, and we were very fortunate to find enough water there to be able to pass.
During the night, the weather was as fine as we could wish, and the winds variable from south to south-south-west. However, the current appeared to us to be fairly strong, since we could not hold with 60 fathoms of cable out and had to pay out 70 to bring the ship head to tide. Perhaps this also comes from the nature of the bottom, which, being hard there, did not allow our anchor to bed itself in the sand.
From the observations made during the night, the speed of the current was 4 tenths of a mile, and its direction to the west-south-west, but neither the decrease nor the increase of the water was perceived, the depth being too considerable.

1803-04-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and calm, squally, with lightning and thunder; calm from ten in the morning until noon. Obs. lat. 3° 38' 24", est. long. 20° 18' 48".
1803-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, 4 April 1803, we got under sail with the intention of coming to make out some portion of the coast in this part, so as to fix approximately its direction, not having been able to sight it during our first voyage in Thermidor Year 9. The winds, which were then at south-south-west, variable to south, gave us hope of reaching it promptly, should they hold in this quarter. But we were disappointed in our expectation, for shortly after sunrise they passed to south-south-east and drew nearer and nearer to east as it rose above the horizon. Nevertheless, the breeze was very weak, and the distance we made on the course east towards north was not very considerable. This did not prevent the bottom from increasing rapidly and putting us in 28 fathoms at noon.
The latitude observed this day fixed the ship's position at 19° 21' 9" and the longitude of No. 35 was 117° 30' 20". As our horizon had an extent of at least six leagues and no land was to be seen, one may reasonably put forward that it makes here a fairly deep indentation to the south, and that its direction should not be from east towards north as the charts indicate.
