However, this is only a conjecture, of which only so much account should be made as one wishes.
In the afternoon, the winds passed, as usual, to north-west, to west, and to south-west, but so weak, until sunset, that we could scarcely take advantage of them. We steered east-south-east to close with the land, and the bottom we then had, having decreased six fathoms since noon, we recognised that we were beginning to approach it. From six o'clock to half past eight, the east-south-east course was continued with a pleasant breeze from the south-west, which made us run four knots, and which we greatly regretted not having had during the day. The bottom holding always above 20 fathoms, I continued the same course, but at half past eight, having suddenly passed from 21 to 17, I anchored on a bottom of fine sand and small broken shells, very suitable for anchoring. The Casuarina did likewise, and we again passed this night very quietly at anchor, the sky being constantly fine and the breeze moderate.
From the night's observations, we were astonished to find the current possessed of as much speed as it had, for, at the time we anchored, its speed was 2 miles 2 tenths. So that we could not bring the ship head to tide with 60 fathoms of cable and were obliged to pay out 70. Its direction appeared to us to be due east. From ten o'clock until five o'clock in the morning, it kept continually decreasing, and by this latter hour made no more than one mile. The bottom, in this interval, had decreased by 3 fathoms, for having anchored in 17 fathoms, we had only 14 at the moment we got under sail, the ship having swung to the same quarter as when we anchored.

1803-04-05.journal_anonyme: A flat calm, the weather dark and misty. Wore onto the starboard tack. The winds, which had drawn round to the west during the manoeuvre, came back to the ENE. Obs. lat. 3° 55' 15", est. long. 20° 40' 19".
1803-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, 5 April 1803, in the morning, being under sail at sunrise, we steered east to close with the land, of which we had had a good sight at daybreak, but only from the mastheads. According to the lookouts' report, we had an uncovered sandbank abeam of us at a short distance, and a second, further to the east, on which there appeared to be very little water. As I have not seen these banks with my own eyes, I can say nothing of them, but I am all the more inclined to believe in their existence in that I strongly urge navigators who succeed us to search for them with caution. Another reason which may likewise lead one to believe in the existence of these banks is that the bottom decreased rapidly when we steered east, and at seven o'clock, having no more than nine fathoms, without seeing the land from the deck, we bore up more to the north to have more water.
In the morning, the weather was very fine and the breeze fairly fresh, from south by south-east to south-east, but as the sun approached the meridian, it slackened imperceptibly, and at noon the ship was scarcely answering her helm.
The latitude observed was 19° 27' 0" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 118° 3' 38"; the bottom was then 18 fathoms.
From noon until three o'clock, we were almost in a flat calm, but then a light breeze came to us from the north, variable to north-north-west, which allowed us to make a little headway.
We steered east, drawing a little to the north, to run along a bank which lay to us from east-north-east to west-north-west. We judged it to be such by the colour of the water, which was of a very pale green, and by the various irregularities of the soundings, which varied from 18 fathoms to ten, from ten to fifteen, and which at last appeared constant for two hours' time, between ten and eleven.
At sunset, the men I had sent as lookouts reported to us that we should not doubt the existence of this bank, that they had made it out plainly, and that we should not clear it by steering east-north-east. This advice made me bear up a little more to the north, and I continued this course until seven o'clock. Seeing that the bottom kept decreasing, and that it was very uneven, between twelve and eight fathoms, I had the anchor let go, all the more since the breeze was weak and a strong current was visibly carrying us to the north-east. The bottom where we anchored was white sand, in twelve fathoms.
The speed of the current, measured at the moment we anchored, was two miles and three tenths, and it then set to the east. During the night, it kept continually decreasing and took its direction to the W.NW. The decrease of the water was not very perceptible and fell only two fathoms, a change to which the ship's swinging may have contributed as much as the current itself, on so uneven a bottom.

1803-04-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from SSE to SSW and WNW. In the 24 hours changed tacks twice. Est. lat. 4° 11' 51", est. long. 20° 50' 36".
1803-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, 6 April 1803, having got under sail, we steered north-east to run along the land, of which we had a perfect view, and which was borne from south to south-south-east at three leagues' distance. As the course we were making was bound continually to lose us sight of the land, we could keep it in view only until about ten o'clock in the morning, when it ceased to be seen even from the mastheads. The quantity of tide-rips among which we found ourselves from the moment we got under sail obliged us to various courses to avoid them, warning us of them. And all the soundings decreasing to as much as ten fathoms, I resolved, from fear of being for a third time carried onto some shoal from which we might perhaps not have got out as easily as on the two previous occasions when it happened to us to become entangled in them.
During the morning the breeze was very weak. The bottom, which we had at only ten fathoms at eight o'clock, was 14 at eleven o'clock.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 19° 4' 45" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 118° 29' 16".
From noon until two o'clock, we were in a flat calm, as had happened to us every day for some time past, and then the winds passed to north-north-west. By means of this light breeze, which freshened a little towards evening, we steered east-north-east to close with the land, on which several columns of smoke were beginning to be made out. Nevertheless, at sunset, we did not see the land even from the mastheads. As it could not be very far off, we continued our course until half past seven, when, having 13 fathoms of water, bottom of white sand and suitable for anchoring, we anchored. The wind was then almost calm and the current appeared to us to have its direction to the south-south-east, at a speed of a mile and a half.
Throughout the whole day, a great quantity of snakes of the two kinds I have already spoken of were seen passing alongside, two or three turtles, and a great quantity of porpoises.
During the night, the little freshness there was came from the north-west, but in the east the sky appeared stormy, and a great quantity of lightning came from that direction. However, the sound of thunder was not heard. Neither was any decrease or increase perceived in the depth of the water, which remained always the same as at the moment we anchored. The strength of the current decreased gradually to seven tenths of a mile, and at eleven o'clock the tide appeared slack. At two o'clock, its speed was one mile three tenths and its apparent direction to the NW.

1803-04-07.journal_anonyme: Almost continual rain and a flat calm. At 1.30 a.m. a fresh breeze from ESE; at 11 went onto the port tack. Est. lat. 4° 30' 3", long. 21° 8' 6".
1803-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, 7 April 1803, at sunrise, we saw the land, which bore from south by south-west to east-north-east. Having got under sail, we steered north-east by east to run along the coast, which appeared to us higher in this part than in all the other places we had just passed. On this course we passed through several violent tide-races which carried us to the east towards the south, but we did not, for that, change course, although they made us approach very close to the coast. The bottom appeared clean, between thirteen and eleven fathoms.
Throughout the whole morning, the breeze was from the south-south-east, very weak, and we made little headway until one o'clock, when we were entirely becalmed. This seemed to announce to us that the breeze from the west or north-west would come to us this day earlier than it was accustomed to do.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 18° 51' 31" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us, at No. 35, at 119° 4' 36". The land, borne at the same moment, extended from SE ¼ E to east ¼ north-east. The coast nearest to us was no more than four or five miles at most, and the Casuarina was between us and the land.
The winds having then passed to the west, we continued the north-east course. The lookouts reported the land to us in this quarter. Although at a short distance from the coast, the lead was between 13 and 14 fathoms, bottom of coarse sand.
From noon until four o'clock, we ran along the coast at a short distance, the depth allowing us to follow its contours, which form several coves, but of little depth. I was surprised to see that the land had a direction quite different from that I supposed it to have, judging, in truth, by the bearing given it by our charts, on which I knew from experience one could not rely, for we were obliged continually to bear away to the north to round the points as each one opened before us in turn.
At four o'clock, a shoal was sighted, running out from a point which then bore from us north-east. To round it at a good distance, we put the helm to north, but the bottom continuing to decrease, we were obliged to hold as close to the wind as possible. This shoal appeared to have its direction from south by south-east to north by north-west. It appears that, on the course we made, we passed over its northern extremity, on which we found no more than eight and nine fathoms of water. At five o'clock, this reef shoal became visible from the deck, and the sea there was strongly agitated. The Casuarina, which was closer inshore than us, signalled to us that there was no water, and wore round to work out to sea so as to be able to round it. Having passed this bank, the bottom increased rapidly from nine to 18 fathoms, and we successively resumed the north-east course, so as to gain an anchorage for the night, and at half past seven we anchored in 15 fathoms, two leagues from the coast, on a bottom of sand mixed with broken shells. Although the sky was fine in the west, it was not so in the east, and we often heard thunder rumbling.
(in the margin, vertically) Strong gusts from the south-west sometimes passed, without our being able to come head to wind; the speed of the current seemed to us, however, less strong than on the preceding days, and it was found to be only (no figures) miles when we anchored.

1803-04-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, continual rain, the wind variable in force and direction from SW, SSE, WNW and SSW. At 3.30 went onto the starboard tack; at 10.30 onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 4° 55' 52", est. long. 21° 7' 23".
1803-04-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, 8 April 1803, in the morning, we resumed the north-east course to run along the coast, from which we were not very far. This course was followed until noon, the bottom being fairly regular between 13 & 14 fathoms.
Throughout the whole morning, we saw a considerable quantity of birds, several schools of porpoises, and a few sharks. One of the latter was taken, and our scientists say that in this instance it is a new and undescribed species.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 18° 19' 33" and the longitude at No. 35 put us at 117° 35' 20". The winds, since eleven o'clock, had passed to south-west, and the breeze was beginning to gather strength. But to the east, the sky became very stormy and thunder was often heard rumbling. The course we were obliged to make in the evening drew much more to the north than that of the morning, having the land directly to the north.
The whole coast we ran along is of moderate height, even, and of a fairly pleasant aspect. About four o'clock, we found ourselves abeam of a fairly deep indentation, having the two extremities of the land to the north-east and to the south-east. I think there may be found in this part a bay whose low lands are visible only from very close, which is why I am not of the opinion of those who think that there are two islands there with the mainland behind them. Moreover, as the depth of water was beginning to decrease rapidly, I did not judge it proper to go and examine it, especially at the end of the day.
A little before sunset, the storm which had formed in the east gave us the winds from that quarter, but we had only a passing gust of it, and at seven o'clock we were almost becalmed. We then anchored in 10 fathoms, bottom of grey sand mixed with shells, and spent the rest of the night there.
From the observations made during the night to learn the speed of the current, it was found, at its greatest strength, to be 1 mile 3 tenths; its direction was at first to the north-north-east, and at four o'clock it was found to be to the north-west.
The differences found in the soundings must rather be attributed to the irregularities of the bottom than to the fall or rise of the waters; at least this is my opinion, founded on the fact that our anchor was let go in ten fathoms, and that with the 50 fathoms of cable veered out, there were twelve abeam of the ship. From midnight to four o'clock, the breeze was fresh, but the ship held fast.

1803-04-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from N to NNE. The stay of the middle staysail having parted, it was refitted. Est. lat. 5° 15' 40", est. long. 22° 18' 44".
1803-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, 9 April 1803, we took the course from north towards east to follow the direction of the coast. We had hopes of making a fine day's run, as it blew a pleasant breeze at sunrise, but it did not hold through the morning, for at eleven o'clock we were almost becalmed, while awaiting the arrival of the winds from the west or north-west, which had, up to now, been accustomed to succeed the south-east or east winds.
During the morning, it seemed to us that the current was carrying us rapidly to the east, for we approached the land very closely, which obliged us to steer from north towards west. The lead varied constantly between eleven and fifteen fathoms, on a bottom of sand very suitable for anchoring.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 17° 39' 27" and the longitude of No. 25 (sic) put us at 119° 35' 20".
At one o'clock, the breeze from west to west-north-west having gathered a little strength, we made a little headway, but the current served us better than the wind, which we could easily judge by the manner in which we passed the various bearing points taken ashore.
The whole part of the coast we ran along at a very short distance this day, without being very elevated, is of good height and of an aspect agreeable to the eye. It appears, from the freshness of the trees, whose foliage was of a fine green and thick, that we were at the moment of their greatest beauty, which the dry season, about to begin, will doubtless tarnish little by little. The places, along the seashore, that appeared covered with grass, were not fanciful and seemed to indicate good soil. The edge of the shore, formed sometimes by dunes of very white sand and sometimes by earth of a deep red colour, was likewise not without charm. In front of the dunes, as of the other parts of the coast which were not of the same nature, a long sandy beach was to be seen, scattered here and there with a few rocks of a very dark colour. We had already seen this part of the coast on our first voyage, but at a greater distance than we were then.
At six o'clock, finding myself too near the land, I wore round to work off the coast a little. My intention, should the weather be fine at eight o'clock, was to anchor as I had done every night. Until this time, after sunset, the breeze slackened considerably, and the change of course took us only a little way from the coast. Fear of being carried closer to it by the current made me anchor at a quarter to eight in 12 fathoms, good bottom of sand and shells, and we passed the night there very quietly.
The speed of the current, at the moment of anchoring and during the night, was one mile three tenths, on the flood as on the ebb. It set to the south-south-east until eleven o'clock; from eleven o'clock until one o'clock it set to the north-west. The lead brought up various bottoms which I think it useless to mention.

1803-04-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the breeze light from NNW to north. At 3.15 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 18' 33", est. long. 21° 43'.
1803-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, 10 April 1803, we continued to run along the coast, which still showed itself under a very agreeable aspect, well wooded and fairly high. The bottom was very variable between eight, nine and fifteen fathoms, and we passed successively from one to the other, taking care only to stand a little further out when it decreased too rapidly, so as to try to keep between ten and fifteen. The various views taken of the coast will make it very recognisable to those who may frequent it after us.
We had, during the morning, the winds from south to south-east, a light breeze, and a fine sky.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 17° 16' 45" and the longitude of timekeeper No. 35 put us at 119° 39' 48". The first time we crossed these waters, we sighted the land we are now running along, but we were further to the west of it and saw it less well than this last time, and the charting of this part will be well made; we have only to regret that it is not more extensive.
In the afternoon, the winds followed their usual course and came to us from the south-west, but they drew nearer to the south than they had done until then. We continued to run along the coast at a distance convenient for the charting work, and at half past seven we anchored in twelve fathoms, bottom of clean sand.
For two or three days past, storms had always been forming towards the end of the evening in the east, which followed the land and lasted an hour and a half or two hours, and then dissipated. During this interval, the lightning was continual, and thunder was heard rumbling fairly loudly, but none of it reached us. It seemed to us that it must be raining abundantly in the places where they passed, and it is to this cause that we attributed the freshness of the trees and the beauty of the greenery that we could plainly make out.
During the night, the winds returned to the south-east, a pleasant breeze, and the sky was constantly fine though very damp. The current having prevented the Casuarina from being able to close with us, she anchored at a fairly great distance from us, so that we did not sight her again until the following morning.
At the moment we anchored, the current had more speed than we had found in it until then, being two miles and a half. At ten o'clock, it was no more than one and four tenths, and it seemed to us, until four o'clock in the morning, to set to the north-east and north-east by north. At this time it took its course to the south-west. The soundings were from 12 ½ to 14 fathoms ½, but I do not know whether this should be attributed to the rise of the waters or to the unevenness of the bottom, for the reasons I have already spoken of.

1803-04-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NNE to north. At noon went onto the starboard tack; at 2 onto the port, and at 9 onto the starboard. Obs. lat. 5° 39', est. long. 21° 49' 0".
1803-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, 11 April 1803, as soon as we had got under sail, I had the ship steered north 31° west so as not to run onto a great bank which I knew was not far from our anchorage of the previous night, and on which I had found myself fairly seriously entangled the first time I visited this coast, in the month of Thermidor of Year Nine. From the moment we got under sail until eight o'clock, the bottom was variable between 15 and 17 fathoms, which led me to believe that I was sufficiently out to sea to work round it at my ease. So that I changed course a little and steered north 22° west. But this was not for long, for at forty minutes past eight, the sounding passed from 14 to 11, and five minutes after, to six and to five. We very quickly hauled close-hauled, and as the winds were at south-south-west, variable to south, we were able to steer west, which made the bottom increase as promptly as its decrease had been rapid. When we had come back to 14, 15 & 16, we again bore a little more to the north, without, however, passing north-west, but this course leading us to too rapid a decrease, having no more, at eleven o'clock, than 10 and 11 fathoms, we resumed close-hauled and steered west until noon, with a very weak breeze and the ship making little headway. On this course, the bottom was fairly regular between eleven and twelve fathoms, sand and coral mixed with fragments of shells.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 16° 43' 8" and the longitude at 119° 39' 28". All lands were out of sight, even the islands that had been seen in the morning until nine o'clock. The expanse of sea over which we sailed all morning was of so white a colour that one could be persuaded, only by the result of the lead, that there was sufficient water for the ship to pass.
At sunrise, considerable flocks of sea birds set out set out (sic) from the lands we had to starboard, and directed their course to the west and west-north. Their quantity was so great that this was what made us notice them. It seemed to be a complete migration, and that they were changing country.
From noon to one o'clock, although we were almost becalmed, the bottom passed from 12 to 18 fathoms; from one o'clock to half past one, the same, from 18 to 23, and from half past two to three o'clock, to 27. As there could no longer be any doubt that we were entirely clear of the banks we had, at times crossed and at times skirted, during the morning, we sought to close with the land by steering successively as far as east, but the bottom, instead of decreasing, kept continually increasing, and we had thirty fathoms at half past seven, when I anchored on a bottom of coarse sand and broken shells.
From a remark that is perhaps not without likelihood, although founded, however, on rather uncertain grounds, it is that in the afternoon of this day, the same innumerable quantity of flights of sea birds in flocks, which had set out from the mainland in the morning,
making for the west or west-north-west, and which I believed to be migrating to another country, began, from three o'clock until sunset, to return and rejoin the mainland. This seemed to me so peculiar that I sought to guess its cause, for it seemed to me that the course they had followed was too extraordinary not to depend on some circumstances unknown to us.
In reflecting, then, on what had happened to us in the morning, and on the banks we had met with off the coast, I am inclined to believe that there still exist others, lying still further out than those over which we passed. I also believe that these banks, whose position is not known to us, dry out at low tide, and that they then furnish an abundant food supply to the birds that frequent them. Gathering together various circumstances, we saw that, according to our calculations, the tide must have been low from six o'clock in the morning until noon, and that after noon, the banks, if they exist, becoming covered as the tide rose, the birds abandoned these waters until it should uncover them again.
If these remarks are false, so much the better for navigators, in that they will have one danger the less to fear in these waters. But until it is better known, I think they will do well to keep on their guard and to navigate, whether by day or by night, with the greatest caution and always with the lead in hand. The change in the colour of the waters not being sufficient, in several places, to make known the approach of a danger, any more than their depth, since in an instant one may pass from 25 to 12, and from 12 infinitely below, as has happened to us several times.
As, in the course of the morning, we also saw a fairly great quantity of small turtles, no larger than a six-franc crown, we were necessarily led to conclude that they were newly hatched and could not have come from very far. Thus it would not be ridiculous to believe that some sandy islets, which the sea does not entirely cover, in the vicinity of the place where we saw them, are the ones that saw them born.
Such is the remark that a particular circumstance led me to make, and of which I should certainly not have spoken on another occasion, since we are no longer in the season when the flight of birds can indicate whether or not there exist, in the direction they take, lands. However, everyone knows that the Portuguese, and even the Spanish, have often made important discoveries by this means.
I have already observed that throughout the whole day we sailed over very white water, and that had the lead not told us there was good bottom, I should have believed myself, at every moment, on the point of touching. Nevertheless, it is no less true that this water, white as it was, offered from time to time yellow patches to the eye, which had the same
effect as if the ship had ploughed the bottom. Although the sun must have had a part in this phenomenon, and the sky was very cloudy, I would think the cause should be particularly attributed to the strength of the currents and tide-races we met with in these waters, and especially to the edges of the banks, which, being of sand, must sweep away a great part of it and carry it in different directions.
When we anchored at eight o'clock in the evening, the current then had only six tenths of a mile of speed, and its direction was to the south-west and west-south-west. From nine o'clock until midnight, it increased to a mile and took that of the south-east until one o'clock, when the tide turned and set to the north-west. At daybreak, the greatest speed of the current was a mile and a half.
Little difference was found in the soundings indicated by the lead, which was constantly between 29 and 30.
The Casuarina, which had anchored too close to us, wishing to change her position, fell athwart our port cathead, but as it was calm, she was promptly pushed off, and no harm was done.
1803-04-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: We passed through tide rips running NE and SW. The crew, who since Mauritius had had rice or beans for supper, had no more; the rice and beans were used up, so that we are now reduced to half a pound of beef or 6 ounces of salt pork and 18 ounces of biscuit a day, with water to drink. We have three meals of fresh bread every ten days.

1803-04-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NNE. Obs. lat. 5° 45' 14", est. long. 22° 37' 56". Var. 8° 29' 15" NW.
1803-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, 12 April 1803, in the morning, having no land in sight, I steered east-south-east so as to try to sight it in the course of the day, if it were possible. But as we met only fleeting decreases in the depth of the waters, it was easy to judge that we were still fairly far from it. But as I wished to make out the direction of the coast in this part, not having seen it during my first voyage at this latitude, I continued the same course as long as the winds allowed me.
In the morning, the breeze was weak and we made little headway. The latitude observed at noon was found to be 16° 27' 20" and the longitude of our No. 35 put us at 119° 46' 41". We then had 34 fathoms of water, bottom of sand.
During the evening, the sky became very cloudy and stormy, especially in the south. The lightning was continual and the thunder made a great deal of noise. This state of the atmosphere made the breeze very weak, and we made little headway, at least in appearance. The course east towards south was continued until half past seven, when we anchored in 21 fathoms, without having had any sight of land at sunset.
About ten o'clock at night, a storm passing over the ship gave us a gust strong enough to make our anchor drag, but it was of short duration. Nevertheless, as the sky did not have a fine appearance, cable was paid out for the rest of the night. This measure, taken as a precaution, proved unnecessary, for, after the squall we had just received had passed, the wind fell entirely calm, although under a very stormy sky.
At eight o'clock, the speed of the current was found to be one mile two tenths, and its direction to the south-south-west. From ten to eleven o'clock, it was one mile and a half to the east-south-east and south-east. Afterwards it passed to east and east-north-east, and from there to north-west, with a speed nearly equal, having successively decreased to half a mile.
The lead was never below 20 fathoms nor above 23 ½, which would lead one to believe that the flood tide was perceptible to us at this anchorage.
For several days past, my health continually weakening, I saw myself on the eve of a third illness. Until this moment, I had made little of the pains and the discomfort I felt, but I was, on this day, so fatigued that, being scarcely able to keep myself on my legs, it was necessary to have recourse to medicine. Independently of a general lassitude in all my limbs, I suffered greatly in the chest, and a dry and almost continual cough decided me to try to rid myself of it by the remedies customary in such a case.
1803-04-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: We passed through tide rips running N and south.

1803-04-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NE to N, NNW and north. At 4 and at 8 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 42' 32", est. long. 22° 44' 50".
1803-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, 13 April 1803, we got under sail at sunrise, and at the same instant we sighted one, or rather several separate lands, which lay to us in the south, and which I have no doubt must be the islets at the extremity of which are the banks over which we passed on the twenty-first, and which obliged us to bring our course to the west in order to get clear of them.
During the morning, the breeze was very weak and variable. As the course was brought as far east as possible, we soon perceived the land in the south-east by east and south-south-east. But we could not approach it closely enough to make it out from the deck before noon. The winds, which had moreover passed to north-east by east, drew us away from it again.
As the sky had been very cloudy and stormy since morning, we had no observations at noon, but the reckoning of the course made in the 24 hours put us at 16° 22' 45" and 120° 4' 47".
The greater part of the evening having passed in calm, with very weak and variable winds from east to south and from south to south-south-west, we made little headway. However, at sunset, the land was perceived from the mastheads, and was borne east-south-east, at five leagues' distance according to reckoning. As the lands are extremely low in this part, this is assuredly the greatest distance at which they can be seen.
After sunset, we continued on our course until eight o'clock, when, having fallen becalmed again, we anchored in 27 fathoms, good bottom of sand.
During the night, it was a flat calm, but we did not lack for lightning, which hurt the eyes and came from different points of the horizon. The sky was very cloudy, and the atmosphere so filled with damp vapours that the men not on watch could not sleep on deck, as they ordinarily did.
We found in this anchorage the current less strong than it had been, and its speed was not above 7 tenths of a mile. Its direction was very changeable. It was at first to the south, for about an hour, and from south to south-east and to east. At midnight it took to the east-north-east, and at three o'clock to north-east by east, at which time the sea appeared slack. At five o'clock its speed was five tenths of a mile to the north-west. The shallowest sounding was 25 fathoms, the ship swung with her head to east, and the deepest 28, her head to north-west. The anchor had been let go in 27, her head to south-east.
1803-04-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: At noon a Spanish ship was sighted in the N 45° W, steering S 22° E.

1803-04-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNE to north and NE. At 9 sighted a Spanish ship in the NW. At 3 a.m. and at 6 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 59' 22", obs. long. 23° 22'.
1803-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, 14 April 1803, we had no sight of land on getting under sail. But at seven o'clock it was sighted from the mastheads, and was borne in the east-south-east quarter, at four or five leagues' distance. As we had the winds in the south, variable now towards the west and now towards the east, we steered east, drawing a little to the south, to close with the coast, which in this place appears to form a fairly deep cove. But the winds having passed to south-east as the sun rose above the horizon, we could not approach it as closely as we could have wished. However, by noon we were not far from it, and it was plainly made out from the deck. From the bearing then taken of it, the point nearest the ship bore east, and the two extremities belonging to it were borne, one south 58° east, and the other east-north-east.
At noon, we observed the latitude at 16° 17' 17" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 120° 21' 47". The bottom was, at noon, 21 fathoms and a half.
In the afternoon, the sky, which had been very cloudy and stormy at various points of the horizon, seemed to want to turn fine, and the south-east quarter was the only one that experienced no change.
About two o'clock in the afternoon, we sighted the uncovered sandbank, at the edge of which the sea broke a little, but as we had 33 fathoms of water, we bore away only a point, to round this bank, until the lead, which was going continually, should warn us to bear away more, which did not happen, for the bottom continuing to increase, we passed from 33 to 35. Having rounded this bank, we sought to close with the land to gain a less considerable depth of water by steering more to the east. The bottom then decreased progressively, and at sunset we had no more than 29 fathoms, bottom of sand and gravel. The same course was continued until seven o'clock in the evening, when, having no more than 27, and reckoning ourselves only two leagues from the coast, which at sunset bore east ¼ north, we anchored to await daylight. The bottom on which we anchored appeared to us very clean, and we had no worry for the safety of our cable.
Throughout the whole night, the sky was very stormy and the breeze weak, but we found, at the moment we anchored, the current fairly strong, its speed being two miles two tenths, to the west-north-west. It afterwards decreased to one mile seven tenths and changed no further. At midnight the sea appeared slack, and the current reversed, setting to the east, without taking a speed above one mile seven tenths. The sounding, the ship having swung to west-north-west, was 27 and a half, and swung to east, 26, which gave little difference from the moment we anchored.
From midnight until 2 o'clock, the wind was very weak, but at this time a storm came upon us from the south-east, which made us drag and put the ship adrift for some time. Twenty fathoms of cable were paid out and the ship held fast. When the height of the storm had passed, the sky turned to rain, and it was abundant until the following day. The wind then fell entirely calm, and we constantly had thunder for company.

1803-04-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from NE. Obs. lat. 6° 46', obs. long. 24° 26' 0".
1803-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, 15 April 1803, in the morning, the rain began to cease a little before daybreak, and we made ready to get under sail. We began by hoisting the topsails, and I gave orders to heave in half the cable and to remain hove short until such time as the breeze should decide itself, for we were then in a flat calm and the ship swung head to the current. As a light breeze sprang up from the south-east, we continued to heave short so as to get under sail at once. And it was not without astonishment that, after having strained hard, we suddenly saw it slacken and come in with the greatest ease. From the moment we were hove short, it was again necessary to strain hard to break out our anchor, which was soon weighed. But it appears that our cable had been badly damaged, either by its own anchor, around which it had turned in various directions during the storm, or by some rock at the bottom of the water, for we suddenly felt a jolt which told us that the weight of the anchor alone had broken it. This fear was soon confirmed, for shortly after we took in the end of our cable and our anchor remained at the bottom. As the Casuarina, which was anchored quite close to us, experienced no mishap of this kind, it is therefore very likely that our cable was cut by our own anchor and not by any rocks at the bottom of the water. I regretted the loss of this anchor all the more since we now had no more than three left, including the bower anchor, which was of little resource to us in the circumstance in which we found ourselves.
Having got our topsails set, we steered we steered (sic) north-east by east to run along the coast, which we made out perfectly although the horizon was of little extent. This course brought us to the edge of a great uncovered sandbank, in the middle of which a considerable quantity of rocks was to be seen, which at a league's distance appeared to form as many small detached islets. The direction of this bank, which appeared to extend from north-north-west to south-south-east, made us bear away successively to round it, and we passed it at a good league to the west, without having less than 37 fathoms of water. At ten o'clock, its north extremity bearing from us south-east, we successively came up to the wind, and at eleven o'clock we lost sight of it.
At noon, there was no observation, the sky being too dark and cloudy. In the morning, we prepared and let go the last anchor we had left on board, which it is very much in our interest to preserve as long as possible, so as not to be obliged to turn back. I cannot refrain from mentioning here what took place on this subject, and it will be seen, from the satisfaction shown by some of those who accompany me, how agreeable the voyage is to them and the interest they take in it. I have no doubt that, were it left to them, they would have the other anchors thrown into the sea, or at least anchored among the rocks, in the hope of seeing them stay at the bottom. And by this means put an end to the expedition.
Be that as it may, in the afternoon we continued to run along a part of the coast that was very low, seeing the land from time to time from the deck, and at other times able to perceive it only from the mastheads, so little elevated is it above the level of the sea. However, we constantly had a great depth of water, but the winds did not allow us to range along it more closely. At sunset, the land nearest to us resembled perfectly an island, and I am even persuaded that it was one, in that other lands were to be seen to the east, lying on a much more distant plane.
My intention was to anchor for the night, as I had done up to this time, the bottom being good, or at least appearing so from the indication given by the lead, but as the depth of water was very considerable, and it seemed to me it must decrease as we advanced to the north towards the east, I put it off until such time as we should have no more than 25 to 30 fathoms. Accordingly, we continued our course, but at eight o'clock, having passed from 32 to 45, there was no longer any means of thinking of it, and I gave the course north by north-east until midnight, at which time I reckoned on lying to until daylight, now on one tack, now on the other;
At nine o'clock, a blackness awash was sighted, which was at first thought might be a bank. The lead was immediately cast, and it was 35 fathoms, down from the 45 we had had at eight o'clock. At half past nine, we had no more than 29 fathoms, and we then steered north-west. The bottom increased so promptly that at ten o'clock we were in 40. Orders were given to follow the north-west course until midnight and then take that of north-north-east. But the wind did not allow it, and the officer of the watch, not having informed me of this, continued on the north-west course, which could not fail to carry us well out to sea.
Moreover, during the night, the weather was fairly fine and the breeze weak, but whether the current carried us to the north-west or otherwise, the bottom kept continually increasing, and we passed, in this last watch, from 40 to 53 fathoms.

1803-04-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NE to ENE. Saw many fish. Obs. lat. 7° 11' 8", est. long. 25° 19' 36". Var. 9° 59' 0" NW.
1803-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, 16 April 1803, in the morning, the weather the weather (sic) was fine but the breeze so calm that we made very little headway. The winds, which were moreover from the east, suited but little the course we had to make to approach the land, of which, however, we had lost sight since the previous day.
In the morning, steering close-hauled in the hope that we should have, during the evening, the breeze from north-west to south-west, as had been the case ever since we had been running along the coast, we saw a great quantity of birds taking flight to the north-west, as if there were there, in this quarter, some banks that attracted them there. We met, on the course we made, several shoals of fish, without having the skill to take any of them, except, however, a porpoise which was clumsy enough not to avoid the harpoon-thrust aimed at it. These shoals of fish made no change in the course the birds were taking, which seemed to indicate that they must find easier means of subsistence in the places towards which they were heading.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 15° 7' 10" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 120° 21' 6".
In the afternoon, the breeze held a little until about six o'clock in the evening, and then began to slacken. The winds having been continually in the east, variable to east-north-east, we were obliged to continue on the northern board, which little suited the desire we had to close with the land. Throughout the whole day we were in a great depth of water, never having less than 45 fathoms, and often more. The night passed in an absolute calm, without our being able to make the ship answer her helm. At six o'clock, we had gone about to close with the Casuarina, which was much to the south of us, and we came up with her about nine o'clock in the evening. As the lead was cast every hour, notwithstanding that the wind was calm, it was thought that the current set to the north-west with a speed of about half a mile. We had much lightning at various points of the horizon during the night, but the calm was none the less constant for it, and the sky fine, save for a great dampness which much inconvenienced those who were on deck.

1803-04-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a pleasant breeze from NNE to NE. The course NW by [W]. Saw many fish of various kinds. Obs. lat. 7° 28' 8", est. long. 26° 16'. Var. 12° 25' 0" NW.
1803-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, 17 April 1803, the calm continued all morning, save for a few light breezes which came to us from the north, but which rarely had force enough to make the ship answer her helm and allow us to lay the course to the east. The bottom varied so little that we were constantly between 55 and 56 fathoms of water.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 14° 56' 16" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 120° 16' 12", which seemed to confirm the observation made by the chief quartermasters on the direction of the currents, for the officers of the watch took no account of it whatever, as is easy to be convinced by the report of their watch in the log book. It was, however, in order to know it, that I had given orders for soundings to be taken every hour. But this practice, which they regarded as troublesome to themselves and useless in its results, meant that they did it only under constraint and not from reflection.
About three o'clock in the afternoon, we had a light breeze from the south-west, which allowed us to lay the course to east-south-east. It lasted until eight o'clock and began to slacken, although the winds still held in the same quarter. My intention was to let go a kedge anchor for the night, should I find a good bottom and a sounding between twenty-five and thirty fathoms. But as the waters were always very deep, I remained under sail. Moreover, as we had not yet reached the grey marl bottom which I expected to meet with the next day, I knew that the bottom over which we were then sailing was not very clean.
At sunset, we thought we saw land to the south-south-east, running to the east, but several among us believed we were mistaken, and that what was taken for land was a curtain of clouds on the horizon, which, however, showed itself to us in the same form until nightfall, without any alteration whatever.
During the night, I made my course, all sail set, to east-south-east and south-east by east, to come and reconnoitre the islands and islets which lay to us very nearly in this quarter, but from which I reckoned myself still more than 25 leagues distant.
During the night, the weather was fine and the breeze fairly weak; nevertheless it was perceived by the log that the ship was making a fair amount of headway, which verifies the first remark we had made in finding that, in these waters, the current sets briskly to the east.

1803-04-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from NE to SE. At 8 p.m. it fell calm; at 10 trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack. Obs. lat. 7° 54' 19", est. long. 27° 3' 48". Var. 11° 4' 0" NW.
1803-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, 18 April 1803, we had no sight of land at sunrise nor even during the morning. I was the less surprised at this in that this part of the coast having been well determined on our first run, we were not to see it yet. We therefore continued on the same course, well persuaded that we should see it in the course of the day, provided the breeze, which was, nevertheless, weak, should hold.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 15° 10' 38" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 121° 29' 18". We were then come upon the marl bottom of which I have spoken, and which we knew must begin a little to the west of this longitude.
In the afternoon, about two o'clock, we began to have sight of the land from the mastheads, but we did not see it well from the deck until sunset. According to the bearing then taken of it, it extended from south 30° east to south 70° east. As it was strongly broken up in this part, I had no doubt that this was the beginning of the islands and islets we had recognised on our first voyage, and that the lands seen there on a more distant plane, in the same direction, were those of the mainland. My intention was to spend the night at anchor, the bottom being very firm, but the sky was so stormy at various points of the horizon that, about eight o'clock, seeing no appearance of fine weather for the night, I took advantage of remaining under sail and standing out to sea, so as to draw a little away from the coast, on which a strong current, setting to the south-east, was making us drift.
From eight o'clock until ten o'clock, the thunder made a great noise, and the lightning repeated itself with unequalled vividness. Great black clouds, which rose little by little above the horizon, were not long in developing. The storm began to make itself felt with abundant rain, and the wind absolutely calm, but as the rain decreased, we had it in squalls and gusts strong enough to make us lower our topsails right down and clew up our fore topgallant sail. This storm lasted about two hours at its greatest strength, and made the whole round of the horizon several times, obliging us to various manoeuvres. The rest of the night, from one o'clock until daylight, was scarcely any finer. The thunder, although in the distance, rumbled continually, and the lightning much troubled my sight.
This storm was the first we had met with since we had been running along the north coast of New Holland.

1803-04-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NNE to NE. Obs. lat. 8° 21' 33", est. long. 27° 56' 36". Est. var. 11° 30' NW.
1803-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, 19 April 1803, in the morning, having lain to an hour before daylight in 35 fathoms of water, we made sail to close with the land, which the lookouts had sighted at sunrise, although the horizon was not very fine, at least at several points of its extent, which was from east-south-east to south by south-east.
All morning, the sky was very cloudy, the atmosphere thick, and I feared some serious squalls, as sometimes happens to meet with in the first months of the changing of the monsoons. However, the clouds, toward the middle of the day, dissipated little by little, and the air became less heavy. The barometer, which had fallen several times to 28 inches one line, began to rise again, and I flattered myself with seeing fine weather return. Moreover, we spent the morning in a calm, making no other way than that given us by the current, which appeared fairly strong and to set to the east, to judge by the weed and bunches of grapes that passed alongside.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 14° 58' 11" and the longitude of the timekeeper was 121° 42' 58". We then had a light breeze from west-south-west, with the help of which we steered east to draw nearer to the land, which, at four o'clock, was borne from the deck from south as far as east by south-east.
In the afternoon, the weather turned entirely fine and the clouds disappeared. In front of the mainland, which could be made out, were several islets of moderate elevation.
After sunset, it continued to blow a pretty breeze, and I made my course all night, steering north 67° east. As these waters were known to me, I feared meeting with nothing in this quarter that might expose me to any danger. Nevertheless, soundings were taken every hour, and the bottom was very regular, between 40 and 35 fathoms.
At eight o'clock, having perceived a great brightness on the horizon, I sent a man to look out, and it was recognised to be a great fire ashore; it bore from us south 15° east.
During the night, the weather was fine, and yet very damp. The winds varied little from west-south-west, but they were very weak. My health, which for several days had been fairly bad, was beginning to mend, which allowed me to resume my ordinary occupations.

1803-04-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from NE. Obs. lat. 9° 22' 5", est. long. 29° 16'. Var. 10° 20' NW.
1803-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, 20 April 1803, from the beginning of the day we had sight of the land in the south-east by east, at a distance of about two leagues, and, at sunrise, we saw it extend to the north-east by east. We were not long in recognising that this was the archipelago of islands, islets and rocks which we had wished to reconnoitre in more detail in Germinal-Fructidor of Year Nine, but into which the lack of water did not permit us to penetrate. We therefore confined ourselves to coasting along this chain of islands, as we had done the first time, and to verifying whether their positions, as assigned by us, were exact, according to the correction made to the longitudes indicated by our timekeepers. We saw with pleasure that there was so little difference that we changed nothing in them.
As the breeze was very weak in the morning, we made little headway. However, the current served us well, and we passed this first archipelago, of which it is likely that the number of islets is greater than the chart indicates. But they are so numerous, and in directions so little convenient for all to be taken with the same exactness, that I have confined myself to those which are most conspicuous, as being furthest advanced to seaward, for the safety of navigation.
At noon, we observed the latitude at 14° 37' 24" and the longitude was 122° 24' 12".
Having doubled this first archipelago, we began to have sight of the second, which lies about five or six leagues off. Although less numerous, in the quantity of islands, islets and rocks belonging to it, than the first, it is more remarkable, not only for their strange shapes, but also for a fairly extensive reef which lies in front of these islands, at about the middle of their extent. This reef appeared to us to be a long sandbank on which several rocks awash are raised, on which the sea breaks heavily. The middle is formed by a small sandy islet, over which the tide does not appear to rise when it is high. Its whole extent is about two leagues from north-east to south-west, as far as it was possible to judge. Having doubled this reef, we drew near to two fairly flat and even islands, and at eight o'clock, the weather being very fine and the breeze weak, we anchored in 37 fathoms of water, bottom of marl, and passed the night there very quietly. On this occasion I sent aboard the Casuarina fresh bread, a turtle, and her sick men who had recovered. In exchange for my presents, she sent me back two other sick men, and the news that she had lost one of her anchors the same day as I had, so that of the five she had had, she now had no more than one left, and a cable in bad condition. She also let me know that in the last storm we had received, her compasses had been entirely deprived of their magnetic properties, and that she could no longer make use of them.

1803-04-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from NE by E to NE by N. Obs. lat. 10° 47', est. long. 30° 40'. Var. 11° 24' 30" NW.
1803-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Floréal, 21 April 1803, as soon as we were under sail, the winds being very weak from the south-west quarter, we found a strong current which, setting to the south and to the east, made us drift onto part of the islands we had to starboard, so that about eight o'clock we were no more than five miles from them. However, the bottom was still 37 fathoms and very suitable for anchoring, so that if, in the course of the morning, the wind did not come to our assistance, we still had the resource of being able to anchor.
The wind did not increase in the morning, but about ten o'clock the current took another direction and carried us to the north and to the west, so that we passed part of the islands with much greater speed than the log indicated. We then fell into 40 fathoms, clear proof that the current was carrying us briskly to the north-west.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 14° 20' 2" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us, at No. 35, at 122° 37' 6".
In the afternoon, the breeze continued very weak, and we coasted, at a short distance, the islands we had in sight, steering north-east, for fear that too unexpected a change in the current might carry us again onto the coast, from which we were then about two leagues and a half distant. As my intention was to anchor about eight o'clock, the dangers being too numerous on this coast to remain under sail during the night, I had the course laid to north-east by north after sunset. The breeze had then freshened a little, and we were making two miles an hour, not counting what the current might make us do in whatever direction, it being impossible to judge on account of the darkness of the night.
In running along the islands, islets and rocks of which I have just spoken, we did not lose sight of the mainland, and it was seen on a more distant plane behind the islands, without any interruption sufficiently noticeable to lead us to believe that what was still seen might be other islands. The columns of smoke, moreover, which were seen rising at intervals, confirmed us in this opinion, although it is not without objection, since the islands may be just as well inhabited as the mainland itself.
Having anchored, I sent to fetch the Captain of the Casuarina, who confirmed to me what he had told me the day before concerning his situation. I had two compasses given to him in place of his own, and promised to send him, the next day, when we should be at anchor, a 6-inch cable and a ninety-pound grapnel, the only one I had left for my longboat.
During the night, the weather was fine and the breeze almost calm. As we were anchored in too great a depth of water for its rise or fall to be perceptible to us, we contented ourselves with observing the speed of the current, which, at the moment of its greatest action, was one mile seven tenths. It set at first to the south, then to the north-east and to the north, decreasing in speed.

1803-04-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. At 1.30 shaped the course NNW. Est. lat. 12° 6' 12", est. long. 31° 59' 24". Var. 9° 4' NW.
1803-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second of Floréal, 22 April 1803, we were no more favoured by the wind than on the preceding days, and it blew so little throughout the whole day that we made headway only by the help of the current, whose change of direction during the day was often contrary to us and carried us further out to sea than we should have wished. And on other occasions it brought us far too close to the coast. The extent of the islands in sight at the moment of getting under way was from south 67° east as far as south. Among them were seen several isolated rocks and the mainland behind, or at least lands we supposed to form part of it.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 14° 6' 33" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us, at No. 35, at 123° 0' 46".
In the afternoon, we were in a flat calm, and often on the point of anchoring so as not to approach too closely the islands that were abeam of us. But we persevered in remaining under sail, and at four o'clock a light breeze came to us from north-north-west, by means of which we were able to stand a little further out to sea and come to a good anchorage for the night. The little freshness we had lasted until about eight o'clock, and then the calm beginning again, we anchored in 30 fathoms, on a good bottom of mud.
As, on my first voyage, I gave an exact account of the lands we saw on this coast, and as, independently of that, I have all the views of them drawn in colour, I do not repeat here what I have already said of them, this second account being superfluous.
During the night, the weather was very fine and the winds calm. The speed of the current was one knot three tenths when we anchored, and it then set to the south. From eleven o'clock until midnight, it was only six tenths, setting to the south-south-east. It then took its direction to the (no indication) at first with little speed, and afterwards to the north-west, making one knot and one knot three tenths at its greatest strength for us.
My health, which was still very unsteady and little assured, suffered various alterations. Sometimes I experienced only a very bearable discomfort, and sometimes I was tormented by fairly sharp pains, and especially by a dry cough which left me no rest during the night.
The Casuarina having anchored too far from us, I could not send her the grapnel and the hawser which I had had prepared for her.

1803-04-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from ENE. At daybreak set up the main and fore topgallant shrouds. Obs. lat. 13° 57', est. long. 33° 2' 24". Var. 8° 37' NW.
1803-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the third of Floréal, 23 April 1803, the same vexation as on the preceding days on the part of the winds. And it was not until about half past seven that, with the help of a light freshness from the south to south-south-east, we were able to get under sail, directing our course to north-east by north.
I flattered myself, in the course of the day, with being able to reach the two islands that lie at the northern extremity of the land in this part, and of which we already had sight from the deck. But the breeze was so weak that it was uncertain whether we should even be there by the beginning of the night.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 13° 58' 58" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 123° 8' 0". This longitude leads me to believe that the timekeeper is fast, and I base myself on this fact, which does not seem doubtful, and which is as follows.
When, on our first voyage, we determined the position of this island, it was found to be in (no figures) south latitude, and its longitude, according to the correction made to the timekeeper at Timor, was (no figures).
The longitude indicated by today's reckoning being found 3 minutes further east, and our distance from the coast being greater than it was then, I therefore believe myself justified in thinking that the timekeeper is fast, and that a great part of our second course draws more to the east than it should. Our first port of call will show us whether this reasoning is correct or not.
In the afternoon, although it was almost a flat calm, the current favoured us so much that it made us drift as far as abeam of the two islands of which I have just spoken, and which we clearly recognised as being those which terminate the land to the north in this part. At four o'clock, the middle of the first island bore from us east by north-east, at about two leagues' distance. There then sprang up, as on the previous evening, a light breeze from south-south-west, variable, very variable, of which we took advantage to work up a little to the north and to the east, so as to reconnoitre, the next morning, the banks and reefs which we know to lie to the north and to the east of these islands.
At eight o'clock, we anchored as usual in 33 fathoms, bottom of mud, and passed the night very quietly. The current appeared slack at the moment we anchored, or rather the officer of the watch neglected to have its strength and direction observed.
At midnight, its speed was one mile, setting to the north-east, until two o'clock, after which it did nothing until it was found to be nine tenths of a mile to the north-west.
Having furled our sails, the grapnel and the hawser which I had promised were sent aboard the Casuarina.

1803-04-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from ENE, freshening a great deal. At noon shaped the course north. Obs. lat. 15° 48' 18", est. long. 33° 50' 0".
1803-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth of Floréal, 24 April 1803, in the morning, we did not have, at sunrise, the light breeze from south to south-south-east which we had had every day before, which obliged us to remain hove short on our anchor until such time as it should declare itself, which did not happen until about nine o'clock. We then at once got under sail. But the current being much stronger than the wind, was carrying us briskly to the south, so that, unable to stem it and not wishing to lose more ground, we anchored again on the same bottom as before, without furling our sails, in the hope that the breeze might come to us. But it did not occur the whole day, and the rest of the day passed in a flat calm.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 13° 52' 0" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 123° 13' 32".
In the afternoon, seeing no appearance of setting out, I had my longboat put to sea to go and reconnoitre the island opposite which we were at anchor. I entrusted the command of it to the coxswain alone, being well persuaded that he would carry out the orders I gave him much better than any officer, to whom such chores are infinitely displeasing.
He therefore had orders to go ashore, but also to return on board at once should he not have reached it before nightfall. I had two rockets given to him so that he might let me know when he had got there, which he did not fail to make known to me, after sunset.
I had embarked in this boat the gardener Guichenot and Citizen Barbe, the one to bring us back the productions of the country in plants, and the other to kill some birds, should any be found.
During the night, the wind was absolutely calm and the sea as smooth as ice. Nothing particular occurred, except that we observed that the current was stronger than usual, and that the sea rose and fell for us about four fathoms. This remark seems to confirm what Dampier says, that several days after the new or full moon, the tides are stronger than at their reciprocal changes.
The greatest speed of the current was not, however, more than a mile and a half, setting sometimes to the south-south-west and sometimes from south to south-east, on the ebb, and from north-north-west to north-east, on the flood.

1803-04-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to ENE. Obs. lat. 17° 30' 35", est. long. 34° 32' 6".
1803-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fifth, in the morning, we sighted our boat, which was trying to reach the ship. As no fire had been seen ashore during the night, I thought they had not been able to land, although the signal agreed upon to let me know they had got ashore had been made.
About seven o'clock, the wind being absolutely calm, I was astonished to see that my boat entirely changed course, and that instead of returning to the ship, it it (sic) was making its way into a sort of bay formed by two islands and some rocks. I thought they were looking for an anchorage to wait for the turn of the tide, and I felt no uneasiness, the coxswain in command of her being an intelligent man and of good will to carry out his duties properly.
On board, the morning passed in an absolute calm, without the least breath of air from any point of the horizon.
At noon, we again sighted our boat coming back out of the inlet it had gone into, and at two o'clock she was on board.
The news she brought us was of the most extraordinary kind. They had sighted four large canoes which had made sail at sunrise and steered for the third island we had in view. They had set out from a sandy cove about two hundred paces from where the boat was at anchor. As soon as it sighted them, it made sail to give them chase, in the hope of catching up with them, but as they went along much better than the boat, they were soon far off by dint of their paddles. On opening up the point of the cove from which they had set out, two more were seen, one making sail and the other still at anchor. Course was then changed to close with one of these last two. The one that had made sail got away, but the third was finally brought to by the show of firing a musket-shot at her if she went on paddling. The canoe and the boat being alongside one another, everyone was quite astonished to see that the five men aboard her were all of Malay origin and dressed entirely in the manner of the Timorese, and armed likewise. Their clothing consisted of a piece of cloth girded about their loins and passing between the thighs, raised up behind. Their headgear was a handkerchief about the head. All were armed with a dagger, or a kind of kris in the Malay fashion. Their canoe was long, raised at both ends and very neatly kept, as well as newly painted black and white. At the after end of the canoe, bows about four or five feet long were hung up, along with several wooden cases holding arrows.
The Malays were at first very much afraid of our men, but they soon grew more familiar when they saw when they saw that all that was wanted was to speak with them, and that no harm was meant them. Some of our men went into their canoe, just as one of them came over into our boat.
The little likelihood there had been of making such an encounter meant that there was nothing to give them as a present, and only biscuit was exchanged with them for turtle eggs. They made it understood that they wished to have some rum, but they were told that they could only get it on board, where they would never consent to go. They offered the boat's crew some water, which they had in a kind of jar similar to those we had
bought at Timor, and such as are made in most of the islands to the north of New Holland. They also made signs to our men to urge them to follow them. But as they were poorly armed and almost without means of defence, unable to imagine that this island might be frequented, they did not think it proper to trust to their guide, preferring to return on board to give me an account of what had just befallen them.
Some of the Malays in the canoe gave our gardener Guichenot some tobacco cut very fine, in the same manner as they are accustomed to prepare it for their daily use. To this present they added a betel leaf, though it was entirely dried out, as well as an areca nut.
The five men in this canoe were tall, well made, and of a reddish colour, having very black teeth, as generally have all the Malays through the use of betel and areca. Four gun ramrods were seen in their canoe, but no firearms. The last two canoes were much smaller than the other four. A very fine fish was also found with them, gutted and very neatly wrapped in a mat, which they seemed to be keeping for someone, at the place to which they were withdrawing.
Such unexpected news having at once made me resolve to find out how it came about that there were Malays in this part, I made up my mind to learn whether they were permanently settled there, or whether they only frequented it at a certain time of year for the turtle fishery, of which our men told me they had seen great numbers at the edge of the banks that surround the island, leaving a few small openings by which one may make one's way into the coves.
I therefore at once had the boat armed, the command of which I gave to the coxswain of the helm Fortin, with orders to go and reconnoitre the place to which the canoes had withdrawn, which the coxswain knew, observing to him above all not to compromise himself in any way. For greater safety, I gave orders to the Casuarina to follow him and to be continually on her guard, and always ready to be able to protect the boat in every circumstance. Both were informed that I myself would make sail the next day to follow them, if the breeze should have force enough for the ship to answer her helm.
At four o'clock, the boat and the Casuarina made sail, but Citizen Freycinet manoeuvred so badly that the current, which then set to the north-east, made her drift to leeward of the island, which the boat reached that same evening, leaving her then to her own resources, which would not have happened had Citizen Freycinet taken the tack to the south with the little wind there was. For in that way the current would have set her across and made her close with the first island.
The night had nothing particular about it, and the calm was as deep as it had been during the day. The direction of the current was the same as that observed the day before, and the tide was no stronger than it had been remarked to be.

1803-04-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 19° 20' 0", est. long. 33° 50'.
1803-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Sixth Floréal, 26 April 1803. The day of the sixth passed in a dead calm, like the preceding days, and had nothing worthy of note. The strength and direction of the current had no doubt prevented the Casuarina from following my boat, which she had orders to protect in case the Malay craft in those waters should come to trouble it. But as she was separated from it for the time being, she could be of no use to it, should the case require it, that ship being at anchor to the south-east by east of us, at about a league and a half. After sunrise, she made sail, and in the morning we lost sight of her, notwithstanding how little wind there was.
Toward evening, a little before sunset, we were told of several Malay praus in sight. Some were under sail and others at anchor. At sunset we made out four of them plainly, under sail, which showed themselves off the eastern point of the island abreast of which we lay at anchor. But we had no sight either of our boat or of the Casuarina.
During the night, the sky continued fine and the breeze always calm. I waited impatiently for the next day, the time at which the Casuarina and my boat were to return on board.
The direction of the current observed during the night was the same as on the preceding days, and the tide rose and fell about two fathoms and a half.

1803-04-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from ENE to E by N. Obs. lat. 20° 40' 36", est. long. 34° 27' 18".
1803-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventh Floréal, 27 April 1803. On the seventh of Floréal, at sunrise, we had the pleasure of seeing the Casuarina and the boat, under sail, off the eastern point of the island where we had seen the Malay praus the day before. I had no doubt that they had communicated with one another, and that we should soon receive some interesting news of them.
As the large boat had orders to bring us branches of foliage for our kangaroos, she parted company with the Casuarina to go ashore, and that ship came in to join us at the anchorage. When she was at anchor, I sent for the Captain, and after he came on board he told me that he had not been able to communicate with the praus, but that my boat had spent half a day with them, and had received from them various pieces of information which appeared to prove that they only frequent this coast at certain times for the fishery, and that they have no settlement there at all.
I shall make known in more detail, from the report that will be made to me by the coxswain of the helm, what draws the Macassans to these waters, the kind of fishing they carry on there, and the time they spend at it.
My boat having arrived, we made sail at once with the help of a light air from south-south-west, which held in that quarter until about four o'clock, when the calm set in again. The land we had left in the morning could be seen at sunset from east-south-east to east by north-east.
We passed the night, as usual, very quietly at anchor, being moored in 34 fathoms, muddy bottom.

1803-04-28.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the wind from NE to east and ENE, variable in force and direction. Obs. lat. 22° 28' 4", est. long. 35° 9' 12".
1803-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighth Floréal, 28 April 1803. On the eighth, in the morning, we made sail, steering north-east by north to run along the great bank, part of which we had coasted along the evening before. Several places on this bank had been seen bare, and we had known of its existence since our first voyage, having coasted along its whole extent, and we had even, more than once, found ourselves caught upon it.
At eight o'clock, the direction of this bank stretching ahead of us, we put our head to the north, with winds from the south, variable to south-south-west, and very light.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 33' 22" and the longitude by No. 35 put us at 123° 23' 20".
In the morning, a little after sunrise, No. 31 stopped, or at least it was noticed at that time. On taking it out of its box to observe it, it started going again, but at noon it was recognised that it must have been stopped for about half an hour. The cause of this mishap is quite unknown to Citizen Bernier, who is in charge of the timekeepers.
At noon, the bank or reef which we had been coasting since yesterday stretched from east-north-east to east-south-east as far as the eye could reach.
(blank)
Particular remarks concerning the longitude
of the bay of Coupang, and the placing on the old and even
modern charts of the south-west point of Timor, as of that of the islands
of Semau, Rottie, and Savu.
From a lengthy series of observations made during our stay at the settlement the Dutch have in the bay of Coupang, island of Timor, it results that the longitude of Fort Concordia is 121° 30" by the rate of our timekeepers, corrected for the errors they have shown since our departure from Paris.
By the observations taken of the moon and sun, both to the east and to the west, the results were absolutely the same, so that it must follow that the determination we have given for the bearing of this settlement is very close to its true position.
Its latitude 10° 9' 55".
Supposing, as there is reason to believe, that our observations are good, it follows that the longitude given by the Connaissance des Temps for the south-west point of Timor is faulty, since it places it at 121° 39' 0". This would put this point to the east of Coupang, whereas we are quite certain that it lies to the west of it, since, to reach it by passing through the Strait of Semau, our course was north-east, and after rounding the south point that forms the bay in question, one must steer east toward south to reach the anchorage.
On leaving Timor on the 14th of Prairial of the 11th year (3 June 1803), I resolved to resume the survey of the north coast of New Holland by making my course to the south of the island of Rottie, persuaded that once I had reached between the 13th and 14th degree of latitude, I would find winds from the south quarter to south-east, and perhaps even south-west, which would allow me easily to work up the coast. Although several seamen whom I had consulted were persuaded that it would be impossible for me to work up to the east with the south-east monsoon, I nonetheless persisted in my plan, and preferred to follow the course I had proposed to myself rather than the more usual one of passing to the north of the equator.
It was not, however, out of stubbornness in an opinion opposed to that of everyone else that I took this course, for having twice worked up this coast, I have always found favourable winds there, and the land and sea breezes have appeared to me very regular there, and we went few days without having them. So I am far from believing that the coast of New Holland, to the north as to the south, is subject to the winds that generally prevail offshore.
On leaving Port Jackson, the English were persuaded that it was impossible to work up the straits and the south coast of New Holland
without exposing themselves to every sort of danger and inconvenience. This prejudice, without any foundation, has meant that all their ships returning home go round Cape Horn.
