I hope that the two voyages I have just made there will change their opinion, and that they will see that, in the favourable season, this course ought to be preferred to any other.
In running along the island of Rottie at a short distance, we have satisfied ourselves that its direction is further west than our charts give it, as it is also certain that this island does not extend as far south as it is marked. Unless it has an extension of coast to the south-east of which the charts make no mention.
Three islands and several reefs, which lie in its south-west part, are shown on Robertson's chart, but wrongly placed. We had sight of the two small islands that lie to the south.
It is probable that the island of Savu is likewise wrongly placed, and that the channel separating it from that of Rottie is much wider than it is marked, since we had no sight of it at all. This land is, however, very high, and can easily be seen at ten or twelve leagues and even more.
By the course we made, we would not have passed out of sight of it, all the more as the sky was fine and the horizon far-reaching.
Departure from Timor. Second port of call in the bay
of Coupang.
1803-04-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: We crossed the Tropic of Cancer. From the 8th to the 15th we saw a great deal of gulfweed lying E and W.

1803-04-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 24° 19', obs. long. 39° 9'.

1803-04-30.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather with a little rain, a good breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 25° 57' 36", est. long. 40° 16' 0". Obs. var. 6° 50' NW.

1803-05-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a good breeze from NE to ENE and east, variable in force and direction. Obs. lat. 27° 47' 33", est. long. 41° 20' 0". Var. 11° 29' NW.

1803-05-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze. Saw a great deal of gulfweed. The breeze at ENE. Obs. lat. 29° 36' 51", est. long. 42° 9' 18". Var. 9° 20' NW.

1803-05-03.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sea smooth. A pleasant breeze in puffs from ESE to NE, east and E by S. Set up the main topmast shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 31° 41' 49", est. long. 42° 18' 36".
1803-05-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: The fore topgallant mast was struck.

1803-05-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from ESE to east. Obs. lat. 33° 43', est. long. 42° 29'. Var. 10° 59' NW.

1803-05-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from ESE to east and ENE. Struck the main topgallant mast to shift the sail. Obs. lat. 35° 43' 55", est. long. 42° 53' 24". Var. 10° 11' NW.

1803-05-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze variable from ESE to ENE and SE. Obs. lat. 37° 26' 50", est. long. 42° 37'.

1803-05-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. Shifted the mizzen topsail. Obs. lat. 39° 4' 58", est. long. 41° 26' 30". Var. 1° 30' NW.

1803-05-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. Saw an American ship to windward of us; we hove to to wait for her, and our small boat went aboard. Obs. lat. 40° 23' 8", est. long. 40° 22'. Est. var. 7° 0' NW.
1803-05-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: We communicated with the American ship Thomas of Charleston, from Liverpool bound for Philadelphia with a cargo of salt; she had English passengers of distinction. We asked her for 6 casks of wine or 2 of rum; she could give us nothing.

1803-05-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze in puffs from SE to ESE. Repaired the main staysail, which had split where it bears on the fore braces. Obs. lat. 42° 6' 24", est. long. 39° 32' 30". Est. var. 7° NW.
1803-05-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Two Spanish ships were sighted standing S 22° E. At 4 p.m. the sea changed colour completely; we sounded at 9.30 without finding bottom at 180 fathoms — though from the way the captain sounded, we should have found no bottom even at 50 fathoms.

1803-05-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from E by S to ESE and SE. Saw several ships. Obs. lat. 43° 50' 52", est. long. 38° 36'. Est. var. 9° NW.
1803-05-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the morning the sea had recovered its natural colour. At 4 p.m. we communicated with an English brig from Dartmouth bound for Newfoundland in ballast; we asked her for wine or rum, which she had not, and she offered us a little salt pork, which we refused. At 6.30 we spoke an English sloop from Jersey bound for Newfoundland in ballast. The ship was painted.

1803-05-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SE to south and S by E. Several ships in sight. On the morning of the 21st set up the main topmast shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 45° 16', est. long. 37° 22'. Var. 10° NW.

1803-05-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south, SE and SSE. Saw several ships. Shifted the main and fore topsails. Obs. lat. 46° 6' 27", est. long. 36° 10' 26".
1803-05-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: New sails were bent. At 7 p.m. we communicated with the Danish corvette Frederikssteen of 26 guns and 32-pounder carronades, whose captain gave us 1 barrel of 21 pots of brandy and 600 lb of biscuit; he sent 27 bottles of rum or wine for the captain and the officers. The corvette was from Saint Croix (in the Virgin Islands) bound for Copenhagen. Captain Hamelin forbade the officer who went aboard her to say that we had called at Mauritius, and told him to say that we came from the coasts of New Holland. We have 4 men sick.

1803-05-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from south to S by E. Several ships in sight; we spoke one which gave us biscuit and brandy. Obs. lat. 47° 2', est. long. 34° 27' 26". Est. var. 20° NW.
1803-05-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Several ships were in sight, one of them the Danish corvette. The coffee shipped for the crew at Mauritius being used up, the second sailmaker Auvray, who had a bale of it weighing 85½ lb, let the captain have it for the crew, payable at Le Havre at the current price.

1803-05-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south, SSE and SSW. Five ships in sight. Hove to and sent our small boat aboard to fetch the captain. Obs. lat. 48° 11' 50", est. long. 32° 19' 26". Est. var. 20° NW.
1803-05-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: We saw 5 ships and communicated with one of them, the Concorde of Le Havre, 58 days out from Saint-Domingue and bound for Le Havre; she could give us nothing. The salt pork shipped at Port Jackson is used up; we have nothing left but beef.

1803-05-15.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a good breeze from SSE. At 1.30 the main topmast backstay having parted, it was repaired at once. Struck the main topgallant mast to shift its sail. Est. lat. 49° 39' 26", obs. long. 36° 25'. Var. 20° NW.

1803-05-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. During the night the weather turned overcast, the wind variable and unsteady. Four ships in sight. Est. lat. 51° 2' 38", est. long. 33° 58' 2". Var. 20° NW.
1803-05-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: The same brig, made out to be French, and three other ships in sight.

1803-05-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from SSE, SSW and south, in gusts; the sea rather high. Saw birds and porpoises. Est. lat. 51° 59' 38", est. long. 31° 49' 30". Var. 30° NW.

1803-05-18.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze and variable from SSW to SW, in gusts. The sea smooth enough. Obs. lat. 52° 34' 12", est. long. 29° 5' 30". Est. var. 30° NW.
1803-05-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 6 p.m., after a squall, the mainmast — long since sprung, and which the captain would not spare — cracked abaft between the masthead rigging and the trestletrees. The officer of the watch at once had the main topsail and the staysails taken in, with which the captain was not pleased; the staysails (according to him) having never carried away a mast, because they did not strain it. The main topgallant mast was struck. In the afternoon two ships were in sight.

1803-05-19.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from SSW, SW and WSW in gusts. At 6, in a squall, the mainmast cracked below the masthead rigging; lowered the main topsail on the cap and took 2 reefs in it and 1 in the fore. Struck the main topgallant mast and got it down. At daybreak sighted a ship to windward of us. We set about rigging preventer backstays and unbending the main topsail. Obs. lat. 52° 14' 13", est. long. 25° 29' 12". Obs. var. 34° 46' NW.
1803-05-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: The damage to the mainmast was made good. Two preventer backstays were set up to starboard and two to port abaft to support the masthead. The main topmast was lowered about 9 feet; it rested on a stout woolding passed over the cap (the turns of the woolding could not be passed over the trestletrees, the port one being broken). Two fishes were put on the masthead; good woolding was passed round the mast, the fishes, the heel of the topmast and its woolding; wedges were driven between these wooldings and the mast, and a preventer woolding passed. The main topsail and the staysails were unbent. A ship was in sight during the day.

1803-05-20.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind falling away from SW, SSW and WSW. Lowered the main topmast about 9 feet and refitted the lashings of the [one word illegible] shrouds and backstays; meanwhile two fishes for the mainmast were got out of the spare spars. From 5 to 8 went on passing the wooldings on the mainmast fish. From 8 until midnight set up the main topmast rigging, and at 11.45 set the main staysail and bent the main topsail; by midnight it was set. At daybreak worked on the main topmast woolding and on woolding the mainmast. Est. lat. 51° 29', est. long. 22° 31'.
1803-05-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: The main topsail was bent with the three reefs taken in, the middle staysail in place of the main staysail, and the topgallant staysail in place of the middle staysail. The eyebolts to which the mainmast preventer backstays and the main topmast backstays were secured being neither strong nor sound enough, they were brought inboard through the after ports. A ship was in sight during the day.

1803-05-21.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather with rain at intervals, the sea smooth, a strong breeze from WSW to SW. We were busy setting up the mainmast shrouds, finishing the wooldings and refitting the preventer backstays, the eyebolts they had been secured to not being strong enough. At 5.30 all was ready. A ship in sight. We got up our main topgallant mast, swayed it up and rigged it; the shrouds and backstays of that mast were set up. Est. lat. 50° 48' 49", est. long. 19° 59' 42". Est. var. 34° NW. [No more follows.]
1803-05-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: A fore topgallant mast was rigged as a main topgallant mast, and a small staysail set to serve as a topgallant staysail. A reef was added to the main topsail. At 3.30 p.m. we sounded without finding bottom at 160 fathoms. Two ships were in sight during the day.

1803-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Fourteenth of Prairial, 3 June 1803, of the eleventh year of the French Republic, seeing no further likelihood of rejoining the deserters I was missing, I resolved to make sail, and at nine o'clock we made our course to get out of the bay of Coupang, passing between the small island of Sem des Tortues, and to the north of the one we ran close along at three-quarters of a league's distance.
My intention, in leaving Coupang, was to pass through the Strait of Semau, so as to pass further to the east and not be carried to leeward of the island of Rottie or even of Savu. But the breeze was so light that it was not possible to attempt this passage, which, though easy with a good wind, is dangerous in a calm. The anchorage being everywhere very deep and not clean means that one is often exposed either to the loss of one's anchor, or at the very least to considerable damage to one's cables, as had already happened to us.
Having rounded the north part of Semau, I went round it to the west, and found myself, at the beginning of the night, off the middle of its western part, hoping to make, the next day, the channel that separates it from that of Rottie. But the currents making us drift heavily to the south-south-west, another passage had to be sought, which decided me to take that which the charts show between Rottie and Savu.
During the night, the wind was very light and the weather fine. We kept as close as possible on the course to the south, and coasted along the western shore of this last island in sight.
The Casuarina, doubtless too heavily laden and encumbered, sailed so badly that we carried no more than our topsails with a reef in them, and even then it was necessary, from time to time, to set the mizzen topgallant.

1803-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fifteenth, 4 June 1803, we continued to run along the coast of Rottie Island at a small distance, and the course we made to follow its contour enabled us to judge that its configuration is badly drawn on our sea charts. I think that which Arrowsmith gives it, in his great chart of the South Seas, is the best.
At noon, we observed the latitude at 10° 44' 49" and the longitude of our marine timekeeper No. 35 put us at 120° 44' 56". At the same time we found ourselves at the opening of a channel formed by several islands which lie to the west of the coast of Rottie. This channel appears wide, but it is obstructed by reefs which must render its navigation difficult, all the more as breakers were plainly distinguished there in several places. Robertson's chart makes mention of these islands, which are three in number,
but it places them much further south than they ought to be.
In the report made to me by the surgeon, I was informed that many persons of the crew were affected with venereal diseases. Citizen Bernier, who for four days had had a fever, appeared likely to have a serious illness, as did the draughtsman Petit. Both had always kept well during the port of call, and it was only two or three days before our departure that they began to feel slightly unwell. Nevertheless, each of them separately had a fairly violent attack of fever, which appeared to have no after-effects, according to the report made to me of it at the time.
When I paid my visit to Citizen Bernier, during the morning, I found him much less well than the day before, and began to fear that he might have a truly serious illness, so cast down and altered did he appear, whereas the day before we had talked and conversed together for more than an hour and he was very well.
In the afternoon, the winds, after having gone the whole round of the compass, settled, passing from south-east to east-south-east, and it blew a good breeze. Several rain clouds fell upon the land and did not reach us. We successively doubled the three islands of which I have spoken, and a reef, on which the sea rose to a great height, which lies at the extremity of the south point of the last of them. After having passed it, we saw the lands of Rottie Island at a fairly considerable distance, and the lands of the great island extended, at sunset, from north 43° east as far as south 72° east.
I am far from believing that Rottie Island extends as far to the south as our charts carry it. Or, if it be so, its configuration must be very different from that given it, and it must advance considerably to the south-east.
During the evening, the surgeon came to warn me that Citizen Bernier had just shown the most distressing signs, which announced a near end. A considerable hiccup had seized him, and the violent and irregular agitations of his pulse gave cause to fear for his life. He judged it proper to apply blistering plasters to him. I went at once to see him. But I found him without consciousness, and every symptom of death was depicted upon his face. Unable to bear such a sight, I withdrew. He was, moreover, without consciousness. I was so struck by so sudden a change that I felt throughout my whole body a distress which obliged me to go to bed much earlier than usual, but I did not find there, for all that, the rest I needed. During the night, I was seized with a spitting of blood similar to those which had already happened to me on two different occasions, and the sputum I brought up was so thick that one would have said some parts of the lungs were separating themselves from my body.
The weather was fine and clear during the night. I had soundings taken several times without finding bottom at 100 fathoms. We sometimes experienced very violent tide-rips, which made as much noise as if the sea had been breaking against reefs.

1803-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
The sixteenth 5 June 1803, about five o'clock in the morning, I was informed that Citizen Bernier was no more. This death, which one might almost regard as a sudden death, made so strong an impression upon me that it would be hard to express all that I suffered by it. The loss of Citizen Bernier is an unfortunate event, not only for us, but also for the Government, for there is no doubt that he would have become an accomplished astronomer, useful to his country. He had, for that science, which was both his occupation and his pleasure, a natural aptitude which he turned to good account through assiduous and continual work. His labours, up to the eve of his death, will doubtless be found to be in good order, and I am, as it were, certain that the Government will be satisfied with them.
This young man, who besides had excellent qualities of heart, was of a gentle and honest character, and if at times it happened that he departed from it, it was only through being led on by example or wearied by bad advice; but as soon as the first moments of ill humour had passed, he was not ashamed to admit his faults and to be the first to blame his own conduct. I regret him, for my own part, sincerely, and I do not hesitate to say that of all the scientists who have been given me, he is the one of them all who worked the hardest, whether to acquire new knowledge or to fulfil the Government's intentions. It is unfortunate that he was of a very delicate constitution, ill suited to bear the fatigues of a long voyage, during which one often lacks the things necessary to a temperament like his.
I will do him the justice of saying, to his credit and to the credit of his zeal for his profession, that despite having been ill at various ports of call, he never once showed the least wish to remain ashore, conduct very much opposed to that of several of his fellows.
At ten o'clock, the officers and the naturalists paid him their last (respects), and his body was cast into the sea.
In the morning, the weather was fine and the winds at east-north-east, a light breeze. At noon, we observed 11° 34' 32" of latitude, and the longitude by our timekeeper No. 35 put us at 120° 33' 16".
During the evening, the breeze, which had been in the morning at east drawing toward north, went round to east and even to east-south-east, which gave me hope that as we advanced to the south, they would take this direction. The breeze was very light all evening, and we made little headway during the night. We had the winds at east.
Before sunset, we saw considerable flights of birds of the black-and-white booby kind, and of gulls, coming from the west and heading toward the south-east. It might be that they came from some banks or islets that lie in that direction, and that they withdrew for the night to the coast of New Holland.

1803-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
It is through an error of date that I entered the death of Citizen Bernier, our astronomer, under the sixteenth; it took place on the 17th at half past four in the morning, and as I was myself very unwell that day from a spitting of blood, these two days of my journal were not in order.
In the morning of this day, we had the winds at east by south-east, variable to east-south-east, and the breeze light. We continued the southern board, conforming to the sailing of the Casuarina, which, going very badly, occasioned us a considerable drift, the vessel not having enough sail to avoid being carried away by the current. We found, nevertheless, that the tide-rips which passed from time to time were beginning to be less long and less strong than we had found them until then.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 12° 24' 0" and the longitude was 120° 34' 6". If we had gained nothing to the east in these 24 hours, at least we had lost nothing, and that was already a good deal.
We saw, as the day before, many of the birds of which I spoke yesterday, which, setting out from the south-east, went off to the west. The latitude observed at noon placed us very nearly at that which Captain Nacht gives to the sandbank of which he had knowledge; I had soundings taken in these waters without finding bottom at 100 fathoms.
During the evening and throughout the night, the winds varied little, and we continued our course to the south, keeping as close to the wind as possible.

1803-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
The eighteenth, 7 June 1803, the weather was much as the day before, and the breeze still very light. We continued the same course. We did not see, in the morning, the same quantity of birds we had seen the day before.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 13° 2' 46" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 120° 38' 18", which gave a fairly great difference from the dead reckoning.
In the evening, the winds varied from east toward south, but I did not change course until midnight, when, believing them settled at south-south-east, I took the eastern board, in the hope of having them the next day at south and perhaps at south-west.
During the day, an inventory was made of Citizen Bernier's effects, and all his papers were gathered and placed in a particular chest, to be handed over to the Government on our arrival.
Of the nineteenth Prairial.

1803-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
The nineteenth, 8 June 1803, in the morning, the winds passed from south-south-east to south-east, and we were able to continue our course to the east, but the breeze was light and we made little way in the morning.
At noon, the latitude was observed at 13° 17' 5" and the longitude of No. 35 put us at 120° 58' 48".
In the afternoon, the winds continued to be variable from south to south-south-east and the breeze still light. But at the beginning of the night, they passed to south-south-west and afterwards to south-west, freshening a little, so that I no longer doubted that we should have, in future, favourable winds to work up to the east, and perhaps even also to follow the north coast of New Holland. We continued during the night our course to the east, conforming to the sailing of the Casuarina, which was making us lose very fine weather.
As we were making our way in the vicinity of the sandbank which was seen by Captain Nacht, I had soundings taken at midnight, but we found no bottom at eighty fathoms straight down.

1803-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twentieth 9 June 1803, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the winds varied from south-west to south-south-west. They even came round to south by east, but only for a short while. The breeze was very light in the morning, or rather, we spent the greater part of it in a calm.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 1' 16" and the longitude, according to the rate of our timekeeper, was 121° 35' 43".
During the evening, the breeze freshened a little and we made our course east by south, having noticed, from the difference in latitude over these 24 hours, that the currents were setting to the north.
The night had nothing had nothing (sic) particular about it; it blew a fine breeze from south to south-south-west, which was what we wished for. We sounded at eight o'clock and at midnight without finding bottom at 80 fathoms straight down.

1803-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-first 10 June 1803, the winds continued favourable to us and the breeze from south-south-west was tolerable. We took advantage of it as much as was possible with regard to the Casuarina.
As the colour of the water changed a great deal in the morning, and as to all appearance we were over the bottom, I had the lead cast at eleven o'clock and we found ourselves in 45 fathoms, somewhat coarse grey sand. At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 1' 17" and our longitude was 121° 23' 14", which put us, near enough, at the position we were in when I made for Timor.
During the evening, the breeze was less strong than it had been in the morning, and there was every appearance of a calm for the night. We sounded at two o'clock in the afternoon; the depth was the same as at eleven in the morning, that is, 45 fathoms, grey sandy bottom.
After sunset, being in 43 fathoms of water, we continued our course, but at ten o'clock, having only 31 fathoms left, we brought to, on the port tack, and held that same tack for the rest of the night. The sounding then increased gradually, and at four in the morning we had 50 fathoms, the currents and the leeway setting us to the north-east.

1803-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-second 11 June 1803, as soon as day began to break, we made sail, steering east until sunrise, when we then took that of south-east by south. It blew a good breeze in the morning, and we took advantage of it to regain to the south the ground that the previous night's lying-to must have made us lose by setting us to the north. I had resolved upon this course for fear that, by making way during the night, we might be set upon one of the banks and reefs that we knew existed to the east of the westernmost north point of this part of the coast.
During the morning we crossed several fairly considerable tide-rips, whose direction was north-north-east and south-south-west.
At noon, the observed latitude was 12° 54' 32" and the longitude by our timekeeper No. 35 put us at 124° 22' 54". The result of several series of lunar distances gave 124° 38' 22".
In the afternoon, the breeze continued favourable to us, the winds being variable from south-west toward south, but as the sun sank toward the horizon, it kept almost steadily dropping, so that at sunset we found ourselves nearly becalmed, which fortunately did not last long, for at seven o'clock it came to us again and was stronger than usual, which lasted until the middle of the night, when the winds came to us again from the west-south-west, a fine breeze. We made our course to the south-east during the night, under little sail, to wait for the Casuarina, which was well astern, though we had no sight of her at all. Otherwise, the night was very fine and clear, but damp.

1803-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-third 12 June 1803, the weather continued fine, but we were sorry to see the breeze fall off a great deal. At sunrise, we made our course south to close with the land, of which it was possible we might have sight during the day, judging by the depth, which was 55 fathoms, grey muddy bottom. At eleven o'clock, we thought we had sight of it from the masthead, without being certain of it. But at one (o'clock) in the afternoon, we saw it perfectly from the topgallant crosstrees. At that distance it showed itself in a fairly high and regular shape.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 26' 6" and our longitude by the timekeeper was 125° 8' 47". That of the lunar distances put us at (no figures).
In the afternoon, we continued our course to the south, and at one o'clock we clearly made out the land from the masthead. The breeze dropped gradually until sunset, with every appearance of a calm for the night. At sunset the two extremities of the land most in view stretched from south 85° west to south 35° east. In this position we were steering south 52° east, and we had abeam of us, at a distance of about two leagues, a small sandy island which we at first took for a bank uncovered by the sea. But as we drew nearer to it, we recognised
that it was indeed a small (island) with some greenery on its highest part, and a fairly long reef off the ends of its south-east and north-west points, along the length of which one could see, here and there, points of rock clear of the water. There were likewise, to the south-west of the ship's position at that time, two other bodies of land which had the appearance of islands, but we could not be sure whether they were points of the mainland thrust further out, or islands.
The stretch of coast off which we made land is of good height and cut sheer down to the sea in the form of a cliff. Accordingly the waters were deep, since having come to anchor at seven o'clock, we were in 45 fathoms of water over a good muddy bottom, and at a league and a half at most from the small island I have just spoken of.
The uniformity of the coast in this part offers few landmarks, and the interior of the country offers nothing pleasing to the eye. The land nearest the sea's edge is thinly wooded. But in the distance, as it rises, one could see trees of tall timber in fairly great quantity. We also saw, during the evening, some smoke rising well within the interior of the land.
The greater part (of the night) passed in a calm; nevertheless the Casuarina, which had remained well astern, rejoined us between eleven o'clock and midnight. From the observations made during the night on the strength and direction of the current, its speed was 6 to 7 tenths of a mile, and its direction south-south-east until midnight, when the tide turned and it then set to the west. Until two o'clock the speed was 8 tenths of a mile, and from three o'clock to five, one mile. I was surprised not to find it stronger, from what I had already experienced, read, or heard said.

1803-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-fourth 13 June 1803, at six o'clock in the morning, we made sail to run along the coast, of which the survey now began. The winds were then from the south-west, fairly light, but the tide, which must have turned about the same time we got under way, was to be favourable to us, or at least I hoped so. As we ran along the coast, we recognised that the two bodies of land which the day before I had suspected to be two islands and not points of the mainland thrust forward, formed two quite distinct from one another. During the morning the winds varied from south-west to north-west, and the breeze was so light that we made very little way. The appearance of the coast was much the same as the day before, still sheer and formed by cliffs, in which are found several coves more or less large, but which do not appear to offer good places of shelter in time of need.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 51' 41" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us at 125° 17' 35". The soundings were very regular, between 55 and 45 fathoms, always a muddy bottom.
In the afternoon, the winds shifted from north-west to north-east, and the breeze freshened a little. And as we were making our course to the south-east, the wind was favourable to us. Nevertheless we made very little headway. The ship's progress was checked by a strong current that kept us from going ahead. The colour of the water changed to such a degree during the evening that I was astonished by it. Indeed, within two hours we went from 45 fathoms to 20, although we had made little way. And the nature of the bottom, which until then had been mud, turned out to be rock, which made me fear that we might be in the neighbourhood of some breakers, though nothing that had that appearance was seen from the masthead. We continued our course to the south-east until six o'clock in the evening, during which time (the bottom) was 20 to 23 fathoms, but then it began to lessen, and within half an hour we went from 20 to 12, coarse gravel mixed with mud. On this sounding we steered at once to the north-east, and even to the north as the winds allowed us to lie that way, and the bottom went from 12 to 15 fathoms. The calm that followed decided me to let go a kedge anchor and remain in that spot, should the breeze during the night not prove too strong.
As soon as the ship was brought up and the sails furled, a boat was put into the water and I sent to sound around the ship, particularly to the east and north-east, the directions in which I supposed the bank must lie, if, as I thought, there was one in our neighbourhood. On the boat's return, I was informed that around the ship, at two cables' length, they had everywhere found 15 fathoms, the same bottom as that on which we lay at anchor, but that in standing off at that distance between east and north-east, the bottom kept lessening, and they had gone as far as 13 fathoms. The report would seem to confirm my opinion.
The night had nothing particular about it, and we passed it almost in a calm, with a light air from north-west to west.
From eight o'clock until eleven, the greatest speed of the current was one mile 8 tenths to the south-east, and from ten o'clock to 3 in the morning, one mile 2 tenths to the north-west and north-west by west. The sea appeared to us, by the soundings, to have risen two fathoms and fallen one.

1803-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-fifth 14 June 1803, after making sail, we made our course north-east, the lead in hand. I had, the day before, given orders to the Casuarina to make sail as soon as day began to break and to steer on that point of the wind, from which she was not to depart to take the course to the south until she was in twenty fathoms. We continued the course north-east to east until about eight o'clock, sounding continually. The first hour, the bottom held between 15 and 16 fathoms; then it went to 17 and to 22. At nine o'clock it was thirty, and at ten, 35, all mud, as we had found it on our arrival off the coast. I therefore remain persuaded that there is a shoal to the south-east and east-north-east of our anchorage, but perhaps there is, upon it, sufficient water
to be able to cross it. At least we saw nothing to indicate the contrary. The wind, moreover, was so light and the sea so calm that we could not judge of it any better.
During the morning the winds varied from south-south-west to south by south-east, almost calm. We ran along the coast as close as was possible, taking bearings of its principal points.
At noon, the observed latitude was 14° 5' 18" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us at 125° 38' 6".
The breeze continued very light in the afternoon, and the winds, having gone from south-south-east to east, then came round from east to north-west, but by then it was beginning to be too late to profit by it, as we did not wish to make way during the night, so as not to be carried by the currents in a direction contrary to our dead reckoning. The night had nothing particular about it. The breeze was very moderate, with winds variable from west to north-west.
The depth at which we lay at anchor being too considerable, no observation was made on the rise or fall of the waters, as it would not have been perceptible at that depth. But the speed of the current was found, from eight o'clock until one in the morning, to be (no figures) in the (no direction), and from one o'clock until five, (no figures) in the (no direction).

1803-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-sixth 15 June 1803, the winds were south-south-east in the morning, which obliged us to make our course east after making sail. The breeze was at first light, but afterwards became fairly strong, and we were even compelled to take two reefs in our topsails. The tack to the east, which we had to hold, made us lose sight of the land, and at noon it could only be seen from the masthead. The wind and the current made the sea run high. From the moment we got under way until noon, the sounding had been very regular, between 35 and 36 fathoms, and we were greatly astonished to find only 25 at the last cast. I had given orders to go about at noon to close with the land, but wishing to make sure whether we had not some shoal ahead of us to the east, I continued on the same course for half an hour, to see whether the bottom would increase or lessen. Having then found it to be 37, we went about and passed for the second time over the bottom where we had found only 25 fathoms, which lasted no more than another half hour, after which we had 32 fathoms. At 3 o'clock the bottom was still 32. It appears that there exists in this spot a fairly considerable rise, but of little extent.
At noon, the observed latitude was 13° 59' 25" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us at 125° 58' 46".
In the afternoon it continued to blow a strong breeze until about two o'clock, but from that time on it kept lessening, and the sea fell off in proportion. After sunset, the winds holding steady enough to counter the current, which then seemed to us to set to the north-west, we did not come to
(anchor), and continued on the tack to the south toward the west, until nine o'clock, when, judging ourselves not far from the land, we took that of east toward the north, which we followed until three o'clock. When we went about, the first time, the sounding was 24 fathoms, muddy bottom, as we had almost always had it until then.
During the night, the weather was fine though hazy at the horizon, and the breeze moderate.

1803-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-seventh 16 June 1803, we expected to see as strong a breeze as the day before, since the sun had set very red the evening before and had appeared in the same guise at its rising, but we learned on this occasion that the Remarks of the old navigators are not always to be trusted, for we had all day a fine breeze, and a very moderate one. We had only to complain of the nature of the winds, which varied little from south-east, either toward east or toward south.
In the morning, the Casuarina asked to pass under our stern, which was granted her. She then begged me to send her a boat and to receive on board a man of her crew whom she judged to be very ill and even in danger. I sent for him at once and he was placed in the sick bay, which was growing larger day by day without our knowing to what to attribute the cause.
At noon, the observed latitude was 14° 20' 30" and our longitude was 125° 47' 5", so that we had lost to the west what we had gained to the south. We went about at the same time, and took the tack of east toward the north, waiting until the winds should allow us to make a more direct course.
During the evening the winds were exactly the same as in the morning, but calmer, which gave us hope that we should have those from the west or south-west by the close of day and during the night, but nothing of the sort occurred. About six o'clock they went round to east-north-east and made us change tacks, but they were so light that the current, carrying us swiftly to the north-west, obliged us to let go a kedge anchor in 22 fathoms, muddy bottom.
During the night, the wind was calm. The current appeared to us to have a constant direction from south-south-east to south-east. The ship scarcely changed her heading, or at least very little, and her greatest speed was, according to the log, one knot two tenths; the depth varied between 22 and 24 fathoms.

1803-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-eighth 17 June 1803, about three o'clock in the morning, we had a light air from west-south-west to south-west. We made sail at five o'clock, steering south toward east, but the wind did not allow us to keep it up for long. Shortly after sunrise, it went round to south and then to south-east by east, which obliged us to make our course east toward north until noon, when we resumed the tack to the south. During the morning the breeze was moderate, but very strong tide-rips made themselves felt so often that the ship had difficulty answering her helm.
At noon we observed the latitude to be 14° 8' 40" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us at 126° 4' 21", so that we had, that day, gained to the east very nearly what we had lost to the south.
In the afternoon we did not have, as we had expected, the breeze from the west or south-west. The winds remained steadily in the quarter from south-east by east to east-south-east, which obliged us to keep to the offshore tack, all the more as the bottom was shoaling rapidly and we were already in 15 fathoms, though quite far from the land, of which nevertheless we still had good sight.
At sunset, the lands in sight stretched from south 85° west to south 5° east. From the masthead, an island could be seen, and a rock close beside it, to the south-south-east.
At about half past eight, being in a dead calm and seeing that the current was carrying us swiftly to the north-west, we came to anchor on a bottom of mud mixed with small pebbles. At midnight, the winds went round to south-south-east, a fresh breeze, and made us drag on our anchor. The bell was rung at once and we got under way. No officer appeared on deck, and none were present but the two midshipmen Baudin and Debrévedent. For the rest of the night it blew a fresh breeze, and the winds varied from south-south-east to south-east by east. We kept between 16 and 24 fathoms of water, over a very uneven bottom.

1803-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-ninth 18 June 1803, the winds went round to east-south-east, a strong breeze. We resumed the tack to the south. At sunrise, the lands in sight bore from south 75° west to south 11° east. The breeze held all morning, with no appearance of wind from the west quarter for the afternoon. The bottom remained uneven throughout, between 24 and 18 fathoms.
At noon, the observed latitude was 14° 23' 49" and our longitude was 126° 8' 25". The winds varied little in the afternoon, and the bottom was even more irregular than we had found it in the morning. We went about after the sun observation, having our heading upon a bank awash with the water, on which the sea did not break, but by its very yellow colour it was easy to perceive that there was very little water over it. The bottom was then 15 fathoms and mud.
At sunset, a piece of land which seemed to me to be an island, and which had been reported as such on the previous days, bore from me east 80° south.
We took, for the night, the offshore tack. The wind was moderate and often light until midnight, but then so strong a breeze came upon us from east to east-south-east that we were obliged to take a second reef in our topsails, lying as close as possible on the tack to the north toward east. The sky, though fine, was very hazy all round the horizon. The bottom, during the night, was between 18 and 22 fathoms, almost always mud and fit for anchorage.

1803-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth 19 June 1803, in the morning, the winds being still the same with no appearance of change, I continued the tack to the east towards the north. During the morning it continued to blow a fresh breeze, but it calmed as the sun gained strength, which was greatly contrary to my expectations. For I expected to see it increase and perhaps be obliged to heave to. The sea had already become heavily agitated and the vessel was much fatigued by it.
At noon we observed the latitude of 13° 52' 29" and our longitude was 126° 32' 0".
The winds being still to the south-east and varying only to the east-south-east, almost calm in the afternoon, I did not change course in order to endeavour to make as much easting as possible, so as to make better the tack to the south-south-west when the wind would allow us to take it. But the breeze was so light in the morning that the current was carrying us with violence to the north, which we could easily judge by the lead and the drift of the vessel.
What we had experienced up to then of the violence of the currents and the constancy of the winds in the south-east to east-south-east part since we had entered into the bend that the coast makes here, made me know that it (is) impossible or at least very difficult to penetrate there coming from the west. And in consequence, I continued to make northing and especially easting as much as possible, preferring to return on my steps when I should have reached the coast between 13 and 12 degrees of latitude.
At sunset the vessel could hardly be steered, although we were making two knots, and went only abeam. From eight o'clock to midnight the breeze was fairly steady but then it became very heavy and we had again to take a second reef in the topsails, and it continued in the same manner for the rest of the night. The bottom on which we sailed was between 24 and 29 fathoms, mud less soft than that of the preceding days.

1803-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first 20 June 1803 messidor, in the morning, the winds followed the course they had taken for two days, that is to say they began at night between ten o'clock and midnight and went on increasing until the following day at about eleven o'clock in the morning. After which they calmed gradually, so that at sunset it was almost calm.
I was very surprised to see it take this course and I am still persuaded that it is only accidental since it is so contrary to that which they follow in every other country and at the same latitudes. Events will show us if it is a constant rule, which I would greatly regret. The breezes, in the middle of the night, which pass in calm everywhere else, were so fresh that they obliged us to make two reefs in the topsails. And, as in places where the waters are not deep, the sea becomes rough quickly, this together with the sail we had to carry to keep the Casuarina, did not little contribute to giving us much drift, increased still further by the currents. Also, we had each day very great differences in the dead reckoning in the course travelled.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 9' 38" and the longitude from No. 35 put us at 127° 2' 54".
In the afternoon the weather was fine and the wind almost calm. As they were from the east part we were constrained to follow the tack to the north which we followed until nine o'clock in the evening, then taking that to the south with winds to the east-north-east very variable. The bottom had considerably incre(ased) and we were in 40 fathoms. In the night which was fine and almost calm it came to 34. We did not have the strong breezes of the preceding days and I hope ( ! ) that the new moon will bring us back, with fine weather, the winds of the south-west and west which we would see return with pleasure.

1803-06-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second 21 June 1803, the breeze was very moderate and did not rise with the rising of the sun nor when it had gained strength. The winds being to the east, variable to east-north-east, we continued on the course to the south, making easting as much as was possible or as the winds allowed us.
At eight o'clock we were still in 30 fathoms of water, but at ten o'clock there were no more than twenty-two and at noon, 21. I was surprised! () at so sudden a decrease and attributed the cause to some elevation of the bottom, which had already several times happened to us to encounter. I still reckoned myself at a fairly great distance from the land according to my charts, to believe that we were still far from it.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 35' 29" and our longitude was only 127° 5' 13" which gave very little distance to the east when compared with that of the day before.
In the afternoon the winds gained a little strength and drew imperceptibly towards the north. We made course to the east. At three o'clock the lookouts announced (land) ahead of us which could not fail to surprise me, for in admitting that the hydrographic office's chart had placed the northern extremity of the land as was the point which is found to the south of Timor which we had ascertained to be placed more than two degrees too far west, it followed that this other part of the coast should be affected by the same difference, which, in all probability will not exist, since we now have land in sight.
At four o'clock we distinguished the coast perfectly from the deck and at five we were no more than two leagues at most from it. It presents itself in a very uniform manner, less elevated than that seen the preceding days and without any point of recognition except for the fires which were seen in different places and which were fairly considerable. The bottom was then between fifteen and sixteen fathoms, very fine grey sand, mixed with a little mud.
As night was falling we bore away to the east-north-east, the bottom not increasing, we stood to the north-east. The winds were then to the south-west very faint. My intention not being to anchor, I ordered the vessel to steer north at seven o'clock, the direction which the coast was to take!** We sailed with all sail set, the lead in hand, on fairly regular bottom between 15 and 16 fathoms.
But at a quarter to nine o'clock, the winds having entirely failed us, we let go a kedge anchor in 14 fathoms, bottom of very fine sand and mud. As several fires were seen on the coast, it was easily perceived that the current was carrying us to the north-west.
During the night it was calm until about two (o'clock) when a light breeze came from the east. According to the observations which were made, the force of the current, with the vessel heading south-east, was one mile 1 tenth, and heading north-east of 1 mile 3 tenths. The rise of the sea decreased by one fathom and rose only by the same amount.

1803-06-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third messidor 22 June 1803, in the morning, the winds being from the east to the south-east, we got under sail at five o'clock and made course as close to the wind as possible. At about nine o'clock they passed to the east-north-east and obliged us to make the course more to the north than we should have wished. The lead, which was 14 fathoms at the moment we weighed, passed successively to eighteen. The land which in the morning remained to us from the SE to the E. NE was lost sight of on this course, and we did not see it again until the afternoon.
At this time the latitude was observed as 13° 27' 48" and the longitude of our timekeeper was 127° 18' 28". We had had throughout the morning a hazy sky and a limited horizon.
The calm which began at about eleven o'clock in the morning lasted until two o'clock in the afternoon. We had afterwards a light breeze from the north-east which was of short duration. At six o'clock they passed to the north and were no less calm than they had been to the north-east. However, we closed with the land by means of the current which at sunset remained to us to the east-south-east at about six leagues' distance. The whole part of the coast which we had seen up to then is low and very uniform without any particular point that could serve as a landmark.
According to the report of the lookouts, they had sight of a sand bank uncovered, remaining to us to the south-east which they assured us they saw very distinctly and of which, according to their reckoning, we were not more than two leagues away. As I was very ill that day I could not see for myself what it was. I ordered the officer who is to replace me in case of death to anchor at eight o'clock if the wind was calm or if it did not allow us to make course to the north, the announced bank remaining to the north-east according to the report made to me. At seven o'clock the wind being calm we anchored in 18 fathoms on a bottom of sand similar to that which we had had in the preceding days.
The rest of the night had nothing of particular note. The force of the current was about the same as the day before and its direction from north to north-west. There was little variation in the rise or fall of the waters.

1803-06-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth 23 June 1803, we got under sail at four o'clock in the morning, making course to the north-north-east while waiting for day and having only fifteen fathoms of water. At sunrise we had sight of the coast which was borne from north 33° east to south 32 east. This extent of coast appeared to us to form several bays some of which seemed to be deep. In the northern part of the land we saw a second one which we judged should be an island by its distance from the continent, or if it touches it, the land must be so low that it cannot be seen from the top of the masts. Although we were fairly close to it the whole of this coast moreover is extremely low and scarcely visible at three leagues' distance and in 14 fathoms of water.
The sky was finer this day than usually and the sun warm which had not happened to us to feel for several days.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 23' 15". There was no hour angle the hazy clouds having robbed us of the view of the horizon and of the sun throughout the evening while the sky had been very fine in the morning. At the end of the day the lands in sight extended from the south to the east 28° north.
At eight o'clock, the winds being perfectly calm and the current causing us to drift in (the) north-west with considerable force to judge by the log, we anchored in 15 fathoms, bottom of coarse gravel and broken shells mixed with a little mud.
During the night the calm continued until three o'clock in the morning when a light breeze came from the east-south-east. The weather was always overcast and hazy yet the sea nevertheless became a little rough an effect no doubt produced by some current.
During the night according to the observations which were made the current had little speed and did not exceed 6 tenths of a knot in the north-west and north-north-west. The tide having reversed at about three o'clock in the morning they took their direction to the south-south-east. The height of the water was about the same.

1803-06-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth 24 June 1803 messidor, we weighed at five o'clock in the morning having the winds from the south-south-east to the south-east a fine breeze. We made to the north-north-east until eleven o'clock having the land in sight in the north-east a quarter north and extending for our view as far as the south-east a quarter south. This land like that of the day before was low and could scarcely be seen at three leagues' distance although we were in fifteen and eighteen fathoms of water.
In the morning the sky was fine and cloudless although hazy at the horizon. At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 44' 56" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 127° 43' 8".
From eleven o'clock we had made the course a little more to the east to not lose sight of it but in the evening the winds coming to us from the east a quarter north-east and then to the north-east obliged us to move away from it. As it was calm the greater part of the evening we made little progress and at sunset the currents carrying us to the north-west we lost sight of it having sight only at six o'clock of a bright and brilliant fire which was borne to the south 30° west.
As the weather had become overcast and there was appearance of wind for the night I kept under sail until ten o'clock when the calm obliged me to anchor the bottom going on increasing. We then had nineteen fathoms bottom of mud which should should (sic) according to our preceding observations put us at a considerable distance from the coast.
During the night if the wind was not entirely calm it was at least very light from the south-south-west to the west. The currents were so little noticeable on the log during the night that we did not think we needed to account for them. Nevertheless the sounding decreased by two fathoms which was rather attributed to inequalities of the bottom than to the tide. The sky during the night was constantly damp and hazy.

1803-06-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth 25 June 1803, after getting under sail we steered to the north-east to close with the land which we had lost sight of the evening before and of which nevertheless we should not have been far away according to the knowledge we had of the fires at the beginning of night. Nevertheless we did not see it at daybreak nor even at about ten o'clock although the bottom was only 15 fathoms.
At noon it was announced to us by the lookouts who had sight of it from the top of the masts and according to our dead reckoning we could not have been more than three or four leagues at most from it. At the same moment the latitude was observed as 12° 25' 44" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 127° 52' 37". The weather was then fine and the wind almost calm from the south-east.
In the afternoon they passed to the north and varied to the west-south-west without gaining much strength so we made little progress.
At four o'clock the land extended for our view from the east-south-east to the south-east a quarter south. It was like that of the preceding days very low and of (more) little easy to distinguish. We held under sail during the night to profit by the wind if it should develop as the appearances seemed to indicate to us. It did indeed blow a little and we held the tack to the north towards the west with winds from the north-east the bottom going on increasing. The sky during the night was as usual hazy and covered with clouds but the breeze increased a little during the night.

1803-06-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh 26 June 1803, at four o'clock in the morning, the winds having passed to the north-north-east, we went about on the tack to the north. A fine breeze blew in the morning, comparatively to that of the preceding days. We were very surprised at sunrise to hear the lookouts announce land to the north-north-west especially according to the course we had made during the night. At first I thought there was a mistake and that what had been taken for land was some cloud at the horizon which had the appearance of it. But having had it examined more carefully I was confirmed in the report.
At eight o'clock we had perfect (knowledge) of the land from the deck. It presented itself to us in a much more elevated form than that seen in the preceding days. And one could distinguish in several places elevated points which if necessary could serve as landmarks.
The sky although fairly fine was covered and laden with hazy clouds which often hid from us the view of the coast although we were not then more than three leagues from it.
We had no observed latitude this day the sky being too covered and at noon we took bearings of the lands of which the most northern remained to us at north 20° west and the most southern at north 70° east. One could distinguish in the part of coast in sight several points which formed between them bays more or less deep.
In the afternoon the winds were extremely variable. From the east-north-east they passed to the north and north-west accompanied by rain and fairly strong squalls. The sky which had not a fine appearance from the morning became dark and laden with very dark clouds which gave us towards the middle of the evening winds to the south-west. We profited by this to draw away from the coast and after having (doubled) the point which relative to our position took from the north towards the west we resumed the course north a quarter north-east to ascertain other lands which then remained to us to the north-east but the sky was so covered dark and laden that at the end of the day we could distinguish nothing.
The appearance of bad weather for the night made me take a second reef in the topsails and had it not occurred I would have done it anyway compelled to do so not to lose the Casuarina which was much astern.
At the beginning of night the weather was in squalls the sky covered and rainy. We were making course to the west towards the south to draw away from the land and I reckoned to follow the same direction until midnight to then take that of the north towards the east. The bottom on this course was between twenty-seven and 30 fathoms until ten o'clock when we found no more than twenty. We then made the course take more of the south and the bottom increased until thirty-two fathoms. But at midnight it was no more than twenty. Not knowing what could be meant by soundings so unequal and disproportionate in a small space of time. The course north towards the east the soundings which we took hour by hour varied no less but they were deep that is to say above twenty fathoms. We continued on this tack until four o'clock in the morning the time at which we took that south towards the east which were equally little regular. We held it until daylight. Although the bottom was almost always decreasing which did not fail to fatigue & to cause me anxiety having passed the greater part of the night on deck and being in poor health attacked again by a coughing of blood which had recurred for the third time since our departure from Port Jackson.

1803-06-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth 27 June 1803, in the morning at six o'clock I expected all the more (to) have sight of land since the lead was bringing up no more than 18 and 19 fathoms of water. We then took the course north towards the east while waiting for sunrise. The weather was not fine and even had a fairly bad appearance. Nevertheless at sunrise we had no sight of the lands although our horizon was fairly extended. On this course the bottom going on increasing and even very rapidly we bore in hugging the wind as close as possible.
During the morning the weather turned fine and we were surprised to see it change so quickly. At noon the latitude was observed as 11° 20' 32" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 127° 29' 19". This longitude confirmed our observations of the past night on the direction of the currents which according to the tidal streams which we encountered should carry us violently to the south-west.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine but the winds passing to the east. We had to steer more to the north than I should have wished. At two o'clock although we still had no sight of the coast from the top of the masts we nevertheless saw very distinctly from the deck two columns of smoke coming from land. One was borne to the south-east and the other to the south-east a quarter east. We continued during the evening to make course to the north making easting as much as the winds allowed. The lead in the evening always reported a great depth and seemed by that alone to indicate to us that we were moving much away from the land.
At the beginning of night the weather became very misty and the winds calmed. The sea which up to then had been fairly fine became rough which led me to believe that we had passed the northern point of the western coast of Van Diemen's Bay.
At midnight the sky which had become covered with clouds since sunset set in to rain and squalls. These gave us at first little wind but rain in abundance and as heavy as that which falls in great showers. At about two o'clock the squalls were not only rainy but also accompanied by winds which obliged us to furl our topsails. The first were furled by us by winds from the east but the second gave us winds winds (sic) from the south-south-east to the south-east and allowed us to make course to the east-north-east. As we sounded hour by hour we passed from three o'clock to four o'clock from eighteen to forty fathoms. A decrease so prompt and so rapid causing me to fear the vicinity of some shoal or shallow water such as those that Arrowsmith shows on his chart although we had much passed the latitude which he gives them I at once ordered to steer north-west and the bottom within the hour passed from 18 to 36 fathoms. We then came successively to the course north and the bottom was always increasing so that at six o'clock we were in 48 fathoms.
These irregularities of bottom on a coast of which almost all nautical charts give a different position is very disquieting for navigators and those who succeed us will doubtless experience them in the same way until the waters are better known and determined. Which in all probability we shall not be able to do if the weather and winds do not favour us more.

1803-06-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth 28 June 1803 in the morning being in forty-six fathoms of water (at) sunrise and having (no mention) we resumed the course to the east-north-east with a fine breeze from the south-south-east variable to the south-east. The bottom was increasing until seven o'clock when it was sixty-four fathoms. At eight o'clock as the vessel was going forward much we did not find it at 30 and continued consequently our course. But at nine o'clock we found ourselves with astonishment in 18 fathoms. And the sea calm although a good breeze blew we let her bear away two points. Nevertheless we decreased still by one fathom. We bore away again and it increased in proportion as we advanced to the north. What had just happened to us leads me to believe that we were following the edge of the bank which the Dutch have indicated on the chart which they have given of this part of the coast and which others have left out. As it also places the northern coast of the western land of Van Diemen's Bay further north than any of the other nautical charts which are known to us my opinion would be that it (is) better placed. The extent which the Dutch chart gives to the bank which we have been coasting does not allow of seeing the coast in that one must go too far away from it to pass it and it is presumable that the other navigators who will have succeeded Tasman will have taken some other points for that of the north of this part. Otherwise they must have had sight of this bank.
Be that as it may the weather was not fine in the morning and had no better appearance for the afternoon. A good breeze blew and we took two reefs in the topsails which did not prevent us from losing sight of the Casuarina which we then had to wait for by remaining two hours abeam the wind.
At noon the latitude was observed as 27° 10° 25' 5" and the longitude of the timekeeper put us at 127° 30' 35".
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze from the south-east and as we had passed the northern point of the bank shown on the chart of Valentyn we resumed again the course to the east-north-east the bottom being then fifty-five fathoms fine sand and mud. This course was was (sic) followed until the following day.
The weather was fairly bad during the night which was dark and with strong squalls.

1803-06-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth 29 June 1803, in the morning the weather was even worse than the day before. The winds varied from the south-east to the south-south-east a fresh breeze and the sea became heavy but the squalls were less frequent than during the night. We sounded several times in the morning without finding bottom at 60 and 50 fathoms.
At noon we did not have sight of the sun which did not even show itself throughout the day. According to our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves at 9° 45' 57" of latitude 128° 13' 44" of longitude. We then took the tack to the south towards the west to maintain ourselves between the ninth and tenth degrees of latitude while waiting for the weather to turn fine which did not appear to be very near according to the state of the atmosphere and the sea. Nevertheless the movement of the barometer varied little.
During the night the weather continued to be bad and the sea heavy. We followed the tack to the south until midnight when we took that to the north.

1803-06-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh 30 June 1803 gave us no change in the weather whose state resembled that which it presents to view on the worst day of winter in Europe. Continuously laden with fogs and heavy dark black and thick clouds it appeared as certain that we would have some squalls. And I decided to wait in the waters where I found myself until it should be passed before proceeding further to the east. At ten o'clock we took the tack to the south which I continued until night when we resumed that to the north.
During the morning we furled the topgallant sails and we made our preparations for the bad weather which seemed to me inevitable and which indeed did not fail to occur during the night which obliged us to heave to. The wind was not however very violent and we would easily have carried our four major sails all reefed in the topsails if we had not had to wait for the Casuarina which could not carry hers without too much fatiguing her vessel. There were nevertheless some heavy gusts but of short duration. Towards the end of the night the weather turning to rain the wind was less strong and the sea was no less agitated by it.
As we did not see the sun at noon our estimated latitude was 9° 41' 33" and the longitude 128° 18' 44". However by two altitudes of sun which were taken in the afternoon at moments when the sun showed itself very obscured the latitude which was thence concluded for the time of noon was found to be 9° 43' 23" and the longitude 128° 17' 12". These results appear to me too doubtful to have great confidence in them.

1803-07-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth 1st July 1803, in the morning the weather was even worse than the preceding days the rain was almost continuous and the gusts began again and lasted without interruption until about ten o'clock when they became less frequent. From six and a half o'clock we had taken the under sail to the south to not be too much driven to the north of the latitude in which I wished to remain until the bad weather should be past. We also set the main topsail at the lower reef so that (that) the arrivals of the vessel should be less considerable. At eleven o'clock the wind seeming to want to calm we hoisted the mainsail and the foresail. We furled the main topsail a second time moving the Casuarina too far away with this sail plan.
At noon the sun having appeared between the clouds we took it about noon and the result put us at (no figures). This latitude although doubtful should differ little from that which we should have had had the weather been fine.
According to our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves at (no figures) and at (no figures) of longitude.
In the evening the weather was less thick and the clouds began to become clearer. Those which being dark and obscure gave us a fine rain
when the winds made them pass in the direction of our course. We continued the tack to the south towards the west until six o'clock when we took that to the east towards the north for the night. During the twenty-four hours we sounded several times on both tacks without finding bottom at 50 and 60 fathoms. The drift was too considerable to pay out more line.
During the night the weather which had cleared a little towards the end of the day became dark and rainy again accompanied by squalls and squalls which had very little interruption.

1803-07-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth 2 July 1803 the sky although always laden with clouds and covered took a better appearance in the morning and it seemed we were going to have a change in our favour. We had need of it all the more since the weather we had been having for four days occasioned to the vessel such violent movements that all our livestock which I desired so much to preserve for the benefit of France were very much incommoded by it and particularly the emus which had to be forcibly made to eat so that they would not die of hunger. The loss of these animals will certainly not be made up for by the little geographical knowledge which it appears we shall be able to have on the part of the coast which remains for us to visit and I am decided if the weather does not turn fine after the full moon to make course for the Isle of France rather than lose them entirely.
The sun having appeared a few moments in the morning an hour angle was taken very doubtful and it was the same for the latitude at the time of noon. Nevertheless the result of these observations preferable to dead reckoning put us at 9° 53' 40" of latitude and 127° 47' 53" of longitude. According to the dead reckoning we were at 9° 44' 54" and 128° 18' 6" of longitude.
During the evening the sky became covered again with clouds and mist. A fresh breeze blew but unevenly and by squalls. The winds were variable from the east-south-east to the south-east which made us hold the tack to the south towards the west. At seven o'clock in the evening we went about and during the night the course took a little more of the east the winds having drawn towards the south. The breeze was much less strong than during the day but the sea did not cease to be agitated and rough.

1803-07-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth 3 July 1803 the weather was finer than usual. The sky although misty had taken a good appearance and I still reckoned on a change in our favour at the full moon. When the sun had gained a little strength the winds passed to the south-east variable towards the east. We held during the morning the tack to the south towards the west hugging the wind as close as possible.
The sea sea (sic) become calmer remained always rough and a long heavy swell which had little appearance at the surface of the water occasioned to the vessel very violent movements although a fresh breeze blew and it was well supported by its sails although there were two reefs in each topsail.
Having had good observations in the morning and an exact latitude at noon we found ourselves at 9° 59' 18" and 128° 9' 52" of longitude so that for six days we had gained almost nothing to the east and it appeared useless to persist any longer in trying to gain it if the winds did not change direction. A thing which appeared fairly probable from the course they had followed since we were north of the lands and as in the middle of the channel which separates New Holland from the other lands which are to the north of it between the eighth and ninth degrees of latitude. It is in all probability to this direction of the coast in this part that must be attributed the different course which they follow south of the tenth degree where we never failed to have breezes from the south to the south-west and even from the west.
During the morning a fresh breeze blew but it was less strong in the afternoon. The winds varied little from the south-east to the east-south-east until sunset when they drew towards the south. We took after having closed with the Casuarina the tack to the east towards the north. This vessel did not little contribute to occasioning to us not only a strong drift by the little sail we had to make to wait for her but also by the course we were obliged to make to the west every evening to close with her which I estimate at two leagues a day. Despite all these inconveniences which did not fail (to) cause me much bad humour I could not bring myself to abandon her and to give her order to make course for the Isle of France foreseeing that I shall essentially need her if by and by I should succeed in gaining the Gulf of Carpentaria.
During the night the hazy and damp clouds made themselves felt and seemed to announce to us that the sky would not be too fine the following day.

1803-07-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth 4 July 1803 the sky was fairly clear although misty but our horizon was laden with misty and thick vapours which gave it little extent. At six o'clock the breeze being then faint we had the bottom at 70 fathoms. I think we would have had it about the same in the soundings of the preceding days if the strong drift of the vessel the heavy sea and the wind (not) had allowed us to pay out so much line.
At sunrise the breeze gained strength but it did not follow the same course of the preceding days. The winds which between seven and eight o'clock in the morning ranged towards the east remained to the south-east variable to the south-east a quarter east until the middle of the day when they took more of the south.
At noon the latitude was observed as 9° 43' 21" and our longitude was found to be 128° 41' 19" so that we had for this time advanced a little to the east.
In the afternoon the winds continued to be variable from the south-south-east to the south and the sea always heavy and rough which did not announce to us imminent the end of the strong breezes which we had been experiencing for several days.
The night had nothing of particular note we continued the tack to the east towards the north with the precaution of sounding every two (two hours) without having bottom at 60 nor 45 fathoms. The sky was always damp and hazy but the winds less strong than during the day.

1803-07-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth 5 July 1803 the winds having allowed us to come nearer to the course to the east we profited by this and took courage in the hope that they would end by becoming if not entirely favourable at least reasonably good so as not to lose on one tack what we gained on the other.
Although the state of the atmosphere was always the same the sea was less agitated and the squalls of wind more bearable than the preceding days.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 55' 40" and our longitude was 129° 44' 44" which gave us a great difference from our dead reckoning according to the courses travelled. But we were far from complaining of it since we found ourselves to have advanced nearly one degree to the east which had not happened to us for a long time.
During the evening we continued the tack to the north towards the east until six o'clock in the evening when not wishing to go further north from our longitude I made the course take that to the south towards the west. The winds being to the south-east moderate we continued it during the night and we did not find bottom at 50 nor 70 fathoms. Besides the weather was fairly fine although misty and very damp.

1803-07-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth 6 July 1803 as soon as it was day we resumed the tack to the north-east and the winds served us a little in the morning in that they came sometimes as far as the south. But this was only passing. At sunrise the sky had a very bad appearance being laden with dark and thick clouds at all points of the horizon. I thought we would have some squalls in the morning but I was deceived in my expectation for as the sun gained strength the clouds dispersed and the weather became fine.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 58' 49" and our longitude was found to be 130° 2' 23". So that we had gained very little to the east in the 24 hours and it appears that the course of the night had taken more of the west than the dead reckoning indicated or that the currents which had favoured us the day before had become contrary or against us when we took the tack to the south.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine but the breeze from the south-south-east having increased the sea became quickly heavy. Towards evening the sky became covered with clouds and there was little appearance that the weather remain fine during the night. We continued the tack to the east towards the north until midnight until midnight that the winds allowed us to bear away for some time to the east towards the south. The breeze was moderate and the weather was not bad despite appearances only the sea was heavy and agitated which occasioned to us much drift.

1803-07-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth 7 July 1803 in the morning although the sky was dark and covered the weather had nothing disagreeable nevertheless we had from time to time fairly good squalls from the south-south-east the point to which the winds had returned.
In the morning I was informed that several of our quadrupeds and emus were very ill.
