We could not attribute the cause to anything but the violent and multiplied movements of the heavy sea which left them not an instant's rest. This news was all the more disagreeable to me as I saw myself on the eve of losing them after care which should have merited for them a happier fate. As the emus refused to eat we made them take food by force by opening their beaks and introducing into their stomachs pellets of rice paste. We gave them as we did to the kangaroos which were indisposed wine and sugar and although I was very much at a loss for these same things for myself I would be very well content to have deprived myself of them for them if they could contribute to bringing them back to health.
I experienced on this day a coughing of blood more considerable than those which had already occurred. I could not say to what cause to attribute it for this ailment had left me about eight days before and I believed myself freed from it for some time. Either the continuation of this illness or some other cause this coughing of blood was accompanied by such weakness in all my limbs that I was constrained to take to my bed and I found not great relief in it.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 26' 33" and the longitude was 131° 11' 14". These observations are very doubtful for the weather was not suited to having good ones.
In the afternoon the winds having passed to the south-east we went about to take the tack to the south-south-west. This course was continued until eight o'clock when we laid to to wait for the Casuarina which did not catch up with us until ten o'clock. As it was necessary to send her back persisting in wanting to gain the entrance to the Gulf of Carpentaria or renounce achieving it while keeping her I made up my mind to take the course for the Isle of France and gave her order to steer to the south-west a quarter west which I took myself. It was not without sorrow that I decided to take this course. A thousand reasons would even have made me take it earlier. But without detailing them all I shall content myself with saying that we had no more than a month's biscuit at six ounces per man and two months' water at the consumption of those of our birds and quadrupeds. Twenty men were on the sick list several attacked by dysentery and the others out of service by serious venereal diseases contracted at Timor no one to replace me. The Casuarina which I was never able to get to sail ahead in any way that I set about it and which alone is the cause that I have not gained this gulf for a long time &a &a &a.
This resolution taken I made course to pass through the channel which separates Roti from Timor in order not to be thwarted in passing south of this first island by the winds from the west and north-west which I was almost certain to find there having for me the experience of two voyages in these waters.
I leave you to imagine the effect which this change of course had on people to which no one was expecting for no one ever knew neither where I was going nor what I intended to do (). During the whole voyage several of those who spent the whole night on deck were often on the compass from fear of being deceived in what they had been told and this night was that on which there was the most people on deck although the weather was not fine.

1803-07-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth 8 July 1803 we continued the course to the south-west a quarter west and the Casuarina was no less troublesome with the wind on the quarter than it had been burdensome close-hauled. To not abandon it we had to keep two reefs in the topsails furl the foresail and constantly have the flying topgallant on the mast. However it had all its sails set except for one reef which it carried on its main topsail. The breeze being strong and the sea heavy.
At noon the latitude was observed as 9° 10' 44" and the longitude was 129° 37' 52" just as doubtful as those of the preceding days.
According to the observed latitude we continued our same course until eight o'clock in the evening when I took that to the west and which was followed during the night. Being then abeam of the wind to wait for the Casuarina I had soundings taken and we had bottom at 85 fathoms. The night had nothing of particular note. The sky was very misty damp and dark.
As it was perceived the day before that the wine with sugar given to our sick animals had done them good and they had regained a little strength we continued to give them the same quantity twice a day.

1803-07-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth 9 July 1803 we had a strong breeze from the east-south-east to the east which quickly made the sea heavy and rough and during the morning we experienced strong squalls accompanied by heavy gusts and rain.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures) and the longitude according to our timekeepers was for No. 35 of (no figures).
In the afternoon the weather was finer than it had been in the morning but the sea continued to be heavy rough and agitated the winds varied little from the east to the east-south-east.
The night had nothing of particular note and the breeze calmed. We continued the course to the south 78° west conforming to the rate of the Casuarina.

1803-07-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first 10 July 1803 the sky was fine and clear and the sea became fine although the winds were about the same as the day before for strength but the breeze which had gained strength at daybreak was steady and not by squalls as most of the preceding days.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures) and according to our longitude we reckoned ourselves at (no figures).
In the afternoon we took the course to the south 84° 30' west which we followed until the following day. At sunset the horizon became laden with clouds and damp vapours nevertheless the night was fine and was troubled only by the great dampness which was felt. At midnight we sounded without finding bottom at one hundred fathoms.

1803-07-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second 11 July 1803 the weather continued fine and the winds varied from the east to the south-east a fine breeze. We made all sail to ascertain the land of which we should not have been be (sic) far away according to the rate of our timekeepers.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures) and our longitude was (no figures) for No. 35 and (no figures) for No. 31.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and at about five and a half o'clock in the evening the horizon which was laden with clouds in the south-east part having cleared we had good sight of the lands of Timor of which the lands most in view extended from the north 71 west to the north 66 west. The other parts of the coast were too hazy to distinguish them well. We continued to make course on the land until eight o'clock in the evening when we turned close-hauled on the tack to the south which was followed until midnight when we took that to the north towards the east waiting for day. During the night the sky although misty was fine and the dampness less strong than the day before.

1803-07-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third 12 July 1803 we closed with the southern coast of Timor which we followed in the course of the morning at short distance with winds from the east-south-east variable to east very light.
At noon by a later observation of the sun our latitude was (no figures) and the longitude of the timekeepers put us at No. 35 at (no figures) and at No. 31 at (no figures). But it seemed to us from the sight of the lands which we believed we could recognize that the rate of No. 35 put us more to the west than we really were not having yet sight of the island of Roti which we should have seen had it been regular.
During the morning evening we made course in the direction of the coast relative to the position of the vessel. And at sunset we had sight of a part of the island of Roti from the top of the masts.
As my intention was not to enter the channel during the night we made course along the coast only until seven and a half o'clock in the evening and then took the closest to tack at the entrance of the channel during the night which was fine and the wind by squalls of short duration.

1803-07-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth 13 July 1803 before daylight we closed with the coast of Timor in order to enter the channel early but at daybreak we found ourselves two or three leagues further away from it than our dead reckoning put us. It appears that the reversal of the tide or a more regular current had carried us to the east on the two tacks which were made during the night. Nevertheless we had perfect sight of the island of Roti and directed our course to pass through the middle of the channel which we crossed between ten and eleven o'clock.
At noon we found ourselves to have passed the small island which is found at the southern point of Semau and at the same instant the latitude was observed as (no figures) and the longitude indicated by our timekeepers was for No. 35 of (no figures) and for No. 31 of (no figures).
This longitude referred to that of Kupang fixed by our observations at (no figures) gave a difference in longitude of (no figures) for No. 35 and of (no figures) for No. 31. So that it appears that since our last departure from Timor this watch had advanced in its ordinary rate of (no figures) a change to which I know not what cause to attribute it unless perhaps to the difference in the manner of setting them each noon and which in the long run may have influenced its movement being more or less rapid by him who is now charged with it than it was when they were set by Citizen Bernier.
Be that as it may when we had passed the small island of which I have just spoken each one expected that I would make course to put in a third time to Timor. For no one could conceive why I had come to seek this channel to go to the Isle of France. This course according to all being very bad since it did nothing but prolong our stay at sea while we had very many good reasons to diminish it as much as would be possible.
It was not at me that all these remarks were addressed but they were the subject of the confidential conversation of our learned officers of the Navy. I was displeased to have been informed of it in that it convinced me more than ever that they had gained no instruction nor profit from the navigation which they had already done at three different periods and which should have taught them that south of the third degree of latitude one is certain to encounter winds very variable from the north-west to the south-south-west since at the three different periods of the year that we have visited these waters we have always found them in this direction while north of the twelfth degree they are constantly from the south-east to the east.
I make mention of this incident only to warn sailors who by and by might find themselves in the same case that the route which appears the shortest is not always that which one should prefer and that it is better to rely on experience than on insignificant and unreflecting remarks of young people who see only superficially or according to their little judgment.
After having passed the small island south of Semau we followed the coast of the island of Roti my intention being to pass during the night through the channel which separates it from Savu. We made all sail in the afternoon to come and ascertain before night the islands which are at the western point of Roti which we saw at sunset. Although the Casuarina was astern I did not reduce sail to wait for her and made course until midnight when finding myself in the middle of the channel and abeam of Savu I hove to to give her time to catch up with me. We spent the rest of the night there occupied in making signals to her by fires and rockets to which she did not reply.

1803-07-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth 14 July 1803 after having passed half the night abeam to wait for the Casuarina we had no sight of her either by daylight which persuaded me that she had not continued the course which she was making at sunset being in our waters at one league's distance. For had she followed it she could not have passed us without having sight of our signals and we of her. I therefore made up my mind and not reckoning on meeting her anymore we resumed the course to the west-south-west.
At daybreak we had in sight the small island of Savu which remained to us from the north-west a quarter west to the north-north-west at a distance of 4 to 5 leagues. In the course of the morning we saw the islet which is to the west a quarter north-west of it and which I spoke of when we passed north of Savu on our first departure from Timor.
At noon the latitude was observed as 11° 6' 31" and the longitude was at No. 35 of 118° 46' 40" and at No. 31 of 119° 14' 53". The lands of Savu could be seen then from the north 15° east to the north 45° east.
During the evening the weather continued fine and at about four o'clock in the afternoon the lookouts announced a sail ahead of us. We had no doubt that it was the Casuarina and we made all sail to join her before night without being able to succeed. As this vessel appeared to be bearing more to the south than we we made the same course in the hope of joining her but we had no sight of her during the night which the weather was fine and the view fairly extended.

1803-07-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth 15 July 1803 in the morning we had again sight of the vessel seen the evening before but it remained to us abeam on the starboard at about two leagues' distance. Having recognized it for the Casuarina we closed with her and I made signal to keep ahead of us from then on and to make all sail.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 0' 58" and the longitude of No. 35 was 116° 32' 28" and that of No. 31 117° 1' 32".
Although I had given order to the Casuarina to keep ahead of us it still let itself fall so much astern although we had almost no sail that I was led to believe that it truly had the desire to separate and I was confirmed in this opinion on learning that its intention was to put in at Batavia. This warning made me observe it so well that I forbade under any pretence to lose sight of it during the night and not even to follow the course which I had given if she departed from it to make another route and to warn me about it observing especially not to pass ahead of her.
We had during the whole day a heavy swell from the south-west which announced to us that the winds were fresh in that part further to the south. The sky was very covered during the night and we had from time to time squalls which were not of long duration.

1803-07-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh 16 July 1803 the weather turned fine again and we had a fine breeze from the east to the east-south-east of which we profited little having most of the time our topsails on the tone to wait for the Casuarina.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 33' 32" and the longitude at No. 35 was 114° 31' 48" and at No. 31 115° 2' 0". Not wishing to go further south to not encounter the winds of the south-west I signalled the course to the west but there was an error in the signal for instead of hoisting the upper ensign it was hoisted lower this error was not perceived until about four o'clock the Casuarina not steering (not) as we to the west. A new signal was made to her accompanied by a gun as she had reduced sail I know not why.
During the evening the sky was fairly fine and we continued our course with little sail to always have the Casuarina ahead and in sight. The manoeuvre of the night was the same.

1803-07-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth 17 July 1803 continuation of fine weather and fine sea we continued to steer to the west. The crew greatly discontented at having such fine weather without profiting by it said that we would not fail as punishment to soon experience some squalls and that we would have no cause to complain since it was by choice that we were keeping them at sea reduced to 6 ounces of bread a day. They perhaps had not wholly wrong to complain but I did not want to leave the Casuarina astern unless forced to do so by some particular circumstance.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 19' 45" and the longitude of No. 35 was 112° 20' 13" that of No. 31 112° 50' 45".
The rest of the day had nothing of particular note nor did the night.

1803-07-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth 18 July 1803 the weather was less fine than usual we had at times during the morning squalls accompanied by rain which were of little consequence but which made the state of the sky not pleasant to look upon. Our course during these twenty-four hours was the same as that of the preceding days except for the courses changes which had to be made to close with the Casuarina which rarely steered on the course indicated.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 27' 40" and the longitude at No. 35 was 110° 4' 22" and for No. 31 110° 36' 3".
In the evening the sky took on a stormy aspect and kept it during part of the night without however giving us lightning or thunder but only a heavy damp and unhealthy air which lasted until the middle of the night when the clouds dispersed.

1803-07-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth 19 July 1803 the sky without being fine had a better appearance than the day before. Nevertheless a thick vapour extending all around the horizon rendered it not extended for us. This situation of the atmosphere lasted until about ten o'clock when the breeze from the east having increased rendered it more extended by dispersing in great part the fog which had formed there.
We had the displeasure of losing on this day one of our emus dead without any sign of illness. This loss was all the more considerable in that on plucking it to stuff it we recognized that it was a female and that in the three which remain to us there are perhaps none.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 30' 19" and the longitude of No. 35 was 107° 28' 29" that of No. 31 108° 1' 14".
In the evening the sky became entirely fine and we began to no longer feel the effects of the heavy swell from the south-west which we had had for several days. The night had nothing of particular note.

1803-07-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first 20 July 1803 we had very fine weather and a fine breeze from the east. We continued the course to the west which I had decided to follow between twelve and thirteen degrees of latitude until abeam of the western point of the island of Java.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 38' 6" and the longitude of our timekeepers put us according to No. 35 at 105° "3' 12" and according to No. 31 at 105° 36' 46".
In the afternoon the sky which had been fine in the morning became covered with clouds a little before sunset and at night we had it very misty and sometimes in small squalls accompanied by a little rain which was not of long duration. But we found the sea very rough and a heavy swell from the south-west occasioned to us movements of rolling very multiplied and very lively. Besides nothing occurred which merits particular remarks.

1803-07-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second 21 July 1803 the winds were very variable and unequal in the part from east towards the south-east. The sky was covered the greater part of the morning and it was not until about eleven o'clock that the clouds began to separate.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 44' 2" and the longitude of our timekeepers was for No. 35 of 102° 35' 0" and for No. 31 of 103° 9' 0".
At sunset After the observation of the sun I signalled the course to the west a quarter south-west. During the evening the sky became covered again with clouds and did not have a fine appearance in several points of the horizon. As the obser officers of the watch made little attention to observe what I had prescribed to keep the Casuarina they were warned that the one that the one who in the watch from six o'clock to eight o'clock did not bring her into sight would continue that watch until he had brought her back in the determined position. The sky remained dark during the night and we had the breeze from the east a quarter south-east fresh and strong.

1803-07-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third 22 July 1803 the sky was not finer than the preceding days and I was surprised to see it for so long have such a very bad appearance and stormy dispositions in several points of the horizon. The sea always heavily rough and elevated by a heavy swell from the south-west gave reason to presume that some gale must have passed from this part in a latitude further south than ours.
At noon we observed the latitude of 13° 13' 1" and the longitude of our timekeepers was for No. 35
of 99° 54' 45" and for No. 31 of 100° 31' 4".
In the afternoon and during the night the sky was the same as in the morning without any appearance of wanting to turn fine.

1803-07-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth 23 July 1803 there was no change in the state of the atmosphere and I was truly surprised to see in these waters the sky for so long covered and laden with stormy and unhealthy vapours which did not contribute to the recovery of our sick who were at that time numbering twenty.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 44' 43" and the longitude of our timekeepers was for No. 35 of 97° 51' 44" and for No. 31 of 98° 29' 36".
In the afternoon the weather was fairly fine although dark and covered until sunset. But then the whole circumference of the horizon enveloped itself in thick mist which until eight o'clock in the evening gave us much dampness and sometimes rain but little wind. It was not the same during the rest of the night. From nine o'clock the lightning announced to us the approach of thunder and the squalls began to be felt. They were at first little to fear from the strength of the wind but they were so abundant in rain that we were inundated from all sides. From eleven o'clock to midnight a squall passed which made (sic) the winds vary as far as the north-north-west it forced us to furl our topsails down low and to run before it during its great violence.
The rest of the night passed in continuous rain but the wind calmed entirely and the winds returned successively to the east.

1803-07-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth 24 July 1803 the sky was not finer than the preceding days and we were almost continuously surrounded by mist or inundated with rain. As what I had observed for several days in the state of the atmosphere reminded me of that form in which the hurricanes declare themselves which commonly make themselves felt at the islands of France and Bourbon I began to fear that the sky would not turn fine before we should have experienced some squalls and I took my precautions in consequence.
At about eight o'clock the Casuarina having asked to pass astern we closed with her and after having spoken to her Citizen Freycinet informed me that it no longer had any wood to burn. He also announced to me that the hook of its boom having broken the past night in the squall which we had received it could no longer use its mainsail. I was surprised to hear him speak thus for what he told me only served to demonstrate to me how little resource it has in itself not to know how to repair an avarie so little consequential and of this nature.
Be that as it may I had one of the boats lowered and the carpenter went to repair its boom. We also sent it a rope of wood and even more and I observed to it to use it carefully in that I would not give it any more this vessel had embarked more than four months' supply when leaving Timor.
When this work was finished we re-embarked our boat and continued our course.
At noon the sky being very covered and laden we did not have sight of the sun nor in the rest of the day. The weather announced itself on the contrary as about to be very bad during the night. Towards the end of the day I closed with the Casuarina and to make known to it that I feared bad weather during the night I had a second reef taken in the topsails and it set its own. As the weather was very dark and it was raining continuously I expressly recommended to the watch officers not to pass it during the night and that it was better to let it go ahead than to have it astern. In consequence we made very little sail. During the night the winds were often by gusts and squalls in the squalls which obliged us to furl our small topsail and to take a third reef in the large one. As the sea began to become heavy we furled the mainsail at ten o'clock and we made course under the foresail and the mizen. As we kept a fire during the whole night and we had no sight of that of the Casuarina I began to fear losing it especially as it will without doubt have run with the wind to more easily withstand the squalls which occurred.
This night was for us one of the worst of those we have spent since our departure from Europe. The wind although violent did not have the character nor the variety of those experienced in a hurricane and we had more to suffer from the rain and the heavy sea than from anything else.

1803-07-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth 25 July 1803 in the morning the weather was the same as during the night. The squalls and gales had few intervals between them and the sea was very heavy and elevated. We had no sight of the Casuarina but as we had made little sail during the night I presume that it was ahead of us and that I would find it again in the day if however it had followed the course which had been signalled to it which in truth I greatly doubted.
In the morning although the weather was always in squalls and rain the sun showed itself sometimes and at noon we had the latitude of 14° 8' very doubtful which put us at 94° 31' 17" of longitude at No. 35 and at 95° 12' 12" at No. 31.
In the afternoon and during the night the weather was always in squalls with strong gusts but we could carry our two topsails all reefs taken. As in the course of the day we had no sight of the Casuarina it is to be presumed that we will not meet it again except at the port of call of the Isle of France.
The squalls during the night were less frequent than they had been during the day and the rain less abundant but the sea being very heavy and rough the vessel fatigued a little and made water through the upper works.

1803-07-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, 26 July 1803, the sky, though still dark and laden with vapours, had a better appearance than on the preceding days, and we believed ourselves to be at the end of the bad weather, which I also supposed must change at the first quarter of the moon. In the morning we let out a reef of our topsails and set the fore topgallant sail. The sea also grew calmer, and the winds, which had been at south-south-east for a long time, were less violent.
At noon we observed the latitude at 14° 33' 8" and our longitude was found to be 91° 27' 28" for No. 35 and 92° 9' 57" for No. 31.
In the afternoon it blew a good breeze and the squalls began again, but the rain which accompanied them was not as disagreeable to receive as that of the past days. We kept the same sail set and continued our course, steering west 11° 15' south.
The night had nothing particular about it, only it was less dark than usual and gave us hope that the weather would soon turn fine again.

1803-07-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth 27 July 1803 the sky did not have a fine appearance in the morning but it became fairly(ment) clear during the day and the return of fine weather appeared to us to be decided. A good breeze blew during the day but the sea was still too agitated to increase our sail.
At noon the latitude was observed as 15° 3' 16" and our longitude was 87° 47' 45" for No. 35 and 88° 31' 43" for No. 31.
Despite the appearance we had had in the morning of seeing the weather turn fine it became covered again with dark and thick clouds in the evening. The breeze which had passed to the south-east had become stronger and the sea had little lost of its elevation and its swell. Nevertheless we had no bad weather during the night which was only very dark and during which we had sometimes rain of short duration.

1803-07-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
The ninth 28 July 1803 the sea was less heavy than usual and the wind more steady and without squalls or strong gusts which allowed us to set our mainsail but the sky was always dark with bad appearance.
At noon we observed the latitude of 15° 40' 59" and the longitude indicated by No. 35 was 84° 13' 0" and for No. 31 84° 58' 41".
During the evening the clouds having dispersed again we loosened a reef of our topsails and even set our staysails. During the night the weather having turned entirely fine we changed nothing in the sail and we followed our same course the course to the west 11° 15' south.

1803-07-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth 29 July 1803 the sky continued to be fine and although very misty the clouds did not have (more) the sad and disagreeable aspect of those which had accompanied us for so long.
In the morning general quarters was called and orders were given to all to bring their clothes up to dry them. We also perfumed the decks and between decks.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 18' 0" and our longitude was for No. 35 of 80° 37' 30" and of 81° 25' 55" for No. 31. As the sea became fairly fine we hoisted the topgallant sails which we set as soon as they were hoisted.
The night had nothing of particular note. Only a few squalls passed which made us furl our topgallant sails. The winds varied to the east-south-east and were moderate although by squalls.

1803-07-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh 30 July 1803 the sky although misty and fine was not as pleasant to look upon as that of the day before and one could see in different parts of the horizon rainy clouds which announced yet another change of weather.
At the morning inspection the carpenters reported to me that our main topmast having been fatigued in the squalls which we had endured was somewhat damaged in the mortise where passes the key and that it was to be feared that there (us) happen what we had already experienced in our small topmast in the passage from France to the Isle of France. The key had worn the mortise by more than an inch despite the iron bracket which prevents it from pressing on the wood. This inconvenience was remedied by passing a brace under the foot of the mast which was then fitted with wedges driven home with a hammer.
In the morning I addressed to the Staffs geographical and naturalists the following letter:
Citizen,
"In conformity with the imperative orders of the Government you are warned to have to gather all the journals memoirs and notes which each one of you in particular must have drawn up from the beginning of the campaign to this time. These works being the property of the Government it is expressly ordered to me to claim them.
"You will therefore be so good as to deliver to me all these papers when we shall
"have reached the longitude of the island of Rodriguez. They will be placed in your presence in a case which will be sealed and addressed to the Minister of the Marine.
"Each one of you in response to this letter will have to declare on your word of honour that you have not reserved any journal nor writing which is relative to the expedition".
Salute. N. B.
This letter will be transcribed on the journal as soon as the reading of it shall have been made by the watch officer.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 59' 29" and our longitude according to our timekeepers was 77° 26' 47" for No. 35 and 78° 16' 53" for No. 31.
In the afternoon the sky was fairly fine but the sea always heavily rough did not resemble at all that which is ordinarily encountered in these waters. At the beginning of night (the sky,) which had appeared to want to turn fine became covered again with clouds which gave us continuous rain although not abundant and sometimes a few squalls. The wind having considerably increased it was necessary to furl the bonnets and the topgallant sails.

1803-07-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth 31 July 1803 in the morning the sky continued to be covered and rainy but the winds were less strong than during the night. We constantly followed the course to the west a quarter south-west under easy sail so as not to fatigue too much our masts nor the body of the vessel which the continual agitation of the heavy sea much incommoded.
Our sick who were numbering twenty experienced little relief from the remedies which were being administered to them which was attributed to the damp and unhealthy air with which we had been surrounded for so long.
Our quadrupeds were no less fatigued by the bad weather and the movements of the vessel than we all and I greatly fear losing several of them if it continues still without at least some intervals which allow them to regain strength.
At noon we did not have sight of the sun and according to our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves at 18° 1' 38" of latitude and 75° 21' 17" of longitude. As for several days we had always found differences to the north in the latitude of 15 to 18 minutes it is to be presumed that the estimated latitude of 18° 1' 38" is greater than that which we should have found had the sun shown itself.
In the afternoon a strong breeze blew accompanied by rain and squalls and the sky took on such a bad appearance for the night that we took at the end of the day a second reef in our topsails. This precaution was not useless for the night was bad and we had almost continuously squalls rain and strong gales which made us make good progress on the course of the wind which we were following.

1803-08-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth 1st August 1803 the rain squalls and gales continued as the day before and with the same strength. Nevertheless in the morning the sky cleared a little. And at noon we could observe the latitude which was 18° 32' 24" and our longitude of 71° 27' 55" for No. 31 and of 70° 34' 21" for No. 35. These results compared to the course reckoned for 48 hours gave a difference of 30 minutes to the north which corresponded fairly well with that which we had found in the preceding days. The greatest part of the cause of these differences should according to me be attributed to the heavy swell which the bad weather occasioned rather than to a particular current which would carry us to the north. Perhaps also these two causes are united.
In the afternoon the sky although misty was fairly fine and although the sea remained heavily agitated we loosened a reef in our topsails at the end of the day. And during a part of the night we could carry the topgallant sails but it was not for long for the rain and squalls were not slow to begin again when the moon had passed its meridian.

1803-08-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth 2 August 1803 the winds although fresh were unequal and variable sometimes from the east towards the north and sometimes from the east towards the south. The rain did not cease until about nine o'clock but then the sky became clear and in such a way as to promise us fine weather at least for the rest of the day.
At noon the latitude was observed as 19° 26' 47" and our longitudes were 67° 13' 29" for No. 35 and 68° 8' 26" for No. 31. These twenty-four hours contrary to ordinary gave only 3 minutes to the north from the dead reckoning.
During the evening the weather continued fine and the sea appeared to have fallen a little. We lost on this day one of our emus which was stuffed for the Museum. It was the second since the heavy weather had accompanied us which became its victim. Despite the displeasure I would consider myself very happy if I succeed in preserving the two of this species which remain to me.
At sunset the sky being decidedly fine we set our bonnets and our topgallant sails which we kept all night making course to the west 5° south the course of the wind on which one had begun to steer since noon. The sky was very pleasant during all the night and the sea fairly fine although always rough and agitated.

1803-08-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth 3 August 1803 in the morning the weather continued fine and although the sea was always rough and agitated we made all sail to carry us to the west as much as would be possible while the sky had a fine appearance.
At noon the latitude was observed as 20° 7' 51" and our longitude was 64° 24' 19" for No. 35 and 65° 20' 11" for No. 31. We did not experience in the twenty-four hours the differences of the preceding days and as the sea was hardly less heavy nor rough than that which we had passed it appears probable that the differences of 15 to 18 minutes to the north which we had for five to six days in succession should be attributed to a current which was carrying us in that direction.
During the rest of the day the weather continued fine. A fine breeze blew and we changed nothing in our sail during the night. At noon the course had been given to the west a quarter north-west.

1803-08-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth 4 August 1803 the sky although very misty was fairly fine and the sea which for so long we had found rough heavy and agitated became calmer. We continued our same course all sail set.
At noon the latitude was observed as 20° 3' 1" and our longitude was for No. 35 of 61° 36' 47" and of 62° 33' 30" for No. 31. There was only two minutes' difference from the dead reckoning to the altitude.
As according to our No. 35 which had always given good results we should have sight of the island of Rodriguez before night at the progress we were making we continued to make all sail and at five o'clock we had sight of this island which then remained to us to the north-north-west at eight or nine leagues' distance. At eight o'clock it was borne to the north and we took from this last bearing our departure point for the approach to the Isle of France.
During the night a fresh breeze blew and we had often squalls which obliged us to furl our topgallant sails. The sea was not slow in becoming heavy and the vessel was fairly troubled by it.
Towards the end of the night having had sight of two vessels on the starboard of us which appeared to be sailing together we reduced sail until daybreak so as to recognize them.

1803-08-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth 5 August 1803 in the morning the vessels seen during the night found themselves astern sailing less well than we who had only our topsails on the tone of the masts although they carried their major sails. The nearest to us was a three-master and the other a small brig. Both of them seemed to me to be American vessels from their sails and their form. At seven o'clock seeing that they were not approaching us although they had set their topgallant sails we made sail and left them astern.
During the morning the sky was fine but the sea very agitated and rough the vessel rolling much.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures) and our longitude was for No. 35 of (no figures) and for No. 31 (no figures).
